W001.plain_title: John Bell's travels from St Petersburg across Asia
W001.one_line: A Scottish doctor's eyewitness account of Russian embassies to Persia, Peking, Derbent and Constantinople, 1715 to 1738.
W001.summary: John Bell (1691-1780), a Scottish physician in Russian service, travelled with Peter the Great's embassy to Isfahan (1715 to 1718), with the Izmailov embassy across Siberia and Mongolia to the Kangxi emperor at Peking (1719 to 1722), with Peter's Persian campaign to Derbent (1722), and to Constantinople (1737 to 1738). He published his journals in 1763. He describes Kalmyk and Tatar life on the Volga, Siberian Tatar villages and shamans, the Mongols, and the Manchu court at Peking. Volume 2 also prints Lorenz Lange's journal of his stay in Peking, with footnotes. This corpus copy is the first edition (Glasgow, 1763), two volumes.
W001.tartar_means: Bell calls many peoples Tartars: the Muslim Tatars of Kazan, Kasimov, Astrakhan and Tobolsk, the Volga Kalmyks, the Siberian 'Tartar tribes' of the Irtysh and Baraba, the Mongols, and the Manchus ('Mantzur Tartars') who ruled China. He treats Kalmyks and Mongols as one people.
W001.why_read: A careful, often sceptical eyewitness who slept in Tatar log huts, watched Kalmyk tents go up, went looking for the vegetable lamb himself, and lodged in the 'Tartar' city of Peking.
W001.watch_out: Some material, such as the Seven Palaces and the grave digging, comes from informants, and his Chinese history was told to him in Peking. Footnotes in volume 2 belong to Lange's journal, not to Bell. The OCR prints the long s as f.

W002.plain_title: Strahlenberg's description of Russia, Siberia and 'Great Tartary'
W002.one_line: A Swedish officer, prisoner in Siberia for over a decade, maps and describes 'Great Tartary', its peoples, tombs and languages.
W002.summary: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (1676-1747), a Swedish officer captured at Poltava in 1709, spent the years to 1721 as a prisoner, mostly at Tobolsk, travelling in Siberia and joining Messerschmidt's expedition. His book (German 1730, English 1738) goes with his famous map of Russia and 'Great Tartary'. It mixes firsthand notes on Siberian peoples, tombs and antiquities with long learned arguments about the origins of names and nations, a history of Russia, an alphabetical glossary, and a 'polyglot table' of 32 'Tartarian' languages. This corpus copy is the 1738 London English translation.
W002.tartar_means: A deliberately wide label. He sorts the peoples 'called Tartars' into classes: Turkic Muslims (Crimean, Kazan, Nogai, Siberian Tatars, Uzbeks and others), Finno-Ugrians, Samoyeds, Mongols and Kalmyks, Tungus and Manchus, and others. He insists the Mongols and Kalmyks do not call themselves Tartars.
W002.why_read: The key eighteenth-century source for how 'Great Tartary' was mapped and named, written by someone who lived there and was openly sceptical of the label itself.
W002.watch_out: Much is compiled from books (Abulghazi, Isbrand Ides, Witsen) or hearsay, and his etymologies (Gog and Magog, Behemoth, Kremlin) are speculative. Captivity in Siberia does not make every claim firsthand. The OCR is good but prints the long s as f.

W003.plain_title: Jonas Hanway's history of British trade over the Caspian
W003.one_line: An English merchant's own journey down the Volga to Persia in 1743 to 1745, bundled with other travellers' journals to Khiva, Bukhara and Derbent.
W003.summary: Jonas Hanway (1712-1786), a London merchant of the Russia Company, travelled in 1743 to 1745 from St Petersburg down the Volga to Astrakhan and across the Caspian to Persia, trying to open a silk trade, and was robbed in a rebellion at Astrabad. His 1753 book mixes his own journal with a history of the trade, a life of Nadir Shah, and journals by others: Captain Woodroofe (Moscow to Kazan, 1740), the factors Reynold Hogg and George Thompson (Kazakh steppe, Khiva and Bukhara, 1740 to 1741), and the Russian embassy to Persia of 1746 (Astrakhan to Derbent and Shirvan). This corpus copy is the 1753 London edition, volumes 1 and 2 in one scan.
W003.tartar_means: A broad label for the Muslim and nomadic peoples around the Volga and Caspian: Kalmyks, Nogais, settled Tatars of Crimean descent near Astrakhan, Kazakhs ('Kirgeese'), Turkmens, Uzbeks of Khiva and Bukhara, Kumyks and Lezgins of Dagestan, and even the Cossacks.
W003.why_read: Vivid scenes of Kalmyk tents, Tatar graves and marriage signals near Astrakhan, and rare British eyewitness pictures of Khiva, Bukhara and the ruins of Urgench.
W003.watch_out: Keep apart Hanway's own travels (Volga, Astrakhan, Persia) and the journals he reprints from others, and the compiled histories. He is quick to call Tartars treacherous. The OCR of this Indian-library scan is rough and has no printed page numbers.

W004.plain_title: Captain John Perry on the state of Peter the Great's Russia
W004.one_line: An English canal engineer's report on Russia, 1698 to 1712, with eyewitness notes on the Kalmyks and Tartars of the Volga.
W004.summary: John Perry (1670-1732), an English naval engineer, was hired by Peter the Great in 1698 and spent some fourteen years in Russia, above all trying to cut a canal between the Volga and the Don at Kamyshin, and later at Voronezh. His book (London, 1716) is mostly about Peter's reforms, the navy and Russian customs, but its survey of the tsar's lands describes the Kalmyks who camped across the river from his works, the raiding Kuban Tartars, the Crimean khanate, and the Mordva and Cheremis 'Tartars' who dug his canal. This corpus copy is the first edition of 1716.
W004.tartar_means: The steppe and frontier peoples of Russia's south and east: Kalmyks, Kuban Tartars (Nogais), Crimean Tatars, the Finnic Mordva and Cheremis (Mari) of the Kazan province, and further away the 'Bogdoi' (Manchu), Uzbek and Bukharan Tartars.
W004.why_read: Short but precise eyewitness pictures of Kalmyk lattice tents, wagon homes and camps laid out like towns, from a practical engineer who lived beside them for years.
W004.watch_out: Only a small part of the book concerns Tartars; his history of the Crimean khanate is second hand and contains errors (Moscow burned in 1571, not 1671). The OCR keeps the long s (ſ) and is patchy in places.

W005.plain_title: Pallas's travels through southern Russia and the Crimea
W005.one_line: A great German naturalist's survey of the lower Volga, the Caucasus steppe and the Crimea, 1793 to 1794.
W005.summary: Peter Simon Pallas (1741-1811), a Berlin-born naturalist in Russian service, had led a famous Siberian expedition in 1768 to 1774. In 1793 to 1794 he travelled from St Petersburg to the lower Volga, the Caucasus lines, the Don and the Crimea, where he then settled. His careful, measured notes cover plants, rocks and peoples, including the brick ruins of the Golden Horde capitals on the Akhtuba, the Madzhary tombs, Kalmyk and Nogai camps, and Crimean Tatar towns, law and customs. He sometimes quotes his own earlier Travels. This corpus copy is the 1812 second edition of the English translation, two volumes.
W005.tartar_means: Mostly the Nogais and Crimean Tatars, whom he treats as heirs of the Mongol armies, plus the Kundure Tartars of the lower Volga; he also speaks of 'Tartar' ruins of the Golden Horde, and distinguishes the Buddhist Kalmyks and the Kirghiz (Kazakhs).
W005.why_read: The most exact eighteenth-century descriptions of Golden Horde brick ruins, with measurements, materials and glazed tiles, plus a detailed portrait of the Crimean Tatars soon after Russian annexation.
W005.watch_out: Pallas often insists that nomads built tombs rather than towns, a view later archaeology has overturned at Sarai and Madzhary. He writes from inside Russian imperial service and can be contemptuous of the Tatars. Some passages are quoted from his older travels.

W006.plain_title: An envoy's overland journey from Moscow to Peking
W006.one_line: Peter the Great's envoy Isbrand Ides describes the peoples, towns and ruins between Moscow and Beijing, 1692 to 1695.
W006.summary: Evert Ysbrants (Isbrand) Ides, a Holstein-born merchant in Russian service, led Peter the Great's embassy to the Kangxi Emperor of China. He left Moscow in March 1692, crossed the Urals, Siberia and Dauria, reached Peking in November 1693 and was home in 1695. He wrote down what he saw of each people on the road, and added what guides, Cossacks and Chinese officials told him. The book appeared in Dutch in 1704 under the direction of Nicolaes Witsen; this corpus copy is the English translation of 1706, which also annexes 'A Short Description of China', said to be by a Chinese author, with European commentary.
W006.tartar_means: A catch-all for the non-Russian peoples of Siberia (even the Ugric Voguls, the Muslim Tatars of Tobolsk and Tyumen, the Bashkirs and the Baraba), plus the Mongols ('Mongalian Tartars'), the Kalmyks ('West Tartars') and the Manchu rulers of China ('East Tartars').
W006.why_read: A first-hand look at the lands where Russia and Qing China had just met: wooden Tatar villages and a mosque at Tobolsk, pole-and-felt tents, ruined walled towns with carved brick towers in Inner Mongolia, and a Manchu 'Tartar' emperor serving kumis at court.
W006.watch_out: Ides uses 'Tartar' very loosely and takes his history from guides and Chinese informants, with some mistakes. The book was shaped by the Dutch editor Witsen, and the annexed description of China is not Ides's own work. The OCR prints the long s as f.

W007.one_line: A young Russian scientist's field report on Kamchatka, its animals and its Itelmen people, gathered 1737 to 1741.
W007.summary: Stepan Krasheninnikov (1711-1755), a Moscow-born student attached to the Great Northern Expedition, was sent ahead to Kamchatka in 1737 and spent four years travelling the peninsula with interpreters and reading the records of the Russian forts. His Description of the Land of Kamchatka appeared in Russian in 1755, the year he died, with material from the naturalist Georg Steller. This corpus copy is James Grieve's shortened English translation, published at Gloucester in 1764. It covers geography, animals, plants and the Kamchadals (Itelmen), Koryaks and Kurils; the Tartars appear only when he asks where the Kamchadals came from.
W007.tartar_means: The peoples of the Amur valley (the 'Tartars who live upon the river Amur'), kept distinct from the Mongols ('Mungals'). The Kamchadals themselves are never called Tartars.
W007.why_read: A good example of eighteenth-century scholars sorting Siberian peoples into families by language, looks and tools: Krasheninnikov argues that the Kamchadals came from the Mongols, not the Tartars.
W007.watch_out: Very little here is about Tartars. The origin theory is learned guesswork (partly Steller's), not tradition, and it rests on racial stereotypes of the time. Grieve's English is an abridgment.

W008.plain_title: Martin Sauer's account of the Billings expedition
W008.one_line: The secretary of Russia's Billings expedition describes the road across Siberia and the Yakuts, 1785 to 1794.
W008.summary: Martin Sauer, an Englishman, was secretary to Joseph Billings's Russian naval expedition to the Kolyma, the Chukchi coast and the Aleutians (1785 to 1794). He travelled overland from St Petersburg through Kazan, Tobolsk and Irkutsk to Yakutsk and Okhotsk, and spent winters among the Yakuts gathering their history and customs 'from personal inquiry and research'. The book was published in London in 1802; this corpus copy is that edition. The Tartars appear as the Muslim Tatars of Kazan and Tobolsk and, more often, as the Yakuts, whom Sauer and the Russians of his day still called Tartars.
W008.tartar_means: Two different peoples: the Muslim Volga and Siberian Tatars around Kazan, Tobolsk and Tara, and the Turkic-speaking Yakuts (Sakha) of the Lena, whom he calls 'wandering tribes of Tartars' and 'Tartars tributary to Russia'.
W008.why_read: The Yakut chapter is one of the fullest eighteenth-century accounts of a Siberian 'Tartar' people: their own migration legend, kumis festival, shamans, oaths and houses, plus honest notes on how Russian rule was impoverishing them.
W008.watch_out: Sauer's Yakut material is gathered from informants and Russian officials, not only his own eyes. He shares the anti-shaman scepticism of his time. The Sarychev volume (W009) covers the same expedition, so the two are not fully independent.

W009.one_line: A Russian naval officer's account of the Billings expedition, with notes on the Yakuts, 1785 to 1793.
W009.summary: Gavriil Sarychev (1763-1831) was a young Russian naval officer on Joseph Billings's expedition to north-east Siberia, the Arctic coast and the Aleutians. Sent ahead in 1785 to prepare the ships at Okhotsk, he crossed Siberia by road and rode from Yakutsk with Yakut guides, lodging in their houses. His account appeared in Russian in 1802; this corpus copy is the shortened English translation published by Richard Phillips in London in 1806, with notes by the translator. Most of it is about sea voyages; the Tartars come in only with his early pages on the Yakuts.
W009.tartar_means: The Yakuts (Sakha), whom Sarychev calls a branch of 'an ancient race of Tartars' not yet converted to Islam, comparing them with the Muslim Tatars of European Russia and western Siberia.
W009.why_read: A clear early statement, backed by a real test, that the Yakuts speak a Tatar (Turkic) language, and a builder's description of their winter and summer houses.
W009.watch_out: The English edition is a translation with added notes by the translator, so check whose voice you are reading. Sarychev travelled with Sauer (W008), so the two accounts are not independent.

W010.plain_title: Wrangel's expedition to the Polar Sea
W010.one_line: A Russian naval officer's narrative of three years on the Arctic coast of Siberia, with a close look at the Yakuts, 1820 to 1823.
W010.summary: Ferdinand von Wrangel (1797-1870), a Baltic German officer in the Russian navy, led a survey of the Arctic coast east of the Kolyma from 1820 to 1823, travelling by horse, dog sled and boat and wintering at Nizhne Kolymsk. His long introduction reviews earlier Russian voyages and reports, including tales of ruins and mammoth bones on the Arctic islands. The German text was prepared by Engelhardt from the officers' journals (Berlin, 1839); this corpus copy is the shortened English translation by Mrs Sabine, edited by Edward Sabine (London, 1840). The Tartars appear through the Yakuts, whom Wrangel treats as Tartars by descent.
W010.tartar_means: The Yakuts (Sakha), whom Wrangel says descend from the Tartars, and in passing the steppe peoples of 'Tartary' who make kumis.
W010.why_read: Sharp, sympathetic observation of Yakut houses and herding life, a Yakut elder's own memory of lost writing and southern origins, and a rare explicit warning not to read ordinary ruined huts as relics of a vanished race.
W010.watch_out: The book was written up by an editor from several officers' journals and then abridged in translation, so 'Wrangel' is partly a composite voice. Much of the introduction repeats earlier reports second-hand.

W011.plain_title: Adolph Erman's scientific travels across Siberia
W011.one_line: A young German physicist's journey from Kazan to Kamchatka, full of Tatar towns, mosques, graves and history, 1828 to 1829.
W011.summary: Adolph Erman (1806-1877), a Berlin physicist, crossed Russia and Siberia in 1828 to 1830 to measure the earth's magnetism, travelling with the Norwegian Hansteen's expedition and then on his own to Yakutsk, Okhotsk and Kamchatka. A trained scholar, he mixed careful eyewitness notes with history (he used Surovzov's 1778 study of the Russian chronicles for the siege of Kazan) and word origins. The German account appeared from 1833; this corpus copy is W. D. Cooley's two-volume English translation (London, 1848), which covers the journey as far as Yakutsk and the Lena. Tatars appear on almost every page from Kazan to Tobolsk.
W011.tartar_means: Mainly the Muslim, Turkic-speaking Kazan Tatars and Siberian Tatars of Tobolsk, Tyumen and Tomsk, plus 'Tatar' as a family name for Turkic peoples such as the Bashkirs and Yakuts. Erman himself protests that Western scholars misuse 'Tatar' for peoples unconnected with Kazan, and he separates the Mongols of Chinggis Khan from the Tatars.
W011.why_read: The richest eyewitness picture in this batch of Tatar towns as they really looked around 1828: log houses, mosques, wooden jetties for ablutions, graves boxed in logs, the Kazan Kremlin and a vivid retelling of its fall in 1552.
W011.watch_out: Erman is a learned and generally careful observer, but his history of Kazan comes from Russian chronicles via Surovzov, and some of his word derivations are guesses. The English is a translation and abridgment by Cooley.

W012.plain_title: Captain Cochrane's walk across Siberian Tartary
W012.one_line: A British naval captain's mostly on-foot journey from St Petersburg to Kamchatka and back, 1820 to 1823.
W012.summary: John Dundas Cochrane (1793-1825), a Royal Navy captain on half pay, set out in 1820 to walk across Russia and Siberia, largely alone and with little money. He was robbed near St Petersburg, helped by officials and villagers all the way, reached the Kolyma and Kamchatka (where he married), and came back through Yakutsk, Irkutsk, Kiakhta, Tomsk and Tobolsk in 1822 to 1823. His lively, opinionated narrative first appeared in London in 1824; this corpus copy is the American edition published in Philadelphia the same year. He uses 'Siberian Tartary' and 'the wilds of Tartary' for all of Siberia.
W012.tartar_means: Mostly the Muslim Tatars of Kazan, Tobolsk, Tara and Tomsk and the Bashkirs, but also a loose family label for Yakuts, Yukaghirs and 'other Tartar nations' of Siberia. 'Tartary' is his word for Siberia as a whole.
W012.why_read: A warm, first-hand portrait of Tatar village hospitality and houses on the Siberian road, plus the popular Russian lore he picked up (crescents on church domes, Tatar cave-dwellers, Omsk as a Tatar stronghold).
W012.watch_out: Cochrane travelled fast and often repeats local claims without checking them; his history of Yermak is, as he admits, translated from a note on a map. He is often scornful of the peoples he meets, and some of his 'facts' are wrong.

W013.plain_title: The blind traveller's journey through Siberia
W013.one_line: James Holman, a blind former naval officer, crosses western Siberia to Irkutsk and is escorted back as a suspected spy, 1822 to 1824.
W013.summary: James Holman (1786-1857), a Royal Navy lieutenant who lost his sight at twenty-five, set out in 1822 to travel alone through Russia and Siberia, hoping to go on around the world. He reached Irkutsk, but in January 1824 the Russian authorities, suspicious of him, sent him back to the frontier under the guard of a courier. He learned about places through touch, sound, conversation and the help of hosts and interpreters. This corpus copy is volume 2 of his Travels (London, 1825), covering Tobolsk to Irkutsk and the return through Omsk, Kazan and central Europe. Tartars appear mostly as his servant, as villagers, and as the Kazakhs near Omsk.
W013.tartar_means: A mixed label: his Siberian Tatar servant and the Tatars of Kazan and the Baraba steppe, the Kazakhs ('Kirguise Tartars') near Omsk, and the Buryats and Mongols ('Mongul Tartars') near Irkutsk and Kiakhta; 'Mongul Tartary' is his name for the lands between Lake Baikal and China.
W013.why_read: A rare view of Siberia from a traveller who could not see, including his hands-on visit to a Kazakh felt tent, a governor's collection of excavated 'Tartar' antiquities, and a clear example of the Tartary and Tartarus pun.
W013.watch_out: Holman was blind, so his descriptions rest on touch, sound and what companions told him; he says so himself. He repeats ugly prejudices and rumours (for example about Tatar cooking and trading), and the OCR of this volume is poor in places.

W014.plain_title: Peter Dobell's travels across Kamchatka and Siberia
W014.one_line: An Irish-born merchant in Russian service describes crossing Kamchatka and eastern Siberia by dog sledge and horse, about 1812 to 1813.
W014.summary: Peter Dobell, a merchant who had lived for years in China and then served the Russian crown, published this travel memoir in London in 1830. He journeyed himself through Kamchatka, the Koryak lands and on to Okhotsk and Yakutsk, writing about reindeer herders, fishing villages, dwellings, food and the hardships of the road. The Tartars are barely present: the word appears only when he compares the faces of Siberian peoples with 'the Tartars', meaning the Manchus who ruled China. This corpus copy is volume I of the 1830 London edition (Colburn and Bentley), a Google scan.
W014.tartar_means: Mainly the Manchu rulers of China ('the Tartars, who have conquered China', 'Pekin Tartars'), used as a yardstick for describing the faces of Koryaks and Tungus.
W014.why_read: Shows how, by 1830, a well-travelled merchant used 'Tartar' almost as a racial type and as a name for the Manchus, rather than for any Siberian people he met.
W014.watch_out: Only volume I is in the corpus and it says very little about Tartars; the 'cream of tartar' mentions are a medicine, not a people. His physical comparisons are impressions, not evidence of descent.

W015.plain_title: A Russian mission crosses Mongolia to Peking, 1820 to 1821
W015.one_line: The escort officer of a Russian church mission records the Mongol steppe, Urga and Peking as he rode through them in 1820 and 1821.
W015.summary: George (Egor) Timkovsky was the Russian official who escorted the 1820 relief of the Russian Orthodox mission from Kiakhta across Mongolia to Peking and back. His journal, first printed in Russian in 1824, came out in English in 1827 from the French version revised and heavily annotated by the orientalist Julius Klaproth. Timkovsky describes felt tents, the camp-city of Urga, ruined temples of Mongol princes, burial, shamans, lamas, food and the Chinese frontier forts. This corpus copy is volume I of the 1827 London edition, which also includes Klaproth's notes and extracts translated from Chinese works.
W015.tartar_means: Mostly the Mongols (Khalkhas, Tsakhars, Sunits), whom he usually just calls Mongols; 'Tartar' appears for Genghis Khan's people, for the Manchu-era 'Tartar town' of Peking, and for the Turkic Tartars of Kazan.
W015.why_read: One of the best eyewitness pictures of Mongolia around 1820: a nomad capital made of tents, ruined brick temples that local Mongols credit to their own princes, and even rock outcrops that only look like ruins.
W015.watch_out: Klaproth's footnotes are a separate voice and often correct Timkovsky; some passages are Timkovsky's own translations from Chinese books, which Klaproth calls faulty. Mongol informants' stories (loadstone rocks, the living Buddha's changing face) are hearsay.

W016.plain_title: A Qing envoy's journey to the Torghut khan on the Volga, 1712 to 1715
W016.one_line: A Manchu official sent by the Kangxi emperor records crossing Siberia and Russia to visit Ayuki Khan of the Torghut Mongols near the Caspian.
W016.summary: Tulishen, a Manchu official, led the Kangxi emperor's embassy of 1712 to 1715 through Mongolia, Siberia and European Russia to Ayuki Khan of the Torghuts (Kalmyks) on the lower Volga. His report, known in Chinese as Yiyu lu, was published by imperial authority in 1723. It describes Russian towns such as Irkutsk, Tobolsk and Kazan, the Tatars living among the Russians, and a long, formal conversation with Ayuki Khan. This corpus copy is George Thomas Staunton's 1821 English translation, which adds many footnotes quoting John Bell's Russian embassy of 1719 to 1722; the corpus also holds the Chinese text (T1072).
W016.tartar_means: Several groups: the Manchus (Staunton's 'Mantchoo Tartars', including the author himself); the Mongols and the Torghut Kalmyks ('Tourgouth Tartars'); and the Turkic-speaking Tatars of Tobolsk and Kazan, whom the Chinese text calls Ta-ta-la (搭搭拉), after the Russian name.
W016.why_read: A rare view of Siberia, Russia and the Kalmyks through Chinese and Manchu eyes, with sober descriptions of towns and a telling moment when a Kalmyk khan asks whether Manchus and Mongols share one origin.
W016.watch_out: Staunton's footnotes quote John Bell at length; those passages are Bell, not Tulishen. The narrative follows Qing court conventions (every foreign ruler 'receives an edict kneeling'), and some place names are garbled Chinese renderings of Russian ones.

W017.plain_title: Two French priests cross Mongolia on the way to Tibet, 1844 to 1846
W017.one_line: Lazarist missionaries Huc and Gabet travel by camel through Inner Mongolia, living in tents among Mongols, on their famous journey to Lhasa.
W017.summary: Évariste Huc and Joseph Gabet, French Lazarist missionaries based north of the Great Wall, set out in 1844 dressed as lamas and travelled by camel across Inner Mongolia, the Ordos and Kokonor to Lhasa, arriving in 1846. Huc's lively account, published in French in 1850, describes Mongol tents, food, marriage, burial, lamaseries, towns, ruins and the pressure of Chinese settlers on Mongol pasture. This corpus copy is volume I of William Hazlitt's English translation (London, National Illustrated Library, 1852), which covers the Mongolian part of the journey.
W017.tartar_means: Chiefly the Mongols ('Tartar-Mongols', 'Western Tartars'), but Huc also calls the Manchus 'Eastern Tartars' and follows Chinese usage (Ta-Dze) for both.
W017.why_read: The most vivid close-up of Mongol daily life in the 1840s, and it includes a half-buried abandoned city, cave-houses dug by Chinese settlers, and a Mongol herder's own view of tents versus houses.
W017.watch_out: Huc is a sharp observer but a storyteller who sometimes embroiders, and he writes as a Catholic missionary with strong opinions about lamas and Chinese. Some chapters mix what he saw with what he read in Chinese or European books.

W018.plain_title: Bogle's mission to the Panchen Lama and Manning's journey to Lhasa
W018.one_line: An East India Company envoy in Tibet in 1774 to 1775 and an English scholar in Lhasa in 1811 to 1812, gathered with older missionary reports by Clements Markham.
W018.summary: This 1876 volume, edited by the geographer Clements R. Markham, prints the journals and letters of George Bogle, sent by Warren Hastings to the Panchen (Teshu) Lama in 1774 to 1775, and the diary of Thomas Manning, the first Englishman to reach Lhasa (1811 to 1812). It adds Hastings's own memorandum on Tibet and, in an appendix, older Catholic accounts: the Jesuit Grueber's crossing in 1661 and the Capuchin della Penna's description of Tibet (about 1730). Tartars appear as Mongol and Kalmyk pilgrims and traders, as the Mongol and Dzungar rulers and invaders of Tibet, and as the Manchu officials at Lhasa.
W018.tartar_means: A loose word: Mongol and Oirat 'Kalmuk' pilgrims and traders at Tibetan monasteries; the Khoshut and Dzungar Mongols who ruled or invaded Tibet; the Manchu (Qing) officials at Lhasa; and in one case 'Turki Tatars' from Central Asia. Markham's own footnote calls this 'the indiscriminate use of the word Tatar or Tartar'.
W018.why_read: Shows the Tartars from the Tibetan side: as chess partners, pilgrims, traders in Siberian furs, and as the armies that fought over Lhasa, with a Tibetan-Mongol contrast between house dwellers and tent dwellers.
W018.watch_out: Several voices share one book: Bogle, Manning, Hastings, Markham's footnotes, and the older missionary reports in the appendix, which are summaries or translations at second or third hand. Keep each speaker separate.

W019.plain_title: Moorcroft and Trebeck's travels to Ladakh, Kabul and Bukhara, 1819 to 1825
W019.one_line: Two British travellers journey through the Himalaya, Ladakh, Afghanistan and Uzbek Turkestan to Bukhara, where their expedition ended in death.
W019.summary: William Moorcroft, superintendent of the East India Company's horse stud, and his young companion George Trebeck travelled from 1819 to 1825 through the Himalayan hill states, Ladakh, Kashmir, Kabul, Kunduz and Balkh to Bukhara, hoping to open trade and buy horses. Both died on the way home. The orientalist Horace Hayman Wilson edited their journals and letters, published in two volumes in London in 1841; both volumes are in this corpus. Tartars appear as the Tibetan-speaking peoples of Lahoul, Spiti and Ladakh, the 'Kalmak Tartars' who once invaded Ladakh, and the Uzbeks and Kazaks of Turkestan.
W019.tartar_means: Very loose: Tibetan-speaking hill peoples of Lahoul, Spiti and Ladakh ('Hither Tatary'); the Kalmak (Oirat) Mongols; and, in Wilson's preface, the Uzbek ruler of Kunduz.
W019.why_read: A careful eyewitness record of how people in Ladakh and Uzbek Turkestan actually built and lived: brick and poplar-beam houses, domed clay towns, felt and reed tents, and the crumbled ruins of Balkh.
W019.watch_out: Wilson assembled the text after both men died, and some sections are Trebeck's journal, not Moorcroft's. 'Tartar' here often means Tibetan-speaking highlanders, not steppe nomads. Moorcroft's commercial and political aims colour his judgments.

W020.plain_title: Alexander Burnes's journey from India to Bukhara, 1831 to 1833
W020.one_line: A young British officer rides in disguise from the Indus over the Hindu Kush to Bukhara and home through the Turkmen desert and Persia.
W020.summary: Alexander Burnes, a lieutenant in the East India Company's army, travelled in 1831 to 1833 from Lahore through Kabul, Bamiyan, Balkh and Bukhara, then across the Turkmen desert to Persia, largely disguised as an Afghan. His Travels into Bokhara (London, John Murray, 1834) became a bestseller. It gives eyewitness descriptions of Uzbek towns, Turkmen tent camps, Bamiyan's caves and statues and the bazaars of Bukhara, plus chapters of general history and ethnology. All three volumes of the 1834 edition are in this corpus. Burnes uses 'Tartary' for Turkestan north of the Hindu Kush and 'Tartar' for Uzbeks, Turkmen, Hazaras, Kalmyks, Nogais and the historic conquerors from Genghis Khan to Timur.
W020.tartar_means: Mainly the Turkic and Mongol peoples of Central Asia: Uzbeks, Turkmen, Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, Kalmyks, the Tatar Hazaras and Nogais, and the armies of Genghis Khan and Timur. 'Tartary' is his name for Turkestan north of the Hindu Kush.
W020.why_read: Burnes tells you exactly where 'Tartary' began on the ground, what Turkmen felt tents and Uzbek towns looked like, and which ruins locals credited to whom, from Bamiyan's Buddhas to Timur's Samarkand.
W020.watch_out: Burnes was a political agent gathering intelligence, and his general chapters mix eyewitness notes with book learning, Persian manuscripts and sweeping ideas about race. Some towns (Samarkand) he never reached and describes from report.

W021.plain_title: Arthur Conolly's overland journey from England to India, 1829 to 1831
W021.one_line: A young British cavalry officer travels through Russia, Persia, Herat and Afghanistan to India, and weighs a Russian march on Khiva.
W021.summary: Arthur Conolly, a lieutenant of Bengal cavalry, returned to India overland in 1829 to 1831 through Russia, the Caucasus, Persia, Herat, Kandahar and Sindh, often travelling disguised as a merchant or physician. His Journey to the North of India was published in two volumes in London in 1834. The corpus holds only volume II, which covers Herat, Afghanistan, Sindh, Afghan history and an essay on a possible Russian invasion of India through Khiva. His vivid chapters on Turkmen tents, marriage and funerals are in volume I, which is not in the corpus.
W021.tartar_means: Only in passing: the Turkmen of the desert between Persia and Khiva ('these Tartars'), their Uzbek overlords, and 'Chinese Tartars' as the supposed source of an Afghan court custom.
W021.why_read: Useful mainly for Herat's Timurid ruins and for a British officer's view of the Turkmen and Uzbeks as a problem of Russian expansion.
W021.watch_out: Only volume II is in the corpus, so the rich Turkmen material of volume I is missing. Conolly does not call the Timurids 'Tartars'; the Herat buildings are included here because Timur's dynasty is often so called in other sources.

W022.plain_title: A British officer's winter ride from Herat to the Khan of Khiva
W022.one_line: A young British artillery officer's eyewitness account of Turkmen camps, the court of Khiva and the Kazakh steppe, 1839 to 1840.
W022.summary: James Abbott, a British artillery officer, was sent from Herat in December 1839 to the Khan of Khiva, whose country a Russian army was then marching against. He rode through Turkmen country and Merv, spent weeks at the Khivan court, and then set out across the Kazakh steppe toward the Caspian as the Khan's go-between with Russia, where he was attacked and wounded. He wrote from notes and memory, with frank personal feelings. This corpus copy is Volume I of the 1843 first edition, which runs from Herat to the Kazakh country east of the Caspian.
W022.tartar_means: Abbott uses 'Tartar' as a broad label for the Turkic-speaking peoples of Central Asia: Turkmens, Uzbeks, Kazakhs (whom the Russians called Kirghiz) and even the Jamshidis near Herat. 'Tartary' is the steppe country as a whole, and the Khan of Khiva is 'a Khaun of Tartary'; the Nogais are 'Russian Tartars'.
W022.why_read: A vivid, first-person look inside felt tents, rammed-clay manor houses, the brick citadel of Khiva and the ruins of Old Urgench, written by someone who slept, ate and negotiated there.
W022.watch_out: Abbott often mocks the people he meets and their looks, and he could barely speak the languages, so much of what he learned came through interpreters. Stories he was told (giants' bones, who built a tomb) are hearsay, and he says so.

W023.plain_title: Lieutenant Wood's winter journey to the source of the Oxus
W023.one_line: A British naval officer's eyewitness account of the Uzbek state of Kunduz, Badakhshan and the Kirghiz nomads of the Pamirs, 1836 to 1838.
W023.summary: John Wood, a lieutenant of the East India Company's navy, served on Alexander Burnes's mission to Kabul and in 1837 to 1838 travelled north across the Hindu Kush to the court of the Uzbek ruler Murad Beg at Kunduz, through Badakhshan and Wakhan, and in midwinter up onto the Pamir plateau, where he reached Lake Sir-i-kol (Zorkul), which he took to be the source of the Oxus. He wrote the book from notes made on the spot. It gives close descriptions of Kunduz, Uzbek customs, the slave trade, and the felt tents and way of life of the Kirghiz. This corpus copy is the 1841 first edition (London, John Murray).
W023.tartar_means: Wood uses 'Tartar' for the Turkic and Mongol peoples of Turkistan in general: the Uzbeks of Kunduz, the Kirghiz, the Hazaras (whom he calls 'quite a Tartar race' by their looks), and the old conquerors Genghis Khan, Timur and Shaybani Khan. He notes that 'Tartary' had become a general word for ancient Scythia, and that the Uzbeks themselves did not use it.
W023.why_read: One of the best early descriptions of a Kirghiz felt tent, inside and out, plus a frank picture of an Uzbek capital that was mostly mud huts and tents, and a thoughtful note on where the word 'Tartar' came from.
W023.watch_out: Wood often judges faces and 'races' by the standards of his day and repeats hostile gossip about the Kirghiz from their neighbours, though he usually says when he is doing so. The book was later revised by his son (1872); this is the original 1841 text.

W024.plain_title: Joseph Wolff's mission to Bukhara to find two missing British officers
W024.one_line: An eccentric missionary's account of his dangerous 1843 to 1845 journey to the Emir of Bukhara, mixing eyewitness scenes, desert tales and borrowed statistics.
W024.summary: Joseph Wolff, a German-born Jewish convert who became an Anglican clergyman, had already visited Bukhara in 1832. In 1843 he set out again, alone and in clerical robes, to learn the fate of Colonel Stoddart and Captain Conolly, two British officers held by the Emir of Bukhara. He found they had been executed and was himself held for months before being released. The book mixes his own experiences in Persia, the Turkmen desert and Bukhara with his earlier travels, long religious digressions, Turkmen and dervish tales, and descriptions of Khiva, Kokand and Bukhara copied from Burnes and others. This corpus copy is the enlarged London edition of 1846, which calls itself the fourth edition (p. 353).
W024.tartar_means: Wolff uses 'Tatar' in several senses: the Uzbeks ('Usbeck Tatars'), the Nogai Tatars of Russia, Turkic people from Yarkand in 'Chinese Tartary', the historic Tatars of Genghis Khan and Timur, and even the Ottoman courier called a 'tatar' who guided him in Turkey.
W024.why_read: A lively picture of Bukhara's crowded streets and colleges, plus rare glimpses of how local people talked about Genghis Khan, Timur and Russia, including a Turkmen tale of Timur's pyramid of skulls and dervishes calling Russia Gog and Magog.
W024.watch_out: Wolff was a zealous missionary with strong religious opinions, a love of legends and a taste for self-dramatisation. Many figures about Khiva, Kokand and Bukhara are copied from Alexander Burnes and other writers rather than observed.

W025.plain_title: James Baillie Fraser's journey into Khorasan and the Turkmen frontier
W025.one_line: A Scottish traveller's 1821 to 1822 journey through Persia to Mashhad and the Turkmen camps of the Gorgan plain, with long appendices on Bukhara, Samarkand, Merv and Khiva gathered from informants.
W025.summary: James Baillie Fraser, a Scottish traveller and artist, crossed Persia in 1821 to 1822 hoping to reach Bukhara and Samarkand. Disguised in Persian dress, he got as far as the shrine city of Mashhad but could not go on, and returned west through the camps of the Goklen and Yomut Turkmens on the Gorgan plain to Astarabad. He describes Turkmen tents, dress, music and customs from his own stay, and retells the Mongol destruction of Nishapur from Persian histories. A long appendix on Merv, Khiva, Bukhara and Samarkand is compiled from informants, including an exiled Bukharan prince living in Mashhad, and from earlier travellers. This corpus copy is the 1825 first edition (London, Longman).
W025.tartar_means: For Fraser 'Tartary' is the steppe and desert north of Persia ('Oozbeck Tartary' for the lands of Bukhara), and 'Tartars' are the Turkic and Mongol peoples there: the Mongols of Genghis Khan who sacked Nishapur, the Turkmen and Uzbek 'Tartar tribes', and people with 'Tartar features'. He notes that the Mughals (Moghuls) were properly one tribe of Tartars.
W025.why_read: One of the most exact early descriptions of how a Turkmen felt tent is built, plus first-hand scenes of Turkmen camp life and a clear, sceptical retelling of what the Mongols did to the cities of Khorasan.
W025.watch_out: Fraser is openly hostile to the Turkmens as raiders and slavers. Everything about Bukhara, Samarkand, Khiva and Merv is second-hand, from informants and books; he says so himself.

W026.plain_title: The Russian embassy's march from Orenburg to Bukhara
W026.one_line: A Baltic German officer's account of crossing the Kazakh steppe with a Russian embassy to Bukhara in 1820 to 1821, in a short, selective English version printed in Madras.
W026.summary: Georg von Meyendorff, a staff officer, travelled with the Russian embassy of Alexander Negri from Orenburg across the Kazakh steppe and the Kyzylkum desert to Bukhara in 1820 to 1821. He described the Kazakh (Kirghiz) nomads, their tents, tombs, laws and feuds, the ruins along the Syr Darya, the audience with the Emir, and, from informants, the towns of Central Asia. His French book appeared in 1826. This corpus copy is the 1840 English abridgement made in Madras by Colonel William Monteith, who added his own preface and notes and an extract from Muraviev's 1819 journey to Khiva.
W026.tartar_means: Following Russian usage, Meyendorff calls the Turkic peoples of Central Asia 'Tartars': Kazakhs (Kirghiz), Karakalpaks ('black cap Tartars'), Uzbeks and Turkmens, and also the Tatars of Kazan, Crimea and Siberia. He argues that the Mongols absorbed the original Tatars and took up their Turkic language, and proposes 'Central Asia' as a better name than 'Tartary'.
W026.why_read: Clear eyewitness scenes of Kazakh camp life, justice and clay tombs, plus an early European argument that the label 'Tartary' is misleading and should give way to 'Central Asia'.
W026.watch_out: This is a partial English translation; Monteith says the French was obscure and he left much out, and some notes are his. The OCR of this Indian printing is rough in places. Descriptions of Tashkent, Kokand, Kulja and Samarkand are from informants.

W027.plain_title: Muraviev's embassy to the Khan of Khiva
W027.one_line: A young Russian officer's account of crossing the Turkmen desert to Khiva in 1819, being held prisoner for 48 days, and meeting the Khan in his felt tent.
W027.summary: Nikolai Muraviev, a Russian staff officer, was sent by General Yermolov in 1819 to win over the Turkmens of the eastern Caspian and open relations with Khiva. He crossed the Karakum by caravan with Turkmen guides, was held for 48 days in a small fort near Khiva, and finally had an audience with Muhammad Rahim Khan before returning to the Caspian. The second half is a general survey of the khanate: its peoples, towns, forts, trade, slaves, customs and beliefs, partly from his own observation and partly from informants. This corpus copy is Captain W. S. A. Lockhart's 1871 English translation, printed in Calcutta, made from Philipp Strahl's German version of the 1822 Russian original.
W027.tartar_means: Muraviev uses 'Tartary' for the great steppe between Russia and India, and 'Tartars' for Turkic peoples such as the 'Tartars in Georgia' (Azerbaijani Turks) and the Tatars of Kazan, whose language he says is close to Khivan Turkic. He insists the Turkmens are 'most incorrectly' called a Tartar race by European writers.
W027.why_read: A vivid first-hand look at a Central Asian court where the ruler lived in a felt yurt beside his mud palace, plus clear descriptions of mud forts, towns and ruins, and what local people believed about them.
W027.watch_out: This is a translation of a translation (Russian to German to English), and the translator sometimes notes Muraviev's contradictions. Muraviev was a Russian agent writing for his government and is hostile to the Khivans and Turkmens.

W028.plain_title: Elphinstone's account of Kabul and its Tartar neighbours
W028.one_line: A British envoy's survey of the Afghan kingdom, 1808 to 1809, with chapters on the Uzbeks, Aimaqs and Hazaras built from informants.
W028.summary: Mountstuart Elphinstone (1779-1859), an East India Company official, led a British embassy to Shah Shuja, King of Kabul, in 1808 to 1809. The mission met the king at Peshawar and never reached Kabul, so Elphinstone built this book from what he saw on the road, from reports by his officers, and from long interviews with Afghan, Uzbek and other travellers, some carried on afterwards at Delhi. Most of it describes the Afghans. A final part covers the Uzbeks of Balkh and Bukhara and the Aimaq and Hazara hill peoples, whom he describes as Tartar in features and descent. This corpus copy is the first edition, London 1815, in a Google scan with heavy OCR damage on some pages.
W028.tartar_means: Mainly the Turkic and Mongol-descended peoples north and west of Afghanistan: the Uzbeks of Balkh and Bukhara, the Kalmyks, and the Aimaq and Hazara hill tribes he traces to Mongol armies. 'Tartary' is the European map name for Turkestan, which he says is not used there.
W028.why_read: A careful, fair-minded observer who says plainly that the word 'Tartary' is a European label, describes the lattice-and-felt tent used 'over all Tartary', and pushes back against the image of the Uzbeks as savage nomads.
W028.watch_out: Elphinstone never visited Balkh, Bukhara or the Hazara country: everything about the Uzbeks, Aimaqs and Hazaras comes from informants. The Google scan is badly garbled on many pages, so several quotes are OCR-normalized.

W029.plain_title: Vigne's travels in Kashmir and Little Tibet
W029.one_line: An English traveller's account of Kashmir, the Punjab hills and Baltistan in the 1830s, with glimpses of the Mughal (Timurid) past.
W029.summary: Godfrey Thomas Vigne (1801-1863), an English barrister, artist and traveller, spent 1835 to 1839 in north India, Kashmir, Ladakh and Baltistan ('Little Tibet'), crossing the mountains from the Punjab several times. His two-volume book (1842) mixes route notes, sketches, politics of the Sikh kingdom, geology, and history of the Mughal emperors, whose roads, rest-houses and gardens he followed into Kashmir. This corpus copy is volume I only, which ends before his journeys into Ladakh and Baltistan. The word Tartar hardly appears in it; the relevant material concerns the Mughal emperors, whom Vigne calls Timurians and traces to Chagatai, son of Genghis Khan.
W029.tartar_means: Almost never used. Where it appears it means Central Asian nomads in general (in a Milton quotation) or a style of dress. The nearest 'Tartar' subject is the Mughal dynasty of Delhi, which Vigne calls Timurians, descended from Timur and the Chagatai line of Genghis Khan.
W029.why_read: Shows what the 'Mogul' (Mongol-descended) emperors actually left in Kashmir: paved roads, brick rest-houses and palaces, many of them in ruins by the 1830s, and a living Timurid wedding custom Vigne claims no European had seen.
W029.watch_out: Only volume I is in the corpus; the Ladakh and Baltistan chapters, where Tibetan peoples appear, are in volume II. Vigne's 'Moguls' are the Indian Mughal emperors, not steppe Mongols.

W030.plain_title: Gerard's account of Kinnaur and the 'Tartars' of the Tibetan frontier
W030.one_line: A Scottish surveyor's first-hand description of the Himalayan valley of Kinnaur and its Tibetan-speaking 'Tartar' neighbours, 1817 to 1821.
W030.summary: Alexander Gerard (1792-1839) was an East India Company surveyor who, with his brothers James and Patrick, mapped the upper Sutlej valley (Koonawur, now Kinnaur in Himachal Pradesh) between 1817 and 1821 and pushed repeatedly to the closed Chinese-Tibetan frontier. This posthumous book, edited by George Lloyd and printed in London in 1841, has a general account of the country followed by his survey journals. A whole book of it is 'Remarks upon that part of Koonawur inhabited by Tartars': the Tibetan-speaking Buddhist villages of upper Kinnaur and Spiti, and the lands under Chinese rule beyond. Gerard learned some of their language and collected about 1,500 words.
W030.tartar_means: Tibetans and Tibetan-speaking Buddhist highlanders of upper Kinnaur, Spiti, Ladakh and western Tibet ('Chinese Tartary'). Gerard himself notes that neither 'Tartar' nor 'Tibet' was used locally.
W030.why_read: An unusually warm eyewitness portrait that deliberately contradicts the 'ferocious Tartar' image, with precise notes on stone and sun-dried brick houses, prayer walls, prayer wheels, butter tea and the closed Chinese frontier.
W030.watch_out: 'Tartar' here is a British label for Tibetans, not steppe nomads. Gerard admits he may have taken 'too favourable a view'. Some information on places he could not reach (Garoo, Yarkand, Lake Manasarovar) comes from informants.

W031.plain_title: Turner's embassy to the Panchen Lama in Tibet
W031.one_line: A British officer's eyewitness account of Bhutan and Tibet in 1783, with reports on Mongol pilgrims and the 'Tartars' beyond.
W031.summary: Samuel Turner (c. 1759-1802), an East India Company officer, was sent by Warren Hastings in 1783 to greet the newly found infant Panchen Lama ('Teshoo Lama') at Tashilhunpo. With the surgeon Robert Saunders he crossed Bhutan and spent about three months in Tibet, talking at length with the Regent and with the Lama's Manchu-born chamberlain, who had travelled in Mongolia and China. His book (London, 1800) describes Bhutanese and Tibetan buildings, religion and daily life, and passes on what he heard about Mongols, Kalmyks and Siberia. It also includes Saunders's botanical notes and a closing account of events in Tibet up to 1793. This corpus copy is the 1800 first edition.
W031.tartar_means: A wide label. Turner uses 'Tartar' for Tibetan nomad herders (the Dukba), for the dress and tea of Tibet, for Manchus ('Mantchieux Tartar'), for Kalmyk and Khalkha Mongols ('Calmuc Tartars'), and for all of Inner Asia as 'Tartary'.
W031.why_read: A calm first-hand witness who asked his Tibetan hosts directly about a supposed lost ancient nation of Inner Asia and was told that no ancient monuments were known there. He also reports the mammoth bones of Siberia and why northern nomads avoided houses.
W031.watch_out: Much of what Turner says about Mongolia, Siberia and the Kalmyks comes second-hand from his hosts. His 'Tartars' are usually Tibetans or Mongols, not Turkic Tatars. Parts of the scan are rough.

W032.plain_title: Clarke's travels: the Greek and Balkan volume
W032.one_line: The Cambridge traveller's account of Greece, Macedonia, Thrace and the road to Vienna in 1801 to 1802, where 'Tartars' are mostly Ottoman couriers.
W032.summary: Edward Daniel Clarke (1769-1822), a Cambridge mineralogist and antiquary, travelled from 1799 to 1802 through Russia, the Crimea, Turkey, the Levant, Greece and the Balkans, and published his Travels in six parts from 1810. The catalogue card is for Part I (Russia, Tartary and Turkey, 1810), with its famous Crimean chapters. The corpus copy, however, is a different volume: Part II, Section III (London, 1816), covering Greece, Macedonia, Thrace, Constantinople and the ride to Vienna in 1801 to 1802. Here Tartars appear mainly as the Ottoman mounted couriers called 'Tatars', plus a few backward glances at the steppe tumuli and Crimean peoples Clarke had seen earlier.
W032.tartar_means: In this volume, mostly the Ottoman government couriers, a job title not an ethnic name, as a quoted footnote explains. Elsewhere 'Tartary' means the southern Russian steppe and Crimea Clarke had crossed earlier, known for its burial mounds.
W032.why_read: A vivid eyewitness picture of the 'Tartar' couriers who carried the Ottoman post, and a clear statement that this 'Tartar' was a profession, not a people.
W032.watch_out: This is not the Crimea volume named on the catalogue card: the Crimean and steppe material of Part I is not in this corpus copy. Clarke refers back to it only in passing.

W033.plain_title: The Hommaire de Hells in the Caspian steppes and the Crimea
W033.one_line: A French engineer and his wife describe the Kalmyks, Nogais and Crimean Tatars they lived among in southern Russia, 1838 to 1841.
W033.summary: Xavier Hommaire de Hell (1812-1848), a French civil engineer and geologist, spent about five years in southern Russia, partly on Russian government missions, travelling with his wife Adèle (1819-1883). They crossed the Kalmyk and Nogai steppes, stayed with the Kalmyk Prince Tumene near Astrakhan, and toured the Crimea. The preface says Adèle wrote all the descriptive parts; Xavier supplied the science, history and statistics. The French original appeared 1843 to 1845. This corpus copy is the condensed English edition, 'with additions from various sources', London 1847. It has whole chapters on the Kalmyks, on the origin of the Tatars and Mongols, on the Nogais, and on Bakhchysarai and the history of the Crimean khanate.
W033.tartar_means: 'Tatar' (they refuse to write 'Tartar') for the Turkic Muslim peoples of southern Russia: Crimean Tatars of the mountains and coast, Nogais of the steppe, and the Tatars of Astrakhan. They argue these are mostly Turks once ruled by Mongols, and that 'Tatar' is really a European name. The Kalmyks are treated as Mongols.
W033.why_read: One of the clearest pre-1850 discussions of where the name Tatar came from, including the Tartarus pun, plus eyewitness detail on felt kibitkas, Nogai mud-brick cottages, the wooden palace of Bakhchysarai and the Russian demolition of Tatar and Genoese buildings in Caffa.
W033.watch_out: The English edition is shortened and adds material from other sources. The history chapters rely on Klaproth, D'Ohsson and others. The authors openly dislike Russian officialdom, and they record, without shame, robbing a Kalmyk tomb.

W034.plain_title: Baron von Haxthausen's travels through Russia in 1843
W034.one_line: A Prussian expert on peasant life tours Russia in 1843 and visits the Tatars of Kazan, the Volga ruins and a Nogai village.
W034.summary: August von Haxthausen (1792-1866), a Westphalian baron who studied rural institutions, toured Russia in 1843 with the backing of Nicholas I's government. He travelled from Moscow and Yaroslavl down the Volga to Kazan and Saratov, then south to the Mennonite colonies and the Crimea. He writes as an eyewitness, helped by officials and local informants such as the Kazan naturalist von Fuchs. His Tatar material covers the Tatar quarter of Kazan, Tatar villages, the ruins of Bolgar, reports about Sarai, and a Nogai village rebuilt on a German model. This corpus copy is volume I of Robert Farie's English translation (London, 1856) of the German original (1847 onward).
W034.tartar_means: Mainly the Muslim Volga Tatars of Kazan and its villages, plus Tatar military settlers near Penza and the Nogai Tatars of the southern steppe. In history passages he uses 'Tatars' and 'Mongols' together for the Golden Horde.
W034.why_read: A calm, close-up picture of settled Tatar townspeople and farmers in the 1840s: their houses, food, schools, marriage customs and mosques, and what a traveller then saw of the ruined Tatar and Bulgar cities of the Volga.
W034.watch_out: Haxthausen travelled as a guest of officials, pushed his own theories about Russian communal life and Christian mission, and uses the race language of his time. His remarks on Sarai and Bolgar history are secondhand.

W035.plain_title: Herberstein's Notes upon Russia (Muscovy and its Tartar neighbours)
W035.one_line: A Habsburg ambassador's description of Muscovy in 1517 and 1526, with a long chapter on the Tartars of Kazan, the Nogai steppe, Astrakhan and the Crimea.
W035.summary: Sigismund von Herberstein (1486-1566), a diplomat from Carniola, went to Moscow as envoy of the Holy Roman Emperor in 1517 and 1526. His Latin Rerum Moscoviticarum Commentarii (1549) became Western Europe's standard book on Russia. He combined what he saw at court with Russian chronicles, a Russian route book for Siberia, and interviews with soldiers, merchants and exiles. His Tartar chapter covers origins, the hordes, food, horses, warfare, law, Kazan's wars with Moscow, the 1521 Crimean raid on Moscow, the Nogais, Astrakhan and the Crimean khans. This corpus copy is R. H. Major's two-volume English translation for the Hakluyt Society (1851-52), with Major's notes.
W035.tartar_means: The Muslim Turkic-speaking peoples of the steppe and Volga: the Kazan Tatars, the Nogai, the Crimean (Taurida, Precop) khanate, Astrakhan, and the 'Savolha' (Great Horde) khans descended from the Golden Horde. He says outright that the name covers many different nations.
W035.why_read: The classic Renaissance portrait of the Tartars as Muscovy's neighbours and rivals, full of concrete detail on horses, food, tactics and politics, plus the famous 'vegetable lamb'.
W035.watch_out: Much is hearsay from Russians who were at war with the Tartars, so hostile stereotypes (no justice, gluttony, huge captive numbers) are common. The Siberian marvels come from a Russian itinerary he translated and did not believe.

W036.plain_title: Fletcher's Russe Common Wealth and Horsey's Travels
W036.one_line: Two Elizabethan Englishmen on Russia under Ivan the Terrible and his son: an envoy's survey (1591) and a merchant's memoir (1573 to 1591), both full of the Crimean Tartar threat.
W036.summary: Giles Fletcher (1546-1611), Elizabeth I's envoy to Moscow in 1588-89, published Of the Russe Common Wealth in 1591, a survey of Russian land, government, church and neighbours, including a long chapter on the Tartars. Jerome Horsey (d. 1626) lived in Russia for the Muscovy Company from 1573 to 1591 and later wrote a vivid, self-serving memoir. Fletcher mixes his own observations with Russian hearsay and older books (Herberstein, Laonicus Chalcocondylas, medieval friars). Horsey writes from memory of events he claims to have witnessed. This corpus copy is the Hakluyt Society edition by Edward A. Bond (1856), which prints both texts with Bond's notes.
W036.tartar_means: Mostly the Crimean Tartars ('the Chrim'), whose khan raided Russia yearly and burned Moscow in 1571. Fletcher also uses 'Tartar' for the Nogais, Cheremis (Mari), Mordvins and Circassians, and says the Tartars are the ancient Scythian nomads.
W036.why_read: Eyewitness English views of the great 1571 burning of Moscow and of Russia's yearly war with the Crimean khanate, with Fletcher's classic portrait of Tartar nomad life and warfare.
W036.watch_out: Fletcher's general Tartar ethnography borrows from much older writers on the 13th-century Mongols (wagon houses, felt idols, horse blood), so it may not describe 16th-century Crimean Tatars, who did have towns. Both authors repeat inflated casualty figures, and Horsey is boastful and prejudiced.

W037.plain_title: Johann Schiltberger's thirty years as a captive among Turks and Tartars
W037.one_line: A Bavarian squire captured at Nicopolis in 1396 serves the Ottoman sultan, Timur and a prince of the Golden Horde, and comes home in 1427 to tell the tale.
W037.summary: Johann Schiltberger (born c. 1380) was taken prisoner as a teenager at the battle of Nicopolis in 1396. He served Sultan Bayezid, then Timur after 1402, then Timur's heirs, and around 1405 to 1410 rode with the Golden Horde prince Chekre and the warlord Edigü, even into 'Ibissibur' (Siberia). He escaped in 1427 and dictated his book from memory. It mixes what he saw in the Horde with lists of places and hearsay marvels. This corpus copy is J. Buchan Telfer's English translation (Hakluyt Society, 1879) of the Heidelberg manuscript, with long notes by Philipp Bruun and Karl Neumann.
W037.tartar_means: Mainly the Golden Horde ('Great Tartary') on the Volga and steppe, and the Turkmen and Mongol nomads of Anatolia ('White Tartary'). He also treats Timur's realm in Central Asia as part of the same world.
W037.why_read: One of very few medieval Europeans who actually lived and campaigned inside the Golden Horde: he describes khans raised on white felt, mare's milk, meat cured under the saddle, a woman warlord and the Horde's cities.
W037.watch_out: Written from memory decades later by a man with little education; names are garbled and dates slip. His Siberian wild men and his notion that some Tartars were Christians (probably Buddhist Uighurs) are hearsay or misunderstanding. Many notes are by the 19th-century editors.

W038.plain_title: Abu'l Ghazi's Genealogical History of the Tatars
W038.one_line: A 17th-century khan of Khiva tells the Turkic and Mongol peoples' own story of their origins, from Adam and the Flood through Chinggis Khan and his heirs.
W038.summary: Abu'l Ghazi Bahadur Khan (1603-1663), Uzbek ruler of Khiva (Khwarazm), wrote this dynastic history in Chaghatai Turkic near the end of his life. He compiled it from earlier Persian histories (he names Rashid al-Din) and from oral tradition, adding his own Islamic framing. Volume I covers the descent of the Turks and Mongols from Noah's son Japheth, the rival lines of Tatar Khan and Mogul Khan, the tribes, the Irgana-kon legend, Chinggis Khan, and his sons' realms, including Batu's Kipchak (Golden Horde). This corpus copy is the anonymous English translation of 1730, made through the French edition, with a translator's preface and notes.
W038.tartar_means: For Abu'l Ghazi, the Tatars are one ancient Turkic tribe descended from a prince named Tatar Khan, rivals and later partners of the Mongols; he writes of Tatars and Mongols as distinct peoples. His English translator uses 'Tatar' in the broad European way for all the peoples of 'Tatary'.
W038.why_read: A rare chance to hear an insider's version: the Turkic and Mongol peoples' own origin legends as a Chinggisid khan told them, including the melting of the iron mountain and the Tatar and Mogul twins.
W038.watch_out: The early chapters are legend and genealogy, not eyewitness history, and the English passed through several translations. The corpus OCR for this volume is unusable (English read as Cyrillic), so every quote here was transcribed from the page images and should be checked against them.

W039.plain_title: The Oriental Geography of 'Ebn Haukal' (a 10th-century Islamic geography)
W039.one_line: A 10th-century Arabic geography of the Islamic world, in a Persian version translated by William Ouseley in 1800, with an early description of the Khazar capital on the Volga.
W039.summary: This is a Persian version of a 10th-century Arabic 'Routes and Realms' geography, attributed by the translator William Ouseley to Ibn Hawqal. Scholars now link it more closely to al-Istakhri, whose work Ibn Hawqal revised. The author describes the lands of Islam province by province, from Arabia to Transoxiana, with notes on the peoples beyond, including the Khazars, Volga Bulgars and Rus. Its information comes partly from travel and partly from earlier books and merchants' reports. It uses 'Turks' (glossed by the translator as 'Tartars') for the Turkic peoples; it predates the Mongol conquests. This corpus copy is Ouseley's English translation (London, 1800), made from his own manuscript collated with one at Eton College.
W039.tartar_means: The original text speaks of 'Turks', not Tartars; the 1800 translator adds '(or Tartars)' in brackets for Turkic peoples such as the Khazars and the Khalaj.
W039.why_read: An eyewitness-era description of the Volga before the Mongols: the Khazar capital Atil with its tents and single brick palace, and the Muslim town of Bulgar, both later part of what Europeans called Tartary.
W039.watch_out: The attribution to Ibn Hawqal is uncertain (the text is closer to al-Istakhri), much is secondhand, and the '(or Tartars)' glosses are the 1800 translator's, not the medieval author's.

W040.plain_title: The Book of Ser Marco Polo (Yule's edition)
W040.one_line: The Venetian merchant who served Kublai Khan for some seventeen years describes the Mongol 'Tartars', their camps, capitals, customs and empire, c. 1271 to 1295.
W040.summary: Marco Polo (1254-1324) travelled with his father and uncle across Asia to the court of Kublai Khan, stayed about seventeen years, and returned to Venice in 1295. In a Genoese prison around 1298 he dictated his book to the romance writer Rustichello of Pisa. It mixes his own observation (much of China and the Mongol court), information gathered in service, and hearsay about distant lands. His Tartar chapters cover Karakorum, Mongol houses and wagons, marriage, religion, war, law, Kublai's palaces at Shangdu and Khanbaliq, and the Golden Horde. This corpus copy is Henry Yule's 1871 English translation in two volumes, with very extensive notes by Yule.
W040.tartar_means: The Mongols of Chinggis Khan and his heirs, including Kublai's court in China ('Tartars of the Levant' for the Ilkhans of Persia, 'Tartars of the Ponent' for the Golden Horde on the Volga). He also tells a legend of the Tartars' early days under 'Prester John'.
W040.why_read: The most famous medieval account of the Mongols at the height of their power, from someone who served them: felt houses on carts beside marble and cane palaces, planned capitals and the empire's customs.
W040.watch_out: Polo's text survives in many differing manuscripts and passed through Rustichello's romance style. He repeats hearsay and legends (Prester John, Gog and Magog, the Land of Darkness) alongside what he saw. Many notes quoted on the same pages are Yule's 19th-century commentary.

W041.plain_title: Yule's Cathay, volume I: Friar Odoric and other medieval notices of China
W041.one_line: Henry Yule's 1866 Hakluyt Society collection of medieval writings on China, centred on Friar Odoric's travels of the 1320s.
W041.summary: Henry Yule, a British scholar of medieval Asia, gathered and translated early European and Asian notices of China for the Hakluyt Society in 1866. This first volume holds his long preliminary essay (with extracts such as the Persian embassy of Shah Rukh to the Ming court in 1419 to 1422), the travels of the Franciscan Friar Odoric of Pordenone, who dictated his account in 1330 after about three years at Khanbaliq (Beijing) under the Mongol Yuan dynasty, and letters of missionary friars. Yule's footnotes are dense and learned. For Tartars, the prize is Odoric's eyewitness picture of the Great Khan's capital and court.
W041.tartar_means: In Odoric, the Tartars are the Mongols of the Yuan dynasty who ruled China from Khanbaliq. Yule's notes also use 'Tartar' for the Khitan and the Jurchen (Kin) peoples, and for the 'Tartar city', the walled inner city of Qing-era Peking.
W041.why_read: Odoric gives one of the few Western eyewitness views of the Mongol palace at Beijing, and Yule's notes trace how the 'Tartar city' of later Peking descends from the city the Mongols built.
W041.watch_out: This is an anthology, so each extract has its own author and reliability. Odoric's text survives in many differing manuscripts (some passages are only in the 'Minor Ramusian' version), and he mixes what he saw with things he was told.

W042.plain_title: The Travels of Sir John Mandeville
W042.one_line: A hugely popular fourteenth-century book of travels to the Holy Land, Cathay and the Great Khan's realm, largely assembled from other writers.
W042.summary: The Travels of Sir John Mandeville appeared in French in the mid-1300s and became one of the most widely read books of the late Middle Ages. Its narrator claims to have served the Sultan of Egypt and the Great Khan, but scholars have long shown that most of the Asian material is borrowed, especially from Friar Odoric and Carpini, and no real traveller behind it has been proved. This corpus copy is A. W. Pollard's 1900 modern-spelling edition of the English Cotton manuscript, with three narratives from Hakluyt appended: Carpini, Rubruck and Odoric. The Tartar chapters cover Genghis Khan's rise, Tartar customs and the Khan's court.
W042.tartar_means: The Mongols of the Great Khan of Cathay and their subject peoples. 'Tartary' is the whole Mongol-ruled north of Asia, 'holden of the great Caan of Cathay'.
W042.why_read: It shows what most late-medieval Europeans actually 'knew' about the Tartars: real details copied from friars, woven together with Bible genealogy, marvels and hearsay.
W042.watch_out: Treat nothing here as eyewitness. Compare each passage with the friars it was taken from (Odoric and Carpini are in this batch). The appended Hakluyt texts are separate works and should be cited under their own authors.

W043.plain_title: Friar William's journey to the Mongol court, with Carpini and Benedict the Pole
W043.one_line: Three friars' eyewitness reports from the Mongol empire: Carpini and Benedict in 1245 to 1247, William of Rubruck in 1253 to 1255.
W043.summary: William Woodville Rockhill, an American diplomat who had himself travelled among Mongols and Tibetans, translated these Latin reports for the Hakluyt Society in 1900. John of Pian de Carpine and Benedict the Pole went as papal envoys to the enthronement of Guyuk Khan in 1246. The Flemish Franciscan William of Rubruck travelled for King Louis IX of France to Batu on the Volga and then to Mongke Khan at Karakorum, living there for months. Rubruck is the richest early European witness to Mongol daily life. Rockhill's long introduction quotes panicked European chronicles such as Matthew Paris, and his footnotes compare Carpini, Marco Polo, Chinese annals and later travellers.
W043.tartar_means: The Mongols and the peoples of their empire (Rubruck's 'Moal'), including the Golden Horde of Batu on the Volga. Rubruck explains that the Tartars were originally a separate neighbouring tribe whose name the Mongols now wished to erase.
W043.why_read: Here are the famous first-hand descriptions: felt tents on giant carts, the ordu that looks like a city, kumiss, women's tall headdresses, Karakorum's mud-walled town with its Chinese artisans, and the silver drinking fountain made by a captured Parisian goldsmith.
W043.watch_out: Keep the friars' own words apart from Rockhill's introduction and notes, which quote many other writers. The friars depended on poor interpreters, disliked what they saw as idolatry, and repeat some hearsay about distant peoples.

W044.plain_title: Early English voyages to Russia and Persia, volume II
W044.one_line: Letters, charters and travel reports of Anthony Jenkinson and other Muscovy Company Englishmen in Russia, on the Volga and in Persia, 1557 to 1581.
W044.summary: The Muscovy Company sent English merchants down the Volga and across the Caspian in search of trade with Persia and Central Asia. E. Delmar Morgan and C. H. Coote edited their papers for the Hakluyt Society in 1886. This corpus scan is volume II only, so Anthony Jenkinson's famous 1558 journey to Bukhara (in volume I) is not here. What is here: Jenkinson's later letters, including one on the Crimean Tatar burning of Moscow in 1571, the Tsar's charters and letters, company instructions, Sir Humphrey Gilbert's discourse, and Hakluyt's narratives of later Persian voyages that passed Kazan, Astrakhan and the Nogai steppe.
W044.tartar_means: Mostly the Crimean Tatars ('Crims', 'Krim Tartars') and the Nogais ('Nagaians') of the Volga steppe, both enemies or uneasy vassals of Muscovy. Jenkinson also calls the Central Asian khanates between the Caspian and Bukhara 'kingdoms of the Tartars', and 'Tartaria' still labels Kazan and the northern coast of Asia.
W044.why_read: It shows Tatars as sixteenth-century neighbours rather than legends: raiders who burned Moscow, river pirates, vassal townsfolk outside Astrakhan, and the ruins of an older stone town on the Volga.
W044.watch_out: Only volume II is in the corpus. The OCR of the old spelling is often badly garbled, and several pieces are later compilations in Hakluyt rather than direct letters; the editors' footnotes are nineteenth-century additions.

W045.plain_title: The Tarikh-i-Rashidi: a Moghul prince's history of Central Asia
W045.one_line: Mirza Haidar Dughlat's Persian history of the Mongol (Moghul) khans of eastern Central Asia, written about 1546.
W045.summary: Mirza Muhammad Haidar Dughlat (1499 or 1500 to 1551), a cousin of the emperor Babur, belonged to the noble Dughlat clan of the Moghuls, the descendants of Chagatai's Mongols in the Tian Shan and the Tarim basin. He wrote this history in Persian while ruling Kashmir, mixing older written chronicles, family traditions and his own memories of Kashgar, Yarkand and Moghulistan. This corpus copy is the 1895 English version, translated by E. Denison Ross and edited by Ney Elias, whose long introduction and notes discuss the names Moghul, Turk and Tatar and compare the text with later travellers.
W045.tartar_means: Mirza Haidar himself speaks of 'Moghuls', the Mongol tribes of Moghulistan who had become Muslims. 'Tatar' and 'Tartar' appear mainly in the editor's introduction and notes, which quote Rashid al-Din and others on how the name Tatar spread to all the Mongols and nomads of inner Asia.
W045.why_read: A rare view from inside the Mongol world: how nomad khans felt about towns, how they became Muslims, what they built, and local stories of cities swallowed by desert sand.
W045.watch_out: Keep Mirza Haidar's text apart from Ney Elias's introduction and footnotes, which are nineteenth-century commentary. Much of the early history is family tradition or copied from Timurid chronicles, and the translation of some passages was adjusted to make sense.

W046.plain_title: Clavijo's embassy to Timur at Samarkand
W046.one_line: A Castilian envoy's day-by-day account of his journey to Timur's court at Samarkand, 1403 to 1406.
W046.summary: Ruy González de Clavijo, a knight of Madrid, was one of three envoys sent by King Henry III of Castile to Timur (Tamerlane). They sailed from Seville in May 1403, crossed Armenia, Persia and Khorasan, and spent the autumn of 1404 at Samarkand, attending Timur's feasts in great tent camps and touring his new buildings. Clavijo wrote in the third person about 'the ambassadors', recording what they saw and what they were told. The account was first printed in Seville in 1582. This corpus copy is Clements R. Markham's 1859 English translation for the Hakluyt Society, with a life of Timur and notes.
W046.tartar_means: Clavijo calls Timur's own people 'Zagatays', whom he says descend from the 'Zagatay Tartars' who came from Tartary with Genghis Khan's son Chagatai. 'Tartary' and its 'emperor' mean the Golden Horde of Tokhtamysh and Edigu north of the Caucasus, and 'white Tartars' are a nomad people Timur fought between Turkey and Syria.
W046.why_read: The best eyewitness picture of a Mongol successor state at its height: tent palaces beside a city of brick and glazed tile, built largely by craftsmen Timur carried off from Damascus, Turkey and elsewhere.
W046.watch_out: Clavijo reports court gossip about Timur's origins and far-off lands as fact. He needed interpreters, and Markham's notes and life of Timur are nineteenth-century additions.

W047.plain_title: Xuanzang's Records of the Western Regions
W047.one_line: A Chinese Buddhist pilgrim's country-by-country description of Central Asia and India, 629 to 645, with the Western Turks as overlords of the Silk Road.
W047.summary: Xuanzang (about 602 to 664), a Chinese Buddhist monk, travelled from Chang'an across Central Asia to India and back between 629 and 645. At the emperor's request his disciple Bianji compiled this record of the countries he passed or heard of from his reports in 646: distances, cities, crops, customs and many local legends, some places visited and some only heard of. The corpus copy is volume 2 of Samuel Beal's English translation (1884), covering books 6 to 12, which end with the return journey through Afghanistan, the Pamirs and Khotan. The Chinese text (Siku quanshu copy, Kanseki Repository) is also in the corpus and adds book 1, the outward route through the lands of the Western Turks.
W047.tartar_means: Xuanzang never says 'Tartar'. He writes of the Tujue (Beal's 'Tu-kiueh', the Turks), whose Western Turkic khaganate ruled the oasis states in his day, and of the ancient Xiongnu ('Hiung-nu'). Beal's index and notes use 'Tartar' for the Hu and for the Toba Wei, and 'High Tartary' for the Tarim Basin.
W047.why_read: A rare seventh-century view of Central Asian steppe rulers from the Chinese side: Turkish kings who own towns but live in tents, subject cities, captives, and the legends told along the road.
W047.watch_out: Only volume 2 of Beal is in the corpus; the book 1 passages here are quoted from the Chinese with my own working translation. Many stories are local legend that Xuanzang reports as 'the common story'. Beal's 1884 glosses (such as 'Hu people (Uighurs)') are his own.

W048.plain_title: Olearius's embassy down the Volga to Persia
W048.one_line: A German scholar-diplomat's eyewitness account of the Tatars of Kazan, Astrakhan, Dagestan and the Terek, 1633 to 1639, with Mandelslo's travels appended.
W048.summary: Adam Olearius (1599-1671) was secretary to the Duke of Holstein's embassy to Moscow and Persia. In 1636 the embassy sailed down the Volga from Nizhny Novgorod past Kazan to Astrakhan and across the Caspian; in 1638 it returned overland through Dagestan and Terki. Olearius published his account in German in 1647 and an enlarged edition in 1656, mixing his own observations with history from older books. This corpus copy is John Davies's English translation, second edition 1669, which also contains J. A. von Mandelslo's travels to the East Indies, edited and enlarged by others.
W048.tartar_means: Mainly the Tatars of Kazan, Astrakhan (Nogais) and Crimea. Olearius also calls the Mari (Cheremis), the Kumyks of Dagestan, the Kabardian 'Circassians' of the Terek, the Kalmyks and the Uzbeks 'Tartars'; the appended Mandelslo volume uses it for the Mongols and Manchus who conquered China.
W048.why_read: A careful observer on the spot: what Tatar towns, huts, food and princes looked like just after the Russian conquest of the Volga, and how Russians policed where Tatars could live and build.
W048.watch_out: Eyewitness scenes sit beside history copied from Herberstein, Miechow and others, so check whether he says 'we saw' or 'they say'. The Mandelslo part is not Olearius and its China history is compiled. OCR of the 1669 type is rough, with long s read as f.

W049.plain_title: Chardin's journey through Crimea and the Caucasus to Persia
W049.one_line: A French jeweller's eyewitness account of Crimean Tatar towns and tents, Georgia and Persia, 1672 to 1673.
W049.summary: Jean Chardin (1643-1713), a Huguenot jeweller from Paris, made two long trading journeys to Persia. On the second he sailed from Constantinople to Caffa in Crimea in 1672, spent forty days there, crossed to Mingrelia and Georgia, and rode through Armenia to Isfahan in 1673, writing as he went. The first volume appeared in French and English in 1686. This corpus copy is the English edition of 1691, which also contains his earlier 'Coronation of Solyman III', with court history on Uzbeks and Kalmyks. Tartars are a side subject here, but he saw them close up.
W049.tartar_means: The Crimean Tatars and Nogais of 'Lesser Tartary', the Uzbeks of Central Asia, the Kalmyks, and the medieval Mongol conquerors of Persia (Hulagu, Arghun, Ghazan, Tamerlane), all called Tartars.
W049.why_read: A sharp eye on building materials: Caffa built entirely of earth, a Tatar hamlet of a few houses ringed by felt tents and wagons, and ruined Persian cities credited to Mongol founders or Tartar raids.
W049.watch_out: Crimea is only a few pages of a long book on Persia and the Caucasus. History and etymologies come from Persian informants and books; the Amazon and Abu'l-Ghazi stories are hearsay. The 1691 OCR is rough, with long s read as f.

W050.one_line: A German naturalist's eyewitness diary of Kazan, Tobolsk and the Tatar, Kalmyk and Teleut lands of western Siberia, 1733 to 1735.
W050.summary: Johann Georg Gmelin (1709-1755), a chemist and botanist from Tübingen working for the St Petersburg Academy, travelled with the historian G. F. Müller on the Second Kamchatka Expedition from 1733 to 1743. This first volume of his 'Reise durch Sibirien' (Göttingen, 1751) is a dated day-by-day diary from Petersburg through Kazan to Tobolsk, up the Irtysh past the steppe forts to Semipalatinsk and Ust-Kamenogorsk, then to Kuznetsk and Tomsk and on toward the Yenisei. He records towns, villages, houses, weddings, shamans, graves and ruins alongside plants and minerals. The corpus copy is the German original, volume 1; no English translation was checked.
W050.tartar_means: Mostly the Muslim Tatars of Kazan and of Tobolsk and the Irtysh (with Bukharan settlers), and a range of Turkic-speaking, largely non-Muslim peoples of the Kuznetsk and Altai region he also calls Tatars (Teleuts, Abinsk and Kondoma Tatars). The Kalmyks (Oirats) are a separate people to him. His preface mocks the old habit of calling all of northern Asia 'Tartary'.
