W050.why_read: A careful, often wry scientist who checks older claims on the spot: timber and clay villages, two-fireplace Tatar houses, reed yurts, an ironworks in a yurt, ruined Kalmyk temples and plundered steppe graves, all dated and placed.
W050.watch_out: German only (quotes here are in the original with working translations). Some sites he knew only from his men's reports. He is openly scornful of shamans and 'idol-worship'. Fraktur OCR confuses s and f and garbles umlauts.

W051.plain_title: Du Halde's Description of China and Chinese Tartary
W051.one_line: A Jesuit compendium of 1735 on China and the lands of the Manchus and Mongols, built from missionaries' journals and the great Qing map survey.
W051.summary: Jean-Baptiste Du Halde (1674-1743), a Paris Jesuit, never went to China. His Description (French, 1735) compiles letters and journals sent home by Jesuits at the Qing court. This corpus copy is the English translation (London, 1738) in two volumes. Volume 1 covers China and the Manchu conquest; volume 2 has a geographical account of Manchu and Mongol 'Tartary' drawn from the map-makers of 1709 to 1711, and the travel journals of Ferdinand Verbiest and Jean-François Gerbillon, who rode into Mongolia with the Kangxi emperor and the 1688 embassy to the Russians. The English editor adds footnotes.
W051.tartar_means: Mainly the Manchus ('Eastern Tartars', rulers of China since 1644) and the Mongols ('Western Tartars': Khalkhas, Ordos and others), plus the Oirats (Eluths) and many forest and river peoples of Manchuria. 'Tartar' and 'Chinese' are the two ruling nations of the Qing court.
W051.why_read: The Jesuit surveyors walked the ground: they describe felt tents from the inside, tent 'cities' round great lamas, and ruined cities in Mongolia and Manchuria, and they argue about who built them.
W051.watch_out: A compilation: always check which missionary is speaking. The 1738 English editor adds footnotes that correct or expand the Jesuits. Religious hostility to lamas colours the tone. Two very long volumes; only the Tartary parts were sampled here.

W052.one_line: An English aristocrat's letters from newly Russian Crimea in April 1786: Tatar towns, houses, women and the khan's palace.
W052.summary: Elizabeth Craven (1750-1828), an English writer and traveller, went by sledge and carriage from St Petersburg through Moscow and Kherson into Crimea in the spring of 1786, three years after Russia annexed the khanate. Escorted by Russian officers and Cossacks, she stayed at Karasubazar, Bakhchysarai and Sevastopol, visited Tatar women at home, lodged in the khan's palace, and sailed on to Constantinople. The book is a series of letters addressed to the Margrave of Brandenburg-Ansbach, published in London in 1789; this is that first edition. It mixes quick, lively first-hand scenes with a history of Crimea summarised from books.
W052.tartar_means: The Crimean Tatars (and the Nogais the khans brought into Crimea), just after the Russian annexation of 1783. She keeps Cossacks and Kalmyks separate.
W052.why_read: A rare woman's view from inside Tatar households, with sharp detail on houses, dress, the Bakhchysarai palace and what Tatars told her about their land, at the very moment the khanate ended.
W052.watch_out: She saw Crimea as a guest of the Russian administration preparing for Catherine II's visit, so her informants were mostly Russian officials. She is frank about her prejudices (dirt, 'mummery'). Letters were edited for publication, and the history is second-hand.

W053.plain_title: Baron de Tott's memoirs of the Crimean Tatar court
W053.one_line: A French officer's memoir of his years as consul to the Crimean Khan, 1767 to 1769, including a Tatar winter campaign.
W053.summary: François, Baron de Tott (1733-1793), a French officer of Hungarian descent, served French diplomacy in Constantinople and in 1767 to 1769 was consul at the court of the Crimean Khan. He crossed the Nogai steppe, lived at Bakhchysarai, built himself a house in the Tatar manner, and rode with Khan Krim Giray on the winter raid into New Serbia in January 1769. His memoirs (French 1784) mix eyewitness scenes with essays on Turkish and Tatar government and his own theories about Tartar antiquity. This corpus copy is the three-volume English translation 'by an English gentleman at Paris', 1785; almost all the Tatar material is in volume 2.
W053.tartar_means: The Crimean Tatars and their Giray khans (whom he calls descendants of Genghis Khan), and the Nogai hordes of the steppe north of Crimea and in the Budjak (Bessarabia). He also uses 'Tartar' as a wide label, comparing a Manchu with a Budjak Tartar.
W053.why_read: One of the most vivid eyewitness pictures of Crimean Tatar life shortly before Russian annexation: felt tents, wattle-and-daub houses, the khan's palace, food, law, marriage and war.
W053.watch_out: De Tott is vain and loves anecdotes in which he is the hero; his essays on Tartar origins and government are opinion, not observation. The 1785 OCR prints the long s as f, and his Franco-Ottoman viewpoint colours his judgments.

W054.plain_title: Maria Guthrie's letters from a tour of the Crimea
W054.one_line: Letters of a Scottish woman living in Russia, written on a journey through the newly Russian Crimea and Nogai steppe in 1795 to 1796.
W054.summary: Maria Guthrie, former acting directress of the imperial school for noble girls in St Petersburg, toured southern Russia and the Crimea in 1795 to 1796 for her health, writing letters in French to her husband, the physician and antiquary Matthew Guthrie. After her death he translated them into English, added ancient history, footnotes, a supplement and appendices on antiquities, and published the book in London in 1802, the edition in this corpus. She describes Bakhchysarai, Tatar houses, food, marriage, burial, religion and law, Nogai tents and steppe monuments; he adds learned and sometimes far-fetched theories.
W054.tartar_means: Mainly the Crimean Tatars ('Crim Tartars') and the Nogai Tatars of the steppe north of Perekop, a dozen years after Russian annexation. In Matthew Guthrie's appendices 'Tartars' is a generic name for all steppe nomads, used interchangeably with 'Scythians'.
W054.why_read: A rare woman's eyewitness view of Crimean Tatar homes, food and customs just after annexation, plus early descriptions of kurgans, steppe stone statues and the ruined Golden Horde town of Madzhary.
W054.watch_out: The English is Matthew's translation, and many footnotes, the supplement and the appendices are his own antiquarian theories (for example that Russians descend from Cumans or Hyperboreans). Keep Maria's observations apart from his speculation; she also repeats merchants' hearsay.

W055.plain_title: Jean Reuilly's travels in the Crimea, 1803
W055.one_line: A young Frenchman's survey of the Crimea twenty years after Russian annexation, with chapters on the Tatars.
W055.summary: Jean Reuilly travelled through the Crimea and along the Black Sea coast in 1803 and published his account in Paris in 1806; this corpus copy is the English translation of 1807, from an Indian library scan with poor OCR. He describes towns such as Perekop, Bakhchysarai, Karasubazar, Eski-Krym and Kozlov (Yevpatoria), gives a history of the peninsula, and devotes chapters to the Tatars: their three groups, houses, dress, language, hospitality, medicine and government. He stayed with the Tatar noble Atai Myrza. Much of the history and some descriptions, such as the Nogai tents credited to Thunmann, come from earlier writers.
W055.tartar_means: The Crimean Tatars, whom he divides into Nogais of the steppe, Tatars of the plain and Tatars of the mountains; also the 13th-century 'Mongholes or Tartars' and the Giray khans descended from Genghis Khan.
W055.why_read: A compact first-hand snapshot of Tatar towns, fountains, houses and hospitality in 1803, including notes on what Russian rule was already destroying.
W055.watch_out: The OCR is poor, so a few words are uncertain. Reuilly borrows history and some ethnography from Thunmann and others, and the notes on the titles khan and sultan are by the numismatists Langlès and Millin.

W056.plain_title: Julius Klaproth's travels in the Caucasus and Georgia
W056.one_line: A German orientalist's scientific expedition through the North Caucasus and Georgia in 1807 to 1808, with a close study of Golden Horde ruins.
W056.summary: Julius Klaproth (1783-1835), a linguist in Russian academic service, was sent by the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences to study the peoples, languages and history of the Caucasus in 1807 to 1808. His book (German 1812 to 1814) appeared in English in 1814, the edition in this corpus. Besides Circassians, Ossetes and Georgians, it covers the Nogai, Kumyk, Karachay and Balkar 'Tartars', and gives the fullest early account of the ruined town of Madzhar on the Kuma, combining Gmelin's 1772 description, Klaproth's own excavation of a vault, dated gravestones, coins of the Golden Horde khans and a Nogai-language history.
W056.tartar_means: Turkic-speaking peoples of the North Caucasus and steppe (Nogais, Kumyks, and the Karachay and Balkar 'mountain Tartars'), and the Kipchak Tatars of the Golden Horde and their Genghisid khans; he notes that Batu's army had few actual Mongols.
W056.why_read: Shows how an early 19th-century scholar used bricks, inscriptions and coins to prove that a ruined stone town on the steppe was a 14th-century Golden Horde city, and how settlers and officials then quarried it away.
W056.watch_out: Long passages quote earlier travellers (Gmelin, Güldenstädt, Gerber) or informants rather than Klaproth's own eyes, and he is combative toward rivals like Reineggs. The OCR mangles the Arabic-script inscriptions and some names.

W057.plain_title: Henry Ellis's journal of the Amherst embassy to China
W057.one_line: A British diplomat's journal of the failed 1816 Amherst embassy to the Qing court and its long journey back to Canton.
W057.summary: Henry Ellis (1788-1855) was third commissioner of Lord Amherst's embassy to the Jiaqing Emperor in 1816. The embassy was expelled without an audience after refusing the full kowtow, and then travelled by river and Grand Canal from near Beijing to Canton. Ellis's journal, published in London in 1817 (the edition in this corpus), records negotiations with Manchu and Mongol officials and remarks on towns, temples and customs along the way. 'Tartar' here almost always means the Manchu ruling people of Qing China and their institutions.
W057.tartar_means: The Manchus and their Mongol allies who ruled Qing China: the 'Tartar' dynasty, bannermen and officials; 'Tartary' is the Manchu and Mongol land beyond the Great Wall.
W057.why_read: Shows what 'Tartar' meant in 1816 China: the 'Tartar ceremony' (kowtow), milk served at court in memory of Manchu origins, four races of Tartars, and Manchu troops.
W057.watch_out: Ellis never went north of Beijing; nearly everything about Tartars is second-hand from officials or missionaries, and he shares the embassy's contempt for the Qing court.

W058.one_line: The Macartney embassy's comptroller on China, its Manchu 'Tartar' rulers and Chinese society, 1792 to 1794.
W058.summary: John Barrow (1764-1848) went to China as comptroller of Lord Macartney's embassy (1792 to 1794), spent weeks at the Yuanmingyuan palace outside Beijing setting up gifts for the Qianlong Emperor, then travelled overland to Canton. His Travels in China (London 1804, the edition in this corpus) is arranged by topic rather than as a diary: government, language, science, religion, architecture, army and people, often combative. He contrasts Manchu 'Tartars' with Chinese, quotes Macartney's journal of the visit to Jehol in Tartary, and speculates about Tartar origins and the Flood.
W058.tartar_means: Mainly the Manchus who conquered China in 1644 and ruled it (the 'Tartar' dynasty, officials, soldiers and the women of Beijing), sometimes the Mongols of Genghis and Kublai; 'Tartary' is the land beyond the Great Wall.
W058.why_read: A sharp eyewitness contrast of Manchu and Chinese manners in 1793, and a view of who built China's great works: the Great Wall, the Grand Canal and the Jehol temples.
W058.watch_out: Barrow was openly hostile to the Qing and to missionary praise of China, and mixes observation with sweeping theories about race, the Flood and Noah's Ark. His evidence overlaps with Staunton's and Macartney's accounts of the same embassy.

W059.plain_title: Staunton's official account of the Macartney embassy to China and Tartary
W059.one_line: The British embassy's official history of its 1792 to 1794 mission, including the journey through the Great Wall to the Qing emperor's summer court at Chengde.
W059.summary: Sir George Leonard Staunton (1737-1801) was secretary and second-in-command of Lord Macartney's embassy to the Qianlong emperor. His official account (1797) was compiled from his own experience and from the journals of Macartney, Captain Parish, Dr Gillan and others, whom he often quotes. This corpus copy is Volume II, which covers Beijing, the ride north through the Great Wall into 'Chinese Tartary', the audience in a tent at Zhe-hol (Chengde), the lama temples there, and the return south. 'Tartar' here almost always means the ruling Manchus and their Mongol allies.
W059.tartar_means: Mainly the Manchus, the conquering 'Tartar dynasty' of the Qing, and their bannermen; also the Mongol princes tributary to the emperor, and 'Tartary' as the lands beyond the Great Wall. Once, the 'Mongol Tartars' of the thirteenth century.
W059.why_read: A close, dated eyewitness picture of Manchu 'Tartar' power at its height: who ruled China, how Tartars and Chinese differed, and what the court at Chengde looked like.
W059.watch_out: Staunton blends his own observations with other members' journals and with what mandarins told him, and he writes as a British official judging a foreign court. Only Volume II is in this corpus.

W060.plain_title: Afanasy Nikitin and other fifteenth-century travellers to India
W060.one_line: An 1857 Hakluyt Society anthology of four fifteenth-century journeys to India, including the Russian merchant Nikitin's trip down the Tatar-held Volga around 1466 to 1472.
W060.summary: R. H. Major edited this collection for the Hakluyt Society in 1857. It gathers the Persian envoy Abd-er-Razzak (1442), the Venetian Niccolò de' Conti as told to Poggio Bracciolini (c. 1440), the Russian merchant Afanasy Nikitin of Tver (c. 1466 to 1472, translated by Count Wielhorski), and Hieronimo di Santo Stefano. Almost all of it concerns India. The Tartar material is mainly Nikitin's opening pages, where he sails down the Volga past Kazan, the Horde and Sarai and is robbed by Tatars near Astrakhan, plus editorial footnotes and one remark in Poggio's Conti narrative.
W060.tartar_means: For Nikitin and his translator, the Tatars of the Volga khanates (Kazan, Astrakhan, the Great Horde) and a Daghestan tribe, the Kaitaks. For Poggio, 'Tartars' is the modern name for the northern Scythians of Asia. The editor's notes use 'Uzbeck Tartars' for Central Asia.
W060.why_read: Nikitin gives a rare Russian merchant's view of the Volga in the last years of the Golden Horde's successor states, when Tatar khans still controlled the river route to the Caspian.
W060.watch_out: Nikitin's Tatar passages are short, and the translator admits parts of the Russian text are obscure. The vivid details about Sarai and the Horde are in 1857 footnotes, not in Nikitin's own words.

W061.plain_title: Two Venetians among the Tatars: Barbaro at Tana and Contarini at Astrakhan
W061.one_line: Venetian merchant-diplomat Giosafat Barbaro's sixteen years at Tana (Azov) from 1436, and envoy Ambrogio Contarini's perilous return through Tatar Astrakhan in 1476.
W061.summary: Giosafat Barbaro lived as a merchant at the Venetian colony of Tana on the Don from 1436 to about 1452, dealt daily with the Golden Horde, rode out to its camp, and later went as envoy to Persia (1473 to 1478). He wrote his account in 1487. Ambrogio Contarini, another Venetian envoy to Persia, crossed the Crimean Tatar steppe in 1474 and came home in 1476 via Derbent, Astrakhan and Moscow. This 1873 Hakluyt Society volume, edited by Lord Stanley of Alderley, prints Barbaro in William Thomas's Tudor English translation (c. 1550) and Contarini in a new translation by S. A. Roy.
W061.tartar_means: The Tatars of the Golden Horde and its successors: the great camp ('Lordo') of khans like Küchük Muhammad on the Don and Volga steppe, the khans of Astrakhan and Kazan, the Crimean Tatars, and the Nogai-like 'wild Tartars' beyond the Volga. Barbaro also lumps northern forest peoples in with 'Tartariens'.
W061.why_read: The best fifteenth-century eyewitness pictures of a Tatar horde on the move: houses on carts, a camp like a city, nomads who still sowed grain, their justice and food, and what Tatar towns such as Astrakhan looked like.
W061.watch_out: Barbaro wrote decades after the events, and Thomas's Tudor English is abbreviated and hard to read in OCR (quotes here expand marks like 'w^th'). Contarini travelled frightened and hostile, and his disgust colours his descriptions.

W062.plain_title: Count Benyowsky's memoirs, volume two: from Kamchatka to Madagascar
W062.one_line: The second volume of a Hungarian-Polish adventurer's much-doubted memoir, covering his 1771 voyage from Kamchatka to Macao and his Madagascar colony.
W062.summary: Maurice (Móric) Benyovszky (1746-1786), a Hungarian-Polish nobleman, fought with the Bar Confederation, was captured by the Russians and exiled to Kamchatka, then led a mutiny and escape by ship in 1771. His memoirs were published in English in 1790, 'translated from the original manuscript'. This corpus copy is Volume II only: it opens at Formosa in August 1771 and covers Macao, the voyage to France and the Madagascar settlement. The Siberian and Kamchatka chapters are in Volume I, which is not in this corpus, so there is nothing substantial here about Tartars.
W062.tartar_means: In this volume the word appears only once, for Qing ('Tartar') soldiers or attendants who rode with him near Canton in January 1772.
W062.why_read: Only as a reminder that this famous Siberian adventure has a second volume that leaves Tartary behind; learners wanting Kamchatka and Siberia need Volume I.
W062.watch_out: Benyowsky's claims are notoriously embroidered and much of his narrative cannot be verified. The 1790 OCR prints the long s as f and is badly garbled in places.

W063.plain_title: Father Avril's search for an overland road to China
W063.one_line: A French Jesuit's 1680s journey through Armenia and Persia to Astrakhan and Moscow, with everything he could learn about 'Great Tartary' on the way.
W063.summary: Philippe Avril (1654-1698), a French Jesuit, was sent in 1685 to find a land route to China. He travelled through Armenia and Persia, reached Astrakhan in June 1686, spent four months there and went up the Volga to Moscow, where the Russians would not let him go on to China. His book (Paris 1692) mixes what he saw at Astrakhan and on the Volga with information gathered in Moscow from merchants and Russian officials about the Kalmyks, Mongols, Manchus and Siberian peoples. This corpus copy is the 1693 English translation (London, Tim Goodwin), which adds a supplement of older overland routes from Hakluyt and Purchas.
W063.tartar_means: A wide label. At Astrakhan he meets Nogai and Kalmyk Tartars. From Moscow reports he describes the Bogdoi or 'Eastern Tartars' (Manchus, rulers of China since 1644), the Mongols, the Kalmyks, and Siberian peoples (Ostyaks, Buryats, Yakuts, Tungus) whom he thinks are offshoots of the Kalmyks.
W063.why_read: It shows 'Great Tartary' being broken down into named peoples by the 1680s: nomads in felt tents, Nogai suburbs with a mosque, Manchu earth houses, the Dalai Lama and mammoth ivory, all from someone who got as far as the Volga.
W063.watch_out: Avril never reached China or inner Asia; everything east of the Volga is hearsay filtered through Russian informants and his own theology (Prester John, crosses). The 1693 OCR is poor, with long s printed as f and some pages unreadable; quotes here are normalised.

W064.plain_title: Peter Henry Bruce's memoirs of service under Peter the Great
W064.one_line: A British-descended officer's memoir of Russian service, including the 1722 Volga voyage and Persian campaign and a 1723 expedition among the Kalmyks.
W064.summary: Peter Henry Bruce (1692-1757), of Scottish family but raised in Prussia, served in the Russian army from 1711 to about 1724, including Peter the Great's 1722 expedition down the Volga to Astrakhan and into Dagestan, and a 1723 mission from Astrakhan to settle a Kalmyk succession fight. His memoirs were published posthumously in London in 1782. The Tartar material mixes his own observations (Kazan, Astrakhan, Kalmyk camps, Tarki) with long descriptive passages that closely follow earlier travel books, plus reports he heard at court, such as the massacre of the Bekovich expedition in Khiva.
W064.tartar_means: A broad label for the peoples along the Volga and Caspian: Kazan Tatars, Nogais ('Nagayans') of Astrakhan, Kalmyks, Crimean and Kuban Tatars, the Uzbeks of Khiva, the Kumyks and others of Dagestan ('Dagestan Tartars'), and even the Finnic Mari ('Ceremisse Tartars').
W064.why_read: A soldier's close look at Kalmyk felt tents and camp life, Tatar towns under Russian control, and the ruined brick city on the Volga that local tradition credited to Tamerlane.
W064.watch_out: Written up long after the events and published by others after his death; some general descriptions of the Volga peoples echo Olearius and other earlier writers almost word for word. Hearsay (Khiva, Siberia) is mixed with what he saw. The 1782 OCR prints long s as f.

W065.plain_title: John Cook's travels as a doctor on Russia's Tartar frontier
W065.one_line: A Scottish physician's memoir of Russian service at Astrakhan in the 1740s and a Russian embassy through Dagestan to Nadir Shah's Persia.
W065.summary: John Cook (c. 1712 to after 1770), a Scottish doctor from Hamilton, served in Russia from 1736, spent years as a physician at Astrakhan, and in 1746 to 1747 went with a Russian embassy through Kizlyar, Dagestan and Derbent into Persia. He published his memoirs at Edinburgh in 1770. This corpus copy is Volume II only, which covers 1741 onward: Astrakhan politics, the Kalmyk khanate and its princess, raids on the Volga, and the embassy's march south. Most Tartar material is about Kalmyks, Karakalpaks and the Muslim peoples of Dagestan, drawn from his own experience plus local report.
W065.tartar_means: A general word for the non-Russian peoples of the steppe and Caucasus: Kalmyks (whom he calls Tartars alongside Cossacks), Karakalpaks, Nogai and other Muslim Tatars serving Russia as irregular cavalry, the 'Dagestan Tartars' of the hills north of Derbent, the 'Lezgi Tartars' to the south, Turkmen, Uzbeks and Crimean Tatars.
W065.why_read: A doctor's-eye view of steppe politics in the 1740s: a Kalmyk princess in her felt tent, salted butter tea, Kalmyk and Karakalpak raiding on the ice, and Tatar villages with houses on the Caucasus frontier.
W065.watch_out: Only Volume II is in this corpus. Cook writes decades later, has personal quarrels (notably with Jonas Hanway), and reports much hearsay about Kalmyk 'barbarities'. The 1770 OCR prints the long s as f.

W066.plain_title: Edmund Spencer's 1836 voyage round the Black Sea, volume one
W066.one_line: A British travel writer's letters from a Danube and Black Sea voyage in 1836, including the south coast of 'Krim Tartary' and the Russian forts of Circassia.
W066.summary: Edmund Spencer, a British travel writer, went down the Danube to Constantinople in 1836, then sailed from Odessa with Count Mikhail Vorontsov, governor-general of New Russia, along the Crimean coast to Kerch and on to the Russian forts of the Circassian coast. His letters were published in London in 1837. This corpus copy is Volume I, which reaches Crimea and Circassia only in its last hundred pages; the fuller description of Crimean Tatar towns belongs to Volume II. What is here is brief: Tatar villages and fishermen glimpsed from the deck, Tatar names for kurgans, and a Tatar-English-Circassian vocabulary.
W066.tartar_means: The Crimean Tatars ('Krim Tartars') and the Nogai Tatars, including those who fled Russian rule into the Caucasus; he also calls the Natukhai of the Kuban 'originally Tartars'. 'Tartar' is also his name for the Turkic language spoken there.
W066.why_read: A snapshot of the Crimean Tatars fifty years after Russian annexation, seen from a Russian governor's steamer: small villages with mosques among the new villas of Russian nobles, and Tatar traditions about the steppe mounds.
W066.watch_out: Spencer travelled as a guest of the Russian governor, wrote with strong pro-Circassian and anti-Muslim opinions, and saw the Tatars mostly from the ship. Volume II is not in this corpus.

W067.plain_title: A soldier's diary of the Macartney embassy to China and Tartary
W067.one_line: Sergeant Samuel Holmes's plain diary of the 1792 to 1794 British embassy, including the march through the Great Wall to the emperor's summer town of Jehol.
W067.summary: Samuel Holmes was a trooper (later serjeant-major) of the 11th Light Dragoons who served in Lord Macartney's guard on the 1792 to 1794 embassy to the Qianlong emperor. His diary was printed in London in 1798, the publisher claiming it was 'without addition, abridgment, or amendment'. It is short and practical: the voyage, soldiers' impressions of Beijing, the four-day ride through the Great Wall into 'Tartary' to Jehol (Chengde), and the return. Holmes was kept outside the palace gates, so his Tartary is what an ordinary soldier saw from the road.
W067.tartar_means: The Manchu rulers of China and their people ('the Tartars' who inhabit Beijing's inner city) and 'Tartary' as the land north of the Great Wall; also the historic northern raiders the Wall was built against.
W067.why_read: A rank-and-file counterpoint to Staunton's official account (W059): the same Great Wall and Jehol seen by a soldier who measured the wall and pocketed its bricks.
W067.watch_out: Very brief on Tartary; Holmes saw little of the court and repeats what he was told. Same expedition as Staunton and Barrow, so not an independent source on the court.

W068.plain_title: Two Moravian missionaries among the Kalmyk hordes of the lower Volga
W068.one_line: A German missionary's day-by-day account of three months in Kalmyk tent camps north of the Caspian, May to August 1823.
W068.summary: Heinrich August Zwick and Johann Gottfried Schill, Moravian Brethren from the colony of Sarepta on the Volga, travelled for the Russian Bible Society from 26 May to 21 August 1823 through the Kalmyk hordes of the Astrakhan steppe, trying to hand out Kalmyk translations of the Gospels. Zwick wrote the narrative. They lived beside the princes' camps, moved with a horde on migration, and on the way home walked through the ruins of Golden Horde towns on the Akhtuba. The book opens with a potted history of the 'Moguls' drawn from earlier writers. This corpus copy is the London English edition of 1831.
W068.tartar_means: The book's title uses 'Calmuc Tartary' for the Kalmyk steppe, but inside Zwick usually keeps 'Calmucs' (Kalmyks, a Buddhist Mongol people) apart from 'Tartars', by which he means the Muslim or baptised Turkic Tatars of Kazan and Astrakhan, including his own drivers, merchants and a small 'Mountain Tartar' clan. For the medieval ruins he speaks of the 'Tartars' of the Golden Horde.
W068.why_read: A close, dated eyewitness picture of a living tent society, down to how a yurt is lashed together and how a princely camp is laid out, set beside the brick and tile ruins of real Golden Horde cities that the same traveller walked through.
W068.watch_out: Zwick writes as an evangelist and judges Kalmyk Buddhism harshly; his historical introduction is second-hand and has errors of date and name. The OCR of this copy is poor in places (E for K, Russian letters for Latin ones), so check the page image.

W069.plain_title: A Jesuit rides with the Kangxi emperor to Manchuria, 1682
W069.one_line: Ferdinand Verbiest's letter describing the emperor's spring journey from Beijing to the Manchu homeland on the Sungari River.
W069.summary: Ferdinand Verbiest (1623-1688), a Flemish Jesuit who ran the imperial astronomical bureau in Beijing, was ordered to ride beside the Kangxi emperor on a three-month progress into 'Eastern Tartary' in 1682, taking latitudes and compass readings along the way. The emperor had just crushed the revolt of the three southern 'kings' and went to honour his ancestors' tombs near Shenyang, then hunted and travelled on to Jilin and Ula. This corpus copy is the English version of Verbiest's letter printed in a learned journal in 1686 (JSTOR Early Journal Content), with his list of daily stages.
W069.tartar_means: The Manchus, the ruling 'Tartars' of the Qing dynasty whom Verbiest served (he calls them 'our Tartars'), and 'Eastern Tartary' as their homeland of Liaodong and Manchuria beyond it.
W069.why_read: A dated eyewitness look at Manchuria in 1682, from ruined Chinese towns in Liaodong to the sacred mountain of the Manchu ancestors, written by a man measuring the route with instruments.
W069.watch_out: This is an English translation of a letter passed on through Europe, not Verbiest's original Latin. The OCR renders the old long s as f throughout.

W070.plain_title: A Jesuit rides with the Kangxi emperor into Mongolia, 1683
W070.one_line: Ferdinand Verbiest's second letter, on the emperor's great summer hunt beyond the Great Wall among the Mongol 'Western Tartars'.
W070.summary: Ferdinand Verbiest, the Flemish Jesuit astronomer at the Qing court, was again ordered to follow the Kangxi emperor in 1683, this time with Father Philippe Grimaldi, on a summer progress north of the Great Wall with the emperor's grandmother, some 60,000 men and 100,000 horses. He explains the reasons for the trip (military training, keeping the Mongols in awe, the emperor's health, escaping Beijing's heat), describes the land and its tent-dwelling herders, and praises the Great Wall. This corpus copy is the English version printed in a learned journal in 1686 (JSTOR Early Journal Content), followed by an editor's note on geography.
W070.tartar_means: 'Western Tartars' are the Mongols north and west of the Great Wall; 'Eastern' or 'Oriental Tartars' are the Manchus who ruled China. The emperor himself is 'the Tartarian Monarch that Conquered China'.
W070.why_read: A court insider's eyewitness picture of Mongol pastoral life in 1683 and of how the Manchu emperor managed the Mongols, with a flat statement that their country had no towns or houses.
W070.watch_out: Verbiest is openly scornful of the Mongols and their lamas, and writes as a missionary eager for converts. Same author as W069, so not an independent witness; English translation of a communicated letter.

W071.plain_title: A 'voyage into Tartary' that finds a philosophers' City of the Sun
W071.one_line: A 1689 English book, presented as a Frenchman's true travels, describing a perfect classical city called Heliopolis somewhere in Tartary.
W071.summary: Published in London in 1689 under the name 'Heliogenes de L'Epy, Doctor of Philosophy', and said in its preface to be translated from a French original. The narrator, born near Lyons, tells of a childhood shipwreck, travels through Greece and Turkey, and a journey across the Caspian 'to see Tartary, of which Country there has been so little said'. The heart of the book is a long description of Heliopolis, a round city of learned sun-honouring philosophers living under the protection of the 'Great Kam'. The corpus copy is a microfilm scan (Early English Books) with very poor OCR.
W071.tartar_means: Tartary is a vague, far-off land reached across the Caspian. 'Tartarians' are the peoples surrounding the imaginary city, and 'wild Tartars' are huntsmen met on the road; the 'Great Kam' is their overlord.
W071.why_read: A rare seventeenth-century English example of a gleaming, domed, classical city placed in Tartary, useful for seeing how an imaginary 'great city of Tartary' could enter print long before modern theories.
W071.watch_out: The author's name ('Sun-born') and his City of the Sun mark this as an imaginary voyage in the utopian tradition, not a travel record, though the preface insists it is true; the catalogue keeps its status open. The OCR is badly broken; check every quote against the page image.

W072.one_line: An 1830 English translation of Persian memoirs said to have been written by Timur himself, covering his rise in fourteenth-century Central Asia.
W072.summary: The Mulfuzat Timury claims to be Timur's (1336-1405) own account of his life, found in a Turki manuscript and put into Persian in the seventeenth century by Abu Talib al-Husayni. Major Charles Stewart translated the early part, to Timur's accession at Samarkand in 1369, from a manuscript once owned by Major William Davy, for the Oriental Translation Fund in 1830. It tells of Timur's youth among the Barlas tribe near Kesh, his omens, his wars with the Chaghatayid khans and his rivals, and his taking of Samarkand. Its authenticity has long been doubted.
W072.tartar_means: The translator uses 'Tartary' for the whole steppe world once called Scythia and 'Tartars' for its Turkic and Mongol nomads, including Timur's own people. In the text, 'Tatar' is also the name of a legendary ancestor, twin brother of 'Moghul'.
W072.why_read: It shows how Timur's world told its own origin story (Tatar and Moghul as twin brothers descended from Japhet) and gives glimpses of felt tents, palaces, fortresses and mosques in Transoxiana, even if the voice is not truly Timur's.
W072.watch_out: Most modern scholars regard the memoirs as a seventeenth-century Persian composition passed off as Timur's own; treat the first-person voice as a literary device. Stewart's preface quotes Davy arguing for authenticity.

W073.plain_title: Ibn Battuta's travels, in Samuel Lee's 1829 abridged translation
W073.one_line: The Moroccan traveller's account of the Golden Horde, Central Asia, India and China in the 1330s and 1340s, from an Arabic abridgement.
W073.summary: Ibn Battuta of Tangier (1304-1368/9) travelled for nearly thirty years across the Islamic world and beyond, and dictated his memories to the scholar Ibn Juzayy in Fez about 1355. Samuel Lee, Cambridge professor of Arabic, translated a shortened Arabic version of that book for the Oriental Translation Committee in 1829, with long learned footnotes; this is that edition. For the Tartar world it covers the Kipchak steppe and Crimea, the moving camp and court of Uzbek Khan, Astrakhan, Sarai, Khwarezm, Bukhara, Samarkand and the Chaghatayid sultan Tarmashirin, the ruins Genghis Khan left at Balkh, and Mongol-ruled China.
W073.tartar_means: Ibn Battuta keeps 'Tartars' mainly for the Mongols of Genghis Khan who invaded and destroyed Muslim lands, and for the Mongol rulers of Iran and China. The Muslim Golden Horde and Chaghatayid peoples he usually calls 'Turks'; the running head 'TARTARY' in this book is the translator's.
W073.why_read: A Muslim insider's eyewitness picture of the Golden Horde at its height: a camp that moved like a city with its own mosques, unveiled royal women, mare's milk, and the great towns of Sarai and Khwarezm, alongside the ruins the first Mongol invasion left behind.
W073.watch_out: Lee worked from an abridgement, so much is missing and some wording differs from modern translations of the full Rihla. The book was written down from memory years later, and scholars doubt some episodes (the trip to Bulgar, and how far into China he really went).

W074.plain_title: The memoirs of Babur, Timurid prince and founder of Mughal India
W074.one_line: Babur's own Turki memoir of his wars in Fergana, Samarkand, Kabul and India, in the 1826 Leyden and Erskine translation.
W074.summary: Zahir al-Din Muhammad Babur (1483-1530), descended from Timur on his father's side and from Genghis Khan on his mother's, wrote the Baburnama in Chaghatai Turki. It follows his boyhood as king of Fergana, his repeated capture and loss of Samarkand to the Uzbeks, his years in Kabul, and his conquest of north India in 1526. This corpus copy is the 1826 English translation begun by John Leyden and completed by William Erskine from Persian and Turki manuscripts, with Erskine's long introduction on the 'Tartar tribes' and the geography of Central Asia, and a supplement covering gaps in the text.
W074.tartar_means: Babur himself speaks of Turks, Moghuls (Mongols) and Uzbeks, not 'Tartars'. The word comes from Erskine, the editor, who calls Babur 'of Tartar race' and devotes pages to explaining that 'Tartar' was a European label for Turks and Mongols alike, and that the peoples themselves did not use it.
W074.why_read: A ruler's first-hand descriptions of Samarkand's stone mosques, palaces, observatory and bazaars, of felt tents and steppe customs, and an 1826 scholar's careful discussion of where the name 'Tartar' came from, including the Tartarus pun.
W074.watch_out: Parts of the memoir are lost and the translators worked from differing manuscripts, often noting where copies disagree. Erskine's introduction is his own synthesis of earlier European and Oriental authors, and carries the racial assumptions of his day.

W075.plain_title: Mohan Lal's journey from Delhi to Balkh, Bukhara and Mashhad
W075.one_line: An Indian munshi's diary of travelling with Alexander Burnes through Afghanistan and Turkestan to Bukhara in 1832, and on into Persia.
W075.summary: Mohan Lal (1812-1877), a Kashmiri Pandit from Delhi trained at the English college there, went as Persian secretary to Alexander Burnes on his 1831-1833 mission through Kabul and over the Hindu Kush to Balkh and Bukhara. He then travelled on alone to Mashhad and the Persian camp at Herat. His diary, first printed in Calcutta in 1834, is here in the enlarged London edition of 1846, which adds his later visit to Britain and Germany. He writes as an eyewitness with an ear for local legends, and his own disgust at the slave trade he saw runs through the Turkestan chapters.
W075.tartar_means: 'Tartary' is a loose name for Turkestan, the lands of Bukhara and the Turkic peoples north of the Hindu Kush. He calls one legendary conqueror from Badakhshan 'a Tartar', and once uses 'the Tartars' for the Turkmen raiders who seized villagers as slaves.
W075.why_read: A non-European eyewitness view of Bukhara, 'the largest and most populous and wealthy city in the whole region of Tartary', built of mud, wood and mats, and of the ruins and tall tales of ancient Balkh.
W075.watch_out: Mohan Lal travelled with Burnes, so his account is not independent of Burnes's Travels into Bokhara. He writes in an English that is not his first language, and he repeats local legends alongside what he saw.

W076.plain_title: Gutzlaff's voyage on a Chinese junk to the edge of Manchuria
W076.one_line: A Prussian missionary's journal of sailing up the China coast on a trading junk in 1831, as far as Liaodong on the frontier of 'Mantchou Tartary'.
W076.summary: Karl Gützlaff (1803-1851), a Prussian Protestant missionary, lived in Siam and in 1831 sailed north aboard a Chinese junk from Bangkok, dressed as a Chinese and working as a doctor while handing out Christian tracts. He reached Tianjin and then Jinzhou in Liaodong, on the southern fringe of Manchuria, before winter drove the junk south. This corpus copy is the small Canton edition of 1832, first printed in the Chinese Repository. Despite the title, he saw only the Liaodong coast and says little about the Manchus themselves.
W076.tartar_means: 'Mantchou Tartary' is Manchuria, homeland of the ruling Qing Manchus, and 'Mantchou Tartars' are the Manchus, many of them bannermen living on imperial pay. 'Western Tartary' means the Qing's Central Asian frontier, where a war was then going on.
W076.why_read: A short eyewitness glimpse of how 'Tartary' looked from the deck of a trading junk in 1831: Manchus hardly different from Chinese in appearance, granite towns and heated brick beds.
W076.watch_out: Gützlaff writes as a zealous missionary and judges Chinese religion harshly. He stayed only in the port and relied on what people told him about Mukden and the Manchus inland, as the catalogue caution warns.

W077.plain_title: Pétis de la Croix's History of Genghis Khan
W077.one_line: A French court orientalist's life of Genghis Khan, compiled from Persian, Arabic and Turkish histories and European travellers, in its 1722 English translation.
W077.summary: François Pétis de la Croix the elder (1622-1695), secretary-interpreter in Turkish and Arabic to Louis XIV, spent years compiling a history of Genghis Khan from Oriental chronicles (Mirkhond, Fadlallah, Abulfeda, Abu'l-Ghazi and others) and from European travellers such as Carpini, Rubruck and Marco Polo, whose words he often gives in the margins. His son published it in Paris in 1710; this is the London English translation of 1722. It covers the Mongol rise, the conquest of Central Asia and China, Mongol laws and customs, and the geography of 'Eastern and Western Tartary'. It is a compilation, not a witness.
W077.tartar_means: The 'antient Moguls and Tartars' are the Mongols of Genghis Khan. The book explains 'Tartar' as the name of one Mongol people, the Tatars of the river 'Tata', later spread to all the Scythian nations Genghis ruled.
W077.why_read: An early modern synthesis showing how Europe around 1700 understood the Mongols: where the name 'Tartar' came from, how their wagon-houses were built, and how Prester John was identified with a real steppe king.
W077.watch_out: Every passage is second-hand, stitched together from sources centuries apart; the author gives marginal source references but blends them freely. The OCR mixes marginal notes into the text.

W078.plain_title: A French officer's account of the Cossacks and the Crimean Tartars
W078.one_line: A 1663 French description of Ukraine's Cossacks and the Tartars of Crimea, with a history of the Cossack wars against Poland, in a 1672 English translation.
W078.summary: Pierre Chevalier, a French officer who (his English translator says) served as a commander and lived long in Poland, published this short book in French in 1663; Edward Brown's English version appeared in London in 1672. It has three parts: the Cossacks' country and customs, a 'Discourse of the Precopian Tartars' (the Crimean Tatars, named after their fortress town Perekop), and a history of Bohdan Khmelnytsky's Cossack revolt of 1648 to 1651, in which the Crimean Khan fought as the Cossacks' ally. The Tartar chapter mixes things Chevalier saw in Poland (Tartar prisoners, captives) with general descriptions of Crimea, its towns, raids and slave trade.
W078.tartar_means: Mainly the Crimean Tatars ('Precopian Tartars') ruled by the Khan (Cham) of the Giray dynasty, a Muslim people and vassals of the Ottoman Sultan, plus the Nogai hordes of Budjak. Chevalier also uses 'Tartary' for all of northern Asia, divided into five parts.
W078.why_read: A compact seventeenth century portrait of the Crimean Khanate from the Polish side: its towns and houses, the Khan's court at Bakhchysarai, raiding and the Caffa slave market, food, arms and morals, and the Khan's army at the siege of Zbarazh.
W078.watch_out: Chevalier writes as a soldier in the service of the Tartars' Polish enemies; some Tartar material overlaps with the engineer Beauplan's earlier description of Ukraine, which Chevalier names, so not every detail is his own observation. The 1672 print uses the long s and the OCR is rough.

W079.plain_title: Nicolaas Witsen explains his new map of Great Tartary to the Royal Society
W079.one_line: A 1686 exchange of letters in the Philosophical Transactions in which the Amsterdam burgomaster Witsen tells how he gathered the information for his map of 'Great Tartary'.
W079.summary: This short notice in the Royal Society's Philosophical Transactions (1686) prints two letters. Sir Robert Southwell, President of the Society, thanks Nicolaas Witsen for copies of his new map of Tartary and asks how it could possibly have been made. Witsen, then a leading burgomaster of Amsterdam, answers that he travelled to Muscovy about 28 years earlier, talked there with 'Tartars of all sorts', and has since kept up correspondence with Moscow, Astrakhan, Isfahan, Constantinople and even Peking, collecting journals and commissioned drawings. He also admits his doubts about the coastlines. It contains no description of Tartar life itself.
W079.tartar_means: 'Tartary' here is the whole vast, little-known interior of northern and central Asia between Muscovy and China; 'Tartars of all sorts' are the many Asian peoples Witsen met in Muscovy.
W079.why_read: It shows exactly how a famous seventeenth century map of 'Great Tartary' was built: from interviews, letters, travellers' journals and drawings, not from a surveyed empire, and with the mapmaker openly flagging what he was unsure of.
W079.watch_out: A four-page notice, not Witsen's map or his great book Noord en Oost Tartarye. The letters are printed in English in the journal; Witsen's is summarised 'to the effect following'.

W081.plain_title: Strabo's Geography, volume II (Scythians and the Black Sea and Caspian lands)
W081.one_line: The Greek geographer Strabo's description of the northern nomads, the Sea of Azov and Central Asia, written about 2,000 years ago, in an 1854 English translation.
W081.summary: Strabo, a Greek geographer from Amaseia in Asia Minor, compiled his Geography around 7 BCE to 23 CE, mostly from earlier writers such as Eratosthenes and Theophanes. This corpus copy is volume II of the Bohn's Classical Library translation by H. C. Hamilton and W. Falconer (1854). The pages relevant here, Book XI, describe the Don, the Greek cities of the Bosporus, the Scythians, Sarmatians and 'waggon-dwellers' of the steppe, and the Sacae and Massagetae of Central Asia. Strabo lived more than a thousand years before the name 'Tartar' reached Europe, so he never uses it; the word appears only once, in an 1854 editor's footnote.
W081.tartar_means: Strabo himself never mentions Tartars. The single use of 'Tartars' is in a translator's footnote, where it means the Crimean or Nogai Tatars who later lived around the Sea of Azov and renamed its ancient sites.
W081.why_read: Background for the steppe before the Tartars: Strabo's nomads who live on meat and milk and in 'waggon-houses' show that later European writers who called the Tartars 'Scythians' were borrowing an ancient template.
W081.watch_out: Context only. Strabo's Scythians, Sarmatians and Sacae are not the medieval Tatars or Mongols, and his information is itself secondhand. The bundle includes publisher's catalogue pages at the back of the volume, which are irrelevant.

W082.plain_title: Mary Holderness's four years among the Crimean Tatars
W082.one_line: An Englishwoman's close, first-hand notes on the daily life of the Crimean Tatars in their village of Karagoss, 1816 to 1820, published with her journey from Riga.
W082.summary: Mary Holderness lived at the village of Karagoss, in the eastern Crimea near Feodosia, from 1816 to 1820. She first published 'Notes Relating to the Manners and Customs of the Crim Tatars' in 1821; this corpus copy is the second edition of 1827, which adds her 'Journey from Riga to the Crimea', chapters on the other colonists of New Russia (Nogays, Greeks, Bulgarians, Germans), and the revised Tatar notes. She attended Tatar weddings and funerals, visited Tatar cottages daily, and questioned her neighbours, so most of her detail is eyewitness, though she flags what she was 'told'. The Crimea had been annexed by Russia in 1783, a generation before she arrived.
W082.tartar_means: Almost always the Crimean Tatars (mountain, valley and steppe villagers, now Russian subjects), plus the Nogay Tatars of the Molochna steppe north of Crimea, whom the government had settled in villages.
W082.why_read: One of the best early close-ups of ordinary Crimean Tatar life: how their wattle-and-daub cottages were built, what was inside, weddings, burials, superstitions, dress and markets, from someone who lived next door for four years.
W082.watch_out: Holderness writes as a devout English Protestant and sometimes judges Tatar religion and character; her population figures and some history come from others. The volume mixes the 1821 notes with later travel chapters, and the OCR occasionally garbles words.

W083.plain_title: James Webster's ride through the Crimea in 1827
W083.one_line: A young Scottish lawyer's travel journal of the Crimea in 1827, with Tatar villages, the Khans' palace at Bakhchysarai and a dervish ceremony, published after his death.
W083.summary: James Webster, a Scottish barrister of the Inner Temple, travelled with W. H. Newnham through Poland, southern Russia, the Crimea, Turkey and Egypt between 1825 and 1828. He died young, and an editor published his journals in two volumes in 1830 as the work of 'the late James Webster'. This corpus copy is Volume I; the Crimean chapters (pages 48 to 90) record late summer 1827: Tatar caravans at Perekop, the old Tatar quarter of Simferopol, village hospitality, Alushta, the cave dwellings of Inkerman, and a long visit to Bakhchysarai with its palace, mosque, tombs and a dervish ritual. Most of it is his own observation, told with youthful wit and some condescension.
W083.tartar_means: The Crimean Tatars: Muslim villagers, townspeople and carters of the peninsula under Russian rule since 1783, and the memory of their former Khans of the Giray dynasty.
W083.why_read: Clear descriptions of what Crimean Tatar towns and buildings actually looked like in 1827: walled courtyard houses, terraced flat-roofed villages, a wood-and-clay mosque, and the Khans' palace and domed tombs at Bakhchysarai.
W083.watch_out: Webster often mocks what he does not understand (Tatar singing, the call to prayer, the dervish rite) and relies on guides and Russian hosts for history. The book was edited after his death.

W084.plain_title: J. G. Kohl's Russia, from St Petersburg to the Crimean Tatar villages
W084.one_line: A German travel writer's lively picture of the Russian Empire in the late 1830s, including Tatars in Moscow and St Petersburg and a horseback tour of Tatar Crimea, in an 1844 English abridgment.
W084.summary: Johann Georg Kohl (1808-1878), a German geographer and travel writer, spent several years in the Baltic provinces and Russia in the 1830s and published four works in nine German volumes. This 1844 London volume (Chapman and Hall) is an English abridgment of all of them by an unnamed editor, strongest on St Petersburg. The Tartar material is scattered: Tatar coachmen, traders and a small mosque in Moscow; Tatar leatherwork and 'dressing-gown Tartars' in the capital; kurgans plundered in the south; and an eight-day ride through the Crimea with village stays, Tatar songs, and a visit to Bakhchysarai and the Khans' tombs. Most Crimean passages are eyewitness.
W084.tartar_means: Mostly the Crimean Tatars of the mountain villages and Bakhchysarai; also Muslim Tatars (largely from Kazan and the Volga) working as coachmen and traders in Moscow and St Petersburg; historically, the Mongol-Tatar armies that burned Moscow and the Crimean Khanate as 'the last fragment of the great Mongolian empire in Europe'.
W084.why_read: Kohl notices how Tatar buildings and towns worked: flat roofs you could ride over, windowless houses with fold-down wooden fronts, a Tatar-only Bakhchysarai, a mosque in Moscow paid for by a Tatar merchant, and tombs that overturned his idea of 'barbarian' Khans.
W084.watch_out: This is an abridged translation, so wording is the English editor's as much as Kohl's. Kohl has a German nationalist streak and sometimes romanticises; the stories behind the Khans' tomb inscriptions were presumably explained to him by guides.

W085.plain_title: Captain Jesse's Crimea: Tatar villages and Bakhchysarai in 1839 to 1840
W085.one_line: A British half-pay officer's travel notes on Russia, Circassia and the Crimea, 1839 to 1840, with nights in Tatar houses and a visit to the Khans' old capital.
W085.summary: Captain William Jesse, a British army officer on half pay, travelled in southern Russia, the Caucasus coast and the Crimea in 1839 and 1840, officially for his health, and published these notes in 1841 (this is Volume I). He is openly critical of Russia and says in his preface that most of his facts came 'under my own observation'. His Crimean chapters cover the south coast estates of the Russian nobility, Tatar villages on the mountainsides, the cave fortress of Mangup, Bakhchysarai with its palace, fountain and a Tatar wedding, the Karaite town of Chufut-Kale, and nights as a guest in Tatar homes, with Colonel Upton's son as interpreter.
W085.tartar_means: The Crimean Tatars: Muslim villagers and townspeople of the peninsula, conquered by Russia in 1783, and their former Khans; also Tatar pilgrims returning from Mecca on a Black Sea steamer.
W085.why_read: Short, concrete snapshots of Tatar building and village life around 1840: clay-roofed houses set into hillsides, two-storey tiled houses in the valleys, a wooden minaret used to call up post horses, the Khans' fountain inscription, and a host's bitter remark about the conquerors.
W085.watch_out: Jesse is sharply anti-Russian and at times crudely disdainful of 'dirty' peoples, including some Tatars; he relied on an interpreter. Only Volume I is in the corpus, and the OCR of this Indian scan is uneven.

W086.plain_title: William Coxe on the Russian conquest of Siberia and the China trade
W086.one_line: An English clergyman's 1780 compilation of Russian voyages to Alaska, the Cossack conquest of the Siberian Tatar khanate, and the Russia and China border trade at Kiakhta.
W086.summary: William Coxe (1747-1828), a Cambridge fellow and tutor who travelled in Russia, compiled this book in 1780 from Russian and German sources, above all G. F. Müller's Sammlung Russischer Geschichte, J. E. Fischer's Sibirische Geschichte and P. S. Pallas's travels, which he footnotes. It covers Russian fur-hunting voyages to the Aleutians, then 'The Conquest of Siberia': Yermak's Cossack campaign of 1579 to 1582 against Kuchum Khan of the Siberian Tatars and his capital Sibir. A final part describes Russia and China relations, the Treaty of Nerchinsk and the frontier towns of Kiakhta and Maimachin. Coxe witnessed none of the Siberian events himself.
W086.tartar_means: Mainly the Siberian Tatars of Kuchum Khan's khanate on the Irtysh and Tobol rivers, and the other native 'Tartar tribes' of western Siberia; also the Kazan and Astrakhan Tatars conquered by Ivan IV, and, loosely, Mongols, Kalmyks and Buryats (the 'Tartar nations' described by Pallas).
W086.why_read: A clear eighteenth century English account of how a real Tatar state in Siberia, with a small fortress capital at Sibir, fell to a Cossack band, and how Russia then built Tyumen, Tobolsk and other towns on its lands.
W086.watch_out: Secondhand throughout: Coxe condenses Müller and Fischer, who drew on seventeenth century Siberian chronicles. His language about 'barbarians' and 'idolatrous' subjects reflects his time and sources, and the Russian conquest is told from the conquerors' side.

W087.plain_title: What pilgrims from 'Chinese Tartary' told a Bombay official in 1835
W087.one_line: A British official in Bombay writes down what Muslim pilgrims from Yarkand, Kashgar and Khotan told him about their Qing-ruled homeland.
W087.summary: W. H. Wathen, Persian Secretary to the Bombay Government, published this memoir in the Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal in December 1835. He never went to the region. Instead, over many friendly conversations, he questioned at least ten natives of 'Chinese Tartary' (the Tarim Basin, in today's Xinjiang) who were passing through Bombay on pilgrimage to Mecca, among them a prince from Aksu and a pirzada, and he checked one informant against another. The memoir covers the towns of Yarkand, Kashgar, Aksu, Khotan and others, Qing garrisons and taxes, trade routes, a volcano, recent Muslim revolts against the Chinese, and a short Turki word list.
W087.tartar_means: 'Chinese Tartary' is the Qing-ruled Tarim Basin (Altishahr, today's southern Xinjiang); 'Independent Tartary' is the Central Asian khanates such as Kokand. Wathen calls the settled Turki-speaking Muslims 'Usbeks' (the ancestors of today's Uyghurs) and also mentions Kalmuks (Oirats), Manchus and Tungans (Chinese Muslims).
W087.why_read: Rare testimony from people of the region itself, around 1830: what Yarkand's forts and houses were built of, what people ate and drank, a rain-making stone, and local anger at forced labour on Chinese walled towns.
W087.watch_out: Everything is oral report retold by Wathen, and he says himself that such information needs 'great caution'. The corpus OCR of this Indian scan is badly garbled on several pages, so two quotes below were transcribed from the page images.

W088.plain_title: A reported road from Phari to Lhasa, 1848
W088.one_line: The Darjeeling superintendent's stage-by-stage itinerary of the road from the Tibetan frontier to Lhasa, compiled from informants, with notes by B. H. Hodgson.
W088.summary: Archibald Campbell, Superintendent of Darjeeling, published this itinerary in the Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal in April 1848. He did not make the journey: he built it, through interpreters, from the recollections of travellers and traders, and he calls it a contribution to 'conjectural Geography'. It lists about forty stages from Phari to Lhasa with notes on monasteries, lakes, hide boats, stone rest houses and bridges, crops and Qing garrisons, and the orientalist B. H. Hodgson added footnotes. It is about Tibet, not Tartary; 'Tartars' appear only as Manchu soldiers in the Qing garrison at Gyantse.
W088.tartar_means: 'Mantchoo Tartars': Manchu bannermen of the Qing army stationed in Tibet. In a footnote Hodgson also notes that Tibetan nomad robbers were wrongly called 'Kalmaks' (Kalmyks).
W088.why_read: A reminder of how widely 'Tartar' was used in the 1840s: here it simply means the Manchu soldiers of the Qing empire, posted as far away as southern Tibet.
W088.watch_out: Informant testimony gathered through interpreters, which Campbell himself calls laborious and uncertain. Almost nothing here concerns Tartars.

W089.plain_title: A surgeon's notes on the plants and minerals of Bhutan and Tibet
W089.one_line: An embassy surgeon's field notes on plants, rocks, springs and diseases along the road from Bengal through Bhutan into Tibet, 1783.
W089.summary: Robert Saunders, an East India Company surgeon, travelled with Samuel Turner's embassy from Bengal to the Panchen Lama in 1783. His report, read to the Royal Society in 1789 and printed in the Philosophical Transactions, is a day-by-day naturalist's diary: thermometer readings, limestone and chalk beds, wild strawberries, firs, rhubarb, poisoned arrows, goitre, borax and salt. Tartars barely appear. The only mention is a remark that true rhubarb grows in the northern provinces of China, in Tartary and in the Russian dominions. This corpus copy is the 1789 journal printing.
W089.tartar_means: Tartary is used only once, as a geographical label for the cold lands north of China where rhubarb grows. No Tartar people are described.
W089.why_read: A reminder that for an eighteenth-century naturalist, Tartary was simply the name of a region on the map, the home of the rhubarb trade.
W089.watch_out: Almost nothing here is about Tartars. The OCR prints the long s as f and garbles some plant names.

W090.plain_title: An early report on Tibet from George Bogle's letters
W090.one_line: A Royal Society letter of 1777 summarising what George Bogle learned on his mission to the Panchen Lama, 1774 to 1775.
W090.summary: John Stewart, a Company official in Bengal, wrote this letter to Sir John Pringle in March 1777, and it was printed in the Philosophical Transactions. Stewart never went to Tibet. He retells what George Bogle reported from his mission to the Panchen (Tashi) Lama, adds what he saw of Tibetan and Bhutanese envoys in Calcutta, and prints a translation of the Lama's letter to Warren Hastings. Tartars appear as the wider Buddhist world around Tibet: Mongols, Kalmyks, the Manchu emperor, and the 'Tartar subjects of Russia' who came as pilgrims. This corpus copy is the 1777 journal printing.
W090.tartar_means: Mostly the Buddhist peoples of Inner Asia (Mongols, Kalmyks and their kin) who revered the Dalai Lama, plus the Manchu ('Mantchou Tartar') emperor of China and the 'Ehatli' (probably Eluth, that is Dzungar Oirat) Tartars who had once held Tibet. He also uses 'Tartar' as a style label for faces and religious images.
W090.why_read: It shows how an educated Briton in 1777 pictured a vast 'Tartar' religious world centred on Lhasa, stretching from the Volga to Korea, and it relays Bogle's firsthand picture of a Tibetan lama's stone castle.
W090.watch_out: Stewart is a second-hand reporter working from Bogle's letters, and he says so; only the envoys in Calcutta are his own observation. His remarks on 'superstition' reflect Protestant prejudice. OCR prints the long s as f.

W092.plain_title: An earthquake on the Siberian frontier, 1761
W092.one_line: Reports from Russian forts on the Irtysh and Altai frontier of a widespread earthquake on 28 November 1761, sent to St Petersburg and printed in London.
W092.summary: W. W. Weymarn, writing from Fort Omsk in March 1762, sent Dr James Mounsey, the Russian emperor's chief physician, a set of garrison reports on an earthquake felt along the fortified lines of the Irtysh, Kuznetsk and Kolyvan on 28 November 1761 (old style), plus a tremor on 22 October. He added his own theory that 'combustible matter' in the Altai caught fire. The French letter was translated and read to the Royal Society in 1763. Tartars appear only once, as makers of gunpowder from Altai saltpetre. This corpus copy is the 1763 Philosophical Transactions printing.
W092.tartar_means: The Turkic peoples of the Altai and upper Irtysh frontier, mentioned alongside the Kalmyks (Dzungar Oirats); the Kazakhs beyond the Irtysh are called 'Kirgis Kaisacks'.
W092.why_read: A precise, dated disaster report from the Siberian frontier: timber forts shaking, turf roofs cracking, and no mention of any buried cities. It also has a one-line glimpse of Tartar and Kalmyk gunpowder making.
W092.watch_out: Only one passing mention of Tartars. The earthquake theory is the author's own speculation. The 'monstrous lamb' skin sent earlier is mentioned but not described.

W094.plain_title: A Spanish bishop's history of the Manchu conquest of China
W094.one_line: A history of the Manchu ('Tartar') conquest of Ming China in the 1640s, compiled in Mexico from reports sent via the Philippines, in the English edition of 1676.
W094.summary: Juan de Palafox y Mendoza (1600-1659), bishop of Puebla and for a time viceroy of New Spain, gathered reports that reached Mexico from Manila about the fall of the Ming and the Manchu takeover. The history was found among his papers after his death and published posthumously; this corpus copy is the 1676 English edition. Besides the campaigns, the sack of Canton and the Shunzhi emperor's rule, later chapters describe the Tartars' tents, food, war habits, dress and hair. Palafox never went to China.
W094.tartar_means: The Manchus (the 'Tartars' of the north-east beyond the Great Wall) who conquered China and founded the Qing dynasty; their ruler is 'the Cham of Tartary'.
W094.why_read: It shows how the Manchu conquest reached European readers as a 'Tartar' conquest, and it gives a vivid picture of a Tartar army camp laid out like a town of leather tents.
W094.watch_out: Palafox relies on missionary and merchant reports from Manila, not his own eyes, and he moralises about Chinese softness and Tartar vigour. The OCR of this early printed book is very poor; only short readable passages can be quoted.

W095.plain_title: Tamerlane's court history, in English via French
W095.one_line: The official Persian history of Timur (Tamerlane), written about 1424 to 1425, in the 1723 English translation made from Pétis de la Croix's French.
W095.summary: Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi wrote the Zafarnama (Book of Victory) for Timur's grandson Ibrahim Sultan about twenty years after Timur's death, using court records and earlier accounts. François Pétis de la Croix translated it into French (1722), adding footnotes, and an English version followed in 1723. The volume in this corpus begins at Book IV: Timur's invasion of India and sack of Delhi (1398), the building of the great mosque at Samarkand, the wars in Syria, the sack of Baghdad (1401) and the war with the Ottoman sultan Bayezid. Throughout, Timur's own army is 'the Tartars'.
W095.tartar_means: Timur's own Turkic and Mongol army and people of Transoxiana (the Chaghatay 'Tartars'), as the court historian and his French translator call them. A translator's footnote distinguishes Turks (descended from Moguls and Tartars) from Tajiks.
W095.why_read: A rare view from inside the 'Tartar' camp: the conqueror's own historian describes his stone mosque at Samarkand and the craftsmen who built it, and records enemies mocking Tartar homes of rope and canvas.
W095.watch_out: This is court propaganda written for Timur's family, filtered through a French translation and its footnotes. The manifest calls this volume I, but the text begins at Book IV. The OCR prints the long s and has many broken words.

W096.plain_title: Mir Izzet Ullah's journey from Kashmir to Bukhara
W096.one_line: An Indian Muslim traveller's route journal through Ladakh, Yarkand, Kashgar, Kokand, Samarkand and Bukhara in 1812 to 1813.
W096.summary: Mir Izzet Ullah, a Persian-writing agent of the English traveller William Moorcroft, was sent ahead in 1812 to scout the road from Kashmir over the Karakoram to Chinese Turkestan and on to Bukhara. He kept a Persian journal of stages, towns, taxes, horses and peoples. H. H. Wilson translated part of it for a Calcutta magazine in 1825 and reprinted it, with notes, in the Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society in 1843; this corpus copy is that reprint. It includes a route from Peking to Kashgar copied from a local man's journal. He meets Kalmyks, Kirghiz, Kazakhs, Uzbeks and Nogais, and describes Timur's tomb at Samarkand.
W096.tartar_means: Izzet Ullah names peoples precisely (Kalmaks, Kirghiz, Kazzaks, Kapchaks, Uzbeks, Nogais) and the English word 'Tartar' appears only a few times, for nomad camps on the road and in the translator's notes. The Kalmaks are the Oirat Mongols (Dzungars) who once ruled Yarkand and raided Ladakh.
W096.why_read: A non-European eyewitness of 1813 shows Inner Asia as a patchwork of named peoples, Chinese-run oasis towns and ruined Timurid monuments, with no one called simply 'the Tartars'.
W096.watch_out: This is an English translation by H. H. Wilson of a Persian journal, with Wilson's notes and some omitted sections. Parts, such as the Peking route, are copied from another man's journal, and some wonders (the rain stone) are hearsay, which the traveller admits.

W097.one_line: A Persian official in Mongol service writes the history of Chinggis Khan and his heirs, about 1252 to 1260.
W097.summary: Ata-Malik Juvaini (1226-1283) came from a family of Persian administrators and served the Mongols. He travelled twice to Mongolia and the court at Karakorum around 1249 to 1253, began his Tarikh-i Jahangushay there, and later governed Baghdad for Hülegü's dynasty. Volume I covers the Mongols before Chinggis Khan, the Yasa (law code), Chinggis's sons, the Uighurs, the conquest of Transoxiana and Khorasan (Bukhara, Samarkand, Merv, Nishapur) and Ögedei's court. The Boyle translation named in the catalogue is not in the corpus. This copy is the Persian text edited by Mirza Muhammad Qazvini (Gibb Memorial Series, volume I, 1912). The translations below are our own working versions.
W097.tartar_means: Juvaini usually says 'Mongol' (مغول), but he uses 'Tatar' (تاتار, تتار) as a plain synonym for the Mongols and their armies: 'the Tatar army', 'the hoof of the Tatar horse', 'the Tatars had no script'.
W097.why_read: The inside view from a Muslim bureaucrat who worked for the conquerors: how poor the Mongols had been, how they borrowed writing from the Uighurs, how they built Karakorum with Chinese and Muslim craftsmen, and the famous one-line report of Bukhara's fall.
W097.watch_out: Juvaini praises his Mongol masters while mourning the ruin of Muslim cities, and his figures are often inflated. The Persian OCR is noisy; quotes are lightly normalized and the printed page numbers are uncertain, so only scan pages are given. The translations are working translations, not Boyle's.

W098.plain_title: Grosier's General Description of China and Tartary
W098.one_line: A French abbé's survey of China and 'Chinese Tartary' compiled from Jesuit reports, in the English translation of 1788.
W098.summary: Abbé Jean-Baptiste Grosier (1743-1823) never went to China. In 1785 he published a general description of the Qing empire built from the Jesuit letters, maps and histories of the previous century, especially the Kangxi-era survey missionaries and Du Halde. The English translation (London, 1788) in this corpus covers Peking and the provinces, then Book II on 'Chinese Tartary': the Manchu homeland and the Amur peoples in the east, and the Mongols (Ordos, Chahar, Khalkha) and Eleuths in the west. Only the first volume is read here.
W098.tartar_means: Grosier uses 'Tartars' for all the peoples north of the Great Wall: the ruling Manchus ('Mantchew or Eastern Tartars'), the Mongols ('Moungal or Mogul Tartars'), the Eleuths or Kalmyks, and small Tungusic peoples of the Amur and Ussuri such as the Yupi-tatse ('fish-skin Tartars') and the Solons.
W098.why_read: A compact eighteenth-century map in words of who the 'Tartars' of Qing China were, with vivid details: felt yurts, fish-skin clothes, dog sleds, and the ruined cities of the Mongol emperors on the Kerulen.
W098.watch_out: Everything is second hand, drawn from Jesuit reports of the 1690s to 1720s, often quoted without naming the missionary. Grosier's aim was partly to defend China's reputation. The OCR prints the long s as f.

W099.plain_title: Martino Martini's history of the Tartar War in China
W099.one_line: A Jesuit missionary's history of the Manchu ('Tartar') conquest of Ming China, much of it witnessed, first printed in Latin and English in 1654.
W099.summary: Martino Martini (1614-1661), an Italian Jesuit, worked in China from 1643 to 1651, mostly in Zhejiang, and lived through the fall of the Ming and the Manchu advance. Sent back to Europe in 1651, he published De bello Tartarico (Antwerp, 1654), a short history of the wars from the Ming expulsion of the Mongols in 1368 to 1651, plus an appendix from later letters. It was translated into English the same year. It includes a sketch of Manchu dress and manners, military organisation, and the fight over the head-shaving order. This corpus copy is a scan of the 1654 London English edition (catalogued by the archive as 1939).
W099.tartar_means: Mainly the Manchus (the 'Eastern' or 'Oriental Tartars' of Niuche, that is the Jurchen), and also the Mongols ('Western Tartars'), whom he treats as one ancient nation north of the Great Wall. He explains that the Chinese call them 'Tata' because they cannot say R.
W099.why_read: The first widely read European book on the Manchu conquest, by a man who was there. It shows what 'Tartar' meant in 1654 to European readers: not a lost global empire but the new rulers of China, with their shaved heads and queues.
W099.watch_out: Martini saw some episodes himself (he says so) but reports most of the campaigns second hand. He writes as a missionary, praising those who favoured Christians. The OCR prints the long s as f and has marginal notes mixed into the text.

W100.one_line: A British China hand's 1836 survey of the Qing empire, its 'Manchow Tartar' rulers and the Mongol lands beyond the Great Wall.
W100.summary: John Francis Davis (1795-1890) worked for the East India Company at Canton for some twenty years, went with Lord Amherst's embassy to Peking in 1816, and later became governor of Hong Kong. The Chinese (London, 1836) is a general description of the empire, built from his own experience, Chinese books he read, and earlier accounts such as Gerbillon, Macartney's embassy and Timkowski. Volume I, read here, covers European contact, geography (including Manchu and Mongol Tartary), history from legend to the Qing conquest, government, army, law, manners, dress and Peking's Tartar and Chinese cities.
W100.tartar_means: Mostly the ruling Manchus ('Manchow Tartars', 'the Tartar dynasty', 'Tartar troops'), and also the Mongols ('Western or Mongol Tartars', the Kalkas, Ordos and Eleuths or Kalmyks) and, loosely, the Tibetans as 'Tartar races' who follow the Lamas. 'Banished to Tartary' means exile beyond the Wall.
W100.why_read: It shows how, by 1836, 'Tartar' in English had become a working political term: the Manchu ruling class of China with its own army, pay, punishments and city in Peking. It also gives precise, measured descriptions of the Great Wall and Peking's walls.
W100.watch_out: Davis mixes his own observations with quotations from Jesuits and embassy books, often without clear breaks. He is openly scornful of Buddhism and of Chinese 'effeminacy'. Only volume I is in the corpus.

W102.plain_title: The Han histories on the Western Regions and the steppe
W102.one_line: Sima Qian's Shiji (about 91 BCE) and Ban Gu's Hanshu (1st century CE) on the Xiongnu nomads and the oasis kingdoms reached by Zhang Qian.
W102.summary: The catalogue card points to an English web selection (Wylie, Hirth and a University of Washington edition), which is not in the corpus. What the corpus holds is the full Chinese text of both histories from the Kanseki Repository (CC BY-SA 4.0). The Shiji chapters on the Xiongnu (ch. 110) and on Dayuan (ch. 123), built on the envoy Zhang Qian's report of his journeys around 139 to 126 BCE, describe herding peoples of the northern steppe and the walled farming towns of Central Asia. These books are more than a thousand years older than the name 'Tatar' and never use it. They matter here as the oldest Chinese template for describing steppe nomads, which later writers applied to the 'Tartars'. The translations below are our own working versions.
W102.tartar_means: The word does not occur. The northern nomads are the Xiongnu (匈奴) and, more loosely, Hu (胡). Much later Chinese sources call the Tatars 韃靼 (Dada).
W102.why_read: The contrast Zhang Qian drew over two thousand years ago, between herders who 'follow water and grass' with no walled cities and settled oasis peoples with 'walled cities and houses', is the same one later European travellers drew for the Tartars.
W102.watch_out: Not about Tartars as such. The Shiji is an official court history, hostile to the Xiongnu. The web selection named in the catalogue is a separate, condensed English edition that was not read here.

W110.plain_title: Ibn Fadlan's mission to the Volga, as preserved by Yaqut
W110.one_line: An Abbasid envoy's eyewitness account of the Rus, Bulghars and Khazars of the Volga in 921 to 922, in C. M. Frähn's editions of 1822 and 1823.
W110.summary: Ahmad ibn Fadlan went from Baghdad in 921 as secretary of the caliph al-Muqtadir's embassy to the king of the Volga Bulghars. His report survived mainly in excerpts quoted by the geographer Yaqut (13th century). The catalogue names the Library of Arabic Literature bilingual PDF, but the corpus holds Christian Martin Frähn's editions: De Chasaris (St Petersburg, 1822), the Khazar excerpts with Latin translation, and Ibn-Foszlan's und anderer Araber Berichte über die Russen (1823), the Arabic Rus passage with German translation and long notes. They cover Rus traders camped on the Volga, a Rus ship cremation, a giant said to have lived at Bulghar, and the Khazar capital Itil.
W110.tartar_means: Ibn Fadlan wrote three centuries before the Mongol conquest and never uses the word Tatar. His Volga peoples (Bulghars, Khazars, Rus) lived in lands later called Tartary; the Kazan Tatars count the Bulghars among their ancestors. The only 'Tatars' in these volumes are in Frähn's notes: the Tatars of Russia he knew around Kazan.
W110.why_read: It is the earliest eyewitness picture of the middle Volga, the heartland of the later Kazan Tatars. It shows a mixed world of felt huts and one brick palace, wooden houses and burial mounds, with no lost stone cities.
W110.watch_out: What survives is Yaqut's excerpts, so the text is second-hand. The Khazar section may partly come from other geographers, since Ibn Fadlan probably never reached Itil. The Rus passages reflect a Muslim envoy's disgust. The German and Latin are Frähn's 1820s translations, and his notes are editorial.

W111.plain_title: Yelü Chucai's Record of a Journey to the West
W111.one_line: A Khitan scholar in Chinggis Khan's service describes the road west with the Mongol army, 1218 to about 1224, in Bretschneider's English translation.
W111.summary: Yelü Chucai (1190-1243), a Khitan noble captured when the Mongols took the Jin capital in 1215, became Chinggis Khan's adviser and rode with his army to Central Asia. His own book, the Si yu lu, is lost except for an abstract kept in a Yuan-era miscellany. Emil Bretschneider translated that abstract with long notes in Mediaeval Researches from Eastern Asiatic Sources (London, 1888); the corpus holds that book (1888 and 1910 printings), not the web transcription named in the catalogue. The short text runs from the Altai past Bishbalik, Almaliq and Talas to Otrar, Samarkand, Bukhara and Urgench, with hearsay about India and the Kipchak steppe.
W111.tartar_means: Yelü Chucai's abstract never uses 'Tatar'; it speaks of Chinggis's army and of 'Western people'. The word appears only in Bretschneider's notes, where he explains that 'Tartar' in European sources comes from the Tatar tribe's name.
W111.why_read: A view of the Mongol conquest from inside Chinggis Khan's camp by a highly educated East Asian writer. It shows the great garden cities the Mongols overran, not cities they are said to have built.
W111.watch_out: The text is a later abridgement, and Bretschneider notes that its directions and distances are often wrong. The India and Kipchak sections are hearsay mixed with older Tang-era material. Names are in 19th-century transliteration.

W115.plain_title: Friar John of Marignolli's mission to the Great Khan
W115.one_line: A Florentine friar and papal legate remembers the Tartar courts, Khanbaliq and the roads between them, 1338 to 1353, in asides scattered through his chronicle of Bohemia.
W115.summary: Giovanni de' Marignolli, a Florentine Franciscan, led the embassy Pope Benedict XII sent to the Great Khan in answer to a Mongol embassy. Travelling by Constantinople, Caffa, the Golden Horde court of Ozbeg Khan, Almaliq and Kamul, he reached Khanbaliq (Beijing) in 1342, stayed about three years, and came home by sea through Zayton, Quilon and Ceylon, reaching Avignon around 1353. Later, as chaplain to Emperor Charles IV, he wrote a rambling universal chronicle of Bohemia and dropped memories of the journey into it.
