This corpus copy is the Latin text printed by Gelasius Dobner in Monumenta historica Boemiae, vol. 2 (Prague, 1768), plus a second scan of the same edition. A third volume (Fontes rerum Bohemicarum) contributes only unrelated Bohemian chronicle pages.
W115.tartar_means: The Mongols and their empires: the Great Khan at Khanbaliq (the Yuan emperor of China), Ozbeg Khan of the Golden Horde, whom he calls the first emperor of the Tartars he reached, and the Chagatai 'middle empire' at Almaliq. He also uses 'Tartars' as a religious group next to Jews and Saracens.
W115.why_read: One of very few Western eyewitnesses to the Yuan court in its last decades. The Tartar rulers appear as masters of great cities, generous hosts and patrons of Christian churches with bells beside the imperial palace.
W115.watch_out: The travel notes are digressions in a chronicle full of biblical legend, and he reports miracles and prophecies as fact. The Latin OCR prints long s as f, and the 1768 editor's footnotes contain real howlers (Almaliq and Sarai placed in Japan, Hangzhou confused with Cambay in India).

W116.plain_title: A Florentine merchant's handbook for the road to Cathay
W116.one_line: Practical trade advice, compiled around 1340, for merchants going from Tana on the Sea of Azov across the Tartar lands to Khanbaliq.
W116.summary: Francesco Balducci Pegolotti, an agent of the Bardi banking company of Florence, compiled his Pratica della mercatura around 1340: a handbook of weights, measures, coins, customs dues and routes across the Mediterranean and Black Sea world. Its first chapters give the overland route from Tana (Azov) through Astrakhan, Sarai, Urgench, Otrar and Almaliq to Cathay, with advice on interpreters, food, costs and paper money. Pegolotti gathered this from merchants who had used the road; there is no evidence he went himself. This corpus copy is the Italian text printed by G. F. Pagnini in Della decima, vol. 3 (1766), with poor OCR.
W116.tartar_means: The Mongol rulers and their men along the route: the 'Signore del Gattajo' (the Yuan emperor), the 'Signore de' Tartari' of Persia (the Ilkhan), and the 'Moccoli', Mongol armed men and brigands on the road.
W116.why_read: It shows the Tartar empires as merchants met them: a single long road, safe by night and day, with customs posts, paper money and a capital a hundred miles round.
W116.watch_out: Secondhand trade knowledge, not a travel diary, so do not treat it as a personal journey. The 1766 OCR is badly garbled, and several Italian words have been restored from obvious misreadings.

W117.plain_title: Brother Bento de Góis and the search for Cathay
W117.one_line: How a Jesuit lay brother crossed from Mughal India over the Pamirs to the Chinese border, 1603 to 1607, and proved that Cathay was China, told in Ricci's Latin history of the China mission.
W117.summary: Bento de Góis, a Portuguese Jesuit lay brother at the Mughal court, set out in January 1603, disguised as an Armenian merchant, to find the Christian kingdom of Cathay that Muslim traders described. He crossed Kabul, Badakhshan and the Pamirs to Yarkand, then went east by Cialis, Turfan and Hami to Suzhou (Jiuquan) inside the Great Wall, where he died in 1607 just after a messenger from Matteo Ricci in Peking reached him. His diary was destroyed, so Ricci rebuilt the story from his companion Isaac the Armenian and surviving letters. Nicolas Trigault published it in Latin in De Christiana expeditione apud Sinas (Augsburg, 1615), the book that also carries Ricci's own long account of China. This corpus has two scans of that 1615 edition.
W117.tartar_means: Mostly the Mongols: the Yuan conquerors who ruled China until 1368, and the steppe nomads who still raided the frontier beyond the Great Wall in 1605. Chinese Muslims are described as Tartar remnants, and the Latin word also shades into 'tartareus', hellish.
W117.why_read: This is the book that settled that Marco Polo's Cathay and Cambalu were China and Peking, names Europe had learned from the Tartars. It also gives a Jesuit's view of the Mongol past and of the nomads beyond the Wall.
W117.watch_out: Goes's own words are lost: the route was pieced together by Ricci from Isaac's testimony and letters, then Latinised and edited by Trigault. The Latin OCR runs words together and misreads letters, and some place names are uncertain.

W121.plain_title: A British officer's ride through 'Crim Tartary' in 1829
W121.one_line: A Scottish officer's travels through Russia and the Crimea during the Russo-Turkish war of 1828 to 1829, with close views of Crimean Tatar towns, villages, palace and people.
W121.summary: James Edward Alexander (1803 to 1885), a Scottish officer of the East India Company's army, travelled in 1829 from St Petersburg and Moscow through Ukraine to the Crimea, hoping to join the Russian forces in the war with Turkey. Held under suspicion for a time at Sevastopol, he eventually reached the Balkan front. Volume 1 carries his tour of the Crimea: the Nogay steppe, Simferopol (Akmetshet), the khans' palace at Bakhchysarai, the mountain ruins of Mangup and the Tatar villages of the south coast, where he dressed in Eastern clothes and used his Turkish. Volume 2 covers the war and his return by Kiev. The corpus holds the 1830 London first edition: one scan of volume 1 and four copies of volume 2.
W121.tartar_means: Mainly the Crimean Tatars, Muslim townspeople and mountain villagers of the peninsula he still calls 'Crim Tartary', and the nomadic Nogays of the steppe north of Perekop. In Russia 'Tartar' means the medieval Mongol-Tatar invaders, and 'Tartaric' is his label for a style of battlement.
W121.why_read: A late, vivid eyewitness picture of Crimean Tatar life half a century after Russian annexation: stone houses, mosques, bazaars, the khans' palace and tombs, food, dress and music, with his notes on who built the ruins he passed.
W121.watch_out: A romantic traveller writing for British readers, fond of classical parallels and 'Oriental' colour. The revolt story is hearsay, and his architectural labels (Tartaric, Genoese) are impressions, not research. The Google OCR of volume 1 is patchy.

W118.plain_title: The Secret History of the Mongols
W118.one_line: The Mongols' own 13th-century chronicle of Chinggis Khan's family and rise, preserved only in a Ming Chinese transcription.
W118.summary: An anonymous Mongol author, writing in the 13th century (the colophon's Year of the Rat is usually read as 1228, though 1240 and 1252 are argued), told the story of Chinggis Khan's ancestors, his rise to power and the reign of his son Ogedei. The Mongolian original is lost. It survives only because Ming court translators, around the 1380s, wrote it out in Chinese characters with word glosses and a running Chinese summary. This corpus holds poor scans of a Peking University Library copy and of Li Wentian's 1896 commentary, the Kanseki Repository text of the Chinese summary, and Igor de Rachewiltz's open-access English translation from the Mongolian (2015 abridged edition), which is quoted here.
W118.tartar_means: In the Mongolian text 'Tatar' is one particular rival steppe people east of the Mongols (the Ca'an, Alci, Duta'ut and Aruqai Tatar), hereditary enemies whom Chinggis destroyed in 1202. The Ming Chinese summary, however, calls the Mongols themselves Dada (逹逹, 'Tatars'), and writes the Tatar tribe separately as 塔塔児.
W118.why_read: It is the only long narrative of the early Mongols written by Mongols, full of tents, carts, feuds and oaths, and it shows the moment when the word Tatar passed from one enemy tribe to the Mongols as a whole in Chinese usage.
W118.watch_out: It is epic and partisan, written to glorify Chinggis's line, and its dating is disputed. The English quoted is de Rachewiltz's translation from the reconstructed Mongolian; the Chinese summary is a Ming paraphrase, not a word-for-word version.

W130.plain_title: The official History of the Yuan (Mongol) dynasty
W130.one_line: The Ming court's official history of Mongol rule in China, compiled in 1369 to 1370 from Yuan state records.
W130.summary: When the Ming drove the Mongol Yuan dynasty out of China, the new court ordered Song Lian and a team of scholars to write its official history, which they did in a hurry in 1369 to 1370 from the Yuan veritable records and archives. The annals of Chinggis Khan (juan 1) give a dated framework for his rise, and the treatise on geography (juan 58 to 63) describes the provinces of the empire, including Lingbei (Mongolia with Karakorum) and the peoples of southern Siberia. The corpus holds poor CADAL scans and the full Kanseki Repository transcription of the Siku quanshu manuscript copy, which is quoted here.
W130.tartar_means: In the passages read here the Yuan shi calls the Mongols 'Mongols' (蒙古) and uses Tatar (塔塔兒, spelled 塔塔爾 in this copy) for the Tatar tribe that Chinggis's father fought, not for the Mongols as a whole.
W130.why_read: It is the Chinese state record of the Mongol empire, and it treats Karakorum as a real capital with walls and a palace and describes Siberian forest peoples in birch-bark tents.
W130.watch_out: Hastily compiled and sometimes repetitive. This Siku copy (1770s to 1780s) systematically re-spells Mongol names (和琳 for 和林 Karakorum, 竒爾濟蘇 for 吉利吉思 Kyrgyz, 特穆津 for 鐵木真 Temujin), so older prints show different forms. Translations are working translations.

W131.plain_title: The official History of the Ming: the Tatars, the Oirats and the Western Regions
W131.one_line: The Qing court's official history of the Ming dynasty, with chapters on the Mongols (Dada, 'Tatars') and Central Asia, completed in 1739.
W131.summary: The Qing history office under Zhang Tingyu finished the History of the Ming in 1739, drawing on the Ming veritable records and private histories. Its 'foreign countries' chapters include juan 327 on the Dada (Tatars, meaning the Eastern Mongols after 1368), juan 328 on the Oirats and the Three Guards, and juan 329 to 332 on the Western Regions from Hami and Turfan to Samarkand and Tibet. The corpus holds poor CADAL scans and the Kanseki Repository transcription of the Siku quanshu manuscript copy, which is quoted here.
W131.tartar_means: Dada (韃靼, Tatar) is the official Ming name for the Eastern Mongols, the descendants of the Yuan court after 1368, as distinct from the Oirats (Wala, here re-spelled Weilate). The chapter opens by saying so, and later (p. 536-6b) explains that after a usurper named Guilichi dropped the Yuan dynastic name around 1400 'they were called Dada'.
W131.why_read: It records in the Chinese state's own words that 'Tatar' meant the Mongols, and gives a vivid episode of Chinese renegades building a walled town and palace for the Tumed Mongol ruler Altan Khan in the 16th century.
W131.watch_out: Written by the Qing (a Manchu dynasty) about the Ming, from a frontier-defence point of view. The Siku copy re-spells Mongol names (諳達 for 俺答 Altan, 衛拉特 for 瓦剌), so older prints differ. Translations are working translations.

W132.plain_title: Fine Talk from the Jade Hall: two Chinese journeys through the Mongol world
W132.one_line: Wang Yun's notebook preserving a Chinese scholar's 1247 to 1248 journey to Khubilai's camp in Mongolia and an envoy's 1259 ride west to Hulegu in Persia.
W132.summary: Wang Yun (1227 to 1304), a Yuan Hanlin academician, filled his notebook Yutang jiahua (also printed in his collected works, the Qiujian ji) with things he heard and copied. Two pieces matter here. Zhang Dehui's Record of a Journey tells how he was summoned in 1247 from Zhending to the camp of the prince (Khubilai) and lived ten months at his court in the Orkhon and Tamir country, dated summer 1248. Liu Yu's Record of an Embassy to the West, written in 1263, retells what the envoy Chang De saw and heard riding from Karakorum to Hulegu's army in Iran in 1259. The corpus holds Kanseki Repository texts of the Siku Yutang jiahua and the Sibu congkan Qiujian ji, poor scans, and Bretschneider's Mediaeval Researches vol. 2.
W132.tartar_means: Neither traveller uses the word Tatar: they speak of Mongol clans (蒙古部族), 'the northern tongue', the prince and the imperial army. The Bretschneider volume held with this record shows the Chinese term Ta-ta (Tatars, Dada) in later Ming geography, as in the 'Water Tatars' of Manchuria.
W132.why_read: Zhang Dehui is the closest thing to a Chinese Rubruck: he describes felt tents and felt carts, earth-roofed farm huts on the Kerulen, walls and towns built by earlier dynasties, and the round of the Mongol year. Chang De's report shows the cities of the Mongol West as full of Uighur and Chinese settlers, and adds legends such as the Assassins' paradise and the lamb that grows from the ground.
W132.watch_out: Zhang saw what he describes; Chang De's account comes second-hand through Liu Yu and mixes observation with hearsay about distant lands. The Siku copy re-spells many names (for example 博囉 for 孛羅), so the older Sibu congkan text is quoted where possible. Translations are working translations.

W139.plain_title: The Comprehensive Gazetteer of the Great Qing: Mongolia and the outer lands
W139.one_line: The Qing court's official geography of its empire, including Mongolia, Qinghai, Xinjiang and Tibet, the lands Europeans called Chinese Tartary.
W139.summary: The Da Qing yitong zhi was the Qing empire's official gazetteer, compiled by court commissions from provincial records, frontier surveys and the Jesuit-Qing mapping of 1708 to 1718. It went through three recensions: 1744, 1784 (424 juan, the Siku quanshu copy named in the catalogue, of which the corpus holds only poor scans of juan 401 to 403 and 423 to 424) and the Jiaqing recension of 560 juan, extended to 1820 and completed in 1842. The readable full text in the corpus (Kanseki Repository, from the Sibu congkan reprint) is the 1842 recension, and that is what is quoted here. Its Mongolia sections give the history, rivers, towns, ruins and products of each banner.
W139.tartar_means: The gazetteer calls the Mongols Menggu and their lands the Outer Mongol domains; it uses Dada (韃靼, Tatar) only in its history, for the Mongols who fled north after the Yuan and 'again called themselves Dada'.
W139.why_read: It shows how the Qing state described the heart of 'Chinese Tartary': where the ruined Yuan capital Karakorum lay, when Hohhot was walled, and the old line that the steppe peoples 'have no houses'.
W139.watch_out: The quotes come from the 1842 recension, not the 1784 Siku copy named in the catalogue; wording can differ between recensions. Mongol names are in the Qianlong-era re-spellings. Much of the text quotes older histories rather than reporting new observation.

W140.one_line: The Qing court's official geography of Manchuria, the land European maps called Eastern or Manchu Tartary, in its 1784 recension.
W140.summary: First compiled in 1684 and revised in 1736, the Shengjing tongzhi was expanded by a Qianlong commission under Agui and Liu Jinzhi into the 130-juan edition of 1784. It covers the Manchu homeland of Shengjing (Liaoning), Jilin and Heilongjiang: imperial edicts, cities and walls, rivers, ancient sites, officials and the tribute peoples of the Amur and Ussuri. It draws on banner records, earlier editions, Yuan and Ming geographies and travel diaries. The corpus holds poor scans of juan 1 and 129 to 130 and the full Kanseki Repository transcription of the Siku copy, which is quoted here.
W140.tartar_means: The gazetteer does not use Tatar for any people it describes. It names Manchus, Mongols, the Solon, Daur, Hezhe and Fiyaka, and calls the Russians Luocha; old names such as the 'Water Tatars' of Yuan sources appear only in re-spelled form.
W140.why_read: It shows the land Europeans called Chinese or Eastern Tartary as the Qing saw it: dog sledges and skis on the Amur, ruined palace cities of earlier dynasties, and the Kangxi emperor building wooden forts against Russian raiders.
W140.watch_out: An official compilation that often quotes older works rather than reporting observation; the Qianlong editors re-spelled Mongol, Jurchen and Khitan names. Translations are working translations.

W141.plain_title: Researches on the Origins of the Manchus
W141.one_line: The Qianlong emperor's official study, finished 1777 to 1783, tracing the Manchus back through the Jurchens, Bohai and Sushen of Chinese records.
W141.summary: In 1777 the Qianlong emperor ordered his officials, led by Agui and Yu Minzhong, to compile a history proving that the Manchus were heirs of the Jurchen Jin and of older peoples of the northeast named in Chinese histories: the Sushen, Yilou, Mohe and the Bohai kingdom. The 20 juan cover peoples, territory, mountains and rivers, and customs, and re-spell old names according to Manchu etymologies. The corpus holds poor scans of juan 1 to 2 and 17 to 20 and the Kanseki Repository transcription of the Siku copy, quoted here.
W141.tartar_means: The work does not call the Manchus Tatars. It re-spells the Yuan 'Water Tatars' (水達達) of Manchuria as Shuo Dalda, explained as Manchu for 'a hidden place', so the Tatar name disappears from its pages.
W141.why_read: It is the Manchu court's own answer to 'who are we?': a sacred origin legend, an etymology of the name Manchu, and ruined palace cities in the homeland claimed as ancestral, to set beside European talk of 'Manchu Tartars'.
W141.watch_out: An ideological compilation meant to give the ruling house an ancient and noble pedigree. Its etymologies and re-spellings of old names are the editors' own and often contested. Translations are working translations.

W150.plain_title: Sumpa Khenpo's Wish-fulfilling Tree: a Tibetan history of Buddhism
W150.one_line: A Mongol-born Amdo lama's 1748 history of Buddhism in India, China, Tibet and Mongolia, with a year-by-year chronological table.
W150.summary: Sumpa Khenpo Yeshe Peljor (1704 to 1788), a lama of Mongol descent from Amdo who studied in Lhasa and spent years at the Qing court in Beijing, finished his Dpag bsam ljon bzang in 1748. It narrates Buddhism in India, Tibet, China and Mongolia and ends with a chronological table (re'u mig) dating events by the Tibetan sixty-year cycle. The corpus holds Sarat Chandra Das's Calcutta edition of 1908, whose Tibetan text is badly garbled in the OCR; the quotes here come from Das's English index and his analytical list of contents for the Tibetan history (Part II), so they are the editor's summaries, not Sumpa's own words.
W150.tartar_means: In Das's English, 'Tartar' renders Tibetan Sog po and Hor, meaning Mongols: the Khoshut and Oirat (Oelod) armies and khans who ruled Tibet from 1642, and Chinggis Khan.
W150.why_read: It shows the Mongols from the Tibetan side, as the 'Tartar kings' of Tibet who made the Dalai Lama's government possible, and the index explains how Tibetan words were turned into 'Tartar' in English.
W150.watch_out: Everything quoted is Das's English paraphrase of the contents, not a translation of Sumpa's text; the Tibetan OCR is largely unreadable. The chronological table itself was not found in readable form in this copy.

W151.plain_title: Jigme Namkha's History of Buddhism in Mongolia
W151.one_line: A Mongol lama's 1819 Tibetan-language history of the Mongol khans and of Buddhism among the Mongols, in Georg Huth's German translation.
W151.summary: Jigme Namkha, a Mongol lama writing in Tibetan, completed his History of Buddhism in the Great Land of the Hor (Mongols) in 1819, drawing on Mongolian chronicles such as Sagang Sechen and on Tibetan histories. It retells the Mongol royal line from its legendary Tibetan ancestor to Chinggis Khan, Khubilai and the later khans, then the spread of Buddhism among the Mongols. The corpus holds the Tibetan text volume and Georg Huth's German translation (Strassburg, volume 2 dated 1896 in the corpus manifest), quoted here with working English translations.
W151.tartar_means: The author writes of Hor and Sog po, the Tibetan words for the Mongols, which Huth renders 'Mongolen'. The word Tatar does not appear in the translation.
W151.why_read: It is the Mongols' own 19th-century picture of their past: a Tibetan prince as ancestor, Chinggis named by a magic bird, Khubilai as a builder of cities, and a subject world that includes dog-headed people.
W151.watch_out: A pious chronicle mixing legend with history; Huth's translation has known errors, and the German OCR is imperfect. Quotes are in German with my own English translation.

W153.plain_title: The Chronicles of Ladakh and minor chronicles
W153.one_line: The royal chronicle of Ladakh in western Tibet, with A. H. Francke's 1926 edition and translation, including the Mongol-Tibetan invasion of the 1680s.
W153.summary: The Ladakh royal chronicle (La dvags rgyal rabs) was compiled by court writers from the 17th century onward and continued into the 1840s, telling the story of the kings of Ladakh from legendary origins to the Dogra conquest of 1834 to 1842. The Moravian missionary and scholar A. H. Francke edited the Tibetan text from several manuscripts and translated it, with notes by himself and Karl Marx, as Antiquities of Indian Tibet, Part II (Calcutta, 1926), which also prints minor chronicles and land grants. The corpus holds two scans of this edition.
W153.tartar_means: The chronicle speaks of Sog po (Mongols) and Hor, which Francke translates as Mongols, Turks, Turkomans or Mughals depending on context. The word Tartar is used only once by Francke, for Timur. The Mongols who invaded Ladakh were Tibetan-led forces with Khoshut or Dzungar Mongol troops sent from Lhasa.
W153.why_read: It gives the Ladakhi side of the war with the 'Mongol army' from Lhasa in the 1680s, ending with the Mongols building a moated fort, and shows how Tibetan 'Hor' could mean several different peoples.
W153.watch_out: The early sections are legendary, the manuscripts differ, and Francke's dates are estimates. Notes by Francke and Marx are 20th-century commentary, not the chronicle, and are labelled as such.

W119.plain_title: Rashid al-Din's Compendium of Chronicles: the Mongol emperors after Chinggis
W119.one_line: The great Persian history of the Mongols, written c.1300 to 1310 by the vizier of the Mongol rulers of Iran.
W119.summary: Rashid al-Din Fadl Allah (d. 1318), a physician who became chief minister of the Mongol Ilkhans of Iran, compiled the Compendium of Chronicles c.1300 to 1310. He worked from Mongol court informants such as Bolad Chingsang, lost Mongol records and earlier Persian histories, above all Juvaini. The catalogue card names a Tehran 1994 edition, which is not stored here. The pages actually read are E. Blochet's Persian edition of the history of Chinggis Khan's successors (Ogedei to Temur), Leiden and London 1911, with long French notes. It covers the founding of Karakorum, the conquest of north China, the Jochid khans of the Golden Horde and Qubilai's China.
W119.tartar_means: Rashid's usual word for the conquerors is Mughul (Mongol). Tatar is for him one particular steppe tribe, also used as a personal name in the ruling family, and in reported speech it can stand for the Mongol armies as a whole. Blochet's French notes use 'Tartares' and 'Tartarie' in the older European sense.
W119.why_read: It is the nearest thing to an official Mongol history: stories of Ogedei's new capital at Karakorum, of Qubilai's palace at Shangdu (Xanadu) built on a drained lake, and of how Persian writers used the words Mongol and Tatar.
W119.watch_out: Rashid wrote two to three generations after many of these events and copied Juvaini's anecdotes. The corpus OCR of the Persian is unreadable, so quotes were transcribed from the page images; Blochet's French notes are his own and are labelled as such.

W198.plain_title: Mustawfi's Delight of Hearts: a geography of Mongol Iran
W198.one_line: A Persian tax official's gazetteer of the Ilkhanid realm and its neighbours, written in 1340.
W198.summary: Hamdallah Mustawfi of Qazvin (d. after 1340) was a finance official of the Mongol Ilkhans of Iran. The geographical part of his Nuzhat al-Qulub (1339 to 1340) lists the provinces, towns and revenues of Iran, many of them rebuilt, founded or ruined under the Mongols, and closes with shorter notes on foreign lands copied from earlier geographers. The corpus holds G. Le Strange's English translation (Gibb Memorial XXIII, 2, Leiden and London 1919) in two scans, and a seventeenth-century Persian manuscript not read here.
W198.tartar_means: Mustawfi writes of Mongols (Mughul), meaning the Ilkhans and their people settled in Iran. The word Tatar appears once, in a twelfth-century poem about Turkish slave soldiers, where Le Strange notes it is the name of a people. The steppe north of the Caspian is the Dasht-i Qipchaq.
W198.why_read: It shows Mongol rulers as city founders and builders in Iran (Sultaniyyah and its stone tomb), keeping Mongol burial custom, and it describes the Qipchaq steppe as a land of nomads with few towns.
W198.watch_out: The Iranian entries rest on his own official knowledge; the foreign-lands chapters are compiled from Yaqut, Ibn Khurradadhbih and others. Le Strange's footnotes are his own.

W200.plain_title: Vassaf's History: the Mongol Ilkhans of Iran and their rivals
W200.one_line: A Persian court historian's ornate chronicle of the Mongol rulers of Iran and the other Mongol khanates, 1257 to 1328.
W200.summary: Vassaf (Shihab al-Din Abdallah of Shiraz, 1264 to c.1330) was a tax official who presented his history to the Ilkhans Ghazan and Uljaytu. It continues Juvaini from 1257 and covers the Ilkhans' wars with the Golden Horde and the Chaghadaids, the Yuan court in China and India. He knew Iran at first hand and relied on envoys and merchants for the other Mongol states. The corpus holds three BULAC manuscripts: MS.PERS.116 (1670), MS.PERS.64 (1856) and MS.PERS.65 (1840, part only). All are in nastaliq script, and the machine OCR of all three is unreadable.
W200.tartar_means: Vassaf writes of the Mughul (Mongols) and their uluses; European readers later called the same rulers the Tartars of Persia. No passage could be read in this corpus copy to show his own usage.
W200.why_read: It is the main contemporary Persian narrative for the Ilkhanid court c.1300 and one of the few Persian sources on the Qipchaq steppe wars. Readers should use a printed edition or translation.
W200.watch_out: The OCR of all three manuscripts is illegible and the handwriting cannot be searched, so no passage could be checked or quoted. Vassaf's prose is famously ornate even in good editions; the Bombay 1853 lithograph and the Hammer-Purgstall German translation of volume 1 (1856) are the usual ways in.

W202.plain_title: Ibn Rusta's Book of Precious Records: the peoples of the Volga c.900
W202.one_line: An Arabic geography of about 903 to 913 describing the Khazars, Volga Bulghars, Magyars and Rus before the Mongol age.
W202.summary: Ibn Rusta, a Persian scholar of Isfahan, compiled his Book of Precious Records c.903 to 913. Its chapters on the northern peoples (Pechenegs, Khazars, Burtas, Volga Bulghars, Magyars, Slavs, Rus) copy a lost report of the later ninth century, probably from the Samanid vizier al-Jayhani. It is not firsthand. The corpus copy is M. J. de Goeje's Arabic edition in the Bibliotheca Geographorum Arabicorum VII (Leiden 1892), a University of Toronto scan whose Arabic OCR is unreadable, so quotes were read from the page images.
W202.tartar_means: The word Tatar does not appear in these chapters, which predate the Mongols by three centuries. They describe Turkic and other peoples (Khazars, Volga Bulghars, Magyars, 'a race of the Turks') of the lands later labelled Tartary.
W202.why_read: It shows the steppe and Volga before the Mongols: a Khazar state whose king was Jewish, towns with mosques and Quran schools, Muslim Bulghar farmers trading furs with the Rus, and Magyars moving with their tents.
W202.watch_out: Second-hand information, a century old when copied; names are uncertain in the unique manuscript. Quotes are transcribed from the printed Arabic and the translations are working translations.

W203.plain_title: Ibn Khurradadhbih's Book of Routes, with Sallam's journey to the Wall of Gog and Magog
W203.one_line: An Abbasid postmaster's route book (c.846 to 885), including an envoy's tale of a great iron wall in the far north-east.
W203.summary: Ibn Khurradadhbih (d. c.912) was director of posts under the Abbasid caliphs and compiled the Book of Routes and Realms from official itineraries, c.846 and revised c.885. It lists roads from Iraq to Central Asia and China and the Turkic peoples along them. It also records the story he says Sallam the Interpreter told him: in 842 to 844 the caliph al-Wathiq sent Sallam to inspect the wall Alexander built against Gog and Magog. The corpus copy is de Goeje's Arabic text with French translation (BGA VI, Leiden 1889), quoted here from the French.
W203.tartar_means: The word Tatar is not used. The 'Turks' of the steppe (Toghuzghuz or Uyghurs, Kimek, Ghuzz, Pechenegs, Kipchaks, Kirghiz, Qarluqs) live in the lands that later maps called Tartary, and Gog and Magog are placed beyond them.
W203.why_read: This is the root of the medieval 'Wall of Gog and Magog' that European maps placed in Tartary. It includes a traveller's claim to have passed twenty-seven days of ruined cities blamed on Gog and Magog.
W203.watch_out: Scholars disagree whether Sallam reached a real Chinese frontier fort (perhaps near the Jade Gate or Hami) or whether the story is largely literary. The OCR of the French has lost its accents, which were restored in the quotes.

W204.plain_title: Abu'l-Fida's Survey of the Countries, with Reinaud's introduction
W204.one_line: A Syrian prince's gazetteer of 1321, with notes on Sarai and the Golden Horde, in Reinaud's French edition of 1848.
W204.summary: Abu'l-Fida (1273 to 1331), prince of Hama in Syria, fought against the Ilkhanid Mongols as a Mamluk commander and in 1321 finished a gazetteer of the world arranged as tables with coordinates. For the north he copied earlier writers, above all Ibn Sa'id, but added news from travellers and merchants, including a man from Sarai. The corpus holds the Arabic text (Paris 1840) and J. T. Reinaud's French translation with a long introduction on Arabic geography (Paris 1848); the French is quoted here.
W204.tartar_means: Tartares (Arabic al-Tatar) means the Mongols and their armies: the Ilkhanid 'Tartars of Persia' whom Abu'l-Fida fought in Syria, and the Golden Horde khans of 'the country of Berke' at Sarai. Reinaud uses Tartarie in the European sense for all of inner Asia.
W204.why_read: An eyewitness Muslim soldier's account of fighting the Tartars, a clear description of Sarai as a new Mongol-founded trading city, and Reinaud's plain explanations of the names Tatar and Horde.
W204.watch_out: Most of the northern entries are compiled, not seen. Reinaud's introduction and footnotes (1848) are his own and are labelled as such.

W206.plain_title: al-Umari's Routes of Insight: a Mamluk encyclopedia of the known world
W206.one_line: A Cairo chancery official's world encyclopedia of c.1340 to 1349; this copy is the first volume only, on general geography.
W206.summary: Ibn Fadl Allah al-Umari (1301 to 1349) served in the Mamluk chancery in Cairo and Damascus. His vast encyclopedia gathers geography and history, with famous chapters on the Mongol states (the Golden Horde, the Chaghadaids, the Ilkhans) built from merchants and envoys he questioned. The corpus copy is volume 1 of Ahmad Zaki Pasha's Cairo edition (Dar al-Kutub, 1924), which covers the earth, climes, seas, rivers and mountains. The Mongol chapters (in later volumes, and in Tiesenhausen's 1884 Russian extracts) are not in this volume.
W206.tartar_means: al-Tatar or al-Tatar (Tatars) means the Mongols and their subjects, especially the Ilkhanid enemies of the Mamluks; 'the land of the Tatars' is a broad region of inner Asia between China and Fergana. The steppe of the Golden Horde is 'the deserts of the Qipchaq'.
W206.why_read: Brief but telling glimpses: the sultan hailed as conqueror of the Tatars, a mountain chain crossing 'the land of the Tatars', the Volga as the river of Sarai, and old Gog and Magog lore about ruined lands in the far north-east.
W206.watch_out: This volume is general geography, largely copied from earlier Arabic writers; the rich informant-based chapters on the Golden Horde are elsewhere and were not read.

W207.plain_title: Ibn Arabshah's hostile life of Timur, with the Golden Horde from inside
W207.one_line: An Arab captive's rhymed-prose biography of Timur (1435 to 1437), with memories of Sarai and the Qipchaq steppe.
W207.summary: Ahmad ibn Arabshah (1389 to 1450) was carried off from Damascus to Samarkand as a boy in 1401. He later lived in Transoxiana, Khwarazm, the Golden Horde lands (Sarai, Astrakhan, Crimea) and Edirne before settling in Cairo. His Wonders of Destiny (1435 to 1437) is a savage, witty life of Timur in rhymed Arabic prose, drawing on his own memories and on informants. It includes a memorable description of the Dasht-i Qipchaq and Sarai. The corpus copy is an Arabic print catalogued as 1842, probably the Calcutta edition of 1818 or a reprint.
W207.tartar_means: Tatar (al-Tatar, al-Tatar al-Tagham, 'the rabble Tatars') means the Turkic and Mongol peoples of the Golden Horde steppe, the Dasht of Berke. Timur's own people are the Chaghatay, and Ibn Arabshah also lumps them with the Tatars of the Dasht as followers of Chinggis Khan's law.
W207.why_read: A rare view from inside the steppe: Sarai as a great Islamic city founded by a Muslim khan, caravans crossing the Dasht by cart, and plain statements that Timur destroyed the Horde's cities and carried Damascus craftsmen off to build Samarkand.
W207.watch_out: Ibn Arabshah hated Timur and wrote in ornate rhymed prose, so his anecdotes are often exaggerated. The corpus OCR is unreadable; every quote was transcribed from the page images.

W210.plain_title: Evliya Celebi's Book of Travels: Crimea, the Kalmyks and the Volga (vol. 7)
W210.one_line: An Ottoman traveller's vivid, embroidered account of Crimea, the Kalmyk steppe, Kazan, Astrakhan and the Tatars, 1665 to 1667.
W210.summary: Evliya Celebi (1611 to c.1685) travelled across the Ottoman world for four decades and wrote his ten-volume Book of Travels in Cairo in the 1670s and 1680s. Volume 7 covers his journeys with the Crimean khan Mehmed Giray IV in 1665 to 1667: the Crimean capital Bahcesaray and other towns, campaigns against Cossacks, Kalmyks and Russians, and a journey he says he made to the Kalmyks and up the Volga to Astrakhan, Sarai and Kazan. He writes from what he saw mixed with hearsay and embroidery. The corpus copy is the 1928 Istanbul printed edition (Kilisli Rifat), whose OCR is partly readable; quotes were checked against the page images.
W210.tartar_means: Tatar means above all the Crimean Tatars (subjects of the Giray khans) and the Nogays, but Evliya also uses it for the Volga Tatars of Kazan ('Hashdek'), Astrakhan and Sarai. He calls the Kalmyks a separate people, not Muslims, but groups them with Chinggis Khan's heirs.
W210.why_read: The richest non-European picture of 'Little Tartary' in the 1660s: a stone-and-tile Tatar capital, the khan's palace, the slave market, Kalmyk houses on carts, and Kazan's mosques and madrasas standing in ruins under Russian rule.
W210.watch_out: Evliya exaggerates numbers and sometimes invents episodes; the Volga, Kazan and some Kalmyk passages are doubted by scholars. The 1928 print is uncritical and censored; quotes follow its text.

W211.plain_title: Katib Celebi's Cihannuma: an Ottoman geography of Asia (printed 1732)
W211.one_line: The Ottoman 'Mirror of the World', a geography of Asia that mixed Islamic tradition with European atlases, printed in Istanbul in 1732.
W211.summary: Katib Celebi (1609 to 1657), an Ottoman scholar and bureaucrat, wrote the Cihannuma in the 1650s, combining the Islamic geographers with European atlases (Mercator-Hondius, Ortelius) translated for him. Ibrahim Muteferrika, the first Ottoman Muslim printer, published it in 1732 with additions and engraved maps. The corpus copy is a modern facsimile (Boyut) of the 1732 print whose OCR is badly garbled, so quotes were read from page images. It is compiled throughout, and its 'Tatarestan' material is taken from European sources.
W211.tartar_means: Tatar is used in two layers: the Islamic genealogy (Tatar and Mongol as twin sons of a Turkish khan) and the European atlas label 'Tatarestan' (Tartary) for all of inner Asia beyond the Imaus. The Nogay and Crimean Tatars appear as real neighbours of the Ottomans.
W211.why_read: It shows the European 'Tartary' being translated into Ottoman Turkish, alongside a plain statement that 'Turk, Tatar and Mongol' had become interchangeable names.
W211.watch_out: Two authorial layers (1650s and 1732) and heavy dependence on European atlases; it is not independent evidence for inner Asia. The printed page numbers in the facsimile are Arabic numerals at the top of each page.

W212.plain_title: Rosebud of the Khans: a Crimean prince's history of his own dynasty
W212.one_line: Biographies of the Giray khans of Crimea, 1441 to 1783, written in 1811 by an exiled member of the family.
W212.summary: Halim Giray (1772 to 1823), a prince of the Giray dynasty that ruled the Crimean khanate, wrote Gulbun-i Hanan ('Rosebud of the Khans') in 1811 while living in Ottoman exile after Russia annexed Crimea in 1783. It is a chain of short biographies of every khan from Haci Giray to Sahin Giray, compiled from Crimean and Ottoman chronicles. The main corpus copy is the Istanbul 1911 print, whose publisher added footnotes from other writers (Evliya Celebi and European authors) and the text of the 1774 Kucuk Kaynarca treaty; a manuscript of Halim Giray's collected works (1827) is also held. The OCR is badly garbled, so passages were read from the page images.
W212.tartar_means: The Crimean Tatars and the Nogay hordes of the Kuban, Budjak and Yedisan steppes: the Muslim, Turkic-speaking subjects of the Giray khans, who were descendants of Genghis Khan. 'Tatar' is an ordinary ethnic and military label here, not a mysterious empire.
W212.why_read: It is the Crimean khanate's history told from the inside by one of its own princes, and its notes show Bakhchysarai as a real town of mosques, baths, madrasas and a palace built by named khans.
W212.watch_out: A late compilation (1811) that depends on earlier chronicles; the 1911 print mixes Halim Giray's text with an editor's footnotes, which are marked here. Dates in the notes can be misprinted, and the corpus OCR is unusable, so every quote was transcribed from the page image.

W218.plain_title: The Cuman Codex: a phrasebook from the Golden Horde
W218.one_line: A Latin-Persian-Cuman word list made by Italian merchants in 1303, with Franciscan prayers and riddles in the steppe Turkic language.
W218.summary: The Codex Cumanicus is a small manuscript now in Venice. Its first part, dated 11 July 1303, is a Latin-Persian-Cuman glossary compiled by Italian (probably Genoese) merchants trading in Crimea and the Golden Horde; its second part, of about 1330 to 1340, holds German Franciscan missionaries' Cuman translations of prayers and hymns, and a set of Cuman riddles. Cuman (Qipchaq) was the Turkic language of the Horde's steppe population. The corpus copy is Count Geza Kuun's first complete edition (Budapest 1880), whose long Latin introduction gathers medieval testimony about the Cumans and their being called 'Tartars'.
W218.tartar_means: In the Codex's own Cuman, 'Tatar' means 'Turkic', and the 'Tatar tongue' is the Qipchaq language itself. In Kuun's introduction, medieval Latin and Hungarian writers use 'Tartar' both for the Mongol invaders and, loosely, for the Cumans and for their Islam ('the Tartar rite').
W218.why_read: It records the everyday words of the Golden Horde's people (for yurt, city, palace, court, shaman) as written down by outsiders who lived among them, and shows 'Tatar' in use as the name of a real Turkic language.
W218.watch_out: The manuscript is a working phrasebook, so it gives words, not descriptions. Kuun's 1880 readings were corrected by later scholars (Radloff, Bang, Gronbech), and much of the quoted material here comes from Kuun's introduction, which assembles earlier authors.

W220.plain_title: Wisdom of Royal Glory: a Turkic mirror for princes from Kashgar
W220.one_line: A long Turkic poem of advice to rulers written at the Qarakhanid court in 1069 to 1070, in Vambery's 1870 edition.
W220.summary: Yusuf Khass Hajib wrote the Kutadgu Bilig ('Wisdom that brings good fortune') in Balasaghun and Kashgar in 1069 to 1070 and presented it to the Qarakhanid ruler, a Muslim Turkic dynasty. It is a verse dialogue about how a king should rule and how he should treat each class of subjects: scholars, merchants, farmers, herders. The corpus copies are Hermann Vambery's partial edition of the Herat manuscript (written in Uighur script in 1439), with German translation, glossary and introduction (Innsbruck 1870). It is literature, not a travel account.
W220.tartar_means: The poem itself does not use 'Tatar'; its people are 'Turks'. Vambery, writing in 1870, uses 'Chinese Tartary' as an alternative name for East Turkestan and 'Tatar' for the Mongol conquerors.
W220.why_read: It shows a settled, literate, Muslim Turkic court in Kashgar two centuries before the Mongols, with its own views of nomads, herders, merchants and palaces.
W220.watch_out: Vambery's text and translation are only a selection and his readings are superseded (Radloff 1891 to 1910, Arat 1947). Several quotes come from his glossary and introduction, not from a continuous text.

W221.plain_title: The Orkhon inscriptions: the Turks write their own history in stone
W221.one_line: Royal memorial stones of the Turk khagans in Mongolia (c.720 to 735), deciphered in the 1890s, where the name 'Tatar' first appears in writing.
W221.summary: The Orkhon inscriptions are carved stone memorials for the Turk prince Kul Tegin (732), his brother Bilge Qaghan (735) and the minister Tonyukuk (c.720 to 726), found in the Orkhon valley of Mongolia in 1889. They are written in Old Turkic runic script, with a Chinese text on the Kul Tegin stone. The corpus holds Radloff's German edition (1894 to 1899), Thomsen's decipherment and French translation (1896), Heikel's report of the 1890 Finnish expedition (1892), and a Yenisei glossary. The editors' introductions add Chinese annals and site descriptions.
W221.tartar_means: In the inscriptions, the Otuz Tatar ('Thirty Tatars') and Toquz Tatar ('Nine Tatars') are a real people on the eastern edge of the Turk empire, which Thomsen identifies as Mongols. In the 1890s editions, 'Tatar' also means Siberian Turkic groups (Abakan Tatars) and the Tatars of the Volga.
W221.why_read: These are the oldest dated texts in a Turkic language and the first written appearance of the name Tatar, and they show nomad khans hiring Chinese builders and warning their people against settled life.
W221.watch_out: The 1890s readings have been much improved since (Tekin 1968 and later), and Radloff and Thomsen often disagree. Many quotes here are from the editors' own notes or from Chinese annals they cite, which are marked.

W222.plain_title: Four Ottoman state papers on the end of the Crimean khanate
W222.one_line: An Ottoman copy (c.1775 to 1780) of memoirs and a treaty text about Russia, Crimea and the Tatar khans in the 1770s.
W222.summary: This small manuscript in the BULAC library, Paris, gathers four Ottoman chancery pieces from the Russo-Turkish war of 1768 to 1774 and its aftermath: a memoir on Russia since 1763, a memoir of 1773 on Russian demands (apparently translated from French), a treaty text on the Crimean frontier, and a memoir on the Tatars and their khans, the last two put into Turkish by the reis ul-kuttab Abd al-Razzaq Efendi. The copy is anonymous and undated, perhaps by a European hand. The corpus text is the library's scan on Internet Archive, whose OCR is unusable, so passages were read from the images. A diary of Pierre Ruffin, French interpreter at Bakhchysarai in 1767, is also filed under this record but was not read.
W222.tartar_means: The Crimean Tatars and the Nogay hordes (Budjak, Kuban, Yedisan, Jamboyluk, Yedichkul): Muslim subjects of the Genghisid Giray khans, whose status was being fought over by Russia and the Ottomans.
W222.why_read: It shows 'Tartary' as it looked to Ottoman officials in its last years: a Muslim khanate with Genghisid rulers, real fortresses, and a religious tie to the sultan as caliph.
W222.watch_out: Some pieces are translations of Russian or French texts, so the Ottoman voice is partly mediated. They are diplomatic documents with a political aim, and the transcriptions from a handwritten copy may contain small errors.

W123.plain_title: Spafarii's 1675 journey across Siberia to the Chinese border
W123.one_line: The travel diary of the tsar's envoy to China, crossing Siberia from Tobolsk to Nerchinsk in 1675.
W123.summary: Nicolae Milescu, called Spafarii, a learned Moldavian Greek in Russian service, led Tsar Aleksei's embassy to the Qing emperor in 1675. This is his road diary from Tobolsk down the Irtysh and Ob, up the Ket to Yeniseisk, across Baikal to Selenginsk and Nerchinsk, with his long description of the Irtysh, the Moscow instructions for the embassy and his dispatches to the tsar. The Irtysh-to-Baikal stretch is his own eyewitness; the upper Irtysh, Mongolia and China come from earlier envoys, traders and local informants. This corpus copy is Yu. V. Arsenyev's 1882 edition (Zapiski of the Imperial Russian Geographical Society, ethnography section, vol. 10.1) with his introduction and notes, in two scans of the same printing.
W123.tartar_means: Spafarii uses 'Tatars' for the Muslim Turkic peoples of western Siberia (Tobolsk, Irtysh and Baraba Tatars, once Kuchum's subjects), for the Kirghiz of the upper Yenisei, and for the Manchu conquerors of China ('the Bogdykhan's Tatars'). Mongols he calls Mungaly and western Mongols Kalmyks, although the Moscow instructions printed with the diary call the Mongols 'Mughal Tatars'.
W123.why_read: A Russian-side eyewitness of Siberia less than a century after Yermak: Tobolsk as a mixed Russian and Tatar town, the empty capital of Kuchum kept alive by a mosque, the earth-houses of the Baraba Tatars, and brick and stone buildings in Kalmyk and Mongol country whose builders he names as Chinese craftsmen.
W123.watch_out: Only the river route he travelled is eyewitness; the upper Irtysh comes from the reports of the envoys Baikov and Ablin, and Mongolia and China from traders. He writes as an Orthodox envoy and calls Islam an 'unclean faith'. The OCR of this pre-reform Russian text is damaged, so quotes are normalized to the printed spelling.

W164.plain_title: The Novgorod First Chronicle: the Tatars arrive
W164.one_line: Year-by-year records kept in Novgorod, with the closest Russian testimony to the Mongol arrival in 1223 and 1237 to 1238.
W164.summary: Monks and clergy in Novgorod kept these annals year by year. The oldest copy, the Synodal manuscript, dates from the 13th and 14th centuries, and the younger version runs to 1447. They record the first appearance of the 'Tatars' at the Kalka in 1223, Batu's campaign of 1237 to 1238, which stopped about 100 versts short of Novgorod, the Mongol census of 1257 to 1259 and later dealings with the Horde. The corpus copy is the 1841 Archaeographic Commission volume (PSRL vol. 3), which prints the Synodal text with variants from the younger copies and adds the Second and Third Novgorod chronicles.
W164.tartar_means: The Mongol armies and later the Golden Horde, its khans, envoys and tax officials. The chroniclers also call them by biblical names (Ishmaelites, sons of Hagar) and once, at Kulikovo, by the older steppe name Polovtsy. The 16th-century entries use 'Tatars' for Kazan Tatars and Crimean raiders.
W164.why_read: Here the Tatars appear as the Rus saw them: at first unknown strangers, then besiegers with palisades and siege engines, and then census takers riding through Novgorod's streets. The concrete details of how cities fell are close to the events.
W164.watch_out: The annalists were churchmen who read the Tatars as God's punishment for Rus sins and used hostile religious language. Some later entries were written up long after the events, and the 1841 edition mixes several copies. The OCR is damaged, so quotes have been normalized against a second scan of the same printing.

W162.plain_title: The Laurentian Chronicle: the Mongol storm over Suzdal Rus
W162.one_line: The oldest surviving Russian chronicle codex (copied 1377), with year-by-year entries on the Tatar conquest of Vladimir-Suzdal and life under the Horde to 1305.
W162.summary: The monk Lavrentii copied this chronicle in 1377 for Prince Dmitrii of Suzdal-Nizhnii Novgorod. It opens with the Primary Chronicle and continues with the annals of Vladimir-Suzdal, some of them written close to the events. For the Tatars it records the first appearance of 'unknown peoples' in 1223, the fall of the Volga Bulgar capital in 1236, the winter campaign of 1237 to 1238 against Riazan, Moscow, Vladimir and Suzdal, princes' journeys to Batu and the Great Khan, the census of 1257 and revolts against Muslim tax farmers. The corpus copy quoted here is the 1846 first edition (PSRL vol. 1), which also prints a continuation headed 'Troitskaia letopis'; the 1926 to 1928 second edition is in the corpus too.
W162.tartar_means: The Mongol armies of Batu and the later Golden Horde: its khans ('tsars'), envoys, census takers and tax officials. The chronicler also calls them godless, pagans, Ishmaelites and 'Taurmens', and calls the Muslim tax farmers who came with them 'besermen'.
W162.why_read: This is the Suzdal side of the conquest in the words of churchmen who lived through it or wrote soon after: dated sieges, named towns, palisades and catapults, the census and the first protests against Horde tax farming. There is nothing here about a Tartar empire building cities in Rus; the Tatars arrive as outsiders who burn them.
W162.watch_out: The chroniclers read the invasion as God's punishment and use hostile religious language. The 1377 codex has lost leaves (for example 1263 to 1283), so some stories begin or end in mid-sentence. The OCR of the 1846 printing is damaged; quotes have been normalized letter by letter (restoring the old letter yat) against the scan.

W163.plain_title: The Hypatian Chronicle: Kiev, Galicia and the Horde
W163.one_line: The southern Rus chronicle, whose Galician-Volhynian part describes the fall of Kiev in 1240, Prince Daniil's visit to Batu and a century of living beside the Tatars.
W163.summary: The Hypatian codex (about 1420s) joins the Primary Chronicle, the Kievan Chronicle and the Galician-Volhynian Chronicle, a court history of Prince Daniil of Galicia and his heirs written in the later 13th century. Its authors knew Daniil's household and sometimes cite eyewitnesses. For the Tatars it gives the Kalka campaign, the siege of Kiev with the names of Batu's generals, the storming of Volhynian towns, Daniil's humiliating visit to Batu on the Volga in 1245 to 1246, the Tatar general Burundai forcing the princes to tear down their town walls, and the disastrous campaigns of Nogai and Telebuga. This corpus copy is the 1843 first edition (PSRL vol. 2), checked against the 1908 Shakhmatov edition.
W163.tartar_means: The Mongols of Batu's army and afterwards the Golden Horde, its khans, generals (Kuremsa, Burundai, Nogai, Telebuga) and their subjects. The chronicler also calls them godless Moabites, Hagarenes and pagans.
W163.why_read: Here the Tatars are seen from a princely court that dealt with them for decades: the sounds of Batu's camp outside Kiev, drinking kumiss in Batu's tent, and a Tatar general ordering Rus towns to demolish their own walls. It also shows the Rus prince Daniil building a new stone and timber town, Kholm, which the Tatars could not take.
W163.watch_out: The Galician-Volhynian text was written without dates, and a later copyist added years that are often wrong by a year or more. It is a court history, hostile to the Tatars and flattering to Daniil. The 1843 OCR is damaged; quotes are normalized and checked against the 1908 edition where doubtful.

W165.plain_title: The Nikon Chronicle: Moscow's grand history of the Horde and the khanates
W165.one_line: Muscovy's largest 16th-century chronicle compilation, retelling the Mongol conquest with added tales and recording Kazan, Nogai and Siberian affairs down to 1558.
W165.summary: Compiled in Moscow around 1526 to 1530 (traditionally linked with Metropolitan Daniil) and continued to 1558, the Nikon or 'Patriarchal' Chronicle stitches together older chronicles, saints' lives and heroic tales. For the 13th and 14th centuries it is a retelling, sometimes embellished (epic heroes at the Kalka, a sorceress envoy of Batu). For the 1530s to 1550s it is close to official record: Nogai horse traders in Moscow, the siege and mining of Kazan in 1552, and the first envoys from the Siberian prince Ediger offering tribute in 1555. The corpus copies are the Archaeographic Commission volumes 9 to 13 (1862 to 1906); quotes come from vols. 10, 11 and 13.
W165.tartar_means: The Mongol invaders and the Golden Horde and its khans ('tsars') for the early centuries; later the Kazan Tatars, Crimean Tatars, Nogais and the Tatars of the Siberian prince Ediger. 'Tsar' is used for any Chinggisid khan.
W165.why_read: It is the official Muscovite story that New Chronology authors quote and reinterpret, so it is worth seeing what it actually says: foreign khans and their envoys, the Tatars' way of fighting, Moscow's stone walls under siege, Kazan's timber and earth defences and a Siberian ruler counting his taxpayers.
W165.watch_out: A late compilation: for events before about 1500 it is not an independent witness and it adds legends and speeches. It is written from the Moscow court's point of view. The OCR of the 1885 to 1904 volumes is fair to poor; quotes are normalized.

W166.plain_title: The History of the Kazan Tsardom: a captive's story of Kazan
W166.one_line: A Russian account of the Kazan khanate from its legendary founding to its conquest in 1552, by an author who says he spent twenty years at the Kazan khan's court.
W166.summary: Written in 1564 to 1565 by an anonymous Russian who says he was taken captive, given as a present to the khan of Kazan, and served at his court for twenty years until Kazan fell in 1552, when he went over to the Moscow tsar, who had him baptized and gave him a small estate. He admits he found little on Kazan's origins in Russian chronicles and asked 'the wisest and most honoured Kazan people' and the khan himself. The book mixes legend (a serpent's nest burned by a sorcerer), Kazan's history under Ulu-Mehmed and his heirs, portents, and a triumphal account of Ivan IV's siege. The corpus copy is PSRL vol. 19 (1903), which prints several redactions in parallel columns; page references below are column numbers.
W166.tartar_means: Mainly the Kazan Tatars and their khans ('tsars'), whom the author also calls Saracens, pagans and barbarians; also the Golden Horde ('Great Horde'), Nogais, Crimean Tatars and Astrakhan princes. He distinguishes the Tatar ruling class from the Chuvash, Cheremis (Mari), Votiaks (Udmurts) and Mordva of the Kazan land.
W166.why_read: It is the only Russian book devoted to the Kazan khanate, and it credits the building of Kazan to named khans: a town on Batu's camping ground for tribute envoys, then a new timber fortress built by Ulu-Mehmed. It also shows how a Russian who lived there imagined its past, with serpents, sorcerers and a demon-haunted ruin of the 'old Bulgars'.
W166.watch_out: The captivity claim cannot be checked, the early history is legend with muddled dates (it has Kazan founded in 1172 by a 'Tsar Sain' after Batu), and the whole book celebrates Ivan IV's conquest. Redactions differ; the OCR is fair, and quotes are normalized.

W167.plain_title: The Book of the Great Map: Muscovy's road book of the steppe
W167.one_line: A 1627 government description of a lost map of Muscovy and its steppe borderlands, listing rivers, fords, Tatar raiding roads, ruined mosques and Crimean palaces.
W167.summary: Clerks of the Razriad (Military Chancellery) wrote this book in 1627 to describe the 'Great Map' (Bolshoi Chertezh) of about 1600, which had worn out, together with a new map of the southern steppe. It is a dry, systematic list of rivers, distances, towns, fords and roads, compiled from service route books and scouts' reports rather than from travel by the authors. Along the way it notes Tatar raiding routes and the watch posts set against them, the Crimean khan's stone palaces at Bakhchysarai, the stone mosques of the ruined Golden Horde on the Akhtuba and on the Kuma, and stone idols in the steppe. The corpus copy is D. I. Yazykov's 2nd edition (1838), with the first edition of 1773 ('Drevniaia rossiiskaia idrografiia') alongside.
W167.tartar_means: Crimean Tatars and their khan ('tsar'), the Nogais (Great and Lesser Nogai), the Tatars of Belgorod (Akkerman) on the Dniester, and more loosely the builders of the Golden Horde; the 'Nogai side' and 'Crimean side' of rivers are the steppe banks where these nomads roamed.
W167.why_read: It shows what Moscow's officials actually knew about the steppe around 1600: which Tatar roads led into Rus, where the fords were, and what stood on the land. Where it finds ruins of stone mosques it calls them Tatar and names the Golden Horde; it lists the Crimean khan's palaces as stone and Crimean villages as wood daubed with clay.
W167.watch_out: A description of a lost map, not an eyewitness journey; distances are rough and some names are garbled between manuscripts (the 1838 editor prints variants in brackets). The book describes places, not people, so its notes on customs are brief.

W168.plain_title: The Siberian Chronicles: Yermak and the fall of Kuchum's khanate
W168.one_line: Seventeenth-century Russian chronicles of the Cossack conquest of the Siberian Tatar khanate (1581 to 1585) and of the towns and rulers that came before it.
W168.summary: This 1907 Archaeographic Commission volume gathers the main Russian accounts of Siberia's conquest: the Stroganov chronicle (1620s to 1630s), the chronicle of Savva Esipov, a Tobolsk church clerk (1636), and the chronicle associated with Semen Remezov (about 1700), with the 'Kungur' articles. None is by an eyewitness. Esipov drew on the Tobolsk archbishop's 1622 collection of Cossack memories and on local tradition about the Siberian khans; the Kungur-Remezov text adds folk stories heard from Tatars, Ostyaks and Cossacks. For the Tatars they give an origin legend of the Siberian rulers, the towns of Chingi-Tura and Sibir, Kuchum's khanate and its fall, and later Tatar memories of Yermak. The corpus holds the 1907 volume and an 1880 edition of the Kungur chronicle.
W168.tartar_means: The Siberian Tatars of the Tura, Tobol and Irtysh and their khans (Kuchum, his sons, the Taibugid princes), described as Muslims; the chronicles distinguish them from Ostyaks (Khanty), Voguls (Mansi), Samoyeds, Kalmyks and Mongols, and mention Bukharan merchants and a prince of the 'Kazakh horde'.
W168.why_read: They show what 17th-century Russians in Siberia believed about the land before them: a Muslim khanate with its own dynasties and towns (Chingiden where Tyumen now stands, Sibir on the Irtysh), a tribute system in furs, and Tatar songs, sacred stones and relics told to Russian writers.
W168.watch_out: Written 40 to 120 years after the conquest by the victors' church and military circles; they glorify Yermak and mix Cossack memory, Tatar legend and miracle stories. Dates and names in the dynastic legend are muddled (Chinggis Khan appears as a local commoner). The OCR of both volumes is fair and has been normalized.

W169.plain_title: The Kungur Chronicle: Yermak's conquest of Tatar Siberia
W169.one_line: A short illustrated Siberian chronicle, written around 1700, telling how Yermak's Cossacks took Kuchum's Tatar khanate in the 1580s.
W169.summary: An anonymous short chronicle of Yermak's campaign against Khan Kuchum of Sibir (1580s), preserved in a manuscript with 154 drawings that G. F. Müller brought from Tobolsk to the Academy in 1744 and attributed to the Tobolsk nobleman Semyon Remezov. It was written more than a century after the events, from older chronicles, Cossack tradition and Tatar hearsay, and mixes plausible detail (towns, rivers, tribute) with visions and miracles. This corpus copy is the 1880 St Petersburg photolithographic facsimile, which prints the text in ordinary type at the back; the drawings themselves are not readable in the OCR.
W169.tartar_means: The Siberian Tatars of Kuchum's khanate on the Tobol, Irtysh and Ishim, clearly distinguished from Voguls, Ostyaks, Samoyeds, Kalmyks and the Kazakh horde.
W169.why_read: It shows how Russians around 1700 remembered the Tatar capital Kashlyk (Isker) and the Tatar towns along the Irtysh, and how miracle stories were woven into the conquest.
W169.watch_out: Written about 120 years after 1582 by a Russian Orthodox author hostile to Kuchum; the preface warns that it mixes reliable facts with legends and that the copyist garbled the language. OCR of the pre-reform type is imperfect.

W171.plain_title: Fyodor Baikov's embassy from Tobolsk to Beijing
W171.one_line: The official route diary of the first Russian envoy sent to the Qing court, travelling up the Irtysh through Oirat (Kalmyk) and Mongol lands to Beijing, 1654 to 1657.
W171.summary: Fyodor Baikov led Tsar Alexei's embassy from Tobolsk to China in 1654 to 1657. His stateinyi spisok, the formal report every Muscovite envoy filed, is a day-by-day itinerary: river mouths, forts, where he waited for carts, what he was fed, and short notes on the towns, fields and buildings he passed. He wintered among the farming Bukharans of the Oirat prince Ablai taisha, crossed the Mongol steppe, and spent half a year shut in a Beijing compound after refusing Qing court protocol. This corpus copy is the 1788 printing in Novikov's Drevniaia rossiiskaia vivliofika, part 4, from a manuscript copy.
W171.tartar_means: Baikov uses 'Tatars' only for the tribute-paying and service Tatars of the Tobolsk and Tara districts on the Irtysh. Kalmyks (Oirats), Mongols and Bukharans are named separately, and he calls the Manchu Qing emperor 'of Mongol race'.
W171.why_read: A sober, practical eyewitness who notes exactly what buildings were made of and who built them, including an Oirat prince's new town raised by craftsmen sent from China.
W171.watch_out: The 1788 text follows a later copy (the 1966 critical edition uses the archival original), and the OCR of this old typeface is badly garbled; quotes here have been normalized letter by letter.

W174.plain_title: Captain Unkovsky's embassy to the Dzungar khan
W174.one_line: A Russian artillery captain's day-by-day journal of ten months at the felt-tent court of the Dzungar ruler Tsewang Rabtan on the Ili river, 1722 to 1724.
W174.summary: Ivan Unkovsky, a captain of artillery, was sent by Peter the Great in 1722 to Tsewang Rabtan, ruler of the Dzungar (western Mongol, Oirat) state, whom Russians called the Kontaisha. His brief was to talk the ruler into Russian protection, gain leave to prospect for gold, and free Russian prisoners. He travelled from Moscow via Tobolsk up the Irtysh, lived beside the ruler's moving camp in the Ili valley from November 1722 to September 1723, and kept a plain, careful journal of audiences, festivals, trade, rumours and landscape. This corpus copy is N. I. Veselovsky's 1887 edition, with an introduction, archive documents and a letter by A. M. Pozdneev on Oirat history.
W174.tartar_means: Unkovsky calls the Dzungars Kalmyks, never Tatars. His 'Tatars' are the Muslim service Tatars of Tobolsk and Tara who travelled in his suite, Siberian Tatar captives, and the Crimean and Kuban Tatars he describes to the Dzungar ruler.
W174.why_read: The best close-up of a great steppe state that Western maps folded into 'Tartary': a capital made of felt tents and reed fences, lama dances, wrestling, courts, new farms and workshops, and robbed burial mounds on the steppe.
W174.watch_out: Unkovsky was a diplomat on a political errand and often repeats what interpreters, captives and Bukharan merchants told him; he calls the Kalmyks deceitful from childhood. Veselovsky prints variant readings from a Moscow copy in footnotes.

W175.one_line: A provincial official's description of the Orenburg frontier (southern Urals and the Kazakh steppe) and its peoples, published in 1762.
W175.summary: Pyotr Rychkov served for decades in the Orenburg administration and became a correspondent of the Academy of Sciences. His Topography (1762) describes the province region by region: towns and forts, Bashkirs, Kalmyks, Kazakhs (then called Kirghiz-Kaisaks), Nogais and Tatars, rivers, minerals, and the ruins of old towns on the steppe. He drew on his own travels, government files, and questions put to Muslim scholars, interpreters and envoys who had been to Khiva and Bukhara. This corpus copy is the 1762 Academy printing.
W175.tartar_means: For Rychkov 'Tatars' are the Muslim Turkic peoples of Kazan, Orenburg and the Volga, the Nogais of the old steppe towns, and the Siberian Tatars. He notes that in Khiva and Bukhara the word was an insult and that these peoples called themselves Turks.
W175.why_read: A candid 18th century discussion of where the name 'Tatar' came from and who used it, plus early notes on steppe ruins and the traditions about who built them.
W175.watch_out: The OCR of this 1762 typeface is badly garbled and quotes here have been normalized word by word; some place names in the ruins list could not be read securely. Much of what he reports about ruins is hearsay from Kazakhs, Cossacks and old men.

W176.plain_title: Gerhard Friedrich Müller's History of the Siberian Tsardom
W176.one_line: The first scholarly history of Siberia, written from archives, chronicles and Tatar informants gathered on the Academy expedition of 1733 to 1743.
W176.summary: G. F. Müller, a German historian of the St Petersburg Academy, spent ten years in Siberia copying archives and interviewing Tatars, Mongols and others. Book 1 of his Description of the Siberian Tsardom (1750) covers the Siberian Tatar khanate from its legendary origins to Kuchum and Yermak's conquest. He compares Tatar, Mongol and Chinese traditions with Abu al-Ghazi and European travellers, visits the ruins of Tatar towns, and argues openly with legends he thinks unfounded. This corpus copy is the 1787 reissue of the Russian text.
W176.tartar_means: Müller uses 'Tatars' for the Turkic Muslims of the Tobol, Irtysh, Ob and Tom (Siberian Tatars), and also for the realm of Chinggis Khan's heirs, whom he treats together with the Mongols. He notes that the Chinese call all lands beyond the Great Wall 'Tartary'.
W176.why_read: A careful 18th century scholar who visited the ruins of Tatar towns, recorded Tatar oral traditions, and explained where names like Isker, Sibir and 'Tartary' came from.
W176.watch_out: Müller wrote with the Russian state's archives and outlook; his account of the khanate depends partly on late chronicles like the Kungur and Esipov texts. OCR of the 1787 type is poor and quotes are normalized.

W177.plain_title: Father Iakinf Bichurin's Notes on Mongolia
W177.one_line: A Russian monk-sinologist's route diary from Beijing to Kiakhta in 1821, with a survey of Mongol life and an essay on who the 13th century 'Tatars' really were.
W177.summary: Nikita (Father Iakinf) Bichurin headed the Russian Orthodox mission in Beijing from 1808 to 1821 and read Chinese fluently. Volume 1 of his Notes on Mongolia (1828) is the diary of his journey home across Inner Mongolia, the Gobi and Urga to Kiakhta in 1821, followed by a general description of Mongolia drawn from his own observation and Qing sources: geography, government, yurts, food, customs, religion. It closes with an essay answering the question 'Who were the Tatars of the 13th century?'. This corpus copy is the 1828 St Petersburg first edition, volume 1.
W177.tartar_means: Bichurin argues that the invaders Europeans called 'Tatars' were Mongols, and that the name was a Russian mistake passed on to the West. In his own day 'Tatars' means the Turkic Muslim peoples of Kazan, Astrakhan and Crimea, who, he notes, did not call themselves by that name.
W177.why_read: A clear, first-hand picture of how Mongols built and lived in yurts, what a Mongol monastery town looked like in 1821, and a pioneering explanation of how 'Tatar' and 'Great Tartary' became labels.
W177.watch_out: Bichurin relied heavily on Chinese sources and could be uncritical of them; his theory of the name is his own reasoning (he calls it a conjecture). The 1828 OCR is fair but patchy.

W178.plain_title: Bichurin's History of the First Four Mongol Khans
W178.one_line: A Russian translation (1829) of the Chinese official history of Chinggis Khan, Ögedei, Güyük and Möngke.
W178.summary: Father Iakinf Bichurin translated into Russian the annals of the first four Mongol great khans from the Yuan shi, the official history compiled for the Ming court in 1370, together with the commentary of the Tongjian gangmu, and added his own notes and a glossary of Mongol names. It gives the Chinese court view of the Mongol rise, the wars in China, the building of Karakorum and the western campaigns, including the attack on Rus. Nothing in it is eyewitness. This corpus copy is the 1829 St Petersburg edition.
W178.tartar_means: The text speaks of Mongols throughout. 'Tatar' appears only as the name of one steppe tribe (the Tatars, with branches like the 'White Tatars' in Bichurin's glossary) and, in the glossary key, as another word for Turkic speech.
W178.why_read: It lets a reader set the Chinese official record of the Mongol empire beside the Russian chronicles and the European friars, including the Chinese account of who first built Karakorum.
W178.watch_out: A translation of a history written more than a century after the events, with Bichurin's additions not always marked off from the source; the bundle pages were mostly glossary and some quotes were found by searching the volume.

W179.plain_title: Bichurin's Description of Dzungaria and Eastern Turkestan
W179.one_line: A Russian translation (1829) of Qing Chinese geographies of the region Europeans called 'Chinese Tartary' or 'Little Bukharia'.
W179.summary: Father Iakinf Bichurin translated Qing gazetteers of the 'Western Region' (Dzungaria and the Tarim Basin oases), written after China conquered the area in 1759, into Russian, with a translator's preface and notes. The book gives the Qing view of the towns, garrisons, taxes, products and peoples of Kashgar, Yarkand, Khotan, Aksu, Turfan and Ili. In his preface Bichurin discusses the name 'Great Tartary' and what 'Tatar' meant to Central Asians he met in Beijing. The corpus also holds his separate History of the Oirats or Kalmyks (1834) under this record. This corpus copy of the Description is the 1829 St Petersburg edition, part 1.
W179.tartar_means: In the translated Qing texts the peoples are Dzungars, Turkestanis, Kazakhs and Kyrgyz. In his preface Bichurin reports that Turkestani Muslims used 'Tatars' only for their Turkic kin in Tobolsk, Kazan and Astrakhan, and that no people in Central Asia called itself Tatar.
W179.why_read: A rare first-hand testimony, gathered in Beijing, on how Central Asians themselves used the word 'Tatar', plus the Qing record of brick-built oasis cities in the heart of so-called Chinese Tartary.
W179.watch_out: The Qing texts were written by the conquerors after 1759 and Bichurin abridged them; his preface remarks are his own. OCR of the 1829 print is patchy.

W180.plain_title: Bichurin's Collection of Information on the Ancient Peoples of Central Asia
W180.one_line: Russian translations (published 1851) of the chapters on the steppe peoples in the Chinese dynastic histories, from the Xiongnu to the Uighurs.
W180.summary: Father Iakinf Bichurin's last big work gathers, in Russian translation, what the Chinese standard histories from the Shiji onward say about the Xiongnu, Wuhuan, Xianbei, Turks (whom he calls the Dulga house), Uighurs, Tungusic peoples and the western oasis states, with his own historical notes and comparisons with Abu al-Ghazi and European scholars. It is a translation of ancient Chinese court records, not a travel account, and covers roughly the 2nd century BCE to the 10th century CE. This corpus copy is the 1851 St Petersburg edition in three parts.
W180.tartar_means: In the Chinese texts 'Tatar' hardly appears. In Bichurin's notes 'Tatar' means Turkic speech (the 'Tatar language') and the Tatars of the Yenisei, and he explains that Persian and Turkic historians called the eastern Mongols 'Tatars' and the northern ones 'Mongols'.
W180.why_read: It shows what the oldest written records say about the lives of the steppe peoples long before anyone spoke of 'Tartary': no cities, felt tents, mare's milk, and a failed plan to build a Xiongnu town.
W180.watch_out: Bichurin's translations were later criticised for omissions, and he treats the Xiongnu as ancestors of the Mongols, which is disputed. The Chinese sources are an enemy's view.

W181.plain_title: Levshin's Description of the Kazakh Hordes and Steppes
W181.one_line: A Russian official's three-part geography, history and ethnography of the Kazakhs (then called 'Kirghiz-Kaisaks'), 1832.
W181.summary: Aleksei Levshin served on the Orenburg frontier commission in 1820 to 1822, questioning Kazakh elders and Tatar interpreters and reading the Orenburg archives. His Description (1832) covers the land, the history of the three Kazakh hordes, and their way of life: yurts, food, Islam, burial, beliefs, law. The geography volume has a whole chapter on the ruined buildings of the steppe and who might have built them. This corpus holds the 1832 St Petersburg edition, parts 1, 2 and 3.
W181.tartar_means: Levshin writes about Kazakhs, not Tatars. 'Tatars' for him are the Muslim Tatars of Russia, whom he notes the Kazakhs, Bukharans and Khivans called Nogais, since 'Tatar' was to them an insulting name. Old graves and ruins the Kazakhs credited to the Nogais.
W181.why_read: A clear-eyed survey of steppe ruins (Buddhist, Muslim and ordinary dwellings, in stone, brick and clay) with the Kazakhs' own views on who built them, plus a detailed picture of yurts and graves.
W181.watch_out: Levshin was a Russian administrator and often condescending about nomads; much of the ruins chapter is compiled from earlier travellers (Müller, Pallas, Rychkov, Shangin) rather than seen by him. Printed page numbers are read from the OCR.

W186.plain_title: Zadonshchina: the Russian poem of the battle of Kulikovo
W186.one_line: A 14th to 15th century Russian prose-poem celebrating Grand Prince Dmitry's victory over the Horde leader Mamai on Kulikovo field in 1380.
W186.summary: The Zadonshchina ('the tale beyond the Don') is an Old Russian poetic lament and victory song about the battle of Kulikovo (8 September 1380), traditionally attributed to Sofony of Ryazan and closely modelled on the Lay of Igor's Campaign. This corpus copy is I. I. Sreznevsky's 1858 Academy edition, which combines the 15th century Kirillo-Belozersk manuscript with the later Undolsky copy, adds variant passages from the prose tales of the 'Mamai battle', and a long commentary. Sreznevsky argues the poem circulated orally and was written down from memory. The 1959 Academy edition listed on the card is not stored in this corpus.
W186.tartar_means: The Tatars are the army of the Golden Horde under the emir Mamai, called 'pagan Tatars', 'Muslims' (busormane) and, in poetic language, 'Khinova'. Batu, the conqueror of 1237 to 1240, is remembered as the model of Horde power.
W186.why_read: The Russian literary memory of the Horde at the moment its hold began to break: Tatars as grey wolves, the loot of their camp, Mamai fleeing to Genoese Kaffa, and (in Sreznevsky's notes) the chronicle scene of Batu's siege of Kiev.
W186.watch_out: This is poetry, not a battle report: numbers and speeches are rhetorical and hostile to the 'pagans'. Some quotes come from Sreznevsky's editorial matter and from later prose tales he prints alongside, and are labelled as such.

W120.plain_title: Jesuits crossing Tibet and 'Tartary', 1603 to 1721 (with Desideri's account of Tibet)
W120.one_line: Jesuit travellers' letters and Ippolito Desideri's Tibet memoir, quoted and checked by a 1924 editor, on the 'Tartars' who ruled, raided and invaded Tibet.
W120.summary: Ippolito Desideri, an Italian Jesuit, crossed Ladakh and western Tibet to Lhasa in 1715 to 1716 and lived there until 1721, witnessing the Dzungar invasion of 1717. His Italian memoir (Notizie istoriche del Thibet, finished 1728 to 1733) stayed unpublished for nearly two centuries. The open text in this corpus is not the 1930s De Filippi translation (still in copyright) but C. Wessels, Early Jesuit Travellers in Central Asia 1603 to 1721 (The Hague, 1924), which quotes Desideri's manuscript at length in English and also covers Bento de Goes, Antonio de Andrade, Estevao Cacella, Joao Cabral and John Grueber, printing some Portuguese letters in the original. Its 'Tartars' are the Mongol powers around Tibet and, after 1720, the Manchus.
W120.tartar_means: Mostly Mongols: the Qoshot Mongol rulers and garrisons of Tibet, and the Dzungar Mongols of 'Independent Tartary' (Giongar) who invaded in 1717. For the Portuguese Jesuits 'Tartary' (Sopo) is Mongolia and even includes Tibet; after 1720 'Chinese Tartars' means the Manchus of the Qing court.
W120.why_read: It shows 'Tartar' as a living political label in 1600s and 1700s Tibet: Tartar princes, princesses and armies, a Tartar monastery in Lhasa, and the local names Europeans matched to 'Tartary' on their maps.
W120.watch_out: Most quotations are Wessels's English renderings of Italian and Portuguese manuscripts, and some passages are Wessels's own summaries; the authoritative Italian text of Desideri is not in this corpus. Wessels also adds a great deal of modern commentary.

W225.plain_title: Matthew Paris's Great Chronicle on the Tartars, 1238 to 1247
W225.one_line: An English monk's chronicle recording rumours, letters and interviews about the Tartars as news of the Mongol invasion reached England.
W225.summary: Matthew Paris, a Benedictine monk of St Albans, kept the Chronica majora from about 1240 until his death in 1259. For 1238 to 1247 he records how news of the Mongol invasions reached England: embassies begging for help, even the collapse of herring prices at Yarmouth because Baltic fishermen stayed home, and copies of letters from Frederick II, Hungarian and Dominican writers, a cleric called Ivo of Narbonne, and the testimony of a fugitive Russian archbishop named Peter. Matthew never met a Tartar; he compiled, commented and drew. This corpus has H. R. Luard's Rolls Series edition (1872 to 1883), Latin text with English margin notes, volumes 3 to 6.
W225.tartar_means: The Mongols of Batu's western campaigns (1237 to 1242) and the wider Mongol empire, spelled Tartari, Tattari or Tatari in the letters Matthew copied.
