W225.why_read: It shows how Latin Europe first imagined the Tartars: the Tartarus pun that gave the name its extra 'r', the idea that they were the lost tribes shut up by Alexander, and the mix of real intelligence and horror stories that reached England.
W225.watch_out: Everything here is second hand. Matthew mixes apocalyptic and biblical ideas with reportage, and some letters he copies (especially Ivo of Narbonne's) are of doubtful reliability. The Latin text is Luard's nineteenth-century edition.

W226.plain_title: Master Roger's lament for Hungary, destroyed by the Tartars (1241 to 1242)
W226.one_line: An Italian cleric's eyewitness account of the Mongol invasion of Hungary, written after a year as their captive.
W226.summary: Master Roger (Rogerius) of Torre Maggiore, an Italian churchman serving as archdeacon of Várad (Oradea) in Hungary, lived through the Mongol invasion of 1241 to 1242. He fled Várad, hid in woods and a fortified island, was taken by the Mongols, worked for a Hungarian who had gone over to them, and escaped as they left Hungary. About 1243 to 1244 he wrote this 'Sorrowful Song' as a letter to a bishop. No manuscript survives; the text comes from the 1488 printings. This corpus has it in the 1600 Bongars collection of Hungarian historians and, used here for clearer print, in the 1885 Budapest edition in Chronica minora.
W226.tartar_means: The Mongol armies of Batu, Kadan and their fellow princes who invaded Hungary in 1241, together with Cumans, Russians and captives serving in their host.
W226.why_read: It is the closest look we have at Mongol war and Mongol occupation inside a European kingdom: sieges, tricks, the treatment of towns, and the officials they set over captured villages.
W226.watch_out: Roger writes a lament and dwells on atrocities; numbers such as 500,000 invaders are guesses or rumours. He saw some events but reports others from survivors, and the text survives only in late printed editions.

W227.plain_title: Thomas of Split on the Tartars (History of Salona and Split, 1241 to 1242)
W227.one_line: A Dalmatian archdeacon's account of the Mongol invasion of Hungary and their pursuit of King Béla to the Adriatic, with a chapter 'On the nature of the Tartars'.
W227.summary: Thomas (about 1200 to 1268), archdeacon of Split in Dalmatia, wrote a history of the bishops of Salona and Split in the 1260s. Its chapters on 1241 to 1242 tell how the Mongols destroyed the Hungarian army at the river Sajó (Mohi), sacked Pest and chased King Béla IV to the Dalmatian coast, where Thomas himself saw the refugees and the Tartar army before Split and Trogir. He adds a chapter describing the Tartars' looks, arms and customs, from what he could learn from informants. This corpus has the first printed edition, in Ivan Lučić (Lucius), De regno Dalmatiae et Croatiae (Amsterdam, 1666; several scans and a 1758 reprint), plus Lučić's Italian history of Trogir (Venice, 1674).
W227.tartar_means: The Mongol armies of Batu and Kadan, whom Thomas notes call themselves 'Mangoli' in their own language; 'Tartar' is for him an outsiders' name.
W227.why_read: A vivid, fairly sober contemporary picture of the Mongols in Europe: their appearance, weapons, felt tents and hide boats, hidden graves and methods of war, alongside eyewitness scenes on the Adriatic coast.
W227.watch_out: Only the Dalmatian scenes are eyewitness; the battle, the sack of Pest and the ethnographic chapter come from informants, and Thomas mixes in stock ideas about barbarians and the end of the world. The 1666 print survives in scans with heavy OCR errors, which have been corrected in the quotes.

W228.plain_title: Friar Riccoldo's pilgrimage book, with chapters on the Tartars of Persia and Baghdad
W228.one_line: A Florentine Dominican who lived under Mongol rule in Tabriz and Baghdad around 1288 to 1300 describes the Tartars' looks, laws, women, funerals, legends and conquests.
W228.summary: Riccoldo of Monte Croce, a Dominican friar from Florence, sailed to Acre around 1288, crossed Cilician Armenia and Anatolia into Ilkhanid Persia, preached for half a year at Tabriz and lived for years in Baghdad before returning to Florence and writing his Liber peregrinationis around 1300. Chapters 9 to 13 are a small treatise on the Tartars: their appearance and hatred of cities, their customs and funerals, the owl legend of how they left their mountains, Genghis Khan and the arrows, the sack of Baghdad in 1258, and their drift to Islam. This corpus holds J. C. M. Laurent's Latin edition (Peregrinatores medii aevi quatuor, Leipzig 1864 and 1873, with the pilgrim Burchard of Mount Sion in the same volume), a 1793 Florentine Italian version and his 1511 anti-Islamic tract.
W228.tartar_means: The Mongols of the Ilkhanate (Hulegu, Abaqa, Arghun and their armies and officials) whom Riccoldo met in Anatolia, Tabriz and Baghdad. He also treats 'Mogoli' as their own name and ties them to Gog and Magog.
W228.why_read: A rare Latin eyewitness from inside Mongol-ruled Baghdad: part sharp observation (armed women riding into towns, funeral horses on poles, the name left blank in letters), part hearsay and legend (the owl, Gog and Magog, the Lost Tribes).
W228.watch_out: Riccoldo is a missionary who openly despises the Tartars and mixes what he saw with tales he heard; some stories (the owl, the caliph made to eat gold, the officer boiled and eaten) are legends or rumours. The Latin OCR is noisy, and the 1793 Italian text in this corpus is a shorter Tuscan version that stops before the Tartar chapters.

W229.plain_title: Hayton's Flower of the Histories of the East
W229.one_line: An Armenian prince who knew the Mongol court dictates, in 1307, a geography of Asia and a history of the Tartar khans from Genghis to his own day.
W229.summary: Hayton (Het'um) of Corycus, a prince of Cilician Armenia and nephew of King Het'um I, served alongside the Mongol Ilkhans, became a Premonstratensian canon, and in 1307 at Poitiers dictated this book in French to Nicolas Falcon, who also made the Latin version. Book I surveys the kingdoms of Asia, Book III tells the history of the Tartars, and Book IV proposes a crusade allied with them. Hayton himself says he knew Book III in three ways: from the Tartars' own histories up to Mongke, from his uncle King Het'um's accounts through Hulegu, and from his own eyes from Abaqa onward. The corpus copy is Charles Kohler's edition of both texts with variants, in Recueil des historiens des croisades, Documents armeniens II (Paris, 1906), in four scans.
W229.tartar_means: The Mongols as a whole: the 'seven nations called Mogols', of which the Tartars proper are the first, and the realms of Genghis Khan's heirs (the Great Khan in Cathay, Chagatai lands in Turkestan, the Golden Horde in Comania, the Ilkhans in Persia). The Latin text usually spells them Tatari.
W229.why_read: The most influential medieval European overview of 'Tartary' as a system of kingdoms, from an Armenian insider who attended khan elections, with famous stories (the black felt, the owl, the drowned khan) that later books copied for centuries.
W229.watch_out: Hayton wrote to win papal support for an Armenian-Mongol alliance, so he flatters the Tartars' friendship with Christians (he calls Qubilai a Christian) and garbles early Mongol history (his 'Octota Can' is made Genghis's heir and Jochi's father). The OCR mixes the main text with dense variant footnotes.

W230.plain_title: Letters of 1241 on the Mongol invasion, printed in the Golden Chronicle of Hohenschwangau
W230.one_line: Latin letters written in 1241 by kings, dukes, bishops and a Dominican friar as the Tartars overran Poland and Hungary, printed by Joseph von Hormayr in 1842.
W230.summary: Joseph von Hormayr's local history of Hohenschwangau castle in Bavaria (Munich, 1842) includes an appendix, 'The Great Mongol Flood', where he tells the story of the 1241 invasion in romantic German and then prints Latin documents supplied by J. F. Boehmer: letters from King Bela IV of Hungary and King Wenceslas of Bohemia to Conrad IV, from Duke Frederick of Austria, Duke Otto of Bavaria and the bishops of Freising and Augsburg, and, notably, a text of the Hungarian Dominican Julian's report to the papal legate on the Tartars' origin and way of war. The corpus holds two scans of the book; the letters sit on scan pages n346 to n359 of T0566 (n364 to n372 of T0565).
W230.tartar_means: The Mongol armies of Batu and his generals that invaded Rus', Poland, Hungary and Moravia in 1240 to 1242; the letters call them 'Tartari', and Hormayr's German calls them Mongolen or Tataren.
W230.why_read: You hear the invasion in the voices of people living through it: a king writing from Vienna after losing his kingdom, dukes counting the enemy dead at their borders, and a friar relaying what he learned on the Russian frontier, including the khan's threatening letter to the king of Hungary.
W230.watch_out: The Latin letters are contemporary, but Hormayr's German narrative is a nineteenth-century patriotic retelling full of local legends. The OCR of the Latin is very poor in places, so quotes are cleaned heavily. The card doubted that Julian's letter was here; it is (letter no. 5), though in a garbled text.

W231.plain_title: Guagnini's Description of European Sarmatia, with a section on Tartary
W231.one_line: An Italian soldier in Polish service describes Poland, Lithuania, Muscovy and the Tatar hordes on their borders, 1578 to 1581.
W231.summary: Alessandro Guagnini of Verona served for decades as a soldier and commander in Poland-Lithuania, including at Vitebsk on the Muscovite frontier, and published this Latin description of 'European Sarmatia' at Krakow in 1578. It ends with a survey of the 'Campestrian' (steppe) Tatars divided into hordes: Kazan, Nogai, the Volga horde, Astrakhan, the Circassians and the Crimean or Perekop Tatars, followed by a chapter on Tatar customs, warfare and law. The corpus holds three scans of the Speyer 1581 edition and the 1768 Polish version. Much of the text is compiled from Herberstein, Miechowita and Polish chronicles, and Maciej Stryjkowski accused Guagnini of taking his work.
W231.tartar_means: The Turkic and Mongol-descended peoples east and south of Poland-Lithuania and Muscovy: Crimean (Perekop) Tatars above all, plus the Kazan, Astrakhan, Nogai and Volga hordes, Kalmyks, and remoter groups such as the Kirghiz; in the Polish history section, the Mongols of 1241.
W231.why_read: A compact sixteenth-century 'map in words' of the Tatar world as Poles saw it, which shows 'Tartary' as a set of hordes and khanates, some living in timber towns and fields, most in camps on the steppe.
W231.watch_out: Largely second-hand and borrowed; Guagnini's own frontier experience is hard to separate from what he copied. Hostile framing is common, and the Latin OCR renders the long s as f and is often run together.

W232.plain_title: Michalo the Lithuanian on the customs of the Tartars, Lithuanians and Muscovites
W232.one_line: A Lithuanian envoy who had been in the Crimean khanate holds up the Crimean Tatars as a mirror of sober virtue to shame his own nobles, c. 1550.
W232.summary: The author, writing as 'Michalo the Lithuanian', was a Lithuanian nobleman and envoy who says he was present in the Crimea in the late 1530s. Around 1550 he wrote a treatise for King Sigismund Augustus comparing the Crimean (Perekop) Tatars and the Muscovites with the Lithuanians, mostly to the Lithuanians' shame. Johann Jacob Grasser printed it at Basel in 1615 as ten fragments from a manuscript, with Jan Lasicki's tract on Samogitian gods. The corpus copy is that 1615 edition, plus the 1627 Elzevir Respublica Poloniae, which reprints extracts from Michalo on Lithuania. The fragments cover Crimean geography, the Giray dynasty, nomad life, law, marriage, religion and, at harrowing length, the slave trade in Lithuanian captives.
W232.tartar_means: Chiefly the Crimean Tatars, whom he calls 'Precopenses' after Perekop, the fortified gate of the peninsula; also the other hordes (Nogai, Volga, Kazan, Bukhara, Samarkand) in passing, and the Volga ('Zavolhenses') Tatars who once ruled Muscovy.
W232.why_read: A rare Latin insider's view of the sixteenth-century Crimean khanate that praises Tatar sobriety, justice and charity while describing the slave markets of Perekop and Kaffa where his own countrymen were sold. It also records a Lithuanian claim that the Giray khans owed their throne to Lithuania.
W232.watch_out: The book is a moralising tract, so it idealises the Tatars to scold Lithuanians; it survives only as fragments chosen by a later editor; and the author's identity is disputed. The OCR of the 1615 print is fair but has many broken words.

W233.plain_title: A papal envoy's report on Muscovy, bound with a Polish envoy's description of the Crimean Tatars
W233.one_line: Jesuit legate Antonio Possevino's report on Ivan IV's Muscovy (1581 to 1582), with Marcin Broniewski's eyewitness account of the Crimean khanate (1578 to 1579) in the 1595 edition.
W233.summary: Antonio Possevino (1533 to 1611), an Italian Jesuit, went to Moscow as Pope Gregory XIII's legate in 1581 to 1582, met Ivan IV and brokered the truce of Yam Zapolsky with Poland. His Moscovia (Vilnius 1586) gathers his reports, debates and letters, with much on Kazan, Astrakhan, the Crimean raids and the tsar's title. The corpus holds three scans: the 1586 Vilnius edition (with an unrelated 18th-century German geography of Russia by Busching bound in after it, not used here), the 1587 Cologne collected works, and the 1595 Cologne edition, which adds Marcin Broniewski's Tartariae descriptio, written in 1579 after nine months as Polish envoy to Khan Mehmed II Giray. Broniewski's passages are labelled as his; that work also has its own catalogue record, W237.
W233.tartar_means: For Possevino, the Tatars of the former Kazan and Astrakhan khanates, the Nogais and the Crimean ('Precop') Tatars who burned Moscow in 1571, plus the Muslim Tatars of Lithuania and a rumoured Christian 'Cham' in Asia. For Broniewski, the Crimean Tatars of the Giray khanate and their Nogai and steppe neighbours.
W233.why_read: Two diplomats who were really there: Possevino shows how Moscow saw its new Tatar conquests and the 'Czar' title, and Broniewski gives one of the fullest 16th-century eyewitness pictures of Crimean Tatar houses, towns, food, law and religion, including who built the stone buildings.
W233.watch_out: Possevino writes as a Counter-Reformation polemicist and relies on informants and Herberstein for background. Broniewski is a separate author printed in the 1595 volume; both texts survive here only as rough OCR, so quotes were checked against the page images.

W234.plain_title: Kircher's China Illustrated: Jesuit reports on China, Tibet and Tartary
W234.one_line: A Roman Jesuit scholar's 1667 compendium of missionary reports, including the first European crossing from Beijing through the Kalmyk steppe to Lhasa.
W234.summary: Athanasius Kircher (1602 to 1680), a German Jesuit polymath in Rome, never went to Asia. China illustrata (Amsterdam 1667) compiles Jesuit sources: Bento de Goes's overland journey of 1602 to 1607, which proved Cathay was China; Martino Martini on the Manchu conquest; and above all what Johann Grueber and Albert Dorville told him and drew after travelling from Beijing via Xining, the Kokonor desert and Lhasa to India in 1661. It adds Kircher's own theories that Chinese and Asian idolatry came from Egypt. The corpus holds four scans of the 1667 Latin edition and the 1668 Dutch translation; quotes here are from the Getty copy.
W234.tartar_means: Several peoples: the Kalmyk (Oirat, Khoshut) Mongols of the Kokonor steppe, the peoples of the 'Tangut' kingdom around Lhasa loosely counted as Tartary, the Manchus who had just conquered China (the 'Sino-Tartar' monarch), and Marco Polo's medieval Mongol khans.
W234.why_read: The best-known 17th-century picture of inner Asia, with engraved plates of Kalmyk dress, tents and the Dalai Lama drawn from eyewitness sketches, and the Manchus shown rebuilding Beijing.
W234.watch_out: Everything is second-hand and filtered through Kircher's missionary hostility and speculative theories (Egyptian origins, Prester John). OCR of all copies is fair only, so quotes were checked against page images.

W238.plain_title: Ramusio's second volume of voyages: Marco Polo, Hayton, Barbaro and the Muscovy texts
W238.one_line: The Venetian editor Ramusio's 1574 collection of the classic Italian texts on Tartary, with his own commentaries.
W238.summary: Giovanni Battista Ramusio (1485 to 1557), a Venetian official, gathered travel accounts in Italian; this second volume, published after his death (1559, this copy Venice 1574), holds his recension of Marco Polo, Hayton the Armenian's Flower of the Histories of the East, the Venetian envoys Barbaro and Contarini to the Tatars and Persia, Herberstein on Muscovy, and, in this printing, the 'Due viaggi in Tartaria' (the papal envoys of 1245 to 1247, via Vincent of Beauvais). Ramusio adds his own discourses, including a report from a Persian merchant about western China. The bundle pages were mostly index; accounts here come from the texts themselves.
W238.tartar_means: Varies by text: the Mongols of Chinggis and Kublai (Polo, Hayton, Carpini), the Golden Horde Tatars on the Don (Barbaro), Crimean and Volga Tatars (Muscovy texts), and even the ruler of Ming China ('Daimir Can, great Emperor of the Tartars') in Ramusio's merchant report.
W238.why_read: It is the form in which most Renaissance readers met the Tartars, and it carries rare material such as Barbaro's eyewitness Tana and Ramusio's own notes on maps, Prester John and China.
W238.watch_out: An anthology: each text has its own date and reliability, and Ramusio's Polo is a distinct recension. The 1574 copy does include the 'Due viaggi in Tartaria' (from n601). OCR is rough, so quotes were checked against page images.

W239.plain_title: Gemelli Careri's round-the-world journey: China under the 'Eastern Tartars'
W239.one_line: A Neapolitan traveller's eyewitness account of Kangxi's China in 1695 to 1696, including the Great Wall and Beijing's 'Tartar City'.
W239.summary: Giovanni Francesco Gemelli Careri (1651 to 1725), a Neapolitan lawyer, travelled round the world between 1693 and 1698, paying his own way. Part IV of his Giro del Mondo (Naples 1699 to 1700) covers China: he went from Canton to Beijing in 1695 to 1696, met the Kangxi emperor, visited the Great Wall and talked with Jesuits such as Filippo Grimaldi. He adds compiled chapters on religion and on the origin of the 'Eastern Tartars', the Manchu dynasty. The corpus holds the 1699 and 1700 printings of part IV and a 1727 edition; quotes come from the 1699 copy and one from the 1700 copy.
W239.tartar_means: Mainly the Manchus ('Eastern Tartars') ruling China as the Qing, and the Mongols of 'Imperial Tartary' under them; also the 'Western Tartars' (Oirat Dzungars, 'Eluth') and Chinese Muslims said to come from 'Great Tartary'.
W239.why_read: A lay eyewitness who walked on the Great Wall, saw the Tartar and Chinese cities of Beijing, and records how the Manchu conquest changed Chinese dress and hair.
W239.watch_out: Critics once doubted he went at all; his journey is now generally accepted, but he borrows freely from Jesuit books, especially on Tartar history, religion and the Dalai Lama.

W240.plain_title: Sanudo's crusade plan: the Secrets of the Faithful of the Cross
W240.one_line: A Venetian merchant-noble's crusade treatise of c. 1321, with a history of the Tartars and advice on using them against Egypt.
W240.summary: Marino Sanudo Torsello (c. 1270 to 1343), a Venetian nobleman who travelled widely in the eastern Mediterranean, wrote the Liber secretorum fidelium crucis between 1306 and 1321 and presented it to Pope John XXII. It proposes a trade embargo on Mamluk Egypt, an alliance with the Mongol Ilkhans, and a crusade by sea, and includes a history of the crusades with chapters on the origin, conquests and customs of the Tartars, largely compiled from Carpini and Hayton, plus merchant knowledge of trade routes. The manuscripts carry Pietro Vesconte's maps. The corpus copy is Jacques Bongars's first printed edition in Gesta Dei per Francos, vol. 2 (Hanau 1611), in two scans; quotes come from the stand-alone scan.
W240.tartar_means: The Mongols and their successor states: Chinggis Khan's people, the Ilkhans who ruled Persia and Iraq ('the Tartars who rule Persia and Chaldea'), the Golden Horde under Uzbek in Gazaria and the north, and the Great Khan in Cathay.
W240.why_read: It shows how a practical Venetian saw the Tartars around 1320: as trading partners controlling the spice road through Tabriz, potential allies against Egypt, and a people whose history was already wrapped in Prester John legend.
W240.watch_out: Most of the Tartar history and customs are copied from Carpini and Hayton, and the book is a piece of crusade advocacy. The Vesconte maps are reduced or absent in this printed edition (note for the maps team).

W241.plain_title: Mendoza's History of the Great Kingdom of China
W241.one_line: The best-selling 16th-century European book on China, compiled in 1585 by a Spanish friar who never went there, with Tartary as China's northern enemy.
W241.summary: Juan González de Mendoza (1545 to 1618), a Spanish Augustinian, was chosen for a mission to China that never went; instead he compiled this history in Rome (first edition 1585) from Chinese books brought to Mexico and Manila, the reports of Martín de Rada (1575) and the Franciscans (1579), and Portuguese writers such as Gaspar da Cruz. It went through dozens of editions and translations. Tartary appears as China's northern neighbour and enemy, behind the Great Wall. The corpus holds the 1585 Rome first edition (quoted here), another 1585 copy, a 1596 edition, the 1586 Itinerario and a 1589 Latin version.
W241.tartar_means: The Mongols of the northern steppe beyond the Great Wall, China's traditional enemies, and loosely 'Tartaria' as the whole land north and northwest of China; the viceroy's guard of 'Tartars by nation' may be Mongols or other northerners in Ming service.
W241.why_read: It fixed for European readers the picture of Tartary as the hostile land beyond the Wall, and preserves a Franciscan eyewitness note of Tartar soldiers guarding a Ming viceroy.
W241.watch_out: Entirely second-hand and often copied closely from Gaspar da Cruz and Rada; Mendoza himself flags some reports as hard to believe.

W242.plain_title: Mendes Pinto's Peregrination: a Portuguese adventurer's claimed journey through China and Tartary
W242.one_line: A famous and unreliable Portuguese memoir (written c. 1569 to 1578, printed 1614) claiming capture by a 'King of Tartary' besieging Beijing in 1544.
W242.summary: Fernão Mendes Pinto (c. 1509 to 1583) spent some twenty years as a trader, soldier and envoy in Asia and later wrote the Peregrinaçam, published after his death in Lisbon in 1614. Its trading episodes rest on real experience, but his account of being enslaved in China, working on the Great Wall, and being taken by a vast Tartar army besieging Beijing in 1544 and travelling through Tartary is widely regarded as invented or built from hearsay. The corpus holds the 1614 first edition (quoted here) and a 1725 edition (the bundle's source pages).
W242.tartar_means: A 'King of Tartary' ruling an empire north of China, with a capital 'Lançame' and a Buddhist-style religious centre; probably a literary composite of the Mongols (perhaps echoing Altan Khan's 1550 raid on Beijing), with touches of Tibet.
W242.why_read: A classic case of 'claimed travel': a bestseller that gave Europeans a vivid but fictional Tartary of giant armies, captured idols and royal tombs.
W242.watch_out: Chronology, place names and numbers cannot be reconciled with history; use it to show what Europeans read about Tartary, not what Tartary was like.

W243.plain_title: Gaspar da Cruz's treatise on China
W243.one_line: The first European book devoted to China, by a Portuguese friar who was in Canton in 1556, with a chapter on China's Tartar neighbours and the Wall.
W243.summary: Gaspar da Cruz (died 1570) was a Portuguese Dominican who worked in India, Malacca and Cambodia and spent some weeks in Canton (Guangzhou) late in 1556. Back in Portugal he printed this treatise at Évora in 1569, shortly before he died of plague. It mixes what he saw in Canton with the written account of Galeote Pereira and reports from Portuguese prisoners held in China around 1549 to 1553. Chapters 2 and 3 discuss the lands bordering China: the Tartars beyond the Wall, the Mughals ('Mogores') of Samarkand, and even Germany and Russia. This corpus copy is a Google scan of the original 1569 blackletter print.
W243.tartar_means: Mostly the Mongols beyond China's northern Wall, with whom the Ming were at war (he reports the great raid of 1550), plus Tartar prisoners serving as soldiers in Canton. He also ties Tartary to the Mughals ('Mogores') of Samarkand and to the Scythians and Magog of classical and biblical learning.
W243.why_read: A rare mid-sixteenth-century view of the Tartars from the Chinese side of the Wall, from a man who actually saw Tartar captives in Canton. It shows how a learned friar stitched Chinese hearsay, prisoners' stories and Bible-based geography into one picture.
W243.watch_out: Most Tartar material is second hand (Chinese informants and Portuguese captives), and his geography of Tartary, Russia and 'Germany' is speculation. The corpus OCR of this blackletter print is nearly unreadable, so all quotes here were read from the page images.

W244.one_line: A Portuguese Jesuit's description of late Ming China, written after two decades there, with the first Manchu ('Tartar') attacks seen from inside the empire.
W244.summary: Álvaro Semedo was a Portuguese Jesuit who reached China in 1613 and lived there, with breaks, until about 1637, at Nanjing, in Jiangxi and elsewhere. Back in Europe he wrote an account of the country and the mission in Portuguese; that manuscript is lost, and the text first appeared as this Spanish edition by Manuel de Faria e Sousa (Madrid, 1642), followed by Italian (1643) and English (1655) versions, all in the corpus. It covers the provinces, customs, government and army, then the Christian mission year by year. The Tartars appear as the old Mongol (Yuan) rulers of China and as the new enemy in Liaodong from 1618. This entry quotes the 1642 Spanish copy, plus one page of the 1655 English.
W244.tartar_means: Two groups: the Mongol conquerors who ruled China from the thirteenth century until 1368, and the Manchus (Jurchen) of the north-east, whose war on the Ming began in Liaodong in 1618. Semedo calls both simply 'Tartaros'.
W244.why_read: It shows how a well informed resident of Ming China understood the Tartars just before the Manchu conquest: an old dynasty of foreign rulers, and a frightening new enemy beyond the Wall. It also preserves the text of a Chinese war memorial of 1618 in translation.
W244.watch_out: Semedo saw little of the frontier himself; the war news comes from Chinese documents and Jesuit letters. The 1655 English edition adds Martino Martini's Bellum Tartaricum on the Manchu conquest, which is Martini's work (catalogued separately) and is not used here.

W245.plain_title: Friar Jordanus's Wonders of the East
W245.one_line: A Dominican bishop's short book of marvels from Armenia, Persia and India, c. 1330, with a hearsay chapter on the 'Great Tartar' of Cathay and the other Mongol empires.
W245.summary: Jordanus Catalani, a Dominican from Séverac in southern France, went east around 1320, worked from Tabriz and Sultaniyeh in Mongol-ruled Persia, then preached on India's west coast. In 1329 Pope John XXII made him bishop of Columbum (Quilon, Kerala), and around then he wrote the Mirabilia descripta, a brisk list of wonders country by country. He describes Armenia, Persia and India from his own travels, and the 'Great Tartar' of Cathay only from what trustworthy people told him. The Latin survives in one manuscript; this corpus copy is its first printing (Paris, 1839), with Henry Yule's English translation (Hakluyt Society, 1863).
W245.tartar_means: The Mongols and their four successor states: the 'Great Tartar' (the Yuan emperor in Cathay), the Tartar rulers of Persia (the Ilkhanate, whose Tartars had become Muslims), the empire of 'Osbet' (Uzbek Khan of the Golden Horde) and the Chagatai lands. 'Tartary' also names the Golden Horde country around Tana on the Don.
W245.why_read: In a few pages it shows how a missionary on the edge of the Mongol world pictured it around 1330: a real, organised set of Tartar empires with cities, paper money, temples and strange funerals, set among dragons, the Roc and dog-headed islanders.
W245.watch_out: Everything on Cathay is hearsay and echoes Marco Polo. The 1839 Latin comes from a single fourteenth-century manuscript, and some names are garbled; Yule's 1863 notes help but are his own guesses.

W223.plain_title: Vincent of Beauvais's Mirror of History on the Tartars
W223.one_line: A thirteenth-century Dominican world history that preserves the lost report of Simon of Saint-Quentin, who met the Mongol general Baiju in 1247, alongside Carpini's account.
W223.summary: Vincent of Beauvais (died c. 1264), a French Dominican, compiled the Speculum historiale, a huge history of the world, in the 1240s and 1250s. He says he received a 'history of the Tartars' from Simon of Saint-Quentin, a friar of the papal embassy led by Ascelin (Anselm) that reached the Mongol army of Baiju in Persia in 1247, and he spread Simon's material through his chapters by date, adding extracts from John of Plano Carpini. Simon's own text is lost, so Vincent is its only witness. This corpus copy is the Douai 1624 printing, where the Tartar chapters fall in books 29 and 31.
W223.tartar_means: The Mongols: the armies of Chinggis Khan and his heirs, above all Baiju's army in Persia and Armenia and the court of Güyük. The text also calls them Mongals, and notes two Tartar peoples with different languages but one law.
W223.why_read: It is the only surviving source for an eyewitness Dominican mission to a Mongol army, with sharp, hostile detail on dress, food, law, warfare and a tense audience at which the friars refused to kneel. It also shows medieval legend (Prester John, the enclosed nations of the Caspian) being repeated and, in one case, tested.
W223.watch_out: Simon's words reach us through Vincent's editing, and the tone is often hostile propaganda (charges of cannibalism, lust and cruelty). The 1624 chapter numbers differ from earlier editions, and the OCR of this folio needs checking against the page images.

W224.plain_title: The Tartar Relation of C. de Bridia
W224.one_line: A Franciscan's 1247 Latin history of the Mongols, written from the reports of the Carpini mission, surviving in one fifteenth-century manuscript bound with the Vinland Map.
W224.summary: The 'Tartar Relation' (Hystoria Tartarorum) was written by a Franciscan who signs himself C. de Bridia, dated 30 July 1247, at the request of his Franciscan superior. He drew on oral reports from members of John of Plano Carpini's mission to the Mongol court (1245 to 1247), especially Benedict the Pole. It covers Mongol history, customs and campaigns, including details not in Carpini. The only known copy is a paper manuscript of about 1440 now at Yale (Beinecke MS 350A), famous because it was bound with the disputed Vinland Map. The atlas does not hold the text: the corpus has only a catalogue description of the manuscript, and the 1965 edition with translation is lending-only.
W224.tartar_means: The Mongols of the empire of Güyük and Batu, whose armies had invaded Russia, Poland and Hungary in 1240 to 1242, along with the peoples they ruled.
W224.why_read: It is an independent early witness to what the first papal envoys learned about the Mongols, parallel to Carpini, and a good example of how a manuscript's history (here, the Vinland Map controversy) can overshadow its content.
W224.watch_out: The atlas has no text of this work, so nothing here is quoted. The account is second hand, from travellers' oral reports, and survives in a single late copy.

W122.one_line: An Amsterdam burgomaster's huge 1705 compilation describing every land then called Tartary, from Crimea to Korea.
W122.summary: Nicolaes Witsen (1641-1717), burgomaster of Amsterdam and a director of the Dutch East India Company, visited Moscow in 1664-1665 but never went to Siberia. For decades he gathered Russian route books, Jesuit letters, Dutch embassy diaries, maps, objects and interviews, and published them as Noord en Oost Tartarye (1692, enlarged 1705). It moves region by region from Manchuria (Niuche) and Mongolia through Siberia, the Kalmyk and Kazakh steppes and the Caucasus to Crimea, often printing his informants' reports word for word. The corpus copy is the DBNL transcription of the 1705 second edition, so the Dutch is clean and page references are printed pages.
W122.tartar_means: A very wide umbrella. Witsen follows the European habit of calling all lands east of the Ob and the Caspian 'Tartarye', covering Manchus, Mongols, Kalmyks and Siberian peoples, while noting that Siberia strictly speaking is not Tartary and that the peoples properly called Tartars now live mostly in Crimea and around Kazan.
W122.why_read: It shows exactly what the word Tartary meant to the best-informed European of the 1690s, and it names its sources, so a reader can see where each claim came from.
W122.watch_out: A compilation of many voices of uneven reliability, so credit each passage to the informant or book Witsen is quoting; his own theories (Egyptians in Siberia, for example) are speculation. The bundle page covered only the Great Wall, so these accounts come from searching the full text.

W246.plain_title: Nieuhof's Dutch embassy to the 'Great Tartar Khan' in Beijing
W246.one_line: A Dutch steward's illustrated eyewitness account of travelling from Canton to Beijing in 1655 to 1657, just after the Manchu ('Tartar') conquest of China.
W246.summary: Johan Nieuhof (1618-1672) was steward of the Dutch East India Company embassy of Pieter de Goyer and Jacob de Keyzer, which travelled by river and canal from Canton to Beijing in 1655-1656 to seek trade with the new Qing emperor. His journal, reworked by his brother Hendrik and the publisher Jacob van Meurs, appeared in 1665 with about 150 engravings and became a best-seller. Part one is the eyewitness journey; part two is a general description of China and of the Manchu conquest, compiled mostly from the Jesuit Martino Martini. The corpus holds the 1665 Dutch first edition and John Ogilby's 1669 English translation, which also carries an appendix taken from Athanasius Kircher.
W246.tartar_means: The Manchus who had just conquered China (the Qing), their emperor being the 'Great Tartar Cham'; in the historical chapters also the earlier Mongol conquerors (the Yuan) and the people of Niuche or East Tartary (Manchuria).
W246.why_read: The fullest early eyewitness picture of 'Tartars' as the new masters of China: their soldiers, lords, women and court, and the ruined cities they left along the road.
W246.watch_out: Keep the eyewitness journey apart from the compiled general description and from Kircher's appendix. The printed text was edited and embellished by others, and the English OCR is poor in places, so quotes here are normalized from the scans.

W248.plain_title: Dapper's record of the Dutch in Qing China, 1662 to 1668
W248.one_line: An Amsterdam writer's 1670 compilation of Dutch embassy and fleet journals from Qing China, with a general description of China and 'East Tartary'.
W248.summary: Olfert Dapper (1636-1689), an Amsterdam physician and writer who never left the Netherlands, worked up the journals of Dutch East India Company missions to the new Qing ('Tartar') rulers of China: the 1662 embassy of Jan van Kampen and Constantijn Nobel to the Fujian viceroy, Balthasar Bort's fleet that fought beside the Qing against the Zheng (Koxinga) regime in 1662-1664, and Pieter van Hoorn's embassy to the young Kangxi emperor in Peking in 1666-1668. A long general description of China, drawn from Martini, Kircher and others, follows. The corpus copy is the 1670 Amsterdam first edition by Jacob van Meurs; the OCR of its double columns is often scrambled.
W248.tartar_means: The Manchu Qing dynasty, its army and officials (the 'Tartars' allied with the Dutch against Koxinga), and their homeland Oost-Tartarye (Manchuria); the emperor is 'Tartar Emperor of China and East Tartary'.
W248.why_read: It shows 'Tartar' used as plain everyday language for the Manchu state in Dutch commercial and military reports, and records the damage the conquest left along the Fujian coast.
W248.watch_out: The embassy journals reach us only through Dapper's rewriting, and the general description is copied from Jesuit books. The English version in Ogilby's Atlas Chinensis (1671) was wrongly credited to Montanus.

W249.plain_title: Struys's three calamitous voyages: the Volga, Astrakhan and slavery in Daghestan
W249.one_line: A Dutch sailmaker's adventure story of sailing down the Volga to Astrakhan in 1669 and being enslaved by 'Tartars' in Daghestan in 1670.
W249.summary: Jan Janszoon Struys (c. 1629-1694) was a Dutch sailmaker hired for the Tsar's new warship Oryol, built on the Oka and sailed down the Volga to Astrakhan in 1669. He saw Stenka Razin's Cossack rising, fled across the Caspian, was captured and sold as a slave in Daghestan and Persia, and came home in 1673. His book (Dutch 1676) was written up by others for the publisher Jacob van Meurs and padded with material from Olearius and other authors. The corpus has the Dutch 1677 edition, whose black-letter OCR is hard to use, and French translations of 1681 and 1718; these accounts quote the 1681 French version by Glanius.
W249.tartar_means: Almost every Muslim or pagan people of the Volga and Caucasus: the Cheremis (Mari) and Mordvins, Kazan Tatars, the Nogais of Astrakhan, the Kalmyks, Circassians and the mountain peoples of Daghestan are all 'Tartares' to Struys.
W249.why_read: A vivid first-person view of the lower Volga in 1669-1670: Tatar Kazan and Astrakhan under Russian rule, Nogai and Kalmyk camps, Golden Horde ruins and local legends, and what captivity among 'Tartars' felt like.
W249.watch_out: The book was ghost-written and borrows heavily from Olearius (see Kees Boterbloem, The Fiction and Reality of Jan Struys, 2008), so treat general descriptions as copied unless Struys clearly speaks for himself; it is also full of contempt for the peoples it describes. The Dutch 1677 OCR is garbled, so the French translation is quoted here.

W250.plain_title: Massa's report on the Russian road into Siberia, 'in Tartary'
W250.one_line: A Dutch merchant's 1612 report, from Russian informants, on how Muscovy was taking over Siberia and the Samoyed and Tungus lands 'in Tartary'.
W250.summary: Isaac Massa (1586-1643), a Haarlem merchant who lived in Moscow from 1601 to 1609, secretly gathered Russian accounts and a Russian map of the routes into Siberia. The Amsterdam map-maker Hessel Gerritsz printed them in 1612, in Dutch and Latin, beside tracts on Hudson's strait and De Quirós's southern continent. Massa never went to Siberia himself: he tells how Russian merchants and officials found the way, founded forts and towns, and brought Samoyeds, Tungus and 'Tartars' under the Tsar. The corpus has the Latin 1612 and 1613 prints and two copies of the 1878 facsimile edition with F. J. Millard's English translation.
W250.tartar_means: Mostly the Siberian Tatars along the Tura, Tobol and Irtysh, who live beside Russians and Samoyeds; also traders from 'Tartary' further south and the Tatars remembered at Tomsk. 'Tartary' itself is the whole northern Asian region where the Samoyed and Tungus lands lie.
W250.why_read: It is the earliest printed Western report of Russian Siberia, and it shows that in 1612 'Tartary' simply meant the unknown north of Asia that Muscovy was just then exploring and settling.
W250.watch_out: Second-hand throughout: Massa relies on Russian informants and says his sources risked death for sharing state secrets. The English is an 1878 translation of the Dutch.

W251.plain_title: De Bruyn's travels down the Volga to Astrakhan, 1703
W251.one_line: A Dutch painter's eyewitness account, with drawings made on the spot, of the Tatars and Kalmyks of the Volga and Astrakhan in 1703 and 1707.
W251.summary: Cornelis de Bruyn (1652-1727), a trained painter from The Hague, travelled through Russia to Persia and the East Indies from 1701 to 1708. In spring 1703 he sailed down the Volga from Moscow to Astrakhan, where he spent weeks sketching the Tatar camps and portraying a Tatar noblewoman, and he returned up the river in 1707. His friend and patron Nicolaes Witsen helped him. The book appeared in Dutch in 1711; the corpus copy is the French translation of 1718 (with a 1725 edition as a second copy), whose editors also inserted a summary of Evert Ysbrants Ides's embassy across Siberia to China in 1692-1695.
W251.tartar_means: Chiefly the Nogai-descended 'Yurt' Tatars camped around Astrakhan and the Kalmyks of the lower Volga; also the Tatars of Kasimov and Kazan, the Muslim Siberian Tatars of Tobolsk (in the Ides section), the medieval Mongols in his history notes, and Crimean Tatars who came to Astrakhan to sell horses.
W251.why_read: A trained artist describes, and drew, exactly what Tatar tents, carts and dress looked like, and records local legends about ruined Golden Horde cities and burial mounds along the Volga.
W251.watch_out: Keep de Bruyn's own observations apart from the Ides section, which he did not witness, and from history copied out of older books. This is a French translation of the Dutch original.

W252.plain_title: Bergeron's 1634 French collection of the friars' journeys into Tartary
W252.one_line: The first French edition of Rubruck, Carpini and Ascelin's reports on the Mongols, bound with Bergeron's own treatise on the Tartars, Paris 1634.
W252.summary: Pierre Bergeron, a Paris scholar, gathered French translations of three thirteenth-century mission reports: William of Rubruck's journey to the Mongol court (1253 to 1255), John of Plano Carpini's embassy to Güyük Khan (1245 to 1247) and the Dominican Ascelin's mission to the Mongol general Baiju in Persia (1247). The friars saw the Mongols for themselves; Bergeron translated their Latin as printed by Hakluyt and Vincent of Beauvais. He added his own Traicté des Tartares, a compiled history of the Tartars' origin, customs and empires down to his own day. The corpus holds two scans of the 1634 Paris first edition: T0621 (the journeys) and T0564 (journeys plus the Traicté).
W252.tartar_means: In the friars' reports 'Tartares' means the Mongols of the 1240s and 1250s, including Batu's Golden Horde on the Volga and the court of the Great Khan in Mongolia. Bergeron uses the word more widely for all the steppe peoples he derives from the Scythians, down to the Crimean 'Precopite' Tatars of his own time.
W252.why_read: Here are the eyewitness classics in French dress: felt houses on wagons, kumiss, a woman from Metz married to a Russian builder, and Karakorum with its silver drinking-fountain tree, next to a seventeenth-century scholar's struggle to explain where the Tartars and their name came from.
W252.watch_out: The friars' words reach us through Bergeron's French translation of printed Latin texts, so the phrasing is Bergeron's, not theirs. His Traicté is armchair compilation that mixes solid history with Gog and Magog and lost-tribes speculation. The OCR is rough 1634 type with long s and margin notes run into the text.

W253.one_line: A Paris editor's anthology of travel reports and translations, 1663 to 1696, with pieces on the Crimean Tatars, the Manchu 'Tartars' who had just conquered China, and Tibet.
W253.summary: Melchisédech Thévenot, a Paris scholar and collector, published four parts of 'curious voyages' (1663 to 1672, reissued 1696): translations from Hakluyt, Purchas, Dutch, Portuguese and oriental writers, many printed in French for the first time. He travelled nowhere himself; each piece has its own author and route to print. For Tartary the corpus copies hold the Dominican Jean de Luca's description of the Crimean and Nogai Tatars (c. 1625), the Dutch embassy to the Manchu emperor at Peking (1656 to 1657) with Thévenot's margin notes, Jesuit reports on the Manchu conquest, and the Jesuit Grueber's overland return through Tibet. Copies: 1663 part I (T0622), 1664 (T0623) and 1696 (T0624, T0625).
W253.tartar_means: It depends on the piece: in de Luca's report 'Tartares' are the Crimean ('Percopite') and Nogai Tatars; in the China pieces 'Tartares' are the Manchus (Thévenot's 'Tartars of Kin'), now masters of China; in Grueber's account the rulers of Tibet descend from 'Tartars of Tangut'.
W253.why_read: A good place to see three different 'Tartaries' side by side in one seventeenth-century book: Crimean khans with walled palaces, Manchu conquerors in Peking, and a Tibetan king in a four-storey castle.
W253.watch_out: Entirely secondhand, with each item translated at least once; part contents differ between issues. The 1663 scan (T0622) has very poor OCR with margin notes run into the text, so place names in it are often garbled.

W254.plain_title: Gaubil's history of Genghis Khan from the Chinese annals
W254.one_line: A Jesuit in Peking retells the rise and rule of the Mongols from Chinese histories, Paris 1739.
W254.summary: Antoine Gaubil, a French Jesuit who lived in Peking from 1723 to 1759, translated and condensed the Chinese annals of the Mongol (Yuan) dynasty into a French history of 'Gentchiscan' and his successors, with his own footnotes on geography and names. He never saw Mongolia; his knowledge comes from Chinese books and informants in Peking. The book follows Chinggis Khan's wars, the fall of the Jin and Song, the building of Mongol capitals and the reign of Khubilai. This corpus copy is the 1739 Paris edition (Briasson and Piget), Wellcome Library scan.
W254.tartar_means: Gaubil uses 'Tartarie' for the whole steppe north of China and 'Tartares' for its peoples in general, but he separates the 'Horde des Tatars' (one tribe) from the 'Mongous', and calls the Jin (Jurchen) emperors 'Eastern Tartars'.
W254.why_read: The Chinese side of the Mongol story: who walled Karakorum, who designed Khubilai's summer capital, and how Chinese historians judged Mongol rule.
W254.watch_out: It is a condensed translation of official Chinese histories, which have their own dynastic bias; Chinese transcriptions of names are hard to match with Persian and European forms, and the OCR mangles some names.

W255.plain_title: Deguignes' general history of the Huns, Turks, Mongols and western Tartars
W255.one_line: A Paris orientalist's four-volume history of the steppe peoples from the Xiongnu to the Ottomans, built from Chinese, Arabic and Persian books, 1756 to 1758.
W255.summary: Joseph de Guignes (Deguignes), a Paris scholar of Chinese and Arabic, set out to write one continuous history of the 'western Tartars': the Huns, Turks, Mongols and their successor states from antiquity to his own century. He argued that the Huns who reached Europe were the Xiongnu of the Chinese annals. He travelled nowhere; he worked from Chinese histories (partly via Gaubil and Visdelou), Arabic and Persian manuscripts and European travel books. This corpus has the 1756 to 1758 Paris edition (Desaint and Saillant) in several Getty scans (T0628 to T0632) and the 1751 prospectus (T0627).
W255.tartar_means: For Deguignes 'Tartares' is an umbrella for all the nomadic peoples of inner Asia and their descendants, from the Xiongnu and Uighurs to the Mongols, the Uzbeks, the Nogais and Timur's armies, divided into 'Eastern' and 'Western' Tartars.
W255.why_read: The great eighteenth-century synthesis that fixed the idea of 'Tartary' as a single history; it shows how much (and how little) a learned European of the 1750s thought he knew.
W255.watch_out: Derivative by design, and argued: the Xiongnu-Hun identification and his tidy genealogy of peoples were his theories, not settled facts. Passages on later peoples (Uzbeks, Nogais) are borrowed from travel books and older compilations.

W256.plain_title: Mailla's General History of China, translated from the Chinese annals
W256.one_line: A Peking Jesuit's multi-volume French version of the Chinese annals, including the Mongol (Yuan) and Manchu (Qing) conquests, printed in Paris 1777 to 1785.
W256.summary: Joseph de Mailla, a French Jesuit in Peking from 1701 to 1748, translated the great Chinese chronicle Tongjian gangmu (from its Manchu version) and continued it through the Ming and early Qing from other Chinese works. The abbés Grosier and Deshauterayes edited it in Paris long after his death, adding notes; some notes on the Qing emperors' journeys into Mongolia draw on Jesuit travel journals. Mailla saw Peking and parts of Tartary, but the history itself is translation and compilation. This corpus has volumes 1, 9, 10, 11 and 12 of the 1777 to 1785 Paris edition (Pierres and Clousier).
W256.tartar_means: 'Tartares' covers every northern people in the Chinese record: the Mongols (Mongous) of the Yuan, the Khitan and Jurchen, the Khalkha and other Mongol princes of Kangxi's day, and above all the Manchus (Mantchéous) who conquered China in 1644.
W256.why_read: It gives the Chinese court's view of two 'Tartar' conquests of China, and some vivid editor's notes on Qing emperors meeting Mongol princes in the steppe.
W256.watch_out: A translation of a translation, heavily edited and annotated in Paris; the Chinese annals are dynastic and moralising. Editorial notes are not Mailla's and are labelled here.

W257.plain_title: Visdelou's history of Great Tartary from the Chinese records
W257.one_line: A Jesuit's abridged history of the northern peoples from Chinese dynastic histories, written c. 1719 to 1728 and printed in 1779 as a supplement to d'Herbelot's Bibliothèque orientale.
W257.summary: Claude de Visdelou, a French Jesuit who lived in China from 1687 to 1709 and later in Pondicherry, translated and abridged what the Chinese dynastic histories say about the peoples north of China: the Xiongnu, Turks (Tou-kiue), Uighurs, Khitan, Jurchen and Mongols. He wrote it partly to correct d'Herbelot's Islamic sources, adding 'Observations' on d'Herbelot's articles. He had no firsthand knowledge of the steppe; his authority is Chinese books. It was printed fifty years later as the fourth, supplementary volume of the Bibliothèque orientale. This corpus copy is the Hague printing (IA dates it 1777; the card gives 1779), DLI scan T0640, with other copies T0638 and T0639.
W257.tartar_means: Visdelou's 'Tartarie' is the whole northern steppe and forest belt beyond China; 'Tartares' are all its peoples as the Chinese recorded them, and he explains that the Chinese name Tha-tha (Tatar) was itself used in several senses.
W257.why_read: The best place to see what Chinese records said about the 'Tartars' before the eighteenth century, including their insulting names for them and origin legends of wolves and deer.
W257.watch_out: Abridged translation from Chinese, printed decades after composition from a manuscript, with the editor's and d'Herbelot's material around it; Chinese sources were hostile to the northern peoples.

W258.plain_title: Memoirs of the Peking missionaries, with Amiot on the Dzungars and the Torghut exodus
W258.one_line: The Peking Jesuits' learned series on China (from 1776), with Amiot's translations of the Qianlong emperor's monuments on the destruction of the Dzungars and the flight of the Volga Torghuts, 1771.
W258.summary: The Mémoires concernant les Chinois were essays, letters and translations sent from Peking by French Jesuits and printed in Paris from 1776. Volume 1 carries Joseph-Marie Amiot's French versions of two stone inscriptions by the Qianlong emperor: on the Qing conquest of the Dzungar (Eleuth) state around 1755 to 1759, and on the Torghut Kalmyks' trek from the Volga to Ili in 1771. Amiot, a court insider for decades, added many notes of his own and a critique of a French traveller's account. Other volumes discuss Peking's history and the Manchu 'Tartars' in China. Copies here: vol. 1 (T0641, 1776), vol. 2 (T0642, 1777), vol. 4 (T0643, 1779; T0644 duplicate).
W258.tartar_means: Several at once: the Eleuths (Dzungars, western Mongols) and Torghuts (Volga Kalmyks) are 'Tartars'; the ruling Manchus are 'Tartares Mantchoux'; and the writers also use 'Tartares' for the Manchu banner people living in Peking, as against 'nos Chinois'.
W258.why_read: The Chinese imperial side of how 'Tartary' was redrawn in the 1750s and 1770s, with a well-informed Jesuit correcting both the emperor's rhetoric and European newspapers.
W258.watch_out: The emperor's texts are victory propaganda (calling the Dzungars worse than bears and monkeys); Amiot admired Qianlong and softened some phrases. The Paris editors cut and arranged the letters. Unsigned essays in later volumes are by anonymous missionaries writing as if Chinese.

W259.plain_title: Edifying and curious letters: Jesuit reports from China and Tartary
W259.one_line: Letters from French Jesuits in Qing China, 1690s to 1770s, reporting on Manchu and Mongol 'Tartary', in Querbeuf's Paris edition of 1780 to 1783.
W259.summary: The Lettres édifiantes et curieuses were letters sent home by Jesuit missionaries and printed in Paris to inform and inspire readers. The China volumes include men who lived at the Qing court and travelled in Manchuria and Mongolia with the Kangxi and Qianlong emperors or on the imperial map survey: Parrenin, Jartoux, Fontaney, Noël and Amiot. They mix firsthand observation with court news and pious stories. The letters were cut and rewritten by Paris editors. This corpus has Querbeuf's new edition (Paris, Mérigot, 1780 to 1783, vols 17 to 25) and a Toulouse reprint of vol. 18 (T0654; IA dates it 1707, but it prints letters of 1711 in nineteenth-century spelling, so it is evidently the Toulouse edition of about 1810).
W259.tartar_means: Mostly the Manchus ('Tartares Mantcheoux', 'Tartares orientaux') who ruled China, and the Mongols ('Tartares occidentaux', 'Mongous', Khalkhas), with the Dzungars (Eleuths) on the far frontier; the writers also speak of 'Chinese made Tartar' in the Manchu banners.
W259.why_read: Direct reports from Europeans who rode with the Qing emperors into Tartary: a palisade across Manchuria, ten thousand ginseng hunters, a Tartar city inside Peking, and the Manchu script debated with a prince.
W259.watch_out: Letters were chosen, cut and polished in Paris to edify readers; missionary aims colour what is reported. Volume numbers differ between editions, and the OCR of the 1780 set is fair but uneven.

W260.plain_title: D'Ohsson's History of the Mongols from Genghis Khan to Tamerlane
W260.one_line: A diplomat-scholar's four-volume history of the Mongol empire built from Persian and Arabic manuscripts, The Hague and Amsterdam 1834 to 1835.
W260.summary: Constantin d'Ohsson, a Swedish diplomat of Armenian-Ottoman background, wrote the standard nineteenth-century history of the Mongols from Persian and Arabic historians (Rashid al-Din, Juvaini, Ibn al-Athir, Wassaf and others) read in Paris manuscripts, with Chinese material taken from Gaubil and Mailla. He saw none of the places; he compiled, translated and compared sources, often quoting them at length in notes. The work runs from the steppe tribes before Chinggis Khan to the Ilkhans and the Golden Horde. This corpus has the 1834 to 1835 Van Cleef edition, 4 vols (T0656 to T0659), and the 1852 reissue (T0655).
W260.tartar_means: D'Ohsson uses 'tatare' for a whole 'race' of steppe peoples (Mongols, Turks and others) and 'Tatares' for the Mongol armies as Muslim writers named them, while keeping 'Tatars' also as the name of one tribe, the enemies Chinggis destroyed in 1202.
W260.why_read: A clear, source-based narrative that lets the reader hear the medieval Persian and Arabic historians, with the original chroniclers quoted in the notes.
W260.watch_out: Derivative, and d'Ohsson read no Mongolian or Chinese; he could be severe on the Mongols, reflecting his Muslim sources. The 1852 reissue repeats the 1834 text.

W261.plain_title: Abel-Rémusat's Researches on the Tartar languages
W261.one_line: A Paris professor of Chinese defines the 'Tartar' peoples by their languages (Manchu, Mongol, Uighur-Turkic, Tibetan) and reviews what Chinese and European writers said about them, 1820.
W261.summary: Jean-Pierre Abel-Rémusat, first professor of Chinese at the Collège de France, published this first (and only) volume of research on the grammar and literature of the Manchus, Mongols, Uighurs and Tibetans in 1820. He never travelled; he worked from Chinese books, Jesuit manuscripts and printed grammars in Paris. His opening chapter asks who the 'Tartars' are and where the name came from, and he surveys Chinese descriptions of northern peoples and the Turkic peoples of Siberia. The corpus has four Google scans of the 1820 Imprimerie royale edition (T0660 to T0663) and his 1832 review of Schmidt's Mongol chronicle (T0664).
W261.tartar_means: For Rémusat 'Tartares' is a vulgar, collective European label for the peoples of high Asia, borrowed from the name of one tribe, the Tatars; he sorts them into four 'Tartar races' by language (Manchu-Tungus, Mongol, Turkic, Tibetan).
W261.why_read: The moment the word 'Tartar' was turned from a map label into a scholarly category, by a scholar who also cleared away older fanciful etymologies.
W261.watch_out: A philologist's book, heavy on grammar; the ethnographic passages are Chinese texts in his translation, and his 'races' reflect early nineteenth-century classification. Google OCR lacks page mapping, so printed pages are read off the scans.

W263.one_line: A German orientalist's 1826 history of Inner Asia, people by people, built from Chinese, Persian and Arabic sources.
W263.summary: Julius Klaproth (1783-1835), a German-born orientalist working in Paris, had crossed the Siberian-Mongolian frontier with a Russian embassy in 1805-1806 and toured the Caucasus in 1807-1808. In 1826 he published this text volume to go with an atlas of 27 historical maps, tracing which peoples held which parts of Asia from Cyrus to his own day. It rests mainly on Chinese dynastic histories, Rashid al-Din, Abu'l-Ghazi and Arabic travellers, which he read in the original languages. The corpus copy is the 1826 Paris edition (Google scans); the atlas itself is a separate item.
W263.tartar_means: Klaproth insists that 'Tatar' properly means the Mongols, a tribe first named in Chinese annals in the 9th century, and that calling the Turkic-speaking peoples of Kazan, Astrakhan and Crimea 'Tatars' is a later confusion. He still uses 'Tatarie' loosely as a geographical name for Inner Asia.
W263.why_read: It shows a leading scholar of the 1820s taking apart both the loose use of the word Tatar and the romantic idea of a lost high civilisation on the 'plateau of Tatary'.
W263.watch_out: Everything here is compiled from written sources, and some of Klaproth's racial and language groupings are his own guesses that have not all held up. In the Google scan, marginal headings run into the text.

W264.one_line: Collected essays of 1824 to 1828 in which Klaproth translates Chinese, Manchu and Persian texts on Siberia, Mongolia and the Tatars and argues about what the names mean.
W264.summary: Julius Klaproth (1783-1835) gathered his shorter studies into three volumes of Memoires relatifs a l'Asie (Paris, 1824-1828). They include his own French translations from Chinese and Manchu (a Qing description of Russia, Chinese notices of Siberian peoples, a Manchu account of the Long White Mountain), a paper on Siberian antiquities read to the Asiatic Society in 1822, reviews of other scholars, and a short essay 'Sur les Tatars' on who the real Tatars were. A little comes from his own trip to the Russian-Chinese frontier in 1805-1806. The corpus holds several scans of volume 1 (cited here from the DLI copy) and one of volume 2.
W264.tartar_means: For Klaproth the 'true Tatars' are the Mongols; the Turkic peoples of Kazan, Astrakhan and Crimea only inherited the name from their Mongol rulers. Older sources he translates use 'Tartare' more loosely, for Siberian tribes such as the Kistym Tatars.
W264.why_read: It lets a learner watch a scholar of the 1820s sort out the name Tatar from Chinese and Persian sources, and see how he explained Siberian graves, mines and inscribed stones without any lost empire.
W264.watch_out: Most of the material is translated or compiled, and Klaproth was quarrelsome and sure of himself; some of his identifications (for example that Mongol and Tatar are simply the same people) are now thought too simple. IA metadata mislabels the volume numbers of the Google scans.

W265.one_line: Alexander von Humboldt's 1843 survey of the mountains and climate of inner Asia, which retires the old 'plateau of Tartary'.
W265.summary: Alexander von Humboldt (1769-1859) travelled through the Urals, the Altai and the Russian-Chinese frontier in Dzungaria in 1829. In 1843 he published Asie centrale in French, three volumes that combine his own barometer readings and observations with a critical review of everything written about inner Asia: Greek and Roman geographers, Chinese sources supplied by Klaproth and Stanislas Julien, Marco Polo, the Jesuit maps and Russian and Tatar caravan itineraries. Much of it is geology, but he repeatedly explains why he drops the name 'Tartary' and the idea of a single high central plateau. The corpus has several scans of the 1843 Paris edition.
W265.tartar_means: Humboldt uses 'Tartarie' mainly to describe the older map label and the discredited 'plateau of Tartary'; in the present he speaks of Tatars of Orenburg and Semipalatinsk (Volga and Siberian Muslims working as traders and guides), Kalmyks, Kirghiz (Kazakhs) and Dzungars.
W265.why_read: It is the clearest 19th-century statement that the idea of a lost ancient civilisation on the high plains of Tartary was an 18th-century dream, written by the most respected scientist of the age after he had measured the ground himself.
W265.watch_out: Most of the book is technical geography. His Chinese material is second-hand, some of his own conclusions about the interior were revised by later explorers, and the stories he collected from Tatar and Kazakh informants are clearly marked by him as reports.

W266.one_line: A French astronomer's account of his 1761 journey from Paris to Tobolsk for the transit of Venus, and of the Tatar villages and towns he passed.
W266.summary: Jean Chappe d'Auteroche (1722-1769), an astronomer of the Paris Academy of Sciences, was sent by Louis XV to Tobolsk to observe the transit of Venus of 6 June 1761. He crossed Russia by sledge in winter, came back through the Urals and Kazan in the autumn, and published Voyage en Siberie in 1768 with engraved plates. Besides astronomy, levelling and natural history, it gives sharp and often hostile remarks on Russian society, first-hand notes on Tatar, Votyak and Kalmyk people he met, and an account of the destruction of the Zunghar Kalmyks learned from refugee envoys in Tobolsk. Catherine II's circle answered it with the Antidote (1770). The corpus copy is the 1768 Paris edition; the Kamchatka volume is a translation of Krasheninnikov and is not used here.
W266.tartar_means: Chappe calls 'Tartares' the Muslim Tatar villagers of the Urals and the Kazan region, the nomads who raided the Siberian frontier lines, and, loosely, the Kalmyks and Mongols as heirs of Chinggis Khan's armies.
W266.why_read: It gives a vivid eyewitness picture of Tatar villages and of Kazan as a Tatar town under Russian rule in 1761, alongside the rumours about steppe nomads and the vegetable lamb that a traveller picked up on the way.
W266.watch_out: Chappe's contempt for Russian society was notorious and was attacked at the time; his stories about the steppe nomads are hearsay and he says so. The OCR prints the long s as f, silently normalised in the quotes.

W267.one_line: A young French consul's diary of carrying La Perouse's dispatches overland from Kamchatka to Paris in 1787 to 1788.
W267.summary: Jean-Baptiste Barthelemy de Lesseps (1766-1834), a Russian-speaking vice-consul attached to La Perouse's round-the-world expedition, was put ashore at Petropavlovsk in Kamchatka in September 1787 with the expedition's journals. He crossed Kamchatka, the Okhotsk coast, Yakutsk, Irkutsk, Tobolsk and Kazan by dog-sled, reindeer, horse and boat, and reached France on 17 October 1788. His Journal historique (Paris, Imprimerie royale, 1790, 2 vols) describes Kamchadals, Koryaks, Yakuts and Tungus in detail; Tatars proper appear mainly near the end, between Tobolsk and Kazan. The corpus copy is the 1790 edition.
W267.tartar_means: For Lesseps 'Tartares' are the settled Muslim Tatars of the Urals and Volga, the 'Tartares Mantchoux' who conquered China, and the 'Tartares Mongols' on the Chinese frontier. He compares the Yakuts' looks and language to those of the Tartars without calling them Tartars.
W267.why_read: It shows everyday Siberia in 1788 through a traveller's eyes: Yakut houses of timber and earth, kumiss making and horse burials, Tobolsk rebuilding in stone after a fire, and clean, prosperous Tatar farming villages.
W267.watch_out: Lesseps travelled fast and often through interpreters, and he judges shamans and 'idolatry' as an 18th-century Catholic. Only a small part of the book concerns Tatars.

W268.plain_title: Peyssonnel on the peoples of the Danube and Black Sea
W268.one_line: A French consul to the Crimean khan reconstructs, in 1765, the peoples who held the Black Sea steppe from the Huns to the Tatars.
W268.summary: Charles de Peyssonnel (1727-1790) was French consul to the khan of the Crimean Tatars at Bakhchysarai from 1753 to 1757. In 1765 he published Observations historiques et geographiques on the 'barbarian peoples' of the Danube and Black Sea: Huns, Avars, Bulgars, Khazars, Pechenegs, Cumans, Walachians and Tatars. He draws mostly on Byzantine and classical writers and matches ancient Crimean place names to modern ones, but his own knowledge of the khanate and the Nogai hordes shows in asides. The corpus copy is the 1765 Paris edition (Tilliard), with Google scans of the same.
W268.tartar_means: Mainly the Crimean Tatars, their khan and the Nogai hordes subject to him; he also calls earlier Turkic steppe peoples (Alans, Uzes, Cumans) 'Peuples Tartares' in a broad sense.
W268.why_read: It shows an 18th-century expert who had lived among the Crimean Tatars fitting them into a long line of steppe peoples, and explaining Crimean ruins by earlier Greek, Genoese and 'Cimmerian' builders.
W268.watch_out: Mostly compiled history. Some etymologies (such as Krim from Cimmerium) are guesses, and 'Tartare' is used very broadly for Turkic and steppe peoples.

W270.plain_title: Jaubert's journey in Armenia and Persia
W270.one_line: A French orientalist's account of his 1805 to 1806 mission from Napoleon to the Shah of Persia, including months in a Kurdish dungeon.
W270.summary: Pierre-Amedee Jaubert (1779-1847), orientalist and interpreter to Napoleon, carried letters to Fath Ali Shah in 1805-1806. Seized by the pasha of Bayazid, he spent months in an underground cell before reaching Tehran and the Shah's summer camp at Sultaniyeh. His Voyage en Armenie et en Perse (Paris, 1821) describes Kurds, Armenians, Persians and the Qajar court, and ends with a notice on Gilan and Mazandaran by Colonel Trezel of the Gardane mission (1807-1808). Tartary proper lies off his route: 'Tartars' appear as Ottoman couriers, as claimed ancestors, and in passing on the Turkmen frontier. The corpus holds two scans of the 1821 edition.
W270.tartar_means: Several things at once: in Ottoman usage a 'Tartare' is an official courier and travel contractor; Kurds and the people of Khoy claim 'Tartar' (Mongol, Uzbek or Turkic) descent; Turkish is called a dialect of 'Tartar'; and a prince's Khwarazmian mother gives him 'Tartar blood'.
W270.why_read: It shows how stretchy the word Tartar was in the Middle East around 1800, from a job title to a claim of ancestry to a slur, on the southern edge of what French maps called Independent Tartary.
W270.watch_out: Peripheral to Tartary. Turkmen material is reported, not seen, and the Gilan notice is Trezel's work. Jaubert's reasoning from faces and 'blood' reflects the prejudices of his day.

W271.plain_title: Carpini and Rubruck in the original Latin
W271.one_line: The Paris Geographical Society's 1839 volume printing the Latin reports of the friars John of Plano Carpini (1245-1247) and William of Rubruck (1253-1255), with Jordanus and learned notes.
W271.summary: Volume 4 of the Recueil de voyages et de memoires (Paris, 1839) gives the first critical Latin texts of the two great Franciscan eyewitness reports on the Mongols: John of Plano Carpini's History of the Mongols (his mission to Guyuk's court, 1245-1247), edited by Armand d'Avezac, and William of Rubruck's Itinerary (to Mongke Khan at Karakorum, 1253-1255), edited by Francisque Michel and Thomas Wright from manuscripts in Paris, Leiden, Cambridge and London. It adds the Mirabilia of the missionary bishop Jordanus (c. 1330) and d'Avezac's long study of the missions. The corpus holds two scans of volume 4; volume 1 (1824, a Latin Marco Polo) is cited once.
W271.tartar_means: For Carpini and Rubruck 'Tartari' are the Mongols of the Chinggisid empire (Batu's Golden Horde and Mongke's court). Rubruck records that the Mongols themselves refused the name, saying the Tartars had been another people. Jordanus's 'Great Tartar' is the Mongol emperor in China.
W271.why_read: These are the two best 13th-century eyewitness accounts of the Mongols, in the friars' own Latin: houses on carts, kumiss, Karakorum's mud walls and quarters, a silver fountain-tree made by a Parisian goldsmith, and the friars' doubts about monsters and Prester John.
W271.watch_out: Manuscript variants crowd the pages and the OCR mixes notes with text; d'Avezac's Carpini text was later superseded (Wyngaert, 1929). Carpini's monster stories are hearsay he flags himself, and some editorial notes quote hostile medieval propaganda.

W272.plain_title: D'Anville's maps of China and Chinese Tartary
W272.one_line: The atlas of d'Anville's maps of China, Chinese Tartary and Tibet (1737), with a foreword on how the Jesuit survey was made and an eyewitness 'Relation of Bukharia'.
W272.summary: Jean-Baptiste Bourguignon d'Anville (1697-1782), the French king's geographer, drew the maps for du Halde's Description of China (1735) from the survey that Jesuit missionaries made for the Kangxi emperor between 1708 and 1717. The catalogue record is for d'Anville's 1776 memoir defending those maps, but the corpus copy under this record is the related Nouvel atlas de la Chine, de la Tartarie chinoise et du Thibet (1737), issued as a fifth, atlas volume to a quarto edition of du Halde. Its foreword explains which maps were measured and which compiled, and it prints an anonymous 'Relation de la Boucharie' by a writer who says he had been in Little Bukhara under Kalmyk rule.
W272.tartar_means: 'Tartarie' is the map label for the lands north and west of China proper (Manchuria, Mongolia, Dzungaria). In the Relation, 'Tartares' are corrected to 'or rather the Kalmyks' who ruled Little Bukhara, and the Manchus are the 'Tartars' who conquered China.
W272.why_read: It shows how the standard 18th-century map of 'Chinese Tartary' was made, from Jesuit triangulation and Gerbillon's travel notes, and admits that the lands towards the Caspian were known only imperfectly. The Relation adds a rare eyewitness look at town life in Kashgaria.
W272.watch_out: This is not the 1776 memoir named in the catalogue. The atlas OCR is poor, and the Relation de la Boucharie is anonymous and undated.

W124.plain_title: Pallas's journey through the provinces of the Russian Empire
W124.one_line: A German naturalist's day-by-day journal of the Academy expedition from the Volga to Siberia and back, 1768 to 1774.
W124.summary: Peter Simon Pallas (1741-1811), a Berlin-born naturalist in the service of the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences, led one of Catherine II's great scientific expeditions from 1768 to 1774. His journal runs from Moscow down the Oka and Volga, through the Orenburg steppe and the Urals, across western Siberia to the Altai, Krasnoyarsk and Lake Baikal, and back by the Volga delta. It mixes botany and geology with close descriptions of Kalmyks, Kazakhs, Bashkirs and many Tatar groups, and with measured drawings of ruins at Kasimov, Bolgar, Saraichik and the Akhtuba. This corpus holds the first edition (St Petersburg, 1771-1776, three parts in five volumes) and a later abridged edition.
W124.tartar_means: Pallas uses 'Tataren' for Turkic-speaking Muslim or shamanist peoples: Kasimov, Kazan and Tomsk Tatars, the Nogai Kundurov Tatars, and the Siberian Kachin, Beltir and other Khakas 'Tatars'. He keeps Kalmyks, Kazakhs (Kirgis) and Bashkirs as separate peoples, though he calls some of their customs 'Tatar'.
W124.why_read: A trained scientist who measured ruins and described dwellings with plates: he credits stone and brick buildings to Tatar khans, Bolgars, Nogais, Kalmyks and Bukharans, and shows living Tatars in log houses, felt tents and birch-bark yurts.
W124.watch_out: Some sections come from his students (Sokolov, Zuev) or from informants, and he sometimes judges peoples harshly. The Fraktur OCR is damaged and the printed page numbers in the scans do not always match the catalogue page numbers.

W273.plain_title: Strahlenberg's advance notice of his book on Great Tartary and Siberia
W273.one_line: A Swedish prisoner of war's 1726 prospectus for his great description of Tartary and Siberia.
W273.summary: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (1676-1747), a Swedish officer captured at Poltava in 1709, spent about thirteen years as a prisoner in Siberia, mostly at Tobolsk, and joined an expedition south-east toward the Kalmyk and Mongol borders. Back in Sweden he printed this short 'Vorbericht' (Stockholm 1726) to announce the book that appeared in 1730. It describes his map of Siberia and Great Tartary, a comparative table of thirty 'Tartarian' languages, his notes on Abulghazi's Tatar history (translated from a Tobolsk manuscript by Swedish prisoners), and his views on names, Prester John and Marco Polo. This corpus copy is the 1726 first edition.
W273.tartar_means: For Strahlenberg 'Tartarey' is the vast region of Siberia and Central Asia, and 'Tatern' are its Turkic Muslim peoples; he treats Kalmyks and Mongols as related but distinct, and warns that not all the peoples of the region can properly be called Tartars.
W273.why_read: It shows an eyewitness scholar sorting out names: Tatar and Mongol as brothers in Abulghazi's legend, the meaning of 'Kalmyk', Prester John as the Dalai Lama, and how a Tatar manuscript from Tobolsk became a European source.
W273.watch_out: This is a prospectus, full of promises and arguments rather than description, and several etymologies are Strahlenberg's own guesses. The OCR of this copy is severely garbled, so every quote here has been restored from damaged text and should be checked against the scan.

W274.plain_title: Adam Brand's journey with the Russian embassy to China
W274.one_line: A German secretary's eyewitness account of the Russian embassy from Moscow through Siberia and Mongolia to Beijing, 1692 to 1695.
W274.summary: Adam Brand, a merchant from Lübeck, travelled as secretary to Eberhard Isbrand Ides, envoy of Peter the Great to the Kangxi emperor, from 1692 to 1695. His short journal, first printed in Hamburg in 1698 and soon translated into English and French, follows the route over the Urals to Tyumen and Tobolsk, down the Ob and across Siberia to Nerchinsk, then through Manchuria and Inner Mongolia to Beijing. He describes Voguls, Siberian Tatars, Tungus and Mongols, ruined cities along the way, and the imperial audience. This corpus copy is the enlarged 1734 Lübeck edition, with Paul Jacob Marperger's preface and added compiled chapters; the 1698 English translation and a 1699 French version are also in the corpus.
W274.tartar_means: Brand uses 'Tartar' very widely: the Voguls are 'the first Siberian Tartars', the Muslim townspeople of Tyumen and Tobolsk are Tartars, the Mongols are 'Mongalen oder Tartern', and the Manchu emperor Kangxi is a 'Mongal oder Ost-Tartar'.
W274.why_read: A brisk eyewitness who records how people lived and what they said back to him, from Vogul grave houses to a Tobolsk mosque, ruined 'Tartar' cities in Inner Mongolia and kumis at the Kangxi emperor's table.
W274.watch_out: The 1734 edition mixes Brand's journal with compiled chapters on Russia, Tartary and China taken from books; some local histories were told to him through interpreters. The English OCR of the 1698 edition is very poor, so German pages are cited.

W275.plain_title: Weber's 'Russia Transformed', with reports on Siberia, the Kalmyks and the Tatars
W275.one_line: A Hanoverian diplomat's account of Peter the Great's Russia, 1714 to 1720, stuffed with other people's reports from Siberia, Astrakhan, China and Bukhara.
W275.summary: Friedrich Christian Weber was the Hanoverian resident at St Petersburg from 1714 to 1719. His 'Das veränderte Russland' (part 1, Frankfurt 1721; parts 2 and 3, 1739 and 1740) describes Peter the Great's court, army and reforms from his own observation, and prints many documents and reports he collected: Lorenz Lange's 1715 journey to Peking with a description of China, informants' news from Astrakhan about Kalmyks and Tatars, anonymous descriptions of the Kalmyks and Mongols, the journal of a painter-traveller who went down the Volga in 1703 (evidently Cornelis de Bruyn), and in part 2 an account of Bukhara. This corpus has the 1721 first edition, a 1744 reissue and parts 2 and 3.
W275.tartar_means: 'Tartar' covers the Muslim Tatars of Kazan and Astrakhan, the Siberian and Baraba Tatars, the Kuban Nogais, the Crimean Tatars, the Mongols (and the medieval Mongol empire), the Manchu rulers of China, and in 'Tartarian Bukhara' the oasis peoples of Central Asia.
W275.why_read: A cabinet of first-hand snapshots from the edges of Peter's empire: pit houses on the Baraba steppe, Kalmyk tents like hooped petticoats, a Tatar camp outside Astrakhan, a burial mound said to be piled up with helmets, and frozen dumplings in Little Bukhara.
W275.watch_out: Much of the material is second-hand, often from unnamed authors, and Weber rarely says where he got it; the historical notes on the Mongols repeat medieval books. Quotes are from the 1721 edition or its 1744 reissue (same text), and the OCR is often damaged.

W276.one_line: An anonymous German compilation of 1720 on Siberia and its 'Tartar peoples', built from Swedish prisoners' reports and earlier travel books.
W276.summary: This anonymous Nuremberg book of 1720 gathers what was then known about Siberia: its government, towns, rivers and animals, the customs of the Samoyeds, Voguls, Ostyaks, Tungus, Buryats, Mongols and Kalmyks, and the story of the Swedish prisoners of war held at Tobolsk after 1709 and their school there.
