Its core firsthand piece is Johann Bernhard Müller's account of the Ostyaks, written at Tobolsk in 1716, but much else is lifted from earlier travellers, especially Adam Brand and E. Ysbrants Ides, and from Marco Polo. This corpus copy is the 1720 first edition.
W276.tartar_means: 'Tartarische Völker' is a catch-all for the non-Russian peoples of Siberia and its borders: Voguls, Ostyaks, Tungus, Buryats, Mongols and Kalmyks, as well as the Muslim Tatars around Tobolsk.
W276.why_read: It shows how a German reader of 1720 learned about Siberia: by stitching Marco Polo, Brand and prisoners' letters together under the heading of 'Tartar peoples'.
W276.watch_out: Largely second-hand and often copied word for word from Brand and Ides without saying so; the OCR is uneven.

W277.plain_title: Lorenz Lange's caravan journals from Kiakhta to Peking
W277.one_line: A Russian trade agent's journals of two caravan journeys across Mongolia to Peking, 1727 to 1728 and 1736, edited by Pallas in 1781.
W277.summary: Lorenz Lange, a Swedish-born official in Russian service, led Russian state caravans to Peking after the Treaty of Kiakhta. These two journals, kept in 1727 to 1728 and 1736, record the route from Kiakhta and Tsurukhaitu across Khalkha and Inner Mongolia to Peking, the Mongol and Solon posts and camps along the way, the caravan's troubles with Qing officials, and a long geographical and historical description of Peking. Pallas obtained a Russian manuscript at Selenginsk, translated and abridged it, and added footnotes marked 'P.'. This corpus copy is the 1781 Leipzig edition.
W277.tartar_means: The book speaks of 'tatarische Völker' for the Mongols and other peoples north of China, and calls the northern part of Peking the 'Tatar city'; in the journal itself the people met are Khalkha and Inner Mongol tribes and Solons.
W277.why_read: A practical traveller's view of Mongol life on the caravan road, plus Pallas's note on how the moving camp of Urga turned into the walled monastery town that became Ulaanbaatar.
W277.watch_out: Pallas says he shortened the journals when translating them from Russian; footnotes marked 'P.' are his, not Lange's. The bundle held only the Peking description, so the Mongol passages come from the 1781 BSB copy.

W278.plain_title: Müller's Collection of Russian History, with his history of Siberia
W278.one_line: The St Petersburg Academy's historical serial (1732 to 1764), including G. F. Müller's archive-based history of the Tatar khanate of Siberia and its conquest.
W278.summary: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (1705-1783), a German historian at the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences, spent 1733 to 1743 in Siberia with the Second Kamchatka Expedition, copying town archives, collecting chronicles and questioning Tatars, Mongols and others. His 'Sammlung Russischer Geschichte' (9 volumes, 1732 to 1764) printed his own and colleagues' studies; volume 6 (1761 to 1762) contains the opening of his 'Description of the Siberian Kingdom', covering the Tatar princes of Tyumen and Isker, Kuchum Khan and Yermak's conquest, with his own descriptions of the ruins. This corpus has the nine volumes of the first edition, a 1777 reprint, and the English 'Conquest of Siberia' derived from it.
W278.tartar_means: Müller's 'Tataren' are chiefly the Turkic Muslim Tatars of Tyumen, Tobolsk and the Baraba, heirs of the Siberian khanate; 'the former Tatars' also means the Mongol empire of Chinggis Khan, which he says united Mongols and Tatars.
W278.why_read: A careful scholar who both walked the ruins and cross-examined the chronicles: he measured the ramparts of Isker, asked Tatars what they called their own capital, and still relayed the chronicles' omens and miracles, labelled as such.
W278.watch_out: Much of the narrative follows the Siberian chronicles (especially Remezov's), which mix history with legend; Müller flags this but sometimes theorises beyond the evidence. The bundle held only the later English 'Conquest of Siberia', so the German volume 6 is cited directly.

W279.one_line: An Academy historian's 1768 history of the Russian conquest of Siberia, with a long introduction on who the Tatars and Mongols were.
W279.summary: Johann Eberhard Fischer (1697-1771), a German historian at the St Petersburg Academy, travelled in Siberia from 1740 to 1747 with the Second Kamchatka Expedition. His 'Sibirische Geschichte' (St Petersburg 1768, 2 volumes) tells the story of Siberia from its discovery to the Russian conquest, drawing heavily on G. F. Müller's unpublished archive work, which Müller resented. Its long introduction compares Chinese, Persian, Arabic and European sources and Siberian observations to sort out Mongols, Tatars and their religions. This corpus has two BSB copies of the 1768 first edition and the 1774 Russian translation.
W279.tartar_means: Fischer insists 'Tatar' was misused by Europeans for all peoples of inner Asia; he separates Mongols from Tatars and uses 'Tataren' for Turkic peoples such as the Siberian, Kacha, Chulym and Baraba Tatars.
W279.why_read: A sharp, sceptical discussion of the word 'Tatar' itself, including the Tartarus pun and the Chinese 'Ta-ta', written by someone who had lived among Siberian peoples.
W279.watch_out: The narrative history leans on Müller's work, often without credit; the introduction is book learning with some firsthand comparison. Only the introduction was read here.

W280.plain_title: Pallas's historical collections on the Mongol peoples
W280.one_line: Pallas's two-part study (1776 and 1801) of the history, laws, religion and learning of the Kalmyks, Mongols and Buryats.
W280.summary: Peter Simon Pallas lived among the Volga Kalmyks and the Buryats and Selenga Mongols during his expedition of 1768 to 1774, and later collected Kalmyk and Mongol texts, translations and informants' reports. Part 1 (1776) covers the origins, history, law and way of life of the Kalmyks, including the flight of the Torghuts in 1771; part 2 (1801) covers Tibetan Buddhism among the Mongol peoples: its gods, clergy, temples, festivals, calendar, writing and learning, with plates. This corpus has both parts in Google scans; part 1's OCR is unusable (German read as Cyrillic), so the accounts here come from part 2.
W280.tartar_means: Pallas uses 'Tataren' for the Turkic Tatars (Crimean, Nogai, Kazan, Siberian) and keeps Kalmyks, Mongols and Buryats as 'Mongol peoples'; 'tatarisch' also appears loosely for inner Asian customs shared with the Mongols.
W280.why_read: A scientist's close look at how Mongol peoples actually built and worshipped, from portable felt temples to brick pagodas, with sharp asides on European fantasies about the East.
W280.watch_out: Pallas mixes his own observation with reports and translations, and his judgements of taste are blunt. The OCR of part 2 is fair, of part 1 unusable; page numbers in the appended literary section are not reliable.

W281.plain_title: Pallas's 'New Northern Contributions', a journal of reports from Russia's frontiers
W281.one_line: A serial edited by Pallas (1781 to 1796) printing field journals, letters and reports from Siberia, the Altai, the Crimea, Mongolia and beyond.
W281.summary: Pallas edited the 'Neue Nordische Beyträge' (7 volumes, St Petersburg and Leipzig, 1781 to 1796, the last as 'Neueste') as an outlet for reports that would otherwise stay in Russian or in manuscript. Pieces used here include Vasily Zuev's notes on the Crimea (1783), the Altai journal of the mine official Peter Shangin (1786), the botanist Johann Sievers's letters from Siberia and the Mongolian border (early 1790s), and J. G. Stritter's description of Peking. Pallas translated many of them from Russian and added footnotes. This corpus has volumes 1 to 4 (Russian State Library scans) and volumes 5 and 7 (CIHM microfiche).
W281.tartar_means: Each author uses 'Tatar' for the people in front of him: the Muslim Crimean Tatars under their khans, the shamanist 'mountain Tatars' of the Altai, the Sagai and Kuznetsk Tatars of the Abakan steppe (Khakas), and in general the Turkic peoples as distinct from Kalmyks and Mongols.
W281.why_read: Vivid reports from people on the spot, including a clear statement of who built the Crimean fortresses, Siberians crediting the steppe's ancient graves to an unknown 'Chud' people, and Altai burial customs.
W281.watch_out: Every article has a different author and quality; several are translations from Russian, and Pallas himself warns that Zuev's history is not fully reliable. The microfiche OCR is often cropped or scrambled.

passages.headline: Kalmyk felt tents at a Volga horse fair
passages.people: Kalmyk Tartars (Torghut Kalmyks of the Volga)
passages.gloss: Crossing the Volga at Saratov to a great horse market held by the Kalmyks, Bell describes their tents step by step: leaning poles fixed into a smoke-hole ring, a frame of light rods tied with thongs, and a covering of felt. On the next page he adds that the felt is coarse wool and hair, that the tents fold up quickly, and that one camel can carry five or six of them.
passages.quote: These tents are of a conical figure; there are several long poles erected, inclining to one another, which are fixed at the top into something like a hoop, that forms the circumference of an aperture for letting out the smoak, or admitting the light; across the poles are laid some small rods… this frame is covered with pieces of felt,
passages.speaker: John Bell (Travels, 1763)

passages.headline: Log huts with windows made of ice
passages.place: Irtysh valley between Tobolsk and Tara
passages.gloss: Travelling up the Irtysh in midwinter, Bell's party passes many Tatar villages and sleeps in their huts. He describes one- or two-room log houses chinked with moss, a broad bench for sitting and sleeping, and, in place of glass, a pane of ice cut to fit the window. The next page adds that these Tatars are very clean and use open hearths rather than Russian stoves.
passages.quote: These houses consist generally of one or two rooms, according to the ability of the landlord. … The walls are built of wood and moss, consisting of large beams, laid one above another, with a layer of moss between every two beams. All the roofs are raised. A square-hole is cut out for a window, and to supply the want of glass, a piece of ice
passages.speaker: John Bell (Travels, 1763)

passages.headline: The 'Seven Palaces' in the steppe
passages.gloss: Bell did not visit this building on the upper Irtysh, but reports what he was told: a regular brick or stone edifice of seven rooms under one roof, standing alone in the steppe. Local Tartars credited it to Tamerlane or to Genghis Khan. Its rooms were full of scrolls in the writing of the 'Tongusts, or Kalmucks' (probably meaning Tanguts, that is Tibetans, or Kalmyks); Bell bought a bundle from a soldier in Tobolsk and gave some to Sir Hans Sloane. The Tibetan or Kalmyk writing suggests a Kalmyk (Oirat) Buddhist building rather than a work of Tamerlane, and the ruin, 'Sem Palaty', later gave the city of Semipalatinsk (Semey) its name.
passages.quote: It is very surprising to find such a regular edifice in the middle of a desert. Some of the Tartars say it was built by Tamerlane, called by the Tartars Temyr-Ack-Sack or Lame-Temyr; others by Gingeez-Chan. The building, according to the best information I could obtain, is of brick or stone, well finished, and continues still entire. It consists of seven apartments under one roof,
passages.speaker: John Bell (Travels, 1763)
passages.caution: Hearsay: Bell never saw the building, and the Tamerlane and Genghis Khan attributions are local legend.

passages.headline: Treasure-hunters in the grave mounds
passages.place: Upper Tom and Ob steppe, south of Tomsk
passages.people: ancient steppe peoples; Kalmyks and other Tartars
passages.gloss: South of Tomsk lie many burial mounds of earth and stones. Bell was told that Russians went out every summer to dig them for gold, silver and weapons, and he saw some of the finds himself, including a brass horseman and gold deer figures. From the horse bones and weapons he concludes that great men were buried with their horse and servant, a custom he says the Kalmyks still keep; the Kalmyks, who hate disturbing the dead, sometimes robbed the grave-robbers. His Baraba Tartar informants credited the battles to Tamerlane.
passages.quote: Many persons go from Tomsky, and other parts, every summer, to these graves; which they dig up, and find, among the ashes of the dead, considerable quantities of gold, silver, brass… Whence it appears, that when any general or person of distinction, was interred, all his arms, his favourite horse and servant, were buried with him in the same grave;
passages.speaker: John Bell (Travels, 1763)
passages.caution: The digging is reported by informants; Bell saw only objects brought back. The link to Tamerlane is a local tradition.

passages.headline: A land without a single house
passages.gloss: Waiting at Selenginsk on the Mongolian border, Bell sums up Mongol life: in all of Mongolia there is not one house, and even the prince and the high lama live in tents that move with the herds. He adds that they do not plough at all, and admits that he finds this simple life pleasant in so dry a climate. The prince's camp at Urga, he explains a few pages later, is a moving city of several thousand tents.
passages.quote: …of Mongalia, there is not so much as a single house to be seen. All the people, even the prince and high priest, live constantly in tents; and remove, with their cattle, from place to place, as conveniency requires. These people do not trouble themselves with ploughing, or digging the ground in any fashion;
passages.speaker: John Bell (Travels, 1763)

passages.headline: Kazan, old capital of a Tartar kingdom
passages.gloss: Bell wintered at Kazan. He describes the Russian brick citadel with its cathedral and palaces, and then the Muslim Tatars who live in a street or two of the suburbs as 'posterity of the ancient natives', free to practise their religion and some of them rich from trade with Turkey and Persia. He recalls that the city was the capital of a Tartar kingdom until Ivan the Terrible took it in 1552.
passages.quote: The suburbs are inhabited chiefly by mechanics, except a street or two possessed by Mahometan Tartars, the posterity of the ancient natives. … Cazan was anciently the capital of a part of Tartary, and the seat of government, where the royal family resided. It was taken from the Tartars by Czar Ivan Vasiloviz, in the year fifteen hundred and fifty two,
passages.speaker: John Bell (Travels, 1763)

passages.headline: Tobolsk: Russian brick above, Tartar streets below
passages.gloss: Bell notes that the Tartar princes of Siberia once lived about thirty versts from Tobolsk at a place now 'neglected and ruinous' (he does not name it; it is probably the old khanate capital Isker, or Kashlyk). The Russian town on the hill has a brick wall, the governor's palace and brick churches, while the Tatars, descendants of the old inhabitants, live in several 'Tartar-streets' in the lower suburb along the river, with freedom of religion and trade.
passages.quote: Formerly the Tartar princes had their abode at a place about thirty verst south from Tobolsky, which is now neglected and ruinous. … Under the hill in the suburbs, along the banks of the river, are several large streets, called the Tartar-streets, occupied by the remains of the ancient inhabitants of these parts.
passages.speaker: John Bell (Travels, 1763)

passages.headline: Lodging in the 'Tartar's town' of Peking
passages.gloss: Entering Peking with the Russian embassy, Bell's party rides for two hours through crowded streets to lodgings in the part of the city called the 'Tartar's town', near its centre. This is the inner walled city where the Manchu garrison families lived, so called because Europeans called the Manchu rulers of China 'Tartars'.
passages.quote: After a march of two hours from the gate where we entered, we, at last, came to our lodgings, in that part of the city called the Tartar's town; which is near the center of Pekin,
passages.speaker: John Bell (Travels, 1763)

passages.headline: Wishing an enemy a house and a job
passages.gloss: Bell describes the Volga Kalmyks as herders who despise settled work. They have no craftsmen except armourers, and their worst curse is that a man should live in one place and labour like a Russian. On the same page he praises their language for lacking oaths and quotes their proverb 'Though a knife be sharp it cannot cut its own handle'.
passages.quote: They have no mechanics, except those who make arms. They avoid all labour as the greatest slavery; their only employment is tending their flocks, managing horses, and hunting. If they are angry with a person, they wish he may live in one place, and work like a Russian.
passages.speaker: John Bell (Travels, 1763)

passages.headline: Horse meat is cooked, not eaten raw
passages.gloss: Bell corrects a common European belief that Tartars eat raw meat. On campaign the Kalmyks live on balls of dried curd dissolved in water, and when that fails they kill spare horses and roast the meat on broken arrows. Their smoked or sun-dried horse meat, he says, cannot fairly be called raw, and he tasted it himself.
passages.quote: They broil or roast the flesh before the fire, on pieces of broken arrows, and never eat it raw, as is commonly believed, unless compelled by necessity. They have indeed large thick pieces of horse-flesh, smoked or dried in the sun, which they eat; but this cannot properly be called raw.
passages.speaker: John Bell (Travels, 1763)

passages.headline: A woman shaman of the Baraba steppe
passages.place: Baraba steppe (between Tara and the Ob)
passages.people: Barabintsy, 'a mixture of different Tartar tribes'
passages.gloss: The ambassador made a point of testing the shamans he met. In the Baraba the party visited a famous female shaman who ignored them until she had smoked, drunk brandy and received presents. She then brought out her spirit image and a ringed drum and sang with her neighbours. Bell judged her answers as ambiguous as any oracle's, and noted she was young and very handsome.
passages.quote: First, she brought the shaytan; which is nothing but a piece of wood, wherein is cut something resembling a human head, adorned with many silk and woolen rags, of various colours; then, a small drum, about a foot diameter, to which were fixed many brass and iron rings, and hung round also with rags.
passages.speaker: John Bell (Travels, 1763)
passages.caution: Bell's tone is openly dismissive; he treats all shamans as frauds.

passages.headline: 'Fish-skin coats' and 'louse-eaters'
passages.gloss: Walking in Peking, Bell records the insults exchanged between Chinese and Manchus. The Chinese call a Tartar 'fish-skin coat' because the Manchus of the Amur live by fishing and wear fish-skin coats in summer. It is a small but telling glimpse of how the ruling 'Tartars' of China were still seen as northern forest people.
passages.quote: When a Chinese and Tartar are angry at one another, the Tartar, in reproach, calls the Chinese louse-eater; and the latter, in return, calls the other fish-skin coat; because the Mantzur Tartars, who live near the river Amoor, subsist by fishing, and, in summer, wear coats made of the skins of fishes.
passages.speaker: John Bell (Travels, 1763)

passages.headline: The Kalmyk khan dines with Peter the Great
passages.gloss: On the way to Derbent, Peter the Great met Ayuka, khan of the Volga Kalmyks, on a galley on the river. Bell watched the khan arrive on horseback with his sons and fifty horsemen, and the queen arrive in a covered wagon with her daughter. He describes Ayuka as a wise old man, the princess as a Kalmyk beauty in Persian brocade, and notes that the khan promised Peter five thousand horsemen on the spot.
passages.quote: Soon after the Ayuka-Chan was got on board the galley, the Queen arrived on the shore, in a covered wheel-machine, attended by one of the princesses her daughter, and two ladies, who were also escorted by a troop of horsemen. … The Ayuka-Chan is an old man, about seventy years of age, yet is hearty and chearful.
passages.speaker: John Bell (Travels, 1763)

passages.headline: Hunting the vegetable lamb
passages.gloss: German authors claimed that a 'Tartarian lamb' (barometz) grew as a plant near Astrakhan, half animal and half vegetable, eating the grass around it. Bell walked many miles with local Tartars to find it and found only a dry prickly bush. The Tartars themselves, he reports, laughed at the story. A rare case of a traveller testing a legend on the spot.
passages.quote: In search of this wonderful plant I walked many a mile, accompanied by Tartars who inhabit these deserts; but all I could find out were some dry bushes, scattered here and there, … After further enquiry of the more sensible and experienced among the Tartars, I found they laughed at it as a ridiculous fable.
passages.speaker: John Bell (Travels, 1763)

passages.headline: The mammoth that hides under the water
passages.people: Tartars of the Baraba; Siberian peoples
passages.gloss: Bell saw many 'mammon's horns' (mammoth tusks) in Siberian towns and brought one home to Hans Sloane. He thought they were elephant teeth and could not explain how they got so far north. His Tartar informants, however, said the mammoth was a living beast the size of an elephant that appears at dawn by lakes and dives into the water when seen, and tunnels under marshes with its horns.
passages.quote: The Tartars tell many fables of its having been seen alive. But to me it appears that this horn is the tooth of a large elephant. … I have been told by Tartars … that they have seen this creature, called mammon, at the dawn of day, near lakes and rivers; but, that on discovering them, the mammon immediately tumbles into the water,
passages.speaker: John Bell (Travels, 1763)

passages.headline: A high lama who ages with the moon
passages.gloss: Bell reports what Mongols told him about their chief lama, the Kutuchtu at Urga. On the previous page he describes how a boy successor is 'found' by making him pick out his predecessor's belongings. Here he adds the popular belief that the Kutuchtu had lived fourteen generations and grew young and old again with each month.
passages.quote: The Mongalls relate, that their Kutuchtu has now lived fourteen generations, and renews his age every moon; for, at the new moon, he appears like a youth; when she is full, like a full-grown man; but, when near the change, he is an old man with grey hairs.
passages.speaker: John Bell (Travels, 1763)
passages.caution: Popular belief reported second hand; Bell himself thinks it ridiculous.

passages.headline: Two different 'Tartar' conquests of China
passages.gloss: In Peking Bell retells the history as it was told to him: about five hundred years earlier 'western Tartars' (the Mongols) broke through the Great Wall and ruled China until driven out; then in the 1640s the Manchus conquered the whole empire. The passage shows that 'Tartar' covered both peoples, centuries apart.
passages.quote: However, about five hundred years ago, the western Tartars found means to get through the wall, and, with a powerful army of horse, entered the country, carrying terror along with them wherever they went. … From this time they enjoyed long peace, till the fatal year one thousand six hundred and forty, when the Mantzur Tartars conquered the whole empire of China; which conquest they retain to this day;
passages.speaker: John Bell (Travels, 1763)
passages.caution: Bell's dates are approximate: the Manchu conquest of Beijing was in 1644.

passages.headline: Three khans, one people
passages.gloss: Bell names the three great 'Tartar princes' between the Volga and China: Ayuka Khan of the Volga Kalmyks, the Kontaysha of the Dzungars and the Tushetu Khan of the Khalkha Mongols. He treats all their subjects as one Kalmyk nation with the same looks, religion and language, and marvels at how far a traveller could go with that one language.
passages.quote: From the river Volga, to the wall of China, there are three great Tartar princes; the Ayuka-Chan, the Kontaysha, and the Tush-du-Chan. These three mighty nations have almost the same features, religion, and language; and live in the same manner. … whose subjects go by the general name of Kalmuks.
passages.speaker: John Bell (Travels, 1763)

passages.headline: The Mongols do not call themselves Tartars
passages.gloss: Strahlenberg insists that the Mongols and Kalmyks, whom Europeans call Tartars, do not use the name and dislike it. In his view the name belonged to the 'original Tartars' near China and was stretched to cover the Mongols because they allied with them long ago. He adds that the Chinese used 'Tata' much as the Romans used 'barbarian'.
passages.quote: But to return to the Mungal Nations: We must know, that these are the People whom the Chinese, with Respect to their Situation, call West Tartars, and others West Mungals: But they do not reckon themselves Tartars, neither would they, by any Means, be thought so by others.
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)
passages.caution: His explanation of how the name spread rests on his own reading of Abulghazi and Chinese sources, and on guesswork about Oghuz Khan.

passages.headline: Blame Marco Polo and the friars
passages.gloss: Strahlenberg blames Marco Polo and the thirteenth-century friars (Carpini, Rubruck) for spreading the 'Chinese conceit' that every steppe people is a Tartar. It is an early and explicit statement that 'Tartary' was an outsiders' label, not a nation's own name.
passages.quote: And because Marcus Paulus Venetus, when he was in China, was not rightly inform'd of the State of Things, he, as well as the Monks sent into Tartary, viz. Plan, Carpin, Rubriquis, &c. have themselves taken up, and misled us Europeans, with the Chinese Conceit, that all those People, whether Kalmucks or Mungals, must go under the Denomination of Tartars:
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)

passages.headline: No river called Tatar
passages.gloss: Medieval writers such as Vincent of Beauvais said the Tartars took their name from a river Tata or Tatar. Strahlenberg asked the Tungus peoples in Siberia and reports that they had never heard of such a river. He himself thought the Tungus and the Manchus were the 'original Tartars' from whom the name spread to others.
passages.quote: But then his Conjecture as to the Derivation of the Name Tartar, is erroneous, when he supposes they have taken it from a River call'd Tata, which, according to him, runs thro' their Country; … For after all possible Enquiry made among these Nations, I have been able to procure no Intelligence of any such Thing; Their Answer being constantly; that they know of no River call'd either Tata or Tatar.
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)
passages.caution: His claim that the Tungus and Manchus were the first Tartars is his own theory.

passages.headline: Turkic peoples who are called Tartars
passages.place: Crimea, Volga, Caucasus, Siberia, Central Asia
passages.people: Turkic-speaking 'Tartars' (Crimean, Kazan, Nogai, Siberian, Uzbek and others)
passages.gloss: Strahlenberg lists the Turkic-speaking peoples who 'are call'd Tartars': the Budjak, Crimean, Kuban, Kazan and Kasimov Tatars, the Nogais, the Astrakhan and Bashkir Tatars, the Tatars of Tyumen, Tobolsk and Tomsk, the Uzbeks, Turkmens, Kazakhs and others. On the same page he adds that, according to learned Bukharans, they took the name from the original Tartars without being descended from them.
passages.quote: Secondly, we find, in Europe, the Budziack, and Crimm-Kubann … Casan- and Cassinowan Tartars, and, in little Nagai, Nagaian Tartars: And in Asia and Great Nagai, the Astracan, Ovinian and Baskirian Tartars. … All these are Mahometans: … However, they, like the former, have, as it were, one Dialect with the Turks. All the Nations mention'd in this Paragraph are call'd Tartars.
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)

passages.headline: Tartar towns of wood and sun-dried brick
passages.gloss: Explaining why old place names in Marco Polo and Rubruck cannot be found on the ground, Strahlenberg says that most Tartar peoples roamed, their khans never stayed long in one place, and their towns were built of wood or sun-dried brick. Centuries of wars, he says, destroyed them so thoroughly that not even ruins remain. This is his general judgement, not a report of a particular site.
passages.quote: …because most of the Tartarian Nations roving about, and the Residences of their Chams being never fix'd long in one Place, their Cities and Towns being also compos'd of Houses or Huts, built either of Wood or Bricks, slightly dry'd in the Sun, it is, therefore, no Wonder that … their Cities and Towns have been so destroy'd, that even the Ruins of them are no more to be seen.
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)

passages.headline: The 'pyramids' of Tartar kings on old maps
passages.place: Southern Siberia (Yenisei, Irtysh and Tobol steppes)
passages.people: ancient peoples of the Siberian steppe (Strahlenberg's 'Scythians')
passages.gloss: Strahlenberg describes the burial mounds of southern Siberia: some are earth heaps as high as houses, lying so thick that they look like a ridge of hills; others are ringed with rough or squared stones, and some are built entirely of stone. He explains that the 'pyramids' drawn on old European maps of Great Tartary, labelled 'Pyramidal Sepulchres of the Tartarian Kings', must mean these tombs, which are not really pyramids.
passages.quote: Some are only raised up of Earth, as high as Houses, … that, at a Distance, they appear like a Ridge of Hills. … In some Places these Tombs are entirely built of Stone. Hence we find in the ancient Maps of Tartary the Greater, a Number of Pyramids, with these Words, in Latin; viz. The Pyramidal Sepulchres of the Tartarian Kings,
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)

passages.headline: Stone statues and ruined cities he never saw
passages.place: Between the Tobol and Ishim rivers, south of Tobolsk
passages.gloss: In a footnote Strahlenberg records that Russian regiments going up the Irtysh in 1720 found antiquities and 'Temples of Idols', and that Tobolsk Tatars and Russians told him of many stone figures of men and beasts and the ruins of several cities in the little-visited steppe between the Tobol and Ishim. He links them to obelisks said to have been set up by Tamerlane and to the seat of Oghuz Khan, and regrets he could never go to see them.
passages.quote: …and I have also been told, by the Tobolskian Tartars and Russians, that, from this River, farther towards the West, South, and South-west from the City of Tobolsky, between the Sources of the Rivers Toboll and Ischim, whither very few People frequented, there were to be found great Numbers of Images, cut in Stone, of Men and Beasts; and that the Ruins of several Cities were discernible in those Desarts.
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg, author's footnote (English translation, 1738)
passages.caution: Pure hearsay: he says himself he never had the chance to visit. The Tamerlane and Oghuz Khan links come from his reading.

passages.headline: 'Kremlin' as a Tartar word for fortress
passages.gloss: In his alphabetical glossary Strahlenberg claims that 'Kremlin' is a Tartar word meaning fortress, and that the Tatars call the Crimea 'Crimm' because of the ancient rampart and ditch at Perekop. He adds that western Tartars and Uzbeks call the Great Wall of China the 'white fortress'. This is his own word-guessing, but it shows how 'Tartar' origins were read into Russian names early on.
passages.quote: Cremmelin, or Crimmelin; the Name of the Czar's Palace, in the City of Muscow. This is a Tartarian Word, and signifies a Fortress, But not a Flint, as Kremm does in the Sclavonian Language. Thus the Precopensian Tartary is call'd, by the Tartars, Crimm or Cremm, on Account of a Rampart and a Mote, which was there in ancient Times,
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)
passages.caution: An etymology offered without evidence; it should not be taken as established.

passages.headline: A ruined city on the upper Yenisei
passages.people: unknown builders; Strahlenberg links it to Kublai Khan's time
passages.gloss: Under 'Kemtschyk' Strahlenberg notes the ruins of an ancient city where the Kemchik joins the upper Yenisei, and guesses that it was the place in Marco Polo where Kublai Khan's people went to meet the Venetian envoys. Elsewhere he says a Russian from Krasnoyarsk found old writings there, where a chapel once stood.
passages.quote: Kemtschyk, A River, which falls into the River Yenisei, near its Source, where formerly stood an ancient City, the Ruins of which are yet to be seen.
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)
passages.caution: The link to Marco Polo is Strahlenberg's own conjecture.

passages.headline: The ruined city of Taiminzin
passages.gloss: Discussing old silver mines on the Argun, Strahlenberg quotes the Dutch envoy Isbrand Ides that the Jurchens and Mongols once mined silver there. He then identifies the 'large and ancient city' of Alackzin in Abulghazi's Tartar history with the ruined city of Taiminzin that Ides described, once the seat of 'Chan Utay'.
passages.quote: But that large and ancient City, which this Tartarian Author calls Alackzin, is the now ruin'd City of Taiminzin; … See the Description which Isbrand Ides gives of the ancient City of Taiminzin, (p. 75.) formerly the Residence of Chan Utay:
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg, author's footnote (English translation, 1738)
passages.caution: An identification made from books (Ides and Abulghazi), not from a visit.

passages.headline: Mare's-milk brandy thrown on the fire
passages.people: Yakuts, a Turkic people he counts among the Tartars
passages.gloss: Strahlenberg confirms, from questioning Yakuts himself, Isbrand Ides's report that at a set time of year they sprinkle a brandy distilled from mare's milk into a great fire, towards the east, as an offering to heaven. On the same page he says Yakuts wore their hair long, unlike their neighbours, and until recently buried a faithful servant alive with a dead master, a custom the Russians had forbidden.
passages.quote: …That, at a certain Time of the Year, they make a great Fire, into which they sprinkle a Sort of Brandy distill'd from Mare's Milk, towards the East, and thereby make an Offering to Heaven. I took an Opportunity of enquiring into the Truth of this Relation, of several of the Jakutians themselves, who all confirmed it.
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)

passages.headline: Jumping through fire after childbirth
passages.gloss: A Mongol or Kalmyk mother, Strahlenberg says, is purified after childbirth by jumping three times through a fire before the lama and her relatives. He adds that they wear or keep a small three-headed idol, made of clay or metal, brought from Tibet and the Dalai Lama. He collects these customs to show a sacred number three.
passages.quote: It is a Custom, to this Day, with the Mungals and Kalmucks, that when a Woman bears a Child, and is afterwards re-admitted into the Community of the People, she must, in the Presence of their Lama, or Priest, and her nearest Relations, jump Three Times thro' a Fire; Which they call the Purification.
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)
passages.caution: He does not say he saw this himself.

passages.headline: Printed scrolls from Kalmyk temples
passages.gloss: Strahlenberg corrects another author: the idols and manuscripts sent to Europe did not come from Samarkand or the Caspian but from pagan temples and tombs in the Kalmyk lands along the upper Irtysh. The writings are in Tangut (Tibetan), Mongol and Kalmyk script, printed rather than written, in gold or silver letters on varnished cotton or silk paper. In a footnote he says he saw a wooden printing block for Kalmyk letters in the governor's house at Tobolsk in 1723.
passages.quote: …were brought from the Desarts of the Kalmucks, on each Side of the River Irtisch, upwards, out of the Pagan Temples and Tombs; And as to the Manuscripts, … they consist of Tanguthian, Mungalian and Kalmuckian Characters, not upon Parchment, but upon a thick Paper, made of Cotton or Silk, done over with black and blew Varnish; Upon which the Characters or Letters are not wrote, but printed,
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)

passages.headline: The Kalmyk story of Shakyamuni
passages.gloss: In a footnote Strahlenberg records the Kalmyk account of 'Xacamuni', that is the Buddha Shakyamuni: once a prince in India, taken up to heaven alive for his holiness, whose celibate sons explain why lamas may not marry, and one of whom brought the religion to Tibet. It is a garbled but recognisable outline of Buddhist teaching as told to a Swedish captive.
passages.quote: They say that 4000 Years ago, he was only a Soveraign Prince, in India; But on Account of his unparallel'd Sanctity, God had taken him up to Heaven alive; But the Place whither he was translated, none of them pretend to know.
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg, author's footnote (English translation, 1738)

passages.headline: Gog and Magog in Tartar speech
passages.gloss: Strahlenberg says the Tobolsk Tartars told him they call peoples on this side of the mountains 'Ma-Tschudi' and those beyond 'Ja-gougi and Ma-gougi', and he concludes that these words are the same as the biblical Gog and Magog. Elsewhere he suggests that Gog was the Tartars' legendary ancestor Oghuz Khan. It is a learned attempt to find the Bible's northern nations among the Tartars.
passages.quote: The same Tartars have also told me, that they use, in the like Manner, the Name Ma-Tschudi, … And when they, at the same Time, would denote the Heathen roving Scythian Nations, who inhabited the other Side of that Mountain, they call them Gaed-Tschudi, Ma-schudi or Ja-gougi and Ma-gougi; And these Words then signify the very same as Gog and Magog,
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)
passages.caution: The informants' words are filtered through his own etymologies, which are speculative.

passages.headline: Prester John is the Dalai Lama
passages.gloss: Dividing 'Tartary' into six parts for his map, Strahlenberg makes the sixth Tibet and Tangut, 'where Dalai Lama, or Prester John, has his Residence'. The legendary Christian priest-king of the East has here become the Dalai Lama, head of the Buddhism of the Mongols and Kalmyks.
passages.quote: For the sixth Part, I have taken the Kingdoms of Thibet and Tanguth, where Dalai Lama, or Prester John, has his Residence, the Civil Government of which is entrusted to two Viceroys or Chans; but the Soldiers are a Sort of Kalmucks, call'd Coschuith, or Coschioth.
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)

passages.headline: Governors licensed the looting of tombs
passages.gloss: Before the tsars took an interest, Strahlenberg says, the governors of Tara, Tomsk, Krasnoyarsk and other towns let townsmen go out in caravans to rob the steppe graves in return for a tenth of the gold and silver. The looters smashed the finds and shared the pieces out by weight. He owned only a broken fragment of a bell-metal mirror to show for it.
passages.quote: …the Governours of the Cities of Tara, Tomskoi, Crasnoyahr, … used to give Leave to the Inhabitants, to go in voluntary Caravans, to these Tombs, in Order to ransack them, on Condition that … the Governour should have an Allowance, generally the Tenths. These Caravans, … used, … to knock to Pieces these choice Antiquities, and give to each Person his Share, by Weight.
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)

passages.headline: Mammoth from 'Behemoth'
passages.gloss: Strahlenberg argues that the word 'mammoth' comes from the Behemoth of the Book of Job, brought into Tartary by Arabs who found the bones of huge beasts and called them 'Mehemot'. He says the Tartars call the animal 'Khir', and cites an exiled Russian priest who said the old Siberian form was 'Memoth'. He admits he could not find out what kind of animal the bones came from.
passages.quote: And these Arabs coming into Tartary, and finding there the Relicks of some monstrous great Beasts, not certain of what Kind they might be, they called these Teeth Mehemot, which afterwards became a Proper Name, among the Tartars; and, by the Russians, is corruptly pronounced Mammoth.
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)
passages.caution: His Behemoth etymology is speculation and is not accepted today.

passages.headline: Kalmyk fishing camps of felt tents
passages.gloss: Sailing down the Volga to the Caspian, Hanway slept within pistol-shot of a Kalmyk settlement and describes their round tents (kibitkas) of canes covered with thick camel-hair felt, with the fire in the middle and the smoke going out at the top. These were poor Kalmyks living by fishing, seven or eight tents together under a chosen chief; others migrated south for the winter.
passages.quote: At night we slept within pistol-shot of a Khalmuck settlement. The habitations of these people are round tents, which they call khabitka's, raised with canes in the form of a cone, and covered with wilocks. These tents are of 10, and some of 15 yards in circumference, and about 12 feet high; they make their fires in the center of the tent,
passages.speaker: Jonas Hanway (Historical Account, 1753)

passages.headline: Brick-lined graves of the Astrakhan Tatars
passages.people: Tatars of Crimean descent settled around Astrakhan
passages.gloss: Around Astrakhan Hanway found settled farmers 'of the race of the Crim Tartars', tributary to Russia. He contrasts their burial with the Kalmyks': they dig deep graves, line them with sun-dried bricks and whitewash them, build a cover over them, and raise mud walls around the tomb topped with white flags. The same page describes their marriage custom of the white tent (see below).
passages.quote: They dig their graves very deep, and after lining them with bricks dried in the sun, and whitewashing them in the inside, they build a cover over them. They also raise thick walls of mud round each tomb, on the top of which are fixed one or more white flags, according to the character of the deceased.
passages.speaker: Jonas Hanway (Historical Account, 1753)

passages.headline: Khiva: walls of earth and houses of mud
passages.gloss: The British factors Hogg and Thompson reached Khiva in 1740. They describe it as the khan's seat on rising ground, defended by a very thick earth wall higher than the houses, with turrets and a wet ditch. The houses are low, mostly mud-built, with flat roofs covered in earth. On the same page they note that the Khivans live in towns while their Kazakh neighbours live in tents.
passages.quote: It is situated on a rising ground, has three gates, and is defended by a strong wall of earth, very thick, and much higher than the houses: it has turrets at small distances, and a broad deep ditch full of water. The place is large, but the houses are low, the greatest part of them being built with mud; the roofs are flat, and covered with earth.
passages.speaker: British factors Reynold Hogg and George Thompson, their 1740 journal as printed by Jonas Hanway (1753)

passages.headline: Bukhara's brick mosques and ruined bazaars
passages.gloss: George Thompson went on alone to Bukhara. He describes low mud houses inside a slender earth wall, but caravanserais and many mosques of brick, and a college for priests of brick and stone. The bazaars had been 'stately buildings' but were now mostly in ruins. He adds a lurid note about guinea worms ('rishtas') from the bad water.
passages.quote: …the houses are low, and mostly built of mud: but the caravanserais and the mosques, which are numerous, are all of brick: the bazars, or market-places, have been stately buildings, but are now the greatest part of them in ruins; these are generally built of brick and stone.
passages.speaker: British factors Reynold Hogg and George Thompson, their 1740 journal as printed by Jonas Hanway (1753)

passages.headline: Astrakhan, city of a Tartar founder
passages.gloss: Hanway gives the history as he heard it: Astrakhan was named after a Tartar founder, Hadgee Terkan, was ruled by Tartars for ages and taken by Ivan the Terrible in 1554. In his day it had some 70,000 people, including many Armenians and 'Tartars of various denominations', an 'epitome of Asia'. The old brick wall was ruinous and the houses mostly mean wooden ones.
passages.quote: …and derives its name from Hadgee Terkan a Tartar by whom it was founded. It was for many ages subject to the Tartars, from whom it was taken by Ivan Wassilowitz czar of Muscovy in 1554, … It contains about 70,000 inhabitants, among whom are many Armenians and Tartars of various denominations, with a few Persians and Indians.
passages.speaker: Jonas Hanway (Historical Account, 1753)
passages.caution: The founder story (Hadji Tarkhan) is a traditional etymology repeated by Hanway.

passages.headline: The ruined city of Urgench and its gold
passages.gloss: On the way to Khiva the factors passed the old city they call 'Jurgantz' (Urgench), once large but now all in ruins except a mosque. Their Tartar companions prayed there and then went looking for gold that, they said, rains often washed out of the ruins. Urgench had been the great capital of Khwarazm destroyed by the Mongols in 1221 and again by Tamerlane.
passages.quote: …we came to the city Jurgantz, which appeared to have been a large place; but now was entirely in ruins, no other building remaining than a mosque. Here our company were very devout: they offered their prayers to heaven for their safe journey, and then went in search of gold, which they said, they had frequently found washed out by the rains from amongst the ruins of this city.
passages.speaker: British factors Reynold Hogg and George Thompson, their 1740 journal as printed by Jonas Hanway (1753)

passages.headline: A Tartar town with whitewashed clay walls
passages.place: North Caucasus lowlands north of Derbent (Dagestan)
passages.gloss: The Russian embassy of 1746 passed a Tartar town under Russian protection, ruled by a prince called Alt Sheff, on a high river bank on the road north of Derbent. It had about 300 houses with clay walls whitened with lime. The diarist grumbles that its people were the most skilful thieves in the world.
passages.quote: …arrived at a tartar town under the Russian protection; though otherwise a kind of independent state. The prince of it was called Alt Sheff: it stands on a high bank on the north side of the river …, and contains about 300 houses; the walls of which are of clay whitened with lime. The inhabitants are the most acute thieves in the world,
passages.speaker: Anonymous journal of the Russian embassy to Persia of 1746, extract printed by Jonas Hanway (1753)

passages.headline: A white tent for a daughter who may marry
passages.people: Tatars of Crimean descent settled around Astrakhan
passages.gloss: When a daughter of these settled Tatar farmers was ready to marry, her family covered her tent with white linen tied with red strings and set a painted cloth on top, with a painted wagon beside it as her dowry. Suitors took the hint, and the girl generally went to the man who offered her father the best present.
passages.quote: When any of their daughters become marriageable, they cover her tent with white linen, and put a painted cloth on the top, which is usually tied with red strings: they have also a painted waggon on the side of the tent; and this is to be her marriage portion. Those who design to marry observe this signal,
passages.speaker: Jonas Hanway (Historical Account, 1753)

passages.headline: Honoured by the number of dogs
passages.gloss: Hanway reports that the Kalmyks threw their dead into open fields for dogs to eat, and that a body eaten by more than six dogs did honour to the dead. He also describes their small wooden idols dressed in rags, caressed in good seasons and beaten in bad ones. Near Astrakhan he later saw many human skulls lying on the steppe, 'for the Khalmucks always leave their dead uninterred'.
passages.quote: They throw their dead into open fields, to be devoured by dogs; of which many run wild, and some are kept for this purpose. If their bodies are thus devoured by any number exceeding six, they think honourably of the state of the deceased; otherwise he is a disgrace to his relations.
passages.speaker: Jonas Hanway (Historical Account, 1753)
passages.caution: Partly hearsay; Hanway admits he could not talk with them and judges only 'the externals of a religion'.

passages.headline: Kumiss in the tent of a Kazakh chief
passages.place: Kazakh steppe, about 800 versts east of the Ural (Yaik) river
passages.people: Kazakh ('Kirgeese') Tartars of the Lesser Horde
passages.gloss: Travelling in Tartar dress with Kazakh guides, the factors reached the horde of the chief Jean Beek (Janibek Batyr). He sat on a carpet in his tent, rose to welcome them, drank a large dish of kumiss and made them drink too. The next page describes Kazakh felt tents, horse meat, drunkenness on fermented mare's milk, the dried cheese called 'crute', and their rule of never harming a guest while he is under protection.
passages.quote: This Tartar-chief was sitting on a carpet in his tent; he rose, and bid us welcome, and making us sit down with him, he took a large dish of kumees, which he drank, and made us do the same. We gave him some small presents, which he immediately divided amongst the company.
passages.speaker: British factors Reynold Hogg and George Thompson, their 1740 journal as printed by Jonas Hanway (1753)

passages.headline: No images in the mosque
passages.gloss: After visiting the Indian temple at Astrakhan, Hanway contrasts the Muslim Tatars, who abhor image worship so much that they will not carry coins stamped with a man, bird or beast into their temples. Their worship is silent prostration, with the priest calling on the lord of nature through Muhammad. He adds that the Nogais are Muslims who look like the Kalmyks 'but better favoured'.
passages.quote: The Tartars hold this image worship in the utmost abomination; they will not carry even money which has any impression of man, bird, beast, creeping thing, or insect, into their temples. Their devotion is in silence and prostrations,
passages.speaker: Jonas Hanway (Historical Account, 1753)

passages.headline: Where the Chuvash smear fat on the shrine
passages.place: Middle Volga, between Moscow and Kazan
passages.gloss: Captain Woodroofe's journal calls the Chuvash 'the poorest and most wretched of all mortals', tributary to Russia and heavily taxed. He could not learn their beliefs, but saw that they stick part of their food over doors and windows, and that when they kill an animal the priest eats some of the fat, greases himself and smears their place of worship with it. He adds that the neighbouring Tartars eat horse meat.
passages.quote: We could not discover what notions the chuvashins have of religion, but observed when they dress victuals, they stick part of it over their doors and windows; and when they kill an animal, … their priest takes out the fat, and after eating some of it and greasing himself, he smears over their place of worship,
passages.speaker: Captain Thomas Woodroofe, his 1740 journal as printed by Jonas Hanway (1753)

passages.headline: Forty Christian Tartar princes buried at Derbent
passages.gloss: On the hills around Derbent the 1746 embassy saw many ancient graves and tombstones six to nine feet long, with inscriptions no one could read. Persians told them forty of these belonged to Christian Tartar princes who died for their faith, and that each stone was cut to the exact height of the dead man. The diarist warns that the Persians 'deal much in the marvellous'. (These are probably the Kirkhlyar, the 'Forty' cemetery linked to the early Arab conquest.)
passages.quote: …the Persians report, that of these are not less than 40 belonging to Christian Tartar princes, who have died fighting for their religion. There are many antient tomb-stones, from 6 to 9 feet long, … with inscriptions not intelligible to any of the present inhabitants. The Persians, who deal much in the marvellous, endeavoured to persuade us, that these stones were cut in length exactly to the stature of the deceased
passages.speaker: Anonymous journal of the Russian embassy to Persia of 1746, extract printed by Jonas Hanway (1753)
passages.caution: Local Persian tradition, which the diarist himself doubts. The identification with the Kirkhlyar cemetery is ours, not the source's.

passages.headline: A tower of 282 heads
passages.place: Shirvan, between Shamakhi and the Kura River (Azerbaijan)
passages.gloss: Marching from Shamakhi towards the Kura, the embassy passed a circular 'pyramid' about fifty feet high with niches holding the heads of 282 Persian and Tartar chiefs of the Shamakhi rebellion, all beheaded in one morning on Nadir Shah's orders. The diarist notes that these Tartars had never accepted Persian rule, yet were punished as rebels.
passages.quote: …here is a circular pyramid of near 50 feet high; in which are niches filled with 282 human heads, of the late Persian and tartar chiefs of the Shamakie rebellion, who were all beheaded in one morning. These Tartars had not acknowledged subjection to Persia, and yet they were treated as rebels.
passages.speaker: Anonymous journal of the Russian embassy to Persia of 1746, extract printed by Jonas Hanway (1753)

passages.headline: Skulls without sutures on the Kalmyk steppe
passages.gloss: Riding back from Astrakhan, Hanway saw many human skulls lying about, as if on a battlefield, because the Kalmyks leave their dead unburied. He examined several and claims he could find no sutures in them. A footnote adds that surgeons doubted any race lacked sutures. A small, odd moment of amateur anatomy on the steppe.
passages.quote: I observed here many human sculls, as if the place had been a field of battle; for the Khalmucks always leave their dead uninterred. Upon examining several of these sculls, I could not discover any sutures,
passages.speaker: Jonas Hanway (Historical Account, 1753)
passages.caution: Hanway's anatomical claim is his own impression; his footnote records that surgeons doubted it.

passages.headline: 'The Cossacks are a species of Tartars'
passages.gloss: Passing through Cossack villages on the Khoper, Hanway describes clean, well-dressed people and women with crescent-shaped caps. He then files the Cossacks under 'Tartars', explaining that their name means freebooters. It shows how loosely an eighteenth-century Englishman used 'Tartar' for any steppe people on Russia's frontier, even Orthodox Russians.
passages.quote: The Cossacks are a species of tartars: their name signifies free-booters; but in these parts they are civilized, and faithful to the Russian government,
passages.speaker: Jonas Hanway (Historical Account, 1753)

passages.headline: Kuban means wild hog
passages.gloss: Woodroofe says the Chuvash were descended from the Kuban Tartars and explains that 'Kooban' means a wild hog in Russian, a name given for their fierce nature, because Ivan the Terrible found them harder to subdue than the Crimean or Nogai Tartars. It is a folk etymology (the Kuban is a river), but a vivid example of how names for Tartar groups were explained.
passages.quote: Kooban, in the Russian language signifies a wild hog; which name was given to these Tartars on account of their fierce and savage nature, having cost Ivan Wassilowitz more trouble to subdue them,
passages.speaker: Captain Thomas Woodroofe, his 1740 journal as printed by Jonas Hanway (1753)
passages.caution: A folk etymology: the Kuban Tatars were named after the Kuban river, and the Chuvash are not descended from them.

passages.headline: Tents 'round like a pigeon-house'
passages.gloss: Perry, an English engineer, watched Kalmyk hordes camp across the Volga every summer while he dug the Volga to Don canal. He describes their tents as round lattice-work frames that fold into narrow panels, covered with thick felt ('wylock'), with a door, a smoke hole and a fire in the middle; with the door and hole shut, he says, the tent is 'as warm as a stove'. He adds that a chief's tent could be lined with Persian silk.
passages.quote: The common Tents, in which the Cullmicks and other forementioned Tartars live and move, with their Camps, from Place to Place, are made of small Lettice-Work, round like a Pidgeon-House, … and which when they strike, folds together in narrow Pannels. They cover them over with Wylock, … matted together like Felt or Hat-Work,
passages.speaker: Captain John Perry (The State of Russia, 1716)

passages.headline: Homes on eight-foot wheels
passages.gloss: When the camp moves, Perry says, women and children ride in covered carriages on two great wheels about eight feet across, high enough to ford small rivers, and they live in these as well as in their tents 'like as in Houses'. Bactrian camels ('dromedaries') pull them. People of rank have several such carriages for baggage and servants.
passages.quote: …Wives and their Children are drawn on covered Machines fixed on two large Wheels of about 8 Foot diameter, … so that they can easily ford over small Rivers; in which, as well as their Tents, they live like as in Houses; and Persons of Distinction have several of these for their Baggage and Retinue. They are drawn by Dromedaries,
passages.speaker: Captain John Perry (The State of Russia, 1716)

passages.headline: Some Tartars in houses, others in tents
passages.place: Central Asia and the Volga steppe
passages.people: Manchus ('Bogdoi'), Uzbeks and Bukharans versus Kalmyks and western hordes
passages.gloss: Perry sorts the Tartars into those who live in houses and stay put all year (the 'Bogdoi', Uzbek and Bukharan Tartars towards China) and those who live in tents and migrate north and south with the seasons (the Kalmyks and western hordes). He compares the nomads' life to the patriarchs in Moses: they neither plough nor sow.
passages.quote: The Bogdoi, Yousbeck, and Bucharsky Tartars, more towards China, live in Houses, and continue Winter and Summer in the same place; but the Cullmick, and several Hordes of Western Tartars, who border more towards the C'zar's Dominions, live in Tents, and move Northward and Southward, according to the Seasons of the Year,
passages.speaker: Captain John Perry (The State of Russia, 1716)
passages.caution: He saw the Kalmyks himself; what he says of the Uzbeks and 'Bogdoi' is from report.

passages.headline: A camp laid out in streets and lanes
passages.gloss: Travelling in bands of up to twenty thousand, the Kalmyks pitched their tents 'in Streets and Lanes' like a town or village, each family knowing its place. Perry's homely proof: he saw their cows stop at their own tents when driven home to be milked. A clear eyewitness picture of the steppe camp as a moving town.
passages.quote: …sometimes 20000 of them or more in a Body, and pitch their Tents in Streets and Lanes, in the same regular Manner as in a Town or Village, and every one knows their due Place and Order; so that I have seen the Cows stop at their own Tents, when they drive them home to milk them.
passages.speaker: Captain John Perry (The State of Russia, 1716)

passages.headline: The ruins of 'Saroff Gorod'
passages.people: unnamed builders; Perry reports 'a Scythian King'
passages.gloss: About forty Russian miles below Tsaritsyn Perry notes the ruins of a large city called 'Saroff Gorod', said to have been the ancient seat of a 'Scythian King'. The name points to Sarai, the capital of the Golden Horde on the Akhtuba, though Perry does not connect it with the Tartars at all. Pallas (W005) describes the same brick ruins in detail.
passages.quote: …there is to be seen the Ruins of a large City, call'd Saroff Gorod, in a very pleasant Situation, and which is said to have been the ancient Residence of a Scythian King.
passages.speaker: Captain John Perry (The State of Russia, 1716)
passages.caution: He gives only a report ('is said'); the identification with Sarai is ours, not his.

passages.headline: When the Crimean Tartars burned Moscow
passages.gloss: Perry recalls that the Crimean Tartars once penetrated to the heart of Russia and burned Moscow, and that the tsars had been forced to pay tribute and even to agree to hold the khan's stirrup if they met. Perry's date is wrong by a century: Khan Devlet Giray burned Moscow in 1571. The tribute to the Crimean khans was indeed paid until the 1680s to 1700.
passages.quote: The said Tartars were formerly victorious against the Russes. They have often penetrated into the Heart of Russia, and in Anno 1671, they burnt the City of Mosco, and by the Articles of Peace … the Russes were obliged to submit to very scandalous Terms; not only to be tributary to the said Tartars, but even … that the Czar's of Russia should hold the Stirrup to the Great Cham,
passages.speaker: Captain John Perry (The State of Russia, 1716)
passages.caution: Perry's year 1671 is a mistake for 1571. The stirrup clause is what he was told.

passages.headline: Raiders with two horses each
passages.place: Steppe between Saratov and the Caspian
passages.gloss: Perry explains why the rich land west of the lower Volga lay empty: raids by the Kuban Tartars, who plundered and burned villages and carried off cattle and people. They came in summer, each man with two horses to change as he rode, with sentries all round, and were gone before the Russians could react. A page later he tells how three to four thousand of them reached his own camp at dawn and drove off about 1400 horses.
passages.quote: The said Tartars when they make their Incursions, it is usually in the Summer time, when there is Grass enough on the Ground; and each Man for Expedition sake takes two Horses, which they change as they ride, sometimes sitting upon one, and sometimes upon another. They always travel with Centinels at a convenient Distance from all Sides of their main Body,
passages.speaker: Captain John Perry (The State of Russia, 1716)

passages.headline: 'If their religion be right, why do they not do right?'
passages.people: Mordva, 'Morsie' and Cheremis (Mari), whom Perry calls Tartars
passages.gloss: Half the labourers on Perry's canal were Mordva and Cheremis 'Tartars', long under Russian rule. Asked why they would not be baptized, they told him that images terrified them, because God is one and cannot be pictured, and he lives in heaven. They taunted Russians with the question, 'if their Religion be right, why do they not do right?' Perry adds that he found them more honest than the Russians.
passages.quote: …they say, that the Ruses using of Images, is a Terror to them to think of embracing their Religion; for that there is but one God, and that he cannot be pictured or described by Men; they look up towards the Heavens, and say, that he resides there, and of whom they are afraid to do Evil;
passages.speaker: Captain John Perry (The State of Russia, 1716)
passages.caution: Perry's 'Tartars' here are mainly Finnic peoples (Mordvins, Mari), not Turkic Tatars.

passages.headline: Barrels of gold, some of them fake
passages.gloss: Perry repeats the story of why Prince Vasily Golitsyn's army turned back from the Crimea in 1689: the Tatars brought him barrels of gold ducats, 'amongst which, as 'tis said, there were many Counters', and he made peace in the field. On the page before, he reports that the Crimean khan would inherit the Ottoman throne if the sultan's male line failed.
passages.quote: …being tempted by a great Sum of Ducats of Gold, which they brought to him in Barrels (amongst which, as 'tis said, there were many Counters) he concluded Conditions of Peace in the Field, and withdrew his Army.
passages.speaker: Captain John Perry (The State of Russia, 1716)
passages.caution: Court rumour, marked as such by Perry ('as 'tis said').

passages.headline: The 'Bogdoi Tartars' who rule China
passages.gloss: Describing the borders of Siberia, Perry notes that the Great Wall was built against the 'bordering Tartars', who about seventy years before had conquered China anyway, and that the 'Chams of Great Tartary', called the Bogdoi Tartars, were still emperors of China. 'Bogdoi' comes from the Mongol title Bogd Khan used for the Qing emperor.
passages.quote: …to defend them from the Incursions of the bordering Tartars, who have notwithstanding, about 70 Years since, made themselves Masters of the Countrey; and the Chams of Great Tartary, who are called the Bogdi Tartars, continue Emperors of China to this Day.
passages.speaker: Captain John Perry (The State of Russia, 1716)

passages.headline: A great khan at Samarkand, heir of Tamerlane
passages.place: Samarkand and the steppe east of the Volga
passages.people: Bukharans, Mongols, Kalmyks and other 'Hordes of Tartars'
passages.gloss: Perry reports that the lands between Siberia and the Caspian hold many hordes of Tartars, each with its own chief, but many recognise one principal khan at Samarkand said to descend from Tamerlane. He adds that their religion is close to Islam, except that they eat horse meat, which the Turks and Crimean Tartars refuse. By 1700 Samarkand had no such overlord; this is hearsay.
passages.quote: Many of them acknowledge one principal Cham as their Chief, who has his Residence at Samarcand, … and derives his Pedigree, as 'tis said, from the Great Tamerlane.
passages.speaker: Captain John Perry (The State of Russia, 1716)
passages.caution: Hearsay; Perry never went east of the Volga steppe.

passages.headline: The ruined city at Selitrennoye
passages.people: 'Nagays' in Pallas's words; the site is Sarai, capital of the Golden Horde
passages.gloss: On the Akhtuba, a branch of the lower Volga, Pallas found an abandoned saltpetre works standing among the ruins of a great city: rubbish heaps, traces of buildings and brick tombs spread over a strip one to two versts wide and more than ten versts long. He calls it 'an extensive city of the Nagays'. Historians today usually identify the site as Sarai, the capital of the Golden Horde founded in the thirteenth century.
passages.quote: …here, along the banks of the Akhtouba, on a place from one to two versts broad, we discovered in every direction heaps of rubbish, traces of buildings, and tombs of brickwork, being the ruins of an extensive city of the Nagays. There had been a small fort erected on a hill, which unquestionably contained the principal and most elegant buildings of the place,
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas, quoting his own earlier Travels (vol. 3), in the English translation (1812 edition)
passages.caution: Pallas credits the city to 'Nagays'; the identification with Sarai is modern, not his.

passages.headline: Glazed tiles and mosaic on a khan's tomb
passages.gloss: Pallas describes the finest building at the Selitrennoye ruins as a khan's family mausoleum with a prayer house above, its foundation walls two fathoms high. The brickwork was the most elegant he had seen among any Tartar ruins, set with glazed tiles in green, yellow, white and blue, with stucco flowers, shell-work and mosaic panels. He adds that whole cargoes of its bricks had been carried off to build Astrakhan.
passages.quote: In the whole brickwork, which consists of beautiful broad squares, disposed in the most regular manner, there is a degree of taste and elegance of which I have no where seen an instance among the ruins of the Tartars. The outside of the walls is not only embellished in all the interstices between the bricks with glazed earthen ornaments, of a green, yellow, white, and blue colour,
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas, quoting his own earlier Travels (vol. 3), in the English translation (1812 edition)

passages.headline: Mortar harder than the bricks
passages.people: Mongol Tartar princes of the Golden Horde
passages.gloss: At Tsarevy Pody ('the royal residence') on the Akhtuba, Pallas examined a flat vaulted tomb mound inside a sandstone wall. The vaults were of six layers of square bricks joined with a grey cement so hard that the bricks broke before the mortar did. He analysed it as lime, powdered charcoal and ground sandstone, and wondered whether sour milk, plentiful among a pastoral people, had been mixed in.
passages.quote: It has, however, acquired such a solid consistence, that it is easier to break the well-burnt bricks, than to separate the mortar. This grey cement appears to be a mixture of unslacked lime, pulverized charcoal, and pounded sandstone, instead of the sand used for building.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)
passages.caution: The sour-milk idea on the next page is his own guess.

passages.headline: A royal valley of tombs, not houses
passages.gloss: Local tradition said the khan's palace had stood at Tsarevy Pody. Pallas disagreed: the mounds and brick vaults were, in his view, tombs of Mongol Tartar princes, mosques and walled cemeteries. A wandering people like the Golden Horde, he argues, would no more live in houses than the Kalmyk khans who refused the houses built for them at Yenotaevsk. (Most historians now identify Tsarev with New Sarai, a real city of the Horde, so here the naturalist's judgement went too far.)
passages.quote: In my opinion, the ruins are not the remains of dwelling-houses, but partly of mosques, and partly of vaulted chapels, … A wandering nation, such as were called the golden horde of these countries, could no more be induced to reside in houses, than the Khans and Princes of the Kalmuks along the banks of the Volga;
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)
passages.caution: This is Pallas's interpretation; later excavation showed the Golden Horde capitals had real houses, workshops and streets.

passages.headline: Madzhary: streets of tombs, not a town
passages.people: a Muslim people 'perhaps of Tartar origin'
passages.gloss: On the Kuma River Pallas visited the famous ruins of Upper Madzhary. In 1780 there were still thirty-two buildings, but settlers had since carted away the fine bricks. The ruins stood in rows, which made 'the ignorant' think they were the streets of a large town; Pallas concludes it was a great cemetery of domed sepulchral mosques. (Madzhar is now known to have been a Golden Horde trading town of the 1300s.)
passages.quote: …they have formerly stood in rows; a circumstance that has induced the ignorant to suppose they were the streets of a large town. But, upon close investigation, it appears that this place was a famous cemetry appropriated to persons of distinction;
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)
passages.caution: His 'cemetery, not a town' verdict reflects his view that nomads did not build towns.

passages.headline: Felt huts that ride on carts
passages.place: Molochnaya River steppe, north of the Crimea
passages.gloss: The Nogais, Pallas says, live in small felt huts four to five and a half arshines across that cannot be taken apart; two men lift the whole hut onto a two-wheeled cart to move it. The next page adds that the huts have a smoke-hole cover worked by a cord and are lined with reed mats, and that the Nogais must buy hazel poles from the Crimean mountain Tatars because the steppe has no timber. A footnote compares them to the ancient 'wagon-dwellers' of the Sea of Azov.
passages.quote: The Nagays, as well as their kinsmen near the Lines of Caucasus, and the Akhtouba, live in small huts constructed of felt, the largest of which are from about four to five and a half arshines in diameter, and, like those of the Kundure Tartars, cannot be taken to pieces, but are placed by two men upon a carriage, and thus removed from one place to another.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)

passages.headline: The khan's palace at Bakhchysarai
passages.gloss: Pallas walks the reader through the Crimean khans' palace, which he calls a jumble of dwellings and offices round several courtyards. Upstairs the rooms are Turkish in style, with carpets, divans, wall paintings and stained glass, partly redone in European taste for Catherine the Great's visit in 1787. He notes the rose garden and fountain, the decayed harem, and a cage-like kiosk where the khan kept his falcons.
passages.quote: The apartments and galleries above-stairs, are decorated totally after the Turkish manner, with carpets and divans, or low sofas, oriental landscapes, clumsy paintings on the walls, artificial flowers, chimney-pieces, and stained glass windows. The alterations we noticed in some of these apartments, were made for the reception of the Empress in 1787,
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)

passages.headline: Mountain houses half dug into the rock
passages.people: Crimean mountain Tatars (called 'Tat' by other Tatars)
passages.gloss: Pallas describes the Tatars of the southern Crimean valleys, a mixed people other Tatars scorn as 'Tat'. Their houses are built against steep slopes, half excavated from earth or rock, with only the front raised in rough stone, under flat earth roofs. On the page before he says the steppe Tatars, lacking stone, build with unbaked clay bricks like the people of Bukhara.
passages.quote: Their houses, or huts, are partly formed under ground; being generally constructed against the steep precipices of mountains, one half excavated from the earth, or rock, and only the front raised with rough stones; having at the same time flat roofs covered with earth.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)

passages.headline: Stone statues on the burial mounds
passages.place: Steppe between the Kuban, Terek, Don and Dnieper
passages.gloss: Along the Tashla Pallas saw the rough-hewn stone statues that stand on burial mounds across the steppe from the Kuban to the Dnieper, always facing east. From their dress and faces he judged that a people related to the Mongols made them. In a footnote on the next page he quotes Rubruck, who credited them to the Cumans, and argues that different monuments on the steppe came from different nations. (Most are now thought to be Cuman (Polovtsian) work of the eleventh to thirteenth centuries.)
passages.quote: If we may judge from the costume and form of the face, they uniformly appear to have been made by a people related to the Mongolians, who formerly inhabited those countries. … All these statues are erected on moderately large sepulchral hills, and their faces are exposed towards the East.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)

passages.headline: Bakhchysarai: 31 mosques and 517 shops
passages.gloss: Pallas counts the old khans' capital: thirty-one mosques, most of well-built freestone with elegant minarets, Greek and Armenian churches, two synagogues, Turkish baths, sixteen inns (six of stone) and 517 shops. Among them are makers of famous Tartar knives, saddlers, felt-makers and sellers of buza (millet beer). On the next page he adds that Catherine II let the Tatars keep sole possession of the town.
passages.quote: There are thirty-one metshets in this town, most of which are well built of free-stone, and surrounded with lofty towers of elegant workmanship; … twenty-three, in which large and small Tartar knives, of great celebrity on account of their superior temper, together with other cutlery, are manufactured in great perfection;
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)

passages.headline: Kaffa, 'Little Constantinople', in ruins
passages.gloss: Kaffa (Feodosia), called by the Tartars 'Little Constantinople', had been the Genoese capital in the Crimea and stayed populous under Tartar rule. After the Russian conquest and mass emigration it was 'a prodigious heap of ruins'. Pallas credits the strong freestone walls and towers, still almost whole, to the Genoese, and admires the great mosque in the centre of the town.
passages.quote: …though it was also called by the Tartars Kutshuk-Stambul, or Little Constantinople. Being erected in an excellent situation very favourable to commerce, it was the principal place in the Crimea, possessed by the Genoese. Even under the Tartar government, it was a populous town, flourishing by its trade,
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)

passages.headline: A bride for forty mares
passages.place: Molochnaya River steppe, north of the Crimea
passages.gloss: Among the Nogais, Pallas reports, the bride price (kalym) paid to a rich bride's father is forty mares, two horses fully harnessed, a suit of armour, a gun and a sabre. They live mainly on horse meat and mare's milk 'like the ancient Mongoles', a diet the Crimean Tatars have given up, and keep a love of wandering.
passages.quote: Conformably to the usage of all Asiatic nations, a Kalim or marriage portion, which, with the opulent, consists of forty mares, two horses completely caparisoned, a suit of armour, a gun, and a sabre is, on the celebration of the nuptials, delivered to the father of the bride. Their food, like that of the ancient Mongoles, consists principally of horse-flesh and mares' milk;
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)

passages.headline: Painted wagons for the women
passages.people: Kundure Tartars (a Nogai remnant) and Kirghiz
passages.gloss: Pallas notes that each wealthy Tartar family on the lower Volga keeps two tents, one for guests and one for the women, and one or more covered two-wheeled chariots painted in various colours, with a chest of best clothes on the front. The women ride in them on migrations, drawn by oxen, while carts called araba carry the tents and chests.
passages.quote: …each wealthy Tartar family commonly has two tents, one for the reception of their visitors, and the other appropriated to their females. … they usually have one or more covered two-wheeled chariots for their wives and daughters. These chariots are painted of various colours; and on the fore-part there is commonly placed a chest covered with ornamental tapestry,
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)

passages.headline: An oath sworn on one's marriage
passages.gloss: Pallas, who lived in the Crimea, says the Muslim clergy quietly taught that an oath on the Koran did not bind towards an infidel. The Russian governor therefore introduced the 'Dallak' oath, by which a man who swore falsely renounced his wife, so that 'a Tartar, who has any conjugal affection, will not easily forswear himself'. Pallas adds that even this was sometimes broken.
passages.quote: But a more solemn form of swearing, termed Dallak, is at present, on important occasions, adopted even in Turkey, by which the person taking such oath binds himself, in case of perjury, to renounce his wife; so that a Tartar, who has any conjugal affection, will not easily forswear himself,
