passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)
passages.caution: Pallas writes as a Russian official's friend and is openly suspicious of the Tatar clergy.

passages.headline: A Mongol twelve-year calendar in the Crimea
passages.gloss: Pallas finds that the Crimean Tatars still use the Mongol twelve-year animal cycle, though some names have lost their meaning (the 'tiger' year became a small grey insect). They use it to forecast the weather and harvests of coming years, and Pallas, who lived among them, says their forecasts were generally wrong.
passages.quote: This aera, which recommenced in 1792, and will terminate with the year 1803, serves chiefly for predicting the nature and fertility of future years; but, in such conjectures, the Tartars are generally mistaken, as far as I could judge during my residence among them.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)

passages.headline: A pillar built of horse skulls
passages.people: Kalmyks of the Russian frontier posts
passages.gloss: On a conical hill above the Akhtuba, Kalmyks stationed at the military posts had built a circular column entirely of horse skulls and jawbones, with a low wall and ditch decorated with more bones and a huge horse head on top pointing east. The bones came from an epidemic that had killed the post's horses and those of the wintering Kirghiz.
passages.quote: …the Kalmuks who were stationed here at the military posts have erected a singular monument. It is a circular column, raised on the very summit of the hill, and constructed entirely of the skulls and jaw-bones of horses, closely adapted to one another:
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)

passages.headline: The camel's tower and a pipeline of mare's milk
passages.people: Kalmyk tradition about Janibek Khan of the Golden Horde
passages.gloss: Pallas was told of a great heap of bricks on the steppe, called by Russians the 'hill of the house of prayer' and by Kalmyks 'the camel's tower'. The Kalmyks said that Janibek Khan (who ruled the Golden Horde 1342 to 1357) kept mares here and piped their milk to his residence. Pallas dryly replies that the burial mounds all around show what the building was really for.
passages.quote: …there is a large heap of bricks, called by the Russians, Metshetnoi Bugor, or the hill of the House of Prayer, and by the Kalmuks, Temahne Balgasum, or the camel's tower. The Kalmuks give the following account of this place: Dshanibek-Khan kept here a number of mares, whose milk was conveyed by tubes, from this tower to his residence.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)
passages.caution: A Kalmyk legend that Pallas reports and rejects.

passages.headline: A city driven out by tarantulas
passages.people: local tradition about the Madzhary ruins
passages.gloss: A story said the people of the 'city' at Madzhary had been driven away by swarms of great tarantulas, which is why the stream is called Byvalla, from the Tartar 'by' (tarantula) and 'valla' (bad). Pallas says there is no basis for it: despite searching diligently, he never found a single tarantula there.
passages.quote: There is no foundation for believing what is related of this supposed city, that its inhabitants have been expelled by great numbers of the large tarantula, or Phalangium araneodes, from which traditionary account the rivulet Byvalla has received its name; By, being the Tartar word for the tarantula, and valla, signifying bad or evil.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)

passages.headline: Nogais: 'unmixed descendants' of Genghis Khan's army
passages.people: Nogais, steppe Tatars and mountain Tatars of the Crimea
passages.gloss: Pallas divides the Crimean Tatars into three classes. The Nogais, as their faces show, are 'unmixed descendants' of the Mongol tribe that formed the bulk of Genghis Khan's invading army. The steppe Tatars keep some Mongol features and build with unbaked clay bricks; the nobles and the mountain people are mixed with Turks and other nations.
passages.quote: All these Nagays are, as their features evince, the unmixed descendants of the Mongolian tribe, who formed the bulk of the army of Tshingis-Khan, which invaded Russia and the Crimea.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)
passages.caution: His judgement rests on facial features, a method no longer accepted.

passages.headline: 'Tat': the Tatars' word for outsiders
passages.gloss: In the southern Crimean valleys Pallas finds people descended from Greeks and other settlers, strangers to the Tatar and above all the Mongol race. The 'original natives' of the Crimea, he says, look on them as aliens and call them by the scornful name 'Tat'. A later footnote derives it from the Turkish 'Mur-Tat', renegade.
passages.quote: …and who were strangers to the Tartar race, but especially to that of the Mongoles: hence the original natives of Crim-Tartary consider them as aliens, and point them out by the contemptible name of Tat.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)

passages.headline: The 'first Siberian Tartars' are Voguls
passages.gloss: As soon as he crosses from Europe into Asia, Ides meets his first 'Siberian Tartars' on the Chusovaya river and names them Wogulski. These are the Voguls, today's Mansi, who speak an Ugric language and are not Turkic Tatars at all. The passage shows how 'Tartar' worked for travellers: it meant almost any native, non-Russian people east of the Urals.
passages.quote: we came too, and touched at a pleasant Shoar on the 25th of May, amongst the first Siberian Tartars, called Wogulski. … But the Wogulskian Tartars to which this River led us, are stupid Heathens
passages.speaker: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)
passages.caution: Ides's scorn ('stupid Heathens') is his own; he spent one night among them.

passages.headline: Log houses with windows of ice
passages.gloss: The Vogul 'Tartars' lived in square log rooms like Russian peasant huts, with an open hearth instead of an oven. Once the fire burned down to coals, they sealed the smoke-hole with a sheet of ice, which kept the heat in and let daylight through. Wide benches around the walls served as seats by day and beds by night.
passages.quote: Their Dwellings are quadrangular wooden Rooms, like those of the Russian Peasants; only instead of Ovens they use Hearths, on which they burn Wood, and dress their Victuals. The Smoak-hole which is in the Roof, is covered with Ice, as soon as the Wood is burnt to a Coal, which keeps the warmth in the Room, and the light strikes through the bright and clear Ice.
passages.speaker: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)

passages.headline: Praying once a year is enough
passages.gloss: Ides lodged a night with the Voguls and asked about their religion. Once a year they go into the woods, kill one animal of each kind, hang the carcass on a tree and bow to it, then feast; and they saw no reason to pray more often. On the same page he notes that a good hunting dog was laid to rest in its own little wooden hut raised on four props of earth.
passages.quote: Their whole Religious Worship consists in making an Offering according to their Custom once each Year: When they go in crouds into the Woods, and kill one of each Species of Beasts … they flea off the Skins, hang up the Carcass on a Tree, and fall prostrate to the Earth, and in their way, Pray to it … What need of Praying any oftner than once a Year, say they?
passages.speaker: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)
passages.caution: Based on one night's conversation through interpreters.

passages.headline: Tobolsk: Russian hilltop, Tatar lower town
passages.gloss: Ides reached Tobolsk, the capital of Siberia, on 1 July 1692. The upper town on the hill was Russian, strengthened by a stone monastery with watchtowers; the lower town along the Irtysh belonged to Muslim Tatars and Bukharan merchants who traded up the river to the Kalmyks and on to China. He adds that several thousand Tatars served the tsar as horsemen.
passages.quote: Tobolesk: Which City, besides its own strength, is re-inforced with a large Stone Cloyster, with high Watch-Towers, which may pass for a Fortification. This place is situate on a high Hill … the bottom of which along by the River Rhitisch, is inhabited by the Mahometan Tartars and Buchars, which drive a great Trade up the Rhitisch or Irtis, into the Kalmakian Territories, and carry their Goods to China.
passages.speaker: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)

passages.headline: How Yermak took the Tatar prince's town
passages.gloss: Ides retells the conquest of Siberia about a century after it happened. The Cossack outlaw Yermak, backed by the Stroganov family, sailed up the rivers, razed Tyumen and took the town where a twelve-year-old 'Tartarian Prince' lived, sending him captive to Moscow. The prince's grandson, Ides says, still lived in Moscow with the title 'Siberian Czarevitz'. Yermak later drowned in his heavy armour during a Tatar night attack.
passages.quote: advanced up the River Tobol to Tobolska, where then resided a Tartarian Prince, aged about twelve Years, whose Name was Altanai Kutzjumowitz (whose Grandson at present lives at Muscow, and is honoured with the Title of the Siberian Czarewitz.) This City he likewise attacqued and took with small loss, after which he carried the Prince Prisoner to Muscow
passages.speaker: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)
passages.caution: Hearsay a century after the events. The Tatar capital Yermak took in 1582 was Isker (Sibir); Tobolsk itself was founded by the Russians nearby in 1587, so Ides compresses the story.

passages.headline: Inside a Tatar mosque at Tobolsk
passages.gloss: With the governor's help, Ides was allowed into a Tatar mosque, which he says outsiders were normally not shown. It was plain: large open windows and carpets on the floor, nothing more. Worshippers left their shoes at the door and sat in rows; the imam wore white calico and a white turban. He adds that the chief mullah was an Arab, and that anyone who could read Arabic was highly respected.
passages.quote: Metschets, called by other Authors Mosques, or Churches, had large Windows round them, all which were set open: The Floor was covered with Tapistry, besides which there was no other Ornament. All Persons at their entrance leave their Shoes or Slippers at the Door … The chief Priest sat there, in a white Calico Habit, and a white Turkish Turbant on his Head.
passages.speaker: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)

passages.headline: Hundreds of fallen stone castles in Dauria
passages.people: Tungus informants; Mongol and 'Western Tartar' raiders
passages.gloss: Travelling from Nerchinsk toward the Argun, Ides saw hundreds of old, half-fallen castles of rough stone scattered through the valleys. His Tungus guides said warriors built them long ago, when Mongols and 'Western Tartars' raided the old kingdom of Nieucheu (the Jurchen or Manchu country). Iron-bound wagon wheels and millstones had also been dug up, which Ides took as a sign that a settled people once farmed and worked there.
passages.quote: In several scattered places in the Valleys, I observed hundreds of old, and partly fallen Castles, built with Rock-stones, which, as the Tunguzians told me, were built by several Warriours long since, when the Mongalian and Western Tartars made joint incursions into this Kingdom of Nieucheu. … And it is not long since that Waggon Wheels bound with Iron, and large Milstones were found in this Country
passages.speaker: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)
passages.caution: Ides saw the ruins himself, but the story of who built them comes from his Tungus guides, and the idea that the Nieucheu people once lived there is his own guess.

passages.headline: A carved brick tower in a dead city
passages.people: Unknown builders (a 'Tartarian King' in Chinese tradition)
passages.gloss: After days of travel without seeing a single house, the embassy passed two deserted walled cities. At the second, Taimingzingh, stood two towers, the larger an octagon faced in brick, with carved stone panels telling 'several Histories' set on all eight sides. The description fits the octagonal brick pagodas that still stand at ruined towns of the Khitan Liao dynasty (907-1125) in this part of Inner Mongolia, though Ides himself gives no date or builder.
passages.quote: we reached another old desolate City, called Taimingzingh, fortified with a square Wall, and necessary Bulwarks: There are in it two Towers or Turrets, one very high and the other less: The largest was an Octagon, whose Front was built with Brick, and about ten Fathom from the Ground there was on each of the eight sides Stones placed, in which were carved several Histories.
passages.speaker: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)
passages.caution: Linking the ruin to the Liao is a modern comparison, not something Ides says, and which ruined town he saw is uncertain.

passages.headline: Haloed figures: 'built by Christians'?
passages.gloss: Looking at the carvings on the ruined tower, Ides saw kings seated cross-legged, crowned queens with folded hands, and attendants with rays around their heads 'as Saints are commonly painted'. From the haloes he concluded that Christians must have built the tower. Other panels showed warriors with pikes 'after the Chinese manner' and figures with 'hideous Diabolical Visages'. Seated, haloed, crowned figures with guardians are typical of Buddhist pagoda reliefs, so this is Ides's own guess, not a local tradition.
passages.quote: Others shew us several Figures seeming to represent Queens folding their Hands together, with their Servants on each side: The Queens having Crowns on their Heads, and the other being adorned with Rays or Lustres, as Saints are commonly painted, and also folding their Hands: all which hints that this Tower must needs be built by Christians.
passages.speaker: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)
passages.caution: The carvings are eyewitness; the Christian builders are Ides's inference from haloes.

passages.headline: Stone lions, giant tortoises and a vanished Tartar king
passages.gloss: Inside the ruined city lay heaps of brick, life-size stone statues, gravestones, stone lions and huge stone tortoises, and hares ran in through the four empty gates. Ides guessed a khan had once lived there. His Chinese companions said that many centuries earlier a Tartar king called Utaichan ruled here until a Chinese king drove him out. In the hills nearby he saw brick turrets that he took for old Tartar tombs.
passages.quote: Several large heaps of Bricks lay in the City, besides a great many Stone Statues, as big as the Life, of Men, and Idols, Grave-Stones, great Stone Lions, and Tortoises of an uncommon largeness … The Chinese relate that many hundred Years past Utaichan, a Tartarian King, governed here, but was conquered and driven out of his Country by a Chinese King.
passages.speaker: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)
passages.caution: The ruins are eyewitness; the story of King Utaichan is Chinese oral tradition relayed through interpreters and cannot be matched to a known ruler.

passages.headline: Jurten: tents that pack up and move
passages.gloss: Around Nerchinsk the mounted Tungus lived in portable huts they called jurten (yurts): a frame of jointed wooden poles that could be packed and carried whenever they moved, covered with hair and other material, with a smoke-hole at the top and the fire in the middle. Ides says religion was much alike 'throughout all great Tartary' up to the Mongols.
passages.quote: They all live in Hutts, called in their Language Jurten, the inside of which is composed of wooden Poles jointed together, that whenever they are willing to remove their Dwellings, as they frequently do, they may conveniently pack and carry them altogether. This wooden work when set up is thatched all over with Hair and Rubbish, except only the Smoak-hole left open at the top.
passages.speaker: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)

passages.headline: Distilling brandy from mare's milk
passages.gloss: The same people drank water, or black brick tea boiled with mare's milk and butter, and they distilled a clear spirit from mare's milk called arak. Ides records the method: boil fresh milk, sour it with old milk, stir it hourly, then distil it twice in sealed pots joined by a reed. He notes that Siberian cows gave no milk once the calf was weaned, which is why mare's milk was so important.
passages.quote: They also draw off a sort of Brandy from Mares-Milk, which they call Kunnen, or Arak, and is distilled in the following manner. The New-Milk is first boiled, then put into a Fat, to which is added some Stale-Milk, and this mixture is stirred every Hour … then it is fit to drink, being as clear, and strong, as Malt Spirits, and very soon intoxicates.
passages.speaker: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)

passages.headline: The emperor serves kumis in a gold cup
passages.people: The Manchu court of the Kangxi Emperor
passages.gloss: At his audience in Peking, after questions translated by the Jesuit Gerbillon, Ides was handed a gold cup of 'Tartarian Liquor called Kumis' by the Kangxi Emperor himself, through the viceroy. The attendants told him it was a spirit made from mare's milk. His whole retinue was then served the same drink. The steppe drink had a place of honour at the Manchu court.
passages.quote: Upon which he gave the Viceroy a Gold Cup of Tartarian Liquor called Kumis, in order to hand it to me; which with due respect I accepted, and having tasted, returned it. This Kumis according to the report of the Attendants is a sort of Brandy distilled from Mares Milk.
passages.speaker: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)

passages.headline: Peking's inner city belongs to the Tartars
passages.gloss: During the New Year festival Ides noticed that women rode openly through the streets on donkeys and in carts, some ladies smoking pipes in public. He explains this by the fact that the walled inner city of Peking was lived in by 'Tartars', meaning the conquering Manchus, while the Chinese had to live around the walls and in the suburbs, where the markets were.
passages.quote: The Women never appear in publick in all China, except the Province of Peking only, and more especially the City, which is inhabited by Tartars; the Chinese being obliged to live all about the City Wall, and the Suburbs, where all the chief Markets, and publick Places of Sale, are.
passages.speaker: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)

passages.headline: The emperor of China is an 'East Tartar'
passages.gloss: Ides calls the Kangxi Emperor 'King of China and Tartary' and 'an East Tartar, or Mongalian', and says he favours his own people over the Chinese. On the next page he adds that a Chinese man seeking high office had to 'naturalize himself a Mansur or Tartar', and that most people inside Peking's walls were Tartars. Here 'Tartar' means the Manchus.
passages.quote: The present … or King of China and Tartary, is an East Tartar, or Mongalian, born in Nieucheu, near the River Sagahen Oula, or Amoer: He governs his Subjects very well, tho' he doth not heartily love the Chinese, but on all occasions prefers his own Nation before them
passages.speaker: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)
passages.caution: Two errors: the Manchus were not Mongols, and Kangxi was born in Beijing in 1654, not in Manchuria near the Amur.

passages.headline: Mongolia: land of the race of Gog and Magog
passages.gloss: Sketching the borders of the Mongol lands from Lake Khövsgöl to the Argun, Ides says that this is what 'hath been formerly said' to be the realm of the race of Gog and Magog, the wild nations of the Bible and the Alexander legends. He then gives an accurate current picture: three ruling brothers, the chief being the Khutughtu, the Buddhist high priest, who had placed themselves under the Chinese emperor after suffering from the Kalmyk (Dzungar) ruler in 1688 and 1689.
passages.quote: is the circumference and boundary of the whole Mongalian Territories, or as hath been formerly said of the Jurisdiction of the Race of Gog and Magog, which is governed by three Regents, the chief of which is the Kuttugt, who is also the High Priest of the Nation.
passages.speaker: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)
passages.caution: Ides repeats the old Gog and Magog label as something said by earlier writers, not as his own claim.

passages.headline: Summer huts, winter log houses on the Baraba steppe
passages.people: Barabinsky (Baraba), whom Ides calls a sort of Kalmyks
passages.gloss: The Baraba people between the Irtysh and the Ob lived in villages of low wooden houses 'like those of the Siberian Tartars', heated by an open fire with a smoke-hole that was stopped once the wood burned down. In summer they moved into tall huts. They farmed oats, barley, millet and buckwheat and paid tribute in furs to both the tsar and the Kalmyk khan. Ides calls them insolent and villainous, a judgment coloured by frontier politics.
passages.quote: they live in low built wooden Houses, like those of the Siberian Tartars; they are not at all acquainted with the use of Stoves or Ovens … Their Houses are ranged into Villages; they set up high Hutts in the Summer, but in Winter retire into their warm wooden dwellings. They are very much addicted to Agriculture, and sow Oats, Barley, Millet, and Buck-wheat.
passages.speaker: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)
passages.caution: Ides's own route followed the Irtysh and Ob rivers north of the Baraba steppe, so this part of his closing survey is probably based on reports.

passages.headline: A wooden idol dressed like a Russian woman
passages.gloss: Baraba hunters took a small carved wooden idol called a Saltan into the forest on its own sled, dressed in bright cloth in imitation of Russian women's clothes. The first catch was offered to it. After a good season they hung the idol all over with sables and other furs, which were left to rot, because selling them was thought an unforgivable crime. Ides regrets the waste of fine skins.
passages.quote: When they go into the Woods in order to hunt furred Animals, they carry their Saltans along with them; which is a rough Image, as well carved in Wood as they can do it with a Knife: This they cloath in a Stuff dress of all sorts of colours, in imitation of the Habit of the Russian Women
passages.speaker: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)
passages.caution: Ides's own route followed the Irtysh and Ob rivers north of the Baraba steppe, so this part of his closing survey is probably based on reports.

passages.headline: Descended from the Mongols, not the Tartars
passages.gloss: Asking where the Kamchadals came from, Krasheninnikov separates the 'Mungals' from the 'Tartars who live upon the river Amur'. His reasoning: if they had come from the Tartars they would have settled on the empty, fertile Lena rather than cold Kamchatka. He also claims the Mungals had used iron for two thousand years while 'the other Tartars' made knives and daggers of copper, yet the Kamchadals knew no iron at all.
passages.quote: The following reasons incline us to think that they take their origin from the Mungals, not from the Tartars who live upon the river Amur, nor from the Kuriles or Japanese; for if they had sprung from the Tartars it is probable they would have settled about the river Lena
passages.speaker: Stepan Krasheninnikov (translated by James Grieve, 1764)
passages.caution: Scholarly speculation. The Kamchadals' own tradition, as he reports on the previous page, was that they were created on the spot.

passages.headline: Proof by word endings and faces
passages.gloss: He concludes that the Kamchadals once lived in 'Mungalia beyond the river Amur' and were one people with the Mongols, pushed out to the edge of the world by 'Eastern conquerors', much as the Lapps and Samoyeds were pushed north in Europe. His evidence is a list of word endings he thought sounded 'Mungal Chinese', and a list of shared bodily features and supposed character traits.
passages.quote: Thus it appears likely, that the Kamtschadales lived formerly in Mungalia beyond the river Amur, and made one people with the Mungals, which is farther confirmed by the following observations, such as the Kamtschadales having several words common to the Mungal Chinese language, as their terminations in ong, ing, oang, chin, cha, ching
passages.speaker: Stepan Krasheninnikov (translated by James Grieve, 1764)
passages.caution: Resemblance in word endings is weak evidence, and the character traits he lists are prejudice, not observation.

passages.headline: Rats that migrate 'like the wandering tartars'
passages.gloss: Describing the root voles of Kamchatka, which store roots in neat many-roomed nests, Krasheninnikov compares their mass migrations to the moves of 'the wandering tartars'. When the rats left, the Kamchadals feared a wet year and poor hunting; when they came back, messengers ran to spread the good news. The simile shows that by the 1750s 'Tartar' was shorthand for nomads who move with the seasons.
passages.quote: These rats change their habitations like the wandering tartars, and sometimes for a certain number of years they all leave Kamtschatka, and go to some other place. This retirement is very alarming to the Kamtschadales, who think it forebodes a rainy season and a bad year for the chace
passages.speaker: Stepan Krasheninnikov (translated by James Grieve, 1764)

passages.headline: Kazan's Tatars: clean, honest, better farmers
passages.gloss: Sauer found Kazan a well-built trading city of Russians, Tatars and Armenians, and at the governor's dinner on 6 January 1786 the Muslim chief priest sat at table with the Orthodox bishop and a Lutheran pastor. Riding east from the city, he praises the Tatar villagers: Muslims, clean, honest and hard-working, whose land yielded nearly twice what Russian farmers got from the same ground.
passages.quote: The Tartars are Mahometans, and very clean in their persons and habitations. The women are, in general, very handsome, and dress extremely neat. They are industrious, honest, and peaceable; and, under their management, a piece of ground of a given extent will produce nearly twice as much as the Russians obtain from an equal quantity. All the villages are built in vallies on the borders of rivers
passages.speaker: Martin Sauer (1802)

passages.headline: Tatar women spinning thread from nettles
passages.gloss: On the road to Tobolsk in 1786, Sauer noted Tatar farmers who also made and sold neat worsted carpets. Coming back in 1794, he saw Tatar women near Tara spinning thread from nettle fibres, making linen as good as flax. The Siberian settlers also told him that trade with the Mongols was not as open as before.
passages.quote: The Tartar women about Tara were preparing nettles, and spinning thread from the fibres; the linen made of which was fine and good, apparently equal to that made of flax. I have already mentioned the neat carpets then made by these industrious people.
passages.speaker: Martin Sauer (1802)

passages.headline: Yakut horse-breeders: 'very opulent Tartars'
passages.gloss: Sauer and the Russians around him still called the Yakuts and their neighbours Tartars. Describing the Lena valley, he says the little Russian posts existed to collect fur tribute from 'the wandering tribes of Tartars' nearby. Here, crossing the Aldan on horseback with Yakut guides, he describes the plains as home to 'very opulent Tartars' with huge herds of horses and cattle: the cattle- and horse-breeding Yakuts.
passages.quote: The woods abound in wild beasts and game; and the plains are inhabited by very opulent Tartars, who possess immense numbers of horses
passages.speaker: Martin Sauer (1802)
passages.caution: The sentence continues 'and herds of cattle' on the next page.

passages.headline: The Yakuts' own story: fleeing from Lake Baikal
passages.gloss: The Yakuts told Sauer they call themselves Sakha and came from the south. Their chief Omogai Bey led his tribe and cattle from the plains west of Lake Baikal to escape a stronger horde, fought the Buryats, and followed the Lena north to the meadows around today's Yakutsk. A related people near Krasnoyarsk, which Sauer calls Mongols, also called themselves Sakha and spoke the same language.
passages.quote: The nation known among the Russians by the name of Yakuti call themselves Socha, and say that they came originally from the south. … The Toyon (i.e. Chief) Omogai Bey, with all his tribe and cattle, left the fertile plains situated to the west of the lake Baical, or Baighal, to make way for a more powerful horde
passages.speaker: Martin Sauer (1802), relating Yakut tradition
passages.caution: Oral tradition recorded through interpreters. The Sakha language is Turkic, so calling the Krasnoyarsk kin 'Mongals' is Sauer's loose label.

passages.headline: Aley the shaman, father of twelve sons
passages.gloss: The Yakut founding story continues with Aley, a runaway from the Buryats who became Omogai's overseer and was thought to have supernatural powers. He declared himself a shaman, prophesied that Omogai's daughter would bear no children, and chose the chief's adopted girl instead. After Omogai's death most of the tribe followed Aley, who is said to have had twelve sons; the eldest founded a named tribe.
passages.quote: He observed, that all his tribe esteemed Aley to adoration; for they supposed him to possess supernatural powers, and attributed his continual good fortune and success to the immediate influence of spirits. … Aley now avowed himself a Shaman, and assumed the powers of divination.
passages.speaker: Martin Sauer (1802), relating Yakut tradition
passages.caution: Oral legend, not history.

passages.headline: How the Russians built their fort among the Yakuts
passages.gloss: Sauer gives a short history of the conquest: Cossacks first heard of the Yakuts in 1620; a chief named Millach went over to the Russians and gave them forty archers to defeat his rival Tygin. Tribute was collected from 1630, and in 1632 the first ostrog (fort) was built on a hill, later moved to where Yakutsk stands. The Russian town grew out of a local feud.
passages.quote: Millach is the first chief reported to have gone over to the Russians. … He supplied the Russians with food, and gave them 40 archers to subdue Tygin and his tribe, which was accomplished on Tygin's falling in the field. Tribute was collected in 1630, and in 1632 the first ostrog was built among them on the mountain Tshebedal, but afterwards removed to the place where the town now stands.
passages.speaker: Martin Sauer (1802)
passages.caution: Sauer's history comes from local informants and records he does not name.

passages.headline: Birch-bark cone for the kumis festival
passages.gloss: Each June, Yakut chiefs held a feast to bless their herds. Mare's milk was fermented into kumis in large leather bags, and a summer hut was raised on a meadow: a cone of thin poles covered with birch bark, decorated inside and out with birch branches, with a hearth in the middle. Guests of any nation were welcome; the shamans took the head seats. The shaman then poured kumis on the fire to each of the gods.
passages.quote: A summer hut is built of thin poles of a conical form, covered with the inner bark of birch, on some extensive meadow. It is ornamented inside and out with branches of the birch-tree, and a hearth is made in the centre. Relations and acquaintances are invited to the banquet; but all guests are welcome of every nation indiscriminately.
passages.speaker: Martin Sauer (1802)
passages.caution: Presented as general custom; Sauer does not say he attended a festival himself.

passages.headline: Doors to the east, men south, women north
passages.gloss: Inside a Yakut winter hut the door always faced east, the fireplace stood near the middle with room to walk around it, and benches and small sleeping cabins lined the walls. Men sat on the south side and women on the north. A hut where someone had died was abandoned to ruin as a home of demons.
passages.quote: They always take care that the doors of their huts shall face the east. The fire-place is nearly in the middle; the back of the chimney towards the door, and a free passage quite round it. The sides of the hut are furnished with benches and small cabins, which serve for sleeping places. … The men keep the south side, and the women the north.
passages.speaker: Martin Sauer (1802)

passages.headline: An oath sworn over the shaman's drum
passages.gloss: A Yakut accused of stealing cattle could clear himself by oath. He stood before the fire facing the sun, called down the loss of family, cattle, sunlight and life if he were guilty, stepped over the shaman's drum and robe, and breathed smoke from butter thrown on the coals. Some tribes also made him bite a bear's head, believing a bear would kill the perjurer. Many innocent men preferred to pay rather than swear.
passages.quote: A magician places his tambour and dress before the fire, the embers of which are burning. The accused stands before it, facing the sun, and says: "May I lose during my life all that man holds dear and desirable, father, mother, wives, children, relations; all my possessions and cattle; the light of the sun, and then my own life
passages.speaker: Martin Sauer (1802)

passages.headline: Shamans no better than an English conjurer
passages.gloss: Sauer explains that shamans could be men or, more rarely, women, trained by an old master in lonely woods. He heard wonderful stories of their power even from Russians, but after watching them many times he was not impressed. He then describes a healing ritual in detail, with a horsehair switch, a sacrificed mare or cow, and a drum.
passages.quote: I have heard most wonderful relations of their power, even from the Russians; but, notwithstanding I have seen their enchantments or incantations many times, I never could discover any of their feats equal to that of a common conjurer in England.
passages.speaker: Martin Sauer (1802)
passages.caution: Sauer's judgment reflects his Enlightenment scepticism.

passages.headline: Fleeing to China: 6,000 Yakuts in one year
passages.gloss: Sauer reports that Yakuts and Tungus unhappy under Russian rule were slipping away to the upper Amur valleys under Chinese protection, where they had reportedly built strong places. Russian officials told him more than 6,000 Yakuts moved to China in 1787 with all their goods, and his footnote remarks that such migrations reduced 'the number of Tartars tributary to Russia'. Elsewhere he blames heavy exactions by Russian officials for the Yakuts' decline.
passages.quote: In the year 1787, there migrated to China, from the districts of Olekma, Yakutsk, and the Vilui, more than 6000 Yakuti, with all their possessions
passages.speaker: Martin Sauer (1802), citing Russian officials Evers and Kyshkin
passages.caution: The figure is second-hand, from two Russian assessors.

passages.headline: A priest flogs his Tartar guides
passages.people: 'Tartar' guides (on this road, most likely Yakuts)
passages.gloss: In a footnote Sauer tells why he calls the expedition's priest 'more than savage'. On the road to Okhotsk the priest lost some food, assumed his two Tartar guides had stolen it, and had them tied to trees and flogged so badly that one died. Runaway exiles turned out to be the thieves. The priest said no harm was done because the guides were not Christians.
passages.quote: On a mere supposition that his two Tartar guides had taken it, he tied each of them up by an arm to a tree, and had them flogged to such a degree, that one of them died, and the other never recovered the use of his arm: it was afterwards known, that some runaway exiles hid in the woods were the thieves.
passages.speaker: Martin Sauer (1802), footnote
passages.caution: Sauer was not present; he tells it to show the priest's character. The same priest burned the Aleuts' carved masks, as Sauer reports on this page.

passages.headline: My Tatar servant understood the Yakuts
passages.gloss: Sarychev argues that the Yakuts descend from 'an ancient race of Tartars' who never became Muslim. His proof is practical: one of his own attendants was a Tatar, and he understood most of what the Yakuts said without difficulty. Modern linguists agree that Sakha is a Turkic language, related to Tatar.
passages.quote: The Jakuts are probably derived from an ancient race of Tartars not yet converted to Mahometanism. This appears evident from a similarity of their features, their mode of life, and still more their language, which approaches so nearly to the Tartar dialect, that one of my attendants, who was a Tartar, understood most of what they said without any difficulty.
passages.speaker: Gavriil Sarychev (English translation, 1806)

passages.headline: Horse-flesh: better than the tenderest beef
passages.gloss: Many poorer Yakuts had been baptised, Sarychev says, perhaps to escape the poll-tax for a few years. The rich stayed pagan because Orthodox fasts would forbid their many wives and their food: meat, butter, milk and above all horse-flesh, their greatest delicacy. In summer they made kumis from mare's milk 'after the manner of the Tartars'.
passages.quote: The rich are not disposed to renounce a plurality of wives, nor the use of meat, butter, milk, and above all, horse-flesh, during the fasts … The latter is the greatest delicacy they can possibly conceive; and they often tell the Russians, that if they were once to make a proper meal from the flesh of a horse, they would in future prefer it to the tenderest beef.
passages.speaker: Gavriil Sarychev (English translation, 1806)

passages.headline: Yakut winter house of poles, planks and dung
passages.gloss: Sarychev, who slept in these houses on the road, explains how a Yakut winter jurt is built: three rows of posts, beams laid across and sloping, rough planks, then a covering of grass, earth and dung. A hearth with a pitch-lined chimney of sticks burns all winter, and the cattle live in an attached shed. Summer houses are different: conical frames of poles covered with bark.
passages.quote: On these poles they lay five beams crossways and sloping, which are covered with rough planks, and afterwards with herbs, mould, and dung. … The summer jurts are altogether different from the winter ones, and have another name, being called masses; they are round and conical, made of long poles, and covered on the outside with the bark of trees.
passages.speaker: Gavriil Sarychev (English translation, 1806)
passages.caution: The OCR (and perhaps the 1806 print) reads the name of the summer house as 'masses'; the Yakut word is urasa.

passages.headline: Yakutsk: a decaying wooden fort and ice windows
passages.people: Russians, with Yakut (Sakha) huts among them
passages.gloss: Sarychev describes Yakutsk as the oldest town in the region, grown up around a wooden ostrog of 1647 whose towers still stood but were falling into decay. There were a few stone churches, but all the houses were wooden, 'in the old Russian taste', with Yakut huts scattered between them. For windows they used mica or bladders in summer and slabs of ice in winter.
passages.quote: The ostrog, or wooden fortress, was erected in the year 1647, and soon afterwards the building of the town commenced. This old edifice, with its towers, is still standing, but in some places is fallen very much to decay. … All the dwelling-houses are built of wood, in the old Russian taste, with here and there Jakutish huts interspersed between them.
passages.speaker: Gavriil Sarychev (English translation, 1806)
passages.caution: Sarychev's date of 1647 differs from Sauer's (W008) story of a first fort in 1632 that was later moved.

passages.headline: A Tartar named Sachalar, forefather of the Yakuts
passages.gloss: Wrangel writes that the Yakuts' faces and language confirm their tradition of descent from the Tartars. In a footnote he gives the tradition itself: their ancestor was a Tartar called Sachalar, who crossed the mountains to Kirenga on the Lena, settled and married a Tungus woman. That, he explains, is why the Yakuts still call themselves Sachalary (Sakha).
passages.quote: Their countenance and language fully confirm the tradition of their descent from the Tartars. … According to this tradition, their ancestor was a Tartar, named Sachalar, who came from his own country on the other side of the mountains, to Kirenga on the Lena, where he settled and married a Tungusian woman; the Jakuti still call themselves Sachalary.
passages.speaker: Ferdinand von Wrangel (English translation by Mrs Sabine, 1840), text and footnote
passages.caution: An origin tradition as reported to Wrangel. It differs from the Omogai legend recorded by Sauer (W008).

passages.headline: Once they had writing, and knew lions and tigers
passages.gloss: Near Sredne Kolymsk Wrangel befriended an 82-year-old Yakut who read and wrote Russian. The old man said his people had been more civilised before they split from 'the other Tartar races', and had once had their own writing, since lost. As proof that they once lived far to the south, he quoted old sayings that mention gold, gems, lions and tigers, things Yakuts no longer knew.
passages.quote: He complained of the ignorance of his countrymen, who he said, had been formerly more civilized; and that before they separated from the other Tartar races, to whom they are allied, they had possessed written characters, and consequently means of intellectual cultivation, which they have since lost. He maintained, that his race had once inhabited far distant southern regions
passages.speaker: Ferdinand von Wrangel (English translation by Mrs Sabine, 1840), reporting a Yakut elder
passages.caution: One elder's memory of lost traditions, which he himself says were fading. Old Turkic peoples of the south did use runic writing, but the elder gives no specifics.

passages.headline: Kumis, but not the intoxicating kind
passages.gloss: In a footnote Wrangel says the Yakuts make kumis from mare's milk 'in the same manner as in Tartary', except that they have not learned, like the Tartars, to make it intoxicating. It is so nourishing that a couple of skins of kumis hung from the saddle are often the only food carried on a hunting trip of several days.
passages.quote: This well known beverage, prepared from mares' milk, is made here in the same manner as in Tartary; only the Jakuti have happily not learnt, like the Tartars, to make it intoxicating. It is an agreable beverage, and so nourishing, that a couple of large skins full of kumys hung to the saddle, are often the only provisions taken for a foraging excursion of a few days.
passages.speaker: Ferdinand von Wrangel (English translation by Mrs Sabine, 1840), footnote
passages.caution: Sauer (W008) reports that Yakut kumis could intoxicate if drunk in quantity, so accounts differ.

passages.headline: A half-millionaire who still lives in a yurt
passages.place: Yakutsk region, between the Lena and the Aldan
passages.gloss: In an oval valley once held by a Tungus chief and later taken by Yakuts from the south, Wrangel found a thriving settlement: many yurts, some as big as Russian houses, two good churches with towers, and big herds of cattle and horses. The Yakut headman had paid for both churches and was said to be worth half a million roubles, yet he still lived in a yurt by an open hearth, drank kumis and ate horse-flesh.
passages.quote: Numerous Jurti, some approaching to the dimensions of Russian houses, two good churches with towers … owes much of its prosperity to the Jakutian Golowa or superintendent, who has built and endowed the two churches at his own expense. His fortune is said to amount to half a million of roubles, nevertheless he has in no respect altered his original national customs. He lives in a Jurte
passages.speaker: Ferdinand von Wrangel (English translation by Mrs Sabine, 1840)
passages.caution: The size of the headman's fortune is hearsay ('is said to').

passages.headline: Summer tents of boiled birch bark
passages.gloss: The Yakuts had two kinds of home. For summer they used the urasa, a light round tent of poles covered with sheets of birch bark that were boiled to soften them and then sewn together. White outside and yellow inside, they looked from a distance like canvas tents. The herders moved with them to the best pastures while they cut hay for the winter.
passages.quote: In summer they use Urossy, which are light circular tents formed of poles, and covered with birch-bark, which they strip from the trees in large pieces. These strips are first softened by boiling, and are then sewed together; the outside being white, and the inside yellow, the Urossy have a very pleasing appearance, and at a distance resemble large white canvas tents.
passages.speaker: Ferdinand von Wrangel (English translation by Mrs Sabine, 1840)

passages.headline: Winter houses shaped like cut-off pyramids
passages.gloss: In winter the Yakuts moved into their jurti: cottages of thin boards shaped like a truncated pyramid and covered thickly with branches, grass and mud. The small windows were closed with plates of ice in winter and fish-skin or oiled paper in summer. The floor was beaten mud sunk a few feet into the ground, or boarded in richer homes, with an open hearth burning all winter. Wrangel thought these suited the climate better than Russian-style houses.
passages.quote: These are cottages formed of thin boards in the shape of a truncated pyramid, and covered thickly on the outside with branches, grass, and mud. A couple of small openings which admit a scanty light are closed in winter by plates of ice, and in summer by fish-membrane, or oiled paper. The floor is generally of beaten mud, and is sunk two or three feet below the ground
passages.speaker: Ferdinand von Wrangel (English translation by Mrs Sabine, 1840)

passages.headline: Horsehair for the spirit of the mountain
passages.place: Road from Yakutsk to the Kolyma
passages.gloss: Crossing a mountain, Wrangel's lead Yakut driver pulled a few hairs from his horse's mane and tied them to a tree as an offering to the spirit of the mountain. Travellers on foot planted a stick instead. Even baptised Yakuts kept the custom, and the drivers sang songs praising the landscape, which his sergeant explained was meant to flatter the spirit.
passages.quote: Our leading postilion got off his horse, plucked a few hairs from the mane, and fastened them to the tree with much solemnity of manner. He told us that this was a customary offering to the spirit of the mountain, to obtain his protection during the journey, and that foot-passengers placed a stick in the ground with the same intention.
passages.speaker: Ferdinand von Wrangel (English translation by Mrs Sabine, 1840)

passages.headline: A priest who burned the idols
passages.gloss: Wrangel reports that the Kolyma Yakuts were now all baptised. A priest named Slezzow, twenty years earlier, had destroyed every idol and pagan altar he found, by fire or water. Yet shamans still had followers and were consulted, even by Russians, to find stray animals or thieves. A footnote adds that newborn girls had once often been left in baskets hung in trees.
passages.quote: The Jakuti are now all baptized. A priest from Sredne Kolymsk visits these settlements every year. An ecclesiastic named Slezzow, who lived here twenty years ago, showed undaunted and unwearied zeal in the abolition of Schamanism. Wherever he discovered idols or heathen altars, they were destroyed by fire or by water, and none such are now to be met with.
passages.speaker: Ferdinand von Wrangel (English translation by Mrs Sabine, 1840)
passages.caution: Wrangel approves of the conversion; the destruction he describes means few Yakut sacred objects survived to be seen.

passages.headline: Not the ruins of a departed race
passages.gloss: Sergeant Andreyev reported in 1763 a ruined timber 'fortress' on the Bear Islands, its beams seemingly cut with stone tools, built by 'what other nation cannot now be determined'. A German writer, von Berg, later saw such ruins as signs of great changes over many centuries. Wrangel disagrees in a footnote: these half-buried wooden huts are just like those still used in the region and are far too flimsy to have survived for centuries. This passage is not about Tartars, but it is an early, direct warning against reading ordinary ruins as relics of a lost people.
passages.quote: A hasty glance at these half-subterranean WOODEN jurti is quite enough to convince any one, that they are not the remains of any remote antiquity, but merely huts resembling those still in use among the population of these regions, and of too slight a construction, and too perishable a material, to permit of their having remained for centuries as the monuments of a departed race.
passages.speaker: Ferdinand von Wrangel (English translation by Mrs Sabine, 1840), footnote
passages.caution: Andreyev's description is quoted from his 1763 journal (pages n99 to n100); Wrangel's own survey in 1820 found no trace of the fortress.

passages.headline: Claws of a giant bird, or a rhinoceros?
passages.gloss: Summarising the explorer Hedenstrom, Wrangel says one of the Lyakhov Islands seemed to be made of mammoth bones, which hunters had carried off by the boatload for eighty years. Along the Arctic shore lay skulls of two unknown beasts, one found with what looked like three-foot claws of a giant bird. The Yukaghirs used these 'claws' to strengthen their bows and told marvellous tales about the bird. A footnote says Dr Kyber believed they came from a kind of rhinoceros.
passages.quote: Near these last-named skulls something like the claw of an enormous bird is generally found. These claws are often three English feet long … The Jukahiri, who make use of these horny claws, to give increased force to their bows, maintain that the head and claws have both belonged to an enormous bird, respecting which they relate a number of marvellous stories.
passages.speaker: Ferdinand von Wrangel (English translation by Mrs Sabine, 1840), summarising Hedenstrom's journal
passages.caution: Not about Tartars. The 'claws' are almost certainly the horns of the extinct woolly rhinoceros, as Kyber suspected; the giant bird is Yukaghir legend.

passages.headline: 'Tatar' should mean Kazan
passages.gloss: At Torzhok, famous for embroidered Russia-leather boots, Erman notes that the Russians learned the craft from the Tatars and still call the boots 'Kasan boots'. For Russians, he says, Kazan was the land of the Tatars, and he complains that Western European scholars too often call peoples 'Tatars' who had nothing to do with Kazan.
passages.quote: The Russians learned this art from the Tatars, whom they soon surpassed, and the name "Kasan boots," now usually given to the boots and shoes made in Torjok, points to a Tatar origin; for among the Russians, Kasan was originally the land of the Tatars; and the learned men of Western Europe too often give the name of Tatars erroneously to tribes who had no connexion with Kasan.
passages.speaker: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)

passages.headline: Chinggis's men were Mongols, not Tatars
passages.gloss: Writing about Russian fortune-telling customs, Erman says the tribes of Chinggis Khan who overran Russia were really a branch of the Mongols from the Irkutsk region, who later joined with the 'Tatar hordes'. Over time, he says, Russian historians wrongly gave the Tatars the whole glory of the conquest.
passages.quote: In point of fact, we know that the tribes under Chingis Khan, who overran that country, were really a branch of the Mongol nation from the government of Irkutsk, who subsequently formed a union with the Tatar hordes; and to the latter the Russian historians, in process of time, incorrectly attributed the whole glory of the conquest.
passages.speaker: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)
passages.caution: Erman's placing of the Mongol homeland 'from the government of Irkutsk' is his own view; the Mongol heartland lay farther south, in today's Mongolia.

passages.headline: A Kremlin wall 'built by the Tatars'
passages.people: Kazan Tatars (the former Khanate of Kazan)
passages.gloss: Erman describes Kazan's fort, or kremlin, on a steep tongue of land between the Kazanka and the Bulak, 'still surrounded by the stone wall built by the Tatars'. On the next page he adds that inside it stood 'ruins of Tatar edifices, very solidly constructed of brick', beside Russian barracks, prisons and the cathedral.
passages.quote: Close to the steepest part of the bank lies the fort, or kreml, which is still surrounded by the stone wall built by the Tatars.
passages.speaker: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)
passages.caution: Modern historians date Kazan's white-stone kremlin walls to after the Russian conquest of 1552, built by masons from Pskov; Erman's own account of the siege (T0013 n171) describes the Tatar walls as oak timber filled with stones and clay. The brick Tatar ruins he saw are more securely Tatar work.

passages.headline: Oak walls twenty-eight feet thick
passages.gloss: Using Professor Surovzov's 1778 study of the chronicles and of old gate sites, Erman reconstructs the Tatar city before 1552. It was nearly as big as the Kazan of his own day. Its walls were two parallel fences of very thick oak timbers, twenty-five feet apart, with the space between filled with stones and clay, and it had thirteen gates with towers.
passages.quote: The walls round the town measured in thickness twenty-eight feet, and were formed of two parallel wooden fences twenty-five feet asunder, and having the space between them filled up with stones and clay. The wooden fences, as well as the towers over the gates, were formed of oak timbers of extraordinary thickness. The gates, with their towers, were thirteen in number
passages.speaker: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848), after G. S. Surovzov (1778)
passages.caution: Reconstructed from chronicles and excavations of gate sites, not seen by Erman.

passages.headline: The last stand at Kazan, 12 October 1552
passages.people: Kazan Tatars and the army of Ivan IV
passages.gloss: Following the chronicles, Erman describes Ivan IV's mines blowing up two towers of the kremlin, a last charge by the Muslim clergy in front of a mosque, and the khan Yediger making his final stand. The defenders handed Yediger over and died fighting. The chronicle also says Yediger set a thousand beautifully dressed young women in the Russians' path to tempt them, without success.
passages.quote: They surrendered Yediger into the hands of the Russians, exclaiming, "Take our ruler, and treat him as befits his rank; but we die with arms in our hands." It happened as they said; not one of the warriors survived the fall of Kasan, and the independence of the nation terminated on the 12th of October, 1552.
passages.speaker: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848), following the Russian chronicles
passages.caution: Russian chronicle tradition, told from the victors' side; the thousand women and the defenders' words are literary touches that cannot be checked.

passages.headline: Queen Suyumbike, the rain-making enchantress
passages.gloss: During the siege, the Russian soldiers in the trenches suffered from constant heavy rain, and everyone blamed the magic of the Tatar queen Sumbyeka (Suyumbike), 'celebrated as an enchantress', and the city's sorcerers. Inside Kazan, people hid in cellars and caves dug in the courtyards, and the defenders shot at their own captured kinsmen tied to the Russian palisades rather than surrender.
passages.quote: The Russian warriors who were stationed in the trenches without tents, suffered much from the constant heavy rains; and this annoyance was universally ascribed to the arts of the Tatar queen Sumbyeka, who was celebrated as an enchantress, and to the subordinate kolduni, or sorcerers of the city.
passages.speaker: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848), following the Russian chronicles
passages.caution: A belief of the besiegers recorded in the chronicles. Historically, Suyumbike had already been sent to Moscow before the final siege.

passages.headline: Evening prayer at the Kaban Lake mosque
passages.gloss: Erman was allowed into the great mosque of the Tatar quarter by Lake Kaban for evening prayer. In the entrance hall stood old gravestones dug up nearby, before which worshippers prayed in silence. Inside the plain round hall, men in white sat 'as motionless as statues' while the imam chanted the Koran; then the visitors were politely asked to leave. Erman was deeply moved by the simplicity and piety.
passages.quote: We entered first into a wide quadrangular hall: along the walls are placed rows of tall grave-stones, dug up in the vicinity, and set up here to perpetuate the memory of some saintly characters. The Tatars, as they came in, stood for a little time in silent prayer before these stones.
passages.speaker: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)

passages.headline: Log houses with curtained windows
passages.gloss: The houses of Kazan's Tatar town were small plain log cabins like Russian village houses, but inside they always had window curtains, behind which the women hid when anyone passed. On the next page Erman notes the many wooden jetties the Tatars built over Lake Kaban for their ritual washing before prayer.
passages.quote: The houses of the Tatar town are small and unadorned, like those of Russian villages, constructed of rough logs, without exterior planking. But in their internal arrangements they differ from the Russian cabins; they have, for example, always window curtains, behind which the women are careful to conceal themselves when any one passes by.
passages.speaker: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)

passages.headline: Graves boxed in logs, like little houses
passages.gloss: At the post village of Metyeshka, east of Kazan, Erman saw a Tatar burial ground. Each grave was covered by a man-length box about four feet high, filled with earth and built exactly like the dwelling houses, of rough-hewn logs laid one on another. The graves lay side by side, their long sides running east to west.
passages.quote: about the length of a man, and filled with earth. It is formed in the same manner as the dwelling houses, with rough-hewn posts laid one upon the other. The graves were in general parallel to one another, the longer sides lying nearly east and west.
passages.speaker: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)
passages.caution: The sentence begins on the previous page (n177): 'On every grave there is a rectangular chest, raised about four feet above the ground'.

passages.headline: Tatar villagers with carpets and cushions
passages.gloss: In the Tatar farming villages beyond Kazan, Erman found people neatly dressed, the men with shaved heads under tight caps and trimmed beards, in contrast to the wild hair of Russian peasants. Their houses always had good carpets and cushions, and the women, in loose white gowns, never helped with rough work like harnessing horses.
passages.quote: Men and women here are neatly clothed. The smooth-shorn pate of the former, covered with the tight-fitting cap, and the precise cut of their beards, form a striking contrast with the savage head of hair, completely in a state of nature, which is usually worn by the Russians. Their houses are never without some good carpets and cushions to cover the seats and beds.
passages.speaker: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)

passages.headline: Tyumen, the 'city of Chinggis'
passages.gloss: Erman reports that the Tatars still called Tyumen 'Chingistora', the city of Chinggis, from the time followers of the Mongol khan settled on the Tura. Khan Kuchum later moved his capital to Isker, near today's Tobolsk, which Yermak attacked. The first Russian town in Asia, he says, was founded on the site of Chingistora in 1586.
passages.quote: This city is, to this day, called by the Tatars Chingistora, the city of Chingis, the name it was known by when some followers of the Mongolian Khan, Chingis, fixed their residence on the Tura. In 1571, Yermak, with 500 of his followers, marched against the Tatar city of Isker, eastward of this place, near where Tobolsk now stands
passages.speaker: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)
passages.caution: Yermak's campaign is usually dated 1581 to 1582, not 1571. Chingi-Tura was the old Tatar town on the site of Tyumen.

passages.headline: Yurts of 'the former rulers of the country'
passages.gloss: Near Tobolsk, on the steep bank of the Irtysh, Erman entered sooty Tatar yurts at Philatefsk. They were shaped like Ostyak (Khanty) huts but cleaner, with a clay hearth (chubal), a built-in cauldron, and woven cloth, Bukharan carpets or felt in the sleeping recesses. The families sat cross-legged round brick tea, with horse-flesh cooking. He calls them 'descendants of the former rulers of the country'.
passages.quote: The Ostyak mode of living cannot be confounded with that of these people, yet the yurts of both are shaped alike; but those of the Tatars have always the advantage in cleanliness, and, besides the chubal of beaten clay, there is also the well-set boiler: in the recesses, too, instead of skins there lies usually some woven fabric
passages.speaker: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)
passages.caution: Here 'yurt' means a small fixed winter hut, not a felt tent.

passages.headline: Kurgan graves of 'a race now extinct'
passages.people: Tatars of the Minusinsk basin (Khakas); unknown ancient builders
passages.gloss: At Krasnoyarsk Erman studied a collection of bronze objects dug from the kurgans (burial mounds) of the Minusinsk district, including round mirrors decorated with animals. The local Tatars told him the mounds belonged to 'a race now extinct, and totally different from theirs'. Erman noted that similar mirrors were still used in Buryat Buddhist rites, and wondered whether the builders were really so different from living Siberians.
passages.quote: The most important consideration, however, is, that these mirrors are found in graves which, as the present Tatar inhabitants of the circle maintain, belong to a race now extinct, and totally different from theirs.
passages.speaker: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)
passages.caution: Erman saw the objects in a private collection, not the graves; the 'extinct race' is local Tatar belief. Modern archaeology links most Minusinsk bronzes to Bronze and Iron Age cultures (such as Tagar) long before the Turkic-speaking Khakas.

passages.headline: Bashkirs, 'the shaven heads'
passages.gloss: Erman argues that the Bashkirs are the 'bald-headed' Argippaei described by Herodotus, and that Herodotus's travellers mistook their shaved heads for natural baldness. He rejects the usual explanation of the name Bashkir as 'bee-head' and offers his own: bash (head) plus a word for shaven, so 'shaven heads'.
passages.quote: Thus, we shall render the gentile name, Bashkir, as written by the Russians Bashkuirtsi, by its natural synonym, shaven heads
passages.speaker: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)
passages.caution: Learned speculation. The origin of the name Bashkir is still debated, and 'shaven heads' is not generally accepted.

passages.headline: Yakut words are 'pure Turkish'
passages.gloss: In Yakutsk Erman compared the Yakuts with the Tatars of western Siberia in looks and language. Their words for God, iron and other metals and fishing gear were 'all pure Turkish', and they named their milk spirits as the Turkish Tatars did. So he rejects the idea that the Yakuts owed their culture to Mongol neighbours.
passages.quote: It cannot by any means be maintained, that the Yakuts have received the better part of their civilisation, at some time or other, from Mongolian neighbours; their names for the Deity, for iron, and the other metals, (excepting the tin of the Buraets), for their fishing gear, &c. are all pure Turkish.
passages.speaker: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)

passages.headline: The vegetable lamb was really cotton
passages.people: Bukharan traders; Russian and European writers
passages.gloss: Watching Bukharan cotton being sold at the Nizhny Novgorod fair, Erman explains the old story of the Baranets, a plant that grew a living lamb, told near the Caspian and repeated by Herberstein in the 1500s. He was sure it came from an embellished description of the cotton plant, and he quotes Herberstein's Latin, including Herberstein's remark that nothing is impossible for the Creator.
passages.quote: It appears to me quite certain that the story of the zoophytic plant, called Baranez, or lamb-plant, (formed as a diminutive, from Baran, a sheep,) originated in some embellished account of the cotton plant. Herberstein relates it at full length and unchanged, just as he had heard it
passages.speaker: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)
passages.caution: Erman's cotton theory is one explanation among several; others point to a fern (Cibotium barometz) whose woolly rhizome was sold as the 'Tartarian lamb'.

passages.headline: Tomsk's Tatar suburb of slender minarets
passages.gloss: At Tomsk Erman found the Tatar and Bukharan quarter south of the main streets, its low but regular wooden houses broken by 'the slender towers of several mosques'. The richer Russian town stood on the hill above the river.
passages.quote: The suburb inhabited by the Tatarian and Bukharian part of the population lies upon the south of the main line of streets, displaying from between its low but regular wooden houses, the slender towers of several mosques.
passages.speaker: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)

passages.headline: 'Never so happy as in the wilds of Tartary'
passages.people: All Siberian peoples ('Tartary' as a region)
passages.gloss: In his preface Cochrane calls all of northern Asia 'Tartary' and invites scientists to explore 'the vast fields of Tartary' after him. He closes by saying he was never so happy as in the wilds of Tartary. For him, as for many readers in the 1820s, 'Tartary' simply meant Siberia and the lands beyond it, not a country or a state.
passages.quote: I may be allowed to add, that after such a journey, I might be supposed cured of the spirit of travelling, at least in so eccentric a way; yet the supposition is far from the fact, for as I am conscious that I was never so happy as in the wilds of Tartary, so have I never been so anxious to enter on a similar field as at this moment.
passages.speaker: John Dundas Cochrane (1824), preface

passages.headline: Why Novgorod's crosses have no crescent
passages.gloss: Cochrane was told that Novgorod was proud of the plain crosses on its steeples: they meant the Tartars had never entered the city. Cities re-conquered from the Tartars, he says, carry a crescent under the cross. This is a popular explanation that Russians told travellers; historians usually read the crescent at the foot of Orthodox crosses as an older Christian symbol, not a mark of Tatar rule.
passages.quote: The steeples of Novgorod present a monument of considerable pride in the estimation of its inhabitants. Their distinction is in the cross, at the top, standing alone, unaccompanied by the crescent, and this is an emblem intimating, that the Tartars, in all their invasions, never succeeded so far, as to enter the city.
passages.speaker: John Dundas Cochrane (1824)
passages.caution: Local lore repeated as fact. Novgorod was indeed never taken by the Mongols, but the cross-and-crescent explanation is a legend.

passages.headline: Kazan: a noble city rising from its ashes
passages.gloss: Cochrane found Kazan still rebuilding after a great fire five years earlier. A cathedral had stood on the site of the ancient mosque, and the old palace had been destroyed by an explosion in the citadel. Wooden houses and even wooden street paving had fed the fire, and the emperor was now encouraging brick. Of about 40,000 people, he says 12,000 were Tatars, living mainly in the marshy suburbs, with many mosques.
passages.quote: It had formerly a cathedral on the site of the ancient mosque, as also a palace; both were destroyed by an explosion in the citadel. The destruction of the city was indeed nearly complete, and it is difficult to conceive how any vestige could remain, a high wind driving a mass of flame over houses built, and streets absolutely paved with wood.
passages.speaker: John Dundas Cochrane (1824)
passages.caution: The fire is real (Kazan burned in 1815), but the history of the cathedral and palace is what Cochrane was told.

passages.headline: Princes of Tartar origin
passages.gloss: Among his hosts in Kazan were Prince Davydov, head of the post, and Prince Tenishev, an army general; Cochrane notes that both princes were 'of Tartar origin'. He then explains that Russian titles of Tatar or foreign origin did not by themselves give noble rank. The passage is a reminder that many Russian noble families traced their roots to Tatar ancestors.
passages.quote: Both the princes are of Tartar origin, though their character and conduct would do honour to the proudest rank of polished society.
passages.speaker: John Dundas Cochrane (1824)
passages.caution: The 'though' reflects Cochrane's prejudice.

passages.headline: 'No purse being necessary among these Tartars'
passages.gloss: Walking toward Tyumen with sore feet, Cochrane stopped at a small Tartar village where he was fed for nothing. He shook hands with his host, received the Muslim blessing 'Peace be with you', and squatted on his heels with the family to eat. Hospitality to strangers comes up again and again in his account of the Siberian Tatars.
passages.quote: At the last station, a small Tartar village, I was regaled with pork, bread and eggs, at free cost, no purse being necessary among these Tartars. I partook of the wholesome fare a la Tartare, shaking hands first with the host, and receiving his blessing of "Peace be with you," then squatting on my hams, like the rest of the company.
passages.speaker: John Dundas Cochrane (1824)
passages.caution: A Muslim household serving pork is surprising; Cochrane may have misidentified the meat or the village.

passages.headline: White plastered chimneys and a raised sleeping floor
passages.gloss: Near Tara Cochrane passed neat Tatar villages whose white plastered chimneys and ovens reminded him of home. Inside, half the room was raised about fourteen inches and used for sitting, sleeping and storage; there were no chairs, only clean bedding and many pillows, which were always offered to a guest. A few pages earlier he stayed in a Tatar district of seventy miles without a single Russian, praising the clean houses and well-kept land.
passages.quote: At Kamenski I quitted the great Siberian road not far from Tara, passing several neat Tartar villages, whose white plastered chimneys and ovens reminded me a little of those in my own country. The furniture consists of a few earthenware utensils, and a set of tea things: one half of the room is elevated above the other about fourteen inches
passages.speaker: John Dundas Cochrane (1824)
passages.caution: On the same page Cochrane calls the Tatars near the Vagai river 'of the Bashkire race'; they were Siberian Tatars.

passages.headline: Sibir, 'the capital of the Tartars'
passages.gloss: Cochrane retells the Cossack Yermak's conquest: after taking Tyumen he marched on Sibir, 'the capital of the Tartars', twelve miles from where Tobolsk now stands, entered it in triumph on 26 October and 'from the head of a banditti, became a sovereign prince'. He notes that the town's name 'seems to have given name' to all Asiatic Russia. He admits the history is translated from a note printed on a map given him by the governor of Tobolsk.
passages.quote: Yermak instantly directed his march against Sibir, the capital of the Tartars, distant twelve miles, and on the 26th October entered it in triumph, received the oath of allegiance of his new subjects, and, from the head of a banditti, became a sovereign prince.
passages.speaker: John Dundas Cochrane (1824), translating a biographical note on a map
passages.caution: Second-hand history, as Cochrane says on n112.

passages.headline: Conquest 'like the Spaniards in South America'
passages.people: Siberian Tatars and other native peoples
passages.gloss: Summing up the Russian conquest of Siberia, Cochrane writes that Tartar tribes who would not readily submit 'were at once exterminated', with a cruelty like that of the Spaniards in the Americas. Only Chinese resistance on the Amur, ending in the treaty of 1689, stopped the Russians from taking Mongolia.
passages.quote: Those tribes of Tartars who were not readily reducible to obedience, were at once exterminated; and something like the same merciless cruelty which characterised the Spaniards in South America, was practised in Siberia.
passages.speaker: John Dundas Cochrane (1824), translating a biographical note on a map
passages.caution: A sweeping judgment from a second-hand history; it is not clear whether the words are the map note's or Cochrane's own.

passages.headline: Omsk, once a Tatar stronghold
passages.gloss: Cochrane says Omsk was 'one of the strong places of the Tartars' and held out against Yermak. Across the Irtysh lay the land of the wandering Kazakhs (whom he calls Kirgeese), with no fields or houses, and he says Kazakh and Kalmyk children could be seen in Omsk as slaves, sold by their parents for tobacco or spirits.
passages.quote: Omsk was one of the strong places of the Tartars, and successfully withstood the attacks of the great Yermak. The country round is fertile as to its soil, though not extensively cultivated: it is one vast plane as level as a floor.
passages.speaker: John Dundas Cochrane (1824)
passages.caution: Doubtful: the Russian fortress of Omsk was founded in 1716, long after Yermak, and no Tatar fortress there is known to have resisted him.

passages.headline: Yakuts are Tartars: the Kazan test
passages.gloss: Arriving in Yakutsk in October 1822, Cochrane states that the Yakuts are 'evidently of Tartar origin, as their language is understood by the Tartars of Kazan'. He praises them as ingenious smiths who make their own knives, guns and kettles, living mostly on horse-flesh, but also describes them with the harsh prejudice of his day.
passages.quote: They are evidently of Tartar origin, as their language is understood by the Tartars of Kazan. Their complexion is a light copper colour; they are generally of low stature, with more regular and pleasing features, than the Tongousi
passages.speaker: John Dundas Cochrane (1824)
passages.caution: He repeats a common claim rather than testing it himself (compare Sarychev, W009). The rest of his character sketch is prejudiced.

passages.headline: Kungur's Tatar caves, now ice-cellars
passages.gloss: On his way home Cochrane stopped at Kungur, a town of 1,100 houses. Before it became a provincial capital, he says, it was a favourite place of the Tartars, and the caves where they lived were still shown to visitors, now used as ice-cellars and storehouses.
passages.quote: Formerly it was the capital of a province, and previous to that period, a favourite place of the Tartars. The caves where they resided, are still shewn in the light of useful curiosities, inasmuch as they are converted into ice-cellars, and storehouses.
passages.speaker: John Dundas Cochrane (1824)
passages.caution: Local tradition. Kungur is famous for its natural ice cave; the idea that Tatars lived in it is folklore, not evidence of Tatar cave cities.

passages.headline: Remains of large 'Tartar ovens' near Chinggis's birthplace
passages.gloss: In the Onon valley east of Lake Baikal, Cochrane passed Kondou, 'an ancient place' held to be the birthplace of the 'conqueror of China' (Chinggis Khan). There he saw 'many remains of large Tartar ovens', but gives no more detail, being more interested in a lively 93-year-old woman who cooked him dinner.
passages.quote: I saw many remains of large Tartar ovens, but nothing that excited my curiosity so much as an old lady of ninety-three years of age.
passages.speaker: John Dundas Cochrane (1824)
passages.caution: Cochrane does not describe the 'ovens' or say how he knew they were Tartar. The Onon valley is indeed linked with Chinggis Khan's birth in Mongol tradition.

passages.headline: A Kazakh tent of folding trellis
passages.gloss: On the steppe four miles from Omsk, Holman and an interpreter visited a family of Kazakhs in their tent. He learned that the frame was made of neat trellis-work that folded up small for moving, covered with thick matting, with woollen beds round half the wall separated by fine cane screens. A pit dug near the centre kept the lambs warm, while sheep and horses had tents of their own. The family let him examine whatever he liked.
passages.quote: The frame of the tent was made of neat trellis-work, so constructed as to admit of being folded up into a small compass, for the convenience of conveyance, whenever they think proper to change their habitations; this was surrounded by thick matting; around one half of the inner circumference of the tent were placed beds of a coarse woollen stuff
passages.speaker: James Holman (1825)
passages.caution: Holman was blind; his description comes from touch and from what his interpreter told him.

passages.headline: The Baraba steppe, 'this earthly Tartarus'
passages.people: 'A few sickly Tartars' of the Baraba steppe
passages.gloss: Holman crossed the marshy Baraba steppe in the rain, having been told of poisonous lakes, fevers, swarms of stinging flies and a disfiguring local disease. He calls it 'this earthly Tartarus', playing on the old pun between Tartary and Tartarus, the Greek underworld. On the next page he describes it as fit only for wild animals, reptiles 'and a few sickly Tartars', and compares it to the land of the legendary poison tree, the Upas.
passages.quote: The above, however, is one of the minor evils of this earthly Tartarus; the insalubrious quality of its atmosphere, loaded with malaria, or miasmatic impregnation, is not only abundantly productive of typhus and intermittent fevers, but gives rise to a disease peculiar to this horrid Steppe.
passages.speaker: James Holman (1825)
passages.caution: Much of this is what Holman was told in advance; he admits his imagination was 'excited by the accounts it had previously imbibed'.

passages.headline: Yermak's armour: too heavy to swim in
passages.gloss: In the arsenal at Tobolsk, which smelled more like a stable, Holman was shown the portrait and armour of the Cossack conqueror Yermak. He handled the chain shirt and found it so heavy that he understood why Yermak sank for good when, in his last battle, he stepped short of 'the Tartar king's galley'. He adds that he cannot say whether the story is fable or history.
passages.quote: the portrait and armour of Yermack; the former a miserable daub; the latter consisting chiefly of a chain shirt, so heavy that one cannot wonder at his going irretrievably to the bottom, when, in his last battle, he stepped short of the Tartar king's galley, and fell into water.
