Whether the history of this banditti leader be fabulous or not, it is at least interesting
passages.speaker: James Holman (1825)
passages.caution: Holman handled the armour but could not judge the portrait; he calls it a daub on others' word. Whether the armour was really Yermak's is not tested.

passages.headline: A governor's cabinet of dug-up antiquities
passages.people: Unknown ancient peoples of the Yenisei region
passages.gloss: At Krasnoyarsk the governor showed Holman his collection of 'Tartar' dresses, weapons and armour, along with objects dug up around the province: metal vases that Holman guessed once held the ashes of great chiefs, copper and stone hatchets, knives and arrowheads. These are the kind of finds that came from the kurgans (burial mounds) of the Yenisei and Minusinsk region.
passages.quote: The governor, on the Tuesday, most obligingly submitted to my inspection his cabinet of curiosities, comprising a large collection of Tartar dresses, weapons, and armour, as also many curious remains that had been dug up in different parts of his government; amongst the rest, metal vases, which had probably been the depositaries of the ashes of the great and powerful of their day
passages.speaker: James Holman (1825)
passages.caution: The idea that the vases held ashes is Holman's guess. Compare Erman's report of Minusinsk kurgan bronzes (W011, T0014 n152).

passages.headline: Mongol chiefs made Knights of Malta
passages.gloss: Near Irkutsk, Holman heard of a settlement of 'Mongul Tartars' at Tunka near the Chinese frontier, whose chiefs had been made Knights of Malta by Emperor Paul (Paul was Grand Master of the Order from 1798 to 1801). Holman doubts they could have understood the honour beyond the star and ribbon.
passages.quote: The Emperor Paul made some of the chiefs of these Mongul Tartars Knights of Malta! It must be difficult to conceive how these people would contemplate the nature or duties of such a creation, or appreciate the honour conferred upon them
passages.speaker: James Holman (1825)
passages.caution: Reported to Holman, not seen; his dismissive comment is his own. Holman puts 'Toonga' about sixty miles from Irkutsk; the identification with Tunka is ours.

passages.headline: Rumour: Tatars stir the pot with a candle
passages.gloss: Holman's Tatar servant often offered to cook for him, especially fish, but Holman refused because he had heard that Tatars stirred their cooking with a candle 'to give it gout' (flavour). He had also blamed the man's illness on the 'disgusting trash' Tatars liked to eat. The passage shows the kind of gossip about Tatars that travellers passed on without checking.
passages.quote: The Tartar often wanted to prepare dinner for me, particularly when fish was to be met with, but having heard that his countrymen were in the habit of stirring up their cookery with a candle in order to give it gout, I could not reconcile myself to take advantage of his culinary talents.
passages.speaker: James Holman (1825)
passages.caution: Pure hearsay and prejudice; Holman never tested it. (Tallow candles were sometimes eaten as fat in Siberia, which may lie behind the rumour.)

passages.headline: 'Mongul Tartary' beyond Lake Baikal
passages.gloss: Holman calls the whole country between Lake Baikal and the trading towns of Kiakhta (Russian) and Maimachin (Chinese) 'Mongul Tartary', wild and rugged and full of wild animals. Here the old map name Tartary survives as a regional label. A page earlier he describes the Buryats as 'of Mongul origin'.
passages.quote: The whole country between these points and the Baikal, which has the name of Mongul Tartary, is wild and rugged in the extreme, and often dangerous to the traveller in consequence of the great number of wild animals that inhabit it.
passages.speaker: James Holman (1825)
passages.caution: Holman did not travel to Kiakhta himself; this is a general description.

passages.headline: Tungus who looked like the 'Pekin Tartars'
passages.people: Tungus (Evenki), compared with the Manchus of Beijing
passages.gloss: Dobell says the Tungus he met on the Okhotsk to Yakutsk road looked strikingly like 'the Tartars, who have conquered China', meaning the Manchus. His two Cantonese servants, who had seen Manchu bannermen in Beijing, agreed, and the servants and the Tungus greeted each other as 'brats', Russian for brothers. It is a vivid glimpse of 'Tartar' meaning Manchu in an English book of 1830.
passages.quote: means of my two Chinese servants, who were born in Canton, and had seen many of the Pekin Tartars, and were themselves struck with the likeness between them and the Tongusees. They always called each other brats (which means, in Russian, brothers) when they met
passages.speaker: Peter Dobell
passages.caution: A comparison of faces made by the author and his servants; it proves nothing about ancestry.

passages.headline: Reindeer Koryaks with 'Tartar' features
passages.people: Reindeer Koryaks, compared with Tartars and northern Chinese
passages.gloss: Meeting a Chukchi man and the Reindeer Koryaks in northern Kamchatka, Dobell sorts them by looks: the Chukchi resemble North American Indians, while the Koryaks have the high cheekbones and small eyes 'by which the Tartars are distinguished'. Here 'Tartar' is simply a label for an East Asian face type, not a nation he met.
passages.quote: The Reindeer Karaikees, on the contrary, have those very high cheek bones and small eyes, as well as those features generally by which the Tartars are distinguished; and they certainly resemble much the Northern Chinese.
passages.speaker: Peter Dobell
passages.caution: A racial generalisation typical of the period.

passages.headline: Ruined brick temples of a Mongol prince
passages.gloss: Invited by their Mongol guide Idam, members of the mission rode out to a hillside covered with ruins of stone buildings about two versts long. Idam said a Mongol prince called Sain Koung had lived there about 300 years earlier and that the buildings were temples. Timkovsky records the materials exactly: granite foundations, walls of sun-dried brick, and clay mixed with gravel instead of mortar. On the next page he adds stone cornices, vaulted niches, a stone-paved court and broken green tiles, and says the Mongols now rarely visit these 'monuments of their former splendour'.
passages.quote: we reached a mountain, the declivity of which was covered with ruins of stone-buildings, about two wersts in extent. … The buildings, of which the ruins lay before us, were temples. … The foundations were of granite, like that of the neighbouring mountain; the walls are of bricks, dried in the sun.
passages.speaker: George Timkowski (English translation, 1827)
passages.caution: The date and builder come from the guide Idam's oral tradition; Timkovsky could not check them.

passages.headline: Rocks that look like ruined buildings
passages.gloss: A day before seeing the real ruins, Timkovsky camped by a granite ridge that from far off looked like a forest and close up looked like altars, a sarcophagus, a tower and 'the ruins of a house with a stone floor'. He calls it a 'lusus naturae', a freak of nature, and explains it as decomposed granite lying in slabs. On the following page his Mongol hosts add that the rock is full of loadstone that pulls at any gun brought near it.
passages.quote: At a distance it looks like a forest; but when seen near at hand, it presents an extraordinary lusus nature. These rocks resemble, now an immense altar, now a sarcophagus; here a tower, there the ruins of a house with a stone floor. The rock, a decomposed granite, lies in large masses from three to nine inches thick
passages.speaker: George Timkowski (English translation, 1827)
passages.caution: The author himself judged these to be natural rock, not buildings.

passages.headline: A Mongol official's belief about Genghis Khan's houses
passages.place: Mongolia (on the road south of Urga)
passages.gloss: A Mongol officer (the zakiroktchi) told the Russians he was sure several European kings descended from Genghis Khan, since Genghis had reigned in Russia, and that ruins of Genghis Khan's houses still stood in Mongolia and probably in Russia too. Timkovsky dismisses the royal descent as absurd but records the belief. It is an early example of a local legend crediting ruins to Genghis Khan.
passages.quote: The zakiroktchi was persuaded that several sovereigns of Europe must be descendants of Gingis Khan, … because he had reigned in Russia, and other foreign countries; a conjecture of which it seems unnecessary to shew the absurdity. He informed us that there still existed in Mongolia ruins of houses that belonged to Gingis Khan, and he supposed there must be some in Russia.
passages.speaker: George Timkowski (English translation, 1827)
passages.caution: Hearsay from a Mongol official; Timkovsky himself rejects part of it.

passages.headline: Urga, a capital made of tents
passages.people: Khalkha Mongols; Manchu and Chinese officials
passages.gloss: Urga (modern Ulaanbaatar), the seat of the Khalkha living Buddha and of the Qing governors, was mostly a town of felt tents. Timkovsky says every dwelling, including the Russian house, stood inside a palisade, with tents in the courtyards and only a small Chinese-style house of two rooms. Elsewhere he describes its temples and a separate Chinese trading quarter, the maimatchin.
passages.quote: Ourga consists chiefly of kibitkas: the evening being foggy we did not see it till we were within three wersts of it. … Our abode, like all the habitations in Ourga, was surrounded with palisades; in the first court there was a tent for the guard; in the second four very spacious tents had been erected for us, behind which was a small Chinese house
passages.speaker: George Timkowski (English translation, 1827)

passages.headline: Gher, ourto and ordo: words for Mongol dwellings
passages.gloss: In a footnote Timkovsky explains the vocabulary: the felt tent the Russians call a jourta or kibitka is a gher in Mongol; a cluster of tents forming a village or station is an ourto; oulous means empire or people; and ordo (the root of 'horde') means a chateau or imperial palace. It is a neat reminder that the famous Tartar 'horde' was originally the ruler's camp-palace.
passages.quote: Such a tent (made of felt,) … is in Mongol called gher; several tents together, forming a kind of village or station, are called ourto. Oulous, or olos, signifies in Mongol, empire, people; ordo, a chateau, or imperial palace.
passages.speaker: George Timkowski (English translation, 1827)

passages.headline: A Buddhist monument of stone, clay and grey brick
passages.gloss: On a walk near Urga the Russians climbed to a soubourgan (suburgan, a Buddhist stupa) built by a Mongol prince. Timkovsky notes how it was made: a square base of unhewn stone bound with clay and straw, grey brick walls, and a core of sand and stones. It shows Mongol nobles commissioning permanent religious buildings even while living in tents.
passages.quote: we ascended an eminence, on which stands a soubourgan, or sacred pyramid, of the disciples of Boudha, erected by a Mongol prince. The pedestal, which is of a square form, is made of unhewn stone, cemented with a composition made of clay and straw: the walls are made of gray bricks, and the interior filled with sand and stones.
passages.speaker: George Timkowski (English translation, 1827)

passages.headline: Ashes kept in monuments of wood or stone
passages.gloss: Explaining Mongol funerals, Timkovsky says the lama decides how each body is disposed of, and that the devout or wealthy raise monuments of wood or stone to hold the ashes. He backs this up by quoting the thirteenth-century friar Rubruck (Ruysbroek) on Tartars keeping ashes in 'high pyramids', a sign that he read his Mongols through older European books.
passages.quote: Those who wish to show their devotion or their riches, cause monuments of wood or stone to be erected, in which they deposit the ashes of the deceased. This custom has been observed in Mongolia from the remotest times. Ruysbroek, says expressly: "The Tartars (Mongols), like the nations of antiquity, burn their dead, and preserve their ashes in high pyramids."
passages.speaker: George Timkowski, quoting William of Rubruck from Bergeron's French collection
passages.caution: The Rubruck line is quoted secondhand from a French anthology, not checked against Rubruck's text.

passages.headline: A child's body left in a leather sack
passages.gloss: On the road the mission was startled to find a dead child sewn in a leather sack, with a scrap of sheepskin, millet and bread laid on top. Timkovsky says this was the usual Mongol way of disposing of the dead, and goes on to explain that lamas chose between burning, water burial, exposure on a platform or leaving the body on the steppe for animals and birds.
passages.quote: We were greatly surprised at seeing on the road, six wersts from Elesoutou, the dead body of a child in a leather sack. Upon the sack was a little piece of sheep-skin, some millet, and some bread. This is the usual manner of burying the dead among the Mongols.
passages.speaker: George Timkowski (English translation, 1827)

passages.headline: Shamans and the household god Ongon
passages.gloss: Passing the Ongon mountains, named for the 'king of the Shamans', Timkovsky notes that shamanism survived among the Mongols despite the Buddhist lamas. He gives the Mongol words for male and female shamans and describes Ongon, a household guardian made of scraps of red cloth that women kept in the tent and appeased with offerings when things went wrong.
passages.quote: Among these people a man is called beg, and a woman ouddogoun, in the Mongol language. They are distinguished by an ardent imagination in the evocation of spirits, which throws them into wild transports. Ongon is their household divinity, which watches over their families and flocks. These remnants of the Shamanic faith have still many zealous partisans among the Mongols
passages.speaker: George Timkowski (English translation, 1827)

passages.headline: Milk, dried cheese and milk brandy
passages.gloss: A tall lama told the travellers about a cattle plague that had left the steppe people short of food. Timkovsky records their diet: meat when herds were large, otherwise milk, dried cheese (kourout) and millet, with a milk brandy drunk in summer. On the facing page he adds that they made coarse felt from sheep's wool, twisted horsehair into ropes, and had 'neither handicrafts nor manufactures'.
passages.quote: When they possess many cows and sheep, they subsist upon their flesh, otherwise they content themselves with milk and dried cheese (bissalak and kourout), they likewise make use of a kind of millet (shara bonda). To exhilarate their spirits they drink, though only in summer, a kind of brandy, which they extract from milk.
passages.speaker: George Timkowski (English translation, 1827)

passages.headline: A living Buddha whose face follows the moon
passages.gloss: Timkovsky reports what the Khalkhas believed about their koutouktou (Jebtsundamba Khutughtu), the reincarnating high lama of Urga: that he had already lived through sixteen generations and that his face aged and grew young again with the moon. He presents it as their belief, not his.
passages.quote: The Kalkas affirm, that their koutouktou has already seen sixteen generations, and that his physiognomy changes with the phases of the moon. At new moon, he has the appearance of a youth; at the full, of a man in the prime of life; and appears quite old in the last quarter.
passages.speaker: George Timkowski (English translation, 1827)
passages.caution: A popular belief reported secondhand.

passages.headline: The 'Tartar town' of Peking was first built by the Mongols
passages.gloss: As the mission reached the walls of Peking, Klaproth added a note on the history of the 'Tartar town', the northern inner city where the Manchu garrison lived. It was first walled by the Mongols in 1267 with eleven gates; the Ming cut it down to nine gates, which is why its governor was called governor of the nine gates. So the 'Tartar' city of Beijing was a Mongol Yuan foundation reshaped by the Chinese Ming.
passages.quote: the Mongols, in 1267; it was then sixty li in circumference, and had eleven gates. The first emperor of the dynasty of Ming took off five li from its northern side, and took away two of the gates, so that only nine remained. It is for this reason that the governor of the Tartar town bears the title of governor of the nine gates.
passages.speaker: Julius Klaproth (editor's footnote in the 1827 English translation)
passages.caution: An editor's footnote drawn from Chinese sources; the first words of the sentence are on the previous page (n337).

passages.headline: A ruined earth fort on the Mongol frontier
passages.place: Inner Mongolia (Tsagan Balgas, north of Kalgan)
passages.gloss: Near the end of the desert crossing the mission sheltered at Tsagan balgassou, the 'white walled town', a small square fort of rammed earth, now in ruins and used to shelter cattle. Timkovsky describes its bastions and a stone circle he took for the site of a khan's tent, and reports that people credited such forts to the Kangxi emperor's campaigns of the late 1600s.
passages.quote: The ramparts, which are in ruins, are five toises high, and have small bastions at the four corners. In the interior, in the north-west angle, there is a circular space enclosed with unhewn stones: it was probably the site of the Khan's tent. … Some persons affirm that this fort, as well as those situated farther to the south, served as encampments during the expeditions of the celebrated Emperor Kanghi
passages.speaker: George Timkowski (English translation, 1827)
passages.caution: The attribution to Kangxi is hearsay, which Timkovsky reports without endorsing.

passages.headline: Turkestan speech sounds like Kazan Tatar
passages.people: Turkic peoples of Eastern Turkestan; Kazan Tatars
passages.gloss: While in Peking, Timkovsky talked through an interpreter with men from Little Bucharia (the Tarim basin towns) and noticed that their language was very like that of the Kazan Tatars, 'who are also of Turkish origin'. Here 'Tartar' means the Turkic-speaking Muslims of the Volga, a different people entirely from the Mongols he had just crossed.
passages.quote: In the conversations I had in China, through the medium of an interpreter, with natives of Little Bucharia who had come to Peking, I observed that their language much resembles that of the Tartars of Kasan, who are also of Turkish origin.
passages.speaker: George Timkowski (English translation, 1827)

passages.headline: The Tartars of Tobolsk, once subjects of Kuchum Khan
passages.gloss: At Tobolsk the envoys asked about a people the Russians called Tartars (Ta-ta-la), who lived from the Irtysh to Kazan. Russians told them these people had once been subjects of Kuchum Khan (Ku-tching Khan), the last khan of Sibir, and had spread out after Tobolsk became Russian. Tulishen noted that those who had not become Orthodox Christians looked like Chinese Muslims (Hui): short hair, small caps, no pork.
passages.quote: the Russians said: "This people was formerly subject to the Ku-tching Khan, otherwise called Ho-tung. … Some among them have conformed to our religion, but others have not." Such of this people as have not conformed to the religion of the Russians, have the appearance of being (Hoei-tse) Mahometans. They wear small caps, and their hair cut short. They eat no pork
passages.speaker: Tulishen (translated from the Chinese by George Thomas Staunton, 1821)
passages.caution: The origin story is what Russians told the envoys. The last clause of this passage in the Chinese text (T1072, juan 1, 46a: 别供佛像) differs from Staunton's 'offer no sacrifices to their Divinities', so that detail is uncertain.

passages.headline: Tatar boat-haulers flogged by Russian soldiers
passages.place: Tobol river, between Tobolsk and Tyumen
passages.gloss: Going up the Tobol river from Tobolsk to Tyumen, the embassy's boats were towed the whole way by Tatars. In Tulishen's own Chinese words, there was no towpath, the men waded through mud until their legs bled, and the Russian soldiers kept whipping them until the envoy, unable to watch, told them to stop. It is one of the few moments where the author shows personal feeling.
passages.quote: 途中皆搭搭拉之人挽縴岸傍林木叢宻無縴路俱行泥水之中兩足肌膚破損血水淋漓俄羅斯兵丁猶加笞楚催促余不忍視呵責方止
passages.translation: All along the way the Ta-ta-la (Tatar) people hauled the towropes. The banks were thick with trees and there was no towpath, so they all walked in mud and water; the skin of their legs and feet was torn and blood ran down, yet the Russian soldiers still flogged them on. I could not bear to watch, and only when I rebuked them did they stop.
passages.speaker: Tulishen (Chinese text, Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)
passages.caution: Staunton's English version of the same scene is on T0019 n156 (p.112).

passages.headline: Kazan in 1714: a wooden city of Russians and Tatars
passages.gloss: Tulishen describes Kazan, the old Tatar khanate capital, as a Russian provincial seat: no stone walls but wooden palisades with eight gates, a ditch and wooden spikes, three public buildings of wood, five brick churches, and two-storey wooden houses for about 5000 families. The people were a mix of Russians, Tatars, Cheremis and Torghuts.
passages.quote: Instead of regular walls, Cazan is surrounded with wooden palisades. It has 8 gates … Within the city there is a market, three public edifices of wood, and five churches built of brick. The population consists of about 5000 families. The dwelling houses are all built of wood, and raised to the height of two stories. The inhabitants are a mixture of Russians, Tartars, Tzeremish, and Tourgouths.
passages.speaker: Tulishen (translated from the Chinese by George Thomas Staunton, 1821)

passages.headline: Tobolsk: a timber capital with two brick buildings
passages.gloss: The capital of Russian Siberia, as Tulishen saw it, had no walls; about a thousand families lived in houses of large timber, with two big brick public buildings and wooden government offices, and a lower town of about 2000 families by the river. It is a plain eyewitness picture of Tobolsk as a Russian timber town seven years after its first stone kremlin was begun.
passages.quote: It contains above a thousand families, who live in houses constructed of large timber. There are also two large public buildings of brick, and several Government offices built of wood in the usual manner. On the low ground, along the banks of the river, there is another portion of the town, built also of wood, and containing above 2000 families.
passages.speaker: Tulishen (translated from the Chinese by George Thomas Staunton, 1821)

passages.headline: Arriving at Ayuki Khan's camp by Lake Manuto
passages.place: Lower Volga steppe (Kalmyk lands east of the Volga)
passages.gloss: After ten days' ride from Saratov the envoys reached the headquarters of Ayuki Khan, not a town but a camp 'at present' on the shore of a lake. The Torghut nobles, priests and chiefs lined the road with their followers, displayed their flocks and herds, set out tables of food, and knelt to offer provisions. The next day the envoys were received in the khan's 'great tent of ceremony'.
passages.quote: we at length arrived at the head-quarters of A-yu-ke, the Khan of the Tourgouth nation, which are situated at present upon the banks of the lake Ma-nu-to. … Their flocks and herds were also collected and displayed, and tables, covered with provisions, laid out before us. All the people had come out to a very considerable distance to meet us
passages.speaker: Tulishen (translated from the Chinese by George Thomas Staunton, 1821)

passages.headline: A Kalmyk khan asks if Manchus and Mongols were once one people
passages.gloss: In his long interview Ayuki Khan asked the envoys a question about origins: Manchus and Mongols look so alike that they must spring from one source, so how did they become separate nations? He asked them to put it to the emperor. The envoys promised to do so. He went on to ask about Manchu writing and why there were 'old' and 'new' Manchus.
passages.quote: "The Mantchoos and the Mongals bear a great resemblance to each other: I imagine therefore that they sprang anciently from the same origin. But how has it happened that they have since formed separate states and nations? The causes of this, are no doubt well known to your Emperor.
passages.speaker: Ayuki Khan, as reported by Tulishen (Staunton translation, 1821)

passages.headline: A khan who 'received the edict kneeling'
passages.gloss: Tulishen writes that Ayuki Khan knelt to receive the Chinese emperor's letter and turned north to wish him well. The translator Staunton adds a sharp footnote: it is very unlikely that an independent prince would humble himself so in his own court; the Chinese claim to rule the whole world simply required every letter from the emperor to be described as received on bended knee.
passages.quote: Nothing certainly can be more improbable than that an independent prince, in the midst of his own court, should have voluntarily subjected himself to such a humiliation; … but it seems that the assumed attribute of universal sovereignty, which occasions every communication from the Emperor of China to claim the authority of an Edict, also requires that such an edict should be supposed to have been received
passages.speaker: George Thomas Staunton (translator's footnote)
passages.caution: The translator doubts the author's official version of events.

passages.headline: The mammoth: a giant beast that lives under the earth
passages.people: Russians and Siberian natives (reported to the envoys)
passages.gloss: Near Yeniseisk the envoys heard of a huge animal in the coldest north that burrowed underground and died if exposed to sun and air. Its white, ivory-like bones were dug from river mud and carved by Russians into cups and combs, and its flesh was eaten against fever. The foreign name was Ma-mien-tou-va (mamont), the Chinese called it kee-shoo (the 'hidden rat'). Staunton notes that John Bell heard the same tale and that frozen mammoth flesh had since been found.
passages.quote: In the very coldest parts of this northern country, a species of animal is found which burrows under the earth, and which dies if it is at all exposed at any time to the sun and air. Its bones are very white and shining, like ivory. … The Russians collect the bones of this animal, in order to make cups, saucers, combs
passages.speaker: Tulishen (translated from the Chinese by George Thomas Staunton, 1821)
passages.caution: Hearsay reported by the envoys; the belief that the animal lives underground is a folk explanation for frozen mammoth remains.

passages.headline: The envoy himself: a man 'from Ye-ho in Tartary'
passages.gloss: Tulishen opens by introducing himself as coming originally from Ye-ho in Tartary, meaning the Yehe lands of the Manchu (Jurchen) confederation north-east of China. John Bell, who met him in 1720, called him 'a Mandshu Tartar by birth'. In this book the Chinese court's envoy to the 'Tartar' Kalmyks was himself a 'Tartar', a reminder of how loosely Europeans used the word.
passages.quote: am originally from the country of Ye-ho in Tartary. My ancestor, O-yen … was a man honorably distinguished in the country of Ye-ho by his fidelity and exertions.
passages.speaker: Tulishen (translated from the Chinese by George Thomas Staunton, 1821)

passages.headline: 'Not so much as a single house' in all Mongolia
passages.gloss: Staunton footnotes the embassy's entry into Mongol lands with John Bell's description of the Mongols. Bell says that in all Mongolia there was not a single house: everyone, even the prince and the high priest at Urga, lived in tents and moved with their herds. It is a clear eyewitness statement, from a Scot who crossed the region, that the Mongol heartland had no built settlements in his day.
passages.quote: It is very remarkable that in all the vast dominions of Mongalia, there is not so much as a single house to be seen. All the people, even the prince and high priest, live constantly in tents, and remove all their cattle from place to place as conveniency requires.
passages.speaker: John Bell of Antermony, quoted in a footnote by the translator G. T. Staunton
passages.caution: These are Bell's words from his own journey, not Tulishen's.

passages.headline: Kalmyks who pity people tied to one place
passages.gloss: Another footnote quotes Bell on the Dzungar Kalmyks of Tsewang Rabdan (the 'Kontaysha'), who could field 100,000 horsemen. Bell, relying on Russians who had visited, says they lived in tents all year and found it amusing to pity settled people who had to work for a living, which they considered 'the greatest slavery'.
passages.quote: These Tartars live in tents, all the year, removing from place to place, as called by necessity or inclination. This is the most ancient and pleasant manner of life. It is entertaining to hear them commiserate those who are confined to one place of abode, and obliged to support themselves by labour, which they reckon the greatest slavery.
passages.speaker: John Bell of Antermony, quoted in a footnote by the translator G. T. Staunton
passages.caution: Bell's information came from Russian officials who had been sent to the Kontaysha.

passages.headline: The Kuban Tartars, raiders subject to the Turks
passages.gloss: Describing the Torghut country between the Volga and the Yaik, Tulishen places to the west the Ho-pang, which Staunton identifies as the Cuban Tartars, also called Mang-vu-te (Mangyt, a Nogai clan name). He says they were subjects of the Turkish sultan and constantly raided both Russians and Torghuts. It shows a Chinese writer mapping the Nogai Tatars by their own clan name.
passages.quote: lies the country of the Ho-pang (Cuban Tartars) otherwise called Mang-vu-te, a nation subject to Kung-ke-eur Khan, king of the Tu-li-ye-se-ko, (Turks). This people are constantly in the practice of coming across the boundary, in order to attack and plunder their Russian and Tourgouth neighbours.
passages.speaker: Tulishen (translated from the Chinese by George Thomas Staunton, 1821)
passages.caution: The identification 'Cuban Tartars' is Staunton's gloss in brackets.

passages.headline: How a Mongol tent is built
passages.gloss: Huc visited Mongol families and describes their tent exactly: a cylinder about three feet high topped by a cone, a folding lattice of crossed bars below, a ring of poles meeting at the top like umbrella ribs, a thick covering, and a low folding door with a beam across the bottom. The next page describes the smoke-hole flap of felt and the men's and women's sides inside.
passages.quote: The Mongol tent, for about three feet from the ground, is cylindrical in form. It then becomes conical, like a pointed hat. The woodwork of the tent is composed below of a trellis-work of crossed bars, which fold up and expand at pleasure. Above these, a circle of poles, fixed in the trellis-work, meets at the top, like the sticks of an umbrella.
passages.speaker: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)

passages.headline: 'No towns, no edifices' in the land of grass
passages.gloss: Crossing the prairies of the Chakhar, Huc sums up what makes Tartary unlike anywhere else: no towns, no buildings, no crafts, no farming and no forests, only endless grassland, lakes, rivers and mountains. A page later he describes encampments of tents appearing and vanishing as herders moved to fresh pasture.
passages.quote: There are no towns, no edifices, no arts, no industry, no cultivation, no forests; everywhere it is prairie, sometimes interrupted by immense lakes, by majestic rivers, by rugged and imposing mountains; sometimes spreading out into vast limitless plains.
passages.speaker: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)
passages.caution: A literary generalisation; elsewhere Huc describes lamaseries, trading towns and ruins in the same region.

passages.headline: A Mongol: 'We Mongols are formed for living in tents'
passages.gloss: In Gechekten, where Chinese settlers had turned grassland into poor sandy fields, the priests asked a Mongol rider why his people did not farm. He answered that Mongols were made for tents and herds; since they had started farming and building houses they had grown poor, and the Chinese (Kitat) had taken their land, herds and houses. It is a Mongol's own verdict on houses versus tents.
passages.quote: "We Mongols are formed for living in tents, and pasturing cattle. So long as we kept to that in the kingdom of Gechekten, we were rich and happy. Now, ever since the Mongols have set themselves to cultivating the land, and building houses, they have become poor. The Kitats (Chinese) have taken possession of the country; flocks, herds, lands, houses, all have passed into their hands.
passages.speaker: A Mongol horseman, as reported by Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)

passages.headline: An abandoned city half buried in the soil
passages.place: Inner Mongolia (between Tolon-Noor and the Blue Town)
passages.gloss: On the road to the Blue Town (Hohhot) the priests came upon a large abandoned walled city with towers and four gates facing the cardinal points. It was three-quarters buried by wind-blown soil and covered in turf, so that streets and buildings showed only as bumps in the ground. The only person there, a young Mongol shepherd, knew nothing except that it was called the Old Town.
passages.quote: we came, in the solitude, upon an imposing and majestic monument of antiquity, … a large city utterly abandoned. Its turreted ramparts, its watch towers, its four great gates, facing the four cardinal points, were all there perfect, in preservation, except that, besides being three-fourths buried in the soil, they were covered with a thick coating of turf.
passages.speaker: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)
passages.caution: Huc blames 'gradual accumulations of wind-borne soil' for the burial; he does not suggest any flood or catastrophe.

passages.headline: Who built the lost cities of Mongolia
passages.gloss: Reflecting on the Old Town, Huc says such ruined cities are common in Mongolia and that their story is unknown locally. His best guess, from Chinese annals, is that the Mongols built many large cities in 'Northern Tartary' while they ruled China, and that after their expulsion the Ming emperor Yongle burned their towns in three campaigns deep into the desert.
passages.quote: the probabilities are, that they date no earlier back than the 13th century, the period when the Mongols rendered themselves masters of the Chinese empire … During their domination, say the Chinese annals, they erected in Northern Tartary many large and powerful cities. … the Emperor Young-Lo, who desired to exterminate the Tartars, invaded their country, and burned their towns
passages.speaker: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)
passages.caution: Huc's explanation is an educated guess from Chinese histories, not local tradition.

passages.headline: A city built for a Mongol prince by imperial slaves
passages.people: Khalkha Mongols; Manchu imperial family; Chinese artisans
passages.gloss: The Qianlong emperor married a daughter to a Khalkha prince, who hated court life and longed for his tents. As a compromise the emperor carved out land in the Chakhar, 'built for him' a small handsome city, and gave him a hundred families of slaves skilled in Chinese arts and crafts. The princess got her court; the prince could go back to the tent. Huc credits the city to the emperor and Chinese craftsmen, not to the Mongols.
passages.quote: He dismembered a portion of the Tchakar, and assigned it to the Mongol prince; he built for him, amid these solitudes, a small but handsome city, and presented to him a hundred families of slaves skilled in the arts and manufactures of China.
passages.speaker: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)

passages.headline: Cave houses dug by Chinese settlers
passages.gloss: Caught in a freezing storm in the Ordos, the priests found a ravine lined with man-made caves, neatly plastered, with windows, stoves and heated beds (kang). Huc explains that Chinese settlers in Tartary dig such homes into hard hillsides. A Mongol sheltering in the next cave told them he had known the Chinese families who dug them, and that the local Mongols had driven them out two years before for encroaching and stealing.
passages.quote: not simple caves formed by nature, but fine, spacious apartments excavated by the hand of man. … When the Chinese establish themselves anywhere in Tartary, if they find mountains, the earth of which is hard and solid, they excavate caverns in their sides. These habitations are cheaper than houses, and less exposed to the irregularity of the seasons.
passages.speaker: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)

passages.headline: The Great Kouren: a monastery city of 30,000 lamas
passages.people: Khalkha Mongols and pilgrims of many peoples
passages.gloss: Huc describes the Great Kouren (Urga, today's Ulaanbaatar) on the Tula river: temples with gilded roofs, 30,000 lamas, and a plain always covered with pilgrims' tents from every people of the Qing north, including 'Fish-skin Tartars' from the Amur and Torghuts. The next page adds a fortified Chinese trading post of wooden and mud huts, where everything was priced in bricks of tea.
passages.quote: Thirty thousand Lamas dwell in the Lamasery itself, or in smaller Lamaseries erected about it. The plain adjoining it is always covered with the tents of the pilgrims who resort hither from all parts to worship Buddha. Here you find the U-Pi-Ta-Dze, or "Fish-skin Tartars," encamped beside the Torgot Tartars
passages.speaker: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)

passages.headline: Ningxia, a Tartar capital ruined by Genghis Khan
passages.gloss: Passing through the half-deserted city of Ning-Hia, Huc gives its history: a prince 'of Tartar race' from Tou-Pa founded a small state near the Yellow River in the tenth century with Ning-Hia as its capital (the Tangut Xi Xia kingdom). It flourished for two centuries until 1227, when it was ruined by Genghis Khan. Here 'Tartar' covers the Tanguts too.
passages.quote: In the tenth century, a prince of Tartar race, a native of Tou-Pa, … having induced a few hordes to follow him, came, and formed, despite the Chinese, a small state not far from the banks of the Yellow River. He chose for his capital, Hia-Tcheou, which afterwards came to be called Ning-Hia. … in 1227, it was involved in the common ruin, by the victories of Tchinggiskhan
passages.speaker: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)

passages.headline: Women do all the work, men ride
passages.gloss: Huc is blunt about the division of labour: Mongol women milk the cows, make butter and cheese, fetch water, gather and dry dung fuel, make clothes, tan skins and full cloth. The men's work is herding on horseback, which Huc calls more amusement than labour. The page opens with the Chinese nickname Tsao-Ta-Dze, 'Stinking Tartars'.
passages.quote: Among the Tartars, household and family cares rest entirely upon the woman; it is she who milks the cows, and prepares the butter, cheese, &c.; who goes, no matter how far, to draw water; who collects the argol fuel, dries it, and piles it around the tent. The making of clothes, the tanning of skins, the fulling of cloth, all appertains to her
passages.speaker: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)

passages.headline: Marriage as a contract of sale
passages.gloss: Huc says Mongol marriages were arranged by parents through go-betweens, and that the bride's family was paid in horses, oxen, sheep, cloth, butter, brandy and flour. The Mongols themselves spoke of 'buying' and 'selling' a daughter. He goes on to describe a mock fight at the bride's door, a gallop to the new tent, polygamy and easy divorce.
passages.quote: The thing is indeed very clearly expressed in their language; they say, "I have bought for my son the daughter of so and so." "We have sold our daughter to such and such a family." The marriage contract is thus simply a contract of sale.
passages.speaker: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)

passages.headline: A minstrel's song: 'Return, O Timour!'
passages.gloss: At a feast for the Moon festival a Mongol bard (toolholos) played a three-stringed fiddle and, at the priests' request, sang the 'Invocation to Timour', a lament for lost greatness that begs a hero to return and make the Mongols warriors again. Huc reproduces it in translation. It shows nineteenth-century Mongols remembering their imperial past in song.
passages.quote: "When the divine Timour dwelt within our tents, the Mongol nation was redoubtable and warlike; its least movements made the earth bend; its mere look froze with fear the ten thousand peoples upon whom the sun shines.
passages.speaker: A Mongol minstrel, as rendered by Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)
passages.caution: Huc gives a free French rendering of an oral song; the 'Timour' of the song may not be the historical Tamerlane.

passages.headline: Brick tea, 'the grand luxury of the Tartars'
passages.gloss: Huc explains 'Tartar tea': coarse tea leaves pressed into bricks, broken off, boiled until red, salted and mixed with milk. He says the Tartars (with the Russians) were its only consumers. Elsewhere he notes that at Urga bricks of tea served as money.
passages.quote: the coarser leaves, with which are mixed up the smaller tendrils, are pressed together in a mould, in the form and of the size of the ordinary house brick. Thus prepared, it becomes an article of considerable commerce, under the designation of Tartar-tea, the Tartars being its exclusive consumers, with the exception of the Russians
passages.speaker: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)

passages.headline: Burning the dead in an earthen pyramid
passages.gloss: Huc describes several Mongol funerals: nomads left the dead on hilltops or in ravines for eagles and wolves, while rich families built a pyramid-shaped earth furnace around the standing body, burned it, and had the Grand Lama knead the powdered bones with meal into cakes that were stacked and placed in a small tower.
passages.quote: The richer Tartars sometimes burn their dead with great solemnity. A large furnace of earth is constructed in a pyramidical form. Just before it is completed, the body is placed inside, standing, surrounded with combustibles.
passages.speaker: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)

passages.headline: Royal tombs with poisoned children and arrow traps
passages.gloss: Huc passes on a lurid report about Tartar kings' burials: a brick building with statues, a central cavern full of treasure, children killed with mercury to keep their faces fresh and set up around the corpse holding the king's pipe and snuff, and a spring-loaded battery of bows to shoot any grave robber. He says bow-makers sold such traps and that Chinese sometimes bought them to guard their houses.
passages.quote: These monstrous interments sometimes cost the lives of a great number of slaves. They take children of both sexes, remarkable for their beauty, and make them swallow mercury till they are suffocated; in this way they preserve, they say, the freshness and ruddiness of their countenance, so as to make them appear still alive.
passages.speaker: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)
passages.caution: Huc did not see this; 'they say' marks it as hearsay, and it echoes older Chinese tomb legends.

passages.headline: The mooncake massacre of 1368
passages.gloss: Huc tells the Chinese tradition behind the Moon festival: in about 1368 the Chinese rose against the Mongol dynasty, passing the signal in letters hidden in the festival cakes, and killed the Mongol soldiers billeted in their homes. When the priests told this to a Mongol family, the old man wept and said a day of vengeance would come. The massacre story is a legend, not established history.
passages.quote: The signal was given by a letter concealed in the cakes which, as we have stated, are on that day, mutually interchanged throughout the country. The massacre was effected, and the Tartar army dispersed in the houses of the Chinese, utterly annihilated. This catastrophe put an end to the Mongol domination
passages.speaker: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)
passages.caution: A Chinese folk tradition that Huc repeats as history.

passages.headline: Eastern Tartars and Western Tartars
passages.gloss: Huc sets out how he uses the word: following the Tartars and Chinese themselves, he divides 'the Tartar people' into Eastern Tartars (Toung-Ta-Dze), the Manchus, and Western Tartars (Si-Ta-Dze), the Mongols. He dismisses European map labels such as 'Kalmoukia' and 'Great and Little Bukharia' as 'purely imaginary'.
passages.quote: we will divide the Tartar people into Eastern Tartars (Toung-Ta-Dze), or Mantchous, and Western Tartars (Si-Ta-Dze), or Mongols. … Great and Little Boukaria, Kalmoukia, Great and Little Thibet … all these denominations seem to us purely imaginary.
passages.speaker: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)

passages.headline: Manchu soldiers who no longer speak Manchu
passages.gloss: At the garrison town of Koukou-Khoton (Hohhot), Huc found that the 10,000 'Mantchou Tartars' stationed there hardly spoke their own language. Two centuries after conquering China, he says, the Manchus had become Chinese in manners, language and even homeland.
passages.quote: The soldiers of the New Town of Koukou Khoton are Mantchou Tartars; but if you did not previously know the fact, you would scarcely suspect it from hearing them speak. Amongst them there is perhaps not a single man who understands the language of his own country.
passages.speaker: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)

passages.headline: Tibet: 'the kingdom of dwellers in houses'
passages.gloss: The Capuchin della Penna, who lived in Lhasa for many years, explains the name Tibet as a Tatar (Mongol) word: Tangat katzar, which he says means the kingdom of people who live in houses, because the Tatars lived in tents of felt or yak-hair cloth while Tibetans lived in houses. Whatever the real etymology, it shows how people at the time drew the line between the two peoples by their dwellings.
passages.quote: The word Tibet is a Tatar corruption, the proper term being Thobot, or Tangat katzar. Tangat means dwellers in houses, and katzar country or kingdom; so the whole expression signifies "the kingdom of dwellers in houses," the Tatars dwelling in tents of felt, or of a coarse material woven from the hair of the yak or hairy ox, and the Tibetans in houses.
passages.speaker: Francesco Orazio della Penna, Capuchin missionary (English version in Markham's appendix, from Klaproth's edition)
passages.caution: The etymology is della Penna's and is doubtful; the contrast in ways of living is the useful part.

passages.headline: Chess with the Kalmuks at Teshu Lumbo
passages.people: Kalmuks (Mongol pilgrims; Markham glosses them as Sokpas of north-east Tibet)
passages.gloss: Bogle's happiest hours at the Panchen Lama's monastery were spent playing chess with a party of Kalmuk pilgrims. He notes their rules (no castling, no stalemate) and how they played as a team: whenever a 'Siberian' sat down to play, two or three friends put their 'great bare heads together' over every move. Bogle learned to recruit his own team of Tatars and beat them.
passages.quote: In my first trials of skill with the Tatars, I used often to come off loser. For when a Siberian sits down to chess, he gets two or three of his countrymen to assist him; they lay all their great bare heads together canvassing and consulting about every move.
passages.speaker: George Bogle (edited by Clements R. Markham, 1876)

passages.headline: Kalmuk pilgrims bring silver, furs and camels
passages.gloss: While Bogle stayed at Teshu Lumbo a large Kalmuk caravan arrived to worship the Panchen Lama, offering silver, furs, silk and dromedaries. They stayed a month, went on to Lhasa, and then went home, about three months' journey north. Elsewhere Bogle says Kalmuk tribes came every year with camels loaded with Siberian furs and hides.
passages.quote: Among the rest of his votaries were a large caravan of Kalmuks, who offered up to his shrine talents of silver, furs, pieces of silk, and dromedaries. They remained about a month at Teshu Lumbo, and then proceeded to Lhasa, where, having spent about ten days, they returned to their own country, which was about three months' journey to the northward.
passages.speaker: George Bogle (edited by Clements R. Markham, 1876)

passages.headline: A Tatar gift that made Bogle look Russian
passages.gloss: An eccentric official decided that English dress was exactly like Russian dress, because Bogle wore a tunic and square cap that the Lama had been given by 'some Turki Tatars'. Markham adds a footnote calling this 'an instance of the confusion caused by the indiscriminate use of the word Tatar or Tartar'.
passages.quote: the tunic which I wore, and also my cap, the cut of which was four-square instead of being round, had been made a present of to the Lama by some Turki Tatars.
passages.speaker: George Bogle (edited by Clements R. Markham, 1876)

passages.headline: The Torghut flight to China, as told by the Panchen Lama
passages.people: Torghut Kalmyks (a tribe of Tatars subject to Russia)
passages.gloss: The Panchen Lama told Bogle he had been busy with Kalmuk business, and explained that some years before 'a tribe of Tatars' subject to Russia had gone over to China (the Torghut exodus from the Volga in 1771), that the Chinese emperor had imprisoned Russian envoys sent to reclaim them, and that war might follow. It shows news of the steppe travelling through Tibetan religious networks.
passages.quote: He told me that he had been so much engaged with some Kalmuks, and had so much to write on their account, that he had not been able to see me sooner; that several years ago a tribe of Tatars, who were subject to Russia, had gone over to the Chinese
passages.speaker: The Panchen (Teshu) Lama, as reported by George Bogle (edited by Markham, 1876)

passages.headline: Fighting on horseback 'the Kalmuk way'
passages.gloss: The Panchen Lama told Bogle that the Lhasa regent did not want Gorkha envoys to enter Tibet in case they learned 'the manner of the Kalmuks fighting on horseback', which Tibetans practised too, and showed him the style with his hands. It hints at how Mongol cavalry methods were treated as a military secret.
passages.quote: Gesub, among other reasons, objects to their coming into Tibet lest they should learn the manner of the Kalmuks fighting on horseback, which is practised in this country (describing it at the same time by motions), and should teach it to the Gorkha Rajah's people.
passages.speaker: The Panchen (Teshu) Lama, as reported by George Bogle (edited by Markham, 1876)

passages.headline: Holy relics sold among the Tatar tribes
passages.gloss: Warren Hastings's briefing memorandum for Bogle passes on what he had been told about Tibetan Buddhism: each Tatar tribe had its own living Buddha (Kutuktu), all of whom deferred to the Dalai Lama, 'so that his excrements are sold as charms at a great price among all the Tatar tribes of this religion'. It is a startling piece of hearsay from a governor who had never been there.
passages.quote: Among the different Tatar tribes which are of this religion, there are persons called Ku-tchuck-tus, who are likewise esteemed living Fos. … it is even pretended that the Ku-tchuck-tus admit a superiority in the Dalai Lama, so that his excrements are sold as charms at a great price among all the Tatar tribes of this religion.
passages.speaker: Warren Hastings (memorandum on Tibet, 1774)
passages.caution: Hearsay collected in Calcutta; Hastings himself hedges with 'it is even pretended'.

passages.headline: Every northern empire was a 'Tatar confederacy'
passages.people: Tuoba, Turks and Mongols, all called Tatars
passages.gloss: In his memorandum Hastings sketches Tibetan history from Chinese sources and calls every northern power a 'Tatar confederacy': the Typa (Tuoba) in the fourth century, the Turks in the eighth and ninth, and on the next page the Mongols under Möngke Khan. It shows 'Tatar' used as a catch-all for any steppe people in the 1770s.
passages.quote: In the fourth century, the Tatar confederacy of the Typa subdued the north and east of Tibet. In the eighth and ninth centuries, when the Tatar confederacy of the Turks became feeble, the power of those nations, which now acknowledge the supremacy of the Dalai Lama, was very great.
passages.speaker: Warren Hastings (memorandum on Tibet, 1774)

passages.headline: Dzungar 'Tatars' seize Lhasa, 1717
passages.people: Dzungar (Oirat) Mongols; Qing army of Chinese and Tatars
passages.gloss: Della Penna records how the 'Gionkar Tatars' (Dzungars) invaded Tibet, plundered it and took Lhasa in November and December 1717, and how in 1720 a Qing army of 107,000 Chinese and 30,000 Tatars retook the city and installed a new Dalai Lama. Before this, he says, Tibet had a 'Tatar king' from the Kokonor chiefs as its protector. Here Tatars are the armies competing for Lhasa.
passages.quote: the Chinese army, composed of 107,000 Chinese soldiers and 30,000 Tatars, retook the metropolis of Lhasa, and made themselves masters of the whole of the kingdom of Tibet, on the 20th September, and overthrew completely the Gionkar Tatars, who had treacherously invaded Tibet, and with the connivance of a great part of its people, had plundered the country, and taken Lhasa, in November and December, 1717.
passages.speaker: Francesco Orazio della Penna, Capuchin missionary (English version in Markham's appendix, from Klaproth's edition)
passages.caution: Della Penna was in Tibet in these years; the troop figures are his and may be exaggerated.

passages.headline: A king's palace amid Tatar tents at Dam
passages.gloss: Describing the northern province of Chang, della Penna says that at Dam, the summer seat of the Tatar king of Tibet, there was nothing but the king's palace; everyone else, mostly Tatars and some Tibetans, lived in tents of felt and of cloth woven from hair. Beyond that, at Nakchu, there was a last fortress and again only tents.
passages.quote: in Dam there is nothing else but the palace belonging to the King and his court, the remainder of the inhabitants (which are mostly Tatars and the other Tibetans) dwelling in tents of felt and of cloth woven out of hair. Two days distant from Dam is Nak chu ka, where is the last fortress of Tibet, but no other dwellings except tents
passages.speaker: Francesco Orazio della Penna, Capuchin missionary (English version in Markham's appendix, from Klaproth's edition)

passages.headline: The Tatars' mare's-milk beer
passages.gloss: Della Penna compares Tibetan barley brandy with 'the beer which the Tatars make from the milk of mares', which he says looks and tastes like water but is surprisingly strong. It is a passing but clear reference to Mongol distilled milk spirit (arkhi) or kumiss.
passages.quote: a kind of brandy (mixed with the beer referred to), which does not differ greatly from the beer which the Tatars make from the milk of mares, and which is like water in appearance and taste, but is of considerable strength.
passages.speaker: Francesco Orazio della Penna, Capuchin missionary (English version in Markham's appendix, from Klaproth's edition)

passages.headline: Kalmuk Tatars with 'portable cities'
passages.gloss: The appendix summarises the letters of the Jesuit Johann Grueber, who crossed from China to Lhasa in 1661. Past the Yellow River his party entered the Kalmuk desert, whose people raided caravans and 'at certain seasons settle with their portable cities' on riverbanks. Their houses were tents of plaited sticks covered with coarse woollen cloth tied with cords, and the Jesuits sketched the people they met.
passages.quote: they immediately entered that vast and barren desert of Kalmuk, inhabited by the Kalmuk Tatars (the Eluths or Tatars of Koko-nor), who rove up and down it to rob the caravans, and at certain seasons settle with their portable cities on the banks of the rivers. … Their habitations are tents made with small sticks twisted or plaited together, and covered with a coarse woollen stuff bound together with cords.
passages.speaker: Account of Johann Grueber's travels, from Astley's Collection of Voyages (reprinted in Markham's appendix)
passages.caution: A compiler's paraphrase of Grueber's letters as abstracted by Athanasius Kircher; the bracketed gloss is part of the printed text.

passages.headline: Manning's 'Tatar mandarin' at Lhasa
passages.gloss: Thomas Manning, travelling to Lhasa in disguise, was dismayed to learn that the chief imperial official there was 'the identical Tatar chieftain' who had been disgraced at Canton over the British occupation of Macao in 1808. Throughout his diary 'the Tatar' means this Manchu amban, whom Manning also calls 'the Tatar dog'.
passages.quote: I had learnt now, to my great sorrow and discomfort, that the chief mandarin at Lhasa was the identical Tatar chieftain who had been disgraced at Canton for his management during the Bengal expedition to Macao. That he was a man of a particular suspicious temper, detested at Lhasa, and that he certainly would give us all the trouble in his power.
passages.speaker: Thomas Manning (diary, edited by Markham, 1876)

passages.headline: The Kalmak Tartars once occupied Leh
passages.gloss: Moorcroft summarises Ladakh's history as he heard it: about 150 years earlier the 'Kalmak Tartars' invaded and occupied Leh, and the raja fled to Kashmir to ask the Mughal governor for help. The Mughals drove the Tartars out on condition the raja became a Muslim, and a mosque was built in Leh that still stood in Moorcroft's day (next page).
passages.quote: About a century and a half ago, the Kalmak Tartars invaded Ladakh, and occupied Lé, and the Raja flew to Kashmir, and implored the aid of Ibrahim Khan, the governor of that province in the reign of Aurangzeb.
passages.speaker: William Moorcroft (edited by H. H. Wilson, 1841)
passages.caution: Local history reported to Moorcroft; the invasion matches the Tibet-Mongol war with Ladakh of 1679 to 1684.

passages.headline: Leh: houses of unburnt brick and poplar beams
passages.people: Ladakhis (people of what Moorcroft called Hither Tatary)
passages.gloss: Moorcroft describes the walled capital of Ladakh: towers on the hills, a labyrinth of streets, and houses of one to three storeys built mostly of large unburnt bricks, a few of stone, whitewashed outside. On the next page he explains the flat roofs of poplar trunks, willow shoots, straw and earth, which leaked in rain.
passages.quote: The walls are in a few instances wholly, or in part of stone, but in general they are built with large unburnt bricks: they are whitened outside with lime, but remain of their original colour inside.
passages.speaker: William Moorcroft (edited by H. H. Wilson, 1841)
passages.caution: Ladakhis are Tibetan, not Turkic or Mongol; they count here only because Moorcroft placed Ladakh in 'Hither Tatary'.

passages.headline: 'Tartar cookery' on the road to Ladakh
passages.gloss: Moorcroft saw his Lahouli porters cook a sheep that had died in the night: skinned, cut up and boiled whole in a big cauldron with all the innards, together with cakes of flour mixed with the blood. He calls it 'Tartar cookery' and admits he did not care to join in.
passages.quote: We had an opportunity here of witnessing Tartar cookery on a more sumptuous scale than usual, but it was not of a character to invite a participation in the meal. A sheep belonging to some of the carriers having died in the night, the carcase was skinned and cut up, and boiled in a large cauldron, together with all the viscera
passages.speaker: William Moorcroft (edited by H. H. Wilson, 1841)

passages.headline: The people of Spiti are 'completely of Tartar appearance'
passages.gloss: On his side trip to Spiti (Piti), Trebeck described the people as 'completely of Tartar appearance in form and face', then went on to their dress, drinking, and the braided hair of the women decorated with amber and coral. It shows 'Tartar' used by British travellers for any Tibetan or Central Asian looking highlander.
passages.quote: The people of Piti are completely of Tartar appearance in form and face; the men are less robust and better grown than those more to the north, and the women are far from good looking.
passages.speaker: George Trebeck (journal, edited by H. H. Wilson, 1841)
passages.caution: A physical stereotype, not an ethnic identification.

passages.headline: Kalmak Tatars moved to Ili as horse breeders
passages.gloss: From merchants' reports Moorcroft learned that many 'Kalmak Tatars' had once lived around Khotan but had been deported by the Chinese to the Ili valley, where some 200,000 families bred cattle, camels and horses and paid one head in a hundred as tax. They brought ten to twenty thousand geldings a year to Ili for sale.
passages.quote: A considerable portion of the population of Khoten consisted formerly of Kalmak Tatars, but it is said that when the Chinese subjugated the province, they deported the Kalmaks to the cities which collectively constitute the modern city of Ila, on the river of the same name, and to the adjacent districts.
passages.speaker: William Moorcroft (edited by H. H. Wilson, 1841)
passages.caution: Secondhand information; the population figure is a trader's estimate.

passages.headline: A Kazak camp of felt tents and reed huts
passages.place: Amu Darya (Oxus) crossing, south of Karshi
passages.gloss: Just across the Oxus, Moorcroft passed through a Kazak owal (aul, a tent village) of khirgahs (felt tents) and kappahs, round huts of mats and reeds with conical tops. Saddled horses waited at the doors, and the cattle were stabled in pits dug in the ground and roofed with branches, grass and sand.
passages.quote: we passed through an owal, or station of Khirgahs and Kappahs, or circular huts of mats and reeds, with a conical top. Horses stood saddled at the doors of the tents, and mares and foals, and many camels, were grazing in the adjoining jangal. The cows were stabled in holes made in the ground, roofed with branches of trees and grass, and covered with sand and bushes.
passages.speaker: William Moorcroft (edited by H. H. Wilson, 1841)

passages.headline: Tash Kurghan: domed houses of clay and sun-dried brick
passages.gloss: Moorcroft describes the Uzbek-ruled market town of Tash Kurghan: about 20,000 one-storey houses of clay and sun-dried brick, domed 'in the usual fashion of the country', each in its own walled yard with fruit trees, along straight streets that crossed at right angles with water running down them.
passages.quote: Tash Kurghan is about three miles in circumference, and may comprise about twenty thousand houses. They are built of clay and sun-dried bricks, of one story, with domes in the usual fashion of the country, and each stands by itself in a walled enclosure, often containing fruit-trees.
passages.speaker: William Moorcroft (edited by H. H. Wilson, 1841)

passages.headline: Balkh, 'mother of cities', in ruins
passages.gloss: Approaching Balkh, once capital of Bactria, Moorcroft passed ruins said to be the elephant stables of the old kings of Turkestan, then entered through a broken gate into streets of rubbish, broken bricks and crumbling clay walls. On the next pages he says only one covered bazaar was still inhabited, the population was under a thousand families, and there were no relics of antiquity apart from one tiled shrine.
passages.quote: A short distance in advance brought us to the ruins of some buildings, said to have been the elephant stables of the kings of Turkistan: similar remains accompanied the road to the wall of the modern town, which we entered by a mean gateway, the folding-doors of which were off their hinges and lying in the mud, no insignificant type of neglect and decay.
passages.speaker: William Moorcroft (edited by H. H. Wilson, 1841)

passages.headline: Murad Beg of Kunduz, 'a Tartar' and a robber
passages.gloss: In his preface Wilson blames the failure of the expedition on Murad Beg, the Uzbek chief of Kunduz, whom he calls 'a Tartar of activity and ambition, but a barbarian and a robber'. Moorcroft's own journal (T0023, n459, p.446) quotes Murad Beg answering a plea to keep his word: 'What have I, what has an Uzbek to do with character?' Here 'Tartar' means an Uzbek.
passages.quote: His death, and the dissensions which ensued amongst his sons, transferred the ascendancy to Murad Beg, a Tartar of activity and ambition, but a barbarian and a robber.
passages.speaker: Horace Hayman Wilson (editor's preface, 1841)
passages.caution: The editor's judgment, written from Moorcroft's papers and hostile to Murad Beg.

passages.headline: Reading Gibbon on Genghis Khan to an Uzbek holy man
passages.gloss: Sheltering with a respected Uzbek pir (khaja) at Talikan, Moorcroft tried to translate into Persian the chapters of Gibbon's Decline and Fall about Genghis Khan and Timur. His host corrected the Persian style, was surprised a European knew so much about the 'Moguls', and admitted many facts were new to him. A European history of the Mongols thus travelled back to Central Asia.
passages.quote: Whilst under his protection, I attempted to render into Persian, for his use, the chapters of Gibbon which treat of Jangez Khan and Timur, in which the khaja took much interest, and corrected the style of the translation. He was much surprised that a European should have known so much of the history of the Moguls, and admitted that many of the facts were new to him
passages.speaker: William Moorcroft (edited by H. H. Wilson, 1841)

passages.headline: Where 'Tartary' begins on the ground
passages.gloss: Crossing the Akrobat pass north of Bamiyan, Burnes notes that he was leaving the kingdom of Kabul and entering Turkestan, 'which is denominated Tartary (more properly Tatary) by Europeans'. At the next village the first ruler was an Uzbek who paid his overlords partly in slaves taken in raids.
passages.quote: Toorkistan, which is denominated Tartary (more properly Tatary) by Europeans.
passages.speaker: Alexander Burnes (1834)

passages.headline: Beehive houses of the first 'Tartar' villages
passages.gloss: North of the Hindu Kush Burnes saw houses with domes instead of flat roofs, a hole in the top for smoke, so that a village looked like 'a cluster of large brown beehives'. He explains the style by the lack of timber. The people too had changed: conical skull-caps, long brown boots, and unveiled village women he calls fair and handsome, 'though they were Tartars'.
passages.quote: they have domes instead of terraces, with a hole in the roof as a chimney; so that a village has the appearance of a cluster of large brown beehives. The inhabitants adopt this style of building, as wood is scarce.
passages.speaker: Alexander Burnes (1834)

passages.headline: The caves and giant statues of Bamiyan
passages.gloss: At Bamiyan Burnes found a valley honeycombed for eight miles with caves, still home to most of the people, and the two great statues. He reports local traditions: the caves were the work of a king named Julal, the statues were made by 'Kaffirs' (infidels) about the time of Christ, or by the Pandavas of Hindu epic. He notes a theory that they were Buddhist, which the long ears made likely. He does not credit them to Tartars.
passages.quote: A detached hill in the middle of the valley is quite honeycombed by them … It is called the city of Ghoolghoola, and consists of a continued succession of caves in every direction, which are said to have been the work of a king named Julal.
passages.speaker: Alexander Burnes (1834)
passages.caution: The builders are given only as local tradition and conjecture.

passages.headline: A Turkmen tent that travels on two camels
passages.gloss: Invited into a Turkmen home at Sarakhs, Burnes found a khirgah (felt tent) twenty-five feet across with lattice sides, a roof of laths springing from a hoop three feet wide, and floors spread with felt and velvety carpets woven by the women. His host told him the whole house could go on one camel and its furniture on another.
passages.quote: The tent or khirgah was spacious, and had a diameter of about twenty-five feet. The sides were of lattice-work, and the roof was formed
passages.speaker: Alexander Burnes (1834)
passages.caution: The description continues on the next page (n83, p.60), where the host says the house and furniture travel on two camels.

passages.headline: A Turkmen camp of 150 black 'beehives'
passages.place: Turkmen desert (between the Murghab and the Oxus)
passages.gloss: On the desert road Burnes halted at a Turkmen oba (camp) of about 150 conical, movable huts called khirgahs, scattered on a rise with no order, like giant beehives with black roofs, with the children swarming like bees. A Turkmen settlement of this size was a whole mobile town.
passages.quote: It consisted of about 150 conical moveable huts, called "khirgahs," which were perched on a rising ground. There was no order in the distribution, and they stood like so many gigantic beehives
passages.speaker: Alexander Burnes (1834)

passages.headline: Bukhara's brick bazaars and the Registan
passages.people: Uzbeks and the peoples of Central Asia
passages.gloss: Burnes describes Bukhara as a city of lofty, arched brick bazaars, each trade in its own quarter, massive colleges, mosques and minarets, twenty caravanserais and about a hundred ponds and fountains of squared stone. People believed the tallest minaret, about 150 feet, reached the level of Timur's Samarkand. In the Registan square a visitor could meet Turkmen, Kalmyks and Kazakhs from the deserts.
passages.quote: when the traveller passes its gates he winds his way among lofty and arched bazars of brick, and sees each trade in its separate quarter of the city; here the chintz sellers, there the shoemakers; one arcade filled with silks, another with cloth. Every where he meets with ponderous and massy buildings, colleges, mosques, and lofty minarets.
passages.speaker: Alexander Burnes (1834)

passages.headline: Samarkand, Timur's capital, shrunk to a provincial town
passages.gloss: Burnes could not safely visit Samarkand, so he describes it from report: once Timur's capital, now a town of 8000 to 10,000 people, with gardens and fields where streets and mosques had been. Three colleges survived, including Ulugh Beg's with enamelled bricks, and Timur's tomb under a lofty dome decorated with agate. Its possession still made a Bukhara king legitimate.
passages.quote: The city has now declined from its grandeur to a provincial town of 8000, or at most 10,000, inhabitants, and gardens and fields occupy the place of its streets and mosques; but it is still regarded with high veneration by the people.
passages.speaker: Alexander Burnes (1834)
passages.caution: Burnes did not see Samarkand; this is hearsay from Bukhara.

passages.headline: Balkh: slaughtered by Genghis, built of frail brick
passages.people: Inhabitants of Balkh; Mongols under Genghis Khan
passages.gloss: Burnes lists Balkh's fate: its people 'butchered in cold blood by Jenghis Khan', then ruled by the house of Timur, the Mughals, Nadir Shah, the Afghans and Bukhara. In 1832 it had under 2000 people. Looking at its crumbling remains he doubts it was ever a substantial city, since its buildings rested only on brick foundations.
passages.quote: Its inhabitants were butchered in cold blood by Jenghis Khan; and under the house of Timour it became a province of the Mogul empire. … and from the frail materials of which its buildings are constructed, the foundations being only brick, I doubt if Balkh ever were a substantial city.
passages.speaker: Alexander Burnes (1834)

passages.headline: The Tatar Hazaras, said to descend from Genghis's army
passages.place: Hazarajat (between the Hindu Kush and Bamiyan)
passages.gloss: Burnes notes a Hazara tribe of about a thousand families called Tatar Hazaras, whom tradition made descendants of Genghis Khan's army. He points out that the only other people who called themselves Tatar were the Nogais on the Russian frontier. Earlier (vol. I, p.178) he says the Hazaras looked like Chinese and were 'Tartars by descent'.
passages.quote: Tradition states these people to be descendants of Jengis Khan's army, but their name of Tatar deserves remark, since the only other tribe so denominated by the people themselves is the Nogai on the frontiers of Russia.
passages.speaker: Alexander Burnes (1834)
passages.caution: The descent from Genghis's army is tradition, which Burnes reports without proving.

passages.headline: The Tartar invasions, from Attila to the Uzbeks
passages.people: Tartars as a catch-all for steppe conquerors
passages.gloss: Burnes opens a chapter 'On the Inroads of the Tartars' by lumping together Attila, Alaric, Genghis, Timur and the Uzbeks as expressions of 'the ever-wandering spirit of the Tartar people'. He places their homeland beyond the Jaxartes (Syr Darya) rather than in northern China. It shows the romantic, racial idea of 'the Tartar' that educated Britons held in the 1830s.
passages.quote: Attila and Alaric spread devastation in the empire of the Caesars. Jengis and Timour have succeeded them in more modern but equally destructive inroads. Through these great revolutions we trace the ever-wandering spirit of the Tartar people
passages.speaker: Alexander Burnes (1834)
passages.caution: Burnes's own generalisation; Alaric was a Goth, not a steppe nomad.

passages.headline: Kalmyk chiefs who wear deer antlers
passages.gloss: From Bukhara merchants Burnes heard that Kalmyk Tartars settled around Ili and Yarkand marked their chiefs and nobles by fixing deer's horns on their skull-caps, the size of the antlers showing rank. He adds a crude rumour about their women, and says the Chinese used Kalmyks to guard the frontier.
passages.quote: There are Calmuk Tartars settled around Eela and Yarkund, who have a singular custom to distinguish their chiefs and grandees, by fixing deer's horns on their skull-caps.
passages.speaker: Alexander Burnes (1834)
passages.caution: Hearsay; the next page adds a sexual slander Burnes 'was assured' of.

passages.headline: Turkmen roadside grave mounds
passages.gloss: Riding with a sayyid near the Caspian, Burnes asked about mounds of earth with a pole in the centre. They were 'yoozka', marking where someone had died or been laid out, and Turkmen said a blessing as they passed. Burnes remarks that they were not graves but barrows raised in honour of the dead, and suspects the custom was 'Tatar'.
passages.quote: They are not graves, but mounds or barrows raised in honour of the dead. I entertain an impression that the usage is Tatar; but I had no opportunity of further investigation.
passages.speaker: Alexander Burnes (1834)
passages.caution: Burnes's 'Tatar' origin is an untested hunch, as he admits.

passages.headline: A petrified city on the Aral Sea
passages.gloss: In Bukhara Burnes heard tales of an enchanted, petrified city on the south-west shore of the Aral Sea called Barsa-gil-mis, Turkic for 'go and never return', because curious visitors never came back. He files it with Bukharan belief in magic and remarks that 'distance gives countenance to most of the fables'.
passages.quote: tales of an enchanted and petrified city which was described by the Bokharees as lying on the south-western corner of the Sea of Aral, and between Orgunje and Orenburg. They call it "Barsa-gil-mis;" which, in Toorkee, means, to go and never return; since such is said to be the fate of the curious.
passages.speaker: Alexander Burnes (1834)
passages.caution: A local legend that Burnes reports with open scepticism.

passages.headline: Greek soldiers' descendants in 'Chinese Tartary'
passages.gloss: Listing people who claimed descent from Alexander the Great, Burnes adds that Tungan soldiers from western China garrisoning Yarkand claimed descent from Alexander's soldiers. He notes the claimants in the Oxus hills were Tajiks, who lived there 'before it was overrun by Toorkee or Tartar tribes', and doubts the claims against the historical record.
passages.quote: the soldiers of the Toonganee tribe, who are sent from the western provinces of Chinese Tartary, and garrison Yarkund and the neighbouring cities, claim also a Grecian origin. They, however, seek, with greater modesty, a descent from the soldiers of Alexander's army
passages.speaker: Alexander Burnes (1834)
passages.caution: Reported claims that Burnes himself questions.

passages.headline: The ruined Musalla of Herat, built by a Timurid king
passages.gloss: North of Herat Conolly explored a 'pile of magnificent ruins', the Musalla, which he was told was built by a king of the house of Timur to receive the body of Imam Reza, then abandoned when the saint was buried at Mashhad. He describes a towering iwan, a court a hundred paces square decorated with mosaic of white quartz and coloured enamel tile, and domed halls. On the next page he counts the remains of twenty minarets.
passages.quote: A mile to the north of the city are the remains of what anciently was the wall of Heri, … is a pile of magnificent ruins, … the "Moosullah," or place of worship, built by a pious king of the house of Timour, to receive the remains of the Imaum Reza
passages.speaker: Arthur Conolly (1834)
passages.caution: The reason given for its building is local tradition; historically the Musalla complex was built by Timurid rulers in the fifteenth century.

passages.headline: White marble tombs of Timur's descendants at Gazur Gah
passages.gloss: At the shrine of the Sufi saint Khwaja Abdullah Ansari on the hills above Herat, Conolly walked through a walled garden where trees shaded 'several tombs of white marble built over the dust of the descendants of Timour-lung'. He adds that Timur's descendants built summer palaces and gardens on the same hill.
passages.quote: We deposited our slippers here, and then passed into a walled garden, the trees of which shaded several tombs of white marble built over the dust of the descendants of Timour-lung.
passages.speaker: Arthur Conolly (1834)

passages.headline: An Afghan court ceremony 'borrowed from the Chinese Tartars'
passages.people: Durrani Afghans; Chinese Tartars (Manchus) as supposed source
passages.gloss: Conolly retells a Persian anecdote about presentation at the court of Ahmad Shah Durrani: two officers ran the visitor up to the king at a trot, shouted his name and whisked him away again. He calls the ceremony 'borrowed, apparently, from the Chinese Tartars', then admits this is only 'the Persian account'.
passages.quote: The Dooraunee ceremony of presentation at court is a very strange one, borrowed, apparently, from the Chinese Tartars, … the person upon whom the honour is to be conferred, being placed between two of the officers of the court, who run him up at a trot to within a certain distance of the king
passages.speaker: Arthur Conolly (1834)
passages.caution: A secondhand Persian story; the 'Chinese Tartar' origin is Conolly's guess.
