passages.headline: The Turkmen: 'these Tartars' under Uzbek rule
passages.gloss: In his essay on a possible Russian invasion of India, Conolly weighs whether Russia could win over the Turkmen, who then gave unwilling allegiance to 'their Oosbeg conquerors' at Khiva. He concludes the Turkmen would follow their interests, and that Russia, as in the Caucasus, might in time 'subdue these Tartars'. It shows 'Tartar' as a British strategic label for the Turkic peoples of the desert.
passages.quote: I am sure that the Toorkmuns would be chiefly influenced by what they thought their interests; and when I look to what we have done in Hindoostan, or, to speak nearer to the point, what the Russians have done in Persia, I cannot decide that they may not subdue these Tartars
passages.speaker: Arthur Conolly (1834)
passages.caution: A political argument, not an observation.

passages.headline: Why a felt tent beats a house
passages.place: Turkmen country between Herat and Merv
passages.gloss: Lodged in a Turkmen camp of about 300 black tents, Abbott was won over by the felt tent. He explains that the felt can be lifted in summer, a central fire warms it in winter with the smoke escaping through a roof opening, and the whole home can be moved to a better spot.
passages.quote: These Toorcumun tents are the most comfortable of dwellings … by removing a portion of the felt covering, this tent is open to the air in summer ; and in winter a fire lighted in the centre makes it the warmest of retreats, all the smoke rising through the skylight in the roof.
passages.speaker: James Abbott

passages.headline: Khiva's manor houses of rammed clay
passages.gloss: Riding into the Khiva oasis, Abbott describes the country houses of the nobles: tall clay-walled compounds with towers at the corners, locally called 'castles'. He explains how the walls were built by ramming wet clay between hurdles of branches, which left a fluted pattern on the surface.
passages.quote: The houses have all one character, being an enclosure of very lofty clay walls, flanked by ornamental towers at the angles, which give them the appearance of castles. This name (Gullah) they bear at Khiva. … The walls, built with great regularity of rammed clay, are generally fluted, an effect given them perhaps by the hurdles of straight branches, between which the clay is supported whilst soft
passages.speaker: James Abbott

passages.headline: The Khan holds court in a felt tent
passages.people: Allah Quli Khan of Khiva and his Uzbek court
passages.gloss: At his first audience Abbott found the ruler of Khiva not in a hall but in a plain black felt tent pitched inside his court, with a wood fire burning in the middle. Even a settled king with a brick citadel kept the nomad's tent as his reception room.
passages.quote: He was seated upon a carpet, and supported by cushions. Before him a wood fire blazed up, sending its smoke and sparks through the sky-light of the tent. … The black tent of felt which he occupied, was of the usual dimensions, i. e. about 24 feet in diameter, and quite unadorned, its sole furniture being the carpet and cushions, on which he reclined.
passages.speaker: James Abbott

passages.headline: A brick tower said to be Genghis Khan's
passages.gloss: Among the ruins of Old Urgench Abbott saw a tall, tapering brick column that he says was put up by Genghis Khan, decorated only with bands of patterned brick and leaning from the wind. Nearby he describes a saint's tomb with a conical roof of coloured tiles on a 24-sided base, and a tiled tomb said to have been built by a lady of Genghis Khan's family for her lover.
passages.quote: On the north of the site, (I speak at hazard,) stands a brick column, erected by Chenghis Khaun. It is the frustrum of an extremely taper cone, surmounted by a cylinder, and is very sufficiently ugly. It has no base, and its sole ornaments have been zones of bricks, of alternating patterns.
passages.speaker: James Abbott
passages.caution: The attribution to Genghis Khan is what Abbott was told or assumed; the tall minaret standing at Konye-Urgench today is usually dated to the 14th century.

passages.headline: A capital made of black tents
passages.gloss: The 'capital' of the Jamshidi tribe was mostly a spread of round black felt tents on a light wooden frame, darkened by smoke. Abbott notes only a few mud huts and a so-called fort that looked like a run-down farmyard.
passages.quote: The black tents which form the capital of the Jumsheedees are of thick felts, supported by a light and moveable framework of wood. Their shape is circular, and their dark hue is received from the smoke of fires lighted within : but sometimes from the colour of the wool. Khooshk however has a few mud huts and a fort, (so called) resembling a dilapidated farm yard.
passages.speaker: James Abbott

passages.headline: Entering walled Khiva
passages.gloss: Abbott rode to his first audience through a suburb, a bazaar and a fortified gateway, with women crowding the rooftops to stare. The royal citadel itself he found to be a modest brick building set into a corner of the town walls.
passages.quote: On approaching the town, we entered a considerable suburb, and afterwards passed through a miserable bazaar to the gateway ; for Khiva is fortified. … It was not long before we reached, through some very poor streets, the citadel, within which resides the "Father of Victories," the king of Khaurism. It is a poor, brick building, forming an angle of the city defences.
passages.speaker: James Abbott

passages.headline: Old Urgench, a brick fort melted into mounds
passages.people: Khwarazm (former capital); Turkmens and Kazakhs at the market nearby
passages.gloss: Abbott paced out the ruins of the old capital of Khwarazm: a town about a mile long with a square brick citadel and round bastions on a raised platform. The town walls, which he guessed were of unbaked brick, had slumped into low mounds.
passages.quote: The extent of this city was perhaps one mile by half a mile, with extensive suburbs on the north. At the east angle is the citadel, a brick fort of square figure, flanked by eight circular, and projecting bastions. … but the whole is now a ruin, as is the ancient city ; the walls of the latter, which were probably of unbaked brick, having subsided into mere mounds.
passages.speaker: James Abbott

passages.headline: Merv abandoned when its dam broke
passages.people: Turkmens under the Khan of Khiva
passages.gloss: Abbott gives a short history of Merv: founded, he says, by fire-worshippers, long Persian, and fought over by Turkic tribes. He explains that the old city emptied when the dam on the Murghab river was neglected and swept away during decades of disorder, leaving a deserted ruin beside a new village of mud huts.
passages.quote: Merv was one of the most ancient cities of Asia. … Merv has probably changed masters as often as any city in the world. … During the misrule and anarchy of the last sixty years the ancient dam of the Moorghaub was neglected and carried away. The city in consequence became uninhabitable, and was utterly abandoned.
passages.speaker: James Abbott
passages.caution: The founding by fire-worshippers is local tradition that Abbott repeats; the abandonment story is what he learned on the spot.

passages.headline: A Kazakh feast: mutton, broth and thumbs for napkins
passages.place: Ustyurt plateau, between Khiva and the Caspian
passages.gloss: At a Kazakh host's tent, the guests ate boiled mutton with no bread or vegetables, the men first and the women afterwards. Abbott is squeamish and scornful, but he records exactly how the meal was served and cleaned up.
passages.quote: It consisted of boiled mutton, soused in its own soup. Bread and vegetables are things quite unknown in these parts. Kuzzauks are exclusively carnivorous. … The bowls were handed to the women, who scraped them clean with their thumbs … The thumb and tongue are the only napkins in Khaurism … The Tartars are right not to eat with their women.
passages.speaker: James Abbott
passages.caution: Abbott's sneering tone is his own; the facts of the meal are what he saw.

passages.headline: Slave caravans on the road to Khiva
passages.people: Turkmen traders and their captives from Herat
passages.gloss: Abbott travelled alongside caravans that had carried grain south and were returning to Khiva with captives, many from Herat. He describes the women riding with their captors and the men walking the whole way, chained by the neck at night.
passages.quote: They had brought grain from Khiva, and are returning thither laden with slaves, many of whom are natives of Heraut. … But the men are chained together by the throats at night, so that rest is scarcely possible, whilst the contact of the frozen iron with their skin must be torturous. For them also no carriage is found, they walk the whole way
passages.speaker: James Abbott

passages.headline: Singing kites over Khiva
passages.gloss: For weeks Abbott heard a strange humming music over Khiva at night. It turned out to be paper kites with a taut string stretched across a bent crosspiece, which hummed in the wind and were left flying all night. He thought the idea worth copying in England.
passages.quote: Seeing some children on the road with their paper kites, I approached to examine the contrivance, by which these toys emit a musical sound, whilst floating in the air. … And, as numbers of these kites are left floating in the air all night, the effect is that of aerial music ; monotonous, but full of melancholy interest.
passages.speaker: James Abbott

passages.headline: A cemetery of giants at Umbarr
passages.people: Khivans, Turkmens; Kalmyks (as former rulers in the story)
passages.gloss: Passing an abandoned walled town, Abbott's interpreter told him it had been a Kalmyk capital, and that the late Khan stopped rebuilding it when diggers found huge human bones. The interpreter claimed to have seen skulls too big to hug that crumbled to powder in the air. Abbott doubts the giants but thinks the bones deserve study.
passages.quote: He said, it was supposed to have been the capital of Khaurism, under the Culmauks, whom we call Calmucks. That these were slain, in an invasion by Russia. That the late Khaun purposed rebuilding this city, and had walled it accordingly ; but that, in digging, some monstrous human bones were found, which proved it to have been a cemetery of giants.
passages.speaker: Ali Muhummud, Abbott's interpreter, as reported by James Abbott
passages.caution: Hearsay. Abbott did not see the bones and on the next page says few would accept the giants theory.

passages.headline: An Uzbek map of the world
passages.gloss: The Khivan minister showed Abbott a world map by an Uzbek scholar that put Italy north of England and Russia south of China. Abbott, tongue in cheek, decided not to argue.
passages.quote: A map of the world, the production of a profound Oozbeg philosopher, was then produced ; I begged a clue to this singular chart, and was rather surprised to find, that Italy lay north of England ; and Russia south of China.
passages.speaker: James Abbott
passages.caution: Abbott is being sarcastic about the map.

passages.headline: Kazakh, Kirghiz or Cossack?
passages.gloss: Abbott explains a naming tangle: the steppe people between Khiva and Orenburg call themselves Kazakhs (Kuzzauks), but the Russians call them Kirghiz to tell them apart from Russia's own Christian Cossacks. The people themselves, he says, do not know the name Kirghiz.
passages.quote: The kingdom of Khaurism is separated from the Russian district of Orenburgh by a considerable belt of steppe, held by Kuzzauks, whose chief, or Sooltaun, is nominally tributary to Russia. The Russians call this people Kirgheez, to distinguish them from their own Kuzzauks, or Cossacks, who are Christians, but the name is unknown to the people themselves.
passages.speaker: James Abbott

passages.headline: 'Tartar' as a look, not a nation
passages.gloss: Abbott calls the Jamshidis Turkish by descent and 'decidedly Tartar' in their features, using 'Tartar' as a racial type. He adds an insult that recurs in the book: that all Tartars fear artillery.
passages.quote: The Jumsheedees are of Toorkish descent, as their habits and physiognomy imply. They are short, stout, very dark, with decidedly Tartar features. … They are arrant cowards, and like all Tartars, superstitiously fearful of artillery.
passages.speaker: James Abbott
passages.caution: Prejudiced generalisation. The Jamshidis are usually counted today among the Persian-speaking Aimaq peoples, not as Turks.

passages.headline: Inside a Kirghiz felt tent on the Pamirs
passages.gloss: Wood and his party were invited into one of the best tents of a Kirghiz camp of 100 families. He describes its coarse dun felts held by broad white bands, the ice-bag by the door that served as the family's water supply, a Russian iron cauldron on a tripod over the fire, and the measurements of the tent.
passages.quote: Close to the door lay a bag filled with ice … the water of the family. On drawing aside the felt which screened the entrance, the air of tidiness and comfort that met our eyes was a most agreeable surprise. … The Kirgah had a diameter of fourteen feet, a height of eight, and was well lighted by a circular hole above the fire-place.
passages.speaker: John Wood

passages.headline: A house that three yaks can carry
passages.gloss: Wood continues his tour of the tent: a willow frame lined with reed mats knitted over with coloured wool, embroidered bands hung with saddles and sewing things, a curtained corner for the women, and fifty lambs tethered on a line inside. The whole home, he adds, packs onto three yaks.
passages.quote: The opposite segment was allotted to the young lambs of the flock. A string crossed the tent to which fifty nooses, twenty-five of a side, were attached, to each of which a lamb was fastened. … Three yaks are able to carry the tent and all its contents. One takes the oostakhan, literally the bones or frame-work, another the felts, and a third its furniture
passages.speaker: John Wood

passages.headline: Kunduz: a capital of mud huts and tents
passages.gloss: The capital of the powerful Uzbek ruler Murad Beg was, Wood says, one of the most wretched towns in his lands: a few hundred mud hovels mixed with straw sheds and Uzbek tents, with fields running into the town and a fortress that was just a walled mound. On the next page he describes the ruler's citadel as an irregular building of kiln-dried brick with a moat.
passages.quote: Kunduz, though the capital of Murad Beg, is one of the most wretched in his dominions. Five or six hundred mud hovels contain its fixed population, while dotted amongst these, and scattered at random over the suburbs, are straw-built sheds intermixed with the Uzbek tent or Kirgah. … Nothing, in short, can be imagined less resembling a metropolis.
passages.speaker: John Wood
passages.caution: Wood openly links the town's poverty to his low opinion of Uzbek character; the physical description is what he saw.

passages.headline: Roadside buildings of the Mughal emperors
passages.place: Between Kunduz and Khulm (Tashkurgan), northern Afghanistan
passages.people: Mughal emperors of India (Babur's line), called 'Mongol' by Wood
passages.gloss: On the road west from Kunduz, Wood found a domed water cistern and a guard tower that he credits to the 'Mongol' emperors, meaning the Mughal dynasty of India founded by Babur. He admired them as public works for travellers, and notes that the emperors had kept post-houses all the way to Balkh.
passages.quote: At the bottom of their western slope stands a water-cistern, a dome-covered building, and a guard-tower … remnants of Mongol munificence, evincing, by their usefulness rather than their beauty, the philanthropic spirit of the monarch who erected them. … for during the palmy days of Baber's line the emperors of Hindustan had post-houses
passages.speaker: John Wood
passages.caution: The attribution to the Mughals is Wood's own judgment.

passages.headline: Where the word 'Tartary' came from
passages.people: Peoples of Central Asia: Kalmyks, Kirghiz, Uzbeks, Turkmens
passages.gloss: Wood suggests the peoples of Central Asia descend from the ancient Huns and that most of their names came from a person: Tartar, Nogai, Uzbek, Moghul. 'Tartar', he says, had been turned into 'Tartary', a catch-all word for what the Romans called Scythia, yet he never heard the Uzbeks of Kunduz use it, and he blames the habit for much confusion.
passages.quote: Most of their names have had a personal origin, such as Tartar, Noghai, Uzbek, and Moghul. The first, corrupted to Tartary, has now become a generic term for the Scythia of the Roman historians, though I do not remember to have heard it used by the Uzbeks of Kunduz. From this custom much ambiguity has resulted.
passages.speaker: John Wood
passages.caution: The Hun ancestry and the 'personal origin' of the names are Wood's own theories from reading, not local testimony.

passages.headline: The three great 'Tartar invaders'
passages.people: Genghis Khan, Timur and Shaybani Khan
passages.gloss: Wood groups Genghis Khan, Tamerlane (Timur) and the Uzbek conqueror Shaybani Khan together as 'Tartar invaders', and says none of them seems to have reached the high valleys of Badakhshan. It shows how loosely 'Tartar' was used for Mongol and Turkic conquerors alike.
passages.quote: None of the three great Tartar invaders, Jangez Khan, Tamerlane, or Shebani Khan, seem to have penetrated so high up the valley of the Oxus, though some of the followers of Baber, when expelled from the rich plains of Soghdiana by the Uzbeks, sought shelter here
passages.speaker: John Wood

passages.headline: Kimiz: mare's milk that makes you drunk
passages.gloss: Wood explains how the Kirghiz and Uzbeks make kimiz (kumiss) from mare's milk, churned overnight and ready by sunrise. A spoonful, he was told, makes a man drunk, but their spoons are huge. He also passes on, while flagging it as hostile gossip, a claim that kimiz season brought drunken excess.
passages.quote: The Kirghiz, as well as the Uzbeks, keep brood mares, according to their means, and the acidulated milk of these animals yields them in spring the intoxicating liquor called kimiz. … A spoonful will produce inebriety, but their kashuk or spoon is much more capacious than the largest upon our tables.
passages.speaker: John Wood

passages.headline: Why the Kirghiz prefer daughters
passages.gloss: Among the Kirghiz, Wood learned, a daughter was more welcome than a son: herding needs few men, and a girl brought a large bride price. He also records that a widow passed to her husband's brother, and that a stranger who married her started a blood feud.
passages.quote: With the Kirghiz, a daughter is more desired than a son. Their flocks and herds, though large, do not require many men to manage them … But for a daughter a large sum is obtained … often as much as £40, if she be not above fifteen years of age.
passages.speaker: John Wood

passages.headline: Shamans turned Muslims
passages.gloss: Wood reports that the Kirghiz had converted from shamanism to Islam in the early 1600s, and that his Uzbek companion claimed the old beliefs lingered. Their chiefs, called Bai, had patriarchal rather than despotic authority.
passages.quote: They were converted from the Shamanian superstition to Mohamedanism early in the seventeenth century. The former belief, if I may credit Abdal Ghani, is not yet thoroughly eradicated ; though in our intercourse with the people, they seemed like all proselytes to erring creeds, to be filled with the most abject reverence for their new doctrines.
passages.speaker: John Wood
passages.caution: The date of conversion is Wood's statement without a source; the survival of shamanism is his guide's claim.

passages.headline: Sell your wife, never your dog
passages.gloss: Wood notes a twist in Uzbek manners: asking a man to sell his wife was no offence, but asking to buy his dog was an insult, and 'dog-seller' was about the worst name one Uzbek could call another. He goes on to praise Uzbek women as fine housekeepers.
passages.quote: To ask an Uzbek to sell his wife would be no affront, but to ask him to sell his dog would be an unpardonable insult, "Suggee ferosh," or dog-seller, being about the most offensive epithet that one Uzbek can apply to another.
passages.speaker: John Wood

passages.headline: Priests who dealt in slaves
passages.people: Uzbeks of Kunduz and their mullahs
passages.gloss: Wood says the Sunni Uzbeks of Kunduz treated persecution of Shia Muslims as proof of faith, and that their religious leaders were the biggest slave dealers, buying Shia captives and justifying it as good for the soul. Elsewhere he describes chained slave tributes on the road to Kunduz.
passages.quote: These mullahs, or priests, are the most notorious slave dealers in the land, and encourage the odious traffic among their disciples, by readily purchasing of them whatever victims of the Shiah creed they may entrap. The good of the soul is assigned as ample extenuation
passages.speaker: John Wood
passages.caution: Wood writes as a hostile Protestant observer; the slave trade itself is confirmed by many sources.

passages.headline: The Kazakh chief who ordered prayers in a jar
passages.people: Kazakhs, as described by Kirghiz storytellers
passages.gloss: The Kirghiz told Wood joke stories about their Kazakh neighbours as simple folk. In one, a Kazakh chief sent to Kokand to buy Muslim prayers for his horde and was given a sealed jar of bees, to be opened by the fire in a closed tent with all the elders undressed. Wood repeats it as a comic tale, not as fact.
passages.quote: A jar carefully covered, containing a swarm of bees, was delivered to the dull Kazak, with instructions to his chief not to open it till all the head men of the horde were assembled. … The chief himself, literally stung to madness, swore that never again should a Mussulman's prayer issue from a Kazak kirgah.
passages.speaker: Kirghiz storytellers, as retold by John Wood
passages.caution: A folk joke told by one people about another.

passages.headline: Kirghiz and Uzbeks: cousins by blood
passages.gloss: The Kirghiz horde Wood visited had come down to winter in Wakhan at the invitation of the Uzbeks of Kunduz, whom they claimed as blood relatives. Wood agrees they are one stock, and puts their differences in build down to climate.
passages.quote: They had been solicited to do so by the Uzbeks of Kunduz, with whom the Kirghiz profess to be connected by blood. The two people are evidently of the same stock, though the effects of location, or in other words, the difference between a temperate and a rigorous climate is observable in the well proportioned frame of the Uzbek and in the stunted growth of the Kirghiz.
passages.speaker: John Wood
passages.caution: The climate explanation is Wood's own theory.

passages.headline: Bukhara: eleven gates and 360 mosques
passages.gloss: Wolff gives a thumbnail sketch of Bukhara: a walled city of fifteen miles' circuit with eleven gates, hundreds of mosques, caravanserais, baths and about a hundred colleges, and the old citadel (the Ark), which he says was built a thousand years earlier by Arslan Khan.
passages.quote: It has eleven gates, and a circumference of fifteen English miles; three hundred and sixty mosques, twenty-two caravanserays, many baths and bazaars, and the old palace called Ark, built by Arslan Khan one thousand years ago, and has about one hundred splendid colleges. The houses have neither roofs nor windows.
passages.speaker: Joseph Wolff
passages.caution: The number 360 is a traditional round figure, and the date and builder of the Ark are local tradition. 'Neither roofs nor windows' probably means flat roofs and no outward-facing windows.

passages.headline: A street full of 'Tatars' of every kind
passages.people: Nogai Tatars, Kazakhs, Kirghiz, Turkic people of Yarkand, Uzbeks, Jews, Afghans
passages.gloss: As Wolff rode into Bukhara in his clerical robes, crowds lined the streets and rooftops. His list of onlookers shows how many different peoples could be called 'Tatar' in one city: Nogai Tatars from Russia, Kazakhs and Kirghiz from the steppe, and a 'Tatar' from Yarkand in Chinese Turkestan.
passages.quote: It was a most astonishing sight ; people from the roofs of the houses, the Nogay Tatars of Russia, the Cassacks and Girghese from the deserts, the Tatar from Yarkand or Chinese Tartary, the merchant of Cashmeer, the Serkerdeha or grandees of the king on horseback, the Affghauns, the numerous water-carriers, stopped still and looked at me
passages.speaker: Joseph Wolff

passages.headline: Samarkand, 'Ornament of the Face of the Earth'
passages.gloss: Wolff describes Samarkand, Timur's old capital, as a clay-walled town of 40,000 people with a palace, marble houses, mosques, colleges and Timur's tomb. He adds stories that Chinese once lived there making paper from silk, and that the city took its name from a conqueror called Samar.
passages.quote: It has a wall of clay, and forty thousand inhabitants; a beautiful palace, and many houses of marble; many mosques and colleges. It was formerly inhabited by Chinese, who manufactured paper of silk; and it once had the name of Bokhara-Tsheen, but received the present name from the conqueror Samar, after Christ 643. Oologh Beyk erected there an observatory.
passages.speaker: Joseph Wolff
passages.caution: Wolff did not describe visiting Samarkand on this journey; the name story and the Chinese paper-makers are traditions he repeats.

passages.headline: Genghis Khan takes Bukhara
passages.people: Mongols under Genghis Khan; Jews of Bukhara
passages.gloss: In a later addition to the book Wolff notes that Genghis Khan besieged Bukhara in 1219 and took it in 1220, and repeats a tradition that thousands of Jews then fled to China. He adds that the city's houses were mostly of mud.
passages.quote: The town of Bokhara is situated one day's journey to the north of the river Jehoon or Amoo ; Ghengis Khan besieged it in 1219, and took it in 1220. Thousands of Jews emigrated at that time to China. The houses are mostly built of mud.
passages.speaker: Joseph Wolff
passages.caution: The Jewish migration to China is Wolff's claim, probably from Bukharan Jewish tradition, not a documented event.

passages.headline: Khiva and Kokand: towns of mud
passages.people: Uzbek khanates of Khiva and Kokand
passages.gloss: Drawing on Alexander Burnes and other authors, Wolff describes the capital of Khiva as a town of mud huts with three stone mosques and a mud palace, living largely by the slave trade, and says Kokand was likewise built of mud except for three stone bazaars.
passages.quote: The capital of Khiva is a town of mud huts, with three stone mosques, and a mud palace. Its chief trade is in slaves, of whom there are about forty thousand in the Khanat ; and it is said there are many captured Russians, who are slaves in Khiva. … It is, like Khiva, built of mud, with the exception of three stone bazaars.
passages.speaker: Joseph Wolff, summarising Alexander Burnes and other writers
passages.caution: Second-hand; Wolff did not visit Khiva or Kokand on this journey.

passages.headline: Bukhara's sun-dried brick and arched bazaars
passages.gloss: Quoting Burnes's figures, Wolff describes Bukhara's massive buildings, the Khan's fortress-palace, houses of sun-dried brick, narrow dirty streets and lofty arched bazaars where each trade had its own section.
passages.quote: It has massive buildings, three hundred and sixty mosques, three hundred schools, the Khan's palace, or rather fortress ; houses built of bricks dried in the sun ; very narrow and dirty streets ; lofty arched bazaars, in which the different trades have their distinct sections ; and ponds and fountains for the supply of water.
passages.speaker: Joseph Wolff, summarising Alexander Burnes
passages.caution: Taken from Burnes, as the page says.

passages.headline: Twin brothers named Mogul and Tatar
passages.people: Muhammad Khan Qarai, a Khorasani chief claiming descent from Genghis Khan
passages.gloss: In a Tabriz prison Wolff met a captive chieftain who wrote out his family tree for him. It calls him a 'Tatar of the family of Genghis Khan' and gives a traditional origin story: an ancestor had twin sons, Mogul Khan and Tatar Khan, from whom the Moguls and the Tatars descend.
passages.quote: Muhammed, son of Izhak Khan Kerahe, Tatar of the family of Ghengis Khan. The ancestors of Ghengis Khan were Oolinjah Khan and Olamgoo, a Mogul, who had twins : the name of the one was Mogul Khan, and the other Tatar Khan, from whom all the Tatars descend, as the Moguls do from Mogul Khan.
passages.speaker: Muhammad Khan Qarai (in Wolff's translation of his autograph)
passages.caution: A traditional genealogy (a version of the Mongol origin story found in Persian and Turkic histories), not history.

passages.headline: Uzbeks replace the 'Turks or Tatars'
passages.gloss: Wolff says that after the 'Turks or Tatars' were driven out, the Uzbeks became the ruling people, brought to the Oxus by Shaybani Khan with their first centre at Urgench in Khiva. He treats 'Turk' and 'Tatar' as one name for the earlier rulers.
passages.quote: Since the expulsion of the Turks or Tatars, the Usbecks are the dominant people. Sheybek Khan brought them to the country of the river Amoo in the year 1498, when they had the centre of their empire at Organtsh, in Khiva.
passages.speaker: Joseph Wolff
passages.caution: Wolff's date is approximate; Shaybani Khan's conquest of Transoxiana is usually dated to about 1500 to 1507.

passages.headline: Timur's pyramid of skulls, as the Turkmens told it
passages.people: Turkmens of the Merv desert; Timur (Tamerlane)
passages.gloss: Snowed in at a desert camp, Wolff listened to Turkmens talk of Alexander and Timur as if they had lived yesterday. One told how Timur punished the Khan of Khwarazm by building a pyramid of human skulls cemented with clay at Urgench, sparing only dervishes, scholars and poets.
passages.quote: It is remarkable to hear these Turkomauns speak of the exploits of Alexander and Timur, exactly as if of modern occurrence. … He made a pyramid at Organtsh entirely of skulls of men, cemented with clay. He spared the lives of none, except those of holy derveeshes, of the learned, and of poets, around whose houses he placed Karawl, i. e. guards.
passages.speaker: A Turkmen in the Merv desert, as reported by Joseph Wolff
passages.caution: Oral tradition. Timur's skull towers are recorded elsewhere (Wolff also mentions one at Sabzevar), but this telling is folk memory.

passages.headline: Russia is Gog and Magog
passages.gloss: In a caravan leaving Bukhara, a Turkmen told Wolff that Russia would conquer the world, having built a fort in the sea near Khiva. A dervish added that the great mullahs of Samarkand said Russia was Gog and Magog, the destroying peoples of the end times.
passages.quote: A Turkomaun present said, "The Russians shall be the conquerors of the world. They have now built a strong castle almost in the midst of the sea, not far from Khiva. … A derveesh sitting among us made the following remark ; "The great mullahs of Samarcand assert that Russia is the Jaaj-Majooj, i. e. Gog and Magog
passages.speaker: A Turkmen and a dervish, as reported by Joseph Wolff
passages.caution: A prophecy repeated in conversation, reflecting fear of Russian expansion.

passages.headline: The rumour that Wolff had been to Tartarus
passages.gloss: Wolff found a rumour running through Bukhara that he knew 72 languages and 72 religions, had spoken with 72 nations, and had even visited the 'land of darkness', which he glosses as Tartarus. The word play between Tartary and Tartarus here comes from Wolff's own gloss.
passages.quote: A report was spread abroad, I found, throughout the whole country of Bokhara, that Mullah Joseph Wolff, the grand derveesh from England, was acquainted with seventy-two languages, with seventy-two religions, and had conversed with seventy-two nations of the earth. That, further, I had been in Sulmistaun, i. e. the ' land of darkness," Tartarus
passages.speaker: Joseph Wolff
passages.caution: Gossip about Wolff himself; the 'Tartarus' gloss is his.

passages.headline: Turkmens pray without mosques
passages.gloss: On his first journey Wolff noted that the Turkmens had no mosques, praying alone in the open or in their tents and gathering twice a year in the desert for common prayer. He also records a claim by the Jews of Turkestan that the Turkmens descend from the biblical Togarmah.
passages.quote: All the Jews of Turkistaun assert that the Turkomauns are the descendants of Togarmah, one of the sons of Gomer, mentioned in Genesis x. 3. The Turkomauns have no mosque; they pray apart from each other, either in the field or the tent. Twice in the year they assemble in the desert, and prefer their prayer.
passages.speaker: Joseph Wolff
passages.caution: The biblical ancestry is a Jewish tradition Wolff repeats.

passages.headline: Turkmen elders who could advise but not punish
passages.gloss: Wolff describes his Turkmen guides as truly 'masterless': their greybeards (aqsaqals) could give advice and lead raids, but had no power to punish anyone.
passages.quote: The Turkomauns my guides were, in the strictest sense of the word, masterless : for their Aga Sakals, ' lords with the beard,' have only a right to give advice, and to conduct them on their plundering expeditions, but they have no power to punish.
passages.speaker: Joseph Wolff

passages.headline: Were the Mohicans Tatars?
passages.people: Mohican people of North America, compared with Tatars and Turkmens
passages.gloss: On a trip to America Wolff thought he saw signs that Native Americans were of 'Tatar race': a shared word for 'great', a fondness for the number nine, and a custom of playing a mournful flute outside a sweetheart's tent like the Turkmens. It is a striking example of how far the Tatar idea could stretch.
passages.quote: Many of their customs, besides words in their language, and their physiognomy, rather seem to me to betray a Tatar race. Thus, for instance, they have the word kelaun, great, which is also used in the same sense at Bokhara. They have nine as a favourite number, which the Tatars also have.
passages.speaker: Joseph Wolff
passages.caution: Wolff's own speculation from a few coincidences.

passages.headline: How a Turkmen tent is built
passages.gloss: Fraser says no one had yet described exactly how the 'portable wooden houses' of the Turkmens are made, and does so: a folding lattice of thin laths pinned with rawhide that opens out like a child's toy, curved roof poles, black felt (numud) coverings, a reed screen outside and a broad woven band holding it all together.
passages.quote: The frame is curiously constructed of light wood, disposed in laths of about an inch broad, by three quarters thick, crossing one another diagonally … and pinned at each crossing with thongs of raw hide, so as to be moveable ; … over which is thrown a covering of black numud, leaving in the center a large hole to give vent to the smoke, and light to the dwelling
passages.speaker: James Baillie Fraser

passages.headline: Uzbek 'black houses' of felt
passages.people: Nomadic Uzbeks of the emirate of Bukhara
passages.gloss: In his appendix on Bukhara, Fraser reports that the tents of the country Uzbeks were like those of the Turkmens: a lath frame under thick black felts, called kara-ui ('black house') or kirgah, with a lattice smoke hole that could be covered with felt when it rained.
passages.quote: The tents, or rather houses, of the Oozbecks resemble those of the Toorkomans, of which a description has already been given, a frame work of thin laths covered with thick, black felts, and they are called karaooees (black houses) or kirghahs. The floors of the rich are spread with carpets and numuds, those of the poor with a blanket or mat of camels' hair
passages.speaker: James Baillie Fraser
passages.caution: From informants, not seen by Fraser.

passages.headline: Bukhara's houses of raw brick and timber
passages.gloss: Fraser's informants described Bukhara's houses as two or three storeys of raw (unfired) brick strengthened with timber frames, with poorer houses of timber filled with mud and broken brick. The city's roughly eighty colleges, by contrast, were mostly of stone and lime.
passages.quote: The houses in Bockhara are in general two and even three stories high, built of raw brick, and often strengthened by wooden frame work ; those of inferior description are constructed of the same frames of timber, filled up with mud and fragments of brick.
passages.speaker: James Baillie Fraser
passages.caution: Second-hand description.

passages.headline: At Merv, only the burnt brick survived
passages.people: Former Seljuk and Timurid rulers; Merv then under Bukhara
passages.gloss: Fraser doubts the tales of marble palaces at Merv. His informants said the main surviving ruins were a mosque and college credited to Timur, the tomb of the Seljuk sultan Sanjar and an arsenal, which lasted because they were built of fired brick.
passages.quote: there are no ruins to prove the existence of the marble palaces, and baths, and tombs, which have been vaguely attributed to it ; the chief remains are those of a fine large mosque, with a medressa, built by Timoor Shah ; of the mausoleum of Sooltaun Sanjer, and of a fine arsenal, all of which having been constructed of burnt brick, have partly escaped
passages.speaker: James Baillie Fraser
passages.caution: From informants. On the same page a footnote doubts the huge death tolls given for the Mongol sack of Merv.

passages.headline: A brick tower among the Turkmen pastures
passages.people: Goklen Turkmens (camped around it); builders unknown to Fraser
passages.gloss: Riding through Goklen Turkmen pastures, Fraser reached the Gonbad-e Kavus, a hollow brick tower on a mound that he guessed at 150 feet high. He admired its fired bricks and lime mortar, and judged it to be of early Islamic ('Arabic') origin, though he could not read its inscription. The nomads grazing around it were not credited with building it.
passages.quote: It has been built of the finest fire-baked bricks, large, square, and about two inches and a half thick, with which also, placed flat, the roof has been covered ; and so well have they stood, that not above one or two of the whole have been yet displaced. The whole is cemented with lime, and of the most excellent masonry
passages.speaker: James Baillie Fraser
passages.caution: Fraser could not read the date. The tower is now known to be the tomb of the Ziyarid ruler Qabus, built around 1006 to 1007.

passages.headline: Nishapur levelled by the Tartars
passages.people: Mongols (called Tartars) under Tolui, son of Genghis Khan
passages.gloss: Fraser retells, from Persian histories via Pétis de la Croix, how Genghis Khan's son Tolui took Nishapur after three days, plundered it, killed or enslaved the people, and levelled the site so that a horse could ride over it without stumbling. He openly doubts the historians' death toll of 1,747,000.
passages.quote: the Tartars having found means to enter the place after a siege of only three days, spent a day and night in plundering it, and in massacring and reducing to slavery its wretched and defenceless inhabitants; the city was razed, and the ground on which it stood levelled so completely, that it is said a horse might have ridden over the whole site without stumbling
passages.speaker: James Baillie Fraser, following historians quoted by Pétis de la Croix
passages.caution: Based on later Persian histories; Fraser himself rejects the huge casualty figure.

passages.headline: Bukhara burned: wood gone, brick left standing
passages.gloss: In his history of Bukhara, Fraser writes that Genghis Khan ordered the city burned when he found enemy officers hidden there. Because most houses were of wood, he says, nothing survived except mosques and public buildings of brick. He adds that Genghis's son Ögedei rebuilt the city.
passages.quote: as the greater part of its habitations were constructed of wood, its destruction was complete ; the sun, which rose upon its rich and crowded bazars, and thickly inhabited edifices, went down at night upon a waste of smoking ashes, among which, there was not one house standing, except some mosques and public buildings, that being built of brick, remained unburned.
passages.speaker: James Baillie Fraser
passages.caution: A retelling from Persian histories, not an eyewitness account.

passages.headline: Samarkand: Timur's capital in ruins
passages.gloss: Relying on the Indian traveller Mir Izzatullah and other reports, Fraser says Samarkand had been almost deserted until Shah Murad of Bukhara repopulated it. It had a mud wall and citadel but stone public buildings, and Timur's tomb still stood under a tall dome whose gold covering Shah Murad had removed.
passages.quote: This venerable city, often the seat of empire, once the favourite capital of the great Timoor, is now little better than a mass of ruins … In this place may yet be seen the Mausoleum of the Ameer Timoor ; it is a large building with a very lofty dome, which once was covered with gold ; but that was taken off by Shah Muraud.
passages.speaker: James Baillie Fraser, drawing on Mir Izzatullah
passages.caution: Second-hand; Fraser never reached Samarkand.

passages.headline: Turkmens: no chiefs, no nobles
passages.gloss: Fraser says Turkmen camps of 30 to 200 families followed an elder but had no rulers or nobles, and anyone who tried to seize power would be destroyed. Only a rare figure like Genghis Khan or Timur, he adds, could force such people into a single powerful union.
passages.quote: But they have no governors, chiefs, or nobles among them : and if any one should attempt to arrogate superior consideration to himself, or openly aim at power or authority, it would be the signal for his destruction. … Such an event can only occur, when some individual supereminently endowed with talents and courage, like a Chengiz, or a Timour, arises to force into union substances naturally repellent
passages.speaker: James Baillie Fraser

passages.headline: Guests seized by the reins
passages.gloss: Turkmen hospitality, Fraser was told, was so insistent that people ran out of the first tent a stranger reached, grabbed his horse and made him their guest; going on to another tent was an insult. In a footnote he warns that his informant made the tribes sound more trustworthy than they were.
passages.quote: When any stranger (who is not an acknowledged enemy) enters a camp, he is saluted at the first tent he approaches by its inhabitants, who run out, seize his reins, and insist on his alighting, and becoming their guest; even should the tent contain but a single
passages.speaker: James Baillie Fraser, quoting informants
passages.caution: Fraser says this part came almost word for word from informants and may overstate Turkmen trustworthiness.

passages.headline: Unveiled women in coin-covered caps
passages.gloss: Turkmen women did not hide from strangers or wear full veils, only a cloth over the lower face. Fraser describes their tall shako-like caps covered in gold coins, silver bells and set stones, which he thought looked more like horse trappings than jewellery.
passages.quote: The Toorkoman women are not shut up, or concealed like those of most Mahometan countries, nor do they even wear veils … most of them wear a lofty cap, with a broad crown resembling that sort of soldier’s cap called a shako … The front of this is covered with ornaments of silver or gold, in various shapes ; most frequently gold coins, mohrs or tomauns, strung in rows
passages.speaker: James Baillie Fraser

passages.headline: A Turkmen singer like an Aeolian harp
passages.people: Goklen Turkmens at the camp of Khallee Khan
passages.gloss: After dinner in a Goklen chief's tent, two musicians played until past midnight. Fraser found the singing far sweeter than Persian music: the singer's voice imitated the vibrating string of the tar, and the audience rocked and shouted with delight.
passages.quote: the measure was always closed by a single line or chorus that died away in a very sweet and singular cadence, infinitely more agreeable than any music I ever heard in Persia, for the singer did not strain his voice in the way usual in that country, but taught it most curiously to follow the inflections of the tarr, imitating the sound and undulations of the wire
passages.speaker: James Baillie Fraser

passages.headline: A pole on a mound where a Turkmen died
passages.gloss: Fraser records that when a Turkmen died, the body was washed on the spot and a small mound with a tree or pole was raised there, while the body itself was buried further out on the plain. He saw the plain dotted with these markers.
passages.quote: When one of these Toorkomans dies, they wash the body on the spot where he breathed his last, or as near it as possible; and on that spot they raise a little mound, by digging a circular trench, two or three feet wide, throwing the earth up in the centre; and in this mound they plant a tree, or pole, to mark the place.
passages.speaker: James Baillie Fraser

passages.headline: Kimmiz and horse flesh among the Uzbeks
passages.gloss: Fraser's informants told him the Uzbeks were fond of kimmiz (kumiss), fermented mare's milk shaken in a skin for hours, and often got drunk on it in season. He also heard, and heard denied, that they preferred horse meat to beef.
passages.quote: it is said they are fond of horse flesh, which they prefer to beef : I have heard this denied ; but I do not know which statement is the true one. There is no doubt of their fondness for the national and intoxicating drink, called kimmiz, prepared from mares’ milk, by shaking it violently in a skin for several hours.
passages.speaker: James Baillie Fraser

passages.headline: Turkmens with 'Tartar' faces
passages.gloss: Fraser sorts the Turkmen tribes by how 'Tartar' they looked: the Teke most, the Goklen less, the Yomut least, with big differences even within one family. It shows 'Tartar' being used as a physical type rather than a nation.
passages.quote: The Tuckehs have a great deal of the Tartar physiognomy; many of the men were tall, stout and well made, with scanty beards, eyes small, and drawn up at the corners ; high cheek bones, and small flat noses: some on the contrary had handsome features, more resembling those of Europeans than Asiatics.
passages.speaker: James Baillie Fraser
passages.caution: Racial typing typical of the period.

passages.headline: 'Moghuls are a tribe of Tartars'
passages.gloss: Correcting an earlier traveller who listed 'Moghuls' among the people of Herat, Fraser explains that Moghuls are properly one tribe of Tartars, and that in India the word was used loosely for Muslims in general because many descended from the Mughal conquerors.
passages.quote: Moghuls are, in truth, a certain tribe of Tartars, very few of whom could possibly be in Herat as part of its permanent population. Probably Captain Christie inserted this word in his journal somewhat loosely, annexing to it the same meaning which is given to it in Hindostan, where it is often applied to Mussoolmans in general
passages.speaker: James Baillie Fraser (footnote)

passages.headline: The poet who carried his own head
passages.people: Sheikh Farid al-Din Attar, captured when the Tartars (Mongols) took Nishapur
passages.gloss: Local legend held that the Sufi poet Attar was captured when the Mongols sacked Nishapur and later beheaded by his owner. His headless body then picked up its head, ran a mile to the site of his tomb and wrote its own epitaph in blood. The tomb's guardians, Fraser adds, told of villagers who stole lead from it and died.
passages.quote: he drew his sword, and smote off the sheikh’s head ; but no sooner had it rolled to the ground than the body taking it up, ran with it a full mile, to the spot where the tomb now is, and with its own finger for a pen, and its blood for ink, wrote upon a stone the epitaph which has since been engraved upon the tomb.
passages.speaker: Local tradition, as retold by James Baillie Fraser
passages.caution: A saint's legend, reported as such.

passages.headline: A wall against the Tartar tribes
passages.gloss: Riding along a long raised bank near Gorgan, Fraser heard that the rich plain had once been shielded from the Tartar tribes by a mighty wall from the mountains to the sea. He dismissed it as a legend about 'fabulous kings'.
passages.quote: It is said that this rich tract was once separated from the desert beyond it, and protected from the incursions of the Tartar tribes by a wall of great strength, which ran from the mountains to the sea. I believe, however, this great work is attributed to some of the fabulous kings, and is probably fabulous itself.
passages.speaker: James Baillie Fraser (footnote)
passages.caution: Fraser's doubt was misplaced: archaeologists have since traced a real brick barrier across this plain, the Great Wall of Gorgan, usually dated to the Sasanian period (5th to 6th century), long before any 'Tartars'.

passages.headline: How Tatars and Mongols merged
passages.people: Tatars and Mongols; Kazakhs, Uzbeks, Turkmens, Kazan and Crimean Tatars
passages.gloss: Meyendorff offers his theory of the name: Genghis Khan's Mongols conquered the Tatars, who were more numerous, and took up their Turkic language. From that mixture, he says, came all the peoples called 'Mongol Tartars', and he sees no real difference in looks between a Kazakh, an Uzbek, a Turkmen and a Tatar of Kazan or Crimea.
passages.quote: The Asiatic people to whom the Russians give the name of Tartars, have the nose slightly flattened, the cheek bones prominent, little beard on the chin, and small eyes … Gengis Khan, at the head of the Mongols, subjugated the Tartars, who became incorporated with his army, and those of his successors. As they were the most numerous, the conquerors adopted the Turkish language, barbarous as it was
passages.speaker: Georg von Meyendorff (translated by William Monteith, 1840)
passages.caution: Meyendorff's own theory, mixed with racial typing of the period.

passages.headline: Call it 'Central Asia', not 'Tartary'
passages.gloss: Meyendorff objects that the usual map label 'Tartary' covers lands never settled by Tartars while leaving out places where Tartar (Turkic) was actually spoken. A country, he argues, should only be named after a people who live there, so he proposes 'Central Asia' instead.
passages.quote: If in geography we give to a country the name of a people, it should be conditional on such people inhabiting that country. It appears to me then, that Central Asia would be a more appropriate name to introduce in lieu of Tartary, since I have found it more correct, and more geographical.
passages.speaker: Georg von Meyendorff (translated by William Monteith, 1840)
passages.caution: The translator notes that this chapter was obscure even in French.

passages.headline: 'We are Kazakhs, not Kirghiz'
passages.gloss: Meyendorff noticed that the steppe people the Russians called Kirghiz never used that name themselves. They called themselves Kazakh, which some said meant 'horseman' and others 'warrior', and they believed the Bashkirs had given them the name Kirghiz.
passages.quote: they never make use of this name among themselves ; they invariably style themselves Kasak ; which, according to some, signifies horseman, and to others warrior. They say the Bachkirs call them Kirghiz, but are ignorant from whence the name is derived
passages.speaker: Georg von Meyendorff (translated by William Monteith, 1840)

passages.headline: Clay tombs that looked like cities
passages.gloss: The nomadic Kazakhs built lasting tombs of clay mixed with chopped straw, sometimes of unburnt brick, with a small prayer chamber inside. Rich families brought craftsmen from Bukhara to make them. Near the Syr Darya they were so many that from a distance they looked like cities.
passages.quote: All the tombs are of clay, mixed with chopped straw, except that of Khodja, which is of unburnt bricks. In the interior of these sepulchres there is another, smaller, where the Kirghiz pray. These monuments become more numerous as you approach the Sir, and appear like cities. The rich Kirghiz frequently bring artificers from Bokhara to make their clay tombs
passages.speaker: Georg von Meyendorff (translated by William Monteith, 1840)

passages.headline: Inside a Kazakh sultan's tent
passages.gloss: At the Ilek River the embassy met its first Kazakh camp: about 50 tents of white or brown felt. Meyendorff then visited the sultan's large round tent, which mixed luxury and plain nomad gear: carpets, tiger skins, a woman's tall gold headdress set with turquoise and rubies, raw meat on hooks and leather bags of mare's milk.
passages.quote: the floor was covered with a carpet, wearing apparel hung on a cord, and skins of tigers were stretched against the sides; a rich diadem of gold, very high, and ornamented with turquoise and rubies, the head dress of Kirghiz women ; by their side might also be seen raw meat hanging on hooks, large leather bags of mare's milk, and some wooden vessels of different kinds
passages.speaker: Georg von Meyendorff (translated by William Monteith, 1840)

passages.headline: Mud ruins the Kazakhs credited to the Nogais
passages.gloss: Along a dried-up river channel Meyendorff saw long earth mounds with canals and broken pottery, the remains of buildings of sun-dried brick. The Kazakhs could not say when or why they were built but guessed they were the work of the Nogais, who had held the steppe before them. The best-known ruin, Djankend, was of fired brick and said to be the seat of an Oghuz chief.
passages.quote: It is clear these buildings, whatever they may have been, were built with sun-burnt bricks; near these ruins are small canals about 1 toise or 6 feet broad and two deep; a great quantity of broken pottery is also to be met with. … The Kirghiz could give us no account of their use or date, but supposing they must have been erected by the Nogais
passages.speaker: Georg von Meyendorff (translated by William Monteith, 1840)
passages.caution: The attribution to the Nogais is the Kazakhs' guess, as Meyendorff says.

passages.headline: Entering Bukhara: earth houses and a brick palace
passages.gloss: The Russian embassy entered Bukhara through a tall gate and narrow streets of gloomy, flat-roofed earth houses to the great square with its mosques and colleges. The palace was reached through a vaulted brick corridor lined with soldiers, and the audience hall had white plaster walls and a painted plank ceiling.
passages.quote: after passing the gate which was very lofty, we continued our route through a narrow winding street, of gloomy houses, built of earth, and flat roofed. At last we arrived at the great square, surrounded with mosques, colleges or madrissa, and the enclosure of the palace. After dismounting, we entered a vaulted corridore built of brick
passages.speaker: Georg von Meyendorff (translated by William Monteith, 1840)

passages.headline: Khiva's mud walls and towns
passages.gloss: In the extract from Muraviev's journal that Monteith appended, Khiva appears as a walled capital of 10,000 to 15,000 people with mud walls 20 feet high, a palace and a fine mosque. The other towns of the khanate were of flat-roofed mud with a few brick mosques, and lasted well because the climate was so dry.
passages.quote: The walls of the city are built of mud and 20 feet in height … The buildings in all these towns are only of mud with flat roofs, some few mosques are of brick and mortar. They are however very permanent from the dryness of the climate.
passages.speaker: Nikolai Muraviev, in William Monteith's English extract
passages.caution: Not Meyendorff's text: Muraviev's journal as extracted by the translator. The full Muraviev translation is record W027.

passages.headline: Samarkand's marble and Timur's jasper tomb
passages.people: Emirate of Bukhara; Timur and his descendants
passages.gloss: Meyendorff was told that Samarkand's mosques and squares were finer than Bukhara's, built of white marble from nearby quarries, with fronts of glazed tiles, and that Timur's tomb of jasper still stood though Ulugh Beg's observatory had vanished. He adds that each new Khan of Bukhara was raised three times on a bluish stone called the Kok-tash.
passages.quote: The mosques and squares are handsomer than those at Bokhara, they are all built of white marble of which there are quarries at a trifling distance from this ancient residence of Timour. The fronts of the houses are covered with varnished tiles like those of Bokhara … The tomb of Timour, built of Jasper is still to be seen at Samercand, but the Observatory of Olong-Bey no longer exists
passages.speaker: Georg von Meyendorff (translated by William Monteith, 1840)
passages.caution: Second-hand; the embassy did not visit Samarkand. Most of Samarkand's great buildings are actually of fired brick faced with tile, so 'all built of white marble' is an exaggeration.

passages.headline: 'Houses mean slavery'
passages.gloss: Meyendorff explains why well-off Kazakhs refused to farm: they feared becoming serfs tied to the soil and liked to say they were as free as the birds. An old saying warned that they would lose their freedom once they began living in houses and farming, and the fate of the Bashkirs under Russia seemed to prove it.
passages.quote: It is therefore easy to imagine why Kirghiz in easy circumstances never cultivate the ground … they have an ancient tradition which says "The Kirghiz shall lose their liberty whenever they begin to live in houses
passages.speaker: Georg von Meyendorff (translated by William Monteith, 1840)
passages.caution: The OCR garbles the end of the saying on this page; the quote stops at 'houses' (the saying continues 'and to follow agricultural pursuits').

passages.headline: A horse thief's punishment
passages.gloss: A Kazakh horse thief was sentenced to death, but the elders asked for mercy as a good omen for the journey with the Russians. Instead he was blackened with soot, tied to a horse's tail and whipped by a laughing crowd, while his own horse was slaughtered and shared out among the onlookers.
passages.quote: The robber, half naked, having about his neck some stripes of black felt, was forced by two men on horseback who carried large whips, to run to the nearest tent, where his face was blackened with soot and marched through a group of Kirghiz; they then tied him to the tail of a horse, and forced him to hold a cord between his teeth.
passages.speaker: Georg von Meyendorff (translated by William Monteith, 1840)

passages.headline: A khan who rules by consent
passages.gloss: A Kazakh khan held power of life and death, Meyendorff says, but his only real check was public opinion: unhappy followers simply rode off and chose another leader. A khan kept power through courage, gifts and a friendly mullah to interpret the law.
passages.quote: The khan has in fact the power of life and death among the Kirghiz, who have no security against his tyranny, except public opinion, and no where is it so powerful as among the pastoral tribes. The discontented party quickly desert an unjust judge, and choose another for themselves.
passages.speaker: Georg von Meyendorff (translated by William Monteith, 1840)

passages.headline: Songs to the moon by the Syr Darya
passages.gloss: Wintering among the reeds of the Syr Darya was the Kazakhs' great wish. Meyendorff describes men sitting half the night on a stone, gazing at the moon and singing sad improvised songs, and regrets never hearing the heroic songs that only professional bards performed.
passages.quote: The Kirghiz often pass half the night seated on a stone, gazing at the moon, and singing melancholy impromptu words to airs not less so. They also have historical songs, which celebrate the great actions of their heroes, but these are chaunted only by professional singers, and I greatly regret not having heard them.
passages.speaker: Georg von Meyendorff (translated by William Monteith, 1840)

passages.headline: Solomon's rock at Osh
passages.gloss: From informants Meyendorff heard of Takht-i-Suleiman, the rock above Osh, where tradition said Solomon had sacrificed a camel and a stone still showed the blood. Sick people lay on a flat stone there hoping to be cured. He treats the story as superstition and notes that reports of ruins there were disputed.
passages.quote: Tradition states that Solomon sacrificed a camel on this spot; where the blood is shewn on a stone still perfectly red. It is, however, particularly frequented by people suffering rheumatic or other pain ; who are said to be cured by extending themselves on a flat stone near the building.
passages.speaker: Georg von Meyendorff (translated by William Monteith, 1840)
passages.caution: A local legend reported at second hand.

passages.headline: The Khan receives the envoy in a yurt
passages.gloss: After weeks of waiting, Muraviev was led through a fine brick gateway and a series of mud-walled courtyards. In the last, weedy courtyard stood the Khan's yurt, and the ruler sat inside it cross-legged on a carpet while the Russian envoy stood at the entrance.
passages.quote: On reaching the end of this corridor, we had to go down two steps into a fourth court-yard, larger than the other three, but surpassing them all in filth, and covered here and there with weeds. In the middle of this stood the Khan's Yurt.
passages.speaker: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)

passages.headline: A khan who lived in a felt tent
passages.gloss: Muraviev says the Khan of Khiva lived in a felt tent all year round and kept his houses only for his wives, spending most of his time hawking and hunting on the steppe. He also notes the Khan had banned alcohol and tobacco on pain of having one's mouth slit.
passages.quote: His mode of living is quite nomadic, for he occupies a felt tent all the year round, keeping his houses for his wives only. The greater part of his time is passed in the steppe, hawking or hunting, snipe and wild goats being his favourite game.
passages.speaker: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)

passages.headline: Mud houses, felt tents, bricks from old ruins
passages.people: Uzbeks and other people of the Khiva khanate
passages.gloss: Many Khivans, even the rich, lived in felt tents all year because they were used to nomad life. Houses were of cheap mud with a hole in the roof for smoke. The fine buildings were a few mosques, above all the turquoise-domed great mosque, and bridges were built of fired bricks taken from old ruins.
passages.quote: The houses are very bad and wretched, and a great portion of the people live in felt tents all the year round. Even the wealthy do this, although they possess houses, because they are so accustomed to a nomadic life. The houses are of mud … Bridges are numerous, and are constructed of the burnt bricks which they get from old ruins.
passages.speaker: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)

passages.headline: Mud castles of the Khivan landowners
passages.gloss: Constant feuds had led landowners to build square fortified farmsteads with granaries, tanks, mills and stables for 100 to 150 people. Muraviev gives their size and materials: mud walls 18 to 20 feet high, sometimes of masonry, with domed corner towers and battlements that were only for show. He was himself held in one of these forts.
passages.quote: The buildings are in the form of a square, and are surrounded by walls generally of mud, but sometimes of masonry. The walls are 8 feet thick at the base, diminishing to 3 at the summit, and are from 18 to 20 feet high. They are supported on the exterior faces by round buttresses, also of mud, and are crenelated, but the battlements are merely for show
passages.speaker: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)

passages.headline: Khiva: a turquoise dome and mud streets
passages.gloss: Muraviev describes Khiva as a walled town between two canals whose chief buildings were the great mosque with its turquoise-blue dome, a rather insignificant palace and some smaller mosques. Most building was in mud, the streets were narrow, and a market was held twice a week. Locals said its old name was Khivak and that it existed before the Amu Darya changed course.
passages.quote: The principal buildings are the great mosque, with its dome of turquoise-blue (a colour revered by Mussulmans) ; the Khan's palace, which is, however, an insignificant structure, and several smaller mosques. Mud is the material in general use for building purposes. The streets are narrow.
passages.speaker: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)

passages.headline: Mud-walled towns that last because it rarely rains
passages.place: Khiva khanate (New Urgench, Shavat, Kat, Gurlen)
passages.people: Sarts, Uzbeks and Turkmens of Khiva
passages.gloss: Muraviev lists the five towns of the khanate, with New Urgench larger and busier than Khiva itself. All were walled, but their buildings were mean and made almost entirely of mud, with walls faced with stone only here and there. They survived for years only because so little rain fell.
passages.quote: The buildings in all the above towns are very mean (the only ones approaching to anything like size being a few mosques), and mud is the almost universal material of the houses, as it may also be said to be that of the town walls … In spite of this perishable material, the buildings stand for many years, owing to the very scanty rain fall.
passages.speaker: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)

passages.headline: The 'Silver Hill': a buried brick fortress
passages.place: Gorgan River mouth, southeast Caspian coast
passages.people: Yomut Turkmens (living around it); builders unknown
passages.gloss: What looked like a hill on the coast turned out to be the sand-covered shell of a huge fired-brick building with a wall about 600 feet long. Muraviev dug for coins and found Muslim-style graves and broken glass. The local Turkmens told him it had been built by the Russians, and a translator's footnote links it to an ancient wall along the Gorgan River.
passages.quote: The Silver Hill is, as above mentioned, only the shell of some huge building or fortress, which has been covered with sand from the eastern side ; nevertheless within those walls I found tombs, and, indeed, got at some human remains, buried after the Mahomedan fashion … The great wall is about 600 feet long and over 12 feet in height. It consists of beautiful burnt bricks
passages.speaker: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)
passages.caution: The site lies at the western end of the brick barrier now called the Great Wall of Gorgan, usually dated to the Sasanian period. The claim that Russians built it is local belief, and the footnote rejects it.

passages.headline: Five doors in the cliff and a hidden king
passages.gloss: Along the dry old bed of the Amu Darya, Muraviev passed five neat openings cut in a cliff, called Besh Dishik. The Turkmens said they led to caverns where a king with his family and treasure had lived since ancient times, and that intruders were strangled by an unseen hand. When one man doubted, another pointed to the cliff's echo as proof.
passages.quote: The nomadic Turcomans of the surrounding country are all assured that these apertures are the approaches to vast caverns in which from time immemorial there has dwelt a King with a numerous family, countless treasure, and beauteous daughters, but that once when some inquisitive persons tried to intrude into the caverns, they were immediately seized by an unseen hand and strangled.
passages.speaker: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)
passages.caution: A local legend; Muraviev tried to climb up but could not reach the openings.

passages.headline: A Russian hut on the old Oxus nobody dares touch
passages.gloss: The Turkmens told Muraviev that at the mouth of the dry river bed stood a hut built in the Russian style that no one would pull down out of superstitious fear, and whose builder nobody knew. Muraviev guessed it dated from Prince Bekovich's expedition sent by Peter the Great a century earlier.
passages.quote: Kiat informed me that the mouth of this old river bed, although choked with sand, is still distinguishable on the Caspian, and that by it there stands a hut (isba) constructed on the Russian plan. No one knows who the builder of this was, but the neighbouring Turcomans are restrained from demolishing it by superstitious dread.
passages.speaker: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)
passages.caution: Muraviev did not see the hut; the link to Bekovich is his guess.

passages.headline: 'Most incorrectly' called Tartars
passages.gloss: Muraviev says the scattered Turkmen tribes share a common origin but have been 'most incorrectly' called a Tartar race by European writers. He suggests the word came from Tatar, the founder of a tribe of that name still living in the far steppes.
passages.quote: This people has been most incorrectly denominated the Tartar race by several European authors. The term was probably borrowed from Tatar, the Chief who founded the tribe of that name, existing in the remoter steppes to the present day.
passages.speaker: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)
passages.caution: The eponymous chief 'Tatar' is a traditional explanation, not established history.

passages.headline: Uzbek means 'own master'
passages.gloss: Muraviev explains the Uzbek name as 'own master' (uz = self, beg = master) and adds, with some irony, that since Muhammad Rahim Khan made himself absolute ruler, the Uzbeks of Khiva now called themselves 'khidmatgar', servants.
passages.quote: "Us" in Turkish signifies "self" and "Beg" master, so Usbeg may be translated as "Own Master." The name was appropriate enough up to the time of the reigning Khan, Mahomed Ragim, who, by ability, craft, and force, established himself as uncontrolled Ruler, since when his countrymen in Khiva style themselves "Khidmatgar" (servant) instead of "Usbeg."
passages.speaker: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)
passages.caution: A popular folk etymology; the name probably comes from the 14th-century Golden Horde khan Özbeg.

passages.headline: A note hidden in a gun barrel
passages.gloss: Preparing to leave, Muraviev found a slip of paper secretly pushed into his gun barrel by Russian captives, begging him to tell the Tsar of more than 3,000 Russian slaves suffering in Khiva. Elsewhere he says most were kidnapped on the Orenburg frontier by Kazakhs and sold at Khiva, and that Russian slaves were the khanate's only smiths.
passages.quote: As I was preparing to clean this gun, I discovered a slip of paper in one of the barrels, on which the following was written in Russian : "We venture to inform your Honor that there are over 3,000 Russian slaves in this place, who have to suffer unheard-of misery from labour, cold, hunger, &c. Have pity on our unhappy situation and reveal it to the Emperor.
passages.speaker: Nikolai Muraviev, quoting a note from Russian slaves (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)

passages.headline: Bards who sing all night
passages.gloss: Rich Khivans kept bards who sang the deeds of ancient heroes on a lute, growing more ecstatic as the audience applauded, sometimes through the whole night while the listeners sat still and silent.
passages.quote: The wealthy Khivans generally keep a bard in their service, who entertains them with stories and songs, and airs played on a sorry kind of lute. Sometimes they compose ballads relating the deeds of ancient heroes. … This singing is kept up the whole night not unfrequently, during which the host and his guests sit attentively listening, motionless, and apparently buried in meditation.
passages.speaker: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)

passages.headline: Oaths at a saint's tomb and fortune-telling sticks
passages.gloss: The Yomut Turkmens settled disputes by swearing an oath over a saint's tomb, believing a perjurer could only escape damnation by dying on the spot. Muraviev also describes Khivan fortune-tellers who read letters from a book, or threw sticks onto a circle of other sticks each standing for a letter.
passages.quote: The Yomud Turcomans adore a Saint over whose tomb they settle their differences by an oath. A false oath under those circumstances is unknown, for it is firmly believed that whoever forswears himself over the tomb can only save himself from eternal punishment by dying on the spot.
passages.speaker: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)

passages.headline: The devil's claws on the moon
passages.gloss: Muraviev says that even the court astronomer who could calculate eclipses believed, like everyone in Khiva, that an eclipse happened when the devil grabbed the sun or moon, and that shouting and firing guns would drive him off. They called the North Star the 'iron point' at the end of the earth's axis and compared the earth to a watermelon.
passages.quote: he does not even know the cause of an eclipse, but believes with the rest of the people that it is brought about by the devil fastening his claws on to the sun or moon, and thinks a loud noise and the firing off of guns necessary to get rid of this dreadful enemy. The earth they believe to be round and compare it to a water-melon.
passages.speaker: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)
passages.caution: Muraviev writes condescendingly about Khivan learning.

passages.headline: Turkmen tents like those of the Georgian Tartars
passages.gloss: On the Caspian coast Muraviev compared Turkmen dwellings to those of the 'Tartars in Georgia' (Turkic-speaking Muslims of the Caucasus): reed mats on long poles covered with felt. He also notes that Turkmen women did not hide from strangers and wore very tall headdresses edged with gold or silver.
passages.quote: The dwelling-places of the Turcomans are constructed like those of the Tartars in Georgia, that is to say, they consist of rush mats stretched on long poles, the whole being covered with felt. Their women are not kept in privacy
passages.speaker: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)

passages.headline: 'The name of Tartary is unknown in those regions'
passages.people: Uzbeks and other Turkic peoples of Central Asia
passages.gloss: Setting out the geography north of the Hindu Kush, Elphinstone divides the lands into Turkestan (west of the Pamirs) and 'Chinese Turkestan' (east of them), using the local name for Turk-speaking country. Then he adds a blunt note: the people who live there do not call it Tartary. The word was a European map label, not a local one.
passages.quote: All the country west of Beloot Taugh, and north of the Oxus, is called Toorkistaun, a term which may be extended to the east of Beloot Taugh, as far as there is reason to think the Turkish language is spoken … The name of Tartary is unknown in those regions.
passages.speaker: Mountstuart Elphinstone (1815)
passages.caution: Based on what his Central Asian informants told him, not on a visit.

passages.headline: The Uzbeks sweep south and take Bukhara
passages.gloss: Elphinstone explains who the Uzbeks were: a people who crossed the Jaxartes (Syr Darya) around 1500 and drove the heirs of Tamerlane out of Bukhara, Khwarazm and Ferghana. The next sentence is badly damaged in the scan, but it seems to say that the Uzbeks belong to the great division of mankind known in Asia as Turks, who together with the Moguls (and a third people whose name is illegible) 'compose what we call the Tartar nation'. So for him 'Tartar' is a European umbrella word for Turks and Mongols together.
passages.quote: The Uzbeks first crossed the Jaxartes about the beginning of the sixteenth century, and pouring on the possessions of the descendants of Tamerlane, soon drove them from Bokhaura, Khoarizm, and Ferghauna, and spread terror and dismay to the remotest parts of their extended empire.
passages.speaker: Mountstuart Elphinstone (1815)
passages.caution: Page is heavily garbled; the words after this sentence can only be read in part.

passages.headline: The round felt tent used 'over all Tartary'
passages.gloss: Elphinstone contrasts two ways of living among the Uzbeks. Their houses, villages and towns look just like Afghan ones, but their tent is the round lattice tent covered with felt (the yurt), which he calls the kirgah and says is used across all of Tartary. On the same page he adds that it is warmer than the Afghan black tent and hardly harder to carry.
passages.quote: Their houses, villages, and towns, exactly resemble those of the Afghauns, but their tents are widely different The Uzbek tent is of the kind called Kirgah, which appears to be in use over all Tartary, in part of Persia, and even in part of China. It is round, and formed of lattice work … covered with black or grey felts.
passages.speaker: Mountstuart Elphinstone (1815)
passages.caution: From informants; Elphinstone did not visit Uzbek country.

passages.headline: Kumiss: drunk all summer, never sold
passages.gloss: Elphinstone describes how the Uzbeks make kimmiz (kumiss) by leaving mare's milk overnight in a skin and then beating and rolling it until morning. He notes that it can only be had in the last two months of summer, that people who can afford it stay drunk for much of that time, and that it is never sold. Nearby he adds that Uzbeks love horse-flesh but usually have to make do with beef.
passages.quote: The liquor thus made is of a whitish colour and a sourish taste: it is only to be had in plenty during the two last months of summer, and those who can afford it are generally drunk for the greater part of that period; but kimmiz is not sold, and those only can enjoy it who have mares enough to make it in the house.
passages.speaker: Mountstuart Elphinstone (1815)

passages.headline: Not savages: a defence of the Uzbeks
passages.gloss: Elphinstone argues that the European picture of the Uzbeks as ferocious barbarians comes from confusing them with the Kalmyks (the garbled word in the scan) and 'other rude Tartar tribes' further north. He does not hide the slave trade in Bukhara, but on the word of Afghan and Tajik travellers he calls the Uzbeks 'as good a people as any in Asia'. The rest of the page, badly scanned, says that anyone who imagines the Uzbeks as savages will be surprised to learn that Bukhara rivals Peshawar in population, has numerous colleges and caravanserais, and tolerates all religions.
passages.quote: of the Uzbeks, appear to be unjust, and is probably owing partly to our confounding them with … other rude Tartar tribes between them and Russia … men are sold in Bokhaura like cattle; but in other respects, by all that I can learn, both from Afghaun travellers, and from Taujiks of Bulkh and Bokhaura, I have reason to think the Uzbeks as good a people as any in Asia.
passages.speaker: Mountstuart Elphinstone (1815)
passages.caution: Second-hand; he names his sources as Afghan travellers and Tajiks of Balkh and Bukhara.

passages.headline: Balkh: a great ruin with one corner lived in
