passages.gloss: Balkh, the old capital of the Uzbek-populated province south of the Oxus, is called by Asians the oldest city in the world and the 'mother of towns' (the scan is garbled here). By Elphinstone's day it had shrunk to a small inhabited corner inside a vast walled ruin, with a citadel held by the Afghan governor. The rich countryside was still watered by eighteen canals.
passages.quote: Its ruins still cover a great extent, and are surrounded with a wall, but only one corner is inhabited.
passages.speaker: Mountstuart Elphinstone (1815)
passages.caution: The page does not say who ruined Balkh; the surrounding text is badly garbled.

passages.headline: Hill people with 'Tartar' faces who say they came from the Moguls
passages.gloss: Elphinstone is puzzled by the Aimaqs and Hazaras: they live in the heart of Afghanistan but look, speak and behave quite differently. They have no history of their own origin and speak a dialect of Persian, yet their features and a tradition point to Mongol ancestry. He goes on to cite the historian Abu'l-Fazl, who says they are remnants of a Mongol prince's army.
passages.quote: Their features, however, refer them at once to the Tartar stock, and a tradition declares them to be the offspring of the Moguls. They are, indeed, frequently called by the name of Moguls to this day, and they are often confounded with the Moguls and Chagatyes, who still reside in the neighbourhood of Heraut.
passages.speaker: Mountstuart Elphinstone (1815)

passages.headline: Hazara villages guarded by loop-holed towers
passages.gloss: Most Hazaras live in villages, not tents, though some use 'Tartar tents' like the Aimaqs. Each village has a defensive tower with a kettle-drum to sound the alarm. On the page before, Elphinstone says their houses are thatched and half sunk into the hillsides.
passages.quote: The Hazaurehs generally live in villages of from twenty to two hundred houses, though some live in Tartar tents like the Eimauks. Each village is defended by a high tower, capable of containing ten or twelve men, and full of loop-holes.
passages.speaker: Mountstuart Elphinstone (1815)

passages.headline: Hazara wives who run the household
passages.gloss: Elphinstone is surprised to find that among the Hazaras, a tribe he calls nearly savage, women have more standing than anywhere nearby. They manage the house and property, are consulted on everything, are never beaten and are not secluded. He also records, from hearsay, lurid claims about their morals which he admits are contradictory.
passages.quote: The wife manages the house, takes care of the property, does her share of the honors, and is very much consulted in all her husband's measures. Women are never beaten, and they have no concealment.
passages.speaker: Mountstuart Elphinstone (1815)
passages.caution: From informants; the same page repeats gossip about Hazara women that Elphinstone himself calls inconsistent.

passages.headline: Victims' blood smeared on faces and beards
passages.gloss: The Aimaqs are quiet under their chiefs, Elphinstone says, but savage in war. He reports throwing prisoners off cliffs and shooting them with arrows, and one occasion, told him by a man who was there, when they drank their victims' blood. A footnote (garbled) compares this to the Mongols' treatment of prisoners.
passages.quote: I have authentic accounts of their throwing their prisoners from precipices and shooting them to death with arrows; and on an occasion at which a … with whom I have conversed assisted, they actually drank the warm blood of their victims, and rubbed it over their faces and beards.
passages.speaker: Mountstuart Elphinstone (1815)
passages.caution: An atrocity story from a single informant, the kind of tale told about enemies; Elphinstone could not check it.

passages.headline: The evil eye that eats a man's liver
passages.gloss: In a footnote Elphinstone records an Afghan belief that some Hazaras have a power of 'fascination': reading the damaged scan, they can eat out the liver of anyone they stare at. He calls it a fable, common in India and Persia and pinned on various tribes. It is a good example of a travelling rumour attached to a people seen as outsiders.
passages.quote: who … the liver of any person on whom they fix their eyes. This fable is very common in India and Persia, and is attributed to various tribes.
passages.speaker: Mountstuart Elphinstone (footnote, 1815)
passages.caution: The words describing the power itself are badly garbled in the scan; the gloss gives the most likely reading.

passages.headline: 'Timurians', not 'Moguls'
passages.gloss: Attending the marriage of a Delhi prince, Vigne insists on calling the Indian imperial house 'Timurians', after their ancestor Timur (Tamerlane), rather than the usual 'Mogul'. It is a small but telling point: the word Mogul (Mongol) had become a name for an Indian Muslim dynasty that itself descended from Central Asian conquerors.
passages.quote: I was fortunate in being present at the marriage of his grandaughter with Unjim Shikoh, one of the Princes of Delhi, or Timurians, as they are generally called … a much more correct name for the Indian Emperors than that of Mogul.
passages.speaker: Godfrey Thomas Vigne (1842)

passages.headline: A goat's blood on the bride's toe
passages.gloss: At the same wedding Vigne is allowed to watch a rite he says belongs only to the Timurid family. The bride pushes her bare, henna-dyed foot out of her palanquin and the groom, still in his wedding clothes, kills a goat and touches her great toe with its blood. Vigne presents this as something he saw with his own eyes and believes no European had seen before.
passages.quote: I was admitted, as a great favour, to see a custom peculiar, I believe, to the Timurians, and which, perhaps, no European ever saw before … she thrust her bared foot … through the sliding doors, and the bridegroom touched her great toe with the blood of a goat, which I saw him kill with his own hands
passages.speaker: Godfrey Thomas Vigne (1842)
passages.caution: Vigne's claim that the custom is peculiar to the Timurids is his belief, not something he checked.

passages.headline: Why the emperors were called 'Cheguthai'
passages.gloss: In a footnote Vigne explains the name Zagatai (Chagatai) that Kashmiris still used for the old imperial rule: it comes from a son of Genghis Khan who founded the Chagatai branch in Transoxiana. This links the Indian Mughals directly to the Mongol conquests of the 1200s.
passages.quote: Or Cheguthai, the Mogul Emperors ; so called from Zagatai Khan, a son of Jenghiz Khan, who founded the Zagatai branch in Transoxiana.
passages.speaker: Godfrey Thomas Vigne (footnote, 1842)

passages.headline: Akbar's red-brick rest-house on the road to Kashmir
passages.gloss: On the old imperial road over the Pir Panjal, Vigne finds loose stones that are all that remain of a causeway laid by Akbar's pioneers, and a large brick serai (caravan rest-house) Akbar built for the imperial retinue. He credits the building plainly to the Mughal emperor and describes its material. He chose to sleep in a humbler house prepared for Ranjit Singh instead.
passages.quote: A large Serai built by him, of red brick, is conspicuously placed on the right bank of the stream, near Thana, and its quadrangle was well adapted to the reception of a cortege of a Mogul Emperor
passages.speaker: Godfrey Thomas Vigne (1842)

passages.headline: Shahbad: 'the abode of the king' in ruins
passages.gloss: Shahbad, once the largest town at the south end of the Kashmir valley and named as a royal seat, had become a ruin by Vigne's visit. The Mughal palace was hardly worth a remark and its grounds were overgrown. Vigne blames much of Kashmir's decay on recent Sikh rule, famine and earthquake rather than on any lost civilization.
passages.quote: Shahbad, the abode of the king, which was the largest place at the southern end of the valley, is now a ruin ; and the palace of the Moguls is scarcely worth a remark. Its environs are overgrown with nettles and wild hemp.
passages.speaker: Godfrey Thomas Vigne (1842)

passages.headline: Milton's 'roving Tartar' on the Himalaya
passages.gloss: Standing on the Pir Panjal pass, Vigne quotes in a footnote Milton's famous simile of a vulture bred on Imaus (the Himalaya), 'whose snowy ridge the roving Tartar bounds'. It shows the English literary picture of the Tartar that travellers carried with them: a wandering herdsman on the far side of the great mountains.
passages.quote: On Imaus bred, Whose snowy ridge the roving Tartar bounds, Dislodging from a region scarce of prey. To gorge the flesh of lambs or yeanling kids, On hills where flocks are fed, flies towards the springs Of Ganges or Hydaspes, Indian streams
passages.speaker: John Milton, Paradise Lost iii.431, quoted in a footnote by Vigne
passages.caution: A poem, not a report; included for the image of the Tartar it carries.

passages.headline: Dressed 'a la Tatare' for a winter ride
passages.gloss: Crossing eastern Turkey in deep winter, with the thermometer at 15 degrees below zero, Vigne kept warm by dressing in Tatar style: five pairs of stockings under big travelling boots. In the Ottoman lands 'Tatar' dress meant the outfit of the government couriers, which European travellers often copied (see Clarke, W032).
passages.quote: On the plain of Erzeroum, the thermometer, on a morning in the middle of February, fell to 15° below zero ; but I was clothed a la Tatare, with five pairs of stockings and large travelling boots drawn over them, so that I felt perfectly warm
passages.speaker: Godfrey Thomas Vigne (1842)
passages.caution: Vigne does not describe the costume further; the link to the courier dress is an explanation, not his words.

passages.headline: 'Tartar or Tatar is unknown here, and so is Tibet'
passages.people: Tibetans of upper Kinnaur and western Tibet
passages.gloss: Gerard lists what the people actually call themselves and their land: Bhoteeas or Zhads to the lowlanders, Bhot for the country, Keao for the people of Gnaree, and he notes that Zhad is an insult. Then he says flatly that neither 'Tartar' nor 'Tibet' was known there. 'Tartar' was the European name he was using for convenience.
passages.quote: The Tartars are called by the inhabitants of the lower parts, Zhads, Bhoteeas or Bootuntees, and their country is often named Bhot and Bootunt … Zhad is reckoned a term of reproach, and is applied by the Hindoos to those who eat bullock's flesh … Tartar or Tatar is unknown here, and so is Tibet.
passages.speaker: Alexander Gerard (ed. George Lloyd, 1841)

passages.headline: 'Very far removed from the ferocity' of the Tartar legend
passages.gloss: Gerard spent days travelling with boys from Tibetan villages as guides and describes them with real affection. He directly rejects the reputation for ferocity that the word Tartar carried in Europe. When he fell ill with rheumatism at Peenoo in Spiti, the villagers brought medicine, sugar, spices and tea.
passages.quote: They are of a mild and benevolent disposition, very far removed from the ferocity commonly attached to the character of a Tartar. I have had many instances of their humanity. At Peenoo, in Speetee, where I was confined to my bed for two days with rheumatism, I never experienced more attention
passages.speaker: Alexander Gerard (ed. George Lloyd, 1841)
passages.caution: Gerard himself warns that he may have taken 'too favourable a view' of them (p.109).

passages.headline: Houses of stone below and sun-dried brick above
passages.gloss: Gerard describes the flat-roofed, two-storey houses of Spiti: stone on the ground floor and unburnt (sun-dried) brick on the upper floor, which he hears is the rule across Ladakh too. In a footnote elsewhere he explains that the climate is so dry that such brick houses last as well as stone. Firewood is so scarce it is brought by yak and stacked on the roofs.
passages.quote: The lower half of the houses here, and I have heard, throughout most part of Ludak, is built of stone, and the upper of unburnt bricks : they are two stories high, and flat roofed.
passages.speaker: Alexander Gerard (ed. George Lloyd, 1841)

passages.headline: Prayer walls you must always pass on the right
passages.gloss: Gerard describes mani walls: long dykes of loose, uncemented stone, topped with slates carved with the prayer 'Om mani padme hum'. The Tartars always keep them on the right hand, even if it means a detour of a quarter of a mile. On nearby pages he describes chortens, prayer flags on every house, and prayer wheels turned by water and wind.
passages.quote: the most common are tumuli, named Mane, consisting of a dyke of different lengths from ten to two hundred feet, two broad, and three or four high; they are constructed of loose stones without cement, and upon their tops are numerous pieces of slate of all shapes and sizes, carved with sentences in the Oochen or sacred character.
passages.speaker: Alexander Gerard (ed. George Lloyd, 1841)

passages.headline: A nine-foot prayer wheel worked by a winch
passages.gloss: At Soongnum Gerard saw three prayer cylinders kept turning by water, and at Nisung others turned by the wind. The largest, about nine feet high, stood in a square house with a wooden dome, lined with China silk, and needed two people to work it with ropes and a winch.
passages.quote: At Soongnum there are three cylinders kept constantly in motion by water, on the same principle as the water mills, and at Nisung several are turned by the wind.
passages.speaker: Alexander Gerard (ed. George Lloyd, 1841)

passages.headline: Tea that tastes like soup
passages.gloss: Tibetan butter tea, bought at the Gartok fair, is made with butter, salt, spices and a little meal instead of milk and sugar. Gerard grew to love it. Every traveller arriving at a Tartar village was offered a dish of it, and it was kept ready most of the day.
passages.quote: During my stay at Soongnum, Putee Ram insisted on bringing me daily tea, prepared after the Tartar fashion, which tastes like soup, and I took a great liking to it. The Tartars drink it in large quantities ; and when they arrive at their encamping ground, their first occupation is to make the tea
passages.speaker: Alexander Gerard (ed. George Lloyd, 1841)

passages.headline: 'I'll make you a real Tartar': travelling on sheep
passages.gloss: When Gerard could not find porters for his grain on the empty high plateau, his friend Putee Ram brought a flock of sheep. The trick was to load the grain on the sheep, eat the grain first, and then eat the sheep. It is a neat picture of how people actually crossed the high Tibetan uplands.
passages.quote: I'll make you a real Tartar: you have grain for ten or twelve days, and now you have no use for porters; load the sheep with the grain, finish it first, and then kill and eat the sheep : this is the way we travel on the uninhabitable tracts ; we never think of grain as long as we have plenty of sheep.
passages.speaker: Putee Ram of Soongnum, quoted by Alexander Gerard (footnote)

passages.headline: Gartok: a famous market town of black tents
passages.gloss: Gartok (Garoo), the chief wool mart of western Tibet, is not a town of houses at all but a camp of black tents occupied for six months of the year. In winter the people move downstream and the Chinese governors live in a fort. Each July a fair of 10,000 to 12,000 people gathers there. Gerard never got there; this comes from informants.
passages.quote: Is a collection of black tents inhabited by pastoral tribes for six months. In winter, the Tartars retire chiefly to Eegoong on the bank of the river, two stages down the stream, and the Chinese governors reside at the Fort of Tuzheegung, where they have houses. Garoo is the most famous mart for wool in Chinese Tartary
passages.speaker: Alexander Gerard (ed. George Lloyd, 1841)
passages.caution: From informants; Gerard was refused entry to Chinese territory.

passages.headline: Yarkand, a magnificent city 'under the Chinese'
passages.gloss: Gerard passes on what he was told about Yarkand, forty days north of Leh. It is described as a large, magnificent city of lofty buildings, ruled by China, where the people are 'Moguls' who speak Turkish and Russian merchants often come. He had not seen it himself.
passages.quote: Yarkund is described as being a large and magnificent city, containing many splendid and lofty buildings ; it is under the Chinese, and the inhabitants are Moguls, and speak the Turkish language. It is said that Russian merchants often visit Yarkund.
passages.speaker: Alexander Gerard (ed. George Lloyd, 1841)
passages.caution: Pure hearsay; Gerard never went north of the Himalaya.

passages.headline: Leh: a town of a thousand houses
passages.gloss: Gerard describes Leh, the capital of Ladakh, standing a few miles from the Indus, as a town of nearly 1,000 houses built like those of Spiti, with Muslim and Hindu shopkeepers but mostly Tartar (Tibetan) people. It holds fairs attended by Punjabis, Yarkandis, Kinnauris and Kashmiris.
passages.quote: … contains nearly 1,000 houses, built like those in Speetee. There are some Mahommedan and Hindoo shop-keepers, but the greater part of the inhabitants are Tartars.
passages.speaker: Alexander Gerard (ed. George Lloyd, 1841)
passages.caution: Gerard does not say he visited Leh; the description reads as gathered from others.

passages.headline: A frontier chief who refused 150 rupees
passages.people: Tibetans of Spiti; officials of Chinese-ruled Tibet
passages.gloss: At Peenoo in Spiti, Gerard asked the headman (styled Lafa) for leave to return by the Taree pass. The man sent back his 150 rupees and said the travellers were welcome to goats, sheep and blankets, but not to that road, though he would not fight them. Gerard admired his firmness and goes on to say that the Tartars of the Chinese frontier were as strict about strangers as officials at Peking; he had been turned back at four different points the year before.
passages.quote: The Chinese Tartars, on this remote frontier of their vast empire, are just as vigilant respecting the non-admission of strangers as their countrymen at Pekin : no sum of money, however great, will bribe them to infringe the orders of their superiors.
passages.speaker: Alexander Gerard (ed. George Lloyd, 1841)

passages.headline: Brothers sharing one wife
passages.gloss: Explaining his population figures, Gerard notes that polyandry (several husbands for one wife) was common in Kinnaur and in 'Chinese Tartary'. His footnote adds that so many people became celibate monks and nuns that in some villages they were almost half the population.
passages.quote: Polyandry also exists in Chinese Tartary and in the hilly tracts towards the plains. Besides this drawback on the increase of the population, there is another peculiar to Chinese Tartary and the adjoining countries ; that is, celibacy, which is professed by numbers of the inhabitants : and in some villages the monks and nuns form almost half the population.
passages.speaker: Alexander Gerard (footnote; ed. George Lloyd, 1841)

passages.headline: Flags that frighten away hobgoblins
passages.gloss: At the corner of almost every Tartar house flew a long flag printed with 'Om mani padme hum' and topped with a tuft of black yak hair. Gerard reports that these flags and the stone piles on the roofs were believed to scare off ghosts and evil spirits.
passages.quote: The Durchuts and Lapchas are considered efficacious in frightening away ghosts, hobgoblins, and evil spirits, which are universally believed in.
passages.speaker: Alexander Gerard (ed. George Lloyd, 1841)

passages.headline: The lost ancient nation of Lake Baikal: no trace
passages.gloss: Turner had read a European theory, fashionable in the 1700s, that a lost ancient people near Lake Baikal had taught arts and sciences to India and Europe. He asked the Manchu-born chamberlain Soopoon Choomboo, who had travelled along the Baikal, about it. The answer: the area was thinly peopled and he knew of no monument showing remote antiquity. A striking early test of a 'lost civilisation of Tartary' idea.
passages.quote: My inquiries respected an ancient nation, supposed to have once inhabited the borders of the Baikal sea, in the interior of Tartary, and from which some persons conjecture, the learning, arts, and sciences of India, and even of Europe, to have been originally derived. If such a nation ever existed, the remembrance of it seems now to be buried in deepest oblivion.
passages.speaker: Samuel Turner (1800)
passages.caution: The same page adds Soopoon Choomboo's answer: 'nor to his knowledge, was any monument existing, that bore marks of remote antiquity.' Turner's own view is only that the tradition, if real, is forgotten.

passages.headline: Heaps of monster bones across Tartary and Siberia
passages.gloss: Discussing why lions are carved on Tibetan buildings though none live nearby, Turner remarks that if lions ever lived there wild, it was in the age of the huge animals whose bones lie in heaps in Tartary and Siberia. He takes the bones (mammoths) as proof of a great convulsion of the globe. This is Turner's own speculation, a common idea in his day.
passages.quote: it must have been at the same time with those vast monsters, whose bones are found in huge heaps in various parts of Tartary and Siberia at this day, and clearly point to some great convulsion, and change, in the order of our globe.
passages.speaker: Samuel Turner (1800)
passages.caution: Turner's own inference from reports of mammoth bones; he did not see them.

passages.headline: Nomads who fear that houses will fall on them
passages.gloss: Soopoon Choomboo told Turner that the wandering people beyond the desert disliked entering houses. Turner passes on the explanation he heard (fear that houses would fall, perhaps from earthquakes) and adds his own guess: that the ability to flee smallpox made a mobile life attractive. Either way, he says, large hordes still live in tents with their herds.
passages.quote: This prejudice is said to have its foundation in a dread of their falling; an apprehension which may perhaps have originated, in remote times, from the calamitous effects of earthquakes … Thus large hordes of Tartars are still found to dwell in tents, tending upon cattle, and placing their chief dependance upon their herds
passages.speaker: Samuel Turner (1800)
passages.caution: Both explanations are guesses; the second (smallpox) is Turner's own.

passages.headline: Tents woven from yak hair
passages.gloss: On the high plain beyond Phari and the Tongla mountain, Turner saw herds of yaks and 'Tartar tents' made entirely from the animals: the tent cloth woven from yak hair, and the guy ropes spun from it too. These are the black tents of Tibetan herders, quite different from the round felt yurts of the Mongols.
passages.quote: On its skirts were large herds of the bushy-tailed cattle, grazing; and we saw some Tartar tents, formed from the hair of these cattle, woven into cloth; the ropes also which fastened them to iron pins driven into the ground, were spun from the same materials.
passages.speaker: Samuel Turner (1800)

passages.headline: A Lama's tomb with 'Chinese, or Tartar' decoration
passages.gloss: Turner describes the mausoleum of the previous Panchen Lama at Tashilhunpo. He sorts its style carefully: Indian-looking pillars and arches inside, Chinese or 'Tartar' decoration outside (the tented canopy and imperial dragon), and a plain but solid stone building with cement. It is a good example of a traveller naming the traditions a building borrowed from.
passages.quote: the external decorations are of Chinese, or Tartar origin, similar to those of the watch tower, or temple of the former; the tented canopy and imperial dragon. As far as the mason has been concerned … a plain substantial building of stone, with cement.
passages.speaker: Samuel Turner (1800)
passages.caution: The scan of this page is rough; the wording has been cleaned from obvious OCR noise.

passages.headline: Kumiss dried in bags under a horse's belly
passages.gloss: Served soured milk (dhy) by the Lama of Phari, Turner compares it with the kumiss of the Tartars, made from mare's milk in the same way. He adds a hearsay detail: it is sometimes dried into chalk-like lumps, and the drying is done by hanging it in cloth bags under the horses' bellies.
passages.quote: The Kummuz of the Tartars is mare's milk, prepared by the same process: this is sometimes dried in masses till it resembles chalk; and is used to give a relish to the water which they drink, by solution with it. I have been told, that the operation of drying it, is sometimes performed by tying the Dhy tight in bags of cloth, and suspending it under their horses' bellies.
passages.speaker: Samuel Turner (1800)
passages.caution: The drying detail is hearsay ('I have been told').

passages.headline: Tartar herdsmen and their yaks
passages.gloss: Near his camp Turner met Dukba herders who lived only in tents. One brought him milk and butter. Their 200 to 300 yaks, owned by three families, grazed the mountains by day and at dusk were called in, tied in a double line before the tents and guarded by two big Tibetan mastiffs. They moved north to south with the seasons.
passages.quote: Near our encampment, was a party of Tartar herdsmen, called Dukba, whose sole occupation is tending cattle, and who always live in tents. One of them brought me a large quantity of milk, which was excellent, and some very good butter.
passages.speaker: Samuel Turner (1800)

passages.headline: Mongol pilgrims bow nine times before the Lama
passages.gloss: Turner watched a party of 'Kilmauks' (Kalmyk or Oirat Mongols) waiting outside the palace for a sight of the infant Lama. When he appeared they prostrated themselves nine times and then handed over bullion and goods. Turner learned that such offerings were one of the main sources of the Lamas' wealth.
passages.quote: There came this day, a party of Kilmauks, (Calmuc Tartars) for the purposes of devotion, and to make their offerings to the Lama … they dropped upon their knees, and struck their heads against the ground. This, with the same motions, was repeated nine times.
passages.speaker: Samuel Turner (1800)

passages.headline: A Mongol monastery town where Russians trade furs
passages.place: Khalkha, Mongolia (seat of the Taranaut Lama)
passages.people: Khalkha and Kalmyk Mongols; Russian traders
passages.gloss: The Regent told Turner that Russia had courted the Taranaut Lama (the head lama of the Khalkha Mongols) with embassies and presents, including an illustrated Russian Bible Turner saw. As a result Russian traders visited the lama's seat at 'Kharka', where hides from 'Calmuc Tartary' and the furs of the Russia-China trade changed hands. The same page describes a Kalmyk pilgrimage bringing 200 to 300 horses to the Panchen Lama.
passages.quote: the Russian traders have since resorted occasionally to Kharka, the place of Taranaut Lama's residence, where they still carry on by their agents a considerable traffic. This principally consists in the sale of bulgar hides, which are prepared in the adjacent districts, and brought also from Calmuc Tartary to the same mart
passages.speaker: Samuel Turner (1800)
passages.caution: Reported by the Regent; 'Kharka' is probably the Khalkha lama's monastery town (later Urga, now Ulaanbaatar), but Turner does not locate it.

passages.headline: A Manchu 'Tartar' at the Tibetan court
passages.gloss: Turner's most important informant, Soopoon Choomboo, the Panchen Lama's cup-bearer and second officer of the court, was Manchu by birth. Turner calls him a 'Mantchieux Tartar', using the European habit of calling the Manchu rulers of China Tartars. Two pages on he describes his 'Tartar' features: small eyes, thin eyebrows, high cheek bones, no beard.
passages.quote: Soopoon Choomboo, who was styled also Sadeek, held the second rank in the court of Teshoo Loomboo. He was by birth a Mantchieux Tartar
passages.speaker: Samuel Turner (1800)

passages.headline: Yellow caps and red caps across all Tartary
passages.gloss: Watching monks in yellow robes and conical yellow hats, Turner explains that Tibetan Buddhism is split into yellow-hat and red-hat sects that between them cover 'almost the whole of Tartary'. The red hats allow their priests to marry. The yellow, favoured by the Emperor of China, is the most orthodox and powerful.
passages.quote: I notice this peculiarity of colour in their dress, as it is a distinction adopted, to mark one of the two religious sects that divide almost the whole of Tartary, from Turkistan to the eastern limits of this continent. The other colour is red; and the tribes are known as belonging to the red, or the yellow cap.
passages.speaker: Samuel Turner (1800)
passages.caution: The claim that these sects cover all Tartary 'from Turkistan' is a large generalisation from what he was told.

passages.headline: Dice worn on every Tartar belt
passages.gloss: Turner says that no journey, marriage or naming was done in Tibet without first seeking an omen, often from a monk skilled in divination. For small decisions people simply threw dice, which is why a pair of dice hangs from a Tartar belt. He cheerfully admits he travelled only when his own monk-diviner said so.
passages.quote: in trivial affairs, the mind is often governed by a casual cast of the die; and hence, dice are almost always found to constitute an appendage to a Tartar dress.
passages.speaker: Samuel Turner (1800)

passages.headline: Ten minutes, a pipe and a spoonful of coffee
passages.gloss: At a khan in Pharsalus Clarke watched 'Tartar' couriers change horses. Each squatted against the wall for about ten minutes, smoked hard, gulped a spoonful of muddy coffee, said 'God be praised' and rode on, travelling night and day. Clarke says no couriers in the world could match their endurance, and that Europeans travelling alone in Turkey disguised themselves in their dress.
passages.quote: the Tartar squats (for it cannot be called sitting) with his back against the wall, supporting himself upon the soles of his feet, and inhaling rapidly the fumes of his pipe upon his lungs; sending it back in curling volumes through his nostrils. Then, if he can procure about as much muddy coffee as would fill the bowl of a table-spoon, he utters his Alhandilla! (God be praised !)
passages.speaker: Edward Daniel Clarke (1816)

passages.headline: 'Their name by no means indicates their origin'
passages.gloss: In a footnote Clarke quotes Thomas Thornton's book on Turkey (1809) to explain the couriers: 'Tartar' was the name of the job, not of a nation. The men came from every province and were marked out by the Tartar calpac (fur cap) they wore instead of a turban. A good reminder that 'Tartar' could mean a role or a costume.
passages.quote: The Tartars are public couriers, much respected for their good conduct and fidelity. Their name by no means indicates their origin, as they are taken indifferently from all the provinces in the empire, and are distinguished by the Tartar calpac, which they wear instead of the turban.
passages.speaker: Thomas Thornton, The Present State of Turkey (1809), quoted in a footnote by Clarke

passages.headline: Burial mounds 'precisely similar to those of Tartary'
passages.people: (ancient mound builders; comparison with the steppe)
passages.gloss: Riding across the bare plains of Thrace, Clarke is reminded of the steppes of southern Russia and its tumuli (kurgans), which he had seen on his earlier journey. He does not say who built either set; he treats them simply as the same kind of ancient earth mound.
passages.quote: This part of Thrace resembles the steppes in the South of Russia ; and to add to the similitude of the two countries, there are here tumuli precisely similar to those of Tartary.
passages.speaker: Edward Daniel Clarke (1816)

passages.headline: Unrobbed mounds, unlike those of Tartary
passages.people: (ancient Greek mound builders; comparison with the steppe)
passages.gloss: On the plain near Larissa Clarke saw many large tumuli in good condition, some with shepherds' huts built on top. He notes that, unlike the mounds of 'Tartary', they did not seem to have been dug open for treasure. The steppe kurgans were well known for being plundered for their gold.
passages.quote: They did not seem to have been opened and ransacked for the hidden treasure which it is possible some of them contain, as it has often happened in Tartary ; but, upon some of them, small huts had been constructed, as dwellings for the shepherds.
passages.speaker: Edward Daniel Clarke (1816)

passages.headline: Russian treasure hunters in 'Tartarian tombs'
passages.gloss: In a long footnote on tomb treasures, Clarke suggests that Turkish beliefs about gold hidden in ancient ruins may come from real finds in tombs. He adds that the Russians had found 'immense treasure' in 'Tartarian tombs', referring readers to his earlier book on the Tomb of Alexander (1805). The graves he means are the steppe kurgans, not necessarily Tatar at all.
passages.quote: The immense treasure found by the Russians in Tartarian tombs has been alluded to by the author, upon a former occasion.
passages.speaker: Edward Daniel Clarke (footnote, 1816)
passages.caution: 'Tartarian tombs' is a loose label for any ancient burial mound on the steppe; the footnote does not say who was buried in them.

passages.headline: Chufut-Kale, the 'Castle of Miscreants'
passages.gloss: Contrasting the Jews of Constantinople with the Karaite Jews of the Crimea, Clarke praises the Karaites' character. He notes that their town was known by a Turkish insult, Tchufut-kaleh, the 'Castle of Miscreants' (his footnote glosses Tchifuit as 'a vile miscreant'), and says their good name had turned it into an honourable title.
passages.quote: How different from the character borne by the Karaite Jews of the Crimea! whose virtues have rendered even the opprobrious name, derived from their Turkish brethren, an honourable title ; for their place of residence is called Tchufut-kaleh, the "Castle of Miscreants."
passages.speaker: Edward Daniel Clarke (1816)
passages.caution: A passing remark; Clarke's full description of Chufut-Kale is in Part I, not in this volume.

passages.headline: No poets on the flat steppe
passages.gloss: Admiring the mountains near Thebes, Clarke argues that great poetry needs great scenery, and that flat countries like Scythia or Belgium never produced it. Even Homer, he says, would not have been a poet if raised in 'oriental Tartary'. It is a period prejudice, not an observation, but it shows how Tartary served as a byword for dull, flat emptiness.
passages.quote: Even Homer himself, if he had been a native of oriental Tartary, and had been cradled and brought up under the impressions made by such scenery, and under the influence of such a climate, would never have been a poet.
passages.speaker: Edward Daniel Clarke (1816)
passages.caution: Clarke's own opinion and prejudice, not a report about any real people.

passages.headline: Why 'Tartar' is a pun, not a name
passages.gloss: In a footnote to their chapter on the origin of the Tatars, the authors refuse to use the spelling 'Tartar' at all. They say it comes only from a play on words by St Louis, King of France, who in the 1240s punned on Tatar and Tartarus, the classical underworld. This is the famous Tartarus pun, stated plainly by a 19th-century writer.
passages.quote: We have entirely rejected from our discussion the word Tartar, which owes its origin only to a jeu de mots, of which St. Louis was the author.
passages.speaker: Xavier Hommaire de Hell (footnote, English translation, 1847)
passages.caution: The St Louis story is traditional (it is told in Matthew Paris's chronicle of the 1240s). The pun was widespread, and the story does not prove where the spelling began.

passages.headline: A people made famous by those who destroyed it
passages.people: the Tatar tribe and the Mongols of Genghis Khan
passages.gloss: Drawing on the historian D'Ohsson, the authors explain that 'Tatar' was first the name of a real Mongolian tribe, whom Genghis Khan wiped out. Yet the name spread from nation to nation and stuck to Genghis's own armies. By a strange accident, they say, a destroyed people became famous through the conquests of its destroyers.
passages.quote: It is a fact established by the statements of many writers, and by D'Ohson himself, that Genghis Khan annihilated the white Tatars, and thus it has come to pass by a most curious freak of accident, that this extinguished people became celebrated all over the East by the conquests of its very destroyers.
passages.speaker: Xavier Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)
passages.caution: A summary of 19th-century scholarship, not the authors' own research.

passages.headline: Europeans kept calling the Muslim Turks 'Tatars'
passages.people: Turkic Muslims of Russia and Central Asia
passages.gloss: The authors argue that after the Mongol conquests Europeans went on calling all the Muslim, Turkic-speaking peoples of Kazan, Astrakhan, the Crimea and Turkestan 'Tatars', which caused endless confusion. On the same page they conclude that the name lost all meaning in Asia and survives 'only in the European vocabulary', and that the Tatars of southern Russia are really Turks, Cumans or Pechenegs once ruled by the Mongols.
passages.quote: After the Mongol torrent had subsided, Europeans persisted in giving the appellation of Tatars to all those Mussulman nations originally of Turkish origin, that to this day occupy the territory of Kasan and Astrakhan, the Crimea and the region called Turcomania
passages.speaker: Xavier Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)

passages.headline: 'Mayst thou never know happiness': where the Nogais got their name
passages.gloss: European books said the Nogai horde was named after a Tatar general called Nogai. Xavier collected the Nogais' own traditions, which say nothing of such a general and derive the name from 'neogai', a curse on their hard wandering life. He prefers the Nogai version, arguing that a people so proud of their ancestry would have remembered a founder.
passages.quote: their chronicles allege that the name of the nation is derived from neogai (which may be translated by the phrase, mayst thou never know happiness), and that it was bestowed on them in their old country, on account of their precarious and vagabond life.
passages.speaker: Xavier Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)
passages.caution: A folk etymology; modern historians generally connect the name with the 13th-century Mongol commander Nogai, the view Xavier rejects.

passages.headline: The Kalmyk kibitka: a felt house two camels can carry
passages.gloss: A precise description of the felt tent (kibitka) from people who stayed in them: a cylinder as high as a man's shoulder, a conical roof open at the top for smoke, a wooden ring held up by many spars. The whole thing comes apart and can be carried by two camels. On the next page they add that the felts kept out the fiercest storms, as they learned from experience.
passages.quote: Their dwellings are felt tents, called kibitkas by the Russians. They are four or five yards in diameter, cylindrical to the height of a man's shoulder, with a conical top, open at the apex to let the smoke escape. The frame is light, and can be taken asunder for the convenience of carriage.
passages.speaker: Xavier and Adèle Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)

passages.headline: A Nogai cottage of sun-dried brick and reeds
passages.gloss: Settled by Russian officials only a generation earlier, the Nogais now built their own cottages. The walls are sun-dried brick, whitewashed yearly; the roof is rafters covered with reeds and branches loaded with earth and ashes. Inside are two rooms, and a man with two wives builds a separate room for each.
passages.quote: The Nogai constructs his own cottage with bricks dried in the sun, and whitewashes it regularly once a year within and without. Its dimensions are scarcely more than two or three-and-thirty feet by thirteen. The roof consists of a few rafters on which are laid reeds and branches of trees loaded with earth and ashes.
passages.speaker: Xavier Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)

passages.headline: 'To us he has given wheels'
passages.gloss: Describing the Nogais before their settlement in villages, Xavier says a family could pack wife, children and goods into its felt-covered wagon (araba) within an hour and roll off towards the horizon. He quotes a Nogai saying that sums up the old nomad view of the world: God gave wheels to them and houses and ploughs to others.
passages.quote: Such is the order established by God himself," cried the Nogai, " to us he has given wheels, to other nations fixed dwellings and the plough."
passages.speaker: a Nogai saying, quoted by Xavier Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)

passages.headline: Terraced Tatar villages with clay roofs
passages.gloss: In the mountain villages of Toklouk, Kooz and Otouz, Xavier found flat-roofed Tatar houses built against the valley sides, so that the roofs formed terraces where people worked and visited each other. The roofs are stout timber covered with a thick bed of clay. At evening whole villages gathered on them.
passages.quote: the terrace tops of their houses, where they regularly carry on their work, and which are formed of stout carpentry covered with a thick bed of clay. Nothing can be more picturesque than the appearance, at evening, of all these terraces rising in gradations one above the other.
passages.speaker: Xavier Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)

passages.headline: The Khan's palace: 'an assemblage of wooden houses'
passages.gloss: Adèle defends the palace of the Crimean khans against visitors who sneered that it was only a cluster of wooden houses with crude paintings, divans and carpets. She agrees that is what it is made of, but says its charm lies in feeling, not materials. It is a useful witness to how the Tatar capital's palace was actually built: timber, painted walls, fountains and gardens.
passages.quote: " How," said they, " can any one apply the name of palace to that assemblage of wooden houses, daubed with coarse paintings, and furnished only with divans and carpets?" And these people were right in their way.
passages.speaker: Adèle Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)
passages.caution: The palace had been restored under Tsar Alexander I, as the authors say on p.363, so not everything seen was original.

passages.headline: Bakhchysarai kept for the Tatars by imperial decree
passages.gloss: The old Tatar capital, the authors explain, kept its eastern look because Catherine II granted the Tatars sole possession of the town. Walking its narrow streets of mosques, shops and cemeteries felt like the old quarters of Constantinople. On the same page they give a potted history: Batu Khan's Tatars founded the kingdom in the 1200s, and Bakhchysarai became the capital in the early 1500s.
passages.quote: Bagtche Serai has completely retained its national character in consequence of an ukase of Catherine II., empowering the Tatars to retain exclusive possession of their own capital. You would fancy yourself in the heart of the East, in walking through the narrow streets of the town, the mosques, shops, and cemeteries of which so much resemble those of the old quarters of Constantinople.
passages.speaker: Xavier and Adèle Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)

passages.headline: Astrakhan, 'ancient capital of the Tatar kingdom'
passages.people: Tatars of the Golden Horde and the Astrakhan khanate
passages.gloss: The authors sketch Astrakhan's history: part of Batu Khan's Kipchak empire (the Golden Horde), then an independent Tatar khanate, taken by Ivan the Terrible in 1554, after which its prosperity faded. In their day it was a provincial town, but its old walls and battlemented towers still recalled its past. Over 5,000 Tatars lived there as traders, and their mosques and bath domes gave the town an oriental look.
passages.quote: At present the ancient capital of the Tatar kingdom is merely the chief town of a government … It contains a great number of squares, churches, and mosques. Its old embattled towers and its walls, which still include a considerable space of ground, remind the traveller of its ancient warlike renown.
passages.speaker: Xavier and Adèle Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)
passages.caution: The history is the authors' summary; they do not say who built the walls and towers they saw.

passages.headline: Caffa: Tatar and Genoese buildings blown up by Russian officials
passages.gloss: Xavier describes what happened to Caffa after the Russian annexation of 1783. The Genoese walls and towers were pulled down for barracks, the great Turkish baths and the old cathedral-turned-mosque were demolished with pickaxe and gunpowder in 1833, and the Tatar population was expelled. It is a first-hand record of who actually destroyed the old buildings of a Tatar-era city.
passages.quote: In 1833, the ignorance of a civil governor, Kasnatcheief, completed this afflicting work of destruction, which extended at the same time to the great baths that still remained untouched. A fortnight's work with the pickaxe and gunpowder razed to the ground the two admirable monuments with which the Genoese and the Turks had adorned the town.
passages.speaker: Xavier Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)
passages.caution: The authors are hostile to Russian officials; the demolition itself is widely recorded, but the blame is their own judgement.

passages.headline: A Buddhist temple of stuccoed brick on the Volga
passages.gloss: At Prince Tumene's island seat, Adèle attended a service in the Kalmyk 'pagoda'. She describes the din of drums, gongs, conch shells and three-metre trumpets, and the building itself: large windows, slender columns of stuccoed brick, a domed gallery and walls hung with painted tapestries of spirits and monsters. This was a settled Kalmyk prince's temple, not a tent.
passages.quote: The temple, lighted by a row of large windows, is adorned with slender columns of stuccoed brick work, the lightness of which reminds one of the graceful Moorish architecture. A gallery runs all round the dome, which is also remarkable for the extreme delicacy of its workmanship.
passages.speaker: Adèle Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)

passages.headline: A ten-year-old breaks a wild stallion
passages.gloss: At Prince Tumene's, Kalmyk riders lassoed wild horses from the herd and rode them bareback, clinging to the mane, until they were caught up by other horsemen. Then a boy of about ten did the same on a huge white stallion. Adèle adds that even Kalmyk women practise the sport.
passages.quote: But what was our amazement when we saw a boy of ten years come forward to undertake the same exploit! They selected for him a young white stallion of great size, whose fiery bounds and desperate efforts to break his bonds, indicated a most violent temper.
passages.speaker: Adèle Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)

passages.headline: The price of a Nogai bride
passages.gloss: Among the Nogais a groom never saw his bride before the wedding and bargained with her family for her price. Xavier gives the going rates: four or five hundred rubles and a couple of score cows for a handsome girl of good family, less for widows. On the same page he adds that Crimean mountain Tatar and Kalmyk wives cost less and were bought by poorer men.
passages.quote: A handsome girl of good family costs four or five hundred rubles, besides a couple of score of cows and a few other beasts. Young widows are cheaper, and old women are to be had for nothing. The bride's price is paid on the spot by the wooer
passages.speaker: Xavier Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)
passages.caution: Written from outside and with some disdain; how widely these prices applied is not stated.

passages.headline: Breaking into a Kalmyk tomb
passages.gloss: Adèle describes how the party tricked their Kalmyk camel-drivers, broke into a satza (a small tomb-shrine for a high priest's ashes) through a window, 'took possession' of it with a silk handkerchief, and carried off two clay statues and some images. She knows the Kalmyks would see it as the worst sacrilege and treats it as a lark. A startling reminder of how European travellers collected 'curiosities'.
passages.quote: Like generous victors we contented ourselves with taking two small statues, and a few images. According to the notions of the Kalmucks, no sacrilege can compare with that of which we were now guilty. Yet no celestial fire reduced us to ashes
passages.speaker: Adèle Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)

passages.headline: The white elephant with thirty-three heads
passages.gloss: Summarising Kalmyk Buddhist books, the authors describe the world-mountain and its guardian elephant, two leagues long and white as snow, with thirty-three red heads, six trunks each spouting fountains, and a young virgin on every star above them. They note, in a footnote, similar marvels in medieval European cosmography. This is religious myth they report, not something anyone claimed to see.
passages.quote: where dwells an elephant two leagues long, white as snow, and named Gasar Sakitschin Koven (protector of the earth). This fabulous animal has thirty-three red heads, each furnished with six trunks, whence spout forth as many fountains, all surmounted with six stars.
passages.speaker: Xavier Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)
passages.caution: A second-hand summary of Kalmyk religious books; the authors do not name the text they used.

passages.headline: Kazan, a city of log houses, burned to the ground
passages.gloss: Arriving in June 1843, Haxthausen calls Kazan 'the gloriously situated old Tatar city', but finds it still in ruins from the great fire of 1842. His count is striking: only about one house in nine was stone, the rest were timber, and wooden plank walkways carried the flames from street to street.
passages.quote: Kazan still lay for the most part in ruins ; a great fire the year before had reduced the vast city to ashes. … Of 4500 houses in Kazan only about 500 were built of stone; the rest were log-houses. The streets, with few exceptions, were unpaved
passages.speaker: August von Haxthausen (translated by Robert Farie, 1856)

passages.headline: Once the rulers, now pushed to the suburbs
passages.gloss: Haxthausen notes that the Tatars, who ruled Kazan before the Russian conquest of 1552, now live in their own quarter outside the Russian town proper. They are mostly traders, and he met rich merchant families among them.
passages.quote: The Tatars in Kazan live mostly together, in a separate quarter of the town. Formerly the ruling people, they have been driven into the suburbs, whilst the town proper is inhabited by Russians. They are traders rather than artisans ; among them are merchants of all the guilds.
passages.speaker: August von Haxthausen (translated by Robert Farie, 1856)

passages.headline: Sarai, the lost capital of the Golden Horde
passages.people: Khans of the Golden Horde (Mongols and Tatars)
passages.gloss: In Saratov a local official showed Haxthausen coins and ornaments dug from the 'supposed ruins' of Sarai. He then retells its history: Batu founded the city, the khans built magnificent palaces, and Russian grand dukes came to kneel there. On the next page he marvels that nobody could yet say for certain where this great capital had stood.
passages.quote: Batu Khan, the Grand Khan of the Golden Horde, who ruled over the half of two hemispheres, founded in the thirteenth century a powerful city, Sarai, and fixed his residence there. He and his successors built palaces of fabulous magnificence. Princes, among others the Grand Dukes of Russia, were obliged to come and bend the knee before their lord and swear fealty to him
passages.speaker: August von Haxthausen (translated by Robert Farie, 1856)
passages.caution: The history is Haxthausen's summary of received accounts, not something he saw; 'palaces of fabulous magnificence' is his phrase, not a description of surviving remains.

passages.headline: Ruined Tatar towns along the Volga
passages.place: Lower Volga (Akhtuba valley, Kazan to Astrakhan)
passages.gloss: On the left bank of the Volga, Haxthausen says, the Tatars were not only nomads: they had fixed towns and farms, as shown by ruins and by place names. The Akhtuba valley where Sarai stood is covered with ruins for about 85 versts (roughly 90 km). When the Horde broke up, the towns were destroyed and the settlers driven off by Kirghiz and Bashkir raiders, leaving only ruins and broken mosques.
passages.quote: This is evident not merely from the ruins of cities (the whole district on the Akhtuba, where Sarai stood, for eighty-five versts, is covered with ruins), but the names of nearly all denote that the Tatars had fixed settlements here. When the Mongol-Tatar empire was dissolved, the cities were destroyed … only here and there a ruin or dilapidated mosque bore witness to their former existence.
passages.speaker: August von Haxthausen (translated by Robert Farie, 1856)
passages.caution: He reports this from local knowledge and place names while passing through the Saratov region; he did not visit the Akhtuba ruins himself.

passages.headline: The minaret of Bolgar, built by a vanished people
passages.gloss: Haxthausen climbed the surviving minaret at Bolgar, which he credits to the old Bulgarian state destroyed by the Mongols and Tatars. The ruins stand beside a Russian church, Kazan Tatars still make pilgrimages to the saints' tombs there, and Alexander von Humboldt had scratched his name on the minaret wall.
passages.quote: The powerful and civilized Bulgarian people who founded this important city have quite disappeared, and the Russians, Tatars, Tchuvash, etc. have taken their place ; all trace of their physiognomy, customs, and language is lost. … We ascended the lofty minaret, which commands an extensive view over boundless forests.
passages.speaker: August von Haxthausen (translated by Robert Farie, 1856)
passages.caution: His claim that the Bulgars left no trace is his own opinion; the Kazan Tatars themselves (see his p.323) were often described as partly descended from them.

passages.headline: Inside a Tatar merchant's house in Kazan
passages.gloss: Hoping to see a 'genuine national household', Haxthausen is taken to the home of two merchant brothers and finds the rooms furnished in European style, with Chinese porcelain, mirrors, a Persian carpet and a stone bowl inscribed with Koran verses. He glimpsed a six-foot-wide family sleeping bench, but the women's rooms were closed to him.
passages.quote: I wished to see a genuine national household, but this no longer exists, at least in Kazan, as the people here too are already affected by European cultivation. The furniture of the rooms into which we were conducted was quite European … In one of the glass cases was a stone bowl, inscribed with texts from the Koran.
passages.speaker: August von Haxthausen (translated by Robert Farie, 1856)

passages.headline: Russian stoves, Tatar benches: a village house
passages.gloss: Lodging in a large Tatar peasant house, Haxthausen found it split into a men's half and a women's half. He noticed it looked much like a Russian house and honestly admits he cannot tell who borrowed from whom. The rooms mixed Russian stoves, Tatar sleeping benches, a samovar, European chairs and a Black Forest clock, with 'God is great' written over the door.
passages.quote: This was divided into two parts ; the right half is the dwelling of the men (our host lived with four of his brothers), the left that of the women and children. It bore much resemblance to Russian arrangements : whether the Russians borrowed of the Tatars, or the latter of the former, cannot be determined. In the rooms the stoves were Russian, the sleeping-benches Tatar
passages.speaker: August von Haxthausen (translated by Robert Farie, 1856)

passages.headline: A Nogai village built on a Mennonite plan
passages.gloss: Near the Mennonite colonies on the Molochna, Haxthausen visited a Nogai Tatar village that looked 'perfectly German'. The Mennonite farmer Johann Cornies had persuaded the formerly nomadic Nogais to build this way and, Haxthausen was told, had already settled 17,000 of them. Solid houses with chimneys, poplars, gardens and Mennonite ploughs had replaced the old steppe life.
passages.quote: The houses in this village were all built with regularity and solid structure ; they had chimneys and enclosed courtyards. In front of the house-doors generally stand two poplars, with small flower-beds on each side ; in the gardens I noticed a great many fruit-trees, and in the courtyard ploughs, harrows, and carts of Mennonite construction
passages.speaker: August von Haxthausen (translated by Robert Farie, 1856)
passages.caution: The figure of 17,000 settled Tatars was told to him, not counted.

passages.headline: Bulgars and Mongols merged into Tatars
passages.gloss: Haxthausen explains who the Kazan Tatars are: a mixed people in whom the old Volga Bulgar population and the Mongol conquerors have blended. He quotes Herberstein calling them 'half Mongols', but his own description (oval faces, curved noses, light complexions) mostly contradicts a Mongol look, apart from the eyes.
passages.quote: The Kazan Tatars belong, both mentally and physically, to the nobler races of mankind ; they are a mixed people, and possess high mental qualities, but Mohammedanism only permits their development in a limited degree. The ancient Bulgarian and Mongol population has been completely merged in the Tatar. The aspect of the Tatars clearly indicates their consanguinity with the Mongols : Herberstein describes them as half Mongols.
passages.speaker: August von Haxthausen (translated by Robert Farie, 1856)
passages.caution: Uses the racial ranking language of the 1840s; his origins theory is his own opinion.

passages.headline: Horseflesh, honey mead and the tea trade
passages.gloss: Kazan Tatars, Haxthausen reports, avoid pork as Muslims but prize horseflesh above all, brew mead, and control much of the tea trade. On the same page he admires Kazan leather boots embroidered with gold and silver and calls Tatar peasants excellent beekeepers.
passages.quote: They live principally upon animal food, avoiding pork, which is forbidden by the Koran ; horseflesh is considered by the common Tatars the choicest food. They are very fond of honey, and make good mead from it. The higher classes drink much tea ; and a large proportion of the tea-trade being in their hands, the best sorts are found among them.
passages.speaker: August von Haxthausen (translated by Robert Farie, 1856)

passages.headline: Bride price and wives in Tatar villages
passages.gloss: In the village he notes that women walked about unveiled, that village men rarely had more than one wife, and that a bride price (kalym, which he writes 'halim') was paid, sometimes 500 roubles even among peasants. He adds that the Tatars kept some village arrangements secret from Russian officials.
passages.quote: In the Tatar villages the men have rarely more than one wife ; in the towns, particularly among the rich merchants, bigamy frequently occurs, but to have more than two wives is very rare. The women are sold, and the halim paid for them, which even in the case of peasants frequently amounts to five hundred roubles.
passages.speaker: August von Haxthausen (translated by Robert Farie, 1856)
passages.caution: 'The women are sold' is his gloss on the bride-price custom, based on what villagers told him.

passages.headline: Tatar, the French of the East
passages.people: Kazan Tatars and Turkic speakers generally
passages.gloss: Haxthausen was impressed that nearly all Kazan Tatars could read and write, that their village schools were run by mullahs, and that students went to Orenburg and Bukhara. In a footnote he claims their Turkic language worked as a common tongue from Persia to China and even Tunis.
passages.quote: The Tatar language occupies the same place in the East as the French in the West. Eastwards from Persia to China, westwards throughout all the Turkish countries, and even in Tunis, any one can make himself understood by means of it.
passages.speaker: August von Haxthausen, footnote (translated by Robert Farie, 1856)
passages.caution: An enthusiastic generalisation: related Turkic languages were widely understood, but not one single 'Tatar' language everywhere he names.

passages.headline: The cathedral for Kazan and the blinded architect
passages.people: Ivan IV; the conquered Kazan Tatars
passages.gloss: St Basil's Cathedral on Red Square was built to celebrate Ivan the Terrible's capture of Kazan, the Tatar capital, in 1552. Haxthausen compares it to a rainbow-coloured dragon and repeats the tale that Ivan had the architect blinded so he could never build anything finer. He clearly marks it as hearsay ('is said to').
passages.quote: Ivan Vasilievitch ordered it to be erected in 1554 by an Italian, to commemorate the conquest of Kazan. After it was completed, he is said to have asked the architect whether he would undertake to make a plan for a still more singular building ; and when the latter in his vanity answered in the affirmative, he ordered his eyes to be put out
passages.speaker: August von Haxthausen (translated by Robert Farie, 1856)
passages.caution: Russian tradition names the builders as the Russian masters Barma and Postnik, not an Italian, and the blinding story is a legend with no contemporary evidence.

passages.headline: One name for many nations
passages.gloss: Herberstein warns his readers that 'Tartar' is not the name of one people. It is a label drawn from one group and stretched over many nations living far apart. It is a useful early statement that the word was an umbrella term.
passages.quote: He who attempts to describe the Tartars will have to describe many races ; for they derive this name from one sect alone, while they consist of various nations lying wide apart from each other.
passages.speaker: Sigismund von Herberstein (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)

passages.headline: Moabites from the desert: a Russian origin legend
passages.gloss: From the Russian chronicles Herberstein copies a story that the Tartars were 'Moabites' who came out of the north-eastern deserts, driven by a prophet named Gideon who preached the end of the world. The chronicle's date of AD 1025 for the Kalka battle is wrong (it was 1223), and the editor Major notes the attribution to Bishop Methodius is an anachronism.
passages.quote: They say that the Moabites, who were afterwards called Tartars, and who differed from the rest of mankind in language, manners, and dress, came to the river Calka ; but that no one knew whence they came, or what religious doctrine they held.
passages.speaker: Sigismund von Herberstein, retelling the Russian annals (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)
passages.caution: A biblical-style legend from the chronicles; Herberstein reports it without endorsing it.

passages.headline: Hordes that hate being called Turks
passages.gloss: Herberstein explains that 'horde' means a multitude, that the Tartars are split into hordes (Savolha, Precop, Nogai and others), all Muslim, and that they take offence at being called Turks, preferring 'Besermani' (Muslims). He then describes their looks: broad faces, shaved heads, and black hair kept only by the great men.
passages.quote: The word " horde" among them signifies a concourse or multitude. But although each horde has its peculiar name, such as the horde of Savolha, Precop, Nahaisa, and many others, and all are of the Mahometan religion, yet they are highly offended if they are called Turks, and consider it a reproach, but delight in being called Besermani
passages.speaker: Sigismund von Herberstein (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)

passages.headline: Khan, sultan, murza: Tartar titles explained
passages.gloss: Herberstein closes his Tartar chapter with a little glossary of ranks: khan (king), sultan (a king's son), murza (a duke's son) and said (chief priest), with other noble grades in between. The same titles run through later Russian records of Tatar nobles. He also names the four great councillors of the Tartar kings.
passages.quote: The titles of dignity amongst the Tartars are nearly as follows : khan, as I have said above, signifies a king ; sultan, the son of a king ; … mursa, the son of a duke ; … said, a chief priest.
passages.speaker: Sigismund von Herberstein (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)
passages.caution: The OCR garbles several of the rarer titles on this page (bey, noble ranks); check the page image for them.

passages.headline: Drinking their horses' blood, prizing mare's milk
passages.gloss: On long rides, Herberstein was told, Tartars open a vein in their horse and drink the blood, believing it does the animal good. They steer by the Pole Star, which they call the 'iron nail'. On the same page he describes their love of mare's milk and how chiefs share out the entrails of a slaughtered animal and lick the knife clean.
passages.quote: Moreover, if during a long ride they are troubled with hunger or thirst, it is a practice to lance the veins of the horses on which they sit, and relieve their craving by drawing their blood ; and they think that this is an advantage to the animals. As they nearly all wander on uncertain tracks, they are accustomed to direct their course by the observation of the stars
passages.speaker: Sigismund von Herberstein (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)
passages.caution: Reported from Russian and Lithuanian informants, not seen by Herberstein.

passages.headline: The feigned flight, which they call a dance
passages.place: Steppe frontier of Muscovy and Lithuania
passages.gloss: Herberstein explains the classic steppe tactic: attack from a distance, pretend to flee, shoot backwards at the pursuers, then wheel round and charge. The Tartars fight in a wheeling circle rather than a battle line and, he says, call this manoeuvre 'a dance'. Without shield, lance or helmet they avoid close combat in narrow places.
passages.quote: they do not, however, continue this mode of warfare long, but pretending flight, take an opportunity while their enemies are pursuing them to discharge their arrows backwards, and then, when the ranks of the enemy are broken, turn their horses suddenly round and attack them.
passages.speaker: Sigismund von Herberstein (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)

passages.headline: 'May you stay in one place like a Christian'
passages.gloss: Herberstein reports that the roving Tartars thought staying put was a misfortune, and that their worst curse on a child was to wish it a fixed home like a Christian's. He is careful to add that Tartars who live in towns and cities live differently, so he is describing the herders, not all Tartars.
passages.quote: They never stay for any length of time in one spot, for they consider it a great calamity to be obliged to remain long in the same place ; hence, when they are angry with their children, and wish to utter a heavy imprecation against them, they are accustomed to say, " may you abide in one place continually like a Christian, and inhale your own stink !"
passages.speaker: Sigismund von Herberstein (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)
passages.caution: A saying reported secondhand; the next lines note that Tartars in towns and cities live otherwise.

passages.headline: Kazan: Tartars who farm, trade and live in houses
passages.gloss: Herberstein sets the Kazan Tartars apart from the steppe herders: their kingdom has a city and fortress on the Volga, an army of 30,000 largely made up of Cheremis and Chuvash archers, and settled farming and trade. He says Moscow controlled their kings largely through the river routes and trade they depended on.
passages.quote: The kingdom of Kazan, with the city and fortress of the same name, is situated on the further bank of the river Volga, nearly seventy miles below Lower Novogorod. … These Tartars are more civilized than the rest, in as much as they cultivate their lands, live in houses, and carry on various branches of merchandize.
passages.speaker: Sigismund von Herberstein (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)
passages.caution: 'Seventy miles' is in German miles (each roughly 7 km).

passages.headline: Kazan's wooden fortress burns
passages.gloss: During a Russian campaign against Kazan, bribed Russians set fire to the Tartar fortress, which was built of wood, and it burned to the ground in sight of the Russian army. Herberstein, relying on soldiers' reports, scorns the Russian commander for letting the Tartars rebuild it. It is a clear statement that the Khanate's fortress in the 1520s was timber, not stone.
passages.quote: In the meanwhile the fortress of Kazan, which was built of wood, was set on fire by some of the Russians who had been bribed for that purpose, and was burnt to the ground under the eyes of the Russian army.
passages.speaker: Sigismund von Herberstein (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)

passages.headline: The Tartar embassy house inside the Kremlin
passages.people: Envoys of the Golden Horde; Ivan III and Sophia Palaiologina
passages.gloss: Even the mighty Ivan III, Herberstein says, had to go out and stand before seated Tartar envoys. The Tartars kept a house inside the Moscow citadel. His Byzantine wife Sophia, claiming a dream, persuaded the Tartar queen to give the plot for a church, and the Tartars were never given a house in the fortress again.
passages.quote: There was within the citadel of Moscow a house in which the Tartars lodged for the purpose of learning what was going on at Moscow, and as this also gave great offence to his wife, she sent messengers with liberal presents to the queen of the Tartars, begging her to give up that house to her
passages.speaker: Sigismund von Herberstein (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)
passages.caution: A court story told to Herberstein decades after the event.

passages.headline: Moscow in panic as the Crimean khan approaches
passages.people: Crimean Tartars under Mehmed Giray; Kazan Tartars
passages.gloss: In 1521 the Crimean khan Mehmed Giray and his brother, the khan of Kazan, raided up to Moscow. Herberstein, drawing on witnesses including German gunners, describes the Grand Duke fleeing (reportedly hiding under a haystack) and crowds crushing each other at the fortress gates. The city bought off the khan with gifts, above all mead, and a written promise of tribute.
passages.quote: On the 29th of July the Tartars made a farther advance, and devastated the country with fire in all directions ; and such was the terror which they inspired amongst the people of Moscow, that they had little confidence in their security even in the city and the fortress.
passages.speaker: Sigismund von Herberstein (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)

passages.headline: Astrakhan, the great emporium of the Tartars
passages.gloss: Herberstein calls Astrakhan a wealthy city and the Tartars' main trading hub near the Volga delta, which he pictures splitting into some seventy branches. On the same page he lists forest-dwelling Siberian Tartars and says the Kalmyks are called that because they alone let their hair grow.
passages.quote: Astrachan is a wealthy city, and the great emporium of the Tartars, which gives its name to all the surrounding country. It lies on this side of the Volga, near to its mouth, ten days' journey below Kazan.
passages.speaker: Sigismund von Herberstein (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)

passages.headline: The vegetable lamb of the Volga
passages.place: Lower Volga (lands of the Savolha khans)
passages.gloss: Herberstein's most famous marvel: a Russian informant said his father, on an embassy to the Tartar king, saw a seed that grew into a lamb-like plant called 'boranetz' (little lamb) with wool, blood and hoofs, which grazed until the grass around it ran out. Herberstein admits it sounds incredible but repeats it because trustworthy people vouched for the wool. Editor Major adds that it was a fern (Polypodium baromez) trimmed to look like a lamb.
passages.quote: he had seen in the island a certain seed, somewhat larger and rounder, but not unlike the seed of a melon, from which, when planted, grew up something very like a lamb, of the height of five palms, and that it was called in their language " boranetz", which signifies a lambkin
passages.speaker: Sigismund von Herberstein, reporting Dimitry Danielovich (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)
passages.caution: Thirdhand (informant's father); Herberstein calls it 'almost incredible'.

passages.headline: 800,000 captives and old men given to boys
passages.gloss: After the 1521 raid the Crimean khan is said to have driven off more than 800,000 prisoners, selling many to the Turks at Kaffa. Herberstein repeats the lurid claim that old captives, worth little at market, were handed to Tartar youths for practice in killing. He flags the numbers himself ('scarcely be considered credible', 'they say').
passages.quote: But he took with him from Moscow so great a multitude of prisoners as would scarcely be considered credible ; they say that the number exceeded eight hundred thousand, part of whom he sold in Kaffa to the Turks, and part he slew.
passages.speaker: Sigismund von Herberstein (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)
passages.caution: The figure is a rumour and far larger than is plausible; the slave trade through Kaffa itself is well documented.

passages.headline: Dining with the last khan of the Great Horde
passages.people: Sheikh Ahmed (Scheachmet), khan of the Great Horde (Savolha)
passages.gloss: Herberstein says the Crimean khans came from the old 'Savolha' royal line and fought its last king, Sheikh Ahmed. Defeated, the khan fled to Lithuania, was held in the island castle of Trakai, and there Herberstein met him at dinner. He writes that this ended the line of the Great Horde kings, heirs of the Golden Horde.
passages.quote: was apprehended in the attempt and taken back to the castle of Troky, four miles from Vilna, where I saw him and dined with him. This was the termination of the reign of the kings of Savolha, and together with them ended the race of the kings of Astrachan, who derived their origin from the same royal line.
passages.speaker: Sigismund von Herberstein (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)
passages.caution: His claim that the Astrakhan line ended here is contradicted a few pages later, where a king of Astrakhan regains his throne.

passages.headline: No towns, only houses on wheels
passages.gloss: Fletcher says the Tartars build no towns or standing buildings. They live in wheeled 'walking houses' which they park in rows to form streets and the shape of a town, and even the khan's capital is a moving 'town of wood'. They reportedly think fixed buildings unhealthy.
passages.quote: Townes they plant none, nor other standing buildings, but have walking houses, which the Latines call veii, built upon wheeles like a shepheards cottage. … And when they come to their stage or standing place, they plant their cart houses very orderly in a ranke ; and so make the forme of streetes and of a large towne.
passages.speaker: Giles Fletcher (1591; ed. E. A. Bond, 1856)
passages.caution: This echoes medieval accounts of the 13th-century Mongols; the Crimean khans of Fletcher's day actually ruled from the town of Bakhchysarai, which Fletcher never visited.

passages.headline: Moscow burned by the Crimean khan, 1571
passages.gloss: Fletcher tells how the Crimean khan reached Moscow unopposed in 1571 and fired the suburbs. Because the city was built of wood, the blaze consumed most of it in about four hours, and crowds crushed each other at the gates. He gives the rumoured death toll of 800,000, which is far too high.
passages.quote: (which is all of wood, without any stone, brick, or lime, save certein out roomes) … consumed the greatest part of the citie almost within the space of foure houres, being of thirty miles or more of compasse. Then might you have seene a lamentable spectacle
passages.speaker: Giles Fletcher (1591; ed. E. A. Bond, 1856)
passages.caution: The sentence begins on p.85 ('The citie he tooke not, but fired the suburbs'); only the p.86 part is quoted here, and the OCR of that page is broken by margin notes. The 800,000 dead is hearsay and far too high.

passages.headline: Horsey's eyewitness of the great fire
passages.gloss: Horsey describes the same disaster: the khan's men fired a church, a storm spread the flames, and the timber city burned in six hours. People drowned in the river with their valuables, and for a year afterwards survivors dredged for jewels. The khan watched from the Simonov monastery.
passages.quote: The enyme fiers St. Johns church high steple : at which instant happened a wounderfull stormye wynd, through which all the churches, howses and palaces, within the cittie and suberbs 30 miells compas, built most of firr and oak tymber, was sett one fier and burnt within six howers space
passages.speaker: Sir Jerome Horsey (memoir; ed. E. A. Bond, 1856)
passages.caution: Horsey arrived in Russia in 1573, two years after the fire, so despite the vivid detail this is what he was told.

passages.headline: The Tsar feeding the khan's horse from his cap
passages.gloss: Fletcher says the Crimean khan claimed Moscow itself as his right, and repeats a Russian story that the Russian ruler once had to stand on foot and feed the khan's horse with oats from his own cap as yearly homage. On the next page he says this homage was later turned into a tribute of furs.
passages.quote: that tell of a certeine homage that was done by the Russe emperour every yeare to the Great Chrim or Cham, the Russe emperour standing on foot and feeding the Chrims horse (himselfe sitting on his back) with oates out of his owne cap, in stead of a boule or maunger
passages.speaker: Giles Fletcher (1591; ed. E. A. Bond, 1856)
passages.caution: A story Fletcher gives 'by the report of the Russes themselves'. Margin notes break the OCR of this passage and have been removed; check the page image.

passages.headline: Olla Billa: the Tartar war cry
passages.gloss: Fletcher describes Tartar raiders setting dummy riders on spare horses to look more numerous, and charging with the cry 'Olla Billa' (Allah, bi-llah), which he translates 'God help us'. He contrasts their refusal to surrender with the behaviour of Russian and Turkish soldiers.
passages.quote: When they make any onset their manner is to make a great shoote, crying all out together, Olla Billa, Olla Billa, God helpe us, God helpe us. They contemne death so much as that they chuse rather to die then to yeeld to their enimie, and are seene when they are slaine to bite the very weapon
passages.speaker: Giles Fletcher (1591; ed. E. A. Bond, 1856)

passages.headline: Pigs as a border defence
passages.gloss: Russian borderers, Fletcher says, kept almost nothing but pigs, because Muslim Tartar raiders would not touch or drive them off. He also notes that the Crimean khan was now largely picked by the Ottoman sultan and paid him a tenth of his war booty.
