passages.quote: The Russe borders (being used to their invasions lightly every yeere in the sommer) keepe fewe other cattel on the border parts save swine onely, which the Tartar will not touch nor drive away with him ; for that he is of the Turkish religion, and will eate no swines flesh.
passages.speaker: Giles Fletcher (1591; ed. E. A. Bond, 1856)

passages.headline: Two horses each: one to ride, one to eat
passages.gloss: Tartar soldiers, says Fletcher, bring two horses, one to ride and one to eat, and horseflesh is their main food. He adds something he saw himself: when the Crimean prince Kiriach Murza came to Moscow with 300 Tartars, he was welcomed with two fat horses, ready skinned, for supper.
passages.quote: every man with his two horse at the least, the one to ride on, the other to kill, when it commeth to his turne to have his horse eate. For their chiefe vittaile is horse flesh, which they eate without bread or any other thing with it.
passages.speaker: Giles Fletcher (1591; ed. E. A. Bond, 1856)
passages.caution: The general claim is hearsay; the Moscow banquet for Kiriach Murza is what Fletcher himself witnessed.

passages.headline: Felt idols on the doors of their wagons
passages.gloss: Fletcher says that, unlike Turks, Tartars keep silk or cloth human figures fastened to the doors of their 'walking houses' as house guardians, made by religious women, and bow to a huge image of their khan when the army marches. He also calls them much given to witchcraft and omens.
passages.quote: Herein they differ from the Turkish religion, for that they have certeine idole puppets, made of silke or like stuffe, of the fashion of a man, which they fasten to the doore of their walking houses, to be as Janusses or keepers of their house. And these idols are made not by all, but by certeine religious women
passages.speaker: Giles Fletcher (1591; ed. E. A. Bond, 1856)
passages.caution: This closely follows 13th-century friars' descriptions of pagan Mongols; the Muslim Crimean Tatars of 1590 are unlikely to have kept such idols.

passages.headline: The Tartars are the old Scythian shepherds
passages.gloss: After a harsh description of Tartar looks and singing, Fletcher identifies the Tartars with the 'Scythian nomads' of Greek and Latin writers. Following the Byzantine historian Laonicus Chalcocondylas, he adds that the Turks may have sprung from the Crimean Tartars, since 'Turk' was said to mean shepherd.
passages.quote: They are the very same that sometimes were called Scythae Nomades, or the Scythian shepheards, by the Greekes and Latines. Some thinke that the Turkes tooke their beginning from the nation of the Chrim Tartars.
passages.speaker: Giles Fletcher (1591; ed. E. A. Bond, 1856)
passages.caution: A bookish identification drawn from classical and Byzantine writers.

passages.headline: Nogais, Cheremis, Mordvins and Circassians: other 'Tartars'
passages.gloss: Fletcher files several quite different peoples under 'Tartar': the Nogais (fierce warriors), the Cheremis (actually the Finnic-speaking Mari), the Mordvins (also Finnic) and the Circassians of the Caucasus. He says they differ more in name than in way of life, except the Circassians, whom he calls more 'civil' and partly Christian.
passages.quote: There are divers other Tartars that border upon Russia, as the Nagais [Nogais], the Cheremissens, the Mordwites, the Chircasses, and the Shalcans, which all differ in name more then in regiment or other condition from the Chrim Tartar, except the Chircasses
passages.speaker: Giles Fletcher (1591; ed. E. A. Bond, 1856; bracketed words are Bond's)
passages.caution: A good example of 'Tartar' as a catch-all: the Mari and Mordvins are not Turkic peoples at all.

passages.headline: Three hundred Tartars drowned in a forced baptism
passages.gloss: Fletcher reports that Russians offered captured Tartars their lives if they accepted baptism, but few agreed. The year after the 1571 fire, a captured Tartar noble and 300 of his men refused, and were 'baptized' by being knocked on the head and thrust into the river.
passages.quote: The yere after Mosko was fired by the Chrim Tartar, there was taken a Dwoymorsey, one of the chiefe in that exploit, with 300 Tartars more : who had all their lives offered them, if they would be baptized after the Russe manner. Which they refused all to doo … they were all baptized after a violent manner, being thrust downe with a knock on the head into the water.
passages.speaker: Giles Fletcher (1591; ed. E. A. Bond, 1856)

passages.headline: 'Away with those new devils and their thundering puffs'
passages.gloss: Horsey claims he persuaded Ivan IV to arm captured Scottish mercenaries and send them against the Crimean Tartars. Twelve hundred Scots with guns, he boasts, did better than 12,000 Russian archers, and the Tartars, unused to firearms, fled crying out against the 'new devils'.
passages.quote: Twelve hundred of them did better service against the Tartor then 12 thowsand Russes, with their shortte bowe and arowes. The Crim, not knowinge then the use of peece and pistolls, stroken dead of their horses with shott they sawe not, cried : " Awaye with those new divells that com with their thunderinge puffs ;"
passages.speaker: Sir Jerome Horsey (memoir; ed. E. A. Bond, 1856)
passages.caution: A boastful anecdote; the Crimean khanate had firearms and Ottoman gunners by this time.

passages.headline: Kazan, Astrakhan and Siberia conquered
passages.people: Kazan, Astrakhan, Nogai and Circassian Tartars
passages.gloss: In his summing up of Ivan the Terrible's reign, Horsey lists the conquest of the Tatar 'kingdoms' of Kazan and Astrakhan and the peoples along the Volga to the Caspian, the end of tribute to the Crimean khan, and the conquest of the 'kingdom of Siberia'.
passages.quote: he conquered the kingdom of Casan and the kingdom of Astracan, and all the regions and great people of the Nagaie and Chercas Tartors, and many other of that kinde, inhabitinge above two thowsand miells of each side that famous river of Volga, sowthward eaven to the Mare Caspian Sea.
passages.speaker: Sir Jerome Horsey (memoir; ed. E. A. Bond, 1856)
passages.caution: Horsey overstates: the Nogais and Circassians were never fully conquered in Ivan's lifetime.

passages.headline: Raising a khan on white felt
passages.gloss: Schiltberger says the Great Tartars sow only millet, eat no bread and drink no wine, but drink mare's and camel's milk and eat horse and camel meat. The khan and his people live in the open fields winter and summer. A new khan is set on a white felt and lifted up three times, carried round the tent, and given a golden sword.
passages.quote: It is also to be noted, that when they choose a king, they take him and seat him on white felt, and raise him in it three times. Then they lift him up and carry him round the tent, and seat him on a throne, and put a golden sword in his hand.
passages.speaker: Johann Schiltberger (translated by J. Buchan Telfer, 1879)
passages.caution: He witnessed several quick changes of khan while with Chekre, but does not say which enthronement he saw.

passages.headline: Meat cured under the saddle
passages.gloss: Here Schiltberger insists he saw it himself: on long journeys Tartars bleed their horses and cook and drink the blood, and they slice meat, salt it and ride on it under the saddle until it dries and softens. Every morning the khan drinks mare's milk from a golden cup on an empty stomach.
passages.quote: I myself have seen them bleed [their horses] and drink the blood after they have cooked it. … I have also seen when they are long on a journey, that they take a piece of flesh, cut it into slices, place it under the saddle, and ride on it, and eat it when they were hungry ; but they salt it first
passages.speaker: Johann Schiltberger (translated by J. Buchan Telfer, 1879; bracketed words are the translator's)

passages.headline: Sarai, Astrakhan, Bolgar and Kaffa: the cities of Great Tartary
passages.people: Golden Horde Tartars and their subject towns
passages.gloss: Schiltberger lists the towns he visited 'that belong to Great Tartary': Urgench, Haitzicherchen (Hajji Tarkhan, old Astrakhan), Sarai 'the residence of the kings of the Tartars', Bolgar, Ibissibur, Tana on the Don, Solkhat in Crimea, and Kaffa with its double walls and its Italian, Greek, Armenian and Jewish quarters. So the Horde of his day had real cities as well as camps.
passages.quote: Item, a city called Haitzicherchen, which is a large city, and in a good country. Another city called Sarei ; there, is the residence of the kings of the Tartars. There is also a city called Bolar, in which are different kinds of beasts.
passages.speaker: Johann Schiltberger (translated by J. Buchan Telfer, 1879)
passages.caution: He says he was in these places but gives almost no description of Sarai itself; editor Bruun's notes (p.173) add that its ruins lie on the Akhtuba.

passages.headline: Kaffa: a walled port of many nations
passages.people: Genoese colony within Golden Horde territory
passages.gloss: The fullest city description in his Tartary chapter is of Kaffa, the Genoese port in Crimea. He counts six thousand houses inside the inner wall and eleven thousand within the outer walls, three bishops (Roman, Greek and Armenian), Muslim and Jewish places of worship, and four thousand houses in the suburbs.
passages.quote: A city called Kaffa, which lies by the Black Sea, and is surrounded by two walls. Within one wall are six thousand houses, in which are Italians, Greeks, and Armenians; it is a chief city on the Black Sea
passages.speaker: Johann Schiltberger (translated by J. Buchan Telfer, 1879)
passages.caution: Kaffa was built and run by the Genoese, not by the Tartars, though it lay in lands they claimed.

passages.headline: A hundred thousand huts, and no wood or stone
passages.gloss: Describing the Horde under the kingmaker Edigü, Schiltberger says the people roam winter and summer with families and herds, and a hundred thousand huts go up whenever the khan camps. Elsewhere (p.50) he says Tartary stretches three months' journey with no wood or stones, only grass and shrubs.
passages.quote: The vassals in Tartary wander about in winter and summer, with their wives and children, and their cattle, and when the king encamps, there must be erected one hundred thousand huts.
passages.speaker: Johann Schiltberger (translated by J. Buchan Telfer, 1879)
passages.caution: 'One hundred thousand' is a round, probably exaggerated figure.

passages.headline: Hairy wild people in Siberia
passages.people: Peoples of Siberia under Edigü's campaign
passages.gloss: Riding with Edigü and Prince Chekre into 'Ibissibur' (this is one of the earliest uses of the name Siberia), Schiltberger heard of a mountain range that ends in a desert at the end of the earth, and of hairy wild people who eat grass. A captured wild man and woman were sent to Edigü. He also describes sled dogs as big as donkeys.
passages.quote: On the same mountain there are savages, who are not like other people, and they live there. They are covered all over the body with hair, except the hands and face, and run about like other wild beasts in the mountain, and also eat leaves and grass, and any thing they can find.
passages.speaker: Johann Schiltberger (translated by J. Buchan Telfer, 1879)
passages.caution: The 'end of the earth' desert is what locals told him; the wild people may be his garbled view of forest peoples or a traveller's tale.

passages.headline: A funeral like a wedding
passages.gloss: He describes the funeral of a young unmarried man: the body in his best clothes on a bier under a canopy, musicians and young people in finery, feasting and merrymaking at the grave while the parents weep, so that it becomes the wedding he never had. He adds firmly: 'All this I have seen.'
passages.quote: It is also the custom in the country, that when a young man, who has not had a wife, dies, he is dressed in his best clothes, and players carry him, and he is laid on a bier, and a canopy is placed over him.
passages.speaker: Johann Schiltberger (translated by J. Buchan Telfer, 1879)
passages.caution: On the same pages he calls these people Christians who worship a nativity picture; editor Neumann suggests they were Buddhists he mistook for Christians.

passages.headline: A widow warlord with four thousand women archers
passages.gloss: A powerful Tartar widow named Sadur Melik came to Edigü with four thousand women and girls to avenge her husband. Her women rode to war with sword and bow like men. When the kinsman who had killed her husband was captured, she beheaded him herself. Schiltberger says he was there.
passages.quote: He was brought before the woman ; she ordered him to kneel, and drew her sword, and cut off his head at one blow, and said : " Now am I revenged." I was present there, and I also saw this.
passages.speaker: Johann Schiltberger (translated by J. Buchan Telfer, 1879)
passages.caution: The number of women (four thousand, on p.37) is likely inflated.

passages.headline: Three tribes of the Great Tartars
passages.gloss: Schiltberger names three tribes among the 'Great Tartars': Kayat, Inbu and Mugal. The editors identify these as the Kerait, the Uighurs and the Mongols, so he correctly grasped that the Horde was a mix of peoples with the Mongols as one part. He also notes that Russia paid tribute to the Tartar king.
passages.quote: Item, the kingdom of Rewschen, which is tributary to the Tartar king. It is to be noted, that there are three tribes amongst the Great Tartars. One is called Kayat, the other Inbu, the third Mugal.
passages.speaker: Johann Schiltberger (translated by J. Buchan Telfer, 1879)
passages.caution: The tribe identifications (Kerait, Uighur) are the editor's footnotes.

passages.headline: Why 'Tartar' and not 'Tatar'?
passages.gloss: In a long note, the editor explains why he writes 'Tatar' rather than the manuscript's 'Tartar': Russians, Armenians and the peoples themselves say Tatar, and the extra 'r' came in Western Europe by association with Tartarus (he cites the story about St Louis). He also records the theory that the name goes back to a Chinese name for the Mongols.
passages.quote: The Russian word Tatarui, or Tatars, says Ralston … modified in Western Europe by a reference to Tartarus into Tartars, is now generally applied by Russian writers to what used to be the Turkish subjects of the Mongol Empire.
passages.speaker: Editor's note (J. Buchan Telfer, 1879), citing W. R. S. Ralston
passages.caution: This is a 19th-century editor's discussion, not Schiltberger's own words.

passages.headline: The Lord's Prayer in Tartar
passages.gloss: Schiltberger ends his book with the Lord's Prayer written phonetically in Armenian and in 'Tartar', a rare early European sample of a Turkic language as a captive heard it. It begins 'Atha wysum' ('our father').
passages.quote: This is the Tartar Pater Noster. Atha wysum chy chockta sen algusch ludur senung adung kel suii senung hauluchig belsun
passages.translation: Roughly: 'Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name, thy kingdom come...' in a Turkic language.
passages.speaker: Johann Schiltberger (translated by J. Buchan Telfer, 1879)
passages.caution: The phonetic spelling is his German ear's rendering; the translation given here is a rough gloss of the opening only.

passages.headline: Tatar and Mogul: twin brothers
passages.gloss: In Abu'l Ghazi's genealogy, a king named Alanza Khan, descended from Japheth son of Noah, had twin sons, Tatar and Mogul, and split his realm between them. So the Tatars and the Mongols begin as two rival brother nations. A footnote in the printed edition insists that the Tatars are named after this prince, not after a river 'Tata'.
passages.quote: Alanza Chan had two Twin-Sons, the one called Tatar, and the other Mogull … 'Tis from this Prince the Tatars take their Name, and not from the River Tata, as the Mogulls from Mogull.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this volume is unreadable); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Abu'l Ghazi Bahadur Khan (English translation, 1730); the second sentence is a footnote in the English edition
passages.caution: A genealogical legend; the twins are not historical people.

passages.headline: The Tatars: one of the oldest Turkic tribes
passages.place: Mongolia and the borders of northern China
passages.people: Tatar tribe (a Turkic people in Abu'l Ghazi's scheme)
passages.gloss: In his chapter on the tribes, Abu'l Ghazi describes the Tatars as a specific tribe, once 70,000 families under one powerful khan, that split into branches and declined. The main branch lived on the frontier of 'Kitay' (northern China) and was subject to its emperor, rebelling often. This is the historical Tatar confederation that Chinggis Khan later crushed, not the later Volga or Crimean Tatars.
passages.quote: The Tribe of the Tatars is one of the most antient and famous of the Turkish Nations; it was heretofore above 70000 Families strong, and had only one Chan who was very potent: But being afterwards divided into several Branches, its Power by degrees began to decline.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this volume is unreadable); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Abu'l Ghazi Bahadur Khan (English translation, 1730)

passages.headline: Kipchak: the boy born in a hollow tree
passages.people: Kipchaks (ancestors of the Golden Horde's Turkic subjects)
passages.gloss: The legendary conqueror Oghuz Khan's officer died in battle, and his pregnant widow gave birth inside a hollow tree. The khan raised the boy and named him Kipchak, said to mean 'hollow tree' in old Turkish. The Kipchaks gave their name to the Dasht-i Kipchak, the steppe that later became Batu's Golden Horde.
passages.quote: she could find no other Place to retire to when her Time was come but an old Hollow-Tree; into which having crept when her Labour came on, she there brought forth a Son. … and gave him the Name of Kipzak, which signifies in the antient Turkish, an Hollow-Tree.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this volume is unreadable); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Abu'l Ghazi Bahadur Khan (English translation, 1730)
passages.caution: A folk etymology from the Oghuz legend.

passages.headline: 'We are no other than a Colony of Tatars'
passages.people: Europeans and 'Tatars' in the translator's broad sense
passages.gloss: The anonymous English translator argues that Europeans should despise the Tatars less because Europeans descend from them: the Cimbrians, Celts, Gauls, Goths, Huns, Vandals and Franks were all 'swarms from the same hive' out of Tatary. On the next page he even toys with the idea that the Saxons were akin to the Uzbeks. This is 18th-century speculation about 'Scythian' origins, using 'Tatar' for any northern Asian people.
passages.quote: Our Contempt for the Tatars would still lessen perhaps, did we consider how nearly we stand related to them: that our Ancestors came originally from the North of Asia, and that our Customs, Laws, and way of Living were formerly the same with theirs: In short, that we are no other than a Colony of Tatars.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this volume is unreadable); long s normalized
passages.speaker: The anonymous English translator's preface (1730), not Abu'l Ghazi
passages.caution: The translator's own theory, offered without evidence; nothing in Abu'l Ghazi's text says this.

passages.headline: Tatar Khan's realm by the powerful town of Dsurdsut
passages.place: Borders of northern China and Manchuria
passages.people: Tatars under the legendary Tatar Khan; the Jurchen (Dsurdsut)
passages.gloss: When Oghuz Khan forced his neighbours to accept the true faith, a few refugees fled to Tatar Khan, who lived near 'Dsurdsut'. Abu'l Ghazi calls it a very powerful town ruling several smaller ones, near China's frontier. Dsurdsut is most likely the Jurchen, the people of Manchuria, so here the early Tatars are placed beside a town-dwelling kingdom.
passages.quote: a very few who retir'd into the Dominions of Tatar Chan, who resided in the Neighbourhood of Dsurdsut. The Town of Dsurdsut is very powerful, having several small Towns under its Jurisdiction: 'Tis situate towards the Frontiers of Kitay, being called Zinu in the Indian and Persian Language.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this volume is unreadable); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Abu'l Ghazi Bahadur Khan (English translation, 1730)
passages.caution: Part of the Oghuz Khan legend; identifying Dsurdsut with the Jurchen is a modern reading, not the text's.

passages.headline: A town of pied horses and silver plate on the Yenisei
passages.people: A branch of the Tatar tribe
passages.gloss: Another branch of the Tatars, Abu'l Ghazi says, settled on the river Ikar (glossed in the margin as the Yenisei). Near its mouth stood a great town called Alachzin ('pied'), ruling smaller ones, whose people rode only piebald horses and, thanks to local silver mines, used nothing but silver plate. He adds that the Uzbeks had a tradition of such a nation but could not say where it was.
passages.quote: Near its Mouth there is a great Town, which commands several small ones thereabouts, call'd Alachzin, that is to say, pied; because the Inhabitants of that Town have none but pied Horses … There are rich silver Mines in the Neighbourhood of that Town; and 'tis for that reason that nothing is seen there but silver Plate.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this volume is unreadable); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Abu'l Ghazi Bahadur Khan (English translation, 1730)
passages.caution: Hearsay bordering on legend; Abu'l Ghazi himself says the Uzbeks know of it only 'by Tradition'. The page footnote compares a Russian tale of a 'pied people' in Siberia.

passages.headline: Batu's campaign west and his capital, Coc-orda
passages.people: Batu Khan and the Mongols of the Golden Horde
passages.gloss: Abu'l Ghazi tells how Ögedei gave Batu an army to conquer the Russians ('Uresses'), Circassians and Bulgars. After a forty-day feast Batu set out, 'filled all the West' with his exploits, returned to the Kipchak steppe and died in his capital, which Abu'l Ghazi calls Coc-orda (probably Kök Orda, the 'Blue Horde'). The name shows the royal camp, the orda, serving as the capital.
passages.quote: gave him a numerous Army to go and subdue the Uresses, the Zerkass, the Bulgars, and other neighbouring Nations … Batu-sagin Chan after he had filled all the West with the Glory of the great Exploits which he atchieved upon that Occasion, at length return'd happily into his own Country of Dasht Kipzak, where he died some time after in the Capital of the Country called Coc-orda.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this volume is unreadable); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Abu'l Ghazi Bahadur Khan (English translation, 1730)
passages.caution: Written four centuries after Batu; he does not describe the capital or mention Sarai here.

passages.headline: Melting a mountain of iron with seventy bellows
passages.gloss: After a crushing defeat by the Tatars, the last two Mongol princes fled with their wives and herds into a valley ringed by mountains, Irgana-kon, reached only by a goat track. Four hundred years later their crowded descendants wanted out. A blacksmith noticed the mountain was thin and made of iron ore, so they piled wood and charcoal against it and melted a road through with seventy leather bellows.
passages.quote: a Farrier, who thought he had observ'd that the Mountain was not over thick in a certain Place, and also that it entirely consisted of Iron-Mine, propos'd to apply Bellows to it … they so effectually blew up by the help of 70 Leathern Bellows, that the Mountain at last coming to melt in this Place, left a Road large enough for the Passage of a loaded Camel
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this volume is unreadable); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Abu'l Ghazi Bahadur Khan (English translation, 1730)
passages.caution: A famous Mongol origin legend (also in Rashid al-Din), not history.

passages.headline: The khan strikes the red-hot iron
passages.gloss: To remember the escape from Irgana-kon, Abu'l Ghazi says, the Mongols held a yearly ceremony: a piece of iron was heated red-hot, the khan struck it first with a hammer, then the tribal chiefs and officers in order of rank, then the common people. It ties Mongol kingship to smithing and iron.
passages.quote: They kindle upon that Day a great Fire, wherein they put a Piece of Iron to make it red-hot; after which the Chan gives the first Stroke with a Hammer upon the Piece of Iron, and then all the Heads of the Tribes and other Officers of Distinction, each according to his Rank, give it a Stroke with a Hammer
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this volume is unreadable); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Abu'l Ghazi Bahadur Khan (English translation, 1730)
passages.caution: He says the Mongols 'still' observe it, but gives no date or place for the rite.

passages.headline: Berke, first Muslim khan of the Golden Horde
passages.gloss: Batu's brother and successor Berke ('Burga'), Abu'l Ghazi says, met merchants from Bukhara on the road, was won over by their explanations of Islam, adopted it on the spot, and on his return ordered his subjects to follow. It is an early step in the Horde's move to Islam, the religion of the later Volga and Crimean Tatars.
passages.quote: he met upon the Road with several Merchants of Great Bucharia and falling into discourse with some of them, particularly upon the Articles of the Mahometan Faith, he was so pierced with the Explanations which these Men gave him of it, that he resolv'd off-hand to embrace that Religion
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this volume is unreadable); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Abu'l Ghazi Bahadur Khan (English translation, 1730)
passages.caution: A simplified story told four centuries later. The page ends 'but he died before...', so check the next page for how far the conversion got.

passages.headline: A being of light enters through the tent's roof opening
passages.people: Alancu (Alan Qo'a), ancestress of Chinggis Khan
passages.gloss: The widowed princess Alancu refused to remarry. One morning, she said, a shining orange-coloured man came down through the opening at the top of her chamber (in a felt tent, the smoke-hole), lay with her and vanished. In Mongol tradition the sons born after this were the ancestors of Chinggis Khan. The English margin calls it a 'Fable of an Incubus'.
passages.quote: having slept all Night long, she saw something as she awak'd in the Morning, as bright as the Sun, fall into her Chamber thro' the Opening a-top, and approach her in the Form of a Man, of an Orange Colour, with Eyes of a singular Beauty
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this volume is unreadable); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Abu'l Ghazi Bahadur Khan (English translation, 1730)
passages.caution: The Alan Qo'a legend, known from the Secret History of the Mongols; a sacred origin myth, not history.

passages.headline: The translator: Irgana-kon is borrowed from Gog and Magog
passages.gloss: The English translator is openly sceptical: he calls the origin of the Tatars 'fabulous', Oghuz Khan 'a mere Legend', and the bellows story 'a whimsical Invention'. In a footnote he suggests the enclosed-valley tale grew out of Arabic legends of Gog and Magog (Yajuj and Majuj) shut up behind the mountains of the far north.
passages.quote: Their melting their way out of the Mountains with seventy Bellows, is a whimsical Invention. … In all likelihood this Fiction of the Moguls being inclosed in the Mountain of Irgana Kon, took its Rise from one of the like kind, which we find in Arabik Authors relating to the People of Yajuj and Majuj, or Gog and Magog
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this volume is unreadable); long s normalized
passages.speaker: The anonymous English translator's preface and footnote (1730), not Abu'l Ghazi
passages.caution: The Gog and Magog link is the translator's guess.

passages.headline: Atil: a capital of tents with one brick palace
passages.gloss: The Khazar capital on the Volga is described as mostly tents. Only a few market halls and bathhouses were of clay, and the king's residence was the only burnt-brick building in the country, because nobody else was allowed to build in brick. It is a precise picture of a steppe capital before the Mongols, on the same river where Sarai and Astrakhan later stood.
passages.quote: Here are many tents ; and in this country there are but a few edifices of clay, such as bazars (market-places) and bathing houses. … it is constructed of burnt bricks ; and this is the only building of such materials in all the country : they will not allow any body but the king to erect such a dwelling.
passages.speaker: The 10th-century author attributed to Ibn Hawqal (translated by William Ouseley, 1800)
passages.caution: The Khazars are not called Tartars in the original; this is the pre-Mongol Volga.

passages.headline: A Jewish king ruling Muslims, Christians and pagans
passages.gloss: The author describes Atil's four gates and a king who is Jewish, with judges from each faith: Muslim, Jewish, Christian and pagan. Most inhabitants were Muslims and Christians, and the leading citizens were Muslim merchants. On the same page he notes that their language resembles that of the Turks, glossed by the translator as 'Tartars'.
passages.quote: The king of this country is a Jew : he has in his train four thousand Mussulmans, and Khozrians (Christians), and Idolaters ; but his principal people are Jews … The principal persons of Atel are Mussulmans and merchants: their language is like that of the Turks (or Tartars), and is not understood by any other nation.
passages.speaker: The 10th-century author attributed to Ibn Hawqal (translated by William Ouseley, 1800; bracketed words are Ouseley's)
passages.caution: '(or Tartars)' is the translator's gloss for 'Turks'.

passages.headline: Crowning a khagan by half-strangling him
passages.gloss: When a new Khazar khagan was made, a silk cord was tied tight around his throat and he was asked how many years he would reign. If he outlived the number he named, he was put to death. The author also says the khagan had a golden throne and pavilion, and that nobles would kill themselves on his order.
passages.quote: they bring him forth, and tie a piece of silk about his throat, so tight that he can scarcely draw his breath. At that moment they ask him, how long he will hold the sovereignty ? He answers, " so many years." … when that space is fulfilled, they put him to death.
passages.speaker: The 10th-century author attributed to Ibn Hawqal (translated by William Ouseley, 1800)
passages.caution: Reported by hearsay; similar sacred-kingship customs are described by other Arabic writers.

passages.headline: Bulgar on the Volga: mosques and wooden houses
passages.gloss: The author notes that the Burtas live in wooden houses, and that Bulgar is a city with Muslims and mosques, with a second Muslim town nearby, about ten thousand people in all. This is the Bolgar whose later ruins Russian and German travellers credited to the Tatars or the Bulgars. He also remarks on the very short summer nights.
passages.quote: In the district of Bertas the houses are built of wood. … Bulgar is the name of a city, where there are Mussulmans and mosques ; and near Bulgar is another town called *, where there are also Mussulmans and mosques. In these two cities there are about ten thousand inhabitants.
passages.speaker: The 10th-century author attributed to Ibn Hawqal (translated by William Ouseley, 1800)
passages.caution: The asterisk marks a town name the translator could not read in his manuscripts (probably Suvar).

passages.headline: Round houses of wands and felt, doors to the south
passages.gloss: Polo describes the classic Mongol dwelling: a round frame of light, tightly bound wands covered with felt, carried from camp to camp, always pitched with the door facing south. Families also had felt-covered wagons, rainproof and drawn by oxen and camels, in which women and children travelled. Yule's note compares the Kirghiz yurts of his own day.
passages.quote: Their houses are circular, and are made of wands covered with felts. These are carried along with them whithersoever they go ; for the wands are so strongly bound together, as well as so well combined, that the frame can be made very light. Whenever they erect these huts the door is always to the south.
passages.speaker: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871)
passages.caution: Yule notes the manuscripts differ on 'felts' (one reads 'ropes'); he chose felt as the right reading.

passages.headline: Karakorum: an earthen rampart, for stone is scarce
passages.gloss: Polo calls Karakorum a city about three miles round, enclosed by an earthen rampart because stone was scarce, with a citadel and a governor's palace, and 'the first city that the Tartars possessed'. Yule's note adds that Ögedei built its walls and palace in 1234, and quotes Rubruck's famous verdict that apart from the palace it was no better than the village of St Denis.
passages.quote: Caracoron is a city of some three miles in compass. [It is surrounded by a strong earthen rampart, for stone is scarce there. And beside it there is a great citadel wherein is a fine palace in which the Governor resides.] 'Tis the first city that the Tartars possessed after they issued from
passages.quote_note: Sentence continues on p.204 ('their own country')
passages.speaker: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871; square brackets mark Yule's additions from other manuscripts)
passages.caution: Polo may never have visited Karakorum himself; the bracketed description comes from the Ramusio version only.

passages.headline: Once a land with no towns at all
passages.gloss: Polo begins his history of the Tartars by saying they originally lived on wide plains near 'Chorcha' (Manchuria) with no towns or villages, only rich pastures, and paid tribute to 'Unc Can', whom Europeans called Prester John. Yule's note identifies Chorcha as the Jurchen country and Unc Can as Toghrul, Wang Khan of the Keraits.
passages.quote: Originally the Tartars dwelt in the north on the borders of Chorcha. Their country was one of great plains ; and there were no towns or villages in it, but excellent pasture-lands, with great rivers and many sheets of water ; in fact it was a very fine and extensive region.
passages.speaker: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871)
passages.caution: Polo's early Mongol history is second- or thirdhand and mixed with the Prester John legend.

passages.headline: Xanadu: a marble palace and a portable palace of cane
passages.gloss: At his summer capital Kublai had a marble palace with gilded, painted rooms inside a sixteen-mile walled park. He also had a second palace made of bamboo cane: gilded, roofed with split-cane tiles, held up by gilt dragon columns, and designed to be taken down and moved, with more than 200 silk cords to hold it against the wind. It is the steppe tent reimagined as palace architecture. This passage later inspired Coleridge's 'Kubla Khan'.
passages.quote: The construction of the Palace is so devised that it can be taken down and put up again with great celerity ; and it can all be taken to pieces and removed whithersoever the Emperor may command. When erected, it is stayed [against mishaps from the wind] by more than 200 cords of silk.
passages.speaker: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871; bracketed words from other manuscripts)
passages.caution: The marble palace and the park are described on the previous page (p.263).

passages.headline: Kublai builds Taidu (Beijing) beside the old city
passages.gloss: Polo explains that Kublai, warned by astrologers that the old city of Cambaluc would rebel, built a new, square city called Taidu (Dadu, the core of later Beijing) right beside it and moved the people there. He gives its walls as 24 miles round, of rammed earth ten paces thick. Yule's notes compare the plan with the Beijing of his own day and adjust the figures.
passages.quote: So he caused the present city to be built close beside the old one, with only a river between them. And he caused the people of the old city to be removed to the new town that he had founded ; and this is called Taidu. … it is all walled round with walls of earth which have a thickness of full ten paces at bottom
passages.speaker: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871)
passages.caution: Polo's measurements are too large; Yule's survey-based estimate is about 18 miles round. The city was designed and built by Chinese and other craftsmen for the Mongol court.

passages.headline: Natigay, the felt god of the household
passages.gloss: Polo says the Tartars worship a high god of heaven and an earth god, Natigay, who guards children, cattle and crops. Every household had felt figures of him, his wife and children, and at meals they greased the idols' mouths with fat and sprinkled broth outside the door. Yule links Natigay to the Mongol 'ongon' spirit figures that Pallas later saw among the Buryats.
passages.quote: They show him great worship and honour, and every man hath a figure of him in his house, made of felt and cloth ; and they also make in the same manner images of his wife and children. … And when they eat, they take the fat of the meat and grease the god's mouth withal, as well as the mouths of his wife and children.
passages.speaker: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871)

passages.headline: Units of ten, blood from a horse's vein and dried milk
passages.gloss: Polo explains the decimal army (officers over ten, a hundred, a thousand and ten thousand, the 'toman'), scouts on every side, and how little gear a rider carried: two leather milk bottles, a small pot and a small tent. In emergencies they rode ten days without a fire, drinking blood from their horses' veins, and carried dried milk paste that churned into a meal inside the bottle as they rode.
passages.quote: And in case of great urgency they will ride ten days on end without lighting a fire or taking a meal. On such an occasion they will sustain themselves on the blood of their horses, opening a vein and letting the blood jet into their mouths, drinking till they have had enough, and then staunching it.
passages.speaker: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871)
passages.caution: Blood-drinking is also reported by Herberstein, Schiltberger and others; Polo describes the practice rather than a scene he witnessed.

passages.headline: The 'genuine Tartars' are going native
passages.people: Mongols settled in China and in the Ilkhanate
passages.gloss: After praising Tartar warfare, Polo adds a striking remark: in his day the Mongols were changing. Those settled in China had taken up the religion and ways of the Chinese, and those in the Middle East had adopted Muslim customs. It is an eyewitness observation that the conquerors were being absorbed by the settled peoples they ruled.
passages.quote: But I must add also that in these days they are greatly degenerated ; for those who are settled in Cathay have taken up the practices of the Idolaters of the country, and have abandoned their own institutions ; whilst those who have settled in the Levant have adopted the customs of the Saracens.
passages.speaker: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871)
passages.caution: 'Idolaters' means Buddhists and followers of Chinese religion; 'Saracens' means Muslims.

passages.headline: Ghost weddings for dead children
passages.gloss: Polo reports that when a boy and a girl died unmarried, their families arranged a marriage between them, drew up a contract, burned it so the couple would know in the next world, and burned paper pictures of the dowry. Yule notes this is really a Chinese custom, though he trusts Polo that Mongols practised it too.
passages.quote: And marry them they do, making a regular contract ! And when the contract papers are made out they put them in the fire, in order (as they will have it) that the parties in the other world may know the fact, and so look on each other as man and wife.
passages.speaker: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871)

passages.headline: Twenty thousand killed on the road to a khan's grave
passages.place: Altai mountains (burial ground of the khans)
passages.gloss: Polo says all the Great Khans were carried, however far away they died, to a mountain called Altay for burial, and the funeral escort killed everyone they met on the road to serve the dead ruler in the next world, along with his best horses. He claims more than 20,000 people died this way on Möngke's funeral journey. Yule notes Rashid al-Din reports the same custom for Chinggis.
passages.quote: When they are carrying the body of any Emperor to be buried with the others, the convoy that goes with the body doth put to the sword all whom they fall in with on the road, saying : "Go and wait upon your Lord in the other world !" … when Mongou Kaan died, more than 20,000 persons, who chanced to meet the body on its way, were slain
passages.speaker: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871)
passages.caution: Möngke died in 1259, years before Polo arrived; the figure is hearsay and likely exaggerated.

passages.headline: Gog and Magog are really Ung and Mungul
passages.place: Tenduc (Inner Mongolia, near the Yellow River bend)
passages.gloss: In Tenduc, which he says was once Prester John's capital, Polo meets the legend of Gog and Magog, the wild nations Alexander walled in. He offers a down-to-earth explanation: the local names Ung and Mungul, two peoples who lived there before the Tartar migration, had been misheard in the West as Gog and Magog. Yule's notes identify the Ung as the Ongut.
passages.quote: Here also is what we call the country of Gog and Magog ; they, however, call it Ung and Mungul, after the names of two races of people that existed in that Province before the migration of the Tartars. Ung was the title of the people of the country, and Mungul a name sometimes applied to the Tartars.
passages.speaker: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871)
passages.caution: Polo's 'Prester John' line here is King George of the Ongut, a Nestorian Christian prince.

passages.headline: The khan's daughter who wrestled her suitors for horses
passages.gloss: Kaidu Khan's daughter Aijaruc ('Bright Moon') refused to marry anyone who could not beat her. Each challenger staked horses, and she won more than 10,000. When a handsome prince staked 1,000 horses and her parents begged her to lose, she threw him on the palace floor anyway. She then rode to war with her father, snatching enemies from their ranks 'as deftly as a hawk'.
passages.quote: When both had taken post in the middle of the hall they grappled each other by the arms and wrestled this way and that, but for a long time neither could get the better of the other. At last, however, it so befel that the damsel threw him right valiantly on the palace pavement.
passages.speaker: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871)
passages.caution: Polo was not present; Persian sources confirm a warrior daughter of Kaidu named Khutulun.

passages.headline: The Tartars of the West and their kings
passages.gloss: Polo calls the Golden Horde the 'Tartars of the Ponent' (of the West). Their first king, 'Sain', conquered Russia, the Cumans, Alans, Circassians, Goths of Crimea and Khazaria. He lists the later khans down to Toqta, who reigned in Polo's time. Yule's note points out that 'Sain' (the Good) was really Batu's own surname, so Polo turned one khan into two.
passages.quote: The first lord of the Tartars of the Ponent was Sain, a very great and puissant king, who conquered Rosia and Comania, Alania, Lac, Menjar, Zic, Gothia, and Gazaria ; all these provinces were conquered by King Sain.
passages.speaker: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871)

passages.headline: Raiding the Land of Darkness on mares with foals
passages.people: Tartars (Golden Horde raiders) and northern fur hunters
passages.gloss: Far to the north, Polo says, lies a Land of Darkness where no sun, moon or stars are seen. Tartars raid it riding mares whose foals they leave at the border, trusting the mares to find the way back to their young. The pale inhabitants hunt sables, ermine and black fox for the fur trade. Yule suggests the story garbles the Arctic winter night.
passages.quote: The Tartars however sometimes visit the country, and they do it in this way. They enter the region riding mares that have foals, and these foals they leave behind. After taking all the plunder that they can get, they find their way back by help of the mares, which are all eager to get back to their foals
passages.speaker: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871)
passages.caution: Pure hearsay; the mare-and-foal trick is an old travellers' tale also told of Alexander the Great.

passages.headline: The Tartars build a new city beside old Beijing
passages.gloss: Odoric says the Tartars captured the ancient city of Cambalech and then built a second city half a mile away, called Taydo (Dadu, 'Great Court'). Yule's footnote dates the new city to Kublai Khan in 1267 and explains that it became the 'Tartar city' of later Peking. A clear case of a Tartar-built capital, recorded by someone who lived there.
passages.quote: I came to that noble city Cambalech, an old city of that famous province of Cathay. The Tartars took the city, and then built another at a distance of half-a-mile, which they called Taydo.
passages.speaker: Friar Odoric of Pordenone (translated by Henry Yule, 1866)
passages.caution: Odoric's figures for the size of the two cities (more than forty miles round together) are rough; Yule discusses them in the notes.

passages.headline: Golden columns and a Green Mount in the Khan's palace
passages.people: The Great Khan (Yuan emperor) and his court
passages.gloss: Odoric describes the palace: a raised basement, twenty-four golden columns, walls hung with red leather, and a giant jade jar hooped with gold and fed by conduits of drink. On the page before he describes an artificial hill planted with trees, the Green Mount, with a lake and bridge. Yule notes that the hill still stood inside the Peking palace walls in his day.
passages.quote: But his own palace in which he dwells is of vast size and splendour. The basement thereof is raised about two paces from the ground, and within there be four-and-twenty columns of gold ; and all the walls are hung with skins of red leather, said to be the finest in the world.
passages.speaker: Friar Odoric of Pordenone (translated by Henry Yule, 1866)
passages.caution: Yule notes that Mongol palace arrangements followed older Chinese and Asian royal traditions.

passages.headline: Dancing golden peacocks and ladies crowned with a 'foot'
passages.gloss: In the palace hall are golden peacocks that flap their wings when Tartars clap their hands, which Odoric thinks is done by devilry or hidden machinery. He then describes the court seating and the tall headdress of married Mongol women, which he likens to a man's foot topped with crane feathers and pearls. Yule's note links this to the bogtak headdress also described by Rubruck and Ibn Battuta.
passages.quote: In the hall of the palace also are many peacocks of gold. And when any of the Tartars wish to amuse their lord, then they go one after the other and clap their hands ; upon which the peacocks flap their wings, and make as if they would dance. Now this must be done either by diabolic art, or by some engine underground.
passages.speaker: Friar Odoric of Pordenone (translated by Henry Yule, 1866)

passages.headline: Melons that burst open with a lamb inside
passages.gloss: Odoric reports the 'vegetable lamb': melons on the 'Caspean Mountains' that ripen and split to reveal a little lamb. He admits he did not see it and heard it from others. Yule's note traces the later 'Tartar lamb' or borametz legend, which Scaliger placed among the Tartars of the Zavolha horde, and identifies the likely source as a woolly fern root.
passages.quote: Another passing marvellous thing may be related, which however I saw not myself, but heard from trustworthy persons. For 'tis said that in a certain great kingdom called Cadeli there be mountains called the Caspean Mountains, on which are said to grow certain very large melons. And when these be ripe, they burst, and a little beast is found inside like a small lamb
passages.speaker: Friar Odoric of Pordenone (translated by Henry Yule, 1866)
passages.caution: Hearsay, and Odoric says so himself. Yule identifies Cadeli with the Volga (Athil) country.

passages.headline: The Tartars descend from Noah's son Cham
passages.gloss: Mandeville explains the title 'Chan' by making the Tartars descendants of Noah's cursed son Cham (Ham). He says that only about 160 years earlier the Tartars were subject herdsmen, and that of their seven 'lineages' the noblest was called Tartar. He then tells how a poor old man, Changuys (Genghis), was chosen emperor after a vision of a white knight.
passages.quote: Natheles, the sooth is this ; that Tartars and they that dwell in the great Asia, they came of Cham ; but the Emperor of Cathay clepeth him not Cham, but Can, and I shall tell you how. It is but little more but eight score year that all Tartary was in subjection and in servage to other nations about.
passages.speaker: 'Sir John Mandeville' (Cotton manuscript, modern spelling ed. A. W. Pollard, 1900)
passages.caution: The Cham genealogy is a Christian learned invention; the list of seven lineages and the Genghis story draw on Hayton and similar sources.

passages.headline: Caydon, the city the men of Tartary built
passages.people: Men of Tartary (Mongols of the Yuan dynasty)
passages.gloss: Mandeville describes the Great Khan's capital: beside an old city of Cathay the Tartars built a new one, Caydon, with twelve gates and a palace with a tree-covered hill, lakes and a bridge. This is almost word for word Friar Odoric's 'Taydo' (Dadu, Beijing), and makes a good exercise in spotting a borrowed passage.
passages.quote: After go men yet to another old city toward the east. And it is in the province of Cathay. And beside that city the men of Tartary have let make another city that is clept Caydon. And it hath twelve gates, and between the two gates there is always a great mile
passages.speaker: 'Sir John Mandeville' (Cotton manuscript, modern spelling ed. A. W. Pollard, 1900)
passages.caution: Copied from Odoric (see W041, Taydo), not an independent witness.

passages.headline: An emperor buried in his tent with a mare and foal
passages.gloss: When a Tartar emperor dies he is seated in his tent with a table of meat and a cup of mare's milk, a mare with her foal and a saddled horse, then buried in a great pit, tent and all, so he will have a house, horses and milk in the next world. Mandeville adds that graves were sometimes hidden under replaced turf. The details match Carpini's report, which Mandeville used.
passages.quote: And when the emperor dieth, men set him in a chair in midst the place of his tent. And men set a table before him clean, covered with a cloth, and thereupon flesh and diverse viands and a cup full of mare's milk. And men put a mare beside him with her foal, and an horse saddled and bridled.
passages.speaker: 'Sir John Mandeville' (Cotton manuscript, modern spelling ed. A. W. Pollard, 1900)
passages.caution: Borrowed from Carpini's eyewitness-based account (compare W043, Rockhill's note at p. 81).

passages.headline: 'Of that fruit I have eaten': the lamb that grows in a gourd
passages.gloss: Mandeville improves on Odoric's melon-lamb: in Caldilhe gourds are cut open to reveal a little beast of flesh, bone and blood, and he claims to have eaten it. He then swaps marvels with his hosts, telling them of the barnacle trees of Britain whose fruit turns into birds. The next page places the enclosed peoples of Gog and Magog in the Caspian mountains of the same region.
passages.quote: And there groweth a manner of fruit, as though it were gourds. And when they be ripe, men cut them a-two, and men find within a little beast, in flesh, in bone, and blood, as though it were a little lamb without wool. And men eat both the fruit and the beast. And that is a great marvel. Of that fruit I have eaten
passages.speaker: 'Sir John Mandeville' (Cotton manuscript, modern spelling ed. A. W. Pollard, 1900)
passages.caution: Odoric only heard the story; Mandeville turns it into a personal tasting. The editor's index tentatively places Caldilhe in Korea, but the tale is the Volga 'Tartar lamb' legend.

passages.headline: Poured forth from Tartarus, so rightly called Tartars
passages.gloss: Rockhill's introduction quotes the English chronicler Matthew Paris, writing from St Albans, who never met a Mongol. He plays on the name: the Tartars burst out like devils from Tartarus, the classical underworld, so the name fits. The same passage goes on to call them monsters who drink blood and eat the flesh of dogs and men, a good example of wartime rumour.
passages.quote: a detestable nation of Satan, to wit, the countless army of the Tartars, broke loose from its mountain-environed home, and piercing the solid rocks (of the Caucasus), poured forth like devils from the Tartarus, so that they are rightly called Tartari or Tartarians.
passages.speaker: Matthew Paris, Chronica Majora, quoted in W. W. Rockhill's introduction (1900)
passages.caution: Hearsay and propaganda from a monk in England; the pun on Tartarus is why Europeans wrote 'Tartar' with an extra r.

passages.headline: The Mongols would like to erase the Tartar name
passages.gloss: Rubruck, told at the Mongol court, explains that the Tartars were a separate poor people living next to the Moal (Mongols). Chingis (Genghis) united both and sent the Tartars ahead in every war, so Europeans heard only 'The Tartars are coming!'. By Rubruck's time the Tartars had mostly been killed off and the Mongols disliked the name. Rockhill's note quotes Rashid al-Din saying the same.
passages.quote: Now this Chingis used to despatch the Tartars in every direction, and so their name spread abroad, for everywhere was heard the cry : "The Tartars are coming !" But through the many wars they have been nearly all killed off, and now these Moal would like to extinguish even the name and raise their own in its stead.
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)
passages.caution: Rubruck's story of Genghis's rise (as a blacksmith, and Prester John's brother 'Unc chan') mixes real events with legend.

passages.headline: Water-Mongols who took their name from the river Tatar
passages.gloss: In a footnote Rockhill quotes Carpini's account of the four nations of Mongolia before Genghis Khan. One, the Su-Mongal or 'Water-Mongols', called themselves Tartars after a river named Tatar. Rockhill's longer note on the next page traces the name Tatar back to a Turkic inscription of AD 732 and to Chinese annals.
passages.quote: That country had once four nations : one called Yeka Mongal, or the Great Mongals, the second called Su-Mongal, or Aquatic-Mongals, though they called themselves Tartars from a certain river which flows through their country and which is called Tatar (or Tartar)
passages.speaker: John of Pian de Carpine, quoted in W. W. Rockhill's footnote (1900)
passages.caution: Editorial footnote quoting Carpini; the river etymology is one of several medieval guesses.

passages.headline: A round frame of sticks covered with white felt
passages.gloss: Rubruck describes the Mongol dwelling (the yurt or ger): a circular frame of interlaced sticks meeting in a hoop at the top with a chimney collar, covered in felt. The felt is whitened with chalk, clay or bone powder and embroidered with vines, trees, birds and beasts. Rockhill's note adds Carpini's description of the same round felt tents.
passages.quote: converging into a little round hoop on the top, from which projects above a collar as a chimney, and this (framework) they cover over with white felt. Frequently they coat the felt with chalk, or white clay, or powdered bone, to make it appear whiter, and sometimes also (they make the felt) black.
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)

passages.headline: A house thirty feet wide, pulled by twenty-two oxen
passages.gloss: Some Mongol houses were never taken down but rode on huge carts. Rubruck measured one cart himself and counted the oxen. The axle was as thick as a ship's mast and a driver stood in the doorway of the house. On the next pages he describes felt-covered chests on carts and a rich man's camp of one or two hundred carts.
passages.quote: I myself once measured the width between the wheel-tracks of a cart xx feet, and when the house was on the cart it projected beyond the wheels on either side v feet at least. I have myself counted to one cart xxii oxen drawing one house, eleven abreast across the width of the cart, and the other eleven before them.
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)
passages.caution: Rockhill thinks these carts were exceptionally large ones.

passages.headline: Batu's camp looked like a great city
passages.gloss: Arriving at Batu's camp on the Volga, Rubruck was amazed: the ordu spread out like a city for three or four leagues, with every family knowing its place. He explains that orda means 'middle', because the court stands in the middle of the people, with its doors opening south. This is the moving 'city' of the steppe, the ancestor of the word 'horde'.
passages.quote: When I saw the ordu of Baatu, I was astonished, for it seemed like a great city stretched out about his dwelling, with people scattered all about for three or four leagues.
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)

passages.headline: Karakorum: smaller than the village of Saint-Denis
passages.gloss: Rubruck lived for weeks at Karakorum, the Mongol capital founded by Ogedei in 1235. His verdict is famously unimpressed: apart from the Khan's palace the town was smaller than the village of Saint-Denis outside Paris. Rockhill's note records that the ruins were located on the Orkhon river in 1889 by the Russian traveller Yadrintsev.
passages.quote: Of the city of Caracarum you must know that, exclusive of the palace of the Chan, it is not as big as the village of Saint Denis, and the monastery of Saint Denis is ten times larger than the palace.
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)

passages.headline: Karakorum's mud wall and its Chinese artisans
passages.people: Mongols, with Muslim merchants and Chinese (Cathayan) craftsmen
passages.gloss: Rubruck describes who lived in and built up Karakorum: a Muslim ('Saracen') quarter with the markets, and a quarter of Cathayans (northern Chinese), all artisans. There were twelve temples of various peoples, two mosques and one church, inside a mud wall with four gates, each gate with its own market. Rockhill's note adds that the Mongols themselves mostly lived in tents even at the capital.
passages.quote: one of the Saracens in which are the markets … the other is the quarter of the Cathayans, all of whom are artisans. … There are there twelve idol temples of different nations, two mahummeries in which is cried the law of Machomet, and one church of Christians in the extreme end of the city. The city is surrounded by a mud wall and has iiii gates.
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized; edition page marker dropped
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)
passages.caution: 'Mahummeries' means mosques; 'idol temples' are mostly Buddhist.

passages.headline: A silver fountain-tree made by a captive Parisian goldsmith
passages.people: Mongke Khan's court; Guillaume Boucher of Paris
passages.gloss: At the entrance of Mongke Khan's palace stood a silver tree built by 'master William', a Paris goldsmith taken captive in Hungary. Four silver lions spouted mare's milk, and pipes in the tree poured wine, clarified kumiss, honey mead and rice wine when a hidden man blew a trumpet-blowing angel on top. On the next page Rubruck says the palace itself was laid out like a church with a nave and two rows of pillars.
passages.quote: master William the Parisian had made for him a great silver tree, and at its roots are four lions of silver, each with a conduit through it, and all belching forth white milk of mares. … And from one of these pipes flows wine, from another caracosmos, or clarified mare's milk, from another bal, a drink made with honey, and from another rice mead
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)

passages.headline: Mounds, statues and brick towers over the dead
passages.people: Comans (Cumans or Kipchaks), subjects of the Tartars
passages.gloss: Crossing the steppe, Rubruck saw the tombs of the Comans: great mounds (kurgans) topped by a stone statue holding a cup, small pointed 'pyramids', tiled towers and stone houses, though there was no stone nearby. Just before, he notes that the burial places of Mongol nobles of Genghis's family were kept secret and guarded. Rockhill's note quotes Carpini on Mongol nobles buried with a horse and a mare.
passages.quote: raise a great tumulus over the dead, and set up a statue to him, its face to the east, and holding a cup in its hand at the height of the navel. They make also pyramids to the rich, that is to say, little pointed structures, and in some places I saw great tiled covered towers, and in others stone houses, though there were no stones thereabout.
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)
passages.caution: These tombs are Cuman, not Mongol; the subject 'The Comans' is on the previous page.

passages.headline: The Golden Orda: a tent on gold-plated pillars
passages.people: Mongols at the enthronement of Guyuk Khan
passages.gloss: Carpini attended the enthronement of Guyuk near Karakorum. After a first great tent called the Sira Orda, the court moved to the Golden Orda, a tent whose pillars were plated in gold with gold nails and whose roof and sides were hung with precious cloth. Guyuk was then seated on the throne and everyone drank until evening.
passages.quote: where another tent was set up, and it is called by them the Golden Orda … This tent rested on pillars covered with gold plates, fastened with gold nails and other woods, and the top and sides of it were covered with baldakins; the outside, however, being of other kinds of stuff.
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized; edition page marker dropped
passages.speaker: John of Pian de Carpine (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)

passages.headline: Ruined cities on the Syr Darya
passages.people: Bisermins (Muslims of the Khwarazmian lands), conquered by the Tartars
passages.gloss: Riding east, Carpini crossed the old Khwarazmian lands the Mongols had conquered in 1219 to 1221 and found them full of ruins. He names Ianckint, Barchin and Ornas. Rockhill's footnote on the same page quotes Carpini's longer account of how the Mongols took Ornas by diverting the river and flooding the city, and on the page before Carpini describes skulls and bones lying on the steppe 'like cattle-dung'.
passages.quote: We found in that country innumerable ruined cities, overthrown villages, and many deserted towns. There is a great river in that country whose name I do not know, and on which stands a city called Ianckint, and also another called Barchin, and still another called Ornas
passages.speaker: John of Pian de Carpine (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)
passages.caution: Identifications of Ornas (Otrar or Urgench) are uncertain; see Rockhill's note.

passages.headline: Omyl, a city the Mongols rebuilt
passages.people: Mongols in the land of the Kara-Khitai
passages.gloss: In the country of the Black Kitayans (Kara-Khitai), Carpini found a city the Mongols had built anew, with a house put up by the Emperor, where the friars were invited to drink. Rockhill's note explains that Imil was first built by the Kara-Khitai around 1125 and was Guyuk's own appanage.
passages.quote: After that we entered the country of the Black Kitayans, in which they (i.e., the Mongols) have built anew, as it were, a city called Omyl, in which the Emperor has erected a house where we were invited to drink
passages.speaker: John of Pian de Carpine (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)

passages.headline: Sarai, 'the new town that Baatu is making'
passages.gloss: On his way home Rubruck asked about his lost books and vestments. Coiac, an official of Batu's son Sartach, said he had left them near Sarai, a town Batu was then building on the Volga. It is a rare contemporary glimpse of the founding of the Golden Horde's capital, and Rubruck later travelled south toward it.
passages.quote: I left your things at my father's, who stays near Sarai, the new town that Baatu is making on the Etilia
passages.speaker: Coiac, an official of Sartach, as reported by William of Rubruck (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)

passages.headline: Derbent's stone towers, cut down by the Tartars
passages.gloss: Rubruck passed through the Iron Gate (Derbent) on the Caspian. He credits Alexander the Great with building it, following medieval legend, and describes a narrow town with strong walls and towers of dressed stone. The Tartars had levelled the tops of the towers and the parapets, making them even with the walls. Rockhill's note says Muslim geographers credited the Persian king Khosrow Anushirvan.
passages.quote: The next day we came to the Iron Gate, which Alexander the Macedonian made … It has very strong walls without moats, and towers of great dressed (politis) stones ; but the Tartars have destroyed the tops of the towers and the parapets of the walls, making the towers even with the walls.
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)
passages.caution: The Alexander attribution is legend; the walls are Sasanian Persian work.

passages.headline: How kumiss is made
passages.gloss: Rubruck gives a step-by-step account of kumiss, fermented mare's milk: foals tied to a rope, mares milked, the milk churned in a skin with a club until it bubbles like new wine and turns pungent. He found it tasted of almond milk and 'intoxicates weak heads'. On the next page he says Batu received the milk of three thousand mares every day.
passages.quote: When they have got together a great quantity of milk, which is as sweet as cow's as long as it is fresh, they pour it into a big skin or bottle, and they set to churning it with a stick prepared for that purpose
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)

passages.headline: Women whose headdresses look like helmets and lances
passages.gloss: Married Mongol women wore the bocca (bogtak), a tall bark frame covered with silk and topped with a tuft of quills and peacock feathers. Rubruck says a group of ladies riding in the distance looked like soldiers in helmets with lances raised, and that women rode astride like men. He adds, less kindly, that the fattest women with the smallest noses were thought the most beautiful.
passages.quote: and one sees them from afar, they look like soldiers, helmets on head and lances erect. For this bocca looks like a helmet, and the tuft above it is like a lance. And all the women sit their horses astraddle like men.
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)

passages.headline: Mongke Khan: one God, many ways, like fingers on a hand
passages.gloss: After a debate between Christians, Muslims and Buddhists at his court, Mongke Khan explained the Mongol faith to Rubruck. The Moal believe in one God, he said, but God gives different peoples different ways, as he gives the hand different fingers. It is a vivid statement of the Mongol court's religious tolerance, spoken through an interpreter.
passages.quote: "We Moal," he said, "believe that there is only one God, by whom we live and by whom we die, and for whom we have an upright heart." … "But as God gives us the different fingers of the hand, so he gives to men divers ways.
passages.speaker: Mongke Khan, as reported by William of Rubruck (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)
passages.caution: Mongke's words reached Rubruck through an interpreter, William Boucher's son.

passages.headline: Were the Tartars the lost tribes shut up by Alexander?
passages.people: Tartars (Mongols), imagined as the ten lost tribes
passages.gloss: Matthew Paris repeats the belief that the Tartars were the ten lost tribes of Israel, whom Alexander the Great walled up in the Caspian mountains, the peoples who would break out at the end of the world (the Gog and Magog legend). Interestingly, he admits a doubt: these Tartars speak no Hebrew and do not know the law of Moses.
passages.quote: having forsaken the Mosaic law, followed after the golden calves, and whom Alexander the Macedonian endeavoured at first to shut up in the rugged mountains of the Caspians with bitumen-covered rocks. … There arises, however, a doubt whether the Tartars now coming from there be really they, for they do not use the Hebrew tongue
passages.speaker: Matthew Paris, Chronica Majora, quoted in W. W. Rockhill's introduction (1900)
passages.caution: Legend repeated by a chronicler far from the events; the sentence begins on the previous page ('these Tartars, of cursed memory, are of the ten tribes who').

passages.headline: No monsters, but hairy little men who cry 'chin, chin'
passages.people: Priests at the Mongol court; Cathay
passages.gloss: Rubruck asked priests at Karakorum about the dog-headed and one-eyed monsters described by Isidore and Solinus. They told him they had never seen any, which surprised him. Then a priest from Cathay told him of tiny hairy creatures with stiff knees living among rocks east of Cathay, caught by leaving out mead to get them drunk, whose blood made a red dye.
passages.quote: They told me they had never seen such, which astonished me greatly, if it be true. … in the countries east of Cathay there are high rocks, among which dwell creatures who have in all respects human forms, except that their knees do not bend, so that they get along by some kind of jumping motion
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)
passages.caution: The creature story is hearsay from a single informant; the denial of monsters is a useful check on older book-learning.

passages.headline: Dog-headed men and people who live on smells
passages.people: Peoples on the northern edge of the Tartar lands
passages.gloss: Benedict the Pole's short report lists the peoples beside the friars' route: Mordvins, Bashkirs, and then the Cynocephali with dogs' heads and the Parossites who cannot chew and live on the smell of food. He also notes the rich city of Ornarum taken by the Tartars with floods of water. Rockhill's note traces the monsters to Pliny and Solinus.
passages.quote: then the Cynocephales, who have dogs' heads ; and then the Parocitae, who have a small narrow mouth, who can masticate nothing, but who live on liquids and sustain themselves on the odours of meats and fruits.
passages.speaker: Benedict the Pole (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)
passages.caution: Book-learned legend placed on the map, not something Benedict saw.

passages.headline: The Crimean Tatars burn Moscow, 1571
passages.people: Crimean Tatars under Khan Devlet Giray
passages.gloss: Writing to Lord Burghley from Kholmogory in August 1571, Jenkinson lists Russia's woes: famine, the Tsar's executions, plague, and then the Crimean Tatars, who in late May routed the Tsar's army and set Moscow on fire. He reports that not one house was left standing and that more than 300,000 were said to have been burned or carried off as captives. The figures are hearsay, but the event is real.
passages.quote: a valyante natyon of Tartars, in the latter ende of May laste, inuadid this realme, gaue the Prynce an ouerthrowe in the feildes, cawsed him to retyre, burnte and consumed all the countrye before theim, and came to the cyttye of Musko, sett fyer one the same, not leauinge one house standinge
passages.speaker: Anthony Jenkinson, letter to Lord Burghley, 8 August 1571 (ed. E. Delmar Morgan and C. H. Coote, 1886)
passages.caution: Jenkinson arrived after the fire and repeats reported numbers; he calls it 'a juste punyshment of God for such a wycked natyon' (the Russians).

passages.headline: Whirlwinds of fire: three hours that ended a city
passages.gloss: A second account, printed by the chronicler John Stow and apparently drawn from a letter of the English survivor Thomas Glover, describes the fire as a storm of 'whirl wynds' that died down after three hours, leaving streets full of dead men and horses. Twenty-five people died in the English Company's house. The 'Tartar dog', the Crimean khan, retreated across the Oka that same night.
passages.quote: This crewell and sodayne destructyon cam vpon ye moscow in great and wonderfull whirl wynds, and at ye ende of thre owrs very calme agayne, and fayre wether, that men myght walke and se ye dede bodyes of men & horses to no small nomber … ye same daye that the tartar dogge had done this myscheffe, the nyght following he, with all his power, fled ouer the ryuar oca
passages.speaker: Account printed by John Stow, apparently from a letter of Thomas Glover (ed. E. Delmar Morgan and C. H. Coote, 1886)
passages.caution: The editors' note (p. 340) explains the chain of letters behind this text.

passages.headline: Tsar Ivan counts his years from the conquest of Kazan and Astrakhan
passages.people: Former Tatar khanates of Kazan and Astrakhan, now Russian
passages.gloss: Ivan IV's letter to Queen Elizabeth is dated not only by the year of the world and his reign but by his two great conquests of Tatar khanates: Kazan (1552) and Astrakhan (1554 to 1556). The seizure of these Tatar cities was so important to Muscovy that it became part of the Tsar's official dating and of his title.
passages.quote: the 23 yere of our Empire, since the wynning of Casane xvii yere, and of Astrecane XV yere.
passages.speaker: Tsar Ivan IV, letter to Queen Elizabeth written at Vologda, 1569 (contemporary English version; ed. Morgan and Coote, 1886)

passages.headline: 70,000 Turks and Tatars besiege Astrakhan
passages.gloss: The English merchants Banister and Ducket were held up at Astrakhan for six weeks by a great army of Turks and Tatars sent by the Sultan to take the town from Russia. Winter and news of a Russian relief army made them give up. The editors' note adds that this was the Ottoman campaign that also tried to dig a canal between the Volga and the Don.
passages.quote: In this towne of Astracan they were somewhat hindered of their iourney, and staied the space of 6. weekes by reason of a great armie of 70,000. Turkes and Tartares, which came thither vpon the instigation of the great Turke, hoping either to haue surprised it suddenly, or by continuance of siege to win the same.
passages.speaker: Narrative written by 'P. I.' from the report of Lionel Plumtree, in Hakluyt (ed. Morgan and Coote, 1886)

passages.headline: Nogai river raiders attack an English barge
passages.gloss: Forty miles above Astrakhan, the English barge was attacked by about 300 Nogai Tatars in eighteen boats, armed with swords, spears and bows. After a two-hour fight the English firearms drove them off, and the English later heard from an escaped Russian prisoner that 120 raiders had died. Banister, the editors note, survived thanks to a mail shirt.
passages.quote: the Nagaian Tartares, being a kind of theeuish and cruell people, made an assault vpon them with 18. boates of theirs, each of them being armed, some with swords, some with speares, and some others with bowes and arrowes, and the whole number of them they discouered to bee about 300. men.
passages.speaker: Narrative written by 'P. I.' from the report of Lionel Plumtree, in Hakluyt (ed. Morgan and Coote, 1886)
passages.caution: Written down secondhand from a participant; the casualty figure came from a prisoner.

passages.headline: A Nogai town outside Astrakhan's walls
passages.people: Nogai Tatars (vassals of the Tsar) and raiding Crimeans
passages.gloss: Wintering at Astrakhan, Christopher Burrough's party saw half of the Nogai Tatar settlement beside the Russian castle burn by accident. He notes that these Nogais were the Tsar's vassals, some seven thousand men, women and children. Weeks later other Nogais and Crimeans camped around Astrakhan with 1,400 horsemen but did not attack.
passages.quote: The Nagayes that inhabit that towne are the Emperour of Russia his vassals. It is supposed there are of them inhabiting that place, of men, women, and children, the number of seuen thousand. … The seuenth of March 1580. the Nagayes and Crims came before Astracan to the number of one thousand foure hundred horsemen, which incamped round about
passages.speaker: Christopher Burrough's reports, in Hakluyt (ed. Morgan and Coote, 1886)
passages.caution: The town's name (given on the previous page as the 'Yurt') is badly garbled in this OCR.

passages.headline: Ruins of a stone castle and horseman tombs at Uvek
passages.people: Unnamed former inhabitants (the editors' index calls Uvek an 'old Tartar town')
passages.gloss: Sailing down the Volga, Burrough's party stopped at Uvek on the 'Crims side' (west bank) and saw the ruins of a fine stone castle and tombs of important people. One tombstone showed a mounted archer, and inscriptions the English took for Armenian letters. The narrative does not say who built it; the editors' index labels Uvek an old Tartar town, and it was in fact a Golden Horde city.
passages.quote: At this place had beene a very fayre stone castle, called by the name Oueake … There remaineth, at this day, to be seene a part of the ruines of the castle and certain tombs, wherein, as it seemeth, haue beene laid noble personages ; for vpon a tombe stone might be perceiued the forme of a horse, and a man sitting on it with a bowe in his hand
passages.speaker: Christopher Burrough's reports, in Hakluyt (ed. Morgan and Coote, 1886)
passages.caution: The 'Armenian' reading of the inscriptions is the travellers' guess.

passages.headline: A town swallowed by the earth for its wickedness
passages.people: Russians' legend about a ruined Volga town
passages.gloss: Next to the ruined castle of Uvek, the Russians told the English, there had stood a town they called Sodom, which God had swallowed into the earth with part of the castle because of its people's wickedness. It is a local legend attached to real ruins, and the narrator clearly labels it as Russian report.
passages.quote: adioyning to the same was a towne called by Russes Sodom. This towne & part of the castle (by report of the Russes) was swallowed into the earth by the iustice of God, for the wickednesse of the people that inhabited the same.
passages.speaker: Christopher Burrough's reports, in Hakluyt (ed. Morgan and Coote, 1886)
passages.caution: Legend reported by Russian boatmen, not observed.

passages.headline: Five 'kingdoms of the Tartars' on the road to Bukhara
passages.people: Turkmen and Uzbek khanates of Central Asia
