passages.gloss: In a late summary of his travels, Jenkinson says he went forty days beyond the Caspian through five kingdoms 'of the Tartars' and the lands of the Turkmen and 'Zayatay' (Chagatai) to the great city of Bukhara. The editors' note names the five as Mangishlak, Vazir, Urgench, Kath and Bukhara. Here 'Tartar' covers the Muslim Turkic states of Central Asia.
passages.quote: of the Tartars, and all the land of Turkenian and Zayatay, and so to the great citie of Boghar, in Bactria, not without great perils and dangers sundry times.
passages.speaker: Anthony Jenkinson, summary of his travels (ed. Morgan and Coote, 1886)
passages.caution: The sentence begins on the previous page ('passed through 5. kingdomes').

passages.headline: Crimeans, Nogais and 'the whole nation of the Tartarians'
passages.people: Crimean Tatars, Nogais and other Tatars
passages.gloss: An English visitor to Ivan IV's court lists the Tsar's usual enemies: Lithuania, Poland, Sweden, Denmark, Livonia, and three kinds of Tatars. He separates the Crimeans and the Nogais from 'the whole nation of the Tartarians' and praises them all as tough fighters.
passages.quote: His enemies, with whom he hath warres for the most, are these : Litto, Poland, Sweden, Denmarke, Liefland, the Crimmes, Nagaians, and the whole nation of the Tartarians, which are a stoute and a hardie people as any vnder the Sunne.
passages.speaker: Narrative of the 1557 voyage with the Russian envoy Osep Napea, attributed to Robert Best (ed. Morgan and Coote, 1886)
passages.caution: Authorship attribution to Robert Best is the editors' (following Hamel).

passages.headline: A unicorn's horn on the coast of Tartaria
passages.people: 'Barbarous Tartarians' of the northern coast of Asia
passages.gloss: Arguing for a sea route to China round the north of Asia, Jenkinson pointed to a unicorn's horn found on the 'coast of Tartaria', which he thought must have floated there from the east. Sir Humphrey Gilbert, reporting the debate, scoffs that the 'barbarous Tartarians' might not know a unicorn's horn at all, and that such a horn would not float. The editors note the many forms of the unicorn legend across Asia.
passages.quote: His second reason is, that there was an Vnicornes horne … found vpon the coast of Tartaria, which could not come (sayd … he) thither by any other meanes then with the tides
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized; printed margin notes omitted
passages.speaker: Sir Humphrey Gilbert, reporting Anthony Jenkinson's argument (ed. Morgan and Coote, 1886)
passages.caution: Nobody here saw the horn; it may have been a walrus or narwhal tusk, but the source does not say.

passages.headline: Why the Mongols are still called Tatars
passages.gloss: Ney Elias's introduction quotes the Persian historian Rashid al-Din (writing about 1300 to 1310). The Tatars were once so powerful that other Turkic peoples called themselves Tatars for the prestige, just as in Rashid's own day everyone wanted to be a 'Mongol'. That, he says, is why the Mongols are still called Tatars in China, India, the Kipchak steppe, Arabia, Syria and Egypt.
passages.quote: Previous to this period it was the same with the Tatars, on account of their power, and this is the reason why the Mongols are still called Tatars in China and in India, by the Kirghiz, the Bashgirds, in the Kapchak country, in the north of Asia, in Arabia, in Syria, in Egypt, and in Africa.
passages.speaker: Rashid al-Din, quoted (via d'Ohsson's French) in Ney Elias's introduction (1895)
passages.caution: Editorial introduction quoting a fourteenth-century source at second hand.

passages.headline: Turkistan after the Tatars: nothing but ruins
passages.people: Tatars (Mongols) and the nomads who followed them
passages.gloss: The editor quotes the fourteenth-century Arab geographer Shihab al-Din (al-Umari), who was told by a traveller that the land had been ruined 'by the arms of the Tatars'. From a distance a village looks well built, but up close its houses are empty, and the people are now all herders. Elias adds that the towns had been built by earlier settled peoples such as the Uighurs and Kara-Khitai, before the Mongol nomads made it their home.
passages.quote: Since the region has been devastated by the arms of the Tatars," he writes, "it is inhabited only by a scanty population. According to what I have been assured by a man who has travelled through the country, there is nothing to be seen in Turkistan but ruins, and more or less obliterated remains.
passages.speaker: Shihab al-Din (al-Umari), Masalik al-Absar, quoted in Ney Elias's introduction (1895)
passages.caution: Hearsay at two removes, quoted from Quatremère's French translation.

passages.headline: A khan who loved towns, and chiefs who would not stay
passages.people: Moghuls (Muslim Mongols of Moghulistan) under Yunus Khan
passages.gloss: Mirza Haidar explains why his grandfather Yunus Khan kept leaving Kashgar and Aksu: the Khan liked cities and houses, but his amirs and soldiers refused to live in towns, so he had to follow them back to the steppe. It is a clear statement from inside a Mongol dynasty of the nomads' dislike of town life.
passages.quote: The substance of the whole matter is that the Khan was very fond of cities and houses, but the Amirs and soldiers of Moghulistan always avoided the towns, and for this reason the Khan spent most of his time in Moghulistan.
passages.speaker: Mirza Haidar Dughlat (translated by E. Denison Ross, 1895)
passages.caution: Mirza Haidar says the accounts he heard of these events differed.

passages.headline: No true Muslims until they settle in towns
passages.gloss: At the start of Yunus Khan's reign, the Moghuls still lived in the old way, shunning towns and farmland, and were Muslims in name only; neighbours even sold them as slaves like unbelievers. Yunus decided that they would never be good Muslims until they settled, and led them to Tashkent, though some rebelled and stayed on the steppe. Elsewhere (p. 58) Mirza Haidar records that an earlier khan had a horseshoe nail driven into the head of any Moghul who refused to wear a turban.
passages.quote: At the beginning of the reign of Yunus Khan, all the Moghuls dwelt, according to their old custom, in Moghulistan ; they avoided all towns and cultivated countries [and regarded them] with great repugnance. They were Musulmans in nothing but the name
passages.speaker: Mirza Haidar Dughlat (translated by E. Denison Ross, 1895)

passages.headline: Tash Rabat: a Moghul khan's stone caravanserai
passages.gloss: Mirza Haidar credits Muhammad Khan, the khan who pushed the Moghuls into Islam, with building a rabat (travellers' lodge) of huge stones north of the Chadir Kul pass, with a tall entrance hall, a dome, cells and a mosque. He had seen it himself. The editor's note matches it with the ruin now called Tash Rabat and rejects a later claim that it was a converted Hindu temple, since no manuscript says so.
passages.quote: In the construction of this building he employed stones of great size, the like of which are only to be seen in the temples … of Kashmir. The Rabat contains an entrance hall 20 gaz in height. … The whole building is of stone, and over the doors there are huge solid blocks of stone, which I thought very wonderful, before I had seen the temples in Kashmir.
passages.speaker: Mirza Haidar Dughlat (translated by E. Denison Ross, 1895)
passages.caution: The editor's note weighs the identification with the surviving ruin and rejects a later story that it was a converted Hindu temple.

passages.headline: Yarkand's new citadel and the old town dug up for treasure
passages.people: Mirza Aba Bakr, Dughlat ruler of Kashgar
passages.gloss: Mirza Haidar describes how Aba Bakr made Yarkand his capital: he dug out the old town, finding much treasure, brought in water channels, laid out gardens and built a citadel thirty gaz high with six gateways guarded by paired towers. It is a local ruler's building programme described by a man who knew the city well.
passages.quote: The old town was dug out by Mirza Aba Bakr ; it was among the excavations [kazihka] which we have spoken about, and much treasure was found [in it]. … Mirza Aba Bakr built a citadel which, in most places, is thirty statute gaz in height.
passages.speaker: Mirza Haidar Dughlat (translated by E. Denison Ross, 1895)
passages.caution: Mirza Haidar himself doubts the report of 12,000 gardens.

passages.headline: The town of Katak, buried by a rain of sand
passages.people: Muslim townspeople of Katak in the Tarim basin
passages.gloss: A holy man warns the town of Katak of God's wrath and leaves. The muezzin goes back for a last call to prayer, sees sand falling like dry snow, and finds the town buried up to the minaret, from which he jumps to escape. Mirza Haidar adds that winds sometimes uncover the minaret or a house where everything is in order but the owner is white bones. The editor notes that sand does not fall like snow but that dunes do bury towns.
passages.quote: So he again ascended and, looking round, discovered that it was raining sand, and to such a degree that the whole town was covered ; after a little while he noticed that the ground was rising, and at last only a part of the minaret was left free.
passages.speaker: Mirza Haidar Dughlat, retelling a story from Maulana Khwaja Ahmad (translated by E. Denison Ross, 1895)
passages.caution: A pious legend passed down in one family; the editor's note compares it with real sand-buried ruins seen by Forsyth, Bellew and Przhevalsky.

passages.headline: Hunters glimpse castles and minarets under the sand
passages.people: Unknown former townspeople of the Tarim basin
passages.gloss: Describing the deserts east and south of Kashgar and Khotan, Mirza Haidar says great towns once stood there, of which only the names Lob and Katak survive. Hunters of wild camels told of seeing foundations, castles, minarets, mosques and colleges that vanished under the sand again soon after. He does not say who built them.
passages.quote: In ancient times there were large towns in these [wastes] … all are buried under the sand. Hunters, who go there after wild camels, relate that sometimes the foundations of cities are visible, and that they have recognised noble buildings such as castles, minarets, mosques and colleges, but that when they returned a short time afterwards, no trace of these was to be found
passages.speaker: Mirza Haidar Dughlat (translated by E. Denison Ross, 1895)
passages.caution: Hunters' reports; the buildings named (minarets, mosques, colleges) are Islamic types, so these towns were not prehistoric in Mirza Haidar's mind.

passages.headline: Better than a dog? A khan's conversion to Islam
passages.people: Tughluk Timur Khan of the Moghuls
passages.gloss: The young Moghul khan, feeding his dogs pork during a hunt, asks a captured Persian-speaking holy man whether he is better than the dog. The shaikh answers that with faith he is better, without it the dog is. Moved, the khan promises to become a Muslim when he rules, and years later the shaikh's son holds him to it. Mirza Haidar heard it from the holy man's descendants.
passages.quote: He was, at that time, feeding some dogs with swine's flesh, and he asked the Shaikh angrily : "Are you better than this dog, or is the dog better than you ?" The Shaikh replied : "If I have faith I am better than this dog ; but if I have no faith, this dog is better than I am."
passages.speaker: Mirza Haidar Dughlat (translated by E. Denison Ross, 1895)
passages.caution: Family and religious tradition, told about two centuries after the event.

passages.headline: The first kumiss of spring, and a cup that fell
passages.gloss: Mirza Haidar's father told him of a spring feast held, by old Moghul custom, when the new kumiss (fermented mare's milk) came in. Just as the amir offered the khan a cup, news came of an envoy from Timur demanding tribute, and the cup fell from the khan's hands. The amir consoled him with verses about not grieving over tomorrow.
passages.quote: I have frequently heard my father (upon whom rest the mercy of God) relate that in the beginning of the spring the new kimiz had come in, and on that day, according to an ancient Moghul custom, a great feast had been prepared.
passages.speaker: Mirza Haidar Dughlat (translated by E. Denison Ross, 1895)

passages.headline: A Moghul khan with a full beard and a Tajik face
passages.gloss: A Muslim scholar expected Yunus Khan, as a 'Moghul', to be a beardless desert Turk, and was surprised to find an elegant man with a full beard and a Persian-looking (Tajik) face. The editor uses the story to show how far the ruling Moghul families had mixed with their Turkic and Persian neighbours.
passages.quote: I had heard that Yunus Khan was a Moghul, and I concluded that he was a beardless man, with the ways and manners of any other Turk of the desert. But when I saw him, I found he was a person of elegant deportment, with a full beard and a Tajik face
passages.speaker: Maulana Muhammad Kazi, as reported by Mirza Haidar Dughlat (translated by E. Denison Ross, 1895)
passages.caution: The editor's racial reading ('Aryan') belongs to his time, not to the source.

passages.headline: Eyes that could bore through brass: a captive poet's Tatars
passages.gloss: Elias quotes the Persian poet Amir Khusrau of Delhi, who had been a prisoner of Mongol raiders and describes them with hatred: narrow piercing eyes, faces set on necks, noses spreading from cheek to cheek. Elias warns that the poet was 'burning with dread and resentment' and omits 'offensive details'. On a later page Elias notes that Khusrau calls the same people Tatars, Turks and Moghuls.
passages.quote: There were more than a thousand Tatar infidels and warriors of other tribes, riding on camels, great commanders in battle, all with steel-like bodies clothed in cotton ; with faces like fire, with caps of sheepskin, with heads shorn. Their eyes were so narrow and piercing that they might have bored a hole in a brazen vessel
passages.speaker: Amir Khusrau, quoted in Ney Elias's introduction (1895)
passages.caution: Hostile caricature by a former captive, quoted in translation by the editor.

passages.headline: The Zagatays: Tartars who stayed and gave their name
passages.people: Zagatays (Chagatai Mongols and Turks of Timur's realm)
passages.gloss: Clavijo explains Timur's people. An 'emperor of Tartary' divided his lands among four sons, and Zagatay (Chagatai) received Samarkand; when the locals killed him, his followers who stayed were called Zagatays. Timur descends from these 'Zagatay Tartars', and many Samarkand people now call themselves Zagatays to share in the famous name. Markham's note corrects the details of the story.
passages.quote: Timour Beg, and the other Zagatays who follow him, are descended from these Zagatay Tartars; and many people of the land of Samarcand have now taken this name of Zagatay, that they may share in the great name which the Zagatays have now attained.
passages.speaker: Ruy González de Clavijo (translated by Clements R. Markham, 1859)
passages.caution: Local tradition as told to the envoys; Markham notes that Chagatai was not killed by his subjects.

passages.headline: Tent people who sow melons by the rivers
passages.gloss: Among the Zagatay tents of Khorasan, Clavijo notes that these people have no other homes. In summer they camp by rivers and sow corn, cotton and melons, in winter they move to warm districts, and Timur and his army wander the same way. On the next page he describes their food of sour milk boiled with bits of dough, cooked over dung fires.
passages.quote: The people of these tents have no other dwelling place, and they wander over the plains, during both winter and summer. In summer they go to the banks of the rivers, and sow their corn, cotton, and melons … The lord, with all his host, wanders in the same way over the plains, winter and summer.
passages.speaker: Ruy González de Clavijo (translated by Clements R. Markham, 1859)

passages.headline: Timur's palace at Kesh: glazed tiles, and a doubt about who began it
passages.people: Timur (Timour Beg) and an earlier lord of Samarkand
passages.gloss: At Kesh (Shahrisabz), Timur's birthplace, the envoys toured palaces said to have been under construction for twenty years: brick arches covered in glazed tiles, a court paved with white stone around a great pool, and a gateway in gold and blue tiles. Clavijo noticed the lion-and-sun device over the door and argued that an earlier lord of Samarkand must have begun it, since Timur's own device was three circles. A rare case of a medieval visitor questioning a building's attribution.
passages.quote: On the top of this doorway there was the figure of a lion and a sun, which are the arms of the lord of Samarcand ; and, though they say that Timour Beg ordered these palaces to be built, I believe that the former lord of Samarcand gave the order
passages.speaker: Ruy González de Clavijo (translated by Clements R. Markham, 1859)
passages.caution: Clavijo's reasoning about the arms is his own inference.

passages.headline: Craftsmen carried off to build Samarkand
passages.people: Captives from Damascus, Turkey and elsewhere, under Timur
passages.gloss: Clavijo explains how Timur filled Samarkand: he brought captives from every land he conquered, above all skilled workers. Silk weavers, bow-makers, glass and pottery makers came from Damascus; archers, masons and silversmiths from Turkey. So many arrived, some 150,000 of many nations, that many lived under trees and in caves outside the city. The page before says the villages around the city were peopled with captives too.
passages.quote: From Damascus he brought weavers of silk, and men who made bows, glass, and earthenware, so that, of those articles, Samarcand produces the best in the world. From Turkey he brought archers, masons, and silversmiths. He also brought men skilled in making engines of war
passages.speaker: Ruy González de Clavijo (translated by Clements R. Markham, 1859)
passages.caution: Clavijo saw the crowded city; where the craftsmen came from and the figure of 150,000 were told to him.

passages.headline: Samarkand: an earth-walled city a little bigger than Seville
passages.gloss: Clavijo compares Samarkand to his own Seville: an earthen wall, a city a little larger, but with suburbs and gardens stretching for leagues and more people outside the walls than within. Timur's palaces stood among the gardens. Elsewhere he watches Timur drive a vaulted market street through the city in twenty days, pulling down houses in its path.
passages.quote: The city of Samarcand is situated in a plain, and surrounded by an earthen wall. It is a little larger than the city of Seville, but, outside the city, there are a great number of houses, joined together in many parts, so as to form suburbs.
passages.speaker: Ruy González de Clavijo (translated by Clements R. Markham, 1859)

passages.headline: A tent palace on thirty-six poles and five hundred cords
passages.gloss: Outside Samarkand Timur held his feasts in a vast camp. Clavijo measured the great pavilion by eye: square, three lances high, a hundred paces across, raised on twelve painted poles each as thick as a man's chest, with cart-wheel winches to lift them, porticoes on twenty-four more poles, and silk hangings inside. It shows that the tent tradition of the steppe survived as palace architecture beside Timur's brick buildings.
passages.quote: there was a great and lofty pavilion, which was like a tent, only square, and three lances high. It was a hundred paces broad, and had four corners, and the ceiling was round, like a vault. It was pitched against twelve poles, each as large round as a man, measured round the chest.
passages.speaker: Ruy González de Clavijo (translated by Clements R. Markham, 1859)

passages.headline: A tent city with streets, butchers and bath-houses
passages.gloss: When Timur called his army together for his festivals, some twenty thousand men pitched their tents in their assigned places without confusion. Clavijo describes the result as a moving town: streets of stalls selling cooked sheep, fruit, barley and bread, and even tents for hot baths with boilers. Compare Rubruck's description of Batu's ordu 150 years earlier (W043).
passages.quote: In this horde there are always butchers and cooks who sell cooked sheep, and others who sell fruit and barley, and bakers who sell bread. Every division of the horde is provided with all that the troops require, and they are arranged in streets. There are even baths and bath men in the horde
passages.speaker: Ruy González de Clavijo (translated by Clements R. Markham, 1859)

passages.headline: The best drinker is called Bahadur
passages.gloss: At Timur's feasts, cup-bearers made guests drain full cups in one pull, and refusing was an insult to the lord. The heaviest drinker earned the title bahadur, 'valiant'. Timur even sent the envoys a jug of wine beforehand so they would arrive in a jovial mood. The food was roast horse, sheep and rice.
passages.quote: They call the man who drinks the most wine Bahadur, which is as much as to say "a valorous man" ; and he who does not drink, is made to do so, although he does not wish it.
passages.speaker: Ruy González de Clavijo (translated by Clements R. Markham, 1859)
passages.caution: Markham's footnote on the same page adds a Victorian moral comment of his own.

passages.headline: The first city after the Flood, sacked by the 'Emperor of Tartary'
passages.people: Golden Horde army ('Tetani, Emperor of Tartary')
passages.gloss: In Armenia the envoys reached Calmarin, a strong city in sight of Mount Ararat, which locals said was the first city built after Noah's flood. Its people told them that eight years earlier an 'Emperor of Tartary' had besieged it, broken the terms of surrender, and sacked and burned it. A few days later Clavijo passed Cusacana, 'half destroyed', which he says Toktamish, Emperor of Tartary, had ruined.
passages.quote: This city of Calmarin was the first city that was built in the world, after the flood, and it was built by the lineage of Noah. The people of the city said that, eight years ago, Tetani, Emperor of Tartary, besieged
passages.speaker: Ruy González de Clavijo (translated by Clements R. Markham, 1859)
passages.caution: The Noah origin is local legend; the siege story continues on the next page.

passages.headline: Women in helmets: how Timur beat the Emperor of Tartary
passages.people: Tokhtamysh and the Tartars of the Golden Horde
passages.gloss: Clavijo tells how Tokhtamysh, 'emperor of Tartary', raided Tabriz and was chased home by Timur. Finding the ford guarded, Timur marched upstream for three days, then had the camp women put on helmets to look like soldiers while the men doubled back, crossed at night and routed the Tartar camp. The next page tells how Tokhtamysh's servant Edigu then became the new lord of Tartary with a horde of 200,000 horsemen.
passages.quote: on the third night Timour Beg ordered the women to put helmets on their heads, that they might look like men ; and all the men rode on, with two horses a piece, leaving the royal encampment, the women who looked like men, the servants, and the prisoners.
passages.speaker: Ruy González de Clavijo (translated by Clements R. Markham, 1859)
passages.caution: A campaign story told at Timur's court, not witnessed by Clavijo.

passages.headline: Towers built of the heads of 'white Tartars'
passages.when: 1404 (towers seen); event a few years earlier
passages.gloss: Outside Damghan the envoys saw towers of mud and human heads. They were told these were the heads of 'white Tartars', nomads from between Turkey and Syria whom Timur had deported to Damghan; when they tried to ride home, plundering as they went, his army killed them, and Timur ordered every white Tartar found to be put to death. Locals said lights burned on the towers at night.
passages.quote: These towers, which are made of heads, are built of the heads of a race of people called "white Tartars," natives of a country between Turkey and Syria. … The people of the city say, that they often see lights burning on the top of these towers in the night.
passages.speaker: Ruy González de Clavijo (translated by Clements R. Markham, 1859)
passages.caution: The towers were seen; the story, the figure of 60,000 dead and the lights at night were told to the envoys.

passages.headline: A golden tree with jewel fruit inside a tent
passages.people: Timur's chief wife Cano (Saray Mulk Khanum) and her court
passages.gloss: At a feast given by Timur's chief wife, the envoys were shown a tent containing a golden oak as tall as a man, with a trunk as thick as a leg, fruit of rubies, emeralds, turquoises, sapphires and pearls, and enamelled golden birds pecking at it. It echoes the silver tree Rubruck saw at Karakorum (W043), and Rockhill's note to Rubruck mentions Clavijo's tree.
passages.quote: there was a golden tree, made to resemble an oak ; with the trunk as big as a man's leg, from which many branches spread out in all directions, with leaves like those of an oak ; and it was as high as a man … The fruit of this tree consisted of rubies, emeralds, turquoises, sapphires, and wonderfully large pearls
passages.speaker: Ruy González de Clavijo (translated by Clements R. Markham, 1859)

passages.headline: Amazons beyond Samarkand, subject to Timur
passages.people: A women's nation said to live toward China
passages.gloss: Clavijo repeats what he heard at Samarkand: fifteen days toward China lived a land of women who met men once a year, kept their daughters and sent their sons to the fathers. He adds that they were Greek Christians, once subjects of the emperor of Cathay, now of Timur, and descended from the Amazons of Troy. A classic legend attached to a real direction on the map.
passages.quote: These women are subject to Timour Beg ; they used to be under the emperor of Cathay, and they are Christians of the Greek Church. They are of the lineage of the Amazons who were at Troy, when it was destroyed by the Greeks.
passages.speaker: Ruy González de Clavijo (translated by Clements R. Markham, 1859)
passages.caution: Hearsay of a classical legend; no one in the party went there.

passages.headline: The Horse Lord's people live in felt domes
passages.people: Northern nomads (the 'Horse Lord' peoples, in practice the Turks)
passages.gloss: The preface divides the known world among four 'lords': elephants in the south, treasure in the west, men (China) in the east, and horses in the cold north. The northern horse peoples are fierce, live in felt tents and domed yurts, and move 'like birds' after their herds. It is a learned Buddhist scheme rather than an eyewitness scene, but it is a compact Chinese picture of steppe housing.
passages.quote: 北馬主寒勁宜馬…馬主之俗天資獷暴情忍殺戮毳帳穹廬鳥居逐牧
passages.translation: In the north is the Horse Lord, whose land is bitterly cold and suited to horses... The ways of the Horse Lord's people: fierce by nature, hardened to killing; they live in felt tents and domed yurts, dwelling like birds and following their herds.
passages.speaker: Xuanzang and Bianji, preface to book 1 (Chinese text, Siku quanshu copy)
passages.caution: A cosmological scheme from Buddhist and Chinese learning, not a description of one place.

passages.headline: The Turkish khan's tame deer at the Thousand Springs
passages.gloss: The meadows of the Thousand Springs were where the khan of the Western Turks came every summer to escape the heat. Herds of deer there wore bells and rings and were so tame they barely ran from people, because the khan loved them and decreed death without pardon for anyone who killed one. Xuanzang passed this way on his outward journey.
passages.quote: 突厥可汗每来避暑中有羣鹿多飾鈴鐶馴狎於人不甚驚走可汗愛賞下命羣屬敢加殺害有誅無赦故此羣鹿得終其夀
passages.translation: The khan of the Turks comes here every year to escape the summer heat. There are herds of deer, many decorated with bells and rings, so tame with people that they hardly startle and run. The khan loves them and has ordered his followers that anyone who dares to kill one will be executed without pardon, so these deer live out their natural lives.
passages.speaker: Xuanzang and Bianji, book 1 (Chinese text, Siku quanshu copy)

passages.headline: A walled town of Chinese captives taken by the Turks
passages.people: Chinese captives living under the Western Turks
passages.gloss: A little south of the merchant city of Taraz stood a small walled town of some 300 households whose people were originally Chinese. They had been carried off by the Turks, then gathered their countrymen together and held this town. They had taken up Turkish dress and ways, though the next page adds that they still kept the speech and manners of their homeland. A glimpse of who actually lived in towns under steppe rule.
passages.quote: 南行十餘里有小孤城三百餘户本中國人也昔為突厥所掠後遂鳩集同國共保此城於中宅居衣服去就遂同突厥
passages.translation: Ten li or so to the south is a small isolated town of more than 300 households. They were originally people of China, carried off long ago by the Turks. Later they gathered together their fellow countrymen and jointly hold this town, living inside it. In clothing and bearing they have become like the Turks.
passages.speaker: Xuanzang and Bianji, book 1 (Chinese text, Siku quanshu copy)

passages.headline: A town emptied by Turkish soldiers near Kucha
passages.people: Turks, called in by the king of Kucha
passages.gloss: On Kucha's eastern border lay a town with no wells, whose people drank from a dragon pool. The story went that dragons had fathered a race of strong, swift men there who defied the king, so the king called in the Turks, who killed everyone, young and old. The town was now waste, with no smoke of hearths. A dragon legend wraps what may be a real memory of a Turkish massacre.
passages.quote: 城中無井取汲池水龍變為人與諸婦㑹生子驍勇走及奔馬如是漸染人皆龍種恃力作威不恭王命王乃引搆突厥殺此城人少長俱戮畧無噍類城今荒蕪人煙㫁絶
passages.translation: There were no wells in the city; they drew water from the pool. The dragons turned into men and lay with the women, who bore sons brave and fierce, able to outrun a galloping horse. Gradually all the people became of dragon stock; trusting in their strength they defied the king's orders. So the king called in the Turks to slaughter the people of this city, young and old alike, leaving hardly a soul. The city is now a waste, with no smoke of hearths.
passages.speaker: Xuanzang and Bianji, book 1 (Chinese text, Siku quanshu copy)
passages.caution: Told as a tradition from 'earlier records'; the dragon ancestry is legend, the ruined city was there to see.

passages.headline: A Turkish prince speared in a dream for raiding a monastery
passages.people: Western Turks (son of the Yabghu khan)
passages.gloss: The New Monastery at Balkh was so rich that rulers coveted it. A son of the Turkish Yabghu khan (named on the previous page) led his whole horde to plunder it and camped nearby. That night he dreamed that the guardian god Vaisravana drove a long halberd through his chest; he woke in pain, sent for the monks to beg forgiveness, and died before the messenger returned.
passages.quote: 其部落率其戎旅奄襲伽藍欲圖珍寳去此不逺屯軍野次其夜夢見毗沙門天曰汝有何力敢壊伽藍因以長㦸貫徹胷背可汗驚寤便苦心痛
passages.translation: [He gathered] his tribes and led his troops to fall on the monastery by surprise, meaning to seize its treasures. He camped in the open not far from here. That night he dreamed he saw the god Vaisravana, who said: 'What power have you, that you dare to destroy this monastery?' and drove a long halberd through him from chest to back. The khan woke in terror, with a pain in his heart.
passages.speaker: Xuanzang and Bianji, book 1 (Chinese text, Siku quanshu copy)
passages.caution: A monastery's protective legend, told to discourage raiders.

passages.headline: A Turkish king who will not stay in his own capital
passages.gloss: Kunduz (Huo) had a walled chief town and farmland, but its king was a Turk who ruled all the small kingdoms south of the Iron Gates. He did not live in the town: he kept moving 'like a bird'. Chains of neighbouring states in the old Tukhara lands are each described as having a capital but 'no chief ruler', being dependent on the Turks.
passages.quote: The king is of the Turkish clan; he governs all the little kingdoms to the south of the Iron Gates. He constantly shifts his dwelling, like a bird (his bird-dwelling), not constantly occupying this town.
passages.speaker: Xuanzang and Bianji (translated by Samuel Beal, 1884)

passages.headline: Dressed like the Turks, crowned with a wooden horn
passages.people: People of Himatala, living like the Turks
passages.gloss: In Himatala, near Badakhshan, people behaved and dressed like the Turks, in wool, skin and felt. Married women wore a wooden horn about three feet long on the head, with two branches standing for the husband's father and mother; when one parent-in-law died a branch was removed, and when both were dead the horn was given up.
passages.quote: In respect of their modes of behaviour and forms of etiquette, their clothes of wool, and skin, and felt, they are like the Turks. Their wives wear upon their head-dress a wooden horn about three feet or so in length. It has two branches (a double branch) in front, which signify father and mother of the husband.
passages.speaker: Xuanzang and Bianji (translated by Samuel Beal, 1884)

passages.headline: Dozens of fortified towns, yet the people live in felt tents
passages.people: People of Himatala, neighbours of the Turks
passages.gloss: Because the land bordered the Turks, its people took up Turkish ways and were raided by them. They scattered, held dozens of strong walled towns each under its own chief, and lived in domed felt tents, moving about. Towns and tents side by side, in the same breath. Beal's English of this passage runs across pages 290 to 291.
passages.quote: 其俗又見侵掠自守其境故此國人流離異域數十堅城各别立主穹廬毳帳遷徙往來
passages.translation: [They took on] their [the Turks'] customs, and were also raided by them, and so defended their own borders. Therefore the people of this country are scattered in different districts, in several tens of strong walled towns, each with its own chief. They live in domed felt tents and move about from place to place.
passages.speaker: Xuanzang and Bianji, book 12 (Chinese text, Siku quanshu copy)

passages.headline: Sacred rats that gnawed a Xiongnu army's harness
passages.gloss: West of Khotan stood mounds made by rats 'as big as hedgehogs', with gold and silver fur. Long ago, the story went, a Xiongnu army camped there; the king of Khotan prayed to the rats, and in the morning the raiders found every strap, bowstring and fastening gnawed through. Khotan built the rats a temple, and travellers still got down from their carts to bow as they passed.
passages.quote: The Hiung-nu, hearing their approach, were overcome by fear. They hastened to harness their horses and equip their chariots, but they found that the leather of their armour, and their horses' gear, and their bow strings, and all the fastenings of their clothes, had been gnawed by the rats.
passages.speaker: Xuanzang and Bianji (translated by Samuel Beal, 1884)
passages.caution: Xuanzang introduces it as 'the common story' he heard. Beal notes a parallel in Herodotus (mice gnawing an Assyrian army's bowstrings).

passages.headline: A city buried overnight by a rain of sand and earth
passages.gloss: East of Khotan Xuanzang heard of Ho-lo-lo-kia, a rich city that mistreated a holy man and was buried when 'it rained sand and earth' for a night. One man escaped by a tunnel. The town was now a great sand mound; kings who came to dig for its treasure were driven off by sudden winds and darkness. Beal's note points to other sand-buried towns reported by nineteenth-century travellers in the region.
passages.quote: The town of Ho-lo-lo-kia is now a great sand mound. The kings of the neighbouring countries and persons in power from distant spots have many times wished to excavate the mound and take away the precious things buried there; but as soon as they have arrived at the borders of the place, a furious wind has sprung up
passages.speaker: Xuanzang and Bianji (translated by Samuel Beal, 1884)
passages.caution: A moral legend about punishment for disrespecting a Buddhist saint. It has nothing to do with Tartars; the region is the one 19th-century English writers called 'High Tartary'.

passages.headline: Empty cities of an old kingdom in the desert
passages.place: Southern Tarim Basin, between Niya and Cherchen, Xinjiang
passages.gloss: Crossing the drifting sands east of Niya, travellers piled up bones to mark the way, and people heard singing or wailing that led them astray, which Xuanzang blames on demons. After 400 li he reached the 'old country of Tukhara', long empty, its cities all desolate. He credits the ruins to a vanished kingdom, not to any Turks or Tartars.
passages.quote: 是以往來者聚遺骸以記之乏水草多熱風…時聞歌嘯或聞號哭視聽之間怳然不知所至由此屢有喪亾蓋鬼魅之所致也行四百餘里至覩貨邏故國國久空曠城皆荒蕪
passages.translation: So those who come and go pile up the bones of the dead to mark the way. Water and grass are lacking and hot winds are frequent... At times one hears singing and whistling, or wailing and crying, and between what is seen and heard one is bewildered and does not know where one is going; many die this way, which is the work of demons and goblins. Going 400 li or so one reaches the old country of Tukhara. The country has long been empty and its cities are all in ruins.
passages.speaker: Xuanzang and Bianji, book 12 (Chinese text, Siku quanshu copy)
passages.caution: Beal's English (page 325) is badly garbled in this OCR, so the Chinese is quoted.

passages.headline: 'Hu': the Chinese word the translator turns into Uighurs or Tartars
passages.people: Hu (western and northern foreigners), glossed by Beal as Uighurs
passages.gloss: The royal family of Tashkurgan in the Pamirs looked Chinese but dressed like the 'Hu'. Hu was a broad Chinese word for foreigners of the west and north. Beal adds '(Uighurs)' here, and in his index he lists 'Tartar (Hu) pilgrims', so the English 'Tartar' in this book is often the translator's choice for a Chinese catch-all word, not Xuanzang's.
passages.quote: The members of the royal family in appearance resemble the people of the Middle Country (China). They wear on their heads a square cap, and their clothes are like those of the Hu people (Uighurs).
passages.speaker: Xuanzang and Bianji (translated by Samuel Beal, 1884; '(Uighurs)' is Beal's gloss)
passages.caution: The bracketed identification is the translator's, not the pilgrim's.

passages.headline: Reed huts shaped like chicken coops, outside Astrakhan's walls
passages.people: Nogai and Crimean Tatars under Russian rule
passages.gloss: At Astrakhan the Tatars were not allowed to live inside the Russian-held city or to build walled towns. They lived in round huts of reeds or canes about twelve feet across, with a smoke hole and a cloth flap turned to the wind. In summer they loaded the huts onto carts and followed the pasture, which is why, Olearius says, the Russians called them wanderers.
passages.quote: The Inhabitants of the Country, who are the Tartars of Crim and Nagaia, are not permitted to live within the City … because they are not suffer'd to build Cities, nor to fortify their Towns nor Villages with walls. Their Huts are made either with Bull-rushes or Canes, being about twelve foot diameter, round, and towards the top, like the Coops wherein Chickens are kept in Europe.
passages.speaker: Adam Olearius (English translation by John Davies, 1669)

passages.headline: Kazan: a wooden town with a stone castle Tatars may not enter
passages.gloss: Olearius stopped at Kazan on the way down the Volga. The town was large but built of wood, houses, towers and ramparts alike; only the castle was stone. Russians and Tatars lived in the town, but the castle was all Russian and Tatars were forbidden to enter it on pain of death. He goes on to tell how Ivan IV took the city by mining its walls in 1552.
passages.quote: It is of a considerable bigness, but all its Houses, as also the Towers and Rampiers, are of wood. Only the Castle and its Fortifications are of stone … the Inhabitants, who are Muscovites and Tartars: But in the Castle they are all Muscovites, and the Tartars are prohibited entring into it upon pain of death.
passages.speaker: Adam Olearius (English translation by John Davies, 1669)

passages.headline: Ruined cities on the Volga, blamed on Tamerlane
passages.place: Middle Volga below the Kama mouth, near Tetyushi
passages.people: Former Tartar (Volga Bulgar and Golden Horde) towns
passages.gloss: Sailing below the Kama, the embassy passed rich, empty grassland where only the ruins of cities and villages could be seen. Olearius was told they had been destroyed by Tamerlane; nearby hills were named after vanished cities, and on the previous page he notes the site of a former 'City of Tartary' with a saint's tomb still visited by locals. A treasure stone with a joke inscription on its underside is told on the same page.
passages.quote: On the right hand, we had the view of a spacious and very delightful Champain Country, the ground very rich, with a high grass on it; but it was not inhabited, and there could be seen only the ruins of Cities and Villages, which had been heretofore destroy'd by Tamberlane.
passages.speaker: Adam Olearius (English translation by John Davies, 1669)
passages.caution: He saw the ruins from the ship; who destroyed them is local tradition.

passages.headline: A Tartar emperor buried under his soldiers' helmets of sand
passages.gloss: Near Samara the Russians showed Olearius a sand hill called Sariol Kurgan. They said a Tartar emperor named Momaon, who meant to invade Muscovy with seven kings, died there, and his soldiers heaped sand over him with their helmets and shields until the grave became a hill. A tale about a burial mound, told to him by Russians.
passages.quote: The Muscovites call it Sariol Kurgan, and affirm, that a certain Tartarian Emperour, named Momaon, who had a design to enter Muscovy, together with seven Kings of the same Nation, dy'd in that place, and that his Soldiers, instead of burying him, fill'd their Head-pieces and Bucklers with Sand, and so cover'd the body that it became a Mountain.
passages.speaker: Adam Olearius (English translation by John Davies, 1669)
passages.caution: Russian folk explanation of a natural or man-made hill; 'Momaon' may be a memory of Mamai, the Horde commander of the 1370s, but the source does not say so.

passages.headline: 'The dead are really dead': a Volga 'Tartar' on the afterlife
passages.people: Cheremis (Mari), whom Olearius counts among the Tartars
passages.gloss: Olearius lodged at Kazan in the same house as a Cheremis man of about 45, and when talk turned to the resurrection the man laughed. The Cheremis, he writes, lived in poor huts, kept no churches, priests or books, sacrificed horses and hung the skins on poles, and feared spirits rather than a hell. They were Mari, a Finnic-speaking people, but to Olearius they were one more kind of Tartar.
passages.quote: and said to me, Those who are dead are really dead, and will never return again, no more than my Horses and Cows, which are long since rotten. I asked him whether he knew who Created this World, and made Heaven and Earth? his answer was, … The Devil may haply know.
passages.speaker: Adam Olearius (English translation by John Davies, 1669)

passages.headline: Dried fish for bread, and mare's milk from a leather bag
passages.gloss: The Nogais near Astrakhan lived on their herds, hunting and fishing. Sun-dried fish served them as bread, they ate camel and horse meat, and they prized mare's milk, which they offered the ambassadors from a leather bag. On the same page he describes their fat-tailed sheep, two-humped camels and small tough horses, and the white linen coifs hung with Russian coins worn by the women.
passages.quote: Their ordinary food is fish dry'd in the Sun, which serves them instead of bread. … They eat Camels and Horse-flesh, and drink water and milk. Mares milk they much esteem; with this they treated our Ambassadors, when we gave them a Visit, taking it out of a … Leather-bag, to present it to us.
passages.speaker: Adam Olearius (English translation by John Davies, 1669)

passages.headline: Tartars as runaway 'Indian lords' who came in 1212
passages.gloss: Before describing Astrakhan, Olearius turns to the Polish scholar Matthias of Miechow. Miechow said the Tartars must not be confused with the ancient Scythians and Sarmatians, since they were only known from the thirteenth century; a comet of 1211 foretold their coming, and they were 'Indian lords' who had killed their king David and fled west. Olearius then says he will stick to what he saw himself.
passages.quote: a Physician, and Canon of Cracow, who liv'd at the beginning of the last age, says that those, who confound the Tartars with those Nations, which the Antients called Getae, Scythae and Sarmatae, are much mistaken, in as much as the Tartars have not been known, but since the thirteenth Age. … They were certain Indian Lords, who having kill'd their King, David, got away
passages.speaker: Adam Olearius (English translation by John Davies, 1669)
passages.caution: Book learning passed on second-hand; the 'King David' story echoes medieval Prester John legends.

passages.headline: 'Tata', because the Chinese cannot say R
passages.people: Mongols (1206) and Manchus (1600s), both called Tartars
passages.when: compiled 1650s to 1660s, about events of 1206 to 1640s
passages.gloss: The appended East Indies volume includes a history of the Tartar conquests of China. It explains that the Chinese called the Tartars 'Tata' because they could not pronounce R, and then tells how the Mongols ruled China until 1368 and how a new Tartar kingdom, the Manchus of 'Niuche', overran it in the 1640s. The same word covers both conquests.
passages.quote: For in the year 1206, the Tartars, whom the Chineses call'd Tata, because they do not pronounce the Letter R, entred China with a powerful Army, and after a War of seventy two years became Masters of it
passages.speaker: Appended section of Mandelslo's travels in this edition (compiled history, source not named)
passages.caution: Not Olearius or Mandelslo as eyewitnesses: a compiled history added to Mandelslo's travels in this edition. Mandelslo never went to China.

passages.headline: Tarku, an unwalled capital of a thousand houses
passages.gloss: On the way home the embassy spent five weeks at Tarku (Tarki), capital of Dagestan, whose people Olearius calls Tartars. The town had no walls and about a thousand houses built in the Persian manner, set among rocks full of fossil shells. He found the local lords frightening: over dinner, he says, they talked only of robbing and selling people.
passages.quote: The City is not wall'd. It may contain a thousand houses, built according to the Persian way, but not so well. These Tartars, as also those of … and the others who live more Northerly, are called Kaitacks
passages.speaker: Adam Olearius (English translation by John Davies, 1669)

passages.headline: Circassian houses of earth and boughs, and no walled towns
passages.place: Terki, on the Terek river, North Caucasus
passages.people: 'Circassian Tartars' (Kabardians of the Terek) under Russian rule
passages.gloss: At Terki the Tsar kept garrisons in all the towns, leaving the Circassians only open towns and villages under their own lords. Their houses were poor ones of earth and branches, plastered inside with clay. Olearius adds that they spoke the common Tartar language and were Muslims in name, though without Koran or priests.
passages.quote: he hath put Garrisons into all the Cities, leaving the Circassian Tartars, for their habitations, but only open Towns and Villages … Their houses are but poor ones, built, for the most part, of earth and boughs of trees, and within, plaister'd over with Clay.
passages.speaker: Adam Olearius (English translation by John Davies, 1669)

passages.headline: A princess with an ox-bladder at her neck
passages.place: Terki, on the Terek river, North Caucasus
passages.gloss: The ambassadors visited Princess Bike, mother of the Tartar prince Mussal, in a hall with earthen walls lined with vaulted niches full of silk bedding and Persian carpets, weapons hung on the pillars. She and another lady wore a blown-up ox-bladder wrapped in an embroidered scarf behind the neck: the badge of widowhood. Her servants still bore the scratches of mourning on their faces.
passages.quote: She wore, at her neck behind, an Ox-bladder, blown to the utmost, which was wound about towards her hair, with a rich Scarf embroider'd with Gold and Silk … Behind the Chair stood a Lady, who had also a Bladder at her neck, and we were told afterwards that it was the Badge of Widdowhood.
passages.speaker: Adam Olearius (English translation by John Davies, 1669)

passages.headline: The khan's statue in Moscow
passages.gloss: Olearius retells the great Crimean raid of 1521: the khan besieged Moscow and forced the Grand Duke to sign himself a tributary. To prove it, the story goes, the khan set up a statue of himself in Moscow before which the Grand Duke had to bow to the ground each time he paid tribute; when the charter was later recovered, the Muscovites smashed the statue.
passages.quote: Mendligeri, to make it appear he was Sovereign Lord of Moscou, caused a Statue of his to be erected in the heart of the City, and would needs oblige the Great Duke, to express his subjection, to smite the ground with his head, before that Statue, as often as he paid Tribute
passages.speaker: Adam Olearius (English translation by John Davies, 1669)
passages.caution: History retold from older books a century after the event; the khan's name is garbled and the statue detail is not confirmed.

passages.headline: A Tatar boy prince in an old stone castle at Kasimov
passages.gloss: At Kasimov on the Oka the embassy met its first Muslims. A twelve-year-old Tatar prince lived with his mother and grandfather in an old stone castle that had once been a fort, under the Tsar's protection. He politely refused baptism until he was old enough to choose, and sent the travellers sheep, mead, beer and butter his mother had churned herself.
passages.quote: This City lies on the right side of the River Occa, in the Principality of Cassinon in Tartary, and there it was we first met with any Mahometans. Not far from the City, in an old stone Castle, which had sometime been a Fort, lived a young Prince of that County
passages.speaker: Adam Olearius (English translation by John Davies, 1669)

passages.headline: 'Tartary full of towns' and the meaning of 'horde'
passages.gloss: Arriving at Caffa, Chardin explains the map names. Geographers call Crimea 'Crim Tartary', which he takes to mean 'Tartary full of towns', because Crimean Tatars mostly live in towns, at least in winter, unlike the Nogais outside the peninsula, who live in hordes. Horde, he adds, is a Turkish and Persian word for an army camp or a court's train. Together they make 'Lesser Tartary', as against the Asian Tartars beyond the Sea of Azov.
passages.quote: The Modern Geographers call it Crim Tartary and Precopensian Tartary. As much as to say Tartary full of Towns; to distinguish the Tartars of this Peninsula that live for the most part in Cities, especially all the Winter long, from those other European Tartars, which inhabit without the Peninsula, call'd Nogays … Hordes or Hordou, a word which signifies an Assembly
passages.speaker: Jean Chardin (English translation, London, 1691)
passages.caution: This etymology is Chardin's own and is not the usual explanation of the name.

passages.headline: Caffa: 4,000 houses, all of earth
passages.people: Turks and Crimean Tatars (with Greek and Armenian Christians)
passages.gloss: Chardin spent forty days at Caffa, the Ottoman port in Crimea. He counted about 4,000 houses, 3,200 of them Muslim (Turks and Tartars) and 800 Christian. Houses, markets, mosques and baths were all built of earth; the only stone buildings were eight decaying churches left by the Genoese. The strong walls and castles he describes were the Ottoman garrison's.
passages.quote: They reck'n about 4000 Houses to be in Caffa; of which 3200 are inhabited by Mahumetans, Turks and Tartars, and 800 by Christians, Greeks and Armenians
passages.speaker: Jean Chardin (English translation, London, 1691)

passages.headline: Earth-built mosques and baths, stone only from the Genoese
passages.gloss: In the same description Chardin is precise about materials: every house, bazaar, public building, mosque and bath in Caffa was built of earth. The only stone buildings were eight old churches the Genoese had built, now decaying. He credits the town's founding to the Greeks (as Theodosia) and its later growth to the Genoese.
passages.quote: The Houses are but small, and all built of Earth, as are also their Bazars or Market-places, their Publick Structures, Mosquees, and Baths. There is not one Building of Stone in all the City, except eight Churches somewhat gone to decay, formerly built by the Genoeses.
passages.speaker: Jean Chardin (English translation, London, 1691)

passages.headline: A Tatar village of ten houses and many felt tents
passages.place: Salt pits near Caffa, eastern Crimea
passages.gloss: While his ship loaded salt, Chardin walked to a nearby Tatar settlement to buy food. He saw only ten or twelve houses and a little mosque, but round them many tents, round and square, and closed covered wagons that served as houses. The best tents were made of poles laid crosswise and covered with light felts, with an opening at the top for light and smoke, a felt door, and carpets on walls and floor.
passages.quote: About a Mile from the Shoar there is a Habitation of the Tartars, whither I went with some of my Servants to buy Provisions, but I did not see in all that place above Ten or Twelve Houses with a little Mosquee. Only round about it there was a great Number of Tents, Round and Square
passages.speaker: Jean Chardin (English translation, London, 1691)

passages.headline: Hidden grain pits and a camp struck in half an hour
passages.place: Salt pits near Caffa, eastern Crimea
passages.gloss: The same Tatars stored grain and fodder in deep pits in the ground, covered so skilfully that only the diggers could find them again, dug either inside the tents or out in the fields. When they moved on, tents came down and were loaded in less than half an hour, carried by oxen and horses. He adds they were Muslims 'intermix'd with strange superstitions' about fortune-telling.
passages.quote: The Tartars store up their Corn and their Forrage, as do all the Country-People in the East, in deep Pits under Ground which they call Amber, or Magazines. Which they cover so exactly, that you cannot discern where they have remov'd the Earth
passages.speaker: Jean Chardin (English translation, London, 1691)

passages.headline: Why no empire can conquer people who move every month
passages.gloss: Explaining why the Ottomans do not try to rule the Caucasus and the steppe directly, Chardin argues that settled people in towns can be conquered and held, but people who move all their lives cannot. It is his own reflection, but it neatly explains why steppe peoples were so hard for empires to pin down.
passages.quote: For if the People that inhabit those parts, were united into Cities and strong Places, there might be a way found to reduce 'em, and keep 'em in Subjection. But which way is it possible to subdue a People that change their Habitations every Month, and all their Life-time wander up and down the Country?
passages.speaker: Jean Chardin (English translation, London, 1691)
passages.caution: Chardin's own opinion, not a report of what he saw.

passages.headline: Amazons near the Kalmyks, and an Amazon's dress in the palace
passages.people: Kalmyks (as the Georgians called them) and a legendary people beyond
passages.gloss: In Georgia Chardin asked about the Amazons of classical legend. He met no one who had been to their country, but many told stories, and in the prince's palace he was shown a large woman's garment of coarse wool said to have belonged to an Amazon killed near Kakheti. The Georgian prince's son told him a numerous unknown people lived five days north, always at war with 'the Tartars, which they call Calmac'.
passages.quote: I confess, I never saw any Person in Georgia who had been in the Country of the Amazons; but I have heard many of 'em tell Stories of those People. And they shew'd me in the Prince's Palace, a large Female habit of a course Woollen Stuff
passages.speaker: Jean Chardin (English translation, London, 1691)
passages.caution: Chardin reports the stories but, on the next page, rejects the classical details as Greek fables.

passages.headline: Sultaniyeh, a royal city founded by Hulagu's descendants
passages.gloss: Passing Sultaniyeh, Chardin saw fine public buildings, about 3,000 houses and vast ruins of churches, mosques and towers stretching west. Some said no one knew its founder; others said Arghun Khan, grandson of Hulagu, laid its foundations and his son finished it and named it 'the Royal City'. He adds on the same page that it was later wrecked by Tamerlane and by other Turkish and Tartar princes.
passages.quote: Others on the other side affirm, that the foundations of it were laid when the Sun was in Leo, by the order, and in the Reign of Ergon Can, the Son of Abkei-Can, and Grand-child of Halacou-Can; and that because it could not be finish'd in his days, his Son Jangou-Sultan compleated the work and call'd it Sultania, or the Royal City.
passages.speaker: Jean Chardin (English translation, London, 1691)
passages.caution: Chardin gives competing traditions about the founder; he saw the ruins himself.

passages.headline: An Armenian monastery levelled by the Tartars and rebuilt in brick
passages.gloss: At Etchmiadzin, seat of the Armenian patriarch, Chardin was told the first monastery was built by the patriarch Nerses and ruined by the Tartars, and that it had been levelled five times in all. What he saw was built of brick. Here Tartars appear as destroyers, not builders.
passages.quote: The first Monastery of this Church was built by Nierses the Twenty Ninth Patriarch of Armenia: This the Tartars ruin'd; and if we may believe the Chronology of the Place, it had been Five times levell'd with the Ground: It is at present built of Brick
passages.speaker: Jean Chardin (English translation, London, 1691)

passages.headline: Rey, 'the Market of the Universe', brought to nothing
passages.gloss: Near Saveh Chardin passed the scattered traces of Rey, once, the Persian histories said, the greatest city in Asia, with incredible numbers of streets, baths and mosques. He blames its fall on sectarian wars together with Tartar incursions, and notes that a later prince tried to rebuild it after making peace with 'Cazan-Can, King of Persia, of the Race of the Tartars' (the Ilkhan Ghazan), but failed.
passages.quote: These Wars, together with the Incursions of the Tartars, destroy'd the Potent Rey, and reduc'd it to nothing before the end of the sixth Age of the Mahumetan Epoche.
passages.speaker: Jean Chardin (English translation, London, 1691)
passages.caution: Taken from Persian and Arabic histories; the huge figures for Rey on the previous page Chardin himself doubts.

passages.headline: 'Yusbek': a hundred lords, or 'he is the lord'?
passages.people: Uzbeks, whom Chardin calls the Tartars of Lesser Tartary
passages.gloss: Chardin gives two etymologies for the Uzbeks. Persians derived it from 'yuz' (a hundred) and 'bek' (lord), mocking a land split among a hundred petty princes; the Uzbeks rejected that and said it meant 'he is the lord'. He adds that Tartar and Turkish are one language, Turkish being a dialect of it.
passages.quote: They are called Yusbecks, at least if the Persian Etymology be true, by reason of the great number of Sovereign Princes by which the Tartars are Govern'd; for Yus, as well in the Language of the Tartars as Turks, which is but a Dialect of it, signifies a hundred, and Bek, Lords
passages.speaker: Jean Chardin, 'The Coronation of Solyman III' (appended to the 1691 English edition)

passages.headline: 'Turk' means a man from the highlands of Tartary
passages.people: Turkmens and Turks, as seen from Persia
passages.gloss: Chardin insists that the true 'Turkey' is the vast highland of Tartary, homeland of both the Turkmen herders and the Ottomans' ancestors. In the East, he says, 'Turk' simply means someone from those highlands, and Ottoman subjects find the name barbarous. He also scolds European travellers who write about countries without knowing the language.
passages.quote: For that among them Turk signifies one that comes from those High-lands of Tartary, let it be from what part it will.
passages.speaker: Jean Chardin, 'The Coronation of Solyman III' (appended to the 1691 English edition)

passages.headline: A captive Tartar prince who galloped home from Isfahan
passages.gloss: Chardin tells the court story of 'Abouel-Kazi', a prince of Khwarazm captured in a Persian victory over the Uzbeks. Shah Safi treated him as royalty in Isfahan for ten years, until he feigned illness, went to a spa, and rode off with twenty Uzbek horsemen sent to fetch him. He became khan and stayed a friend of Persia. This is Abu'l-Ghazi Bahadur, khan of Khiva, later author of a famous history of the Turks.
passages.quote: To whom the Yusbeck Prince thus briskly answer'd; I am highly oblig'd to the King of Persia, but I owe more my own Country and Relations that call me back. 'Tis my Father that sends me these Men, to facilitate my return to my Native soil
passages.speaker: Jean Chardin, 'The Coronation of Solyman III' (appended to the 1691 English edition)
passages.caution: Court gossip retold decades later; details such as the role of the prince's father may not match other accounts.

passages.headline: 'All the land was Tartary, and all the peoples Tartars'
passages.people: Everyone in northern Asia, as European maps saw them
passages.gloss: In his preface Gmelin explains why Peter the Great sent the expedition. Before it, he says, European geographers knew nothing of the far north: every land there was simply 'Tartary' and every people 'Tartars'. On the next page he adds that in Russia itself people talk far less about 'Tartary' than elsewhere, the way real experts talk less about hidden qualities than those still in the dark.
passages.quote: In den Nordlichsten Ländern war bey den Erdbeschreibern nichts als Dunkelheit. Alles Land war Tatarey, und alle Völker selbiger Gegenden Tataren.
passages.translation: In the northernmost lands the geographers had nothing but darkness. All the land was Tartary, and all the peoples of those regions Tartars.
passages.speaker: Johann Georg Gmelin, preface (German original, Göttingen, 1751)

passages.headline: Kazan's kremlin: Tatars not only may enter, they must
passages.gloss: Gmelin describes Kazan's stone fortress with its cathedral, a monastery founded by Ivan IV, and a stone arsenal. Anyone could go in, Tatars included; indeed they often had to, because the government chancery was inside. Nobody he asked had heard that Tatars were ever barred, as Olearius had written a century before. The next page adds that Tatars had their own shops in the stone merchants' hall, selling Persian silks.
passages.quote: Es ist jedermann erlaubet, in die Festung zu gehen, auch den Tataren. Ja sie müssen zuweilen wider ihren Willen hinein, weil die Regierungskanzeley darin ist, vor welcher sie sich öfters zu stellen haben. Es wuste auch niemand, den wir darüber befragten, daß der Eingang in die Festung den Tataren jemahls verboten gewesen wäre, wie Olearius zu seiner Zeit vorgiebt.
passages.translation: Everyone is allowed to go into the fortress, the Tatars too. Indeed they sometimes have to go in against their will, because the government chancery is inside, before which they often have to appear. Nor did anyone we asked know that entry into the fortress had ever been forbidden to the Tatars, as Olearius claims for his time.
passages.speaker: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)
passages.caution: A direct check on Olearius (W048, n154): the rule may have lapsed in the hundred years between them, or Olearius may have been misinformed.

passages.headline: Clean Tatar rooms with two fireplaces and calf-skin windows
passages.place: Tatar villages east of Kazan (Kursa to Seredni Shun)
passages.gloss: Riding east from Kazan through a string of Tatar villages, Gmelin lodged in Tatar houses. They had no 'black rooms' (smoky rooms without a chimney): every room had two fireplaces side by side, one for heat and one for cooking, and broad low benches laid with a carpet and a cushion for guests. The sentence that follows says that instead of window glass they stretched the outer skin of a calf's stomach over the frames.
passages.quote: Die Tatarn haben keine Schwarz-Stuben, sondern in einer jeden Stube sind 2. Camine neben einander, in deren einem eingeheizt, und in dem andern Essen gekocht wird. Ihre Stuben sehen sehr reinlich aus. Es sind sehr breite niedrige Bänke darin
passages.translation: The Tatars have no 'black rooms' [rooms without a chimney]; instead, in every room there are two fireplaces side by side, one used for heating and the other for cooking. Their rooms look very clean. There are very broad, low benches in them
passages.speaker: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)

passages.headline: A goose and a loaf on the table: 'the fearsome name of the Tatars'
passages.place: Tatar villages east of Kazan (Kursa to Ulga)
passages.gloss: Gmelin admits the travellers had feared the very name of the Tatars. After a few days among them it sounded quite different: everywhere a gift was waiting, usually a plucked goose and a baked loaf, and at Ulga also honey and hazelnuts. He is honest that the courtesy had limits: one host hid rather than hand over his horses, and the soldiers found him and took them anyway.
passages.quote: Wir haben sie überhaupt als leutseelige Leute befunden, und der uns ehemahls fürchterliche Name der Tataren kam uns nun ganz anders vor. An allen Orten, wo wir hinkamen, fanden wir auf dem Tische schon ein Geschenke vor uns, welches gemeiniglich in einer abgefederten Gans und einem gebackenen Brodte bestund
passages.translation: On the whole we found them friendly people, and the name of the Tatars, once so frightful to us, now sounded quite different. Everywhere we came we found a gift already waiting for us on the table, usually a plucked goose and a baked loaf
passages.speaker: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)

passages.headline: Horse races before a Tatar wedding
passages.gloss: Gmelin and Müller drove out to a Tatar wedding at Sabanaka near Tobolsk. Before any wedding, he was told, riders race their horses to the bride's house for prizes put up by both families; this time they included red damask, a fox pelt, cotton cloths brought from the Kalmyk lands and a red horsehide. A few pages on, the akhun (Muslim cleric) told the groom his chief duty: not to take another wife without the consent of the one he was marrying.
passages.quote: Es ist dieses eine alte hergebrachte Gewohnheit bey allen Tatarischen Hochzeiten, daß viele Pferde, ehe die Hochzeit angehet, vorher dieses Schauspiel machen müssen. Und damit es allezeit Reuter und auch Leute, die die Pferde dazu lehnen, geben möge, so sind sowohl von Seiten des Bräutigams, als der Braut verschiedene Preise ausgesetzt
passages.translation: It is an old custom at all Tatar weddings that many horses must first put on this show before the wedding begins. And so that there may always be riders, and people to lend horses for it, various prizes are put up both by the bridegroom's side and by the bride's
passages.speaker: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)

passages.headline: A wedding song called 'Yermak'
passages.gloss: At the same wedding two Tatar musicians, one with a reed pipe with finger holes (its end taken wholly into the mouth) and one with an ordinary violin, played for the guests. They singled out one tune they found moving. It was called 'Yermak', after the Cossack leader who conquered Siberia in the 1580s, and they said it dated from the time he brought their forefathers under Russian rule.
passages.quote: Sie nennten das Lied Jermak und sagten, daß es zu der Zeit gemacht wäre, da Jermak Sibirien eingenommen, und ihre Voreltern durch seine Dienste unter die Russische Bothmäßigkeit gebracht hätte.
passages.translation: They called the song 'Yermak' and said it had been composed at the time when Yermak took Siberia and, through his services, brought their forefathers under Russian rule.
passages.speaker: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)

passages.headline: Old Sibir: a rampart and a name
passages.people: Former rulers of Siberia (the Siberian Tatar khanate)
passages.gloss: Gmelin and Müller rode 18 versts up the Irtysh from Tobolsk to where, by common report, the old town of Sibir had stood, seat of Siberia's former rulers. Apart from traces of a rampart they saw nothing at all. Gmelin suggests that both the little Sibirka stream and the whole province of Siberia took their names from this vanished town.
passages.quote: wo der gemeinen Sage nach die alte Stadt Sibir gestanden hat, welche der Sitz der ehemahligen Sibirischen Beherrscher gewesen seyn soll. … Außer einigen Spuren von einem Walle, der daselbst aufgeworfen war, konnten wir nichts sehen.
passages.translation: where, according to common report, the old town of Sibir stood, which is said to have been the seat of the former rulers of Siberia... Apart from some traces of a rampart that had been thrown up there, we could see nothing.
passages.speaker: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)

passages.headline: Two villages for every village: summer and winter
passages.gloss: Sailing up the Irtysh, Gmelin passed Uttus aul, which was really three villages: two for summer and one for winter. This, he says, was the general custom of the local Tatars, who moved into the winter village when the cold set in. He adds that 'aul' is the Tatar word for village, and that Russians call every Tatar village 'yurty', a Tatar word that simply means 'house'.
passages.quote: Dieses ist unter den hiesigen Tataren eine allgemeine Gewohnheit, daß sie ein anderes Dorf für den Sommer, ein anderes für den Winter haben. Sobald die Kälte einfällt, ziehen sie in ihr Winterdorf, und sobald die Wärme kommt, in das Sommerdorf.
passages.translation: It is a general custom among the Tatars here that they have one village for the summer and another for the winter. As soon as the cold sets in they move into their winter village, and as soon as the warm weather comes, into the summer village.
passages.speaker: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)

passages.headline: Clay ruins in the steppe, credited to Bukharan farmers
passages.place: Irtysh steppe south of Semey (Semipalatinsk), Kazakhstan
passages.gloss: South of Semipalatinsk the party saw the foundations of a house of six rooms, which Gmelin calls the former dwelling of a Kalmyk 'idol-worshipper'. Others had stood there, but weather had destroyed them because all were built only of clay. Irrigation channels in the fields he credits to Bukharans, since, he explains, the Kalmyks do no farming at all and even their ruler has no fixed seat but is always on the move.
passages.quote: allein das Wetter hatte sie ganz zernichtet, weil alle Gebäude bloß von Leim aufgeführet gewesen waren. Auf dem Felde dabey sahe man einige Rinnen in dem Erdreiche, in welche die Einwohner dieser Gegend, welche Bucharen gewesen seyn sollen, Wasser geleitet haben
passages.translation: but the weather had destroyed them entirely, because all the buildings had been made only of clay. In the field nearby one could see some channels in the ground, into which the inhabitants of this area, who are said to have been Bukharans, had led water
passages.speaker: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)
passages.caution: Who built the houses is Gmelin's inference from hearsay and from what he knew of Kalmyk life.

passages.headline: Grave-robbers melt the gold of the old steppe graves
passages.place: Upper Irtysh between Yamyshevo and Ust-Kamenogorsk, Kazakhstan
passages.people: Ancient graves, thought to be Kalmyk or Bukharan
passages.gloss: All along the Irtysh Gmelin saw very many graves, which he took for remains of former Kalmyk or Bukharan settlement, and nearly every one had been dug open. Local people treated them as a mine for 'grave silver': horse ornaments, big seals, bracelets, sometimes idols. The unopened ones near Ust-Kamenogorsk were ringed with upright field stones or slates and filled with stones and earth.
passages.quote: Allein diejenigen, die hier zu Lande die Gräber eröffnen, haben die Gewohnheit, daß sie zu ungemeinem Verlust der Historie das Gold und Silber gemeiniglich schmelzen, das Kupfer und Eisen aber wegwerfen.
passages.translation: But those who open the graves in this country have the habit, to the uncommon loss of history, of generally melting down the gold and silver and throwing away the copper and iron.
passages.speaker: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)
passages.caution: The attribution of the graves to Kalmyks or Bukharans is a guess; many such steppe graves are far older.

passages.headline: Ablai-kit: a brick temple full of books in the steppe
passages.gloss: Gmelin did not go himself: he sent a corporal, soldiers and a scribe, with orders to measure the place and 'carry off everything'. They reported a rectangle walled with broken rock, buildings on a raised base, a hall with two bellied furnaces, a great clay idol with sixteen smaller ones, and heaps of Tibetan ('Tangut') and Kalmyk manuscripts and woodblocks; nearly twenty cartloads still lay there. Gmelin names it the idol temple of the Kalmyk prince Ablai of the Khoshut, driven out about 1671.
passages.quote: In eben diesem Gebäude war ein großer Schrank mit vielen Fächern, worin bey der ersten Entdeckung viele Schriften gelegen haben, die nun in dem ganzen Gebäude zerstreuet sind. … Alle diese Gebäude sind von gebackenen Ziegelsteinen aufgeführet
passages.translation: In this same building was a large cupboard with many compartments, in which many writings lay when the place was first discovered, and which are now scattered through the whole building... All these buildings are built of baked bricks
passages.speaker: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)
passages.caution: Second-hand: the description is the soldiers' and scribe's report. It also records the expedition removing manuscripts from the site.

passages.headline: A man with four heads and twenty-four arms
passages.gloss: On the walls behind the idols at Ablai-kit were paintings that baffled Gmelin. He says he has not the patience to describe them and refers the curious to alchemical pictures, as equally absurd. His examples: figures with several heads and many arms, one trampling a man's head, and a many-headed man embracing a woman.
passages.quote: Man siehet z. E. einen Mann mit 4 Köpfen und 24 Armen, einen andern mit 2 Köpfen und 8 Armen. Der erstere tritt mit einem seiner rechten Füße einem Menschen auf den Kopf und hat noch zween andere Menschen zu seinen Füßen liegen.
passages.translation: One sees, for example, a man with 4 heads and 24 arms, another with 2 heads and 8 arms. The first treads with one of his right feet on a man's head and has two more men lying at his feet.
passages.speaker: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)
passages.caution: Gmelin does not identify the figures; they match the many-armed deities of Tibetan Buddhist art. He knew them only from his men's report and the pieces they brought back.

passages.headline: Round reed huts for summer, other houses for winter
passages.gloss: Three versts from Kuznetsk Gmelin visited a village of Teleut Tatars with two kinds of houses, one for summer and one for winter. The summer huts were round and pointed, about three fathoms across, with a small door on the east side, a smoke hole at the top, benches all round and a cooking hollow in the middle. They were built of reeds woven onto thin poles, with birch bark tucked in against the rain.
passages.quote: Das Dorf bestehet aus zweyerley Art Häusern, in der einen wohnen sie des Sommers, in der andern des Winters. … Die Sommerhütten sind von Figur rund, und oben zugespitzt … Der Bauzeug dieser Häuser ist Schilf, welches an die inwendig zusammen verbundenen dünnen Stöcke angeflochten
passages.translation: The village consists of two kinds of houses: in the one they live in summer, in the other in winter... The summer huts are round in shape and pointed at the top... The building material of these houses is reed, woven onto thin poles bound together on the inside
passages.speaker: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)

passages.headline: A stuffed horse on four birch poles, facing east
passages.gloss: The Teleuts, Gmelin notes, were not Muslims; each morning they turned to the rising sun and prayed 'do not strike me dead'. By the village stood their 'taülga', four birch posts in a square. Once or more a year they killed a horse, ate it in a circle, stuffed the skin and set it on the posts facing east. They now built these close to the village, he says, because they had noticed the Russians knew better uses for the hides.
passages.quote: Sie schlachten ein Pferd, ziehen demselben die Haut ab und verzehren das Fleisch nahe bey dem Taülga … Die Haut stopfen sie aus, und setzen das Pferd … oben auf den Taülga … Sie haben gemerckt, daß die Russen ihre Häute besser zu gebrauchen wissen, deswegen bauen sie ihre Taülga jetzo allzeit nahe bey dem Dorfe.
passages.translation: They slaughter a horse, strip off its skin and eat the flesh near the taülga... They stuff the skin and set the horse... on top of the taülga... They have noticed that the Russians know how to make better use of their skins, so they now always build their taülga close to the village.
passages.speaker: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)

passages.headline: An ironworks inside a family yurt
passages.place: Gadöwa, on the Kondoma river, Kemerovo region
passages.people: Tatars of the Kondoma valley (the people now called Shors)
passages.gloss: Gmelin rode to see a Tatar ironworks and at first could not find it: no building looked any different. The furnace was simply the cooking hollow found in every yurt, topped with a clay cone about a foot high and blown by two bellows, and the family went on living around it. Two men did all the work; from three pounds of ore they got about two pounds of iron, impure-looking but, he thought, very good.
passages.quote: Wir konnten auch gleich sehen, daß man wegen des Schmelzofens nicht nöthig habe, eine besondere Jurte zu bauen, sondern daß eine jede Jurte darzu tüchtig sey. Ja es hinderte auch die Leute nicht in eben dieser Jurte zu wohnen, welches alles schon ein großer Vortheil vor den Europäischen Eisenhütten ist, die man mit großen Kosten aufführen muß.
passages.translation: We could see at once that no special yurt needs to be built for the furnace, but that any yurt will serve. Indeed it did not even stop people living in that same yurt, which is already a great advantage over European ironworks, which have to be built at great expense.
