passages.speaker: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)

passages.headline: A Mongol tent 'like the roof of a round tower'
passages.place: Inner Mongolia, north of the Great Wall
passages.gloss: On his first journey beyond the Great Wall with the Qing embassy to the Russians, the Jesuit Gerbillon went into a Mongol tent 'the better to know how they were built'. He describes a round cage of small sticks about 13 or 14 feet across and 8 or 9 feet high, with a pointed roof, covered with felt ('woollen stuff, not woven, but mill'd'). Inside: a plank bed, a bench, a cupboard and wooden bowls.
passages.quote: It is a sort of Cage, made of pretty small Sticks, round, and about 13 or 14 Foot Diameter. … the Roofing begins at about four Foot from the Ground, and ends in a Point like the Roof of a Round Tower, or Pigeon-house: They are covered with Pieces of Woollen Stuff, not woven, but mill'd.
passages.speaker: Jean-François Gerbillon, Jesuit (journal compiled by Du Halde, English translation, 1738)

passages.headline: Ruined cities in Mongolia credited to Kublai's successors
passages.gloss: The map-making Jesuits found ruins of a large city on the Kherlen and of cities 'in above 20 different places'. They argue these were not ancient: the Mongols preferred tents to the most convenient houses, but after Kublai conquered China they began to build cities in Tartary so as not to look inferior to the Chinese, and all were destroyed or abandoned within a century. They compare this to the Manchu emperor Kangxi building towns and summer palaces in their own day.
passages.quote: Rubraquis speaks of Kara koram as a Village; but it is the Genius of that Nation to prefer Tents to the most convenient Houses: However, when they took to the Chinese Customs … they begun to build Cities in Tartary, the Ruins of which are still to be seen in above 20 different Places.
passages.speaker: Jesuit map-makers of 1709 to 1711 (Régis, Jartoux, Fridelli and others), compiled by Du Halde (English translation, 1738)
passages.caution: Their dating of the ruins is an argument, not a finding; the English editor's footnotes add material from Abu'l-Ghazi and Gaubil and disagree on details.

passages.headline: A city made of tents around a living Buddha
passages.place: Iben river, northern Mongolia (near the Selenga)
passages.people: Khalkha Mongols and their Hutuktu (Jebtsundamba Khutuktu)
passages.gloss: The Khalkha Mongols revered a lama called the Hutuktu, a 'living Fo' (Buddha), brother of one of their khans, who had built a costly temple of yellow glazed bricks on the Tula with workmen from Beijing; the Oirat ruler Galdan destroyed it in 1688. Now the Hutuktu lived in tents, and his camp drew Russian traders, monks from India, Pegu, Tibet and China, and lamas of every rank: 'a large City made of Tents'.
passages.quote: One may call it a large City made of Tents, the Hurry being much greater there than any where else in this Part of Tartary. The Russians of Selinghinskoy, which is not far distant, trade thither; there you meet also with Bonzas from Indostan, Pegu, Tibet, and China
passages.speaker: Jesuit map-makers of 1709 to 1711 (Régis, Jartoux, Fridelli and others), compiled by Du Halde (English translation, 1738)
passages.caution: The Jesuits boast of rebuking the lama to his face, and their account of Mongol Buddhism is hostile.

passages.headline: Stone stairs of a palace no Manchu built
passages.people: Jurchen (Kin) of the 12th century, ancestors of the Manchus
passages.gloss: Near Ningguta the Jesuits found ruined cities, one reachable only by a narrow causeway through water, with great stone staircases and palace remains finer than anything in Ningguta itself. They concluded these were the work not of the present Manchus but of the twelfth-century Kin (Jurchen), who ruled north China, built towns and palaces, and were then destroyed by the Mongols and the Chinese.
passages.quote: Here are also found great Stone Stair-cases, with some other Remains of a Palace … So that it is very probable, all the Monuments of Antiquity in Eastern Tartary were not the Work of the present Manchews, but of those of the 12th Century, who, under the Name of Kin chau, were Masters of the North of China
passages.speaker: Jesuit map-makers of 1709 to 1711 (Régis, Jartoux, Fridelli and others), compiled by Du Halde (English translation, 1738)

passages.headline: Underground huts and a village in a circle
passages.place: Northern Crimea, between Perekop and Karasubazar
passages.gloss: South of Perekop the post stations were sometimes in deserted Tatar villages, and sometimes the stable-keeper lived in a hut dug underground, which she calls common in this treeless, sun-baked country. At sunset she reached a Tatar village of huts straggling in a circle with no fence, while herds of horses, cows and sheep drifted home across the downs: 'a simple and majestic landscape'. A few lines earlier she had called Perekop's Tatar village the dirtiest place she ever saw.
passages.quote: The posts were sometimes in a deserted Tartarian village, and sometimes the only habitation for the stable-keeper was a hut made under ground, a common habitation in this country, where the sun is so extremely hot, and there is no shade of any sort.
passages.speaker: Elizabeth Craven (letters published London, 1789)
passages.caution: Villages were emptied by emigration after the Russian annexation of 1783; Craven does not say why these were deserted.

passages.headline: A Tartar house: one storey, cushions, and cupboards behind the panels
passages.gloss: At Karasubazar Craven visited the wife of the kadi (judge). The house, she writes, was a very light building of a single storey with no wooden furniture at all, only large cushions round the room. What impressed her was that the panelling slid back to reveal storage space larger than the room itself, so that 'every necessary' was hidden behind the walls.
passages.quote: A Tartar house is a very slight building of one story only … no chair, table, or piece of furniture in wood to be seen … large cushions are ranged round the room, on which we sat or reclined
passages.speaker: Elizabeth Craven (letters published London, 1789)

passages.headline: The kadi's wife examines an English arm
passages.gloss: Only the interpreter and a twelve-year-old boy were allowed into the women's room. The kadi's wife wore a turban with diamonds and pearls, scarlet-dyed nails and a face painted white and red with the veins drawn in blue. Craven's gloves seemed to trouble her, and once they were off the lady took her hand and felt her arm up to the shoulder, nodding approval, before coffee and rose-petal sweetmeats signalled the end of the visit.
passages.quote: She made me a sign to sit down; and my gloves seeming to excite much uneasiness in her I took them off … upon which she drew near, smiled, took one of my hands between her's, and winked and nodded as a sign of approbation
passages.speaker: Elizabeth Craven (letters published London, 1789)

passages.headline: A 'mosque' of whirling, groaning devotees
passages.people: Crimean Tatar Muslims (a Sufi dervish circle)
passages.gloss: Craven watched men going round in a circle in a mosque, groaning and flinging their heads to the ground until they fell senseless and were dragged into side recesses; one had lain there forty hours without food. She calls it 'mummery' and was disgusted. She also notes the tall, narrow minarets and the town's trade in coloured Morocco leather.
passages.quote: I went to a Mosque, where several pious Mussulmen were going round in a circle in the midst of the building, groaning and flinging their heads almost to the ground and them up again, a constant motion which with the moving round one way soon put them into a kind of torture
passages.speaker: Elizabeth Craven (letters published London, 1789)
passages.caution: She did not understand what she saw and says so with open contempt; this was a dervish ritual (dhikr), not ordinary mosque worship.

passages.headline: Bakhchysarai: five thousand Tatars line the streets
passages.people: Crimean Tatars of the khan's former capital
passages.gloss: Craven rode into Bakhchysarai, 'formerly the chief residence of the Khans', escorted by some hundred well-dressed Tatar horsemen. She was told the town had 5,000 Tatar inhabitants and thought every man was out lining the streets; most looked at the ground rather than at an unveiled woman's face, while some laughed at the novelty. She adds that the town made sword blades said to rival Damascus work.
passages.quote: There are five thousand Tartar inhabitants here; I do not believe there was a man left in his house, the streets being lined with Tartarian men on each side; their countenances were very singular, most of them kept their eyes fixed on the ground, as we passed
passages.speaker: Elizabeth Craven (letters published London, 1789)

passages.headline: The khan's palace, 'perfectly in ruins', regilded for the Empress
passages.gloss: Craven lodged in the khans' palace. She describes an irregular building mostly of one floor raised on pillars of painted and gilded wood, a finely proportioned doorway with a gilt inscription, courts within courts, a harem higher than the rest, and marble-paved rooms with fountains playing. She was told it had been in ruins until the Russian governor had it repaired, regilded and repainted for Catherine II's coming visit.
passages.quote: The Khan's palace is an irregular building, the greatest part of it is one floor raised upon pillars of wood painted and gilt in a fanciful and lively manner
passages.speaker: Elizabeth Craven (letters published London, 1789)
passages.caution: What she saw was a Russian restoration of 1786, not the palace as the khans left it.

passages.headline: A khan's dome for a beloved Christian wife
passages.gloss: From her window Craven saw a domed building and was told a khan built it as the tomb of a Christian wife he loved so much he could not be consoled, placing it where he could always see it. It is the story later attached to the Dilara Bikeç mausoleum. A footnote adds ruined baths and summer houses near the town; she went into one round bath lined with white marble, with niches for bathers.
passages.quote: I saw from the windows a kind of dome which raised my curiosity, and I am told it is a monument built to the memory of a Christian wife, which the Khan loved so tenderly that he was inconsolable for her loss
passages.speaker: Elizabeth Craven (letters published London, 1789)
passages.caution: A romantic local story told to her; the source does not name the khan or the wife.

passages.headline: 'The sea once lay at the foot' of the cliffs
passages.gloss: The house of the chief minister's sister stood below extraordinary rocks full of springs. On their summits, Craven says, were marks where huge cables had 'certainly passed and been tied', and the Tatars insisted the sea had once reached the foot of the cliffs and ships were moored there. At dinner she found Tatar cooking 'much grease and honey', and her hostess served two quarts of sherbet, coffee and sweets.
passages.quote: The Tartarians insist upon it that the sea once lay at the foot of them … and ships were fastened to them
passages.speaker: Elizabeth Craven (letters published London, 1789)
passages.caution: The belief is the Tatars'; the 'cable' marks were probably natural weathering grooves, but Craven gives no more detail than this.

passages.headline: Choosing exile rather than an oath to the Tsaritsa
passages.people: Crimean Tatars after the Russian annexation of 1783
passages.gloss: Craven's host, the Russian governor, was said to have reconciled the Tatars to their new ruler by gentleness and firmness. She adds, 'to their honour', that those who could not bear to swear allegiance did not stay but left for the Caucasus, and had since repented. A rare note, from the Russian side, of the emigration that followed annexation.
passages.quote: I am told he has conciliated the Tartars to their change of sovereign very much by his gentleness and firmness … To their honour, I find none would stay who could not bear the idea, of taking the oaths of allegiance
passages.speaker: Elizabeth Craven (letters published London, 1789)
passages.caution: Told her by Russian officials; she hears nothing from the emigrants themselves.

passages.headline: 'Cream of Tartar' and the cream of the Tartars
passages.gloss: Explaining the title 'Kaima-Kan' (the khan's first minister), Craven confesses in a footnote that someone in her party called him 'cream of Tartar', after the chemist's powder. Afraid he would hear of it, she turned it into 'the cream of the Tartars'. A reminder of how English ears played with the word.
passages.quote: a person called him cream of Tartar … which I fearing he should be told of, turned into the cream of the Tartars
passages.speaker: Elizabeth Craven, footnote (letters published London, 1789)

passages.headline: How the peninsula got the name Krim
passages.people: Mongols or Tartars of the Golden Horde
passages.gloss: In a history letter written before entering Crimea, Craven summarises its past: the Mongols or Tartars conquered it in 1237, and because they traded heavily at the town of Krim, the whole peninsula took that name, the only one Eastern peoples used. When she later reached the site (n198) she found 'not a vestige' of the ancient town left.
passages.quote: and, as the Tartars carried on a great trade in the town of Krim, the peninsula took the name of Krim, by which only it is known to the Orientals at this hour
passages.speaker: Elizabeth Craven (letters published London, 1789)
passages.caution: A second-hand summary of history from books she does not name.

passages.headline: A Tartar house like a giant poultry basket
passages.gloss: On his first night among the Nogais, de Tott is given a brand-new felt tent (oba) and inspects how it is made: a circular lattice wall, a dome open at the top, and a covering of camel-hair felt. On the next page he admires the lattice joined with rawhide and learns that the tent was part of a new bride's dowry.
passages.quote: I employed myself, in the mean time, in examining the structure of my Tartar house. It was like a large poultry basket, built in lattice work, and formed in a circular inclosure, over which was a dome, open at the top; a felt of camel's hair covered the whole on the outside, and the hole at the top, intended occasionally as a vent-hole for the smoke.
passages.speaker: Baron de Tott (English translation, 1785)

passages.headline: Building a house the Tartar way
passages.gloss: Facing winter in a poor hut at the khan's capital, de Tott rebuilt it himself 'without departing from the method of building pursued by the Tartars'. On the next page he explains the method: a timber frame of posts, closely set uprights woven with hazel rods like a basket, packed with pounded earth and chopped straw, then plastered with lime and hair and painted. He thought it more solid and healthy than European peasant houses.
passages.quote: I drew the plan, I collected the materials, and superintended the work, without departing from the method of building pursued by the Tartars… I shall take this opportunity of describing the structure of the houses in Crimea; but these details, or the architecture of the Tartars, will be of more service to the lovers of oeconomy, than to disciples of Vitruvius.
passages.speaker: Baron de Tott (English translation, 1785)

passages.headline: The khan's palace, once 'entirely in the Chinese' style
passages.gloss: De Tott describes the palace of the Crimean khans at the edge of Bakhchysarai, ringed by rocks and fed by streams channelled into kiosks and gardens. He says it was first built in a 'Chinese' manner and later repaired in Turkish fashion. On the same page he claims crime was rarer in Tartary than anywhere, so the capital had no guards but the khan's.
passages.quote: The Palace he inhabits, formerly built entirely in the Chinese, but repaired in the Turkish fashion, still retains some of the beauties of its former stile of construction. It is placed at one of the extremities of the town, and is surrounded by very high rocks, from whence flows an abundance of streams, which are conveyed into the kiosks and gardens in a most delightful manner.
passages.speaker: Baron de Tott (English translation, 1785)
passages.caution: 'Chinese' is de Tott's impression of the painted, wide-eaved style; he gives no source for who built it.

passages.headline: A capital that grew from a garden palace
passages.gloss: In a footnote de Tott explains that Bakhchysarai ('Palace of the Gardens') began as a country house of the khans; people settled round it and it eclipsed the old capital, Krim (Eski-Krym), which had shrunk to a village whose tombs alone showed its past importance.
passages.quote: This town, at present considered as the capital of the Crimea, was formerly nothing but a country house, called the Palace of the Gardens. The sovereigns by living there have drawn together a number of inhabitants; and this town… has successively usurped the pre-eminence over the ancient town of Crimea, which is now no more than a paltry village, where the tombs alone testify its ancient importance.
passages.speaker: Baron de Tott (his own footnote, English translation, 1785)

passages.headline: Villages of felt tents strung along the valleys
passages.place: Budjak and Nogai steppe (Bessarabia to the Sea of Azov)
passages.people: Nogai Tatars; Budjak and Crimean Tatars
passages.gloss: After defining 'Little Tartary' (Crimea, the Kuban, part of Circassia and the steppe between Russia and the Black Sea) on the previous page, de Tott contrasts the settled Tatars of the Budjak and Crimea, who live in villages, with the Nogais, who have only felt tents. Yet the Nogais are not aimless wanderers: their tents stand in single lines along valleys, forming 'villages' tens of leagues long that mark out each horde.
passages.quote: The latter province, called at present the Boudjak, is inhabited by Tartars settled in villages, as well as those of the peninsula, but the inhabitants of the three other provinces have only tents made of felt, which they remove at pleasure… their tents ranged along them in one line, form a kind of villages
passages.speaker: Baron de Tott (English translation, 1785)
passages.caution: The exact length he gives for these tent-villages is damaged in the OCR.

passages.headline: The khan's campaign tent, big enough for sixty
passages.gloss: Before the winter campaign de Tott describes Tartar tents in detail: folding lattice walls, roof rods hooked to a ring, felt covering bound with a girth, and snow banked against the walls instead of posts or ropes. The khan's own tent was the same design on a huge scale, hung inside with crimson cloth and ringed by twelve smaller tents for his officers.
passages.quote: This covering is bound with a girth, and a few shovels full of snow, thrown up against the walls, prevents the external air from penetrating, and perfectly consolidates these tents, without either posts or cordage… The tent of the Kam was of this kind, but so large, that more than sixty persons might conveniently sit round the wood fire.
passages.speaker: Baron de Tott (English translation, 1785)

passages.headline: Supper cooked by the best cook of the horde
passages.gloss: Curious about Nogai food, de Tott watches a young cook stir roasted millet flour into boiling water, then crumble in balls of salted, dried mare's-milk cheese until the mixture turns to a dough he turns out by hand. He liked the dish better than expected, but admits he could not bring himself to enjoy the mare's milk.
passages.quote: he then asks for one of the white balls, which was cheese, made of mare's milk, saturated with salt, and dried… he then draws out his flat knife, empties the kettle on his hand, and presents me with a cylinder of puff-paste in a spiral form. I was anxious to taste it, and was really better pleased with the mess than I expected.
passages.speaker: Baron de Tott (English translation, 1785)

passages.headline: Dung fuel, millet and a whole sheep at one sitting
passages.gloss: Crossing treeless plains, de Tott explains that the Nogais burn cakes of dung kneaded with sandy earth. He reports (as hearsay) that they had uprooted the old forests so no enemy could surprise them. Their everyday diet is millet and mare's milk, yet a Nogai could eat a whole sheep for a wager.
passages.quote: each family carefully collects the dung of the cattle, which they knead with a sort of sandy earth, and produce a turf which unfortunately smokes the Tartars more than it warms them. No people live more soberly. Millet and mares milk are their usual diet… A Noguais might lay a wager that he eat a whole sheep, and win his wager, without having an indigestion.
passages.speaker: Baron de Tott (English translation, 1785)
passages.caution: The claim that the Nogais tore up the forests is something he was 'assured' of, not something he saw.

passages.headline: Tartar law: the victim's family carries out the sentence
passages.gloss: A Jew's slave murdered his master and then converted to Islam hoping for pardon. De Tott explains that under Tartar law the injured family must execute the criminal themselves. Khan Maksud Giray refused to spare the convert, saying he would hand over his own brother if guilty; in the end the Jews were allowed to stone the murderer according to the law of Moses.
passages.quote: by the Tartar law the criminal must perish by the hand of the injured person, or by his heirs. It was objected then, but in vain, that a Turk could not be delivered up to the Jews. “I would deliver up my brother to them,” replied the Kam, “if he was guilty; I leave Providence to reward his conversion, if it be sincere; it is my duty to do justice.”
passages.speaker: Baron de Tott (English translation, 1785)

passages.headline: A bride's dowry measured in a pyramid of millet
passages.gloss: In a footnote de Tott describes an old Tartar wedding custom: a dish was set on the veiled bride's head and millet poured over it until the heap reached the dish. Small brides fared badly, so by his day families simply counted measures of millet. He then speculates that European nuptial crowns and sugar-plums come from this rite.
passages.quote: they placed a flat dish… on the head of the new married woman; they stretched a veil over her head… after this they poured millet on the trencher, which, spreading all around her, formed a cone… her dowry was not complete until the pyramid of millet reached up to the trencher, the veil still allowing her to breath. This custom was not favourable to little persons
passages.speaker: Baron de Tott (his own footnote, English translation, 1785)
passages.caution: Told in the past tense; the link to European wedding customs is de Tott's own guess.

passages.headline: How a raider carried off his captives
passages.people: Crimean and Nogai Tatars (Krim Giray's army)
passages.gloss: Riding with the khan's army on its last great slave raid into Russian New Serbia, de Tott watches a single Tartar manage a whole captured family and flock: children in a sack at the saddle, the girl in front, the mother behind, the father and son on led horses. He admires the skill but calls the scene an image of 'avarice' and 'the most cruel injustice'. He reckons about 20,000 captives were taken.
passages.quote: Five or six slaves, of different ages, sixty sheep, and twenty oxen, the prize of a single man, do not embarrass him. The children, with their heads peeping out of a sack, hanging by the pummel of the saddle; a young girl sitting before, leaning on her left hand; the mother behind on the crupper, the father on a led horse, the son upon another
passages.speaker: Baron de Tott (English translation, 1785)

passages.headline: Electric shocks at the khan's court taken for magic
passages.people: Crimean Tatars (Khan Maksud Giray and courtiers)
passages.gloss: After a fireworks show for the khan's birthday, de Tott staged 'a little chamber fire-work' of electrical experiments. The courtiers thought it sorcery; the khan asked to be shocked himself, and next day the whole town talked of nothing but electricity.
passages.quote: The first effects of this phenomenon excited such astonishment, that I had some difficulty in destroying the opinion of magic I saw arising in their minds… The Kam, however, had the air of comprehending me, and was himself desirous of being electrified. I gave him the stroke very moderately, but I handled the courtiers in such a manner as to obtain the Prince's approbation.
passages.speaker: Baron de Tott (English translation, 1785)
passages.caution: A self-flattering anecdote; only de Tott tells it.

passages.headline: The khan who died to music, poisoned by his doctor
passages.gloss: De Tott tells how Krim Giray, suffering 'hypochondriac' fits, took a draught from the Greek physician Siropolo despite de Tott's warnings. The khan sent for his friend, said farewell, and had six musicians play as he went to sleep; he died within the hour. The doctor left freely, and de Tott says embalming showed clear signs of poison.
passages.quote: Prince breathed his last to the sound of music… Siropolo obtained, without difficulty, a passport, and the necessary order for post-horses, to return quietly to Wallachia. The symptoms of poison appeared very manifest, however, on embalming the body; but the present interest of that Court, stifled every idea of vengeance, and of the punishment of the offender.
passages.speaker: Baron de Tott (English translation, 1785)
passages.caution: De Tott was present at the death, but the poisoning is his suspicion and a report from the embalming; no trial followed.

passages.headline: Tartary as the first land after the Flood
passages.gloss: Touching on the 'Atlantis' debate of his day, de Tott argues that the high plateau of Tartary must have been the first land inhabited in Asia, the source of the swarms that later poured into Europe as Goths, Ostrogoths and Visigoths. He says a Tartar tradition told him by Khan Krim Giray supports this, and on the next page traces the Crimean dynasty back to Genghis Khan.
passages.quote: this country, possessed at present by the Tartars, must have been the first discovered land in Asia, and the earliest inhabited; the source of that population which first sent forth those swarms which, constantly driven back by the wall of China, and the defiles of Thibet and of Caucasus, fell upon the northern parts of Asia, and overflowed our Europe, under the name of Goths, Ostrogoths, and Visigoths.
passages.speaker: Baron de Tott (English translation, 1785)
passages.caution: A speculative 18th-century theory based on geography and one conversation, not on evidence; de Tott himself calls it a 'hypothesis'.

passages.headline: A Manchu and a Budjak Tartar: one name, 1,500 leagues apart
passages.gloss: In his opening essay de Tott argues that government shapes peoples more than climate. His example shows how widely 'Tartar' stretched in his day: a Manchu from beyond China and a Tatar from Bessarabia share the name and, he claims, the same kind of government.
passages.quote: Bring together a Manchou and a Bass-Arabian Tartar, you will search in vain the interval of fifteen hundred leagues that separates their countries: the climate differs but little; the government is the same.
passages.speaker: Baron de Tott (Preliminary Discourse, English translation, 1785)
passages.caution: A rhetorical generalisation, not an observation.

passages.headline: Bakhchysarai: a city shaped like a funnel
passages.gloss: Maria Guthrie calls the former khans' capital a 'romantic city' hidden in a valley: Tatar houses stacked in rings up the slopes around the palace, like an amphitheatre, beneath overhanging rocks carved by wind and water into shapes like towers and obelisks. On the previous page she complains that the streets are dirty, badly paved and too narrow for anything but a horseman or a small cart.
passages.quote: Only figure to yourself, my good friend, in a deep valley, bounded by a huge chain of pendant rocks, an assemblage of Tartar houses of uncouth forms, stuck as it were against the sides of the mountains, and placed in circles one above another, round the palace of their Chan (situated at the bottom of the valley), so as to represent a large amphitheatre, or rather funnel
passages.speaker: Maria Guthrie (letter, translated by Matthew Guthrie, 1802)

passages.headline: The khan's palace: 'painted Chinese structure'
passages.gloss: Like Baron de Tott thirty years earlier, Maria Guthrie reaches for 'Chinese' to describe the painted palace of the khans. She says its interior is a maze (a 'Scythian labyrinth') with separate women's quarters, and on the next page describes the court mosque whose slender minaret sways under the climber.
passages.quote: The palace, which, as said before, rises in the middle of this curious Tauric city, to add greatly to the singularity and romantic appearance of the scene, is a curious species of painted Chinese structure, well suited to such a group of oddities.
passages.speaker: Maria Guthrie (letter, translated by Matthew Guthrie, 1802)
passages.caution: She admits she lacks the vocabulary of 'oriental architecture'; 'Chinese' is an impression, not a statement about builders.

passages.headline: Tombs of the khans and a monument to a Christian wife
passages.gloss: In the palace courtyard she sees two domed rotundas holding the remains of generations of khans, and a small mausoleum said to honour a khan's beloved Christian wife, probably a captive. Inside, a marble vestibule has three fountains, and vine-and-rose bowers fill a small garden.
passages.quote: Near the handsome mosque in the court of Batcheferai palace, mentioned in my last, we perceived a couple of pretty rotundos, in which repose the ashes of a long line of Chans; but what most attracted our eyes… was a pretty little mausoleum, dedicated “To Conjugal Fidelity and Attachment,” erected by one of the Crimean Chans on losing a beloved christian wife, probably a fair captive
passages.speaker: Maria Guthrie (letter, translated by Matthew Guthrie, 1802)
passages.caution: The story of the Christian wife is what she was told; 'probably a fair captive' is her guess.

passages.headline: Stone houses that turn their backs to the street
passages.gloss: In her general letter on the 'Crim Tartars' she says their houses are single-storey stone buildings bonded with limy clay and roofed with tiles. They have no street windows: the fronts face an inner courtyard so that the women can take the air unseen behind muslin screens.
passages.quote: The Tartar houses are of one story, constructed of stone, cemented together by a calcareous clay, and covered with tiles. Toward the street they have no windows; polygamy, and its natural consequence, jealousy, having turned the facade of Tauric dwellings to the inner court, where the women may breathe the fresh air through muslin blinds.
passages.speaker: Maria Guthrie (letter, translated by Matthew Guthrie, 1802)

passages.headline: Felt tents on carts, as in Herodotus
passages.gloss: Leaving the Crimea, the party came on a few nomad tents: round, about four feet high and eight feet across, covered in rushes and thick felt, with a smoke-hole and a banner marking the horde. She notes they ride on carts called kibitkas, just like the cart-dwelling Scythians of Herodotus, and that women live in separate tents.
passages.quote: the very tents that I have been describing, called Kabitkies, are placed on carts of the same name, and drawn with their inhabitants from one grazing ground to another, as the difference of season, or a want of pasture for their numerous flocks, demands a change of place. The women are kept in separate tents pitched near those of the men
passages.speaker: Maria Guthrie (letter, translated by Matthew Guthrie, 1802)
passages.caution: The link to Herodotus's Scythians is a learned comparison, not evidence of descent.

passages.headline: Kurgans: graves or ash heaps from Tartar tents?
passages.gloss: Crossing the steppe she notes many conical mounds (kurgans) like those on the plain of Troy. She reports a view that they are heaps of ash from Tartar camps and adds her own twist: that the Tartars buried their dead beneath the ash to make cheap monuments. On the next page she suggests this is the origin of mound burial across Europe.
passages.quote: Some people contend that they are not tombs, but hillocks formed by the ashes thrown out of the Tartar tents while encamped on the spot; which is a fact, and a very wise measure too, as, by making the graves of their companions the bases of these conic hillocks, they prevent putrid exhalations, while they raise a rude monument to departed friends without either trouble or expence
passages.speaker: Maria Guthrie (letter, translated by Matthew Guthrie, 1802)
passages.caution: A speculation presented as fact; most steppe kurgans are ancient burial mounds far older than the Tatars.

passages.headline: Stone statues on the steppe that today's Tartars know nothing about
passages.place: Nogai steppe east of the Dnieper
passages.gloss: She examined upright stone figures scattered over the steppe, each carved with a man's or woman's bust. From their dress and faces she judges them 'Tartar workmanship' of Kalmyk or Hun type, but notes that the living Tatars know nothing of them and she cannot tell whether they marked graves or grazing bounds. Matthew Guthrie adds a whole appendix on them.
passages.quote: They are standing perpendicularly in the ground, bearing each the bust of a man or woman tolerably sculptured for Tartar workmanship; which there can be no doubt of their being, from the particular dress in which they are represented, and the marked features of the Calmouks, or Huns. But whether these rude monuments of antiquity (for the present race of Tartars know nothing about them,)…
passages.speaker: Maria Guthrie (letter, translated by Matthew Guthrie, 1802)
passages.caution: Attribution by dress and 'features' is guesswork; these stone figures (kamennye baby) belong to several earlier steppe peoples.

passages.headline: Ruins 'all of Tartar origin', and a palace the Kalmyks would not live in
passages.gloss: In his appendix Matthew Guthrie lists brick ruins on the Akhtuba, at Madzhary on the Kuma (32 buildings in 1780, only four by 1793) and near the Terek, which Pallas had drawn, and calls them all of Tartar origin from their shape, construction and inscriptions. He follows Pallas in thinking them tombs or shrines, because Mongols so loved camp life that the Kalmyk princes of his day would not live in a palace Russia built for them.
passages.quote: all of Tartar origin, as is evident from several kinds of proof, viz. shape, construction, and inscriptions… I am of Pallas's opinion with regard to the sepulchral or religious destination of all those ruins, from the known attachment of the Monguls to a camp residence, which to this day prevents their descendants, the Calmuc princes, from inhabiting a palace built for them by the crown of Russia
passages.speaker: Matthew Guthrie (editor's Appendix, 1802)
passages.caution: Second-hand from Pallas; Klaproth (W056) later argued Madzhary was a real town, not just a cemetery.

passages.headline: How to make koumis
passages.gloss: At a steppe village hospitable Tatars brought koumis and a brandy distilled from mare's milk. Maria took down the recipe for her husband: warm mare's milk, a sixth part warm water and a starter of old koumis, sour milk or rye leaven, churned and left to ferment a day and a night. She found it sourish-sweet and pleasant.
passages.quote: To any given quantity of warm Mares' Milk, the Crim Tartars add a sixth part warm water of the same temperature, with a little old Koumis, sour cows' milk, or a piece of sour leaven of their rye-bread, as a ferment; and mix all together in a species of churn… The koumis has a sourish sweet taste by no means unpleasant to my palate
passages.speaker: Maria Guthrie (letter, translated by Matthew Guthrie, 1802)

passages.headline: Marriage sight unseen
passages.gloss: She explains that a Crimean Tatar groom never saw his bride before the wedding and relied on a matron go-between. The groom then bargained with the father, usually offering a cow and some sheep; the imam married the couple with little ceremony, and the groom treated his friends to pipes, coffee and sherbet outside the house.
passages.quote: for an inhabitant of the Taurida never sees his bride till the nuptial torch is lighted up; so that if it were not for the friendly ministry of a grave matron, or go between (the Pronuba of the Antients), who has the privilege of taking a peep at the bride, a man might marry the grandmother instead of the daughter.
passages.speaker: Maria Guthrie (letter, translated by Matthew Guthrie, 1802)
passages.caution: She says herself that 'all is mystery' about women's lives; this is what she was told.

passages.headline: Nailed by the ear to his own shop door
passages.gloss: Describing justice under the khans, she says judges ruled on the spot and punished at once: cheating shopkeepers were nailed by the ear to their doors, small offences got the bastinado and serious ones the bowstring for Muslims but a halter for Christians and Jews. She adds that Turks and Tatars rarely cheated.
passages.quote: A shopkeeper caught in the act of cheating with false or short weights was nailed by the ear to his own shop-door, that the whole market might know the knave, and watch him in future… Lesser offences were instantly punished with the bastinado, and greater with the bow-string, if a true believer; for a halter was the portion of an infidel
passages.speaker: Maria Guthrie (letter, translated by Matthew Guthrie, 1802)
passages.caution: Describes the system before Russian rule, which she did not see.

passages.headline: The Nogais: a splinter of the Golden Horde
passages.gloss: Crossing the Nogai steppe she explains the horde's name: the Nogais split from the Golden Horde under a leader called Nogai, which, she suggests, let them escape Timur's destruction of the Horde in the 1380s and 1390s. She adds that Russian rule has greatly changed them since earlier travellers' accounts.
passages.quote: The Nogay Tartars, who have wandered for some ages in this desert (a part of the primitive or little Scythia of the ancients), were originally a subdivision of the famous golden horde placed in the Kaptchak by the conqueror Zingis Chan, (properly Tschinghis), who, on some quarrel among themselves, separated from the main body of their nation, under a chief or general named Nogay
passages.speaker: Maria Guthrie (letter, translated by Matthew Guthrie, 1802)

passages.headline: 'Tartar' as a convenient catch-all
passages.gloss: In a footnote Matthew Guthrie admits that scholars like Georgi and Tooke had tried to separate Mongols from Tartars, but says the steppe peoples are so alike that everyone will go on using one generic name, 'Scythians' for ancient times and 'Tartars' for modern ones, simply to save trouble.
passages.quote: Notwithstanding all the trouble taken by Professor Georgi, Mr. Tooke, &c. to distinguish the Monguls, &c. from the Tartars, there is so much similitude… that a generic name for the whole will always be employed by every one who is not minutely treating of their subdivisions, let professed historians do what they please to prevent it
passages.speaker: Matthew Guthrie (editor's footnote in the Appendix, 1802)

passages.headline: A Nogai prince in a little clay town
passages.gloss: An Italian merchant told her he had crossed the Nogai steppe and was welcomed by the Nogai chief Beyazet Beg, who lived in a small clay-built town and ate mostly milk, koumis and mutton. Trying to please a European, the prince served an 'Italian' feast so strange that the guest slipped out to be sick, and promised a French one next day.
passages.quote: He said, he found their chief named Beyazet Beg, i. e. Prince Bajazet, dwelling in a little town built with clay, on the lake and rivulet Bolotchik… This Tartar prince, who lives like his Scythian ancestors… principally on milk and its preparation koumis (which constitutes the food, wine, and brandy of the Tartars), with occasionally the flesh of his flocks
passages.speaker: Maria Guthrie (letter, translated by Matthew Guthrie, 1802), reporting an Italian merchant of Kherson
passages.caution: Second-hand story from a merchant.

passages.headline: Tatars collect money to 'free' a charming Greek lady
passages.gloss: After mocking whirling dervishes, Maria offers a story to the Tatars' credit: a Greek-born countess, married to a Russian general, so charmed the Tatars of Eupatoria with her Turkish that they took her for a Muslim woman held captive by Christians and secretly raised money to buy her freedom.
passages.quote: so charmed the honest Tartars with the graces of her person, and conversation in the Turkish language, that they, ignorant of her rank and quality, conceived an idea of her being a fair daughter of Mahomet, held in Christian bondage by the right of war, and secretly opened a subscription among themselves to purchase her liberty
passages.speaker: Maria Guthrie (letter, translated by Matthew Guthrie, 1802)
passages.caution: An anecdote about another traveller, not something she witnessed.

passages.headline: Tatar waterworks and fountains, and who wrecked them
passages.gloss: Reuilly finds Tatar-built towns narrow, unpaved and dirty, with houses hidden behind high courtyard walls. But he praises the Tatars highly for piping water by canals, sometimes over long distances, to public fountains and into houses, and blames the Russians for destroying the fountains or leaving them to decay.
passages.quote: Too much praise, however, cannot be given to the Tartars for their care in conducting the water by canals, sometimes from a very considerable distance, and the purposes to which they apply it; either by making public springs, or conveying it into their houses… Unfortunately, these fountains have been in a great degree destroyed by the Russians, and those which remain, decay daily for want of necessary repairs.
passages.speaker: Jean Reuilly (English translation, 1807)

passages.headline: Bakhchysarai: thirty-one mosques and seventy-five fountains
passages.gloss: Reuilly describes the old khans' capital packed into a narrow valley, its main street lined with wooden shops. Because Catherine II left the town to the Tatars, no Russian townsmen lived there; the people were Tatars and Jews. He counts its mosques and fountains and describes the one-storey palace with its mosque, stables, terraced garden and cemetery of the khans.
passages.quote: The principal street, which is about a verst and a half in length, contains, almost the whole way along, two rows of miserable wooden shops. As the empress Catherine gave up this town to the Tartars, it contains no Russian burgesses, but is inhabited entirely by Tartars and Jews… Bachtchisarai contains thirty-one mosques, and seventy-five fountains.
passages.speaker: Jean Reuilly (English translation, 1807)

passages.headline: Karasubazar's trading khans and the ruins of old Krim
passages.gloss: At the market town of Karasubazar he counts twenty-three mosques and describes the merchants' khans (warehouses) that look like old Gothic palaces. Eski-Krym, the old Tatar capital that gave the whole peninsula its name, now lies in ruins in a fertile plain, its gardens abandoned.
passages.quote: They reckon in Carasubasar, twenty-three mosques, and three Greek or Armenian churches. The khans, or houses of depôt for commerce, resemble old Gothic palaces… Eski-krym, anciently Krim, which, under the Tatars, gave its name to the whole peninsula, is situated, with its extensive ruins, in a fertile plain at the foot of the mountain
passages.speaker: Jean Reuilly (English translation, 1807)

passages.headline: Portable Nogai huts of twigs and felt
passages.people: Nogai Tatars (remnant of the Kuban Tatars)
passages.gloss: Reuilly describes the seven or eight thousand Nogais roaming between the Berda and the Molochna. Their round huts, about eight feet across, have a wicker wall and dome covered with rush mats and brown felt, a smoke-hole and a tiny door; the furniture is a few cushions, a low table, pots and dishes. He adds that they were starting to build fixed houses and farm.
passages.quote: They encamp themselves in little cabins of felt; their tents, according to Thunmann, are a kind of portable huts, of a circular form, of about eight feet in diameter, made of lath-work or hurdles of twigs, about the size of a thumb, forming a sort of wall about four feet in height, upon which rests a dome or roof of the same structure
passages.speaker: Jean Reuilly (English translation, 1807), citing Johann Thunmann
passages.caution: The tent description is taken from Thunmann's earlier book, not Reuilly's own observation.

passages.headline: Brick houses on the plain, flat turf roofs in the mountains
passages.gloss: Reuilly contrasts two kinds of settled Tatar house. Plains Tatars live in small Turkish-style houses of stone or, lacking stone, brick, and burn dried cakes of turf and dung. Mountain Tatars build on steep slopes with flat turf roofs, packed so closely that each row of roofs forms a street for the row above.
passages.quote: they inhabit small houses built after the Turkish fashion, and make use of bricks, when they cannot procure stone… their houses, which are built on the steep sides of the mountains, are roofed with turf in a flat manner… and they are built so close together, that these flat roofs seem like a street for the row of houses which stands next above them
passages.speaker: Jean Reuilly (English translation, 1807)

passages.headline: How the Nogais came to the Crimea
passages.gloss: In his history chapter Reuilly says that when Mengli Giray became khan under Ottoman protection (1478), few Tatars actually lived in the Crimea; the khan settled thousands of Nogais captured in wars on the Volga, and his successors peopled the Kuban and the lands between the Don and Dniester the same way.
passages.quote: When the sovereignty of the peninsula passed to Menguely Guerai, there were not many Tartars amongst its inhabitants; but the wars which he carried on with them on the banks of the Volga, afforded him an opportunity to bring with him into the Crimea, several thousand Nogays, who were obliged to establish themselves in that country.
passages.speaker: Jean Reuilly (English translation, 1807)
passages.caution: Compiled history from earlier authors; the claim of few Tatars before 1478 is his source's view.

passages.headline: Why the Tatar ruler is 'khan' and a sultan is a mere prince
passages.gloss: In notes on coins of the last Crimean khan, Shahin Giray, the French orientalists Langlès and Millin explain that among Turks and Persians 'sultan' means sovereign and 'khan' a lesser officer, but among the Tartars it is the reverse, perhaps because 'khan' is a Tartar word found in Kalmyk, Mongol and Manchu. They add that Shahin was the 39th and last khan and descended from Genghis Khan.
passages.quote: Among the Tartars on the other side, a directly contrary usage prevails, and the sovereign only has a right to the distinction of khan, which he places before his proper names, either it is because the word is originally Tartar, and is to be found, indeed, in the Calmuc dialects, Monghol, Mantchou, &c.; while sultan is Arabian
passages.speaker: Numismatic notes by L. Langlès and A. L. Millin, printed in Reuilly's Travels (English translation, 1807)

passages.headline: A young mare killed for an honoured guest
passages.people: Crimean Tatar nobility (family of Atai Myrza)
passages.gloss: Reuilly says Tatar nobles still kill a horse to feast a distinguished guest. When he arrived at the house of Atai Myrza's brother, the prince told him a young mare had been slaughtered in his honour; the interpreter explained this was the greatest compliment, since a mare was the most precious thing he could offer.
passages.quote: They still retain the practice of killing a horse, to make a feast on the arrival of a guest of distinction. On my arrival at the house of the brother of Atai Myrza, this prince said to me, “You are very welcome. As soon as I hear that you had come, I ordered a young mare to be killed, to give you a feast.”
passages.speaker: Jean Reuilly (English translation, 1807)

passages.headline: Coffee-houses, hawking and a singer with a guitar
passages.gloss: Noble Tatars love hawking and hare-hunting; in town, men spend whole days cross-legged in coffee-houses, smoking and talking. Sometimes a singer recites stories or verses to a guitar-like instrument while the listeners nod in approval. Reuilly finds Tatar song 'grave, harsh, and discordant' and describes a dance of shaking limbs with the feet barely leaving the ground.
passages.quote: Hawking and hunting the hare, form the greatest delight of the noble Tartars. In the towns their amusements are reduced to meeting in the coffee-houses… Sometimes a singer recites a story or chaunts verses, accompanying himself with a bad instrument, in the shape of a guitar; the assembly listens with the greatest attention, and expresses the pleasure it receives by slight motions of the head.
passages.speaker: Jean Reuilly (English translation, 1807)

passages.headline: A Turkish dialect even Turks struggle with
passages.gloss: Reuilly says the Tatars speak a Turkish dialect so mixed with Mongol and Arabic words that a Turk finds it hard to follow, and the Nogais are hardest of all to understand because they speak fast and gutturally.
passages.quote: Though the general language of the Tartars is only a Turkish dialect, yet it is intermixed with such a number of Mogol and Arabic words, that a Turk has a difficulty to understand it. The Nogays in particular render themselves scarcely intelligible, by the quickness with which they speak, and the guttural pronunciation.
passages.speaker: Jean Reuilly (English translation, 1807)

passages.headline: Broken ribs cured by drinking gruel
passages.gloss: Reuilly watched a Tatar remedy: a servant of Atai Myrza who broke two ribs falling from his horse was made to drink water-gruel until his belly swelled, under threat of the bastinado, so the ribs would push back into place. Reuilly will not vouch for the cure but admits the man was better by the time he left.
passages.quote: A domestic of Atai Myrza having fallen from his horse, and had two of his ribs broken, his master made him drink water gruel till his belly was prodigiously inflated; and when he refused to take more, he was threatened with the bastinado and drenched with the gruel… his master assuring me that the ribs would get into their places spontaneously.
passages.speaker: Jean Reuilly (English translation, 1807)

passages.headline: Madzhar's brick buildings, described in 1772
passages.gloss: Klaproth quotes the naturalist S. G. Gmelin, who saw the ruins in 1772 when they were best preserved: a great city on a plateau, with fortified mansions at the edge. The bricks were like those Astrakhan Tatars still made; walls were bonded mostly with clay and plastered and whitewashed inside; buildings were square, octagonal or round, up to nine fathoms high and topped by pyramids or domes.
passages.quote: The bricks resemble those still made by the Tartars of Astrachan, that is to say, they are broader and thicker than ours. In the external walls, a mortar composed of lime and sand is used only here and there, the cement generally employed being clay alone… The figure of the buildings yet preserved is square, octagonal, and circular.
passages.speaker: Samuel Gottlieb Gmelin (visit of 1772), in Klaproth's extract (English translation, 1814)
passages.caution: Gmelin called it 'a magnificent Scythian city'; Klaproth corrects the attribution to the Golden Horde.

passages.headline: Who pulled down Madzhar
passages.people: Russian and Armenian settlers; Count P. S. Potemkin
passages.gloss: When Klaproth arrived only two burial chapels were left. He explains that nearby colonists tore the ruins down for bricks, and that Count Paul Potemkin had most of what remained demolished to build the fortress-town of Yekaterinograd; peasants carried off the rest, and inscribed stones ended up in their yards.
passages.quote: The destruction of these remains of antiquity has been occasioned chiefly by the settlement of several colonies, which have established themselves in this neighbourhood, and have pulled them down for the sake of the serviceable bricks. Their total demolition, however, is to be ascribed more particularly to Count Paul Ssergeitsch Potemkin, who ordered the greatest part of the buildings remaining in his time to be taken down
passages.speaker: Julius Klaproth (English translation, 1814)

passages.headline: Proof that Madzhar was built by Kipchak Tatars
passages.gloss: Klaproth sets out his evidence that Madzhar was a Tatar town: the shape of its buildings and burial chapels, which match a Tatar cemetery near Tbilisi; walls decorated with coloured glazed tiles, a Tatar and Mongol fashion; Arabic gravestones; coins of the Golden Horde; and mentions in Asian histories. He also opened a brick vault himself and found a wooden coffin.
passages.quote: The following facts, however, afford incontestable proofs that Madshar was a town built and inhabited by Ckipdshack Tartars. I. The form of the buildings and sepulchral chapels is characteristic of Southern Asia… The fashion of adorning the walls with tiles, which are glazed on one side with different colours, is also Tartar and Mongol.
passages.speaker: Julius Klaproth (English translation, 1814)

passages.headline: Coins struck at Sarai, capital of the Golden Horde
passages.gloss: Klaproth reads the coins found at Madzhar: nearly all were minted at Sarai or New Sarai, the Golden Horde capitals, under khans from Mengu-Timur to Tokhtamysh and Pulad (1270s to 1408), some with names in Mongol script. One is struck at Astrakhan. The latest coin helps date the town's end to about 1400.
passages.quote: The great Ssulthan Ghajats Eddunia (the prop of the world) Toktégu-chan, the Just… Coined at Ssarai, the capital, in the year 715; that is, A.D. 1315.
passages.speaker: Julius Klaproth, transcribing coin legends (English translation, 1814)
passages.caution: The Arabic legends are garbled in the OCR; the translations are Klaproth's.

passages.headline: A Tatar history: 'The habitations of the Chans were stone buildings'
passages.place: Golden Horde lands (Sarai, Astrakhan, Kazan, Madzhar)
passages.when: text acquired 1807; describing the 14th to 15th centuries
passages.gloss: At Mozdok Klaproth bought a history of the Tartars in the Nogai dialect and translates its list of where the khans lived: Sarai, the Akhtuba, Madzhar, and vice-khans at Astrakhan and Kazan. He notes that the word he renders 'stone buildings' is 'Madshar' itself. The Nogais near the ruins also told him it had been the residence of Khan Mamai.
passages.quote: The habitations of the Chans were stone buildings. The residence of one Chan was Urisch, and the residence of another Chan was Churssan… Dshan Beg Chan's residence was at Ack Adil, with the name of Ssaray Aldy… Jaick Chan's was Madshar. There were three vice-chans; at Adshdruchan was the place of abode of Timur Ckutlu-Chan, Borki Chan's habitation was at Ckathatdr, and Sheich Aly Chan's residence at Ckasan.
passages.speaker: Anonymous history of the Tartars in the Nogai dialect, as translated by Julius Klaproth (English translation, 1814)
passages.caution: A late native chronicle of unknown date and author; place names are Klaproth's transcriptions.

passages.headline: A Muslim gravestone dated 1346
passages.people: Muslim Tatars of the Golden Horde
passages.gloss: Klaproth read Arabic gravestones at Madzhar: one for 'Sina, son of Mohammed, son of Chalil' of AH 747 (1346-1347), another for a judge of AH 777 (1375-1376), which he carried away. All dated stones he saw belonged to the 8th Islamic century. He notes Pallas missed them because peasants had built them into their yards.
passages.quote: Here is buried the deceased, who needs the mercy of God in eternity, Sina, son of Mohhammed, the son of Chalil..... in the year of the era seven-and-forty and seven hundred.
passages.speaker: Julius Klaproth, translating an Arabic gravestone (English translation, 1814)

passages.headline: The myth that Hungarians came from Madzhar
passages.gloss: Klaproth traces a legend: in 1728 Gerber saw 'handsome stone houses' at Madzhar and guessed from the name that the Hungarians (Magyars) came from there, a notion copied onto maps. Klaproth calls it absurd: the name is Tatar for stone buildings, and the ruins are Golden Horde.
passages.quote: It is yet called Madshar, an appellation which is given by the Poles and Turks to the Hungarians, and by which the latter commonly distinguish themselves. It is probable that the founders of the kingdom of Hungary were originally from this country. Thus we see that Gerber was the first who broached the absurd opinion that the Hungarians derived their origin from Madshar
passages.speaker: Johann Gustav Gerber (1728), quoted by Klaproth, followed by Klaproth's comment (English translation, 1814)
passages.caution: A name-based origin legend that Klaproth rejects.

passages.headline: Mountain Tartars who remember a lost capital
passages.gloss: Klaproth reports the origin tradition of the Turkic mountain peoples the Georgians called Bassiani: their elders say they once lived on the steppe of the Kuma up to the Don, with a magnificent capital, Ckirck Madshar ('forty stone buildings'), which they identify with the ruins at Madzhar, before being driven into the high mountains.
passages.quote: Their elders report that they were long ago settled in the steppe of the Kuma as far as the Don… Their capital, which is said to have been very magnificent, was named Ckirck Madshar, which in their language signifies the forty stone buildings, or the forty four-wheeled waggons… They assert that the ruins of Madshar, which yet subsist, are the remains of this city.
passages.speaker: Julius Klaproth (English translation, 1814), reporting the elders' tradition
passages.caution: An oral tradition; the dates are uncertain even to the tellers.

passages.headline: God called Tagri and sacrifices to the prophet Elijah
passages.gloss: Klaproth says the ordinary Bassian Tartars had no fixed religion: they called God 'Tagri' rather than Allah, offered lambs, dairy and beer to the prophet Elijah on mountain tops with song and dance, ate pork and kept sacred springs. Like other Tartars they foretold the future from sheep's shoulder-blades cracking in the fire. Only their chiefs had been made Muslim by the Circassians.
passages.quote: The common people have, strictly speaking, no established religion, but worship God, whom they call Tagri and not Allah, as the giver of all good, and the prophet Elijah… who, according to them, frequently appears on the summits of the highest mountains, and to whom they offer sacrifices of lambs, milk, butter, cheese, and beer (ssra), accompanied with singing and dancing.
passages.speaker: Julius Klaproth (English translation, 1814)
passages.caution: Based on informants' reports rather than long residence.

passages.headline: The long-haired forest goblin who boiled two children
passages.gloss: Among the Karachay's many tales of mountain demons, Klaproth records the Ssalmasti, a long-haired female spirit of the woods. A villager caught one and enslaved it by hiding its cut hair, until his children revealed the hiding place; the spirit threw them into the boiling pot and fled back to the forest.
passages.quote: A malignant spirit in female shape, and having very long hair, which they call in their language Ssalmasti, is reported to reside in a certain wood. About twenty-five years ago one of the inhabitants of the village caught this goblin, carried it home with him, and cut off its hair, which he carefully hid, and by which means he rendered the spirit subservient to him.
passages.speaker: Julius Klaproth (English translation, 1814), from an Armenian informant who lived among the Karachay
passages.caution: A folk tale passed on through an informant.

passages.headline: Karachay marriage and the 'price of blood'
passages.gloss: Klaproth describes the Karachay as usually monogamous and unusually kind to their wives. As among other Tartars, the bride's parents receive a kalym (bride price), here called 'the price of blood'; a rich groom sends the bride a full outfit and she is brought to him at night, followed by three days of feasting and dancing.
passages.quote: In general they take only one wife… so that here, as among the Europeans, the wife is the companion, and not the menial servant, of the husband… Among them, as among the other Tartars, the parents, on the marriage of a daughter, receive a kalim, which is here termed the price of blood.
passages.speaker: Julius Klaproth (English translation, 1814)
passages.caution: Klaproth's Karachay material came mainly from one Armenian informant.

passages.headline: A name Tatars called dishonourable
passages.gloss: In the written instructions the Academy gave Klaproth, a scholar remarks that peoples sometimes adopt names their neighbours use: just as the Tartar nations in Russia call themselves 'Tartars' for outsiders, though at home they consider the name dishonourable.
passages.quote: They perhaps assume it for the purpose of accommodating their neighbours, as the Tartar nations in Russia give themselves the name of Tartars, which in their own countries they consider as dishonourable.
passages.speaker: Instructions for Klaproth from the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences (section II, probably by A. C. Lehrberg or Ph. Krug), printed in Klaproth's Travels

passages.headline: Batu's 'Mongol' army had very few Mongols
passages.gloss: In footnotes to his account of Batu's conquest of Russia and sack of Kiev in 1240, Klaproth points out that Batu's army contained very few Mongols and that he ruled as prince of the Kipchak Tartars. The khans of Kipchak called themselves Tartar sultans and lived at Sarai on the Akhtuba; after their empire split, the khans of Kazan, Astrakhan and Crimea kept the title.
passages.quote: Batu-chan had very few Mongols in his army, and had become prince of the Kipdschak Tartars… The chans of Kipdschak styled themselves Tartar sultans, and resided in the city of Sarai or Saratschik on the river Achtuba; an arm of the Wolga, till the division of their extensive dominions.
passages.speaker: Julius Klaproth (his own footnotes, English translation, 1814)

passages.headline: An octagonal stone tomb with a Tatar inscription
passages.gloss: Near the rivulet Jaman-Kul, Klaproth describes the oldest monument of Little Kabarda: an octagon of hewn stone about twelve feet high with an arched door, windows and a collapsed vault, ringed by about a hundred earth mounds. Its Tatar inscription names 'Ckoban-Chan son of Berdi-beg' and the Islamic year 860 (1455).
passages.quote: It is an edifice of hewn stone, and round it are about a hundred hillocks of earth called Bugri… The building is an octagon, each of its sides measuring six feet… On the stone inserted over the door is engraved a Tartar inscription in three lines, of which only these words ‘Ckoban-Chan son of Berdi-beg, in the year 860’ (A. D. 1455) are legible.
passages.speaker: Julius Klaproth (English translation, 1814)

passages.headline: Milk at court, in memory of Tartar origins
passages.gloss: Asking about the 'milk-tea' that was to have been served at the cancelled audience, Ellis learns it is simply milk, served to recall the Manchu dynasty's Tartar origins; likewise the emperor carves meat with a knife rather than chopsticks at state meals. Ellis adds that the conquerors profess to value their ancestors' simple ways but have lost their energy.
passages.quote: This milk-tea, it appears, is simply milk; chaya, or tea, being affixed to the names of many beverages besides that made from the tea plant. The milk is given as a record of the Tartar origin of the reigning family. Another instance of the anxiety to preserve these recollections is, that the Emperor, on state occasions, uses a knife to divide his meat, instead of chop-sticks.
passages.speaker: Henry Ellis

passages.headline: Four races of Tartars in China
passages.gloss: The Mongol official Kwang tells Ellis that Tartars can hold office at eighteen and that there are four races of Tartars in China. Ellis's footnote explains the Manchu, Mongol and 'Tartarized Chinese' eight-banner system, and notes that Mongols have long been Buddhists while Manchus adopted Buddhism only after entering China.
passages.quote: Tartars, Kwang informed us, were eligible to office at eighteen; this is said to arise from the wish of government to bring them early into employment: there are four different races of Tartars in China; he himself is a Mongul, or, as called in China, a Mun-koo.
passages.speaker: Henry Ellis, reporting the Mongol official Kwang

passages.headline: The 'Tartar ceremony': nine knocks of the head
passages.gloss: The embassy's quarrel was over the 'Tartar ceremony' demanded before the emperor. Ellis notes that the English word kowtow is loose: the court rite is properly 'thrice kneeling and nine times bowing the head', a Manchu court protocol.
passages.quote: The Tartar ceremonial has perhaps improperly been rendered by the Chinese word ko-tou, which more strictly signifies three simple genuflexions, a mode of salutation practised even in private life. The court ceremony has a different name, implying thrice kneeling and nine times bowing the head, San-kwei-keu-kou.
passages.speaker: Henry Ellis (footnote)

passages.headline: Manchu troops in long robes
passages.gloss: From the boats Ellis sees soldiers under distinctive flags pointed out as Manchu Tartars. Their weapons look like Chinese troops', but they wear long gowns instead of jackets.
passages.quote: Last evening we observed some troops on the opposite bank with peculiar flags, which were described as Man-tchoo Tartars. There did not seem any difference in their arms or accoutrement, but instead of jackets they wore long dresses.
passages.speaker: Henry Ellis

passages.headline: What the Chinese fought to keep at the Tartar conquest
passages.gloss: Ellis notes that the executioners' conical caps kept an ancient shape that the Chinese had been anxious to preserve when the Manchus conquered China, along with the sanctity of their ancestors' tombs. It hints at what the Chinese cared most to keep under their new rulers.
passages.quote: These, I afterwards learnt, were the public executioners, and that the shape of their caps was one of ancient form, which the Chinese, at the Tartar conquest, were most anxious to retain. The sanctity of the tombs of their ancestors was another and more reasonable object of their anxiety.
passages.speaker: Henry Ellis (footnote)

passages.headline: Mukden, the emperor's hunting capital
passages.gloss: An official mentions Mukden (Shenyang), the old Manchu capital in Manchuria, where the emperor goes to hunt; Ellis records its Chinese name. The official feared being summoned to the imperial hunt.
passages.quote: Chang called Moukden, Moulin; but the latter may be the Chinese pronunciation of the name. The Emperor goes there to hunt.
passages.speaker: Henry Ellis

passages.headline: Great monuments were Ming, not Tartar
passages.gloss: Ellis repeats a remark that China's great national monuments and best works of art all date from the Ming dynasty, and adds his own jibe that the Tartar conquerors brought barbarism without their ancestors' energy. It is an opinion about who built China's monuments, not a survey.
passages.quote: It has been remarked that all the great national monuments were executed in the reign of the Ming dynasty; the best works of art of all kinds belong to the same period, so that the last Tartar conquerors of China would seem to have communicated the barbarism without the energy of their ancestors.
passages.speaker: Henry Ellis
passages.caution: A prejudiced generalisation; the Qing built a great deal, including the palaces and temples at Chengde described by Barrow (W058).

passages.headline: Villagers told to hide their women from 'Tartar' brutes
passages.gloss: An imperial edict ordered villagers along the route to stay at work and women to keep out of the foreigners' sight. A Chinese general explained why: an earlier party of Tartars from 'barbarous tribes' passing through had assaulted village women, and all foreigners were suspected of the same.
passages.quote: A party of Tartars belonging to some barbarous tribes, passing through the country on a similar occasion to the present, violated the women of the villages on the route; and as all foreigners are alike despised by the Chinese, we, until known, were suspected of equal brutality.
passages.speaker: Henry Ellis, reporting General Wang
passages.caution: Hearsay from an official; the tribe, date and place are not given.

passages.headline: Are Tartars really great horsemen?
passages.gloss: Told that the emperor loves hunting and excels with the bow, Ellis adds a footnote: the missionaries praise Tartars as superb horsemen, but judging by the horses he saw, he doubts they could manage fast manoeuvres.
passages.quote: The account of the Missionaries represent the Tartars as excellent horsemen, and that the arts of the manege are various, and much attended to. I had no opportunity of verifying the truth of this description; from the appearance of the horses I should doubt their being equal to rapid manoeuvre.
passages.speaker: Henry Ellis (footnote)
passages.caution: Ellis admits he could not check the missionaries' claim.

passages.headline: Tartars who look and dress like the Chinese
passages.gloss: Barrow says the Manchu conquerors took over Chinese dress, manners and laws and, being in his view of the same stock, are hardly distinguishable from the Chinese except that they are shorter and stockier. On the following pages he contrasts their blunt, rough character with Chinese ceremoniousness.
passages.quote: The Tartars, by assuming the dress, the manners, and the habits of the Chinese, by being originally descended from the same stock, and by a great resemblance of features, are scarcely distinguishable from them in their external appearance. And if any physical difference exist, it seems to be in stature only
passages.speaker: John Barrow
passages.caution: The 'same stock' idea is Barrow's racial theory, not an observation.

passages.headline: Fair Manchus with blue eyes and bushy beards
passages.gloss: Barrow noticed some Manchu men and women who were very fair, with blue eyes, straight or aquiline noses, brown hair and big beards, 'more the appearance of Greeks than of Tartars'. He guesses at Greek ancestry from Sogdiana, notes that the Qianlong Emperor boasted of descent from Genghis Khan, and stresses these were exceptions.
passages.quote: The Man-tchoo Tartars would appear to be composed of a mixed race: among these we observed several, both men and women, that were extremely fair and of florid complexions: some had light blue eyes, straight or aquiline noses, brown hair, immense bushy beards, and had much more the appearance of Greeks than of Tartars.
passages.speaker: John Barrow
passages.caution: Barrow himself calls these exceptions; the Greek-descent explanation is pure guesswork.

passages.headline: Beijing's Tartar women ride astride and walk the streets
passages.gloss: In Beijing Barrow saw women in the crowds, in the lanes and on horseback riding like men, and all of them were Tartars (Manchus). Unlike Chinese women, they did not bind their feet: on the next page he describes their thick-soled shoes and painted faces, while Chinese women stayed indoors.
passages.quote: Women in Pekin were commonly seen among the crowd, or walking in the narrow streets, or riding on horseback, which they crossed in the same manner as the men, but they were all Tartars. They wore long silken robes, reaching down to their feet
passages.speaker: John Barrow

passages.headline: Under the bamboo: the Chinese cry, the Tartar is silent
passages.gloss: Travelling south, Barrow saw beatings with the bamboo almost daily. He contrasts the two peoples: a Chinese cries out and thanks the official on his knees, while a Tartar bears it silently and then grumbles, disputing a Chinese official's right to flog him.
passages.quote: In travelling through the country, a day seldom escaped without our witnessing the application of the Pan-tsé, or bamboo… A Chinese suffering under this punishment cries out in the most piteous manner; a Tartar bears it in silence.
passages.speaker: John Barrow
passages.caution: A generalisation from what he happened to see.

passages.headline: Imperial palaces 'modelled after the form of a tent'
passages.gloss: Barrow, who lived weeks inside the Yuanmingyuan, says the palaces of Beijing are a letdown after the missionaries' praise. Like ordinary Chinese houses they follow the shape of a tent: one storey, big roofs, wooden columns, paint and gilding, crowded by mean huts. He compares them to St James's Palace, and not kindly.
passages.quote: Those who should rely on the florid relations, in which the missionaries and some travellers have indulged in their descriptions of the palaces of Pekin and those of Yuen-min-yuen, would experience on visiting them a woful disappointment. These buildings, like the common habitations of the country, are all modelled after the form of a tent
passages.speaker: John Barrow
passages.caution: Barrow is describing Chinese architecture in general, not a Manchu style; his tone is deliberately deflating.

passages.headline: The wall that divides China from Tartary
passages.gloss: Barrow calls the Great Wall, built against the Tartars, China's most stupendous work: a mound of earth faced with brick or stone like Beijing's walls. On the next page he calculates that its masonry would equal all the houses of England and Scotland and credits it to the First Emperor.
passages.quote: But the most stupendous work of this country is the great wall that divides it from northern Tartary. It is built exactly upon the same plan as the wall of Pekin
passages.speaker: John Barrow
passages.caution: Barrow did not cross the wall himself (he stayed near Beijing while Macartney went to Jehol); he relies on Captain Parish's survey for the embassy.

passages.headline: The Grand Canal: a Mongol work, or only a Mongol repair?
passages.gloss: Barrow credits the successors of Genghis Khan with opening a waterway joining the two ends of the empire, praising it as the highest credit to the Mongol Tartars. He records the Chinese counter-claim that the Tartars only repaired older works. Elsewhere he says Kublai 'repaired' the canal.
passages.quote: the successors of Gengis-Khan were induced to open a direct communication between the two extremes of the empire, by means of the rivers and canals; an undertaking that reflects the highest credit on the Mongul Tartars, and which cannot fail to be regarded with admiration, as long as it shall continue to exist. The Chinese, however, say, that the Tartars only repaired the old works that were fallen into decay.
passages.speaker: John Barrow

passages.headline: Temples built in Tartary by the Qianlong Emperor
passages.gloss: Describing the Qianlong Emperor, Barrow cites as proof of his piety the many splendid Buddhist temples he built and endowed in 'oriental Tartary', the grandest being the Potala-style monastery at Jehol (Chengde), where Macartney was received.
passages.quote: The sincerity of his faith may partly be inferred from the numerous and splendid temples he built and endowed in different parts of oriental Tartary, of which the Poo-ta-la, or convent of Budha at Gehol, is the most magnificent.
passages.speaker: John Barrow
passages.caution: Barrow did not go to Jehol himself; he relies on Macartney's party.

passages.headline: The Manchu script, 'more like the Greek'
passages.gloss: Barrow describes the Manchu 'Tartar' language as alphabetic (or syllabic), inflected like European tongues, rich in B and R sounds, written in vertical columns from the left, and 'full, sonorous'. He predicted it would replace Chinese at court within a century.
passages.quote: the Man-tchoo Tartar character, which, if the present family continue on the throne for a century longer, will, in all probability, supplant the Chinese, or will at least become the court language. In the enunciation it is full, sonorous, and far from being disagreeable, more like the Greek than any of the oriental languages
passages.speaker: John Barrow
passages.caution: His prediction proved wrong: Manchu declined and Chinese prevailed at the Qing court.

passages.headline: Noah's Ark grounded in Tartary
passages.gloss: In a chapter on Chinese origins Barrow argues that the 'heights of Tartary' are the highest land in the Old World, so the Ark probably first touched ground there rather than in Armenia, and that Tartars and Chinese share one origin. He suggests Noah's survivors may have followed the rivers down into China.
passages.quote: we may suppose that the ark, instead of resting in Armenia, first struck ground in that part of Tartary which is now inhabited by the Eleuths, as being the most elevated tract of country in the old world. From these heights large rivers flow towards every quarter of the horizon.
passages.speaker: John Barrow
passages.caution: Pure speculation built on the biblical Flood and faulty geography.

passages.headline: Chinese funeral figures as a relic of Scythian burials
passages.gloss: Barrow says the Chinese once buried slaves and concubines with rulers, now replaced by tinfoil figures and statues on graves. He guesses this descends from a Scythian or Tartar custom that Herodotus described, in which horses, slaves and concubines were killed and set around a king's tomb.
passages.quote: Formerly it was the custom to bury slaves with emperors and princes and sometimes also their concubines alive… this seems to be the remains of a Scythian or Tartar custom, which, according to Herodotus, was commonly observed at the funerals of their sovereigns, when their horses, their slaves, and their concubines were impaled alive and placed in order round the tyrant's tomb.
passages.speaker: John Barrow
passages.caution: The Tartar link is Barrow's guess from Herodotus.

passages.headline: Kublai Khan imports astronomers from Balkh and Samarkand
passages.gloss: Barrow credits the Mongol emperor Kublai with welcoming learned men, especially Muslims, surveying the empire, reforming the calendar, bringing astronomical instruments from Balkh and Samarkand, and repairing the canal. He adds that after the Mongols were expelled the Chinese could not keep a correct almanac.
passages.quote: He caused a regular survey to be taken of the whole empire. He adjusted their chronology, and corrected the errors of their astronomical observations; he imported various mathematical and astronomical instruments from Balk and Samarcand; such as were then in use among the Chinese being of a rude construction
passages.speaker: John Barrow
passages.caution: Compiled from Chinese annals and missionary writings.

passages.headline: An emperor who preferred a tent to a palace
