passages.gloss: The Qianlong emperor received the British envoy not in a hall of his summer palace but in a great tent in the garden, with small round tents pitched in front for the tributary princes. Staunton explains the choice: the Manchu rulers had adopted Chinese customs but kept a fondness for their old movable dwellings when they were on 'Tartar ground'.
passages.quote: The Tartar dynasty, in conforming in most instances, to the customs of a much more numerous and more civilized, tho vanquished nation, retained still a predilection for its own ancient manners, in which occasionally, and upon Tartar ground, it took a pleasure in indulging. The moveable dwelling of a tent was, more than a permanent palace of stone and timber, the favourite residence of a Tartar sovereign.
passages.speaker: George Leonard Staunton
passages.caution: The explanation of the emperor's motive is Staunton's interpretation.

passages.headline: A Tibetan temple in Tartary that looked European
passages.people: Manchus and Mongols (Qing court); Tibetan Buddhist lamas
passages.gloss: Near the summer palace the party visited the 'Poo-ta-la', the great lama temple the emperor had built (today's Putuo Zongcheng temple, modelled on the Potala of Lhasa). Staunton found it unlike any Chinese building and oddly like a European front, eleven stories of windows high, with a golden chapel inside whose roof plates were said to be solid gold. He credits the building to the emperor himself.
passages.quote: the outside very much resembling the front of an European edifice. It was of great height, containing eleven rows of windows, implying as many stories, or ranges of apartments, one above another. … The square, or principal building of Poo-ta-la, includes a quadrangle, in the centre of which is the golden chapel, so termed from the materials in which it, apparently at least, abounds.
passages.speaker: George Leonard Staunton
passages.caution: The 'European' look is Staunton's comparison; the page before says the temples round Zhe-hol 'had been erected by the Emperor'. The gold was 'said to be' solid.

passages.headline: A solid brick tower thought to guard against Tartars
passages.gloss: At Tong-choo-foo, the river port of Beijing, the embassy examined an old eleven-storey brick pagoda with no door or window in its solid lower stories. Nobody knew what it had been for; the guess Staunton reports is that it was an ancient watch tower against sudden Tartar raids.
passages.quote: It is built of brick, and in its exterior form resembles what are called in Europe Chinese pagodas … It is thought most probable that this building was erected prior to the existence of Tong-choo-foo, and perhaps of the great Chinese wall, and was intended for a watch tower, to guard against the sudden approach of the Tartar enemy.
passages.speaker: George Leonard Staunton
passages.caution: Staunton admits the tower's 'original destination is not known with certainty'; the watch-tower idea is a conjecture, and many solid brick pagodas in north China were Buddhist relic towers.

passages.headline: Why part of Beijing was called the Tartar city
passages.gloss: Staunton describes Beijing as two walled cities side by side. The northern and larger one, with the imperial palace at its centre, was called the Tartar city; he explains the name by its being laid out anew under the first Tartar (Mongol) dynasty in the thirteenth century. The page after describes the 'Chinese city' adjoining its southern wall, half empty and partly under cultivation.
passages.quote: The principal part of it is called the Tartar city, from the circumstance of having been laid out anew in the thirteenth century in the time of the first Tartar dynasty. It is in the form of a parallelogram … in the centre of which is the imperial palace, occupying within the yellow wall at least one square mile.
passages.speaker: George Leonard Staunton
passages.caution: The origin of the name is Staunton's explanation; other European writers tied 'Tartar city' to the Manchu banner garrison that lived there under the Qing.

passages.headline: Hovels and palaces at the emperor's summer town
passages.gloss: Zhe-hol (Jehol, modern Chengde), beyond the Great Wall, was the Qing emperors' summer capital in Tartary. Staunton contrasts the poor, crooked town with the grandeur of the imperial palaces, gardens and temples just beyond it. He adds that the principal buildings 'in this part of Tartary' differed little from those of China.
passages.quote: The town of Zhe-hol, excepting the houses of mandarines, consisted of miserable hovels full of people. The streets also were crooked, unpaved, and dusty. Immediately beyond it, the imperial garden, the palaces, the temples displayed much grandeur; and magnificence and wretchedness knew no medium.
passages.speaker: George Leonard Staunton

passages.headline: Born in Beijing, but still Tartars
passages.gloss: Staunton explains that the Qianlong emperor, though four generations removed from the conquest and born in Beijing, was seen by everyone, and saw himself, as a Tartar. His ministers, generals, wives and servants were mostly of the same race, and every male of Tartar descent drew a stipend from birth. Here 'Tartar' plainly means the Manchu conquerors.
passages.quote: Tho the Emperor Chen-Lung, be the fourth in descent from him who successfully invaded China in the last age, and tho the last three succeeding generations were all born at Pekin, yet they are universally regarded by their subjects, and they regarded indeed themselves, as Tartars. Their principal ministers, their confidential servants, the chiefs of their armies, most of their wives, concubines, domestics, and eunuchs, are of that race.
passages.speaker: George Leonard Staunton

passages.headline: A story that the Manchu emperors came from Kublai Khan
passages.gloss: The Tartar princes at court, Staunton says, revered the emperor as a descendant of Kublai Khan: Kublai's heirs, driven out of China in the fourteenth century, fled to the Manchus, intermarried, and produced the 'Bog-doi Khans' who conquered China. It shows how the Qing dynasty was presented to, or understood by, its Mongol allies.
passages.quote: They hold the Emperor in the greater veneration, as considering him descended from Kublai-Khan, the conqueror of China in the thirteenth century. His descendants being in the fourteenth century expelled from the throne of that empire, fled into the country of the Man-choos in Eastern Tartary; and from their intermarriages with the natives, sprung the Bog-doi Khans
passages.speaker: George Leonard Staunton
passages.caution: A genealogical belief reported at second hand; the Qing ruling clan is usually traced to Jurchen (Manchu) chiefs, not to Kublai.

passages.headline: Kalmyk chiefs who fled Russia for China
passages.people: Manchus and Mongols at court; Kalmyks from the Volga
passages.gloss: At the emperor's birthday theatricals most of the guests who came to meet the British envoy were Tartars, since few Chinese were invited to Zhe-hol. Among them were two chiefs of 'Calmoucks' whose people had recently left Russian rule on the Caspian and migrated to Chinese Tartary, an event of 1771.
passages.quote: Most of them were Tartars ; few original Chinese being invited to Zhe-hol. There were likewise two Mussulmen, chiefs of some hordes of Calmoucks, who, not long since, on occasion of discontent or misunderstanding with the government of Russia, migrated in great numbers from the northern coast of the Caspian sea into Chinese Tartary, and put themselves under the Emperor's protection.
passages.speaker: George Leonard Staunton
passages.caution: The Kalmyks (Torghuts) who made the 1771 migration were Tibetan Buddhists, so calling their chiefs 'Mussulmen' looks like a confusion.

passages.headline: 'No Chinese may punish me on the Tartar side of the wall'
passages.gloss: Although Chinese and Tartars had one master, Staunton found the Great Wall still treated as the boundary between two peoples. Just past it, a Tartar attendant facing punishment by Chinese mandarins loudly refused, claiming they had no authority over him on the Tartar side. On the next page a Chinese mandarin dares not sit before a Tartar officer of equal rank.
passages.quote: The line it has traced, continues still to be considered as a demarkation between the respective nations of Chinese and Tartars. … one of the Tartar attendants was about to be punished for some misdemeanour, by order of the Chinese mandarines; but he resisted with much vehemence, loudly exclaiming, that no Chinese had a right of exercising authority over him on the Tartar side of the great wall.
passages.speaker: George Leonard Staunton

passages.headline: Tartar women with unbound feet
passages.gloss: Crossing Beijing, the embassy noticed that most women in the watching crowds were said to be of Tartar race. Unlike Chinese women their feet were not bound, and they wore broad-toed shoes with thick soles. On the next page Staunton adds that some Tartar ladies rode on horseback astride, like men.
passages.quote: Among the spectators of the novel sight, some women were observed. The greatest number were said to be natives of Tartary, or of a Tartar race. Their feet were not cramped, like those of the Chinese; and their shoes with broad toes, and soles above an inch in thickness, were as clumsy as those of the original Chinese ladies were diminutive.
passages.speaker: George Leonard Staunton

passages.headline: Tartar soldiers paid double
passages.gloss: From a Chinese officer's figures Staunton reports that much of the cavalry was Tartar, that Tartars held the posts of trust, and that a Tartar horseman drew seven ounces of silver and twenty measures of rice a month, against three and three-tenths ounces and fifteen measures for a Chinese horseman.
passages.quote: Of the troops, especially cavalry, a vast number are Tartars, who have a higher pay than their Chinese fellow soldiers. The principal officers of confidence in the army are Tartars also. … A Tartar horseman, seven similar ounces of silver, and twenty measures of rice for the same period.
passages.speaker: George Leonard Staunton
passages.caution: Figures supplied by the mandarin Van-ta-Zhin, whom Staunton thinks candid but not always careful.

passages.headline: The Tartar princes and their fiefs
passages.gloss: After the birthday festivities the tributary Tartar princes went home. Staunton describes them as chiefs of large clans who owed troops in wartime under the 'grand banners of Tartary', held hereditary fiefs that needed the emperor's investiture, and usually married women of the imperial family.
passages.quote: They were the chiefs of numerous clans dependent on them, and could bring large bodies of troops into the field. They were often called upon in time of war, and had their respective stations, rank, and duty, assigned to them under the grand banners of Tartary. Their lands, or fiefs, were properly hereditary by primogeniture
passages.speaker: George Leonard Staunton

passages.headline: Horses stabled in the emperors' palaces
passages.people: Mongols ('Mongol Tartars'), as remembered by the Chinese
passages.gloss: On the Grand Canal Staunton notes that the Chinese still looked on Tartars in general as barbarians. As proof they told a four-hundred-year-old story about the Mongol capture of Beijing: the conquerors lived in tents and put their horses in the imperial palaces.
passages.quote: they repeat the story, popular amongst them for four centuries, that when the Mongol Tartars seized first upon Pekin, they erected tents for their own accommodation, while they put their horses in the palaces of the Chinese emperors.
passages.speaker: George Leonard Staunton
passages.caution: A popular Chinese tale, reported as such; not evidence of what happened in 1215.

passages.headline: Running the gauntlet past Tatar Astrakhan by moonlight
passages.gloss: Nikitin sails down the Volga past Kazan, the Horde and Sarai, then meets three Tatars who warn of a sultan watching for merchants. Paid to guide the party around Astrakhan, they betray it to the khan ('zar'), and the Russian boats are chased. It is a first-person glimpse of the Volga still ruled by Tatar khanates.
passages.quote: We passed unmolested through Kazan, the Orda, Ooslan, Sarai, and Berekezany, and we entered the river Buzan. Here we fell in with three godless Tartars, who told us false tidings … We sailed by Astrakhan at moonlight. The zar perceived us, and at once the Tartars cried : " Do not fly ;" and the zar ordered the whole orda to chase us.
passages.speaker: Afanasy Nikitin (translated by Count Wielhorski, 1857)
passages.caution: Translated from a difficult late fifteenth-century Russian text; 'zar' is the translator's rendering of the title Nikitin gives the khan of Astrakhan.

passages.headline: Sarai, once the Horde's capital, now a heap of stones
passages.gloss: A footnote to Nikitin's route explains that Sarai, on the Akhtuba branch of the Volga, had been the capital of the Golden Horde, where Russian grand dukes went for two centuries to pay tribute. By the nineteenth century it was reduced to ruins. The note is a useful reminder that the Horde did have a real capital city, and that it was well known to Russian historians.
passages.quote: Sarai, now a heap of stones and the abode of loathsome reptiles, still observable on the borders of the Akhtouba, an arm of the Volga, forty-six miles from the sea, was at that time the capital of the great or Golden Orda, the famous residence of the great conqueror Baty, the place where, during two centuries, the Grand-Dukes of Russia had to pay their allegiance and their tribute
passages.speaker: Editorial footnote in the 1857 Hakluyt Society edition (translator Count Wielhorski or editor R. H. Major)
passages.caution: Nineteenth-century editorial comment, not Nikitin. The neighbouring note on Kazan reads '1052' in this OCR, evidently for 1552.

passages.headline: What 'Orda' meant
passages.people: Tartar khans who ruled Russia; the Golden Horde and Crimean Horde
passages.gloss: Nikitin passes 'the Orda' on the Volga. The editor explains that 'orda' (horde) was the name for the seats of the Tartar kings who ruled Russia, and later for the successor kingdoms such as the Golden Horde and the Crimean Horde. It shows that 'horde' named a royal seat or state, not just a mob of riders.
passages.quote: This is the name formerly given to the seats of the Tartar kings that ruled over Russia ; subsequently it was also applied to the different kingdoms that sprung up from the immense empire of Baty in the beginning of the fifteenth century ; as the Zolotaia Orda (golden or great orda), Krimskaia Orda, the Ordea of Crimea, etc, etc.
passages.speaker: Editorial footnote in the 1857 Hakluyt Society edition

passages.headline: Scythians 'called at the present day Tartars'
passages.gloss: The humanist Poggio Bracciolini, writing up travellers' reports in Rome, describes an envoy from 'upper India' who crossed the lands of the northern Scythians on his way west. Poggio adds that these Scythians are now called Tartars, a typical Renaissance habit of mapping the new name onto the classical one.
passages.quote: Travelling through the country of the northern Scythians, who are called at the present day Tartars, and of the Parthians, for the space of several months, he arrived at length at the Euphrates ; then, having embarked at Tripoli, he proceeded to Venice, and afterwards to Florence.
passages.speaker: Poggio Bracciolini (translated by J. Winter Jones, 1857)
passages.caution: Poggio relays an envoy's report through an interpreter; the Scythian identification is a learned label, not observation.

passages.headline: The Great Khan's square capital, by hearsay
passages.gloss: Conti, as retold by Poggio, describes Cathay, whose lord is the Great Khan, and its capital Cambaleschia (Khanbaliq, the Mongol name for Beijing): a square city with a central palace-fortress and four round corner fortresses linked by a vaulted wall. By Conti's time the Mongols had been expelled and a Ming emperor ruled there, so this is a mix of older fame and report.
passages.quote: The lord of this country is called the Great Khan, which in the language of the inhabitants means emperor. The principal city is called Cambaleschia. It is built in the form of a quadrangle, and is twenty-eight miles in circumference. In the centre is a very handsome and strong fortress, in which is situated the king's palace.
passages.speaker: Niccolò de' Conti as recorded by Poggio Bracciolini (translated by J. Winter Jones, 1857)
passages.caution: Conti did not visit Cathay as far as the text shows; the title 'Great Khan' for the ruler of China was out of date by then.

passages.headline: Plundered by the Kaitaks, 'a Tartar tribe'
passages.people: Kaitaks (called a Tartar tribe by the editor)
passages.gloss: After a storm wrecks one of their boats on the Caspian shore, Nikitin's party is seized and robbed by the Kaitaks near Tarki. The Shah of Shirvan then negotiates with the Kaitak prince, his brother-in-law, for their release. The footnote labels the Kaitaks a Tartar tribe of Daghestan, an example of how widely the label was stretched.
passages.quote: A storm having arisen at sea, the smaller boat was wrecked on shore. Then came the Kaitaks and made the whole party prisoners, and we came to Derbend
passages.speaker: Afanasy Nikitin (translated by Count Wielhorski, 1857); tribe identified in editorial footnote
passages.caution: The Kaitaks of Daghestan were a Caucasian people; 'Tartar tribe' is the 1857 note's label, not Nikitin's.

passages.headline: Tall carts carrying round felt houses
passages.people: Tatars of the Golden Horde (the camp of Küchük Muhammad)
passages.gloss: Barbaro watched the whole horde pass Tana and describes its vehicles: two-wheeled carts taller than Italian ones, closed with reed mats and covered with felt or cloth depending on rank. Some carried a house built on a timber ring with half-hoops above, filled with reed mats and covered in felt, which was lifted off when they camped.
passages.quote: This people carie with them innumerable cartes of twoo wheeles higher than ours be, which are closed with mattes made of reades, and parte covered with felte, parte with clothe … Some of these cartes carie their houses vpon them which are made on this wise. They take a cercle of tymber, whose dyameter is a pase and an halfe, crossed within foorthe with other halfe cercles
passages.speaker: Giosafat Barbaro (Tudor translation by William Thomas, c. 1550)
passages.caution: Scribal abbreviations in the Tudor text (w^th, pte) have been expanded.

passages.headline: 'He that is afraid builds towers'
passages.gloss: Barbaro insists the horde was not a band of vagabonds: it carried clothiers, smiths and armourers, and its camps looked like great fair cities, only without walls. When he showed a Tatar merchant the fine tower over Tana's gate, the man smiled and said towers are built by the fearful. Barbaro thought he was right.
passages.quote: In this armie are many artisanes, as clothiers, smythes, armorers, and of all other craftes and things that they neede. … For (saving that they are not walled about) they seeme verie great and faire cities. … I saied vnto a Tartarien marchant … howe thinkest thou, is not this a faire thinge ? But he, smiling, againe answered, he that is afearde buyldeth towres
passages.speaker: Giosafat Barbaro (Tudor translation by William Thomas, c. 1550)

passages.headline: Burial mounds with stone crosses, credited to the Alans
passages.people: Alans (As), 'chased awaie and destroied by the Tartares'
passages.gloss: Describing the land around Tana, Barbaro says the countless mounds on the steppe are graves, each topped with a pierced stone holding a stone cross. He credits them to the Alans, a Christian people destroyed by the Tartars, not to the Tartars themselves.
passages.quote: These have been Christen men, and were chased awaie and destroied by the Tartares. In that region are hills, ryvers, and plaines : wheare are to be seene an infinite nombre of little hills forced in signe or steede of sepultures, and on the toppe of everie of them a great stone with an hole : wherein standeth a crosse of one peece made of an other stone.
passages.speaker: Giosafat Barbaro (Tudor translation by William Thomas, c. 1550)
passages.caution: The crosses may be later Christian additions or Barbaro's reading of stone markers; most steppe kurgans are far older than the Alans.

passages.headline: Venetian treasure-hunters dig a kurgan
passages.gloss: Tipped off by a story that a Tatar woman in Cairo had told of Alan treasure, Barbaro and six partners hired 120 men and dug into a great mound. Instead of gold they found layers of ash, millet husks and fish scales, then stone vessels, glass-covered brick beads and part of a silver ewer. The dig was so big that locals renamed the mound 'the cave of the Franks'.
passages.quote: we founde in the botome certein vessels of stone, some of them with asshes, some with coles, some emptie and some full of fishe back bones. We founde also v or vi beadestones as bigge as oranges made of bricke and covered with glasse … We founde also halfe the handle of a little ewer of sylver, made with an adders hedde on the toppe.
passages.speaker: Giosafat Barbaro (Tudor translation by William Thomas, c. 1550)
passages.caution: The treasure story came at third hand; Barbaro repeats the local explanation that the Alan lord Indiabu faked a grave to hide his wealth from the Tartar emperor.

passages.headline: Nomads who sowed and reaped
passages.gloss: Barbaro answers the obvious question of where so many people got their grain. Each February the horde announced where sowing would happen; volunteers went with seed, carts and families, ploughed and sowed, and later returned to harvest while the khan's camp circled nearby. He says the yields were huge.
passages.quote: About the mooneth of Februarie they make proclamacons throughout the Lordo, that he which woll sowe shall prepare his things necessarie against the mooneth of Marche, to sowe in such a place. … And there do they eare, sowe, and tarie, till they haue furnisshed that they came for, which doon they retorne to their Lordo.
passages.speaker: Giosafat Barbaro (Tudor translation by William Thomas, c. 1550)

passages.headline: Justice on the spot
passages.gloss: In the camp, Barbaro says, quarrels were settled without violence or paperwork: the parties walked off together and asked the first respectable man they met to judge, and his verdict was accepted, with bystanders as witnesses. He also describes petitioners kneeling repeatedly as they approached the lord's pavilion.
passages.quote: Whan a difference groweth betwene partie and partie, and wordes multiplied (not aftre the maner of our quarters, for these do vse no violence), thei both or moo (if they be moo) arise and go what waie they thinke good : and to the first man of any estimacon that they meete they saie : Master, do vs right, for we here are in controversie
passages.speaker: Giosafat Barbaro (Tudor translation by William Thomas, c. 1550)

passages.headline: Islam arrives, idols linger
passages.gloss: Barbaro says Islam had taken hold among the Tartars only about a hundred years before he wrote, in the time of the warlord Edigu. Before that, some were Muslims but each believed what he liked, and some worshipped idols of wood and rags carried on their carts. On another page a Tatar tells him there are still plenty of secret idolaters.
passages.quote: The faith of Macomett beganne to take place amonge the Tartariens about an C yeres past. In dede some of them were Macomettanes before, but everie man was at his libertie to believe what hym best liked ; so that some worshipped ymags of woode, and of ragges
passages.speaker: Giosafat Barbaro (Tudor translation by William Thomas, c. 1550)
passages.caution: Historians usually date the Golden Horde's official conversion to Khan Uzbek (1313); Barbaro's timeline reflects what he was told.

passages.headline: The 'valiant fool'
passages.gloss: The bravest Tatar warriors, Barbaro says, earned the title 'Tulubagator', which he translates 'valiant fool', an honour like 'the wise' or 'the handsome' in Italy. The editor explains it as tulu bahadur; bahadur is the root of the Russian bogatyr, hero. He follows it with the story of a Tatar merchant who chased forty Circassians alone.
passages.quote: The hablemen are verie valiaunt and hardie, in such wise that some of them for their excellencie are called Tulubagator, which signifieth a valiaunt foole : being a name of no lesse reputacon amongst them than the sernames of wisedome or beaultie with vs
passages.speaker: Giosafat Barbaro (Tudor translation by William Thomas, c. 1550)
passages.caution: 'Fool' is Barbaro's own gloss; the etymological note is the 1873 editor's.

passages.headline: Astrakhan, great before Tamerlane
passages.gloss: Barbaro calls Astrakhan ('Cithercan') a little town almost destroyed, but once great and famous: before Timur (Tamerlane) sacked it, spices and silk came up through it to Tana and were shipped to Venice. It is a clear statement that a Tatar trading city existed, flourished and was ruined by a known conqueror.
passages.quote: the ryver Ledil, whereon standeth Cithercan, which at this present is but a litle towne in maner destroied ; albeit, that in tyme passed it hath been great and of great fame. For, before it was destroied by Tamerlano, the spices and silke that passe nowe through Soria came to Cithercan, and from thense to Tana
passages.speaker: Giosafat Barbaro (Tudor translation by William Thomas, c. 1550)

passages.headline: Kazan, the 'cauldron' town of furs
passages.gloss: Barbaro notes the turn of the tide: the Russians once paid tribute to the Tartar emperor, but Moscow had now subdued Kazan on the Volga. He calls Kazan a town of great trade, the source of most furs sent to Moscow, Poland, Prussia and Flanders, and says its name means 'cauldron'.
passages.quote: nowe they haue subdued a towne called Cassan (which, in our tonge, signifieth a cawldron), that standeth on the ryver Ledil, on the lefte hande as you go towards the Sea of Bachu … This is a towne of great merchaundise. From whense cometh the most parte of the furres that are caried to Musco and into Polonia, Prusia, and Flandres
passages.speaker: Giosafat Barbaro (Tudor translation by William Thomas, c. 1550)
passages.caution: Moscow's 1487 capture of Kazan installed a client khan; the city was not annexed until 1552.

passages.headline: The Crimean Tatars' two walled places
passages.gloss: Barbaro says the Crimean plain was ruled by Tatars who could raise three or four thousand horse and had two walled but weak places: Solkhat, also called Crimea ('Incremin', meaning fortress), and 'Cherchiarde', meaning forty places. These are Eski Kırım and Kırk Yer (Chufut-Kale), early seats of the Crimean khans.
passages.quote: The champaigne of this He of Capha is vnder the Tartariens domynion … they haue twoo places walled, but not stronge, thone whereof is called Sorgathi, which they also called Incremin, that signifieth a forteresse ; and thother Cherchiarde, which signifieth xl placs.
passages.speaker: Giosafat Barbaro (Tudor translation by William Thomas, c. 1550)
passages.caution: 'He' is the OCR's reading of 'Ile' (isle), Barbaro's word for the Crimean peninsula; the identifications with Eski Kırım and Kırk Yer are modern.

passages.headline: A rescued Tatar slave in a Venetian wine cellar
passages.gloss: In a Rialto wine cellar Barbaro found two chained men who looked like Tartars, runaway slaves of the Catalans recaptured by the vintner. He had them freed by the magistrates and took them home. One turned out to be a servant of the khan's customs officer at Tana, who recognised Barbaro's Tana name, Jusuph, and fell to the ground.
passages.quote: I asked him what was his name. He answered, Chebechzi, which signifieth a bulter of meale. And whan I had well behelde him, I saied vnto him, doest thou knowe me ? He answered, no. But, as soone as I mentioned Tana and Jusuph (for so they called me there), he fell to thearthe, and wolde haue kissed my feete : saieng vnto me, thou hast saved my lief twies
passages.speaker: Giosafat Barbaro (Tudor translation by William Thomas, c. 1550)

passages.headline: Cut in half for stealing a pail of milk
passages.people: Chinese of Cathay, as described by a Tartar ambassador's servants
passages.gloss: A Tartar ambassador returning from Cathay lodged in Barbaro's house at Tana. His servant told 'wonders' of Chinese justice: a man who drank a widow's milk in the market was seized and cut in two on the spot. Barbaro passes it on as the ambassador's report, not something he saw.
passages.quote: being on a daye in Madian, which signifieth the markett place, they did see a woman carieng a payle of mylke on her heade, to whom one came that tooke it from her : and beginneng to drynke, she beganne to crye out … Wherevpon, he was incontinently taken, and with a swearde cutt in sonder by the myddest
passages.speaker: Giosafat Barbaro, reporting a Tartar ambassador's servants (Tudor translation by William Thomas)
passages.caution: A traveller's tale told at second hand about Ming China.

passages.headline: A horse stuffed with straw and worshipped
passages.people: The Moxii (Moksha Mordvins), grouped by Barbaro with northern 'idolater' Tartars
passages.gloss: Barbaro says the northern lands of Zagatai and Moxia were inhabited by Tartars who were mostly idolaters, then describes a Moxii rite: a horse staked down and shot with arrows, eaten, its hide stuffed with straw and propped up as if alive. On the next page he says it was set on a scaffold in a tree and worshipped, with furs hung as offerings, and that other idolater Tartars worship images carried on their carts.
passages.quote: At a certein tyme of the yere they vse to take a horse : which they laie alonge on the plaine. … Than they stufe the hyde so full of strawe, that it seemeth hole again ; and in every of his legges putt a pece of woodde ; and so sett him afoote againe, as though he were on lyve.
passages.speaker: Giosafat Barbaro (Tudor translation by William Thomas, c. 1550)
passages.caution: The Moksha are a Finnic people, not Tatars; Barbaro says he 'learned' this, not that he saw it.

passages.headline: Baltracan, the plant that fed travellers
passages.gloss: In a letter to the Bishop of Padua, Barbaro describes 'Baltracan', a wild plant the Tartars depended on when crossing the steppe. When it sprouted, merchants set out saying 'Let us go, for the Baltracan has grown', and no one chased a runaway slave because he could live on it. He says he ate it himself and later found it in Albania and near Padua.
passages.quote: The Tartars have a plant in their country which they call Baltracan, the want of which would cause them great suffering, and prevent them from going from place to place, especially across those great deserts and solitudes, where they find nothing to eat except this plant, which supports them and gives them vigour.
passages.speaker: Giosafat Barbaro, letter of 1491 (translated 1873)
passages.caution: The plant's modern identity is not given in the text.

passages.headline: Astrakhan: a low wall and a few brick houses
passages.gloss: Contarini spent May to August 1476 at Astrakhan ('Citracan'). He says it belonged to three nephews of the Tatar emperor who wintered there and roamed the steppe in summer. The town was small, with a low wall and a few brick houses, but showed signs of larger buildings not long before, and was said to have once been a great trading place.
passages.quote: These three brothers remain in Citracan a few months in the winter, but in the summer do like the rest. Citracan is a small town situated on the Volga, and surrounded by a low wall. The few houses it contains are built of bricks ; but it is evident that it possessed several edifices at no very distant period.
passages.speaker: Ambrogio Contarini (translated by S. A. Roy, 1873)

passages.headline: Unwashed lamb and mare's milk that 'stank most horribly'
passages.gloss: Hiding from the khan's search on a Volga island, the starving Contarini was fed by his Tatar guide's people. They killed a lamb for him and cooked it without washing it, saying washing spoils the flavour. They pressed mare's milk on him as a strengthening drink, and were offended when he refused it.
passages.quote: a lamb was killed in my honour, which was partly roasted and partly boiled, but no trouble whatever was taken to wash the flesh, as they say that washing takes all the flavour away … Mare's milk was also brought, which they hold in great esteem … as they say it gives great strength to man; but, as it stank most horribly, I refused to taste it
passages.speaker: Ambrogio Contarini (translated by S. A. Roy, 1873)

passages.headline: The 'wild Tartars' with waist-long hair
passages.people: Tatars between the Don and Volga; 'wild Tartars' east of the Volga
passages.gloss: Contarini separates the Tatars of the 'Lordo' between the Don and Volga, whom he calls brutes who live on milk and meat, from another numerous people beyond the Volga, called 'wild Tartars', with hair to their waists. He admits he did not visit the Lordo himself and relies on what he was told.
passages.quote: But there is said to be another tribe of Tartars living beyond the Volga, in an east-north-easterly direction, who are supposed to be very numerous. They wear long hair reaching to their waists, and are called wild Tartars. They wander in search of pasturage and water like the others; and, in the winter, when there is much cold and ice, they are said to come as far as Citracan
passages.speaker: Ambrogio Contarini (translated by S. A. Roy, 1873)
passages.caution: Hearsay; Contarini's dislike of the Tatars shows throughout.

passages.headline: Rafts towed by swimming horses
passages.people: Crimean Tatars (escort sent by the khan)
passages.gloss: Travelling to Kaffa with a Lithuanian embassy escorted by Crimean Tatar horsemen, Contarini had to cross the broad river dividing Russia from Tartary. The Tatars built a raft of lashed timbers and branches, then swam their horses across holding their necks, with the raft tied to the horses' tails. He thought he had never been in greater danger.
passages.quote: the Tartars began to cut timbers, which they tied together, and covered with branches to form a raft, and our things being placed on it the Tartars entered the river holding on to their horses' necks, while our raft was attached to their tails by cords. Thus mounted, the horses were driven across the river, which we passed by the help of God.
passages.speaker: Ambrogio Contarini (translated by S. A. Roy, 1873)
passages.caution: The text does not name the river; the Dnieper is the likely crossing on this route.

passages.headline: A Nogai suburb of bulrush houses behind a wooden rampart
passages.gloss: Avril describes Astrakhan as a mixed trading city. The Armenians had one suburb and the Nogai Tartars another, which looked like a town of its own: a wooden rampart, its own governor under the Russian governor, a mosque, and about two thousand houses made mostly of bulrushes. He adds that the Russians treated the Nogais more as allies than subjects because they fought for them.
passages.quote: Armenians possess one of the Suburbs entirely to themselves, and the Nogais Tartars another, which altogether resembles a City, being fortifi'd with a Wooden-Rampart, and having a Governour who commands there, under the Orders of the Chief Governor of Astrakan. Within that Enclosure stands a Mosquee ; but the Houses are for the greatest part made of Bulrushes, of which there may be about two thousand.
passages.speaker: Philippe Avril (English translation, 1693)

passages.headline: 'No Cities nor fix'd Habitations'
passages.gloss: Summing up the Kalmyks, who ranged from Mongolia to the Volga, Avril says plainly that they had no cities or fixed homes, only neat, comfortable felt tents, and that no people could strike camp faster. On the same page he calls them idolaters who, like the Mongols, look to the Dalai Lama.
passages.quote: The Calmoucs have no Cities nor fix'd Habitations, but only live in Tents made of Felts, which are very neat, and very commodious; nor is there any Nation so nimble at Camping and Decamping in an instant as they, there being no Nation so much accustom'd to it, in regard they never stay long in a place, and are always making Incursions.
passages.speaker: Philippe Avril (English translation, 1693)
passages.caution: Avril met Kalmyks near Astrakhan, but this general statement comes from Moscow informants.

passages.headline: Manchu country: 'none but houses of Earth'
passages.gloss: From a Russian report, Avril describes the homeland of the Bogdoi, the Manchus who had conquered China. He says the houses there were all of earth, and that the people traded sables, black fox skins and ginseng, had few cattle and small unshod horses.
passages.quote: In all the Province of Bogdoi, you shall meet with none but houses of Earth … which people drive a great Trade in Sables and Black Fox-Skins, as likewise in Ginseng Roots : But they are not rich in Cattel ; their Horses are very small ; nor do their owners ever shooe 'em.
passages.speaker: Philippe Avril (English translation, 1693)
passages.caution: Second-hand, from a relation Avril says came out of the Moscow treasury (archives).

passages.headline: Why say 'Tartar' when they say 'Totar'?
passages.gloss: Avril reports that the Chinese call the Tartars 'Totai' because of a missing letter in their language, and then wonders why Western Europeans say 'Tartar' at all, when Poles, Russians and the Tartars themselves say 'Totar'. It is a rare early admission that the extra 'r' of 'Tartar' is a Western habit.
passages.quote: This Relation adds, that the Chineses call the Tartars Totai, because they have not the Letter K in their Language. Nor do I know why we call 'em Tartars, seeing that in Poland, Muscovy and even in Tartary it self, they abridge the Name, and call 'em only Totar.
passages.speaker: Philippe Avril (English translation, 1693)
passages.caution: The scan reads 'Letter K'; the sense (Chinese has no r sound) suggests the original printed 'R'.

passages.headline: The Bogdoi, 'Eastern Tartars' who took China
passages.gloss: Avril's first 'nation' beyond China's frontier is the Bogdoi, whom the Chinese call Eastern Tartars and the Mongols 'Niouchi' (Jurchen). The next page gives his version of their history: an early invasion of China, the Yuan family ruling to 1368, the Ming to 1644, and then the Bogdoi returning to conquer China under Shunzhi, first emperor of the reigning Qing.
passages.quote: The first Nation is that of the Bogdoi, by the Chineses call'd the Eastern Tartars, and whom the Monguls call Niouchi
passages.speaker: Philippe Avril (English translation, 1693)
passages.caution: His history is muddled; he credits the 'Tousbecks' (Uzbeks) with putting the Yuan family on the throne, where the Mongols are meant.

passages.headline: A hundred thousand Kalmyks every winter
passages.gloss: At Astrakhan Avril learned that the Kalmyks, though at peace with the Nogais, came every winter into the milder plains between Astrakhan and the Caspian to feed their herds, which were all their wealth. The Russians could not stop these visits of over 100,000 people, and paid yearly presents to prevent raids, which the Kalmyks came to treat as a duty owed.
passages.quote: Which Annual Visits of above a hunder'd thousand men at a time, though they Be no way pleasing to the Muscovites, however they are forc'd to suffer 'em, and not only so, but to humble themselves to that degree, as to make 'em Presents duely every year, to hinder their Incursions
passages.speaker: Philippe Avril (English translation, 1693)
passages.caution: The number is a report, not a count.

passages.headline: Sheepskin vests and a double scalp-lock
passages.people: Ostyaks, Buryats, Yakuts and Tungus (called 'other Tartars')
passages.gloss: Avril lists Siberian peoples, the 'Ostiaks, Bratski, Jacuti and Tongusi', as further kinds of Tartars and guesses they are Kalmyk hordes tamed by contact with the Russians. He then describes their looks and dress: sheepskin vests tied with a cord carrying bow and quiver, heads shaved to the crown with a double lock, and a round bonnet whose coloured silk tuft marked the horde.
passages.quote: Their Habits are for the most part all alike, consisting of several Sheep-skins sow'd together, which they fit to their bodies in the form of Vests, and gird about their Wastes with a Cord, wherein hangs their Bow and Quiver, with which they go always arm'd. They shave their Heads to the very Crown, where they preserve a Tuft thick enough to make a double lock
passages.speaker: Philippe Avril (English translation, 1693)
passages.caution: Hearsay that lumps very different Siberian peoples together; the Kalmyk-origin theory is Avril's guess.

passages.headline: Mammoth tusks shown in Moscow
passages.gloss: Among Siberia's riches Avril lists a fine ivory from creatures the Russians called 'Behemot', found along the Lena and the shores of the 'Tartarian Sea'. He was shown teeth in Moscow ten inches long, finer than elephant ivory. On the next page he says the ivory was believed to stanch bleeding, was prized by Persians and Turks for dagger hilts, and came from a creature 'as big and as dangerous as a Crocodile'.
passages.quote: Several teeth of this Monster were shewn us at Moscow, which were ten Inches long, and two in Diameter at the Root ; Nor are the Elephants Teeth comparable to 'em
passages.speaker: Philippe Avril (English translation, 1693)
passages.caution: He saw the teeth; the living 'monster' is hearsay. This is fossil mammoth (or walrus) ivory; the page OCR is badly garbled around it.

passages.headline: Prester John's kingdom 'still in being'
passages.people: Tartars of Tangut; the Dalai Lama
passages.gloss: Avril takes up the medieval legend of Prester John, the Christian king of the East. Following Marco Polo, he places John's kingdom in Tenduc or Tangut, between China and Mughal India, and a page earlier concludes that the Dalai Lama must be the real 'Prester John', a line of Christian rulers turned idolaters.
passages.quote: For the Kingdom of Tenduc, or as others read it, Tanchut, this Kingdom, I say, where Marcus Paulus places Preste-John, is still in being, if we may believe those who have travell'd through it, and lies between China and the Empire of the Great Mogul.
passages.speaker: Philippe Avril (English translation, 1693)
passages.caution: A legend Avril tries to fit to the facts; he never went there.

passages.headline: 'Lama' means a cross, and the Manchus wear crosses
passages.gloss: To support his idea that the peoples of Tartary were once Christian, Avril claims that 'lama' means 'cross' in the Tartar language, and that the Manchus who conquered China in 1644 always wore crosses they called lamas. It is a striking example of a missionary reading his hopes into reports.
passages.quote: he bears the Name of Lama, which in the Tartar Language signifies a Cross: And the Bogdoi who conquer'd China in 1644, and who are subject to the Dalae in all matters of Religion, wear always Crosses about 'em, which they call Lama's also
passages.speaker: Philippe Avril (English translation, 1693)
passages.caution: 'Lama' is a Tibetan word for a teacher, not a cross; this is Avril's mistaken inference.

passages.headline: A Kalmyk khan said to eat only from gold
passages.gloss: Avril reports that the chief khan of the Kalmyks claimed descent from Tamerlane, forced Russians and Uzbeks to pay him tribute, dressed always in white and ate only from gold plate. On the next page he checks the rumour: a French officer in Moscow who had been in this khan's tent near Astrakhan, with 100,000 Tartars, confirmed his splendour but never saw gold or silver plate.
passages.quote: He is very Potent, and therefore forces the Muscovites and the Yousbecks to pay him a certain Tribute, or else he would be continually Harrassing their Countries. 'Tis also reported that he is very Magnificent, that he goes always clad in White, and never eats but serv'd in Gold Plate.
passages.speaker: Philippe Avril (English translation, 1693)
passages.caution: Rumour, partly contradicted by the eyewitness Avril cites.

passages.headline: How a Kalmyk kibitka is put up
passages.gloss: Camped in bitter cold above Astrakhan, Bruce's detachment was lent sixty kibitkas by the Kalmyk prince Dasan. He describes them closely: 24 feet across, folding lattice walls six feet high, a round wooden crown raised on lances with holes for the rafters, and a felt covering laid from the bottom up. He found them warmer and more weatherproof than a house.
passages.quote: they are all round, the sides being made of a kind of checkered wicker-work, and the cross sticks neatly jointed for folding together or extending … they raise with their lances a round board, three feet diameter, with a hole in the middle of it … the large hole serves for their chimney, the small holes receive the ends of so many strait rafters
passages.speaker: Peter Henry Bruce (published 1782)

passages.headline: A ruined brick city 'built by Tamerlane', quarried for Astrakhan
passages.place: Lower Volga between Kamyshin and Volgograd
passages.people: Golden Horde (credited by local tradition to Tamerlane)
passages.gloss: Sailing down the Volga, Bruce passed the ruins of a great city called Czarefgorod. He reports the local belief that Tamerlane built it, says its palace and walls were brick, and notes that the Russians had been carting the bricks away for years to build Astrakhan's walls, churches and monasteries. It was most likely one of the Golden Horde's Volga towns.
passages.quote: About forty miles from this, and at a small distance from the river-side, are to be seen the ruins of a great city, formerly called Czaresgorod, built, as is related, by Tamerlane : its palace and walls were all of brick, and have served the city of Astrachan with materials, these many years, for building their walls, churches, and monasteries.
passages.speaker: Peter Henry Bruce (published 1782)
passages.caution: The Tamerlane attribution is hearsay ('as is related'); Timur sacked the Horde's Volga cities in 1395 rather than building them.

passages.headline: Nogai round huts of bulrushes, each with its hawk
passages.gloss: Bruce says the Nogais around Astrakhan lived mostly in small round huts of bulrushes or canes with a smoke hole at the top, and that even the smallest had a hawk, since they were great falconers. On the next page he says they packed the huts onto carts in summer and moved with their herds.
passages.quote: The Nagayans live for the most part in round huts made of bull-rushes, or canes, and seldom exceed twelve or thirteen yards in circumference, with a hole at the top to let out the smoak ; yet the least of these huts has a falcon, or hawk, as those Tartars are great masters of this sport
passages.speaker: Peter Henry Bruce (published 1782)
passages.caution: This description closely follows Adam Olearius's account of the 1630s and may be borrowed rather than observed.

passages.headline: Kazan Tatars who 'live all in houses'
passages.gloss: Bruce contrasts the Kazan Tatars with the nomads: they all lived in houses, farmed and supplied the south with food, which made them the most civilised of the Tartars in his eyes. He adds they were mostly Muslims, though many townspeople were Orthodox, and were forbidden to enter Russian fortifications. On the previous page he describes Kazan itself: wooden houses, a stone castle, and a population of Tatars and Russians.
passages.quote: The kingdom of Casan lies on the left side of the Wolga, and its inhabitants live all in houses, and subsist by agriculture : they supply the southern provinces with all sorts of provisions, and by this means they are the most civilized of all the Tartars.
passages.speaker: Peter Henry Bruce (published 1782)

passages.headline: Astrakhan: Tatars kept outside the stone walls
passages.gloss: Bruce describes Astrakhan as a Russian city with high stone fortifications, stone towers and wooden houses. The Tartars, the former inhabitants, were no longer allowed to live inside the walls, only in suburbs fenced with palisades. He dates the Russian capture to 1554, after the fall of Kazan.
passages.quote: The city is of a considerable bigness, and at present inhabited almost entirely by Russians ; the former inhabitants of the country, being Tartars, are not permitted to live within the walls, but in the adjacent suburbs, which are only fenced round with pallisades : the fortifications of the city are all of stone, very high
passages.speaker: Peter Henry Bruce (published 1782)
passages.caution: Astrakhan fell to Ivan IV in 1556; Bruce's 1554 marks the first Russian campaign.

passages.headline: Tarki, capital of 'Dagestan Tartary'
passages.gloss: Peter the Great's army camped below Tarki, seat of the shamkhal. Bruce describes a town of over 3,000 houses on a hillside, without walls, with two-storey flat-roofed houses where women walked in the evening, each with its own garden and spring.
passages.quote: This city of Tarku, being the metropolis of Dagestan, contains above three thousand houses, and is very full of inhabitants ; the houses all two stories high, platformed at top, standing close to each other : the women walk upon them in the cool of the evenings, as the men do in the streets. Every house has a garden stored with all kinds of delicious fruits
passages.speaker: Peter Henry Bruce (published 1782)

passages.headline: Nogais said to be Indians, and Astrakhan named after King Astra
passages.gloss: In his 'short account of the Tartars', Bruce says the ancients knew them only as Scythians and Sarmatians, and that the Tartars were really several nations. He repeats a story that the Nogais and Kazan Tatars were Indians who rebelled around 1212 and migrated to the Sea of Azov, and that Astrakhan was named after its founder, a Tartar king called Astra.
passages.quote: The Nagayans, with the Tartars of Casan, and some others inhabiting between the Wolga and the Don, or Tanais, are said to have been Indians, who revolting from their sovereigns about the year 1212, emigrated … Astrachan, their principal city, they relate to have been built by a Tartar king, whose name being Astra, gave his city the name of Astra chan, or king.
passages.speaker: Peter Henry Bruce (published 1782)
passages.caution: Both stories are origin legends reported as hearsay ('are said', 'they relate'); they appear in earlier writers such as Olearius.

passages.headline: Not a single house between Saratov and Astrakhan
passages.gloss: Below Saratov Bruce entered Kalmyk country on the left bank of the Volga. He says the whole huge tract had not one house: the Kalmyks lived in tents, moved with horses, camels, cattle and sheep, grew no crops and ate meat (especially horse), fish and game, with plenty of milk and a strong clear spirit made from mare's milk.
passages.quote: in all which immense tract there is not so much as one single house to be seen, as they all live in tents, and remove from one place to another in quest of pasturage for their large herds of cattle, consisting of horses, camels, cows, and sheep ; they neither sow, nor reap, nor make hay for their cattle, so that they live without bread
passages.speaker: Peter Henry Bruce (published 1782)

passages.headline: Left behind with a sheep and a jar of water
passages.gloss: Bruce says the Kalmyks feared smallpox like the plague. When someone caught it they struck camp and fled, leaving the sick person in their worst kibitka with a killed sheep, water and firewood; few survived. On the same page he describes being served roast and boiled suckling foal by Prince Dasan, and calls it delicious.
passages.quote: The small-pox is as much dreaded among the Kalmucks as the pestilence amongst us : when any of them are seized with it, they immediately break up their camp and fly, leaving the sick person in one of their worst kibbets with a killed sheep, part of which is roasted and part raw, and a jar of water and some wood for fire
passages.speaker: Peter Henry Bruce (published 1782)

passages.headline: A skin on a pole to plead with God
passages.gloss: Bruce calls the Mari (Cheremis) of the middle Volga 'Tartars' and describes them as heathens without churches or priests. When they sacrificed a horse, cow or sheep they hung its skin on a high pole and prayed to it to intercede with God for more cattle. He adds details on naming, polygamy and dress.
passages.quote: when they offer a sacrifice to God, they kill a horse, cow, or sheep, and extend its skin on a high pole, which they implore to intercede for them with God, that he may increase the number of their cattle. They have a high veneration for the sun and moon … They make use of no churches, priests, or books
passages.speaker: Peter Henry Bruce (published 1782)
passages.caution: The Mari are a Finnic people, not Tatars; this account closely matches Olearius and is probably borrowed.

passages.headline: 'Vagabond Tartars' with huts by the rivers
passages.gloss: Bruce reports what an envoy sent by Peter the Great to the 'northern Tartar princes' found on a journey toward the Lena. He said they were all wandering Tartars in tents, rich only in cattle, but that along the rivers there were some houses or huts and a little corn, where their khans usually lived. The prince of the Yakuts turned him back.
passages.quote: He reported, that they were all vagabond Tartars, living in tents, and shifting their residence from place to place for pasturage, as all their riches consisted in herds of cattle ; but he observed a sort of houses, or huts, on the sides of rivers, and some corn, and in these situations their chams generally resided.
passages.speaker: Peter Henry Bruce, reporting the czar's envoy (published 1782)
passages.caution: Second-hand; the envoy is not named and the peoples are not identified beyond the Yakuts.

passages.headline: The khan who wanted no gold: the Khiva massacre
passages.gloss: Bruce tells how Prince Alexander Bekovich, sent to find gold on the Amu Darya, was lured into quartering his men among the Uzbeks. The khan assured him he had no use for gold or silver, since his people owned only herds and tents and had no castles or towns to lose. That night the troops were massacred and Bekovich cut to pieces. The story reached Peter through a surviving captive officer.
passages.quote: for his own part, he neither valued gold nor silver, as it was of no use in their country, for they lived without that, or even bread, consequently had no use for either ; their whole riches consisting in herds of cattle, which, with their tents, they could remove at pleasure ; and, consequently, could not fear having either castles, towns, or villages, rifled or taken from them
passages.speaker: Peter Henry Bruce, reporting the khan's words via a surviving officer (published 1782)
passages.caution: Hearsay and dramatised; the khanate of Khiva in fact had walled towns, so the khan's speech (if spoken) was a ruse.

passages.headline: A Kalmyk princess in a silk-lined felt tent
passages.gloss: Sent to treat the widowed Kalmyk princess, held under Russian guard in a dispute over the khanate, Cook entered a very large beehive-shaped tent covered with felt and lined with Persian silk. She lay on a down bed covered with silk, with priests and chiefs standing round. He decided her illness was confinement and grief.
passages.quote: In company with the major, the governor's only son, I went to a very large tent, in form of a bee-hive, covered with felt, and lined with Persian silk. When I entered into the tent, the Princess was lying on a bed of down covered with silk; her face was from us. Many Kalmucks well dressed were standing with great decorum
passages.speaker: John Cook (published 1770)

passages.headline: Tea with salt and butter
passages.gloss: The Kalmyk princess offered Cook a dish of tea. The tea was good, he says, but the Kalmyks put salt and butter into it; he drank it out of politeness and then hurried off to get rid of it, while the Russian major laughed at him. It is an early Western description of Mongolian salted milk tea.
passages.quote: Accordingly a cup of tea was brought, but such as I never had tasted before this time. The tea, I dare say, was good, but the Kalmucks put salt and butter into it ; nevertheless I drank it, though extremely disagreeable
passages.speaker: John Cook (published 1770)

passages.headline: Two horses each, and the Volga swum
passages.gloss: After a Kalmyk raid on the Karakalpaks, Cook describes how Kalmyks went to war: bow, quiver and scimitar, at least two horses per man, herds grazing as they marched. He says he had seen thousands cross the Volga by swimming their animals, and that lame or dead horses were cut up and shared as food.
passages.quote: The Kalmucks in time of war are armed with a bow and a quiver full of arrows of different shapes, and a large scymitar. Every man has at least two horses … They need neither bridges nor boats to cross rivers, for I have seen thousands cross the Volga by swimming their cattle over
passages.speaker: John Cook (published 1770)

passages.headline: Prisoners tied beneath the horses' bellies
passages.people: Karakalpaks, Kalmyks, Russian Cossacks and Tatars
passages.gloss: In revenge for a Kalmyk raid, some 15,000 Karakalpaks crossed the frozen Volga, killed Kalmyk old and young and carried off the youths. Cornered by a Russian force, they broke through and fled, leaving about three hundred Kalmyk prisoners bound to horses by their feet. The Kalmyks then rode off with thousands of the Russians' own horses and camels.
passages.quote: they, being about fifteen thousand, made a very sudden unexpected attack upon the Russians, and actually, bravely broke through them, got over the ice, and fled to the desart, leaving about three hundred Kalmuck prisoners fixed to their horses, by tying their feet with cords to one another under the horses bellies.
passages.speaker: John Cook (published 1770)
passages.caution: Cook was at Astrakhan but not with the troops; numbers are reported.

passages.headline: Allies, not subjects: the Kalmyks and Russia
passages.people: Kalmyks and other Tatars serving as Russian irregulars
passages.gloss: Explaining why Russian generals let irregular cavalry plunder freely, Cook says these troops were Cossacks, Kalmyks or other Tartars on the borders. The Kalmyks owned no subjection, only Russian protection, and could not be forced to move; even their khan could not act without the consent of his many elders, some of them lords of five or six thousand fighting men.
passages.quote: The Kalmucks acknowledge no subjection, but only live under the protection of Russia. They are barbarous to a great degree, but yet they must be treated with great lenity ; for, if they do not incline to leave their own country, the whole force of Russia is not able to oblige them, nor even their prince, unless with the approbation of their seniors
passages.speaker: John Cook (published 1770)

passages.headline: A 'Tartarian or Circassian' village of four hundred houses
passages.people: Kumyks or Kabardians (called Tartars or Circassians)
passages.gloss: Marching south from the Terek, the embassy reached a large village of 300 to 400 houses called Andreofske Derevna, ruled by a prince named Alish under Russian protection. Cook is unsure whether to call it Tartar or Circassian. The prince, drunk from celebrating, showed the scars of many raids and boasted of horses stolen from Turkey and Georgia.
passages.quote: at seven o'clock at night we arrived, very cold, in a large Tartarian or Circassian village, called Andreofske Derevna, consisting of between three and four hundred houses. The prince of this village is called Alish, and is under the protection of Russia.
passages.speaker: John Cook (published 1770)

passages.headline: Towers on the hills credited to Alexander
passages.gloss: Cook describes Derbent's huge walls of natural shell-stone and then notes towers on the hills to the west. The inhabitants told him Alexander the Great built them and ran them all the way to the Black Sea to hold back the Dagestan Tartars. This echoes the old legend of Alexander's wall against Gog and Magog.
passages.quote: Upon the tops of the hills, west from Derbent, are to be seen some towers, which the inhabitants say were built by Alexander the Great; and that he continued these towers from Derbent west to the Black Sea, in order to curb the Dagestan Tartars.
passages.speaker: John Cook (published 1770)
passages.caution: Local tradition; the Derbent walls are Sasanian Persian work of the 6th century, not Alexander's.

passages.headline: Muslim Tartars with stone crosses and Christian feast days
passages.people: 'Tartars' between Astrakhan and Derbent (Kumyks and Dagestani peoples)
passages.gloss: Cook says all the Tartars from Astrakhan to Derbent were Sunni Muslims, but he suspected many had once been Christians. They held yearly gatherings they could not explain, which he says fell on Greek Orthodox feast days, and he was told there were many stone crosses in the hills where they still met.
passages.quote: The Tartars from the borders of Astrachan to Derbent, are all Mahometans, of the sect of the Turks; but some things make me believe, that a majority of them had formerly professed the Christian religion. They have meetings at certain times of the year, where they divert themselves, without being able to account for the cause, any other way than that their ancestors did so before them
passages.speaker: John Cook (published 1770)
passages.caution: Cook's inference; the crosses are reported, not seen.

passages.headline: Dagestan Tartars versus Lezgi Tartars
passages.gloss: Cook admits writers were confused about the peoples of the eastern Caucasus and sets his own rule: 'Dagestan Tartars' for the hill people between Derbent and Circassia, 'Lezgi Tartars' for those south and south-east of Derbent to the Kura. It shows 'Tartar' being used simply as a label for Muslim mountaineers who spoke many languages.
passages.quote: The difference between the Dagestan and Lesgee Tartars, I think is not clear in authors; I therefore desire my readers to remember, that I call the Dagestan Tartars, those who inhabit the hills between Derbent and Circassia; and I call those who inhabit the hills south, and south-east of Derbent, all the way to the north banks of Cura, Lesgee Tartars.
passages.speaker: John Cook (published 1770)

passages.headline: A jar of old Tartar coins falls out of a cliff
passages.gloss: Resting under red gravel cliffs on the Volga near Astrakhan, Cook was told by his colonel that merchants picnicking there had seen part of the cliff collapse, releasing an earthen jar full of old Tartar coins in gold and silver. The colonel said he had seen some of them.
passages.quote: when they were taking their dinner, part of the cliff fell down, and with it, an earthen jar full of old Tartar coin, some of which he had seen, both gold and silver.
passages.speaker: John Cook, reporting a Russian colonel (published 1770)
passages.caution: Second-hand; the coins are not described further.

passages.headline: A hundred thousand tents on the Mughan plain
passages.people: Nomadic tent-dwellers of Persia (compared to Kalmyks)
passages.gloss: Crossing the plains near the Aras River, Cook was told that the kings of Persia bred their best horses there, and that the plains had held more than 100,000 tents of roving people 'as the Kalmucks do in Astrachan' when Nadir Shah took the throne. He passed a few of the last groups being moved to Khorasan on Nadir's orders.
passages.quote: these plains were formerly inhabited by roving people living in tents, as the Kalmucks do in Astrachan ; and that upwards of a hundred thousand tents were in these happy plains when Kouli Khan mounted the throne of Persia.
passages.speaker: John Cook (published 1770)
passages.caution: Reported figure.

passages.headline: Tatar cottages and little mosques among the vineyards
passages.gloss: Sailing along the south coast of Crimea past Alupka, where Vorontsov's palace stood, Spencer saw terraced vineyards on the slopes and, in the small valleys below, clustered Tatar cottages with their little mosques and slender minarets. It is a brief glimpse of Tatar villages surviving beside the new estates of Russian nobles.
passages.quote: the whole space between the towering cliffs and the sea, forming a splendid panorama, presented one mass of the richest foliage ; terraced vineyards adorned the hills, mingling their lighter green with the dark cold pine of the mountain; while the miniature valleys beneath glowed with the clustering cots of the Tartars, and their pretty little mosques and slender minarets.
passages.speaker: Edmund Spencer
passages.caution: Seen from the steamer.

passages.headline: Kurgans raised by each mourner's handful of earth
passages.people: Crimean Tatars and older mountain peoples (as tradition-keepers)
passages.gloss: After watching a kurgan being opened at Kerch, Spencer reflects on the countless mounds of the region. He reports the tradition of 'descendants of the aboriginal inhabitants' in the Crimean mountains: when a great warrior or king died, every admirer carried a portion of earth and threw it on his grave. On the next page he calls this 'the tradition of the Tartars' and compares it to Scottish cairns.
passages.quote: these tumuli were voluntarily erected by the people ; as when any of their great warriors or kings expired, his ashes were placed in the tomb, and every man who admired his virtues carried a portion of earth and threw it over his grave.
passages.speaker: Edmund Spencer
passages.caution: A local tradition; the Kerch kurgans are mostly Greek and Scythian burials many centuries older than the Tatars. Spencer credits the builders to 'a great and powerful people' of antiquity, not to the Tatars.

passages.headline: Altyn Obo, the Tatars' 'hill of gold'
passages.gloss: At Kerch's museum Spencer saw finds from a mound opened in 1830 that the Tatars called Altyn Obo, 'hill of gold', and which was claimed to be the tomb of Mithridates. The gold vases and ornaments justified the name, he says, though the best had gone to St Petersburg. The Tatars named the mound; the treasures were Greek work.
passages.quote: we then extended our promenade to the Museum, the collection of which has been considerably augmented since the opening of a tumulus in 1830, called by the Tartars, Altyn Obo, or the hill of gold ; pretended to have been the tomb of Mithridates.
passages.speaker: Edmund Spencer
passages.caution: The 1830 excavation was of the Kul-Oba kurgan; Spencer's 'Altyn Obo' may conflate names. He himself says the finds were 'unquestionably of Grecian workmanship'.

passages.headline: Crimean and Nogai refugees in the Caucasus
passages.gloss: Explaining why his book includes a Tatar vocabulary, Spencer says many Circassians knew the language and that Crimean and Nogai Tatars who had fled Russian rule were settled throughout the Circassian provinces. He adds that the word lists should disprove the common idea that Circassians and Tatars shared an origin.
passages.quote: many of the Circassians are not only acquainted with it, but we every where find, throughout the whole of these provinces, Krim and Nogay Tartars domiciliated, who, on the subjection of their country to the rule of Russia, fled into the Caucasus.
passages.speaker: Edmund Spencer

passages.headline: Anapa: mud cabins and a medley of peoples
passages.people: Nogai Tatars, Kalmyks, Kumyks, Kazan Tatars and others
passages.gloss: Anapa, the first Russian fortress on the Circassian coast, is described from notes by the expedition's historiographer: most houses were cabins of wood and mud thatched with maize leaves or reeds, and its 2,000 people included Circassians, Nogai Tatars, Kalmyks, Kumyks, Kabardians, 'Kazannes', Dagestanis and Bukharans. Spencer admits he did not land there himself.
passages.quote: The greater number of the houses of the town are mere cabins, constructed of wood and mud, thatched with the leaves of Indian corn or reeds. The inhabitants, consisting of Circassians, Nogay Tartars, Kalmucks, Komouks, Kabartis, Kazannes, Demikarponis, Daghistanes, Boukhares, with a few Greeks, Armenians, and Russians, speaking a medley of tongues
passages.speaker: Edmund Spencer, from the expedition historiographer's notes
passages.caution: Second-hand, as Spencer says.

passages.headline: The Natukhai, 'originally Tartars'
passages.people: Natukhai (Circassian tribe said to be of Tatar origin)
passages.gloss: Vorontsov told Spencer he had been visited at Anapa by a prince of the Natukhai, a tribe 'originally Tartars' who had fled into the Caucasus after Russia conquered the lands of the Kuban and Azov. Spencer calls them Russia's most uncompromising enemies there. The Natukhai are usually counted as a Circassian (Adyghe) tribe.
passages.quote: he had been honoured with a visit from a Circassian prince, chief of the Natouhay tribe, originally Tartars, who had fled into the mountains of the Caucasus upon the conquest of the provinces on the banks of the Kouban and the sea of Azov.
passages.speaker: Edmund Spencer, reporting Count Vorontsov
passages.caution: The Tatar origin is a claim reported at second hand.

passages.headline: Soldiers pocketing bricks from the Great Wall
passages.people: Chinese builders; 'the Tartars' as the threat
passages.gloss: Holmes reports what the soldiers were told on the spot: the Wall was built about 1,500 years earlier against Tartar raids on the northern provinces and ran about 1,400 miles. They measured it at 25 feet high and 36 paces thick at the gate, saw it was built of brick, and everyone from the ambassador to the privates collected pieces as souvenirs.
passages.quote: That part of it which we measured and examined, with uncommon pains, was in height 25 feet, and in breadth, through the gate, 36 regular paces, which breadth it carried to the summit. … It was built of brick; many pieces of which were as anxiously collected as if they were wedges of the most precious metal, by all ranks, from his Excellency to the private soldier
passages.speaker: Samuel Holmes (diary printed 1798)
passages.caution: The age and length of the Wall are what he was told, not measured.

passages.headline: Chinese in the suburbs, Tartars in the city
passages.gloss: Shut in covered carts, the soldiers saw little of Beijing except high brick walls and low, rather shabby brick houses. Holmes notes the division of the capital: the Chinese lived in the suburbs, the Tartars in the city proper. He found the suburb's buildings and shops elegant.
passages.quote: we then entered the suburbs, which the Chinese inhabit, as the Tartars do the city. The buildings here were truly elegant, and the shops of the tradesmen well stocked with all kinds of goods.
passages.speaker: Samuel Holmes (diary printed 1798)

passages.headline: Jehol: kept outside the palace gates
passages.gloss: The guard marched through Jehol ('Gehor'), a town about three miles long, to the palace with the presents, but only the ambassador and gentlemen were allowed in. The soldiers went back disappointed, though Holmes says the palace's extent and elegance against the mountains, lit by the rising sun, were beyond description.
passages.quote: none, except his Excellency and the gentlemen, were suffered to enter the gates ; all the others returned mortified and terribly disappointed … the extent and elegance of it was beyond description, and contrasted with the adjacent mountains and precipices, the scene was great and beautiful indeed
passages.speaker: Samuel Holmes (diary printed 1798)

passages.headline: Tartary: herds on the hills, few houses
passages.gloss: From the Wall it was four days' hard travel through hills and valleys to Jehol. Holmes found the country fertile and good pasture for immense herds of sheep and cattle, but thinly peopled, with only scattered houses in the valleys and no place of note until Jehol.
passages.quote: The country appeared fertile, though so rugged, and afforded good pasturage for immense herds of sheep and bullocks. It was but thinly peopled; here and there a few scattered houses in
passages.speaker: Samuel Holmes (diary printed 1798)
passages.caution: The sentence continues on the next page ('the vallies, but no place of note till we entered Gehor').

passages.headline: How a Kalmyk felt tent is put together
passages.gloss: Zwick opens a whole chapter on the Kalmyk tent, called gerr by its owners and kibitka by Russians. He describes a round lattice wall of willow laths, painted in red stripes, that folds flat in seven or eight sections, with poles rising to a wooden crown and the whole covered in large felts tied down with woollen girths. It is one of the most exact eyewitness descriptions of a steppe yurt in English before 1850.
passages.quote: The Calmuc huts or tents, in their own language gerr, and in the Russian kibitka, consist of a number of parts, which are easily put together, and taken to pieces. The tents are round, with a funnel-shaped roof, and a blunt point at the top of it. The frame-work, which is of willow laths about an inch thick, carved and painted in red stripes, forms a circular wall of lattice-work
passages.speaker: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)

passages.headline: A prince's camp laid out like a town
passages.gloss: The horde's headquarters had a fixed plan. The prince's tent, a tent serving as the hall of justice and the princess's tent stood on one side of the wells, the temple tents and the Lama's huts on the other, with the lesser priests in a semicircle around them and the prince's officials and servants ringed outside. Zwick adds that every door faced the main temple. Erdeni's camp held about 100 tents.
passages.quote: To the north of these were the royal tents, viz. that of Erdeni himself, the hall of justice, and the tent of Princess Mingmer ; to the south, the Churulls (or temples) and the huts of the High Priest, or Lama. Round these, in a wide semicircle, were the tents of the inferior priests (or Gellongs,) and these again were enclosed by the ministers and servants of the Prince.
passages.speaker: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)

passages.headline: A tent bazaar between two princes
passages.people: Kalmyks; Russian, Armenian and Tatar traders
passages.gloss: Arriving at the 'place of heroes' whips', where two Torgut princes were camped, the missionaries found a market that had grown up in the gap between the two princely tents. Russian, Armenian and Tatar merchants lived there in their own tents and carts, forming the travelling bazaar of the horde.
passages.quote: Their tents were about a quarter of a mile asunder, and between them was a multitude of tents and cars belonging to the Russian, Armenian, and Tartar merchants, forming the market, or rather bazaar, of the horde.
passages.speaker: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)

passages.headline: Grave mounds and brick foundations on the steppe
passages.people: Golden Horde Tatars (as Zwick supposes), and older peoples
passages.gloss: Crossing the steppe, Zwick stopped at kurgans, the grave mounds Russians call by that name. He thinks they come from many ages and peoples, but credits most of them to the Tartars of the medieval Volga empire whose ruined cities he names, and on the next page notes two mounds holding the remains of a square brick building.
passages.quote: Such tumuli are every where to be found on the steppes, and most plentifully on the willowy shores of the Volga … They probably belong to different ages, and different races of men, but the majority are undoubtedly to be ascribed to the Tartars … I saw a great number of these hillocks, near the ruins of their principal cities Serag and Tschigis.
passages.speaker: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)
passages.caution: The dating and attribution of the mounds are Zwick's guesses; the omitted words name the empire in a garbled form ('Eamschatkan' in the OCR, apparently for Kipchak).

passages.headline: The ruins of a great Tatar city on the Akhtuba
passages.gloss: On the way home the missionaries stopped at the 'saltpetre town', a Russian cordon post among ruins that stretched far along the Akhtuba, a navigable arm of the Volga. Zwick could see the city had once been large and splendid but could not learn its old name. Just before, he says these Tartars were subdued by Russia 'in 1562' and their lands laid waste from Kazan to Astrakhan (Kazan actually fell in 1552 and Astrakhan in 1556).
passages.quote: At noon we arrived at Selitrenoi Gorodok, (which the Tartars call Tschigit) where we stayed till noon the following day. This ancient Tartarian city must, as it is evident from the remains, have been remarkable for its size and splendour; its ancient name I have not been able to learn. … The ruins of the city extend far and wide along the shore of the river.
passages.speaker: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)
passages.caution: Modern archaeologists identify the Selitrennoye ruins as Sarai (often called Sarai-Batu), a capital of the Golden Horde; Zwick did not know this.

passages.headline: Russian towers built from Tatar rubble
passages.people: Golden Horde Tatars; early Russian settlers
passages.gloss: The few towers still standing among the ruins were not Tatar work at all, Zwick decided, but early Russian forts. His reasons are practical: the towers are held together with clay, while the Tatar buildings used a hard mortar, and they were patched together from broken pieces of fine older buildings, with glazed tiles stuck in any which way.
passages.quote: In the first place, they are built with clay cement, whereas the Tartars used a durable mortar; in the next place, they are evidently piled up from the ruins of handsome buildings, as may be seen by the glazed tiles which are stuck on at random, without any respect to the glazed side.
passages.speaker: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)
passages.caution: The judgement that the towers are Russian is Zwick's own reading of the masonry.

passages.headline: Glazed brick and blue mosaic at Sarai
passages.gloss: From the same ruins Zwick describes walls of glazed, pointed brick decorated with coloured mosaic on a deep blue ground, which he compares to the building styles of the Turks and Saracens from the Near East to Egypt and Spain. He says the same was true at 'Seray' further up the river. On the next page he describes a six-foot panel of this work, with a white inscription 'in the Tartarian language', reused in the wall of a peasant's cottage.
passages.quote: We perceived, from the ruins of this city, that here as well as at Seray, … walls were built of glazed brick and pointed, and mosaic work of various colours was employed in decoration here, as throughout the ancient Turkish, Tartar, and Saracen tribes, in the East, in Egypt, and Spain. The ground is usually deep blue, with other colours let in.
passages.speaker: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)
passages.caution: The omitted words call Seray the capital of an empire whose name is garbled in the OCR.

passages.headline: Coins of the Khans dug from the ruins
