passages.gloss: Zwick picked up antiquities at the site: an inscribed alabaster, a copper amulet, a seal, inscribed gems including one bearing the Muslim creed 'There is no God but God', and silver and copper coins of the Khans dated from 710 to 766 of the Hijra, which he converts as 1310 to 1364 AD, from 'Tochtocho-Chan' (Tokhta Khan) to 'Asis Chan' (Aziz Khan). The finds tie the city to the Muslim Golden Horde of the fourteenth century.
passages.quote: I here procured several antiques; amongst others, an alabaster with an inscription, a copper amulet with magical characters, a seal with a name upon it ; a number of ring-jewels, and jewels with inscriptions, … also a quantity of silver and copper coins of the old Chans, from 1310 A.D. (or 710 of the Hegira) to 1364 (or 766.)
passages.speaker: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)
passages.caution: The OCR reads the last date as '1864'; 766 of the Hijra is 1364 to 1365.

passages.headline: Old wells lined with pine and tile
passages.gloss: At the 'Pine-tree Wells' in a treeless steppe, Zwick guessed the name came from a time when the Tartars had boarded the wells with pine floated down the Volga from the north. Bits of tile lay in the sand, and nearby grave mounds showed traces of masonry. He adds that Kalmyk and Tatar tradition credited such works to Janibeg Khan, who ruled from the Akhtuba and died in 1357.
passages.quote: Probably these wells were so called by the Calmucs, because they had been in former times boarded at the sides with pine by the Tartars, and the wood for the purpose might have been brought on the Volga from northern Russia, as it is at this day. Fragments of tiles are still to be found in the sand, and appear also to have been used in forming the wells.
passages.speaker: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)
passages.caution: The explanation of the name is Zwick's guess; the credit to Janibeg is local tradition he heard.

passages.headline: A Tatar cart turned to stone
passages.gloss: Near the same wells the Kalmyks told Zwick they had once cleared an old well and found a Tatar cart (arba) turned to stone, and he heard of similar finds in the Kuma marshes. He did not see it himself, and offers a sober explanation: salty soil hardens wood, as the Volga fishermen knew from their salting tubs.
passages.quote: In an old well in this neighbourhood, which the Calmucs cleared out some years ago, they are said to have found a Tartar arba in a state of petrifaction. Similar cases, as we were elsewhere told, have been found in the Kuma Morass. That the saltness of the soil may have contributed to the preservation of the wood is the more probable
passages.speaker: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)
passages.caution: Hearsay; Zwick reports it and explains it but did not see the cart.

passages.headline: A chapel mortared with a prince's ashes
passages.gloss: The Kalmyks did build in stone and wood, for their dead nobles. Zwick visited a small memorial chapel (zaza) for the late Torgut prince Sandschi-Ubaschi: a wooden room about four paces square on a stone base, reached by steps, with a flat roof and a small tower. He was told that the prince's ashes had been mixed into its mortar and whitewash.
passages.quote: This chapel was erected to the memory of the late Torgud Prince Sandschi-Ubaschi, father of the Prince Zerren Ubaschi, and his ashes, as the Calmucs informed me, are mixed with the mortar which cements and whitens the building. The foundation of this edifice is of stone, upon which is erected a wooden chapel, with steps up to it.
passages.speaker: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)
passages.caution: The ashes in the mortar is what the Kalmyks told him.

passages.headline: Left on the steppe for the dogs
passages.gloss: Zwick found the body of a Kalmyk woman laid out in furs under a felt, with wooden cups and utensils beside her. This, he says, was the normal way of disposing of commoners, whose bodies were eaten by dogs and vultures; the dogs that fed on them were then driven off as unclean. Princes and Lamas, by contrast, were cremated with ceremony, and their ashes mixed with mortar for a chapel or tomb.
passages.quote: At some distance from our tent, we found the corpse of a Calmuc woman, laid out in a fur dress, and covered with coarse felt. Wooden drinking vessels, and other unimportant utensils, were laid by her side. This is the common way of disposing of the dead, amongst the Calmucs of inferior rank, so that the bodies are usually devoured by dogs and vultures.
passages.speaker: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)

passages.headline: A whole horde on the move
passages.gloss: The missionaries travelled with Erdeni's horde as it moved camp. The column was more than a verst wide: strings of camels carrying the tents, goods and children in baskets, then the herds. No one walked; even mothers with babies rode. Zwick describes the migration as a festive show at which families displayed their best clothes and carpets.
passages.quote: The main body of this moving multitude extended more than a verst in breadth, and consisted of single columns of camels, bearing tents, household goods, and children, who were stowed in baskets; next followed troops of horses, cattle and sheep … Nobody performs a migration on foot … we even saw mothers on horseback with infants, who were hardly out of the cradle
passages.speaker: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)

passages.headline: Sour milk for the poor, meat for princes, brick tea for all
passages.gloss: In summer the Kalmyks lived almost entirely on sour milk: mare's milk (tschigan) for the rich, cow's milk for the poor. Only the prince and great men ate meat, because the herds were their whole wealth. Their tea came from China by way of Siberia as hard cakes of coarse leaves and stalks, boiled with butter or sheep's-tail fat and salt.
passages.quote: None but the Prince, and the great men, had flesh in their kettles, for the whole wealth of the nation consists in their flocks and herds, and they are forced to use them sparingly. In winter, when they are short of milk, they buy meal from the Russians who inhabit the shores of the Volga
passages.speaker: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)
passages.caution: The OCR on this page is badly garbled; check the scan.

passages.headline: A Kalmyk prince with a wooden castle and a piano
passages.gloss: Not every Kalmyk lord lived in a tent. Prince Sered-Dscheh, a colonel in the Russian army, had a large wooden castle on the left bank of the Volga, fortified with Russian-style outworks after the Napoleonic wars and furnished with mahogany, mirrors, clocks, a billiard table and a piano. Even so, he held court out on the steppe for part of the summer.
passages.quote: He resides on the left bank of the Volga, in a large wooden castle, thirty paces in front, which he fortified with Russian outworks when he returned from the French war … His castle is well fitted up in the interior, and contains a number of saloons, with mahogany furniture, lustres, mirrors, a billiard table, piano-forte, a number of clocks, &c.
passages.speaker: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)

passages.headline: Mountain Tatars who move house by cart
passages.people: Cunduran-Mangut or 'Mountain Tartars' (a Nogai-type Tatar clan)
passages.gloss: Zwick visited a small Tatar clan that had once been vassals of the Kalmyks and were now Russian crown subjects. Their felt huts were just like Kalmyk ones, but when they moved they carried their women and children in wooden huts set on carts (arbas). He also describes the women's face cloth fastened just under the eyes.
passages.quote: The women wear full cotton dresses, and a cloth hanging from the top of the head to the waist behind, and fastened in front just under the eyes, so as to cover the face. Their manner of removing from one place to another with their herds, differs from the Calmucs, in as much as they make use of a great many arbas, upon which wooden huts are placed
passages.speaker: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)

passages.headline: Our Tartars: the missionaries' drivers
passages.gloss: The 'Tartars' who appear on almost every page of the journey are the two hired drivers of the missionaries' carts, not the Kalmyks of the title. Both spoke Russian; the elder, Andre, also spoke Kalmyk and had been baptised in the Orthodox Church, while the younger was a Muslim. Later Zwick notes that Andre spoke the dialect of the Kazan Tatars.
passages.quote: To transport our copies of Scripture, which were packed in chests, we bought a couple of two-wheeled Tartarian carts, (called arba,) with the requisite horses and tackle, and hired two Tartars as drivers. They both understood Russian, and Andra, the elder of the two, was acquainted with the Calmuc tongue also. He had been baptized into the Greek Church, in his youth ; the other was a Mahometan.
passages.speaker: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)

passages.headline: Karakorum explained as 'the circle of the common people'
passages.gloss: In a footnote Zwick explains that kura means a circle, especially the ring of priests' huts around a Kalmyk temple tent, which served as the centre of a horde without a prince. He then derives the name of Genghis Khan's capital from the same word. It is a striking attempt to read an old imperial capital as a camp word.
passages.quote: Thus, the capital of the famous Genghis Khan, which is known in history under the name of Karakorum, was originally Chara Kura, or, in the Tartar dialect, Kara Kura, the circle of the Blacks, or common people.
passages.speaker: Heinrich August Zwick (footnote, English edition, 1831)
passages.caution: This is Zwick's own etymology; the name is usually explained as Turkic qara qorum, 'black rocks'.

passages.headline: Priest John and the Tartar princes
passages.gloss: Zwick's historical introduction repeats the medieval story of Prester John: a certain Master Philip told Pope Alexander III of marvels in Tartary and of the Christian priest-king there, and the Pope sent a letter east in 1177. Zwick is summarising older histories, not reporting anything he saw.
passages.quote: The first intelligence of the Tartarian Princes at Karakorum, was brought to Alexander the Third, by one "Master Philip," … who professed to have travelled in Tartary, and added many marvels of the might and dominion of Priest John, the head of the church at that place.
passages.speaker: Heinrich August Zwick (historical introduction, English edition, 1831)
passages.caution: Second-hand history. Karakorum was not founded until the 1220s, so placing Priest John there in 1177 is Zwick's anachronism.

passages.headline: Towns wiped out by the Manchu war
passages.gloss: Verbiest saw almost nothing left of the many towns and villages of Liaodong. He was told why: the 'petty King of the Tartars' who started the war, with only a small army, forced the local people to take up arms and then destroyed their homes so his soldiers had nothing to go back to. It is a clear case of a named cause for ruins, reported sixty years after the event.
passages.quote: There is now not the least footsteps remaining of a great number of Towns and Villages which were here before the Warr. Because the petty King of the Tartars, who began to kindle this Warr having but a very small Army, caused the Inhabitants of those places to take Armes, which places he forthwith destroyed
passages.speaker: Ferdinand Verbiest (English translation, 1686)
passages.caution: Verbiest saw the ruins; the explanation of how they came about is what he was told. The 'petty King' is presumably the Manchu founder Nurhaci, whose armies took Liaodong from 1618.

passages.headline: New houses of mud and rubble among old walls
passages.people: Chinese and Manchu settlers in Liaodong
passages.gloss: In place of the old cities, Verbiest saw only broken walls of brick and stone, with a few new houses thrown up on the outskirts. Some were of earth, some built from the rubble of the old buildings, and most were thatched rather than tiled. The capital, which he calls Kin-Yam (Shenyang), was the exception: fairly whole, with the remains of an old palace.
passages.quote: One can see nothing through the whole Country but old ruined Walls with Rubbell, Bricks and Stones. In the out skirts of these Citys there have been of late some few houses built, but without any order. Some of them made of Earth, others of the Rubbish of the old Buildings, the most part of them covered with straw or thatch, and but few with tyles.
passages.speaker: Ferdinand Verbiest (English translation, 1686)

passages.headline: The White Mountain, old home of 'our Tartars'
passages.gloss: At Jilin on the Sungari, Verbiest describes the mountain the Manchus revered as the cradle of their people. He translates its name, Cham-pe (Changbai), as 'the white mountain', and says that when the Kangxi emperor 'saw it' he got off his horse, knelt by the river and bowed three times to the ground towards it. Verbiest calls the Manchus 'our Tartars', the people he served at court.
passages.quote: This Mountain so famous in the East for having been the Antient Seat of our Tartars, is alwayes covered with Snow, from whence it had its name, because Cham-pe signifyes the white Mountaine. So soon as the Emperour saw it, he alighted from his Horse and fell on his knees on the bank of the River, and bowed himself three times to the ground to Salute it
passages.speaker: Ferdinand Verbiest (English translation, 1686)
passages.caution: Verbiest also says the mountain lay 400 miles away, so the emperor was most likely saluting it from afar, as in the Qing rite of worshipping Changbai at a distance.

passages.headline: A ring of 3,000 guards closes on the game
passages.gloss: The emperor hunted almost daily. Verbiest describes the Manchu ring hunt: 3,000 guardsmen spread out in a circle at least 3,000 paces across, then walked inward in step until it was only 300 paces wide, trapping everything inside. He watched two or three hundred hares taken in less than a day, and elsewhere over a thousand deer, besides bears, boars and more than sixty tigers.
passages.quote: they Reduced this great Circle to another much less, which had about 300 paces in the Diameter : So that all the Beasts which had been stayed within the first, found themselves taken in this last as in a Net … I saw taken in this manner two or three hundred Hares in less then one day, without counting an Infinite of Wolves and Foxes.
passages.speaker: Ferdinand Verbiest (English translation, 1686)

passages.headline: No cities, no villages, not even a house
passages.gloss: Verbiest states plainly that in the whole of 'Western Tartary' he found only mountains, rocks and valleys, with no towns and no houses at all. The people lived in tents and moved them from valley to valley as the grazing required, keeping cattle, horses and camels but no pigs or poultry.
passages.quote: there is nothing to be found but Mountains, Rocks, and Vallies, there are neither Cities, Towns, nor Villages, nor so much as any Houses. The Inhabitants Lodge under Tents, pitched on all sides in the open Feilds. They are for the most part Grasiers, and transport their Tents from one Vally to another, according as the Pastures are better.
passages.speaker: Ferdinand Verbiest (English translation, 1686)
passages.caution: He is describing the part of Mongolia the imperial hunt crossed, not all of Mongolia.

passages.headline: Milk, cheese, meat and a steppe spirit
passages.gloss: The Mongols, Verbiest says, grew no crops and lived on milk, cheese and meat, with a distilled drink he compares to European aqua vitae (almost certainly milk spirit), which they drank at feasts. He then turns contemptuous, likening them to the herds they tended.
passages.quote: They pass their Life either in Hunting, or doing nothing. And as they neither Sow nor cultivate the Earth, so they make no Harvest. They Live upon Milk, Cheese, and Flesh, and have a sort of Wine, not much unlike our Aqua-vitae ; with which they make their Feasts, and are often Drunk.
passages.speaker: Ferdinand Verbiest (English translation, 1686)
passages.caution: The food is observed; the judgement that they do nothing but eat and drink is Verbiest's prejudice.

passages.headline: The Great Wall, built by a Chinese emperor against the Tartars
passages.gloss: Verbiest crossed the Great Wall several times and says all seven wonders of the world together could not match it. He credits it to an ancient Chinese emperor who built it as a bulwark against the Western Tartars, and was amazed that water, brick and mortar had been hauled up dry mountains. He measured one stretch with an instrument at 1,037 geometrical feet above the horizon.
passages.quote: 'twas to make a Bulwork against their Incursions, that a Chinese Emperor in Antient times caused this great Wall to be Built, which seperates China from their Countrey. I have passed it several times, and have considered it very attentively, And I can say without Hyperbolizing, that all the seven Wonders of the World put together, are not comparable to this worke.
passages.speaker: Ferdinand Verbiest (English translation, 1686)
passages.caution: The OCR reads 'fewer times', which seems to be a misreading of 'several times'.

passages.headline: Winning the Mongols through their lamas
passages.gloss: Verbiest explains that the 'Tartarian Monarch that Conquered China' won over the Mongols partly by courting their Buddhist lamas, who persuaded their people to submit. The emperor still gave the lamas presents and used them to keep the Mongols obedient, though Verbiest believed he privately despised them. He adds that the land had been divided into 48 tributary units.
passages.quote: one of his first Cares was to engage to his Interest by his Royal Bounties, and by Demonstration of a Singular Affection, the Lamas (or Preists) these Men having a great Repute above all those of their Nation, easily perswaded them to Submit to the Government of so great a Prince
passages.speaker: Ferdinand Verbiest (English translation, 1686)
passages.caution: Court knowledge and Verbiest's own reading of the emperor's motives; as a rival missionary he was hostile to the lamas.

passages.headline: Heliopolis: a round city in Tartary with streets like Amsterdam
passages.when: Claimed travels of the mid-1600s; printed 1689
passages.gloss: From the top of a column like London's Monument, the narrator surveys Heliopolis. It is round, about three miles across, ringed by a moat fed by rivers, with no building over two storeys. It has three wards named after the Sun, the Council and the Schools, and wide, clean, straight streets like Amsterdam's, lined with trees and flushed by running water.
passages.quote: It is divided into three Quarters or Wards, of which the first in the heart of the City, derives its name from the Sun; the second from the Council; and the third from the Schools. The Streets are wide, clean and streight, like those of Amsterdam
passages.speaker: 'Heliogenes de L'Epy' (English translation, 1689)
passages.caution: Almost certainly fiction: the city is an ideal community in the manner of Campanella's City of the Sun, not a place any traveller recorded.

passages.headline: Lead domes, gilded cupolas and three classical orders
passages.gloss: The book dresses its Tartar city in the European classical style of its own day: porticos on pillars and pilasters of the Doric, Ionic and Corinthian orders in the three wards, house roofs of lead shaped like domes with gilded copper cupolas, and at the centre a temple 'like the Pantheon at Rome'. It is a European architect's dream set in Tartary, not a description of anything built there.
passages.quote: The Roof of these Portico's is supported by Pillars without, and Pilasters within … The Doors and Windows observe the same Symmetry. The tops of their Houses are cover'd with Lead, in a Figure of a Duomo
passages.speaker: 'Heliogenes de L'Epy' (English translation, 1689)
passages.caution: Fictional architecture. The OCR on this page mixes lines from two columns; the Pantheon comparison is on the next page (n148).

passages.headline: Philosophers protected by the Great Kam
passages.gloss: The book explains how its peaceful city survives among the Tartars: the Great Kam admires the citizens' honesty and lets them live in peace, and in return they send him a volunteer regiment of 300 young men. That service, the author says, is how they learn the 'Tartarian Language' needed for trade at their fair.
passages.quote: Now altho' they lye surrounded by the Tartarians, yet are they not at War with any body : For the Great Kam, who has always had a high esteem for them, by reason of their Integrity, permits them to live in Peace and Tranquillity one among another.
passages.speaker: 'Heliogenes de L'Epy' (English translation, 1689)
passages.caution: Fiction; the 'Great Kam' is the stock European name for a Tartar emperor, used here without any real ruler in view.

passages.headline: Why can't there be another Heliopolis, in Tartary?
passages.gloss: In his preface the author answers readers who doubted his story. Many cities share a name, he argues (two Frankforts, two Lyons, two Chalons), so why deny that besides Heliopolis in Egypt there could be the one he describes in Tartary? He also compares his doubters to those who laughed at the idea of the Antipodes before Columbus.
passages.quote: Why must it be deny'd, but that besides Heliopolis in Egypt, there may be that other of which I have given the Relation in Tartary.
passages.speaker: 'Heliogenes de L'Epy', preface (English translation, 1689)
passages.caution: The protest of truth is a standard device of imaginary voyages.

passages.headline: Tatar and Moghul, twin sons of a Turkish king
passages.people: Turks, Tatars and Mongols (as legendary ancestors)
passages.when: Legendary antiquity (told as by Timur, c.1350s)
passages.gloss: Timur asks his father for the family history, and hears the Turkic origin legend: the Turks descend from Yafet Aghlan, son of the biblical Japhet, and a later king had twin sons named Tatar and Moghul who split Turkestan between them. Tatar's eight sons and Moghul's nine founded the tribes, who then fought each other on the plains. The same story is told by the Khivan khan and historian Abu'l-Ghazi in the seventeenth century.
passages.quote: when his fifth son Aljeh Khan ascended the throne, the all gracious God bestowed on him twin sons, one of which was called Tatar, the other Moghul ; when they were grown up, Aljeh Khan divided the kingdom of Turkestan between them during his life-time
passages.speaker: Attributed to Timur (Persian text of Abu Talib al-Husayni, translated by Charles Stewart, 1830)
passages.caution: A genealogical legend, retold in a work whose authorship is disputed.

passages.headline: Black felt tents and a room dug underground
passages.gloss: Lost on a freezing night while hunting, young Timur and his companions saw black felt tents that at first looked like sand hills. The family took them for thieves, then gave them a room built underground, lit a fire, fed them soup and lent them flea-ridden blankets. Timur says that after becoming ruler he rewarded them.
passages.quote: About this time we saw some black (felt) tents or huts, upon which my companions said, " these are hillocks of sand and dust," … the inhabitants of which supposing I was a thief, hallooed out and prepared to attack me ; but when I told them all the circumstances, they were ashamed, and having cleared out a room which was constructed under ground, lighted a fire for us
passages.speaker: Attributed to Timur (translated by Charles Stewart, 1830)
passages.caution: The word 'felt' is the translator's addition in brackets. The story may be literary.

passages.headline: Repairing a Mongol khan's palace at Karshi
passages.gloss: Before marching on Samarkand, Timur orders the palace of 'Kepee Khan' at Karshi repaired, a fortress built at the town gate and other buildings put up. The translator's note explains that the old town of Nakhsheb took the name Karshi (Turkic for 'palace') from a palace built there by a Mongol prince, the Chaghatayid khan Kebek.
passages.quote: I prepared for marching to Samerkund, but first gave orders to repair the palace of Kepee Khan, whose name in the Turky language, was Karshy ; and I commanded that a fortress should be erected at the gate of the town, and some other buildings constructed.
passages.speaker: Attributed to Timur (translated by Charles Stewart, 1830)
passages.caution: The wording makes 'Karshy' the palace's Turkic name; the footnote is by the translator.

passages.headline: Reading the future in a mutton bone
passages.gloss: Before helping his ally Malik Husayn retake Herat, Timur strips a leg of mutton to the bone and performs 'the usual ceremonies' to read an omen from it; the sign is good, and the city falls by surprise at dawn. The translator adds a footnote that the Tartars play with sheep bones instead of dice. Omens run all through these memoirs.
passages.quote: At this time there was a stewed leg of mutton before us, the bone of which was sticking out ; I took it, and having stripped it of all the meat, I resolved within myself to draw from it an omen, whether Melk Hussyn would be successful in his enterprize. I performed the usual ceremonies, and the result was favourable
passages.speaker: Attributed to Timur (translated by Charles Stewart, 1830)
passages.caution: The footnote about sheep-shank games is Stewart's, not the text's.

passages.headline: A moving city with mosques and kitchens
passages.people: Golden Horde (Turks and Mongols under Uzbek Khan)
passages.gloss: Ibn Battuta reached Uzbek Khan's camp (the urdu, or horde) at the Five Mountains at the start of Ramadan. He describes it as a city on the move, with streets, mosques and cook-houses whose smoke rose as they travelled, all of which became stationary when the camp halted. He ranks Uzbek among the seven great kings of the world.
passages.quote: at this place, which is termed the urdu, or camp, we arrived on the first of the month Ramadan. Here we witnessed a moving city, with its streets, mosques, and cooking-houses, the smoke of which ascended as they moved along. When, however, they halted, all these became stationary.
passages.speaker: Ibn Battuta (as redacted by Ibn Juzayy; abridged text translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)

passages.headline: Queens on the throne, faces uncovered
passages.gloss: After Friday prayer Uzbek Khan sat in a 'golden alcove' on a gilded, jewelled throne, with his four wives seated on the throne beside him in full view. When each wife came in, the khan rose and led her by the hand to her seat. Ibn Battuta, used to royal women being hidden, was struck by this, and a page earlier he notes that Turkish noblewomen here went unveiled and were highly respected. He was given sheep, a horse and a leather bag of kumiss.
passages.quote: Whenever one of these wives enters, he arises, and taking her by the hand, puts her into her place upon the throne. Thus they are exposed to the sight of all, without so much as a veil.
passages.speaker: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)

passages.headline: A leather bag of kumiss from the khan
passages.gloss: The khan's welcome gift was practical steppe hospitality: sheep, a horse and a skin of kimiz (kumiss), fermented mare's milk, which Ibn Battuta notes was highly valued as a drink. He also explains that each of the khan's wives had her own household, and that a visitor was expected to call on every one of them.
passages.quote: Upon this day I was presented to the Sultan, who received me very graciously, and afterwards sent me some sheep and a horse, with a leathern bag of kimiz, which is the milk of a mare ; and very much valued among them as a beverage.
passages.speaker: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)

passages.headline: Nine animals for one stolen
passages.gloss: Crossing the Kipchak steppe by hired cart (araba), Ibn Battuta noticed huge herds grazing with no herdsmen. He explains it by the harsh law on theft: a thief had to return the animal with nine more, and if he could not, his children were taken, or he himself killed. He also notes that the treeless steppe folk burned dung for fuel.
passages.quote: he is compelled to return it with nine others of equal value. But, if this is not in his power, his children are taken. If, however, he have no children, he is himself slaughtered just like a sheep.
passages.speaker: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)
passages.caution: The sentence begins on the previous page (n102): a man 'convicted of having stolen a beast'. The law is what he was told, not a case he saw.

passages.headline: Silent trade with unseen people in the Land of Darkness
passages.people: Unknown northern peoples; Golden Horde merchants
passages.gloss: At Bulgar he was told of a Land of Darkness forty days north, reached only by dog-sledges over ice, where there were no trees, stones or houses. Merchants left their goods and withdrew; next day they found sable and ermine in their place, and could take the furs or leave them. Nobody ever saw the other party, so the merchants did not know if they traded with men or demons. He did not go.
passages.quote: each man, leaving what he has brought with him, goes back to his appointed station. On the morrow they return to look for their goods, and find, instead of them, sable, ermine, and the fur of the sinjab. … for the merchants know not whether it is with mankind or demons that they have to do ; no one being seen during the transaction.
passages.speaker: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)
passages.caution: Hearsay; he says he decided not to make the journey. Modern scholars also doubt that he reached Bulgar itself.

passages.headline: Astrakhan, where the khan wintered on a road of hay
passages.gloss: Ibn Battuta travelled with the khan's court to Astrakhan, 'one of his cities', on the Volga (Athal). The khan wintered there, and when the river froze the local people were ordered to lay thousands of bundles of hay on the ice as a roadway.
passages.quote: At this place the Sultan resides during the very cold weather ; and when this river, as well as the adjoining waters, are frozen, the King orders the people of the country to bring thousands of bundles of hay, which they do, and then place it upon the ice, and upon this they travel.
passages.speaker: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)

passages.headline: A queen's travelling mosque, left at the border
passages.place: Balkans, on the road to Constantinople
passages.gloss: Ibn Battuta escorted Uzbek Khan's Byzantine wife on a visit to her father in Constantinople. Like her husband, she carried a mosque (evidently a tent) that was set up at every halt for daily prayers. At the first Byzantine fortress she left it behind, and from then on, he says with some dismay, the call to prayer stopped and wine appeared at her table.
passages.quote: The Queen had with her a mosque, which she set up at every stage, just as her husband used to do. In this she had daily prayers. She left it, however, at the fortress. After this the office of the Moazin ceased : wine was brought into the banquet and of this she drank.
passages.speaker: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)

passages.headline: Sarai, the khan's great capital
passages.gloss: Returning from Constantinople, Ibn Battuta found the khan had moved to his capital, El Sarai, which he calls very handsome and very large. He met its leading scholar, a Khwarezmian imam whom the khan visited every Friday. The abridged text gives little more about the city itself.
passages.quote: This city of El Sarai is very handsome and exceedingly large. Of its learned men is the Imam, the learned Nooman Oddin, El Khavarezmi. I met him in this place.
passages.speaker: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)
passages.caution: The full Rihla describes Sarai's quarters and peoples at much greater length; this abridgement cuts it down.

passages.headline: Khwarezm, largest city of the Turks, where skipping prayers meant a whipping
passages.gloss: After forty days across the steppe by camel cart, by way of Saraichuk with its bridge, Ibn Battuta reached Khwarezm (Urgench), which he calls the largest and most crowded city of the Turks, ruled by an emir for Uzbek Khan. He praises its people as the best-mannered he had met, and describes a whip hung in every mosque to punish those who missed prayers.
passages.quote: This is the largest city the Turks have, and is very much crowded, on account of the multitude of its inhabitants. It is subject to the sultan Uzbek Khan, and is governed on his part by a great Emir, who resides within it.
passages.speaker: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)

passages.headline: Bukhara, a century after the Tartars
passages.gloss: Bukhara, the chief city beyond the Oxus, had still not recovered, Ibn Battuta says, from being ravaged by the Tartars more than a century earlier. He found nobody there with any learning. Here 'Tartars' means the Mongol armies of Genghis Khan.
passages.quote: then, after one stage, we came to Bokhara, which is the principal city of the country beyond the Gihon. After it had been ravaged by the Tartars, it almost entirely disappeared : I found no one in it who knew any thing of science.
passages.speaker: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)
passages.caution: Bukhara was sacked again by Ilkhanid Mongol troops in 1273, so not all the damage he saw dated from 1220.

passages.headline: Genghis Khan the blacksmith
passages.gloss: At Bukhara Ibn Battuta retells what was said of the Tartars' founder: that Genghis Khan began as a blacksmith in the country of 'Khota', a big, generous man who won followers by feasting them, then conquered Khota, China, Kashgar and Almaliq before turning on Khwarezm. The translator notes that other histories give his origins very differently.
passages.quote: It is said that Jengiz Khan, who came with the Tartars into the countries of Islamism and destroyed them, was in his outset a blacksmith in the country of Khota.
passages.speaker: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)
passages.caution: A popular story ('it is said'); the blacksmith tale may have grown from Temujin's name, which resembles the Turkic word for iron. The rest of the story continues on the next page (n115).

passages.headline: Twenty-four thousand scholars killed: a story at fourth hand
passages.gloss: The editor Ibn Juzayy inserts a report passed down a chain of four people: a scholar from Iraq, met at Mecca, said that 24,000 learned men died in the Tartar war in Iraq and that he and his nephew were the only scholars who escaped. It is a vivid example of how atrocity figures travelled by word of mouth, and the text is careful to show the chain.
passages.quote: that in the war with the Tartars in Irak not fewer than four and twenty thousand learned men perished ; and that himself, and that man, pointing to his brother's son, were the only learned men who had escaped.
passages.speaker: Ibn Juzayy, the editor, citing a chain of informants (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)
passages.caution: Fourth-hand report added by the editor, not by Ibn Battuta; the number cannot be checked.

passages.headline: Balkh's great mosque, broken open by Genghis Khan for treasure
passages.gloss: Balkh lay in ruins, never rebuilt since Genghis Khan destroyed it; only the outline of the city could be traced. Its mosque had been one of the finest in the world, and Genghis had three of its pillars torn down because he was told treasure was hidden beneath them. Ibn Battuta then tells the legend behind that rumour: a governor's wife built the mosque from the price of a jewelled robe and buried a third of the money under a pillar for repairs.
passages.quote: It has not been rebuilt since its destruction by the cursed Jengiz Khan. … Its mosque was one of the largest and handsomest in the world. Its pillars were incomparable : three of which were destroyed by Jengiz Khan, because it had been told him, that the wealth of the mosque lay concealed
passages.speaker: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)
passages.caution: He saw the ruins; the story of the pillars and the treasure is local tradition.

passages.headline: A khan deposed for breaking Genghis Khan's Yasa
passages.gloss: Ibn Battuta visited the camp of Sultan Tarmashirin, a devout Muslim khan who prayed in a mosque inside his camp. He explains that Genghis Khan's law book, the Yasa, required an annual assembly where nobles could depose a ruler who had broken its rules. Tarmashirin had abolished that assembly, so, after Ibn Battuta left, the Tartars and their nobles deposed him and he was killed.
passages.quote: Now, Tarmashirin had entirely abolished the observance of this day, which gave very great offence. Some time, therefore, after we had left the country, the Tartars, together with their nobles, assembled and deposed him, appointing for a successor one of his relations
passages.speaker: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)
passages.caution: The deposition happened after he left, so he reports it second-hand; his account of the Yasa assembly is not confirmed by other sources.

passages.headline: The King of China is a Tartar
passages.gloss: In China, Ibn Battuta says plainly who ruled: the king was a Tartar, a descendant of the Genghis Khan who had laid waste to Muslim lands. He adds that every Chinese province had a separate town for Muslims, with their own mosques, and that the kings honoured them.
passages.quote: The King of China is a Tartar, and one of the descendants of Jengiz Khan, who entered the Mohammedan countries, and desolated many of them. In all the Chinese provinces, there is a town for the Mohammedans, and in this they reside.
passages.speaker: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)

passages.headline: The rope trick at a Mongol governor's feast
passages.gloss: At a banquet given by the emir Qurtay at El Khansa (Hangzhou), the Khan's jugglers performed. A ball on a strap was thrown up out of sight; a boy climbed the strap and vanished; the master followed with a knife and threw down the boy's limbs, then put them together and the boy stood up. Ibn Battuta says he was so shaken he had palpitations. The Muslim judge beside him swore it was all illusion.
passages.quote: he then threw the hand of the boy upon the ground, then his foot ; then his other hand, then his other foot ; then his body, then his head. He then came down, panting for breath, and his clothes stained with blood. … The juggler then took the limbs of the boy and applied them one to another
passages.speaker: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)
passages.caution: He says he witnessed it; a judge present called it trickery. Some scholars doubt how much of the China section is first-hand.

passages.headline: A khan buried under a hill with slaves and impaled horses
passages.gloss: Ibn Battuta reports that a Mongol khan was killed by rebel kinsmen and buried with about a hundred relatives. The khan was laid on a couch in an underground chamber with his weapons, gold and silver vessels, four slave women and six favourite servants, and earth was heaped over it into a hill. Four horses were impaled on stakes on the mound. Everyone wore white hoods for mourning.
passages.quote: a large sepulchre was dug for him under the earth, in which a most beautiful couch was spread, and the Khan was with his weapons laid upon it. With him they placed all the gold and silver vessels he had in his house, together with four female slaves, and six of his favourite Mamluks … and the earth heaped upon them to the height of a large hill.
passages.speaker: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)
passages.caution: He says the khan was killed before he reached the capital, so the burial is almost certainly reported, not seen; the translator notes he could find no record of such a khan's death, and no Yuan emperor died this way at that date.

passages.headline: A name the conquerors themselves rejected
passages.gloss: In his introduction Erskine explains that 'Tartar' was first used by thirteenth-century European travellers and that Genghis Khan's family disliked it. He cites Rubruck, who was warned at the court of Sartaq (actually Batu's son, not Genghis's grandson) to call him Moal, a Mongol, because the Tatars were a different, conquered tribe. The European name for the whole empire was thus the name of one of its subject peoples.
passages.quote: This name of Tartar, however, by which we are accustomed to designate Chengiz Khan and his successors as well as their empire, these princes themselves rejected with disdain. Rubriquis, who visited the court of Sartakh, Chengiz Khan's grandson, about the year 1254, was cautioned, therefore, to call him Moal (that is Moghul), and not Tartar
passages.speaker: William Erskine, editor's introduction (1826), citing William of Rubruck
passages.caution: Editorial synthesis, not Babur. Sartaq was Batu's son, a great-grandson of Genghis Khan, and in Rubruck's own account the warning was not to call Sartaq a Christian; the remark that the Mongols disliked being called Tartars is Rubruck's general comment.

passages.headline: Tartar and Tartarus: why the name stuck in Europe
passages.people: Mongols and Turks (as named by Europeans)
passages.gloss: Erskine reports that the Mongols (Kalmyks) regarded 'Tatar' as an insult meaning something like 'robber', and asks why a name its bearers rejected became so widespread. His answer is the old pun: 'Tartar' sounded like Tartarus, the classical underworld, and fitted the terror the invaders caused in Europe.
passages.quote: It is singular that a name thus rejected among the nations to whom it is applied, should have had so much currency. The resemblance between Tartar and the infernal Tartarus, joined with the dread and horror in which the Tartar invaders were held, while they scattered dismay over Europe, probably, as has been well conjectured, preserved the name in the west.
passages.speaker: William Erskine, editor's introduction (1826)
passages.caution: Editorial conjecture; Erskine says it 'has been well conjectured' by others.

passages.headline: Babur: a Turk by his father, a Mongol by his mother
passages.gloss: Erskine explains that Babur belonged to 'both races of Tartars'. Through his father he descended from Timur, and so counted himself a Turk; through his mother he descended from Genghis Khan. Erskine adds that Babur's sympathies were entirely with the Turks and that he often speaks of the Mongols with hatred and contempt.
passages.quote: Baber had a close connexion with both races of Tartars, He traced up his descent on the father's side in a direct line to the great Taimur Beg, whence he always speaks of himself as being a Turk ; while by the mother's side he was sprung from Chengiz Khan, being the grandson of Yunis Khan, a celebrated prince of the Moghuls.
passages.speaker: William Erskine, editor's introduction (1826)

passages.headline: 'Were the name Moghul written in gold'
passages.gloss: After his defeat by the Uzbek Shaybani Khan, Babur complains bitterly that the Mongol troops sent to help him did not fight but turned on his own men, unhorsing and stripping them, and he says this was their usual practice. He sums up with a couplet that shows how sharply a Timurid Turk could separate himself from the Mongols, though he was one by descent.
passages.quote: If the Moghul race were a race of angels, it is a bad race ; And were the name Moghul written in gold, it would be odious.
passages.speaker: Babur (translated by John Leyden and William Erskine, 1826)
passages.caution: Written in anger after a defeat; a partisan judgement.

passages.headline: The Uzbek turning charge
passages.gloss: Describing how he lost the battle, Babur explains the Uzbek method: they always tried to turn the enemy's flank (the tulghama), and charged front and rear together, shooting arrows at full gallop, chiefs and common men mixed together, retreating just as fast if driven back. Babur escaped by swimming his armoured horse across the Kohik river.
passages.quote: In battle, the great reliance of the Uzbeks is on the Tulghmeh (or turning the enemy's flank). They never engage without using the Tulghmeh. Another of their practices is to advance and charge in front and rear, discharging their arrows at full gallop, pell-mell, chiefs and common soldiers, and, if repulsed, they in like manner retire full gallop.
passages.speaker: Babur (translated by John Leyden and William Erskine, 1826)

passages.headline: A khan raised up on a white felt
passages.gloss: Babur tells how his Mongol grandfather Yunis Khan was made khan: a leading beg seated him and his new wife on a white felt and proclaimed him, according to the ancient Mongol rules (tore). Erskine's footnote links it to the felt on which Genghis Khan was said to have been proclaimed.
passages.quote: Shir Haji Beg having seated the Khan and Ais-doulet Begum on a white felt, according to the Tureh, or ancient Institutions of the Moghuls, they proclaimed him Khan.
passages.speaker: Babur (translated by John Leyden and William Erskine, 1826)
passages.caution: Family history from before Babur's birth.

passages.headline: The veiled bride and the child who unveils her
passages.gloss: Visiting his uncle in Samarkand at the age of five, Babur found the new bride still veiled 'according to the custom of the Turks', and was told to take the veil off. The translators' note explains the custom: a Turki bride stayed veiled for a time after marriage until a child of the family pulled the veil off and ran, which was thought to bring the child luck in marriage.
passages.quote: she still kept her face covered with a veil, according to the custom of the Turks. He directed me, and I took off her veil.
passages.speaker: Babur (translated by John Leyden and William Erskine, 1826)
passages.caution: The explanation of the custom is in the translators' footnote.

passages.headline: A prince in exile sleeps in a felt tent of cross-poles
passages.gloss: Driven out of his homeland, Babur set off for Khorasan with two or three hundred followers, most on foot. They had only two proper tents; Babur gave his to his mother and slept each night in a small felt tent on flexible poles. Erskine's note explains this alachuq was a felt-covered frame that folded up easily.
passages.quote: Such was our distress, that among us all we had only two tents. My own tent was pitched for my mother, and they erected for me at each stage a felt-tent of cross-poles, in which I used to take up my quarters.
passages.speaker: Babur (translated by John Leyden and William Erskine, 1826)

passages.headline: Towns for Persians, open country for Turks
passages.gloss: Erskine explains why the Turki language absorbed so many Persian words. The cities north of the Oxus were mostly lived in and farmed by the older Persian-speaking people, the Sarts or Tajiks, because the Turks long disliked town life and farming, mocking wheat as 'a weed'. The Turkish rulers held court in these cities, but the townspeople were largely not Turks.
passages.quote: The cities of Samarkand, Bokhara, Ahsi, Andejan, and Tashkend, as well as the other towns to the north of the Oxus and Jaxartes, were chiefly inhabited by Persians, the Turks long retaining their aversion to the life of a town, and refusing to submit to the drudgery of agriculture for the sake of supporting themselves on the top of a weed, as they call wheat in derision.
passages.speaker: William Erskine, preface (1826)
passages.caution: Editorial generalisation; Babur himself says the people of Andijan were all Turks.

passages.headline: Andijan: a stone-faced moat and three gates
passages.gloss: Babur begins his memoirs with his own kingdom of Fergana. Its capital Andijan was, he says, the largest fortress in Transoxiana after Samarkand and Kesh, with three gates, a citadel on the south, a stone-faced moat circled by a pebbled road, and suburbs all round. Its people were all Turks and spoke the same Turki that poets wrote in.
passages.quote: In Maweralnaher, after the fortresses of Samarkand and Kesh, none is equal in size to Andejan. It has three gates. The citadel is situated on the south of the city. … Around the fortress, on the edge of the stone-faced moat, is a broad highway covered with pebbles. All round the fort are the suburbs
passages.speaker: Babur (translated by John Leyden and William Erskine, 1826)

passages.headline: Timur's stone mosque, built by stonecutters from India
passages.gloss: Babur, who took Samarkand more than once, describes the buildings of his ancestor Timur: a four-storey palace, the Gok-serai, in the citadel, and a grand mosque of stone near the Iron Gate, whose Qur'an inscription could be read almost a kos away. He notes that the stonecutters were brought from Hindustan. Erskine's footnote adds that the historian Sharaf al-Din counted 200 masons from Azerbaijan, Fars and India.
passages.quote: There are many other magnificent edifices. One of these is the grand mosque, which is situated near the Iron-gate, within the walls of the city, and is built of stone. A number of stone-cutters were brought from Hindustan to work on it.
passages.speaker: Babur (translated by John Leyden and William Erskine, 1826)

passages.headline: Ulugh Beg's three-storey observatory
passages.gloss: Among the works of Timur's grandson Ulugh Beg, Babur singles out the observatory on the hill of Kohik: three storeys high, fitted with instruments, where the astronomical tables still in use in his day were made. He places it among the seven or eight observatories ever built, alongside Hulagu's at Maragha.
passages.quote: Another remarkable edifice is the observatory, erected on the skirts of the hill of Kohik, which is provided with an astronomical apparatus, and is three stories in height. By means of this observatory, Ulugh Beg Mirza composed the Zich-Korkani (or Korkani Astronomical Tables), which are followed at the present time, scarcely any other being used.
passages.speaker: Babur (translated by John Leyden and William Erskine, 1826)

passages.headline: Forty stone pillars and a house of Chinese porcelain
passages.gloss: In the Garden of the Plain, Babur describes the Chehel Sutun (Forty Pillars), a two-storey hall built entirely on carved stone columns, twisted and fluted, and a throne cut from a single huge stone brought from far away. Nearby stood a pavilion whose walls were covered in Chinese porcelain, for which, he was told, someone had been sent to China.
passages.quote: In this garden, there is another state pavilion, the walls of which are overlaid with porcelain of China, whence it is called the Chinese House. It is said that a person was sent to Khita, for the purpose of bringing it.
passages.speaker: Babur (translated by John Leyden and William Erskine, 1826)
passages.caution: That the porcelain was fetched from China is what Babur was told.

passages.headline: Samarkand: every trade in its own bazaar
passages.gloss: Babur calls Samarkand 'a wonderfully elegant city'. Its markets were arranged so each trade had its own bazaar, its bakers and cooks were excellent, and it made the best paper in the world and a crimson velvet exported everywhere. He also measured the city walls himself at 10,600 paces round.
passages.quote: Samarkand is a wonderfully elegant city. One of its distinguishing peculiarities is, that each trade has its own bazar ; so that different trades are not mixed together in the same place. The established customs and regulations are good. The bakers' shops are excellent, and the cooks are skilful. The best paper in the world comes from Samarkand.
passages.speaker: Babur (translated by John Leyden and William Erskine, 1826)

passages.headline: A Chaghatai prince makes wind and rain
passages.people: Chaghatai Mongol princes in Babur's army
passages.gloss: In India, Babur notes calmly that the Chaghatai prince Tokhta Bugha Sultan 'performed some of his enchantments' in his boat, and a high wind rose and it began to rain. This is the steppe weather magic with a rain-stone (yada) that Erskine's introduction calls wholly of Tartar origin and traces to a legendary stone given by Noah to Japhet.
passages.quote: I sent for the Sultans into the boat ; Tokhteh Bugha Sultan performed some of his enchantments. A high wind having risen, it began to rain.
passages.speaker: Babur (translated by John Leyden and William Erskine, 1826)
passages.caution: Babur records the rain following the rite without comment; the link to the rain-stone is Erskine's (introduction, p. xlvii, n58).

passages.headline: Fifteen hundred stonecutters on Babur's buildings in India
passages.gloss: Babur was scornful of Indian architecture but impressed by India's supply of craftsmen. He compares Timur's famous stone mosque in Samarkand, built with 200 masons from several countries, to his own works: 680 stonecutters at Agra alone, and 1,491 across his building sites. The buildings of this Timurid ruler were raised by local Indian hands.
passages.quote: In Agra alone, and of stone-cutters belonging to that place only, I every day employed on my palaces six hundred and eighty persons; and in Agra, Sikri, Biana, Dhulpur, Gualiar, and Koel, there were every day employed on my works one thousand four hundred and ninety-one stone-cutters.
passages.speaker: Babur (translated by John Leyden and William Erskine, 1826)

passages.headline: Bukhara, the greatest city of Tartary
passages.gloss: Mohan Lal calls Bukhara the largest, most populous and richest city 'in the whole region of Tartary', and says it had 360 mosques and colleges, though he was not impressed by the students' Persian and Arabic. Shops opened only after the owners had finished their morning tea and closed at three, when trade moved to the Registan square.
passages.quote: Bokhara is the largest and most populous and wealthy city in the whole region of Tartary. The splendid mosques and magnificent colleges, which are 360 in number, contain students who are unqualified both in the Persian and Arabic languages, but they write a very good hand.
passages.speaker: Mohan Lal (1846 edition)
passages.caution: The figure of 360 is a traditional round number rather than a count.

passages.headline: Houses of mud, wood and mats, and a roofed bazaar
passages.gloss: Behind its famous mosques, Bukhara was built of humble materials. Most houses had one storey, a few more than two, made of mud, wood and mats. The great roofed bazaar built by the late king, with its long straight line of shops hung with Chinese porcelain and Russian bottles, impressed him most.
passages.quote: The houses are mostly of one story high; some of them of more than two; they are neatly constructed of mud, wood, and mats, which prevent the falling of the dust from the roof. … The large bazar, which is roofed, has a very striking appearance.
passages.speaker: Mohan Lal (1846 edition)

passages.headline: Balkh, 'mother of cities', a mass of ruins and dust
passages.gloss: Mohan Lal found the ancient city of Balkh reduced to ruins and dust among orchards, with a broad bazaar roofed crudely with rafters, hay and mud, whose shops opened only on Tuesdays. An Uzbek customs officer searched their baggage. Locals called Balkh the mother of cities, founded by a son of Noah.
passages.quote: This was formerly a very large and populous city, but at present nothing is to be seen except a mass of ruins and dust. Orchards are scattered in every spot … The bazar of Balk, though broad, is irregularly roofed with rafters, hay, and mud.
passages.speaker: Mohan Lal (1846 edition)

passages.headline: A goat that walked the rooftops from Balkh to Mazar
passages.gloss: Mohan Lal records two local marvels. An old mud fort outside Balkh was said to grow taller at night (he wanted to check, but the caravan left). And the city had once been so vast that its roofs touched all the way to Mazar, so that a goat climbed onto a roof in Balkh and came down the next day in Mazar, some 20 kilometres away.
passages.quote: Without the city of Balk is an old mud fort, called Chihal Gazi, which, people say, in the night increases in its height. I wished to stop and verify the fact, but our caravan started at the very eve. … a goat climbed up one of the roofs in Balk, and descended next day at Mazar, whither his master followed him also.
passages.speaker: Mohan Lal (1846 edition)
passages.caution: Local legends; Mohan Lal takes the goat story as proof of Balkh's former size, but did not test either tale.

passages.headline: Timur's archers could not hit the giant Buddhas
passages.gloss: At Bamiyan, Mohan Lal repeats the local story that Timur, returning from India, ordered his best archers to shoot down the colossal statues, but that not one arrow struck them. He had just recounted that Hindus credited the statues to the five Pandava brothers of the Mahabharata; Muslims linked them with the pre-Islamic idols Lat and Manat.
passages.quote: Being tempted by his religion, he ordered his expert archers to discharge their arrows against the images, which he wished to level to the ground ; but none of the arrows struck them, the cause of which I know not.
passages.speaker: Mohan Lal (1846 edition)
passages.caution: Tradition, not history; the statues were in fact Buddhist, carved around the sixth century AD.

passages.headline: The Tartar and the princess of Ghulghula
passages.gloss: Mohan Lal tells the legend of Shahr-i Ghulghula, the ruined fortress city by Bamiyan, said to have been built by an unbeliever before Muhammad's time. A Tartar from Badakhshan besieged it in vain until the ruler's daughter, in love with him, wrote telling him to cut off the water. He took the fort, married her, and then killed her for betraying her father.
passages.quote: A Tartar, native of Badakhshan, resolved to invade it, and laid siege to it. When he found great difficulty in subduing it, and was on the point of dismissing his camp, he fortunately received a letter, with the following contents, from the beautiful daughter of the Kafar, who had fallen in love with the Tartar
passages.speaker: Mohan Lal (1846 edition)
passages.caution: A folk tale; in history Shahr-i Ghulghula was destroyed by Genghis Khan's army in 1221.

passages.headline: Turkmen tents half-buried in snow
passages.gloss: On the desert road to Bukhara the caravan passed Turkmen tents. Mohan Lal notes that they had large herds, lived on meat, curds and bread, fed their horses on meat and gave them salt water, and spent the winter in tents half-buried in snow. He adds bluntly that plundering caravans was their real trade and that they held many Persian (Qizilbash) slaves.
passages.quote: There we observed a few tents of Turkmans; they possess large herds of cattle, and live upon meat, curd, and bread. They feed their horses generally with flesh, and give them salt-water to drink. They do not much mind the cold of the winter, which they pass in tents, half-buried under the snow. Plundering the caravans is the proper occupation of these Turkmans.
passages.speaker: Mohan Lal (1846 edition)
passages.caution: He saw the tents; the details of winter life and horse-feeding are probably what he was told.

passages.headline: Villages emptied by 'the Tartars'
passages.gloss: Near Mashhad the caravan passed villages wrecked by Turkmen raiders. At Tibris, which Mohan Lal says was 'harassed by the Tartars', most of the people had been carried off as slaves, and the survivors ran up weeping to ask the travellers for news of their captive families. Here 'Tartars' simply means the Turkmen slave-raiders.
passages.quote: Tibris, a fine walled village, contains very few inhabitants, who are harassed by the Tartars. Some time ago it was destroyed by the Alamans, and most of the residents made slaves. On our approach, the villagers ran up to us, shedding a flood of tears
passages.speaker: Mohan Lal (1846 edition)

passages.headline: Manchu 'Tartars' on the emperor's pay
passages.gloss: Arriving at the harbour of Kin-chow (Jinzhou), about fifteen leagues from Mukden (Shenyang), Gützlaff was told the Manchus of the area were numerous but lived idly, mostly in the direct or indirect employ of the emperor, a description of the hereditary banner garrisons. He adds that there seemed little jealousy between them and the Chinese labourers, and that the Manchus looked little different from the Chinese.
passages.quote: The Mantchou Tartars who live hereabouts are numerous, and lead an idle life, being principally in the employ of the Emperor, either directly or indirectly. There seems to be but little jealousy between them and the labouring class of Chinese.
passages.speaker: Karl Gützlaff (1832)
passages.caution: This comes from 'the persons with whom I conversed', not from his own observation inland.

passages.headline: Granite houses and beds heated from below
passages.people: Chinese and Manchu townspeople of Liaodong
passages.gloss: Gützlaff found Kin-chow small and plain. Its houses were built of the local granite, with few comforts apart from brick sleeping platforms warmed by a fire lit underneath (the kang). It is a precise, humble picture of domestic building on the edge of 'Tartary'.
passages.quote: Kin-chow itself has very little to attract the attention of visitors ; it is not a large or handsome place. The houses are built of granite ( which abounds here) ; and are without any accommodations, except a peculiar kind of sleeping places, which are formed of brick; and so constructed, that they can be heated, by fires kindled beneath them.
passages.speaker: Karl Gützlaff (1832)

passages.headline: Grand Cham of the Tartars, named after the river Tata
passages.gloss: At Genghis Khan's proclamation, Pétis says, the new emperor praised the 'Soumoguls', called Tartars after the river Tata that ran through their land, and added 'Grand Cham of the Tartars' to his title to honour them. A footnote explains that this is how all the Scythian nations under Genghis came to be called Tartars, and that the Chinese, lacking an r, said 'Tata'.
passages.quote: And having much cause to praise the Soumoguls (who are particularly called Tartars, by reason of the River Tata that waters their Country) he declared in the Mogul Language, that he would add to his Title of Emperor of the Moguls that of Grand Cham of the Tartars, both to do that Nation Honour
passages.speaker: François Pétis de la Croix (English translation, 1722)
passages.caution: A compiler's explanation drawn from Carpini (who first spoke of 'Su-Mongals' named after a river Tatar) and Oriental histories; the river origin of the name is not accepted today.

passages.headline: Felt houses on wheels, drawn by thirty oxen
passages.gloss: Describing the great assembly Genghis held on the plain of Toncat, Pétis explains that most lords brought their 'moveable houses' on wheels. They had wooden floors, lattice walls, a dome with a smoke hole, and felt covers rubbed with sheep's milk, or among the rich plastered with tallow, to shed the rain. Some were so heavy with furniture that thirty oxen pulled one, and every door faced south.
passages.quote: Some were cover'd with Felt rubbed with Sheep's Milk, so that the Rain might run off without penetrating it. … they are sometimes so heavy, by reason of the Furniture they contain, that they are obliged to put to one of them thirty Oxen to draw it along.
passages.speaker: François Pétis de la Croix (English translation, 1722)
passages.caution: The details closely follow Rubruck's eyewitness description of 1253 and Carpini's; Pétis applies them to Genghis's assembly.

passages.headline: Bukhara burned because it was built of wood
passages.gloss: Retelling the Mongol sack of Bukhara from Persian historians, Pétis explains why the fire was so complete: most buildings were of wood, because stone was hard to get around Bukhara. Only public buildings such as the mosques and caravanserais, built of brick, escaped. It is a clear statement of what one of Central Asia's great cities was built from.
passages.quote: all Parts of the Town were strait on fire, the greatest part of the Building being made of Wood, because of the difficulty of getting Stone in the Country round Bocara. … and all the Houses became a Prey to the Flames, except some publick Buildings, such as the Mosques and Caravansera's, which were made of Bricks.
passages.speaker: François Pétis de la Croix (English translation, 1722), citing Fadlallah (Rashid al-Din) and others
passages.caution: Marginal source notes are mixed into the OCR here and have been dropped. Compiled five centuries after the event.

passages.headline: Prester John unmasked as a steppe king, and his letter as a forgery
passages.gloss: Pétis identifies the famous Prester John of Asia with Ong Khan, king of the Keraits and Genghis Khan's early patron, and summarises the boastful letter in Prester John's name, which claimed seventy vassal kings and rule over Gog and Magog. He then declares the letter a forgery spread by Nestorian Christians. Elsewhere (n126) he notes that the Great Wall of China was called by Arabs the Bank of Gog and Magog.
passages.quote: But 'tis not difficult to discover that this Letter is a Counterfeit, and that it was not writ by Ounghcan. The Nestorians who in that Country were very numerous, having established themselves there in the Year 757. by the means of the Missionaries of Moussoul and Basra, were the Authors of this Letter
passages.speaker: François Pétis de la Croix (English translation, 1722)
passages.caution: The identification of Prester John with Ong Khan goes back to Marco Polo; the claim that Nestorians forged the letter is Pétis's own theory.

passages.headline: Scythians under a new name
passages.people: Tartars in general, including the Crimean Tatars
passages.gloss: Chevalier opens his Tartar chapter by saying the name 'Tartar' was only about four hundred years old and that the people were really the ancient Scythians under a new label. He reports the scholar Leunclavius's view that the name came from a 'River Tartar' in their homeland.
passages.quote: The Tartars have not been known by this name, but for about four hundred years, and are properly the Scythians; some Authors, as Leunclave and others, derive this name from the River Tartar, in the Countrey where they did inhabit
passages.speaker: Pierre Chevalier (translated by Edward Brown, 1672)
passages.caution: The river etymology is reported from earlier authors, not Chevalier's own finding.

passages.headline: Were the Tartars the Lost Ten Tribes?
passages.gloss: Chevalier repeats a learned theory that 'Tartar' was a corruption of 'Tatares', supposedly a Syriac word for 'remnant', making the Tartars the remnant of the Ten Tribes of Israel carried off by the Assyrians. He presents it as what 'some say', not as his own view.
passages.quote: There are some who say that the name of Tartar is improper and corrupted, and that they ought to be called Tatares or Totares, A word which in the Syriack Language signifies a Remnant, supposing that these people are the remnant of the Ten Tribes which Salmanazar and his predecessors led away captive into Assyria
passages.speaker: Pierre Chevalier (translated by Edward Brown, 1672)
passages.caution: A scholarly speculation of the period, reported secondhand.

passages.headline: Five Tartaries on the map
passages.people: Crimean Tatars, Volga Tatars, Nogais, Uzbeks and the peoples of 'Great Tartary'
passages.gloss: Here 'Tartary' is a geographer's label for most of northern Asia, carved into five parts: Crim Tartary, the hordes under the Tsar (including Kazan and Astrakhan), Zagatay or the Uzbek country where Tamerlane reigned, Cathay or Great Tartary, and an unknown far north-east. It shows how loosely the name was spread over many peoples.
passages.quote: Tartary is devided into five parts, the first is the lesser Tartary, or Tartary of Precop, called also Crim Tartary. The second is Sarmatia Asiatica, which containeth many Hordes of the Tartars subject to the Great Duke of Moscovia, as the Czeremisses, the Nagais, Zauolhans, and those of Cazan and Astracan.
passages.speaker: Pierre Chevalier (translated by Edward Brown, 1672)
passages.caution: A textbook geographic scheme, not observation. The list continues on p.35 with Zagatay (where Tamerlane reigned), Cathay or Great Tartary, and an unknown north-east.

passages.headline: No towns outside the peninsula
passages.gloss: Chevalier says Lesser Tartary stretched far beyond the Crimean peninsula across the steppe as far as the Don, but that outside the peninsula there were no towns or villages at all. The Tartars simply moved their camps to wherever the grazing was good; the next page says they used huts and 'travelling sheds' only in winter.
passages.quote: There are no Towns nor yet Villages, but in the Chersonesus, the rest being only incultivated Plains, yet of themselves very fruitful, and the Tartars encamp up and down in them as they find more or less forrage
passages.speaker: Pierre Chevalier (translated by Edward Brown, 1672)

passages.headline: Perekop, Crim and the Khan's court at Bakhchysarai
passages.gloss: A quick census of the Khan's towns in Crimea, counted in houses: Perekop (which the Tartars called Or) had about 400, and Bakhchysarai, where the Khan kept his court, about 2,000. The same page names a Black Sea trading town of about 2,000 houses belonging to the Khan (the name is garbled in the scan; probably Kozlov, today's Yevpatoria), and the next page adds the Khan's second palace at Almasaray, with a town of only 60 to 80 houses.
passages.quote: The Towns of this Peninsula are first Przecop, called Or by the Tartars, where there are about four hundred Houses … Crim, another Town of the Cham … inhabited by few but by the Tartars. Baciasary where the Cham ordinarily keepeth his Court … about two thousand Houses.
passages.speaker: Pierre Chevalier (translated by Edward Brown, 1672)
passages.caution: House counts are estimates; Chevalier does not say he visited Crimea.

passages.headline: Caffa, a fallen Genoese trading city
passages.people: Crimean Tatars, Turks, Greeks, Armenians, Jews and Italians
passages.gloss: Caffa (ancient Theodosia, modern Feodosia) belonged to the Turks, not the Khan. Chevalier describes it as a once-great Genoese trading port that had declined under Ottoman rule but still had five or six thousand houses and a mixed population, mostly Christian, with dozens of churches.
passages.quote: it was one of the most trading Towns of the Levant … yet there are still remaining about five or six thousand Houses; the Inhabitants are Greeks, Italians, the remainder of the Genoeses, Armenians, Jews, Turks and Tartars, but the most part of them are Christians
passages.speaker: Pierre Chevalier (translated by Edward Brown, 1672)

passages.headline: Captives sold at Caffa, as far as Persia and India
passages.gloss: Chevalier says Crimean Tartars left farming to Christians, Jews and their own slaves, and counted their wealth in horses, cattle and captives taken in raids. The captives were sold to merchants at Caffa and shipped east, and Polish women, he says, could end up in harems in Persia and India.
passages.quote: Their Horses and Cattel are their Riches, with the Booty and Slaves of both Sexes, which they take in their incursions and sell to the Merchants of Caffa … especially the Women and Maids of Poland, who are carried away sometimes as far as Persia and India, to furnish the Serraglios of those Countreys
passages.speaker: Pierre Chevalier (translated by Edward Brown, 1672)
passages.caution: Written from the Polish side of a long frontier war.

passages.headline: Sheepskins, bows and whips no European could copy
passages.gloss: The Tartars living out on the steppe wore sheepskins and sheepskin caps and carried a scimitar, bow and about twenty arrows, all homemade from horse parts. Chevalier admires their plaited whips, which he says French and German saddlers could not imitate, and notes they were beginning to use firearms.
passages.quote: The Tartars who live abroad, are habited in Sheep-skins with a Cap of the same Stuffe; their Arms are ordinarily a Cimeter, a Bow and a Quiver, with about twenty Arrows … of which also they make their Whips so neatly, by a particular Art which they have, that our Sadlers in France and Germany have not yet been able to imitate them
passages.speaker: Pierre Chevalier (translated by Edward Brown, 1672)

passages.headline: Horse meat cooked under the saddle
passages.gloss: Chevalier repeats the famous story that Tartars on the march softened horse meat by riding on it under the saddle and ate it with no sauce but the horse's sweat. He adds that they chose worn-out, sick or lame horses for this, not the best ones. At home they ate millet porridge and boiled horse meat.
passages.quote: when they goe to war and are upon their March, they make it ready, or rather mortify, or just heat it, under their Saddles, and eat it afterwards in this condition without any other sauce then the froth upon the Flesh, made by the sweating of the Horse
passages.speaker: Pierre Chevalier (translated by Edward Brown, 1672)
passages.caution: The saddle-meat story goes back to medieval writers and is a stock European image of steppe warriors; Chevalier does not say he saw it.

passages.headline: Water, millet beer and mare's milk
passages.gloss: Here Chevalier speaks as an eyewitness: in Poland he saw Tartar prisoners carry dead horses out of stables to feast on. He then lists their drinks: water, snow in winter, horse broth, 'Breha' (a millet drink, the steppe boza), and for the better-off mare's milk, mead and spirits, even though Islam forbade them wine.
passages.quote: I have seen at my being in Poland, divers Tartar prisoners come and take away dead Horses out of the Stables to feast one another with … their drink is ordinarily clear water, and in winter snow … or else Breha, which is a drink made with boiled Millet, but those who are better accommodated, and more delicate, drink Mares milk, Mead, and Strong waters
passages.speaker: Pierre Chevalier (translated by Edward Brown, 1672)

passages.headline: Honest at home, raiders abroad
passages.gloss: An enemy's surprisingly warm verdict: Chevalier calls the Tartars among the least vicious of nations, chaste, sincere and faithful, with no thieves or false witnesses among themselves. He explains their raids on Christian lands by saying they did not regard robbing 'infidels' as wrong. On the next page he says Polish nobles trusted young Tartar servants with the keys to their money and jewels.
passages.quote: As to their Morals, there are very few Nations to be found less vitious, for besides their continence, they are extremely sincere, and faithful, they have no Thieves or false witnesses amongst them, little injustice or violence, and live in Union and great tranquility
passages.speaker: Pierre Chevalier (translated by Edward Brown, 1672)
passages.caution: A generalisation; on the next page Chevalier adds his own observation that Polish nobles trusted young Tartar servants with their money and jewels.

passages.headline: Tartar captives hauling brick and lime in Poland
passages.gloss: Slavery ran both ways. Chevalier says the Poles kept most Tartar prisoners as chained slaves, used 'as Beasts' to carry building materials, firewood and other loads, living on bread and water. He saw two or three hundred of them in Warsaw, earning a little by making and selling whips.
passages.quote: the rest are kept as Slaves, having always Irons upon their feet, and are made use of as Beasts to carry all manner of burthens, Lime, Brick, and all other materials for building … when I was at Warsaw, I had opportunity to take notice of two or three hundred of them
passages.speaker: Pierre Chevalier (translated by Edward Brown, 1672)

passages.headline: The Khan's army at the siege of Zbarazh
passages.people: Crimean Tatars allied with Khmelnytsky's Cossacks
passages.gloss: In the history section, Chevalier describes the Polish commander Firley fortifying the town and castle of Zbarazh (in today's western Ukraine) before a huge Tartar and Cossack army surrounded it. He compares the host to those of Attila and Tamerlane, and on the next page stresses that the Khan himself was present in person.
passages.quote: the Army of the Tartars and Cossacks came and encompassed them in on all sides in such numbers, that there have been seldom seen the like forces together, since those of Attila and Tamerlan
passages.speaker: Pierre Chevalier (translated by Edward Brown, 1672)
passages.caution: A partisan Polish-side narrative of the siege; the numbers are rhetorical.

passages.headline: A map of a land that 'lay in the dark'
passages.gloss: The Royal Society's president greets Witsen's map as a Columbus-like discovery of a new world, and wonders aloud how anyone could chart deserts, bogs and mountains that seemed made for 'everlasting Solitude'. It is a vivid picture of how unknown 'Tartary' was to western Europe in the 1680s.
passages.quote: I Have lately had a great Effect of your Bounty in the Maps of Tartary. this is Columbus like, the Discovery of a New World; at least Tydings of those Parts, which from the beginning have layn in the Dark.
passages.speaker: Sir Robert Southwell, President of the Royal Society, writing to Witsen

passages.headline: How Witsen gathered his Tartary
passages.people: 'Tartars of all sorts' met in Muscovy
passages.gloss: Witsen answers that the map grew out of a visit almost 28 years earlier to the country of the Tsar, where he talked with local people and 'Tartars of all sorts'. Since then he had kept up letters with Moscow, Astrakhan, Georgia, Isfahan, Poland, Constantinople and Peking, and collected journals and drawings made to his order. He then admits his biggest doubts are about the sea coasts, which he drew in pale colour to show the uncertainty.
passages.quote: I not only Conversed with the Inhabitants of those Countreys, but with Tartars of all sorts … I have maintain'd a constant Correspondence in Mosco, Astracan, Georgia, Ispahan, Polonia, and Constantinople, I have had Letters every year from Peking the chief City of China, I have gathered Volumes of Journals and Registers
passages.speaker: Nicolaas Witsen (letter printed in Philosophical Transactions, 1686)
passages.caution: The country Witsen visited is garbled in the scan; his known journey of 1664 to 1665 was to Muscovy.

passages.headline: Ancient Greek place names 'corrupted by the Tartars'
passages.people: Tatars of the Azov coast (Crimean or Nogai), as seen by eighteenth century French scholars
passages.gloss: In a note on Strabo's temple of Achilles at the mouth of the Sea of Azov, the translators quote the French scholars Du Theil and Peyssonel, who wondered whether the Tatar fort of 'Achou' was the ancient Achilleum, its Greek name worn down in Tatar mouths. It is a small example of how Tatar place names were layered over Greek ones on the Black Sea coast.
passages.quote: Is not the fort of Achou, which is 8 leagues more to the east on the Palus Maeotis, the true Achilleum, the name being corrupted and abridged by the Tartars?
passages.speaker: Footnote by the 1854 translators (H. C. Hamilton and W. Falconer), quoting Peyssonel via Du Theil
passages.caution: Editorial conjecture, not Strabo's text.

passages.headline: How a Tatar cottage was built
