passages.gloss: Holderness gives a builder's-eye account of the ordinary Tatar house: oak stakes driven upright into the ground, woven through with branches, plastered inside and out and whitewashed, with an earth or marl roof, or tiles for richer families. Farm buildings used the same stakes and wattle, plastered with cow dung. This is about as far from 'lost stone cities' as it gets, and she saw it every day.
passages.quote: The cottages of the Tatar peasants, for cheapness of construction, rapidity of building, and simplicity of materials, are perhaps unrivalled … They are constructed of oaken stakes, whose ends are driven perpendicularly into the ground … into these, liggers are entwined, and the whole are well plastered within and without, and white-washed when dry.
passages.speaker: Mary Holderness
passages.caution: 'Liggers' are pliant rods or branches used as wattle.

passages.headline: Steppe houses dug into the ground
passages.gloss: On the treeless steppe, Holderness says, Tatar houses were often dug down into the earth so deeply that they needed only a roof. She notes they were warmer in winter and cooler in summer than the usual plastered wooden huts.
passages.quote: The houses of the Stepp Tatars are often dug in the ground, to such a depth as to require only roofing to complete them. These being impervious to the air, are warmer in winter, and cooler in summer, than the usual huts, which are built of wood and plastered.
passages.speaker: Mary Holderness

passages.headline: A vanished Tatar village turned into an orchard
passages.gloss: Holderness's own estate was a huge wild orchard made from the lands of a Tatar village of 1,700 people that had emptied after the Russian conquest. Only foundations, wells, the ruins of a Tatar bath and a mosque with its minaret remained. She is explicit that these ruins were a recent Tatar village, not something ancient or mysterious.
passages.quote: The village of Karagoss, at the time of the subjugation, contained 1700 inhabitants … Not a single house now remains within its circuit, though the foundations of them are to be found in every part … also the ruins of a Tatar bath, and a Tatar metchet, or mosque, the minaret of which, seen from all parts of the estate, embowered in wood, has a remarkably picturesque appearance
passages.speaker: Mary Holderness
passages.caution: The population figure at the conquest is presumably what she was told.

passages.headline: Karasubazar, 'the first Tatar town'
passages.people: Crimean Tatars with Jews, Armenians, Russians and Greeks
passages.gloss: Arriving in Crimea, Holderness describes Karasubazar (today Bilohirsk) as a crowded market town of narrow, irregular streets and an extraordinary number of shops: about two hundred for fruit alone and as many again for Tatar shoes. Elsewhere she calls its people almost entirely Tatar and its market the cheapest in the Crimea.
passages.quote: This is the first Tatar town, and is much more singular than pleasing: narrow and irregular streets, presenting a most extraordinary number of shops, occupied by Tatars, Jews, Armenians, Russians, and Greeks. For the sale of fruit alone, there are said to be two hundred shops
passages.speaker: Mary Holderness

passages.headline: Bakhchysarai's mosques and fountains
passages.gloss: The old Khans' capital, Holderness reports, was said to have had thirty-one mosques and seventy-five fountains in 1803. She adds that its fine fountains survived, while those of almost every other Crimean town had been destroyed.
passages.quote: Bachtcheserai is said to have contained, in 1803, thirty-one mosques, and seventy-five fountains: except Dr. Clarke, no late travellers have noticed the fine fountains which are still preserved here, though those of almost every other town have been destroyed.
passages.speaker: Mary Holderness
passages.caution: The mosque and fountain count is a reported figure, not her own count.

passages.headline: Staryi Krym, the old capital, in ruins
passages.gloss: Holderness calls Starai Krim, 'once the capital of the peninsula', little better than a heap of ruins, its few inhabitants Armenian shopkeepers. In a footnote she says the ruins were very extensive and that the town had still been flourishing at the Russian conquest.
passages.quote: These ruins are very extensive, and we know that at the first conquest of the country by the Russians, it was a flourishing town, though not to be compared to what it was when held by the Genoese.
passages.speaker: Mary Holderness (footnote)
passages.caution: Staryi Krym (the medieval Solkhat) was a Golden Horde and early Crimean Khanate centre; her remark that it was once 'held by the Genoese' may confuse it with nearby Genoese Caffa.

passages.headline: The Nogays, a wandering horde made to settle
passages.gloss: Holderness explains who the Nogay Tatars were: the old nomads of 'Nogay Tatary', who had roamed the steppes north of Crimea with tents, flocks and herds for ages. By her time the Russian government had gathered them into villages and pushed them to farm, though they still preferred grazing and horses.
passages.quote: The Nogay Tatars, if not the original inhabitants of the country, at least wandered over the immense Stepps of New Russia, with their tents, flocks, and herds, at the time of the Russian Conquest, and for ages before: this remnant of the Nomades of Nogay Tatary, are now collected together in a number of villages
passages.speaker: Mary Holderness
passages.caution: On the next page she describes the Nogays' moral character in very hostile terms, reflecting settler prejudice.

passages.headline: A bride carried home unseen
passages.gloss: Holderness, often invited to village weddings, describes how the bride travelled in a curtained cart and was kept from every eye: she was given sherbet and a lamb at her new door, then, behind screens of blanketing, wrapped in a sheet and carried into the house by her brother.
passages.quote: When she reaches the door of her new prison, sherbet is brought her to drink, and some kind of sweetmeat is given with it. She is next presented with a lamb, which is actually put into the carriage with her … wrapped in a sheet, she is carried by her brother into the house.
passages.speaker: Mary Holderness
passages.caution: 'New prison' is Holderness's own judgement.

passages.headline: Passports for the dead
passages.gloss: At an old woman's burial in Karagoss, Holderness watched the body laid in a side niche of the grave with papers written by the mulla: one on the breast describing the dead woman's character, one in the hand as a passport at the gates of Heaven, and one above the head warning the Evil One away. Stakes, hay, earth and stones then sealed the grave.
passages.quote: some papers written by the Mulla were disposed about it; one being placed on the breast, expressive of the character of the deceased; another in the hand, intended likewise as a sort of passport at the gates of Heaven; and a third above the head, which is said to be an intimation to the Evil One to refrain from disturbing the bones of a true believer.
passages.speaker: Mary Holderness
passages.caution: The meaning of each paper is what she was told; the Arabic texts were never translated for her.

passages.headline: Walking dead for forty days
passages.gloss: Holderness reports a startling belief: the spirits of wicked people walk for forty days after death, and then the grave must be opened and the corpse shot, beheaded or have its heart removed. She follows it with a Tatar neighbour's gentle answer on why every dead person got a good 'passport'.
passages.quote: The Tatars believe that the spirits of the bad walk for forty days after death. In this case, they say, it is requisite to uncover the grave, and either shoot the dead body, cut off its head, or take out its heart.
passages.speaker: Mary Holderness
passages.caution: Reported belief; she does not say she saw a grave opened.

passages.headline: Horse skulls against witchcraft
passages.gloss: Tatars and Bulgarian settlers alike stuck a horse's skull up near their houses to ward off witchcraft. Holderness links it, on hearsay, to the ancient Taurians, said to have used human skulls. On the same page a hired Tatar driver refuses to start a journey on a Tuesday, an unlucky day.
passages.quote: It is a very common custom in the Crimea, with the Tatars as well as the Bulgarian settlers, to stick up a horse's skull near their houses, in order to preserve them from witchcraft.
passages.speaker: Mary Holderness
passages.caution: The Taurian comparison is secondhand ('I am told').

passages.headline: Crimean Tatars deny ever eating horse
passages.gloss: A striking correction to older European books: Holderness says the Crimean Tatars of her day did not eat horse meat and denied that they ever had. Seventeenth century writers such as Chevalier had made horse-flesh the signature Tartar food.
passages.quote: The custom of eating horse-flesh is not in use among the Crim Tatars of the present day, and they indeed deny that it was ever their practice.
passages.speaker: Mary Holderness

passages.headline: Sheepskins, a knife and a pipe, but no guns
passages.gloss: Holderness describes the Tatar winter outfit of felt cloak, sheepskin pelisse and lamb's-wool cap, with a knife, tobacco pouch, flint and steel. Under Russian rule they were not allowed firearms, and few still owned the bows of their forefathers; a local noble, Maksout Murza, had one made entirely of bone.
passages.quote: The sheep-skin pelisses and lamb's-wool caps, which are assumed by the Tatars in winter, increase not a little their savage looks … The use of fire-arms is not allowed them, and few remain possessed of the bows and arrows which were the national weapons of their forefathers. Maksout Murza has a bow which is formed entirely of bone.
passages.speaker: Mary Holderness

passages.headline: Ak-Mechet: a Russian new town beside a walled Tatar town
passages.gloss: Webster found Simferopol, 'called by the Tartars, Ak-Metchet', split in two: the part built by the Russians since the conquest, and what remained of the old Tatar town. In the Tatar quarter every house and yard was surrounded by a wall with no window facing the street, and women rarely appeared, always veiled.
passages.quote: Symferapol, called by the Tartars, Ak-Metchet … consists of two parts, that which has been erected by the Russians, since their possession of the Crimea, and that which remains from the ancient Tartar town. This latter part is dull, dirty, and disgusting: every Tartar house and yard being surrounded by a wall, and not having a single window looking into
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized; a dash in the original replaced by a comma
passages.speaker: James Webster
passages.caution: The sentence ends '... into the streets' on the next page. 'Disgusting' is Webster's own prejudice.

passages.headline: Four hundred ungreased wheels
passages.gloss: At the entrance to the Crimea Webster met a Tatar caravan of about a hundred wagons, drawn by oxen and camels, whose ungreased wheels made an 'excruciating' noise. The Tatars in their black lambskin caps, the camels and the bustards on the plain struck him as a novel eastern scene.
passages.quote: These people never grease the wheels. The creaking of one is sufficiently offensive; but the noise of four hundred was absolutely excruciating. The Tartars, too, were singing, which, with them, is another term for howling … The Tartars, in their black lamb-skin caps and eastern dresses, the camels grazing on each side of the road
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized; a dash in the original replaced by a comma
passages.speaker: James Webster
passages.caution: Mocking tone about Tatar song.

passages.headline: Inside a spotless Tatar house
passages.gloss: After rejecting a filthy Russian post-house, Webster's party lodged with a Tatar family and were 'much surprised' by the cleanliness: double carpets, a row of cushions along the wall to sleep on, an open hearth in a big chimney, cushions piled to the roof and pots ranged on the rafters, all whitewashed. On the next page the host hints he hopes to be paid, unlike some Russian officers who answered with blows.
passages.quote: On entering, we were much surprised at the perfect cleanliness of the house. The room was doubly carpeted, and along the wall was a row of cushions, of sufficient breadth to admit of a traveller's stretching himself with perfect comfort. The fire was on the ground, in a large open chimney.
passages.speaker: James Webster

passages.headline: Alushta: terraced roofs and a mosque of wood and clay
passages.people: Crimean Tatars of the south coast
passages.gloss: Webster describes the Tatar village of Alushta built in terraces up the hillside, so that each house's flat roof served as the street or promenade for the one above. Its mosque, under huge walnut trees, was a 'rude structure of wood and clay' with a projecting roof. It is a precise picture of vernacular Tatar building materials.
passages.quote: Alushta is built on a sort of terrace, so that the flat roof of one house serves as a promenade to the people of the upper one. There are seven or eight rows of these houses, none having more than one flat, and that very low, with a portico in front … The mosque is embowered among old and immense walnut trees. It is a rude structure of wood and clay
passages.speaker: James Webster
passages.caution: 'One flat' here means one storey.

passages.headline: Graves dug for pilgrims to Mecca
passages.gloss: In Alushta Webster watched villagers dig two holes near the mosque for the two oldest men, about to leave on pilgrimage to Mecca. If they did not return, their upright gravestones topped with turbans would be set up there. The whole village was to share a feast paid for by voluntary gifts.
passages.quote: The two oldest, and for whom this ceremony was acting, were to set out, in two days, on a pilgrimage to Mecca, and, should they not return, their monuments, upright stones, surmounted by turbans, would be placed on the spot where the holes were dug.
passages.speaker: James Webster

passages.headline: The bride inside the Red Rock
passages.gloss: Webster records a legend 'implicitly believed by the Tartars': a girl forced to marry against her will prayed to Allah to bury her alive inside the red rock of Keesil-tash, and at every full moon at midnight the rock opens and she walks out in her bridal clothes. The next page adds a Tatar's dry joke about why a Russian count failed to see her.
passages.quote: She besought Allah to hide her from the world, and to bury her alive in the centre of the Keesil-tash. This prayer was granted, and she was snatched away by an invisible hand. She is said to inhabit the rock, but at every full moon, at midnight, the rock, as it is declared, opens, and the lady walks forth in her
passages.speaker: James Webster
passages.caution: Local legend as told to Webster; the sentence ends 'bridal garments' on the next page.

passages.headline: Cave homes at Inkerman, later reused by Tatars
passages.people: Medieval Christian cave-dwellers; later Crimean Tatars
passages.gloss: Webster examined the rock-cut chambers and chapel at Inkerman, near Sevastopol. From the altar, carved cross and style he judged them medieval Christian dwellings, and he noticed rafter marks showing some were part built, with a few 'reinhabited, or reconstructed by the Tartars'. He credits the builders to Christians, not Tatars, and says the Tatars reused them.
passages.quote: Some seem to have been partly excavated and partly built, which is proved by the marks of the rafters in the rocks, as also by these being, in a few instances, reinhabited, or reconstructed by the Tartars … the inference is natural that these excavations were the dwellings of the Christians.
passages.speaker: James Webster
passages.caution: His dating ('middle ages') is his own reasonable guess; the previous page blames damage on 'Mohammedan conquerors' without evidence.

passages.headline: The golden chamber of the Khans' palace
passages.gloss: Webster describes the palace of the Khans set in a great courtyard with the palace, mosque and tombs together. Past a marble fountain, a staircase led to the 'golden chamber' with a ceiling of gilded stars. On the next page he adds the crimson walls, stained glass and divans, faded but still showing 'the magnificence of the Tartar rulers', and notes Russian repairs under way.
passages.quote: The most interesting object is the palace of the Khans, which stands in a large area … We entered the court-yard, which brought into our view the palace, the mosque, and the tombs … In the entrance we passed a marble fountain, and ascended a spacious staircase, which brought us to a large room, called the golden chamber, the ceiling of which, divided into compartments, and studded with gilded stars
passages.speaker: James Webster

passages.headline: Low roofs, minaret chimneys and a wooden harem
passages.gloss: Seen from the garden, the Khans' palace was a low building, in parts only one storey, with white roofs and chimneys shaped like little minarets. The harem was a square building of three lofty rooms with verandas and small wooden-grated windows, behind a high wall. The palace of the Crimean Khans, in other words, was modest in scale.
passages.quote: This harem is a square building, with verandas, having only three rooms: these are large and lofty … Each room has a double range of small windows, with wooden gratings … The appearance of the exterior of the palace, as seen from the garden, is that of a low building, in some parts only one story. Its roof is white, and the chimnies appear like so many minarets
passages.speaker: James Webster

passages.headline: Domed tombs of the Khans
passages.gloss: Beside the palace mosque, the Khans lay in a small burial ground of Turkish-style tombs, some of marble, and in two domed octagonal mausoleums about thirty feet across. Inside were wooden coffins draped in black cloth and topped with the turbans of the dead. Webster also describes the town's one-storey houses and streets of shops grouped by trade.
passages.quote: There are two large octagons, with domes, of about thirty feet diameter, which contain the bodies and monuments of many Khans. In the first are ten or twelve wooden coffins, covered with black cloth, and having at the top the turbans of the deceased.
passages.speaker: James Webster

passages.headline: Dervishes 'snorting' in the Khans' mosque
passages.gloss: For a few rubles, Webster's party had thirteen men, five of them dervishes, perform their ritual (a zikr) in the Khans' mosque. He describes the rhythmic bowing and rasping breath in comic, hostile terms, yet on the next page concedes the rite was 'civilization' next to the flagellations he had seen in Rome.
passages.quote: They first snorted with great fury, then bellowed as furiously; the bellow consisting of three notes, like that of a calf, or a bull. Each time they bent forward with a violent motion. The rite altogether is absolutely terrific, and must be most fatiguing.
passages.speaker: James Webster
passages.caution: A paid performance for tourists, described with open ridicule.

passages.headline: The happiest peasantry possible
passages.gloss: Webster ends his Crimean chapters defending Tatar 'laziness' against Russian complaints: the Tatar sits on his roof under his grandfather's walnut tree and wants nothing more. He honestly adds that, not speaking their language, a traveller may mistake the look of happiness for the real thing.
passages.quote: The Russians exclaim against the laziness of the Tartars: but wherefore should they work? They are the happiest peasantry possible without it … not understanding their language, we may mistake the appearance of happiness for its reality.
passages.speaker: James Webster
passages.caution: A romantic generalisation, which Webster himself qualifies.

passages.headline: A Tatar village you could ride across by the rooftops
passages.people: Crimean Tatars of the south coast
passages.gloss: Guided by a young villager named Ismael, Kohl climbed to the Tatar village of Derekoi near Yalta. Its houses leaned into the hillside so their big flat roofs, made of packed earth and pebbles rolled smooth and resting on thin tree trunks, served as courtyards; there was no window glass, only wooden flaps. On the next page he watches village life going on across the rooftops.
passages.quote: The dwellings lie thickly scattered about among the trees, and leaning on one side against the mountain, so that one may ride over their flat roofs. These are large, as they supply the place of a courtyard covered with earth and small stones, laid smooth with a sort of roller, and supported on thin trunks of trees. Glass windows there are not, but in their place wooden flaps
passages.speaker: J. G. Kohl (English abridged translation, 1844)

passages.headline: Shop songs about Khans and the fall of Kazan
passages.gloss: Hearing singing from a grocer's shop in Yalta, Kohl went in and sat on an apple chest until late at night while two Tatars, an Armenian and a Circassian sang and explained their songs. Besides love songs, some were historical: about Khan Krym Giray, Khan Devlet Giray, the Russian conquest of Crimea and the taking of Kazan. Tatar history lived on in popular song.
passages.quote: Love formed, as usual, the principal theme, but some, to my surprise, were on historical subjects. One treated of Krim-Gerei, the last distinguished Khan of the Crimea, the friend of the well known French ambassador, Baron de Tott, another of Khan Devlet-Gerei, a third of the conquest of the Crimea by the Russians, a fourth of the taking of Kasan
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized; a dash in the original replaced by a comma
passages.speaker: J. G. Kohl (English abridged translation, 1844)
passages.caution: Kohl relied on the singers' own explanations of the words.

passages.headline: Bakhchysarai, 'seraglio of gardens'
passages.gloss: Kohl explains the town's name from the Tatar word for garden and places the Crimean Khanate in history as the last surviving piece of the Mongol empire in Europe. It shows how a nineteenth century writer linked the Crimean Tatars back to the Mongols.
passages.quote: The word “Baktsha,” signifies in the Tartar language “garden” and the name of Baktshiserai would, therefore, signify “seraglio of gardens.” This city was for centuries the capital of the remarkable state which formed the last fragment of the great Mongolian empire in Europe
passages.speaker: J. G. Kohl (English abridged translation, 1844)

passages.headline: A town where only Tatars may live
passages.gloss: Kohl reports that the Russian government had made the old capital a Tatar reserve: apart from officials, only Tatars were allowed to live there. The government had also preserved the Khans' palace. He found the town crowded and noisy with music, and a complete contrast to the new Russian cities of Sevastopol and Simferopol.
passages.quote: Baktshiserai has been declared their exclusive possession, and, with the exception of official personages, no other than a Tartar is allowed to reside in it. The government has also had the good taste to bestow much pains on the preservation of the palace of the ancient Khans, once the dreaded enemies of Muscovy.
passages.speaker: J. G. Kohl (English abridged translation, 1844)
passages.caution: The residence rule is what Kohl was told; he does not cite the decree.

passages.headline: Houses with fold-down wooden fronts
passages.gloss: In Bakhchysarai's single long, narrow street the houses had no windows: the whole front was a set of wooden flaps that could be raised or lowered and used as counters. So every trade was on show, from a baker at his oven to a brewer of 'boussa' (boza, a fermented millet drink) and a tailor with his journeymen.
passages.quote: The houses have no windows, but the entire front wall consists only of wooden flaps, which can be let down or drawn up at pleasure, and which sometimes serve as tables or boards for goods. In one house you may see a baker at work … In the next you may overlook all the manipulations required in the preparation of the Turkish beverage entitled “boussa,”
passages.speaker: J. G. Kohl (English abridged translation, 1844)

passages.headline: The Khans' graves upset a traveller's ideas
passages.gloss: Kohl had been taught to think of the Khans as destroyers who burned Moscow and terrorised Vilna and Warsaw. In their burial ground he found neat white marble monuments among vines, shrubs and flowers, with thoughtful inscriptions, and he concluded that 'the records of history' were imperfect.
passages.quote: In the burial-place of the Khans I found many memorials strikingly at variance with our notions of these barbarians; so many traces of humanity and piety, that I felt more strongly than ever, how imperfect are the records of history.
passages.speaker: J. G. Kohl (English abridged translation, 1844)

passages.headline: A roofless tomb, a walled-up tomb, a vine for a sinner
passages.gloss: Kohl retells the stories behind several Khans' tombs: one left roofless so the dead ruler could look up at heaven, one walled up because its occupant felt unworthy of God's sunlight, and one with a vine planted over the head so that a Khan who bore little fruit in life might do better in death. Another Khan asked to be buried under the mosque eaves so rain could wash away his sins.
passages.quote: without a roof, because “he considered the Heavens so beautiful and sublime, that even from his grave he would wish to look towards the firmament, the abode of God.” Another had had his tomb entirely walled up, because, as the inscription ran, “he did not feel himself worthy to be shone on by the least ray of God's sun.”
passages.speaker: J. G. Kohl (English abridged translation, 1844)
passages.caution: Kohl could not read the Arabic or Turkish inscriptions himself; these explanations were presumably given by guides and read like local tradition.

passages.headline: 'No Tartar has more than one wife'
passages.gloss: Sheltering from rain with a Tatar named Ali Mustapha Oglu, Kohl asked a guest how many wives he had. The answer was firm: one, as for every decent Tatar. The same man then told Kohl about his village's lawsuit against a Russian landowner who had turned a grant of 700 acres into 20,000 by enclosing Tatar woods and meadows.
passages.quote: We inquired of him how many wives he had, and his answer was, “Of course only one! No Tartar has more than one wife, except such as are rascals;” so that it appears Mahomet's indulgent permission to have four is made but little use of.
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized; dashes in the original replaced by commas
passages.speaker: J. G. Kohl (English abridged translation, 1844), quoting a Tatar villager

passages.headline: A stone for a man who lifted her veil
passages.gloss: At Alupka, beside Count Vorontsov's new palace, Kohl saw the Tatar village with a handsome new mosque the count had built 'for his Tartars'. When one of Kohl's companions lifted a passing Tatar woman's veil, she threw a great stone at him, and Kohl says they all took the lesson.
passages.quote: On the top of one stands the handsome new mosque, built by Count W. for his Tartars. One of our party had the temerity to lift the corner of the veil of a Tartar woman who was passing, to get a peep at her face … for the lady took up a great stone and hurled it at him
passages.speaker: J. G. Kohl (English abridged translation, 1844)
passages.caution: 'Count W.' is Count Mikhail Vorontsov, governor-general of New Russia.

passages.headline: Moscow's mosque, rebuilt by a Tatar merchant
passages.gloss: Kohl visited Moscow's small mosque in the Tatar quarter. Its predecessor burned in the fire of 1812, and the poor congregation of about 120 Tatars could not rebuild until a wealthy Tatar paid for new walls. When Kohl saw it, it still had only a temporary roof and bare walls, and Russians had stolen one of its prized carpets.
passages.quote: The little building erected here to the honour of Allah … had a predecessor which in 1812 met with the same fate from the French fire, in which so many Russian churches shared. The flock were long unable to get together the necessary funds for a new temple, till about twelve years ago, when a wealthy Tartar erected the walls that are now standing.
passages.speaker: J. G. Kohl (English abridged translation, 1844)

passages.headline: Leather masters and 'dressing-gown Tartars'
passages.people: Tatars (from Kazan and Central Asia) trading in the capital
passages.gloss: Among the street cries of St Petersburg Kohl heard 'Kazan boots' and 'Bukhara dressing-gowns'. He credits Mongols and Tatars with founding almost every branch of Russian leatherwork, from Moscow's embroidered caps and belts to Kazan's morocco boots, and says Tatar sellers of silk robes were nicknamed 'dressing-gown Tartars'.
passages.quote: The Mongolians and Tartars are distinguished for their skill in the preparation of leather, and almost every branch of manufacture connected with this article in Russia has had its origin from them … Dressing-gowns are almost the only things that do not come through Russian hands, but from those of the Tartar makers … where they are often called “dressing-gown Tartars.”
passages.speaker: J. G. Kohl (English abridged translation, 1844)
passages.caution: The claim that Russian leatherwork originated with the Tatars is Kohl's generalisation.

passages.headline: Moscow 'singed' by the Tartars twelve times
passages.gloss: Kohl says no European city except Constantinople had burned so often as Moscow, and that the Tartars alone had set it alight more than twelve times. He adds that about two-thirds of its 12,000 houses were still wooden, the rest built of soft local limestone and brick.
passages.quote: Constantinople excepted, there is, perhaps, no city in Europe that has been so often burnt to the ground. By the Tartars alone it was well singed more than twelve times.
passages.speaker: J. G. Kohl (English abridged translation, 1844)
passages.caution: A round, popular-history figure.

passages.headline: Kurgans built by others, dug up by everyone
passages.people: Tatars among later plunderers of ancient graves
passages.gloss: Describing the Crimean gold in the Hermitage, Kohl credits the southern burial mounds to the Greeks of Taurida and older peoples of the Caucasus and Siberia. The Tartars appear not as builders but as one of many later peoples, with Goths, Huns and Cossacks, who dug into the kurgans and melted down the treasure.
passages.quote: the countless graves of the Greeks of Taurus, and of the original inhabitants of the Caucasus and Siberia, have been objects of zealous research … the Tartars and the Cossacks of the present day, have plundered them, and melted down the treasures found therein. The greater part of the kurgans and mohilos of South Russia, have been long since burrowed like rabbit-warrens
passages.speaker: J. G. Kohl (English abridged translation, 1844)
passages.caution: The list of plunderers ('Alarics' and a garbled name, probably Huns) is rhetorical.

passages.headline: Moscow as a 'Tartar Rome'
passages.people: Tartars as a byword for the Asiatic side of Russia
passages.gloss: Kohl opens his chapter on Moscow's churches with Madame de Staël's famous exclamation on first seeing the city: 'Voilà Rome Tatare'. It shows how Western Europeans used 'Tartar' as shorthand for Moscow's un-European look.
passages.quote: Madame de Staël, when she beheld Moscow … turned to her companions and exclaimed, “Voilà Rome Tatare.” The Russians themselves like to compare their city to that world subduer
passages.translation: 'Voilà Rome Tatare' means 'There is a Tartar Rome'.
passages.speaker: J. G. Kohl (English abridged translation, 1844), quoting Madame de Staël
passages.caution: An anecdote repeated from De Staël's memoir, not Kohl's observation.

passages.headline: Clay roofs you could walk onto by mistake
passages.place: South coast of Crimea, near Yalta
passages.gloss: Riding along the coast, Jesse saw his first Tatar village close up. The houses were very low, with flat clay-covered roofs set so tightly into the slope that, as the next page says, someone coming down the hill might walk onto a roof without noticing.
passages.quote: Near here I had the first opportunity of seeing a Tartar village, “de près;” the houses are very low, the roofs flat and covered with clay, and frequently so curiously placed against the mountain, that a person coming down from above
passages.speaker: Captain William Jesse
passages.caution: The sentence continues on p.125: 'might easily ride or walk on to the top of one without being the least aware of it.'

passages.headline: The head man calls the horses from the minaret
passages.gloss: Tatar villages had to supply post horses to travellers in turn. Jesse describes the village head man (bashi) climbing the wooden minaret in the middle of the village to shout out the names of those whose horses were due, with replies coming back from around the village.
passages.quote: On arriving at a station, the Bashi, or head man, was not always in the way; when found, he immediately ascended the wooden minaret in the centre of the village, and commenced calling a roster of those whose horses were next for duty, a reply was soon elicited from one corner or another
passages.speaker: Captain William Jesse

passages.headline: Mangup: a Greek, Genoese and Karaite ruin, with a Tatar fountain
passages.people: Crimean Tatars (village below); earlier Greeks, Genoese and Karaites
passages.gloss: Jesse credits the cliff-top ruined town of Mangup to others: first Greek, then a Genoese fortress, then home to Karaite Jews. The Tatars appear in the village at the foot, where women hurried to veil themselves, and in a roadside fountain whose inscription said a 'benevolent Tartar' had built it as an act of charity.
passages.quote: The town was once in the hands of the Greeks, it became afterwards a Genoese fortress, and was subsequently the residence of the Karaite Jews … The inscription informed us that it was erected as an act of charity by some benevolent Tartar.
passages.speaker: Captain William Jesse
passages.caution: His history of Mangup is secondhand and simplified (Mangup was the capital of the Principality of Theodoro before the Ottoman conquest of 1475).

passages.headline: The Tatars' own old capital
passages.gloss: Jesse calls Bakhchysarai one of the few Crimean towns inhabited only by Tatars, who still loved 'the ancient capital of their race'. He lists its trades: leather cushions, slippers, whips and saddles, black lambskin caps, and the shaggy woven cloaks called bourkas.
passages.quote: This is one of the few towns in the Crimea inhabited solely by Tartars, who still cling with affection and reverence to the ancient capital of their race … a few employ themselves in the manufacture of leather cushions, slippers, whips, saddles, &c., fur caps of the black lamb-skin, and cloaks called bourkas.
passages.speaker: Captain William Jesse

passages.headline: Woken by a Tatar bride's procession
passages.gloss: At dawn in Bakhchysarai Jesse was woken by drums, gongs and bagpipes accompanying a Tatar bride in a curtained carriage drawn by two ponies, lit by torch-bearers. The same page gives his unimpressed verdict on the Khans' mausoleum and the palace's 'diminutive apartments'.
passages.quote: the concert was in honour of a Tartar bride, whose equipage, drawn by two ponies, was surrounded by curtains and torch-bearers, lighting her to the hymeneal couch, in a manner truly classical … The mausoleum of the Khans is a wretched edifice after that of the Sultans at Constantinople
passages.speaker: Captain William Jesse
passages.caution: He mocks Tatar music.

passages.headline: The Fountain of Tears inscription: 'never such a fountain'
passages.gloss: Jesse copies the translated inscription on the Selsabil fountain in the palace vestibule (the famous 'Fountain of Tears'). It credits Khan Krym Giray with finding the spring and giving water to his people, and boasts that Damascus and Baghdad never saw its equal. He notes that the palace's rooms were small and the furniture mean and modern.
passages.quote: The town of Bagtché-Serai rejoices in the beneficent solicitude of the luminous Crim-Gheri-Khan: it was he, who with generous hand quenched the thirst of his countrymen … If there exists such another fountain, let it present itself. The towns of Scham and Bagdad have seen many things, but never such a fountain.
passages.speaker: Inscription on the Selsabil fountain, in an English translation printed by Captain Jesse
passages.caution: Jesse does not say who translated the Ottoman Turkish inscription. 'Scham' is Damascus.

passages.headline: A night in a Tatar house
passages.gloss: Lodged by a village head man, Jesse describes a room with a divan running all round it, no tables or chairs, a three-legged low table for meals, and a fireplace so big that six or eight people could stand inside the chimney. Each house had high wattle fences and at least half a dozen dogs; supper was kaimak (thick cream), milk and eggs.
passages.quote: A divan, covered with coarse cotton, ran round the apartment, and the fire-place, in the centre of the side near the door, was large enough to admit six or eight persons within the chimney. Of course, there were no tables or chairs; a low wooden stool or plateau on three legs, as in Turkey, being used for meals
passages.speaker: Captain William Jesse

passages.headline: 'Our conquerors, Sir, have left us very poor'
passages.gloss: In the morning Jesse's Tatar host was surprised to be paid, explaining that most of his guests were Russians travelling on duty, who did not pay. His short reply about the conquerors is a rare recorded Tatar voice on life under Russian rule, a generation after annexation.
passages.quote: Our host appeared rather astonished at being remunerated, in the morning, and said that the generality of his visitors were always on duty; adding, “Our conquerors, Sir, have left us very poor.”
passages.speaker: Captain William Jesse, quoting his Tatar host (through an interpreter)
passages.caution: Heard through an interpreter by a strongly anti-Russian author.

passages.headline: Two-storey tiled houses in the valleys
passages.people: Crimean Tatars of the inland valleys
passages.gloss: Jesse notices that Tatar houses in the inland valleys were better built than the flat-roofed coastal ones: still low, but often two storeys with an outside gallery, raised tiled roofs and carved wooden ceilings. At the village inn of Uzenbash a Tatar barber gave him an expert shave.
passages.quote: The houses in these valleys are much better built than those on the coast, and though very low, have frequently two stories, with a gallery running round them on the outside; the roofs also are raised and tiled, and the ceilings sometimes ornamented with carving in wood.
passages.speaker: Captain William Jesse

passages.headline: The 'Golden Hill' of Kerch
passages.gloss: In the Kerch museum of ancient Greek finds, Jesse reports a Tatar tradition that centuries earlier about forty poods (some 1,440 pounds) of gold had been taken from one of the nearby burial mounds, which they therefore called the Golden Hill. He calls the story 'no doubt fabulous'.
passages.quote: The Tartars have a tradition, that upwards of forty pouds, nearly one thousand four hundred and forty pounds English, of this metal, in ornaments and coin, were, several hundred years ago, taken from one of the tumuli in the neighbourhood; and they call it in consequence the Golden Hill. This is, no doubt, fabulous
passages.speaker: Captain William Jesse
passages.caution: The mounds were ancient Greek and Bosporan burials, not Tatar; the tradition is about finding treasure, not building.

passages.headline: Hajj pilgrims on a Black Sea steamer
passages.gloss: On the steamer to Odessa's quarantine, Jesse shared the deck with forty passengers including Tatars returning from the pilgrimage to Mecca. He sneers at their lack of washing but notes that they prostrated themselves constantly towards the Kaaba.
passages.quote: The Tartars were returning from a pilgrimage which they had made to Mecca; and though Mohammedans, did any thing but observe the ablutions recommended by their religion; but they unceasingly prostrated themselves in the direction of the Caaba.
passages.speaker: Captain William Jesse
passages.caution: Openly contemptuous; the conditions were those of a crowded quarantine deck.

passages.headline: A Khan descended from Genghis
passages.gloss: Coxe describes Muscovy's early raids into western Siberia, when 'Tartar tribes' paid tribute, and one chief, Yediger, promised a thousand sables a year. Yediger was then overthrown by Kuchum Khan, whom Coxe identifies as a direct descendant of Genghis Khan who had only recently founded his realm there.
passages.quote: Some Tartar tribes were indeed laid under contribution; and a chief, whose name was Yediger, consented to pay an annual tribute of a thousand sables. But this expedition was not productive of any lasting effects; for soon afterwards Yediger was defeated, and taken prisoner by Kutchum Chan; the latter was a lineal descendant of the celebrated Zinghis Chan
passages.speaker: William Coxe (compiling G. F. Müller)

passages.headline: Kuchum Khan's realm and his fortress of Sibir
passages.gloss: On the eve of the Cossack invasion, Coxe says, Siberia was split between several princes and independent 'Tartar' tribes. The strongest ruler, Kuchum Khan, held the lands from the Irtysh and Ob to the Tobol and Tura, with his residence at Sibir, a small fortress on the Irtysh. The next page adds that it stood near today's Tobolsk and that some of its ruins could still be seen.
passages.quote: Siberia was at that time partly divided among a number of separate princes; and partly inhabited by the various tribes of independent Tartars. Of the former Kutchum Chan was the most powerful Sovereign … His principal residence was at Sibir, a small fortress upon the river Irtish
passages.speaker: William Coxe (compiling G. F. Müller)

passages.headline: The Tatars called it Isker, not Sibir
passages.gloss: In a footnote Coxe rejects the popular idea that Siberia was named after the captured fortress of Sibir, pointing out that the Tatars themselves called the fort Isker. He suggests the regional name came to the Russians earlier, through the Permian and Zyrian peoples.
passages.quote: Several authors have supposed the name of Siberia to derive its origin from this fortress, soon after it was first taken by the Russians under Yermac. But this opinion is advanced without sufficient foundation; for the name of Sibir was unknown to the Tartars, that fort being by them called Isker.
passages.speaker: William Coxe (footnote, following Müller)

passages.headline: A Khan who spread Islam by force
passages.people: Siberian Tatars and their subject peoples
passages.gloss: Coxe gives one reason Kuchum's khanate was fragile: much of it was newly conquered, and he had alienated his 'idolatrous' (shamanist) subjects by pushing Islam on them with intolerant zeal. It is a useful reminder that 'Tartar' Siberia was religiously mixed, with Islam still spreading in the sixteenth century.
passages.quote: He had newly acquired a large part of his territories by conquest; and had, in a great measure, alienated the affections of his idolatrous subjects by the intolerant zeal, with which he introduced and disseminated the Mahometan religion.
passages.speaker: William Coxe (compiling G. F. Müller)
passages.caution: 'Idolatrous' is the source's word for the region's shamanist peoples.

passages.headline: Yermak enters an empty capital
passages.gloss: After routing Kuchum's army on the Irtysh, Yermak marched on Sibir, 'the residence of the Tartar princes', expecting a hard fight. Instead the news of the defeat had emptied it; he rode in and sat on the Khan's throne unopposed, and neighbouring peoples came in to swear allegiance and pay tribute.
passages.quote: delay to Sibir, the residence of the Tartar princes … But the news of the late defeat had diffused universal consternation, and Sibir was entirely deserted … he himself soon after made his triumphant entry, and seated himself upon the throne without the least opposition.
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized; printed margin notes omitted
passages.speaker: William Coxe (compiling G. F. Müller and J. E. Fischer)
passages.caution: Based on Siberian chronicles written decades later from the conquerors' side.

passages.headline: Miracles at the enemy's grave
passages.people: Siberian Tatars; later a Kalmyk prince
passages.gloss: After Yermak drowned in the Irtysh, his body was first abused on Kuchum's orders, but then, Coxe says, the Tatars came to revere him: they buried him with pagan rites, and stories spread that touching his body cured all illness and that a flame hovered over his tomb. A footnote adds that a Kalmyk prince, Allai, was said to have been cured by drinking earth from the grave.
passages.quote: Many miraculous stories were soon spread abroad, and met with implicit belief. The touch of his body was supposed to have been an instantaneous cure for all disorders; and even his clothes and arms were said to be endowed with the same efficacy. A flame of fire was represented as sometimes hovering about his tomb
passages.speaker: William Coxe (compiling Müller's Siberian history)
passages.caution: Legend preserved in Russian Siberian chronicles; Coxe calls these 'idle fables'.

passages.headline: New Russian towns on Tatar land
passages.people: Siberian Tatars and other native peoples
passages.gloss: After Yermak's death the Russians returned, built the fort of Tyumen and then the fortresses of Tobolsk, Tara and others (previous page). Coxe sums up the following century bluntly: the Tartars were subdued or wiped out, and new towns and colonies went up everywhere. In his account the Siberian towns were new Russian foundations, not inherited 'Tartar' cities.
passages.quote: The Russians pushed their conquest far and wide: wherever they appeared, the Tartars were either reduced or exterminated. New towns were built and colonies were planted on all sides. Before a century had well elapsed, all that vast tract of country now called Siberia … was annexed to the Russian dominions.
passages.speaker: William Coxe (compiling G. F. Müller)
passages.caution: The previous page lists the forts as Tumen, Tobolsk, 'Sungur' (probably a scan error for Surgut) and Tara.

passages.headline: A market at the Mongol camp
passages.gloss: Besides the official caravans to Beijing, Russian merchants traded privately at the headquarters of the Mongols, a moving camp usually pitched where the Orkhon and Tuul rivers meet. An annual fair grew up there, which on the next page becomes a scene of drunken Russian 'riot and confusion' that angered the Kangxi emperor.
passages.quote: private merchants continued as before to carry on a separate trade with the Chinese, not only at Pekin, but also at the head quarters of the Mongols. The camp of these roving Tartars was generally to be found near the conflux of the Orchon and Tola, between the Southern frontiers of Siberia and the Mongol desert. A kind of annual fair
passages.speaker: William Coxe (compiling Müller and Pallas)

passages.headline: Maimachin: a wooden frontier town guarded by Mongols
passages.people: Chinese merchants; Mongol garrison of the Qing
passages.gloss: Following Pallas, Coxe describes the Chinese trading town of Maimachin facing Russian Kiakhta, with frontier posts inscribed in Russian and Manchu. Its only defence was a wooden wall and a small ditch dug in 1756 during the Qing wars with the Kalmyks (Dzungars), and its gates were watched by a garrison of Mongols in tattered clothes armed with clubs.
passages.quote: Maimatschin has no other fortification than a wooden wall, and a small ditch of about three feet broad; the latter was dug in the year 1756, during the war between the Chinese and the Calmucs … over each of these gates there is a wooden guard-house for the Chinese garrison, which consists of Mongols in tattered clothes, and armed with clubs.
passages.speaker: William Coxe (from P. S. Pallas's travels)
passages.caution: The following pages describe the town's one-storey wooden, plastered Chinese houses; those are Chinese, not Tartar, buildings.

passages.headline: 'Tartar nations': Kalmyks, Mongols and Buryats
passages.gloss: In a note Coxe praises Pallas's new work on the 'Tartars' living between Siberia and the Great Wall, whom Pallas divides into Kalmyks, Mongols and Buryats, split in religion between shamanism and the Dalai Lama's Buddhism. It shows 'Tartar' used in 1780 as an umbrella term for Mongolic peoples.
passages.quote: No writer has placed the religion and history of the Tartar nations in a more explicit point of view than Mr. Pallas … concerning the Tartars, who inhabit parts of Siberia, and the territory which lies between that country and the Chinese wall … as they are divided into Calmucs, Mongols, and Burats.
passages.speaker: William Coxe (note on P. S. Pallas)

passages.headline: Raw rhubarb stalks that grip the throat
passages.people: 'Tartars' of the Baikal region (probably Buryats or Mongols)
passages.gloss: In an appendix on rhubarb, Coxe (credited to Pallas) says the Tartars ate the leaf stalks of wild rhubarb raw, and that outsiders who tried them got a spasm of the throat at every meal until they grew used to it. A small, odd detail of steppe diet.
passages.quote: The stalks of the leaves are eaten raw by the Tartars: they produce upon most persons, who are unaccustomed to them, a kind of spasmodic contraction of the throat, which goes off in a few hours; it returns however at every meal, until they become habituated to this kind of diet.
passages.speaker: William Coxe (from information supplied by P. S. Pallas)
passages.caution: Which people Coxe means by 'Tartars' here is not stated.

passages.headline: Yarkand: a clay fort, a stone fort and clay houses
passages.gloss: Wathen's informants described Yarkand, the biggest town of Chinese Tartary, as having two forts: a large, empty one with clay walls, and a smaller, inhabited one with four gates, built of stone and chunam (lime plaster) with a ditch. Ordinary houses were one storey and built of clay, which served well because it hardly ever rained. The same page says the city had many mosques and colleges and two big bazaars.
passages.quote: It has two forts: the principal one is of large extent, but its walls are of clay; and it is uninhabited; the other, which is rather smaller, has four gates, is inhabited, and is considered by the natives as very strong, being built of stone and chunam, and surrounded with a ditch … The houses are generally one story high, and built of clay
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this page is garbled)
passages.speaker: W. H. Wathen, reporting his informants
passages.caution: Second-hand description from pilgrims interviewed in Bombay.

passages.headline: Horse meat at the butcher's, kumiss only on the steppe
passages.people: Townspeople of Chinese Tartary; Kalmuks and other nomads
passages.gloss: In Yarkand horse meat was sold openly in butchers' shops, cost the same as mutton and was not thought unlawful. Kumiss (fermented mare's milk), the classic 'Tartar' drink of older books, was drunk not by the townspeople but by the Kalmuks and other nomadic tribes. The informants also said Islam was not kept very strictly there, and that people were more tolerant than in Kokand.
passages.quote: Horse-flesh is sold in the butcher's shops, and generally eaten: it is not considered unlawful food by the people of the country, and generally sells for the same price as mutton. Kimmiz is not used by the inhabitants of the towns, but by the Kalmuks, and other roving tribes.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this page is garbled)
passages.speaker: W. H. Wathen, reporting his informants

passages.headline: A stone that makes it rain
passages.people: Turki-speaking Muslims of the Khotan road
passages.gloss: The chief of Guma, a town between Yarkand and Khotan, was said to own the 'Yedeh Tash', a rain-stone that made rain fall whenever it was placed in sweet water. Belief in the rain-stone (yada tash) is an old Turkic and Mongol tradition. Wathen reports it as 'popular belief', not as fact.
passages.quote: who was said to be in possession of the stone called “Yedeh Tásh,” (rain-stone,) which, according to popular belief, possesses the extraordinary virtue of causing rain to fall, whenever it is placed in sweet water.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this page is garbled)
passages.speaker: W. H. Wathen, reporting his informants
passages.caution: Popular belief reported at third hand. The sentence begins with the town of Gúma (the spelling is unclear in the scan) and its former chief, a Beg, as the stone's owner.

passages.headline: Walled towns built by forced labour
passages.gloss: The pilgrims told Wathen that Chinese rule was very unpopular, and that resentment had grown because the Chinese were building large fortifications and walled towns with the forced labour of the local people. After the revolts of the 1820s the Qing did build new walled garrison towns in the region. Here the builders of the walls are named plainly: Qing authorities using conscripted local workers.
passages.quote: The feeling of dislike, with which the Chinese are regarded, has been latterly much increased, in consequence of their carrying on vast works of fortification, and building walled towns, by the forced labour of the natives.
passages.speaker: W. H. Wathen, reporting his informants
passages.caution: The informants were Muslim subjects hostile to Qing rule. The corpus lists no printed page here; 662 comes from the page sequence.

passages.headline: Manchu 'Tartars' in a Tibetan garrison
passages.people: Manchu soldiers of the Qing army ('Mantchoo Tartars')
passages.gloss: At Gyantse, a small town on the road to Lhasa, Campbell's informants reported a Chinese officer with three or four hundred soldiers, a few of them 'Mantchoo Tartars of the Chinese army' and the rest local Tibetans. Here 'Tartar' is simply the standard English word for the Manchus who ruled Qing China.
passages.quote: There is a Chinese officer stationed here with 3 or 400 soldiers, a few of whom are Mantchoo Tartars of the Chinese army. The rest are native Tibetans.
passages.speaker: Archibald Campbell, reporting his informants

passages.headline: Tibetan robbers 'erroneously styled Kalmaks'
passages.gloss: On a stage called 'the place of thieves', where robbers hid in underground burrows, Hodgson adds a footnote: the Catholic missionary Huc wrote much about Tibetan robbers, who were black-tent Tibetan nomads, 'erroneously styled Kalmaks'. It shows 'Kalmak' being stretched to cover any nomad raiders of Inner Asia.
passages.quote: M. Huc in his narrative speaks much of the robbers of Tibet, who, he says, are Kalos or black-tent nomadic Tibetans, erroneously styled Kalmaks. They are mounted gang robbers.
passages.speaker: Footnote by B. H. Hodgson, summarising Évariste Huc
passages.caution: An editorial note, not Campbell's informants.

passages.headline: Rhubarb from Tartary
passages.people: none named; Tartary as a region north of China
passages.gloss: After seeing a wild rhubarb near the snowline in Bhutan, Saunders notes that the true medicinal rhubarb grows in cold country: the north of China, Tartary and parts of Russia. He then describes his own experiment drying a root, which lost far less weight than the traders claimed. Rhubarb was one of the great goods Europeans associated with Tartary.
passages.quote: The true rhubarb (Rheum palmatum) is likewise the native of a cold climate ; and though China supplies us with much of this drug, it is known to be the growth of its more northern provinces, Tartary, and part of the Russian dominions.
passages.speaker: Robert Saunders (Philosophical Transactions, 1789)
passages.caution: A general statement of where rhubarb grows, not an observation of Tartary itself.

passages.headline: A god-king for the Tartars from the Volga to Korea
passages.people: Buddhist Tartars (Mongols, Kalmyks and other Inner Asian peoples)
passages.gloss: Stewart explains the Dalai Lama's place in the Tartar world: he is worshipped by the 'heathen Tartars' across the whole breadth of Asia, and the more distant ones treat him as God himself. He adds that even the Manchu emperor of China honours him and keeps a lama envoy at the palace in Peking.
passages.quote: Every body knows that the Delai Lama is the great object of adoration for the various tribes of heathen Tartars, who roam through the vast tract of continent which stretches from the banks of the Volga to Correa on the sea of Japan, the most extensive religious dominion, perhaps, on the face of the globe.
passages.speaker: John Stewart (Philosophical Transactions, 1777)
passages.caution: General knowledge of the day, drawn from books and Bogle's reports, not from travel among the Tartars.

passages.headline: The rumour of the Lama's holy excrement
passages.people: Tartar chiefs (Mongol and other Buddhist rulers)
passages.gloss: Stewart repeats a rumour, common in European books, that Tartar chiefs were given small portions of the Lama's excrement, kept it in gold boxes and mixed it into their food. On the same page he reports that Bogle 'strenuously insists' the Lama never gave such gifts, only little balls of consecrated flour, which credulous followers might then imagine to be something else.
passages.quote: It is even reported, that many of the Tartar chiefs receive certain presents, consisting of small portions of that, from him, which is ever regarded in all other persons as the most humiliating proof of human nature, and of being subject to its laws, and treasure it up with great reverence in gold boxes, to be mixed occasionally in their ragouts.
passages.speaker: John Stewart (Philosophical Transactions, 1777)
passages.caution: Stewart labels it a report, and the eyewitness Bogle denied it.

passages.headline: A lama's castle of stone or brick, with no stairs or windows
passages.gloss: Relaying Bogle, who lived five months with the Panchen Lama, Stewart describes one of the Lama's castles: stone or brick, many courts and halls, rooms finished in Chinese style with gilding and varnish. The surprise is what is missing: upper floors are reached by wooden or iron ladders, and light comes through covered holes in the ceilings. Stewart does not call this a Tartar building; it is the seat of the lama the Tartars revered.
passages.quote: The castle is of stone or brick, with many courts, lofty halls, terraces, and porticos ; and the apartments are in general roomy, and highly finished in the Chinese stile, with gilding, painting, and varnish. There are two conveniencies to which they are utter strangers, stair-cases and windows.
passages.speaker: John Stewart, relaying George Bogle
passages.caution: Second hand, from Bogle's letters. The castle is Tibetan, not built by or for Tartars.

passages.headline: Lhasa, a trading capital with a Chinese garrison
passages.gloss: Stewart describes Lhasa as populous and flourishing, home to Chinese mandarins, Chinese and Kashmiri merchants and craftsmen, and a daily stream of caravans. Just before this he notes that while Bogle was with the Lama, 'several Mongols and Calmucs arrived from Siberia'. Neither Bogle nor Stewart saw Lhasa: the city is 'represented' to them.
passages.quote: The city of Lahassa, which is the capital, is of no inconsiderable size, and is represented as populous and flourishing. It is the residence of the chief officers of government, and of the Chinese mandarins and their suite. It is also inhabited by Chinese and Cassemirian merchants and artificers, and is the daily resort of numberless traders from all quarters,
passages.speaker: John Stewart (Philosophical Transactions, 1777)
passages.caution: Hearsay about a city no Briton had then visited.

passages.headline: Eluth Tartars out, Manchu Tartar emperor in
passages.people: Eluth (Dzungar Oirat) Tartars; Manchu Tartars of the Qing
passages.gloss: Stewart dates Tibet's dependence on China from the 'expulsion' of a Tartar people the OCR prints as 'Ehatli', almost certainly the Eluths (the Dzungar Oirats who seized Lhasa in 1717 and were driven out in 1720). On the same page he calls the Chinese emperor 'a Mantchou Tartar'. Two very different peoples share one label.
passages.quote: ever since the expulsion of the Ehatli Tartars, the kingdom of Thibet is regarded as depending on the empire of China, which they call Cathay; and there actually reside two mandarines, with a garrison of a thousand Chinese, at Lahassa the capital,
passages.speaker: John Stewart (Philosophical Transactions, 1777)
passages.caution: 'Ehatli' is left as the OCR reads it; the identification with the Eluths is ours, not Stewart's.

passages.headline: The Himalaya as a 'Tartar bulwark'
passages.people: none named; Tartary as the lands north of India
passages.gloss: Stewart describes the mountain wall north of Bengal as a continuation of the Caucasus and calls it a 'stupendous Tartar bulwark' that the Mughals and other Muslim conquerors had always thought impassable. On the same page he says the Jesuit account of Tibet in Du Halde was compiled 'from Tartar relations'. Here 'Tartar' simply means everything beyond the mountains.
passages.quote: This stupendous Tartar bulwark had ever been held impassable by the Mogols, and all other Mussulman conquerors of India:
passages.speaker: John Stewart (Philosophical Transactions, 1777)

passages.headline: Tibetans with 'quite the Tartar face'
passages.gloss: This is one of the few things Stewart saw himself. The Tibetan envoys in Calcutta struck him as fairer and ruddier than their neighbours, with 'the Tartar face'. He goes on to describe coarse home-woven woollens, Siberian furs for the rich, a Bhutanese envoy in conical hat and silk tunic, and a diet of milk, cheese, butter and barley.
passages.quote: The Thibetians are of a smaller size than their southern neighbours, and of a less robust make. Their complexions are also fairer, and many of them have even a ruddiness in their countenances unknown in the other climates of the east. Those whom I saw at Calcutta appeared to have quite the Tartar face.
passages.speaker: John Stewart (Philosophical Transactions, 1777)
passages.caution: 'Tartar face' is a stock eighteenth-century physical label, not an ethnic finding.

passages.headline: Tartar pilgrims from Russia, and letters from the Czar
passages.people: Buddhist Tartar subjects of Russia (Kalmyks, Buryats and others)
passages.gloss: According to Bogle, the Panchen Lama knew of only one European empire, Russia, because many of its Tartar subjects came to Tibet and the Czar had sent him letters and presents. The Lama admired Russia but could not believe it was a match for China ('Cathay').
passages.quote: Many of the Tartar subjects of Russia come to Thibet; and the Czar has even, at various times, sent letters and presents to the Lama.
passages.speaker: John Stewart, relaying George Bogle
passages.caution: Second hand, from Bogle's conversations with the Lama.

passages.headline: War booty that looked 'perfectly Tartar'
passages.gloss: After British troops took a place held by the Bhutanese during the Cooch Behar war, the spoils sent to Calcutta included religious images in clay, gold, silver and enamel. To Stewart they looked exactly like the 'Tartar' art he knew from travellers' drawings. 'Tartar' here is a style label for Tibetan Buddhist art.
passages.quote: Images in clay, in gold, in silver, and in enamel, were sent down to Calcutta; all which appeared perfectly Tartar, as we have them represented in the relations and drawings of travellers; and there were besides several pieces of Chinese paintings and manufactures.
passages.speaker: John Stewart (Philosophical Transactions, 1777)

passages.headline: Tartar gunpowder from Altai saltpetre
passages.people: Tartars and Kalmucks of the Altai frontier
passages.gloss: In his notes on the earthquake, Weymarn says the Altai near the Katun river is full of saltpetre that forms like cement in the rock clefts, and that the local Tartars and Kalmyks make strong gunpowder from it by a quick, simple method. It is a small but concrete detail about frontier peoples' technology.
passages.quote: is all full of a kind of Saltpetre, which is found in form of a cement, in great plenty, in the clefts and between the beds of rock ; with this the Tartars and Kalmucks make very strong and good Gunpowder, by an industrious, simple and expeditious method.
passages.speaker: W. W. Weymarn (translated from the French, 1763)
passages.caution: Weymarn does not say he watched the powder being made.

passages.headline: A town of leather tents, with streets and markets
passages.gloss: When the trumpet sounds at night, every soldier pulls his tent from the baggage wagons. Palafox says the tents are made of strong leather or raw hides sewn together, big enough to live in, and pitched in order with streets and market places like a great town. On the next page he adds that the Tartars preferred living in tents to living in Chinese cities, which they felt were bad for their health, though he expects them to grow soft in time.
passages.quote: The Tents are either made of strong Leather or raw hides, which are sewed together; and made up indifferent handsomly… These Tents they pitch in great order, with Market-places and Streets, like as in great Towns,
passages.speaker: Juan de Palafox y Mendoza (English translation, 1676)
passages.caution: Compiled from reports; the OCR on this and the following page is badly garbled.

passages.headline: Horse-flesh for feasts, mutton every day
passages.gloss: Palafox says the Tartars eat and drink heartily, care more for quantity than quality, and count horse-flesh their greatest delicacy. Their daily food is mutton from their great flocks, plus venison they hunt in the mountains, and he claims they eat their meat nearly raw 'according to the custome of Barbarians'. On the page before he says they despise soft music and love only the harsh sound of the trumpet.
passages.quote: They account Horse-flesh their greatest dainty… But their ordinary food is Mutton, and they have great flocks of Sheep : They eat likewise all sorts of Venison,
passages.speaker: Juan de Palafox y Mendoza (English translation, 1676)
passages.caution: Second-hand and coloured by the stock European image of 'barbarian' eating.

passages.headline: The horses announce that the town has fallen
passages.gloss: Describing how the Tartars stormed Chinese walled towns, Palafox says archers lying or kneeling on the wall top drove the defenders from their guns while others scaled the walls or seized a gate. Once horses got inside, their noise and neighing told everyone the town was taken. On the next page he notes that the Tartars stormed first and only brought up artillery afterwards, the reverse of European practice.
passages.quote: they quickly discover, that the Town is taken… Thus the Tartarian horses first proclaim the Victory.
passages.speaker: Juan de Palafox y Mendoza (English translation, 1676)
passages.caution: The OCR on this page is garbled; the quote keeps only the readable words.

passages.headline: 'Their houses are only of cords and canvas'
passages.people: Timur's Tartar army, described by the Mamluk council of Syria
passages.gloss: As Timur approached Syria, the Mamluk governors rejected advice to make peace. Yazdi gives them a proud speech: other kingdoms fell because their towns were mud and brick, but Syria's fortresses are cut from solid rock. The Tartars, they sneer, live in homes and walls of rope and canvas, meaning tents. The boast was followed by defeat.
passages.quote: Their towns were built only of mud and brick ; but ours are all of solid stone, cut out of the almost impenetrable rock ;… The houses and walls of these Tartars are only of cords and canvas ; while we live in good fortresses, which are of hewn stone
passages.speaker: Speech Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi puts in the mouths of the Mamluk emirs (English of 1723, via Pétis de la Croix)
passages.caution: A speech composed by a court historian for enemies of his patron's grandfather, not a transcript.

passages.headline: Foreign masons build Timur's great mosque at Samarkand
passages.people: Timur and craftsmen from Azerbaijan, Persia and India
passages.gloss: Back from India, Timur ordered a congregational mosque for Samarkand. Yazdi says the foundations were laid at an astrologically chosen moment and that the work was done by masons brought from foreign countries, 200 from Azerbaijan, Persia and India inside alone. On the next page he adds 500 men cutting stone in the mountains, 95 elephants hauling blocks, and a finished hall of 480 hewn-stone pillars, a carved marble roof, four minarets and brass doors. Earlier (p. 67) he records that Timur kept the captured masons of Delhi for this very building.
passages.quote: The masons, brought from foreign countrys, as mention'd before, gave the greatest proofs of their art and skill, as well in the solidity and beauty of the angles, as in the strength of the foundations of this noble edifice. In the inside of the mosque were employ'd two hundred masons from Azerbijana, Persia and India:
passages.speaker: Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi (English of 1723, via Pétis de la Croix)
passages.caution: Written by Timur's dynasty's historian about twenty years later; the figures are the court's.

passages.headline: Baghdad razed, except mosques, colleges and hospitals
passages.gloss: After Baghdad fell by storm, each Tartar soldier was ordered to bring a head, and towers of heads were built as a warning. Timur then ordered every house razed but the mosques, colleges and hospitals spared. A footnote from the translator adds Ibn Arabshah's figures: 90,000 killed and 120 towers of heads.
passages.quote: Afterwards Timur gave orders that there shou'd not remain one single house in the city unraz'd ; but that the mosques, colleges and hospitals shou'd be spar'd. Accordingly they ruin'd the markets, caravanseras, hermitages, cells, monasterys, palaces, and other edifices.
passages.speaker: Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi (English of 1723, via Pétis de la Croix)
passages.caution: The official history presents the massacre as justified; the casualty figures in the footnote come from Ibn Arabshah, a hostile writer.

passages.headline: Turks, Tartars, Moguls and Tajiks
passages.people: Timur's Turkic soldiers and the Tajik townspeople
passages.gloss: Two footnotes explain the troops sent to scout the mountains of Kafiristan. 'Turks' are the descendants of Moguls and Tartars; 'Tadgics' (Tajiks) are the Persian-speaking townspeople of Transoxiana and Iran, who are neither. It is a neat 1720s key to how Tartar, Mogul and Turk overlapped.
passages.quote: The Turks are those who descend from the Moguls and Tartars… The Tadgics are the inhabitants of the towns of Transoxiana, and all the country of Iran, who are neither Tartars, Moguls, nor Turks.
passages.speaker: Translator's footnote (François Pétis de la Croix, carried into the 1723 English)
passages.caution: An editorial gloss, not Yazdi's own words.

passages.headline: The rain stone of Yarkand
passages.gloss: Among the curiosities of Yarkand, Izzet Ullah lists the 'Yedeh', a stone taken from the head of a cow or horse that can bring rain or snow. He admits he never saw it work, but says many people swore to it. Rain-stone magic (yada) was an old practice of Turkic and Mongol peoples. His closing line is a neat mix of belief and doubt, and Wilson's footnote praises his honesty.
passages.quote: The individuals who employ the stone are numerous; they are called Yedejis. The stone is to be smeared with the blood of some animal, and then thrown into water: a charm is read at the same time, upon which a strong wind springs up, and then rain and snow ensue… The truth of the story is known to God alone.
passages.speaker: Mir Izzet Ullah (translated by H. H. Wilson)
passages.caution: Hearsay; the traveller says he had 'no opportunity of observing the fact'.

passages.headline: Timur's tomb, stripped of its gold
passages.people: Uzbeks of Bukhara; tomb of Timur
passages.gloss: Izzet Ullah visited the Gur-i Amir, the tomb of Timur (Tamerlane), whose court history calls his army 'the Tartars'. He saw the great dome, the famous dark green stone slab and the inscribed plate, and was told the gilding had been stripped off by the Bukharan ruler Shah Murad. The poor attendants asked him whether any descendants of Timur still lived in India who might help them.
passages.quote: the seat of the sepulchre of Amir Timur ; a lofty building with an immense cupola : within it is a remarkable slab of a brilliant green stone, and above it is a plate with an inscription, with the name of Timur engraved on it. Formerly the dome was gilt, but Shah Murad Be stripped off the gilding, and took it away ;
passages.speaker: Mir Izzet Ullah (translated by H. H. Wilson)
passages.caution: The story of the stripped gilding is what he was told.

passages.headline: Samarkand's colleges, once haunted by lions and wolves
passages.people: Uzbeks of the Emirate of Bukhara
passages.gloss: Timur's old capital had shrunk. Izzet Ullah found it defended only by a mud wall and an earth citadel, Ulugh Beg's observatory reduced to a mound of rubbish, and the great 'Madressa Khanum' (the Bibi Khanum complex) in ruins. He says that before Shah Murad repopulated it, the city had been so run down that lions and wolves haunted the colleges.
passages.quote: Samarkand is defended by a mud wall, as well as a citadel of earth… There are many large colleges in the city ; the largest is the Madressa Khanum, but it is now in ruins… Before the reign of Shah Murad Be, Samarkand was in an entirely dilapidated condition, and the colleges were haunted by lions and wolves.
passages.speaker: Mir Izzet Ullah (translated by H. H. Wilson)
passages.caution: The ruins he saw; the lions and wolves are local report.

passages.headline: Ruined buildings of the Kirghiz, 'a Mongol tribe speaking a Turkish dialect'
passages.gloss: On the road from Ladakh to Yarkand, Izzet Ullah passed a place called Kirghiz Jangal (Kirghiz thicket) with the ruins of Kirghiz buildings. He explains that the Kirghiz had lived there until they were expelled for plundering caravans, before China took the region. Elsewhere on his route the Kirghiz live in felt tents, so the note that these nomads also left buildings behind is worth noticing.
passages.quote: On the road half way is a place called Kirghiz thicket, where are the remains of some of their ruined edifices, that tribe having been resident here before the country was subjected to China: being in the habit of plundering the Kafilas they were expelled. The Kirghizes are a Mongol tribe, speaking a Turkish dialect.
passages.speaker: Mir Izzet Ullah (translated by H. H. Wilson)
passages.caution: He saw the ruins; who built them and why they left is local report.

passages.headline: Felt tents pitched beside a domed tomb
passages.place: Tian Shan, between Kashgar and Osh
passages.gloss: Crossing the mountains west of Kashgar in deep winter, Izzet Ullah notes Kirghiz felt tents lining the road (p. 321). At the stage called Mizar Gumbaz he found a domed building with Kirghiz tombs and the living Kirghiz camped in tents beside it: permanent structures for the dead, portable ones for the living.
passages.quote: Mizar Gumbuz, … west by north, eight hours. A building with a cupola and Kirghiz tombs; their tents were also pitched near the building; supplies plentiful;
passages.speaker: Mir Izzet Ullah (translated by H. H. Wilson)

passages.headline: Kalmyks in Leh, and the mosque that came of it
passages.gloss: The only mosque in Leh, Izzet Ullah was told, was founded by Ibrahim Khan, a Mughal noble sent to help the king of Ladakh when the Kalmaks had seized the city. The king converted to Islam and swore vassalage, then soon went back to his own faith. This is a memory of the Tibet-Ladakh-Mughal war of 1679 to 1684. On the same page he describes Leh's thousand houses of stone or unburnt brick, three or four storeys high.
passages.quote: It was founded by Ibrahim Khan, one of the nobles of the Mogul Court, at a time when the Kalmaks … had got possession of the city, and the Raja of Tibet had recourse to the Sultan of Hindustan for succour. Ibrahim Khan, who was sent to his assistance, defeated the Kalmaks, and restored the Raja;
passages.speaker: Mir Izzet Ullah (translated by H. H. Wilson)
passages.caution: Local tradition about events some 130 years earlier.

passages.headline: Yarkand: from Mughal khans to Kalmyks to China
passages.gloss: Izzet Ullah sketches Yarkand's history: once ruled by Moghul khans, it fell to the Kalmaks, whose chief lived at Ili. Then an epidemic killed the Kalmak ruler, his family and vast numbers of his people, rival Khoja factions fought, and China conquered the country about sixty years before his visit. This matches the collapse of the Dzungar state in the 1750s.
passages.quote: fell into the hands of the Kalmaks. The chief of the Kalmaks, entitled the Tura, resided at Ila, and a deputy on his part was sent to Yarkand. After some time an epidemic occurred amongst the Kalmaks, which carried off the Tura, his children, his chief men, and a vast number of people.
passages.speaker: Mir Izzet Ullah (translated by H. H. Wilson)
passages.caution: Local oral history; Wilson's footnote adds dates from other sources.

passages.headline: Kazan, 'capital of the Khan of the Dasht Kipchaks'
passages.people: Kazakhs, Karakalpaks; the old khans of the Kipchak steppe
passages.gloss: Describing the lands north of Ferghana, Izzet Ullah says the Kazakhs and Karakalpaks there depend on Russia, and that the capital of the Khan of the Dasht-i Kipchak, 'Bulghar, now known by the name of Kazan', lies in Russian territory. He runs together two different Volga cities (old Bulghar and Kazan), but the line shows how the Tatar khanates were remembered in Central Asia.
passages.quote: To the north of the mountains of Andejan the country is a barren plain ; to the north of which are the tribes of Kazzaks and Kara Kalpaks, dependant on Russia. The capital of the Khan of the Dast Kapchaks, Bulghar, now known by the name of Kazan, is in the Russian territory.
passages.speaker: Mir Izzet Ullah (translated by H. H. Wilson)
passages.caution: Bulghar and Kazan were separate cities; the identification is his, and it is wrong.

passages.headline: Turks and Kipchaks versus the Kirghiz
passages.people: Turks, Kapchaks (Kipchaks), Kirghiz and Muslim Kalmaks
passages.gloss: Near Andijan, Izzet Ullah passes the spring and summer pastures of the Turks and Kipchaks, some 10,000 to 12,000 families, whom he admires as prosperous, well dressed and soldierly. He is scornful of the poorer Kirghiz. A page earlier he notes 'many Tartar stations' where herds of horses graze, and just after this he meets Kalmaks who 'are Musalmans', a surprise since most Kalmyks were Buddhist.
