passages.quote: the adjacent country is divided into the pasture grounds of the Turks and Kapchaks… These two tribes amount here to 10,000 or 12,000 families: they are a strong good-looking people, apparently in a prosperous condition, well dressed, and of military bearing, and present a striking contrast to the Kirghizes, who are a mean-looking race, ill-fed, housed, and clothed,
passages.speaker: Mir Izzet Ullah (translated by H. H. Wilson)
passages.caution: His judgement of the Kirghiz is a townsman's prejudice.

passages.headline: Kirghiz snow-treaders keep the pass open
passages.gloss: In winter the snow in the passes west of Kashgar lay a man's height deep or more. Izzet Ullah describes Kirghiz posted along the road whose job was to trample the snow hard so caravans could cross. Even so, several horses died, including his own.
passages.quote: The Kirghizes tread the snow down so as to make it hard, and then the caravans pass; a certain number of Kirghizes are appointed to this duty,
passages.speaker: Mir Izzet Ullah (translated by H. H. Wilson)

passages.headline: Ili: the old Kalmyk capital becomes a Chinese garrison
passages.gloss: In the route copied from a Kashgar man's journal, the note on Ili says the old city by the river, once the Kalmaks' capital, is deserted, and that the name now covers two towns: Gulja, mostly Muslim, and Kura, the Chinese garrison and seat of the governor-general. It also mentions the grave of Tughluk Timur, the first Chaghatai khan to become Muslim, and a burning stone (coal) found nearby.
passages.quote: Ila is properly the name of the river on the borders of which stood the city, thence so called, and which is now deserted. There is the grave of Tughluk Timor, the first of the Chaghatai Sultans who adopted Mohammedanism.
passages.speaker: Mir Izzet Ullah, from Mullah Nazr of Kashgar's route notes (translated by H. H. Wilson)
passages.caution: Not seen by Izzet Ullah; copied from another traveller's journal and oral notes.

passages.headline: Bukhara: 'They came, they dug, they burned, they killed, they plundered, they left'
passages.gloss: After telling how Bukhara's citadel was stormed and its walls levelled, Juvaini says a man who escaped reached Khorasan and was asked what had happened. His answer was six verbs. The clever men who heard it agreed that nothing more concise could be said in Persian, and Juvaini says his whole chapter is only a commentary on those few words.
passages.quote: گفت آمدند و کندند و سوختند و کشتند و بردند و رفتند جماعت زیرکان که این تقریر شنیدند اتفاق کردند که در پارسی موجزتر ازین سخن نتواند بود
passages.translation: He said: 'They came, they dug, they burned, they killed, they plundered, and they left.' The shrewd people who heard this account agreed that nothing could be said more concisely in Persian.
passages.speaker: Ata-Malik Juvaini (Persian text, ed. Mirza Muhammad Qazvini, 1912)
passages.caution: Juvaini reports what a survivor said; he was not at Bukhara in 1220. One stray OCR token has been dropped.

passages.headline: Karakorum built on an old ruin, with craftsmen from China and Islam
passages.people: Ögedei Khan's Mongols; Chinese and Muslim craftsmen
passages.gloss: Juvaini says Ögedei chose the Orkhon valley and the Qaraqorum mountains for his throne, though there was no town or village there, only the trace of a wall of the old Uighur city of Ordu-Baliq. An inscribed stone found there named its founder, Buqu Khan. On top of the ruin Ögedei ordered a new city built, 'known as the city of Qaraqorum', and craftsmen of every kind were brought from Khitai and from the Islamic lands, along with farmers.
passages.quote: در آن موضع شهری و دیهی نبودست مگر رسم دیواری که آن اردو بالیغ بودست … و بر بالای آن فرمود تا شهری بنا نهادند و اردو بالیغ نام … معروف بشهر قراقورم است و از ختای از هر نوع … آوردند و از بلاد اسلام همچنان صناع و زراع
passages.translation: In that place there had been neither town nor village, only the trace of a wall, which had been Ordu-Baliq … and on top of it he ordered that a city be built, and [it was] named Ordu-Baliq … known as the city of Qaraqorum. And from Khitai they brought [workers] of every kind, and likewise from the lands of Islam craftsmen and farmers.
passages.speaker: Ata-Malik Juvaini (Persian text, ed. Mirza Muhammad Qazvini, 1912)
passages.caution: Juvaini visited Karakorum around 1250, but the founding story comes from court tradition. Garbled words in the OCR are marked with ellipses, including the word for the people brought from Khitai.

passages.headline: Before Chinggis: clothes of dog and mouse skins
passages.gloss: Juvaini describes the Mongols' homeland as a barren land bordered by Khitai (north China), the Uighurs, the Kirghiz and Tangut. Before Chinggis Khan, he says, they had no ruler, fought and stole from each other, and paid tribute to the Khan of Khitai. The page also says (in badly garbled OCR) that a chief was marked out only by stirrups of iron. Then comes the twist: now they wear silk and brocade and jewels pour into their tents.
passages.quote: و پوشش از جلود کلاب و فارات و خورش از لحوم آن و میتهای دیگر و شراب از البان بهایم و نقل از بار درختی بشکل ناژ که فسوق گویند
passages.translation: Their clothing was of the skins of dogs and mice, their food the flesh of those animals and of other dead things, their wine the milk of beasts, and their dessert the fruit of a tree shaped like the pine, which they call qusuq.
passages.speaker: Ata-Malik Juvaini (Persian text, ed. Mirza Muhammad Qazvini, 1912)
passages.caution: A rags-to-riches set piece that flatters the dynasty's rise; Juvaini had not seen pre-Chinggis Mongolia.

passages.headline: The Tatars had no writing, so they learned it from the Uighurs
passages.gloss: Explaining Chinggis Khan's laws, Juvaini says that since the Tatars had no script, Mongol children were taught to write by the Uighurs. The laws were then written on rolls called the Great Book of the Yasa, kept in the treasuries of the leading princes. This is also a clear case of Juvaini using 'Tatar' for the Mongols.
passages.quote: و چون … تاتاررا خطی نبوده است بفرمود تا از ایغوران کودکان مغولان خط درآموختند و آن یاساها و احکام بر طوامیر ثبت کردند و آنرا یاسا نامه بزرگ خوانند و در خزانه معتبران پادشاه زادگان باشد
passages.translation: And since the Tatars had no script, he ordered that the children of the Mongols should learn writing from the Uighurs; and those yasas and ordinances were written down on rolls, which they call the Great Book of Yasas, and it is kept in the treasury of the chief princes.
passages.speaker: Ata-Malik Juvaini (Persian text, ed. Mirza Muhammad Qazvini, 1912)
passages.caution: One garbled word before 'Tatars' (probably 'people') is marked with an ellipsis.

passages.headline: A pavilion raised by Muslim architects to outdo the Chinese
passages.people: Ögedei Khan's court; Muslim and Chinese builders
passages.gloss: Juvaini follows Ögedei's yearly round of residences near Karakorum. In spring the khan moved to a palace called Qarshi Suri, which 'Muslim architects' had put up in rivalry with the Khitayans (Chinese builders): a lofty pavilion decorated with paintings and many-coloured carpets, with a throne and jewelled vessels. The Mongol khan's buildings are credited to foreign craftsmen competing for his favour.
passages.quote: که آنرا مهندسان مسلمان بر رغم ختائیان افراشته بودند و آنرا قرشی سوری نام است کوشکی نیک عالی بانواع نقوش و فرشهای متلوّن حالی
passages.translation: which Muslim architects had raised in rivalry with the Khitayans, and which is called Qarshi Suri: a very lofty pavilion, adorned with all kinds of paintings and many-coloured carpets.
passages.speaker: Ata-Malik Juvaini (Persian text, ed. Mirza Muhammad Qazvini, 1912)
passages.caution: Juvaini visited the Karakorum area after Ögedei's death; the description of the khan's routine is partly from informants.

passages.headline: The Sira Ordu: a Chinese pavilion with latticed wooden walls
passages.gloss: In summer Ögedei went up into the mountains, where his people set up a great pavilion brought from Khitai (north China), its walls made of latticed wood, with rich cloth above. It was called the Sira Ordu (Yellow Horde or Yellow Palace). The khan's summer 'palace' was a portable structure, not a stone building.
passages.quote: و از ختای بارگاهی که دیوارهای آن از چوب مشبك ساخته بودند … بر افراشتندی و آنرا سیر اردو نام است
passages.translation: and they would raise a pavilion from Khitai whose walls were made of latticed wood … and it is called Sir[a] Ordu.
passages.speaker: Ata-Malik Juvaini (Persian text, ed. Mirza Muhammad Qazvini, 1912)
passages.caution: The line describing the roof coverings is too garbled in the OCR to quote.

passages.headline: The Uighurs born from a glowing hill
passages.people: Uighurs (as told in their own books)
passages.gloss: Juvaini retells the Uighurs' own origin story. Between two rivers near Karakorum grew two trees; a light from heaven came down on a hill between them, the hill grew day by day, and the Uighurs heard sweet music coming from it. At last, like a woman giving birth, it opened a door, and inside were five chambers. At the head of the Uighur chapter he says he writes down their beliefs to arouse wonder, not because he accepts them.
passages.quote: تا چنانك حاملات‌را وقت وضع حمل … باشد دری گشاده شد اندرون آن پنج خانه بود
passages.translation: until, as happens to women with child when the time of delivery comes, a door opened, and inside there were five chambers.
passages.speaker: Ata-Malik Juvaini, retelling Uighur tradition (Persian text, ed. Mirza Muhammad Qazvini, 1912)
passages.caution: A legend from Uighur books, which Juvaini says he writes down 'for wonder, not for belief'. The OCR is heavily garbled: 'five' restores a broken word, and one unclear word is marked with an ellipsis.

passages.headline: Jochi's share: 'as far as the hoof of the Tatar horse has reached'
passages.people: Jochi (Tushi) and the Mongols, called Tatars
passages.gloss: Describing how Chinggis Khan divided his realm among his sons, Juvaini says the eldest, Jochi, received everything from Qayaligh and Khwarazm to the far edge of Saqsin and Bulghar on the Volga, and westward 'as far as the hoof of the Tatar horse has reached'. This is the land that became the Golden Horde. Here 'Tatar' is simply another word for the Mongol cavalry.
passages.quote: و پسر بزرگتر توشی‌را از حدود قیالیغ و خوارزم تا اقصای سقسین و بلغار و از ان جانب تا انجا که سم اسب تاتار رسیدست بدو داد
passages.translation: And to his elder son Tushi he gave the lands from the region of Qayaligh and Khwarazm to the farthest parts of Saqsin and Bulghar, and in that direction as far as the hoof of the Tatar horse has reached.
passages.speaker: Ata-Malik Juvaini (Persian text, ed. Mirza Muhammad Qazvini, 1912)

passages.headline: Mongol felt tents versus Manchu canvas tents
passages.gloss: Grosier compares the two kinds of Tartar tent. Manchu tents are just single or double canvas, like European army tents. Mongol tents are round, shaped like a cut-off cone, covered in white or grey felt, with a smoke hole above a central fire; warm while the fire burns, freezing at night, stifling in summer. Three pages earlier he states flatly that the Mongols have 'neither towns, villages, nor houses', only wandering hordes living under tents.
passages.quote: These tents are however more commodious than the common tents of the Mantchews, which are composed only of double or single canvass, almost like those of our troops; these of the Moguls are circular, in form of the frustum of a cone, and covered with a large piece of white or gray felt. A round hole in the top gives a passage to the smoke,
passages.speaker: Jean-Baptiste Grosier (English translation, 1788)
passages.caution: Compiled from Jesuit travellers, probably Gerbillon; Grosier did not see these tents.

passages.headline: Ruins of a Mongol city on the Kerulen: 'the City of the Tyger'
passages.people: Khalkha Mongols; ruins left by the Yuan (Kublai's successors)
passages.gloss: In Khalkha country Grosier places 'Karakum', seat of Chinggis Khan's empire, and describes ruins on the north bank of the Kerulen: a square city about two leagues round, built by the Mongol successors of Kublai Khan, with foundations, bits of wall and two half-ruined 'pyramids' (probably stupas or towers) still standing. The locals called it Para-hotun. Ruined cities here are credited to the Yuan emperors.
passages.quote: On the northern side of it are seen the ruins of a large city, built by the Mogul successors of the famous Coblai-kan ; this city was square, and about two leagues in circumference; its foundations, some pieces of the walls, and two pyramids
passages.speaker: Jean-Baptiste Grosier (English translation, 1788)
passages.caution: Taken from Jesuit survey reports. The sentence ends on the next page: 'half in ruins, still subsist; it was called Para-hotun, or The City of the Tyger' (n198).

passages.headline: The fish-skin Tartars of the Ussuri
passages.gloss: On the Ussuri, Grosier says, live the 'Yupi-tatse' (Chinese for 'fish-skin Tartars'). They live almost entirely on fish and dress in fish skins, dyed three or four colours and stitched so finely with thin thongs that the seams look like silk. On the next pages he describes their bark canoes, hair hung with little mirrors, and a lady who drove a sledge pulled by a hundred dogs.
passages.quote: The river Ousouri, on the banks of which these people live, must supply them with abundance of fish, since they have no other food, and scarcely any clothes but what they make of their skins. They have the art of dressing these skins, and of dying them three or four colours ;
passages.speaker: Jean-Baptiste Grosier (English translation, 1788)
passages.caution: From the Jesuit map-makers who surveyed Manchuria about 1709; Grosier calls them 'stupid and clownish', a prejudice he inherits.

passages.headline: How the Mongols split into Mongol and Manchu 'Tartars'
passages.gloss: Grosier explains 'Chinese Tartary' with an origin story: all its tribes were once called Mongol Tartars, and when the Mongols were driven out of China in 1368, some fled east toward the Amur and kept Chinese customs, becoming the Manchus or 'Eastern Tartars', while the rest went back west and stayed Mongols. The Manchus did not in fact descend from the Yuan refugees; the story shows how Europeans tried to make one 'Tartar' family out of different peoples.
passages.quote: Those of the east retain their ancient name of Moungal or Mogul Tartars: the rest are known by the name of Mantchew or Eastern Tartars. Chinese Tartary is therefore divided into two parts, the eastern and western.
passages.speaker: Jean-Baptiste Grosier (English translation, 1788)
passages.caution: The text as printed has 'east' and 'the rest' the wrong way round (it means the western group kept the Mongol name), and the origin story itself is mistaken. The quote swaps the printed long dash for a comma.

passages.headline: Why the Chinese say 'Tata'
passages.people: Tartars in general: Eastern (Manchu/Jurchen) and Western (Mongol)
passages.gloss: Martini defines his subject: the Tartars are simply the people living north of the Great Wall, which for 300 German leagues has served as a rampart against them. He adds that the Chinese, lacking the letter R, have always called them 'Tata', and that the name covers both the Eastern Tartars, unknown in Europe, and the Western ones stretching from Kashgar to the sea above Japan.
passages.quote: I call that Nation Tartars, which inhabiting the Northern parts, behind that famous Wall which stretching out above 300. German Leagues from East to West, hath ever served for a Rampart to hinder their irruptions into the said Empire. This Country the Chineses having a defect of the letter R. antiently called Tata:
passages.speaker: Martino Martini (English translation, London 1654)
passages.caution: Chinese 'Dada' (韃靼) is a real name for the Tatars; the 'missing R' explanation is Martini's.

passages.headline: From Mongol refugees to the kingdom of Niuche
passages.people: Tartars of Niuche (Jurchen, ancestors of the Manchus)
passages.gloss: Martini tells how, after the Ming founder drove the Yuan out in 1368, he carried the war into Tartary itself, and the storm fell chiefly on the province of Niuche 'whither the Tartars of China being expelled were retired'. These Tartars then came to Liaodong every year to trade ginseng, furs and horsehair, multiplied into seven 'Hordes', and about 1550 formed the kingdom of Niuche. Like Grosier later, he blends the Yuan Mongols and the Jurchen into one Tartar story.
passages.quote: This Storm of War fell chiefly on the Tartars of the Province of Niuche, whither the Tartars of china being expelled were retired.
passages.speaker: Martino Martini (English translation, London 1654)
passages.caution: The idea that the Yuan refugees became the Jurchen of Niuche is Martini's mistake.

passages.headline: Shaved heads, queues and horse-hoof sleeves
passages.gloss: When the Tartars took a city in Liaodong, they proclaimed that no one would be killed who cut his hair and wore Tartar dress. Martini then breaks off to describe their manners: head and beard shaved except the moustache, a long braided tuft at the back, a low round cap trimmed with beaver or sable. The next pages add long robes with sleeves cut like a horse's hoof, a sabre hung point forward, silk or horse-skin boots, broad saddles, and the remark that they are like 'our Tartars of Europe' but not so barbarous.
passages.quote: For the Tartars (that I may say something of their Manners, as my subject gives me occasion) doe shave both the Head and Beards reserving only the Mustachoes, which they extend to a great length, and in the hinder part of their heads they leave a Tuft, which being curiously woven and plated, they let hang down carelesly below their shoulders;
passages.speaker: Martino Martini (English translation, London 1654)

passages.headline: Fighting harder for their hair than for their emperor
passages.people: Manchu Tartars and the Chinese of Zhejiang
passages.gloss: The Manchus took the south of Zhejiang easily, Martini says, until they ordered everyone to cut their hair in Tartar fashion. Then soldiers and townspeople alike rose up, fought 'more desperately for their Hair' than for king or kingdom, and drove the Tartars back across the Qiantang river. Elsewhere (p. 108 to 109) he says the Tartars made refusing the haircut high treason, and many Chinese chose death instead.
passages.quote: But when they commanded all by Proclamation to cut off their Hair, then both Souldier and Citizen took up Arms, and fought more desperately for their Hair of their Heads, than they did for King or Kingdom, and beat the Tartars not only out of their City, but repulst them to the River Cienthang
passages.speaker: Martino Martini (English translation, London 1654)
passages.caution: Martini was living in Zhejiang at the time, but he did not witness every battle he describes.

passages.headline: Beds on the ground, horses in the house, beautiful tents
passages.gloss: In a sketch of how the Tartars trained for war, Martini describes their great ring hunts and their camp habits. They sleep on the ground on a horse-cloth and care nothing for houses; if they must live in houses they keep their horses inside and knock holes in the walls. Their tents, he says, are very beautiful and put up and struck so skilfully that they never slow an army's march.
passages.quote: The earth covered with their Horse-cloath is their Bed ; for they care not for Houses, and Chambers ; but if they be forced to dwell in Houses, their Horses must lodge with them, and they must have many holes beaten in the Walls; but yet their Tents are most beautiful, which they fix and remove with such Art and dexterity,
passages.speaker: Martino Martini (English translation, London 1654)
passages.caution: A general portrait; the 'holes in the walls' detail may be hearsay.

passages.headline: The Eight Banners and the ring hunt
passages.gloss: Martini gives an early European description of the Eight Banners: white (the imperial banner), red, black and yellow, and four more made by mixing colours. Every soldier knows his colour and where in the city his arms and horse are kept, so the whole army is ready in half an hour at a horn call. On the next pages he adds that they carry no baggage, eat meat half cooked or their own horses and camels, and hunt by encircling a whole mountain.
passages.quote: under these eight colours are comprehended all the Forces of the Kingdom of China, whether they be Natives or Tartars ; the first of which is White, called the Imperial Banner ; the second is Red, the third is Black, the fourth is Yellow;… so as every Souldier knows his own colours, and to what part of the City to repair, where they have ever their Arms and Horses ready
passages.speaker: Martino Martini (English translation, London 1654)
passages.caution: The real banner colours were yellow, white, red and blue (plain and bordered); Martini's 'black' may be a mistake.

passages.headline: Servants and horses burned with the dead
passages.gloss: When the Chinese ignored his complaints, the Tartar king (Nurhaci) vowed to celebrate his father's funeral with the lives of 200,000 Chinese. Martini explains that when a Tartar of rank died, servants, women and horses, with bows and arrows, were thrown into the funeral fire to serve him in the next life, a custom he says they gave up after conquering China.
passages.quote: For it is the custom of the Tartars when any man of quality dyeth, to cast into that fire which consumes the dead Corps, as many Servants, Women, and Horses, with Bows and Arrows, as may be fit to attend and serve them in the next life: Though now since they conquered China, they have left off this barbarous custome,
passages.speaker: Martino Martini (English translation, London 1654)
passages.caution: Reported, not witnessed; Manchu funeral sacrifice (of wives and servants) is attested, but the scale is probably exaggerated.

passages.headline: Storming a city behind a wooden wall
passages.gloss: Martini describes how the Tartars, armed only with sabres and bows against Chinese muskets, took 'Leaotung', which he calls the chief city of the province of Liaodong. The front ranks carried thick boards as a moving 'wooden wall' to soak up the musket fire, ladder-men followed, and cavalry came behind. Before the Chinese could reload, the Tartars were over the walls. He credits their speed and nimbleness, 'in which they excel all Nations'.
passages.quote: the scaling ladders being applied, before they could charge again, they were upon the Walls and enterd the City ; for such is the quickness and nimbleness of the Tartars (in which they excel all Nations, and in which also they place their chief art) that in a trice, they either prevail in their Designs, or retire :
passages.speaker: Martino Martini (English translation, London 1654)
passages.caution: An event before Martini reached China, told from report; he runs several Liaodong campaigns together.

passages.headline: Nurhaci pulls down unlucky walls and builds new ones
passages.gloss: After taking 'Leaotung' and then Guangning, Martini says, the Tartar king returned to Liaodong rich with plunder. His soothsayers told him the old walls were unlucky, so he pulled them down, built new ones, and proclaimed himself emperor of China though he held only its edge. A page earlier Martini explains that Chinese soldiers and citizens fled their houses because the Tartars destroyed any city that resisted but only plundered those that surrendered.
passages.quote: And because his Southsayers had perswaded him that the standing of the old Walls were unfortunate, he beat them down, and compassed them about with new, fortifying them with new Munitions, and there proclamed himself Emperour of China:
passages.speaker: Martino Martini (English translation, London 1654)
passages.caution: Martini's report; historically Nurhaci moved his capital to Liaoyang in 1621 and to Shenyang in 1625.

passages.headline: Shaoxing, the cleanest city in China, surrenders
passages.gloss: Martini, who knew Zhejiang well, pauses as the Tartars cross the Qiantang to praise Shaoxing: not the largest city but the cleanest and most comely in China, circled by fresh water, with wide streets paved in white square stone, a navigable canal down the middle, stone bridges and arches. On the next page he says its houses are built of the same square stone, 'which I observe no where else in China'. It submitted without resistance.
passages.quote: This City in bigness yields to many others, but in cleaness and comeliness it surpasses all: it is so invironed with sweet waters as a man may contemplate its beauty by rounding it in a Boat ; it hath large and fair Streets paved on both sides with white square stones, and in the middle of them all runs a Navigable Chanel,
passages.speaker: Martino Martini (English translation, London 1654)
passages.caution: A Chinese city, not a Tartar one; it matters here as a city the Tartars took.

passages.headline: Martini watches the Tartars ride back into Peking
passages.gloss: After putting down Jiang Xiang's revolt in Shanxi, the Tartars plundered Datong and burned Puzhou, where the Christians' church was lost. Martini says he saw them return to Peking loaded with riches. Dorgon ('Amavangus') went on to the Western Tartars (Mongols) to ratify the young Shunzhi emperor's marriage and brought back a huge herd of horses.
passages.quote: But yet they Plundered the City Taitung, and burned the City of Pucheu, where the Church of the Christians also perished. From hence the Tartars returned to Peking, where I saw them enter overloaden with Riches and triumphant Laurels ;
passages.speaker: Martino Martini (English translation, London 1654)
passages.caution: Martini says he saw the return himself; the campaign in Shanxi he knew by report.

passages.headline: A Ming emperor hanged with a bowstring
passages.people: Manchu Tartars and the Ming claimant Hongguang
passages.gloss: Martini says the Hongguang emperor, first ruler of the Southern Ming at Nanjing, was betrayed to the Tartars after less than a year on the throne, sent to Peking, and publicly hanged on the town walls with a bowstring, 'which kind of death the Tartars esteem most noble'.
passages.quote: This unfortunate Prince being thus betrayed before he had reigned full one year, was sent to Peking, and there upon the Town Walls was hanged publickly in a Bow string, which kind of death the Tartars esteem most noble.
passages.speaker: Martino Martini (English translation, London 1654)
passages.caution: Reported from a distance; other sources give different details of his death, which came in 1646.

passages.headline: Descended from Kublai Khan? The Manchu origin story
passages.people: Manchu Tartars (the Kin or Jin 'golden race')
passages.gloss: Davis explains that the 'Eastern Tartars' now called their country Manchow, 'the full region'. Earlier, as the Kin or 'golden' race, they had ruled north China before the Mongols drove them out. He then repeats a story that the last Mongol emperors, expelled by the Ming, took refuge among these Eastern Tartars and intermarried, so that the Manchu emperors descend from Kublai Khan.
passages.quote: When the last of the Mongols, descendants of Koblai Khan, were expelled from China by the founder of the Ming, or Chinese race, they sought a refuge among the Eastern Tartars, and from their intermarriages with the natives sprung the Bogdoi Khans, or Manchow princes, who were destined to expel the Ming. It is in this manner that the Emperors of the present dynasty derive their descent from Koblai Khan.
passages.speaker: John Francis Davis (The Chinese, 1836)
passages.caution: This descent from Kublai is a European and dynastic legend, not established history; Davis presents it as fact.

passages.headline: The queue: 'the most open and degrading mark of conquest'
passages.gloss: After the Manchus took Peking, Davis writes, the Chinese were forced to shave their long hair and adopt 'the Tartar fashion of a long plaited tress, or tail', and Tartar dress, on pain of death. He reflects that changing the whole nation's costume touches every single person and is the plainest possible sign of conquest. The old Chinese costume, he notes, now survives only on the stage.
passages.quote: In other respects, too, they were commanded to adopt the Tartar habit on pain of death; and many are said to have died in preference to submission… an entire alteration in the national costume affects every individual equally, from the highest to the lowest, and is perhaps, of all others, the most open and degrading mark of conquest.
passages.speaker: John Francis Davis (The Chinese, 1836)
passages.caution: The sentence begins on the previous page ('The conquered Chinese were now compelled to shave the thick hair...'), n199.

passages.headline: Peking's Tartar city and Chinese city
passages.people: Manchu Tartars (the imperial garrison) and Chinese
passages.gloss: Davis describes Peking as two walled cities: the northern 'Tartarian, or City of Nine Gates', holding the palace and under strict military police, and the southern Chinese city, whose walls are weaker, 'like the ordinary Chinese towns', and which holds the Temples of Heaven and Agriculture. On an earlier page he notes that Amherst's party pulled bricks out of holes in the neglected north-east wall. 'Tartar city' names who lived in it under the Qing.
passages.quote: The Chinese town, which lies to the south of the Tartarian, or "City of Nine Gates," is not subject to the same rigid system of military police as that which contains the abode of the Emperor; and its walls and defences are inferior to those of the other, being, in fact, like the ordinary Chinese towns.
passages.speaker: John Francis Davis (The Chinese, 1836)
passages.caution: Davis saw Peking only briefly in 1816; much of his description comes from Barrow and Father Hyacinth.

passages.headline: Tartar women who ride astride
passages.gloss: Davis quotes the account of Macartney's embassy passing through Peking. Many women in the crowd were said to be Tartars. Their feet were not bound, their thick-soled broad-toed shoes looked clumsy next to Chinese women's tiny ones, they wore a patch of vermilion on the lower lip, and some rode horseback astride like men.
passages.quote: Among the spectators of the novel sight some women were observed; the greatest number were said to be natives of Tartary or of a Tartar race. Their feet were not cramped like those of the Chinese;… A few of the Tartar ladies were on horseback, and rode astride like men.
passages.speaker: Account of Lord Macartney's embassy (Staunton), quoted by John Francis Davis
passages.caution: A quotation from the 1797 embassy account, not Davis's own observation.

passages.headline: The Great Wall measured: earth, brick and blue bricks that were really burned
passages.people: Chinese builders (the wall as a barrier against the Tartars)
passages.gloss: Using Captain Parish's survey for Macartney's embassy, Davis gives the wall's make-up: an earthen core faced on both sides with masonry and brick, a platform of square bricks, 20 feet high including the parapet, 25 feet thick at the base. The bricks are bluish, which made people doubt they were fired, until old kilns were found and Dr Abel showed in 1816 that Chinese clay burns blue. The wall, he says, was a useful barrier until Chinggis Khan overran it.
passages.quote: The body of the wall consists of an earthen mound, retained on each side by walls of masonry and brick, and terraced by a platform of square bricks. The total height, including a parapet of five feet, is twenty feet, on a basis of stone projecting two feet under the brick-work,
passages.speaker: John Francis Davis, summarising Captain Parish's survey (Macartney embassy)

passages.headline: Mongols in tents of coarse felt; a timber stockade around Manchuria
passages.people: Mongol and Kalka Tartars; Manchu homeland
passages.gloss: Drawing on Gerbillon's 1688 journey, Davis says the Mongols and Kalkas are devoted to their Lamas, live in tents of coarse felt, eat half-raw meat and value livestock over money; Timkowski adds that brick tea is their currency. Two pages earlier he describes the Manchu homeland of Mukden, where the emperors are buried, fenced not by a wall but by a timber stockade about eight feet high, wrongly drawn on some European maps as part of the Great Wall.
passages.quote: Entirely devoted to their Lamas, whom even the Emperor of China honours, on account of their influence over the various tribes, the Mongols live in tents of coarse felt, eat nothing but flesh half raw, and exchange their sheep and cattle for a few of the necessaries of life, having no value for money.
passages.speaker: John Francis Davis, summarising Gerbillon (1688)
passages.caution: Second hand, from Jesuit and Russian travellers.

passages.headline: Tartar soldiers paid more than Chinese
passages.people: Manchu Tartar bannermen and Chinese Green Standard troops
passages.gloss: Davis explains the dual army. The 'trusty Tartar troops' are ranged under eight standards, yellow, white, red and blue, plain and bordered, said to be 80,000 men; the Chinese serve under the green flag. A Tartar foot soldier gets two taels a month plus rice, a Chinese only 1.6 taels without rice. He also notes that Tartars under the law are punished with the whip instead of the bamboo.
passages.quote: A great difference seems to exist between the pay of Tartars and Chinese. One of the former, being a foot-soldier, is allowed two taels per month, or about five-pence a day, with an allowance of rice; one of the latter, only one tael and six-tenths, without the rice.
passages.speaker: John Francis Davis (The Chinese, 1836)
passages.caution: Davis says 'seems to exist'; the figures come from report.

passages.headline: Mare's milk and blood soup at the emperor's feast
passages.gloss: Discussing Chinese drinks, Davis says the Tartars still show their pastoral origins in a liking for a strong spirit distilled from mutton, and that one of the soups served at the imperial banquet for Amherst's embassy at Tianjin was said to be made of mare's milk and blood. Davis was on that embassy, but he reports the soup's recipe as hearsay.
passages.quote: The Tartars are said still to preserve a remnant of their pastoral state, in their predilection for a strong liquor which is distilled from mutton. One of the soups, too, presented at the imperial feast conferred on the last British embassy at Tien-tsin, was said to be composed of mare's milk and blood!
passages.speaker: John Francis Davis (The Chinese, 1836)
passages.caution: Both claims are introduced with 'said'.

passages.headline: Kangxi kills a bear with a half-pike
passages.people: Manchu emperors and their hunting army
passages.gloss: Davis says the emperors Kangxi and Qianlong kept up 'the hardy and warlike habits of the Manchows' with great ring hunts north of the Wall, led by a small army with falconers. He quotes Gerbillon: Kangxi shot a bear with an arrow from across a valley, then dismounted and finished it with a half-pike 'used by the Manchows against tigers'. Davis contrasts this with the later emperors who kept cancelling the hunt.
passages.quote: The Emperor, upon this, alighting from his horse took a half-pike, used by the Manchows against tigers, and, accompanied by four of the ablest hunters armed in the same way, he approached the bear and killed him outright with a stab of his half-pike.
passages.speaker: Jean-François Gerbillon, quoted by John Francis Davis
passages.caution: A quotation from Gerbillon's journal, not Davis's own observation.

passages.headline: Du Halde's 'lying miracle' of the earthquake
passages.people: Manchu regents and the Jesuit Adam Schall
passages.gloss: Davis praises the Jesuit astronomer Adam Schall, who kept his post after the Tartars took the empire, but he mocks Du Halde for padding the story with miracles. He quotes Du Halde's claim that when the regents tried to confirm Schall's death sentence, an earthquake scattered them every time, until a general pardon was granted. Davis calls this one of the 'lying miracles' with which Du Halde 'has not blushed to disfigure his work'.
passages.quote: this sentence was carried to the Princes of the blood and to the regent for confirmation; but, as often as they attempted to read it, a dreadful earth quake dispersed the assembly. The consternation was so great, that they granted a general pardon;
passages.speaker: Jean-Baptiste Du Halde, quoted (and rejected) by John Francis Davis
passages.caution: Davis quotes it only to dismiss it. (A real earthquake did strike Beijing in 1665 during Schall's trial.)

passages.headline: The Xiongnu: no walled cities, felt and furs
passages.people: Xiongnu (northern steppe nomads of the Han era)
passages.gloss: Sima Qian opens his chapter on the Xiongnu with their way of life: they move their herds of horses, cattle and sheep in search of water and grass, have no walled cities, fixed homes or farming, though each group has its own pasture land, and they keep no written records. Later in the passage he adds that from the ruler down they eat meat and wear hides, felt and furs. It is the oldest Chinese model of the 'people without cities' that later writers used for the Tartars.
passages.quote: 逐水草遷徙，毋城郭常處耕田之業，然亦各有分地。毋文書，以言語為約束。
passages.translation: They move about following water and grass, and have no walled cities, fixed dwellings or work of tilling fields; yet each has its own allotted land. They have no writing, and make agreements by word of mouth.
passages.speaker: Sima Qian, Shiji ch. 110 (Kanseki Repository text)
passages.caution: The Xiongnu are not 'Tartars'; the passage is included as the earliest Chinese description of steppe nomad life. Archaeology has since found Xiongnu fortified settlements.

passages.headline: Ferghana: walled cities, rice, wine and blood-sweating horses
passages.people: Dayuan (people of Ferghana, reported by Zhang Qian)
passages.gloss: In contrast to the Xiongnu, Zhang Qian reported that the people of Dayuan (Ferghana) were settled farmers growing rice and wheat, made grape wine, and bred fine 'blood-sweating' horses descended from 'heavenly horses'. They had walled cities and houses, some seventy towns large and small, and several hundred thousand people. The same chapter labels the Wusun, Kangju and Yuezhi as 'moving nations' (行國).
passages.quote: 其俗土著，耕田，田稻麥。有蒲陶酒。多善馬，馬汗血，其先天馬子也。有城郭屋室。其屬邑大小七十餘城，眾可數十萬。
passages.translation: Their custom is to stay settled on the land; they plough fields and grow rice and wheat. They have grape wine. They have many fine horses; the horses sweat blood, and their ancestors were the offspring of heavenly horses. They have walled cities and houses; the towns under them, large and small, number over seventy, and the people several hundred thousand.
passages.speaker: Sima Qian, Shiji ch. 123, from Zhang Qian's report (Kanseki Repository text)
passages.caution: Zhang Qian's report as edited by the court historian; 'heavenly horses' is a legend he passes on.

passages.headline: Itil: a city of felt huts with one brick palace
passages.gloss: Yaqut's excerpt describes the Khazar capital Itil on the lower Volga as two towns on either bank. The western part, where the king lived, was walled and about a parasang long, but its buildings were mostly huts of felt, with a few of clay, plus markets and baths. On the next page (n27) it says the king's palace, away from the river, was of fired brick, and that the king let nobody else build in brick.
passages.quote: Haec pars occidentalis in parasangae longitudinem extenditur, muro cincta, sed eo quidem sparsae raraeve structurae. Eorum autem aedificia sunt casae (seu mapalia) ex panno coactili confectae, paucis exceptis, quae e luto constructa. Sunt iis fora et balnea.
passages.translation: This western part stretches for a parasang in length and is enclosed by a wall, but its buildings are scattered and few. Their dwellings are huts (or tents) made of felt, apart from a few built of clay. They have markets and baths.
passages.speaker: Ibn Fadlan as quoted by Yaqut (Latin translation by C. M. Frähn, De Chasaris, 1822)
passages.caution: Yaqut attributes this to Ibn Fadlan, but much of it matches the geographer al-Istakhri, and Ibn Fadlan probably did not visit Itil.

passages.headline: The Khazar king's tomb under a river, its builders beheaded
passages.gloss: The Khazar excerpt says that when the supreme king died, a great building with twenty rooms was raised over a river, with a grave dug in every room, so that no one would know which held the king. The men who buried him were then beheaded. The tomb was called 'paradise'. A page later (n30) it adds that a king was killed if he reigned a day beyond forty years.
passages.quote: Regi supremo mortuo magnum exstruatur palatium in viginti divisum conclavia, inque singulis sepulchrum fodiatur… Sepulto Rege, colla eorum, qui eum composuere, amputantur, ne quis sciat, in quonam eorum conclavium ejus sepulchrum sit.
passages.translation: When the supreme king dies, a great palace divided into twenty rooms is built, and a grave is dug in each one… Once the king is buried, the necks of those who buried him are cut, so that no one may know in which of the rooms his grave lies.
passages.speaker: Ibn Fadlan as quoted by Yaqut (Latin translation by C. M. Frähn, De Chasaris, 1822)
passages.caution: Hearsay about a court the author had not seen.

passages.headline: Rus traders build big wooden houses on the Volga
passages.gloss: Ibn Fadlan says the Rus came downriver with their goods, anchored on the Itil (Volga) and built large wooden houses on the bank, each holding ten or twenty people with a bench for every man. He goes on to describe, with disgust, their public sex with slave girls and a shared washing bowl passed from man to man.
passages.quote: Sie kommen aus ihrem Lande, legen ihre Schiffe im Itil, welches ein großer Fluß ist, vor Anker und bauen sich an dessen Ufern große Häuser von Holz. In so einem Hause leben ihrer zehn oder zwanzig, auch mehr oder weniger, zusammen.
passages.translation: They come from their own country, anchor their ships in the Itil, which is a great river, and build large houses of wood on its banks. Ten or twenty of them, more or fewer, live together in one such house.
passages.speaker: Ibn Fadlan as quoted by Yaqut (German translation by C. M. Frähn, 1823)
passages.caution: The Rus were Scandinavian traders, not Tatars; the place is the Bulghar trading ground where Kazan Tatar history later begins.

passages.headline: A round mound raised over the burned ship
passages.gloss: After the ship cremation, Ibn Fadlan watched the Rus raise something like a round hill over the spot, set a large post of beech wood in the middle, and write on it the dead man's name and the name of the Rus king. It is a rare eyewitness account of a burial mound (kurgan) being built on the Volga.
passages.quote: Darauf führten sie über dem Orte, wo das aus dem Flusse gezogene Schiff gestanden, etwas einem runden Hügel ähnliches auf, errichteten in dessen Mitte ein großes buchen Holz und schrieben darauf den Namen des Verstorbenen, nebst dem des Königs der Russen.
passages.translation: Then, over the place where the ship drawn out of the river had stood, they built something like a round hill, set up in its middle a large post of beech wood, and wrote on it the name of the dead man together with that of the king of the Rus.
passages.speaker: Ibn Fadlan as quoted by Yaqut (German translation by C. M. Frähn, 1823)
passages.caution: 'Büchen Holz' is read here as 'beechwood post'; other translators render the wood as birch (khadank).

passages.headline: 'You Arabs are a stupid people': why the Rus burn their dead
passages.gloss: At the end of the famous ship funeral, in which a slave girl was killed and burned with her master, a Rus man spoke to Ibn Fadlan through the interpreter. Arabs, he said, bury their dearest in the earth to be eaten by worms, while the Rus burn theirs in an instant so they go straight to paradise. Then he laughed and said God's love had sent the wind to speed the fire.
passages.quote: ihr Araber, sagte er, seyd doch ein dummes Volk: ihr nehmt den, der euch der geliebteste und geehrteste unter den Menschen ist, und werft ihn in die Erde, wo ihn die kriechenden Thiere und Würmer fressen. Wir dagegen verbrennen ihn in einem Nu, so daß er unverzüglich und sonder Aufenthalt in's Paradies eingeht.
passages.translation: 'You Arabs,' he said, 'are a stupid people: you take the one who is dearest and most honoured to you among men and throw him into the earth, where crawling creatures and worms eat him. We, on the other hand, burn him in a moment, so that he enters paradise at once and without delay.'
passages.speaker: A Rus man, reported by Ibn Fadlan via an interpreter (German translation by C. M. Frähn, 1823)
passages.caution: Words reported through an interpreter.

passages.headline: Wooden idols with human faces
passages.gloss: When their boats arrived, each Rus trader went to a tall wooden post carved with a human face and ringed by smaller figures, bowed to the ground and listed his slave girls and sable furs, asking for a rich buyer. If trade went well he slaughtered cattle and sheep, left the meat before the idols and hung the heads on the posts; when dogs ate it at night, he said his lord was pleased.
passages.quote: Er tritt zu der großen hölzernen Figur, wirft sich vor ihr zur Erde nieder und spricht: o mein Herr! ich bin aus fernem Lande gekommen, führe so und so viel Mädchen mit mir, und von Zobeln so und so viel Felle,
passages.translation: He goes up to the large wooden figure, throws himself on the ground before it and says: 'O my lord, I have come from a distant land, bringing so many girls with me, and so many sable skins.'
passages.speaker: Ibn Fadlan as quoted by Yaqut (German translation by C. M. Frähn, 1823)

passages.headline: A twelve-cubit giant of Gog and Magog at Bulghar
passages.gloss: Frähn summarises a tale Ibn Fadlan heard from the Bulghar king: traders found a man twelve cubits tall floating in the flooded Volga, with a head like the largest cauldron, a nose over a span long and fingers a span long. The Wisu people told the king he belonged to Gog and Magog, who lived three months away across a sea. The giant died, and the speaker claims to have seen his dreadful bones. Yaqut already refused to vouch for it, and Frähn suggests in a footnote that mammoth bones were the likely source.
passages.quote: der eine Höhe von 12 Ellen gehabt, einen Kopf so gross wie nur der grösste Kessel sey, eine Nase über eine Spanne lang, grosse Augen und Spannenlange Finger;… dass dieser Mensch zu den Jog und Magog gehöre,
passages.translation: who was twelve cubits tall, with a head as big as the biggest cauldron, a nose more than a span long, large eyes and fingers a span long; … that this man belonged to Gog and Magog,
passages.speaker: C. M. Frähn, summarising Ibn Fadlan's report of the Bulghar king's story (1823)
passages.caution: An editor's paraphrase of a story told to Ibn Fadlan; Yaqut himself doubted it.

passages.headline: Could anyone know the name 'Tatar' in the 6th century?
passages.gloss: In a note, Frähn discusses a 16th-century Ottoman writer who claimed the Persian king Anushirvan (6th century) built the Caspian Gates for fear of 'Turks and Tatars'. Frähn replies that although Arab writers mention the Tatars earlier than some scholars thought, the name can hardly have been known that early in western Asia. It is a scholarly warning against reading 'Tatar' back into ancient history.
passages.quote: denn erwähnen gleich Arabische Schriftsteller der Tataren früher, als in den trefflichen Mémoires sur l'Arménie T. II. p. 263 angemerkt ist; so früh kann man wohl kaum Bekanntschaft mit ihrem Namen im westl. Asien annehmen.
passages.translation: for although Arab writers mention the Tatars earlier than is noted in the excellent Mémoires sur l'Arménie (vol. II, p. 263), one can hardly assume that their name was known so early in western Asia.
passages.speaker: C. M. Frähn, editor's note (1823)
passages.caution: Editorial, not Ibn Fadlan.

passages.headline: Sober Tatars who still enjoy a drink
passages.gloss: Commenting on Ibn Fadlan's horror at Rus drinking, Frähn notes that not all Muslims keep the ban on wine. Among the Tatars of Russia, he says, 'sober as this people is', he met many who did not refuse wine and strong drink, though he never saw them drink too much. It is a small firsthand note on real Tatars by a scholar who knew them.
passages.quote: Und so habe ich auch unter den Tataren Russlands, so nüchtern dieses Volk auch ist, nicht wenige gefunden, die Wein und derlei starke Getränke nicht verschmähten, wenn ich sie gleich nie das Maass überschreiten sah.
passages.translation: And so among the Tatars of Russia too, sober as this people is, I have found not a few who did not scorn wine and such strong drinks, though I never saw them exceed moderation.
passages.speaker: C. M. Frähn, editor's note (1823)
passages.caution: Editorial observation, not part of Ibn Fadlan's text.

passages.headline: Samarkand, 'a delicious place'
passages.people: Khwarazmian subjects in Samarkand, reached by Chinggis Khan's army
passages.gloss: Yelü Chucai calls Samarkand 'Sün-sz'-kan', explains that the name means 'fat' because the land is so fertile, and describes gold and copper coins without holes. For miles around the city he saw orchards, flower gardens, aqueducts, springs and pools, melons as big as a horse's head, grape wine, and white cotton clothes, since white was lucky there and black the colour of mourning.
passages.quote: Around the city, to an extent of several tens of li, there are everywhere orchards, groves, flower gardens, aqueducts, running springs, square basins, and round ponds, in uninterrupted succession ; indeed, Sün-sz'-kan is a delicious place ! The water-melons there are as large as a horse's head.
passages.speaker: Yelü Chucai's Si yu lu, in a Yuan-era abridgement (translated by E. Bretschneider, 1888)
passages.caution: An abridged text; Yelü Chucai lived in Samarkand for a time after its capture.

passages.headline: Otrar: where the war began
passages.people: Chinggis Khan's envoys and merchants; the governor of Otrar
passages.gloss: Yelü Chucai names Otrar ('O-ta-la'), ruling more than ten other towns, as the cause of the Mongol invasion of Central Asia. Its governor had Chinggis Khan's envoys and several hundred merchants with them killed and seized their goods. Bretschneider notes that Persian historians tell the same story.
passages.quote: One time the chief of this place ordered several envoys (of Chinghiz), and several hundreds of merchants (who were with them), to be put to death, and seized upon their goods. That was the cause of the army being directed against the Western people.
passages.speaker: Yelü Chucai's Si yu lu, in a Yuan-era abridgement (translated by E. Bretschneider, 1888)

passages.headline: A plain without cities where the sun rises before a chop is cooked
passages.people: Kipchaks (the steppe later ruled by the Golden Horde)
passages.gloss: Far to the north-west lies 'K'o-fu-ch'a', which Bretschneider identifies with the Kipchak steppe north of the Caspian. Yelü Chucai heard that it was endless plain, its people had no cities or towns, bred cattle and horses and made a drink from honey, and that summer nights were so short the sun rose again before a mutton chop could be cooked. Bretschneider shows the short-night detail was copied from a Tang-era account of a Siberian people.
passages.quote: To the north-west of Yin-du (Hindustan) is the realm of K'o fu-ch'a… The people there have no cities or towns. They breed much cattle and horses. They make a fermented beverage from honey. In that country the days (in summer) are long and the nights short. In little more than the time necessary to cook a mutton chop, the sun rises again.
passages.speaker: Yelü Chucai's Si yu lu, in a Yuan-era abridgement (translated by E. Bretschneider, 1888)
passages.caution: Hearsay, partly borrowed from the Tang history; the Mongols did not conquer the Kipchak steppe until 1236.

passages.headline: Tatar, Tartar, Mongol: the editor explains
passages.people: Mongols, called Tatars in Russian annals
passages.gloss: In a footnote to a Russian chronicle's account of the siege of Kiev in 1240, printed in the same volume, Bretschneider explains the names. Russian annals always call the Mongols Tatars, Western chronicles call them Tartars, and so do Carpini, Rubruck and Marco Polo; but the name comes from a real Mongol-era tribe, the Tatar, which is how Muslim and Chinese writers spell it.
passages.quote: The Mongols are invariably termed Tatars in the Russian annals. The Hungarian and other Western chronicles of the thirteenth century call them Tartars. Piano Carpini, Rubruck, M. Polo, also write Tartar. But the original Mongol name of the tribe, from which this appellation is derived, was Tatar. Thus the Mohammedan and the Chinese authors spell the name.
passages.speaker: E. Bretschneider, editor's footnote (Mediaeval Researches, 1888)
passages.caution: An editor's note from another part of the volume, not Yelü Chucai's text.

passages.headline: Lord of half the eastern world
passages.people: Tartars (the Mongol Yuan emperor and his empire)
passages.gloss: Marignolli opens his travel memories by describing the ruler he was sent to: the Great Khan at Khanbaliq, 'supreme emperor of all the Tartars'. For this Florentine friar the Tartar ruler was not a tent chief but the master of countless cities, languages and peoples. The Khan was Toghon Temur, last Yuan emperor of China.
passages.quote: missus fui cum Apostolicis literis & donis nuncius & legatus ad Kaam, summum omnium Thartarorum Imperatorem, qui tenet quasi dominium medietatis orbis orientalis, cujus potestas & copia civitatum, terrarum, linguarum, diviciarum, & regiminis infinitorum quodammodo populorum excedit omnem narracionem.
passages.translation: I was sent with apostolic letters and gifts as envoy and legate to the Khan, supreme emperor of all the Tartars, who holds lordship over almost half of the eastern world, whose power and wealth in cities, lands, languages, riches and rule over countless peoples is beyond all telling.
passages.speaker: Giovanni de' Marignolli (Latin text ed. Gelasius Dobner, 1768)
passages.caution: The printed text dates the departure 1334; the mission is otherwise dated to 1338, when Benedict XII answered the Khan's embassy.

passages.headline: A friar with a cross before the Great Khan
passages.people: The Great Khan of the Tartars (Yuan emperor) and his court
passages.gloss: The Pope's gifts included big European warhorses, and the Khan was delighted with them. Marignolli entered the palace in full vestments behind a cross, with candles and incense, singing the Creed, and blessed the Khan. He adds that the court then lodged the 32 members of the mission and paid for everything, food, drink and even paper for lanterns, for three or four years.
passages.quote: Maximus autem Kaam visis dextrariis, & donis Pape, & literis bullatis … gavisus est gaudio magno … Ego autem solempniter indutus cum Cruce pulcherrima, que me precedebat cum luminaribus & incenso cantando: Credo in unum Deum; intravimus coram illo Kaam in glorioso pallacio residente, & cantu finito, largam dedi recipienti humiliter benediccionem.
passages.translation: The great Khan, seeing the warhorses, the Pope's gifts and the sealed letters … rejoiced with great joy … And I, solemnly vested, with a most beautiful cross carried before me with candles and incense, singing 'I believe in one God', we went in before the Khan as he sat in his glorious palace; and when the singing was over I gave him a full blessing, which he received humbly.
passages.speaker: Giovanni de' Marignolli (Latin text ed. Gelasius Dobner, 1768)
passages.caution: Marignolli's own account of his success; 'humbly' is his view of how the Khan received the blessing.

passages.headline: Khanbaliq, with a cathedral beside the palace
passages.people: The Tartar (Yuan) capital and its Franciscan community
passages.gloss: Marignolli refuses even to try to describe the size, population and military order of the Khan's capital, the seat of the 'Empire of the East'. What he does describe is the Christian presence: a Franciscan cathedral right next to the imperial palace, an archbishopric, several other churches with bells, all supported from the Emperor's table. The city is the Yuan capital (Dadu) on the site of modern Beijing.
passages.quote: pervenimus in Cambalec, ubi est summa Sedes Imperii Orientis, de cujus magnitudine incredibili, & populo, ordine militum sileatur. … Habent etiam fratres Minores in Cambalec Ecclesiam Cathedralem immediate juxta pallacium, & solempnem Archiepiscopatum, & alias Ecclesias plures in civitate, & campanas, & omnes vivunt de mensa Imperatoris honorifice valde.
passages.translation: We came to Khanbaliq, the chief seat of the Empire of the East; of its incredible size, its people and the order of its soldiers, let nothing be said. … The Friars Minor also have in Khanbaliq a cathedral church right next to the palace, and a solemn archbishopric, and several other churches in the city, with bells, and they all live very honourably at the Emperor's expense.
passages.speaker: Giovanni de' Marignolli (Latin text ed. Gelasius Dobner, 1768)

passages.headline: From Ozbeg's horde to a new church at Almaliq
passages.people: Tartars of the Golden Horde (Ozbeg Khan) and of the Chagatai 'middle empire'
passages.gloss: The legates wintered with Ozbeg, khan of the Golden Horde, who fed, clothed and rewarded them and sent them on with his own horses to Almaliq, a city of the Chagatai khanate in the Ili valley (near modern Huocheng, Xinjiang). There, only a year after a bishop and six friars had been killed, they bought a plot, built a church and preached openly. The Tartar khans appear as hosts who moved envoys across their realms at their own cost.
passages.quote: Inde ad primum Tartarorum Imperatorem Usbec pervenimus, & obtulimus literas, pannos, dextrarium, cytiacam, & dona Pape, & post hiemem bene pasti, vestiti, & remunerati magnifice, & cum ejus equis & expensis pervenimus in Armalec Imperii medii, ubi fecimus Ecclesiam, emimus aream, fecimus fontes, cantavimus missas, baptisavimus plures, libere, & publice predicantes
passages.translation: From there we came to the first emperor of the Tartars, Ozbeg, and presented letters, cloth, a warhorse, a 'cytiaca' (the editor guesses a strong liquor) and the Pope's gifts; and after the winter, well fed, clothed and magnificently rewarded, we travelled with his horses and at his expense to Almaliq of the middle empire, where we built a church, bought a plot of ground, made wells (or fonts), sang masses and baptised many, preaching freely and in public
passages.speaker: Giovanni de' Marignolli (Latin text ed. Gelasius Dobner, 1768)

passages.headline: A martyr's prophecy against the Tartars of Sarai
passages.people: Tartars of Sarai (Golden Horde) and of Almaliq (Chagatai khanate)
passages.gloss: Marignolli names the Franciscans killed at Almaliq the year before he arrived and credits one of them, Pascal the Spaniard, with visions and prophecies: that the Tartars of Sarai on the Volga would be destroyed by a flood, that Almaliq would perish, and that the ruler would be killed three days after the martyrdom. He presents the dead friars as holy martyrs 'shining with miracles'.
passages.quote: frater Paschalis Hyspanus, qui fuit Propheta, & vidit celum apertum, & predixit sibi, & Sociis suis martirium, & Thartaros de Saray destruendos diluvio, Armalec perituram, propter ipsorum martirium, Imperatorem illum tercio die occidendum post ipsorum martirium
passages.translation: Brother Pascal the Spaniard, who was a prophet, saw heaven opened and foretold martyrdom for himself and his companions, and that the Tartars of Sarai would be destroyed by a flood, that Almaliq would perish because of their martyrdom, and that that emperor would be killed on the third day after their martyrdom
passages.speaker: Giovanni de' Marignolli (Latin text ed. Gelasius Dobner, 1768)
passages.caution: Pious report: Marignolli arrived after the killings and repeats what the local friars remembered.

passages.headline: The Tartars crossed the 'impassable' torrid zone
passages.gloss: East of Almaliq the legates reached wind-built 'mountains of sand' beyond which, Marignolli says, nobody before the Tartars believed there was habitable land. The Tartars crossed them into a vast plain that philosophers called the Torrid Zone and thought impassable; on the next page he adds that he crossed it twice himself. He is mixing a real desert crossing with the old scholarly theory of uninhabitable climate zones.
passages.quote: pervenimus ad Cyollos Kagon, id est, ad montes arene, quos faciunt venti, ultra quos ante Tartaros nullus putavit terram habitabilem, nec putabatur ultra aliquam terram esse. Tartari autem voluntate Dei mirabili industria transierunt, & fuerunt in campo maximo, ubi dicitur Torrida Zona, & inpertransibilis a Philosophis
passages.translation: we came to the Cyollos Kagon, that is, to mountains of sand made by the winds, beyond which, before the Tartars, nobody thought there was habitable land, nor was it believed that any land lay beyond. But the Tartars, by God's will and with marvellous skill, crossed them and came into a vast plain, the place called the Torrid Zone, held by the philosophers to be impassable
passages.speaker: Giovanni de' Marignolli (Latin text ed. Gelasius Dobner, 1768)
passages.caution: The 'Torrid Zone' is a label from medieval theory, not a real description of a Central Asian desert.

passages.headline: Thirty thousand Christian Alans at the Khan's court
passages.gloss: Among the Khan's great men, Marignolli counts more than thirty thousand Alans, a people from the Caucasus whom the Mongols had taken into their service, who were Christians 'in fact or in name' and called themselves the Pope's slaves. He also explains that the peoples of the East called all Western Europeans 'Franks'. The passage shows how mixed in religion and origin the Tartar empire's elite was.
passages.quote: Summi eciam principes … Imperii tocius, plus quam triginta millia, qui vocantur Alani, … sunt Christiani, re vel nomine, & dicunt se Sclavos Pape, parati mori pro franquis, sic enim vocant nos, non a francia, sed a franquia.
passages.translation: The highest princes of the whole empire, more than thirty thousand, who are called Alans … are Christians, in fact or in name, and they call themselves the Pope's slaves, ready to die for the Franks; for so they call us, not from France but from 'Franquia'.
passages.speaker: Giovanni de' Marignolli (Latin text ed. Gelasius Dobner, 1768)
passages.caution: The number is Marignolli's estimate, and he is keen to show the East as friendly to the Pope.

passages.headline: Chinggis Khan hires the Alans to punish the world
passages.people: Tartars (Mongols) under Chinggis Khan, and the Alans
passages.gloss: In his world history after Noah, Marignolli derives the Alans from Elam, son of Shem, calls them the noblest nation on earth, and says the Tartars won the Empire of the East only with their help. Chinggis Khan, 'first king of the Tartars', hired 72 of their princes when he set out, by God's command, to chastise the world. The Tartars are fitted into Bible history as God's scourge.
passages.quote: a quo nobilis generacio Alanorum in oriente dicitur exorta, & est hodie maior & nobilior nacio mundi, & homines pulcriores, & forciores, quorum auxilio Tartari optinuerunt Imperium orientis, & sine quibus nunquam habuerunt victoriam gloriosam. Conduxit enim Cingwis Caam primus Thartarorum Rex de eis LXXII. principes, quando voluit precepto Dei castigare mundum.
passages.translation: from whom [Elam] the noble race of the Alans in the East is said to have sprung; and it is today the greatest and noblest nation in the world, the handsomest and strongest men, with whose help the Tartars won the Empire of the East, and without whom they never won a glorious victory. For Chinggis Khan, first king of the Tartars, hired seventy-two of their princes when he wished, at God's command, to chastise the world.
passages.speaker: Giovanni de' Marignolli (Latin text ed. Gelasius Dobner, 1768)
passages.caution: Biblical genealogy plus praise of the Alans, who were in fact conquered by the Mongols in the 1220s and 1230s rather than hired by Chinggis.

passages.headline: Baptisms at Kamul, on a promise of no church taxes
passages.people: Tartars and other peoples of Kamul
passages.gloss: In an aside on church tithes, Marignolli recalls that at Kamul (Hami), where there were 'many Tartars and other nations', converts refused baptism until the friars swore they would never demand anything worldly from them afterwards. Once the friars promised, and even helped the poor from their own funds, crowds of men and women were baptised. He uses the story to argue against forcing tithes on new converts.
passages.quote: ubi primo conversi nolebant baptizari, donec juravimus, nihil temporale post baptismum extorquere ab eis, ymo de nostro indigentibus providere, quod & fecimus, sic multitudo civitatis utriusque sexus baptismum libentissime receperunt.
passages.translation: where at first the converts would not be baptised until we swore that we would extract nothing worldly from them after baptism, but would rather provide for the needy from our own; which we did, and so a multitude of the city, of both sexes, received baptism most willingly.
passages.speaker: Giovanni de' Marignolli (Latin text ed. Gelasius Dobner, 1768)
passages.caution: The mention of Tartars at Kamul is on the previous page (n144); conversion numbers are the missionary's own claim.

passages.headline: To Tartars, Latin Christians looked like idol-worshippers
passages.gloss: In a chapter on how idols began, Marignolli admits an uncomfortable fact he learned abroad: Jews, Tartars and Saracens, and even some Eastern Christians, think Western Christians are the worst idolaters. Eastern Christians honour painted images but loathe the carved faces and frightening sculptures found in Latin churches, such as those on Saint Adalbert's tomb in Prague.
passages.quote: Judei tamen, Tartari, & Sarraceni iudicant nos pessimos ydololatras, & non solum gentiles, sed eciam Christiani quidam. Nam licet illi Christiani venerentur picturas, abhominantur tamen larvas, facies, & horrendas sculpturas, sicut sunt in Ecclesiis: patet in sepulcro sancti Adalberti in Praga.
passages.translation: Yet Jews, Tartars and Saracens judge us the worst of idolaters, and not only the heathen but even some Christians. For although those Christians venerate paintings, they abhor masks, faces and horrible sculptures such as there are in our churches, as can be seen at the tomb of Saint Adalbert in Prague.
passages.speaker: Giovanni de' Marignolli (Latin text ed. Gelasius Dobner, 1768)

passages.headline: Robes 'in the Tartar fashion'
passages.people: Tartars (Mongols), as a model for a dress style
passages.gloss: Retelling the old legend of Queen Semiramis, who disguised herself as her son, Marignolli explains her disguise with clothing he had seen on his travels: robes 'in the Tartar fashion', wrapped over across the chest, with long sleeves, long skirts covering the feet and trousers for riding. The legend is classical; the comparison to Tartar dress is his own.
passages.quote: ipsa invenit sibi vestes thartarico modo formatas, ante pectus replicatas, ne mamille apparerent, longas manicas, ne mulieris manus viderentur, longas vestes, ad cooperiendum pedes, bracas, quando equum ascendebat, & precepit nomine filii, quod omnes tali veste uterentur
passages.translation: she devised for herself clothes made in the Tartar fashion, folded over across the chest so that her breasts would not show, with long sleeves so that a woman's hands would not be seen, long robes to cover the feet, and trousers for when she mounted a horse; and she ordered in her son's name that everyone should wear such clothing
passages.speaker: Giovanni de' Marignolli (Latin text ed. Gelasius Dobner, 1768)
passages.caution: A legend about ancient Assyria; only the description of the 'Tartar fashion' reflects what he saw.

passages.headline: Hangzhou's temples and ten thousand stone bridges
passages.people: Chinese of Manzi (southern China) under the Great Khan
passages.gloss: The Khan sent the legates home through Manzi, southern China, with its 'thirty thousand great cities'. Campsay (Hangzhou), the old Song capital, is to Marignolli the finest city in the world, full of buildings and temples, with thousands of monks living together. The ten thousand carved stone bridges he takes from earlier writers and cannot quite believe. These were Chinese buildings in a Chinese city under Mongol rule; he does not credit any of them to the Tartars.
passages.quote: Et inter illas est civitas famosissima nomine Campsay mirabilior, pulchrior, dicior, & maior cum maiori populo, & pluribus diviciis, & deliciis, edificiis, & maxime ydolorum templis … quam aliqua civitas, que sit in mundo, vel forte fuerit unquam. Ubi scribunt scribentes esse decem millia poncium nobilium de lapide cum sculpturis & ymaginibus principum armatorum, incredibile est non videnti, & tamen forte non menciuntur.
passages.translation: And among them is the most famous city called Campsay, more marvellous, more beautiful, richer and larger, with a greater population, more riches and delights, more buildings and above all temples of idols … than any city that exists in the world, or perhaps ever existed. There, writers write, are ten thousand fine bridges of stone with sculptures and images of armed princes; it is incredible to one who has not seen it, and yet perhaps they do not lie.
passages.speaker: Giovanni de' Marignolli (Latin text ed. Gelasius Dobner, 1768)
passages.caution: The bridge count is taken from earlier writers, as he says. Dobner's footnote wrongly identifies Campsay with Cambay in Gujarat.

passages.headline: An editor moves Almaliq and Sarai to Japan
passages.people: Editor's note on the Tartar cities of Almaliq and Sarai
passages.gloss: Faced with unfamiliar names, the Prague editor Gelasius Dobner trusted a Franciscan martyrology that placed the martyrs 'in Japan' and concluded that Almaliq and Sarai were Japanese islands, Sarai being 'Sayrock Xymo' (probably Kyushu, which Jesuit writers called 'Saicoku' or 'Ximo'). In fact Almaliq lay in the Ili valley of Central Asia and Sarai on the lower Volga. By the eighteenth century the geography of the medieval Tartar empires had become hazy even for scholars.
passages.quote: Et cum Martyrologium S. Francisci Seraphici dicat eos passos in Japonia, verosimillime Armalec una ex insulis fuit Japonie, quemadmodum mox supra nominata Saray verosimillime est hodierna insula Sayrock Xymo una inter tres precipuas Japonie insulas in Oceano orientali.
passages.translation: And since the Martyrology of Saint Francis says they suffered in Japan, Almaliq was most probably one of the islands of Japan, just as Sarai, named just above, is most probably the present-day island of Sayrock Xymo, one of the three chief islands of Japan in the eastern Ocean.
passages.speaker: Gelasius Dobner, editor (footnote, 1768)
passages.caution: The editor's error, not Marignolli's.

passages.headline: The road to Cathay is safe, day and night
passages.people: Merchants on the Mongol roads; officials of the Tartar lords
passages.gloss: According to merchants who had used it, the road from Tana to Cathay was perfectly safe by day and by night. The one risk was death: if a merchant died on the way, the lord of the land took everything he carried, unless a brother or close companion was there to claim it. On the same page Pegolotti advises hiring an interpreter and two servants who speak Cuman, the Turkic language of the steppe, and taking flour and salt fish for the journey, since meat is plentiful everywhere.
passages.quote: Il cammino d'andare dalla Tana al Gattajo è sicurissimo e di dì, e di notte secondo che si conta per gli mercatanti, che l'hanno usato: salvo se il mercatante, che va, o che viene, morisse in cammino, ogni cosa sarebbe del Signore del paese, ove morisse il mercatante, e tutto prenderebbono gli uficiali del Signore
passages.translation: The road from Tana to Cathay is perfectly safe, by day and by night, according to what the merchants say who have used it; except that if a merchant, going or coming, should die on the road, everything would belong to the lord of the country where he died, and the lord's officials would take it all
passages.speaker: Francesco Balducci Pegolotti (ed. G. F. Pagnini, 1766)
passages.caution: Reported from merchants' experience; Pegolotti himself is not known to have made the journey.

passages.headline: Khanbaliq, a hundred miles round
passages.people: The Cathay of the Great Khan (Yuan China)
passages.gloss: Cathay, Pegolotti explains, is a province of many towns, and its chief city, where merchants gather and do most of their business, is Cambalecco (Khanbaliq, the Yuan capital on the site of Beijing). He passes on the merchants' claim that the city is a hundred miles round and packed with people and houses.
passages.quote: Il Gattajo si è una Provincia, dove à molte Terre, e molti Casali; infra l'altre si ha una, cioè la mastra Cittade, ove riparano mercatanti … la quale Cittade si chiama Cambalecco. E la detta Cittade gira cento miglia, ed è tutta piena di gente, e di magione
passages.translation: Cathay is a province in which there are many towns and many villages; among them there is one, the chief city, where merchants resort … and this city is called Cambalecco. And the said city is a hundred miles round, and all full of people and houses
passages.speaker: Francesco Balducci Pegolotti (ed. G. F. Pagnini, 1766)
passages.caution: The hundred-mile circuit is merchants' exaggeration; the city name is badly misread in the OCR ('Cam baleito').

passages.headline: The Khan takes your silver and pays in paper
passages.people: The lord of Cathay (the Mongol Yuan emperor)
passages.gloss: All the silver merchants bring into Cathay, Pegolotti warns, is taken by the lord of Cathay into his treasury, and the merchants are given paper money in exchange: yellow paper stamped with the lord's seal. Everyone in the country must accept it, and he adds that prices are not raised because the money is paper. This is the Yuan paper currency that amazed European visitors.
passages.quote: Tutto l'argento, che i mercatanti portano, e che va al Gattajo, il Signore del Gattajo lo fa pigliare per se, e mettelo in suo tesoro, e mercatanti che lui portano ne dà loro moneta di pappiero, cioè di carta gialla coniata della bolla del detto Signore
passages.translation: All the silver that the merchants carry with them to Cathay, the lord of Cathay has taken for himself and put into his treasury, and to the merchants who bring it he gives paper money in exchange, that is, yellow paper stamped with the seal of the said lord
passages.speaker: Francesco Balducci Pegolotti (ed. G. F. Pagnini, 1766)

passages.headline: 'Moccoli, that is, Tartar brigands'
passages.people: Moccoli (Mongols) in the Ilkhanate of Persia
passages.gloss: Listing the tolls on the road from Ayas in Lesser Armenia to Tabriz, the capital of the 'lord of the Tartars' in Persia, Pegolotti adds a last charge for the extortion of the 'Moccoli, that is, Tartar brigands' along the way. 'Moccoli' is the Italian merchants' form of 'Mongols', and he treats it as a plain synonym for Tartars. In the Cathay chapter he likewise warns that the road beyond Tana is full of Moccoli, 'that is, armed men'.
passages.quote: E per forza che fanno i Moccoli, cioè Tartari Scherani per cammino
passages.translation: And for the extortion that the Moccoli, that is, Tartar brigands, practise along the road
passages.speaker: Francesco Balducci Pegolotti (ed. G. F. Pagnini, 1766)
passages.caution: The amount of the charge is illegible in this OCR.

passages.headline: Nomads beyond the Wall who ate only meat
passages.people: Tartars (Mongol nomads north and west of the Great Wall)
passages.gloss: Between Cialis and the Chinese frontier, the account says, the country was notorious for Tartar raids: merchants scouted from the hills by day and travelled silently by night, and passed Muslim travellers who had been murdered for going alone. The Tartars rarely killed the settled locals, calling them their slaves and shepherds whose flocks they could seize. They refused grain and rice as fodder for animals, lived on meat including horse, mule and camel, and were said to live past a hundred.
passages.quote: quanquam raro Tartari indigenas ipsos mactent, asserentes eos esse servos suos ac pastores, quibus arietum greges, & boum armenta eripiunt; sed neque frumento, neque oriza aliove legumine ipsi vescuntur, dicentes hoc iumentorum esse non hominum pabulum: sola igitur carne vesci solent, nec ab equis, mulis, aut Camelis abhorrent, & tamen fama est eos diutissime vivere, & fere annorum centum excedere senectutem.
passages.translation: although the Tartars rarely kill the local people themselves, saying that they are their slaves and shepherds, from whom they carry off flocks of sheep and herds of cattle. They themselves eat neither grain nor rice nor any other pulse, saying that this is fodder for beasts, not food for men; so they live on meat alone, and do not shrink from horses, mules or camels. And yet it is said that they live very long, often past a hundred years.
passages.speaker: Nicolas Trigault, from Matteo Ricci's commentaries, reporting Goes's journey (1615)
passages.caution: Travellers' report passed through Isaac the Armenian and Ricci; the hundred-year lifespan is explicitly rumour ('fama est').

passages.headline: Walls and fortress towns built against the Tartars
passages.gloss: Where the Great Wall ends in the far north-west, the account explains, there was a gap of some two hundred miles through which the Tartars, shut out by the Wall, kept trying to raid China. To stop them the Chinese built two heavily fortified cities, Kanchou (Zhangye) and Suchou (Jiuquan), with picked troops and their own viceroy. Here the walls and forts are Chinese works built to keep the Tartars out.
passages.quote: Ad occiduam Sinensis regni partem, qua in Boream flectitur, celebres illi muri finiuntur, & spatium erat ducentorum fere milliariorum, quo spatio Tartari muris exclusi, saepe in Sinarum regnum excurrentes tentabant ingressum, & etiamnunc, sed minore periculo tentant: extructae sunt enim ad retundendos eorum impetus urbes duae munitissimae
passages.translation: At the western part of the kingdom of China, where it bends to the north, those famous walls come to an end, and there was a stretch of about two hundred miles through which the Tartars, shut out by the walls, often tried to break into China, and still try even now, though with less danger: for two very strongly fortified cities have been built to beat back their attacks
passages.speaker: Nicolas Trigault, from Matteo Ricci's commentaries (1615)

passages.headline: The scrap of paper that proved Cambalu was Peking
passages.people: Muslim merchants returning from Peking; Goes and Isaac
