passages.gloss: At Cialis, Goes met merchants coming back from a trade 'embassy' to Peking who had lodged in the same foreigners' palace as Ricci and his companions. They did not know the Jesuits' Chinese names, but they had rescued from a servant's sweepings a note written in Portuguese. That settled it: Cathay differed from China only in name, and the capital the Muslims called Cambalu was Peking. Cialis is usually identified with Karashahr in Xinjiang.
passages.quote: addiderunt etiam ad fidem acrius exigendam schedulam a Nostris scriptam sermone Lusitano, quam e famuli cubiculum verrentis sordibus eripuerant … his nunciis cum Socio Noster satis recreati sunt, nihilque deinde dubitarunt Cataium a Sinensi Regno solo nomine discrepare, ipsamque Regiam a Saracenis Cambalu appellatam Pechinum esse
passages.translation: to make their story more certain they added a scrap of paper written by our men in Portuguese, which they had snatched from the rubbish of a servant sweeping out a room … with this news our Brother and his companion were much cheered, and from then on they had no doubt that Cathay differed from the kingdom of China in name only, and that the royal city the Saracens call Cambalu is Peking
passages.speaker: Nicolas Trigault, from Matteo Ricci's commentaries, reporting Goes's journey (1615)

passages.headline: Cathay: the Tartars' name for China
passages.people: Tartars (Mongols) who ruled China in Marco Polo's day
passages.gloss: Ricci explains why Europe thought Cathay and China were two countries. Marco Polo came when the Tartars ruled China, perhaps with them, and so Europe learned the country under the names the Tartars used: Cathay, with its royal city Cambalu. The Portuguese later brought home the name China and the city name Peking, and mapmakers drew two kingdoms side by side. On the previous page he offers a folk etymology that splits Campalu into Tartar 'Cam' (great) and the Chinese words 'Pa' (north) and 'Lu' (Tartars); the name is really Turkic Khanbaliq, 'city of the khan'.
passages.quote: inde plane apparet, Marcum Paulum Venetum eo tempore in hoc regnum penetrasse, quo Tartari Sinis imperitabant, & fortasse cum illis ipsis eo penetrasse. Eius deinde commentariis Europae, Sinarum Regnum innotuit eo nomine, quo Tartari utebantur, Cataium videlicet & urbem Regiam Cambalu appellantes. … Hoc tamen tempore nulla extra muros Sinenses Regio reperitur, quae Cataium vocitetur.
passages.translation: From this it is plain that Marco Polo the Venetian entered this kingdom at the time when the Tartars ruled the Chinese, and perhaps entered with them. Through his writings the kingdom of China became known to Europe by the name the Tartars used, calling it Cathay and its royal city Cambalu. … At present, however, no region outside the Chinese walls is found that is called Cathay.
passages.speaker: Matteo Ricci, edited and translated into Latin by Nicolas Trigault (1615)

passages.headline: Was China's Tartar conqueror Tamerlane?
passages.gloss: Ricci writes that China had never been wholly conquered by foreigners until a Tartar leader invaded; his line ruled until 1368, when the Chinese threw off the yoke and the Ming founder Hongwu expelled the Tartars. Some Jesuits guessed this conqueror was Tamerlane, because the Chinese called him 'Tiemor'. Ricci gives up and simply calls him 'the Tartar'. The Chinese name was almost certainly Tiemuzhen, that is Temüjin (Chinggis Khan), not Timur, who lived a century later and never reached China.
passages.quote: nunquam tamen prius ab externis populis legitur universim esse subactum, quam anno nostrae salutis … e Tartaria Dux nescio quis, regnorum domitor, in hoc regnum sese cum exercitu victore immisisset. Eum Ducem nonnulli e nostris, nec levibus, meo iudicio, coniecturis Tamerlanem, vel e successoribus eius aliquem fuisse arbitrantur. Eum enim Sinae Tiemor appellant … Quisquis is fuerit, Tartarum appellabo.
passages.translation: yet we do not read that it was ever wholly conquered by foreign peoples until, in the year of our salvation …, some leader from Tartary, a conqueror of kingdoms, invaded this kingdom with his victorious army. Some of our men, on conjectures that in my judgement are not slight, think this leader was Tamerlane or one of his successors, for the Chinese call him Tiemor … Whoever he was, I shall call him the Tartar.
passages.speaker: Matteo Ricci, edited and translated into Latin by Nicolas Trigault (1615)
passages.caution: The year is illegible in both scans and is omitted. The Tamerlane identification is wrong.

passages.headline: Peking: the Tartar kings' city becomes the Northern Court
passages.people: The Tartar (Yuan) kings and the Ming emperor Yongle
passages.gloss: Ricci explains why China had two capitals. The Ming founder ruled from Nanjing, but his son Yongle, who had guarded the northern frontier against the recently expelled Tartars, seized the throne and moved his seat north, fearing the Tartars would break out again to win back the empire. He chose the very city where the Tartar kings had lived and renamed it Peking, 'Northern Court'. The Mongol capital (Dadu, Khanbaliq) thus became Ming Beijing.
passages.quote: Et quoniam in aquilonaribus provinciis plus habebat virium ac fidei, & Tartaros inde ad recuperandam regni tyrannidem credibile erat erupturos, iis in partibus considere statuit; & quidem ea in Urbe, in qua Reges Tartari, cum Sinis imperitabant, morabantur. Eam Urbem ipse Pequim, id est, Borealem Curiam, ad similitudinem australis, quae dicitur Nanquim nominavit.
passages.translation: And since he had more strength and loyalty in the northern provinces, and it was likely that the Tartars would break out from there to recover their tyranny over the kingdom, he decided to settle in those parts, and indeed in the very city where the Tartar kings lived when they ruled the Chinese. He named that city Pequim, that is, Northern Court, on the model of the southern one called Nanquim.
passages.speaker: Matteo Ricci, edited and translated into Latin by Nicolas Trigault (1615)

passages.headline: Chinese Muslims as 'remnants of the Tartars'
passages.people: Chinese Muslims, described as descendants of the Tartars
passages.gloss: Telling of a clash near Macao, the account notes that one of the Chinese magistrates was a 'Saracen' (Muslim) by origin and religion. Ricci explains that many remnants of the Tartars stayed on in China after the Mongols fell; after four generations they count as natives and may even sit the examinations and hold office. It shows Europeans linking China's Muslim communities with the Mongol period.
passages.quote: Ex iis Magistratibus erat unus origine ac professione Saracenus: nam ex Tartarorum reliquiis multi in eo regno remanserunt, qui post quartam generationem pro indigenis habiti, ne a litterariis quidem gradibus publicisque muneribus prohibentur.
passages.translation: Among these magistrates was one who was a Saracen by origin and religion: for many of the remnants of the Tartars remained in that kingdom, who after the fourth generation are held to be natives and are not barred even from the literary degrees and public offices.
passages.speaker: Matteo Ricci, edited and translated into Latin by Nicolas Trigault (1615)
passages.caution: Ricci's own explanation; many Chinese Muslims descend from Central Asian and Persian Muslims settled under the Mongols rather than from Mongols themselves.

passages.headline: Chinese warhorses that bolt at a Tartar neigh
passages.people: Tartars (Mongol horsemen), compared with the Chinese
passages.gloss: Describing Chinese livestock, Ricci says the Chinese do not know how to break horses and simply geld them to make them docile. Their cavalry horses are countless but so feeble that they flee at the mere neigh of a Tartar horse, which makes them nearly useless in war. It is a Jesuit's jab at Ming cavalry and a measure of the fear the steppe horsemen still inspired.
passages.quote: Eos Sinae domare minime norunt, castrati omnes mansuescunt, quotquot ad usus quotidianos adhibentur. Equi porro militares sunt propemodum innumerabiles, sed ii ita degeneres atque imbelles, ut ne hinnitu quidem equi Tartari sine fuga ferant
passages.translation: The Chinese hardly know how to break them; all those used for everyday work are tamed by gelding. War horses are almost countless, but so degenerate and unwarlike that they cannot bear even the neigh of a Tartar horse without running away
passages.speaker: Matteo Ricci, edited and translated into Latin by Nicolas Trigault (1615)
passages.caution: A sweeping judgement meant to impress European readers.

passages.headline: Bronze star instruments from the Tartar era
passages.gloss: On a hill at Nanjing, Ricci inspected huge bronze astronomical instruments: armillary spheres, a globe, a gnomon on a great marble base. He later saw identical ones at Peking and concluded they came from the same caster, made when the Tartars ruled China. Because they were so well made, he guessed a foreigner trained in European sciences had built them. They were set for the wrong latitude at Nanjing, which he took as a sign they had been moved.
passages.quote: Spectavit etiam P. Matthaeus post annos aliquot similes Pechini machinas, aut easdem potius, ita nihil aliae ab aliis discrepabant, nihil ut dubium videatur, ab eodem fusas artifice: & quidem eo tempore fusas constat, quo Tartari Sinis imperitabant. unde non temere coniectare possumus, eas ab aliquo externo perito disciplinarum nostrarum fuisse conflatas.
passages.translation: Some years later Father Matteo saw similar instruments at Peking, or rather the same, so little did they differ from one another, so that there seems no doubt they were cast by the same craftsman; and it is certain they were cast at the time when the Tartars ruled the Chinese. From this we may reasonably guess that they were made by some foreigner skilled in our sciences.
passages.speaker: Matteo Ricci, edited and translated into Latin by Nicolas Trigault (1615)
passages.caution: Ricci's guess about a foreign maker is doubtful: historians usually credit the designs to the Yuan astronomer Guo Shoujing, and the Peking set he saw was a Ming copy of the Yuan originals.

passages.headline: Fake embassies from 'Tartar princelings'
passages.people: Western merchants posing as envoys; minor Tartar rulers
passages.gloss: At Suzhou, the account explains, caravans from the west entered China as 'embassies' bringing tribute of jade and other goods every six years, with forged letters from their kings offering submission. The emperor paid their costs, so the posts were bought and sold. China received similar embassies from Cochinchina, Siam, the Ryukyus, Korea and some Tartar princelings, at huge cost to the treasury; Ricci thinks the officials knew it was a sham and kept it up to flatter the emperor.
passages.quote: cum tempus legationis advenit publicas Regum suorum litteras effingunt, quibus Sinarum Regi clientelare obsequium deferunt. Similes legationes e variis regnis admittunt Sinae e regnis Caucincino, Sian, Leuchieu, Coriano, & ab aliquot Tartarorum Regulis non sine incredibili aerarii publici sumptu, quibus artibus ipsi Sinae (qui fraudem minime ignorant) Regem suum ludunt
passages.translation: when the time for the embassy comes, they forge official letters from their kings offering the King of China the homage of a vassal. The Chinese admit similar embassies from various kingdoms, from Cochinchina, Siam, the Ryukyus and Korea, and from some Tartar princelings, at an incredible cost to the public treasury; by these tricks the Chinese themselves (who are well aware of the fraud) deceive their own King
passages.speaker: Nicolas Trigault, from Matteo Ricci's commentaries (1615)
passages.caution: A hostile outsider's reading of the tribute system.

passages.headline: A 'Tartar custom': sharing out a dead man's goods
passages.gloss: After Goes died at Suzhou, the Muslim merchants of the caravan seized his goods, destroyed his diary (which recorded their debts) and bound his companion Isaac, threatening to kill him unless he invoked Muhammad. The account explains that among these merchants a 'Tartarea' custom had taken hold: the goods of anyone who died on the road were divided among all. Three centuries earlier Pegolotti (W116) warned that the lord of the land seized a dead merchant's goods on the Tartar road.
passages.quote: Tartarea plane consuetudine inter Negotiatores illos invaluit, ut morientium in itinere Negotiatorum bona inter omnes dividantur, hac ex causa Benedicti Socium Isaac vinxerunt, mortem minati, nisi Mahometem inclamasset.
passages.translation: Among those merchants a thoroughly Tartar custom has taken hold, that the goods of merchants who die on the road are divided among them all; for this reason they bound Benedict's companion Isaac and threatened him with death unless he called on Muhammad.
passages.speaker: Nicolas Trigault, from Matteo Ricci's commentaries (1615)
passages.caution: 'Tartarea' can mean 'Tartar' or 'hellish' in Latin, and here probably carries both. The story comes from the Jesuit side of a dispute.

passages.headline: 'A Tartarean law' and the image of 'some Tartar'
passages.people: Chinese scholars accusing the Jesuits; 'Tartar' as an insult
passages.gloss: At Nanchang, local graduates petitioned to have the Jesuits expelled. In Trigault's Latin their complaint says the foreigners had moved from cramped lodgings to grand houses, preached a 'tartarea' law, and handed out pictures of 'some Tartar or Saracen' they called God come down from heaven. The word play is Latin: tartareus means hellish, from Tartarus, while 'tartarus' here also means a barbarian foreigner. It is Trigault's rendering, not the petition's own Chinese wording.
passages.quote: Eos ipsos primum in angustis sedibus habitasse, nunc vero alias capaces atque magnificas coemisse, legem ab iisdem tartaream praedicari, rude vulgus in fraudem induci … eos certas imagines distribuere, nescio cuius tartari aut Saraceni, quem dicebant esse Deum, qui ad mortales instruendos liberandosque e caelo venerat
passages.translation: that these same men at first lived in cramped lodgings, but have now bought others, roomy and magnificent; that they preach a Tartarean law and lead the ignorant crowd into deception … that they hand out certain images of some Tartar or Saracen, whom they said was God, who had come down from heaven to teach and set free mankind
passages.speaker: Chinese petitioners at Nanchang, as rendered in Latin by Nicolas Trigault (1615)
passages.caution: A hostile petition summarised in Latin by the Jesuits' own historian.

passages.headline: Nogay herdsmen, 'inhabitants of waggons'
passages.gloss: Crossing the sandy steppe on the way to the Crimea, Alexander passed herds of horses guarded by Nogay Tartars and their dogs. He likens them to the wagon-dwellers Herodotus described among the Scythians, notes their two- and four-wheeled carts drawn by horses, oxen or camels, and describes their sheepskin caps, grey coats and sandals of leather or linden bark.
passages.quote: passed several taboons of horses guarded by wild-looking Nogay Tartars and their dogs: these are the Hamaxobitii, or inhabitants of waggons, of Herodotus : their arbas are two or four-wheeled, and drawn by horses, oxen, or camels. The dress of these nomade tribes harmonises well with the Scythian deserts which they frequent ; a rough sheep-skin cap, a grayish surcoat reaching below the knees
passages.speaker: James Edward Alexander (1830)
passages.caution: The Herodotus comparison is Alexander's classical flourish, not evidence that the Nogays descend from Scythians.

passages.headline: The Nogays: a fragment of the Golden Horde
passages.gloss: Alexander describes the Nogays' faces and then explains who they are: a part of the Golden Horde scattered by Timur (Tamerlane), whose wars shattered the Horde in the 1390s. It is a short, fairly accurate piece of steppe history attached to a first-hand description.
passages.quote: Their noses are short, eyes elongated, and beards scanty : such are the Nogays, a party of the Golden Horde dispersed by Timoorlung (Tamarlane).
passages.speaker: James Edward Alexander (1830)
passages.caution: The physical description reflects the racial typing common in travel books of his day.

passages.headline: Akmetshet: stone houses and three mosques
passages.people: Crimean Tatars and the Russian administration
passages.gloss: Simferopol, the Russian capital of the Crimea, still went by its Tatar name Akmetshet ('white mosque'). Alexander lists three Tatar mosques alongside the new cathedral and government buildings, and notes that the houses were of stone with tiled roofs, while in the Tatar quarter houses stood behind courtyards and high walls. His guide was the governor's Tatar interpreter.
passages.quote: The public buildings of Akmetshet, besides three Tartar mosques, are a very handsome cathedral, the halls of justice, residences of the civil officers, &c. The houses are built of stone, and roofed in the ancient Greek style with tiles: in the Tartar quarter courts surround the houses and high walls
passages.speaker: James Edward Alexander (1830)

passages.headline: Koumis, chess and music in a Tartar coffee-house
passages.gloss: Drawn in by music, Alexander entered a Tatar coffee-house in Akmetshet. Greeks and Tatars sat cross-legged on carpets, smoking long pipes and drinking coffee; an old man urged a youth to drink koumis, which Alexander calls a spirit distilled from mare's milk; two men played chess; and three musicians played a stringed instrument and a drum and sang.
passages.quote: on entering it, I found it divided into compartments by railings, and Greeks and Tartars were sitting cross-legged on carpets, and smoking cherry-stick chebouks and drinking coffee. A gray-beard, in a corner, was encouraging a youth to drink koumis or spirits, distilled from mare's milk. A grave-looking pair were engaged at chess ; and in the window-seat were three musicians
passages.speaker: James Edward Alexander (1830)
passages.caution: Koumis is fermented mare's milk; the distilled spirit made from it is a different drink, and Alexander may be running the two together.

passages.headline: Bakhchysarai, the Tartar capital in its valley
passages.gloss: Riding south past Tatar cottages with minaret-shaped chimneys and the domed tombs of the khans, Alexander looked down on Bakhchysarai, the old capital of the Crimean khans. He describes flat-roofed, tiled houses filling a narrow valley and climbing its sides, with the palace in the middle. On the next page he walks streets lined with workshops where Tatar tailors, smiths, shoemakers and saddlers sat cross-legged, smoking as they worked.
passages.quote: we saw beneath us the singular and romantic Tartar capital of the Crimea. Buckteserai, the Palatium of Strabo, is seated in a narrow valley, through which runs the stream of the Tchuruksu. The flat-roofed and tile-covered houses are built in the bottom of the valley, and up the sides of the hills : in the midst of them is a most interesting object, viz. the Tartar Palace.
passages.speaker: James Edward Alexander (1830)
passages.caution: Identifying the town with Strabo's 'Palatium' is a scholarly guess of his time.

passages.headline: The khans' palace: painted walls and a fountain
passages.gloss: Alexander found the palace of the former khans in good repair, though he had been told it was a ruin. He describes gaudily painted walls, minarets and tall pointed chimneys, an oblong courtyard with a marble fountain said to honour a khan's Christian wife, and a mosque by the gate. Inside were painted ceilings, stained-glass windows and brocade divans; he calls it 'a most interesting specimen of Tartaric magnificence' and notes that no Russians were allowed to live in the town.
passages.quote: It is a most grotesque pile : the walls are gaudily painted, and above the roofs rise minarets and numerous tall sharp-pointed chimnies. The buildings of the palace inclose an oblong court, in which is a marble fountain, erected to the memory of the Christian wife of a khan ; on the left of the gateway is a mosque
passages.speaker: James Edward Alexander (1830)
passages.caution: He does not say who built it. The Christian-wife story is the local legend behind the 'Fountain of Tears'.

passages.headline: Black sarcophagi with white turbans
passages.gloss: Two domed mausoleums beside the palace held the remains of a long line of khans. Inside, Alexander was startled to find black sarcophagi on the floor with white turbans at their heads; outside, the graves had carved marble headstones topped with turbans, shaded by cypresses.
passages.quote: a burial ground attached, contained the remains of a long line of khans : on entering the former it was rather startling to see black sarcophagi on the floor, with white turbans at the head. In the open air the tombs were adorned with carved and turbaned headstones of marble, which, with the accompanying cypress, give such effect to Moslem cemeteries.
passages.speaker: James Edward Alexander (1830)

passages.headline: Mangup: a ruined mountain city of many peoples
passages.people: Crimean Tatars and earlier occupants of the site
passages.gloss: With a Tatar guide Alexander climbed to Mangup Kale, a deserted fortress-city on a table mountain. He credits its battlemented walls to the Genoese and reads the ruins as layers of occupation: a Tatar mosque, a synagogue, a small church, and Muslim, Jewish and Christian graves. The only living things were a few grazing Tatar horses.
passages.quote: passed through some noble remains of battlemented walls of Genoese architecture, flanked with square and round towers. Before us were the remains of a Tartar mosque, a Jewish synagogue, a small church, and the tombs of Moslems, Israelites, and Christians, pointing out the successive occupiers of this strange city, the ruins of whose habitations were very numerous
passages.speaker: James Edward Alexander (1830)
passages.caution: 'Genoese' is his guess: Mangup was the capital of the Orthodox principality of Theodoro until the Ottomans took it in 1475.

passages.headline: Village houses built into the hillside
passages.people: Crimean Tatars of the south coast
passages.gloss: On the south coast, below the Baidar pass, Alexander found houses unlike any he had seen: roofs carried on low stone walls on three sides, with the fourth side set against the slope like Swiss chalets, among fruit trees and poplars. The villagers wore the same Tatar dress as before, but he thought their features Grecian and both men and women very handsome.
passages.quote: The houses, as well as their inhabitants, were now totally different from what we had hitherto seen : the roofs were supported on three sides by low stone walls, and the fourth rested against the side of the declivity (after the manner of Swiss chalets) … but their features were Grecian, and both men and women were extremely handsome.
passages.speaker: James Edward Alexander (1830)

passages.headline: An old Tartar woman's welcome
passages.people: Crimean Tatars of the south coast
passages.gloss: At the village of Koochook Koi (Kuchuk-Koy) an old Tatar woman invited Alexander in for bread and bekmes, a thick pear syrup. He records her dress closely: a white headcloth over hair in six long plaits, a coloured petticoat under a blue knee-length coat held by a patterned belt, and silk trousers gathered at the ankle. A little girl nearby wore a red fez with silver coins sewn on the front.
passages.quote: a clean old Tartar woman invited me to eat some bread and bekmis with her : her head was enveloped in a white handkerchief … her hair, in six long plaits ; her coloured petticoat was covered with a blue surcoat reaching below the knees, and confined round her waist with a figured belt ; her trousers were of silk, drawn in at the ancles
passages.speaker: James Edward Alexander (1830)

passages.headline: 'Tartaric battlements' where no Tartars came
passages.gloss: At Novgorod, Alexander saw citadel walls topped with what he calls 'Tartaric battlements', copied from the Kremlin's, and notes that the Tartars never reached Novgorod, so its church crosses have no crescent beneath them. He repeats the popular idea that a crescent under a cross marks the Tatar period, and calls Moscow's Kremlin battlements 'Tartaric' as well. He also uses the label for a tower in the Genoese fortress at Balaklava.
passages.quote: The walls of the citadel were surmounted by Tartaric battlements, in imitation of those of the Kremlin; yet the Tartars in their invasions never penetrated to Novogorod, and the crosses on the churches do not, therefore, surmount a crescent
passages.speaker: James Edward Alexander (1830)
passages.caution: 'Tartaric' is his style label: the Moscow Kremlin's brick walls and swallow-tail merlons were built by Italian masters in the 1480s and 1490s. The crescent-under-the-cross explanation is a popular belief that most historians reject.

passages.headline: Caffa: Tartar songs among the ruins
passages.people: Crimean Tatars; the former Genoese colony
passages.gloss: Arriving at night at Theodosia, the old Caffa, Alexander found ruin on every side. He heard Tatars singing under an arch in a melancholy strain, as if mourning the decay of the once-flourishing city, and noted the crumbling citadel walls by the shore. The town's houses, he says, were built partly in the Tatar and partly in the Genoese style. From there he crossed the steppe by 'the commercial Tartar city of Karasubazar'.
passages.quote: we heard some Tartars under an arch singing in a most melancholy strain, and seemingly mourning over the decay of this once flourishing city: the dilapidated walls of a citadel were on the sea-shore, and near them was the stranded wreck of a Greek mystico. The houses of Caffa were built partly in the Tartar and partly in the Genoese style of architecture.
passages.speaker: James Edward Alexander (1830)
passages.caution: 'Seemingly mourning' is his romantic reading of a song he could not follow.

passages.headline: A khan's descendant from Edinburgh University
passages.people: Sultan Katty Gherry, of the Crimean khans' family (Giray)
passages.gloss: In Simferopol an English gig drove into a courtyard and out stepped an old fellow-student of Alexander's from Edinburgh University: Sultan Katty Gherry Crim Gherry, of a branch of the Tatar khans of the Crimea, born in the Caucasus. On the next page Alexander adds that a missionary brought him to Britain, that he married a Miss Nelson of Edinburgh, and that he now had an imperial pension and estates on the south coast.
passages.quote: One day I was surprised to see an English gig drive into their court, with a mounted servant behind. A dark good-looking gentleman then alighted, and I recognised an old fellow-student at the University of Edinburgh, the Sultan Katty Gherry Crim Gherry. He was born in the Caucasus, of a branch of the Tartar Khans of the Crimea, was brought to Britain
passages.speaker: James Edward Alexander (1830)

passages.headline: A carter's boast exposes a Tartar plot
passages.gloss: Alexander heard from a civilian that in 1828 the Crimean Tatars were ready to revolt, stirred up, he guessed, by the Turks. A Karaite Jewish merchant of Bakhchysarai grew suspicious when his Tatar carter refused well-paid work, followed him home and overheard him telling his mother to wait until the Russians lost at Anapa. The man was arrested and confessed to a plot, spies were set to work and the leaders punished.
passages.quote: Russians are defeated before Anapa, and you'll see that we will be masters of the Crimea again. I have cast an eye at the Karaémee's house and garden; his tribe, as well as the Muscovites, will ere long not possess a foot of the country." On this the Tartar was taken up, and he confessed that there was a plot on foot to rise against the Russians
passages.speaker: Words attributed to a Crimean Tatar carter, in a story Alexander heard from a civilian (1830)
passages.caution: Secondhand anecdote from the Russian side; the 'confession' may have been forced. On the previous page Alexander says he himself saw no cause for Tatar complaint.

passages.headline: Bones of those who hid from a Tartar invader
passages.gloss: In the cave monastery at Kiev, after oil-weeping skulls and a supposed relic of the Holy Innocents, the monks showed Alexander walled-up cells, fitted with glass panes, holding the bones of a thousand priests and townspeople. They were said to have hidden from a Tartar invader and been suffocated in their refuge.
passages.quote: In cells which were built up, with a thick piece of glass in the wall, were the bones of one thousand of the unfortunate priests and people of Kiev, who thought to conceal themselves from a Tartar invader, but who were inhumanly suffocated in their sanctuary.
passages.speaker: James Edward Alexander (1830)
passages.caution: He saw the bones; the story of how they died is the monks' tradition, told alongside other relics he plainly doubted.

passages.headline: 'Those Tatars smell bad': how Chinese turned Mongols into Tatars
passages.people: Mongols, called Dada (Tatars) by the Ming translators; Naiman
passages.gloss: The Naiman ruler Tayang plans to attack the upstart people to his east, and his mother Gurbesu sneers that they stink and wear dirty dark clothes, so only their good-looking women are worth fetching to milk the Naiman herds. In the Mongolian original these people are the Mongols; the Ming Chinese summary calls them Dada, the Chinese word for Tatars, while it keeps a different spelling for the actual Tatar tribe. The same summary has To'oril ask 'how can you Dada be without an emperor?' of Chinggis's people.
passages.quote: 塔陽說這東邊有些逹逹…如今咱去将那逹逹取了其母古児别速說那逹逹百姓歹氣息衣服黒暗取将来要做甚麽教逺有者
passages.translation: Tayang said: 'Over here in the east there are some Dada (Tatars)... Let us go now and take those Dada.' His mother Gurbesu said: 'Those Dada people have a bad smell and their clothes are dark and grimy. What would we do bringing them here? Let them stay far away.'
passages.speaker: Ming Chinese summary translation of the Secret History (Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
passages.caution: The Mongolian text (de Rachewiltz p.105) says 'the Mongol people have always smelt bad'; 'Dada' is the Ming translators' word, not the Mongol author's.

passages.headline: Measured against the linchpin of a cart
passages.gloss: After defeating the Tatar tribes at Dalan Nemurges, Chinggis and his kinsmen met in a single tent and decided the fate of the prisoners. Every Tatar male taller than the linchpin of a cart was to be killed and the rest enslaved and shared out, as revenge for Tatar killings of Chinggis's forefathers (including, in the chronicle's story, the poisoning of his father Yesugei). The chronicle goes on to say the plan leaked, the Tatars barricaded themselves in and fought with knives hidden in their sleeves.
passages.quote: From olden days the Tatar people Have destroyed our fathers and forefathers; To avenge our fathers and forefathers, And requite the wrong, for them We shall measure the Tatars against the linchpin of a cart, And kill them to the last one, We shall utterly slay them. The rest we shall enslave: Some here, some there, dividing them among ourselves!
passages.speaker: Anonymous author of the Secret History (translated by Igor de Rachewiltz, 2015)
passages.caution: The editor's footnote explains that only those taller than the linchpin were to be killed; the scene is told from the victors' side.

passages.headline: Felt-walled tents and wooden doors
passages.people: Mongols and the peoples under them
passages.gloss: When Chinggis made his adopted brother Sigi Qutuqu chief judge, he told him to divide the whole population into those living in felt-walled tents and those living in dwellings with wooden doors, that is nomads and settled folk. Sigi Qutuqu then asked as his reward for people from the towns with walls of pounded earth. The Mongols thus sorted their world by house type, and counted walled-town people as a separate prize.
passages.quote: Splitting up those that live in felt-walled tents, Separating those that live in dwellings with wooden doors. … let him decide in favour of granting me the people from the towns that have walls of pounded earth.
passages.speaker: Anonymous author of the Secret History, words given to Chinggis Qa'an and Sigi Qutuqu (translated by Igor de Rachewiltz, 2015)
passages.caution: The editor's footnote glosses the pairing as 'nomadic or settled populations'.

passages.headline: The Tanguts cannot carry off their walled towns
passages.gloss: When Chinggis fell from his horse on his last campaign against the Tangut kingdom, a commander advised going home to recover, arguing that the Tanguts, unlike steppe people, were tied to their pounded-earth towns and fixed camps and would still be there later. Chinggis refused to withdraw. The passage shows how the Mongols saw walled towns: as something that cannot run away.
passages.quote: The Tang’ut people Are ones who have towns with pounded-earth walls, Are ones who live in permanent camps. They won’t leave, carrying off their towns with pounded-earth walls; They won’t leave, abandoning their permanent camps. Let us withdraw.
passages.speaker: Anonymous author of the Secret History, words given to Tolun Cerbi (translated by Igor de Rachewiltz, 2015)

passages.headline: Karakorum: 'capital for five reigns'
passages.gloss: The geography treatise explains that the Lingbei capital took its name, Helin (Karakorum), from the Qara Qorum river to its west. Chinggis made it his capital in 1220 and it remained the capital of five reigns. A small-character note adds that Ogedei walled the city and built the Wan'an palace in 1235, and goes on to list more halls outside the city built in 1237 and 1238. Khubilai moved the capital to Dadu (Beijing) in 1260.
passages.quote: 始名和琳以西有哈喇和琳河因以名城太祖十五年平定河北諸郡建都於此初立元昌路改轉運和琳使司前後五朝都焉(太宗乙未年城和琳作萬安宫…)
passages.translation: [Hening circuit] was first called Helin; because west of it is the Halahelin (Qara Qorum) river, the city was named after it. In the fifteenth year of Taizu (Chinggis), having pacified the prefectures north of the Yellow River, he established his capital here. At first Yuanchang circuit was set up, later changed to the Helin Transport Commission. It was the capital for five successive reigns. (In the yiwei year of Taizong [Ogedei, 1235] Helin was walled and the Wan'an palace built.)
passages.speaker: Song Lian and the Ming history office, History of the Yuan (Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)
passages.caution: The Siku copy writes 和琳 for the usual 和林. The words 'Taizu established his capital here' in 1220 are the history's claim; the annals date the building of the walls and palace to 1235.

passages.headline: Temujin named after a captured Tatar chief
passages.gloss: The annals of Chinggis Khan say that his father Yesugei had just captured the Tatar chief Temujin when his wife gave birth to a son clutching a clot of blood like a red stone. Yesugei named the boy after the captive to mark his victory. Here Tatar is the name of one rival tribe, not of the Mongols.
passages.quote: 初烈祖征塔塔爾部獲其部長特穆津宣懿太后諤楞適生帝手握凝血如赤石烈祖異之因以所獲特穆津名之志武功也
passages.translation: At first Liezu (Yesugei) campaigned against the Tatar tribe and captured its chief Temujin. Just then the empress Xuanyi, Ogelen (Hoelun), gave birth to the emperor, who held in his hand clotted blood like a red stone. Liezu thought it a marvel and named him after the captured Temujin, to record his military success.
passages.speaker: Song Lian and the Ming history office, History of the Yuan (Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)
passages.caution: The same story is told in the Secret History; the Siku copy re-spells Temujin as 特穆津 and the Tatars as 塔塔爾.

passages.headline: Birch-bark tents and reindeer in the Siberian forests
passages.people: Kyrgyz and forest peoples of Qianzhou (Kem River)
passages.gloss: The note on the Kyrgyz lands of the upper Yenisei describes a forest people whose poor lived in tents of birch bark, loaded their goods on white deer (reindeer), drank deer milk, gathered pine nuts and roots, and hunted in winter on 'wooden horses' (skis). Nearby Qianzhou had a few thousand households of Mongols and Uighurs, and workshops of Chinese craftsmen moved there early in the dynasty.
passages.quote: 貧民無恒産者皆以樺皮作廬帳以白鹿負其行裝取鹿乳採松實及斸山丹芍藥等根為食冬月亦乗木馬出獵…居民數千家悉蒙古囘紇人有工匠數局葢國初所徙漢人也
passages.translation: The poor, who have no fixed property, all make their tents of birch bark and load their baggage on white deer. They take deer's milk, gather pine nuts and dig up the roots of mountain lilies and peonies for food. In winter they also ride 'wooden horses' (skis) to hunt... [In Qianzhou] the inhabitants, several thousand households, are all Mongols and Huihe (Uighurs); there are several workshops of craftsmen, who are Han Chinese moved there at the start of the dynasty.
passages.speaker: Song Lian and the Ming history office, History of the Yuan (Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)
passages.caution: Based on reports of the Yuan official Liu Haoli, sent there in 1270; the Siku copy re-spells the place names.

passages.headline: A Yuan official teaches pottery, metalwork and boats
passages.gloss: The same note says that before the Yuan official Liu Haoli arrived, the local peoples made cups from willow wood and hollowed out logs as troughs to cross rivers, and did not know how to cast farm tools. Liu reported this to the court, which sent craftsmen to teach pottery, metal-casting and boat-building. It is a Chinese state view of 'civilising' the Siberian frontier.
passages.quote: 先是數部民俗皆以杞栁為杯皿刳木為槽以濟水不解鑄作農器好禮聞諸朝乃遣工匠教為陶冶舟楫土人便之
passages.translation: Before this, the custom of these several tribes was to make their cups and dishes of willow and to hollow out logs as troughs for crossing water; they did not know how to cast farm tools. Haoli reported this to the court, which then sent craftsmen to teach them pottery, metal-casting and boats, and the local people found it convenient.
passages.speaker: Song Lian and the Ming history office, History of the Yuan (Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)
passages.caution: Told from the point of view of the imperial administration.

passages.headline: 'The Dada are the Mongols'
passages.gloss: The chapter on the Tatars opens with a flat definition: the Dada are the Mongols, the descendants of the former Yuan dynasty. It then tells how the last Yuan emperor fled Beijing beyond the passes in 1368. For Ming and Qing officials, 'Tatar' was simply the name for the Mongols of the steppe.
passages.quote: 韃靼即䝉古故元後也太祖洪武元年大將軍徐逹率師取元元主自北平遁出塞居開平
passages.translation: The Dada (Tatars) are the Mongols, the descendants of the former Yuan. In the first year of Hongwu (1368), under Taizu, the grand general Xu Da led an army to take the Yuan; the Yuan ruler fled from Beiping (Beijing) out beyond the frontier and stayed at Kaiping (Shangdu).
passages.speaker: Zhang Tingyu and the Qing history office, History of the Ming (Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)

passages.headline: Chinese renegades build a walled town and palaces: 'bansheng' means 'house'
passages.people: Tumed Mongols under Altan Khan; Chinese deserters
passages.gloss: The history says that Chinese outlaws led by Qiu Fu and Zhao Quan, who had gone over to the Mongols, gathered fugitives at Fengzhou, built a walled town to protect themselves, put up palaces and broke irrigated fields. Their settlements were called bansheng, which the history explains as the Mongol word for 'house'. Zhao Quan also taught the Mongols siege warfare.
passages.quote: 時富等在敵招集亡命居豐州築城自衛搆宮殿墾水田號曰拜甡拜甡華言屋也趙全教敵益習功戰事
passages.translation: At that time Qiu Fu and the others, living among the enemy, gathered fugitives and settled at Fengzhou. They built a walled town to defend themselves, put up palaces and opened irrigated rice fields, calling them baisheng; baisheng in Chinese means 'house'. Zhao Quan taught the enemy to become more practised in attack and warfare.
passages.speaker: Zhang Tingyu and the Qing history office, History of the Ming (Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)
passages.caution: The Siku copy writes 拜甡 for the usual 板升 (bansheng, from Mongolian baishing 'building'). 功 is a copyist's slip for 攻 ('attack').

passages.headline: A palace for Altan Khan, and a beam that fell
passages.people: Tumed Mongols under Altan Khan; Chinese deserters
passages.gloss: After Qiu Fu's death Zhao Quan became more powerful among the Mongols. He honoured Altan Khan as an emperor and built him a palace, but on the day the ridge-beam was raised a great wind blew it down, injuring several men, and Altan was too frightened to live there. The Mongol ruler's palace was a Chinese project, built by Chinese hands.
passages.quote: 時邱富死趙全在敵中益用事尊諳達為帝治宫殿期日上棟忽大風棟墜傷數人諳達懼不敢復居
passages.translation: At that time Qiu Fu had died, and Zhao Quan, among the enemy, grew ever more powerful. He honoured Anda (Altan Khan) as emperor and built palaces for him. On the day set for raising the ridge-beam a great wind suddenly blew, the beam fell and injured several men, and Anda was afraid and did not dare to live there.
passages.speaker: Zhang Tingyu and the Qing history office, History of the Ming (Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)
passages.caution: Told as an omen story by a hostile Chinese source; the Siku copy writes 諳達 for 俺答 (Altan).

passages.headline: Horse fairs on the Great Wall
passages.gloss: After Altan Khan made peace in 1571, the Ming set rules for border markets: the Mongols would bring gold, silver, cattle, horses, hides and horsetail, and Chinese merchants satin, silk, cloth and iron cooking pots. Each market ran for a month, with three hundred Mongols camped outside the wall and five hundred Chinese troops guarding the marketplace. Iron pots were a key trade good because the Mongols could not easily make them.
passages.quote: 一立互市其規如𢎞治初北部三貢例蕃以金銀牛馬皮張馬尾等物啇販以縀紬布匹釡鍋等物開市日来者以三百人駐邉外我兵五百駐市場期盡一月
passages.translation: One: establish border markets, on the model of the northern tribes' three tributes at the start of Hongzhi. The fan (Mongols) bring gold, silver, cattle, horses, hides, horse tails and such; the merchants bring satin, silk, cloth and iron pots and cauldrons. On market days three hundred of those who come are to camp outside the wall, and five hundred of our soldiers are to be stationed at the marketplace; the market lasts a full month.
passages.speaker: Zhang Tingyu and the Qing history office, History of the Ming (Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)
passages.caution: A summary of the governor Wang Chonggu's proposals as quoted in the history.

passages.headline: Beyond the pass: felt tents and felt carts
passages.gloss: Travelling north from Beijing, Zhang Dehui crossed the pass beyond Xuande and found that from here on every post station belonged to a Mongol clan and was named after its holder. Climbing the ridge he saw for the first time the felt tents and felt carts of herders who moved with water and grass. For him this line marked the end of the Chinese world.
passages.quote: 自是以北諸驛皆蒙古部族所分主也毎驛各以主者之名名之由嶺而上則東北行始見毳幕氊車逐水草畜牧而巳非復中原之風土也
passages.translation: From here northward, all the post stations are held as shares by Mongol clans, and each station is named after its holder. Going up from the ridge, we travelled northeast and for the first time saw felt tents and felt carts; [people] follow water and grass and herd their animals, and that is all. This is no longer the land and custom of the Central Plain.
passages.speaker: Zhang Dehui, Record of a Journey (Qiujian ji juan 100 = Yutang jiahua juan 8; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)

passages.headline: A princess's walled palace by the lake
passages.people: Mongol court; Chinese and other artisans
passages.gloss: Past the sandy desert, at the Yu'er lakes, Zhang found a walled detached palace belonging to a princess, with a sleeping hall, side chambers, galleries and a lookout tower, and a small settlement of commoners and craftsmen beside it. It is an early glimpse of Mongol-era buildings on the steppe, and of the artisans who lived around them.
passages.quote: 泊之東涯有公主離宫之外垣高丈餘方廣二里許中建寝殿夾以二室背以龜軒旁列兩廡前峙眺樓登之頗快目力宫之東有民匠雜居稍成聚落
passages.translation: On the eastern shore of the lake is the outer wall of a princess's detached palace, more than one zhang high and some two li square. Inside stands a sleeping hall flanked by two chambers, with a 'turtle' gallery behind, two side wings along its flanks and a lookout tower rising in front; climbing it gives a fine view. East of the palace, commoners and artisans live together, forming something of a settlement.
passages.speaker: Zhang Dehui, Record of a Journey (Qiujian ji juan 100 = Yutang jiahua juan 8; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
passages.caution: The text does not name the princess or say who built the palace.

passages.headline: Old walls of 'the former dynasty' and earth-roofed huts on the Kerulen
passages.gloss: Zhang passed the ruined base of a long wall stretching out of sight, which he credits to 'the former dynasty', meaning the Jurchen Jin, as their outer rampart. On the Kerulen he found a mixed population of 'barbarians' and Chinese living in a few houses roofed with earth and growing a little hemp and wheat.
passages.quote: 四驛有長城䫋址望之綿延不盡亦前朝所築之外堡也…瀕河之民雜以蕃漢稍有屋室皆以土冐之亦頗有種藝麻麥而巳
passages.translation: After four stages there is the ruined base of a long wall, stretching on endlessly as far as one can see; this too is an outer rampart built by the former dynasty... The people along the river are a mix of fan (steppe peoples) and Han Chinese. There are a few houses, all roofed with earth, and they also do some farming, of hemp and wheat, and that is all.
passages.speaker: Zhang Dehui, Record of a Journey (Qiujian ji juan 100 = Yutang jiahua juan 8; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
passages.caution: 'Former dynasty' (前朝) here means the Jin, whose border walls ran across Inner Mongolia.

passages.headline: The Karakorum valley: Khitan ruins and irrigated fields
passages.people: Mongols; farmers of the Orkhon valley
passages.gloss: Near a large clear lake (Ugii Nuur) Zhang notes the branch road to Helin, the Chinese name for Karakorum, about a hundred li away, and a small old walled town built by the Khitans. The Orkhon plain itself was farmed: people irrigated their fields (and, the text adds, kept some vegetable gardens), though in early autumn the crops were already killed by three frosts.
passages.quote: 自泊之南而西分道入和林城相去約百余里泊之正西有小故城亦契丹所築也…中即和林川也居人多事耕稼悉引水灌之…時孟秋下旬麻麥皆槁問之田者云巳三霜矣
passages.translation: From the south of the lake a branch road leads west into the city of Helin (Karakorum), about a hundred li away. Due west of the lake there is a small old walled town, also built by the Khitans... In the middle is the Helin plain. Most of the inhabitants farm, bringing water to all their fields... It was then late in the first month of autumn and the hemp and wheat had all withered; when I asked the farmers, they said there had already been three frosts.
passages.speaker: Zhang Dehui, Record of a Journey (Qiujian ji juan 100 = Yutang jiahua juan 8; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
passages.caution: Bretschneider (1888) thought Zhang passed near Karakorum without entering it.

passages.headline: Mare's milk for the gods at the great tent
passages.gloss: The prince's summer camp stood on the sunny side of a ridge beyond the Tamir. Twice a year, on the ninth day of the ninth month and of the fourth month, his followers gathered at the great ordo-tent and sprinkled the milk of white mares as a seasonal sacrifice, using plain birchwood vessels rather than gold and silver.
passages.quote: 其陽帳殿在焉乃避夏之所也…至重九日王師麾下㑹于大矛帳灑白馬湩脩時祀也其什噐皆用禾樺不以金銀為飾尚質也
passages.translation: On its sunny side stands the tent-palace; this is the summer retreat... On the Double Ninth the prince's following assembles at the great ordo-tent and sprinkles white mares' milk, performing the seasonal sacrifice. The vessels used are all of birch, not decorated with gold or silver: they value plainness.
passages.speaker: Zhang Dehui, Record of a Journey (Qiujian ji juan 100 = Yutang jiahua juan 8; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
passages.caution: 大矛帳 is a copyist's slip for 大牙帳 ('great tooth-banner tent', the ordo), as the Siku copy reads.

passages.headline: White furs for the New Year
passages.gloss: At each year's end the whole camp moved its tents to a fresh site to celebrate the New Year. There was a great feast in front of the tents at which everyone from the prince down wore pure white furs, and three days later they went to the great tent to offer New Year greetings. White was the lucky colour of the Mongol New Year (the White Month).
passages.quote: 比歳除日輙迁帳易地以為賀正之所日大晏所部於帳前自王以下皆衣純白裘三日後方詣大牙帳致賀礼也
passages.translation: On the last day of the year they always move the tents to a new site, as the place for celebrating the New Year. That day there is a great banquet for all his people in front of the tents, and everyone from the prince down wears pure white furs. Only after three days do they go to the great ordo-tent to offer their New Year greetings.
passages.speaker: Zhang Dehui, Record of a Journey (Qiujian ji juan 100 = Yutang jiahua juan 8; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)

passages.headline: Almaliq: running water, fruit, Uighurs and Chinese settlers
passages.people: Uighurs/Muslims (Huihe) and Chinese under Mongol rule
passages.gloss: Beyond the Iron Pass, guarded by Chinese soldiers, Chang De reached Almaliq, a Mongol-ruled city of the Chagatai realm. Its streets were crossed by running water and its melons, grapes and pomegranates were excellent. Muslim Turks lived mixed with Chinese and had picked up Chinese ways, and a town further south was full of settlers from Shanxi.
passages.quote: 出関至阿里麻里城市井皆流水交貫有諸菓唯瓜蒲萄石榴最佳囬紇與漢民雜居其俗漸染頗似中國又南有赤木児城居民多并汾人
passages.translation: Leaving the pass he reached the city of Alimali (Almaliq). Its streets and markets are all crossed by running water. There are all kinds of fruit; the melons, grapes and pomegranates are the best. The Huihe (Muslim Turks) live mixed with the Han Chinese, and their customs have gradually been coloured until they are rather like China's. Further south is the city of Chimur, whose inhabitants are mostly people from Bing and Fen (Shanxi).
passages.speaker: Liu Yu, Record of an Embassy to the West, from Chang De's report (Qiujian ji juan 94 = Yutang jiahua juan 2; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)

passages.headline: Houses of earth with windows of glass
passages.gloss: At the city of Bolad (here spelled in its Siku form) Chang De noted fields of wheat and rice, stunted cypresses on the rocky hills, and a town where houses, shops and gardens were interspersed. The houses were built of earth, and the windows and doors were of glass (liuli). Bretschneider rendered the same line 'the houses are built of clay, and the windows furnished with glass'.
passages.quote: 又西南行過博囉城所種皆麥稻山多栢不能株絡石而長城居肆囿間錯土屋忩户皆琉璃
passages.translation: Going further southwest he passed the city of Boluo (Bolad). What they sow is all wheat and rice. The hills have many cypresses, which cannot grow into proper trunks but grow twisting among the rocks. In the city, dwellings, shops and gardens are interspersed; the houses are of earth, and the windows and doors are all of glass.
passages.speaker: Liu Yu, Record of an Embassy to the West, from Chang De's report (Yutang jiahua juan 2, Siku quanshu copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)
passages.caution: The Siku editors re-spelled the name as 博囉; the older text has 孛羅. Liuli can mean glass or glazed material.

passages.headline: Ruined walls, 'the old home of the Khitans'
passages.people: Khitans (Qara Khitai), as local people told it
passages.gloss: Crossing a level, well-watered and crowded land between two mountain ranges, Chang De saw many old ramparts and ruined walls. Asking about them, he was told they were the former home of the Khitans, meaning the Qara Khitai empire that ruled here before the Mongols. He reckoned the place nearly 15,000 li from Karakorum.
passages.quote: 二月二十四日過亦堵两山間土平民夥溝洫映帶多故壘壊垣問之盖契丹故居也計其地去和林萬五千里而近
passages.translation: On the 24th of the second month he passed between the two Yidu mountains. The land is level and the people many, with irrigation channels winding everywhere. There are many old ramparts and ruined walls; when he asked about them, [he was told] they were the old home of the Khitans. He reckoned this land to be a little under 15,000 li from Helin (Karakorum).
passages.speaker: Liu Yu, Record of an Embassy to the West, from Chang De's report (Qiujian ji juan 94 = Yutang jiahua juan 2; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
passages.caution: The identification of the ruins comes from local informants.

passages.headline: The Assassins' paradise
passages.gloss: Describing the Ismaili state the Mongols destroyed in 1256, Chang De repeats the story that its soldiers were all assassins, trained by being drugged, shown music and women in a hidden chamber, and told they would enjoy such bliss after death. It is the Chinese version of the 'Old Man of the Mountain' legend that Marco Polo tells, and it is hearsay.
passages.quote: 其國兵皆刺客俗見男子勇壯者以利誘之令手刄父兄然後充兵醉酒扶入窟室娱以音樂羙女縱其慾數日復置故處既醒問其所見教之能爲刺客死則享福如此
passages.translation: The soldiers of that country are all assassins. Their custom is that when they see a brave, strong man, they lure him with gain and make him kill his own father or elder brother with his own hand; then he is enrolled as a soldier. They make him drunk, carry him into a cave chamber and entertain him with music and beautiful women, indulging his desires for several days, then put him back where he was. When he wakes, they ask what he saw and teach him that if he can become an assassin, at death he will enjoy bliss like that.
passages.speaker: Liu Yu, Record of an Embassy to the West, from Chang De's report (Qiujian ji juan 94 = Yutang jiahua juan 2; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
passages.caution: A hostile legend about the Ismailis, told by their conquerors; not an eyewitness account.

passages.headline: The fall of Baghdad
passages.people: Mongols of Hulegu; the Abbasid caliph
passages.gloss: Chang De's report describes Baghdad as two cities, east and west, divided by a great river, the western one without walls and the eastern one fortified with painted brick. The Mongol army broke the caliph's troops in one battle and slaughtered the people of the western city; the eastern city fell after a six-day siege (the page goes on). It is one of the very few Chinese accounts of the sack.
passages.quote: 丁巳歳取報逹國南北二千里其主曰合里法其城有東西城中有大河西城無壁壘東城固之以甓繪其上甚盛王師至城不一交戰破勝兵四十餘萬西城䧟皆尽屠其民
passages.translation: In the dingsi year they took the country of Baoda (Baghdad), two thousand li from north to south. Its ruler was called the Helifa (caliph). The city has an east city and a west city, with a great river between. The west city has no ramparts; the east city is fortified with brick, painted very splendidly on top. When the imperial army reached the city, in a single battle it broke picked troops more than 400,000 strong; the west city fell and all its people were slaughtered.
passages.speaker: Liu Yu, Record of an Embassy to the West, from Chang De's report (Qiujian ji juan 94 = Yutang jiahua juan 2; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
passages.caution: The dingsi year is 1257; Baghdad fell in February 1258. This text reads 城不 where the Siku copy has 城下 ('below the city'); the translation follows the Siku reading. The troop figure is an exaggeration.

passages.headline: The lamb that grows from the ground
passages.people: Hearsay about peoples of the far west
passages.gloss: Among the marvels Chang De heard of is the 'furrow-planted sheep': a sheep's navel sown in the ground and watered sprouts when it hears thunder, grows up still tied to the earth by its navel, and is freed by a scare so it can graze. This is the Chinese form of the 'vegetable lamb of Tartary' (barometz) that European books later placed on the Volga steppe.
passages.quote: 壠種羊岀西海羊臍種土中溉以水聞雷而生臍系地中及長驚以木臍断嚙草至秋可食臍内復有種
passages.translation: The furrow-planted sheep comes from the Western Sea. A sheep's navel is planted in the soil and watered; when it hears thunder it comes to life, its navel still tied into the ground. When it has grown, they startle it with a piece of wood; the navel snaps and it grazes. By autumn it can be eaten, and inside its navel there is seed again.
passages.speaker: Liu Yu, Record of an Embassy to the West, from Chang De's report (Qiujian ji juan 94 = Yutang jiahua juan 2; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
passages.caution: Liu Yu himself closes the list by saying such strange things 'cannot all be recorded'; it is hearsay.

passages.headline: Sledges from post to post, and Kyrgyz dog teams
passages.place: Between Bolad and the Chu valley, Central Asia (Ma'a)
passages.people: Peoples of the Chagatai realm; Kyrgyz (Qirqis)
passages.gloss: West of Bolad, Chang De found that coins were of gold, silver and copper with inscriptions but no square hole, and that in the land he calls Ma'a horses pulled sledges from one post station to the next, carrying heavy loads at speed. He adds, as a report, that the Kyrgyz used dogs in place of horses. Bretschneider doubted there were sledges on this route but noted that Marco Polo also mentions dog sledges in Siberia.
passages.quote: 至麻阿中以馬撁拖床逓鋪負重而行疾或曰乞里乞四易馬以犬
passages.translation: On coming into Ma'a, they use horses to pull sledges from post station to post station, carrying heavy loads and going fast. Some say that the Qiliqisi (Kyrgyz) use dogs in place of horses.
passages.speaker: Liu Yu, Record of an Embassy to the West, from Chang De's report (Qiujian ji juan 94 = Yutang jiahua juan 2; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
passages.caution: The dog-sledge detail is introduced with 'some say'.

passages.headline: 'Water Tatars' in Manchuria
passages.gloss: Bretschneider summarises the Ming imperial geography of 1461 on the Jurchen homeland: after the Mongols overthrew the Jin, the Yuan set up military posts there, and the country was inhabited by Jurchens and 'Water Tatars', who gave their name to an administrative circuit. His footnote compares Carpini's 'Su-Mongal' or Water Mongols, who Carpini said called themselves Tartars after a river.
passages.quote: The country was inhabited by the Nü-chi and the Shui Ta-ta (Water Tatars), and formed the circuits of Ho-lan-fu and Shui Ta-ta.
passages.speaker: E. Bretschneider, Mediaeval Researches vol. 2 (1888, reissued 1910), summarising the Ming Geography of 1461
passages.caution: A 19th-century summary in English of a Ming source, not the Yutang jiahua itself.

passages.headline: 'No houses': the steppe in the official customs entry
passages.people: Mongols of the Outer Mongol domains
passages.when: quoting sources of the 12th to 14th centuries; compiled to 1842
passages.gloss: The customs entry for the Mongol lands is built from quotations: from the History of the Liao, that the northern deserts live by herding and hunting; and from the History of the Jin, that 'by custom they have no houses', living wherever there is water and grass and moving without fixed places. The Qing editors chose to describe their Mongol subjects in words written centuries earlier.
passages.quote: 朔漠以畜牧射獵為業生生之資於是乎出(遼史)俗無室廬隨水草以居遷徙不常(金史)
passages.translation: The northern deserts make herding and hunting their livelihood; all the means of life come from these (History of the Liao). By custom they have no houses; they live wherever there is water and grass and move about with no fixed place (History of the Jin).
passages.speaker: Qing history office, Comprehensive Gazetteer of the Great Qing (Jiaqing recension, completed 1842; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription), quoting the Liao and Jin histories
passages.caution: Stock phrases copied from older histories, not a fresh description.

passages.headline: From Yuan emperors back to 'Dada'
passages.gloss: The history of the Mongol domains says the Yuan's ancestors, the Mongols, came from the far northwest, conquered the world and unified it. After 1368 the Yuan heir fled north and kept his dynastic title, but a later usurper, Guilichi, called himself khan, dropped the dynastic name and 'again called [them] Dada', Tatars. The Qing record thus treats Tatar as the name the Mongols fell back on after losing China.
passages.quote: 元之先曰蒙古居西北極邊奄有天下遂成一統明初阿裕實哩達喇遯歸朔漠復其故號…果勒齊篡位稱可汗去國號復稱韃靼
passages.translation: The forebears of the Yuan were called Menggu (Mongols); they lived on the far northwestern frontier, took possession of all under heaven and so unified it. At the start of the Ming, Ayushiridara fled back to the northern desert and resumed his old title... Guolegi (Guilichi) usurped the throne, styled himself khan, abolished the dynastic name and again called [them] Dada (Tatars).
passages.speaker: Qing history office, Comprehensive Gazetteer of the Great Qing (Jiaqing recension, completed 1842; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
passages.caution: The second half is in a small-character note drawn from Ming sources.

passages.headline: Where was Karakorum? Between the Orkhon and the Tamir
passages.gloss: In the Khalkha section's list of ancient sites, the gazetteer copies the Yuan history's account of Hening (Karakorum) and then adds its own finding: according to the 'Map of the Northern Desert', the old capital stood east of the Khangai mountains, between the Orkhon and Tamir rivers. A few pages earlier the same section places the Erdene Zuu monastery on the upper Orkhon. Karakorum here is a known Mongol capital with a location, not a mystery.
passages.quote: 朔漠圖和寕北有錫爾格河又北庫庫布哈渡口西有迷河哈刺和林河西南有温泉南有旺吉河按其地在今杭愛山東鄂爾坤塔米爾河之閒
passages.translation: According to the Map of the Northern Desert, north of Hening is the Xiluge (Selenge) river, and further north the Kokebuqa ferry; to the west are the Mi river and the Qara Qorum river; to the southwest is a hot spring; to the south the Wangji river. Note: the place lies east of the present Khangai mountains, between the Orkhon and the Tamir rivers.
passages.speaker: Qing history office, Comprehensive Gazetteer of the Great Qing (Jiaqing recension, completed 1842; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
passages.caution: Listed under 'ancient sites' in the Khalkha section; the ruins of Karakorum lie beside Erdene Zuu on the Orkhon.

passages.headline: Hohhot, the Blue City, and its walls
passages.gloss: Under 'walls and moats' the gazetteer describes Guihua cheng, whose Mongol name is Kokekhota (Blue City): two li around, two zhang high, with north and south gates and an outer wall with three gates. It notes that the Ming gave it its Chinese name when Altan Khan submitted. Nearby was the new Qing fortress of Suiyuan, built in 1739. The gazetteer ties the town's Chinese name to Altan Khan's submission to the Ming in the 1570s.
passages.quote: 歸化城(在殺虎口邊城外二百里蒙古名庫庫河屯周圍二里高二丈南北門各一外郭東西南三面三門明諳逹歸順改賜今名
passages.translation: Guihua city (200 li beyond the frontier wall at Shahukou; its Mongol name is Kuku Hetun [Kokekhota, Blue City]; two li in circuit and two zhang high, with one gate each on the north and south; the outer wall has three gates on its east, west and south sides. When Anda [Altan Khan] of the Ming period submitted, it was given its present name.
passages.speaker: Qing history office, Comprehensive Gazetteer of the Great Qing (Jiaqing recension, completed 1842; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
passages.caution: The gazetteer does not say who built the walls; the Ming history (W131) describes Chinese renegades building walled settlements for Altan Khan in this area.

passages.headline: A ruined palace city with a giant stone Buddha
passages.people: Builders of an earlier dynasty (identified as Jin; now known as Bohai)
passages.gloss: Quoting the diary of Gao Shiqi, who accompanied the Kangxi emperor to Manchuria in 1682, the gazetteer describes Huorong city: a walled site over forty li around with an inner forbidden city, the foundations of three halls strewn with broken green-glazed tiles, and outside it a great stone Buddha about three zhang high on a lotus base, with a leaning stone pagoda. Gao took it for the Jin (Jurchen) upper capital; the gazetteer's editors then use the Jin river name Anchuhu (which they equate with the Alchuka) and Song travellers' distances to argue that the Jin capital lay further west, toward the Sungari.
passages.quote: 沙林東南十五里曰火茸城金之上京㑹寧府也廣四十餘里中間禁城可里餘三殿基址皆在碎碧瓦棊布其上禁城外有大石佛髙可三丈許蓮花承之前有石塔向東小欹
passages.translation: [Gao Shiqi's diary:] Fifteen li southeast of Shalin is Huorong city, the upper capital Huining prefecture of the Jin. It is more than forty li around; in the middle is a forbidden city about a li across, where the foundations of three halls all survive, with broken green tiles scattered over them like chess pieces. Outside the forbidden city is a great stone Buddha about three zhang high, resting on a lotus, and in front of it a stone pagoda leaning a little to the east.
passages.speaker: Agui, Liu Jinzhi and the Qianlong commission, Imperially Commissioned Gazetteer of Shengjing (1784 recension; Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription), quoting Gao Shiqi's diary of 1682
passages.caution: Gao's identification is doubted in the gazetteer itself. Modern archaeology identifies the ruins near Ningguta, with their stone Buddha and stone lantern, as Shangjing, capital of the Bohai kingdom (8th to 10th centuries).

passages.headline: Wooden horses and dog carts on the snow
passages.people: Peoples of the lower Sungari and Amur
passages.when: Yuan period, noted as still in use 1784
passages.gloss: The gazetteer quotes the Yuan imperial geography: the people of Kaiyuan were strong, warlike and practised archers and hunters, and had 'wooden horses' (skis) tied to both feet that could keep up with a galloping horse on snow and ice, and light boat-shaped wooden 'dog carts' pulled by several dogs. The editors add that in Manchu these are called suntaha and sherhe, in Chinese pali (sledges), and that they are still used throughout Jilin and Heilongjiang.
passages.quote: 開元勁健善戰習射獵有狗車木馬輕㨗之便木馬形如彈弓…一左一右繫於兩足激而行之雪中冰上可及奔馬狗車以木為之其制輕簡形如船…以數狗拽之
passages.translation: The people of Kaiyuan are strong, good fighters and practised at archery and hunting. They have the convenience of dog carts and wooden horses, which are light and quick. The wooden horse is shaped like a bow... one on the left and one on the right, tied to the two feet; pushing off, they glide along and on snow and ice can keep pace with a galloping horse. The dog cart is made of wood; it is light and simple, shaped like a boat... and pulled by several dogs.
passages.speaker: Agui, Liu Jinzhi and the Qianlong commission, Imperially Commissioned Gazetteer of Shengjing (1784 recension; Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription), quoting the Yuan Comprehensive Geography (Yuan yitong zhi)

passages.headline: The 'dog-using' and 'deer-using' tribes of the Amur
passages.people: Fiyaka (Nivkh), Kiler, Kuyala and other tribute peoples
passages.gloss: The gazetteer lists the northeastern peoples who brought tribute to the Qing post at Ningguta, measuring each by distance: the Fiyaka seven or eight hundred li beyond the three-river confluence, the Kiler three thousand li away on the sea coast, the Kuyala facing Korea across the Tumen. Beyond the 'dog-using' tribes lay a 'deer-using' (reindeer) tribe. These are the peoples European maps grouped in 'Eastern Tartary'.
passages.quote: 又東北行七八百里曰費雅喀自寕古塔東北行三千里曰奇勒爾東濵大海…庫雅喇其地在圖們江北岸與朝鮮之慶逺相對…而使鹿部又在使犬諸部之外
passages.translation: Another seven or eight hundred li to the northeast are the Fiyaka. Three thousand li northeast of Ningguta are the Kiler, who border the great sea on the east... The Kuyala: their land lies on the north bank of the Tumen river, opposite Kyongwon in Korea... And the deer-using tribe lies beyond the dog-using tribes.
passages.speaker: Agui, Liu Jinzhi and the Qianlong commission, Imperially Commissioned Gazetteer of Shengjing (1784 recension; Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)

passages.headline: Wooden forts against the Russians on the Amur
passages.gloss: In an edict of 1682 the Kangxi emperor weighs the report that the Russians (Luocha) raiding the Amur could be driven out with three thousand men. War, he says, is not a good thing; instead he orders fifteen hundred troops from Ula and Ningguta, with boats, cannon and muskets, to build wooden forts at Heilongjiang (Aigun) and Humar facing the enemy, and to farm so they can hold out. This is the start of the Albazin war that ended with the Treaty of Nerchinsk (1689).
passages.quote: 第兵非善事宜暫停攻取調烏拉寧古塔兵一千五百名並置造船艦發紅衣礮鳥鎗及演習之人於黑龍江瑚瑪爾二處建立木城與之對壘相機舉行
passages.translation: But war is not a good thing; it is fitting to pause the attack for now. Transfer fifteen hundred soldiers from Ula and Ningguta, have boats built, and send red-barrel cannon and muskets with men trained to use them to Heilongjiang and Humar, to build wooden forts in both places, face the enemy's lines and act as opportunity allows.
passages.speaker: The Kangxi emperor, edict of 1682, in Agui, Liu Jinzhi and the Qianlong commission, Imperially Commissioned Gazetteer of Shengjing (1784 recension; Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)
passages.caution: The edict is dated 1682 (Kangxi 21) in the heading on the preceding page.

passages.headline: Three heavenly maidens and a red fruit
passages.gloss: The dynasty's origin legend: three heavenly maidens bathed in Lake Bulhuri below Bukuri mountain, east of the Changbai range. A magic magpie dropped a red fruit on the youngest one's clothes; she put it in her mouth, swallowed it and conceived a boy who could speak at birth. She named him Bukuri Yongshon, of the Aisin Gioro clan, and sent him downriver in a small boat to settle a land at war. The court presents this as sacred history.
passages.quote: 長白山之東有布庫哩山其下有池曰布勒瑚里相傳三天女浴于池有神鵲銜朱果置季女衣季女含口中忽已入腹遂有身尋産一男生而能言
passages.translation: East of the Changbai mountains is Bukuri mountain, and below it a lake called Bulhuri. It is handed down that three heavenly maidens bathed in the lake. A divine magpie, holding a red fruit in its beak, placed it on the youngest maiden's clothes. The youngest held it in her mouth; suddenly it went down into her belly and she conceived. Soon she bore a boy who could speak at birth.
passages.speaker: Agui, Yu Minzhong and the Qianlong commission, Researches on Manchu Origins (Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription), quoting the dynasty's Record of Origins (Faxiang shiji)
passages.caution: A dynastic foundation legend, not history; the editors compare it to the miraculous births of the Shang and Zhou founders.

passages.headline: 'Manchu' from Manjushri, the bodhisattva of wisdom
passages.gloss: The editors argue that the name Manchu (滿洲) was originally Manju, both syllables level in tone, and link it to the Tibetans' custom of addressing the Qing emperor each year as 'Great Emperor Manjushri'. Manju, they say, means 'wonderful auspiciousness'; the Chinese character zhou (continent) was borrowed because it looked like a place name, but Manchu is the name of a people, not a place.
passages.quote: 國書考之滿洲本作滿珠二字皆平讀我朝光啟東土每嵗西藏獻丹書皆稱曼珠師利大皇帝翻譯名義曰曼珠華言妙吉祥也
passages.translation: [Examined in] our national (Manchu) script, Manzhou was originally written Manzhu, both syllables read in the level tone. Since our dynasty arose in the eastern land, every year Tibet presents red-ink letters all addressing 'the Great Emperor Manjushri'. The Fanyi mingyi (a Buddhist glossary) says: Manju in Chinese means 'wonderful auspiciousness'.
passages.speaker: Agui, Yu Minzhong and the Qianlong commission, Researches on Manchu Origins (Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)
passages.caution: The Manjushri etymology is the court's own proposal and is disputed by modern scholars.

passages.headline: Palace ruins of the old capitals near Ningguta
passages.people: Bohai and Jurchen (Jin) builders, claimed as Manchu ancestors
passages.gloss: The Jilin section notes that Ningguta was the Bohai kingdom's Huhan prefecture, later its Upper Capital Longquan, and that sixty li southwest of the Qing town, south of the Hurha river, lay an old city thirty li around with an inner city five li around where palace foundations still survived. Between Lalin and Alchuka was the Jin upper capital, likewise with outer and inner walls and palace remains. The Qing claimed these as the works of their own ancestors.
passages.quote: 古城周三十里内城周五里宫殿舊址猶存金為呼爾哈路亦統於上京拉林勒楚喀之間則金上京城在焉今城南四里尚有古城及子城宫殿遺址
passages.translation: [Sixty li southwest of the present city, south of the Hurha river, is] an old city thirty li around, with an inner city five li around, where the old foundations of palaces still survive. Under the Jin it was Hurha circuit, also under the Upper Capital. Between Lalin and Alchuka stood the Upper Capital of the Jin: four li south of the present town there is still an old city with an inner citadel and the remains of palaces.
passages.speaker: Agui, Yu Minzhong and the Qianlong commission, Researches on Manchu Origins (Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)
passages.caution: The sentence begins on the previous page (012-8a), which identifies Ningguta as Bohai's Upper Capital Longquan.

passages.headline: The 'Water Tatars' re-spelled out of existence
passages.gloss: Quoting the History of the Yuan on the Hailan and 'Water Tatar' circuits of Manchuria, the editors change 水達達 (Shui Dada, 'Water Tatars') to 碩達勒達, explained as Manchu for 'a hidden place', and note that the old form has been 'now corrected'. The Qing court thus removed the Tatar name from the history of its own homeland.
passages.quote: 海蘭府碩達勒達等路元史海蘭(詳前金上京條)府碩達勒達(滿洲語隠避處也舊作水達達)(今改正)等路土地廣濶人民散居
passages.translation: Hailan prefecture, Shuo Dalda and other circuits. The History of the Yuan: Hailan (see the Jin Upper Capital entry above) prefecture, Shuo Dalda (Manchu for 'a hidden, sheltered place'; formerly written Shui Dada, 'Water Tatars'; now corrected) and other circuits: the land is broad and the people live scattered.
passages.speaker: Agui, Yu Minzhong and the Qianlong commission, Researches on Manchu Origins (Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)
passages.caution: The Manchu etymology is a Qianlong-era reinterpretation; Yuan sources clearly meant 'Water Tatars'.

passages.headline: Sog-po and Hor: the Tibetan words for 'Tartar'
passages.gloss: Das's index to the Tibetan history glosses the Tibetan word Sog po as 'Tartary or a Tartar', and Sog yul (Sog land) as 'Mongolia, Hor, Tartary'. The English word Tartar in this edition is therefore a translation of Tibetan words for the Mongols, not a name the Tibetan author used.
passages.quote: Sog-po, the Tibetan for Tartary or a Tartar … Sog-yul Mongolia, Hor, Tartary
passages.speaker: Sarat Chandra Das, index to his edition of Sumpa Khenpo (Calcutta, 1908)
passages.caution: The Tibetan-script headwords are garbled in the OCR (the second reads ཐོག་ཡུལ for སོག་ཡུལ).

passages.headline: Mongols descended from the Asuras
passages.gloss: Among the opening legends of the Tibetan history, Das lists one that gives each great people a different origin: the Indians from the gods, the Chinese from the naga demigods, and the Mongolians from the asuras, the demons who fought the gods. It sits beside the story of the Tibetans' descent from a monkey.
passages.quote: The origin of the people of Aryavartta (India) from the gods, that of the Chinese from the Naga demi-gods, and that of the Mongolians from the Asura (demons who fought with the gods)
passages.speaker: Sarat Chandra Das, English analytical contents to his edition of Sumpa Khenpo's Tibetan text (Calcutta, 1908)
passages.caution: A summary line by the editor; Sumpa reports it as a traditional legend.

passages.headline: Gushri Khan's Tartars take Shigatse fortress
passages.gloss: Das summarises Sumpa's account of how the Khoshut Mongol ruler Gushri Khan invaded Tibet, besieged the fortress of Samdruptse (Shigatse), took thirteen district forts and captured the king of Tsang, who was thrown into the Tsangpo river. Gushri was then proclaimed king of all Tibet and handed religious authority to the Dalai Lama's church. The 'Tartars' here are Oirat Mongols from Kokonor.
passages.quote: The seige of Sam-dub-tse (now fort Shi-ga-tse) by the Tartars and the capture of thirteen Jong by them under the lead of Gucri Khan … The king of Tsang surrendered himself. He was thrown into the river Tsang-po
passages.speaker: Sarat Chandra Das, English analytical contents to his edition of Sumpa Khenpo's Tibetan text (Calcutta, 1908)
passages.caution: Das adds that the king was packed into something before being drowned, but that word is garbled in the OCR.

passages.headline: The Potala's Red Palace, built under the 'Tartar kings'
passages.people: Khoshut Mongol kings of Tibet; the Tibetan regent Sangye Gyatso
passages.gloss: The contents list the regents (desi) who governed Tibet under Gushri Khan's descendants, the 'Tartar kings', and credit the building of the nine-storeyed Red Palace of the Potala to the regent Sangye Gyatso. The Mongol khans held the title of king; the great building is credited to the Tibetan regent.
passages.quote: Succession of Desrid or governors … under the Tartar kings … The erection of the nine-storeyed Red palace (Phodañ Marpo) of Potala during the prime-ministership of Desrid San-gye Gya-tsho
passages.speaker: Sarat Chandra Das, English analytical contents to his edition of Sumpa Khenpo's Tibetan text (Calcutta, 1908)
passages.caution: An editor's summary line; the Red Palace was built in the 1690s.

passages.headline: A Tibetan prince at the sacred mountain: where the Mongol khans came from
passages.place: Burkhan Khaldun and Lake Baikal region
passages.gloss: Jigme Namkha begins the Mongol royal line not with the wolf and doe of the Secret History but with a son of the Tibetan king Drigum Tsenpo, called Borte Chino in Mongolian, who went into Mongolia with his wife and came to the mountain Burkhan Khaldun. The local people, learning of his noble descent, made him their ruler. It is a Buddhist retelling that ties the Mongol khans to Tibet's royal house.
passages.quote: Jener jüngste Sohn des Königs K'ri gum btsan-po, mit Namen Na k'ri oder mongolisch Porta Zeba, nahm sich aus dem Lande rKoii-po eine Gattin G-n-ö Maral mit Namen, ging mit ihr in die Mongolei und kam an den Berg Porhan Galtona am Ufer des Päigal -Seees.
passages.translation: That youngest son of King Khri gum btsan po, named Nya khri, or in Mongolian Borte Chino, took a wife named Go(a) Maral from the land of Kongpo, went with her into Mongolia and came to the mountain Burkhan Khaldun on the shore of Lake Baikal.
passages.speaker: Jigme Namkha (translated from the Tibetan into German by Georg Huth, 1896)
passages.caution: Huth's transliteration of Mongol names is idiosyncratic ('Porta Zeba' for Borte Chino, 'Porhan Galtona' for Burkhan Khaldun), and the OCR garbles some letters; the placing of Burkhan Khaldun by Baikal is the author's.
