passages.headline: A bird cries 'Chinggis!' and a jade seal appears
passages.gloss: The chronicle explains Chinggis Khan's title with a marvel: for three mornings a never-before-seen bird with rainbow feathers sat on a stone in front of his palace and called 'chinggis, chinggis', so his officials gave him the name. Then the stone split open by itself, revealing the old imperial jade seal. The author adds that the name is mispronounced in Tibetan as 'Jingir'.
passages.quote: rief lange mit lieblicher Stimme ‘c'ihgis, chhgis’. Die Beamten fassten dies als ein wunderbares Zeichen und glückliches Omen auf und gaben daher dem Könige den Namen Pogta C'ingis
passages.translation: ...[the bird] called for a long time in a lovely voice 'chinggis, chinggis'. The officials took this as a wonderful sign and a lucky omen, and therefore gave the king the name Bogda Chinggis.
passages.speaker: Jigme Namkha (translated from the Tibetan into German by Georg Huth, 1896)
passages.caution: A legend taken from Mongolian chronicles such as Sagang Sechen.

passages.headline: Khubilai 'built four great cities'
passages.gloss: The chronicle credits Khubilai, who took the throne in 1260, with building four great cities: Daidu (Beijing), Chagan (Chagan Balgasun), Huriyetu and Lanfin (Kaiping, the later Shangdu), and with appointing able prefects. For this Mongol author, the khans were founders of cities, not tent-dwellers only.
passages.quote: Er erbaute vier grosse Städte: die Stadt Täitu, die Stadt C'agan, die Stadt Hnriyet'u und die Stadt Lanfin, er- nannte tüchtige Männer zu Präfekten
passages.translation: He built four great cities: the city of Daidu, the city of Chagan, the city of Huriyetu and the city of Lanfin, and appointed capable men as prefects.
passages.speaker: Jigme Namkha (translated from the Tibetan into German by Georg Huth, 1896)
passages.caution: Written more than five centuries later; the identification of all four cities is not certain.

passages.headline: Subjects of five colours, Amazons and dog-heads
passages.people: Peoples subject to the Mongol khans
passages.gloss: Listing the peoples conquered from Chinggis to Khubilai, the chronicle gives the 'five colours': blue Mongols, red Chinese, black Tibetans, yellow Sartagul (Central Asian Muslims) and white Solongos (Koreans). Then come four more peoples: Amazons, one other, people with an eye on the chest, and dog-headed people. Old wonder-lore sits beside a real map of the empire.
passages.quote: Die blauen Mongolen, über vierhunderttausend Häuser, die roten Chinesen, die schwarzen Tibeter, die gelben Sart'agwol, die weissen Solongwos … ferner vier weitere Völkerschaften: die T sug-te- Amazonen, die j/Yon-ru, die mit einem Auge auf der Brust und die mit Hundeköpfen.
passages.translation: The blue Mongols, over four hundred thousand households; the red Chinese; the black Tibetans; the yellow Sartagul; the white Solongos... and four further peoples: the Tsug-te Amazons, the Yon-ru, those with one eye on the chest, and those with dogs' heads.
passages.speaker: Jigme Namkha (translated from the Tibetan into German by Georg Huth, 1896)
passages.caution: The marvellous peoples are traditional lore repeated by the author, not observation.

passages.headline: A lama general leads the Mongols against Ladakh
passages.people: Mongols (Sog po) sent from Lhasa; Ladakhis
passages.gloss: The chronicle tells how the Lhasa government, fearing the king of Ladakh, chose by divination a Mongol lama at Ganden monastery named Tshewang, who gave up his vows and led the Mongol tribe and a Tibetan army into Ladakh. The Ladakhis held Basgo castle for three years until the king called in the Mughal governor of Kashmir.
passages.quote: At that time there happened to be at Dgah-ldan lamasery a Mongol lama, called Tshe-dban. The calculations pointed out him [as the destined leader]. He, accordingly, turned layman, and, heading the Mongol tribe and a powerful army [of Tibetans], he [soon] reached [Ladakh].
passages.speaker: Chronicles of Ladakh (La dvags rgyal rabs), translated by A. H. Francke (1926)
passages.caution: Francke dates the war to about 1650; modern historians place the Tibet-Ladakh-Mughal war in 1679 to 1684. Square brackets are Francke's.

passages.headline: The defeated Mongols build a moated fort
passages.gloss: After the Kashmiri army routed the Tibetans near Basgo, the Mongol army fled to Tashigang, where, the chronicle says, they built a fort, surrounded it with a wall and ringed it with water, and stayed inside, secure against assault. The builders in this passage are the Mongols themselves.
passages.quote: the Mongol army in its flight [eventually] reached Bkra-sis-sgan. There they built a fort, shut it in with a wall, and surrounded it with water. Inside they made it secure against an assault of armies, and there they abode.
passages.speaker: Chronicles of Ladakh (La dvags rgyal rabs), translated by A. H. Francke (1926)

passages.headline: Ruins blamed on the Mongols, and a Mongol hand on show
passages.gloss: In his notes Francke records that popular tradition connected the many ruins at Mkhar-rdzong in Nubra with the Mongol general Galdan Tshewang, whose portrait head was kept at Diskit monastery in the hands of a guardian demon. Elsewhere in the book a missionary reports that at Phugtal monastery 'a dried human hand, which once was cut off a Mongol' was shown at a festival.
passages.quote: According to popular tradition the numerous ruins at Mkhar-rdzon in Nub-ra are connected with the Mongol general Dgah-ldan-tshe-dban, of whom a portrait head may be seen at the Bde-skyid monastery, where it is placed in the hands of the ogre Mgon-dkar.
passages.speaker: A. H. Francke, translator's note (1926)
passages.caution: Popular tradition reported by the editor; the Phugtal hand is in the Rev. G. Hettasch's notes (p.152), not the chronicle.

passages.headline: 'It is generally asserted that it was built by the Mongols, which is an error'
passages.people: Ladakhi king Nyima Namgyal; Mongols in local belief
passages.gloss: The chronicle credits King Nyima Namgyal with building a long mani wall near Leh. Karl Marx's note adds that local people generally claimed the wall was built by the Mongols, and calls that belief an error. A small but telling case of a structure popularly credited to the Mongols that the written record gives to someone else.
passages.quote: It is generally asserted that it was built by the Mongols, which is an error.
passages.speaker: Karl Marx (Moravian missionary), note to Francke's edition
passages.caution: An editorial note, not the chronicle text.

passages.headline: Ogedei throws open the treasury of his new capital
passages.gloss: Among the anecdotes of Ogedei's generosity, Rashid says that while Karakorum (Qara Qorum) was being founded the khan found about twenty thousand silver ingots (balish) piled in the treasury and saw no point in hoarding them. He had it announced that anyone who wanted balish could come and take it. The story assumes a real city with a population of rich and poor, nobles and commoners.
passages.quote: دیکر بوقت آنك قرا قوروم‌را بنیاد فرموده بود روزی بخزانه در آمد و قرب دو تومان بالش دید فرمود که از اذخار این مارا چه فایده … اهل شهر از شریف و وضیع توانکر و درویش روی بخزانه آوردند و هر کسی نصیبی وافر یافتند
passages.translation: Another story: at the time when he had ordered Qara Qorum to be founded, one day he went into the treasury and saw nearly two tumans [some twenty thousand] of balish [silver ingots]. He said: 'What use to us is hoarding this?' … The people of the city, noble and humble, rich and poor, made for the treasury, and every one of them found a generous share.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this Persian text is garbled)
passages.speaker: Rashid al-Din (Persian text ed. E. Blochet, 1911)
passages.caution: A moralising anecdote about the khan's generosity, taken over from Juvaini, not an eyewitness report.

passages.headline: A radish harvest in a land too cold to farm
passages.gloss: Rashid notes that no crops grew around Karakorum because of the fierce cold, and that farming there only began in Ogedei's reign. When a man managed to raise a few radishes and brought them to the khan, Ogedei had them counted and paid him one silver ingot for each. The story shows a steppe capital fed from outside, where a home-grown vegetable was a marvel.
passages.quote: دیکر چون در حدود قرا قوروم از افراط سرما زراعت نمی باشد در عهد دولت قاآن آغاز آن کردند شخصی ترب کاشت و چندی حاصل آمد آنرا به بندکی قاآن آورد فرمود تا آنرا برکها بشمارند صد عدد بر آمد فرمود تا اورا صد بالش دادند
passages.translation: Another: since there is no farming around Qara Qorum because of the extreme cold, they made a start at it in the reign of the Qa'an. A man sowed radishes and a few came up. He brought them to the Qa'an, who ordered them to be counted, leaves and all; they came to a hundred, and he ordered that the man be given a hundred balish.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this Persian text is garbled)
passages.speaker: Rashid al-Din (Persian text ed. E. Blochet, 1911)
passages.caution: Another generosity anecdote from the Juvaini tradition.

passages.headline: Xanadu: a Chinese-style palace built on a drained lake
passages.gloss: Rashid describes how Qubilai's summer palace near Kaiping-fu was built. On the previous page he says the khan consulted sages and engineers, who chose a lake in a meadow, and that they gathered a local stone burned instead of firewood (coal). Here the lake is filled with rubble and broken brick sealed with molten tin and lead, raised on a platform, and crowned with a palace built 'in the manner of Cathay', inside a marble wall. The builders' style is Chinese, the patron Mongol.
passages.quote: با چشمهٔ آن از حصا و آجرّ خرد کرده پر کردند و قلعی و ارزیز بسیار بر ان کداختند تا محکم شد و بمقدار مرد بالائی از زمین بر آوردند و صفّهٔ بر بالای آن ساختند … و بر سر آن صفّه قرشی بیانك ختای ساخته و پیرامون آن مرغزار از مرمر دیواری کشیده
passages.translation: [the lake] with its spring they filled with rubble and broken brick, and melted a great deal of tin and lead over it until it was firm; they raised it the height of a man above the ground and built a platform on top of it … and on top of that platform they built a palace in the Cathay [Chinese] manner, and round that meadow they drew a wall of marble.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this Persian text is garbled)
passages.speaker: Rashid al-Din (Persian text ed. E. Blochet, 1911)
passages.caution: Rashid never saw Shangdu; he relied on informants from Yuan China. The Persian word qarshi (palace) and the phrase 'Cathay manner' are explained in Blochet's notes.

passages.headline: 'The Tatars are exceedingly numerous'
passages.gloss: When a large Mongol army under Chormaghun crossed the Oxus, Sultan Jalal al-Din of Khwarazm, though on bad terms with the caliph and the rulers of Anatolia and Syria, sent envoys to each of them. Rashid writes 'Mughul' (Mongol) in his own voice, but gives the substance of the warning as 'the Tatars are exceedingly numerous'. The same army is Mongol in the narrative and Tatar in the alarm.
passages.quote: پیش هریك رسول فرستاد و از حال وصول مغول خبر داد و مضمون پیغام آنك تاتار بغایت بسیارند و این نوبت زیادت از هر بار
passages.translation: He sent an envoy to each of them and gave news of the Mongols' coming; the substance of the message was that the Tatars are exceedingly numerous, and this time more than ever before.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this Persian text is garbled)
passages.speaker: Rashid al-Din (Persian text ed. E. Blochet, 1911)
passages.caution: Reported speech summarised by Rashid some seventy years later.

passages.headline: A Mongol capital and a tomb of cut stone
passages.gloss: Mustawfi credits the founding of Sultaniyyah to the Mongol Ilkhan Arghun and its completion to his son Uljaytu, who named it after himself. He gives the circuit of the walls built and planned, and describes a castle of cut stone at the centre that is Uljaytu's tomb. Elsewhere on the page he says the new capital drew settlers of all nations and that only Tabriz had as many great buildings.
passages.quote: The city was founded by Arghun Khan, grandson of Hulagu the Mongol, and his son Uljaytu Sultan completed it, naming it Sultaniyyah after himself … The walls which Arghun built were 12,000 paces in circuit … In the centre stands a Castle built of cut stone, which is the tomb of Uljaytu Sultan
passages.speaker: Hamdallah Mustawfi (translated by G. Le Strange, 1919)
passages.caution: Mustawfi served the dynasty and knew the city well; the 'castle' is the great domed mausoleum still standing today.

passages.headline: A khan's grave hidden in a sacred mountain
passages.gloss: Mustawfi records that the Ilkhan Arghun was buried on the mountain of Sujas and that, following Mongol custom, the grave was concealed and the whole mountain made a forbidden sanctuary (qurugh). His daughter later revealed the grave and founded a dervish lodge there, a Muslim practice laid over a steppe one.
passages.quote: The sepulchre of Arghun Khan was made in the mountain of Sujas, and according to Mongol custom, they concealed the place, making the whole mountain an inviolable Sanctuary (Qurugh), so that people could not without difficulty pass that way. Arghun's daughter, Uljay Khatun, however, made manifest her father's grave, founding a Darvish-house, and settling a community here.
passages.speaker: Hamdallah Mustawfi (translated by G. Le Strange, 1919)

passages.headline: The Qipchaq steppe: pasture, nomads and few towns
passages.people: Nomads of the Qipchaq steppe (Golden Horde lands)
passages.gloss: Mustawfi's short entry on the Dasht-i Qipchaq, the Golden Horde's steppe, says it has rich pasture but few houses, towns or villages, and that most people are nomads. He then lists its towns, including 'Saray Batu', the Horde capital on the Volga. Le Strange's footnote places the ruins of Saray above Astrakhan.
passages.quote: Dasht-i-Qipchaq. This is of the Sixth Clime, its plains bear excellent pasturage, stretching to the north of the Caspian Sea, but there are here few houses or towns or villages. Most of the inhabitants are nomads of the plain. Its most celebrated town is Khazar … then there is Burtas, also Suvar, Muhtal, Saray Batu and Sarir
passages.speaker: Hamdallah Mustawfi (translated by G. Le Strange, 1919)
passages.caution: Compiled at second hand: several of the 'towns' (Khazar, Burtas, Suvar) are names from much older Arabic geographies.

passages.headline: 'Of the Tatar race': a poem about Turkish slave soldiers
passages.people: Turkish ghulams (slave soldiers) of Sultan Sanjar, called Tatars
passages.when: 1141 (battle with the Qara Khitay), quoted c.1340
passages.gloss: Listing places in the East, Mustawfi quotes a mocking poem about the Turkish pages of the Seljuk Sultan Sanjar, who fled before the Qara Khitay cavalry. The poet calls them swordsmen 'of the Tatar race'. Le Strange adds that Tatar is not a place-name but the name of a people. It is a glimpse of the word in Persian a century before the Mongol conquests.
passages.quote: Other places are Kasan, Tatar and Fay which a poet has mentioned in his verses on the Ghulams (Pages) of Sultan Sanjar, who had showed lack of bravery in their attack on the cavalry of the infidel Qara Khitay. He says: Bravo! O ye strong hearted Turkish swordsmen Of the Tatar race from Fay and Kasan
passages.speaker: Hamdallah Mustawfi (translated by G. Le Strange, 1919), quoting a twelfth-century poem
passages.caution: The poem is satire; Le Strange identifies the poet as Sharaf al-Din Kushkaki in his footnote.

passages.headline: The Khazars' Jewish king and Turk-like people
passages.gloss: Ibn Rusta says the Khazars had a king called Isha who ran the army, while the supreme king, the Khazar Khaqan, had only the name. The supreme ruler was of the Jewish religion, as were Isha and the commanders and nobles who followed him; the rest followed a religion like that of the Turks.
passages.quote: ولهم ملك يقال له ايشا والملك الاعظم انما هو خزر خاقان وليس له من طاعة الخزر الا الاسم … ورئيسهم الاعظم على دين اليهود وكذلك ايشا ومن يميل ميله من القواد والعظماء والبقية منهم على دين شبيه دين الاتراك
passages.translation: They have a king called Isha; the supreme king is the Khazar Khaqan, but he has nothing of the Khazars' obedience except the name … Their supreme chief follows the religion of the Jews, and so do Isha and those commanders and great men who lean his way; the rest of them follow a religion like the religion of the Turks.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of the Arabic is garbled); vowel marks omitted
passages.speaker: Ibn Rusta (Arabic text ed. M. J. de Goeje, 1892)
passages.caution: Copied from an earlier report; the Khazar state was destroyed c.965, long before the word Tartar came into use.

passages.headline: Winter in the towns, summer on the steppe
passages.gloss: Having named the Khazar towns (Sarighshin and a second, garbled name) as the people's winter quarters, Ibn Rusta continues that in spring they go out to the steppe and stay there until winter comes. The two towns held many Muslims, with mosques, imams, muezzins and Quran schools. It is a pattern of town and pasture later seen among the Golden Horde.
passages.quote: المدينتين فاذا كان ايام الربيع خرجوا الى الصحارى فلم يزالوا بها الى اقبال الشتاء وفى هاتين المدينتين خلق من المسلمين لهم مساجد وائمة ومؤذنون وكتاتيب
passages.translation: [these two] towns. When spring comes they go out to the steppes and stay there until winter approaches. In these two towns there is a multitude of Muslims, who have mosques, imams, muezzins and Quran schools.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of the Arabic is garbled); vowel marks omitted
passages.speaker: Ibn Rusta (Arabic text ed. M. J. de Goeje, 1892)
passages.caution: The sentence begins on the previous page, which names the towns.

passages.headline: Muslim farmers of the Volga Bulghars
passages.gloss: The Bulghars (written Bulkar) lived on the Itil (Volga), between the Khazars and the Slavs; their king was a Muslim. Ibn Rusta says the Khazars and the Rus came to trade with them in sable, ermine and squirrel, and that they farmed wheat, barley and millet, and that most of them were Muslims with mosques and schools. Their land around Bolgar later became part of the Golden Horde and then the Kazan khanate.
passages.quote: وهم قوم لهم زرع وحراثة يزرعون كل الحبوب من الحنطة والشعير والدخن وغير ذلك واكثرهم ينتحلون دين الاسلام وفى محالهم مساجد وكتاتيب ولهم مؤذنون وائمة
passages.translation: They are a people who have crops and ploughing; they sow every kind of grain, wheat, barley, millet and so on. Most of them profess the religion of Islam; in their settlements there are mosques and Quran schools, and they have muezzins and imams.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of the Arabic is garbled); vowel marks omitted
passages.speaker: Ibn Rusta (Arabic text ed. M. J. de Goeje, 1892)

passages.headline: Magyars: 'a race of the Turks' living in tents
passages.gloss: Before they moved to Hungary, the Magyars lived on the steppe north of the Black Sea. Ibn Rusta calls them a race of the Turks, says their chief rides out with twenty thousand horsemen, and that they have tents (qibab) and move with the grass and pasture. In winter they camped by the rivers and fished.
passages.quote: والمجغرية جنس من الترك ويركب رئيسهم فى مقدار عشرين الف فارس … ولهم قباب يسيرون مع الكلأ والخصب وبلادهم واسعة
passages.translation: The Majghariyya are a race of the Turks; their chief rides out with about twenty thousand horsemen … They have domed tents and travel with the grass and the pasture, and their country is wide.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of the Arabic is garbled); vowel marks omitted
passages.speaker: Ibn Rusta (Arabic text ed. M. J. de Goeje, 1892)
passages.caution: 'Turks' here is a broad label for steppe horsemen; the Magyars spoke a Finno-Ugric language.

passages.headline: A wall of iron bricks bound with copper
passages.place: 'Wall of Gog and Magog' (perhaps the Gansu or Hami frontier, China)
passages.gloss: Sallam describes how the wall was built: foundations dug thirty cubits deep and laid in iron and copper, then two great jambs, all of iron bricks sheathed in copper, carrying a 120-cubit iron lintel. He credits the work to Dhu'l-Qarnayn, the Quran's 'two-horned' king, usually identified with Alexander. Nothing here is credited to the Turks.
passages.quote: La muraille fut construite de la manière suivante. D'abord on creusa le sol jusqu'à une profondeur de 30 coudées et on y jeta les fondements qu'on construisit en fer et en cuivre jusqu'à ras de terre … Toute la construction se compose de briques de fer, revêtues de cuivre, dont chacune a une coudée et demie en long et en large sur 4 pouces d'épaisseur.
passages.translation: The wall was built in the following way. First the ground was dug to a depth of 30 cubits and the foundations laid there, built of iron and copper up to ground level … The whole structure is made of iron bricks faced with copper, each a cubit and a half long and wide and 4 inches thick.
passages.speaker: Sallam the Interpreter, as reported by Ibn Khurradadhbih (French translation by M. J. de Goeje, 1889)
passages.caution: Sallam's account as dictated to Ibn Khurradadhbih; the 'history' of the building is legend.

passages.headline: Twenty-seven days through ruined cities
passages.place: Central Asian steppe, north-east of the Khazars
passages.people: Peoples of the steppe; ruins blamed on Gog and Magog
passages.gloss: After leaving the Khazar king, Sallam says, his party crossed a black, foul-smelling land, then travelled twenty (or twenty-seven) days among ruined cities. They were told these were the remains of cities overrun by Gog and Magog. Near the wall they found forts held by Arabic- and Persian-speaking Muslims with schools and mosques, who had never heard of the caliph.
passages.quote: nous passâmes, durant vingt (vingt-sept) jours, au milieu de villes en ruine. On nous apprit que c'étaient les restes des villes envahies autrefois et dévastées par les peuples de Gog et Magog. Nous arrivâmes enfin à des forteresses bâties dans le voisinage des montagnes … Nous y trouvâmes des personnes qui parlaient l'arabe et le persan. Ils sont musulmans, sachant lire le Koran
passages.translation: we passed twenty (twenty-seven) days in the midst of ruined cities. We were told these were the remains of cities once invaded and laid waste by the peoples of Gog and Magog. At last we came to fortresses built near the mountains … There we found people who spoke Arabic and Persian. They are Muslims and can read the Koran
passages.speaker: Sallam the Interpreter, as reported by Ibn Khurradadhbih (French translation by M. J. de Goeje, 1889)
passages.caution: A ninth-century tale: the ruins are real or imagined, but the explanation (Gog and Magog) is what Sallam was told, not something he could check.

passages.headline: Gog and Magog, a span and a half tall
passages.gloss: Sallam asked the guards at the gate whether they had ever seen one of Gog and Magog. They said they had once glimpsed several on top of the mountain before a violent wind blew them back, and at that distance they looked no more than a span and a half tall. On the same page he describes the wall's striped look, yellow copper and black iron in alternate layers.
passages.quote: Nous demandâmes aux gardiens de la porte s'ils avaient jamais vu un individu de la race de Gog et Magog; ils nous racontèrent qu'ils en avaient aperçu, un jour, plusieurs au-dessus de la montagne, mais qu'un vent impétueux les avait rejetés de leur côté. Vus à cette distance, leur taille ne paraissait pas dépasser un empan et demi.
passages.translation: We asked the guards of the gate whether they had ever seen one of the race of Gog and Magog; they told us that one day they had glimpsed several on top of the mountain, but a violent wind had thrown them back to their own side. Seen at that distance, they seemed no taller than a span and a half.
passages.speaker: Sallam the Interpreter, as reported by Ibn Khurradadhbih (French translation by M. J. de Goeje, 1889)
passages.caution: Hearsay from guards, told by Sallam; de Goeje's footnote discusses which side of the wall the wind blew them to.

passages.headline: The Toghuzghuz khan's city of twelve iron gates
passages.gloss: In his own route list, Ibn Khurradadhbih says the Toghuzghuz khan's capital lay three months' march beyond Upper Nushajan, through pasture land with large villages. The king lived in a great city with twelve iron gates and had a golden tent on top of his palace, visible five parasangs away, while the Kimek king camped among pastures in tents. Steppe Turks here have both cities and tents.
passages.quote: De Nouschadjan la supérieure à la capitale du khakân des Toghozghor, il y a trois mois de marche, à travers un pays de pâturage couvert de vastes bourgades … Leur roi réside dans une grande ville fermée par douze portes de fer … Le roi des Toghozghor possède une tente d'or placée au faîte de son palais; elle peut abriter cent personnes
passages.translation: From Upper Nushajan to the capital of the khaqan of the Toghuzghuz is three months' march, through pasture country covered with large villages … Their king lives in a great city closed by twelve iron gates … The king of the Toghuzghuz owns a golden tent set on the top of his palace; it can shelter a hundred people
passages.speaker: Ibn Khurradadhbih (French translation by M. J. de Goeje, 1889)
passages.caution: From route reports, not a visit. The capital is usually identified with the Uyghur city Ordu-Baliq (Karabalgasun) in the Orkhon valley, near later Karakorum.

passages.headline: Sarai: a new city of merchants and the Turkish slave trade
passages.gloss: Abu'l-Fida's entry on Seray (Sarai), capital of 'the states of Berke', says the present ruler is Uzbek, that the city lies in a plain on the Volga north-west of the Caspian, and that merchants crowd there and do a great trade in Turkish slaves. He calls it a modern city, founded by a descendant of Chinggis Khan named Sain Batu, and adds day-length information from a man of the city.
passages.quote: Le prince qui règne en ce moment s'appelle Uzbek. La situation de Seray est en plaine, au nord-ouest de la mer Caspienne … C'est un lieu très-fréquenté des marchands, et il s'y fait un grand commerce d'esclaves turks. La ville est d'origine moderne. On en attribue la fondation à un descendant de Djenguiz-Khan, appelé Saïn-Batou.
passages.translation: The prince now reigning is called Uzbek. Sarai lies in a plain, north-west of the Caspian Sea … It is a place much visited by merchants, and there is a great trade there in Turkish slaves. The town is of recent origin; its founding is attributed to a descendant of Chinggis Khan called Sain Batu.
passages.speaker: Abu'l-Fida (French translation by J. T. Reinaud, 1848)
passages.caution: The entry opens on the previous page ('Seray, capitale des états de Berké'). Abu'l-Fida never went there; he cites a man from Sarai.

passages.headline: 'They made a rampart of their saddles'
passages.gloss: Reinaud quotes Abu'l-Fida's own chronicle of a skirmish before the battle of Marj al-Suffar in 1303, in which Abu'l-Fida fought. A group of Tartars who had dismounted were surrounded and offered their lives; they answered with arrows, made a barricade of their horses' saddles, and fought until every one was killed. It is an eyewitness picture of Mongol soldiers from the other side.
passages.quote: Une partie des Tartares ayant mis pied à terre, nous les entourâmes et nous leur offrîmes la vie; mais ils reçurent nos propositions à coups de flèches, et, se faisant un rempart des selles de leurs chevaux, ils soutinrent un nouveau combat. Ils furent tous massacrés jusqu'au dernier.
passages.translation: Some of the Tartars had dismounted; we surrounded them and offered them their lives, but they answered our offer with arrows, and, making a rampart of their horses' saddles, fought a fresh battle. They were all killed to the last man.
passages.speaker: Abu'l-Fida's Chronicle, quoted in Reinaud's introduction (1848)
passages.caution: Written by a victorious enemy commander.

passages.headline: Why 'Golden Horde': the khan's gilded tent
passages.people: Mongol khans of the Qipchaq steppe (Golden Horde)
passages.gloss: On Abu'l-Fida's remark that the horde of the Tartar prince of Berke's country comes as far as Ukek, Reinaud explains that horde (Turkish ordu) means tent: the Chinggisid khans moved with the seasons and wherever they pitched their tents was called the horde. He suggests the Russians called the dynasty the Golden Horde because the khan's tent stood on wooden posts plated with gold, citing Ibn Battuta.
passages.quote: Le mot horde, en arabe ordou, appartient à la langue turke et signifie tente. Les princes tartares de la race de Gengiskhan, qui régnèrent sur le Capichac, étaient dans l'usage de changer de demeure, suivant la saison, et le lieu où ils dressaient leurs tentes portait le nom de horde … probablement parce que la tente qu'occupait le khan était appuyée sur des pieux de bois recouverts de lames d'or
passages.translation: The word horde, in Arabic ordu, belongs to the Turkish language and means tent. The Tartar princes of the race of Chinggis Khan who ruled the Qipchaq steppe used to change their residence with the seasons, and the place where they pitched their tents was called the horde … probably because the tent the khan occupied rested on wooden posts covered with plates of gold
passages.speaker: J. T. Reinaud (editor's footnote, 1848)
passages.caution: An editor's explanation drawing on Rubruck, Ibn Battuta and Hammer-Purgstall, not Abu'l-Fida's own words.

passages.headline: Scythians, then Turks, then Tatars
passages.gloss: In his introduction Reinaud explains that the same northern peoples went by different names in different eras: Scythians for ancient writers, Turks for early Arabic writers, and Tartars, or rather Tatars as Arabs, Persians and Turks pronounce it, for later writers. It is a short, clear account of how 'Tartar' became a catch-all label.
passages.quote: Chez les écrivains de l'antiquité, les peuples du nord de l'Asie et de l'Europe étaient des Scythes; chez les anciens écrivains arabes, ce sont des Turks; chez les écrivains postérieurs, ce sont des Tartares ou plutôt, comme prononcent les Arabes, les Persans et les Turks, des Tatars.
passages.translation: For ancient writers, the peoples of northern Asia and Europe were Scythians; for the early Arabic writers they are Turks; for later writers they are Tartars, or rather, as the Arabs, Persians and Turks pronounce it, Tatars.
passages.speaker: J. T. Reinaud (introduction, 1848)
passages.caution: A nineteenth-century scholar's summary, not a medieval statement.

passages.headline: The Volga, 'the river on which the city of Sarai stands'
passages.gloss: In his list of rivers al-Umari describes the Athil (Volga) as the river on which the city of al-Sarai is set, flowing through 'the deserts of the Qipchaq' into the Caspian. Sarai was then the capital of the Golden Horde, with which the Mamluks were allied.
passages.quote: ومن ذلك نهر أثيل . وهو المركب عليه مدينة السراى . ومخرجه من عين تنبع فى ذيل جبل قاقونا ، ثم يقتبل الجنوب آخذا بغرب فى صحارى القبجاق على شمالى معادن الفضة ، حتى يصب فى بحر طبرستان
passages.translation: Among them is the river Athil. It is the river on which the city of al-Sarai is set. Its source is a spring welling up at the foot of Mount Qaquna; then it turns south, heading west through the deserts of the Qipchaq, north of the silver mines, until it flows into the Sea of Tabaristan [the Caspian].
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR is partly garbled); vowel marks omitted
passages.speaker: al-Umari (Arabic text ed. Ahmad Zaki Pasha, Cairo 1924)
passages.caution: Geographical summary; the source and course are partly traditional.

passages.headline: A mountain chain that crosses 'the land of the Tatars'
passages.place: Inner Asia, from China to Fergana
passages.gloss: Tracing the great mountain chain that ends in Syria, al-Umari starts it in China at the encircling ocean and says it cuts across 'the land of the Tatars' along its mines before reaching Fergana. Here 'land of the Tatars' is simply the Mamluk name for Mongol-ruled inner Asia, much as Europeans used 'Tartary'.
passages.quote: فإن أوله بالمشرق من الصين من البحر المحيط . فيقطع بلاد التتر على معادنها إلى أن يأتى فرغانة
passages.translation: Its beginning is in the east, in China, at the Encircling Ocean. It cuts across the land of the Tatars, along its mines, until it reaches Farghana.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR is partly garbled); vowel marks omitted
passages.speaker: al-Umari (Arabic text ed. Ahmad Zaki Pasha, Cairo 1924)

passages.headline: Lands ruined by the raids of Gog and Magog
passages.place: Far north-east of the seventh clime
passages.gloss: Describing the far north, al-Umari says the eastern end is a region peopled by Gog and Magog within the Barrier (the wall). He reports that the Rus lands and the land of the Ankariyya (Hungarians) are inhabited, but that the land of Sisaban was once flourishing and populated and fell to ruin long ago because Gog and Magog raided it.
passages.quote: فأوله من جهة الشرق قطعة معمورة بيأجوج ومأجوج ، فيما هو داخل السد … قالوا : فأما الروسية ، فعامرة آهلة . وكذلك الأنكرية . وأما بلاد سيسبان ، فقد كانت عامرة آهلة مسكونة ، ثم خربت من قديم ، لإغارات يأجوج ومأجوج عليهم
passages.translation: Its beginning on the eastern side is a stretch peopled by Gog and Magog, within the Barrier … They say: as for the Rus lands, they are flourishing and inhabited, and so are those of the Ankariyya; but the land of Sisaban was once flourishing, populated and settled, then fell to ruin long ago because of the raids of Gog and Magog upon them.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR is partly garbled); vowel marks omitted
passages.speaker: al-Umari (Arabic text ed. Ahmad Zaki Pasha, Cairo 1924)
passages.caution: 'They say': copied lore, of the same family as Sallam's ruined cities.

passages.headline: The sultan who 'vanquished the Tatars'
passages.people: Tatars (Ilkhanid Mongols), enemies of the Mamluks
passages.gloss: In the dedication al-Umari praises the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun as king of Arabs, Persians and Turks and 'vanquisher of the Rum, the Franks, the Georgians, the Armenians and the Tatars'. For a Mamluk official the Tatars are one of the great enemy peoples, set beside the Crusaders.
passages.quote: هازم الروم والفرنج والكرج والأرمن والتتار ، سلطان البسيطه
passages.translation: vanquisher of the Rum, the Franks, the Georgians, the Armenians and the Tatars, sultan of the wide earth
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR is partly garbled); vowel marks omitted
passages.speaker: al-Umari (Arabic text ed. Ahmad Zaki Pasha, Cairo 1924)
passages.caution: Court flattery; the Mamluks defeated Ilkhanid armies, notably in 1303, and made peace with them in 1323.

passages.headline: Timur's four tribal vizirs and the Barlas
passages.gloss: Ibn Arabshah opens his life of Timur by explaining that the Turks, like the Arabs, are divided into tribes. The four chief officers of the Chaghatayid sultan came from four tribes, the Arlat, Jalayir, Qauchin and Barlas, and Timur was the son of the Barlas chief. On the same page he reports a Persian genealogy linking Timur to Chinggis Khan through the female line, and explains Timur's title Gurkan as Mongol for 'son-in-law', since he married royal daughters.
passages.quote: والترك لهم قبائل وشعب تكاد توازي قبائل العرب وكل واحد من هؤلاء الوزراء كان من قبيلة … احدهم تسمى ارلات وقبيلة الثاني تدعى جلابر وقبيلة الثالث يقال لها قاوجين وقبيلة الرابع اسمها برلاس وكان تيمور ابن رابعهم
passages.translation: The Turks have tribes and clans that almost match the tribes of the Arabs, and each of these vizirs was from a tribe … the first of them called Arlat, the tribe of the second called Jalabir [Jalayir], the tribe of the third called Qauchin, and the tribe of the fourth named Barlas; and Timur was the son of the fourth of them.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this print is garbled); vowel marks and the asterisk dividers of the rhymed prose omitted
passages.speaker: Ahmad ibn Arabshah (Arabic text, print catalogued 1842)
passages.caution: Ibn Arabshah wrote as an enemy of Timur. The print misspells Jalayir as Jalabir; the tribal list matches other Timurid sources.

passages.headline: The Dasht of Berke: 'a land of the Tatars alone'
passages.people: Tatars of the Golden Horde (Dasht-i Qipchaq)
passages.gloss: Describing the steppe that Timur coveted, Ibn Arabshah calls it the Dasht of Berke (after the Golden Horde khan) and says it was a country belonging to the Tatars alone, teeming with herds and Turkish tribes, well guarded, well peopled and healthy in water and air. He had lived there himself in the 1410s and 1420s.
passages.quote: دشت بركه وكانت بلادا بالتتار خاصه وبانواع المواشي وقبائل الترك غاصه محفوظة الاطراف معمورة الاكناف فسيحة الارجاء صحيحة الماء والهواء
passages.translation: the Dasht of Berke. It was a country belonging to the Tatars alone, and teeming with every kind of livestock and with the tribes of the Turks; its borders guarded, its sides well peopled, its reaches wide, its water and air wholesome.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this print is garbled); vowel marks and the asterisk dividers of the rhymed prose omitted
passages.speaker: Ahmad ibn Arabshah (Arabic text, print catalogued 1842)
passages.caution: Rhymed, flattering prose. One word (al-mawashi, livestock) is blurred in the print.

passages.headline: Caravans on carts with no need for provisions
passages.people: Tatars and Turks of the Golden Horde steppe
passages.gloss: Ibn Arabshah says caravans used to set out from Khwarazm and travel by cart (ajal) across the steppe to Crimea, a journey of about three months, without fear. They carried no food or fodder and took no guide, because the steppe was so thick with peoples and so full of security and food that they only ever stopped at some tribe, and only halted with people who honoured their guests.
passages.quote: وكانت القوافل تخرج من خوارزم وتسير بالعجل وهم آمنون من غير ريب ولا وجل … فكانت القافلة لا تحمل زادا ولا عليقا ولا يصحبون معهم رفيقا وذلك لكثرة الامم ووفور الامن والماكل والمشرب من الحشم فلا يصدرون الا عن قبيله ولا ينزلون الا عند من يكرم نزيله
passages.translation: Caravans used to leave Khwarazm and travel by cart, safe, without doubt or fear … The caravan carried no provisions and no fodder, and took no companion along, because of the multitude of the peoples and the abundance of security, food and drink among the retinues; they set out only from a tribe and halted only with someone who honoured his guest.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this print is garbled); vowel marks and the asterisk dividers of the rhymed prose omitted
passages.speaker: Ahmad ibn Arabshah (Arabic text, print catalogued 1842)
passages.caution: Nostalgic description of the steppe before Timur's invasions, written decades later.

passages.headline: Sarai, an Islamic city built by Khan Berke
passages.gloss: Ibn Arabshah names Sarai as the throne city of the Dasht and calls it 'a city of Islamic building, of marvellous structure'. Khan Berke, he says, built it when he became a Muslim and made it his royal seat. Just before this he laments that today, from Khwarazm to Crimea, nothing stirs of those peoples, and only gazelles and camels are left.
passages.quote: وتحت الدشت سراي وهي مدينة اسلامية البنيان بديعة الاركان … وكان السلطان بركه رحمه الله لما اسلم بناها واتخذها دار الملك واصطفاها
passages.translation: The throne of the Dasht is Sarai, a city of Islamic building and marvellous structure … Sultan Berke, may God have mercy on him, built it when he became a Muslim, and took it as the seat of kingship and chose it.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this print is garbled); vowel marks and the asterisk dividers of the rhymed prose omitted
passages.speaker: Ahmad ibn Arabshah (Arabic text, print catalogued 1842)
passages.caution: Modern scholars credit Batu with founding the first Sarai; Ibn Arabshah gives it to his brother Berke, the first Muslim khan. The first word is printed tht, read as takht, 'throne, capital'.

passages.headline: Sarai: sixty-three years from building to ruin
passages.gloss: Ibn Arabshah says Sarai drew so many scholars, men of letters and wits in a short time that no other city could match it, not even the great mosque of Cairo and its villages. He puts the whole life of the city, from its building to its ruin, at sixty-three years, and calls it one of the greatest and most populous of cities.
passages.quote: فصارت سراي بواسطة هؤلاء السادات مجمع العلم ومعدن السعادات … وبين بنيان سراي وخرابها من الامكنه ثلاث وستون سنه وكانت من اعظم المدن وضعا واكثرها للخلق جمعا
passages.translation: So Sarai, through these masters, became a gathering place of learning and a mine of good fortune … Between the building of Sarai and its ruin there were sixty-three years; and it was one of the greatest of cities in layout and the most crowded with people.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this print is garbled); vowel marks and the asterisk dividers of the rhymed prose omitted
passages.speaker: Ahmad ibn Arabshah (Arabic text, print catalogued 1842)
passages.caution: The sixty-three-year span is Ibn Arabshah's own reckoning; the city's history was longer and more complex.

passages.headline: The runaway slave who hid in Sarai for ten years
passages.gloss: To show how vast Sarai was, Ibn Arabshah tells a story: a slave ran away from one of the city's notables, opened a shop in an out-of-the-way street and made his living there for about ten years, and in all that time his master never came across him or saw him.
passages.quote: حكي ان رجلا من اعيانها هرب له رقيق في مكان منحي عن الطريق وفتح له حانوتا يتسبب فيه ويحصل له قوتا واستمر ذلك الحين نحوا من عشر سنين لم يصادفه فيه مولاه ولا اجتمع به ولا رآه وذلك لعظمها وكثرة اممها
passages.translation: It is told that a slave of one of its notables ran away to a spot off the main road, opened a shop there, traded in it and earned his living; this went on for about ten years, and his master never came upon him there, nor met him, nor saw him, because of the city's size and the multitude of its peoples.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this print is garbled); vowel marks and the asterisk dividers of the rhymed prose omitted
passages.speaker: Ahmad ibn Arabshah (Arabic text, print catalogued 1842)
passages.caution: A 'they say' anecdote, told to make a point about size, not a checked fact.

passages.headline: Timur tears down Sarai, Saraichuk and Astrakhan
passages.place: Sarai, Saraichuk and Astrakhan (lower Volga and Ural)
passages.gloss: After defeating Toqtamish, Timur's raiders reached Azaq (Azov), and he destroyed Sarai, Saraichuk and Hajji Tarkhan (Astrakhan) and the surrounding lands. The line is short, but it records in plain words that the Golden Horde's cities were destroyed by Timur, not lost to any natural catastrophe.
passages.quote: من الاموال والاسرى والمتاع ووصلت طراشته الى ازاق وهدم سراي وسرايجوق وحاجي ترخان وتلك الآفاق
passages.translation: … of wealth, captives and goods; his raiding parties reached Azaq, and he demolished Sarai, Saraichuk and Hajji Tarkhan and those regions.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this print is garbled); vowel marks and the asterisk dividers of the rhymed prose omitted
passages.speaker: Ahmad ibn Arabshah (Arabic text, print catalogued 1842)
passages.caution: Ibn Arabshah was a child in Damascus in 1395; he learned this from others, later.

passages.headline: The craftsmen of Damascus marched off to Samarkand
passages.people: Timur's army and the craftsmen of Damascus
passages.gloss: When Timur took Damascus in 1401, Ibn Arabshah says he carried off its learned men and craftsmen, 'everyone skilled in any art': weavers, tailors, stone-cutters, carpenters, cap-makers, farriers, tent-makers, painters and decorators, bow-makers and falconers. They were shared out among the army commanders, who were ordered to deliver them to Samarkand. Ibn Arabshah, then a boy, was himself taken from Damascus to Samarkand.
passages.quote: واخذ من دمشق ارباب الفضل واهل الصنائع وكل ماهر في فن من الفنون بارع من النساجين والخياطين والحجارين والنجارين والاقباعية والبياطرة والخيميه والنقاشين والقواسين والبازداريه وفي الجملة اهل اي فن كان … وفرق هؤلاء الطوائف على رؤوس الجند وامرهم ان يوصلوهم الى سمرقند
passages.translation: He took from Damascus the men of learning and the craftsmen, everyone skilled and outstanding in any art: weavers and tailors, stone-cutters and carpenters, cap-makers and farriers, tent-makers, painters and bow-makers, and falconers; in short, the people of every craft whatever … He divided these groups among the heads of the army and ordered them to deliver them to Samarkand.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this print is garbled); vowel marks and the asterisk dividers of the rhymed prose omitted
passages.speaker: Ahmad ibn Arabshah (Arabic text, print catalogued 1842)
passages.caution: Ibn Arabshah was among the captives, but wrote some thirty years later and with deep hostility to Timur.

passages.headline: A marble mosque for Samarkand, and a builder dragged to death
passages.gloss: Timur had seen a mosque of white marble in India and wanted one like it in Samarkand. Ibn Arabshah says he ordered solid marble to be quarried and put a man named Muhammad Jald in charge, who raised four minarets and outdid the master builders. When Timur came back from campaign and looked at the mosque, he had Muhammad Jald thrown on his face, his feet tied, and dragged until he was torn to pieces.
passages.quote: وان يقطع له احجار من المرمر الصلد وفوض امره الى رجل يقال له محمد جلد … فلما آب من سفرته وتفقد ما حدث في غيبته توجه الى الجامع لينظر اليه فبمجرد ما وقع نظره عليه امر بمحمد جلد فالقوه على وجهه وربطوا رجليه ولا زالوا يجرونه وعلى وجهه يسحبونه حتى بضعوه
passages.translation: … and that blocks of solid marble be cut for it; and he entrusted the work to a man called Muhammad Jald … When he returned from his journey and inspected what had been done in his absence, he went to the mosque to look at it; the moment his eye fell on it, he gave orders about Muhammad Jald, and they threw him on his face, tied his feet, and kept dragging him on his face until they had cut him to pieces.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this print is garbled); vowel marks and the asterisk dividers of the rhymed prose omitted
passages.speaker: Ahmad ibn Arabshah (Arabic text, print catalogued 1842)
passages.caution: A hostile anecdote about the building of Timur's great mosque in Samarkand; the cruelty may be exaggerated.

passages.headline: Chinggis Khan's law set above Islam
passages.place: Transoxiana, the Dasht, Cathay and Turkestan
passages.people: Timur, the Chaghatay, the people of the Dasht (Golden Horde Tatars)
passages.gloss: Ibn Arabshah says Timur spoke Persian, Turkish and Mongol but no Arabic, and held to the 'Chinggis Khan rules' (the yasa), treating them like branches of Islamic law. So, he says, did all the Chaghatay, the people of the Dasht, Cathay and Turkestan, whom he calls rabble. For this reason, he adds, leading jurists declared Timur an unbeliever.
passages.quote: وكان معتقدا للقواعد الجنكيزخانيه وهي كفروع الفقه من الملة الاسلاميه … وكذلك كل الجغتاي واهل الدشت والخطا وتركستان اولئك الطغام كلهم يمشون قواعد الملعون جنكيزخان على قواعد الاسلام
passages.translation: He held to the rules of Chinggis Khan, which are like the branches of jurisprudence in the Islamic faith … And so do all the Chaghatay and the people of the Dasht, Cathay and Turkestan, that rabble: all of them put the rules of the accursed Chinggis Khan ahead of the rules of Islam.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this print is garbled); vowel marks and the asterisk dividers of the rhymed prose omitted
passages.speaker: Ahmad ibn Arabshah (Arabic text, print catalogued 1842)
passages.caution: Religious polemic. It shows that Chinggisid law still mattered in Muslim Central Asia c.1400, but the tone is hostile.

passages.headline: 'Where would the rabble Tatars learn the sword?'
passages.people: Tatars of the Golden Horde (Toqtamish's army), as seen by the Ottomans
passages.gloss: Ibn Arabshah gives the Ottoman sultan Bayezid a furious reply to Timur's letter. Bayezid scorns the idea that he is like 'the Tatars of the Dasht' and says Toqtamish's army was mostly treacherous: the rabble Tatars, he says, have no skill with the sharp sword and nothing but volleys of arrows, unlike the lions of Rum.
passages.quote: واما توقتاميش خان فان غالب عسكره خان ومن اين للتتار الطغام الضرب بالبتار الحسام وما لهم سوى رشق السهام بخلاف ضراغم الاروام
passages.translation: As for Toqtamish Khan, most of his army betrayed him; and where would the rabble Tatars get striking with the keen, cutting sword? They have nothing but the showering of arrows, unlike the lions of Rum.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this print is garbled); vowel marks and the asterisk dividers of the rhymed prose omitted
passages.speaker: Ahmad ibn Arabshah, putting words in the mouth of the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I
passages.caution: A speech composed by Ibn Arabshah for Bayezid, not a record of real words; useful for how the name Tatar was used as an insult.

passages.headline: Breath that froze on the beard
passages.gloss: On Timur's last march toward China, Ibn Arabshah describes a winter so cold that a man's breath froze on his moustache and beard, and spittle turned to a frozen pellet before it hit the ground. It is a set piece of rhymed prose about the winter in which Timur died at Otrar.
passages.quote: وكان الرجل اذا تنفس جمدت انفاسه على سباله ولحيته … وان لفظ من فيه نخامة لا تصل الى الارض مع ما فيها من الحرارة الا وهي بندقة جامدة
passages.translation: When a man breathed out, his breath froze on his moustache and beard … and if he spat phlegm from his mouth, for all its warmth it did not reach the ground except as a frozen pellet.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this print is garbled); vowel marks and the asterisk dividers of the rhymed prose omitted
passages.speaker: Ahmad ibn Arabshah (Arabic text, print catalogued 1842)
passages.caution: Literary exaggeration; Ibn Arabshah was not on the campaign.

passages.headline: Bahcesaray: a city of red-tiled houses in a gorge
passages.gloss: Evliya describes the Crimean khans' capital as a great city lying in a wide gorge between two cliffs, about eight thousand paces long. The Churuk Su stream runs through the middle, crossed by forty-three stone and timber bridges. On both sides, storey above storey, stand masonry houses roofed with red tiles and set in gardens, climbing to the foot of the cliffs.
passages.quote: بوشهرك تا اورتاسنده کی جریان ایدن صلاجق نهرندن ... و بو چوروك صو اوزرنده شهرك ایچنده قرق اوچ یرده طاش واغاج جسرلرله شهرك بریاندن بریانته کچیلوب بوشهرك یمین ویسارنده قات اندرقات تحتانی وفوقانی جمله کارکیر بنالی وسراپا لعل کون قرمزی کیره‌مت اورتولی
passages.translation: Through the very middle of the city runs the Salachik stream … and over this Churuk Su, inside the city, one crosses from one side to the other at forty-three places by stone and timber bridges; and to right and left of the city, storey upon storey, lower and upper, all are masonry buildings roofed from end to end with ruby-red tiles.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR is partly garbled); bracketed variant markers omitted
passages.speaker: Evliya Celebi (Ottoman text, Istanbul 1928, vol. 7)
passages.caution: Evliya visited in 1666; his figures (bridges, houses) are typically inflated. Crimean Tatars here are settled townspeople, not nomads.

passages.headline: The khan's palace: stone walls and iron gates
passages.gloss: Evliya's tour of the Crimean khan's palace (the Khan Saray) says it is surrounded on all four sides by gardens, like a fortress, with walls of masonry cut stone but no battlements or ramparts. It has four strong iron gates, a mint, kitchens, a garden gate and the harem gate guarded by black eunuchs, and many storeyed pavilions and halls, each built by a different khan.
passages.quote: اولا بوسرای دلکشانك جانب اربعه‌سی باغ ارملر اولدوغیچون باغچه‌سرایدر جانب اربعه‌سی قلعه‌مثال چارکوشه شدادی مثال کارکیر طاش بنا دیوارلی سرای خاص الخاصدر امابو سرایك اطرافنده دندان بدنلری وقلعه یصدقلری یوقدر ... جمله درت یرده قوی ومتین دمیر قپولری واردر
passages.translation: First: because this heart-delighting palace has gardens like Iram on all four sides, it is a garden palace (bagche saray). On all four sides it is a most private palace with walls of masonry cut stone, square like a fortress, like the palace of Shaddad; but around this palace there are no battlements or ramparts … It has strong, solid iron gates in four places in all.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR is partly garbled); bracketed variant markers omitted
passages.speaker: Evliya Celebi (Ottoman text, Istanbul 1928, vol. 7)
passages.caution: The palace he saw was largely rebuilt after a Russian fire in 1736; this is one of the fullest early descriptions.

passages.headline: How Bahcesaray was founded, 'as the Tatar historians say'
passages.gloss: Evliya reports the Crimean Tatars' own story of their origins: the first conquerors of Crimea settled at Eski Yurt near Salachik, coming from Mahan, Ahlat, Kerman and Yesu, and from Kazan, Astrakhan and Sarai. As the Tatars multiplied and the old site grew too small, they settled at Bahcesaray and spread over the whole peninsula, while the 'Genoese infidels' stayed in their seaside fortresses. He names Jochi Khan and 'Artogmuz Khan' as the conquerors behind its first building.
passages.quote: قوم تاتارك مورخلری قوللری اوزره ابتدا فاتح قریم اسکی صلاجق یوردنده ساکن اولوب ماهان واخلاط وکرمان ویسو شهرلرندن وقازان واژدرخان وسرای اولکه‌لرندن قریمه تاتارلر کله‌رك تناسل بوله‌راق اسکی یورده صغمیوب بوباغچه سرای یوردنده توطن ایدوب
passages.translation: According to the Tatar historians, the first conqueror of Crimea settled at the Eski Salachik yurt; Tatars came to Crimea from the cities of Mahan, Ahlat, Kerman and Yesu and from the lands of Kazan, Astrakhan and Sarai, and as they multiplied they no longer fitted into the old yurt, and settled at this Bahcesaray site.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR is partly garbled); bracketed variant markers omitted
passages.speaker: Evliya Celebi (Ottoman text, Istanbul 1928, vol. 7)
passages.caution: A local origin tradition, retold with Evliya's own additions; it links Crimea to Kazan, Astrakhan and the Golden Horde capital Sarai.

passages.headline: The slave market at Karasu
passages.people: Crimean Tatars and captives (Russians, Circassians, Abkhaz)
passages.gloss: Evliya describes a great slave market beside the walls of Shirin Bey's khan at Karasubazar, where mothers were sold away from sons and brothers from sisters amid weeping. He calls the traders a merciless people, cursed in a saying as 'sellers of men', and warns buyers about the tricks of dealers and midwives. The Crimean economy rested heavily on captives taken in raids.
passages.quote: وبیوك جسر باشنده بر واسع میدانده شیرین بکی خانك دیواری دبنده بر عظیم اسیر بازاری دورر بو دخی بر عبرت نما بازار نحوستدرکم حقلرنده ( بایع البشر وقاطع الشجر وخارق الحجر لعن الله فی الدنیا والآخرة ) ... دینلمش اسیرجی قوملریدر زیرا بوقوم زیاده‌سیله بی‌رحم قومدرلر
passages.translation: At the head of the great bridge, in a wide square below the wall of Shirin Bey's khan, there is a huge slave market; this too is an ill-omened market, a lesson to behold, for of them it is said: 'The seller of men, the cutter of trees and the breaker of stone, God curse him in this world and the next' … They are slave-dealing peoples, for this people is exceedingly merciless.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR is partly garbled); bracketed variant markers omitted
passages.speaker: Evliya Celebi (Ottoman text, Istanbul 1928, vol. 7)
passages.caution: Evliya was himself a slave-owner and took captives on raids; he condemns the dealers, not the institution.

passages.headline: Horsemeat, mare's milk and 'no lies' among the Sarai Tatars
passages.people: Nogay and other Tatars of the Volga (the 'Sarai Tatars')
passages.gloss: On the Tatars around old Sarai, Evliya writes that they love horseflesh above all, some boiling it and some eating it raw with the blood running, and drink boza, kumiss (mare's milk) and camel's milk. He claims they know no backbiting, slander or lies, since they fear no one. All these Tatars are desert-dwellers who move with their camel-carts, and they became Muslims (Hanafi and Shafi'i) after Chinggis Khan.
passages.quote: همان جمله‌سی زیاده محبت اتدکلری آت اتیدر ونیجه قبیله‌سی آت اتن بشررلر ونیجه قبیله‌سی قانی آقیده آقیده اتی چیك یرلر صو یرینه بوزا وآت سودی قمزی ودوه سودی ایچرلر ... وجمله تاتار صحرا نشینلردر دوه عربه‌لریله بنوب کوچرلر
passages.translation: What all of them love most is horse meat: many tribes cook horse meat, and many tribes eat the meat raw with the blood running. Instead of water they drink boza, mare's-milk kumiss and camel's milk … and all the Tatars are desert-dwellers; they mount their camel-carts and migrate.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR is partly garbled); bracketed variant markers omitted
passages.speaker: Evliya Celebi (Ottoman text, Istanbul 1928, vol. 7)
passages.caution: Mixes observation with stock claims; Evliya's Volga journey is thought partly invented or exaggerated.

passages.headline: Sarai in 1666: nine thousand reed-roofed houses under Moscow
passages.people: Tatars of Sarai under Muscovite rule
passages.gloss: Evliya says the Sarai of his day was a city full of all kinds of Tatars, now in Muscovite hands. Half the subjects and soldiers were Muslim Kazan Tatars ('Hashdek') and half Muscovite Christians. The town had about nine thousand wretched houses of planks, rushes and reeds and seven monasteries. He names Nogay, Yaman, Teb and Yishdak Tatars living there as subjects of Moscow since its conquest.
passages.quote: ( دربیان عمارت شهر سرای ) جمله طقوز بیك تخته وساز وقامش ایله مستور خانهٔ منحوسلردر جمله یدی عدد دیر معظملر واردر ... حالا بو سرای شهری قوم تاتارك اجناسیله مملو بر شهردر
passages.translation: (On the buildings of the city of Sarai.) In all there are nine thousand wretched houses covered with planks, rushes and reeds, and there are seven great monasteries in all … Today this city of Sarai is a city filled with every kind of Tatar people.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR is partly garbled); bracketed variant markers omitted
passages.speaker: Evliya Celebi (Ottoman text, Istanbul 1928, vol. 7)
passages.caution: Evliya's Volga itinerary is doubted by modern scholars; which town he calls Sarai is unclear, since the Golden Horde capital had long been in ruins.

passages.headline: Kazan: stone ruins of a Tatar capital, now Muscovite
passages.people: Kazan Tatars ('Hashdek') and Nogays under Muscovite rule
passages.gloss: Evliya calls Kazan a former throne city of Chinggis Khan's line, now 'an ill-fated capital in Muscovite hands'. He says thousands of khans (caravanserais), mosques, madrasas, baths and shops lie as domed and arched ruins, while people now live in some three thousand houses roofed with rushes and reeds, with twenty churches and seven mosques for the many Nogay and Hashdek Muslims.
passages.quote: ماتقدم بودخی جنقیز خانك تخت‌گاهی ایمش نیجه ملوکدن ملوکه قالمش حالا دست مسقوده بر دارالملك منحوس اولمش نیجه بیك عدد خان وجامع وعمارت ومسجد ومدرسه وتکیه وحمام ودکاکینلر وبزازستانلرك قبابلری وطاق کسرالری وقلعه‌لری رایکان دورور ... حالا اوچ بیك قدر صاز وقامش اورتولی اولری
passages.translation: Formerly this too was the throne city of Chinggis Khan, passing from king to king; now in Muscovite hands it has become an ill-fated capital. The domes and Chosroes-like arches and fortresses of many thousands of khans, great mosques, charitable foundations, mosques, madrasas, dervish lodges, baths, shops and cloth-halls stand abandoned … Today there are some three thousand houses roofed with rushes and reeds.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR is partly garbled); bracketed variant markers omitted
passages.speaker: Evliya Celebi (Ottoman text, Istanbul 1928, vol. 7)
passages.caution: Scholars doubt that Evliya reached Kazan; the description may rest on hearsay. The picture of stone Islamic buildings left as ruins after the Russian conquest (1552) is striking either way.

passages.headline: Astrakhan: Tatar nomads outside, reed houses inside
passages.people: Astrakhan Tatars and Nogays under Muscovite rule
passages.gloss: Evliya says thousands of Astrakhan Tatars live outside the city along the Volga in their oba (tent camps), moving like the Nogays, and adds the local legend that the name comes from a dragon (azhder) that ravaged the country until a khan killed it. Inside the walls he counts monasteries, churches and a thousand-odd reed-roofed houses, and in the outer town thirteen thousand houses roofed with reeds and earth and seven mosques.
passages.quote: نیجه بیکی شهر خارجنده نهر ادل کنارنده اوبالر ایله ساکن اولورلر بونلرك دخی اصلی تاتاردر همان نوغای کبی اوبالریله قنوب کوچرلر ... زمان قدیمده بوشهر خراب یاتوب بونده براژدرها توره‌یوب ... بعده برخان بهادر بواژدرهایی قتل ایدوب ولایت امن وامان اولدوغیچون بودیاره اژدرخان دیرلر
passages.translation: Many thousands of them live outside the city on the bank of the Volga in their tent-camps; these too are Tatars by origin, and like the Nogays they camp and move with their obas … In ancient times this city lay in ruins, and a dragon was born here … then a heroic khan killed this dragon, and because the land became safe they call this country Azhder-khan.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR is partly garbled); bracketed variant markers omitted
passages.speaker: Evliya Celebi (Ottoman text, Istanbul 1928, vol. 7)
passages.caution: The dragon etymology is folk legend (the name comes from Hajji Tarkhan). Evliya's presence in Astrakhan is doubted by some scholars.

passages.headline: Kalmyks who live in houses on carts
passages.gloss: Evliya says the Kalmyks have no fleas, lice, bedbugs, snakes, scorpions or tarantulas among them, because their round houses stand on carts and they live on the open steppe. He then begins his description of their appearance: small eyes, said to come from the salt mines of the region.
passages.quote: وبونلرده اصلا پیره وکهله وتخته بتی ویلان وچیان وعقرب اولمز زیرا درم اولری عربه‌لر اوزره اولوب صحرا نشینلردر
passages.translation: Among them there are no fleas, lice, bedbugs, snakes, tarantulas or scorpions at all, because their round houses are on carts and they are desert-dwellers.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR is partly garbled); bracketed variant markers omitted
passages.speaker: Evliya Celebi (Ottoman text, Istanbul 1928, vol. 7)
passages.caution: The link between cart-houses and the absence of vermin is Evliya's own explanation. 'Kalmyk' here means Oirat Mongols recently arrived on the Volga, whom he treats as a kind of Tatar.

passages.headline: The Kalmyk 'Kaaba' and Alexander's wall
passages.place: Beyond the Kalmyk steppe (unspecified, far east)
passages.gloss: Evliya records what Kalmyks told him about a domed shrine they call their Kaaba, far to the east beyond a sea of ice. He adds his own learned gloss: Alexander built the Wall of Gog and Magog from every kind of metal, the mountains the Kalmyks call the Yildirak Dag, then built this dome with ancient sages and hid his treasures in it. On a following page Kalmyk elders say their ancestors died from a deafening noise behind the metal mountains.
passages.quote: سد اسکندر داغلرن جمیع معادنلردن بنا ایدوب قوم قالمغك ( یلدراق داغ ) دیدکلری سد یأجوجدر بعده اسکندر بونلرك کعبه دیدکلری قبه‌یی بنا ایدوب
passages.translation: [Alexander] built the Barrier of Alexander, the mountains, out of every kind of metal; it is the Barrier of Gog, which the Kalmyk people call the 'Yildirak Dag' [the glittering mountain]; afterwards Alexander built the dome which they call their Kaaba.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR is partly garbled); bracketed variant markers omitted
passages.speaker: Evliya Celebi (Ottoman text, Istanbul 1928, vol. 7)
passages.caution: Evliya's modern editor adds a long note calling the story an invention; it mixes Kalmyk (Buddhist) pilgrimage tales with Islamic Alexander legend.

passages.headline: Kalmyks and the hadith of the Turks
passages.gloss: Evliya lists the many spellings of the Kalmyk name and says all historians call them the 'yellow folk' (Bani Asfar). He applies to them a hadith about God's soldiers in the east 'whose name is Turk'. He adds that twenty years earlier the Kalmyks were not on this steppe and 140 Nogay tribes grazed it, sending butter to Taman to be sold cheaply in Istanbul; when the Kalmyks arrived the Nogays were routed and butter became dear.
passages.quote: قالمق وقالماق وقلماق وقلماخ وقلماغ جمیع مورخان بونلره بنی عصفر قومی درلر ... حتی بوقالمق قومی یکرمی سنه مقدم بوهیهات صحراسنده وجودلری اولمیوب جمله نوغای قومنك یوز قرق عدد قبیله‌لری صحرای هیهاتده قنوب کوچوب
passages.translation: Kalmuk, Kalmak, Kalmaq, Kalmakh and Kalmagh: all the historians call them the people of Bani Asfar [the 'yellow folk'] … Indeed, twenty years ago this Kalmyk people were not present on this vast steppe, and all the hundred and forty tribes of the Nogay people camped and migrated on the open steppe.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR is partly garbled); bracketed variant markers omitted
passages.speaker: Evliya Celebi (Ottoman text, Istanbul 1928, vol. 7)
passages.caution: The print reads 'Bani Asfar' with a misprint noted by the editor. The dating of the Kalmyk arrival is roughly right (1630s); the religious framing is Evliya's.

passages.headline: Mongol and Tatar: twin sons, and a name that swallowed the rest
passages.gloss: Katib Celebi tells the Islamic-Persian genealogy: the children of Turk son of Japheth spread over Turkestan, most of them nomads living in tents. Later Alinja Khan had twin sons, Mongol and Tatar, who divided the kingdom, so two clans arose. Eight Tatar rulers reigned before their line died out, and the Mongol line followed. Then comes a clear statement of the naming problem: 'Mongol' became a generic name for many tribes, so that by extension people say 'Turk', 'Tatar' and 'Mongol' for all of them, although the Mongols were really one kind of Turk.
passages.quote: مزبور بطن واحددن ایکی اوغلی اولدی بری مغول و بری تاتار تسمیه اولنوب جمله مملکتنی بو ایکی اوغلی بیننده تقسیم ایلدی ... نیجه قبایل واقوامه لفظ مزبور اسم جنس اولمشدر انلردن اولمینه دخی مجاز طریقیله اطلاق وتعمیم ایدوب ترك وتاتار ومغول دیرلر لکن حقیقتده مغول ترکدن برصنف ایدی
passages.translation: From one womb he had two sons, one named Mongol and the other Tatar, and he divided his whole kingdom between these two sons … The said word became a generic name for many tribes and peoples, and it is applied by extension even to those who are not of them, so they say Turk and Tatar and Mongol; but in truth the Mongols were one kind of Turk.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this facsimile is garbled)
passages.speaker: Katib Celebi, Cihannuma (Muteferrika print, Istanbul 1732)
passages.caution: A legendary genealogy from Persian and Chaghatay histories (Abu'l-Ghazi's tradition); the observation about names is Katib Celebi's own.

passages.headline: 'Tartarestan', says Lorenzo: from the river Tartar
passages.place: Inner Asia beyond the Imaus mountains
passages.gloss: Here Katib Celebi reports what the European geographer he calls 'Lorenzo' wrote: the second part of Asia, beyond the Imaus mountains, is Tatarestan (Tartary). Its people are Mongol Tatars who have spread over most of Asia. Their origin is a river named Tatar, from which they took their name, and they were formerly known as Mongols. He is translating a European atlas (Mercator-Hondius), so this is the European 'Tartary' coming back into an Ottoman book.
passages.quote: قسم ثانی که ایماوس طاغلرندن اوته اولان تاتارستاندر لورنسو تحریری اوزره انلر مغول تاتارلری اولوب آسیانك اکثرینه یایلدیلر ... بونلر تاتار اصلیدرکه تاتار نام ارماقدن اسم اخذ ایتدیلر ومونغال دیمکله معروف یرکه
passages.translation: The second part, which lies beyond the Imaus mountains, is Tatarestan. According to Lorenzo's account, they are Mongol Tatars who spread over most of Asia … These are the original Tatars, who took their name from a river called Tatar, and were known by the name Mongal.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this facsimile is garbled)
passages.speaker: Katib Celebi, Cihannuma (Muteferrika print, Istanbul 1732)
passages.caution: Second-hand from European atlases; the 'river Tatar' etymology comes from medieval European writers, not steppe tradition. 'Lorenzo' may be a Latin atlas author as rendered by Katib Celebi's translator.

passages.headline: 'Like wind and water': Katib Celebi on the Tatar character
passages.gloss: Continuing from the European source, Katib Celebi describes the Tatars as steel-natured among mankind, restless as wind and water, with the strength of Ahriman and the might of demons. They roam the deserts like the wind; they neither eat bread nor build houses, their horses need neither shoes nor nails, and they cross rivers by swimming. It is the classic European literary picture of the steppe nomad, translated into Ottoman.
passages.quote: واوصاف تاتار بوقوم بنی نوع انسان میانه‌ده پولاد نهادلر وآب وباد کبی طبیعتلری حرکته معتاد اهرمن قوت ودیو زورلو ... ایل کبی یلرلر نه کندولر یورولور نه اتلری درلر بندکلری آته نه نعل حاجت نه میخ
passages.translation: Qualities of the Tatars: this people are of steel nature among mankind, and like water and wind their nature is used to motion; they have the strength of Ahriman and the power of demons … they run like the wind; neither do they tire nor do their horses; the horses they ride need neither shoe nor nail.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this facsimile is garbled)
passages.speaker: Katib Celebi, Cihannuma (Muteferrika print, Istanbul 1732)
passages.caution: A stereotype copied from European books, not observation; a few words at the line breaks are uncertain in the print.

passages.headline: Siberia, the Nogays and a coin-minting town on the Irtysh
passages.people: Nogay Tatars, Siberian Tatars ('Kesellu' Tatars), Bulghars
passages.gloss: Following 'Lorenzo' again, the Cihannuma says the Nogay Tatars are subject to the Crimean khans, that north of them lived the Bulghars, and north of the Bulghars lies the land of Siberia, mostly forest, where some Nogay Tatars live. There is a town there called Hanam, very prosperous and famous for trade, where jewels are sold, and Tatars of Cathay and Muscovites gather to trade. It gives an Ottoman reader a Siberia of towns and markets, not an empty waste.
passages.quote: بولغار قومندن شماله سیبریا اولکه‌سی دوشر اکثری اورمانلقدر ونوغای تاتارلرینك بعضی انده ساکن اولورلر وهمه خانام برشهرلری وار غایت معمور وتجارتله مشهوردر
passages.translation: North of the Bulghar people lies the land of Siberia; most of it is forest, and some of the Nogay Tatars live there. They have a city called Hanam, very prosperous and famous for trade.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this facsimile is garbled)
passages.speaker: Katib Celebi, Cihannuma (Muteferrika print, Istanbul 1732)
passages.caution: Compiled from European atlases; the town names are garbled forms of names on Western maps.

passages.headline: A khan who built a hundred mosques
passages.gloss: Halim Giray credits Khan Sahib Giray with building a mosque and a bathhouse beside the khan's palace in Bakhchysarai, and about a hundred mosques in other districts. The editor's footnote on the page before adds madrasas, shops, double bathhouses and the fortress at Or Qapi (Perekop) that guarded the isthmus. The builders named are the Tatar khans themselves, and the buildings are ordinary Islamic ones: mosque, bath, madrasa, palace.
passages.quote: صاحب کرای ، باغچه سرای ده ، خان سرایی یاننده جامع ، حمام یاپدردیغی کبی سائر محللرده دخی یوز قدر مسجد بنا ایتمک صورتیله نامنی دنیاده خیر ایله یاد ایتدرمکه موفق اولمشدر .
passages.translation: Sahib Giray, just as he had a mosque and a bathhouse built beside the khan's palace in Bakhchysarai, also built about a hundred mosques in other quarters, and so succeeded in having his name remembered with blessing in the world.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this print is garbled)
passages.speaker: Halim Giray, Gulbun-i Hanan (main text of the Istanbul 1911 print)
passages.caution: Written about 260 years after the events from earlier chronicles; 'about a hundred' is a round figure.

passages.headline: Bakhchysarai: founded 1501, partly burned by the Russians
passages.gloss: An editor's note, citing a writer it calls Brzhinski, gives a short history of the khans' capital: its story begins in 1501, Greeks ('Rum') lived there before the Tatars came into Crimea, a Russian army burned about a quarter of it in a war, and the khans' first palace was at Salacik nearby. The note goes on to say that the one old monument left there is the tomb by the monastery gate, rebuilt in 1510 by Mengli Giray in his father's name. So the town is presented as a dated foundation of the Giray khans on a site with earlier Greek inhabitants.
passages.quote: باغچه سرای تاریخی ( ١٥٠١ ) سنه سندن باشلار . تاتار قریمه کیرمه دن اول اوراده ( روم ) لر واردی . باغچه سرایک ( ١٧٨٦ ) ده روسلرله اولان محاربه ده ، همان ربعی یانمشدر . قریم خانلرینک ایلک سرایی صلاجقده در .
passages.translation: The history of Bakhchysarai begins in the year 1501. Before the Tatars entered Crimea, there were Greeks (Rum) there. In the war with the Russians in (1786), about a quarter of Bakhchysarai burned. The first palace of the Crimean khans is at Salacik.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this print is garbled)
passages.speaker: Editorial footnote in the Istanbul 1911 print of Halim Giray's Gulbun-i Hanan, quoting a writer it names as Brzhinski
passages.caution: The printed '1786' is very likely a misprint for 1736, when a Russian army under Munnich burned Bakhchysarai; Crimea was already Russian in 1786. This is the 1911 editor's note, not Halim Giray.

passages.headline: 'The Tatar peoples' in the 1774 treaty: free, and ruled by Genghis's line
passages.people: Crimean Tatars and Nogays (Budjak, Kuban, Yedisan, Jamboyluk, Yedichkul)
passages.gloss: The 1911 editor prints Article 3 of the Kucuk Kaynarca treaty between Russia and the Ottomans. It lists the 'Tatar peoples' by name, the Crimeans and the Nogay hordes of Budjak, Kuban, Yedisan, Jamboyluk and Yedichkul, and declares them independent, governed by khans of 'the line of Genghis' chosen by the Tatars themselves. Here 'Tatar' is a legal and diplomatic name for real, named peoples north of the Black Sea, and their rulers claim descent from the Mongol conqueror.
passages.quote: قریم وبوجاق وقوبان ویدیسان وجانبویلق ویدیچقول قبائل وبالجمله طوائف تاتار بلا استثنا دولتین طرفندن سربستیت وبغیر تعلق مستقل وجوهله اجنبی بر دولته تابع اولمامق اوزره اعتراف وقبول اولنه لر . طوائف تاتار بالجمله رأی واتفاقلریله آل جنکیز صویندن انتخاب و نصب اولنان کندی خانلری …
passages.translation: The tribes of Crimea, Budjak, Kuban, Yedisan, Jamboyluk and Yedichkul, and all the Tatar peoples without exception, shall be recognised and accepted by the two states as free and entirely independent, subject to no foreign state. Their own khans, elected and installed from the line of Genghis by the common vote and agreement of all the Tatar peoples …
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this print is garbled)
passages.speaker: Editorial footnote in the Istanbul 1911 print of Halim Giray's Gulbun-i Hanan, giving the Ottoman text of Article 3 of the Kucuk Kaynarca treaty (1774)
passages.caution: An official treaty text reproduced by the 1911 editor; the 'independence' it granted was the first step to Russian annexation in 1783, as the main text goes on to say.

passages.headline: Circassian 'fault-fines' paid in goods and slaves
passages.gloss: During the khan's war with the Kabardians, the main text says the Circassians in the khan's own army secretly told the Kabardians to attack the Tatars by night and promised to change sides. A footnote explains a custom of the khanate's relations with the Circassians: when they committed an offence, they paid the khan a fine called 'ayiplik' in goods, slave girls and slaves. It shows tribute, law and the slave trade in the khanate's frontier politics.
passages.quote: چرکسلر بر قباحت ایشله دکلری زمان ( عیبلق ) نامیله خانلره قباحتلرینه کوره اموال ، جواری و کوله لر تقدیم ایدرلردی .
passages.translation: When the Circassians committed an offence, they used to present to the khans, under the name 'ayiplik' (fault-fine), goods, slave girls and slaves according to their offence.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this print is garbled)
passages.speaker: Editorial footnote in the Istanbul 1911 print of Halim Giray's Gulbun-i Hanan
passages.caution: An explanatory footnote in the 1911 print; the custom is described in general terms without a date.

passages.headline: In the Cumans' own language, 'Tatar' simply meant 'Turkic'
passages.gloss: Kuun's index of the Cuman words in the Codex gives the entry 'Tatar' as meaning 'a Turk' or 'Turkish', and the phrase 'tatar til' ('Tatar tongue') as meaning plain, sincere speech. So the merchants and friars who compiled the book heard the steppe people use 'Tatar' for their own Turkic language, not for a lost empire. The phrase occurs on page 229 of the Codex.
passages.quote: Tatar «Turca», «turcicus», tatar til «sermo sincerus» pag. 229.
passages.translation: Tatar: 'a Turk', 'Turkish'; tatar til: 'honest (plain) speech', page 229.
passages.speaker: Geza Kuun, Cuman word index to the Codex Cumanicus (1880)
passages.caution: Kuun's gloss of 'tatar til' as 'sermo sincerus' is his reading of a phrase in the German part of the Codex; later editors (Bang, Gronbech) revised many of his readings.

passages.headline: Hungarian hymns called the Cumans 'Tartars'
passages.gloss: Kuun shows how loosely the name was used in medieval Hungary. Hymns to St Ladislaus sometimes call the Cumans 'Tartars', and the chronicler Thuroczy says the chief of the Cumans whom King Stephen II took in (in 1129) was himself named Tatar.
