This is more than a century before the Mongol invasion of 1241, so 'Tatar' here is a personal name and a label for steppe Turks, not for the Mongols.
passages.quote: In antiquis hymnis latinis et hungaricis sancti Ladislai Cumani interdum Tartari nuncupantur … Thuroczy in suis Chronicis, Cumanorum a rege Stephano II in Hungariam receptorum summum ducem itidem Tatar nominat: «Rex autem Stephanus, diligebat Cumanos tunc temporis; quorum dux nomine Tatar, qui a cede imperatoris (Graecorum), cum paucis, ad regem fugerat»
passages.translation: In the old Latin and Hungarian hymns of St Ladislaus the Cumans are sometimes called Tartars … Thuroczy, in his Chronicle, likewise names the supreme chief of the Cumans received into Hungary by King Stephen II 'Tatar': 'King Stephen loved the Cumans at that time; their chief, named Tatar, had fled with a few men to the king from the slaughter by the (Greek) emperor'.
passages.speaker: Geza Kuun, Latin introduction to his edition of the Codex Cumanicus (Budapest 1880), quoting the Hungarian chronicler Janos Thuroczy (1488)
passages.caution: Kuun is assembling medieval Hungarian testimony; Thuroczy wrote in the 1480s about events of 1129.

passages.headline: Islam among the Cumans was called 'the Tartar rite'
passages.gloss: Kuun notes that Islam had spread among the Cumans and that later Latin church writers called their religion 'the Tartar rite'. He quotes John, deacon of Kukullo, saying that King Louis I of Hungary had the Cuman people, 'wrapped in the Tartar rite', converted to Catholicism. So in church Latin 'Tartar' could simply mean 'Muslim steppe people'.
passages.quote: Religio Muhammedanica … etiam apud Cumanos propagata fuit, eam Cumanorum religionem scriptores ecclesiastici latini posteriores «ritum tartaricum» nominabant, ita e. g. Joannes diaconus Küküllőiensis: «Hic etiam gentem Chomanorum, ritui Tartarico involutam … ad fidem Catholicam converti procuravit (scilicet Ludovicus I. rex Hungariae)»
passages.translation: The Muhammadan religion … spread also among the Cumans, and later Latin church writers called this religion of the Cumans 'the Tartar rite', for example John, deacon of Kukullo: 'He (namely Louis I, king of Hungary) also had the Cuman people, wrapped in the Tartar rite, converted to the Catholic faith'.
passages.quote_note: Checked against the page image; a dash in the printed quotation is replaced by an omission mark
passages.speaker: Geza Kuun, Latin introduction to his edition of the Codex Cumanicus (Budapest 1880), quoting John of Kukullo (14th century)
passages.caution: Kuun's statement that the Cumans were Muslims is his interpretation; many Cumans were pagan.

passages.headline: 'They have tents, you have castles and cities': a Mongol threat
passages.gloss: Kuun quotes a letter from a Mongol commander to King Bela IV of Hungary, brought back by the Dominican Friar Julian. The Mongol calls the Cumans who fled into Hungary 'our slaves' and warns the king: the Cumans live without houses and move about with tents, so they might escape, but a king who lives in houses and has castles and cities cannot. It is a clear contemporary statement of the difference between steppe tents and settled towns, seen from the Mongol side.
passages.quote: Facilius enim est Cumanis evadere quam tibi, quia illi sine domibus cum tentoriis ambulantes possunt forsitan evadere. Tu autem in domibus habitans habes castra et civitates, quomodo effugies manus meas?
passages.translation: For it is easier for the Cumans to escape than for you, because they, going about without houses, with tents, may perhaps escape. But you, living in houses, have castles and cities: how will you escape my hands?
passages.speaker: A Mongol commander's letter to King Bela IV (c.1237), as brought back by Friar Julian; quoted by Geza Kuun (1880)
passages.caution: The letter survives in Friar Julian's Latin report, so its wording is a translation; the original, Julian says, was in 'pagan letters and the Tartar tongue'.

passages.headline: The word for a dwelling was 'yurt'
passages.gloss: In the merchants' glossary the Latin word 'mansio' (dwelling, lodging) is given in Persian as 'manzel' and in Cuman as 'yurt'. Kuun adds that the word is widespread across the Turkic languages and compares the Mongol 'ger' (house). The steppe word for home and camp-place was the same word English later borrowed for the felt tent.
passages.quote: mansio manxel yurt … Vox late patens in dominio linguarum turcicae originis. Cf. mongolicum ger «domus», «habitatio»
passages.translation: dwelling (Latin) / manzel (Persian) / yurt (Cuman) … A word widespread in the domain of the languages of Turkic origin. Compare Mongolian ger, 'house', 'dwelling'.
passages.speaker: Codex Cumanicus, Latin-Persian-Cuman glossary (Italian part, dated 11 July 1303), ed. Geza Kuun 1880, with Kuun's footnote
passages.caution: A glossary entry, not a description; 'yurt' in Cuman meant a dwelling place or homeland rather than specifically a felt tent.

passages.headline: City, castle, palace: the merchants' town vocabulary
passages.gloss: The glossary gives, column by column, Latin, Persian and Cuman words for places. A city (civitas) is 'saar' or 'chent' in Cuman, a castle is 'kalaa', a palace is 'saray', and a house is 'eu' (ev). The words for city, castle and palace are loans from Persian and Arabic (shahr, qal'a, saray), next to the Turkic 'kent' and 'ev'. The Italian merchants clearly needed these words for dealing with towns in the Horde's lands.
passages.quote: ciuitas ghachar saar ul chent castrum kala kalaa casale de gala palacium saray saray domus ghana eu
passages.translation: city: (Persian) shahr / (Cuman) shahr or kent; castle: (Persian) qal'a / (Cuman) qal'a; village: (Persian) deh / (Cuman) qala; palace: saray / saray; house: (Persian) khana / (Cuman) ev.
passages.quote_note: Checked against the page image; 'ul' is the manuscript's abbreviation for Latin 'vel', 'or'
passages.speaker: Codex Cumanicus, Latin-Persian-Cuman glossary (Italian part, dated 11 July 1303), ed. Geza Kuun 1880
passages.caution: The modern equivalents in the translation are the usual identifications of these spellings; the scribe's spellings are Italian.

passages.headline: The court is the 'orda', the queen is the 'khatun'
passages.gloss: A page of ranks and offices shows how the Horde's court looked to Italian traders. Latin 'curia' (court) is Persian 'ordu' and Cuman 'orda', the word behind English 'horde'. An empress is 'khan khatun', a queen 'sultan khatun', a lord is 'bey' or 'khoja'. The khan's court, the orda, was the capital in the steppe.
passages.quote: dominus ghoya bey ul coia corona taz tagz curia ordu orda imperatris xen i padixa can catonj regina xen y patia soltan catonj
passages.translation: lord: (Persian) khwaja / (Cuman) bey or khoja; crown: taj / tagz; court: (Persian) ordu / (Cuman) orda; empress: (Persian) wife of the padishah / (Cuman) khan khatun; queen: (Persian) wife of the king / (Cuman) sultan khatun.
passages.quote_note: Checked against the page image; 'ul' stands for Latin 'vel', 'or'
passages.speaker: Codex Cumanicus, Latin-Persian-Cuman glossary (Italian part, dated 11 July 1303), ed. Geza Kuun 1880
passages.caution: A word list, so it shows the vocabulary the compilers needed, not a description of the court.

passages.headline: A friar goes to Sarai to learn the language
passages.people: Cumans in the Golden Horde capital
passages.gloss: Kuun cites the Franciscan Pascal of Vitoria, who in 1337 went to the 'ancient city of Sarai on the bank of the Volga' to learn Turkish among the Cumans and studied it there for a whole year. Sarai was the capital of the Golden Horde, and the story shows missionaries living in the Horde's own city.
passages.quote: Fra Pascal de Victoria anno 1337 in antiquam urbem Serai ad ripam Volgae, uti ipse ait, linguae turcicae ediscendae causa ad Cumanos contendit et illic per unum annum integrum studiis linguae quam maxime operam navabat.
passages.translation: Friar Pascal of Vitoria in 1337, as he himself says, hurried to the Cumans in the ancient city of Sarai on the bank of the Volga in order to learn the Turkish language, and there worked as hard as he could at the study of the language for one whole year.
passages.speaker: Geza Kuun, Latin introduction to his edition of the Codex Cumanicus (Budapest 1880), citing a letter of Pascal of Vitoria
passages.caution: Kuun paraphrases Pascal's letter; Pascal was killed in Central Asia in 1340.

passages.headline: A sorceress is a 'kam khatun', a shaman woman
passages.gloss: Under the verb 'to divine' the glossary gives the Cuman 'kamlik etermen', literally 'I do shamaning', and a later hand added 'incantatrix' (enchantress) as 'kam katun kisi', a shaman-woman. 'Kam' is the old Turkic word for a shaman. The steppe people living around the Italian colonies still had words for shamans and women diviners.
passages.quote: adiuino ram mecunem kamlik etermen ranzilic etarmen … incantatrix kam katun kisi dir
passages.translation: I divine: (Persian) ram mikunam / (Cuman) kamlik etermen, (also) ranzilik etermen … enchantress: she is a kam khatun person (a shaman woman).
passages.quote_note: Checked against the page image (the corpus OCR misreads 'kamlik' as 'kamhk')
passages.speaker: Codex Cumanicus, Latin-Persian-Cuman glossary (Italian part, dated 11 July 1303), ed. Geza Kuun 1880, entry for 'enchantress' added by a third hand
passages.caution: Kuun notes the 'incantatrix' line was added by a later hand.

passages.headline: The Lord's Prayer in the language of the Horde
passages.gloss: The German Franciscan part of the Codex contains Christian texts turned into Cuman for preaching. This is the start of the Lord's Prayer: 'Our father who art in heaven, blessed be thy kingdom, thy will be done as in heaven so on earth, give us this day our daily bread'. Elsewhere in the Codex the word for God is 'Tengri', the old Turkic name of the sky god, as Kuun's word index shows.
passages.quote: Atamis kim köctä sen. Algiszle bulsun senig hanlechin. bulsû senig tilemegin nezikkim kocta alley ierda. kundegi ötmackimisni bisga bugun bergil.
passages.translation: Our father who art in heaven. Blessed be thy kingdom (khanate). Thy will be done, as in heaven so on earth. Give us today our daily bread.
passages.speaker: Codex Cumanicus, German (Franciscan) part, c.1330 to 1340, ed. Geza Kuun 1880
passages.caution: A missionary translation, so it shows the language, not the beliefs of the people who spoke it. 'Kingdom' is rendered with the Turkic word for a khan's realm.

passages.headline: A riddle: 'like a white tent, with no door'
passages.gloss: The Codex preserves Cuman riddles, the oldest recorded Turkic riddles. This one runs: 'Like a white tent, it has no mouth. That is the egg.' Kuun reads 'akkoy' as 'ak ev', literally 'white house', and renders it 'the tent of a new bride'. The riddle draws on the everyday sight of a tent, the home of the people who told it.
passages.quote: [6,] akkoy mania avzu joh. ol jumurtka.
passages.translation: Like a white tent (ak ev), it has no mouth. That is the egg.
passages.speaker: Codex Cumanicus, German part (riddle 6), ed. Geza Kuun 1880
passages.caution: Kuun's footnote on the page explains 'akkoy' as 'ak ev', 'tentorium novae nuptae' (the tent of a new bride); the gloss depends on his reading.

passages.headline: One language and one script 'in all these kingdoms'
passages.people: Cumans and Tatars of the Golden Horde
passages.gloss: Kuun quotes a Franciscan missionary from the order's annals: he decided first to learn the language of the land, and 'by the grace of God' learned Cuman and the Uighur script, which were used in common 'throughout all these kingdoms'. It shows the Horde as a literate world with a shared Turkic language and an old Uighur script, not a land without writing.
passages.quote: Ego vero, consilio habito, prius volui linguam terrae addiscere, et per gratiam Dei addidici linguam Cumanicam et literaturam Uiguricam, qua quidem lingua et literatura utuntur communiter per omnia regna ista
passages.translation: But I, after taking counsel, wished first to learn the language of the land, and by the grace of God I learned the Cuman language and the Uighur script, which language and script are used in common throughout all these kingdoms.
passages.speaker: An anonymous Franciscan missionary, quoted by Geza Kuun (1880) from the annals of the Franciscan order
passages.caution: The missionary is not named on this page; Kuun cites the annals of the Friars Minor (Rome, vol. VII).

passages.headline: Inscribed Cuman tombstones in a Moravian church? The editor doubts it
passages.gloss: Kuun quotes the Czech Jesuit Bohuslav Balbin, who said that near Ivancice and the Oslavany convent there was a church whose floor was paved almost entirely with Cuman tombs and stones inscribed in their letters, 'as I saw myself'. Kuun says plainly that he hardly believes it. It is a good example of a striking claim reported and then doubted by the editor himself.
passages.quote: «Superest hodieque aliqua barbarorum memoria non procul Evanczicio et Oslovanensi Coenobio, insigne templum Christianorum, in quo plurima Cumanorum sepulchra et saxa litteris illorum incisa spectantur, quibus saxis totum fere Templi solum stratum est, ut ipse vidi.» Ceterum hanc Bohuslavi narrationem ego quidem vix veram esse putaverim.
passages.translation: 'There survives even today some memory of the barbarians not far from Ivancice and the Oslavany convent: a notable Christian church in which very many tombs of the Cumans and stones carved with their letters are to be seen, with which stones almost the whole floor of the church is paved, as I saw myself.' For my part I would hardly think this story of Bohuslav's true.
passages.speaker: Geza Kuun, Latin introduction to his edition of the Codex Cumanicus (Budapest 1880), quoting Bohuslav Balbin, Epitome historica rerum Bohemicarum (Prague 1677)
passages.caution: Balbin claims to have seen the stones; Kuun doubts it, and no such Cuman inscriptions are known.

passages.headline: 'The wanderer builds no farmsteads and no palaces'
passages.people: Turkic nomads of the Qarakhanid realm
passages.gloss: A line of the poem, quoted in Vambery's glossary under the word for 'nomad', says that the person who moves from place to place does not build farmsteads or palaces. The poet is contrasting nomad life with the settled court life of Kashgar, where palaces (saray) were built. It is an eleventh-century Turkic writer's own view that nomads and palace-builders were different ways of living.
passages.quote: köcükli kisi etmes urtu saraj. Der von einem Orte zum andern ziehet, bauet keine Gehöfte und Schlösser. (87)
passages.translation: köchükli kishi etmes urtu saray: he who moves from one place to another builds no farmsteads and no palaces. (chapter 87)
passages.speaker: Yusuf Khass Hajib, Kutadgu Bilig (1069 to 1070), verse quoted with German translation in Vambery's glossary (1870)
passages.caution: A moral saying about the uncertainty of worldly life rather than an ethnographic report; Vambery's readings are now outdated (Arat 1947).

passages.headline: Herdsmen give kumis, milk, wool and cheese
passages.people: Turkic herders of the Qarakhanid realm
passages.gloss: The poem's chapter on how a ruler should treat the keepers of the horse herds lists what they provide: food, drink and horses to ride, and kumis (fermented mare's milk), milk, wool, butter, sour milk and cheese, food and clothing and coarse wool for ropes. The poet calls them useful and honest but 'without knowledge', people from whom a prince should not expect law or manners. It is a courtier's view of the herding life that fed the court.
passages.quote: 3 Zu essen, zu trinken, Pferd zu reiten . . . . . Hengste Stammt von diesen her, so auch . . . . 4 Kimis, Milch, Wolle, Schmalz, saure Milch und Käse, Speise und Kleider, sowohl als grobe Wolle für Stricke.
passages.translation: 3 Food, drink, horses to ride … stallions come from these (people), and also … 4 Kumis, milk, wool, butter, sour milk and cheese, food and clothing, as well as coarse wool for ropes.
passages.speaker: Yusuf Khass Hajib, Kutadgu Bilig (1069 to 1070), in Vambery's German translation (1870)
passages.caution: Vambery's translation leaves gaps where he could not read the manuscript.

passages.headline: Merchants and 'the caravan from Cathay'
passages.people: Qarakhanid Turks and Silk Road merchants
passages.gloss: In the chapter on merchants the poet advises the prince to welcome them: they travel from east to west, bring the finest clothes and 'wonders', and without them nobody could dress well in winter or see strings of pearls. When 'the caravan of Cathay' (China) sets out, thousands of gifts follow. It places the Turkic court of Kashgar on the great trade road between China and the west.
passages.quote: 7 Gäbe es keinen Kaufmann, der die Welt durchzieht, Wie könntest du dich kleiden in der Mitte des rauhen Winters? 8 Wenn Chatai's Karavane dahinzieht, so ist es eine Karavane, Von wo tausendfache Spenden kommen sollen.
passages.translation: 7 If there were no merchant who travels the world, how could you clothe yourself in the middle of harsh winter? 8 When Cathay's caravan sets out, it is a caravan from which thousandfold gifts will come.
passages.speaker: Yusuf Khass Hajib, Kutadgu Bilig (1069 to 1070), in Vambery's German translation (1870)

passages.headline: One book, many names: 'the Turkish Shahnameh'
passages.gloss: The prose preface of the Herat manuscript says the book was finished 'in the land of Kashgar' and presented to Bughra Khan, who made the author his chamberlain, hence his title Khass Hajib. It boasts that the Chinese called it 'The Manners of Kings', the Iranians 'the Turkish Shahnameh', and the 'Turanians' Kutadgu Bilig. The Turks here are a named people with their own literary language, 'the Turkish tongue' of the eastern lands.
passages.quote: Die Leute von Cin haben es Adab ul Muluk, Sitten der Fürsten genannt; die Gelehrten des Fürsten von Macin haben Ajn ul Memleket, das Auge des Reiches geheissen; die Morgenländer haben es Zinet un Umera, Zierde der Fürsten betitelt. Die Iranier hiessen es das türkische Schah Nameh
passages.translation: The people of Chin called it Adab al-Muluk, 'the manners of princes'; the scholars of the prince of Machin called it Ayn al-Mamlaka, 'the eye of the realm'; the easterners called it Zinat al-Umara, 'the ornament of princes'. The Iranians called it the Turkish Shahnameh.
passages.speaker: Anonymous prose preface to the Kutadgu Bilig, in Vambery's German translation (1870)
passages.caution: The preface is a later addition praising the book, not the author's own words; its claims about foreign names are a boast.

passages.headline: Vambery: East Turkestan, 'also called Chinese Tartary'
passages.gloss: In his introduction Vambery places the Uighur homeland in 'today's East Turkestan or Chinese Tartary, as it is also called'. For a nineteenth-century scholar, 'Tartary' is just an older map name for the region where the Kutadgu Bilig was written, next to the modern term. He also claims Samarkand and Karshi as Uighur foundations from the meaning of their names, an etymological guess.
passages.quote: Wenn wir daher als die Heimat der Uiguren das heutige Ostturkestan oder die Chinesische Tatarei, wie es auch genannt wird, bezeichnen, so muss jedoch bemerkt werden, dass einzelne Colonien sich auch ausserhalb der bezeichneten Grenzen befanden
passages.translation: If we therefore describe the homeland of the Uighurs as present-day East Turkestan, or Chinese Tartary as it is also called, it must be noted that some colonies lay outside these borders.
passages.speaker: Hermann Vambery, introduction to his edition Uigurische Sprachmonumente und das Kudatku Bilik (Innsbruck 1870)
passages.caution: Vambery's statement that Samarkand means 'rich city' in Uighur and that it was an Uighur colony is his own speculation.

passages.headline: Lost books blamed on 'Tatar lust for war'
passages.gloss: Vambery laments that Uighur manuscripts on history and religion, such as those Rashid al-Din used for his great history, are lost for ever, destroyed by time and 'the even more devastating fire of Tatar lust for war'. Here 'Tatar' means the Mongol conquerors. It is a nineteenth-century scholar's explanation for missing sources, not evidence of a hidden civilisation.
passages.quote: Vieles hat der eiserne Zahn der Zeit und das noch mehr verheerende Feuer tatarischer Kriegslust zu Grunde gerichtet. Kostbare, unersetzliche Kleinodien der Geschichte jener fernen Gegenden Asiens, wie jene, deren Raschid-ed-Din noch bei Zusammenstellung seines Tag-et-tevarich's sich bediente, sind für uns auf ewig verschwunden
passages.translation: Much has been destroyed by the iron tooth of time and the even more devastating fire of Tatar lust for war. Precious, irreplaceable jewels of the history of those distant parts of Asia, such as those Rashid al-Din still used when compiling his Taj al-Tawarikh, are lost to us for ever.
passages.quote_note: Checked against the page image (the corpus OCR reads 'Kasehid')
passages.speaker: Hermann Vambery, introduction to his edition Uigurische Sprachmonumente und das Kudatku Bilik (Innsbruck 1870)
passages.caution: Vambery's opinion; he gives no specific case of Mongols destroying Uighur books.

passages.headline: The 'Thirty Tatars' mourn the first Turk khans
passages.people: Otuz Tatar (the Thirty Tatars), a Mongolic people east of the Turks
passages.gloss: The Kul Tegin stone opens with the Turks' own origin story and then says that when the first khans, Bumin and Istemi, died, peoples came 'weeping and lamenting' from the east: the Chinese, the Tibetans, the Kirghiz, the Three Qurıqan, the Thirty Tatars, the Kitay (Khitan) and the Tatabi. This is one of the oldest written uses of the name Tatar anywhere, carved in stone by the Turks themselves, and here the Tatars are one steppe people among many.
passages.quote: Pleurant et se lamentant arrivèrent de l'avant, du côté du soleil levant, les puissants peuples du désert (c'est-à-dire étrangers?), les Chinois, les Thibétains, les Apar et Apourim, les Kirghiz, les Trois-Kourikans, les Trente-Tatars, les Kitaï, les Tatabi, … tous ces peuples vinrent se lamenter et pleurer: si vaillants avaient été ces kagans.
passages.translation: Weeping and lamenting there came from the front, from the side of the rising sun, the mighty peoples of the desert (that is, foreign peoples?): the Chinese, the Tibetans, the Apar and Apurim, the Kirghiz, the Three Qurıqan, the Thirty Tatars, the Kitay, the Tatabi … all these peoples came to lament and weep, so valiant had these khagans been.
passages.speaker: Bilge Qaghan (inscription composed by Yollugh Tegin), Kul Tegin inscription, 732, in Vilhelm Thomsen's French translation (1896)
passages.caution: Thomsen marks several words as uncertain; the list of mourners is a royal boast carved some 180 years after the funeral it describes.

passages.headline: Thomsen: the Tatars of the stones were Mongols, not Turks
passages.place: Eastern Mongolia (east and southeast of Lake Baikal)
passages.gloss: In his notes Thomsen comments on 'Otuz Tatar' (Thirty Tatars) and 'Toquz Tatar' (Nine Tatars): the name meets us here 'for the first time in history', appears in Chinese books only in the ninth century, and belongs to the Mongols or one of their tribes, not to a Turkic people. He places them between the Oghuz (Uighurs) to the west and the Khitan to the east, near the Kerulen river. So the original Tatars were a real Mongolic group on the edge of the Turk empire.
passages.quote: nom bien connu que nous rencontrons ici pour la première fois dans l'histoire Dans la littérature chinoise, Ta-ta se présente au commencement du IXe siècle. C'est aux Mongols ou plutôt à une de leurs tribus que revient cette dénomination, et non à aucun peuple de race turque
passages.translation: a well-known name that we meet here for the first time in history. In Chinese literature, Ta-ta appears at the beginning of the ninth century. This name belongs to the Mongols, or rather to one of their tribes, and not to any people of Turkic race.
passages.speaker: Vilhelm Thomsen, commentary in Inscriptions de l'Orkhon dechiffrees (1896)
passages.caution: Thomsen's 1896 identification; later scholars still debate how Mongolic the eighth-century Tatars were.

passages.headline: 'Nine Tatars' join the Oghuz against the khan
passages.gloss: In the Bilge Qaghan inscription the khan says he campaigned against the Oghuz and 'devastated their houses and their buildings', and that the Oghuz then allied with the Nine Tatars and came against him. He fought two great battles at Agu, destroyed their army and enslaved their people. The Tatars appear here as a real political ally of the Oghuz, and the Oghuz are said to have houses and buildings.
passages.quote: j'entrai en campagne et dévastai leurs maisons et leurs bâtiments. Le peuple [ogouz] s'allia avec les Neuf-Tatars, et ils vinrent. Près d'Agou, je livrai deux grandes batailles; je dévastai leur armée et j'asservis là leur peuple.
passages.translation: I went on campaign and devastated their houses and their buildings. The [Oghuz] people allied with the Nine Tatars, and they came. Near Agu I fought two great battles; I destroyed their army and there I enslaved their people.
passages.speaker: Bilge Qaghan inscription, 735, in Vilhelm Thomsen's French translation (1896)
passages.caution: A victor's account; the word Thomsen renders 'bâtiments' (barq) is discussed by Radloff as 'buildings', while 'houses' (eb) may mean yurts.

passages.headline: The khan sent to China for sculptors
passages.people: Turks (Kok Turk) and Tang Chinese craftsmen
passages.gloss: Bilge Qaghan says he brought sculptors from the Chinese emperor, who sent his own palace craftsmen. Through them he had a separate building (a temple or hall) put up, had sculptures carved inside and outside, and had the 'eternal stone' cut and inscribed. The Turk ruler plainly credits Chinese craftsmen with the stonework and the temple beside his brother's grave; his cousin Yollugh Tegin wrote the text.
passages.quote: De chez le kagan des Chinois j'ai fait venir des sculpteurs et je (leur) ai (fait) sculpter. On n'a pas rejeté mon invitation, mais on a envoyé les sculpteurs intérieurs (c.-à-d. attachés à la maison) du kagan. Je leur ai fait ériger à part l'édifice (le temple, la salle), et tailler à part les sculptures à l'intérieur et à l'extérieur, et je leur ai fait tailler la pierre.
passages.translation: From the khagan of the Chinese I brought sculptors and had them carve. My invitation was not refused: they sent the khagan's inner (household) sculptors. I had them put up a separate building (the temple, the hall), carve sculptures inside and outside, and cut the stone.
passages.speaker: Bilge Qaghan (inscription composed by Yollugh Tegin), Kul Tegin inscription, 732, in Vilhelm Thomsen's French translation (1896)
passages.caution: Thomsen's translation of this passage has several question marks in the surrounding lines; the Chinese annals confirm that the emperor sent artists.

passages.headline: Named Chinese builders of the memorial
passages.gloss: Radloff's translation of the end of the Kul Tegin inscription lists the embassies at the funeral and then names the builders: 'to raise the buildings, make the sculptures and the inscribed stone came Tschankany and Tschang-Sangun', both from the Chinese emperor. Radloff's glossary adds that 'barq' here means the temple built by the grave, and that the old pair 'eb barq' meant 'houses (yurts) and other buildings'.
passages.quote: Die Gebäude aufzuführen, die Skulpturarbeiten und den Schriftstein herzustellen, sind Tschänkany und Tschäng-Sängün gekommen.
passages.translation: To raise the buildings, to make the sculptures and the inscribed stone, Chankany and Chang-Sangun came.
passages.speaker: Kul Tegin inscription, 732, in Wilhelm Radloff's German translation (1895)
passages.caution: The names are Turkic renderings of Chinese titles or names; Radloff's page 236 explains that they came 'from the Chinese emperor'.

passages.headline: 'Sweet words and soft silks': a khan's warning about China
passages.gloss: Bilge Qaghan tells his people that the forest of Otuken is the true centre of their realm. The Chinese give gold, silver and silk without trouble, but their words are sweet and their riches soft; with them they lure distant peoples close and many Turks who settled near China died. If the Turks stay in Otuken and send caravans, they will keep an eternal empire. It is the steppe ruler's own argument for staying nomads rather than moving into Chinese-style towns.
passages.quote: Habitant ce pays j'entrai en relations avec le peuple chinois. L'appel du peuple chinois, qui nous donne sans peine tant d'or, d'argent, d'isigti, de soie(?), était doux, ses richesses étaient molles. En s'insinuant par leur doux appel et leurs richesses molles, ils (les Chinois) firent approcher d'eux le peuple lointain.
passages.translation: Living in this land I entered into relations with the Chinese people. The call of the Chinese people, who give us so much gold, silver, isigti and silk(?) without trouble, was sweet, and their riches were soft. Worming their way in with their sweet call and soft riches, they (the Chinese) drew distant peoples close to them.
passages.speaker: Bilge Qaghan (inscription composed by Yollugh Tegin), Kul Tegin inscription, 732, in Vilhelm Thomsen's French translation (1896)
passages.caution: Thomsen marks 'silk' and some verbs as uncertain; the moral is the khan's political advice, not a neutral report.

passages.headline: Chinese annals: felt tents, grazing, and stones for enemies killed
passages.gloss: Thomsen quotes Chinese annals (through Stanislas Julien's translations) on the customs of the Turks, the 'Tou-kioue': they wear their hair loose, fold their robes to the left, and live in felt tents, moving wherever they find water and grass. At burials they set up stones beside the grave, one for each enemy the dead man had killed, sometimes a hundred or a thousand. Thomsen says these notices describe a time somewhat earlier than the inscriptions.
passages.quote: «Les Tou-kioue laissent flotter leurs cheveux, jettent à gauche le pan de leur vêtement, et habitent sous des tentes de feutre. Ils se transportent d'un lieu à un autre, suivant qu'ils y trouvent de l'eau et des herbes. Leur principale occupation est l'élève des troupeaux et la chasse.
passages.translation: 'The Tujue let their hair hang loose, fold the flap of their garment to the left, and live in felt tents. They move from one place to another according to where they find water and grass. Their main occupation is raising herds and hunting.'
passages.speaker: Chinese dynastic annals (6th to 7th century) in Stanislas Julien's French translation, quoted by Vilhelm Thomsen (1896)
passages.caution: An outside Chinese view, translated twice before reaching this page.

passages.headline: The dead in the yurt, faces cut, stones for the slain
passages.gloss: Heikel quotes the Chinese account of Turk funerals: the body is laid in the yurt, relatives sacrifice horses and sheep, ride six times round the tent and gash their faces so that their tears run with blood. The body is burned with the dead man's horse and belongings, and the ashes are buried in autumn or spring. A statue of the dead is placed in a small building by the grave, with a painted record of his battles, and stones are set up for every enemy he killed, 'sometimes up to 100 and even 1000'.
passages.quote: »Le corps du défunt est placé dans la yourte, devant laquelle les enfants et autres parents du défunt des deux sexes déposent en offrandes des chevaux et des moutons qu'on a tués. Ils font à cheval six fois le tour de la tente, en se tailladant le visage avec un couteau, de telle façon que leurs larmes se teignent de sang.
passages.translation: 'The body of the dead man is placed in the yurt, in front of which his children and other relatives of both sexes lay out as offerings horses and sheep that have been killed. They ride six times round the tent on horseback, gashing their faces with a knife, so that their tears are dyed with blood.'
passages.speaker: Chinese annals quoted by Axel Heikel in Inscriptions de l'Orkhon (Helsingfors 1892)
passages.caution: Heikel's version says six circuits; Thomsen's version of the same Chinese text (1896) says seven.

passages.headline: 'No fixed dwelling': why the Turks refused a walled capital
passages.gloss: Heikel retells the Chinese annals: Bilge Qaghan wanted to build a wall round his residence and temples to Buddha and Laozi, but his old adviser Tonyukuk warned him off. The Turks, he said, were not a hundredth of China's population and survived only because they follow grass and water, hunt, have no fixed homes and practise war; Chinese armies live in towns and are captured when beaten, and Buddhism makes men weak. Heikel concludes the khan's camp probably stayed unfortified.
passages.quote: »Le peuple doulgase (c. a. d. les Toukioux) n'atteint pas en nombre la centième partie de la population de la Chine, et si, malgré son infériorité numérique, il a pu résister à cet empire, la raison en est que les Doulgases, ne recherchant que de l'herbe et de l'eau, n'ont d'autre intérêt que la chasse, et n'ont pas de demeure fixe, mais ne s'exercent qu'au métier de la guerre.
passages.translation: 'The Turk people do not amount to a hundredth part of the population of China, and if, despite their small numbers, they have been able to resist that empire, it is because the Turks, seeking only grass and water, have no interest but hunting and have no fixed dwelling, but practise only the trade of war.'
passages.speaker: Chinese annals (Tang history) in Axel Heikel's French retelling, Inscriptions de l'Orkhon (1892)
passages.caution: A speech recorded by Chinese historians, retold second-hand from Father Hyacinth's Russian translations.

passages.headline: Chinese-style roof tiles in a marmot burrow
passages.gloss: Heikel describes the mound beside the Kul Tegin monument. Marmots had dug into it, and from one of their holes he pulled a quantity of half-round roof tiles 'such as are still used in China to cover the roofs of houses', with more scattered on the hill. He concluded the mound was a fallen building, a temple put up when the monument was erected. It is a first-hand archaeological observation that fits the inscription's statement about Chinese builders.
passages.quote: Je retirai d'un des trous faits par ces animaux une quantité de tuiles demi-rondes, telles qu'on les emploie encore généralement en Chine pour couvrir les toits des maisons. Il y en avait plusieurs autres semblables éparpillées sur la colline et aux alentours.
passages.translation: From one of the holes made by these animals I pulled out a quantity of half-round tiles, such as are still generally used in China to cover the roofs of houses. There were several others like them scattered over the hill and round about.
passages.speaker: Axel Heikel, Inscriptions de l'Orkhon (Helsingfors 1892), report of the Finnish expedition of 1890

passages.headline: Headless statues and skull cups
passages.gloss: Heikel found that all the carved stone figures at the first two monuments had lost their heads. He explains this by old Mongolian customs: enemies' heads were carried off as trophies, chiefs' skulls were made into drinking cups (the Irkutsk museum held one), and stones set round a grave stood for enemies killed. So attackers would naturally knock the heads off figures that stood for Turks. His explanation is a guess drawn from old accounts, not something he saw happen.
passages.quote: Celles-là comme toutes les autres statues trouvées auprès de ce 1er monument et du 2e, n'ont pas de tête, ce qui n'a rien d'étonnant pour ceux qui connaissent les anciennes moeurs des peuples de la Mongolie, chez lesquels on avait coutume d'emporter à de longues distances les têtes des ennemis en guise de trophées. On façonnait même en coupes les crânes des chefs tués à la guerre.
passages.translation: These, like all the other statues found near the first and second monuments, have no heads, which is not surprising to those who know the ancient customs of the peoples of Mongolia, among whom it was the practice to carry enemies' heads long distances as trophies. The skulls of chiefs killed in war were even made into cups.
passages.speaker: Axel Heikel, Inscriptions de l'Orkhon (Helsingfors 1892)
passages.caution: The missing heads are observed; the explanation is Heikel's own guess from written sources.

passages.headline: Karakorum built beside ruins of an older Uighur city
passages.gloss: Heikel quotes the Persian historian Juvaini: Ogedei founded Karakorum, and on the Orkhon were found the ruins of a city and palace that had belonged to the Uighurs, with inscribed stones before the palace gate. Heikel argues that Karakorum stood where the Erdene Zuu monastery was built about 1590, and was not the same as the older Uighur ruins of Khara Balgasun. Real cities rose and fell here, and their builders are named.
passages.quote: »Devant l'entrée de ce palais gisent des pierres couvertes de caractères gravés que nous avons vus. Sous le règne du Caan (Khan) Ogotaï on leva ces pierres, et l'on découvrit une fosse, dans laquelle il y avait une grande table de pierre, chargée d'une inscription».
passages.translation: 'Before the entrance of this palace lie stones covered with engraved characters, which we have seen. In the reign of the Qaan (Khan) Ogedei these stones were lifted and a pit was found, in which there was a great stone slab bearing an inscription.'
passages.speaker: Juvaini, History of the World Conqueror (13th century), quoted by Axel Heikel (1892) after d'Ohsson
passages.caution: Juvaini is quoted through d'Ohsson's French; Heikel's placing of Karakorum at Erdene Zuu has since been confirmed by excavation.

passages.headline: From tents to palaces: the Uighur khans' capital
passages.gloss: In notes to the same volume the French sinologist Deveria writes that the Uighur khanate set up its main seat on the Orkhon in 745, but that the khans only later replaced the tents of their royal camp with palaces: the Tang history mentions a palace built for the Uighur ruler in 780 as something new, and in 784 a khan had an inscription carved on a stone stele 'before the gate of his capital'. The capital was burned by the Kirghiz in 841. It is a clear dated sequence from tent camp to built city.
passages.quote: La fondation du Khanat ouïgour et l'établissement du siège principal de ses Khakans sur les bords de l'Orkhoun remonte à l'année 745, mais ce ne serait que plus tard que les Khakans auraient substitué des palais aux tentes de leur camp royal. Ce n'est en effet qu'en 780 que l'histoire des T'ang parle, comme d'une chose nouvelle chez les Ouïgours, de la construction d'un palais
passages.translation: The founding of the Uighur khanate and the setting of its khagans' main seat on the banks of the Orkhon go back to 745, but only later did the khagans replace the tents of their royal camp with palaces. Indeed it is only in 780 that the Tang history speaks, as something new among the Uighurs, of the building of a palace.
passages.speaker: Gabriel Deveria, notes on the Chinese inscriptions, in Inscriptions de l'Orkhon (Helsingfors 1892)
passages.caution: Deveria is summarising Tang annals.

passages.headline: 'Abakan Tatars': the Kirghiz' descendants in 1895
passages.people: Kirghiz (Khakas), called Abakan Tatars in Radloff's time
passages.gloss: Radloff notes that the Yenisei inscriptions were left mostly by the Kirghiz, and that their descendants still form a large part of the Turkic population there, 'the Abakan Tatars and Soyots'. In the nineteenth century Russian usage called many Siberian Turkic groups 'Tatars'. The same people who carved runic stones in the early Middle Ages were called Tatars by the time Radloff wrote.
passages.quote: Als die Russen sie im XVI. Jahrhundert im südlichen Theile des Jenisseischen Gouvernements kennen lernten, waren die Kirgisen vollkommene Türken und noch jetzt bilden Nachkommen der Kirgisen einen grossen Theil der türkischen Bevölkerung desselben Gebietes, der Abakan-Tataren und Sojonen.
passages.translation: When the Russians came to know them in the sixteenth century in the southern part of the Yenisei province, the Kirghiz were complete Turks, and even now descendants of the Kirghiz form a large part of the Turkic population of that area, the Abakan Tatars and Soyots.
passages.speaker: Wilhelm Radloff, Die alttuerkischen Inschriften der Mongolei (1895)
passages.caution: Radloff's own ethnographic judgement; his claim that the Kirghiz were first a non-Turkic people rests on a Chinese remark about red hair and blue eyes.

passages.headline: Only a descendant of Genghis may be khan
passages.people: Crimean Tatars and Nogays ('the Tatar peoples')
passages.gloss: The memoir sets out what happens when a Crimean khan dies or the Tatar peoples agree to depose him. Because it is 'among impossible things' for anyone outside the line of Genghis to hold the rank of khan, they must elect and install another khan from Genghis's descendants, and then notify both Russia and the Ottoman sultan. Five centuries after the Mongol conquest, the Crimean Tatars' rulers still drew their legitimacy from Genghis Khan.
passages.quote: خانك وفاتنده ويا خود طوايف تاتاريه بالاتفاق عزلنی مراد ايدوب سلسله جنکيزيه‌دن غيری اشبو خانلق رتبه‌سنه نايل اولمق مواد ممتنعاتدن اولمغيله اعقاب جنکيزيه‌دن آخر بر خان انتخاب ونصب ايتدکلرنده
passages.translation: On the khan's death, or if the Tatar peoples by common agreement wish to depose him, since it is among impossible things for anyone other than the line of Genghis to attain this rank of khan, when they elect and install another khan from the descendants of Genghis
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the manuscript image (corpus OCR of this manuscript is garbled)
passages.speaker: Ottoman chancery memoir on the Tatars and their khans (item IV in the library catalogue, put into Turkish by the reis ul-kuttab Abd al-Razzaq Efendi), undated copy c.1775 to 1780
passages.caution: A diplomatic text written for the post-1774 arrangements, not a description of daily life; the copyist is unknown.

passages.headline: Muslim Tatars and the sultan as caliph
passages.gloss: Although the Tatars were declared independent of the Ottomans, the memoir keeps a religious tie. Because 'the Tatar nation is of the religion of Islam', and two caliphs cannot coexist under Islamic law, Russia agrees that the Tatars acknowledge the Ottoman sultan, 'caliph and head of all Muslim rulers and protector of the Two Holy Cities', as holding supreme spiritual authority over them. It shows the Crimean Tatars as a Muslim people whose faith linked them to Istanbul.
passages.quote: ولکن تاتار ملتی دین اسلامدن اولمغيله … روسيه دولتی رضاداده اولورکه شفقتلو قدرتلو پادشاه آل عثمان حضرتلری خليفه ورئيس جمله حکمداران مسلمين وحرمين شريفين حاميسی اولمغيله ذات شريفه‌لرنده رخصت علياء روحانيه مرکوز بولنديغی تاتارلر قبول واعتراف ايده‌لر
passages.translation: But since the Tatar nation is of the religion of Islam … the Russian state consents that the Tatars accept and acknowledge that supreme spiritual authority is vested in the noble person of His Majesty the compassionate and mighty Padishah of the House of Osman, as caliph and head of all Muslim rulers and protector of the Two Holy Cities.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the manuscript image (corpus OCR of this manuscript is garbled)
passages.speaker: Ottoman chancery memoir on the Tatars and their khans (item IV in the library catalogue, put into Turkish by the reis ul-kuttab Abd al-Razzaq Efendi), undated copy c.1775 to 1780
passages.caution: Treaty-style wording agreed between two empires; it states a legal position, not what ordinary Tatars believed.

passages.headline: Kerch and Yenikale for Russia, a fortress on a non-existent island for the Ottomans
passages.gloss: The memoir lists Russia's peace terms as the Ottomans understood them: the fortresses and places on the Crimean, Taman and Kuban side would be handed to the Tatars, while Yenikale and the port of Kerch, with their districts, would go to Russia. At most, it says with open sarcasm, the Ottomans would be allowed to build a fortress 'on an imaginary island, whose name and body do not exist' between Yenikale and Taman. The Tatar towns of the strait are real fortresses bargained over by two empires.
passages.quote: قريم وطمان وقوبان جانبنده اولان قلاع وبقاع بالجمله … تاتاره ترك وتسليم اولنه وثانيا یکی قلعه وکرش ليمانی الکا وناحيه‌لريله روسيه دولتنه تمليك اولنوب نهايه یکی قلعه ايله طمان بيننده اسم وجسمی معدوم بر اطه موهومه ده دولت عليه بر قلعه بنا ايتمك جايز اوله
passages.translation: All the fortresses and places on the side of Crimea, Taman and Kuban … shall be left and handed over to the Tatars; and secondly Yenikale and the port of Kerch, with their districts and territories, shall be made over to Russia; and at most the Sublime State may build a fortress on an imaginary island, whose name and body do not exist, between Yenikale and Taman.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the manuscript image (corpus OCR of this manuscript is garbled); one unclear word omitted
passages.speaker: Ottoman memoir on Russia's demands, 1773 (item II in the library catalogue, apparently translated from a French memoir), undated copy c.1775 to 1780
passages.caution: A hostile Ottoman summary of Russian demands, perhaps translated from French; the sarcasm about the island is the memoir's own. Russia did gain Kerch and Yenikale by the treaty of 1774.

passages.headline: Tobolsk: churches on the bluff, Russians and Tatars below
passages.people: Siberian (Tobolsk) Tatars living beside Russian settlers
passages.gloss: Spafarii set out from Tobolsk, then the capital of Russian Siberia, in May 1675. He describes a town in two levels: churches, houses and people in the upper town on the high bluff over the Irtysh, and a large trading quarter under the hill where many Russians and Tatars lived. From here, he adds, roads ran to Bukhara, to Kazan and to other states.
passages.quote: А городъ Тоболескъ построенъ на рѣкѣ Иртышѣ на высокомъ мѣстѣ, на яру, и мѣсто зѣло красивое, и множество церквей Божіихъ, и дворовъ, и людей живутъ въ верхнемъ городѣ; такъ же и подъ горою посадъ великой, въ которомъ живутъ множество Рускихъ людей и Татаръ.
passages.translation: And the town of Tobolsk is built on the Irtysh river on a high place, on a bluff, and the place is very beautiful, and there are many churches of God, and houses, and people live in the upper town; and below the hill there is also a great trading quarter (posad), in which live many Russian people and Tatars.
passages.speaker: Nikolai Spafarii (ed. Yu. V. Arsenyev, 1882)

passages.headline: Kuchum's empty capital and the mosque the Tatars still kept
passages.people: Siberian Tatars (Tobolsk Tatars, former subjects of Khan Kuchum)
passages.gloss: Just up the Irtysh from Tobolsk, by a stream called Sibirka that he thought gave all Siberia its name, Spafarii notes the empty little town and earthworks of Kuchum, the Tatar khan who ruled when Yermak's Cossacks came. The site was naturally strong, an island, but deserted. Only the Tobolsk Tatars still renewed a mosque there and came to worship. The editor adds that the historian Müller later described these ruins.
passages.quote: близъ рѣчки лежитъ пустой городокъ и шанцы Кучюма царя Сибирского, который владѣлъ въ то время, какъ приходилъ Ермакъ въ Сибирь; и мѣсто то самое крѣпкое: островъ есть, однакожъ нынѣ лежитъ пусто, толко Тоболскія Татары для воспоминанія нечистые ихъ вѣры магмецкіе обновили прежъ сего и нынѣ обновляютъ мечеть, въ которой по ихъ нечистой вѣрѣ приходяще дѣйствуютъ.
passages.translation: near the stream lies the empty little town and earthworks of Kuchum, tsar of Siberia, who ruled at the time when Yermak came into Siberia; and the place is very strong: it is an island, yet now it lies empty, only the Tobolsk Tatars, in remembrance of their unclean Mahometan faith, renewed a mosque before this and renew it now, in which they come and perform their rites according to their unclean faith.
passages.speaker: Nikolai Spafarii (ed. Yu. V. Arsenyev, 1882)
passages.caution: Spafarii does not say he visited the site, which lies a short way upriver from Tobolsk where he stayed; 'unclean faith' is his Orthodox hostility to Islam.

passages.headline: Baraba Tatars: houses dug into the earth
passages.gloss: Between Tara and Tomsk lay the Baraba district, home to Tatars who had once paid fur tribute both to the tsar and to the Kalmyk prince Ablai, and now paid only the tsar. They spoke both Kalmyk and Tatar, lived in dwellings dug into the ground like cellars, had their own princelings and small 'dug' towns (earthworks), and lived by hunting of every kind.
passages.quote: и въ той Барабинской волости живутъ Татары, которые прежъ сего платили есакъ Великому Государю и Аблаю тайшѣ, а нынѣ только Великому Государю платятъ. И тѣ Татары говорятъ по калмыцки и по татарски, а жилище ихъ есть, копаютъ въ землѣ погребы, и князцы у нихъ есть, и городки копаные, и звѣриные промыслы всякіе промышляютъ
passages.translation: and in that Baraba district live Tatars who formerly paid tribute (yasak) to the Great Sovereign and to Ablai taisha, but now pay only to the Great Sovereign. And these Tatars speak Kalmyk and Tatar, and their dwelling is this: they dig cellars in the ground; and they have princelings, and dug-out little towns, and they carry on all kinds of hunting.
passages.speaker: Nikolai Spafarii (ed. Yu. V. Arsenyev, 1882)
passages.caution: Baraba was off his route; this is Tobolsk knowledge, not his own observation.

passages.headline: Brick halls in Kalmyk country, built by craftsmen from China
passages.people: Kalmyks (the Oirat prince Ablai taisha); 'Tatars' here means the Manchu rulers of China
passages.gloss: Following the upper Irtysh through Kalmyk country, Spafarii notes its few buildings. The Kalmyk prince Ablai had built two halls of fired brick in a strong place among stone mountains, and the craftsmen had been sent to him from China, because Mongol and Kalmyk princes exchanged envoys and gifts with the Chinese emperor, 'since now a Kalmyk and Tatar race rules in China'. On the same page he mentions the Kontaisha's clay town with two brick halls where Kalmyk lamas lived.
passages.quote: А на той рѣчкѣ Аблай тайша сдѣлалъ 2 палаты изъ зженаго кирпичю въ крѣпкомъ мѣстѣ межъ горъ каменныхъ, а мастеры къ нему присланы были изъ Китайского государства, потому что Мугалскіе и Калмыцкіе тайши ссылаются часто съ Китайскимъ ханомъ и поминки емлютъ и даютъ для того, что нынѣ въ Китаехъ владѣетъ родъ Калмыцкой и Татарской.
passages.translation: And on that stream Ablai taisha built 2 halls of fired brick in a strong place among stone mountains, and the craftsmen were sent to him from the Chinese state, because the Mongol and Kalmyk taishas often exchange envoys with the Chinese khan and take and give presents, since now a Kalmyk and Tatar race rules in China.
passages.speaker: Nikolai Spafarii (ed. Yu. V. Arsenyev, 1882)
passages.caution: Not eyewitness: the editor says Spafarii took the upper Irtysh from the reports of the envoys Baikov (1654) and Seitkul Ablin. Historians link Ablai's buildings to the Ablai-kit monastery of the 1650s; the text does not use that name.

passages.headline: An empty brick hall on the steppe: 'an old work'
passages.people: Kalmyks (Oirats); the builders of the ruin are not named
passages.gloss: The route list down the Irtysh names the Kalmyk lama's two halls of fired brick coated with lime, and then a place the Kalmyks call Kabal-Gasun, which Spafarii renders in Russian as 'stone hall': a building of fired brick, standing empty, 'an old work'. He says nothing of who built it or when.
passages.quote: лама Калмыцкой, живетъ подлѣ рѣки Иртыша на лѣвой сторонѣ; и поставлены у него двѣ палаты кирпичныя, кирпичь зженой смазыванъ известью … Кабалъ-Гасунъ - калмыцкимъ языкомъ, а по руски - палата каменная: кирпичъ зженой, пустая. Дѣло старинное.
passages.translation: the Kalmyk lama lives by the Irtysh river on the left side; and two brick halls have been set up for him, of fired brick coated with lime … Kabal-Gasun in the Kalmyk tongue, and in Russian 'a stone hall': fired brick, empty. An old work.
passages.speaker: Nikolai Spafarii (ed. Yu. V. Arsenyev, 1882)
passages.caution: Taken from earlier envoys' route reports, not seen by Spafarii. Dashes in the printed text are shown as hyphens.

passages.headline: The salt-lake fair where Kalmyks, Bukharans and Tatars sold horses and captives
passages.people: Kalmyks, Bukharans and Tatars trading with Russians
passages.gloss: At the Yamysh salt lakes, where the 'Siberian kingdom' ended, 30 or 40 river boats came every year from Tobolsk, Tomsk and other towns to load natural salt. While the Russians gathered it, a fair sprang up: many thousands of Kalmyks, Bukharans and Tatars came to sell horses, captives and Chinese goods. After two or three weeks everyone left and the place stood empty again, and Spafarii suggests a fort should be built there.
passages.quote: А въ то время, какъ Рускіе люди собираютъ соль изъ озера, учинится ярмарокъ. И приходятъ многіе тысящи людей Калмыки и Бухарцы и Татары и торгуютъ съ Рускими людьми. И они продаютъ лошади, и ясырь, и иные китайскіе товары. И держатъ тотъ ярмарокъ недѣли по 2 и по 3
passages.translation: And at the time when the Russian people gather salt from the lake, a fair takes place. And many thousands of people come, Kalmyks and Bukharans and Tatars, and trade with the Russian people. And they sell horses, and captives, and other Chinese goods. And they hold that fair for 2 or 3 weeks
passages.speaker: Nikolai Spafarii (ed. Yu. V. Arsenyev, 1882)
passages.caution: 'Yasyr' means captives taken in raids and sold as slaves.

passages.headline: Why Siberia's rivers have Tatar names
passages.people: Siberian Tatars of Kuchum's former khanate
passages.gloss: Spafarii notices that the Irtysh, Tobol, Tura and other Siberian rivers have no Russian names: Russians still use the names the Tatars or Ostyaks gave them before the conquest. The Irtysh, he says, took its name from the Tatars because Kuchum, 'the Tatar tsar', ruled widely along it over Tatars, Ostyaks and other peoples. Even under Russian rule, he adds, a great multitude of Tatars and their faith lived along the river.
passages.quote: Рѣка Иртышъ имя руское не имѣетъ, для того что Иртышъ именуется по татарски, а не по руски … Такъ же рѣка Иртышъ приняла имя свое отъ Татаръ, потому что Кучюмъ, царь Татарской, владѣлъ по Иртышу пространно и не токмо надъ Татары, но и надъ Остяками и надъ иными иноземцы
passages.translation: The river Irtysh has no Russian name, because Irtysh is named in Tatar and not in Russian … So too the river Irtysh took its name from the Tatars, because Kuchum, the Tatar tsar, ruled widely along the Irtysh, and not only over the Tatars but over the Ostyaks and other foreign peoples too
passages.speaker: Nikolai Spafarii (ed. Yu. V. Arsenyev, 1882)

passages.headline: The Kirghiz: 'their language and faith are Tatar'
passages.gloss: In the Krasnoyarsk district, Spafarii says, the Russian villages and their thousand or so servicemen were always in danger from the Kirghiz: only about a thousand men, but very warlike, 'and their language and faith are Tatar'. Elsewhere he lists the Kirghiz among the 'Tatars' living at the head of the Ket. In Siberian Russian usage 'Tatar' reached well beyond Kuchum's old realm.
passages.quote: толко всегда опасно отъ Киргызъ: ихъ человѣкъ съ 1000, толко гораздо воисты, и языкъ и вѣра ихъ татарская.
passages.translation: only it is always dangerous from the Kirghiz: there are about 1000 of them, but they are very warlike, and their language and faith are Tatar.
passages.speaker: Nikolai Spafarii (ed. Yu. V. Arsenyev, 1882)
passages.caution: He only sailed two days on the Yenisei, so Krasnoyarsk news is hearsay from Yeniseisk.

passages.headline: A cliff of unknown writing on the Yenisei
passages.gloss: Before the great rapids of the Yenisei, Spafarii was told, a stone cliff carries carved writing in an unknown script, with crosses among the letters and carved men holding maces, and 'many other such works'. Nobody knew what it said or who made it. The upper Yenisei is famous today for its rock art and early Turkic runic inscriptions, but Spafarii could only report the mystery.
passages.quote: А до болшого порогу не доѣзжая есть мѣсто, утесъ каменной по Енисѣю. На томъ утесѣ есть вырѣзано на каменю невѣдомо какое писмо и межъ писмомъ есть и кресты вырѣзаны, такъ же и люди вырѣзаны, и въ рукахъ у нихъ булавы, и иные многіе такія дѣла. … А никто не вѣдаетъ, что писано и отъ кого.
passages.translation: And before one reaches the great rapids there is a place, a stone cliff along the Yenisei. On that cliff there is carved in the stone some unknown writing, and among the writing crosses are carved too, and men are carved as well, and in their hands they hold maces, and many other such works. … And no one knows what is written or by whom.
passages.speaker: Nikolai Spafarii (ed. Yu. V. Arsenyev, 1882)
passages.caution: Hearsay ('as they say'); he did not travel that stretch of the Yenisei.

passages.headline: The Mongols as Gog and Magog
passages.gloss: At Selenginsk, where by his reckoning the Siberian realm ended and the 'Mongol state' began, Spafarii offers a learned identification: the Mongols are the Gog and Magog of the Bible, 'because they call themselves Mogol'. It is an old pun on the name from biblical geography, not something the Mongols told him. He then describes them as a very great people stretching from the Amur to Bukhara and India.
passages.quote: И здѣ скончается Сибирское государство, и начинается государство Мунгальское. Мунгалы суть, о которыхъ пишетъ въ Библіи - Гогъ и Магогъ, потому что они называютъ себя Маголь. И тотъ родъ Мунгальской зѣло великой
passages.translation: And here the Siberian state ends and the Mongol state begins. The Mongols are those of whom the Bible writes, Gog and Magog, because they call themselves Magol. And that Mongol race is very great
passages.speaker: Nikolai Spafarii (ed. Yu. V. Arsenyev, 1882)
passages.caution: A bookish word-play, repeated from the European and Byzantine tradition. The printed dash is shown as a hyphen.

passages.headline: No towns or villages: Mongols in felt yurts
passages.gloss: In the same passage Spafarii sketches how the Mongols lived: under many princes (taishas), with the Saïn khan as overlord and the Khutukhta lama as their high priest. They roamed near Selenginsk, he says, because they had no towns or villages, and so wandered over the steppes in felt yurts to feed their great herds.
passages.quote: и тѣ неподалеку кочуютъ отъ Селенгинского острогу, потому что у нихъ городовъ и селъ нѣтъ; и для того кочуютъ по степямъ въ юртахъ войлочныхъ для прокормленія многаго скота ихъ.
passages.translation: and they roam not far from the Selenginsk fort, because they have no towns or villages; and for that reason they wander over the steppes in felt yurts, to feed their many herds.
passages.speaker: Nikolai Spafarii (ed. Yu. V. Arsenyev, 1882)

passages.headline: The lama's stone temple 'like a city', built by Chinese masters
passages.people: Khalkha Mongols and their chief lama, the Khutukhta; Chinese craftsmen
passages.gloss: Spafarii copies the report of the party of Ivan Porshennikov, who rode from Selenginsk across Mongolia to China and back in 1675. On the Tola (Tuul) river lived the Khutukhta lama, head of all the priests 'like our metropolitan', who had built for his idols a great stone temple 'like a city', with craftsmen brought from China. A little further down the Tola stood an empty stone city, very strong, whose walls needed only a little repair.
passages.quote: и въ томъ мѣстѣ построилъ капище своимъ идоломъ великое каменное, будто городъ, а мастеры, которые дѣлали то капище, приведены были изъ Китаи. Да и по той же рѣкѣ Толѣ пониже немного Кутухты есть городъ каменной пустой, и около стѣны его починки немного надобно, а городъ самой крѣпкой.
passages.translation: and in that place he built for his idols a great stone temple, like a city, and the craftsmen who made that temple were brought from China. And on the same Tola river, a little below the Khutukhta, there is an empty stone city, and around its wall little repair is needed, and the city is very strong.
passages.speaker: Nikolai Spafarii, relaying the report of Ivan Porshennikov's party (ed. Yu. V. Arsenyev, 1882)
passages.caution: Second-hand, from Porshennikov's men; the same page says a nearby gold mine was 'not yet certain'.

passages.headline: Could the empty stone city be Karakorum? The editor wonders
passages.people: Mongols (ruins of the old Mongol capital, as the editor suggests)
passages.gloss: In his notes, the 1882 editor Arsenyev calls the report of an abandoned fortified city on the Tola 'extremely interesting' and suggests it might be the ruins of Karakorum, the old Mongol capital, which the French scholar Abel-Rémusat had placed near where the Tula joins the Orkhon.
passages.quote: Свѣдѣніе о запустѣвшемъ укрѣпленномъ городѣ (у каменныхъ стѣнъ котораго „починки немного надобно“), стоящемъ близъ рѣки Толы ниже Урги, чрезвычайно интересно и могло бы относиться къ развалинамъ Каракорума, который, по свидѣтельству Абеля Ремюза, … находился, вѣроятно, недалеко отъ сліянія р. Тулы съ Орхономъ.
passages.translation: The report of the deserted fortified city (whose stone walls 'need little repair'), standing near the Tola river below Urga, is extremely interesting and could refer to the ruins of Karakorum, which, according to Abel-Rémusat, … probably lay not far from the confluence of the Tula with the Orkhon.
passages.speaker: Yu. V. Arsenyev (editor's note, 1882)
passages.caution: The editor's guess, not Spafarii's. The ruins of Karakorum were identified on the Orkhon at Kharkhorin in 1889, some distance from the Tuul, so the identification is doubtful.

passages.headline: A great stone ghost city near Lake Dalai
passages.people: Mongols nomadising around the lake; the city's builders are not named
passages.gloss: Describing Lake Dalai (Hulun Nur) from what the local peoples told him, Spafarii reports a great stone city a day's ride from the lake, 'with every kind of building', its stone halls still whole. Some said its people all died of plague and left their goods behind, so that no one dared enter and people only looked at it from afar; others said war had emptied it. On the same page he repeats that the lake is so deep it holds whales and seals.
passages.quote: Отъ Далая днище есть городъ великой каменной со всякимъ строеніемъ, и палаты въ немъ каменныя цѣлы; и говорятъ, что въ томъ городѣ отъ мору люди всѣ пропали, и осталось имѣніе ихъ все тамъ; и иноземцы въ тотъ городъ иттить не смѣютъ, а смотрятъ все издали; а иные говорятъ, что отъ войны запустѣло.
passages.translation: A day's journey from the Dalai there is a great stone city with every kind of building, and the stone halls in it are whole; and they say that in that city the people all perished of plague, and all their goods remained there; and the natives dare not go into that city, but look at it all from afar; and others say that it was laid waste by war.
passages.speaker: Nikolai Spafarii (ed. Yu. V. Arsenyev, 1882)
passages.caution: Rumour from local informants; a gap in both manuscripts cuts off the sentence just before, so the river it stood on is lost.

passages.headline: 'Tatars' who seized China thirty years ago
passages.people: Manchus (called Tatars) and the Han Chinese 'Nikan' kingdom
passages.gloss: In a dispatch to Tsar Aleksei from Yeniseisk, Spafarii passes on what Russian traders just back from Peking (Kambalyk) told him. The 'Nikan kingdom' the Chinese were fighting, he explains, is simply the old Chinese kingdom: about thirty years before, 'Tatars' had taken the Chinese realm, the old royal line fled to distant coastal provinces, and 'the Bogdykhan's Tatars' now call it Nikan. Russian deserters in Peking whispered that two thousand soldiers could win all Dauria for the tsar.
passages.quote: И то Никанское царство нѣтъ иного, опричь стараго Китайскаго царства, потому что нынѣ есть лѣтъ съ тридцать завладѣли Китайскимъ царствомъ Татары, а поколѣніе царское бѣжало въ дальніе приморскія китайскія страны, и то нынѣ называютъ Богдыхановы Татары Никанскимъ царствомъ.
passages.translation: And that Nikan kingdom is nothing other than the old Chinese kingdom, because it is now some thirty years since the Tatars took possession of the Chinese kingdom, and the royal line fled into the distant coastal Chinese lands, and the Bogdykhan's Tatars now call that the Nikan kingdom.
passages.speaker: Nikolai Spafarii, dispatch from Yeniseisk to Tsar Aleksei, July 1675, reporting traders' news (ed. Yu. V. Arsenyev, 1882)
passages.caution: Second-hand from traders. The editor's footnote explains that the war was the revolt of the southern provinces led by Wu Sangui, not a restored Ming kingdom; 'Nikan' was the Manchu word for the Han Chinese.

passages.headline: Tatar forts on the Irtysh stormed by Yermak's men
passages.gloss: The 1882 editor matches Spafarii's list of Tatar villages on the Irtysh with the Tobolsk chronicle of Semyon Remezov. In 1582, that chronicle says, Yermak's officer Bogdan Bryazga stormed a fortified Tatar town at the mouth of the Aremzyanka, and further down met resistance at the old Tatar fortress of Turtas, whose traces the historian Müller later searched for in vain. Beyond Turtas, Spafarii's list shows Tatar villages giving way to Ostyak ones.
passages.quote: Слѣдуя внизъ по Иртышу, при устьѣ р. Аримдзянки (гдѣ Спаѳарій называетъ Аримдзянскую волость), Брязга взялъ приступомъ татарскій укрѣпленный городокъ … Здѣсь въ лѣтописи упоминается старинная татарская крѣпость, Туртасское городище, слѣды котораго тщетно разыскивалъ исторіографъ Миллеръ во время своего путешествія по Сибири.
passages.translation: Going down the Irtysh, at the mouth of the Arimdzyanka (where Spafarii names the Arimdzyansk district), Bryazga took by storm a fortified Tatar town … Here the chronicle mentions an ancient Tatar fortress, the Turtas gorodishche, whose traces the historiographer Müller sought in vain during his journey through Siberia.
passages.speaker: Yu. V. Arsenyev (editor's note, 1882), summarising the Tobolsk (Remezov) chronicle
passages.caution: Editorial note resting on the late Remezov chronicle (c. 1700), not on Spafarii. The printed dash is shown as a comma.

passages.headline: 'Unknown peoples': nobody knew who the Tatars were
passages.people: Tatars (the Mongol army of Jebe and Subutai)
passages.gloss: The chronicler's first notice of the Tatars is an admission of ignorance. Nobody knew who they were, where they came from, what language they spoke or what faith they held. People called them Tatars, Taurmens or Pechenegs, and learned men linked them to the prophecy of Pseudo-Methodius about peoples locked away in the desert who would come out at the end of time.
passages.quote: придоша языци незнаеми, ихъ же добрѣ никто же не вѣсть, кто суть и отколѣ изъидоша, и что языкъ ихъ, и котораго племене суть, и что вѣра ихъ; а зовуть я Татары, а иніи глаголють Таурмены, а друзіи Печенѣзи, иніи же глаголють, яко се суть, о нихъ же Меѳодій Паторомьскыи епископъ съвѣдѣтельствуеть: яко си суть изъшли изъ пустыня Етріевьскыя
passages.translation: there came unknown peoples, whom no one clearly knows: who they are and whence they came, and what their language is, and of what tribe they are, and what their faith is; and they call them Tatars, and others say Taurmens, and others Pechenegs, and others say that these are the ones of whom Methodius, bishop of Patara, bears witness: that they came out of the Etrian desert
passages.speaker: Novgorod First Chronicle (Synodal copy; PSRL vol. 3, 1841)
passages.caution: The Methodius reference is to the apocalyptic Revelation of Pseudo-Methodius, a book legend, not an origin the Mongols gave.

passages.headline: The Tatar envoys: 'we have not taken your towns'
passages.people: Tatar (Mongol) envoys to the Rus princes
passages.gloss: Before the Kalka battle the Tatars sent envoys to the Rus princes, who had allied with the Polovtsy (Cumans). They said they had not touched Rus land, towns or villages and had come against 'our slaves and grooms, the pagan Polovtsy'. The princes killed the envoys. The chronicle records the Mongol claim that the steppe nomads were their runaway subjects.
passages.quote: се слышимъ, оже идете противу насъ, послушавше Половьць, а мы вашеи земли не заяхомъ, ни городъ вашихъ, ни селъ вашихъ, ни на васъ придохомъ; нъ придохомъ, Богомъ пущени, на холопы и на конюси свое, на поганыя Половчь.
passages.translation: we hear that you are coming against us, having listened to the Polovtsy; but we have not taken your land, nor your towns, nor your villages, nor have we come against you; but we have come, sent by God, against our slaves and grooms, the pagan Polovtsy.
passages.speaker: Novgorod First Chronicle (PSRL vol. 3, 1841), reporting the envoys' words

passages.headline: A Tatar commander buried alive in a Polovtsian kurgan
passages.gloss: When Prince Mstislav crossed the Dnieper and beat the Tatar vanguard, the survivors fled with their commander Gemyabeg into a Polovtsian kurgan (burial mound). Unable to hold out, they buried him alive in the earth to save his life. He was found, and the Polovtsy begged him from Mstislav and killed him. The steppe was already dotted with mounds that the chronicler credits to the Polovtsy.
passages.quote: а прокъ ихъ въбѣже съ воеводою своимъ Гемябегомъ въ курганъ Половьчьскыи, и ту имъ не бы мочи, и погребоша воеводу своего Гемябега жива въ земли, хотяще животъ его ублюсти, и ту й налѣзоша, испросивъше Половьци у Мьстислава, и убиша й.
passages.translation: and the rest of them fled with their commander Gemyabeg into a Polovtsian kurgan, and there they could not hold out, and they buried their commander Gemyabeg alive in the earth, wishing to save his life; and there they found him, and the Polovtsy, having begged him from Mstislav, killed him.
passages.speaker: Novgorod First Chronicle (PSRL vol. 3, 1841)

passages.headline: A victory feast on top of the captured princes
passages.people: Tatars (Mongols) and the defeated Rus princes
passages.gloss: After the Kalka, the Tatars crushed the captured Rus princes under boards and sat on top to feast, 'and so ended their lives'. Then they turned back from the Dnieper and vanished, and the chronicler confesses he does not know where they came from or where they went: 'God knows whence He brought them upon us, for our sins.'
passages.quote: а князи имъше издавиша, подъкладъше подъ дъскы, а сами верху сѣдоша обѣдати, и тако животъ ихъ концяша. … Татари же възвратишася отъ рѣкы Днѣпря, и не съвѣдаемъ откуду суть пришли, и кдѣ ся дѣша опять; Богъ вѣсть, отколѣ приде на насъ, за грѣхы наша.
passages.translation: and the princes they seized and crushed, putting them under boards, and they themselves sat on top to dine, and so they ended their lives. … And the Tatars turned back from the Dnieper river, and we do not know whence they came nor where they have gone again; God knows whence He brought them upon us, for our sins.
passages.speaker: Novgorod First Chronicle (PSRL vol. 3, 1841)
passages.caution: Reported from survivors' accounts; not seen by a Novgorod writer.

passages.headline: A sorceress envoy demands a tenth of everything
passages.gloss: The Tatars came to Ryazan land 'without number, like locusts'. From their camp they sent envoys to the Ryazan princes, a woman sorceress and two men, demanding a tenth of everything: of people, of princes and of horses. The editor's footnote on this page adds that another copy lists the horses by colour, ten of each. The princes answered that when none of them were left, all would be theirs.
passages.quote: придоша иноплеменьници, глаголеми Татарове, на землю Рязаньскую, множьство безъ числа, акы прузи … и оттолѣ послаша послы своя, жену чародѣицю и два мужа съ нею, къ княземъ Рязаньскымъ, просяче у нихъ десятины во всемъ, и въ людьхъ, и въ князьхъ, и въ конихъ, во всякомъ десятое.
passages.translation: foreigners called Tatars came upon the Ryazan land, a multitude without number, like locusts … and from there they sent their envoys, a woman sorceress and two men with her, to the Ryazan princes, asking of them a tenth of everything: of people, and of princes, and of horses, a tenth of everything.
passages.speaker: Novgorod First Chronicle (PSRL vol. 3, 1841)

passages.headline: The fall of Vladimir: palisade, siege engines, a burning church
passages.gloss: The chronicle describes the Tatar method at Vladimir. They surrounded the city with a palisade (tyn), set up siege engines (poroki), took the city and set it on fire. The prince's family and the bishop, who had taken monastic vows as the end approached, shut themselves in the gallery of the cathedral. The Tatars broke down the doors, piled up timber and burned the church, suffocating everyone inside.
passages.quote: Безаконьнии же Измаильти приближишася къ граду, и оступиша градъ силою, и отыниша тыномъ всь … поставивше порокы взяша градъ и запалиша й огнемь … вбѣгоша въ святую Богородицю и затворишася въ полатѣ; погании же отбивше двьри зажгоша церковь, наволочивше лѣса, и издушиша вся.
passages.translation: And the lawless Ishmaelites drew near the city, and surrounded the city in force, and fenced it all round with a palisade … having set up siege engines they took the city and set it on fire … they ran into the church of the Holy Mother of God and shut themselves in the gallery; and the pagans, breaking down the doors, set fire to the church, having piled up timber, and suffocated them all.
passages.speaker: Novgorod First Chronicle (PSRL vol. 3, 1841)
passages.caution: 'Ishmaelites' is a biblical label, not an ethnic name.

passages.headline: Torzhok's two-week siege and the road to Novgorod
passages.gloss: After Moscow, Pereyaslavl, Yuryev, Dmitrov, Volok and Tver, the Tatars besieged Torzhok. As at other towns, they fenced it with a palisade and battered it with siege engines for two weeks while Novgorod sent no help. They took it on 5 March and chased the fugitives along the Seliger road 'cutting down people like grass' as far as Ignach Krest, 100 versts from Novgorod. There they turned back, which the chronicler credits to God and St Sophia.
passages.quote: придоша безаконьнии и оступиша Торжекъ, на Сборъ чистои недѣли, и отыниша тыномъ всь около, якоже иніи гради имаху, и бишася ту оканнии порокы по двѣ недѣли … Тогда же гоняшася оканьнии безбожници отъ Торжку Серегерьскымъ путемъ оли и до Игнача креста, а все люди сѣкуще акы траву, за 100 верстъ до Новагорода
passages.translation: the lawless ones came and surrounded Torzhok, on the Sunday of Orthodoxy, and fenced it all round with a palisade, as they took other cities, and the accursed ones battered it there with siege engines for two weeks … Then the accursed godless ones pursued from Torzhok along the Seliger road as far as Ignach Krest, cutting down all the people like grass, to within 100 versts of Novgorod
passages.speaker: Novgorod First Chronicle (PSRL vol. 3, 1841)

passages.headline: The 'raw-eaters' come with their wives
passages.people: Tatar officials of the Golden Horde (Berkai and Kasachik)
passages.gloss: In 1257 'evil news' reached Novgorod that the Tatars wanted the tamga (a trade tax) and a tithe. In the winter of 1259 the Tatar officials Berkai and Kasachik arrived with their wives and many others. The chronicler calls them 'accursed Tatar raw-eaters' (syroyadtsy), a standard insult for steppe nomads.
passages.quote: Приде вѣсть изъ Руси зла, яко хотять Татарове тамгы и десятины на Новѣгородѣ, и смятошася люди черезъ все лѣто. … Тои же зимы приѣхаша оканьнии Татарове сыроядци, Беркаи и Касачикъ, съ женами своими, и инѣхъ много
passages.translation: Evil news came from Rus that the Tatars wanted the tamga and the tithe from Novgorod, and the people were in turmoil all through the summer. … That same winter the accursed Tatar raw-eaters arrived, Berkai and Kasachik, with their wives, and many others
passages.speaker: Novgorod First Chronicle (PSRL vol. 3, 1841)
passages.caution: 'Raw-eaters' is an insult, not a description the chronicler checked.

passages.headline: The census: Tatars ride the streets writing down houses
passages.people: Tatar census officials of the Golden Horde
passages.gloss: Novgorod split over the Mongol census. The Tatars threatened to leave ('give us the number, or we go') while the common people swore to die for St Sophia rather than be counted. In the end the boyars gave way, and the census takers 'began to ride through the streets writing down the Christian houses'. The chronicler complains that the boyars made it easy for themselves and hard for the poor.
passages.quote: и рѣша Татарове: даите намъ число, или бѣжимъ проче; и чернь не хотѣша дати числа, но рѣша: умремъ честно за святую Софью и за домы ангелскыя … и почаша ѣздити оканьнии по улицамъ, пишюче домы христьяньскыя
passages.translation: and the Tatars said: give us the number, or we will run away; and the common people would not give the number, but said: let us die honourably for St Sophia and for the houses of the angels … and the accursed ones began to ride through the streets, writing down the Christian houses
passages.speaker: Novgorod First Chronicle (PSRL vol. 3, 1841)

passages.headline: Tver kills the Horde's envoy, and a Tatar army lays the land waste
passages.people: Golden Horde envoy Shevkal (Chol Khan) and a punitive Tatar army
passages.gloss: In 1327 Prince Alexander of Tver killed many Tatars in Tver and other towns, after the mighty envoy Shevkal had come from the Horde with a large Tatar retinue. That winter a huge Tatar army took Tver, Kashin and the Torzhok district and 'laid the whole Russian land waste'. Novgorod escaped by paying the Tatar envoys 2000 in silver and sending gifts to the commanders.
passages.quote: князь Александръ Михаиловичь изби Татаръ много, во Тфери и по инымъ городомъ … пришелъ бо бяше посолъ силенъ изъ орды, именемь Шевкалъ, съ множествомъ Татаръ. … На ту же зиму приде рать Татарьская, множество много, и взяша Тфѣрь, и Кашинъ, и Новоторжьскую волость, и просто рещи всю землю Русьскую положиша пусту
passages.translation: Prince Alexander Mikhailovich killed many Tatars in Tver and in other towns … for a mighty envoy had come from the Horde, named Shevkal, with a multitude of Tatars. … That same winter a Tatar army came, a very great multitude, and took Tver, and Kashin, and the Torzhok district, and, to put it simply, laid the whole Russian land waste
passages.speaker: Novgorod First Chronicle (PSRL vol. 3, 1841)
passages.caution: The OCR prints the year as 6855; the event belongs to 6835 (1327).

passages.headline: Kulikovo: 'Ishmaelites' ruled by Mamai behind a puppet khan
passages.people: Tatars of the Golden Horde under the emir Mamai
passages.gloss: The younger Novgorod text on the battle of Kulikovo explains the politics of the Horde: a weak khan reigned while Mamai did everything. It calls Mamai's army the pagan 'Ishmaelite race' and 'sons of Hagar', and when Dmitry arrays his troops it is 'against the pagan Polovtsy'.
