Old names for steppe enemies were simply reused for the Tatars.
passages.quote: въздвизается на крестьяны Измаилтескии родъ поганыи: нѣкоему убо у нихъ худу царствующу, а все дѣющу у нихъ князю Мамаю … великии же князь Дмитрии, съ братомъ своимъ съ Володимеромъ, изрядивъ полкы противу поганыхъ Половець
passages.translation: the pagan Ishmaelite race rises against the Christians: for a certain feeble man reigns among them, and Prince Mamai does everything among them … and Grand Prince Dmitry, with his brother Vladimir, arrayed his regiments against the pagan Polovtsy
passages.speaker: Novgorod First Chronicle, younger redaction (PSRL vol. 3, 1841)
passages.caution: Written in Novgorod, far from the battle, in a religious register.

passages.headline: Tatar prisoners in Novgorod: baptism or the river
passages.people: Tatar prisoners (Kazan Tatars brought to Novgorod after 1552)
passages.gloss: The Second Novgorod Chronicle, a terse 16th-century town record, notes that in 1552 sixty Kazan Tatars were brought from Moscow and three new prisons were built for them. On this page, under the winter of 7065 (1556 to 1557), it records that clerks handed the Tatars held in the prisons who wished to be baptised over to the monasteries, while 'those who did not wish to be baptised, they threw into the water'.
passages.quote: давали дьяки по монастыремъ Татаръ, которые сидѣли въ тюрмѣхъ и захотѣли креститись; которые не захотѣли креститись, ино ихъ метали въ воду.
passages.translation: the clerks gave out to the monasteries the Tatars who sat in the prisons and wished to be baptised; those who did not wish to be baptised, they threw into the water.
passages.speaker: Second Novgorod Chronicle (printed in the same PSRL volume, 1841)
passages.caution: This is the Second Novgorod Chronicle, not the First, though it is bound in the same volume. The chronicle does not say explicitly that these were the Kazan prisoners of 1552.

passages.headline: 'Unknown peoples': who are these Tatars?
passages.people: Tatars (the Mongol army of Jebe and Subutai)
passages.gloss: The first Suzdal notice of the Tatars admits that nobody knows who they are, where they came from, what language they speak or what faith they hold. People called them Tatars, Taumens or Pechenegs, while bookish men tied them to a prophecy of Methodius of Patara. The chronicler adds that he writes them down only 'for the memory of the disaster of the Rus princes' at the Kalka.
passages.quote: явишася языци, ихже никтоже добрѣ ясно не вѣсть, кто суть и отколѣ изидоша, и что языкъ ихъ, и которого племени суть, и что вѣра ихъ; и зовуть я Татары, а инии глаголють Таумены, а друзіи Печенѣзи, ини глаголють, яко се суть, о нихъ же Меѳодій Патомьскый епископъ свѣдѣтельствуеть
passages.translation: there appeared peoples whom no one clearly knows: who they are and whence they came out, and what their language is, and of what tribe they are, and what their faith is; and they call them Tatars, and others say Taumens, and others Pechenegs, and others say that these are the ones of whom Methodius, bishop of Patara, bears witness
passages.speaker: Laurentian Chronicle (Suzdal annal), PSRL vol. 1 (1846)
passages.caution: The editors note that other chronicles read 'Taurmens' (Turkmens). The Methodius link is a book legend, not anything the Mongols said of themselves.

passages.headline: The end-of-time peoples of Pseudo-Methodius
passages.people: Tatars (Mongols), read as an apocalyptic nation
passages.gloss: Straight after naming the Tatars, the chronicler quotes the prophecy he thinks explains them: peoples driven into the desert by Gideon would come out at the end of time and conquer everything from the east to the Euphrates and from the Tigris to the Black Sea, except Ethiopia. He hedges at once: 'God alone knows who they are.' This is the same book legend that western writers linked to Gog and Magog.
passages.quote: тако бо Меѳодій рече: яко къ скончанью временъ явитися тѣмъ, яже загна Гедеонъ, и поплѣнять всю землю отъ встока до Ефранта и отъ Тигръ до Понетьскаго моря, кромѣ Еѳіопья.
passages.translation: for thus Methodius said: that toward the end of time those whom Gideon drove out will appear, and they will capture all the land from the east to the Euphrates, and from the Tigris to the Pontic Sea, except Ethiopia.
passages.speaker: Laurentian Chronicle, citing the Revelation of Pseudo-Methodius, PSRL vol. 1 (1846)
passages.caution: A prophecy the chronicler read in a book, offered as one guess among several.

passages.headline: The Great City of the Volga Bulgars burned
passages.gloss: A year before they reached Rus, the Tatars came 'from the eastern lands' and took the 'glorious Great City' of the Volga Bulgars, a Muslim trading state on the middle Volga. The chronicler says they killed everyone, took a great quantity of goods and burned the city. The Great City is usually identified by historians with Bilyar.
passages.quote: Тое же осени придоша отъ всточныя страны въ Болгарьскую землю безбожніи Татари, и взяша славный Великый городъ Болгарьскый, и избиша оружьемъ отъ старца и до унаго и до сущаго младенца, и взяша товара множство, а городъ ихъ пожгоша огнемъ, и всю землю ихъ плѣниша.
passages.translation: That same autumn the godless Tatars came from the eastern lands into the Bulgar land, and took the glorious Great City of the Bulgars, and slew them with weapons from old man to youth to the infant at the breast, and took a great quantity of goods, and burned their city with fire, and captured all their land.
passages.speaker: Laurentian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 1 (1846)
passages.caution: Reported from Suzdal at a distance; 'from old man to infant' is a stock phrase for a massacre.

passages.headline: Riazan: through the forest in winter
passages.gloss: The Tatars came 'through the forest' in winter, ravaged the Riazan land as far as Pronsk, burned Riazan and killed its prince. The chronicler describes what they did to captives: some were impaled or stretched, others shot with arrows, others tied with their hands behind their backs. Then the army moved on to Kolomna.
passages.quote: придоша отъ всточныя страны на Рязаньскую землю, лѣсомъ, безбожніи Татари, и почаша воевати Рязаньскую землю, и плѣноваху и до Проньска; поплѣнивше Рязань весь и пожгоша, и князя ихъ убиша, ихже емше овы растинахуть, другыя же стрѣлами растрѣляху въ ня, а ини опакы руцѣ связывахуть
passages.translation: the godless Tatars came from the eastern lands onto the Riazan land, through the forest, and began to make war on the Riazan land, and captured as far as Pronsk; having captured all Riazan they burned it, and killed their prince; of those they seized, some they stretched out, others they shot through with arrows, and others they bound with their hands behind them
passages.speaker: Laurentian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 1 (1846)

passages.headline: Vladimir besieged: scaffolds, catapults and a palisade
passages.gloss: After parading the captured prince Vladimir Iurevich before the Golden Gate so his brothers on the walls could see him, the Tatars camped around the city. On the Saturday before Lent they built scaffolds and set up 'poroki' (stone-throwing engines), and in one night surrounded the whole city with a timber palisade. The next morning they attacked. It is a precise picture of Mongol siege method.
passages.quote: Въ суботу мясопустную почаша наряжати лѣсы и порокы ставиша до вечера, а на ночь огородиша тыномъ около всего города Володимеря; въ недѣлю мясопустную по заутрени приступиша къ городу, мѣсяца февраля въ 7, на память святаго мученика Ѳеодора Стратилата.
passages.translation: On Meatfare Saturday they began to prepare scaffolds and set up siege engines until evening, and in the night they fenced the whole city of Vladimir round with a palisade; on Meatfare Sunday after matins they advanced on the city, on the 7th of February, the feast of the holy martyr Theodore Stratelates.
passages.speaker: Laurentian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 1 (1846)
passages.caution: The editors note that the date and saint's day do not quite match (the feast is 8 February).

passages.headline: The stone cathedral that became a furnace
passages.people: Tatars (Mongols); Bishop Mitrofan and the princely family of Vladimir
passages.gloss: When the new town fell, the bishop, the grand prince's wife, daughters-in-law, grandchildren, boyars and townspeople shut themselves in the stone Cathedral of the Mother of God, built by the Suzdal princes. The Tatars set it on fire. Then they forced the doors, killed the survivors and stripped the wonder-working icon of its gold, silver and gems. The passage shows a Rus-built stone church and who ruined it.
passages.quote: Татарове же силою отвориша двери церковныя, и видѣша овы огнемъ скончавшася, овы же оружьемъ до конца смерти предаша; святую Богородицю разграбиша, чюдную икону одраша, украшену златомъ и серебромъ и каменьемъ драгымъ
passages.translation: The Tatars forced open the church doors, and saw some who had perished by fire, and others they put to death with weapons; they plundered the holy Mother of God [cathedral], and stripped the wonderful icon adorned with gold and silver and precious stones
passages.speaker: Laurentian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 1 (1846)

passages.headline: Fourteen towns in one February
passages.gloss: After Vladimir the army split up: some went to Rostov, some to Iaroslavl, some along the Volga to Gorodets and Galich, others to Pereiaslavl and as far as Torzhok. The chronicler sums up: hardly a village was left untouched, and fourteen towns fell in the single month of February, not counting 'slobodas' (settlements) and 'pogosts' (parish centres).
passages.quote: и оттолѣ всю ту страну и грады многы все то плѣниша, доже и до Торжку, и нѣсть мѣста, ни вси, ни селъ тацѣхъ рѣдко, идѣже не воеваша на Суждальской земли; и взяша городовъ 14, опрочь свободъ и погостовъ, во одинъ мѣсяць февраль
passages.translation: and from there they captured all that country and many towns, as far as Torzhok, and there is no place, nor village, and few hamlets, where they did not make war in the Suzdal land; and they took 14 towns, besides slobodas and pogosts, in the one month of February
passages.speaker: Laurentian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 1 (1846)

passages.headline: Kozelsk, the 'evil city'
passages.people: Tatars (Mongols under Batu); townspeople of Kozelsk
passages.gloss: Batu turned back from the road to Novgorod and besieged the small town of Kozelsk, whose prince was a boy. The townsmen held out for seven weeks, sallied out, cut up the siege engines and killed three sons of a 'temnik' (commander of ten thousand). The chronicle says that afterwards the Tatars would not call it Kozelsk but 'the evil city'.
passages.quote: Оттолѣ же въ Татарѣхъ не смѣяху его нарещи Козелескъ, но зваху его градъ злый, понеже бяше билися у города того по семъ недѣль, и убиша три сыны темничи, Татарове же искаша ихъ, и не обрѣтоша ихъ во множествѣ трупа мертвыхъ.
passages.translation: From then on among the Tatars they did not dare to call it Kozelsk, but called it the evil city, because they had fought at that town for seven weeks, and three sons of a temnik were killed; the Tatars searched for them and did not find them among the multitude of dead bodies.
passages.speaker: Continuation printed as the 'Troitskaia letopis' in PSRL vol. 1 (1846)
passages.caution: Not in the Laurentian codex itself but in the parallel text the 1846 editors printed after it. The 'evil city' name is a report of what the Tatars supposedly said.

passages.headline: A patent from Batu: 'be the eldest of all princes'
passages.people: Batu, khan of the Golden Horde; Grand Prince Iaroslav Vsevolodich
passages.gloss: Five years after the conquest the grand prince rode 'to the Tatars, to Batu', and sent his son Konstantin on to the Great Khan ('Kan') in Mongolia. Batu received him with honour and named him senior over all Rus princes. The chronicle records the start of the system in which Rus princes held their thrones by the khan's word.
passages.quote: Великый князь Ярославъ поѣха въ Татары къ Батыеви, а сына своего Костянтина посла къ Канови; Батый же почти Ярослава великою честью, и мужи его, и отпусти й, рекъ ему: «Ярославе! буди ты старѣй всѣмъ княземъ въ Русскомъ языцѣ.»
passages.translation: Grand Prince Iaroslav went to the Tatars, to Batu, and sent his son Konstantin to the Kan; Batu honoured Iaroslav with great honour, and his men, and let him go, saying to him: 'Iaroslav! be thou the eldest of all princes in the Russian nation.'
passages.speaker: Laurentian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 1 (1846)

passages.headline: Bow to the fire and the idols
passages.gloss: When Mikhail of Chernigov came to Batu's camp, Batu ordered him to bow to fire and to 'their idols'. Mikhail refused, mocked the idols as deaf, and was killed. The episode matches western reports that visitors had to pass between fires and honour Mongol felt images, and it made Mikhail a Russian saint.
passages.quote: посла Батый къ Михаилу князю, веля ему поклонитися огневи и болваномъ ихъ; Михайло же князь не повинуся велѣнью ихъ, но укори й и глухыя его кумиры, и тако безъ милости отъ нечестивыхъ заколенъ бысть
passages.translation: Batu sent to Prince Mikhail, ordering him to bow down to fire and to their idols; but Prince Mikhail did not submit to their command, but reproached him and his deaf idols, and so he was stabbed to death without mercy by the impious ones
passages.speaker: Laurentian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 1 (1846)
passages.caution: Told as a martyr story; the fuller hagiographic version is in later chronicles.

passages.headline: The census: tens, hundreds, thousands and ten-thousands
passages.people: Mongol census officials ('chislenitsy') of the Golden Horde
passages.gloss: The Horde sent census takers who counted the Suzdal, Riazan and Murom lands and set up officers over tens, hundreds, thousands and ten-thousands, the Mongol decimal system, before returning to the Horde. Clergy were not counted, in line with the Mongol practice of exempting religious men from tax.
passages.quote: Тое же зимы пріѣхаша численици, исчетоша всю землю Суждальскую, и Рязаньскую, и Мюромьскую, и ставиша десятники и сотники и тысящники и темники, и идоша въ ворду, толико не чтоша игуменовъ, черньцовъ, поповъ, крилошанъ, кто зрить на святую Богородицю и на владыку.
passages.translation: That winter the census takers came, and counted all the Suzdal land, and the Riazan and the Murom, and appointed chiefs of ten, of a hundred, of a thousand and of ten thousand, and went off to the Horde; only they did not count abbots, monks, priests, choir clergy, whoever looks to the holy Mother of God and to the bishop.
passages.speaker: Laurentian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 1 (1846)

passages.headline: Tax farmers driven out by the town assemblies
passages.people: Muslim ('besermen') tax farmers working for the Horde; townspeople of Rostov, Vladimir, Suzdal, Iaroslavl
passages.gloss: The Horde's tribute had been farmed out to Muslim merchants, who bought the right to collect it and charged interest. In 1262 the towns called their assemblies (veche) and drove them out of Rostov, Vladimir, Suzdal and Iaroslavl. The same entry tells of a renegade monk, Zosima, who became a Muslim under a Tatar official named Kutlubii and was killed in Iaroslavl.
passages.quote: вложи ярость въ сердца крестьяномъ, не терпяще насилья поганыхъ, изволиша вѣчь, и выгнаша изъ городовъ, изъ Ростова, изъ Володимеря, изъ Суждаля, изъ Ярославля; окупахуть бо ти оканьніи бесурмене дани, и отъ того велику пагубу людемъ творяхуть
passages.translation: [God] put fury into the hearts of the Christians, who, not bearing the violence of the pagans, summoned the veche and drove them out of the towns, out of Rostov, out of Vladimir, out of Suzdal, out of Iaroslavl; for those accursed besermen had bought up the tribute, and from that they worked great ruin on the people
passages.speaker: Laurentian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 1 (1846)

passages.headline: The baskak's warning: heads tied to saddle straps
passages.people: Akhmat, Muslim baskak (tax agent) of the Kursk land, and his 'besermen'
passages.gloss: After a quarrel with the local princes, the baskak Akhmat had captured boyars killed, their bodies hung on trees without heads and right hands, and told pilgrims to spread the message that anyone who disputes with his baskak will end the same way. His men then tied the heads to their saddle straps. The Laurentian text starts mid-story because leaves are missing from the manuscript.
passages.quote: «вы есте гости, а паломници, ходите по землямъ; тако молвите: хто иметь держати споръ съ своимъ баскакомъ, тако ему будеть;» а что изъимано людій черныхъ и съ женами и съ дѣтми, то все попровадилъ прочь. А трупья бояръ тѣхъ повелѣ по деревью извѣшати, отъимая голову и правую руку; и начаша бесурмене вязати головы боярьскыя къ торокомъ
passages.translation: 'You are guests and pilgrims, you travel through the lands; say this: whoever will hold a dispute with his baskak, so it will be with him.' And whatever common people were seized, with wives and children, he sent all of them away. And he ordered the corpses of those boyars hung up on the trees, cutting off the head and the right hand; and the besermen began to tie the boyars' heads to their saddle straps
passages.speaker: Laurentian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 1 (1846)
passages.caution: The opening of the story is lost in the codex; the chronicler blames Rus sins and princely feuds as much as the baskak.

passages.headline: The baskak's two settlements empty overnight
passages.people: Akhmat's 'besermen' (Muslim) settlers; Rus princes of Rylsk and Lipovichsk
passages.gloss: Akhmat had founded two 'slobodas' (tax-free trading settlements) in the Kursk land and left two brothers to guard and fortify them. After a Rus prince ambushed their men, the brothers fled to Kursk and on the next day the whole of both settlements scattered. It is a rare glimpse of settlements founded under Horde protection inside Rus, and of how fragile they were.
passages.quote: Того же лѣта, по Велицѣ дни въ недѣлю Фомину, побѣгоста 2 братеника та бесерменина къ Курьску, а на заутрѣи въ понедѣльникъ побѣже вся свобода та, и другая; и тако розоидошася обѣ свободѣ бесерменьскиѣ.
passages.translation: That same year, after Easter on St Thomas Sunday, those two besermen brothers fled to Kursk, and on the morrow, Monday, all that sloboda ran away, and the other one too; and so both besermen slobodas dispersed.
passages.speaker: Laurentian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 1 (1846)
passages.caution: The manuscript spells sloboda as 'svoboda'.

passages.headline: 'Godless Moabites, called Tatars'
passages.gloss: The Galician chronicler opens the Kalka story with an 'unheard-of army': godless Moabites 'called Tatars' who fell on the Polovtsian land. Even the greatest Cuman chief could not stand against them. After the rout the Tatars 'went back to their vezhi', the steppe word for nomad tent camps. The biblical name Moabites shows how the chronicler fitted a new enemy into scripture.
passages.quote: Приде неслыханая рать: безбожніи Моавитяне, рекомыи Татарове, придоша на землю Половецькую. Половцемь же ставшимъ, Юрьгій Кончаковичь бѣ болійше всихъ Половець, не може стати противу лицо ихъ; бѣгающи же ему, и мнози избьени быша, до рѣкы Днѣпра, Татарове же возвратишася, идоша въ вѣжа своя.
passages.translation: There came an unheard-of army: the godless Moabites, called Tatars, came onto the Polovtsian land. The Polovtsy made a stand, but Iurii Konchakovich, who was greatest of all the Polovtsy, could not stand against their face; he fled, and many were killed, as far as the river Dnieper, and the Tatars turned back and went to their tent camps.
passages.speaker: Hypatian Chronicle (Galician-Volhynian part), PSRL vol. 2 (1843)
passages.caution: Written decades after 1223; the date 6732 was added by a later copyist.

passages.headline: A prisoner names Batu's generals, and Guyuk
passages.people: Batu's commanders: Urdiui (Orda), Baidar, Biriui, Kaidan, Bechak, Mengu (Mongke), Kiuiuk (Guyuk), Subutai, Burundai
passages.gloss: During the siege of Kiev the defenders captured a Tatar named Tovrul, who told them who was in Batu's army. The list matches Batu's Chinggisid relatives and generals known from Persian and Mongol sources. The chronicler adds that Guyuk turned back on hearing of the Great Khan's death and became khan himself, though (he believed) not of the khan's family but his first general.
passages.quote: Яша же въ нихъ Татарина, именемъ Товрулъ, и тъ исповѣда имъ всю силу ихъ; се бяху братья его силный воеводы: Урдюй, Байдаръ, Бирюй, Кайданъ, Бечакъ и Меньгу и Кююкъ (иже вратися увѣдавъ смерть канову и бысть каномъ, не отъ роду же его, но бѣ воевода его перьвый), Себѣдяй Богатуръ и Бурунъдай Багатырь
passages.translation: They captured among them a Tatar named Tovrul, and he told them all their strength; these were his brothers, strong commanders: Urdiui, Baidar, Biriui, Kaidan, Bechak and Mengu and Kiuiuk (who returned on learning of the khan's death and became khan, though not of his family, but he was his first commander), Sebediai the Bogatur and Burundai the Bagatyr
passages.speaker: Hypatian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 2 (1843)
passages.caution: Guyuk was in fact a grandson of Chinggis Khan; the chronicler's remark about his descent is mistaken.

passages.headline: Kiev besieged: you could not hear for the carts and camels
passages.gloss: Batu came to Kiev 'in heavy strength' and ringed the city. The chronicler's famous line: inside the walls people could not hear each other for the creaking of Batu's carts, the bellowing of his camels and the neighing of his herds of horses. Batu then set up siege engines by the Liadskie (Polish) Gate, where the ravines came close, and battered the walls day and night.
passages.quote: Приде Батый Кыеву въ силѣ тяжьцѣ, многомъ множьствомъ силы своей, и окружи градъ и остолпи сила Татарьская, и бысть градъ во обдержаньи велицѣ. И бѣ Батый у города и отроци его обсѣдяху градъ, и не бѣ слышати отъ гласа скрипанія телѣгъ его, множества ревѣнія вельблудъ его, и рьжанія отъ гласа стадъ конь его
passages.translation: Batu came to Kiev in heavy strength, with a great multitude of his forces, and surrounded the city, and the Tatar force hemmed it in, and the city was under great siege. And Batu was at the city and his men besieged the city, and one could not hear for the noise of the creaking of his carts, the multitude of the bellowing of his camels, and the neighing of the herds of his horses
passages.speaker: Hypatian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 2 (1843)

passages.headline: The church vaults that collapsed under the refugees
passages.gloss: When the Tatars broke through, the townspeople threw up a last ring of defences around the Church of the Mother of God (the Tithe Church, Kiev's first stone church, built by Prince Vladimir about 990). Next day, as people crowded onto the church and its vaults with their goods, the walls gave way under the weight, and the city fell. The chronicler credits the building to Rus princes and its ruin to the siege.
passages.quote: Наутрѣя же придоша на нѣ, и бысть брань межи ими велика; людемъ же узбѣгшимъ на церковь и на комары церковныя, и съ товары своими, отъ тягости повалишася съ ними стѣны церковныя, и пріятъ бысть градъ сице воими.
passages.translation: Next morning they came against them, and there was a great battle between them; and as the people ran up onto the church and onto the church vaults, with their goods, from the weight the church walls fell down with them, and so the city was taken by the warriors.
passages.speaker: Hypatian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 2 (1843)
passages.caution: The church is not named in this sentence; the identification with the Tithe Church comes from the preceding line and from archaeology.

passages.headline: Twelve catapults at Kolodiazhin, and a town Batu could not take
passages.people: Tatars (Mongols under Batu); towns of Prince Daniil of Galicia
passages.gloss: After Kiev, Batu marched into Volhynia. At Kolodiazhin he set up twelve siege engines but could not break the wall, so he talked the defenders into surrendering and then killed them. Kremenets, Daniil's town, he judged impossible to take and left alone. Vladimir-in-Volhynia was stormed and its people slaughtered. The passage shows that walls and position still mattered against the Mongols.
passages.quote: приде къ городу Колодяжьну, и постави порока 12 и не може разбити стѣны, и начатъ перемолвливати люди; они же, послушавше злого съвѣта его, передашася и сами избити быша. … видивъ же Кремянець градъ Даниловъ, яко невозможно пріяти ему, и отъиде отъ нихъ
passages.translation: he came to the town of Kolodiazhin, and set up 12 siege engines and could not break the wall, and began to talk the people over; they, heeding his evil counsel, surrendered and were themselves slaughtered. … and seeing Daniil's town of Kremenets, that it was impossible for him to take it, he went away from them
passages.speaker: Hypatian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 2 (1843)

passages.headline: Sorcery, Chinggis Khan's dreams and bowing to a bush
passages.place: Pereiaslav and the Volga (Kuremsa's and Batu's camps)
passages.people: Tatars of Kuremsa and Batu; Prince Daniil of Galicia
passages.gloss: On his way to Batu, Daniil passed through the camp of the commander Kuremsa and was horrified by Tatar religion as a Christian saw it: shamans' 'kudesy' (sorcery), the 'dreams' of 'Chigizakon' (Chinggis Khan), and visiting kings and princes being led around a bush to bow to the sun, the moon, the earth and the souls of their ancestors. At Batu's a Rus servant told him to bow to the bush as his brother had done.
passages.quote: видя бо обладаемы дьяволомъ: скверная ихъ кудешьская бляденья и Чигизаконова мечтанья, скверная его кровопитья, многыя его вольшбы; приходящія цари, и князи и велможѣ, солнцю и лунѣ и земли, дьяволу и умершимъ въ адѣ отцемъ ихъ и дѣдомъ и матеремъ, водяше около куста покланятися
passages.translation: for he saw them possessed by the devil: their foul sorcerers' ravings and the dreams of Chigizakon, his foul blood-drinkings, his many witchcrafts; the kings and princes and nobles who came were led around a bush to bow to the sun and moon and earth, to the devil and to their fathers and grandfathers and mothers who have died and are in hell
passages.speaker: Hypatian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 2 (1843)
passages.caution: A hostile Christian description; the chronicler learned it from Daniil's party, not from Mongol informants.

passages.headline: 'Drink our black milk, mare's kumiss'
passages.people: Batu; Prince Daniil of Galicia; Batu's wife Barakchin
passages.gloss: Inside Batu's tent Batu asked Daniil whether he drank 'black milk, our drink, mare's kumiss'. Daniil said he never had, but would if ordered. 'You are now one of us, a Tatar: drink our drink,' said Batu. Then Daniil went to pay respects to Batu's senior wife Barakchin, who sent him a cup of wine because, she said, he was not used to milk.
passages.quote: «пьеши ли черное молоко, наше питье, кобылій кумузъ?» Оному же рекшу: «доселѣ есмь не пилъ, нынѣ же ты велишь, пью.» Онъ же рче: «ты уже нашь же Татаринъ, пій наше питье.» Онъ же испивъ поклонися, по обычаю ихъ
passages.translation: 'Do you drink black milk, our drink, mare's kumiss?' He said: 'Until now I have not drunk it; now, since you order it, I drink.' And he said: 'You are already one of us, a Tatar; drink our drink.' And he drank and bowed, according to their custom
passages.speaker: Hypatian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 2 (1843), reporting Batu's words

passages.headline: 'Worse than evil is Tatar honour'
passages.people: Batu's Horde; Prince Daniil of Galicia
passages.gloss: The chronicler breaks off to lament what homage meant: a great prince who ruled Kiev, Vladimir and Galich now knelt and was called a slave, and paid tribute in fear for his life. He adds that the Tatars had poisoned Grand Prince Iaroslav of Suzdal and knifed Mikhail of Chernigov for not bowing to the bush. Daniil stayed 25 days before he was sent home with his lands confirmed.
passages.quote: О злѣе зла честь Татарьская! Данилови Романовичю князю бывшу велику, обладавшу Рускою землею, Кыевомъ и Володимеромъ и Галичемъ, со братомъ си инѣми странами: нынѣ сѣдить на колѣну и холопомъ называеться, и дани хотять, живота не чаеть и грозы приходять.
passages.translation: O, worse than evil is Tatar honour! Daniil Romanovich was a great prince, who ruled the Russian land, Kiev and Vladimir and Galich, with his brother, and other lands: now he sits on his knees and is called a slave, and they want tribute, he does not expect to live, and threats come.
passages.speaker: Hypatian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 2 (1843)
passages.caution: The poisoning of Iaroslav is the chronicler's claim (Carpini reports a similar suspicion); it is not proven.

passages.headline: Kholm: a new town that craftsmen fled to from the Tatars
passages.people: Prince Daniil of Galicia; craftsmen fleeing the Tatars
passages.gloss: Daniil founded Kholm on a wooded hill he spotted while hunting, and the chronicler notes that the Tatars could not take it when Batu conquered Rus. Daniil invited Germans, Rus, Poles and other foreigners, and young men and master craftsmen of every kind 'fled from the Tatars' to it: saddlers, bowyers, quiver makers, and smiths of iron, copper and silver. Here the arrow runs the other way: craftsmen leave Tatar-held lands to build a Rus prince's town.
passages.quote: нача призывати прихожаѣ Нѣмцѣ и Русь, иноязычникы и Ляхы; идяху день и во день, и уноты и мастеръ всяціи бѣжаху изъ Татаръ, сѣдлници, и лучници, и тулници, и кузници желѣзу и мѣди и сребру, и бѣ жизнь, и наполниша дворы окрестъ града поле и села
passages.translation: he began to invite newcomers, Germans and Rus, foreigners and Poles; they came day after day, and young men and masters of every kind fled from the Tatars, saddlers and bowyers and quiver makers and smiths of iron and copper and silver, and there was life, and they filled the courtyards around the town, the fields and the villages
passages.speaker: Hypatian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 2 (1843)

passages.headline: Kholm's church: carved heads, Roman glass, a floor like a mirror
passages.people: Prince Daniil of Galicia and his craftsmen (one named Avdei)
passages.gloss: The chronicler describes Daniil's Church of St John in Kholm in unusual detail: vaults resting on four carved human heads, windows glazed with 'Roman' glass, a floor cast of copper and pure tin that shone like a mirror, and doors trimmed with white Galician and green Kholm stone, carved by 'a certain craftsman Avdei'. Nearby stood a tower on a stone base 15 ells high, built of hewn timber and whitewashed. The builders are Rus, and the materials are named.
passages.quote: комары, съ каждого угла преводъ, и стоянье ихъ на четырехъ головахъ человѣцскихъ изваяно отъ нѣкоего хытреца; окна украшена стеклы Римьскими … внутрьній же ей помостъ бѣ слитъ отъ мѣди и отъ олова чиста, яко блещатися яко зерцалу; двери же ей двоя украшены каменьемъ Галичкымъ бѣлымъ и зеленымъ Холмъскымъ, тесанымъ
passages.translation: vaults, with an arch from each corner, and their supports on four human heads carved by a certain craftsman; the windows adorned with Roman glass … its floor inside was cast of copper and pure tin, so that it shone like a mirror; its two doors were adorned with hewn stone, white Galician and green Kholm stone
passages.speaker: Hypatian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 2 (1843)
passages.caution: The chronicler writes that the church later burned; the description is of a building he knew.

passages.headline: The wind that turned the catapult stones back
passages.gloss: When Kuremsa's Tatars attacked the unfortified town of Lutsk in a winter flood, the townsmen cut the bridge. Kuremsa set up siege engines, but, says the chronicler, God, St John and St Nicholas worked a miracle: the wind blew the stones back onto the Tatars, and then the sling of the engine broke. The Tatars went back to their camp in the steppe.
passages.quote: Богъ же чюдо створи, и святый Иванъ, и святый Никола, вѣтру же таку бывшу, яко порокомъ вергшу вѣтръ же обращаше камень на нѣ, пакы же мечющимъ на нѣ крѣпко изломися, Божіею силою, пракъ ихъ, и не успѣвше ничтоже вратишася во станы своя, рекше въ поле.
passages.translation: But God worked a miracle, and St John and St Nicholas: there was such a wind that when the engine threw, the wind turned the stone back upon them; and again, as they hurled hard, by the power of God their sling broke, and having achieved nothing they went back to their camps, that is, to the steppe.
passages.speaker: Hypatian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 2 (1843)
passages.caution: Told as a miracle; the wind may have been real, the saints' part is the chronicler's reading.

passages.headline: Burundai: 'tear down all your town walls'
passages.people: Burundai, Tatar general; Princes Vasilko and Lev
passages.gloss: The Tatar general Burundai arrived in Volhynia during a princely wedding and told the princes: if you are at peace with me, raze your towns. Lev dismantled Danilov and Stozhek and then Lviv; Vasilko razed Kremenets and Lutsk. Vladimir-in-Volhynia was too big to pull down quickly, so Vasilko had it burned overnight, and next day Burundai came to see it burned 'with his own eyes' and dined with the prince.
passages.quote: «оже есте мои мирници, розмечѣте же городы своѣ всѣ.» Левъ розмета Даниловъ, и Стожекъ, оттолѣ же пославъ Лвовъ розмета, а Василко пославъ Кремянець розмета и Луческъ.
passages.translation: 'If you are at peace with me, then tear down all your towns.' Lev tore down Danilov and Stozhek, and from there he sent and tore down Lviv, and Vasilko sent and tore down Kremenets and Lutsk.
passages.speaker: Hypatian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 2 (1843), quoting Burundai
passages.caution: 'Razing' here means pulling down fortifications (walls and ramparts), not whole towns.

passages.headline: Telebuga lost in the mountains: a hundred thousand dead
passages.people: Golden Horde army of Nogai and Telebuga
passages.gloss: Returning from a raid on Hungary, Nogai went by Brasov, while Telebuga tried to cross the mountains. A three-day crossing became fifty days of wandering. Famine set in, the soldiers began to eat people and then to die, and 'eyewitnesses said' a hundred thousand perished. Telebuga came out on foot with his wife and a single mare. The chronicler presents it as God's punishment.
passages.quote: Телебуга поиде поперекъ Гору; што бяшеть переити треими деньми, и ходи по 50 дній блудя въ горахъ, водимъ гнѣвомъ Божіимъ. И бысть въ нихъ голодъ великъ; и начаша люде ѣсти, потомъ же начаша и сами измирати, и умре ихъ бесчисленое множьство; самовидци же тако рекоша: умершихъ бысть сто тысячь.
passages.translation: Telebuga went across the Mountain; what should have been crossed in three days, he wandered for 50 days lost in the mountains, led by the wrath of God. And there was a great famine among them; and they began to eat people, and then began themselves to die, and a countless multitude of them died; eyewitnesses said this: the dead were a hundred thousand.
passages.speaker: Hypatian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 2 (1843)
passages.caution: The figure of 100,000 is hearsay attributed to eyewitnesses; the cannibalism report is part of the same account.

passages.headline: Epic heroes die at the Kalka
passages.people: Tatars (Mongols); Rus warriors including the epic heroes Aleksandr Popovich and Dobrynia
passages.gloss: The Nikon Chronicle adds names from Russian heroic poetry to the Kalka disaster: Aleksandr Popovich, his servant Torop, Dobrynia 'Golden Belt' and seventy great bogatyrs all fell to the Tatars. The same page tells how the captured princes were laid under planks while the Tatars sat on top to eat, crushing them. Older chronicles do not name these heroes; the compilers took them from oral epic.
passages.quote: убиша же на томъ бою: и Александра Поповичя, и слугу его Торопа, и Добрыню Рязаничя Златаго пояса, и седмьдесятъ великихъ и храбрыхъ богатырей, вси побіени быша гнѣвомъ Божіимъ за грѣхи наша отъ Татаръ.
passages.translation: and in that battle they killed Aleksandr Popovich and his servant Torop, and Dobrynia Riazanich Golden Belt, and seventy great and brave bogatyrs; all were slain by the Tatars through the wrath of God for our sins.
passages.speaker: Nikon Chronicle, PSRL vol. 10 (1885)
passages.caution: The editors note that this sentence is found in only one manuscript (G). The heroes belong to epic song, not to 13th-century records.

passages.headline: 'Swift to battle and swift to flee'
passages.gloss: Closing its Kalka story, the Nikon compiler sums up the newcomers: nobody knew where these Tatars came from or where they went. They were quick to fight and quick to run, light and not weighed down by baggage; they fled and then turned back again, the feigned retreat that western writers also noticed. The last phrase, 'like demons', shows the chronicler's fear.
passages.quote: Се же первое прихоженіе Татарское на Русь; бѣ же скори на бой, такоже и на бѣганіе, легци же суща, не обременяющеся ничимъ же тяготнѣе, бѣгаеть же и паки возвращается, и злодѣиствени суть аки дѣмони.
passages.translation: This was the first coming of the Tatars on Rus; they were swift to battle and likewise to flight, being light and not burdened with anything heavy; they flee and then return again, and they are evildoers like demons.
passages.speaker: Nikon Chronicle, PSRL vol. 10 (1885)
passages.caution: A 16th-century summary, not a 1223 eyewitness.

passages.headline: Batu's demand: a tenth of everything
passages.people: Batu's envoys; the princes of Riazan, Murom and Pronsk
passages.gloss: Camped on the river Onuza, Batu sent envoys to the Riazan princes asking for a tenth of everything: princes, people, armour and horses. The princes answered: 'when we are gone, all will be yours.' One manuscript printed alongside says the envoys were 'a sorceress woman and two men with her', a detail that may echo Mongol shamanesses or may be later colour.
passages.quote: И оттолѣ послаша послы своя жену чародѣйцу и два мужа съ нею ко княземъ Рязаньскимъ, просяще у нихъ десятины во всемъ: въ князехъ, и въ людехъ, и въ доспѣсехъ, и въ конехъ.
passages.translation: And from there they sent their envoys, a sorceress woman and two men with her, to the Riazan princes, asking of them a tenth of everything: of princes, and of people, and of armour, and of horses.
passages.speaker: Nikon Chronicle, variant text of the Tolstoy (Golitsyn) copy printed in parallel, PSRL vol. 10 (1885)
passages.caution: The 'sorceress' appears only in the parallel copy; the main Nikon text simply says 'envoys'. The tithe demand matches the Novgorod First Chronicle.

passages.headline: Tver rises against the khan's cousin
passages.people: Shchelkan (Chol-khan), son of Diuden and nephew of Uzbek Khan; the people of Tver
passages.gloss: Uzbek Khan's nephew Shchelkan came to Tver as envoy. The Moscow chronicle says he meant to kill the Tver princes, rule Tver himself, put Tatar princes into the Rus towns and bring the Christians to the 'Tatar faith' (Islam). Tver rose, and Shchelkan was burned in the prince's palace; the Horde merchants in the town were killed too. Uzbek's revenge helped Moscow's rise.
passages.quote: Пріиде во Тверь посолъ силенъ зѣло царевичь Щелканъ изъ Орды, отъ царя Азбяка; бѣ же сей братаничь царю Азбяку, хотя князей Тверскихъ избити, а самъ сѣсти на княженіи во Твери, а своихъ князей Татарскихъ хотя посажати по Рускимъ градомъ, а христіанъ хотяше привести въ Татарскую вѣру.
passages.translation: There came to Tver a very powerful envoy, the tsarevich Shchelkan, from the Horde, from Tsar Uzbek; he was Uzbek's nephew, and he wanted to kill the Tver princes and himself sit as prince in Tver, and to set his own Tatar princes over the Russian towns, and he wanted to bring the Christians into the Tatar faith.
passages.speaker: Nikon Chronicle, PSRL vol. 10 (1885)
passages.caution: Shchelkan's plans are the chronicler's allegation, written two centuries later from Moscow's side.

passages.headline: Tokhtamysh, 'a certain tsar from the east, from the Blue Horde'
passages.people: Tokhtamysh, khan from the eastern (Blue) Horde; Mamai
passages.gloss: After his defeat at Kulikovo, Mamai heard that 'a certain tsar from the east named Tokhtamysh, from the Blue Horde' was coming against him. They met on the Kalka and Mamai lost. The passage shows the Rus knew the Horde as several 'hordes' with colours, and treated a new khan from the east as a stranger.
passages.quote: и се пріиде ему вѣсть, что идеть на него нѣкый царь съ востока, именемъ Тахтамышь, изъ Синіе Орды. Мамай же, еже уготова на великого князя Дмитреа Ивановича рать, съ тою ратью поиде противу его, и срѣтошася на Калкахъ
passages.translation: and news came to him that a certain tsar from the east, named Tokhtamysh, from the Blue Horde, was coming against him. And Mamai, with the army he had prepared against Grand Prince Dmitrii Ivanovich, went against him with that army, and they met on the Kalka
passages.speaker: Nikon Chronicle, PSRL vol. 11 (1897)
passages.caution: Historians still argue whether 'Blue Horde' meant the eastern or western wing of the Jochid ulus.

passages.headline: Moscow boasts of its stone walls and iron gates
passages.people: Tokhtamysh's Tatars; the besieged people of Moscow
passages.gloss: When Tokhtamysh marched on Moscow, the townspeople burned their own suburbs so no timber or fence was left for the attackers. Some broke into the boyars' cellars, got drunk on mead and jeered from the walls that the Tatars could not stay long before 'a stone city with iron gates'. The Kremlin walls of white stone had been built in 1367. Four days later the Tatars took the city by a false peace.
passages.quote: И изношаху ис погребовъ меды господскія и упивахуся до пьяна, и шатающеся пьяни, глаголюще: «не устрашимся нахоженіа Татарьскаго, имѣемъ бо градъ каменъ твердъ и врата желѣзна; и не терпятъ Татарове стояти подъ градомъ нашимъ долго
passages.translation: And they carried the lords' mead out of the cellars and drank themselves drunk, and reeling about drunk they said: 'We shall not fear the Tatar invasion, for we have a strong stone city and iron gates; and the Tatars will not bear to stand long under our city
passages.speaker: Nikon Chronicle, PSRL vol. 11 (1897)

passages.headline: Tatar archers who never miss
passages.gloss: The account of the 1382 siege describes Tatar archery: their arrows fell on the walls like rain, some shot standing, others ran back and forth, others galloped and shot to both sides, forward and back, 'without a miss'. The defenders answered with crossbows, stone-throwers, boiling water and even the first cannon mentioned in Moscow.
passages.quote: Бѣ же приступъ ихъ ко граду яръ зѣло и ови отъ нихъ стояще стрѣляху, а друзіи скоро рищуще сѣмо и овамо, тако изучени быша, и стрѣляху безъ погрѣха; а иніи на конѣхъ борзо велми гоняюще, и на обѣ руцѣ и паки напреди и назадъ скорополучно стрѣляху безъ погрѣха.
passages.translation: Their assault on the city was very fierce; some of them shot standing, and others ran swiftly here and there, so well were they trained, and shot without a miss; and others, galloping very fast on horses, shot swiftly to both hands, and again forward and backward, without a miss.
passages.speaker: Nikon Chronicle, PSRL vol. 11 (1897)

passages.headline: Nogai horses for sale below Simonov
passages.people: Nogai envoys and horse traders of Koshum-mirza
passages.gloss: Nogai envoys arrived with letters from their mirzas asking for friendship. The grand prince lodged them at the 'Nogai Court' in Moscow and let them sell their horses on the meadow below the Simonov monastery. That year the horses were cheap: early snow had left no grazing, and many barely arrived alive or died. Steppe horse herds for Moscow's cavalry were the Nogais' great export.
passages.quote: И князь великій пожаловалъ ихъ, дружбу свою хочетъ къ нимъ дръжати, и велѣлъ ихъ поставити на Нагайскомъ дворѣ, а съ коньми торговати подъ Симановымъ на лугу. И быша лошади дешевы, едва и живы пришли, а иныхъ много помроша, понеже снѣгъ палъ рано, безъкорміа ради.
passages.translation: And the grand prince favoured them, and wishes to keep his friendship with them, and ordered them lodged at the Nogai Court, and to trade their horses on the meadow below Simonov. And the horses were cheap, they barely arrived alive, and many others died, because snow fell early, for lack of fodder.
passages.speaker: Nikon Chronicle, PSRL vol. 13, part 1 (1904)

passages.headline: Kazan's earth-filled timber ramparts
passages.gloss: During the siege Ivan IV's clerk Ivan Vyrodkov built a siege tower six sazhens high opposite Kazan's Tsar's Gate and mounted guns on it. The chronicle explains how the Kazan defenders survived: at every gate beyond the moat they had great 'tarasy', timber cribs filled with earth, and they dug holes and burrows under the gates and walls and fought from them 'like snakes'. Kazan's defences were timber and earth, not stone.
passages.quote: Погани же крыющеся въ ямы и рвы копающе подъ врата градцкые и подъ стѣну и рыюще норы подъ тарасы, бѣ бо у нихъ у всякыхъ воротъ за рвомъ тарасы велики, землею насыпаны, изъ-за тарасовъ біющеся по вся дни и изъ норъ, якоже змѣи
passages.translation: And the pagans hid, digging pits and ditches under the city gates and under the wall, and burrowing holes under the tarasy (for at every gate, beyond the moat, they had great tarasy filled with earth), fighting every day from behind the tarasy and from the holes, like snakes
passages.speaker: Nikon Chronicle, PSRL vol. 13, part 1 (1904)

passages.headline: Kazan's wall blown into the sky
passages.people: Kazan Tatars under Khan Ediger-Mahmet; Ivan IV's army
passages.gloss: A foreign engineer called 'Razmysl' had dug gunpowder mines under Kazan's walls. As the deacon in Ivan IV's camp church read the Gospel line 'there shall be one flock and one shepherd', the first mine went off 'like thunder': the tsar saw the wall torn out, earth and logs and people thrown high into the air. A second blast followed, and the army stormed the city.
passages.quote: и абіе якоже силный громъ грянулъ: и велми земля дрогну и потрясеся. Благочестивый же царь изъ церковныхъ дверей мало поступи и видѣ градскую стѣну подкопомъ вырвану, и страшна убо зрѣніемъ земля, яко тма, являшеся и на великую высоту въсходяще и многіе бревна и людей на высоту възметающе поганыхъ.
passages.translation: and at once it was as though mighty thunder crashed: the earth shook greatly and trembled. The pious tsar stepped a little out of the church doors and saw the city wall torn out by the mine, and the earth, terrible to look upon, appeared like darkness and rose to a great height, flinging many logs and pagan people up into the air.
passages.speaker: Nikon Chronicle, PSRL vol. 13, part 1 (1904)
passages.caution: Court narrative written to glorify Ivan IV; the logs thrown up show Kazan's walls were timber.

passages.headline: Siberia asks to pay tribute: a sable per man
passages.people: Ediger, prince of Siberia, and his envoys Tiagriul and Paniady
passages.gloss: Envoys came to Moscow from Ediger, 'prince of Siberia', and from 'all the Siberian land'. They congratulated Ivan IV on taking Kazan and Astrakhan and asked him to take Siberia under his protection and set tribute. They agreed on one sable per 'black' (tax-paying) man, plus a squirrel skin for the collector, and said they had 30,700 such men. This is the first Moscow record of the Siberian khanate that Yermak would later conquer.
passages.quote: били челомъ государю ото князя Едигеря и ото всей земли, чтобы государь ихъ князя и всю землю Сибирьскую взялъ во свое имя и отъ сторонъ ото всѣхъ заступилъ и дань свою на нихъ положилъ … а черныхъ у собя людей сказали 30 тысящь семъсотъ человѣкъ.
passages.translation: they petitioned the sovereign on behalf of Prince Ediger and of all the land, that the sovereign take their prince and all the Siberian land in his name, and defend them from all sides, and lay his tribute on them … and they said they had 30,700 black [tax-paying] people.
passages.speaker: Nikon Chronicle, PSRL vol. 13, part 1 (1904)
passages.caution: Ediger was a Taibugid prince, not a Chinggisid; the head count is what the envoys stated.

passages.headline: Given to the khan as a present: twenty years at court
passages.people: The anonymous author; the khan of Kazan
passages.gloss: The author explains how he knew: for his sins he was captured by 'barbarians', taken to Kazan and given to the khan as a gift. The khan took him into his household to stand before him, and he stayed twenty years, until Kazan fell and he left for the Moscow tsar. He says he often questioned the wisest Kazan nobles and heard things from the khan's own mouth. Captives in service at a Tatar court were common.
passages.quote: Грѣхъ ради моихъ случи ми ся плененну быти варвары и сведену быти въ Казань, и даша мя царю Казанскому въ дарехъ; и взятъ мя царь съ любовію къ себѣ служити, во дворъ свои, постави мя предъ лицемъ своимъ стояти. И бывъ тамо 20 лѣтъ, по взятіи же Казанскомъ изыдохъ исъ Казани, на имя царево Московсково.
passages.translation: For my sins it befell me to be captured by barbarians and taken to Kazan, and they gave me to the tsar of Kazan as a gift; and the tsar took me with love into his service, into his court, and set me to stand before his face. And having been there 20 years, after the taking of Kazan I left Kazan, in the name of the Moscow tsar.
passages.speaker: Anonymous author of the History of the Kazan Tsardom, PSRL vol. 19 (1903)
passages.caution: The author's own claim; no other source confirms his identity.

passages.headline: A town on the khan's camping ground, for the tribute envoys
passages.people: 'Tsar Sain' (Batu's epithet Sain Khan) of the Horde
passages.gloss: The author explains why a Horde ruler built a town near Rus: after the Rus princes bought him off with gifts, 'Tsar Sain' decided to build a town at his nomad camping ground, for his own glory and as a stopping place for his envoys who rode to Rus every year to collect tribute. The book adds that Kazan was long called 'Sain's yurt' and that the khan often came to live there from his capital, Sarai.
passages.quote: И отстави царь Саинъ плѣнити Рускія земля, и восхотѣ близъ ея на кочевищѣ своемъ … поставити градъ, на славу имени своему и на пріѣздъ и на опочиваніе посломъ его, по дань ходящимъ на Русь на всякое лѣто и на земскую управу людскую.
passages.translation: And Tsar Sain gave up ravaging the Russian land, and wished to build a town near it at his nomad camping ground … for the glory of his name, and for the arrival and rest of his envoys going for tribute to Rus every year, and for the governing of the people of the land.
passages.speaker: Anonymous author of the History of the Kazan Tsardom, PSRL vol. 19 (1903)
passages.caution: Legendary history; the author confuses Batu (Sain Khan) with a later ruler and elsewhere dates the founding to 1172. Archaeology dates Kazan's origins to Volga Bulgar times.

passages.headline: The two-headed serpent of Kazan
passages.gloss: Before the town, 'many say', the site was a serpents' nest ruled by a huge two-headed serpent: one head a snake's, which ate people, cattle and beasts, the other an ox's, which ate grass. The khan's sorcerer drew a line around all the snakes, heaped hay, reeds and wood on them with sulphur and pitch and burned them, and the stench killed many of the army's horses and camels. Then the khan built Kazan there. The author reports it as hearsay.
passages.quote: живяше ту вгнездився змій великъ, страшенъ, о двою главу, едину имея змиеву, а другую главу волову; единою пожираше человѣки и скоты и звѣри, а другою главою траву ядяше; а иныя змія около его лежаша, живяху съ нимъ, всяцеми образы.
passages.translation: there lived, having made its nest, a great and terrible serpent with two heads, one a serpent's head and the other an ox's head; with one it devoured people and cattle and beasts, and with the other head it ate grass; and other serpents of every kind lay around it and lived with it.
passages.speaker: Anonymous author of the History of the Kazan Tsardom, PSRL vol. 19 (1903), reporting what 'many say'
passages.caution: A founding legend (related to the Zilant dragon of Kazan's later coat of arms); the author marks it as hearsay.

passages.headline: Who lived in the Kazan land: Bulgars, Cheremis and runaway Rostovians
passages.gloss: The author says the khan drove the Rus out of the district and brought in 'a fierce pagan people' from the Kama, the Bulgar commoners with their princes and elders, as savage, he adds, as the 'dog-headed Samoyeds'. He also claims the Cheremis, called Votiaks, were Rostov commoners who fled there to escape baptism. It shows a Russian view of Kazan as a mix of peoples under a Tatar ruler, with a dose of prejudice and folk etymology.
passages.quote: и наведе исъ Камы языкъ лютъ, поганъ, Болгарскую чернь, со князи ихъ и со старѣишинами ихъ, и много ему сущу убо подобну суровствомъ, обычаемъ злымъ, песьимъ главамъ Самоедомъ. Наполни такими людми землю ту, еже Черемиса, зовемая Отяки, тое жъ глаголють Ростовскую чернь, забежавши тамо отъ крещенія Русково
passages.translation: and he brought from the Kama a fierce, pagan people, the Bulgar commoners, with their princes and elders, much like in savagery and evil custom to the dog-headed Samoyeds. He filled that land with such people, that is the Cheremis, called Votiaks; these, they say, are the Rostov commoners who fled there from Russian baptism
passages.speaker: Anonymous author of the History of the Kazan Tsardom, PSRL vol. 19 (1903)
passages.caution: The Rostov origin of the Cheremis is the author's own folk explanation; 'dog-headed Samoyeds' is a stock insult drawn from marvel literature.

passages.headline: The Bulgar towns dug up to their foundations
passages.people: Prince Iurii Dmitrievich of Moscow; the Bulgar-Tatar towns of the middle Volga
passages.gloss: The first Russian capture of Kazan: Prince Iurii, sent by his brother Vasilii I, took the Bulgar towns on the Volga (Kazan, Bolgar, Zhukotin, Kermenchuk), raided the Golden Horde and 'dug all those towns up to their foundations', killing the Kazan tsar. The author says Kazan then stood empty for forty years. The passage lists real Volga towns of the Golden Horde era.
passages.quote: Тои шедъ взя грады Болгарскія, по Волзе стояща, Казань, и Болгары, Жюкотинъ, Керменчюкъ, и Златую Орду повоева, по совету Крымского царя Азигерея, и вся тѣ грады до основанія раскопа
passages.translation: He went and took the Bulgar towns standing along the Volga, Kazan, and Bolgar, Zhukotin, Kermenchuk, and ravaged the Golden Horde, on the advice of the Crimean tsar Azigerei, and dug all those towns up to their foundations
passages.speaker: Anonymous author of the History of the Kazan Tsardom, PSRL vol. 19 (1903)
passages.caution: The alliance with the Crimean khan Hacı Giray is an anachronism (he ruled in the 1440s to 1460s).

passages.headline: Ulu-Mehmed's new timber fortress, stronger than the old
passages.people: Ulu-Mehmed, exiled khan of the Golden Horde, founder of the Kazan khanate
passages.gloss: After his 'ice town' at Belev melted in the sun, the exiled Golden Horde khan Ulu-Mehmed crossed the Volga and occupied empty Kazan, 'Sain's yurt'. The surviving Bulgars asked him to protect them, and he built a strong wooden town on a new site near the old Kazan that Russian armies had ruined. Settlers came from the Golden Horde, Astrakhan, Azov and Crimea. The builder, material and reason are all named.
passages.quote: Царь же вселися въ жилище ихъ и постави себѣ древяны градъ крѣпокъ, на новомъ мѣсте, крѣпчайше старого, недалече отъ старыя Казани разоренныя отъ Руския рати. И начаша збиратися ко царю мнози варвари отъ различныхъ странъ, ото Златыя Орды и отъ Асторохани, отъ Азуева и отъ Крыма
passages.translation: And the tsar settled in their dwelling place and built himself a strong wooden town, on a new site, stronger than the old one, not far from old Kazan, which had been ruined by the Russian army. And many barbarians began to gather to the tsar from various lands, from the Golden Horde and from Astrakhan, from Azov and from Crimea
passages.speaker: Anonymous author of the History of the Kazan Tsardom, PSRL vol. 19 (1903)

passages.headline: A prefabricated wooden town floated down the Volga
passages.people: Ivan IV's builders; Shah Ali of Kasimov and Muscovite voevodas
passages.gloss: To besiege Kazan, Ivan IV had a whole timber town made in advance upriver, carried it down the Volga on big Beloozero boats, and set it up quickly on a hill at the mouth of the Sviyaga, 15 versts from Kazan. The chronicle adds that churches, monasteries and houses were built inside. The fortress that ended the Kazan khanate was Russian-built and timber.
passages.quote: везущи съ собою готовы градъ древяны на великихъ лодіяхъ Белозерскихъ, тово же лѣта новъ, хитръ сотворенъ. И плывше … придоша въ землю Казанскую на рѣку Свіягу, на мѣсто указное имъ
passages.translation: carrying with them a ready-made wooden town on great Beloozero boats, new that same year and skilfully made. And sailing … they came into the Kazan land to the river Sviyaga, to the place appointed for them
passages.speaker: Anonymous author of the History of the Kazan Tsardom, PSRL vol. 19 (1903)

passages.headline: The Devil's Fort: an empty town of the old Bulgars on the Kama
passages.people: Kazan Tatars, Cheremis and their soothsayers; the 'old Bulgars'
passages.when: 1540s to 1551 (while the author lived in Kazan)
passages.gloss: The author describes an empty little town on the high bank of the Kama, which the Russians called the 'Devil's gorodishche'. A demon lived there, answering questions through soothsayers, and people of the Kazan land came to sacrifice; travellers on the river threw it some of their goods or risked drowning. He credits the ruin to the 'old Bulgars', whose sacrificial prayer-place it had been. Several manuscripts call it a 'small stone town'.
passages.quote: имать градецъ пустъ, на брезе высоцѣ Камы реки стоя, его же Русь имянуетъ Бесовское городище, въ немъ же живяше бѣсъ, мечты творя отъ многа лѣтъ; и то бѣ еще старыхъ Болгаръ молбище жертвеное.
passages.translation: there is an empty little town standing on the high bank of the river Kama, which the Rus call the Devil's Fort, in which a demon lived, working illusions for many years; and it was a sacrificial prayer-place of the old Bulgars.
passages.speaker: Anonymous author of the History of the Kazan Tsardom, PSRL vol. 19 (1903)
passages.caution: The identification with the stone 'Devil's Fort' at Yelabuga is by later scholars; the demon oracle is the author's Christian reading of a local shrine.

passages.headline: A holy fool cries: 'Tatars will not live here'
passages.gloss: Among the omens of Kazan's fall the author lists a Tatar holy fool who walked the streets shouting that Tatars would not live there, only Russians. The khan forbade killing him and had him shut in an empty house, but he broke out. The next chapters tell of a calf born in human shape that turned into an armed man, and a fish-net that brought up a live old man who urged surrender to Moscow.
passages.quote: Нѣкто Татаринъ въ Казани уродивъ, по граду ходя, нача напрасно вопити и непрестанно глаголати: «не жить здѣ Татаромъ, но Рускимъ людемъ». Татарове же хотяху убити его; не повелѣ имъ царь убити его, но въ праздну храмину повелѣ затворити его.
passages.translation: A certain Tatar in Kazan, a holy fool, walking through the city, began suddenly to cry out and say without ceasing: 'Tatars will not live here, but Russian people.' The Tatars wanted to kill him; the tsar did not allow them to kill him, but ordered him shut up in an empty house.
passages.speaker: Anonymous author of the History of the Kazan Tsardom, PSRL vol. 19 (1903)
passages.caution: Prophecies written after the event to show that Kazan's fall was fated.

passages.headline: The people of Kazan, rank by rank
passages.people: Kazan clergy, nobility and subject peoples
passages.gloss: When Kazan surrendered its boy khan Utemish-Girey and his mother Siuiumbike in 1551, the author lists everyone who submitted: mullahs, seyyids, sheikhs, hafizes and other Muslim clergy; ulans, princes, murzas, ichki (court nobles) and 'rear-court' Cossacks; and the subject peoples, Chuvash, Cheremis, Votiaks, Mordva, tarkhans and Mozhars. It shows Kazan as a Muslim state of many peoples, not a single 'Tatar' mass.
passages.quote: Казанцы же молны, и сеиты, и шихъ … и афызы, и уланы, и князи, и мурзы и ички, и задворные казаки, и Чюваша и Черемиса, и Отяки, и Мордва, и тарханы, и Можары, и вся земля Казанская
passages.translation: And the Kazan people, the mullahs, and seyyids, and sheikhs … and hafizes, and ulans, and princes, and murzas and ichki, and the rear-court Cossacks, and the Chuvash and Cheremis, and Votiaks, and Mordva, and tarkhans, and Mozhars, and all the Kazan land
passages.speaker: Anonymous author of the History of the Kazan Tsardom, PSRL vol. 19 (1903)
passages.caution: Some Tatar titles are garbled in the manuscripts; the omitted words are variously spelled.

passages.headline: Kazan taken, its khan seized alive
passages.people: Khan Ediger-Mahmet and the people of Kazan; Ivan IV's army
passages.gloss: After the mines blew open the walls, the Russians stormed the city. The author describes the slaughter, the soldiers taking countless riches and leading away princesses, murzas' wives and children 'from the greatest to the simplest', and the capture of Khan Ediger-Mahmet, found on the wall and nearly killed before some Tatars cried out that he was their tsar.
passages.quote: Во граде же христьянстіи люде взяша неисчетное богатество и въ полонъ многое множество княгинь и мурзиныхъ женъ и детеи, просто рещи, отъ великихъ даждь и до простыхъ всѣхъ плениша.
passages.translation: And in the city the Christian people took uncountable riches, and into captivity a great multitude of princesses and murzas' wives and children; to put it simply, from the great down to the simple, they captured them all.
passages.speaker: Anonymous author of the History of the Kazan Tsardom, PSRL vol. 19 (1903)

passages.headline: A Tatar convert tears his beard
passages.people: A Tatar from the Arsk side, baptized Stefan
passages.gloss: A lame Tatar from the Arsk district came to Kazan to be baptized, saying his legs were healed the moment he heard that the Moscow tsar had taken Kazan and filled it with churches. Warned not to return to his old faith, he tore out some of his beard and crumbled the hairs, saying he would sooner be crumbled like them. Later his kinsmen hacked him to death. It is a story of conversion and of Kazan Tatars' resistance to it.
passages.quote: Татаринъ же абіе рукою напрасно исторже часть власовъ своея брады и раздроби ихъ на малыя крупицы, глаголя: «Азъ тако уразумѣхъ великую силу и милость Бога вашего, яко его ради готовъ есмь не токмо многія скорби терпѣти, но аще и сицевъ раздробленъ буду, яко же раздробихъ власы моя, никако же не отвергуся его».
passages.translation: The Tatar at once suddenly tore out with his hand part of the hair of his beard and crumbled it into small bits, saying: 'I have so understood the great power and mercy of your God that for his sake I am ready not only to suffer many sorrows, but even if I am crumbled like this, as I have crumbled my hairs, I will never renounce him.'
passages.speaker: Anonymous author of the History of the Kazan Tsardom, PSRL vol. 19 (1903)
passages.caution: A pious conversion tale in the hagiographic style.

passages.headline: Kazakh horde, Great and Lesser Nogais: the peoples on the old map
passages.people: Kazakhs ('Kazatskaia orda'), Great Nogai, Lesser Nogai; Bukhara and Urgench
passages.gloss: The preface lists what the old Great Map showed in the south and east: the 'nomad Kazakh horde', the camps of the Great Nogais, the towns of Bukhara and Urgench, the Volga to Astrakhan and the Don to Azov, and the fields between Azov and Astrakhan 'where the Lesser Nogais roam'. The steppe is named by its nomad peoples, not by a single 'Tartary'.
passages.quote: и кочевую Казацкую орду, и большихъ Нагаевъ кочевье, и Бухарскіе и Юргенскіе города, и рѣку Волгу до Астарахани, и рѣку Донъ до Азова, и межъ Азова и Астарахани до Хвалинскаго, и до Азовскаго, и до Чернаго моря, поля и рѣки, что кочують малые Нагаи.
passages.translation: and the nomad Kazakh horde, and the nomad camps of the Great Nogais, and the Bukharan and Urgench towns, and the river Volga to Astrakhan, and the river Don to Azov, and between Azov and Astrakhan to the Khvalyn [Caspian] and to the Azov and Black Seas, the fields and rivers where the Lesser Nogais roam.
passages.speaker: Razriad clerks, preface to the Book of the Great Map (1627), ed. Yazykov (1838)

passages.headline: Perekop: a stone town and a ditch across the isthmus
passages.gloss: At the neck of the Crimea stood Perekop, 'a stone town' where Crimean Tatars and Turks lived, with artillery. A ditch ran from sea to sea across six versts, two sazhens wide and three deep, with stone towers along it. Beyond the ditch people ploughed fields. A precise official description of a Crimean Tatar fortress.
passages.quote: А въ Перекопи городъ каменной, а въ немъ живутъ Крымскіе Татара и Турчаня, и нарядъ въ городѣ есть. А Перекопи отъ моря до моря на 6 верстахъ, а поперегъ Перекопи съ двѣ сажени косыхъ, а въ глубину три сажени, а по рву стоятъ башни каменныяжъ
passages.translation: And in Perekop there is a stone town, and Crimean Tatars and Turks live in it, and there is artillery in the town. And Perekop runs from sea to sea for 6 versts, and across Perekop [the ditch] is some two slanting sazhens, and three sazhens deep, and along the ditch stand stone towers too
passages.speaker: Book of the Great Map (1627), ed. Yazykov (1838)
passages.caution: The editor glosses 'nariad' as artillery.

passages.headline: The khan's stone palaces and clay-daubed wooden houses
passages.gloss: The khan had two residences, one at Bakhchysarai and one on the Alma. At Bakhchysarai the khan's 'palaty' (chambers), kitchens and stables were of stone, set low under a hill, with a church of the Virgin two versts away served by Greeks. The Alma court had one stone chamber and wooden houses plastered with clay, standing in a vineyard. It is a rare early note on Crimean Tatar building materials.
passages.quote: А въ Бакчисараѣ палаты Царевы, поварни и конюшни, каменныя, а стоитъ подъ горою ниско; да за Царевымъ дворомъ версты съ 2, церковь Пречистыя Богородицы въ солончакахъ, а служатъ у нее Гречане. А которой дворъ на рѣкѣ на Алмѣ, и въ томъ дворѣ одна палата, да избы деревянныя, обмазанныя глиною, а стоитъ на берегу въ виноградѣ.
passages.translation: And in Bakhchysarai the tsar's chambers, kitchens and stables are of stone, and it stands low beneath a hill; and about 2 versts beyond the tsar's court is a church of the Most Pure Mother of God in the salt flats, and Greeks serve in it. And the court on the river Alma has one stone chamber, and wooden houses daubed with clay, and it stands on the bank in a vineyard.
passages.speaker: Book of the Great Map (1627), ed. Yazykov (1838)
passages.caution: The church is probably the Uspensky cave monastery near Bakhchysarai; 'palata' in 17th-century Russian usually means a masonry building.

passages.headline: Kozlov, a stone town, and Tatar villages with dug wells
passages.gloss: Coming from Perekop, the book notes on the right, by the sea, the stone town of Kozlov (the 1838 editor adds: now Yevpatoria). Between the Alma, Bakhchysarai and Kozlov, Tatar villages lined both sides of the road, watered by dug wells because there were no rivers. Crimea appears as a settled country of towns and villages as well as nomads.
passages.quote: Да отъ Перекопи ѣдучи, на правѣ, у моря на берегу, городъ Козлевъ каменной. … А отъ Алмы до Бакчисарая, и до Козлева, по обѣ стороны дороги, деревни Татарскія, а воды копаные колодези, а рѣкъ нѣтъ.
passages.translation: And travelling from Perekop, on the right, on the seashore, is the stone town of Kozlov. … And from the Alma to Bakhchysarai and to Kozlov, on both sides of the road, are Tatar villages, and the water is from dug wells, and there are no rivers.
passages.speaker: Book of the Great Map (1627), ed. Yazykov (1838)

passages.headline: 'The Golden Horde': stone Tatar mosques on the Akhtuba
passages.gloss: In one line the book marks the ruins of the Golden Horde's capital: 90 versts along the Akhtuba from Tsaritsyn lies 'the Golden Horde, stone Tatar mosques'. By 1600 the city was a field of ruins, and Muscovite clerks named both the builders (the Horde) and the material (stone).
passages.quote: А по рѣкѣ по Ахтубѣ на 90 верстахъ отъ Царицына, Золотая орда, мечети Татарскія каменныя.
passages.translation: And along the river Akhtuba, 90 versts from Tsaritsyn, is the Golden Horde, stone Tatar mosques.
passages.speaker: Book of the Great Map (1627), ed. Yazykov (1838)
passages.caution: The book gives no date or builder name beyond 'Golden Horde'; the identification with Sarai (Tsarev settlement) is by later scholars.

passages.headline: Seven Tatar mosques at Majar on the Kuma
passages.people: Ruined Golden Horde town of Majar
passages.gloss: On the right bank of the Kuma the book lists '7 Tatar mosques, the Majar yurt', and another mosque across the river, the 'Chrak-Keshen'. These are the ruins of Majar, a Golden Horde town. The word 'keshen' (keshene, a domed tomb) appears again on the Dnieper, where the book records '7 keshens of Tatar mosques'. The clerks credit the ruins to Tatars.
passages.quote: А по рѣкѣ по Кумѣ, съ правыя стороны, 7 мечетей Татарскихъ, Мажаровъ юртъ, да мечеть, по другой сторонѣ рѣки Кумы, Чракъ-Кешень.
passages.translation: And along the river Kuma, on the right side, are 7 Tatar mosques, the Majar yurt, and a mosque on the other side of the river Kuma, Chrak-Keshen.
passages.speaker: Book of the Great Map (1627), ed. Yazykov (1838)

passages.headline: Mamai's Sarai and Uslam's little towns on the Dnieper
passages.people: Tatars (named after the Horde leader Mamai)
passages.gloss: On the lower Dnieper the book lists a little town called 'Mamai's Sarai' (palace), and below it 'Uslam's little towns', while along the Konskie Vody stand '7 keshens of Tatar mosques'. The first name ties the place to Mamai, the 14th-century Horde commander defeated at Kulikovo. The clerks record the ruins as Tatar but say nothing more about who built them or when.
passages.quote: А по правой сторонѣ Конскихъ-водъ, отъ Днѣпра 60 верстъ, 7 Кешеней Татарскихъ мечетей. … Да ниже Московки, съ Крымской стороны 50 верстъ, на Днѣпрѣ городокъ Мамаевъ-сарай. А ниже Мамаева-сарая 50 верстъ, на Днѣпрѣ Усламовы городки.
passages.translation: And on the right side of the Konskie Vody, 60 versts from the Dnieper, are 7 keshens of Tatar mosques. … And below the Moskovka, on the Crimean side, 50 versts, on the Dnieper is the little town of Mamai's Sarai. And 50 versts below Mamai's Sarai, on the Dnieper, are Uslam's little towns.
passages.speaker: Book of the Great Map (1627), ed. Yazykov (1838)
passages.caution: The book gives names only; 'keshen' is the Turkic word for a domed tomb.

passages.headline: The Devil's Fort, 'also Yelabuga'
passages.people: Unnamed builders (a ruin on the Kama)
passages.gloss: Listing places on the Kama below the Ik, the book notes 'the Devil's gorodishche', with the variant reading 'the Devil's town, also Yelabuga'. This is the same haunted ruin that the author of the History of the Kazan Tsardom credited to the 'old Bulgars'. The map book gives only the name and position.
passages.quote: А ниже Ика рѣки 40 верстъ, на рѣкѣ на Камѣ городище Чортово [градъ Чортовъ, Елабуга тожь].
passages.translation: And 40 versts below the river Ik, on the river Kama, is the Devil's gorodishche [the Devil's town, also Yelabuga].
passages.speaker: Book of the Great Map (1627), ed. Yazykov (1838), with a variant reading in brackets

passages.headline: The Pig Road: how the Belgorod Tatars came raiding
passages.place: Ryl'sk, Karachev, Orel and Bolkhov districts
passages.gloss: The book records the raiding roads the Tatars used. Along the 'Svinaia doroga' (Pig Road) the Belgorod Tatars from the Dnieper used to ride on the Rylsk, Karachev, Orel and Bolkhov districts, led by Bakai Murza, 'when there were no steppe towns yet'. They crossed the Seim 40 versts below Kursk, where there were now villages and a watch post. Muscovy's southern towns were built along these routes to block them.
passages.quote: А Свиною дорогою прихаживали отъ Днѣпра Бѣлогородскіе Татарове, на Рыльскіе, и на Карачевскіе, и на Орловскіе, и на Болховскіе уѣзды, хаживали Бакай Мурза, какъ не было Польскихъ городовъ, а Семь рѣку лаживали подъ Городенскимъ городищемъ, ниже Курска верстъ съ 40
passages.translation: And by the Pig Road the Belgorod Tatars used to come from the Dnieper onto the Rylsk and Karachev and Orel and Bolkhov districts; Bakai Murza used to come, when there were not yet the steppe towns; and they used to cross the Seim river below the Gorodensk gorodishche, about 40 versts below Kursk
passages.speaker: Book of the Great Map (1627), ed. Yazykov (1838)
passages.caution: 'Polskie goroda' here means the new towns of the 'Pole' (steppe frontier), not Polish towns.

passages.headline: Bashkirs who live on honey, game and fish
passages.gloss: Along the Belaya and Ufa rivers up to the Ural mountains, the book says, 'all live Bashkirs', and they feed on honey (from forest beekeeping), game and fish, and have no ploughland. It is a one-line ethnographic note from the frontier, about a Turkic people that western maps often put under 'Tartary'.
passages.quote: А отъ устья рѣки Бѣлыя-Воложки, съ верхъ и по рѣкѣ по Уфѣ, по обѣимъ сторонамъ и до Аральтовы горы и далѣе, все живутъ Башкиры, а кормля ихъ медъ, звѣрь, рыба, а пашни не имѣютъ.
passages.translation: And from the mouth of the river Belaia Voloshka, upstream and along the river Ufa, on both sides as far as the Aral'tova mountain and beyond, all live Bashkirs, and their food is honey, game and fish, and they have no ploughland.
passages.speaker: Book of the Great Map (1627), ed. Yazykov (1838)

passages.headline: Stone men by the salt spring
passages.people: Unnamed makers of steppe stone statues
passages.gloss: By a stream in the Manych steppe, opposite the salt that the people of Azov gathered, the book marks 'stone men, idols'. These are the carved stone statues ('kamennye baby') that stood on steppe kurgans, set up by earlier nomads such as the Polovtsy. The clerks give no builder, only the landmark.
passages.quote: А по правой сторонѣ по тому истоку люди каменные болваны, противъ той соли, что емлютъ Азовцы.
passages.translation: And along the right side of that stream are stone people, idols, opposite the salt that the Azov people take.
passages.speaker: Book of the Great Map (1627), ed. Yazykov (1838)
passages.caution: The identification with kurgan stelae is the usual scholarly reading; the book does not describe them.

passages.headline: A giant's grave and a stone table on the Don
passages.people: Unnamed (folk landmarks on the Tatar frontier)
passages.gloss: On the upper Don the book lists a 'Volotova mogila', a giant's grave (volot is the old Russian word for a giant), at the mouth of the Mecha, and further down the 'Don beseda' (Don meeting-place), 'a stone table and stone vessels'. Nearby were the Tatar fords into Rus. These folk names for kurgans and rocks sit side by side with military route data.
passages.quote: а устьѣ рѣки Мечи съ вышія страны Волотова могила. … А ниже устья Сосны, на Дону, Донская бесѣда, каменной столъ и каменныя суды.
passages.translation: and at the mouth of the river Mecha, on the upper side, is the Giant's Grave. … And below the mouth of the Sosna, on the Don, is the Don Meeting-place, a stone table and stone vessels.
passages.speaker: Book of the Great Map, first edition 'Drevniaia rossiiskaia idrografiia' (1773)
passages.caution: The 1838 edition reads 'Bolotova' (marsh) where the 1773 edition reads 'Volotova' (giant's).

passages.headline: Tatars keep the law of Muhammad; the Kalmyks, 'I do not know'
passages.people: Tatars, Kalmyks, Mongols, the 'Piebald Horde', Ostyaks, Samoyeds
passages.gloss: Esipov opens with the peoples living along the Tobol, Irtysh and Ob: Tatars, Kalmyks, Mongols, the 'Piebald Horde' (Selkups), Ostyaks and Samoyeds. The Tatars, he says, keep Muhammad's law; as for the Kalmyks, he honestly does not know their faith, since he found nothing written and could not find out. The Ostyaks and Samoyeds, he adds, have no law and worship idols.
passages.quote: По сихъ же рѣкахъ жителствуютъ мнози языцы: Тотаровя, Колмыки, Мугалы, Пѣгая орда, Остяки, Самоядь и прочая языцы. Тотаровя законъ Моаметовъ держатъ; Колмыки же который законъ или отецъ своихъ преданіе держатъ, невѣмъ, понеже писменно о семъ не обретохъ ни испытати возмогохъ.
passages.translation: Along these rivers live many peoples: Tatars, Kalmyks, Mongols, the Piebald Horde, Ostyaks, Samoyeds and other peoples. The Tatars keep the law of Muhammad; which law or tradition of their fathers the Kalmyks keep, I do not know, since I found nothing written about it and could not find out.
passages.speaker: Savva Esipov, Siberian Chronicle (1636), in Sibirskie letopisi (1907)
passages.caution: The editors restore some words from other copies (printed in brackets in the edition).

passages.headline: Tsar On and a commoner called Chingis
passages.people: Early rulers of the Siberian Tatars: 'Tsar On', 'Chingis', Taibuga
passages.gloss: Esipov's history of the Siberian rulers begins with a Muslim 'tsar named On' on the Ishim river, overthrown by a man 'from the simple people' named Chingis, who killed him 'like a robber' and took his realm. A servant saved On's son Taibuga, founder of the Taibugid princes. In this local legend the world conqueror Chinggis Khan has become a Siberian upstart, and the 'Ong Khan' of Mongol history has become a Muslim tsar.
passages.quote: на сей же рѣцѣ Ишимѣ бѣ царь Моаметова закону именемъ Онъ. И воста на него его же державы отъ простыхъ людей именемъ Чингисъ, и шедъ на него, яко разбойникъ, съ прочими, и уби царя Она, и царство самъ приемлетъ Чингисъ.
passages.translation: on this river Ishim there was a tsar of Muhammad's law named On. And there rose against him, of his own realm, from the simple people, one named Chingis, and he went against him like a robber with others, and killed Tsar On, and Chingis himself took the realm.
passages.speaker: Savva Esipov, Siberian Chronicle (1636), in Sibirskie letopisi (1907)
passages.caution: A dynastic legend told among Siberian Tatars and retold by a Russian; it garbles Chinggis Khan and Ong Khan of the Kereit.

passages.headline: Chingiden, the Tatar town where Tyumen stands
passages.people: Prince Taibuga of the Siberian Tatars
passages.when: Legendary (Chingi-Tura existed by the 14th to 15th centuries)
passages.gloss: After conquering peoples along the Irtysh and Ob for Chingis, Taibuga asked leave to settle where he liked. He went with his household to the Tura river, 'built a town there and named it Chingiden; now on that place is the town of Tyumen'. Another page of the same volume says the Russian voevodas built Tyumen in 1586 'where before there was a Tatar town, Chingidi'. The Tatar builder and the later Russian town are named in sequence.
