passages.quote: Изыде жъ князь Таибуга со всемъ домомъ своимъ на рѣку Туру и тамо созда градъ и нарече его Чингиденъ; нынѣ жъ на семъ мѣсте градъ Тюмень.
passages.translation: Prince Taibuga went off with all his household to the river Tura, and there built a town and named it Chingiden; and now on this place is the town of Tyumen.
passages.speaker: Savva Esipov, Siberian Chronicle (1636), in Sibirskie letopisi (1907)
passages.caution: The founding by Taibuga is legend; Chingi-Tura is attested as a real Tatar town, capital of the Tyumen khanate.

passages.headline: Sibir, 'the chief town', built on the Irtysh
passages.people: Mamet (Muhammad), Taibugid prince; Upak (Ibak), 'the Kazan tsar'
passages.gloss: Esipov continues: Taibuga's descendant Mamet killed Upak (Ibak, khan of Tyumen, whom Esipov calls 'the Kazan tsar'), destroyed his own town of Chingiden, went deeper into Siberia and built a town on the Irtysh, naming it Sibir, 'that is, the chief one'. This is the Tatar capital also called Isker or Kashlyk, which Yermak took in 1582. The Russian name for the whole region comes from this Tatar town.
passages.quote: Маметъ Казанского царя уби Упака и градъ свой Чингиденъ разруши и отиде оттуду внутрь Сибирския земли и постави себѣ градъ на рѣке Иртише и назва его градъ Сибирь, сиречь началный; и живяше в немъ царь лѣта многа
passages.translation: Mamet killed Upak, the Kazan tsar, and destroyed his own town Chingiden and went away from there into the interior of the Siberian land and built himself a town on the river Irtysh and named it the town of Sibir, that is, the chief one; and the tsar lived in it many years
passages.speaker: Savva Esipov, Siberian Chronicle (1636), in Sibirskie letopisi (1907)
passages.caution: Esipov's 'Kazan tsar' Upak is Ibak of the Shibanid dynasty; the meaning 'chief' for Sibir is Esipov's gloss, not a proven etymology.

passages.headline: Out hawking: Seydyak, a Kazakh tsarevich and Karacha
passages.people: Prince Seydyak, Tsarevich Saltan of the 'Kazakh horde', Karacha (Kuchum's counsellor); voevoda Danila Chulkov
passages.gloss: A year after the Russians founded Tobolsk on the hill opposite the Tobol mouth, the Tatar prince Seydyak, a Kazakh tsarevich named Saltan and Kuchum's counsellor Karacha rode out from the old Tatar capital Sibir 'for bird sport' (falconry) with five hundred Tatars. The voevoda invited them to a feast as if for peace talks; when the guests choked on the wine he had offered, he took it as a sign of treachery, had their men cut down and sent the princes to Moscow.
passages.quote: По поставленіи града Тоболска во второе лето, из града Сибири, от Чувашъ вышли для птичной потехи Татара князь Седякъ да царевичь Казачьей орды Салтанъ да царя Кучума думной Татаринъ Карача, с нимъ Татаръ пятьсотъ человекъ.
passages.translation: In the second year after the building of the town of Tobolsk, from the town of Sibir, from Chuvash, there came out for bird sport the Tatars Prince Sedyak and the tsarevich of the Kazakh horde Saltan and Tsar Kuchum's counsellor, the Tatar Karacha, and with them five hundred Tatars.
passages.speaker: Esipov Chronicle (short redaction), in Sibirskie letopisi (1907)
passages.caution: Told from the Russian side, which presents the massacre as a justified precaution.

passages.headline: A golden 'Russian god' in a cup
passages.people: Tatars, Voguls and Ostyaks of Prince Demyan's town; a Chuvash informant
passages.gloss: Yermak's men besieged Prince Demyan's big hill-town on the lower Irtysh, held by 2000 Tatars, Voguls and Ostyaks. A Chuvash who had been Kuchum's captive told them the defenders prayed to 'a Russian god, cast in gold, sitting in a cup'; they poured water in the cup and drank it, called it Christ, and said it had come from Vladimir's baptism of Rus. Sent to steal it, he reported that it stood on a table surrounded by burning fat and sulphur fumes. The Cossacks never found it.
passages.quote: Одинъ же въ нихъ Чювашенинъ былъ у Кучюма, руского полону, сказалъ: молятся де они рускому богу и тотъ де руской богъ литой золотой, въ чашѣ сѣдитъ, и въ ту де чашу наливши воды пьютъ, и зовутъ его Христомъ, а сказываютъ де привезенъ отъ Владимерова крещенія
passages.translation: One of them, a Chuvash who had been with Kuchum, a Russian captive, said: they pray, he said, to a Russian god, and that Russian god is cast of gold, sits in a cup, and they pour water into that cup and drink it, and call him Christ, and they say he was brought from Vladimir's baptism
passages.speaker: Kungur (Brief Siberian) Chronicle, Remezov tradition, 1880 edition
passages.caution: Third-hand: a captive's report retold a century later. Such metal idols (often looted Christian or Iranian vessels) are known from Ob-Ugrian shrines.

passages.headline: Tribute sworn on a bloody sabre
passages.people: Cossack Bogdan Briazga and the Tatars and Ostyaks of the lower Irtysh
passages.gloss: Yermak sent the fifty-leader Bogdan Briazga down the Irtysh to bring the Tatar and Ostyak districts under the tsar and collect yasak (fur tribute). At the first district he stormed a strong little town, hanged the best 'mergens' (warriors) by the leg and shot them, collected tribute 'by the sabre', laid the bloody sabre on the table and made the people kiss it as an oath to pay every year. The terror, says the chronicle, silenced the whole district.
passages.quote: И пріѣхавъ въ первую Аремзянскую волость, и городокъ крѣпкій взялъ боемъ, и многихъ лутчихъ мергеней повѣсилъ за ногу и розстрѣлялъ, и ясакъ собралъ за саблею, и положилъ на столъ кровавую, и велѣлъ вѣрно цѣловати за государя царя, чтобъ имъ служить и ясакъ платить по вся годы
passages.translation: And coming to the first, the Aremzian district, he took the strong little town by battle, and hanged many of the best mergens by the leg and shot them, and collected the yasak by the sabre, and laid it, bloody, on the table, and ordered them to kiss it in faith to the sovereign tsar, that they would serve and pay yasak every year
passages.speaker: Kungur (Brief Siberian) Chronicle, Remezov tradition, 1880 edition
passages.caution: The sabre oath (shert) reflects local oath customs that the Russians adopted; the details come from Cossack tradition.

passages.headline: A Tatar lament: 'five Cossacks'
passages.gloss: At the mouth of the Ishim there was a fierce hand-to-hand fight in which five of Yermak's Cossacks died. The chronicle says the Tatars still sang about it at their gatherings, weeping, with the refrain 'yanym, yanym, bish kazak', which it translates as 'warriors, warriors, five men defeated and ruined'; the song was called 'the tsaritsa's lament'. The Tatar words more likely mean 'my soul, my soul, five Cossacks'.
passages.quote: и о тѣхъ пяти человѣкахъ Татара поютъ съ плачемъ при бесѣдахъ въ пѣсняхъ припѣваючи: янымъ, янымъ, бишь казакъ, бишь казакъ, сирѣчь: воины, воины, пять пять человѣкъ побѣдиша и разориша. И ся пѣсня и словетъ царицынъ плачь.
passages.translation: and about those five men the Tatars sing with weeping at their gatherings, in songs with the refrain: 'yanym, yanym, bish kazak, bish kazak', that is: 'warriors, warriors, five, five men defeated and destroyed'. And this song is called the tsaritsa's lament.
passages.speaker: Kungur (Brief Siberian) Chronicle, Remezov tradition, 1880 edition
passages.caution: The chronicler's translation of the Tatar refrain is loose; the song itself is reported, not transcribed in full.

passages.headline: The sky-stone that makes cold, rain and snow
passages.gloss: Rowing up the Irtysh, Yermak's men came to the little town of Tashatkan, where, they were told, a stone had fallen from the sky, dark red in colour, and from it at times came cold, rain and snow. Yermak and his men marvelled at 'God's work'. Weather stones (the 'yada tash' of Turkic and Mongol lore) were believed to bring rain and snow.
passages.quote: И погребоша къ Ташатканскому городку; и въ томъ городкѣ спалъ камень съ небеси … видомъ багровъ, и отъ него де временемъ восходитъ стужа, дождь и снѣгъ. И о семъ Ермакъ съ товарыщи дивился Божію дѣянію.
passages.translation: And they rowed to the little town of Tashatkan; and in that town a stone fell from the sky … dark red in appearance, and from it, they say, at times there arises cold, rain and snow. And at this Yermak and his comrades marvelled at God's doing.
passages.speaker: Kungur (Brief Siberian) Chronicle, Remezov tradition, 1880 edition
passages.caution: Hearsay reported with 'de' ('they say'); the size of the stone is missing in the manuscript.

passages.headline: Kuchum's hidden ford of stone and sand
passages.gloss: Before Yermak's last night, the chronicle explains the trap: across a swampy stream near the Vagai, Kuchum had built a broad ford, wide enough for three or four carts abreast, in one spot only, packing it firmly with stones and sand; anyone who missed the spot drowned. A Tatar condemned to death was sent across it to spy on the sleeping Cossacks. It is one of the few Tatar-built works the chronicles describe.
passages.quote: понеже Кучюмъ учинилъ бродъ широкой, какъ въ три или въ четыре телѣги проѣхать въ одномъ мѣстѣ, каменьемъ и пескомъ засыпалъ плотно; а кто не угадаетъ, утопаетъ.
passages.translation: because Kuchum had made a broad ford, so that three or four carts could pass abreast, in one place, filled in firmly with stones and sand; and whoever did not hit upon it would drown.
passages.speaker: Kungur (Brief Siberian) Chronicle, Remezov tradition, 1880 edition

passages.headline: Yermak's armour and the Tatars' vow of silence
passages.place: Camp of the Kalmyk taisha Ablai
passages.people: Ablai, Kalmyk (Oirat) ruler; Ulian Remezov, Tobolsk envoy; Siberian Tatars
passages.gloss: In 1651 the Tobolsk officer Ulian Remezov took Yermak's famous mail coat, reclaimed from Tatar princes, as a gift to the Kalmyk ruler Ablai, who kissed it and raised it to his head. Ablai then told his own version of Yermak's death: drowned at the ford, found and shot at, his blood flowing, his armour divided up, miracles from his armour and clothes, and a Tatar oath 'on pain of death' not to tell the Russians about him. Ablai said that as a sick child he was given earth from Yermak's grave to drink and was cured.
passages.quote: И нача Аблай повѣсти дѣяти о немъ по своей исторіи, какъ пріѣхалъ въ Сибирь, и отъ Кучюма на перекопѣ побѣжа, и утопе, и обрѣтенъ, и стрѣлянъ, и кровь течаше, и пансыри раздѣлиша и развезоша, и какъ отъ пансырей и отъ платья чюдесъ было, и какъ Татара смертной завѣтъ положиша, что про него Русакамъ невѣщати
passages.translation: And Ablai began to tell stories about him, according to his own history: how he came to Siberia, and fled from Kuchum at the ford, and drowned, and was found, and was shot at, and blood flowed, and they divided up his armour and carried it off, and how there were miracles from the armour and the clothing, and how the Tatars made a vow on pain of death not to tell the Russians about him
passages.speaker: Kungur (Brief Siberian) Chronicle, Remezov tradition (reporting Ulian Remezov's embassy), 1880 edition
passages.caution: A family story of the Remezovs, told half a century later; the miracles are Tatar and Kalmyk beliefs as Russians reported them.

passages.headline: Who built Kashlyk, the Tatar capital of Sibir
passages.gloss: The chronicle credits a Tatar ruler, Mamet, with founding the town of Kashlyk at the mouth of the little Sibirka river after defeating a khan of Kazan. From this town, it says, the whole land took the name Sibir. The author says he took this from a 'Muslim history', meaning Tatar tradition.
passages.quote: Маметь царь казанскаго царя Алима побѣдилъ, и на усть рѣчки Сибирки градъ Кашлыкъ учинилъ, царство въ Сибири распространивъ и поддани учинилъ; и оттолѣ нача славнѣе зватися Сибирь и цари, ихъ же бусурманская исторія повѣдаетъ.
passages.translation: Tsar Mamet defeated Alim, tsar of Kazan, and built the town of Kashlyk at the mouth of the little river Sibirka, spreading his realm in Siberia and making subjects; and from then Siberia and its tsars began to be more famous, as the Muslim history tells.
passages.speaker: Kungur (Remezov) chronicle, article 17 (1880 printed text)
passages.caution: The chronicler reports Tatar tradition second-hand; Kashlyk is the town known in other sources as Isker or Sibir.

passages.headline: A shining Christian city seen in the sky over the Tatar capital
passages.people: Siberian Tatars (Muslim clergy and nobles of Sibir)
passages.gloss: The chronicle claims that the Tatar khans, princes and Muslim clergy saw, year after year, a glowing Christian city with churches and ringing bells hovering in the air over the spot where Tobolsk cathedral later stood. It is a foretelling legend written to show that God had given the land to the Russians, not an eyewitness report.
passages.quote: При сихъ во вся лѣта видѣнія царь и князи, агуны, муллы и абызы и протчіе бусурманы на томъ мѣстѣ, идѣже нынѣ градъ Тоболескъ и соборная церковь до колоколни, видѣшася христіанскій со свѣтомъ градъ въ воздухѣ, и церкви и звонъ велій, яко ими дивитися и ужасно недоумѣя, что будетъ се.
passages.translation: In their time, every year, the tsar and the princes, akhuns, mullahs, abyzes and the other Muslims saw visions: on the place where the town of Tobolsk and the cathedral church up to its bell tower now stand, a Christian city appeared in the air with light, with churches and a great ringing, so that they marvelled and were terrified, not knowing what it would be.
passages.speaker: Kungur (Remezov) chronicle, article 18 (1880 printed text)
passages.caution: A pious prophecy legend composed after the conquest; the same page adds a pillar of fire and gold and silver sparks on the town site.

passages.headline: A Tatar lament for five slain Cossacks
passages.gloss: After a hand-to-hand fight at the mouth of the Ishim in which five of Yermak's Cossacks died, the chronicle says the Tatars still sang about it at their gatherings, weeping, with a Tatar refrain that it translates. The song was known as 'the Tsaritsa's lament'. It is a rare glimpse of Tatar oral memory of the war.
passages.quote: и о тѣхъ пяти человѣкахъ Татара поютъ съ плачемъ при бесѣдахъ въ пѣсняхъ припѣваючи: янымъ, янымъ, битъ казакъ, битъ казакъ, сирѣчь: воины, воины, пять пять человѣкъ побѣдиша и разориша. И сія пѣсня и словетъ царицынъ плачь.
passages.translation: and about those five men the Tatars sing with weeping at their gatherings, with the refrain: 'yanym, yanym, bit kazak, bit kazak', that is: 'warriors, warriors, five, five men we defeated and destroyed.' And this song is called the Tsaritsa's Lament.
passages.speaker: Kungur (Remezov) chronicle, article 100 (1880 printed text)
passages.caution: The refrain is Tatar in Russian letters; the other scan of this edition (T0442 n95) reads 'бишь', closer to Tatar 'bish' (five), which fits the chronicler's own gloss. The translation of the Tatar words is the chronicler's.

passages.headline: Tatars by the rivers, reindeer people to the north, camel herders on the steppe
passages.people: Siberian Tatars, Voguls, Ostyaks, Samoyeds, Kalmyks, Mongols, Kazakhs
passages.gloss: What Yermak is said to have heard about Siberia before setting out: a map in words that sorts the peoples. The Tatars live along the Tura, Tobol and Irtysh and travel by boat and horse; the Ostyaks and Samoyeds of the Ob ride reindeer and dogs and live on fish; Kalmyks, Mongols and the Kazakh horde ride camels on the steppe. 'Tatar' here is one people among many, not a label for all Siberians.
passages.quote: по Турѣ же и по Тоболу живутъ Татара, ѣздятъ въ лодкахъ и на коняхъ. А Тоболъ палъ въ Иртышъ; и на Иртышѣ царство близь устья и многіе Татара, и Иртышъ палъ въ Обь, а Обь рѣка пала въ море двѣма устьи, а по ней живутъ Остяки и Самоѣдь, ѣздятъ на оленяхъ и псахъ и кормятся рыбами; а по степи Калмыки и Мунгалы и казачья орда, ѣздятъ на вельбудахъ
passages.translation: and along the Tura and the Tobol live Tatars, who travel in boats and on horses. The Tobol falls into the Irtysh; and on the Irtysh near its mouth is a tsardom and many Tatars; the Irtysh falls into the Ob, and the Ob falls into the sea by two mouths, and along it live Ostyaks and Samoyeds, who ride reindeer and dogs and feed on fish; and on the steppe the Kalmyks and Mongols and the Kazakh horde, who ride camels
passages.speaker: Kungur (Remezov) chronicle, article 9 (1880 printed text)
passages.caution: Framed as hearsay Yermak gathered from people on the Chusovaya; written down long afterwards.

passages.headline: An Oirat prince builds a town with craftsmen from China
passages.gloss: Travelling with the camp of the Oirat prince Ablai taisha, Baikov found him building a town on the Beshka stream between stone hills. Baikov could not tell whether it would be of stone or wood, but saw lots of timber cut, and was told the master builders had been sent from China. It is a precise, first-hand note of a steppe ruler commissioning a fixed town from foreign craftsmen.
passages.quote: А на той рѣчкѣ Бешкѣ Аблай-Тайша дѣлаетъ городъ; а про то подлинно не вѣдомо, каменной ли, или деревянной; а лѣсу нарожено много: лѣсъ сосновой тонокъ … а ставитъ тотъ городъ промежь горъ каменныхъ; а мастеры къ нему присланы изъ Китайскаго Царства
passages.translation: And on that stream, the Beshka, Ablai taisha is building a town; whether of stone or of wood is not known for certain, but much timber has been felled, thin pine … and he is putting that town up between stony hills; and the master builders for it were sent from the Chinese Tsardom.
passages.speaker: Fyodor Baikov (1788 Novikov printing)
passages.caution: Baikov saw the works under way; the origin of the craftsmen is what he was told. Historians identify this with the Buddhist monastery-town later known as Ablai-kit, whose ruins survive.

passages.headline: Brick temples and clay houses on the Irtysh
passages.people: Kalmyks (Oirats), a Buddhist lama, Bukharan farmers
passages.gloss: On the way up the Irtysh Baikov noted a Kalmyk 'mosque' (a Buddhist temple) of burnt brick, then a Kalmyk lama with two large 'Burkhan' halls, also of burnt brick, and clay houses to live in. The fields around grew wheat and millet, but the ploughing was done by Bukharans, the settled Central Asian farmers who worked for the Oirats.
passages.quote: а въ Кабанъ-Гусанѣ поставлена мечеть Калмыцкая: кирпичь жженой … А живетъ тутъ Калмыцкой Лама подлѣ Иртыша на лѣвой сторонѣ. А поставлены у того Ламы двѣ палаты Бурханные велики: кирпичь жженой; а избы у нихъ, въ которыхъ живутъ, глиняные; а хлѣба родится у того Ламы пшеницы и проса много, а пашутъ Бухарцы.
passages.translation: and at Kaban-Gusan a Kalmyk mosque has been built: of burnt brick … And a Kalmyk lama lives here beside the Irtysh on the left bank. Two great Burkhan (Buddha) halls have been built for that lama, of burnt brick; and the houses they live in are of clay; and much wheat and millet grows for that lama, and Bukharans do the ploughing.
passages.speaker: Fyodor Baikov (1788 Novikov printing)
passages.caution: 'Mosque' is Baikov's word for a non-Christian temple; Burkhan is the Mongol word for Buddha.

passages.headline: Kokotan (Hohhot): earth walls, brick towers, glazed temple roofs
passages.gloss: The first Chinese-ruled town Baikov reached was Kokotan, today's Hohhot in Inner Mongolia. He says its people spoke Mongol and its governors were sent from Beijing. The wall was of earth with towers of burnt brick and iron-bound oak gates, but no cannon; inside and outside were many brick temples with green-glazed tile roofs, and a big market of stone shops.
passages.quote: а городъ Кококотанъ земляной: башни кирпичные: кирпичь жженой; проѣзжіе башни велики: по двои ворота въ башнѣ; … а ворота дубовые, окованы желѣзомъ; … а огненного бою, пушекъ и пищалей нѣтъ, а кумирницъ въ городѣ и за городомъ много: кумирницы кирпичные, а верьхи у нихъ дѣланы по Руски, а крышы черепицею муравленою.
passages.translation: and the town of Kokotan is of earth, with towers of brick, burnt brick; the gate towers are large, with two gates in each tower; … the gates are of oak, bound with iron; … there are no firearms, cannon or muskets; and there are many idol-temples in the town and outside it: the temples are of brick, their tops made as in Russia, and the roofs of glazed tile.
passages.speaker: Fyodor Baikov (1788 Novikov printing)

passages.headline: A Beijing emperor 'of Mongol race'
passages.people: Manchus (Qing dynasty), called Mongols by Baikov
passages.gloss: Baikov calls Beijing by its old Mongol name Kanbalyk (Khanbaliq) and reports that the reigning emperor, the 'Bogda', was of Mongol race, and that the last Chinese emperor hanged himself when the 'Mongols' took over China. He means the Manchus, who had taken Beijing in 1644. It is the Russian counterpart of the Western habit of calling the Manchus 'Tartars'.
passages.quote: А въ Китайскомъ Царствѣ въ Канбалыкѣ Царь Богда Мунгальскаго рода; а прежде того былъ Царь Китайскаго рода Даба; а какъ одолѣли Мунгальцы Китайскимъ Царствомъ, и тогда тотъ Даба Царь обѣсился
passages.translation: And in the Chinese Tsardom, in Kanbalyk, the tsar is the Bogda, of Mongol race; and before him there was a tsar of Chinese race, Daba; and when the Mongols overcame the Chinese Tsardom, that Tsar Daba hanged himself
passages.speaker: Fyodor Baikov (1788 Novikov printing)
passages.caution: Hearsay gathered while confined in Beijing. 'Daba' is Baikov's rendering of the Ming ruler (the Chongzhen emperor hanged himself in 1644).

passages.headline: A capital of tents laid out like streets
passages.gloss: Riding to his first audience, Unkovsky entered the ruler's urga, the moving headquarters camp. He describes rings of Kalmyk and Bukharan tent-camps (kuri) set out 'like streets', which he was led around for about a verst, and a bazaar in front of the ruler's own tent. This is what the capital of a powerful steppe state looked like: a planned city of portable dwellings.
passages.quote: Какъ въѣхали въ первые кури, которые яко улицами поставлены, калмыцкіе и бухарскіе, и вели насъ между оными около версты не прямо, но вкругъ Урги, и какъ пріѣхали съ лица контайшиной Урги, гдѣ базаръ бываетъ, около ста сажень не доѣхавъ, сказалъ Кашка, что тутъ надлежитъ съ лошадей слезть.
passages.translation: When we rode into the first kuri (tent-rings), which are set out like streets, Kalmyk and Bukharan, they led us among them for about a verst, not straight but around the Urga; and when we came to the front of the Kontaisha's Urga, where the bazaar is held, about a hundred sazhens short of it, Kashka said we must get off our horses here.
passages.speaker: Ivan Unkovsky (ed. N. I. Veselovsky, 1887)

passages.headline: The khan's felt house inside a fence of reeds and willow
passages.gloss: The ruler of the Dzungars received the Russian envoy in a 'felt house' (a large yurt), set inside an enclosure woven from reeds and willow withies, entered through a door made of six planks. Unkovsky had to lift the felt door flap himself. The detail shows the materials of a steppe palace: felt, reed, willow and a little timber.
passages.quote: Какъ дошли сажень за 6 до коши, которая вкругъ контайшиной войлошной избы изъ камыша и талнику сплетена, отворили двери, которыя изъ шести плахъ сплочены.
passages.translation: When we came within about 6 sazhens of the enclosure (kosha), which is woven of reed and willow around the Kontaisha's felt house, they opened the doors, which are joined from six planks.
passages.speaker: Ivan Unkovsky (ed. N. I. Veselovsky, 1887)

passages.headline: A New Year banquet in a felt tent 14 metres wide
passages.gloss: At the Mongol New Year (Tsagan Sar, 'White Month') about 300 nobles feasted in one enormous round felt kibitka, some 20 arshins (about 14 metres) across. The lattice walls were hung with blue cloth and a fire burned on an iron hearth in the middle. Tea, meat and vodka were served and musicians played fiddles, long flutes and a three-stringed instrument.
passages.quote: Кибитка была войлочная зѣло великая, круглая, въ діаметрѣ около 20 аршинъ; внутри термы (на которыхъ крышка утверждена) завѣшаны голубымъ сукномъ; посрединѣ очагъ, на которомъ дрова горѣли, сдѣланъ изъ желѣза.
passages.translation: The kibitka was of felt, very large and round, about 20 arshins across; inside, the lattice walls (on which the roof is fixed) were hung with blue cloth; in the middle was a hearth made of iron, on which wood was burning.
passages.speaker: Ivan Unkovsky (ed. N. I. Veselovsky, 1887)

passages.headline: A Muslim saint-khan's tomb, and the wrestling match that converted his people
passages.people: Chagatai Mongols (Temer khan) and Muslim Bukharans
passages.when: told on 9 November 1722; events c. 1388 by the Bukharans' reckoning
passages.gloss: The Tobolsk Bukharans in Unkovsky's party told him of the tomb of 'Temer khan', a ruler of the Ili who, they said, had worshipped idols until a Muslim merchant threw his strongest wrestler three times. The khan then converted, his people were circumcised and threw the tassels from their caps into the Borotala river, damming it. Muslims built chambers over his grave and still brought offerings. Unkovsky wanted to see it but was not allowed. The tomb is generally identified with the mausoleum of the Chagatai khan Tughluq Timur near Khorgos.
passages.quote: Того ради Темерханъ принялъ Махометской законъ, и всѣ его владѣнія люди обрѣзались и съ шапокъ залы (или кисти) въ рѣку Борталъ побросали, и будто оными рѣку запрудили. И для вышеозначенного махометане оного Темерхана, святымъ почитаютъ, а надъ гробомъ его полаты построены и приносятъ доднесь махометане приносы на гробъ его, и сторожи при томъ гробѣ имѣются.
passages.translation: For that reason Temer khan accepted the Muhammadan law, and all the people of his realm were circumcised and threw the tassels from their caps into the river Borotala, and supposedly dammed the river with them. And for this the Muhammadans revere Temer khan as a saint, and chambers have been built over his tomb, and to this day the Muhammadans bring offerings to his tomb, and there are guards at that tomb.
passages.speaker: Ivan Unkovsky, reporting what the Tobolsk Bukharans told him (ed. N. I. Veselovsky, 1887)
passages.caution: A conversion legend passed on by Muslim merchants; Unkovsky did not see the tomb. The identification with Tughluq Timur is a modern one, not Unkovsky's.

passages.headline: Opened burial mounds all over the steppe: whose were they?
passages.place: Irtysh steppe between Semey (Semipalatinsk) and Yamyshevo
passages.gloss: On the way home Unkovsky saw many burial mounds dug open 'like cellars' across the steppe. The Dzungar envoy Darzha said the dead were of his own people. Unkovsky objected that by their religion Kalmyks burn their dead or give them to dogs and birds, and never bury them with gold, so the mound-builders must have been someone else. An early recorded argument about who built the kurgans.
passages.quote: Ѣдучи въ пути степью, видѣли множество разрытыхъ бугровъ … яко погребы раскрытые, по всей степи видны. … Спрошено у него: Какіе люди тутъ погребены были? Оной сказалъ, будто ихъ народу. На сіе сказано ему, что по ихъ вѣрѣ умершихъ людей жгутъ и въ воду бросаютъ, собакамъ и птицамъ на кормъ отдаютъ, а съ золотомъ и ни съ какимъ богатствомъ не погребаютъ.
passages.translation: Travelling across the steppe we saw a great many dug-open mounds … like opened cellars, visible all over the steppe. … He was asked: what people were buried here? He said: supposedly of their own people. To this he was told that by their faith they burn their dead and throw them in the water, give them to dogs and birds for food, and do not bury them with gold or with any wealth at all.
passages.speaker: Ivan Unkovsky (ed. N. I. Veselovsky, 1887)
passages.caution: Unkovsky saw the robbed mounds; his account of Kalmyk funeral custom is a generalisation made to win an argument.

passages.headline: A Russian envoy guesses that ancient Russians lay under the mounds
passages.place: Irtysh steppe between Semey (Semipalatinsk) and Yamyshevo
passages.gloss: Continuing the argument about the robbed mounds, Unkovsky told Darzha that in pagan times, over seven hundred years earlier, Russians had buried their dead with war-gear under great earth mounds, so perhaps some of 'our peoples' had once lived here. He blamed the digging on Kalmyks, Ostyaks or Kazakhs, and said Russian law punished grave-robbers with death. Darzha, doubtful, replied that his people had only had writing for a hundred years and could not know. A striking early example of a claim about who once lived on the steppe, made on the spot and without evidence.
passages.quote: У насъ погребаются люди съ богатствомъ, а паче что въ древнія времена еще до христіанского закона, лѣтъ слишкомъ за семь сотъ погребалися со всѣмъ военнымъ уборствомъ, и насыпали на нихъ великіе бугры земли, и можетъ быть, что въ древнія времена нѣкоторые изъ нашихъ народовъ въ сихъ мѣстахъ жили … сказалъ, что у насъ де только сто лѣтъ какъ грамота началась
passages.translation: Among us people are buried with their wealth, and especially in ancient times, before the Christian law, more than seven hundred years ago, they were buried with all their war-gear and great mounds of earth were heaped over them; and it may be that in ancient times some of our peoples lived in these places … [Darzha] said that among them writing began only a hundred years ago.
passages.speaker: Ivan Unkovsky, recording his own words and the reply of the Dzungar envoy Darzha (ed. N. I. Veselovsky, 1887)
passages.caution: Unkovsky offers this as a guess in a diplomatic sparring match, not as knowledge; he himself calls it 'perhaps'.

passages.headline: Horned masked dancers and stones thrown at China
passages.gloss: Before the New Year the lamas performed a masked dance (the Buddhist tsam) before a great tent. Unkovsky describes masked dancers wearing caps with horns, one like a cow's, one like a wild goat's, cymbals, drums and long brass trumpets, and an offering blown up in a fire. At the end the whole crowd, the ruler among them, marched east and hurled stones, sticks and earth toward the east with a great shout, 'as if for victory over the Chinese', their enemy at the time.
passages.quote: Вышли два человѣка, закрытыя лица, на шапкахъ по два рога было; у одного коровей, у другого яко у дикой козы … и весь народъ, ухватя что попало въ руки (камень или палку или земли), съ великимъ крикомъ бросали на востокъ, будто бы въ побѣду на Китайцевъ; притомъ и самъ Контайша шелъ.
passages.translation: Two men came out with covered faces, with two horns each on their caps; one had cow's horns, the other horns like a wild goat's … and all the people, seizing whatever came to hand (a stone or a stick or earth), threw it toward the east with a great shout, as if for victory over the Chinese; and the Kontaisha himself walked with them.
passages.speaker: Ivan Unkovsky (ed. N. I. Veselovsky, 1887)
passages.caution: The meaning of the stone-throwing ('as if for victory over the Chinese') is Unkovsky's reading.

passages.headline: Wrestlers in rolled-up trousers
passages.gloss: Invited to watch wrestling, Unkovsky sat near the ruler under awnings on tall poles. He describes bouts between the ruler's side and his son Galdan Tseren's side, with bets and judges who wrote down the results. The wrestlers came out bare but for trousers rolled above the knee, raised their arms, glared to look fearsome, and gripped each other by the trousers. A bout only counted when a man was thrown flat on both shoulders.
passages.quote: И тако съ обѣихъ сторонъ выходятъ борцы нагіе, токмо въ штанахъ, которыя подобраны выше гораздо колѣнъ. И не дошедъ единъ отъ другого сажени за четыре, подымутъ руки вверхъ, и искося глаза (являя себя страшливыми), потихоньку сходятся; и какъ сойдутся, и принаклонясь, схватываются за штаны
passages.translation: And so from both sides the wrestlers come out naked, only in trousers rolled up well above the knee. And when they are about four sazhens from each other they raise their arms, and, rolling their eyes (to make themselves look fearsome), slowly close in; and when they meet they bend forward and seize each other by the trousers
passages.speaker: Ivan Unkovsky (ed. N. I. Veselovsky, 1887)

passages.headline: No bread, only meat and fermented milk; the Tatars will drink it
passages.people: Dzungars (Oirats); Siberian service Tatars in the Russian suite
passages.gloss: Instead of flour the Dzungars sent the embassy chigan, fermented milk, saying they had no grain and ate only meat and drank chigan. Unkovsky answered that some of his people would drink it and some would not, since a Christian fast was about to begin: during it nobody but the Tatars would drink chigan. The 'Tatars' here are the Muslim service Tatars of Tobolsk and Tara travelling with him.
passages.quote: а вмѣсто муки и крупъ привезли чигану, объявляя, что у нихъ нынѣ хлѣба нѣтъ, и люди ихъ нынѣ не ѣдятъ, токмо мясо, и пьютъ чиганы. Сказано имъ, что наши люди иные будутъ пить чиганъ, а иные не будутъ; а особливо съ завтрешнего числа начнется у насъ постъ … и никто, кромѣ Татаръ, чигану пить не будутъ
passages.translation: and instead of flour and groats they brought chigan, declaring that they have no bread now, and their people are not eating now, only meat, and drink chigan. They were told that some of our people will drink chigan and some will not; and especially since from tomorrow our fast begins … and nobody except the Tatars will drink chigan
passages.speaker: Ivan Unkovsky (ed. N. I. Veselovsky, 1887)

passages.headline: Verbal courts and savage punishments
passages.gloss: In his closing description of the Dzungar state Unkovsky says the ruler took no great decision without his council of zaisangs, and that the court (zargo) of ten or more zaisangs judged cases orally, not in writing. Capital sentences were carried out by flogging to death or by tying limbs to horses' tails, though he adds that such executions were rare.
passages.quote: Суды рѣшатъ не письменно, но на словахъ. Ежели за важныя дѣла кого на смерть осудятъ: иныхъ, поставя на колѣнки, плетьми до смерти убиваютъ; иныхъ же, привязавъ къ лошадинымъ хвостамъ руки и ноги, и тако оныя лошади на бѣгу тѣмъ людямъ руки и ноги отрываютъ. Однакожъ, рѣдко у нихъ оныя казни случаются.
passages.translation: They decide cases not in writing but orally. If they condemn someone to death for serious matters, some they kneel down and flog to death with whips; others they tie by the hands and feet to horses' tails, and the horses, running, tear off those people's arms and legs. However, such executions happen rarely among them.
passages.speaker: Ivan Unkovsky (ed. N. I. Veselovsky, 1887)
passages.caution: Part of a general summary built from inquiry, not an execution he witnessed.

passages.headline: Nomads turning farmers on the khan's orders
passages.gloss: Unkovsky notes that thirty years earlier the Kalmyks had little grain because they did not know how to plough, but now fields were multiplying: not only their subject Bukharans (settled Turkestani farmers) but many Kalmyks had taken up farming by the ruler's order. He lists wheat, millet, barley and rice, and melons, apricots, grapes and pomegranates from Yarkand and the other towns under Dzungar rule.
passages.quote: Предъ симъ временемъ лѣтъ за тридцать хлѣба мало имѣли, понеже пахать не умѣли. Нынѣ пашни у нихъ отъ часу умножаются, и не токмо подданные Бухарцы хлѣбъ сѣютъ, но и Калмыки многіе за пашню пріемлются, понеже о томъ Контайши приказъ есть.
passages.translation: Some thirty years before this they had little grain, because they did not know how to plough. Now their fields multiply by the hour, and not only the subject Bukharans sow grain, but many Kalmyks are taking up ploughing, because there is an order from the Kontaisha about it.
passages.speaker: Ivan Unkovsky (ed. N. I. Veselovsky, 1887)
passages.caution: The same page opens with Unkovsky's prejudiced remark that Kalmyks learn cunning and theft from childhood.

passages.headline: A Swedish prisoner casts cannon for the Dzungar ruler
passages.gloss: A Russian soldier freed from Dzungar captivity told Unkovsky that a foreign sub-lieutenant, Renat, captured with the Russians in 1716, had cast seven bronze cannon and three mortars for the ruler, and that other captive officers had taught the Dzungars to make cloth and needles; one was said to be making velvet in Yarkand. It shows a steppe state importing skills through its prisoners.
passages.quote: слышалъ, что иноземецъ штыкъ-юнкеръ Ренотъ, которой взятъ съ ними въ полонъ съ Корякова, вылилъ Контайшѣ семь пушекъ мѣдныхъ, три мортиры. Да у него жъ Контайши въ Ургѣ поручикъ Дебешъ и другіе офицеры научили дѣлать суконъ, иголъ. А нынѣ слышно, что оной Дебешъ дѣлаетъ въ Эркени бархатъ.
passages.translation: he heard that the foreigner, sub-lieutenant of artillery Renat, who was taken prisoner with them at Koryakov, cast for the Kontaisha seven bronze cannon and three mortars. And at the same Kontaisha's Urga, Lieutenant Debesh and other officers taught them to make cloth and needles. And now it is said that this Debesh is making velvet in Erken (Yarkand).
passages.speaker: Ilya Lychagin, freed Russian captive, as recorded in Unkovsky's interrogation records (ed. N. I. Veselovsky, 1887)
passages.caution: Hearsay from a former captive. Renat is the Swedish officer Johan Gustaf Renat, later known for his maps of Dzungaria (a modern identification).

passages.headline: The peoples of the Dzungar realm, none of them called Tatars
passages.gloss: Unkovsky lists the peoples under the Kontaisha: the Dzungars proper ('of the left hand'), Kyrgyz, Uriankhai, Telengits and others, the town-dwelling Bukharans of Yarkand, the Buruts (Kyrgyz) of lake Issyk-Kul and the Barabinians, who paid tribute to both Russia and the Dzungars. No one here is called a Tatar; the same land appears on Western maps of the time as part of 'Great Tartary'.
passages.quote: Подъ его контайшинымъ владѣніемъ обрѣтаются разные народы, а именно: его настоящей народъ, имянуемой Зюнгоры (или лѣвой руки), Киргизы, Урянхайцы, Теленгуты, Мингаты, Каюты, Кошеуты, Эркенскіе Бухарцы (въ городахъ живущіе, а лучше при немъ кочуютъ), Буруты, которые около озера Тускелъ кочуютъ, Барабинцы, которые ясакъ платятъ въ сторону Императорского Величества и Контайшѣ.
passages.translation: Under the Kontaisha's rule are various peoples, namely: his own people, called the Dzungars (or 'of the left hand'), the Kyrgyz, Uriankhai, Telengits, Mingats, Khoits, Khoshuts, the Bukharans of Erken (Yarkand), who live in towns, though the better sort roam with him, the Buruts, who roam around lake Tuskel (Issyk-Kul), and the Barabinians, who pay tribute to His Imperial Majesty and to the Kontaisha.
passages.speaker: Ivan Unkovsky (ed. N. I. Veselovsky, 1887)
passages.caution: The identifications of Kayuty as Khoits and Tuskel as Issyk-Kul are editorial glosses by this reader, not Unkovsky's.

passages.headline: In Bukhara and Khiva, 'Tatar' was an insult
passages.people: Peoples of Central Asia; Tatars as a label
passages.gloss: Rychkov questioned Muslim scholars and Russian envoys sent from Orenburg to Khiva and Bukhara about the names 'Scythians' and 'Tatars'. He concludes that no people there called itself Tatar. The word meant a lawless, inhuman people supposed to live somewhere in far Siberia, and calling someone a Tatar was like calling him a barbarian or a worthless peasant.
passages.quote: ибо я совершенно увѣренъ, что во всѣхъ тамошнихъ сторонахъ ни одного народа нѣтъ, которой бы Татарами имяновался. Подъ именемъ Татаръ разумѣютъ они народъ весьма беззаконной и безчеловѣчной, признавая, якобы жительствуетъ онъ въ Россійскихъ, а паче въ самыхъ отдаленныхъ Сибирскихъ мѣстахъ … И имя Татаръ почитаютъ они за весьма безчестное и поносное, такъ какъ бы сказать, Варваръ, Смердъ, и ни къ чему годной человѣкъ.
passages.translation: for I am fully certain that in all those parts there is not one people that calls itself Tatars. By the name Tatars they understand a very lawless and inhuman people, which they suppose lives in the Russian, and above all in the most remote Siberian, places … And they regard the name Tatar as very dishonourable and abusive, as if to say barbarian, serf, and good-for-nothing.
passages.speaker: Pyotr Rychkov (1762)
passages.caution: Based on Rychkov's interviews with Muslim scholars and returning envoys, not on travel of his own to Khiva or Bukhara.

passages.headline: The 'tailed Tatars' of Turkestan
passages.people: A despised clan near Turkestan called 'tailed Tatars'
passages.gloss: The interpreter Aralov, who had often been to the town of Turkestan, told Rychkov of a despised clan of under a hundred families nicknamed the 'tailed Tatars'. The story went that their ancestors killed the son of a local saint, who cursed them so they could not ride horses, and they grew a tail-like mark. Aralov swore he had seen such a mark on a naked child. Rychkov leaves it to the reader: 'whether this is true or not'. His real point follows: there the name Tatar is an insult, and the Tatars of Orenburg and Kazan are called Nogais.
passages.quote: заклялъ ихъ молитвою, дабы они неспособны были къ верховой ѣздѣ на лошадяхъ, и будтобъ съ того времени получили они на тѣлѣ знакъ подобной хвосту … Помянутой Переводчикъ объявляетъ, яко бы онъ изъ тѣхъ людей одного робенка самъ видѣлъ нагова, и увѣряетъ, что у него назади такой знакъ подлинно былъ. Правдаль сіе, или нѣтъ, остается въ произвольномъ разсужденіи.
passages.translation: he cursed them with a prayer, so that they should be unable to ride on horseback, and supposedly from that time they received on their bodies a mark like a tail … The said interpreter declares that he himself saw one child of those people naked, and assures that it really had such a mark behind. Whether this is true or not is left to free judgment.
passages.speaker: Pyotr Rychkov, reporting the interpreter Aralov (1762)
passages.caution: A second-hand legend; Rychkov explicitly declines to vouch for it.

passages.headline: A ruined stone town with a mosque, credited to the Nogais
passages.people: Nogai Tatars (as builders, per Kazakh tradition); Kazakhs of the Middle Horde
passages.gloss: In a section on 'ruins of ancient towns and buildings' Rychkov lists sites in the Kazakh Middle Horde. At a great ruined town on the Nura river there were chambers still standing, a mosque and much fallen stone building. The Kazakhs told Russian informants that Nogais had lived there in the old days. Nearby entries credit other ruins to Nogai princes or to holy women.
passages.quote: Тутъ же одна мечеть, и весьма много развалившагося каменнагожъ строенія. Киргисцы сказываютъ, что тутъ въ старину живали Нагайцы.
passages.translation: Here too is a mosque, and a great deal of ruined stone building. The Kirghiz (Kazakhs) say that Nogais lived here in the old days.
passages.speaker: Pyotr Rychkov (1762)
passages.caution: Rychkov did not visit these ruins; he relies on Kazakh report and the interpreter Aralov. The OCR of the town's name on this page is unreadable.

passages.headline: Stone ruins that an old Tatar called tombs of a people who left for China
passages.place: Uy river, southern Urals (Chelyabinsk and Kostanay region)
passages.people: Siberian Tatars of Iset province (as informants); unknown earlier inhabitants
passages.gloss: Along the Uy frontier line Rychkov notes ruins of stone buildings, some still whole. An old Tatar of Iset province told Lieutenant-Colonel Rennenkampf, from his ancestors' tradition, that the peoples who once lived here had moved away to China, and that the standing buildings were nothing but cemeteries of their notable men. An early record of local explanations for steppe ruins.
passages.quote: въ разныхъ мѣстахъ находятся развалины каменныхъ строеній, изъ коихъ нѣкоторыя понынѣ еще въ цѣлости. О сихъ изъ живущихъ въ Исетской провинціи Татаръ одинъ престарѣлой человѣкъ Подполковнику Ренненкампфу по преданію предковъ своихъ объявлялъ, яко бы въ древнія времена жившіе въ сихъ мѣстахъ народы отошли въ Китайское государство. Оныя донынѣ видимыя строенія не что иное, какъ знатныхъ ихъ людей кладбища
passages.translation: in various places there are ruins of stone buildings, some of which are still whole. About these, one very old man among the Tatars living in Iset province told Lieutenant-Colonel Rennenkampf, from the tradition of his ancestors, that the peoples who lived in these places in ancient times went away into the Chinese state. The buildings still visible are nothing other than the cemeteries of their notable people
passages.speaker: Pyotr Rychkov, reporting an old Tatar's account to Rennenkampf (1762)
passages.caution: Oral tradition passed through two intermediaries.

passages.headline: Isker, the real Tatar name of the town of Sibir
passages.people: Siberian Tatars (khans of the Taibugid line)
passages.gloss: Müller says Khan Makhmet moved the princely seat from the Tura to a high headland on the Irtysh and fortified it, because the old capital Chimgi (Tyumen), though protected by ravines, a rampart and ditches, lay on flat ground. The ruins could still be seen above Tobolsk. He rejects the idea that 'Sibir' is a Tatar word for 'capital': the Tatars call the fortress Isker, and the name Kashlyk used in the Tobolsk chronicle was, he says, used by no people he knew.
passages.quote: Сіе мѣсто есть такъ именуемое старинной Татарской городъ и крѣпость Сибирь, котораго остатки повыше Тобольска … еще и теперь видны. … Подлинное Татарское имя сей старинной крѣпости есть Искеръ, которымъ именемъ Татаре еще и понынѣ оную называютъ.
passages.translation: This place is the so-called old Tatar town and fortress of Sibir, whose remains can still be seen upriver of Tobolsk … The true Tatar name of this old fortress is Isker, by which name the Tatars call it to this day.
passages.speaker: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Russian edition, 1787 issue)
passages.caution: The distance from Tobolsk is garbled in the OCR and has been left out.

passages.headline: Stone markers, idols and gold from the graves: whose were they?
passages.people: Tatars and Mongols of Chinggis Khan's era (as Müller supposes)
passages.gloss: Müller points to the traces of old towns on the steppes, the many stone markers and 'idols' (stone statues), old grave mounds, and the gold and silver objects dug out of them. He attributes them to the earlier Tatars, reasoning that the treasures of China, Persia, Russia, Poland, Bohemia and Hungary had fallen to them as conquerors. It is a scholar's inference, not a report from the graves themselves.
passages.quote: Сколько не видно слѣдовъ на разныхъ мѣстахъ по степямъ городковъ? Коликое множество въ память поставленныхъ каменныхъ маяковъ, болвановъ, старинныхъ могилъ и другихъ принадлежащихъ къ тому вещей на всѣхъ мѣстахъ не находится? Какихъ дорогихъ вещей, золотыхъ и серебреныхъ, изъ могилъ не выкопано? Откуда можно было имъ произойти, какъ только отъ прежнихъ Татаръ
passages.translation: How many traces of small towns are seen in various places on the steppes? What a multitude of stone markers set up as memorials, idols, old graves and other such things are found everywhere? What precious objects, of gold and silver, have not been dug out of the graves? Where could they have come from, if not from the former Tatars
passages.speaker: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Russian edition, 1787 issue)
passages.caution: Müller's attribution to the Chinggisid Tatars is his own guess; modern archaeology dates many of these kurgans and stone figures far earlier.

passages.headline: Tartary: the Chinese name for everything beyond the Wall
passages.people: Mongols and other peoples north of the Great Wall
passages.gloss: Discussing a Siberian Tatar story that Chinese once lived in Siberia, Müller suggests that at most the Chinese may have built some towns on the Daurian and Mongol frontiers and toward Liaodong, because in China all lands beyond the Wall are called Tartary. The name, in his view, is a broad outsiders' label, not the name of one country.
passages.quote: По всѣмъ обстоятельствамъ разсуждать можно, что развѣ о построенныхъ нѣкоторыхъ городахъ на границахъ Даурскихъ и Мунгальскихъ и къ Леотонгу, о чемъ и въ древнихъ временахъ примѣры имѣются, упоминать хотѣли, по тому что въ Китаѣ всѣ за стѣною находящіяся земли общимъ именемъ Татарія называются.
passages.translation: By all the circumstances one may judge that they perhaps meant certain towns built on the Daurian and Mongol borders and toward Liaotung, of which there are examples in ancient times, because in China all the lands lying beyond the Wall are called by the general name Tartary.
passages.speaker: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Russian edition, 1787 issue)
passages.caution: Müller cites Martini's Chinese atlas and Witsen for this; it reflects European usage of his day.

passages.headline: The Tatar tale of Chinese who fled when the forest grew
passages.people: Siberian Tatars of Tobolsk (tellers); 'Chinese' (in the tale)
passages.gloss: Müller reports a story still told orally by the Tobolsk Tatars: Siberia was once a bare steppe where the Chinese lived, but when forest began to grow everywhere the people took fright, 'as the land became as if horned', and moved away to their present home. He says it was also written down in 1670 on the orders of the Tobolsk governor Pyotr Godunov. Müller calls it a false tale that no reasonable person can believe, and notes that forest could easily grow over abandoned sites in 450 years without any miracle.
passages.quote: Сказываютъ, якобы сперва вся Сибирь была голая степь безъ лѣсу, а какъ въ оное время Китайцы тамъ жительство свое имѣли, то помалу по разнымъ мѣстамъ началъ лѣсъ расти, чего народъ испужавшись, понеже земля подобно какъ рогатая стала, на нынѣшнее жилище переселился. Сію повѣсть еще и нынѣ у Тобольскихъ Татаръ изустно слышать можно.
passages.translation: They say that at first all Siberia was a bare steppe without forest, and when at that time the Chinese lived there, forest little by little began to grow in various places, at which the people took fright, because the land became as if horned, and moved to their present dwelling. This tale can still be heard by word of mouth from the Tobolsk Tatars.
passages.speaker: Gerhard Friedrich Müller, reporting Tobolsk Tatar oral tradition (Russian edition, 1787 issue)
passages.caution: Müller records the tale in order to reject it; the next page adds the claim that ruined towns between the Irtysh and Tobol are overgrown with forest.

passages.headline: The Russians named the Mongols 'Tatars', and Europe copied them
passages.gloss: Bichurin says the invaders of 1237 to 1240 were Mongols of the 'Tatan' confederation, among whom the Tatar tribe near the Argun was only one conquered clan. In his view the Russians made the first mistake by calling the whole army 'Tatars', Carpini copied it through poor interpreters, and geographers without further inquiry called the whole belt from the Caspian to the Pacific 'Great Tartary'.
passages.quote: И такъ, по моему мнѣнію, Россіяне при первомъ нашествіи Татаньцевъ, назвавъ ихъ Татарами, первые погрѣшили и сообщили сію погрѣшность западнымъ народамъ. … а Географы, безъ дальняго изслѣдованія, всю полосу отъ Каспійскаго моря до Восточнаго назвали Великою Татаріею.
passages.translation: And so, in my opinion, the Russians, calling the Tatans 'Tatars' at their first invasion, were the first to err and passed this error on to the western peoples. … and geographers, without further investigation, called the whole belt from the Caspian Sea to the Eastern Sea Great Tartary.
passages.speaker: Iakinf (N. Ya. Bichurin), 1828
passages.caution: Bichurin's own argument; he is disputing Klaproth, who held that the Mongols were rightly called Tatars. 'Tatan' is his rendering of Chinese Dada.

passages.headline: How Mongol conquerors became the Turkic 'Tatars' of Kazan and Crimea
passages.people: Golden Horde Mongols and Turkic peoples
passages.gloss: Bichurin explains how the name moved: the Mongol lords on the Volga were few among Turkic subjects, married into them, took their language, customs and Islam, and so disappeared, reappearing under the Russian name 'Tatars' as a seemingly new people ruling Kazan, Astrakhan and Crimea. A footnote adds that the Tatars do not call themselves by that name but Uzbeks, Nogais and so on.
passages.quote: Побѣдители, перенявъ отъ Туркистанцевъ съ браками ихъ нравы и обыкновенія, ихъ языкъ и религію, мало по малу совершенно потерялись, такъ что наконецъ самое имя Татаньцевъ исчезло, и они подъ Россійскимъ названіемъ Татаръ содѣлались какъ бы новымъ народомъ, который въ послѣдствіи господствовалъ въ царствахъ: Казанскомъ, Астраханскомъ и Крымскомъ.
passages.translation: The conquerors, taking from the Turkestanis through marriage their manners and customs, their language and religion, little by little were completely lost, so that at last the very name of the Tatans disappeared, and under the Russian name of Tatars they became as it were a new people, which afterwards ruled in the tsardoms of Kazan, Astrakhan and Crimea.
passages.speaker: Iakinf (N. Ya. Bichurin), 1828
passages.caution: Bichurin himself calls this a conjecture with probability on its side.

passages.headline: How a Mongol yurt is built
passages.gloss: Bichurin describes the yurt, 'which we call a kibitka': folding lattice walls tied with rawhide instead of nails, which can be widened or heightened, a domed roof of poles set like rays into two half-rings, covered with one layer of felt in summer and two or three in winter and bound with woollen bands. A smoke hole at the top, a felt or wooden door always facing south-east. He gives the sizes too: 12 to 20 feet across.
passages.quote: Монголы кочуютъ въ круглыхъ юртахъ, которыя у насъ иначе называютъ кибитками. … Состоятъ изъ рѣшетчатыхъ складныхъ стѣнокъ, скрѣпленныхъ вмѣсто гвоздиковъ сырымъ ремнемъ; съуживая можно повышать ихъ, разширяя понижать. Полукруглый наметъ, составляющій кровлю, состоитъ изъ двухъ полукружій, къ которымъ лучеобразно прикрѣплены палки, упираемыя въ рѣшетчатыя стѣнки. Сей остовъ оболокаютъ войлоками въ одинъ, а зимою въ два и три ряда
passages.translation: The Mongols live nomadically in round yurts, which among us are otherwise called kibitkas. … They consist of folding lattice walls fastened with rawhide instead of nails; by narrowing them one can make them higher, by widening them lower. The half-round canopy that forms the roof consists of two half-rings to which poles are fixed like rays, resting on the lattice walls. This frame they cover with felts in one layer, and in winter in two and three
passages.speaker: Iakinf (N. Ya. Bichurin), 1828

passages.headline: Urga in 1821: a monastery town of wooden temples and giant yurts
passages.gloss: The ancestor of Ulaanbaatar, as Bichurin saw it: a great monastery (Khüree) built on Tibetan lines, about 12 li round, with many irregular streets. At the centre was the court of the Jebtsundamba Khutukhtu. The temples were of wood, the main one with a gilded dome; the other buildings were huge yurts covered with canvas. The lamas lived in felt tents or mud-plaster huts. A Chinese trading town (Maimaicheng) stood nearby.
passages.quote: Курень, обширный монастырь, построенный по Тибетскимъ правиламъ. … Въ окружности содержитъ около 12 ли, и состоитъ изъ многихъ неправильныхъ улицъ. Въ средоточіи стоитъ обширный дворъ, въ которомъ Чжебцзунь-дамба-хутухта имѣетъ пребываніе. Здѣсь храмы построены изъ дерева и главный съ позолоченымъ куполомъ. Прочія строенія состоятъ изъ огромныхъ юртъ, обтянутыхъ парусиною.
passages.translation: Khüree, a vast monastery built according to Tibetan rules. … Its circuit is about 12 li, and it consists of many irregular streets. In the centre stands a large courtyard in which the Jebtsundamba Khutukhtu resides. Here the temples are built of wood, and the main one has a gilded dome. The other buildings consist of huge yurts covered with canvas.
passages.speaker: Iakinf (N. Ya. Bichurin), 1828

passages.headline: Chagan-balgas: a Mongol emperor's capital abandoned after a year
passages.people: Mongols of the Yuan dynasty; Chahar Mongols
passages.gloss: Crossing Chahar country, Bichurin passed the ruins of Chagan-balgas, 'White Wall', known in Chinese history as Shahen. He says it was begun as the Middle Capital for Chinggis Khan's descendants ruling China, but the work was stopped the next year as too heavy a burden on the people, and it had lain in ruins ever since: an earthen rampart seven li round with four gates. A real Mongol-built city, identified from Chinese records.
passages.quote: Сей городокъ извѣстенъ въ Китайской Исторіи подъ названіемъ Ша-хенъ. Его начали строить … и назначили быть Среднею столицею (по-Китайски Чжунъ-ду) для потомковъ Чингисовыхъ, царствовавшихъ въ Китаѣ; но въ слѣдующемъ году сія работа, какъ чрезмѣру отягчительная для народа, прекращена, и онъ съ того времени донынѣ лежитъ въ развалинахъ. Сей городъ состоитъ изъ землянаго вала и въ окружности содержитъ семь ли
passages.translation: This small town is known in Chinese history under the name Shahen. They began to build it … and designated it to be the Middle Capital (in Chinese Zhongdu) for the descendants of Chinggis reigning in China; but in the following year this work, as excessively burdensome for the people, was stopped, and since then it has lain in ruins to this day. This town consists of an earthen rampart and is seven li in circuit
passages.speaker: Iakinf (N. Ya. Bichurin), 1828
passages.caution: The founding year is illegible in the OCR and is omitted. Bichurin passed the ruins at a distance; the history comes from Chinese sources.

passages.headline: Obo: stone cairns for the spirits of the land
passages.gloss: Bichurin explains the obo cairns he saw on hilltops: small round mounds of stones heaped on every notable height by a main road. Once a year Mongols gather there to honour the guardian spirits of the district with wrestling, horse racing and archery. Every rider passing an obo dismounts, kneels on the south side, bows three times and leaves something: a khadag scarf, an arrow, a scrap of cloth, horsehair or a pebble.
passages.quote: Это суть священныя мѣста, при которыхъ Монголы собираются однажды въ годъ для поклоненія духамъ покровителямъ страны. Здѣсь-то происходятъ ихъ празднества, сопровождаемыя борьбою, конскимъ ристаніемъ и стрѣляніемъ изъ луковъ. Въ прочее время каждый Монголъ, проѣзжающій мимо Обо, сходитъ съ лошади, становится предъ онымъ съ южной стороны на одно колѣно, и, поднося сложенныя ладони ко лбу, дѣлаетъ троекратное поклоненіе.
passages.translation: These are sacred places, where the Mongols gather once a year to worship the guardian spirits of the country. Here their festivals take place, accompanied by wrestling, horse racing and archery. At other times every Mongol riding past an obo gets off his horse, kneels on one knee before it on the south side and, raising his folded palms to his forehead, bows three times.
passages.speaker: Iakinf (N. Ya. Bichurin), 1828
passages.caution: Bichurin's definition of an obo (a small round mound of heaped stones on heights by a main road) is on the preceding page, n95.

passages.headline: Karakorum: an old Uighur town, walled by Ögedei
passages.gloss: The Chinese commentary says that Khorin (Karakorum) had been the town of a Uighur khan in Tang times. The Mongols first used it as their assembly place and in 1235 surrounded it with a wall about five li (Bichurin: about 3.5 versts) round. In the same year, the annal adds, Ögedei built the Wan'an palace there.
passages.quote: Во вторый мѣсяцъ Монголы обвели стѣною Хоринь. Хоринь былъ прежній городъ Хойхорскаго Пиця-Хана, жившаго при династіи Тханъ. Монголы прежде назначили его сборнымъ мѣстомъ, а нынѣ обвели стѣною, имѣвшею около пяти ли окружности.
passages.translation: In the second month the Mongols surrounded Khorin with a wall. Khorin was formerly the town of the Uighur (Khoikhor) Pijia khan, who lived under the Tang dynasty. The Mongols earlier made it their place of assembly, and now surrounded it with a wall about five li in circuit.
passages.speaker: Tongjian gangmu (Chinese commentary), translated by Iakinf Bichurin, 1829
passages.caution: The Chinese compilers are writing long after the event; the Uighur capital (Ordu-Baliq) actually lay some distance from Karakorum, a point this source does not raise.

passages.headline: The wind that dried the sea for Möngke
passages.gloss: In the Chinese biography of Möngke, the Kipchak chief Bachman fled to an island in the sea. When Möngke arrived, a strong wind drove the water off the shallows and his army crossed; Möngke declared that Heaven itself was opening the road. Bachman, captured, refused to kneel, saying 'I was the ruler of a state' and 'am I a camel, that I should kneel?', and warned that the water would soon return. The next sentence says Möngke then marched with Batu against Rus ('Oros').
passages.quote: По счастію, сильный вѣтеръ согналъ морскую воду съ мелкихъ мѣстъ, такъ, что можно было переправиться. Ханъ, обрадовавшись, сказалъ: »Само Небо открываетъ дорогу мнѣ.« … Ханъ приказалъ ему стать на колѣна: но Бацимакъ сказалъ: »Я былъ обладателемъ государства и могу ли дорожить жизнію? Сверхъ сего я не верблюдъ: для чего мнѣ становиться на колѣна?«
passages.translation: By good fortune a strong wind drove the sea water off the shallow places, so that it was possible to cross. The khan, delighted, said: 'Heaven itself opens the road for me.' … The khan ordered him to kneel; but Bachman said: 'I was the ruler of a state, and can I value my life? Besides, I am not a camel: why should I kneel?'
passages.speaker: Yuan shi (biography of Möngke), translated by Iakinf Bichurin, 1829
passages.caution: An official dynastic history that presents the wind as a sign of Heaven's favour; not an eyewitness account.

passages.headline: A Chinese picture of the far north-west: white nights and blue-eyed horsemen
passages.people: Kipchaks (Polovtsy) and neighbours, as described in Chinese annals
passages.gloss: The Chinese annal describing the Mongol attack on the 'tribes of the state of Kincha' (Kipchak) says the land lay 30,000 li from China, that its summer nights were so short the sun barely set before rising, that it bred fine horses, and that its people were brave, with blue eyes and reddish hair. Bichurin notes on the facing page that this is the Mongol invasion of Russia in 1237.
passages.quote: Лѣтомъ ночи бываютъ чрезвычайно коротки. Солнце едва закатится, и тотчасъ всходитъ. Сія страна производитъ отмѣнныхъ лошадей … Мужественны и храбры … Глаза имѣютъ синіе (голубые), волосы рыжеватые.
passages.translation: In summer the nights are extremely short. The sun barely sets and at once rises again. This country produces excellent horses … They are courageous and brave … Their eyes are blue, their hair reddish.
passages.speaker: Tongjian gangmu (Chinese annal), translated by Iakinf Bichurin, 1829
passages.caution: Second-hand Chinese geography of a land its compilers never saw; parts of the OCR on this page are illegible and were left out.

passages.headline: Whom do you call Tatars? A question put to Turkestanis in Beijing
passages.people: Turkestani Muslims (Uighurs of the Tarim oases); Volga and Siberian Tatars
passages.gloss: Bichurin notes that Europeans called the belt from the Caspian to the Pacific 'Great Tartary'. While living in Beijing he asked people from Eastern Turkestan whom they called Tatars. Their answer: a people of their own stock living in Tobolsk, Kazan and Astrakhan. The Tatars themselves, he adds, said the name was given them by neighbours, and no people or clan in Central Asia used it of itself.
passages.quote: Великую полосу земли, простирающуюся отъ Каспійскаго моря до Восточнаго Океана, Европейцы назвали Великою Татаріею. Во время пребыванія моего въ Пекинѣ, неоднократно имѣя случай разговаривать съ жителями Восточнаго Туркистана,
passages.translation: The great belt of land stretching from the Caspian Sea to the Eastern Ocean the Europeans named Great Tartary. During my stay in Beijing, having had more than one occasion to talk with inhabitants of Eastern Turkestan,
passages.speaker: Iakinf (N. Ya. Bichurin), translator's preface, 1829
passages.caution: The answer itself is on the next page (n14): 'now we call Tatars a people of the same stock as us, living in Tobol, Kazan and Astrakhan'.

passages.headline: 'Now we call Tatars our kin in Tobolsk, Kazan and Astrakhan'
passages.people: Volga and Siberian Tatars, as seen by Turkestani Muslims
passages.gloss: The answer Bichurin got from Turkestanis in Beijing, and his conclusion. It shows 'Tatar' as a name used by outsiders for particular Turkic communities under Russian rule, not the name of a vast state.
passages.quote: я спрашивалъ ихъ, кого они называютъ Татарами? Вотъ ихъ отвѣтъ: „нынѣ мы называемъ Татарами единоплеменный съ нами народъ, обитающій въ Тоболѣ, Казани и Астрахани.“ Напротивъ, сами Татары утверждаютъ, что сіе названіе дано имъ отъ сосѣднихъ народовъ. … но только нынѣ нѣтъ ни одного не токмо народа, но и поколѣнія въ Средней Азіи, которое бы называлось симъ именемъ.
passages.translation: I asked them whom they call Tatars. Here is their answer: 'Now we call Tatars a people of the same stock as us, living in Tobol, Kazan and Astrakhan.' The Tatars themselves, on the contrary, assert that this name was given them by neighbouring peoples. … but now there is not a single people, nor even a clan, in Central Asia that calls itself by this name.
passages.speaker: Iakinf (N. Ya. Bichurin), translator's preface, 1829

passages.headline: Kashgar, the 'many-coloured brick' city
passages.gloss: The Qing gazetteer describes Kashgar as one of the great cities of Turkestan, so famous that foreigners called all East Turkestanis 'Kashgarians'. It lists its Manchu and Chinese garrison, taxes paid in cash, grain and cotton cloth, silk and gold-thread products, and skilled jade polishers and goldsmiths. A note explains the name as 'many-coloured brick building', because the city had many buildings of coloured brick.
passages.quote: Кашб значитъ разноцвѣтный, гаръ кирпичное зданіе. Здѣсь много разноцвѣтныхъ кирпичныхъ зданій, отъ чего и названіе дано. Еще говорятъ, что слово Кашгаръ означаетъ богатый.
passages.translation: Kash means many-coloured, gar a brick building. There are many buildings of coloured brick here, which is where the name comes from. It is also said that the word Kashgar means rich.
passages.speaker: Note in the Chinese original ('Author's note'), translated by Iakinf Bichurin, 1829
passages.caution: A folk etymology from the Chinese compiler; the true origin of the name Kashgar is uncertain.

passages.headline: The Xiongnu: no cities, no fields, no writing
passages.people: Xiongnu (Huns), in Bichurin's view ancestors of the Mongols
passages.gloss: Sima Qian's classic description of the Xiongnu, north of China: herders of horses, cattle and sheep who move with the grass and water, with no cities, no settled life and no farming, though each had his own allotted land. No writing: laws are proclaimed orally. Boys ride sheep and shoot birds; all fighting men are mounted archers. It is the oldest template for Chinese and later European pictures of the steppe nomad.
passages.quote: Перекочевываютъ съ мѣста на мѣсто, смотря по приволью въ травѣ и водѣ. Не имѣютъ ни городовъ, ни осѣдлости, ни земледѣлія; но у каждаго есть отдѣленный участокъ земли. Письма нѣтъ, а законы словесно объявляются. Мальчикъ, какъ скоро можетъ верхомъ сидѣть на баранѣ, стрѣляетъ изъ лука пташекъ и звѣрковъ
passages.translation: They move from place to place according to the abundance of grass and water. They have neither cities, nor settled dwelling, nor farming; but each has his allotted piece of land. There is no writing, and laws are proclaimed orally. A boy, as soon as he can sit astride a sheep, shoots little birds and small animals with a bow
passages.speaker: Sima Qian, Shiji (c. 100 BCE), translated by Iakinf Bichurin, 1851
passages.caution: A Chinese court historian writing about an enemy; Bichurin's footnote equates the Xiongnu with the Mongols of his day, a view historians no longer accept.

passages.headline: The Xiongnu town that was never built
passages.people: Xiongnu, with Chinese defector Wei Lü
passages.gloss: The Chinese annals tell how a Chinese defector at the Xiongnu court, Wei Lü, advised the young shanyu to dig wells, build a town and two-storey granaries, and give the grain to Chinese captives to keep. Hundreds of wells were dug and thousands of logs felled, but others argued that the Xiongnu could not defend towns and the grain would only fall to the Chinese, so the plan was dropped. A vivid example of steppe rulers weighing fixed buildings against mobility.
passages.quote: Вэй Люй подалъ Шаньюю совѣтъ выкопать колодцы, построить городъ и двухъ-этажные магазины для содержанія хлѣба, а храненіе хлѣба поручить Китайцамъ династіи Цинь. Тогда хотя и придутъ китайскія войска, ничего сдѣлать не могутъ. Уже выкопано было нѣсколько сотъ колодцевъ, срублено нѣсколько тысячъ бревенъ, какъ нѣкоторые представили, что Хунны не могутъ защищать городовъ
passages.translation: Wei Lü advised the shanyu to dig wells, build a town and two-storey storehouses to keep grain, and to entrust the keeping of the grain to 'Qin Chinese'. Then, even if Chinese troops came, they could do nothing. Several hundred wells had already been dug and several thousand logs cut, when some pointed out that the Xiongnu cannot defend towns
passages.speaker: Chinese dynastic history (Han shu), translated by Iakinf Bichurin, 1851
passages.caution: Bichurin's footnote explains 'Qin Chinese' as descendants of Chinese who had fled to the Xiongnu.

passages.headline: The Wuhuan: round yurts facing east, meat and kumiss
passages.gloss: The Chinese histories describe the Wuhuan as skilled mounted archers and hunters who move with their herds, with no permanent home, living in round yurts with the door facing east, eating meat, drinking kumiss and wearing coloured woollen cloth. Bichurin's summary treats them as a branch of the 'house of the Tatar khan', the Donghu.
passages.quote: Ухуаньцы искусны въ конной стрѣльбѣ изъ лука; занимаются ловлею звѣрей и птицъ, Переходятъ со скотомъ съ мѣста на мѣсто, смотря по достатку въ травѣ и водѣ; постояннаго прибыванія не знаютъ. Живутъ въ круглыхъ юртахъ, изъ коихъ выходъ обращенъ къ востоку. Питаются мясомъ, пьютъ кумысъ; одежду дѣлаютъ изъ разноцвѣтныхъ шерстяныхъ тканей
passages.translation: The Wuhuan are skilled at shooting the bow from horseback; they hunt beasts and birds, move with their livestock from place to place according to the supply of grass and water, and know no permanent dwelling. They live in round yurts whose entrance faces east. They eat meat and drink kumiss, and make their clothing of many-coloured woollen fabrics
passages.speaker: Chinese dynastic history (Hou Han shu), translated by Iakinf Bichurin, 1851
passages.caution: Bichurin's link of the Wuhuan to a 'house of the Tatar khan' is his own reconstruction.

passages.headline: Why 'Tungus' may be a Tatar word for pig-keepers
passages.gloss: In a footnote Bichurin says the word Tungus does not exist in Manchu and no ancient Tungusic ruling house used it. He guesses the Russians took it from the Tatars of the Yenisei, since the Chinese histories say the Tungus peoples bred pigs, still used in shamanic sacrifice, and the Tatar word for pig is 'donguz'. It shows how names for Siberian peoples passed through Tatar speech into Russian.
passages.quote: Слова: Тунгусъ, нѣтъ въ маньчжурскомъ языкѣ: да и ни одинъ изъ древнихъ тунгузскихъ владѣтельныхъ Домовъ не былъ извѣстенъ подъ симъ названіемъ. Вѣроятно, что Русскіе, первоначально достигнувъ Енисея, заимствовали сіе названіе отъ енисейскихъ Татаръ. … а свинья на татарскомъ языкѣ называется Донгусъ.
passages.translation: The word Tungus does not exist in the Manchu language, and none of the ancient Tungusic ruling houses was known by this name. Probably the Russians, when they first reached the Yenisei, borrowed this name from the Yenisei Tatars. … and in the Tatar language a pig is called donguz.
passages.speaker: Iakinf (N. Ya. Bichurin), footnote, 1851
passages.caution: Bichurin's etymology is a guess; linguists still debate the origin of 'Tungus'.

passages.headline: 'Kirghiz-Kaisak' is a foreign name: they call themselves Kazak
passages.gloss: Levshin opens his history by saying that Europe gives the Kazakhs a name neither they nor their neighbours use. They call themselves Kazak, and Persians, Bukharans and Khivans know them by that name; the Chinese say Hasak. Russia too called them the Kazakh horde until the 18th century, when the prefix 'Kirghiz' was added, partly to tell them apart from Russia's own Cossacks.
passages.quote: и что онѣ себя до нынѣ иначе не называютъ, какъ Казаками (Казакъ). Подъ симъ же именемъ извѣстны они Персіянамъ, Бухарцамъ, Хивинцамъ и прочимъ народамъ Азіи. Китайцы, смягчая начальную букву К, говорятъ Хасаки. До XVIII столѣтія и въ Россіи не знали Киргизъ-Кайсаковъ, но именовали ихъ Казаками, Казачьею ордою.
passages.translation: and that to this day they call themselves nothing but Kazakhs (Kazak). Under this same name they are known to the Persians, Bukharans, Khivans and other peoples of Asia. The Chinese, softening the initial K, say Hasak. Until the 18th century Russia too did not know 'Kirghiz-Kaisaks', but called them Kazakhs, the Kazakh horde.
passages.speaker: Aleksei Levshin (1832)

passages.headline: Forty outlaw horsemen: a Kazakh origin legend
passages.people: Kazakhs (in legend, descendants of Crimean exiles)
passages.gloss: Among several Kazakh origin stories Levshin gives one from the journal of Captain Rychkov (1771): seven sons of a Crimean khan, cheated of their inheritance, went into the steppe, joined other exiles to make a band of forty, lived by raiding, stole wives and multiplied. Forty is kyrk in Turkic, so they were called Kyrk-Kazak, 'forty Cossacks' or riders. Levshin himself calls most such traditions absurd but prints them as he found them.
passages.quote: Шайка сія, въ числѣ 40 человѣкъ, долго занимаясь грабежами сосѣдственныхъ съ ними земель; наконецъ, похитила себѣ женъ и размножилась. Сорокъ означается по-Турецки словомъ Кыркъ, а потому и толпа сія названа Кыркъ-Казакъ, то есть, сорокъ Казаковъ, или наѣздниковъ. Потомки ихъ сохранили названіе предковъ.
passages.translation: This band, forty men strong, for a long time lived by plundering the lands around them; at last it stole wives for itself and multiplied. Forty is expressed in Turkic by the word kyrk, and so this crowd was called Kyrk-Kazak, that is, forty Kazakhs, or riders. Their descendants kept the name of their ancestors.
passages.speaker: Aleksei Levshin, from the journal of Captain N. Rychkov (1832)
passages.caution: A folk etymology linking 'Kirghiz' to kyrk (forty); Levshin presents it as one tradition among several.

passages.headline: Russia's Tatars are 'Nogais' to the Kazakhs; 'Tatar' is a cursed name
passages.people: Tatars of Russia (as seen by Kazakhs, Bukharans and Khivans)
passages.gloss: In a footnote to his chapter on ruins Levshin notes that Kazakhs call the Tatars living in Russia only 'Nogais'. The word 'Tatar' itself they did not use; in their view it belonged to some base people cursed by a Muslim prophet. Bukharans and Khivans thought the same. The same story was reported by Rychkov seventy years earlier (W175).
passages.quote: Киргизъ-Казаки иначе не называютъ Татаръ въ Россіи живущихъ, какъ Ногаями. Само Татары совсѣмъ у нихъ не употребительно, и принадлежитъ по ихъ мнѣнію какому то подлому народу, проклятому однимъ Магометанскимъ пророкомъ. Бухарцы и Хивинцы тоже думаютъ, и также называютъ Татаръ Россійскихъ Ногаями.
passages.translation: The Kirghiz-Kazakhs call the Tatars living in Russia nothing but Nogais. The (word) Tatar itself is not used by them at all, and in their opinion belongs to some base people cursed by a certain Muslim prophet. The Bukharans and Khivans think the same, and also call the Russian Tatars Nogais.
passages.speaker: Aleksei Levshin, footnote (1832)
passages.caution: 'Само' is as printed in the OCR; the word 'слово' (word) seems to be implied or garbled.

passages.headline: Grey felt for the poor, red cloth for sultans, reeds for the poorest
passages.gloss: After describing the Kazakh yurt (a round tent of wooden lattice covered with felt, with a smoke hole at the top, 'exactly like the Kalmyk ones', 4 to 8 arshins high), Levshin shows how its covering marked rank. Ordinary Kazakhs used grey felt, the rich and noble white felt, some great sultans red broadcloth lined with silk, and the very poorest covered their homes with matting, turf and reeds.
passages.quote: Кибитки простыхъ Киргизовъ обыкновенно дѣлаются изъ войлоковъ сѣрыхъ; знатные и богатые употребляютъ для сего бѣлые войлоки; а у нѣкоторыхъ сильныхъ Султановъ Средней и Большой Орды, юрты бываютъ обтянуты краснымъ сукномъ и подбиты шелковыми тканями. Въ противоположность послѣднимъ самые бѣдные, вмѣсто войлоковъ, покрываютъ жилища свои рогожами, дерномъ и камышемъ.
passages.translation: The kibitkas of ordinary Kirghiz are usually made of grey felts; the noble and rich use white felts for this; and some powerful sultans of the Middle and Great Horde have yurts covered with red broadcloth and lined with silk fabrics. By contrast, the very poorest cover their dwellings, instead of felt, with matting, turf and reeds.
passages.speaker: Aleksei Levshin (1832)

passages.headline: Who built the ruins of the steppe? 'Not our ancestors'
passages.people: Kazakhs; Mongols and Dzungars; unknown earlier peoples
passages.gloss: Levshin's chapter on ruins begins by admitting that it is hard to say who built them, because they are of different kinds: some are Buddhist temples plainly built by Mongols or Dzungars, some look like mosques, some are ordinary Asian dwellings, some are too ruined to judge. Materials differ too: big stones, brick, clay. The Kazakhs, he says, only agree that the buildings were not their ancestors', and they call old graves and a few ruins 'Nogai'.
passages.quote: Трудно и даже едва ли возможно опредѣлить, какой народъ строилъ сіи зданія: ибо они разныхъ родовъ. Одни, сохранивъ признаки капищъ, Ламайскому служенію посвященныхъ, очевидно принадлежатъ Мунгаламъ, или Зюнгарамъ; другія похожи на Магометанскія мечети; третьи суть остатки обыкновенныхъ Азіатскихъ жилищъ … Нынѣшніе Киргизъ-Казаки вообще не говорятъ объ нихъ ничего правдоподобнаго, кромѣ того, что они не принадлежатъ ихъ предкамъ
passages.translation: It is hard, and hardly even possible, to determine what people built these buildings, for they are of various kinds. Some, keeping signs of temples devoted to Lamaist worship, clearly belong to the Mongols or Dzungars; others resemble Muslim mosques; a third kind are remains of ordinary Asian dwellings … The present Kirghiz-Kazakhs in general say nothing plausible about them, except that they do not belong to their ancestors
passages.speaker: Aleksei Levshin (1832)

passages.headline: Ablai-kit: a walled Buddhist monastery whose books reached Peter the Great
passages.when: built 1650s; leaves sent to Peter I in 1720; described 1832
passages.gloss: The chief ruins of the steppe, Levshin says, are those of Ablai-kit on the left bank of the Irtysh, a stone-walled enclosure about a verst long.
