Inside stood two buildings, one a Buddhist temple where statues, paintings of burkhans (Buddhas) and many manuscripts were still to be seen early in the 18th century. Leaves of those manuscripts were sent to Peter the Great in 1720 and on to the Paris Academy. This is the same town the envoy Baikov saw being built for Ablai taisha by craftsmen from China in 1655 (W171).
passages.quote: Внутри ограды были два зданія; одно служило Ламайскимъ капищемъ, и въ началѣ прошедшаго столѣтія еще видны въ немъ были статуи, живописныя изображенія бурхановъ, и многія письмена, изъ коихъ нѣкоторые листы въ 1720 году были доставлены Императору Петру Великому, а имъ посланы въ Парижскую Академію надписей и изящныхъ искусствъ.
passages.translation: Inside the enclosure there were two buildings; one served as a Lamaist temple, and at the beginning of the last century statues, painted images of burkhans and many writings could still be seen in it, some leaves of which were delivered in 1720 to the Emperor Peter the Great and sent by him to the Paris Academy of Inscriptions and Fine Arts.
passages.speaker: Aleksei Levshin (1832)
passages.caution: Levshin compiles this from Müller, Pallas and others; he does not claim to have visited the site. The name 'Ablai-kit' (Ablai's monastery) itself records who built it.

passages.headline: 'Nogai' graves of heaped stone, with gold horse-trappings inside
passages.gloss: Besides their own cemeteries, Levshin says, the Kazakh steppes hold many ancient graves that the Kazakhs attribute to the Nogais who once lived there. These stand out for their height and size, often being huge heaps of stones brought from far away, and sometimes contain gold and silver horse-harness ornaments and coins. The attribution is Kazakh tradition; archaeologists now date many such kurgans to far older peoples.
passages.quote: Кромѣ кладбищъ, принадлежащихъ Киргизъ-Казакамъ, въ степяхъ ихъ находятся многія древнія могилы, которыя приписываютъ они Ногайцамъ, нѣкогда въ сей странѣ обитавшимъ. Ногайскія могилы отличаются высотою, обширностію и часто состоятъ изъ огромныхъ насыпей такихъ камней, кои перевезены издалека; иногда находятъ въ нихъ золотыя и серебряныя украшенія для конской сбруи, монеты и проч.
passages.translation: Besides the cemeteries belonging to the Kirghiz-Kazakhs, in their steppes there are many ancient graves which they attribute to the Nogais, who once lived in this country. The Nogai graves are distinguished by their height and extent, and often consist of huge heaps of stones brought from far away; sometimes gold and silver ornaments for horse harness, coins and so on are found in them.
passages.speaker: Aleksei Levshin (1832)
passages.caution: The Nogai attribution is Kazakh tradition as reported by Levshin.

passages.headline: Steppe cemeteries of stone and clay: pyramids, towers, a khan's domed tomb
passages.place: Kazakh steppe; Olkeyek river (tomb of Abulkhair Khan)
passages.gloss: Levshin calls a Kazakh cemetery one of the most curious sights for a traveller: after the empty steppe the eye rests on pyramids, towers and high enclosures built of stone and clay, spears hung with horsehair and ribbons, yurt lattices, stone or wooden turbans, a saddle, bow and arrows on a famous rider's grave. Over the grave of Abulkhair Khan stood a square vaulted building. The Kazakhs, a nomadic people, built lasting monuments for their dead.
passages.quote: глаза останавливаются или подъ тѣнью дерева, или на складенныхъ изъ камней и глины пирамидахъ, башняхъ и высокихъ оградахъ. Въ одномъ мѣстѣ видитъ онъ копья съ развѣвающимися на нихъ конскими гривами, лентами и платками; въ другомъ рѣшетки, служившія стѣнами кибиткѣ … Надъ гробомъ Хана Абуль-хайра на рѣчкѣ Улкіакѣ … было построено квадратное зданіе со сводомъ
passages.translation: the eyes come to rest either in the shade of a tree, or on pyramids, towers and high enclosures built of stones and clay. In one place he sees spears with horse manes, ribbons and kerchiefs fluttering from them; in another, the lattices that served as the walls of a kibitka … Over the grave of Abulkhair Khan on the Olkeyek stream … a square vaulted building was built
passages.speaker: Aleksei Levshin (1832)

passages.headline: Winter dead hung in trees until spring
passages.people: Kazakhs of the Middle and Great Hordes
passages.gloss: Levshin reports that in some clans of the Middle and Great Hordes, rich people who died in winter were not buried at once but hung in trees wrapped in felt or linen, and in spring carried to Turkestan to be buried near the shrine of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi, the Kazakhs' revered saint. He then explains how graves were dug with a side niche so the earth would not press on the body.
passages.quote: Богатыхъ людей, умирающихъ зимою, въ нѣкоторыхъ поколѣніяхъ Средней и Большой Орды, вмѣсто погребенія, вѣшаютъ на деревьяхъ, обвернувъ въ войлокъ или въ полотно; весною-же отвозятъ ихъ въ Туркестанъ
passages.translation: Rich people who die in winter, in some clans of the Middle and Great Horde, instead of being buried are hung in trees, wrapped in felt or linen; and in spring they are carried to Turkestan
passages.speaker: Aleksei Levshin (1832)

passages.headline: Muslims without mosques or mullahs
passages.gloss: Levshin describes Kazakh Islam as loose: they count themselves Sunnis alongside Turks, Tatars, Bukharans and Khivans and practise polygamy, but do not keep the fasts or ablutions, find praying five times a day too hard, and have no mosques and no mullahs chosen from among themselves. Sometimes elders read prayers with others kneeling around them.
passages.quote: Постовъ и омовенія, весьма благоразумнаго постановленія Магометова, Киргизы не соблюдаютъ; молиться по пяти разъ на день, находятъ они для себя труднымъ; мечетей и избранныхъ изъ среди себя муллъ не имѣютъ. Иногда молитвы читаются стариками въ присутствіи многихъ стоящихъ около нихъ на колѣнямъ
passages.translation: Fasts and ablution, a very sensible institution of Muhammad, the Kirghiz do not observe; they find praying five times a day hard for themselves; they have no mosques and no mullahs chosen from among themselves. Sometimes prayers are read by old men in the presence of many people kneeling around them
passages.speaker: Aleksei Levshin (1832)
passages.caution: An outsider's judgment of religious practice; Kazakh Islam had its own shrines and holy men that Levshin mentions elsewhere.

passages.headline: Seven wolves chasing two horses: the end of the world in the stars
passages.gloss: In a chapter on Kazakh knowledge of the sky, Levshin says herdsmen navigated the trackless steppe by the stars and told time by them 'as a European looks at his pocket watch'. They saw the Great Bear as seven wolves chasing two horses, a white and a grey gelding; when the wolves catch and eat the horses, the world will end.
passages.quote: Не раздѣляя звѣздъ, составляющихъ Большую медвѣдицу … Киргизы говорятъ, что онѣ состоятъ изъ 7 волковъ, которые гонятся за бѣгущими отъ нихъ двумя лошадьми, Акъ-бузатъ (бѣлый меринъ) и Кукъ-бузатъ (сѣрый меринъ), и что, когда первые, догнавъ сихъ послѣднихъ, съѣдятъ ихъ, то сдѣлается преставленіе свѣта.
passages.translation: Not separating the stars that make up the Great Bear … the Kirghiz say that they consist of 7 wolves chasing two horses fleeing from them, Ak-buzat (the white gelding) and Kuk-buzat (the grey gelding), and that when the former catch the latter and eat them, the end of the world will come.
passages.speaker: Aleksei Levshin (1832)

passages.headline: Stone statues of legendary lovers that received offerings
passages.gloss: On the Ayagoz river, Levshin writes, stood a pointed building carefully built of smooth stone slabs, containing three stone statues. The Kazakhs said two of them showed the lovers famous in their tales (Bayan and Kozy-Korpesh, heroes of a Kazakh epic) and the third their servant, and believers brought them offerings. A building credited not to vanished giants but to a local love story.
passages.quote: Въ немъ три каменныя статуи, изъ коихъ двѣ, по словамъ Киргизъ Казаковъ, изображаютъ прославляемыхъ въ сказкахъ любовниковъ … а третья ихъ служанку. Вѣрующіе въ подлинность сихъ изображеній приносятъ имъ жертвы.
passages.translation: In it are three stone statues, of which two, according to the Kirghiz-Kazakhs, depict the lovers celebrated in their tales … and the third their servant. Those who believe in the authenticity of these images bring them offerings.
passages.speaker: Aleksei Levshin (1832)
passages.caution: The description of the building itself (pointed, of smooth stone slabs) is at the foot of the previous page, n212. The lovers' names are omitted here because the OCR garbles them.

passages.headline: Batu at Kiev: creaking carts, bellowing camels, walls battered day and night
passages.gloss: In his introduction Sreznevsky quotes the Hypatian (Galician-Volhynian) Chronicle's famous account of Batu's siege of Kiev to show the old Russian epic style. The Tatar host was so large that nothing could be heard in the city for the creaking of carts, the bellowing of camels and the neighing of horses. Batu set up siege engines by the Polish Gate and battered the walls day and night until they fell. It shows the Horde as a besieger of cities, with engineers and machines.
passages.quote: Приде Батый Кыеву въ силѣ тяжьцѣ... И бѣ Батый у города, и отроци его обсѣдяху градъ, и не бѣ слышати отъ гласа скрипанія телѣгъ его, множества ревѣнія вельблудъ его, и рьжанія отъ гласа стадъ конь его... Постави же Батый порокы городу подлѣ вратъ Лядьскыхъ … Порокомъ же беспрестани бьющимъ день и нощь, выбиша стѣны.
passages.translation: Batu came to Kiev in heavy force... And Batu was at the city, and his warriors besieged the city, and nothing could be heard for the creaking of his carts, the bellowing of his many camels and the neighing of his herds of horses... Batu set up siege engines against the city by the Polish Gate … The engines battering without cease day and night broke down the walls.
passages.speaker: Hypatian (Galician-Volhynian) Chronicle, quoted by I. I. Sreznevsky in his 1858 introduction
passages.caution: The chronicle was compiled in Galicia-Volhynia some decades after 1240; Sreznevsky quotes it only as a stylistic parallel.

passages.headline: Not grey wolves but the pagan Tatars: the 'Khinova' comes to Rus
passages.gloss: The poet builds the Horde's approach from omens: creaking carts between the Don and the Dnieper, the 'Khinova' marching on the Russian land, grey wolves howling by the river Mecha. Then he turns the image: those were not grey wolves but the pagan Tatars, come to take the whole Russian land. Sreznevsky's commentary suggests 'Khinova', an old poetic name for steppe enemies also used in the Lay of Igor, may hide the name of the Huns.
passages.quote: Идетъ Хинова на Рускую землю. Сѣріе волци воютъ, на рѣкѣ хотятъ на Мечи поступити въ Рускую землю. То ти были не сѣріе волци, придоша поганые Татарове, хотятъ проити воюючи, взяти всю землю Рускую.
passages.translation: The Khinova is marching on the Russian land. Grey wolves are howling; by the river Mecha they mean to cross into the Russian land. Those were not grey wolves: the pagan Tatars have come, they mean to pass through making war and take the whole Russian land.
passages.speaker: Zadonshchina (Kirillo-Belozersk text), ed. I. I. Sreznevsky, 1858
passages.caution: Poetic imagery. The Huns etymology of 'Khinova' is Sreznevsky's guess (commentary, n54 p.49).

passages.headline: The Tatars' lament: no more tribute, and their camels and sugar carried off
passages.people: Golden Horde Tatars (as imagined by the Russian poet)
passages.gloss: The poet gives the defeated Tatars a lament as they flee toward the sea: they will never again see their land or children, never again raid Rus or collect the 'vykhod', the tribute Russian princes paid the Horde. The Russians have plundered their armour, horses, oxen, camels, wine, sugar and treasures. The list shows what a Horde army carried with it: herds, camels and luxury goods from trade.
passages.quote: Уже намъ, братіе, въ земли своей не бывать и дѣтей своихъ не видать, а въ Русь ратью намъ не хаживать, и выхода намъ у Рускихъ людей не прашивать. … уже бо Рускіе сынове разграбиша Татарскія узорочья, и доспѣхи, и кони, и волы, и верблуды, и вино, и сахаръ, и дорогое узорочіе.
passages.translation: Now, brothers, we shall not be in our own land nor see our children, nor march in war on Rus, nor ask tribute of the Russian people. … for the sons of Rus have plundered the Tatar treasures, and armour, and horses, and oxen, and camels, and wine, and sugar, and costly finery.
passages.speaker: Zadonshchina (Kirillo-Belozersk text), ed. I. I. Sreznevsky, 1858
passages.caution: A speech invented by the poet for the enemy; the 'vykhod' was in fact paid to the Horde again after 1382.

passages.headline: Mamai flees to Kaffa, and the Genoese mock him with Batu's memory
passages.people: Mamai and the Golden Horde; Genoese (Fryazi) of Kaffa
passages.gloss: In the poem Mamai escapes from his army 'howling like a grey wolf' and runs to the city of Kaffa, the Genoese colony in Crimea. The Fryazi (Italians) jeer that he is no Batu: Batu had 400,000 armoured men and warred over the whole Russian land, while Mamai came with nine hordes and seventy princes and now flees with eight companions. Historically Mamai did flee to the Crimea and was killed near Kaffa.
passages.quote: А не бывати тебѣ въ Батыя царя, у Батыя царя было четыреста тысячъ кованные рати, а воевалъ всю Русскую землю отъ востока и до запада … И ты пришелъ на Рускую землю, царь Мамай, съ многими силами, съ девятью ордами и семидесятью князьями, а нынѣ ты поганый бѣжишь самъ-девятъ въ лукоморье.
passages.translation: You will never be like Tsar Batu: Tsar Batu had four hundred thousand armoured men, and he made war on the whole Russian land from east to west … And you came to the Russian land, Tsar Mamai, with great forces, with nine hordes and seventy princes, and now, pagan, you flee with eight companions to the sea-shore.
passages.speaker: Zadonshchina (Kirillo-Belozersk text), words the poet gives to the Genoese of Kaffa, ed. I. I. Sreznevsky, 1858
passages.caution: The flight to 'Khafesta grad' (Kaffa) is on the previous page, n31. The figures are poetic, not a muster roll.

passages.headline: Tibet plus Mongolia make 'great Tartary'
passages.gloss: Writing from Tsaparang in 1626, the Portuguese Jesuit Antonio de Andrade lists the kingdoms of Tibet and says that, together with the empire of the 'Sopo' (Mongols), they make up 'great Tartary'. He also demotes fabled Cathay to a single large town ruled by the Mongol king. It is a neat example of how elastic the European label 'Tartary' was: here it swallows Tibet as well as Mongolia.
passages.quote: Together with the great empire of the Sopò [Mongolia], which borders on China on the one side and on Moscovia on the other, they form great Tartary". … "The famous Cathayo is not a separate kingdom but a large town which is called Katay, the capital of a province situated much nearer to China and which is said to be ruled by the great king of the Sopôs"
passages.speaker: Antonio de Andrade, letter of 15 August 1626, in C. Wessels's English translation (1924); bracketed word is Wessels's
passages.caution: Andrade had not been to Mongolia; his picture of 'great Tartary' and Cathay comes from what he was told in western Tibet and from European maps.

passages.headline: In Bhutan, Tartary is called 'Sopo'
passages.people: Sopo (Mongols) as described to Jesuits in Bhutan
passages.gloss: In a Portuguese letter of 1627 from the kingdom he calls Cambirasi (Bhutan), Estevao Cacella reports that the local king says the people of Sopo are more valiant than the Chinese and usually beat them, which Cacella links to the well known wars of the Tartars with China. He then explains why nobody there has heard of 'Cathay': local people use quite different names, calling China 'Guena', Tartary 'Sopo' and Tibet 'Potente'.
passages.quote: porem que a do Sopo he mais esforçada, e assi commummente esta vence os Chinas, o que tudo diz com o que he tão sabido da guerra dos Tartaros com as Chinas … pois nem a China nem a Tartarea, nem o Tibet são conhecidos por estes nomes, dos quaes não tem noticia; e a China chamão Guena, a Tartarea Sopo e ao Tibet Potente
passages.translation: but that the [people] of Sopo are more valiant, and so this one commonly defeats the Chinese, all of which agrees with what is so well known of the war of the Tartars with the Chinese … for neither China nor Tartary nor Tibet is known by these names, of which they have no knowledge; and they call China Guena, Tartary Sopo and Tibet Potente
passages.speaker: Estevao Cacella, S.J., Portuguese letter from Cambirasi (Bhutan), 4 October 1627, printed in Wessels's Appendix II
passages.caution: Cacella is reporting what the Bhutanese king told him and matching it to European ideas about Tartars and Cathay; the equations are his own guesses.

passages.headline: Shambhala placed in 'Great Tartary' on the maps
passages.gloss: Joao Cabral, writing in 1628 after travelling in central Tibet (U-Tsang), says the kingdom is bounded on the north by the Tartars, with whom the king sometimes fights, and that many Tartars come there who say their religion is the same. He then decides that the famous kingdom of 'Xembala', which his companion Cacella had hoped was Cathay, is really the 'Great Tartary' of European maps. Xembala is the European spelling of Shambhala, the hidden kingdom of Tibetan Buddhist tradition, so here a legendary land is being matched to a map label.
passages.quote: Pollo norte confina com os Tartaros com os quaes este Rei as vezes briga, e aqui vem muitos os quaes dizem que a sua Lei he a mesma. … Xembala que a meu ver não he o Catayo, mas aquella que nos Mapas chamão gram Tartarea fica mais desviada para o Norte.
passages.translation: On the north it borders on the Tartars, with whom this king sometimes quarrels, and many of them come here who say that their religion is the same. … Xembala, which in my opinion is not Cathay but that which on the maps they call Great Tartary, lies further off to the north.
passages.speaker: Joao Cabral, S.J., Portuguese letter from Hugli, 17 June 1628, printed in Wessels's Appendix III
passages.caution: The identification of Xembala with Shambhala is a modern one; Cabral himself treats it as a real kingdom he has only heard of. The 'same religion' remark refers to Mongol Buddhists.

passages.headline: 'Sokpo, also called Giongar, that is to say, independent Tartary'
passages.gloss: Describing Ladakh, Desideri lists its neighbours and names the land to the north as 'Sokpo, also called Giongar, that is to say, independent Tartary'. Sokpo is the Tibetan word for the Mongols, and Giongar is the Dzungar state. The same page describes Leh, the Ladakhi capital, as a town climbing a mountain to the palace and fort, with 'no large towns' elsewhere, only villages, farmsteads and castles.
passages.quote: On the former side it borders on Baltistan, towards the north on Caxkar and some parts of the kingdom of Sokpo, also called Giongar, that is to say, independent Tartary.
passages.speaker: Ippolito Desideri, in C. Wessels's English translation of the Italian manuscript (1924)
passages.caution: Translation by Wessels from the manuscript; Desideri knew Ladakh first hand but the Dzungar lands only by report.

passages.headline: A Lhasa ruler 'of ancient Tartar stock'
passages.people: Qoshot Mongols (Gushi Khan and his heirs)
passages.gloss: The Austrian Jesuit John Grueber reached Lhasa in 1661. As Wessels summarises his report, Tibet then had two kings: a secular governor 'of ancient Tartar stock' who ran the government, and the Dalai Lama, worshipped as a god in his palace. Wessels adds that the Potala was begun in 1642 by the Fifth Dalai Lama, who had risen to power 'with the aid of the Tartar prince Gushi Khan'. The Tartars here are the Qoshot Mongols who held military power in Tibet.
passages.quote: There are two kings in this kingdom; one, the Deva (Deba), of ancient Tartar stock, carries on the government; the other, who is worshipped as a deity, lives in seclusion within the precincts of his palace. … the energetic Ngavang Lobsang, who from being the head of the Tashi Lhumpo monastery had, with the aid of the Tartar prince Gushi Khan, worked his way up
passages.speaker: C. Wessels (1924), summarising John Grueber's 1661 report (via Kircher) and adding his own historical comment
passages.caution: The first sentence is Wessels's paraphrase of Grueber as printed by Kircher; the Gushi Khan sentence is Wessels's own history, not Grueber's.

passages.headline: A Tartar prince's widow commands the frontier
passages.gloss: At Gartok on the western frontier Desideri found a permanent force of Tartar and Tibetan soldiers guarding the fortress of Tashigang and watching everyone who entered Tibet. Its commander, a Tartar prince, had died, and his widow had taken over the command until a new governor arrived. Desideri and his companion travelled to Lhasa under her protection; later in the book he says this 'Tartar princess' retired to a nunnery near Shigatse.
passages.quote: in a large plain called Cartoà a strong, permanent force of Tartar and Tibetan soldiers was stationed not only for the defence of the frontier-fortress of Treéscy-Khang and the surrounding settlements, but more especially to watch all those who from that side entered the country. The commander, a Tartar prince, had died and his widow had taken over the command
passages.speaker: C. Wessels (1924), closely paraphrasing Ippolito Desideri's manuscript
passages.caution: Wessels's paraphrase rather than Desideri's exact words; the Tartars here are the Mongol garrison serving the Mongol-descended ruler of Lhasa.

passages.headline: Tartar raiders on the road to the Great Wall
passages.people: Tartars (Mongol and Turkic nomads of the steppe)
passages.gloss: The Portuguese lay brother Bento de Goes travelled overland from India towards China in 1603 to 1605. On the last stretch he found the country between Cialis and the Chinese wall 'notorious for its Tartar raids': merchants crossed it by night in silence, and the bodies of lone Muslim travellers lay by the road. Goes adds a telling detail (in the sentence that follows this excerpt): the Tartars did not usually kill the local people, whom they treated as their servants and herdsmen and occasionally robbed of their flocks.
passages.quote: "The country between Cialis and the Chinese wall," Goes writes, "is notorious for its Tartar raids, so that traders always cross it in the greatest fear, sometimes even under cover of night and in the strictest silence. One often comes across the dead bodies of Mohammedans who have attempted the journey unaccompanied, though on the other hand the Tartars are not wont to kill the native population
passages.speaker: Bento de Goes, as recorded in Matteo Ricci's Commentari and translated by C. Wessels (1924)
passages.caution: Goes died in China in 1607; his account survives through Ricci's reworking of his notes, so the wording is Ricci's.

passages.headline: Decrees in Chinese, Tartar and Tibetan
passages.gloss: After the Qing armies drove the Dzungars out in 1720, Desideri reports, Tibet's government passed to the Emperor of China, run by ministers some of whom were Chinese, some 'Chinese Tartars' and some Tibetans. Every decree had to be issued in three languages: Chinese, Tartar and Tibetan. 'Chinese Tartars' was the usual period term for the Manchus, so within one book 'Tartar' shifts from Mongols to Manchus.
passages.quote: Till October 1720 Tibet was a monarchy under an absolute and independent king. From that time, however, all power has passed into the hands of the Emperor of China and the actual government consists of a body of ministers appointed by him, some of whom are Chinese, some Chinese Tartars, others again Tibetans. All decrees must be promulgated in three languages Chinese, Tartar and Tibetan.
passages.speaker: C. Wessels (1924), summarising Ippolito Desideri's manuscript
passages.caution: A summary by Wessels, not Desideri's own words. Which 'Tartar' language is meant (Manchu or Mongol) is not stated.

passages.headline: Lhasa's walls and gates, built by 'Ginges-Khang'
passages.people: Lhazang Khan ('Ginges-Khang'), the Qoshot Mongol ruler of Lhasa
passages.gloss: Desideri says Lhasa had anciently been an open town, and that 'Ginges-Khang' was the first to protect it with gates and fortifications, with a fort guarding each of the four approaches through the mountains. Ginges-Khang is Desideri's name for Lhazang Khan, the ruler killed by the Dzungars in 1717. The editor's footnote on the same page adds that these defences were built late in the 1600s and pulled down again in 1722 by order of the Kangxi emperor, with only some gates and fragments of wall surviving.
passages.quote: In ancient times, our missionary goes on to tell us, Lhasa was an open place, Ginges-Khang being the first to protect it at various points with gates and fortifications. Situated in a plain the town is enclosed by mountains so as to leave only four approaches each of them defended by a fortification.
passages.speaker: C. Wessels (1924), paraphrasing Ippolito Desideri's manuscript
passages.caution: Wessels's footnote insists Ginges-Khang is 'not the famous Mogul despot' (Genghis Khan) but a Tibetan king; modern historians identify him as Lhazang Khan of the Qoshot Mongols. Dating of the walls comes from Koeppen via the editor.

passages.headline: A Lhasa monastery 'reserved for the Tartars'
passages.gloss: In his tour of Lhasa's temples Desideri notes three more Gelugpa temples and monasteries, one of them in the north-eastern quarter 'reserved for the Tartars', that is for Mongol monks who came to study in Tibet. Elsewhere he says the great monastic universities drew students from Ladakh, Tartary and China. The editor could find no later confirmation that this house was specially for Tartars.
passages.quote: "There are at Lhasa", the narrator continues, "three other idolatrous temples and monasteries of the same sect [the Gelugpa or Yellow-caps]. One is situated in the north-eastern quarter and is reserved for the Tartars. The other two lie towards the east, one near the town-limit, the other just on it, both called by the same name Ramo-cce."
passages.speaker: Ippolito Desideri, in C. Wessels's English translation (1924); bracketed words are Wessels's
passages.caution: 'Idolatrous' is the missionary's own religious judgement. Wessels identifies the house tentatively with the Muru monastery and notes that later writers do not mention its being for Tartars.

passages.headline: The Dzungar 'Tartars' storm Lhasa, 1717
passages.people: Dzungar Mongols ('the Tartar king' and his army)
passages.gloss: Wessels summarises Desideri's eyewitness chapters on the Dzungar invasion. Invited by the discontented great monasteries, 'the Tartar king' of Independent Tartary sent 6,000 men under Tsering Dondup, who reached Lhasa in late 1717; on the night of 30 November the gates were opened to them by allies inside. Lhazang Khan ('Ginghes Khang') fled to the Potala, and the same page says the city was then plundered for two days. Desideri was at Sera monastery and lost only a few things left with the Capuchins.
passages.quote: At their instance the Tartar king crossed into Tibet in 1717 with an army of 6,000 men under the command of General Zze-ring-ton-drup … in the night of November 30 a general assault on Lhasa was delivered the gates were thrown open by their confederates. In a couple of hours there was nothing left for Ginghes Khang but to seek safety in the Potala Palace.
passages.speaker: C. Wessels (1924), summarising Ippolito Desideri's eyewitness account
passages.caution: A summary, not Desideri's own words; Wessels notes that other histories (Waddell) tell the story differently.

passages.headline: A lama builds a new wall against the conquerors
passages.gloss: Describing 'Giegazze' (Shigatse), seat of the lama second only to the Dalai Lama, Desideri praises the lama's courage in 1717. When the conquerors of Lhasa, the Dzungar Tartars, marched on the town to plunder its rich temple and monastery, he quickly fortified both with a new wall, armed his people and drove them off. On the next page Desideri adds that the damage from the siege was repaired and the town enlarged in 1720.
passages.quote: Every one admired his firmness and courage when he offered heroic resistance to the conquerors of Lhasa, who after the sack of this town marched on Giegazze to make the fabulously rich temple and the monastery share the same fate. In a short time he fortified both with a new wall, armed his people and forced the enemy to retreat.
passages.speaker: Ippolito Desideri, in C. Wessels's English translation (1924)
passages.caution: Desideri was at Sera near Lhasa during the invasion, so the defence of Shigatse is reported, not seen.

passages.headline: 'Rightly called Tartars, as if from Tartarus'
passages.gloss: Under the year 1240 Matthew describes the Tartars bursting out of a homeland walled in by mountains 'like demons loosed from Tartarus', and adds that this is why they are rightly called Tartars, as if 'Tartareans'. This pun on Tartarus, the classical underworld, is why Latin writers turned the steppe name Tatar into 'Tartar'. The same paragraph compares them to locusts covering the earth.
passages.quote: eodem anno plebs Sathanae detestanda, Tartarorum scilicet exercitus infinitus, a regione sua montibus circumvallata prorupit; et saxorum immeabilium soliditate penetrata, exeuntes ad instar daemonum solutorum a tartaro, ut bene Tartari, quasi tartarei, nuncupentur, scatebant, et quasi locustae terrae superficiem cooperientes
passages.translation: in that same year a detestable people of Satan, namely a boundless army of Tartars, burst out from its region walled in by mountains; and, having broken through the solid mass of impassable rocks, they came swarming out like demons loosed from Tartarus (so that they are well called Tartars, as if 'Tartareans'), and like locusts covering the face of the earth
passages.speaker: Matthew Paris, Chronica majora, ed. H. R. Luard (Rolls Series, vol. 4, 1877)
passages.caution: A preacher's wordplay, not an etymology; on p. 78 Matthew also offers a river 'Tartar' as the source of the name.

passages.headline: The lost ten tribes, shut in the Caspian mountains by Alexander
passages.people: Tartars as imagined by Matthew Paris
passages.gloss: Matthew reports the belief that the Tartars were descendants of the ten tribes of Israel who abandoned the Law for golden calves, and whom Alexander the Great tried to wall up in the Caspian mountains with stones cemented with bitumen; when the work proved too great, God made the mountain peaks close together. On the next page he admits a problem: these Tartars do not speak Hebrew or know the Law of Moses, which he explains as divine punishment.
passages.quote: Creduntur isti Tartari, quorum memoria est detestabilis, fuisse de decem tribubus, qui abierunt, relicta lege Mosaica, post vitulos aureos; quos etiam Alexander Macedo primo conatus est includere in praeruptis montibus Caspiorum molaribus bituminatis. Quod opus cum videret humanos labores excedere, invocavit auxilium Dei Israel; et coierunt cacumina montium adinvicem
passages.translation: These Tartars, whose memory is detestable, are believed to have come from the ten tribes who went away, abandoning the Law of Moses, after the golden calves; whom Alexander of Macedon first tried to shut up in the steep Caspian mountains with millstones set in bitumen. When he saw that the work was beyond human labour, he called on the help of the God of Israel; and the peaks of the mountains came together
passages.speaker: Matthew Paris, Chronica majora, ed. H. R. Luard (vol. 4, 1877), drawing on Peter Comestor's Historia scholastica
passages.caution: A medieval legend (Alexander's gates and the enclosed nations, linked to Gog and Magog), taken from Peter Comestor; Matthew himself notes the difficulty that the Tartars are not Hebrew speakers.

passages.headline: An exiled Englishman as the Tartars' envoy
passages.people: Mongol army and its English interpreter
passages.gloss: In a letter Matthew copied under 1243, a cleric named Ivo of Narbonne says that among eight Tartars captured in Austria was an Englishman, banished from England for some crimes, who had twice come to the king of Hungary as envoy and interpreter for the Tartar king, threatening disaster unless Hungary submitted. The letter goes on (next page) to give his account of how he drifted east, learned many languages, and was recruited by the Tartars because they needed interpreters.
passages.quote: Ex ipsis vero fugientibus princeps Dalmatiae cepit octo, quorum dux Austriae novit unum, Anglicum natione, sed propter quaedam maleficia de regno Angliae perpetua banniatione proscriptum. Hic ex parte regis nequissimi Tattarorum, bis venerat ad regem Hungariae nuntius et interpres, mala, quae postmodum contigerunt, satis manifeste praemuniendo comminatus est, nisi se et regnum suum Tattareae dederet servituti.
passages.translation: Of those fleeing, the prince of Dalmatia captured eight, one of whom the duke of Austria recognised: an Englishman by nation, but banished from the kingdom of England for ever for certain crimes. He, on behalf of the most wicked king of the Tattars, had twice come to the king of Hungary as envoy and interpreter, and had openly threatened the evils that afterwards happened, unless he surrendered himself and his kingdom to Tattar servitude.
passages.speaker: Letter of Ivo of Narbonne to the archbishop of Bordeaux, copied by Matthew Paris under 1243 (Luard, vol. 4)
passages.caution: Ivo's letter is a contested text and its author admits a shady past; the Englishman's story cannot be checked. The same letter includes lurid cannibalism stories.

passages.headline: A Russian archbishop's report: food, prayer and women archers
passages.people: Mongols (Tartars) as described by a refugee
passages.gloss: Peter, an archbishop who had fled Russia before the Tartars, was questioned in the West, and Matthew records his answers. The Tartars, he said, eat horse and dog meat and in need even human flesh, but cooked, not raw; they drink blood, water and milk. Each morning they raise their hands to heaven to worship the Creator, toss the first morsel into the air and pour the first drink on the ground, and claim John the Baptist as their leader. Their women fight, and are excellent archers.
passages.quote: Carnes comedunt jumentinas, caninas, et alias abominabiles, etiam in necessitate humanas, non tamen crudas, sed coctas. Sanguinem, aquam, et lac bibunt. … Quolibet mane manus ad caelum levant, Creatorem adorantes. Comedentes vero, primum morsellum in aera jaciunt; bibentes, prius partem in terram fundunt, in veneratione Creatoris. Et dicunt se habere sanctum Johannem Baptistam pro duce. … Mulieres bellatrices, praecipue sagittatrices optimae sunt.
passages.translation: They eat the flesh of horses and dogs and other abominable things, even human flesh in necessity, yet not raw but cooked. They drink blood, water and milk. … Every morning they raise their hands to heaven, worshipping the Creator. When eating, they throw the first morsel into the air; when drinking, they first pour part onto the ground, in veneration of the Creator. And they say they have Saint John the Baptist as their leader. … The women are warriors, and especially excellent archers.
passages.speaker: Peter, a Russian archbishop, as recorded by Matthew Paris under 1244 (Luard, vol. 4)
passages.caution: Peter had fled the Tartars and his account mixes real observation (libations, sky worship) with rumour; the John the Baptist claim is unexplained. Luard notes the same account appears in the Burton Annals, given at the Council of Lyons.

passages.headline: "Held not by Tartars but in Tartarus"
passages.gloss: In his opening letter Roger plays on the old pun that made 'Tartars' out of 'Tatars': whoever falls into their hands will feel he is held not by Tartars but in Tartarus, the pit of the underworld. He stresses that he writes from experience, having lived among them 'for a time and half a time', a biblical phrase for a long ordeal. The pun shows how the name itself carried a hellish ring for Latin Christians.
passages.quote: Et sciant cuncti haec me temere non referre; quod quisquis ad manus ipsorum deuenerit Tartarorum, si natus non fuisset melius esset ei; et sentiet se non a Tartaris sed in tartaro detineri. Hoc refero ut expertus. Fui enim per tempus et dimidium temporis inter eos; in quo mori solatium exstitisset, sicut supplicium fuit vita.
passages.translation: And let everyone know that I do not report these things rashly: whoever comes into the hands of these Tartars, it would have been better for him not to have been born, and he will feel himself held not by Tartars but in Tartarus. I report this as one who went through it. For I was among them for a time and half a time, in which death would have been a comfort, just as life was a punishment.
passages.speaker: Master Roger (Rogerius), Carmen miserabile, in the 1885 Budapest edition (Chronica minora)

passages.headline: Batu, 'king of kings', and the princes who invaded
passages.gloss: Roger lists the Tartar leaders who entered Hungary. Batu is the 'king of kings'; under him a commander Roger calls Bochetor held most power, and Kadan was the bravest. Several more names follow in garbled Latin forms, and Roger gives the army as 500,000 men. It shows how a Latin writer who had met the invaders understood their chain of command.
passages.quote: Rex regum et dominus Tartarorum qui Hungariam intrauerunt Bathus suo nomine vocabatur. Rector erat sub ipso in militia potentior Bochetor appellatus. Cadan in probitate melior dicebatur. Coacton Feycan Peta Hermeus Cheb Ocadar maiores reges inter Tartaros censebantur; quamquam essent inter eos alii reges quamplurimi, principes et potentes, qui cum quinquies centenis millibus armatorum regnum Hungariae inuaserunt.
passages.translation: The king of kings and lord of the Tartars who entered Hungary was called by name Bathus [Batu]. Under him the commander more powerful in the army was called Bochetor. Cadan [Kadan] was said to be the most valiant. Coacton, Feycan, Peta, Hermeus, Cheb and Ocadar were counted as the greater kings among the Tartars; though there were among them very many other kings, princes and mighty men, who invaded the kingdom of Hungary with five hundred thousand armed men.
passages.speaker: Master Roger (Rogerius), Carmen miserabile, in the 1885 Budapest edition (Chronica minora)
passages.caution: The figure of 500,000 is a wild overestimate. Only Batu and Kadan are securely identified; the other names are Latin garblings of Mongol princes and generals.

passages.headline: Dummies on spare horses to fake an army
passages.gloss: Bishop Benedict of Várad chased a small Tartar band that had sacked Eger. Knowing they were few but had many horses, the Tartars made dummies and figures, set them on the empty horses like riders and hid them behind a low hill. When they pretended to retreat and the 'army' of dummies came out in battle order, the Hungarians thought they had fallen into an ambush and fled, and were cut down.
passages.quote: Fecerunt autem laruas et monstra quamplurima; ea super equos vacuos tamquam si essent milites ordinando. Et equos illos sub quodam monticulo, paucis cum eis relictis seruientibus dimiserunt … Et dum ipsi cum laruis exierunt sub monte, et ut condictum erat acie ordinata; Hungari hoc videntes, et opinantes eis insidias factas terga dederunt, et fugam velociter inierunt.
passages.translation: They made a great many masks and figures, setting them on the empty horses as if they were soldiers. And they left those horses below a little hill, with a few servants left with them … And when these came out from under the hill with the masks, in battle order as had been agreed, the Hungarians, seeing this and thinking an ambush had been laid for them, turned their backs and quickly took to flight.
passages.speaker: Master Roger (Rogerius), Carmen miserabile, in the 1885 Budapest edition (Chronica minora)
passages.caution: Roger was not at this skirmish; he reports it from those who were.

passages.headline: Arrows like locusts at the river Sajó
passages.gloss: At the battle by the river Sajó (Mohi), the Tartars crossed at night by a ford, surrounded the royal camp at dawn and shot into it. Roger says the arrows were so thick they almost shaded the fighters and flew through the air like swarms of locusts, so that the king could not even draw up his lines. He was not in the battle himself and writes from survivors' reports.
passages.quote: Tanta enim erat crebrosa emissio sagittarum, quod fere umbram pugnantibus faciebant; et sagittae sicut locustae et bruchus congregatim vadunt, per aera volabant. Et sic sagittarum ictus minime sufferre valentes, infra circulum exercitus retro ibant. Rex vero acies non poterat ordinare
passages.translation: For so dense was the shooting of arrows that it almost made shade for the fighters; and the arrows flew through the air as locusts and grasshoppers go in swarms. And so, unable to bear the strikes of the arrows, they fell back inside the ring of the army. The king could not draw up his battle lines
passages.speaker: Master Roger (Rogerius), Carmen miserabile, in the 1885 Budapest edition (Chronica minora)

passages.headline: The fall of Várad: stone-throwers, a new wall, a burning cathedral
passages.gloss: Roger was a canon at Várad and had just had the damaged castle repaired with a broad new wall; he himself fled to the woods. He describes the castle's ditches and wooden towers on the walls. The Tartars set up seven stone-throwing machines against the new wall and battered it day and night until it fell. The noblewomen who had fled into the cathedral were burned inside it.
passages.quote: Nam magnis munitum erat fossatis, et turribus ligneis super muros, et multi loricati milites erant ibi … Et castrum illico circumdantes, ex opposito ad murum nouum septem machinas posuerunt, et die noctuque cum eis emittere lapides, quousque nouus murus dirutus est ex toto, nullatenus cessauerunt. … Et quia kathedralem ecclesiam subito intrare nequiuerunt, igne apposito ecclesiam et dominas, et quidquid erat in ecclesia combusserunt.
passages.translation: For it was fortified with great ditches and wooden towers on the walls, and many knights in mail were there … And at once surrounding the castle, they set up seven machines facing the new wall, and did not stop hurling stones with them day and night until the new wall was completely thrown down. … And because they could not quickly get into the cathedral church, they set fire to it and burned the church, the ladies and whatever was in the church.
passages.speaker: Master Roger (Rogerius), Carmen miserabile, in the 1885 Budapest edition (Chronica minora)
passages.caution: Roger saw the defences, having had the new wall built himself, but fled to the woods before the final assault; the fall of the castle and the burning of the cathedral are reported from survivors.

passages.headline: Tartar bailiffs, markets and justice under occupation
passages.people: Mongol occupiers and their appointed officials
passages.gloss: After the massacres the Tartars lured people back from the woods and set up a working occupation. Each village chose a Tartar 'king'; the invaders appointed about a hundred 'canesii' (Roger glosses them as bailiffs) who kept justice and collected horses, animals, arms and gifts. Roger's own master was one of them and ruled almost a thousand villages. 'We had peace and markets,' he writes. A few lines later the same officials summon villagers with gifts and massacre them.
passages.quote: et quaelibet villa elegit sibi regem de Tartaris quem optauit. … Constituerunt Canesios id est Baliuos, qui iustitiam facerent, et eis equos animalia arma exenia et vestimenta utilia procurarent. Et sic procurator meus de istis dominis erat unus, et pene mille villas regebat. Et erant Canesii fere centum. Pacem habebamus et fora, iustaque unicuique iusticia seruabatur.
passages.translation: and each village chose for itself a king from among the Tartars, whomever it wished. … They appointed Canesii, that is bailiffs, to do justice and to procure for them horses, animals, weapons, gifts and useful clothing. My master was one of these lords, and ruled almost a thousand villages. And there were about a hundred Canesii. We had peace and markets, and justice was kept for each person.
passages.speaker: Master Roger (Rogerius), Carmen miserabile, in the 1885 Budapest edition (Chronica minora)
passages.caution: 'Canesii' probably reflects a local title (compare Slavic knez, 'prince, headman'); the peace was brief and ended in treachery, as Roger goes on to tell.

passages.headline: They spared the houses to winter in them
passages.people: Tartars and Cumans of Batu's army
passages.gloss: Roger watched Tartar and Cuman raiders return from a night of slaughter in the villages, loaded with spoil. Yet they burned neither grain, straw nor houses. He guessed, and later confirmed, that they meant to winter there and needed shelter and food for their horses. It is a telling detail: these herders used the settled country's buildings rather than destroying them.
passages.quote: Verumtamen nec fruges nec stramina nec domos aliquas combusserunt, sed in praeseruationem vitae omnia haec induxerunt. Pro eo conieci firmiter ipsos velle in illis partibus hiemare, vel familias suas dimittere, ut in hieme pro equis domos et victualia inuenirent. Quod totum postmodum didici esse verum.
passages.translation: Yet they burned neither the crops, nor the straw, nor any houses, but brought all these in to keep themselves alive. From this I firmly concluded that they meant to winter in those parts, or leave their families there, so that in winter they would find shelter and provisions for their horses. All of which I afterwards learned to be true.
passages.speaker: Master Roger (Rogerius), Carmen miserabile, in the 1885 Budapest edition (Chronica minora)

passages.headline: Bait on the ice: how they crossed the frozen Danube
passages.gloss: In a hard winter the Danube froze over, which had not happened for many years, but the Tartars did not dare ride onto the ice. They drove horses and cattle onto the bank and left them unguarded for three days. The Hungarians, thinking the enemy gone, crossed and led the animals over the ice, which showed the Tartars that it would bear horses; they then crossed in one rush (as the next page tells).
passages.quote: Et ecce in hieme niuis et glaciei abundantia superuenit, ita quod Danubius, quod non acciderat a multis retroactis temporibus, gelabatur. … Multos equos et animalia super ripam Danubii adduxerunt, et neminem per tres dies ad eorum custodiam dimiserunt; ita quod bestiae sine custodibus pergere videbantur, nec aliquis eorum in illis partibus apparebat.
passages.translation: And then in winter a great deal of snow and ice came, so that the Danube froze, which had not happened for many years past. … They brought many horses and animals onto the bank of the Danube and left no one to guard them for three days, so that the beasts seemed to be wandering without keepers, and none of the Tartars appeared in those parts.
passages.speaker: Master Roger (Rogerius), Carmen miserabile, in the 1885 Budapest edition (Chronica minora)

passages.headline: A wall of brushwood built by captives at Esztergom
passages.gloss: Esztergom, the richest city in Hungary, had fortified itself with ditches, walls and wooden towers. Roger says the Tartars had their captives carry bundles of branches and pile them into a high wall along the edge of the ditch in a single effort, then set thirty stone-throwing machines behind it and pounded the city and its wooden towers day and night. The builders of this siege work, he notes, were the prisoners.
passages.quote: Strigonienses interim se cum fossatis muris et turribus ligneis fortissime munierant. … Ecce una dierum ciuitatem Tartari circumdederunt, et captiui qui cum eis erant tot ramorum fasciculos portauerunt, quibus in una parte ciuitatis supra fossati supercilium altum murum simul et semel de fasciculis construxerunt, et statim post murum illum dictas triginta machinas posuerunt
passages.translation: Meanwhile the people of Esztergom had fortified themselves very strongly with ditches, walls and wooden towers. … Then one day the Tartars surrounded the city, and the captives who were with them carried so many bundles of branches that on one side of the city, on the brink of the ditch, they built a high wall of the bundles all at once, and immediately behind that wall they set the thirty machines already mentioned
passages.speaker: Master Roger (Rogerius), Carmen miserabile, in the 1885 Budapest edition (Chronica minora)
passages.caution: Roger was not at Esztergom; he reports the siege from others.

passages.headline: Wooden houses burned, stone palaces stormed
passages.people: Mongol army; Hungarian, French and Lombard defenders
passages.gloss: Seeing they could not hold the town, the Hungarian, French and Lombard citizens who ran Esztergom burned the suburbs and the many wooden houses right up to the stone palaces, destroyed their cloth and goods, buried their gold and retreated into the palaces. Enraged at losing the plunder, the Tartars stormed the palaces; Roger doubts fifteen people survived. The castle itself, held by a Spanish count with crossbowmen, was not taken.
passages.quote: Hungari vero et Francigenae ac Lombardi, qui quasi erant domini ciuitatis, se non posse defendere aduertentes combusserunt suburbia et domos ligneas, quae multa erant, usque ad palatia ciuitatis. … coeperunt postmodum palatia expugnare. Quibus velociter expugnatis, non credo ut verum fatear quod XV de tota remanserunt ciuitate
passages.translation: But the Hungarians, the French and the Lombards, who were as it were the masters of the city, seeing that they could not defend themselves, burned the suburbs and the wooden houses, of which there were many, right up to the palaces of the city. … Afterwards they began to storm the palaces. These were quickly taken, and I do not believe, to tell the truth, that fifteen people of the whole city survived
passages.speaker: Master Roger (Rogerius), Carmen miserabile, in the 1885 Budapest edition (Chronica minora)
passages.caution: Roger adds that the Tartars 'roasted men alive like pigs'; like other atrocity details it is reported, not witnessed.

passages.headline: Nothing left at Alba but bones and broken walls
passages.people: Ruins left by the Mongol army
passages.gloss: After escaping as the Tartars withdrew, Roger and a companion walked for eight days through empty country, guided by the bell towers of churches, and reached the cathedral town of Alba (Alba Iulia in Transylvania). There they found only the bones and heads of the dead and the broken, undermined walls of churches and palaces, the stones still stained red. It is a rare eyewitness description of a town just ruined by the Mongols.
passages.quote: Tamdem vix octauo die a siluae recessu ad Albam venimus ciuitatem, in qua nihil potuit reperiri praeterquam ossa et capita occisorum, basilicarum et palatiorum muros diruptos et suffossos, quos nimia Christiani cruoris effusio macularat. Et licet terra innoxium sanguinem quem inebriata suxerat non monstraret, ostendebant se lapides adhuc cruore roseo purpurati
passages.translation: At last, hardly on the eighth day after leaving the forest, we came to the city of Alba, in which nothing could be found but the bones and heads of the slain, and the walls of churches and palaces broken and undermined, which the great outpouring of Christian blood had stained. And although the earth, drunk with the innocent blood it had soaked up, did not show it, the stones still showed themselves dyed rose red with gore
passages.speaker: Master Roger (Rogerius), Carmen miserabile, in the 1885 Budapest edition (Chronica minora)

passages.headline: Turning over corpses for buried flour
passages.place: Hungary (a fortified island in the Körös region)
passages.gloss: After the Tartars stormed the island refuge where he had sheltered, Roger lived as a fugitive in the woods. Hunger drove him to creep back onto the island at night and turn over the bodies of the dead in search of buried flour and meat. He hid in caves, dug holes or crept into hollow trees, while (he says on the next page) the Tartars combed the thickets like dogs hunting hares and boars.
passages.quote: Ita quod necessitate famis et sitis me acrius perurgente de nocte compellebar intrare insulam, et corpora euertere mortuorum, ut sepultam farinam et carnes ad esum mihi, vel aliud comestibile inuenirem … Oportebat me inuenire cauernas, vel foveas facere, vel arbores quaerere perforatas in quas me possem recipere
passages.translation: So, with hunger and thirst pressing me hard, I was forced at night to go onto the island and turn over the bodies of the dead, to find buried flour and meat to eat, or anything else edible … I had to find caves, or dig pits, or look for hollow trees in which I could hide
passages.speaker: Master Roger (Rogerius), Carmen miserabile, in the 1885 Budapest edition (Chronica minora)

passages.headline: 'In their own language they are called Mangoli'
passages.gloss: Thomas opens his chapter 'On the nature of the Tartars' by saying he will report what he could hear from people who had looked into the matter closely. Their land lies where the East meets the North, and in their own language they are called 'Mangoli', that is, Mongols. He adds that their country is said to border on 'further India' and names their king in a garbled form. So a Dalmatian writer of the 1260s already knew that 'Tartar' was not what these people called themselves.
passages.quote: Nunc vero de natura, & habitu gentis illius prout ab his audire potui, qui rem curiosius indagarunt, pauca narrabo: Est enim regio illorum in ea parte orbis sita ubi Oriens conjungitur Aquiloni, gentesque illae secundum proprietatem linguae suae Mangoli appellantur. Ferunt tamen quod terra illorum confinis sit ulterioris Indiae
passages.translation: Now I will tell a few things about the nature and dress of that people, as far as I could hear from those who investigated the matter more carefully. Their region lies in that part of the world where the East joins the North, and those peoples, in the proper usage of their own language, are called Mangoli. They say, however, that their land borders on further India
passages.speaker: Thomas, archdeacon of Split, Historia Salonitana, in the first edition by Ivan Lučić (Lucius), Amsterdam 1666
passages.caution: Thomas says plainly that this chapter is hearsay from informants.

passages.headline: 'Tartar' from a river, or from a word for 'multitude'
passages.gloss: Thomas insists that 'Tartar' is not the people's own name. He offers two explanations he had heard: that they were named after a river flowing past their country, or that 'Tatar' means 'multitude'. The river story also appears in Matthew Paris; neither explanation is how historians now explain the name, which came from the Tatar tribe that the Mongols had defeated.
passages.quote: Hoc autem nomen Tartari non nomen est gentis proprium, sed a quadam aqua, quae illorum praeterfluit regionem sic appellati sunt, vel secundum quosdam Tatar idem sonat, quod multitudo
passages.translation: This name Tartars is not the people's own name, but they were so called from a certain river that flows past their region; or, according to some, Tatar means the same as 'multitude'
passages.speaker: Thomas, archdeacon of Split, Historia Salonitana, in the first edition by Ivan Lučić (Lucius), Amsterdam 1666
passages.caution: Both explanations are reports Thomas heard; he does not choose between them.

passages.headline: Broad chests, short legs, white skin: a Tartar portrait
passages.gloss: Thomas describes the invaders as terrifying to look at: short legs but huge chests, broad faces, white skin, beardless cheeks, hooked noses and small eyes set far apart. Their armour was made of ox hide in overlapping plates, light but, he says, impenetrable. It is one of the earliest European portraits of the Mongols, and notably it calls their skin white.
passages.quote: Terrificum valde exhibent faciei aspectum, breves habent tibias, sed vasta pectora, lata est facies, & cutis alba, imberbis gena, & naris adunca, breves oculi spacio longiore disjuncti. Arma eorum sunt quaedam tegmina ex taurinis coriis laminarum more compacta, impenetrabilia tamen, & valde secura.
passages.translation: They present a very terrifying face: they have short legs but vast chests; the face is broad and the skin white, the cheeks beardless and the nose hooked, the eyes small and set wide apart. Their armour consists of coverings made of ox hides fitted together like plates, yet impenetrable and very safe.
passages.speaker: Thomas, archdeacon of Split, Historia Salonitana, in the first edition by Ivan Lučić (Lucius), Amsterdam 1666
passages.caution: Second hand, and 'terrifying' is Thomas's judgement; other writers of the time describe Mongol features differently.

passages.headline: Felt tents, and boats of wicker and raw hide
passages.gloss: Thomas says almost no river could stop them, since they swam their horses across. If a river was too deep, they at once wove wicker baskets like small boats, stretched raw animal hides over them, loaded their baggage and crossed without fear. They lived in tents of felt and of leather. This is the whole of what he says about their dwellings: portable felt and leather, not buildings.
passages.quote: si qua vero immeabilis unda occurrit, continuo in modum lemborum ex viminibus cistas intexunt, superducentes crudas animalium cutes, quibus sarcinas inferentes intrant, & transeunt absque metu, Tentoriis utuntur filtrinis, & ex coriis factis
passages.translation: but if an impassable stream meets them, they at once weave baskets of wicker in the manner of skiffs, stretching raw animal hides over them; putting their baggage in, they get in and cross without fear. They use tents of felt and tents made of hides
passages.speaker: Thomas, archdeacon of Split, Historia Salonitana, in the first edition by Ivan Lučić (Lucius), Amsterdam 1666

passages.headline: Unshod horses like wild goats; mare's blood with curdled milk
passages.gloss: Their horses, Thomas writes, were small but strong, able to bear hunger and toil, running over rocks without iron shoes like wild goats and content with a little straw after three days of hard work. The men too cared little for food: they disliked bread, ate any meat, clean or unclean, and drank curdled milk mixed with horse blood.
passages.quote: equos breves, sed fortes, patientes inediae, & laboris … Per rupes vero, & lapides absque ferramentis discurrunt, ac si caprae forent silvestres: Tribus enim continuis diebus labore quassati parvo stipularum pabulo sunt contenti, homines simili modo nil pene de alimentorum perceptione curantes, sola crudelitate pascuntur, usum panis abhorrent, mundorum & immundorum carnibus indifferenter utuntur, & lac concretum cum sanguine potant equino
passages.translation: their horses short but strong, enduring hunger and toil … They run over rocks and stones without iron shoes, as if they were wild goats; after three days of continuous labour they are content with a little fodder of straw. The men likewise care almost nothing about taking food; they feed on cruelty alone, loathe the use of bread, eat the flesh of clean and unclean animals alike, and drink curdled milk with horse's blood
passages.speaker: Thomas, archdeacon of Split, Historia Salonitana, in the first edition by Ivan Lučić (Lucius), Amsterdam 1666
passages.caution: 'They feed on cruelty alone' is rhetoric; the horse blood detail echoes reports of Mongols bleeding their horses on campaign.

passages.headline: Graves trampled flat so no sign remains
passages.gloss: Thomas says the Tartars did not like to throw away their lives. If one of them fell in battle, the others at once carried him off, buried him in a very hidden place, levelled the mound and trampled the spot with their horses' hooves so that no sign of a grave could be seen. Hidden burial is also reported for Mongol rulers by later writers.
passages.quote: Ipsi Tartari non se libenter morti exponunt, sed si quem eorum in bello mori contingat, statim rapiunt, & efferentes in occultissimo loco terra infodiunt, complanantes tumulum, & locum equorum pedibus conculcantes, ne quod sepulturae appareat signum
passages.translation: The Tartars themselves do not willingly expose themselves to death; but if one of them happens to die in battle, they carry him off at once, and taking him to a most hidden place bury him in the earth, levelling the mound and trampling the spot with the feet of their horses, so that no sign of a burial appears
passages.speaker: Thomas, archdeacon of Split, Historia Salonitana, in the first edition by Ivan Lučić (Lucius), Amsterdam 1666

passages.headline: Forty thousand axemen cut the road
passages.gloss: King Béla had blocked the mountain passes into Hungary with barricades of felled trees. Thomas says the Tartars had forty thousand men with axes marching ahead of the army, cutting down woods, laying roads and clearing obstacles, so that the great barricades of fir and oak were crossed as if they were made of straw, then broken up and burned.
passages.quote: habebant autem quadraginta millia securigeros, qui praeibant exercitum, sylvas caedentes, vias sternentes, & omnia offendicula ab ingressibus removentes. Quamobrem indagines, quas Rex parari fecerat, tam facile transcenderunt ac si non ex ingentium abietum, & quercuum fuissent extructae congerie, sed ex levibus essent stipulis praeparatae
passages.translation: they had forty thousand axe-bearers who went before the army, cutting down forests, laying roads and removing every obstacle from the approaches. Therefore they crossed the barricades that the king had had prepared as easily as if they had been built not of a pile of huge firs and oaks but of light straw
passages.speaker: Thomas, archdeacon of Split, Historia Salonitana, in the first edition by Ivan Lučić (Lucius), Amsterdam 1666
passages.caution: The number is Thomas's figure from report, not a count.

passages.headline: Tartar women fought like men
passages.gloss: Among the cruelties of the occupation, Thomas reports that the Tartars' women armed themselves like men and rode boldly into battle. He adds that they treated captive women even more savagely than the men did, killing good-looking ones out of jealousy and disfiguring others to make them servants. Mongol women travelling and sometimes fighting with the army are also mentioned by Matthew Paris's informants.
passages.quote: Praeterea mulieres Tartarorum virili more armis accinctae in pugnam audacter ferebantur, ut viri, hae in mulieres captivas atrocius saeviebant, si quas enim venustiori vultu cernebant, ex quibus zelotypiae motum possent aliquatenus formidare, statim extracto gladio perimebant
passages.translation: Moreover the women of the Tartars, girded with arms in the manner of men, charged boldly into battle like men; they raged more cruelly against captive women, for if they saw any with a more beautiful face, of whom they might in any way fear jealousy, they at once drew a sword and killed them
passages.speaker: Thomas, archdeacon of Split, Historia Salonitana, in the first edition by Ivan Lučić (Lucius), Amsterdam 1666
passages.caution: An atrocity report Thomas did not witness.

passages.headline: Suzdal, great Christian city, taken by trickery
passages.gloss: Thomas sketches the Mongol advance before Hungary: they had been held back by the Russians, circled the northern lands for twenty years, then returned with Cumans and other subject peoples. Their first great prize was 'a very great city of the Christians called Suzdal', which they besieged and took more by guile than force, killing its king George and many of his people. (Grand Prince Yuri of Vladimir-Suzdal died in 1238.)
passages.quote: Et primo quidem Civ. maximam Christianorum nomine Susdaliam circumdantes obsederunt, & obsessam, diu, non tam vi, quam fraude ceperunt, & destruxerunt, Regemque ipsius nomine Georgium cum magna multitudine sui populi neci dederunt.
passages.translation: And first they surrounded and besieged a very great city of the Christians named Suzdal, and having besieged it for a long time they took it, not so much by force as by fraud, and destroyed it, and put to death its king, named George, with a great multitude of his people.
passages.speaker: Thomas, archdeacon of Split, Historia Salonitana, in the first edition by Ivan Lučić (Lucius), Amsterdam 1666
passages.caution: Thomas's chronology is loose; the capture of Vladimir and Suzdal and Yuri's death were in 1238.

passages.headline: Pest overrun and burned
passages.gloss: After the defeat at the Sajó, crowds gathered in Pest, 'a great township' on the far bank of the Danube, and began to dig a rampart and weave wicker fences, against the advice of Prince Coloman. The Tartars camped around it and shot it to pieces for two or three days, broke in and slaughtered the people; then they set fire to the whole town. Thomas says about ten thousand more burned in the Dominican house where they had taken refuge.
passages.quote: Igitur Tartarorum acies suis castris circa totam Villam defixis, coeperunt eam undique impugnare … & quia locus non satis erat munitus die quadam uno impetu Tartari irruperunt, nec fuit ultra congressio, nec resistentia ulla.
passages.translation: So the Tartar battle lines, having fixed their camps around the whole township, began to attack it from every side … and because the place was not well enough fortified, one day the Tartars burst in with a single rush, and there was no more fighting and no resistance at all.
passages.speaker: Thomas, archdeacon of Split, Historia Salonitana, in the first edition by Ivan Lučić (Lucius), Amsterdam 1666
passages.caution: Thomas's figure of over 100,000 dead in one day, given on the same page, is not credible as a count.

passages.headline: Kadan at Trogir: a muddy channel and a herald shouting in Slavonic
passages.gloss: Here Thomas was close by. King Béla had taken refuge on an island off Trogir. Kadan rode round the town trying to get under the walls on horseback, but found the channel separating Trogir from the mainland too deep in mud to ford. He then sent a herald to the bridge who shouted in Slavonic, 'Kadan, prince of the unconquered army, says this to you': hand over our enemies. On the king's orders the guards gave no answer, and the army left.
passages.quote: Caeterum Dux Caydanus omnibus loci illius circumstantiis perlustratis tentabat, si posset sub moenibus equitando transire, sed cum cognovisset, quod aqua illa, per quam Civitas a terra dirimitur propter limi profunditatem invadabilis erat, retraxit se inde … exclamavit voce magna Sclavonice dicens: Haec dicit vobis D. Caydanus invictae militiae Princeps.
passages.translation: Duke Kadan, having surveyed all the surroundings of the place, tried whether he could pass beneath the walls on horseback; but when he learned that the water by which the city is cut off from the land was unfordable because of the depth of the mud, he withdrew … [the messenger] cried out in a loud voice in Slavonic, saying: 'This says to you Lord Kadan, prince of the unconquered army.'
passages.speaker: Thomas, archdeacon of Split, Historia Salonitana, in the first edition by Ivan Lučić (Lucius), Amsterdam 1666
passages.caution: Thomas was in Split, a few miles away, so he may have learned details from Trogir; the herald's words are as reported.

passages.headline: Rumour: the Tartars will pile up a mountain to overtop the walls
passages.people: Tartars as imagined by frightened citizens
passages.gloss: With the Tartars on the coast, Thomas says the people of Split started 'empty rumours'. Some said the Tartars were building huge siege machines to throw the towns down; others that they were heaping up earth and stones like a mountain, so they could stand higher than the cities and take them easily. Thomas himself calls these rumours vain and baseless: a record of fear, not of what happened.
passages.quote: Coeperunt autem vanos agitare rumores, confingentes opiniones vanas, & inanes. Dicebant alii quod ingentes machinas, & plurima instrumenta bellica Tartari fabricarent, quibus Civitates has deiicere conabantur; asserebant alii, quod ad montis instar terrae, ac lapidum congeriem acervabant, & sic Civitatibus supereminentes, facile eas esse capturos.
passages.translation: They began to spread empty rumours, inventing vain and idle opinions. Some said that the Tartars were building huge machines and many instruments of war with which they were trying to throw down these cities; others asserted that they were heaping up a pile of earth and stones like a mountain, and so, rising above the cities, would easily capture them.
passages.speaker: Thomas, archdeacon of Split, Historia Salonitana, in the first edition by Ivan Lučić (Lucius), Amsterdam 1666
passages.caution: Thomas reports these as rumours he did not believe.

passages.headline: Scholars decide they are the peoples before Antichrist
passages.people: Tartars as seen by Latin scholars
passages.gloss: After the Hungarian disaster, Thomas says, the whole world trembled. Even the emperor Frederick II was said to be thinking not of resistance but of a hiding place. Learned men searched old writings and concluded, above all from the prophecies attributed to Methodius, that these were the peoples who must come before Antichrist, and cities began fortifying themselves in case the Tartars marched on Rome.
passages.quote: Ipse etiam Fredericus Rom. Imperator non de resistendo, sed de latibulo dicitur cogitasse. Tunc litterati plerique viri veteres scrutantes scripturas, conjiciebant maxime ex dictis Methodii Martyris has fore illas gentes, quae praecedere debent antichristi adventum.
passages.translation: Even Frederick, the Roman emperor, is said to have thought not of resisting but of a hiding place. Then many learned men, searching the old writings, conjectured, above all from the sayings of Methodius the Martyr, that these were those peoples who must come before the advent of Antichrist.
passages.speaker: Thomas, archdeacon of Split, Historia Salonitana, in the first edition by Ivan Lučić (Lucius), Amsterdam 1666
passages.caution: The claim about Frederick is gossip ('is said'); the Methodius prophecy is the Pseudo-Methodius apocalypse, which linked enclosed northern nations with the end of the world.

passages.headline: The 'Tartars' Road' over Mount Vlaško
passages.people: Mongol army of Kadan (in local tradition)
passages.gloss: Writing four centuries later, the Trogir historian Giovanni Lucio (Ivan Lučić) explains why King Béla did not trust the island next to Trogir: the Hungarians knew that Tartars swam their horses across huge rivers. He then records a local tradition that the Tartars, leaving, rode past in the king's sight along the slope of Mount Vlaško, and that the road there had been called 'the Tartars' road' ever since, just as a nearby rock is still called the King's Rock.
passages.quote: sapendo gl'Ongari, che li Tartari erano soliti passare con Caualli à nuoto grossissimi fiumi, dubitassero, che passassero anco nell'Isola Bua … i quali nell'andar via passarono à vista sua sopra la costa del monte Vlasco, hauendo lasciato con tal occasione il nome alla strada, che d'indi in qua vien detta strada de Tartari
passages.translation: the Hungarians, knowing that the Tartars were accustomed to cross very large rivers by swimming with their horses, feared that they would cross to the island of Bua as well … who, as they went away, passed in his sight along the slope of Mount Vlasko, having on that occasion left their name to the road, which from then on has been called the Tartars' road
passages.speaker: Giovanni Lucio (Ivan Lučić), Memorie istoriche di Tragurio ora detto Traù (Venice, 1674)
passages.caution: A place-name tradition recorded in 1674, not a medieval report.

passages.headline: A people who seem to hate every city and building
passages.gloss: Riccoldo's first sight of the Tartars, inside 'Turchia' (Seljuk Anatolia under Mongol rule). He describes broad faces, narrow eyes and thin beards, and then claims they 'seem to hate every city and every dwelling building', destroying nearly all the towns, castles and houses they meet. For a source on who built what in 'Tartary', this is a blunt statement from a man who lived among them that the Tartars were destroyers, not builders.
passages.quote: sed videntur odire omnem ciuitatem et omne edificium habitacionis. Nam quasi omnes ciuitates et castra et habitaciones et edificia destruunt, et illum magis ledunt, qui se magis illis humiliat
passages.translation: but they seem to hate every city and every dwelling building. For they destroy almost all cities and castles and dwellings and buildings, and they harm most the one who humbles himself most before them
passages.speaker: Riccoldo of Monte Croce, Liber peregrinationis, ed. J. C. M. Laurent (Leipzig, 1864)
passages.caution: A hostile missionary generalisation; he says they 'seem' to hate cities, and his own later chapters show Tartars ruling from Tabriz and Baghdad.

passages.headline: Women who ride into town with bow and arrows
passages.gloss: Riccoldo says Tartar women are held in great honour, run the realm or the household, buy and sell, and are fierce and warlike. He adds from his own eyes that they ride like men and that he often saw them entering cities armed with bows and arrows. Elsewhere on the same page he explains their tall crowns, topped with a foot to remind them they are still under their husbands.
passages.quote: et ipse sunt, que gubernant regnum vel domum, et emunt et vendunt, et sunt feroces et bellicose. Equitant autem vt viri, et frequenter vidi eas intrantes ciuitates cum arcu et sagittis accinctas vt viros.
passages.translation: and it is they who govern the kingdom or the household, and they buy and sell, and they are fierce and warlike. They ride like men, and I often saw them entering cities girded with bow and arrows like men.
passages.speaker: Riccoldo of Monte Croce, Liber peregrinationis, ed. J. C. M. Laurent (Leipzig, 1873)

passages.headline: A horse on a pole for the dead lord
passages.gloss: Riccoldo describes Tartar funerals: cooked meat, clothes and money buried with the dead, and for a great lord a horse ridden to exhaustion, killed, stuffed with green grass and hung up on a stake, told to be ready whenever its master rises again. He adds that they once buried up to twenty living slaves with a lord until Christians shamed them out of it, and that Tartars even paid bishops to be buried in Christian cemeteries.
passages.quote: et equus cadit, et ipse exenterat eum et euacuat omnia de ventre equi, et implet herba viridi, et postea infigit palum magnum per posteriora, et facit palum exire vsque ad os, et ita dimittit equum impalatum, et suspendit eum et mandat ei, quod sit paratus, quandocumque wlt dominus surgere
passages.translation: and the horse falls, and he guts it and empties everything from the horse's belly and fills it with green grass, and then drives a great stake in from behind and makes the stake come out at the mouth, and so leaves the horse impaled, and hangs it up and orders it to be ready whenever its lord wishes to rise
passages.speaker: Riccoldo of Monte Croce, Liber peregrinationis, ed. J. C. M. Laurent (Leipzig, 1864)
passages.caution: He does not say he watched a funeral; this is presented as general custom. The horse-on-a-pole rite matches steppe burial practice reported by other travellers.

passages.headline: Execution called 'sleep', and a blank space for the lord's name
passages.gloss: Two sharp details of Mongol court manners. When writing to a superior, a Tartar leaves a gap where the lord's name belongs and writes the name out in the margin. When a man is condemned, the lord says 'cut him and make him sleep', because they do not call death death, and the condemned simply holds out his arms to be bound.
passages.quote: Cum scribunt suis maioribus, tantam reuerenciam habent et seruant, quod non scribant nomen sui maioris in suo loco, sed dimittunt spacium vacuum et postea scribunt nomen de foris in margine in alio loco.
passages.translation: When they write to their superiors they keep such reverence that they do not write their superior's name in its place, but leave an empty space and afterwards write the name outside, in the margin, in another place.
passages.speaker: Riccoldo of Monte Croce, Liber peregrinationis, ed. J. C. M. Laurent (Leipzig, 1873)

passages.headline: 'Mogoli' from 'Magogoli': the Tartars and Gog and Magog
passages.gloss: Riccoldo weighs the theory that the Tartars were the Lost Ten Tribes of Israel shut behind the Caspian mountains by Alexander, notes that they hate Alexander's name and that their script looks like Chaldean, then argues against it. He reports that they themselves claim descent from Gog and Magog, which is why they are called Mogoli, as if a corruption of 'Magogoli'. It is a textbook example of how Europeans fitted the Mongols into biblical and Alexander legends.
passages.quote: Ipsi vero dicunt se descendisse de Gog et Magog. Vnde ipsi dicuntur Mogoli, quasi corrupto vocabulo Magogoli.
passages.translation: They themselves say they are descended from Gog and Magog. Hence they are called Mogoli, as if from a corruption of the word Magogoli.
passages.speaker: Riccoldo of Monte Croce, Liber peregrinationis, ed. J. C. M. Laurent (Leipzig, 1864)
passages.caution: A folk etymology. 'Mongol' has nothing to do with Magog; the claim that Mongols themselves said this is Riccoldo's report and is doubtful.

passages.headline: The hare, the owl and the fortress of wind
passages.place: Mountains beyond the Caspian (Caucasus in the legend)
passages.gloss: Riccoldo's origin tale: the Tartars lived shut in by mountains whose only pass held an empty fortress that roared with the noise of horses, men and trumpets, a trick of the wind. A hunter chasing a hare followed it in, saw an owl singing on the gate, reasoned that no one lives where a hare runs and an owl sings, and led his people out. So, Riccoldo says, Tartars honour the hare and paint it on arms and tents, and nobles wear owl feathers and owl skins, which Western merchants now sell them for up to twenty pounds each.
passages.quote: Non est habitacio hominum, vbi lepus fugit et bubo cantat. Et sic fiducialiter intrans neminem inuenit.
passages.translation: 'There is no dwelling of men where a hare flees and an owl sings.' And so, entering confidently, he found no one.
passages.speaker: Riccoldo of Monte Croce, Liber peregrinationis, ed. J. C. M. Laurent (Leipzig, 1864)
passages.caution: A legend Riccoldo heard; Hayton of Corycus (W229) tells a different owl story in which the bird saves Genghis Khan in a bush.

passages.headline: The caliph of Baghdad made to eat his gold
passages.people: Tartars under Hulegu; the Abbasid caliph
passages.gloss: Riccoldo's version of the fall of Baghdad, told a generation later by a man living in the city.
