The Tartars found the caliph in a marvellous palace heaped with treasure, starved him for three days, set gold, silver and jewels before him, and when he said he had only kept what his ancestors gathered, poured molten gold into his mouth. They then killed the people for forty days.
passages.quote: Quo tacente mandauerunt, quod liquaretur aurum et colaretur in os eius, et dixerunt ei: Aurum sitiisti, aurum bibe! Populum autem eius per quadraginta dies continuos occiderunt.
passages.translation: When he fell silent they ordered gold to be melted and poured into his mouth, and said to him: 'You thirsted for gold, drink gold!' And they killed his people for forty days on end.
passages.speaker: Riccoldo of Monte Croce, Liber peregrinationis, ed. J. C. M. Laurent (Leipzig, 1864)
passages.caution: The molten-gold death is a legend; Persian sources say the caliph was rolled in a carpet and trampled, and Hayton (W229) has him starved among his treasure.

passages.headline: Baghdad forty years on: mostly ruined, still crowded, ruled by Tartars
passages.people: Tartars (Ilkhanid rulers); Muslims, Christians and Jews of Baghdad
passages.gloss: Riccoldo lived in Baghdad and describes it after the Mongol conquest: the city is 'for the most part destroyed' yet still full of people, with many thousands of Christians and Jews and over two hundred thousand Muslims, all under Tartar lordship. He also found its Muslim colleges and Sufi houses thriving and admired their scholars.
passages.quote: In ipsa quidem ciuitate, licet sit pro maiori parte destructa, est tamen maxima multitudo populi in ea. Nam preter Christianos et Iudeos, qui sunt ibi multa milia, sunt ibi vltra ducenta milia Sarracenorum, vt probabiliter creditur; omnes tamen sunt sub dominio Tartarorum.
passages.translation: In that city, although it is for the most part destroyed, there is nevertheless a very great multitude of people. For besides Christians and Jews, who are many thousands there, there are more than two hundred thousand Saracens, as is plausibly believed; yet all are under the lordship of the Tartars.
passages.speaker: Riccoldo of Monte Croce, Liber peregrinationis, ed. J. C. M. Laurent (Leipzig, 1864)
passages.caution: Population figures are his estimate ('as is plausibly believed').

passages.headline: Why the Tartars became Muslims
passages.gloss: Riccoldo explains the Ilkhanate's conversion to Islam from a missionary's frustrated point of view: the Tartars had neither law nor prophet, found Islam an easy law, and Muslims gave them rich gifts to convert, so that now 'for the most part' they have become Saracens. He adds that many still like Christians but find Christianity too hard and are offered no presents.
passages.quote: acceperunt legem, et facti sunt Sarraceni, maxime quia ipsi Tartari nec legem nec prophetam habebant. Vnde modo pro magna parte Tartari facti sunt Sarraceni. Nam et Sarraceni eos emunt et dant eis maxima dona, vt ipsi efficiantur Sarraceni.
passages.translation: they took up the law and became Saracens, above all because the Tartars had neither law nor prophet. So now for the greater part the Tartars have become Saracens. For the Saracens buy them and give them very great gifts so that they will become Saracens.
passages.speaker: Riccoldo of Monte Croce, Liber peregrinationis, ed. J. C. M. Laurent (Leipzig, 1864)
passages.caution: A partisan explanation; the Ilkhan Ghazan converted in 1295, within Riccoldo's stay.

passages.headline: A shaman who seemed to fly
passages.people: Tartars and their 'baxitae' (Buddhist or shamanic priests)
passages.gloss: Riccoldo says the Tartars honour above all men certain 'boxitae' (bakhshis), priests of idols from India, wise and grave, who practise magic with the help of demons, show many marvels and foretell the future. One of their leaders was said to fly, but, Riccoldo reports, it was found that he only walked just above the ground without touching it and sat on nothing solid.
passages.quote: Nam et vnus maior inter eos dicebatur volare, sed secundum veritatem repertum est, quod non volauit, sed ambulabat iuxta terram et eam non tangebat, et quando videbatur sedere, nulla re solida sustentabatur.
passages.translation: For one of the greater among them was said to fly, but according to the truth it was found that he did not fly, but walked close to the ground without touching it, and when he seemed to sit he was held up by nothing solid.
passages.speaker: Riccoldo of Monte Croce, Liber peregrinationis, ed. J. C. M. Laurent (Leipzig, 1864)
passages.caution: Hearsay about a wonder, which Riccoldo half-debunks (not flying) and half-repeats (levitating).

passages.headline: The officer boiled alive by the Tartar women
passages.gloss: After Abaqa's army turned tail before the Mamluks in Syria, Riccoldo says, a great Tartar baron was caught plotting revolt. When the khan wanted to execute him, the Tartar ladies asked for him instead, boiled him alive and fed him in tiny pieces to the whole army as a warning.
passages.quote: obstiterunt domine et mulieres Tartarorum, petentes eum sibi dari. Quo accepto coxerunt eum viuum, et dederunt eum comedere incisum per partes minimas toti exercitui in exemplum aliorum.
passages.translation: the ladies and women of the Tartars opposed it, asking that he be given to them. When he was handed over they cooked him alive and gave him, cut into the smallest pieces, to the whole army to eat, as an example to others.
passages.speaker: Riccoldo of Monte Croce, Liber peregrinationis, ed. J. C. M. Laurent (Leipzig, 1873)
passages.caution: A lurid atrocity story Riccoldo did not witness; treat as rumour.

passages.headline: The Tartars were one of seven Mongol nations
passages.people: Tartars and the other Mongol tribes
passages.gloss: Hayton says the Tartars first lived beyond the great mountain of Belgian, 'like beasts' without faith or law, serving other nations, until several tribes 'called Mogols' banded together. He then lists seven nations, and the first is named Tartars. So for Hayton 'Tartar' is both the name of one tribe and the name for the whole confederation, a distinction that matters for anyone asking where the word came from.
passages.quote: La primiere de [ces] VII nacions est nomée Tartars, la secunde Tangot, la tierce Eurach, la quarte Jalair, la quinte Sonit, la sime Mengli, la setime Tebet.
passages.translation: The first of these seven nations is named Tartars, the second Tangot, the third Eurach, the fourth Jalair, the fifth Sonit, the sixth Mengli, the seventh Tebet.
passages.speaker: Hayton of Corycus, La Flor des estoires de la terre d'Orient (French text, 1307), ed. Ch. Kohler (1906)
passages.caution: The editor notes that 'Mengli' should read Merkit; the list mixes real tribes (Tatar, Jalayir, Sunit, Merkit) with Tangut and Tibet.

passages.headline: A poor old blacksmith and the white knight
passages.gloss: Hayton's origin legend of Genghis Khan: a poor old blacksmith named Canguis saw in a dream a white knight on a white horse, who told him that God willed him to rule the seven Tartar nations called Mogols and free them from servitude. The chiefs laughed at him until they saw the same knight the next night. A second vision later sends him west over the mountain.
passages.quote: un veillart, povre home fevre, qui avoit non Canguis, vit en songe un avision; car il vit un chevalier armez sur un cheval blanc qui l'apela par son non, et luy dit: « Canguis, la volenté de l'inmortel Deu est tel que tu doies estre governeor e seignor sur les VII nacions des Tartars qui sunt dites Mogols
passages.translation: an old man, a poor smith, named Canguis, saw a vision in a dream: he saw an armed knight on a white horse who called him by his name and said: 'Canguis, the will of the immortal God is that you should be governor and lord over the seven nations of the Tartars, which are called Mogols'
passages.speaker: Hayton of Corycus, La Flor des estoires de la terre d'Orient (French text, 1307), ed. Ch. Kohler (1906)
passages.caution: A legend; the 'smith' idea echoes Genghis's personal name Temujin, which was linked with 'smith' in later tellings. Hayton says this part comes from the Tartars' own histories.

passages.headline: Raised on black felt: a khan election Hayton saw twice
passages.gloss: Hayton says the Tartars still make their lord the way they made Genghis: the whole people gathers in a field, the chosen man is seated on a black felt, the nobles and Genghis's kin lift him high and set him on a rich throne, and all kneel to him. He adds that he himself was present at two such elections, and marvels that for all their conquests they never changed their first custom.
passages.quote: Quant volent eslire leur seignor, e j'ai esté II foiz à la eleccion de l'empereor des Tartars, e ai veü coment tous les Tartars s'assembloient en un grant champ, e celui qui devoit estre leur seignor faisoient seoir sur un feltre noir, e metoient un riche siege au mi d'eaus.
passages.translation: When they want to elect their lord (and I have been twice at the election of the emperor of the Tartars, and saw how all the Tartars gathered in a great field), they seated the one who was to be their lord on a black felt, and set a rich throne in their midst.
passages.speaker: Hayton of Corycus, La Flor des estoires de la terre d'Orient (French text, 1307), ed. Ch. Kohler (1906)

passages.headline: The owl that saved Genghis Khan
passages.gloss: Unhorsed and alone after a lost skirmish, Genghis hid in a bush. As his enemies came to search it, an owl (the 'duc', eagle owl) landed on the bush, and they left, reasoning that no bird would sit where a man was hiding. Hayton says this is why every Tartar who can get an owl feather wears it on his head. Compare Riccoldo (W228), who tells a quite different owl story to explain the same feathers.
passages.quote: et sur ce un oisel, qui avoit non duc, vint e s'asist sur ce boisson … Les Tartars rendirent graces à Deu, e dès adonques orent en tante reverence cel oisel, qui est apellez duc, que chascun qui poet avoir de la plume de cel oisel la porte sur sa teste.
passages.translation: and at that a bird called the duc (eagle owl) came and sat on the bush … The Tartars gave thanks to God, and from then on held that bird, called the duc, in such reverence that everyone who can get a feather of it wears it on his head.
passages.speaker: Hayton of Corycus, La Flor des estoires de la terre d'Orient (French text, 1307), ed. Ch. Kohler (1906)
passages.caution: A legend explaining a real custom (owl feathers worn on the head).

passages.headline: Tartars learned letters, and idols, from the Uighurs
passages.gloss: Hayton says that before their expansion the Tartars had no letters at all, which is why he cannot give dates for their early history. When their armies reached the kingdom of 'Tarse' (the Uighurs), they learned writing there, and because the people were idolaters they also began to worship idols, while always confessing one immortal God above the others.
passages.quote: En celes [parties] les Tartars apristrent letres, car avant ne avoient letres nules. E por ce que les habiteors de celes contrées estoient touz ydolatres, les Tartars comencierent aorer les ydoles; mès tout adès confessoient le Deu inmortel, plus grant que les autres.
passages.translation: In those parts the Tartars learned letters, for before they had no letters at all. And because the inhabitants of those lands were all idolaters, the Tartars began to worship idols; but they always confessed the immortal God, greater than the others.
passages.speaker: Hayton of Corycus, La Flor des estoires de la terre d'Orient (French text, 1307), ed. Ch. Kohler (1906)

passages.headline: The Great Khan sunk by enemy swimmers
passages.gloss: Hayton's account of the death of the Great Khan Mongke: besieging an island in the sea of Cathay, he was sunk when the clever local people sent swimmers under his ship to bore holes in its hull until it filled and he drowned. The Kohler edition notes that a French manuscript garbled the Latin word for sponge-divers into 'spiongeorges'.
passages.quote: entra par mer au roiaume de Cathaï, e come il assegast une isle, laquele il voloit prendre par mer, la gent de cele terre, qui sont molt engignous, manderent homes noeors, e ceaus entrerent desouz le vaissel où Mango Can estoit
passages.translation: he went by sea into the kingdom of Cathay, and as he was besieging an island which he wanted to take by sea, the people of that land, who are very ingenious, sent swimmers, and they went under the ship in which Mango Can was
passages.speaker: Hayton of Corycus, La Flor des estoires de la terre d'Orient (French text, 1307), ed. Ch. Kohler (1906)
passages.caution: Not true as told: Mongke died in 1259 during a land siege in Sichuan, reportedly of illness or a wound.

passages.headline: Qubilai's new city 'Jong', bigger than Rome
passages.gloss: After Mongke's death the Tartars made his brother Qubilai lord. Hayton says Qubilai founded a city called Jong, 'bigger than Rome', and lived there to the end of his life. The editor identifies Jong with Khanbaliq (Marco Polo's Cambaluc), today's Beijing, the Mongol capital that Qubilai built beside the ruined Jurchen city of Zhongdu.
passages.quote: firent seignor son frere Cobila Can, qui tint la seignorie des Tartars XLII ans, e fu crestien e ferma une cité qui est appellée Jong, que est plus grant que Rome. E en cele cité demora Cobila Can
passages.translation: they made his brother Cobila Can lord, who held the lordship of the Tartars for forty-two years, and was a Christian, and built a city called Jong, which is bigger than Rome. And in that city Cobila Can lived
passages.speaker: Hayton of Corycus, La Flor des estoires de la terre d'Orient (French text, 1307), ed. Ch. Kohler (1906)
passages.caution: Qubilai was not a Christian and reigned 34 years (1260 to 1294); Hayton exaggerates Mongol Christian sympathies throughout.

passages.headline: Sarra, capital of Comania, 'almost all laid waste'
passages.gloss: In his geography of Comania (the Kipchak steppe, the Golden Horde's land) Hayton names its chief city Sarra, 'once a very good city', which the Tartars have almost entirely ruined. The editor identifies Sarra with Sarai on the Volga, and later in the book Hayton says the Tartar king Toqta holds his seat in a city called 'Sera'.
passages.quote: La maistre cité du roiaume de Comaine est apellée Sarra, laquele fu ancienement molt bone cité, mès les Tartars l'ont presque toute gastée.
passages.translation: The chief city of the kingdom of Comania is called Sarra, which was once a very good city, but the Tartars have laid it almost entirely waste.
passages.speaker: Hayton of Corycus, La Flor des estoires de la terre d'Orient (French text, 1307), ed. Ch. Kohler (1906)
passages.caution: Sarai is usually credited to the Golden Horde itself (founded under Batu in the 1240s to 1250s), so Hayton's 'once good, now wasted' is puzzling; he may mean another Kipchak town or be confused.

passages.headline: Baghdad taken, the caliph and his treasure
passages.gloss: Hayton's account of the Mongol sack of Baghdad: Hulegu took the city by force, put men and women to the sword, and found such riches that it was a marvel to see. Asked why he had not spent his treasure on an army, the caliph answered that he thought old women alone were enough to defend his land. Hulegu then shut him in a room with his treasure to eat it, and 'never again was there a caliph in Baghdad'.
passages.quote: Le calif fu amenez vif devant Haloon, e tantes richesses furent trovées en la cité de Baldac que ce fut grant merveille à regarder. … E le calif respondi que il quidoit que veisles fammes soulement estoient soufisables à defendre la terre.
passages.translation: The caliph was brought alive before Hulegu, and so much wealth was found in the city of Baghdad that it was a great marvel to behold. … And the caliph answered that he thought old women alone were enough to defend the land.
passages.speaker: Hayton of Corycus, La Flor des estoires de la terre d'Orient (French text, 1307), ed. Ch. Kohler (1906)
passages.caution: Hayton says his knowledge of Hulegu's reign came from his uncle King Het'um; the starving-among-treasure ending is a widely told story, not a verified fact.

passages.headline: Killing a man is no sin, but leaving the bridle on is
passages.gloss: In his chapter on Tartar customs Hayton says they name God simply and immortal but honour him with no prayers, fasts or penances. A Tartar would not think it a sin to kill a man, yet would think he had sinned mortally if he left the bit in his horse's mouth while it grazed. When they cross lands short of food they drive cows and mares with them, living on the milk and eating horse meat, which they think good.
passages.quote: Le Tartar ne reputaroit avoir fait pechié d'oucivre I home; e se il laissoit le frein en la bouche de son cheval, quant il deüst paistre, il quideroit pechier mortelment. … e vivent du lait, e la char des chevaus mangent, e lur pert bone char.
passages.translation: A Tartar would not reckon it a sin to kill a man; but if he left the bridle in his horse's mouth when it should graze, he would think he had sinned mortally. … and they live on the milk, and eat the flesh of horses, and it seems good meat to them.
passages.speaker: Hayton of Corycus, La Flor des estoires de la terre d'Orient (French text, 1307), ed. Ch. Kohler (1906)
passages.caution: The editor notes this chapter overlaps with John of Plano Carpini's earlier description, so parts may be borrowed rather than observed.

passages.headline: Conquerors who would rather live in tents and carts than towns
passages.gloss: Hayton's summary of the Tartar character includes a line that answers the question of Tartar towns directly: they know how to conquer foreign lands but not how to keep them, because they prefer to live in tents and wagons rather than in towns. The Latin version says the same, that they 'do not know how to live in castles and cities'.
passages.quote: Les Tartars scevent bien conquerre les estranges terres, mès il ne les sevent garder, car miaus volent estre en tentes e en chars que habiter en villes.
passages.translation: The Tartars know well how to conquer foreign lands, but they do not know how to keep them, for they would rather be in tents and in carts than live in towns.
passages.speaker: Hayton of Corycus, La Flor des estoires de la terre d'Orient (French text, 1307), ed. Ch. Kohler (1906)

passages.headline: Shooting backwards while they flee
passages.gloss: Hayton, who fought beside Mongol armies, describes their tactics: when they flee they do so in ordered squadrons, and pursuing them is dangerous because they shoot backwards as they ride, wounding men and horses, then wheel round on careless pursuers. Their army looks smaller than it is because they ride packed close, so a thousand Tartars look like five hundred.
passages.quote: Quando Tatari vertunt in fugam, fugiunt omnes simul per turmas et acies ordinatas; et valde periculosum est sequi eos, quoniam retrograde sagictas jaciunt fugiendo, et equos et homines vulnerant et occidunt. … Exercitus Tatarorum non est magne apparencie, quia omnes simul congregatim incedunt, ita quod acies mille Tatarorum quingentorum apparenciam non habet.
passages.translation: When the Tatars turn to flight, they all flee together in ordered squadrons and lines; and it is very dangerous to follow them, because as they flee they shoot arrows backwards and wound and kill horses and men. … The Tatar army does not look large, because they all ride packed together, so that a line of a thousand Tatars does not look like five hundred.
passages.speaker: Hayton of Corycus, Flos historiarum terre Orientis (Latin version by Nicolas Falcon, 1307), ed. Ch. Kohler (1906)

passages.headline: One great khan in Cathay and three Tartar kings
passages.gloss: Hayton closes his history with the Tartar world as it stood when he wrote: a great emperor, Temur Khan, sixth of the line, ruling from the city of Jong in Cathay, and three other Tartar kings, Chapar in Turkestan, Toqta in Comania and Kharbanda (Oljeitu) in Tabriz, who all owe him reverence and take their quarrels to his court. It is a clear picture of 'Tartary' as a family of Mongol states, not a single city or civilisation.
passages.quote: Le grant empereor des Tartars, celui qui ores tient la seignorie, est només Tamor Can, e est le VI empereor. Au roiaume de Cathaï tient le siege de son empire, en une molt grant cité que est nomée Jong … Encores i a autres trois rois des Tartars, qui ont molt grant puissance, e tous portent reverence e obedience au grant empereor.
passages.translation: The great emperor of the Tartars, the one who now holds the lordship, is named Temur Khan, and he is the sixth emperor. He holds the seat of his empire in the kingdom of Cathay, in a very great city called Jong … There are also three other kings of the Tartars, who have very great power, and all pay reverence and obedience to the great emperor.
passages.speaker: Hayton of Corycus, La Flor des estoires de la terre d'Orient (French text, 1307), ed. Ch. Kohler (1906)

passages.headline: 'Barbarian nations that call themselves Tartars', like locusts
passages.gloss: King Bela IV of Hungary, writing to the German king Conrad IV after the disaster at Mohi, describes the invaders as barbarian nations 'which call themselves Tartars', coming out of the East like locusts from the desert. He lists Greater Hungary, Bulgaria, Cumania, Rus', Poland and Moravia as ravaged, with only some castles and strongholds still holding out, and his own kingdom beyond the Danube occupied.
passages.quote: barbare nationes, que se Tartaros appellant, de plaga orientali velut locuste ex heremo prodeuntes majore Ungaria, Bulgaria, Cumania, Ruscia nec non Polonia et Moravia, castris et munitionibus quibusdam exceptis, que usque hodie se ipsos defendunt, depopulatis
passages.translation: barbarian nations which call themselves Tartars, coming out of the eastern region like locusts from the desert, having laid waste Greater Hungary, Bulgaria, Cumania, Rus' and also Poland and Moravia, except for certain castles and fortifications which still defend themselves to this day
passages.speaker: King Bela IV of Hungary, letter to Conrad IV, Vienna, June 1241 (printed by Hormayr, 1842)

passages.headline: Bela warns that the Tartars are building forts in Hungary
passages.gloss: In the same letter Bela urges the German princes to march with crossbowmen and supplies, warning that a Tartar hold on Hungary would be a heavy threat to the Empire 'because they are raising many fortifications there'. He also says he knows their strength from personal experience of battle, and that their wealth from forty conquered kingdoms could enrich twenty kingdoms if they were destroyed.
passages.quote: cum eorum ibidem receptio, Tartarorum videlicet, esset imperio plurimum honerosa, eo quod munitiones ibidem plurimas erigant
passages.translation: since their being received there, that is of the Tartars, would be most burdensome to the Empire, because they are raising very many fortifications there
passages.speaker: King Bela IV of Hungary, letter to Conrad IV, Vienna, June 1241 (printed by Hormayr, 1842)
passages.caution: A king pleading for help; 'many fortifications' may be an alarm rather than a survey. The Mongols withdrew from Hungary in 1242.

passages.headline: Friar Julian: the Tartars' first land was 'Gothia'
passages.gloss: Friar Julian, a Hungarian Dominican who had travelled to the edge of Rus' looking for the pagan 'Greater Hungarians', tells the papal legate what he learned 'from many': that the Tartars once lived where the Cumans now live, are 'in truth' called Ishmaelites but wish to be called Tartars, and came out of a land called 'Gothia'. He then tells a tangled origin story of a duke named Gurgutha whose vengeance war launched their conquests.
passages.quote: Relatum est enim a pluribus, quod Tartari, qui prius inhabitabant terram quam Cumani nunc inhabitant, dicuntur in veritate illi Ysmahelite, volunt nunc Tartari appellari. Terra autem de qua prius sunt egressi Gothia vocatur
passages.translation: For it is reported by many that the Tartars, who formerly lived in the land the Cumans now inhabit, are in truth called Ishmaelites, but now wish to be called Tartars. The land from which they first came out is called Gothia
passages.speaker: Friar Julian of Hungary, O.P., report to the bishop of Perugia (c. 1238), in the text printed by Hormayr (1842)
passages.caution: Hearsay gathered on the Russian frontier; the 'Ishmaelite' label is biblical classification, and the Gurgutha story has no basis in Mongol history. The OCR is badly garbled and the wording is reconstructed from it.

passages.headline: A khan's palace with golden doors in the city of 'Homah'
passages.gloss: Julian reports that the son of the first Tartar duke, 'Chayn', rules from a great city called Homah, in a palace so large that a thousand horsemen ride in through one door and out again without dismounting, with golden doors and a high golden bed on golden columns. Anyone who touches the threshold with his foot is struck with a sword. It is a vivid second-hand picture of a steppe court, filtered through frontier rumour.
passages.quote: residet in civitate magna Homah … palatium habet ita magnum, quod mille equites intrant per unum hostium et eidem inclinantes equites exeunt nichilominus insidentes.
passages.translation: he resides in the great city of Homah … he has a palace so large that a thousand horsemen enter by one door and, bowing to him, go out again still mounted.
passages.speaker: Friar Julian of Hungary, O.P., report to the bishop of Perugia (c. 1238), in the text printed by Hormayr (1842)
passages.caution: Hearsay; 'Homah' is not identified (Julian also mentions a 'sultan of Homach'), and the golden palace may blend tales of the khan's great tent with rumours of Near Eastern cities. The threshold taboo matches what Carpini and Rubruck saw.

passages.headline: Conquered men made to fight, and the rest 'called Tartars'
passages.gloss: Julian explains how the Tartar army grows: they kill the rulers of conquered lands at once, drive the strong men into battle in front of them, leave the weaker men to farm, give each of them ten or more women of the dead, and order that 'from now on they be called Tartars'. Soldiers who retreat are killed by the Tartars, so they prefer to die fighting. Instead of storming strong castles they strip the land and force the local people to attack the castle.
passages.quote: cuilibet decem vel plures assignantes et imponunt eisdem, ut de cetero Tartari nuncupentur. … Castra munita non expugnant, sed prius devastant terram et populum depredantur et ejusdem terre populum congregatum compellunt ad pugnam ad expugnandum ipsum castrum.
passages.translation: assigning ten or more to each, and they order them that from now on they be called Tartars. … They do not storm fortified castles, but first lay waste the land and plunder the people, and compel the gathered people of that same land to fight to take the castle.
passages.speaker: Friar Julian of Hungary, O.P., report to the bishop of Perugia (c. 1238), in the text printed by Hormayr (1842)
passages.caution: Reported by refugees and the duke of Suzdal, not seen by Julian himself.

passages.headline: The khan's letter: 'You live in houses, how will you escape me?'
passages.people: The Tartar khan ('Chayn', probably Batu) and King Bela IV
passages.gloss: Julian carried to King Bela a letter the Tartar ruler had sent, written in 'pagan letters and the Tartar tongue', which a pagan he met in Cumania translated. The khan, calling himself the messenger of the heavenly king, demands Bela's surrender and the return of the Cumans who fled to Hungary, and draws a sharp contrast: the tent-dwelling Cumans might escape him, but a king who lives in houses, castles and cities cannot.
passages.quote: Facilius enim est Cumanis evadere quam tibi, quia illi sine domibus cum tentoriis ambulantes possunt forsitan evadere. Tu autem in domibus habitans habes castra et civitates, quomodo effugies manus meas?
passages.translation: For it is easier for the Cumans to escape than for you, since they, going about without houses, with tents, may perhaps escape. But you, living in houses, have castles and cities: how will you flee my hands?
passages.speaker: The Tartar khan's letter to King Bela IV, as translated and reported by Friar Julian (printed by Hormayr, 1842)
passages.caution: Known only through Julian's Latin rendering of an oral translation.

passages.headline: They seem to rain arrows rather than shoot them
passages.gloss: Julian's report on how the Tartars fight: they shoot farther than other nations, and in the first clash 'do not seem to shoot but to rain arrows', while swords and lances are said to be less suited to them. Their army is organised so that one Tartar commands ten men and a centurion commands a hundred, so that spies cannot hide among them.
passages.quote: dicitur, quod longius jaciunt, quam alie consueverint naciones. In prima congressione belli, ut dicitur, non sagittant, sed quasi pluere sagittas videntur.
passages.translation: it is said that they shoot farther than other nations are accustomed to. In the first clash of battle, it is said, they do not shoot, but seem as it were to rain arrows.
passages.speaker: Friar Julian of Hungary, O.P., report to the bishop of Perugia (c. 1238), in the text printed by Hormayr (1842)

passages.headline: A people from 'unknown lands' whose reason for coming no one knows
passages.gloss: Duke Otto of Bavaria, writing from Straubing on 11 April 1241, two days after Liegnitz, warns the bishop of Augsburg of a barbarous people 'of infinite multitude, coming from distant and unknown parts', whose reason for coming nobody knows except that they persecute and kill Christians. He reports Cracow's land destroyed, the duke of Poland defeated, and the Tartars at the borders of Bohemia in three armies, and fears for all Germany.
passages.quote: quedam gens barbara Tartarorum crudelis nimium, multitudinis infinite, de longinquis et ignotis partibus adveniens, cujus causam adventus aliam ignoramus, nisi quod christianos universos impie prosequantur et occidant.
passages.translation: a certain barbarous people of the Tartars, exceedingly cruel, of infinite multitude, coming from distant and unknown parts, the cause of whose coming we do not know, except that they wickedly pursue and kill all Christians.
passages.speaker: Duke Otto II of Bavaria, letter to Bishop Siboto of Augsburg, Straubing, 11 April 1241 (printed by Hormayr, 1842)

passages.headline: Hungary after the Tartars: church towers the only signposts
passages.gloss: Hormayr's own nineteenth-century retelling of what King Bela found on his return: church towers the only guides, grass growing in the streets, whole days' journeys without a living soul, thousands of unburied corpses, wolves snatching children, and human flesh sold openly. It is vivid but it is Hormayr's rhetoric, built on chronicles like Master Roger's, not an eyewitness text.
passages.quote: waren Kirchthürme die einzigen Wegweiser, Gras und Gesträuch auf Strassen und Gassen, ganze Tagereisen weit keine menschliche Seele, aber viele tausende, unbegrabene, halb verwesete, grässlich verstümmelte Leichen
passages.translation: church towers were the only signposts, grass and brush on roads and lanes, whole days' journeys without a human soul, but many thousands of unburied, half-rotted, horribly mutilated corpses
passages.speaker: Joseph von Hormayr, editor's narrative (1842)
passages.caution: Editorial narrative written six centuries later; the famine cannibalism detail comes from medieval chronicles and is repeated without a source.

passages.headline: Moravian legends: bakers' 'hands, feet and ears' and Tartar arrows in the fields
passages.gloss: Hormayr collects Moravian memories of the invasion: Stramberk, which alone held out, where bakers every Pentecost bake pastry 'hands, feet and ears' because the Mongols cut these from the dead and sent them to their khan in sacks; a field where tiny horseshoes, swords and very long foreign arrows are dug up; and the legend that Jaroslav of Sternberg killed a Mongol prince at Olomouc. These are local traditions, not medieval evidence.
passages.quote: Stramberg im Preraner-Kreise ist der Ort, der sich der Mongolen allein erwehrte, zu dessen ewigem Gedächtnisse der Bäcker alljährlich um Pfingsten, dem Tage der Erlösung, Hände, Füsse und Ohren bäckt, weil die Mongolen diese den Erschlagenen und wohl auch vielen Lebenden abzuschneiden
passages.translation: Stramberk in the Prerov district is the place that alone fended off the Mongols; in its eternal memory the baker every year at Pentecost, the day of deliverance, bakes hands, feet and ears, because the Mongols were wont to cut these off the slain, and probably many of the living
passages.speaker: Joseph von Hormayr, editor's narrative (1842)
passages.caution: Local folklore reported by a nineteenth-century editor; the Mongol victory at Olomouc and Sternberg's slaying of a khan are later legends.

passages.headline: Rumour: the emperor himself called in the Mongols
passages.gloss: Hormayr notes that German enthusiasm for the crusade against the Mongols was weakened by a slander spread by papal partisans: that Emperor Frederick II, who liked the company of Arabs, Jews and heretics, had himself summoned the Mongols. He also repeats the chronicle story of an old Englishman, expelled from the crusader army, captured serving the Tartars as interpreter and guide.
passages.quote: die von den Päpstlichen überall ausgestreute Verläumdung: der mit Arabern, Juden und Ketzern am liebsten verkehrende, ruchlose Kaiser Friedrich selber, habe die Mongolen herbeigerufen.
passages.translation: the slander spread everywhere by the papal party: that the wicked Emperor Frederick himself, who liked best to keep company with Arabs, Jews and heretics, had called in the Mongols.
passages.speaker: Joseph von Hormayr, editor's narrative (1842)
passages.caution: Hormayr reports the rumour as propaganda; there is no evidence Frederick invited the Mongols.

passages.headline: Kazan Tatars farm and live in houses, unlike the steppe hordes
passages.gloss: Guagnini opens his survey of the hordes with the Kazan Tatars, conquered by Moscow in 1552. He sets them apart from the 'Campestrian' Tatars because they till fields, live in houses rather than in the open steppe, and trade with Muscovites, Turks and other Tatars. At the end of the section he adds that the steppe Tatars proper 'have no houses' and live in bands across the plains.
passages.quote: Hij Tartari Cazanenses reliquis ingeniosiores, & aliquantulum humaniores sunt, circa agriculturam, remque domesticam (qua a caeteris maxime differunt) versantur. In domibus non in campestribus degunt, mercimonia rerumque permutationes varias, cum vicinis Moschovitis, Turcis & caeteris Tartaris exercent
passages.translation: These Kazan Tatars are cleverer and somewhat more civilised than the rest; they occupy themselves with farming and household affairs (in which they differ most from the others). They live in houses, not in the open steppe, and carry on trade and various exchanges with their neighbours the Muscovites, Turks and other Tatars
passages.speaker: Alessandro Guagnini, Sarmatiae Europeae descriptio (Speyer, 1581)
passages.caution: Largely drawn from Herberstein's description of Kazan.

passages.headline: Samarkand, 'once the metropolis of all Tartary', now in ruins
passages.gloss: Guagnini calls Samarkand a very large city that was once the capital of all Tartary but now lies disfigured by ruins, with many traces of antiquity, and the burial place of Tamerlane, 'that king of the Tartars' who, he repeats, carried the captured Ottoman sultan Bayezid round Asia in a cage bound with golden chains. For modern readers interested in 'lost Tartarian cities', this is a sixteenth-century writer naming a real capital and explaining its ruins by Timur's fallen empire.
passages.quote: Sarmacandia Orientem versus procedendo, ultra Turcomaniam, urbs est amplissima, quae olim totius Tartariae Metropolis extitit, nunc vero ruinis deformis iacet, una cum multis antiquitatis vestigijs. In ea sepultus est Tamerlanes ille Tartarorum Rex, qui olim Turcarum Imperatorem Baiazetem … captivum aureis catenis vinctum, in cavea velut avem per totam Aziam circumvehebat.
passages.translation: Going eastward beyond Turkmenia, Samarkand is a very large city, which was once the metropolis of all Tartary but now lies disfigured by ruins, together with many traces of antiquity. In it is buried Tamerlane, that king of the Tartars, who once carried the Turkish emperor Bayezid … captive, bound in golden chains, in a cage like a bird through all Asia.
passages.speaker: Alessandro Guagnini, Sarmatiae Europeae descriptio (Speyer, 1581)
passages.caution: Guagnini never went there. Samarkand in the 1570s was a living Shaybanid (Uzbek) city, and the iron-cage story of Bayezid is a famous legend.

passages.headline: A magic head on a Tartar banner, breathing smoke at the Poles
passages.gloss: In the history of the Polish kings Guagnini tells how the Poles were winning against the Tartars until a Tartar standard-bearer came forward with a banner marked with a Greek X and, on top of the lance, a terrible head made by magic art that breathed foul smoke over the Poles. Bewitched, they lost their strength and were cut down 'like grain by hail', and the Tartars cut off every dead man's right ear and filled nine great sacks.
passages.quote: sed quidam Vexillifer Tartarorum, cum vexillo, in quo erat scripta litera Graeca tali modo, X, processit: superius vero in cuspide hastae erat caput quoddam terribile infixum, arte magica confectum, ore fumum vaporemque sordidum in Polonos evomens: quo velut peste quadam infecti, & incantationum vi fascinati, vires amiserunt.
passages.translation: but a certain standard-bearer of the Tartars came forward with a banner on which was written a Greek letter in this manner, X; and above, on the point of the lance, was fixed a terrible head, made by magic art, spewing smoke and foul vapour from its mouth over the Poles, by which, as if infected with a plague and bewitched by the force of spells, they lost their strength.
passages.speaker: Alessandro Guagnini, Sarmatiae Europeae descriptio (Speyer, 1581), lives of the Polish kings, following Polish chroniclers
passages.caution: A battle legend from Polish chronicles (Dlugosz tells it of Legnica); Guagnini dates the reign from 1243 and does not name the battle. Some historians suspect a smoke or incendiary device behind the tale.

passages.headline: A Tatar curse: 'may you stay in one place like a Christian'
passages.gloss: In his chapter on Tatar customs Guagnini says they never stay long in one place and think doing so a great misfortune. When angry they curse their children with it: may you be stuck in one place forever like a Christian and smell your own stink. He adds that they measure the growth of their realm by how many provinces they have laid waste, since they live in the open fields.
passages.quote: morari, iratique liberis suis sic grave malum imprecantur, dicentes: O utinam eodem in loco perinde ut Christianus perpetuo haereres, propriumque foetorem olfaceres. … Quo vero plures provincias desolaverint, hoc se regna sua (in campis enim sub dio vivere solent) ampliora reddidisse dicunt.
passages.translation: (to) stay, and when angry they call down on their children this grievous evil, saying: 'O may you cling forever to one place, like a Christian, and smell your own stink.' … The more provinces they have laid waste, the larger, they say, they have made their realms (for they are used to living in the fields under the open sky).
passages.speaker: Alessandro Guagnini, Sarmatiae Europeae descriptio (Speyer, 1581)
passages.caution: The sentence begins on the previous page ('they think it a great misfortune to stay long in one place'). The curse also appears in Herberstein, so Guagnini may be copying.

passages.headline: Proud of their Scythian descent and divided into hordes
passages.people: Tatars (Crimean, Nogai, Volga and other hordes)
passages.gloss: The opening of the work: the Tartars, though Lithuanians think them barbarous and poor, pride themselves on their restraint and on the antiquity of their 'Scythian' race, which they claim never served anyone, and are divided into hordes ('Ordas, that is, nations'). Michalo lists the Perekop (Crimean) Tatars and their Budjak neighbours, the Nogai, the Volga horde (homeland of Batu, 'once ruler of the Muscovites and all Ruthenians'), Kazan, Kazakh, Bukhara and Samarkand hordes, and links their twelve rulers to the twelve princes promised to Ishmael.
passages.quote: Etsi Tartari, barbari & inopes habeantur a nobis, gloriantur tamen continentia vitae, & antiquitate gentis suae Scythicae, asseverantes eam semen esse … nemini servivisse unquam … & varias nunc divisam in Ordas, id est, nationes.
passages.translation: Although the Tartars are held by us to be barbarous and poor, they nevertheless glory in the restraint of their life and in the antiquity of their Scythian race, asserting that it is a seed … that has never served anyone … and that it is now divided into various Hordes, that is, nations.
passages.speaker: Michalo the Lithuanian, De moribus Tartarorum, Lituanorum et Moschorum, fragment 1 (c. 1550; Basel, 1615)
passages.caution: The OCR is damaged at 'semen esse'; the omitted words are illegible.

passages.headline: Crimea's ruined Greek cities with a thousand churches
passages.people: Crimean Tatars; earlier Greek Christian inhabitants
passages.gloss: Michalo says the Crimea was once so densely peopled by Greeks that single cities had a thousand churches, and that some cities, though ruined, still show by their walls and ruins how grand they were: Solkhat (called Krym by the Muscovites and once Theodosia by the Greeks) and old Chersonesos (Korsun), where the Rus' were baptised. He is clear about who built them: the Greeks, not the Tatars, who came later as settlers.
passages.quote: Atque nunc etiam urbes ibi nonnullae quamvis pessundatae, amplitudine tamen ambituum suorum & ruinarum, superbae olim fuisse apparent, & praesertim quae a nobis Solhoth; a Moscis Krym; a Graecis Theodosia appellabatur quondam, & metropolis vetusta Korsunij, quae genti Ruthenorum princeps dedit baptisma
passages.translation: And even now some cities there, though ruined, show by the size of their circuits and of their ruins that they were once splendid, above all the one we call Solkhat, the Muscovites Krym, and the Greeks once called Theodosia, and the ancient metropolis of Korsun, which first gave baptism to the Ruthenian people
passages.speaker: Michalo the Lithuanian, De moribus Tartarorum, Lituanorum et Moschorum, fragment 1 (c. 1550; Basel, 1615)
passages.caution: Michalo confuses Solkhat (Staryi Krym) with Theodosia (Kaffa); the 'thousand churches' is a traditional boast he repeats ('it is recorded').

passages.headline: The Giray khans: a dynasty 'planted' by Lithuania
passages.gloss: Michalo claims the Crimean Christians, weak and luxurious, invited a band of Tartars from the Volga horde to defend them, and that this Tatar power grew until it took the peninsula. He adds that the Crimean khans came from Lithuania: the last, 'Aczkirei' (Haci Giray), born near Trakai and sent by Grand Duke Vytautas to rule, whose descendants all bear the name Giray. He calls the dynasty a stock 'planted there by the brave right hand of Your Majesty's ancestors' that now repays Lithuania with endless trouble.
passages.quote: Ultimus vero ex Lituania Caesarum Aczkirei, hic apud Troki natus, & hinc a divo Withowdo ad imperium illud missus, genuit imperans ibi in Taurica filium Menglikirei. … Haec igitur est Kireorum stirps, dextra forti progenitorum S. Mtis Vestrae ibi plantata
passages.translation: The last of the khans from Lithuania, Aczkirei, was born near Trakai and sent from here by the late Vytautas to that throne; ruling there in Taurica he fathered a son, Mengli Giray. … This, then, is the stock of the Girays, planted there by the strong right hand of Your Majesty's ancestors
passages.speaker: Michalo the Lithuanian, De moribus Tartarorum, Lituanorum et Moschorum, fragment 1 (c. 1550; Basel, 1615)
passages.caution: Partly true: Haci Giray, founder of the khanate, did spend time in Lithuania and had Lithuanian backing, but the claim of Lithuanian birth and appointment is a Lithuanian patriotic version.

passages.headline: No houses, only portable huts of wicker and reeds on carts
passages.place: Crimea and the Black Sea steppe
passages.gloss: Michalo describes the Tatars' pastoral life: they follow their herds across the plains, have no enclosures and no houses except portable tents made of wicker and reeds covered with felt and rush mats, which they carry on carts full of wives and children. They do not farm even rich land, live on milk without bread or beer, and own nothing fixed except wells shared by the clan.
passages.quote: Septa nulla habent, nec domos, praeter tabernacula gestatoria, ex viminibus & arundinibus compactis, cilicijs velata storeis, & mattis scirpeis munita, quae uxoribus & pueris referta, vectant secum in plaustris.
passages.translation: They have no enclosures and no houses, only portable tents of wicker and reeds joined together, covered with felts and mats and made fast with rush matting, which, filled with wives and children, they carry with them on carts.
passages.speaker: Michalo the Lithuanian, De moribus Tartarorum, Lituanorum et Moschorum, fragment 1 (c. 1550; Basel, 1615)
passages.caution: Michalo generalises; the Crimean khanate also had towns such as Bakhchysarai and Kaffa (under the Ottomans), which he mentions elsewhere.

passages.headline: Judges who are clerics, and no one carries a sword at home
passages.gloss: Michalo contrasts Tatar order with Lithuanian lawlessness: among the Tatars no one overeats and no one starves, there are no beggars, thieves, false witnesses or corrupt judges, and it is forbidden to carry a sword while travelling inside their land. Justice is given free by religious judges (qadis), with no fee taken, and everyone from nobles to commoners lives under one law and the same dress and food.
passages.quote: Unde minime opus est apud eos angi quenquam sollicita rerum suarum custodia, nec se armis onerare domi ad privatam sui defensionem. Nam iter habenti intra regionem eorum ferre telum, enorme & illicitum est.
passages.translation: So there is no need among them for anyone to worry anxiously about guarding his goods, or to load himself with weapons at home for his private defence. For it is outrageous and unlawful for anyone travelling within their land to carry a weapon.
passages.speaker: Michalo the Lithuanian, De moribus Tartarorum, Lituanorum et Moschorum, fragment 1 (c. 1550; Basel, 1615)
passages.caution: Idealised for moral contrast with Lithuania.

passages.headline: Horses never harnessed to a cart, even for the khan
passages.gloss: Tatars train to ride from the cradle and keep riding into old age, despising carriages even when ill. Michalo says even a leading woman going to the khan's court rides in a closed cart drawn by one or two oxen, glittering with gold and jewels inside, because it is forbidden to harness even the worst horse to a vehicle, though a man may own a thousand horses. He sets this against Lithuanian ladies driven in carriages drawn by six or eight horses.
passages.quote: Et mulier apud illos etiam primaria, & vel Caesaris necessaria regiam accessura, non verecundatur caveae suae obturatae reclusa, auro vel gemmis intro nitens, bove vehi uno; aut propter plaustri grossitiem duobus. Equum autem vel deterrimum iungi vehiculo, nefas est & religio cuilibet eorum
passages.translation: And among them even a woman of the first rank, even one close to the khan, going to the palace, is not ashamed to ride shut in her closed cage, gleaming inside with gold and jewels, drawn by one ox, or by two if the cart is heavy. But to yoke even the worst horse to a vehicle is sacrilege and forbidden to every one of them
passages.speaker: Michalo the Lithuanian, De moribus Tartarorum, Lituanorum et Moschorum, fragment 1 (c. 1550; Basel, 1615)

passages.headline: Kaffa, 'a whirlpool of our blood'
passages.people: Crimean Tatars and Ottoman merchants; Lithuanian and Ruthenian captives
passages.gloss: Michalo describes the sale of captives from his own country in the Crimean markets: led in chained rows of ten, auctioned by criers who shout that they are fresh, 'royal' not Muscovite slaves, stripped and checked for flaws, dressed up to fetch a better price, and resold for profit. This happens in all the peninsula's towns, 'but above all in Kaffa', whose port sends the bought captives straight onto ships. He calls Kaffa an insatiable place, a 'whirlpool of our blood'.
passages.quote: Aguntur haec & in caeteris peninsulae illius urbibus, in Caffa vero praecipue, Contigitque ibi quod globi miserorum illorum coemptorum aguntur ex mercatu ad naves recta. … situ suo insatiabilis illa … urbs sed vorago sanguinis nostri.
passages.translation: These things go on in the other towns of that peninsula too, but above all in Kaffa, and there it happens that crowds of those wretches, once bought, are driven straight from the market to the ships. … by its site that insatiable … city, but a whirlpool of our blood.
passages.speaker: Michalo the Lithuanian, De moribus Tartarorum, Lituanorum et Moschorum, fragment 1 (c. 1550; Basel, 1615)
passages.caution: Kaffa was an Ottoman-held port, not a Tatar town, by Michalo's time. One or two words before 'urbs' are illegible in the OCR (probably 'not a city but'), so they are left out.

passages.headline: A Jewish toll-keeper asks if anyone is left in Lithuania
passages.people: Crimean Tatars; Lithuanian and Ruthenian captives
passages.gloss: At Perekop, the single gate into the Crimea, Michalo met a Jewish toll collector who watched endless columns of Lithuanian captives being brought in and asked whether there were still any people left in their lands, and where so many came from. Michalo then describes how the stronger male captives were mutilated, branded and chained to work by day and locked up by night, while young women were kept for pleasure.
passages.quote: Unde Iudeus quidam ibi in Taurica ad portam eius unicam illam, teloneo praesidens & innumeram semper hominum nostrorum captivorum multitudinem importari illuc cernens, quaerebat ex nobis utrum adhuc homines in regionibus nostris supersint, nec ne, & unde hic tantae mortalium copiae.
passages.translation: So a certain Jew there in Taurica, in charge of the toll at its one and only gate, and always seeing an innumerable multitude of our people brought in as captives, asked us whether there were still any people left in our lands or not, and where so great a supply of mortals came from.
passages.speaker: Michalo the Lithuanian, De moribus Tartarorum, Lituanorum et Moschorum, fragment 1 (c. 1550; Basel, 1615)

passages.headline: Eighty blows for a taste of wine
passages.gloss: Attacking drunkenness in Lithuania, Michalo says more Lithuanians are executed for theft and robbery in a single month in one district than in one or two hundred years across all the Tatar and Muscovite lands where drink is forbidden. Among the Tatars, anyone who so much as tastes wine gets eighty blows with a stick and a fine of as many coins.
passages.quote: Certe apud Tartaros, qui modo vinum gustaverit, is & octoginta fustuarijs ictibus percutitur, & totidem nummis multatur.
passages.translation: Certainly among the Tartars, whoever has merely tasted wine is struck eighty blows with the cudgel and fined as many coins.
passages.speaker: Michalo the Lithuanian, De moribus Tartarorum, Lituanorum et Moschorum, fragment 3 (c. 1550; Basel, 1615)
passages.caution: Eighty lashes is the Islamic penalty for drinking; Michalo states the law, not a case he saw.

passages.headline: Forty brothers, one father: polygamy and a Tatar village
passages.place: Crimea; a Tatar village on the Vaka river (Lithuania)
passages.gloss: Michalo argues that polygamy is why the Perekop Tatars, so often slaughtered by the Lithuanians, keep springing back. He cites a troop of forty full brothers in the army of Sultan Islam Giray, all sons of one Omeldesz by wives and concubines within little more than a year, and a Tatar village on the Vaka river in Lithuania still called 'Forty Tartars', that is, forty brothers. He adds that both Tatars and Muscovites keep their women without freedom.
passages.quote: haec multitudo uxorum facit ut vicini nostri Tartari Precopenses toties a nobis ad internecionem caesi, rursum repullulascant. nec ita pridem in copijs Oslam Soltani fuerunt 40. fratres collectanei eius, cuiusdam Omeldesz 40. filij simul
passages.translation: this multitude of wives is why our neighbours the Perekop Tartars, so often cut down by us to the last man, spring up again. Not long ago in the forces of Sultan Islam there were forty brothers, his comrades, forty sons at once of a certain Omeldesz
passages.speaker: Michalo the Lithuanian, De moribus Tartarorum, Lituanorum et Moschorum, fragment 7 (c. 1550; Basel, 1615)

passages.headline: The Tatars' mocking war cry: 'John, you sleep, I tie you up'
passages.gloss: Michalo complains that Lithuanian soldiers idle in taverns while Muscovite and Tatar frontier troops stand watch in turns, and that the Tatars mock Lithuanian carelessness with a well-known jibe: 'John, you sleep; I am binding you.' He adds that Lithuania even pays yearly gifts to the Perekop khan.
passages.quote: taxant hanc nostram supinam securitatem, hostes nostri Tartari, usitato suo scommate, cum nos post comessationes somno sepultos, his secum verbis invadunt: Iohannes tu dormis, ego te vinciens
passages.translation: our enemies the Tartars mock this lazy carelessness of ours with their usual jibe, falling upon us when we lie buried in sleep after our feasting, with these words: 'John, you sleep; I, tying you up...'
passages.speaker: Michalo the Lithuanian, De moribus Tartarorum, Lituanorum et Moschorum, fragment 8 (c. 1550; Basel, 1615)
passages.caution: The jibe ends on the next page (n36, p. 30) with 'laboro' ('I am at work tying you up'); the quote stops at the page break.

passages.headline: Tatar religion: one God, Christ a prophet, prayer morning to night
passages.gloss: Michalo summarises Tatar Islam as a Christian of his day understood it: a law shared with the Turks and other 'Saracens', professing one simple God, Christ as holy prophet and final judge born of a virgin but not crucified, and circumcision at the age Ishmael was circumcised. On the next page he praises their prayer morning, afternoon and evening, their fasting and their alms, and says they laugh at Christian fasts and churches.
passages.quote: Deum unicum & simplicem profitetur, Christum vero, sanctum Prophetam & iudicem mundi postremum, Virgine pura natum, sed non passum credit. Circumcisionem observat.
passages.translation: It professes one simple God, and believes Christ to be a holy Prophet and the last judge of the world, born of a pure Virgin, but not to have suffered. It observes circumcision.
passages.speaker: Michalo the Lithuanian, De moribus Tartarorum, Lituanorum et Moschorum, fragment 10 (c. 1550; Basel, 1615)

passages.headline: Kazan and Astrakhan fall to Ivan IV
passages.people: Tartars of Kazan and Astrakhan (the Kazan and Astrakhan khanates)
passages.gloss: Possevino sums up how Ivan IV took the two Tatar khanates on the Volga. The king of Poland told him the Kazan Tatars were easy to storm because they were unused to bronze cannon. Astrakhan, 'no mean emporium of the East' on the Caspian, is called the capital of another Tartar Horde or kingdom, and its fall carried Muscovite rule to the Circassians.
passages.quote: vlcisci Tartarorum iniurias, & pedem figere in Liuonia statuit. Casanenses adortus, admotis æneis tormẽtis, facilè fuit ei (vt Stephanus Poloniæ Rex mihi narrauit) siue armorum, seu machinarum generi insuetos expugnare. Inde Astracanum ad ostia fluuij Volgæ situm cœpit, non ignobile Orientis emporium ad mare Caspium. Id cùm alterius Tartarorum Hordæ (seu Regni) esset caput; protulit ditionis suæ fines vsq; ad Circassos
passages.translation: He resolved to avenge the wrongs done by the Tartars and to set foot in Livonia. Attacking the people of Kazan with bronze cannon brought up, it was easy for him (as Stephen, King of Poland, told me) to storm men unused to that kind of arms or engines. Then he took Astrakhan, set at the mouths of the Volga, no mean emporium of the East on the Caspian Sea. Since it was the capital of another Horde (or kingdom) of the Tartars, he pushed the bounds of his realm as far as the Circassians.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR garbled); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Antonio Possevino, S.J. (Moscovia, Vilnius 1586)
passages.caution: Possevino arrived 30 years after these conquests; the Kazan detail is second-hand from Stephen Bathory.

passages.headline: Every Horde has one chief city
passages.people: Kazan and Astrakhan Tatars; Crimean ('Precop') Tatars
passages.gloss: An informant Possevino calls only 'N.' explains why Moscow could swallow Kazan and Astrakhan but not Crimea. The tsar's gunners fired from behind thick perforated planks fixed to carts, and each Tartar Horde had a single chief city or gathering place: take it and the rest submits. It is a neat description of the horde as a people centred on one capital.
passages.quote: Cum enim (dicebat) Moscus aduersùs illos, quos edomuit, Tartaros, maximis tormentis adductis, crassos etiam asseres perforatos curribus præfigi iussisset, per quos Pyxidarij bombardas suas exonerabant, certa hostium pernicie, ipsi à nemine læsi: facilè fuit nouo armorum genere circumuentos opprimere; præterquàm quòd cùm vniuscuiusque Tartarorum Hordæ primaria vna (vt dixi) ciuitas sit, seu conuentus, quo deuicto, reliqua omnia sine difficultate in potestatem veniant.
passages.translation: For (he said) the Muscovite, against those Tartars he subdued, brought up very large cannon and had thick planks with holes in them fixed to carts, through which the musketeers fired their guns, to the sure ruin of the enemy while they themselves were hurt by no one: so it was easy to overwhelm men caught by a new kind of arms; besides which, since each Horde of the Tartars has one chief city (as I said), or gathering place, once that is conquered everything else comes under his power without difficulty.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR garbled); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Antonio Possevino, S.J. (Moscovia, Vilnius 1586), reporting an unnamed informant 'N.'
passages.caution: Hearsay from an unnamed adviser Possevino consulted before his journey.

passages.headline: Moscow shrunk after the Tartar fire of 1571
passages.people: Crimean Tatars (the raid of Khan Devlet Giray)
passages.gloss: Possevino, who saw Moscow himself, says it had been larger and more crowded under the same tsar until the Tartars burned it 'in the seventieth year of this century', killing most of the inhabitants. Traces of the old, larger circuit were still visible, and the city now filled barely five miles round. He means the Crimean Tatar sack of Moscow in 1571.
passages.quote: Et erat sanè eodem hoc Principe augustior, ac numerosior Moscua, sed anno præsentis seculi septuagesimo à Tartaris cõcremata, incolis plerisq; incendio absumptis, res omnis in angustiores terminos adducta est. Extant vestigia maioris circuitus; vt qui octo, vel nouem fortasse fuisset, iam vix quinq; millia passuum impleat
passages.translation: And Moscow was indeed grander and more populous under this same prince, but in the seventieth year of the present century it was burned down by the Tartars, most of its inhabitants consumed by the fire, and everything was reduced to narrower bounds. Traces of a larger circuit remain, so that what was perhaps eight or nine miles round now scarcely fills five thousand paces.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR garbled); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Antonio Possevino, S.J. (Moscovia, Vilnius 1586)
passages.caution: He gives the year as 1570; the raid was in May 1571. The damage and population figures are his estimates.

passages.headline: Walls rebuilt after the Tartar fire, a Kremlin by Italians
passages.gloss: Possevino classifies Muscovite fortresses: some of stone and brick, some of earth banks woven with wicker and rammed hard, some of squared timbers filled with earth. Moscow's outer wall of the wattle and earth kind was put up after 'the Tartar fire', while the two stone citadels of Moscow were built for Ivan's father Vasily by a Milanese architect with Italian workmen. Here the Tartars burn, and Italians build.
passages.quote: Aliæ ex saxis, et lateribus, quales duæ sunt, quæ ciuitati Moscuæ hærent … Aliæ aggeribus vimine contextis, & ad duritiem pressis: quale Smolencium est, ipsiusq; Moscuæ mœnium ambitus, post Tartaricum incendium excitatus. … Arces autem Moscuæ duas Principis huius parens Basilius ædificari iussit, Mediolanense architecto, Italis operarijs.
passages.translation: Some are of stones and bricks, like the two that adjoin the city of Moscow ... Others are of earth banks woven with wicker and pressed hard: such is Smolensk, and the circuit of the walls of Moscow itself, raised after the Tartar fire. ... The two citadels of Moscow were ordered built by this prince's father Vasily, with a Milanese architect and Italian workmen.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR garbled); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Antonio Possevino, S.J. (Moscovia, Vilnius 1586)
passages.caution: The attribution of the Kremlin works to Italian masters is broadly right, though Possevino compresses the history (much was done under Ivan III as well as Vasily III).

passages.headline: Raids that emptied the countryside
passages.gloss: Explaining why Muscovy seemed half empty, Possevino lists plague, wars and the constant Tartar raids, including the burning of the capital twelve years earlier. Abandoned ploughland and young forest showed where people had once lived, while the north stayed well peopled because the Tartars never raided there. He checked this with Italian and Spanish captives freed through him who had walked across the country.
passages.quote: Tartarorumq; continentes excursiones, ipsaq; ab ijsdem ante duodecim annos combusta Regia … At verò dedolati agri, & recentes Syluæ, quæ passim succreuerunt, indicia sunt frequentiorum anteà incolarum: licèt quæ regiones supra Moscuam versùs Septentrionem vergunt, eæ admodùm frequentes incolas habeant, quòd excursiones illuc Tartari non fecerint, & salubriore cœlo fruantur
passages.translation: ... and the continual raids of the Tartars, and the capital itself burned by them twelve years ago ... But the abandoned fields, and the young woods that have grown up everywhere, are signs of formerly more numerous inhabitants: although the regions that lie north of Moscow have a fairly dense population, because the Tartars have not raided there, and they enjoy a healthier climate.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR garbled); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Antonio Possevino, S.J. (Moscovia, Vilnius 1586)
passages.caution: Part observation, part report from freed Italian and Spanish captives; war with Poland and famine also emptied the land.

passages.headline: Muscovites 'descended from Scythians and Tartars'
passages.people: Muscovites; Tartars as their supposed ancestors and former overlords
passages.gloss: In a hostile character sketch of the Muscovites, Possevino claims that most of them descend from or are mixed with Scythians and Tartars, which in his view explains their cunning and suspicion. He adds that the grand princes' pride grew from the time they freed themselves from the Tartars, 'whose tributaries they had been'. This is Counter-Reformation polemic, not ethnography.
passages.quote: Ea in Schytis, & Tartaris perspicuè cernuntur, ex quibus cùm pleriq; Moscorum originem ducant, aut constent, mirum non est, quòd hactenus naturam illam non exuerint, quam pietas in alijs nationibus excoluit, ac vicit. … Quæ tria cùm in Magnis Moscouiæ Ducibus ab eo potissimùm tempore fuerint, quo se à Tartaris, quorum erant tributarij, in libertatem asseruerunt
passages.translation: These things are plainly seen in the Scythians and Tartars, from whom most of the Muscovites take their origin or of whom they are made up, so it is no wonder they have not yet put off that nature which piety has refined and overcome in other nations. ... Since these three things have been in the Grand Dukes of Muscovy above all from the time when they freed themselves from the Tartars, whose tributaries they had been
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR garbled); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Antonio Possevino, S.J. (Moscovia, Vilnius 1586)
passages.caution: A prejudiced generalisation; 'Scythians and Tartars' is a stock label for steppe peoples, not a genealogy he could check.

passages.headline: 'Czar' is a Tartar word, not 'Caesar'
passages.people: Muscovite envoys; the Kazan and Astrakhan khanates as sources of the title
passages.gloss: At the peace talks Possevino mediated, the Muscovite envoys begged that their master be styled 'Czar of Kazan and Astrakhan'. Possevino replied that Kazan and Astrakhan were not important enough to add a new imperial title, and that if the emperor allowed it, it should be understood that 'Czar' did not mean Caesar but a royal title 'used by the Tartars'. A few pages on (n166) the Polish side refuse to call a Christian prince by 'a Tartar or Turkish title, like that Tartar Czar'.
passages.quote: vt ille Czar Casani, & Astracani diceretur … non esse tantam rem Casanum, & Astracanum, vt nouus titulus quasi alterius Cæsaris, Imperatoris, vel Regis addatur. Si Cæsar id fecerit, sciri vocem istam Czar non Cæsarem, sed aliquid aliud à Tartaris vsurpatum, quasi Regium titulum designari.
passages.translation: that he be called Czar of Kazan and Astrakhan ... Kazan and Astrakhan were not so great a matter that a new title, as of another Caesar, Emperor or King, should be added. If the Emperor did it, it should be known that the word Czar does not mean Caesar, but something else used by the Tartars, signifying a kind of royal title.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR garbled); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Antonio Possevino, S.J. (Moscovia, Vilnius 1586) (minutes of the peace congress)
passages.caution: Possevino's etymology serves his argument; the Russian title tsar does derive ultimately from Caesar, though Muscovites also used it for the Tatar khans.

passages.headline: Crimean guides who led a Turkish army to starve
passages.gloss: Asked how the Muscovites had inflicted a great defeat on the Turks when a river diversion was attempted, Possevino's informant said it was not the Muscovites but the Crimean Tatars who did it. Though allies of the Turks, they feared a heavier yoke if the scheme succeeded, so they offered themselves as guides and led the Turkish troops through vast forests and foodless country until nearly all died of hunger and toil.
passages.quote: cladem Moscus intulisset, cùm Tanaim deriuari iussisset in Boristhenem: respondit, hoc non à Moscis, sed à Tartaris Præcopensibus, licèt Turcarum fœderatis, accidisse, ægrè ferentibus id fieri, vnde grauius sibi iugum pendere prospicerent. Quamobrem cùm sese duces itineris Copijs Turcicis exhibuissent, per ingentes syluas, & loca commeatus egena, eas circumduxisse, vt fame, ac labore pleræq; omnes fermè interierint.
passages.translation: ... the Muscovite had inflicted [so great a defeat on the Turks], when he had ordered the Don to be diverted into the Borysthenes: he answered that this was done not by the Muscovites but by the Precop Tartars, though allies of the Turks, who resented the scheme because they foresaw a heavier yoke hanging over them. So, offering themselves as guides to the Turkish forces, they led them round through huge forests and places without supplies, so that almost all of them perished of hunger and toil.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR garbled); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Antonio Possevino, S.J. (Moscovia, Vilnius 1586), reporting an unnamed informant 'N.'
passages.caution: Hearsay. The river named is garbled: the real 1569 Ottoman plan was a Don to Volga canal to reach Astrakhan (a reader of this copy wrote 'Volgam' in the margin).

passages.headline: A Tartar emperor in Asia who keeps Christian rites
passages.people: 'Cham, emperor of the Tartars in Asia'
passages.gloss: The same informant adds that the 'Cham', emperor of the Tartars in Asia, lives not far from the Circassians and still keeps many Christian rites because his people were once converted. This is an echo of the medieval Prester John and Christian khan legends, repeated as current news.
passages.quote: Adiecit autem, Cham, Tartarorum in Asia Imperatorem, non procul ab ea gente abesse, qui multum adhuc rituum Christianorum retineat, cũ olim ad fidem nostram accesserint.
passages.translation: He added, moreover, that the Cham, Emperor of the Tartars in Asia, is not far from that people, and still keeps much of the Christian rites, since they once came over to our faith.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR garbled); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Antonio Possevino, S.J. (Moscovia, Vilnius 1586), reporting an unnamed informant 'N.'
passages.caution: Rumour with no named ruler or place; by 1580 no Christian 'Cham' ruled near the Caucasus.

passages.headline: Muslim Tatars in the streets of Vilnius
passages.gloss: In a polemical letter to King Stephen Bathory, Possevino points to Vilnius, capital of Lithuania, where the king could see on one side 'faithless Tartars' and schismatic Ruthenians and heretics of many kinds, and on the other many Catholics. The Tartars are 'faithless' because they follow Muhammad. It is a glimpse of the settled Muslim Tatar community of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.
passages.quote: Venisti non ita pridem ad hanc ciuitatem Lituaniæ caput. Hic vides ex altera parte perfidos Tartaros & schismaticos Ruthenos, ac varia hæreticorum genera, ipsos autem ex altera parte Catholicos plurimos. Et Tartari quidem, quoniam Mahometem sectantur, Rutheni autem quoniam cum schismate multos errores hauserunt
passages.translation: You came not long ago to this city, the capital of Lithuania. Here you see on one side faithless Tartars and schismatic Ruthenians, and various kinds of heretics, and on the other side very many Catholics. And the Tartars indeed because they follow Muhammad, the Ruthenians because with their schism they have drunk in many errors
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Antonio Possevino, S.J., letter to the King of Poland (Moscovia et alia opera, Cologne 1587)
passages.caution: Religious polemic; it tells us Tatars were a visible Muslim group in Vilnius, not how they lived.

passages.headline: Mud and dung huts in winter, round houses on carts in summer
passages.gloss: Broniewski, the Polish envoy who spent nine months in the Crimean khanate, describes Tatar winter villages called 'ulus': huts of very thin wood daubed with mud and animal dung and roofed with reed. In April the Tatars leave them with wives, children and slaves, carrying round felt-covered houses that barely hold four or five people on two-wheeled carts drawn by camels or oxen, and return in October.
passages.quote: tugurijs Tartaricis, quæ vulgo vlnsi à Barbaris nominantur, ac vt pagi ex tenuissimis lignis, limo vel cœno stercoribusque pecorum seu animalium obliti, facti, & arundine tecti sunt … Verùm æstate & in autumno Tartari in eis tugurijs non degunt, nam in Aprili cum vxoribus, liberis, familia, mancipijs ac domibus, quæ rotundæ penulis obsitæ quatuor vel quinque hominibus ad degendum vix commodæ sunt, & in carris rotis duabus sustentatis … vehũtur.
passages.translation: Tartar huts, which the barbarians commonly call 'vlnsi' (evidently ulus, a misprint), made like villages of very thin wood, plastered with mud or muck and the dung of cattle or animals, and roofed with reed ... But in summer and autumn the Tartars do not live in these huts, for in April, with wives, children, household and slaves, they are carried with their houses, which are round, covered with penulae (felt coverings), and scarcely roomy enough for four or five people to live in, on carts resting on two wheels ...
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR garbled); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Marcin Broniewski (Martin Broniovius), Tartariae descriptio (written 1579), printed in the 1595 Cologne edition of Possevino's Moscovia

passages.headline: Bakhchisaray: a stone palace, and mosques built from Christian ruins
passages.gloss: The khan lives in a stone house in Bakhchisaray, a town between two mountains with a small river through it. Broniewski says the stone mosque and the khans' tombs were built from the ruins of Christian buildings. Next to it lies the town of Salachik, and a palace of the khans that, he says, the early Tatar princes adorned with buildings, mosques, tombs and baths. So he credits Tatars as builders, reusing older stone.
passages.quote: Oppidum non ignobile, & domum lapideam primariam, in qua ille semper residet, Baccasaraium nuncupatam ille habet. … Mahometicum templum lapideũ, & sepulturę Chanorum ex ruinis Christianorum penes oppidum exstructæ sunt. … Chanorum Regia vel domus à priscis Tartarorum Principibus sumptuosè ædificijs, templis, sepulturis, & balneis magnificè exornata est.
passages.translation: He has a not undistinguished town, and a principal stone house in which he always lives, called Bakhchisaray. ... A stone Muslim temple and the tombs of the khans have been built near the town out of the ruins of the Christians. ... The palace or house of the khans was sumptuously and magnificently adorned by the early princes of the Tartars with buildings, temples, tombs and baths.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR garbled); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Marcin Broniewski (Martin Broniovius), Tartariae descriptio (written 1579), printed in the 1595 Cologne edition of Possevino's Moscovia
passages.caution: The claim about Christian ruins is his reading of reused stone; he did not see the building work.

passages.headline: Crim, the old city that gave the Crimean Tatars their name
passages.gloss: Crim had a very old, high wall and many ancient mosques inside and outside the town with Arabic ('Chaldaic') inscriptions carved in large stones. Tatar and Turkish residents told him their ancestors remembered that Persians had once lived there, and that it had been the leading workshop of the mechanical arts. The ruins showed a once famous city, and he notes that the Tatars are now commonly called 'Crimean' after it.
passages.quote: Nam templa seu delubra antiqua Mahometica non solùm in Ciuitate ipsa, verùm & vltra ciuitatem plurima admodũ cum Characteribus Chaldaicis in grãdioribus saxis excisis conspiciuntur. Turcę seu Tartari nõ pauci admodũ incolę, Gręci tamen rariores hoc referũt, quod maiores sui constanter meminerint, eã ciuitatem à Persarum olim gente inhabitatam, præstantem ac primariam ferè officinam Mechanicarum artium quondam eam extitisse. … Tartari ab eo loco Crimenses vulgò nunc appellantur.
passages.translation: For very many ancient Muslim temples or shrines, with Chaldaic characters cut into rather large stones, are seen not only in the city itself but beyond it. Quite a few Turkish or Tartar inhabitants, though fewer Greeks, report that their forefathers constantly remembered that the city was once inhabited by a people of Persians, and was once an outstanding and almost the chief workshop of the mechanical arts. ... From this place the Tartars are now commonly called Crimean.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR garbled); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Marcin Broniewski (Martin Broniovius), Tartariae descriptio (written 1579), printed in the 1595 Cologne edition of Possevino's Moscovia
passages.caution: The 'Persian' founders are local oral tradition; 'Chaldaic' is Broniewski's word for Arabic script.

passages.headline: Ruined castles and cities credited to the Greeks
passages.people: Crimean Tatars (present), ancient Greeks and earlier peoples (builders)
passages.gloss: Broniewski notes very deep wells cut by the old Greeks or the ancient peoples who lived in Crimea before them, and frequent, very large Greek ruins of castles, cities, churches and monasteries in the mountains and forests. They had stood empty so long that their names were lost. He does not credit these ruins to the Tatars.
passages.quote: fontes seu putei altissimi mira profunditate & difficultate à veteribus Græcis seu populis illis antiquissimis & maximis, qui eam Peninsulam ante Græcorum tempora incolebant, quondam excisi & facti … arcium, ciuitatum, templorũ, monasteriorumq; antiquissimæ & maximæ Græcæ ruinæ frequentissimæ admodum reperiuntur, quæ cum multo sęculo habitatoribus caruêre propter antiquitatem temporũ cognomina sua amiserũt.
passages.translation: very deep wells, of wonderful depth and difficulty, cut and made long ago by the ancient Greeks or by those very ancient and great peoples who inhabited the peninsula before the time of the Greeks ... very ancient and very large Greek ruins of castles, cities, churches and monasteries are found very frequently; having lacked inhabitants for many ages, they have lost their names through the antiquity of the times.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR garbled); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Marcin Broniewski (Martin Broniovius), Tartariae descriptio (written 1579), printed in the 1595 Cologne edition of Possevino's Moscovia
passages.caution: 'Greek' covers Byzantine, Gothic and Genoese remains; he guesses builders from style and local lore.

passages.headline: Kurgans on the steppe: battle markers or tombs
passages.place: Steppe between the Southern Bug and Dniester
passages.people: Unknown builders; Tatars and Cossacks roam the area
passages.gloss: Crossing the steppe toward Ochakiv, Broniewski saw very high, large and numerous mounds called 'mogily'. Most people, he says, hold that they mark great and bloody battles or are the tombs of famous men, which he thinks reasonable. He does not say the Tatars built them.
passages.quote: Cozles seu tumuli vulgò Mogilij dicti altissimi maximi & frequentissimi maximorum ac cruentissimorum, vt plurimi asserunt, ac verisimile, rationiq; consonum videtur, quondam bellorum certissima signa; seu illustrium virorum sepulturæ cõspiciuntur.
passages.translation: Mounds or tumuli, commonly called mogily, very high, very large and very numerous, are seen, which, as most people assert, and as seems likely and consistent with reason, are the surest signs of once very great and very bloody battles, or the tombs of illustrious men.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR garbled); long s normalized
