passages.speaker: Marcin Broniewski (Martin Broniovius), Tartariae descriptio (written 1579), printed in the 1595 Cologne edition of Possevino's Moscovia
passages.caution: Explanation from common opinion; most such kurgans are much older burial mounds.

passages.headline: Millet porridge, mare's milk and distilled spirit
passages.gloss: Most Tatars, Broniewski says, neither plough nor sow but live from horses, camels, cattle and sheep. The nobles have bread, meat, distilled spirit and mead; the ordinary people have no bread but eat pounded millet mixed with milk and water, called 'cassa', and drink mare's milk and eat cheese. Worn-out camels, horses and oxen are slaughtered for meat.
passages.quote: plurimi etiam agros non colunt, nec serunt, equis, camelis, bobus, vaccis, pecoribus & ouibus abundant, ac inde victitant. Nobiliores tamen panem, carnes, cibum, vinum crematum & mulsum potum habent, agrestiores verò pane carent, verùm milio concusso, lacte & aqua diluto, quem cassa vulgo nominant, pro cibo, pro potu lacte equino & caseo vtuntur.
passages.translation: many do not till fields or sow, but abound in horses, camels, oxen, cows, cattle and sheep, and live from them. The nobles, however, have bread, meat, food, burnt wine and mead to drink; the rustics lack bread, but use pounded millet diluted with milk and water, which they commonly call cassa, for food, and mare's milk and cheese for drink.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR garbled); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Marcin Broniewski (Martin Broniovius), Tartariae descriptio (written 1579), printed in the 1595 Cologne edition of Possevino's Moscovia

passages.headline: Wooden houses 'in the Turkish style', and crafts left to slaves and foreigners
passages.people: Crimean Tatars; Christian slaves, Turks, Armenians, Jews, Circassians, Roma
passages.gloss: The Tatars build wooden houses much in the Turkish manner, but they themselves very rarely practise crafts. Whatever merchants or artisans are found in the towns are Christian slaves or Turks, Armenians, Jews, Circassians and Roma. Fields are worked by captive Hungarians, Russians, Muscovites and Moldavians. This is a direct statement of who built and made things in the khanate.
passages.quote: Aedificia & domus ligneas similes admodum Turcico more ædificant … mechanicas autem artes rarissimi exercent, & quicunq; mercatores vel artifices ibi reperiuntur, vel Christianorum mancipia, vel Turcæ, Armeni, Iudæi, Cercesij, Petigorenses, qui Christiani sunt, Phylistini vel Cyngani obscurę & extremæ conditionis homines sunt.
passages.translation: They build wooden buildings and houses very much in the Turkish manner ... but they very rarely practise the mechanical arts, and whatever merchants or artisans are found there are either Christian slaves, or Turks, Armenians, Jews, Circassians, Piatigorians who are Christians, 'Philistines' or Gypsies, men of obscure and the lowest condition.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR garbled); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Marcin Broniewski (Martin Broniovius), Tartariae descriptio (written 1579), printed in the 1595 Cologne edition of Possevino's Moscovia
passages.caution: A diplomat's generalisation; it ignores Tatar artisans who certainly existed in towns like Bakhchisaray.

passages.headline: Muslims who learned letters and law from the Turks
passages.gloss: The Crimean Tatars are Muslims with mullahs and mosques and write in Arabic letters, somewhat cruder than the Turks'. Broniewski believes that before they came into Crimea they were a wild steppe people without Muslim laws, letters or customs, and that the nobles learned 'civility' and the faith from the Turks.
passages.quote: Tartari illi Mahometani sunt, presbyteros & templa Mahometica habent, literis Chaldaicis vel Arabicis à Turcis paulò corruptioribus vel rudioribus illi vtuntur, etsi antequam in Tauricam seu Peninsulam venerant, moribus multo agrestioribus gens ea fera & campestris … fuisse videntur: nam illis Mahometicis legibus, iuribus, litteris & moribus illa tum prorsus caruit.
passages.translation: Those Tartars are Muslims; they have priests and Muslim temples, and use Chaldaic or Arabic letters, somewhat more corrupt or rougher than the Turks', although before they came into Taurica or the peninsula that wild steppe people seems to have had much ruder manners ... for it then wholly lacked those Muslim laws, rights, letters and customs.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR garbled); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Marcin Broniewski (Martin Broniovius), Tartariae descriptio (written 1579), printed in the 1595 Cologne edition of Possevino's Moscovia
passages.caution: His view of their earlier 'wildness' is a guess, not something he could observe; the Golden Horde had adopted Islam long before.

passages.headline: Nine months without hearing of a single lawsuit
passages.gloss: Justice follows Muslim law: cadis judge in the towns, beys in the villages, and the khan with his council decides capital and property cases. Even the poorest Tatar or foreigner can put his case to the khan in person without lawyers or delays. Broniewski says that in more than nine months there he never heard of a criminal or civil case or a feud among them.
passages.quote: Extremæ enim conditionis Tartari vel peregrini homines coram Iudicibus & Chano ipso, à quo semper audiuntur, & celeriter expediuntur, iniurias suas ipsi per se liberè admodum exponunt … Mensibus amplius nouem ibi ego mansi, nec audiui prorsus aliquem actum criminalem, nec ciuilem inter eos contigisse, nec inimicitiarum causa compositionem aliquam obtigisse.
passages.translation: For Tartars of the lowest condition, or foreigners, set out their wrongs quite freely by themselves before the judges and the khan himself, by whom they are always heard and quickly dispatched ... I stayed there more than nine months, and never heard that any criminal or civil action had taken place among them, nor any settlement made on account of feuds.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR garbled); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Marcin Broniewski (Martin Broniovius), Tartariae descriptio (written 1579), printed in the 1595 Cologne edition of Possevino's Moscovia
passages.caution: An envoy kept under escort saw little of daily disputes; the praise also serves as a rebuke to his own society.

passages.headline: Descendants of Chinggis, come from the Volga
passages.people: Crimean Tatars and their Giray khans
passages.gloss: Broniewski says the Tatars moved gradually into the steppe between the Don and the Dnieper and reached Crimea about 160 years before his time. Their khans were anciently called the 'Cyngisson' line (descendants of Chinggis Khan), all tracing descent from one khan he calls Lochtonus, the first ruler of Crimea. On the previous page he says these Crimean or Perekop Tatars sprang from and were named after the Volga (Rha).
passages.quote: Porrò inter celebratissimos, altissimos & maximos Tanaim seu Donum & Boristhenẽ Septentrionis fluuios in campos paulatim progressos fuisse, ab annis verò centum sexaginta, vel paulo amplius in Tauricam seu peninsulam eos peruenisse manifestè apparet. … Chanorum vel Principum Tartarorum illorum Cyngissonum genus antiquitus nuncupatum fuit, ex quo Lochtonus quispiam Chanus, à quo vniuersi Chani ortum trahunt.
passages.translation: Further, it is clear that they advanced gradually into the plains between the very famous, deep and great northern rivers Tanais or Don and Borysthenes, and reached Taurica or the peninsula a hundred and sixty years ago or a little more. ... The line of the khans or princes of those Tartars was anciently called the Cyngissons, from which came a certain khan Lochtonus, from whom all the khans take their origin.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR garbled); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Marcin Broniewski (Martin Broniovius), Tartariae descriptio (written 1579), printed in the 1595 Cologne edition of Possevino's Moscovia
passages.caution: 'Lochtonus' is a garbled name (probably Toqtamish); the dates are approximate lore.

passages.headline: Hordes that deserve to be called portable cities
passages.gloss: Crossing the desert beyond the Great Wall at Xining on the way to Lhasa, Grueber and Dorville found it inhabited at set seasons by 'Tartars whom they call Kalmuk', camped along rivers where pasture was best, in hordes 'which not unfittingly deserve to be called portable cities'. The same Tartars roamed the desert as raiders, so caravans needed a strong armed escort.
passages.quote: Hoc desertum quamtumvis squalidum sit, à Tartaris tamen, quos Kalmuk vocant, constitutis anni temporibus, ubi ad ripas fluminum major pascuorum copia est, per hordas quæ portatiles non incongruè civitates dici merentur, habitatur; Tartaris desertum hinc indè longè latéque latrocinandi causâ divagantibus; undè ad Tartarorum insultantium violentiam propulsandam valida manu Caravanam instructam esse oportet.
passages.translation: This desert, however squalid it may be, is nevertheless inhabited at fixed times of the year by the Tartars whom they call Kalmuk, along the banks of the rivers where there is more pasture, in hordes which not unfittingly deserve to be called portable cities; the Tartars roam the desert far and wide here and there for the sake of robbery, so a caravan must be equipped with a strong force to repel the violence of the attacking Tartars.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR partly garbled); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Athanasius Kircher, S.J. (China illustrata, Amsterdam 1667), from the oral report and drawings of Johann Grueber and Albert Dorville
passages.caution: Kircher never travelled; he writes up what Grueber told him and drew. 'Kalmuk' here means the Oirat Mongols then dominant around Kokonor.

passages.headline: The Kalmyk tent: folding sticks inside, rough wool outside
passages.gloss: Describing Grueber's engraving of a Kalmyk dwelling (Figure A), Kircher explains the felt tent: a framework of small folding rods inside, covered outside with a coarse woollen material bound with ropes. This is the yurt, with its collapsible lattice wall, as reported by an eyewitness.
passages.quote: Habitationem eorum Figura A. exprimit, estque tentorium Tartaricum intrinsecùs ex parvis plicatilibus bacillis confectum, exterius verò rudi ex certæ lanæ materia funibusque constricta contectum.
passages.translation: Figure A shows their dwelling: it is a Tartar tent made on the inside of small folding rods, and covered on the outside with a rough material of a kind of wool, bound tight with ropes.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR partly garbled); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Athanasius Kircher, S.J. (China illustrata, Amsterdam 1667), from the oral report and drawings of Johann Grueber and Albert Dorville
passages.caution: Based on Grueber's sketch and account; the engraving was redrawn in Amsterdam.

passages.headline: A living god in Lhasa, and relics made of his excrement
passages.gloss: Kircher says traces of the famous Prester John survive in the 'Tanchut' kingdom that the Tartars call Barantola and the locals Lassa (Lhasa). There are two kings there: one governs, the other, the Grand Lama, sits hidden in his palace and is worshipped as God the Father, so much that people believe even his dung cures all ills. The Jesuits were refused access to him and drew only his portrait.
passages.quote: Sunt & in hoc Regno duo Reges, prior administrationi Regni totius incumbit; alter, quem & Deum patrem sive cœlestem, aut etiam Magnum Lamam, sive sacrificulorum Pontificem vocant, in ultimis Palatii sui recessibus Numinis instar residens, ab omnibus divini cultus recipit cerimonias; tantoque eum in honore habent, ut vel ipsius sordes & excrementa ad omnes infirmitatum adversitates plurimum conducere stultè sibi persuadeant
passages.translation: There are also two kings in this kingdom: the first attends to the administration of the whole kingdom; the other, whom they call God the Father or heavenly Father, or else the Great Lama, or high priest of the sacrificers, lives like a deity in the innermost recesses of his palace and receives the ceremonies of divine worship from all; and they hold him in such honour that they foolishly persuade themselves that even his filth and excrement are of great help against every kind of illness.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR partly garbled); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Athanasius Kircher, S.J. (China illustrata, Amsterdam 1667), from the oral report and drawings of Johann Grueber and Albert Dorville
passages.caution: Hostile missionary framing; the Prester John link is Kircher's own speculation, and the excrement relics are hearsay the Jesuits did not see.

passages.headline: Beijing burned by a rebel, rebuilt by the Tartars in four years
passages.gloss: Explaining that Chinese houses and palaces are almost all of wood and burn easily, Kircher cites Beijing: at the start of the Tartar invasion a rebel and tyrant (Li Zicheng) set it on fire for four days, but the Tartars, meaning the conquering Manchus, restored it to its former dignity with four years of building. Here the 'Tartars' are the rebuilders of a capital.
passages.quote: ut quemadmodum omnia ex ligno ferè constructa sunt, ita quoque incendio alicubi exorto nisi obstetur, integræ sæpè urbes exiguo temporis spatio in cineres rediguntur; uti Pekino accidit, quæ urbs post Nankingum omnium vastissima à Rebelle & Tyranno ad initium irruptionis Tartarorum quadriduano incendio consumpta fuit, à Tartaris tamen quadriennali fabricatione in pristinum dignitatis statum restituta.
passages.translation: since almost everything is built of wood, if a fire breaks out somewhere and is not checked, whole cities are often reduced to ashes in a short time; as happened to Peking, the vastest of all cities after Nanking, which at the beginning of the invasion of the Tartars was consumed in a four-day fire by a rebel and tyrant, but was restored by the Tartars to its former dignity by four years of building.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR partly garbled); long s normalized
passages.speaker: Athanasius Kircher, S.J. (China illustrata, Amsterdam 1667), compiling Jesuit reports (Martini and others)
passages.caution: Second-hand; the palace fire of 1644 was real, but 'four years' is a round figure from Kircher's sources.

passages.headline: 'Whoever is afraid builds towers'
passages.people: Tatars of the Golden Horde (the horde of Küchük Muhammad)
passages.gloss: Giosafat Barbaro, a Venetian merchant who lived at Tana on the Don for sixteen years, watched a whole horde migrate past the town. Asked whether these people wander like gypsies, he says no: apart from having no walls, their camps look like very large and beautiful cities. When he asked a Tatar merchant if Tana's fine gate tower was not beautiful, the man laughed: 'Pah, whoever is afraid builds towers.'
passages.quote: Rispondo di nò: conciosia, ch'eccetto il nõ esser circondati di mura, tali alloggiamenti paiono grossissime, & bellissime città. Ritrouandomi, a questo proposito, vn giorno alla Tana, sopra la porta dellaquale era vna torre assai bella, & essendo appresso di me vn Tartaro mercante, ilquale guardaua la torre, gli domãdai: Ti pare vna bella cosa questa? Et egli, guardandomi, & sorridendo, disse: poh, c'ha paura, fa torre
passages.translation: I answer no: for, except that they are not surrounded by walls, such encampments look like very large and very beautiful cities. Being one day at Tana, speaking of this, over whose gate there was a rather fine tower, and having beside me a Tartar merchant who was looking at the tower, I asked him: Does this seem a fine thing to you? And he, looking at me and smiling, said: Pah, whoever is afraid builds a tower.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR partly garbled); long s and ligatures normalized
passages.speaker: Giosafat Barbaro (Viaggio alla Tana, written 1487), in Ramusio's Italian edition
passages.caution: Barbaro wrote his memoir some fifty years after the events.

passages.headline: Brick houses and a painters' street under the 'Emperor of the Tartars'
passages.people: 'Idolaters' of Campion, subjects of 'Daimir Can, great Emperor of the Tartars'
passages.gloss: Ramusio adds to his Marco Polo commentary what a Persian merchant, Hajji Muhammad ('Chaggi Memet'), told him in Venice about Campion (Ganzhou), a city of idol-worshippers subject to 'Daimir Can, great Emperor of the Tartars'. Its houses were built 'in our manner' of fired brick and stone, two or three storeys high, with painted ceilings, and one whole street was lived in only by painters. He also mentions temples like churches, colossal gilded statues and printing.
passages.quote: La città di Campion è habitata da popoli che sono idolatri: soggetta alla signoria de Daimir Can, grande Imperatore de Tartari … Le fabriche delle lor case son fatte al modo nostro di pietre cotte, & di pietre viue, con due & tre solari, quali sono soffittati & dipinti di pittura di varij & diuersi colori, & di figure: vi sono anco infiniti pittori: & vi è vna contrada doue non habita altri, che pittori.
passages.translation: The city of Campion is inhabited by peoples who are idolaters, subject to the lordship of Daimir Can, great Emperor of the Tartars ... The buildings of their houses are made in our manner, of fired brick and of living stone, with two and three storeys, which are ceiled and painted with pictures of various and different colours and with figures; there are also countless painters, and there is a quarter where no one lives but painters.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR partly garbled); long s and ligatures normalized
passages.speaker: Giovanni Battista Ramusio, Dichiaratione on Marco Polo, reporting the Persian merchant Hajji Muhammad
passages.caution: Second-hand merchant's report. 'Daimir Can' is probably the Ming emperor ('Dai Ming Khan'), so here 'Tartars' is a loose label for the ruler of China.

passages.headline: The 'Water Mongols', named Tartars after the river Tartar
passages.people: Mongols and Tatars (Carpini's four peoples of 'Mongal')
passages.gloss: In Ramusio's Italian 'Two journeys to Tartary', drawn from the papal envoys of 1245 to 1247, the land called 'Mongal, or Tartaria' once held four peoples: the Yeka Mongol ('great Mongols'), the Su Mongol ('water Mongols'), who were the Tartars proper, named after a river Tartar that watered their land, and the Merkit and the Mecrit. Chinggis came from the first and conquered the rest.
passages.quote: Hebbe anticamente quattro Popoli (come si dice) il primo Popolo in lingua loro diceuasi Iekamongal, cioè, grandi Mongali. Il secondo, Summongal, cioè, Aquatici Mongali, che erano essi Tartari da un fiume Tartar cosi nominati, ilquale bagna il suo paese. Il terzo Merkath. Il quarto, Metrith.
passages.translation: It anciently had four peoples (as is said): the first people in their language was called Yekamongal, that is, great Mongols. The second, Summongal, that is, water Mongols, who were the Tartars themselves, so named from a river Tartar which waters their country. The third, Merkath. The fourth, Metrith.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR partly garbled); long s and ligatures normalized
passages.speaker: John of Plano Carpini (and Simon of Saint-Quentin), via Vincent of Beauvais, in Ramusio's Italian 'Due viaggi in Tartaria'
passages.caution: A medieval Latin report reached Ramusio through Vincent of Beauvais's encyclopedia; the river Tartar is a folk explanation of the name.

passages.headline: Prester John between Gog and Magog on the old sea charts
passages.people: Tartars identified with Gog and Magog; 'Uncan' as Prester John
passages.gloss: Ramusio notes that Marco Polo called the northern lord Uncan 'Prester John' and put his seat in two regions, Og and Magog. He adds that on all the sea charts made 200 and 300 years earlier, Prester John is placed in the north above India, between the Ganges and the Indus, with no mention of an Ethiopian Prester John; on the next page he calls these 'the provinces of Gog and Magog, that is, of the Tartars'.
passages.quote: oue dice Messer Marco Polo che sotto la Tramontana v'era vn gran signore detto VmCan che vogliono alcuni questo nome dire Preti Ianni, nella nostra lingua: & che la sua principale sedia era in due regioni, Og & Magog, è da sapere, che in tutte quelle carte da nauigare che si vegghono hoggidi fatte già 200 & 300. anni, v'è posto questo Prete Ianni sotto la Tramontana & sopra l'India
passages.translation: where Messer Marco Polo says that in the north there was a great lord called Uncan, whose name some take to mean Prester John in our language, and that his principal seat was in two regions, Og and Magog: it should be known that on all those sea charts one sees today, made 200 and 300 years ago, this Prester John is placed in the north and above India
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR partly garbled); long s and ligatures normalized
passages.speaker: Giovanni Battista Ramusio, Dichiaratione on Marco Polo
passages.caution: Ramusio is reporting legend and old maps, not asserting the facts himself; useful for the maps team.

passages.headline: The Great Wall is brick, built against the Tartars
passages.place: Great Wall of China (north of Beijing)
passages.people: Chinese builders; Tartars as the enemy it was built against
passages.when: 1696 (visit); wall credited to Qin Shi Huang
passages.gloss: Careri rode out from Beijing and walked four miles up the mountains to see the Wall himself. It stood 15 to 20 feet high, higher and wider in the valleys, room for six horses abreast, built 'of large fire-baked bricks with few stones', with strong square towers two bowshots apart running to the sea. He credits the emperor 'Xi-hoamti' with building it more than 1800 years earlier 'as a defence against the raids of the Tartars'.
passages.quote: Egli è alto quel muro in alcune parti 15. e in altre 20. piedi; ma nelle valli è più alto assai, e più largo, potendovi agiatamente andar sei cavalli di fronte. La fabbrica è di grandi mattoni cotti al fuoco, con poche pietre: & ha di quando in quando le sue Torri bẽ forti, e quadrate, l'una lontana all'altra quanto due tratti di freccia
passages.translation: That wall is 15 feet high in some parts and 20 in others; but in the valleys it is much higher and wider, so that six horses can comfortably go abreast on it. The construction is of large bricks baked in the fire, with few stones, and from time to time it has its towers, very strong and square, one as far from the next as two bowshots
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Giovanni Francesco Gemelli Careri (Giro del Mondo, part IV, Naples 1700)
passages.caution: The 1800-year date and builder are from Chinese tradition via Jesuit books; the brick section he saw is a Ming rebuild.

passages.headline: A wall up a cliff no Tartar horse could climb
passages.gloss: Careri found the Wall one of the greatest and 'most senseless' works ever made. What made him laugh was seeing it carried to the top of a precipitous mountain where 'the Tartar cavalry' could never have climbed; and if the Chinese thought raiders could scramble up the cliffs, it was foolish to think so low a wall would stop them. A rare eyewitness who was unimpressed.
passages.quote: Ma quel, che affatto mi sembrò da ridere, fu a vedere il muro tratto ancor fino alle cime d'un'altissimo, e straripevol monte, ove appena vi sarebbero appiccati i picchi: non che montar vi potesse la cavalleria Tartara per entrar nel paese.
passages.translation: But what struck me as altogether laughable was to see the wall carried even to the peaks of a very high and precipitous mountain, where hardly even woodpeckers could cling, let alone the Tartar cavalry climb up to enter the country.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Giovanni Francesco Gemelli Careri (Giro del Mondo, part IV, Naples 1700)
passages.caution: His own opinion of the defensive logic.

passages.headline: Beijing's two cities: the Tartar City and the Chinese City
passages.gloss: Careri describes Qing Beijing as two joined cities: the old walled 'City of the Tartars' around the palace, where the Manchu bannermen, officials and ministers lived, and the 'City of the Chinese', built later beside it for the overflow of inhabitants, about the same four leagues round and joined to the Tartar City by a single shared wall.
passages.quote: La Città de' Cinesi (che si fabbricò appresso per dar luogo alla moltitudine degli Abitanti) è dell'istessa grandezza, che la Città de'Tartari, tenendo quattro leghe di giro; ma la figura non è somigliante a quella … nel cui lato si unisce con la Città Tartara, con un sol muro, che le divide.
passages.translation: The City of the Chinese (which was built next to it to make room for the multitude of inhabitants) is of the same size as the City of the Tartars, being four leagues round; but its shape is not like that one ... on which side it joins the Tartar City by a single wall that divides them.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Giovanni Francesco Gemelli Careri (Giro del Mondo, part IV, Naples 1700)
passages.caution: The division itself was Ming (Inner and Outer City); the name 'Tartar City' reflects Qing residential segregation.

passages.headline: Tartars in huts, now made to build villages
passages.people: Mongols under Qing rule ('poor Tartars'; Khalkha)
passages.gloss: Describing the lands between Beijing and the Russian frontier, Careri says the vast 'Imperial Tartary' owned by the emperor of China was uncultivated and wooded, and its 'poor Tartars' lived in huts without walled houses, like the ancient nomads with portable dwellings. But the present emperor was now 'civilising' them, beginning to have villages built and gathering them in, with forty tributary princes including the Khalkha.
passages.quote: vivendovi que' poveri Tartari sotto capanne, senza case murate, a modo degli antichi Numidi, o Hamaxobiti, che tutti intesi alla vita pastorale, nè men case avevano, ma con loro portatili mapali, ove più concio era, andavano ad abitare. Ma l'Imperador odierno della Tartaria, bene al presente dirozzandogli comincia a far loro fabbricare Ville, e raccorgli entro a quelle in comunanza
passages.translation: those poor Tartars living there under huts, without walled houses, in the manner of the ancient Numidians or Hamaxobians, who, all given to the pastoral life, did not even have houses but went to live wherever it was most convenient with their portable huts. But the present Emperor of Tartary, now civilising them well, is beginning to have villages built for them and to gather them into these in communities
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Giovanni Francesco Gemelli Careri (Giro del Mondo, part IV, Naples 1700)
passages.caution: Careri did not travel there; this comes from Jesuits at court (Grimaldi, Gerbillon, Pereira). The classical comparison is his own.

passages.headline: The Tartar haircut forced on the Chinese
passages.gloss: Before the Tartars began to rule, Careri says, the Chinese wore their hair long, wound behind the head in a knot pinned with silver. After 'the empire of the Tartar' everyone was ordered, on pain of death, to cut it and adopt the Tartar style: shaved head with one tuft, which the Chinese wore braided, sometimes down to the legs. Loose wide-sleeved robes were also banned for Tartar dress, 'which the Chinese felt, and still feel, in their hearts'.
passages.quote: Prima che cominciassero a dominare i Tartari, portavano i Cinesi lunghi i capelli, avvolgendogli dietro la testa … ma dopo l'Imperio del Tartaro, fu ordinato a tutti, in pena della vita, di tagliarsegli; e di andare alla maniera Tartara, colla testa rasa, e un ciuffo
passages.translation: Before the Tartars began to rule, the Chinese wore their hair long, winding it behind the head ... but after the empire of the Tartar, everyone was ordered on pain of death to cut it, and to go in the Tartar manner, with the head shaved and a tuft
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Giovanni Francesco Gemelli Careri (Giro del Mondo, part IV, Naples 1700)
passages.caution: He saw the result; the history is from Jesuit sources. The corpus OCR reads 'miniera' for 'maniera'.

passages.headline: 'Eastern Tartars': a Manchu dynasty from a small horde chief
passages.people: Manchus ('Eastern Tartars'), as against 'Western Tartars' (Mongols, Oirats)
passages.gloss: Careri opens his chapter on the 'Eastern Tartars' by saying their princes' origin is so obscure that everyone who writes of it tells fables. They began only in this century from 'a small Horde chief, or captain of outlaws or wandering Tartars' called Tien-mim (Nurhaci). He goes on to divide Tartary into Eastern (Manchu lands, poor, with only two or three small towns) and a far more powerful Western Tartary, both mostly living in tents.
passages.quote: E' così oscura di questi Principi l'origine, che chiunque ha voluto parlarne ha dato nelle favole. Eglino hanno avuto principio in questo secolo da un picciol Capo d'Horda, o Capitano di fuorusciti, o Tartari erranti, che si chiamava Tien-mim
passages.translation: The origin of these princes is so obscure that whoever has tried to speak of it has fallen into fables. They had their beginning in this century from a small chief of a Horde, or captain of outlaws or wandering Tartars, who was called Tien-mim
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Giovanni Francesco Gemelli Careri (Giro del Mondo, part IV, Naples 1700), compiling Martini and other Jesuit histories
passages.caution: Compiled from printed Jesuit histories; 'Tien-mim' is Tianming, Nurhaci's reign name, not his personal name.

passages.headline: Two million Muslims 'from Great Tartary'
passages.people: Chinese Muslims (Hui) 'come from Great Tartary'; Manchu garrison
passages.gloss: In Nanjing Careri notes that not all inhabitants are Chinese: there are many 'Moors come from Great Tartary', two million across China according to Father Grimaldi, who marry their daughters only within their own sect and so multiply 'like locusts'. The royal palace sits in a citadel held by a Tartar (Manchu) garrison that let no one in.
passages.quote: Gli abitanti, che sono in Nankin, non son tutti Cinesi, ma vi sono ancor molti Mori venuti dalla G. Tartaria (accertandomi il Padre Filippo Grimaldi, ch'in tutta la Cina ve ne siano due milioni), i quali han per politica di non casar le loro figlie, sol che nella propria Setta
passages.translation: The inhabitants of Nanking are not all Chinese: there are also many Moors who came from Great Tartary (Father Filippo Grimaldi assuring me that in all China there are two million of them), whose policy is not to marry their daughters except within their own sect
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Giovanni Francesco Gemelli Careri (Giro del Mondo, part IV, Naples 1700)
passages.caution: The figure is Grimaldi's estimate; 'from Great Tartary' reflects the belief that China's Muslims came from Central Asia.

passages.headline: A land with no towns except 'Cracurim'
passages.gloss: Sanudo's chapter headed 'the sordid origin of the Tartars' describes the land 'called Mongal or Tartaria' where the East meets the North: mountainous in parts, mostly gravel and sand, short of water, so that there are no villages or cities 'except one called Cracurim', said to be fairly good, though the land is excellent for raising herds. Cracurim is Karakorum.
passages.quote: Terra quæ Mongal siue Tartaria dicitur, in ea parte describitur, vbi Oriens Aquiloni coniungitur … & aquarum copiâ caret: vndè nec villæ ibi sunt aut ciuitates, exceptâ vnâ quæ Cracurim vocatur, & satis bona esse dicitur. In alendis tamen pecoribus terra optima est.
passages.translation: The land called Mongal or Tartaria is described as lying in that part where the East joins the North ... and it lacks plenty of water: hence there are no villages or cities there, except one which is called Cracurim, and is said to be fairly good. For raising herds, however, the land is excellent.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Marino Sanudo Torsello (Liber secretorum fidelium crucis, c. 1321; ed. Bongars, Hanau 1611)
passages.caution: Copied almost word for word from John of Plano Carpini's report of 1247; Sanudo never went to Mongolia.

passages.headline: Seven Tartar nations, and the 'water Mongols' named after a river
passages.gloss: Sanudo lists seven Tartar nations 'of greater excellence': Tartar, Tangoth, Eurath, Ialayr, Sonit, Mengli and Theboth (roughly Tatar, Tangut, Oirat, Jalayir, Sunit, and others). Then, from another source, he says the land of Mongal had four peoples, the second being the Su Mongol or 'water Mongols', who 'call themselves Tartars, from a river of theirs called Tartar'. Chinggis rose from the first people and conquered the rest.
passages.quote: quarum prima vocatur Tartar, secunda, Tangoth, tertia Eurath, quarta Ialayr, quinta Sonit, sexta Mengli, septima Theboth. Præfata quoque terra Mongal, quatuor olim habebat populos: quorum primus Iechamongla, id est, magni Mongali vocabatur: Secundus, Summongal, id est, aquatici Mongali: hii se ipsos Tartaros appellant, à quodam suo fluuio qui Tartar dicitur
passages.translation: of which the first is called Tartar, the second Tangoth, the third Eurath, the fourth Ialayr, the fifth Sonit, the sixth Mengli, the seventh Theboth. The said land of Mongal also once had four peoples: the first of which was called Iechamongla, that is, great Mongols; the second, Summongal, that is, water Mongols: these call themselves Tartars, from a certain river of theirs which is called Tartar
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Marino Sanudo Torsello (Liber secretorum fidelium crucis, c. 1321; ed. Bongars, Hanau 1611)
passages.caution: Stitched from Hayton (the seven nations) and Carpini (the four peoples); the river Tartar is a folk etymology.

passages.headline: Prester John's son cut to pieces, his daughter wed to Chinggis
passages.people: Mongols under Chinggis Khan; 'David, son of Prester John'
passages.gloss: Sanudo tells how the Tartars, once tributaries of 'David, son of Prester John, king of India', rose against him under Chinggis. Their best weapons were clubs with bows and arrows; most fought on foot, some rode oxen, a few rode asses and colts. David was cut limb from limb with all his family except one daughter, whom Chinggis took as wife. A blend of the Prester John legend with the real defeat of the Kereit ruler Toghrul.
passages.quote: Potiora eorum arma, fuere claua cum arcubus, & sagittis: pedites in maxima parte erant; pars minor in bobus sedebat; minima asinis & iumentis & pullis equorum. Rex itaque Dauid eorum aduentum audiens … & cum tota familia, exceptâ vnicâ eius filiâ, membratim truncatur: quam quidem filiam, Cyngis Chaam vxorem accepit.
passages.translation: Their best weapons were clubs, with bows and arrows: for the most part they were on foot; a smaller part sat on oxen; the smallest on asses and beasts of burden and colts. So King David, hearing of their coming ... was cut limb from limb with his whole family except his only daughter: which daughter Chinggis Khan took as his wife.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Marino Sanudo Torsello (Liber secretorum fidelium crucis, c. 1321; ed. Bongars, Hanau 1611)
passages.caution: A legend repeated from older crusade-era books; the Mongols were famously mounted archers, not ox-riding foot soldiers.

passages.headline: The Iron Gate city of Alexander razed by the Tartars
passages.gloss: Sent west with 10,000 horsemen, the Mongol general Jebe ('Gebesagada') took towns before they knew he was coming, killing the armed men but, Sanudo says, sparing the people and leaving gold untouched. At the Caucasus he reached Alexandreta, built by Alexander, later called the Iron Gate, which blocks the way from deep Asia. The Tartars entered it suddenly and 'overthrew both citizens and place from the foundations'.
passages.quote: peruenitque ad magnum montem Caucasum, vbi Alexandretam Alexander ædificauit, quæ postea Portæ ferreæ dicta est. Hæc transitum prohibet de profunda Asia ad maiorem. Hanc autem inexpugnabilem ciuitatem, intrantes subitò terram Tartari, tam ciues quam locum funditus euerterunt.
passages.translation: and he came to the great mountain Caucasus, where Alexander built Alexandreta, which was afterwards called the Iron Gates. This blocks the passage from deep Asia to the greater. This impregnable city the Tartars, entering the land suddenly, overthrew from its foundations, both citizens and place.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Marino Sanudo Torsello (Liber secretorum fidelium crucis, c. 1321; ed. Bongars, Hanau 1611)
passages.caution: Compiled history; the attribution of Derbent's walls to Alexander is medieval tradition (they are Sasanian).

passages.headline: Kublai founds in Cathay 'a city greater than Rome'
passages.gloss: Summing up the khans, Sanudo says Möngke drowned trying to take an island in the sea of Cathay (a garbled report), and his brother 'Cobila Chaam' held the Tartar empire forty-two years, 'was a Christian', and founded in the kingdom of Cathay a city greater than Rome called 'Iong', where he always lived. This is Kublai's new capital, Dadu or Khanbaliq, now Beijing.
passages.quote: & successit illi frater Cobila Chaam, qui annis XLII. tenuit imperium Tartarorum: hic Christianus fuit, & fundauit in regno Catay, Româ ciuitatem maiorem, vocatam Iong, vbi continuè immoratus est.
passages.translation: and his brother Kublai Khan succeeded him, who held the empire of the Tartars for 42 years: he was a Christian, and founded in the kingdom of Cathay a city greater than Rome, called Iong, where he stayed continually.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Marino Sanudo Torsello (Liber secretorum fidelium crucis, c. 1321; ed. Bongars, Hanau 1611)
passages.caution: From Hayton's history; Kublai was not a Christian, and Möngke actually died besieging a Chinese fortress.

passages.headline: Aleppo, Hama and Damascus fall; Acre tears down its towers in fear
passages.gloss: In his year-by-year chronicle Sanudo notes that in 1260 the Tartars broke in violently and took Aleppo, Harim, Hama, Homs and Damascus, killing every Saracen who met them, then entered the kingdom of Jerusalem and took Sidon, but not its sea castle. The people of Acre, afraid of them, cut down their orchards and threw down the orchard towers outside the walls, even carrying off cemetery stones. The Tartars were beaten by the Sultan of Egypt at Ain Jalut (the 'plain of Tiberias').
passages.quote: Tartari autem sequenti anno violenter irrumpentes ceperunt Alapiam, Harenc, Haman, Calamelam, & Damascum: occidentes cunctos factos sibi obuiam Saracenos. Intrant deindè regnum Ierusalem, capiuntq; Sydonem: sed castrum maris nullatenus capere potuerunt. Ptolomenses verò eorum timore præciderunt viridaria extra ciuitatem; & turres viridariorum ad terram proiecerunt, amouentes etiam lapides cimiterii cum lapidibus ædificiorum.
passages.translation: The next year the Tartars, breaking in violently, took Aleppo, Harim, Hama, Homs and Damascus, killing all the Saracens who came against them. Then they entered the kingdom of Jerusalem and took Sidon, but could by no means take the sea castle. The people of Acre, for fear of them, cut down the orchards outside the city, and threw the orchard towers to the ground, removing even the stones of the cemetery along with the stones of the buildings.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Marino Sanudo Torsello (Liber secretorum fidelium crucis, c. 1321; ed. Bongars, Hanau 1611)

passages.headline: One god, many idols, and the sin of a knife in the fire
passages.gloss: Sanudo's chapter on 'the customs of the Tartars' says they believe in one God, maker of all, but do not pray to him; they worship idols that give them answers. They are 'too superstitious': it is a sin to stick a knife in the fire, touch fire with a knife, take meat from the cauldron with it, or chop with an axe near the fire, 'for they think the head is thus cut off the fire'. Killing and invading other lands, he adds, they do not count as sin.
passages.quote: Tartari, vnum Deum colunt, factorem omnium; bonorum, & pœnarum in hoc mundo datorem: eum tamen orationibus vel laudibus aut aliter non colunt; sed idola à quibus habent responsa. … Superstitiosi sunt nimis: peccatū enim putant cultellum in igne figere, vel quomodocunq; cultello tangere, vel cum eo carnes de caldaria extrahere, vel cū securi incidere iuxta ignē: putant enim sic caput igni auferri.
passages.translation: The Tartars worship one God, maker of all things, giver of good and of punishments in this world; yet they do not worship him with prayers or praises or in any other way, but idols from which they get answers. ... They are too superstitious: for they think it a sin to stick a knife in the fire, or touch it in any way with a knife, or take meat out of the cauldron with it, or chop with an axe beside the fire: for they think that in this way the head is taken off the fire.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Marino Sanudo Torsello (Liber secretorum fidelium crucis, c. 1321; ed. Bongars, Hanau 1611)
passages.caution: Condensed from Carpini's report; Sanudo presents it as general knowledge.

passages.headline: No locks on their wagons, and living on mare's milk
passages.gloss: In the same chapter Sanudo, following Carpini, praises Tartar honesty and endurance: there are no robbers or thieves of anything valuable among them, so the tents and carts where they keep their treasure are never locked; they welcome anyone who comes while they eat, can go a day or two without food and still sing and play, and when heading for lands short of food they take mares and cows along and live on the milk.
passages.quote: Prædones vel fures notabilium rerum, inter eos non sunt: ideoq; stationes & currus eorum, vbi thesauros conseruant, seris aut vectibus non firmant. Honorant se mutuò, & sunt ad inuicem familiares; omnem accedentem, dum comedunt, ad conuiuiū recipiunt … & quando ad terram pergunt, vbi putant adesse victualiū inopiam, equas, vaccas & alia animalia secū portant; & de lacte viuunt.
passages.translation: Robbers or thieves of valuable things are not found among them: so their dwellings and carts, where they keep their treasures, they do not secure with locks or bars. They honour one another and are friendly among themselves; everyone who approaches while they are eating they receive at the meal ... and when they go to a land where they think there is a shortage of food, they take mares, cows and other animals with them, and live on the milk.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Marino Sanudo Torsello (Liber secretorum fidelium crucis, c. 1321; ed. Bongars, Hanau 1611)
passages.caution: Copied from Carpini, who also stressed their arrogance and cruelty to outsiders.

passages.headline: Spices come by the Tartar road through Baghdad and Tabriz
passages.people: Mongols of the Ilkhanate (Persia and Iraq)
passages.gloss: Sanudo, a Venetian with merchant experience, argues that the Pope should ban trade with Mamluk Egypt because goods can come instead through the lands of the Tartars. Christian merchants, he says, can travel from the Tartar dominions all the way to India, and many have gone and come back, whereas the Sultan lets no Christian pass; light, precious spices such as cloves, nutmeg and mace already reach the Mediterranean via Baghdad and Tabriz.
passages.quote: ab hac parte scilicet dominii Tartarorum, vsque in Indiam ipsi mercatores Christiani poterunt dirigere gressus suos, cùm multi sint, qui iam iuerunt & redierunt. … sciendum est quod à partibus Tartarorum, scilicet à Baldach & à Thorisio, à magno tempore citra conducta sunt & cōducuntur ad præsens ad Mare Mediterraneum, quasi omnia mercimonia modici ponderis, & magni prætii
passages.translation: from this side, namely the dominion of the Tartars, Christian merchants will be able to direct their steps as far as India, since there are many who have already gone and come back. ... it should be known that from the parts of the Tartars, namely from Baghdad and from Tabriz, for a long time past and at present almost all goods of small weight and great price are carried to the Mediterranean Sea
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Marino Sanudo Torsello (Liber secretorum fidelium crucis, c. 1321; ed. Bongars, Hanau 1611)
passages.caution: A policy argument for a trade embargo; his trade information came from Venetian and other merchants.

passages.headline: Khan Uzbek turns Muslim, with an army counted in tens
passages.gloss: Sanudo warns the Pope that the Sultan of Egypt, with gifts and treaties, had drawn 'the Emperor of the Tartars named Husbecho, who rules in Gazaria and other northern parts' to accept Islam. Trustworthy people told him Uzbek's cavalry was so vast that, his army being organised in tens, he could take just three of every ten and still field an almost unbelievable host.
passages.quote: prædictus Soldanus Imperatorem Tartarorum, nomine Husbecho, qui in Gazaria, & aliis Septentrionis partibus dominatur, immutauit taliter & attraxit, vt legem receperit perfidi Mahumeti … Nam à nonnullis dignis fide asseritur quod dictus Husbecho, habet equitum multitudinem adeò numerosam, vt subtrahendo tres de decem, cum per decuriones habeat exercitum ordinatum, ex solis ternariis in campo ponit ita militiam copiosam, quod quasi incredibile videatur.
passages.translation: the said Sultan so changed and drew the Emperor of the Tartars, named Uzbek, who rules in Gazaria and other northern parts, that he received the law of the faithless Muhammad ... For it is asserted by some trustworthy people that the said Uzbek has so numerous a multitude of horsemen that, taking three out of ten, since he has his army ordered by tens, from the threes alone he puts so large a force in the field that it seems almost incredible.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Marino Sanudo Torsello (Liber secretorum fidelium crucis, c. 1321; ed. Bongars, Hanau 1611)
passages.caution: Uzbek's conversion was his own and not simply the Sultan's doing; the army figure is hearsay.

passages.headline: Why the Tartars could never hold Syria: summer heat and no grass
passages.gloss: Arguing against landing a crusade in Armenia, Sanudo notes that the Tartars had often overrun almost all of Syria but always had to give it up and let the Sultan retake it. They could not cross the desert into Egypt, and could not stay through the summer because of the great heat and the lack of pasture for their horses and herds. It shows how nomad armies were tied to grass.
passages.quote: Et considerandum est quod multoties Tartari cucurrerunt per terram, & cœperunt quasi omnes contratas de Semo, & de Syria: sed quia non potuerunt transire desertum per quod transitur in Ægyptum … Et si dici vellet quod Tartari compulsi fuerunt relinquere acquisita, hoc fuit, quia non potuerunt in æstate commorari propter intensionem caloris, & propter defectum herbatici, quod non habuerunt pro suis equis pascēdis & gregibus
passages.translation: And it should be considered that many times the Tartars overran the land and took almost all the districts of Sham and Syria: but because they could not cross the desert by which one passes into Egypt ... And if one wished to say that the Tartars were forced to give up what they had taken, this was because they could not stay in summer on account of the intense heat, and on account of the lack of grazing, which they did not have for pasturing their horses and herds
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Marino Sanudo Torsello (Liber secretorum fidelium crucis, c. 1321; ed. Bongars, Hanau 1611)
passages.caution: A strategic argument, but it matches what modern historians say about Mongol logistics in Syria.

passages.headline: A 500-league wall against the Tartars, mostly mountains
passages.people: Chinese builders; Tartars (Mongols) as the enemy
passages.gloss: Mendoza reports a wall 500 leagues long running west to east, built by a king 'Tzintzom' (Qin Shi Huang) to protect himself from the Tartars, 'and so the wall takes in the whole frontier of Tartary'. But, he adds, 400 of those leagues are made by nature, very high closed mountains; only the remaining hundred were built by the king, of very strong stone, seven fathoms wide at the base.
passages.quote: Hallase en este Reyno vna cerca, o muralla, que tiene quinientas leguas de largo … Hizo la vn Rey llamado Tzintzom, por ampararse de los Tartaros, con quien tenia guerra, y assi toma la muralla toda la frontera de Tartaria. Pero ha se de entender, que las 400. leguas que tiene la dicha muralla, son hechas por la naturaleza, por que son vnas sierras altissimas muy cerradas.
passages.translation: There is in this kingdom an enclosure or wall five hundred leagues long ... A king called Tzintzom made it to protect himself from the Tartars, with whom he was at war, and so the wall takes in the whole frontier of Tartary. But it must be understood that 400 of the leagues of the said wall are made by nature, for they are very high, very close-set mountains.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Juan González de Mendoza (Historia del gran Reyno de la China, Rome 1585)
passages.caution: Mendoza never saw it; he relies on Gaspar da Cruz, Rada and Chinese books. The natural-barrier claim comes from those sources.

passages.headline: The viceroy's guard: 'Tartars by nation, not Chinese'
passages.gloss: In the account of the Franciscan friars who entered China in 1579, Mendoza describes the Guangdong viceroy's guard of more than two thousand men in silk livery and shining iron helmets with great plumes, swords on the stairs and lances in the courtyards with an arquebusier between each pair. The whole guard, the friars understood, 'was of men who were Tartars by nation, and not Chinese', and they could not find out why, though they asked.
passages.quote: Estaua la guarda del Virey (que passauan de dos mill hombres) puesta en hylera, y todos vestidos de librea de seda, y en las cabezas, zeladas de yerro muy relucientes, con muy grandes plumages. … Toda esta guarda (segun entendieron) era de hombres Tartaros de nacion, y no de Chinos, sin poder sauer la caussa, aunque la inquirieron con diligencia.
passages.translation: The viceroy's guard (which was more than two thousand men) was drawn up in a line, all dressed in silk livery, and on their heads very shining iron helmets with very large plumes. ... This whole guard (as they understood) was of men who were Tartars by nation, and not Chinese, without their being able to learn the reason, though they inquired diligently.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Juan González de Mendoza (Historia del gran Reyno de la China, Rome 1585), from the report of the Franciscan mission of 1579 (Pedro de Alfaro and companions)
passages.caution: The friars saw the guard but could not confirm who the men were; 'Tartars' may mean Mongols or other northern soldiers in Ming service.

passages.headline: The Tartar now fears China and pays a kind of vassalage
passages.gloss: Discussing China's military system, Mendoza says the Chinese had fought continual wars with the Tartars for many years, 'although today the Tartar fears him so much that he thinks it good to be his friend, and acknowledges a kind of vassalage'. Even so, every city was guarded day and night as if the enemy were at the gate. This reflects the 1571 peace in which Altan Khan accepted a Ming title and tribute trade.
passages.quote: aunque el dia de oy le tiene el Tartaro tanto temor que tiene por bien de ser su amigo, y le reconosce vna manera de vasallaje. Y con estar al presente y de algunos tiempos a esta parte sin ocasion de guerra que sea de momento, tiene el mesmo cuidado en la preuençion que si tuuiera muchos y muy grandes enemigos
passages.translation: although today the Tartar fears him so much that he thinks it good to be his friend, and acknowledges to him a kind of vassalage. And though at present and for some time past there has been no occasion for war of any importance, he takes the same care in preparation as if he had many very great enemies
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Juan González de Mendoza (Historia del gran Reyno de la China, Rome 1585)
passages.caution: Compiled from Chinese and missionary sources; the framing flatters the Chinese emperor.

passages.headline: Mass weddings by lot 'toward Tartary'
passages.people: Peoples of the northern provinces and 'Tartary itself'
passages.gloss: Mendoza passes on a story that in the provinces toward Tartary, and in Tartary itself, governors set an age by which men and women must either enter religion or marry. At the appointed time all who are to marry gather in a designated city, where twelve elders record their names and wealth; if there are more men than women, they draw lots, and the surplus wait until next year. He introduces it with 'they say'.
passages.quote: Dizen que en las Prouincias hazia la Tartaria, y en la mesma Tartaria, se acostumbra vna cierta manera de casar muy estraña, y es que los Virreyes, o Gouernadores tienen señalado tiempo, assi a los hombres como a las mugeres paraque hasta llegar a tal edad tengan obligacion, o de meterse en Religion, o de casarse.
passages.translation: They say that in the provinces toward Tartary, and in Tartary itself, a certain very strange manner of marrying is customary, which is that the viceroys or governors have set a time for both men and women, so that on reaching a certain age they are obliged either to enter religion or to marry.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Juan González de Mendoza (Historia del gran Reyno de la China, Rome 1585)
passages.caution: Hearsay introduced with 'they say'; the story echoes older European tales (such as Herodotus's Babylonian bride market) and has no clear Asian source.

passages.headline: The biggest army since Adam marches on Beijing
passages.people: 'The King of Tartary' (Mongol forces, possibly echoing Altan Khan)
passages.gloss: Pinto says that while he was a captive in China, news came at midnight that 'the King of Tartary' was before Beijing with the largest army any king had gathered 'since the time of Adam': twenty-seven kings and 1,800,000 men, 600,000 of them cavalry, with 80,000 rhinoceroses carrying supplies, and the Chinese emperor had fled to Nanjing. The numbers are fantastic and the event cannot be matched to 1544.
passages.quote: auia noua certa de estar el Rey da Tartaria sobre a cidade do Pequim, co mais grosso poder de gente q nenhum outro Rey nũca ajuntara no mundo, desde o tempo de Adão até aquella hora, no qual se affirmaua que vinhaõ vinte & sete Reys, & q se dezia q trazião comsigo hũ conto & oitocentos mil homẽs, de q os seiscẽtos mil eraõ de cauallo
passages.translation: there was certain news that the King of Tartary was before the city of Peking with the greatest force of people that any other king had ever gathered in the world, from the time of Adam until that hour, in which it was affirmed that twenty-seven kings were coming, and it was said that they brought with them one million eight hundred thousand men, of whom six hundred thousand were on horseback
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s and abbreviations normalized
passages.speaker: Fernão Mendes Pinto (Peregrinaçam, Lisbon 1614)
passages.caution: Pinto reports this as rumour in the city; the numbers are impossible, and no such siege took place in 1544 (Altan Khan's raid on Beijing was in 1550).

passages.headline: A Tartar general storms Quansy and burns it to the ground
passages.people: Tartar army of the 'Nauticor of Lançame'
passages.gloss: Pinto describes the Tartars setting more than two thousand scaling ladders against the walls of the city where he was held, breaking the four gates with iron-bound beams, killing the governor and, he says, more than sixty thousand people, then burning every house and temple and carrying off gold and silver. He presents himself as a captive eyewitness.
passages.quote: arremeteraõ a elles com hũa grita taõ espantosa que parecia que se ajuntaua o Ceo com a terra, & aruorando mais de duas mil escadas que para isso trazião, lhe deraõ o assalto a toda em roda, por todas as partes que puderaõ, subindo pelas escadas acima muyto determinadamente, & sem nenhum medo
passages.translation: they rushed at them with so terrible a shout that it seemed heaven and earth were coming together, and setting up more than two thousand ladders which they had brought for the purpose, they assaulted it all around, on every side they could, climbing up the ladders very resolutely and without any fear
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized (checked in part against the page image)
passages.speaker: Fernão Mendes Pinto (Peregrinaçam, Lisbon 1614)
passages.caution: Pinto's Tartar episodes are widely regarded as fictional or built from hearsay; treat as claimed travel. The city and general cannot be identified.

passages.headline: 360 giant bronze gods, one for each day, carried off as trophies
passages.gloss: Brought before the Tartar king, Pinto describes a square courtyard lined with four rows of bronze statues of men 'like savages' with maces and crowns, gilded, 27 palms high, with frizzy hair 'like Kaffirs'. The Tartars told them these were the 360 gods who made the days of the year, taken from a great temple in a Chinese city 'to triumph over them' and show the world he had captured China's gods.
passages.quote: no qual estauão quatro fileyras de estatuas de bronzo em figura de homens a modo de saluagens com maças, & coroas do mesmo, porem tudo cozido em ouro, os quais idolos, ou gigantes, ou o que quer q eraõ, tinhão daltura vinte & sete palmos, & seys de largo nos peytos … & pregũtando nòs aos Tartaros pela significação daquellas figuras, nos disseraõ que eraõ os trezẽtos & sessenta deoses
passages.translation: in which there were four rows of bronze statues in the form of men like savages, with maces and crowns of the same, but all gilded, which idols, or giants, or whatever they were, were twenty-seven palms high and six wide at the chest ... and when we asked the Tartars the meaning of those figures, they told us they were the three hundred and sixty gods
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s and abbreviations normalized
passages.speaker: Fernão Mendes Pinto (Peregrinaçam, Lisbon 1614)
passages.caution: Pinto's Tartar episodes are widely regarded as fictional or built from hearsay; treat as claimed travel.

passages.headline: The Tartar 'Rome': 27 royal tombs and 280 monasteries
passages.gloss: Travelling on with the Tartars, Pinto describes Lechune, 'head of the false religion of this heathendom, as Rome is among us', with a sumptuous temple holding the tombs of twenty-seven kings or emperors 'of this Tartar monarchy' in chapels lined with silver, and nearby a walled enclosure of 280 monasteries with 42,000 priests. It is a vivid and entirely unverifiable picture of Tartar monumental building.
passages.quote: chegamos a hũa cidade que se chamaua Lechune, que he cabeça da falsa religião desta gentilidade, como o he Roma entre nos, na qual està hũ templo muyto sumptuoso, & de edificios muyto notaueis, em que estão sepultados vinte & sete Reys ou Emperadores desta Tartara Monarchia, em jazigos de capellas muyto ricas
passages.translation: we came to a city called Lechune, which is the head of the false religion of this heathendom, as Rome is among us, in which there is a very sumptuous temple, with very remarkable buildings, in which twenty-seven kings or emperors of this Tartar monarchy are buried, in very rich chapel tombs
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s and abbreviations normalized
passages.speaker: Fernão Mendes Pinto (Peregrinaçam, Lisbon 1614)
passages.caution: Pinto's Tartar episodes are widely regarded as fictional or built from hearsay; treat as claimed travel. Lechune may blend reports of Tibetan or Chinese Buddhist centres.

passages.headline: The wall between China and Tartary, 'which I saw and measured'
passages.people: Chinese builders; Tartars as the enemy
passages.gloss: Pinto says a Chinese king, after wars with the Tartar, closed the whole border of the two empires with a wall, built in 27 years by 750,000 men over 315 leagues. He claims to have seen and measured it: six fathoms high and forty palms thick, with an earth rampart faced with mortar at its foot, and watchtowers of two storeys on black ironwood posts instead of towers.
passages.quote: Este muro vy eu algũas vezes, & o medy, que he por todo geralmente de seis braças dalto, & quarenta palmos de largo no mociço da parede, mas das quatro braças para baixo corre hum entulho a modo de terrapleno, alamborado da face de fora de hũ betume como argamassa
passages.translation: This wall I saw several times, and measured it, and it is generally throughout six fathoms high and forty palms wide in the thickness of the wall, but from four fathoms down there runs a fill like an earthen rampart, sloped on the outer face with a cement like mortar
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image; long s and abbreviations normalized
passages.speaker: Fernão Mendes Pinto (Peregrinaçam, Lisbon 1614)
passages.caution: Pinto's Tartar episodes are widely regarded as fictional or built from hearsay; treat as claimed travel. His 'Chinese chronicle' history of the wall is unreliable.

passages.headline: Samarkand, 'the head of Tartary' on the maps
passages.people: Mogores (Mughals), counted by Cruz among the Scythians
passages.gloss: Describing the Mughal rulers of Sind and Delhi, Cruz says the head of their kingdom is 'the great Samarkand', which the maps of his day label 'the head of Tartary'. He then uses Josephus to make these people Scythians descended from Japheth, son of Noah, through Magog. This is book learning, not observation: it shows 'Tartary' already working as a map label in the 1560s.
passages.quote: Ha cabeça de seu reyno se chama ho grã Samarcam, q̃ nos Mappas se chama cabeça de Tartaria: estes sam cõtados antre os Scythas, como testefica Josepho no liuro primeiro das antiguidades, os quaes segũdo elle descendem de Japha filho de Noe por Magog.
passages.translation: The head of their kingdom is called the great Samarkand, which on the maps is called the head of Tartary. These are counted among the Scythians, as Josephus testifies in the first book of the Antiquities, who according to him descend from Japheth son of Noah through Magog.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this blackletter print is garbled); long s normalized, the Tironian sign for 'and' given as 'e', a few contractions (de, per, pro, terra) expanded, other abbreviation marks kept as printed
passages.speaker: Gaspar da Cruz, O.P. (Tractado, Évora 1569)
passages.caution: Cruz is repeating maps and Josephus; he never went near Samarkand.

passages.headline: Mogores, named after Magog
passages.people: Mogores (Mughals and related Central Asian peoples) living beside the Tartars
passages.gloss: Cruz says these peoples trade as far as Hormuz, border the Caspian and have the Tartars at their side. The Greeks called them Scythians, but across Asia they are called Mogores, a name he believes they kept from their ancestor Magog. It is a learned folk etymology linking the Mughals (from 'Mongol') to the biblical Magog.
passages.quote: Vem muitos delles cõ fazendas a Ormuz, confinẽ cõ ho mar Caspio, e ao lado com os Tartaros: e inda q̃ os gregos a estes chamẽ Scythas: por toda Asia mayor e menor sam chamados Mogores perseuerãdo nelles ha primeira denominaçam q̃ tomaram do pay Magog dõde decẽdem e se denominarã.
passages.translation: Many of them come with goods to Hormuz; they border on the Caspian Sea, and at their side are the Tartars. And although the Greeks call these people Scythians, throughout Asia the greater and the lesser they are called Mogores, keeping the first name they took from their father Magog, from whom they descend and take their name.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this blackletter print is garbled); long s normalized, the Tironian sign for 'and' given as 'e', a few contractions (de, per, pro, terra) expanded, other abbreviation marks kept as printed
passages.speaker: Gaspar da Cruz, O.P. (Tractado, Évora 1569)
passages.caution: The Magog derivation is Cruz's own guess; 'Mogor' actually comes from 'Mongol'.

passages.headline: Scythians who will march for the Antichrist
passages.people: Scythians beyond the Caspian (the same peoples as the Mogores)
passages.gloss: Right after the Magog passage, Cruz cites a treatise on the Antichrist by one Pedraza, who says these Scythians live beyond the Caspian, are a huge multitude, and will come to help the Antichrist at the end of time. Cruz offers it as support for his own view. It is the old Gog and Magog end-of-the-world legend, repeated from a book.
passages.quote: Destes diz Pedraza no tractado q̃ fez do Antichristo q̃ sam Scythas e viuẽ alem do mar Caspio, e q̃ he muita gente, ha qual ha de vir em ajuda do Antichristo, ho que refiro pera mostrar que cõforma com ho que tenho dito.
passages.translation: Of these Pedraza says, in the treatise he made on the Antichrist, that they are Scythians and live beyond the Caspian Sea, and that they are a great multitude, which is to come to the aid of the Antichrist; I mention this to show that it agrees with what I have said.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this blackletter print is garbled); long s normalized, the Tironian sign for 'and' given as 'e', a few contractions (de, per, pro, terra) expanded, other abbreviation marks kept as printed
passages.speaker: Gaspar da Cruz, O.P. (Tractado, Évora 1569)
passages.caution: Apocalyptic legend quoted from another author; not a report about real people.

passages.headline: Raw meat, blood and a smell carried on the wind
passages.gloss: Cruz describes the Tartars as reddish, naked from the waist up, eating raw meat and smearing their bodies with its blood, so that they stink. An old Chinese man told him that when Tartar raiders approached with the wind behind them, the Chinese could smell them coming. In war, he adds, they carry raw meat under themselves to eat. This is a Chinese stereotype passed to a Portuguese friar, not something Cruz saw.
passages.quote: da cinta pera cima, comẽ carne crua, e vntã os corpos com ho sangue della: pello qual comũmẽte sam fedorẽtos e tem mao cheiro. Afirmou me hũ China velho q̃ algũas vezes quãdo elles vinham cõtra as terras da China, se ho vento vinha da parte donde elles vinham, que eram sentidos pello cheiro: e quãdo vã aa guerra leuã ha carne crua debaixo de si pera comerẽ
passages.translation: [they go naked] from the waist up, eat raw meat, and anoint their bodies with its blood, for which reason they commonly stink and have a bad smell. An old Chinese man assured me that sometimes, when they came against the lands of China, if the wind blew from where they were coming, they were detected by the smell; and when they go to war they carry the raw meat underneath them to eat.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this blackletter print is garbled); long s normalized, the Tironian sign for 'and' given as 'e', a few contractions (de, per, pro, terra) expanded, other abbreviation marks kept as printed
passages.speaker: Gaspar da Cruz, O.P. (Tractado, Évora 1569)
passages.caution: Hostile Chinese hearsay. The sentence begins at the foot of the previous page, where Cruz calls these people commonly reddish ('bermelha') and says they go naked.

passages.headline: A hundred leagues of wall, with mountains in the gaps
passages.gloss: Cruz reports that the Chinese have a wall of a hundred leagues (some say more) between themselves and the Tartars, always garrisoned against Tartar raids. He reasons that it cannot be continuous but must use mountains to fill the gaps, because a Persian lord told him Persia had similar walls broken by hills. The Wall is credited plainly to the Chinese, built against the Tartars.
passages.quote: como tenho dito tem os Chinas cẽ legoas (dizendo outros que seram mais) de muro ãtre si e elles, õde ha sempre guarnições de gente pera defesa das ẽtradas dos Tartaros. Pode se crer que este muro nam he cõtinuado se nam q̃ se antremetem algũs mõtes ou serras, porq̃ me afirmou hũ señor da Persia que auia semelhantes obras nalgũas partes da persia, cõ se antremeterẽ outeiros ou serras.
passages.translation: as I have said, the Chinese have a hundred leagues of wall (others say it is more) between themselves and them, where there are always garrisons to defend against the incursions of the Tartars. It may be believed that this wall is not continuous, but that some mountains or ranges come in between, because a lord of Persia assured me that there were similar works in some parts of Persia, with hills or ranges coming in between.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this blackletter print is garbled); long s normalized, the Tironian sign for 'and' given as 'e', a few contractions (de, per, pro, terra) expanded, other abbreviation marks kept as printed
passages.speaker: Gaspar da Cruz, O.P. (Tractado, Évora 1569)

passages.headline: The Tartar raid of 1550 and a city retaken
passages.gloss: Portuguese prisoners in China were told that after some years of truce, the Tartars made a great invasion in 1550 and took a very important city. The Chinese besieged it but could not storm it; on the advice of a low-born man they found a way to kill the Tartars and their horses and recovered the city. Cruz does not name the city or the method. The date matches the great Mongol raid on the Beijing region in 1550.
passages.quote: Afirmouse aos Portugueses q̃ estauam catiuos … q̃ ha algũs annos q̃ auia entre os Chinas e Tartaros treguas: e no anno de cincoenta fizeram os Tartaros hũa grãde ẽtrada na China, da qual lhe tomaram hũa cidade muy principal … por cõselho de hũ homẽ de baixa sorte, tiuerã meo cõ que a elles e aos cauallos matarã, e ficarã outra vez señores da cidade.
passages.translation: It was affirmed to the Portuguese who were captives … that for some years there had been truces between the Chinese and the Tartars; and in the year fifty the Tartars made a great incursion into China, in which they took from them a very important city … on the advice of a man of low rank they found a means by which they killed them and their horses, and became masters of the city once more.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this blackletter print is garbled); long s normalized, the Tironian sign for 'and' given as 'e', a few contractions (de, per, pro, terra) expanded, other abbreviation marks kept as printed
passages.speaker: Gaspar da Cruz, O.P. (Tractado, Évora 1569)
passages.caution: Prisoners' hearsay; the city is not named.

passages.headline: The court moved to Beijing to face the Tartars
passages.people: Ming emperors; Tartars on the northern frontier
passages.gloss: Describing the province of Nanjing, Cruz says the king once lived there because the land is fertile and pleasant, but moved his court to Beijing ('Paquim') to be nearer the wars against the Tartars. It is an early European statement of why Beijing became the capital.
passages.quote: Tem esta prouincia dezaseys cidades, residio ãtiguamẽte nesta cidade el Rey por ser terra muy fertil, fresca e apraziuel, e mudou a corte pera ho paquim pera de mais perto acudir aas guerras dos Tartaros.
passages.translation: This province has sixteen cities. The king anciently resided in this city, because it is a very fertile, fresh and pleasant land, and moved the court to Paquim [Beijing] in order to attend more closely to the wars of the Tartars.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this blackletter print is garbled); long s normalized, the Tironian sign for 'and' given as 'e', a few contractions (de, per, pro, terra) expanded, other abbreviation marks kept as printed
passages.speaker: Gaspar da Cruz, O.P. (Tractado, Évora 1569)

passages.headline: Tartar prisoners in Canton, called 'Tatos'
passages.people: Tartar (Mongol) captives serving the Ming as soldiers
passages.gloss: Here Cruz speaks as an eyewitness: in Canton he saw many Tartar captives whose only 'captivity' was serving as soldiers far from home. They wore red caps as a badge but otherwise dressed like the Chinese, and received a fixed royal pay. The Chinese, he says, call them 'Tatos' because they cannot pronounce the letter R. Chinese Dada (Tatar) is real; the missing-R explanation is his.
passages.quote: Na cidade de Cantam vi eu muitos tartaros catiuos, os quaes nã tem mais catiueiro q̃ seruirẽ por homẽs darmas noutras partes longe de tartaria, e trazẽ por diuisa barretes bermelhos, no demais trazem ho trajo dos chinas com quẽ viuẽ … Chamam os chinas a estes Tatos, porque nam podem pronunciar esta letra. r.
passages.translation: In the city of Canton I saw many Tartar captives, whose only captivity is to serve as men-at-arms in other parts far from Tartary. They wear red caps as a badge; otherwise they wear the dress of the Chinese among whom they live … The Chinese call these people Tatos, because they cannot pronounce this letter r.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this blackletter print is garbled); long s normalized, the Tironian sign for 'and' given as 'e', a few contractions (de, per, pro, terra) expanded, other abbreviation marks kept as printed
passages.speaker: Gaspar da Cruz, O.P. (Tractado, Évora 1569)
passages.caution: The explanation of the name is Cruz's own.

passages.headline: Bearded 'Alimenes' guarding the Tartar passes
passages.people: Hired guards on the Tartar frontier, called 'Alimenes' by the Chinese
passages.gloss: Cruz reports that the king of China keeps salaried soldiers to guard the weak passes and walls facing the Tartars: big, bearded men in cut breeches and caps, with curved swords. A Portuguese captive heard the Chinese call them 'Alimenes', which Cruz takes to mean Germans (Alemanes), concluding that China must border Upper Germany. He tells the same story on an earlier page (n25). The identification is his own leap.
passages.quote: dizem os chinas que tẽ el Rey da China muita gente darmas salariada, que lhe guarda os passos fracos e os muros da bãda dos tartaras: dizẽ q̃ sam homẽs grãdes e barbaçudos, e q̃ trazẽ calças cortadas e gorras e espadas rõbas, e disse me hũ portugues q̃ pola terra dentro fora leuado catiuo, q̃ ouuira dizer aos chinas q̃ lhe chamauã a estes Alimenes
passages.translation: the Chinese say that the King of China has many salaried men-at-arms who guard for him the weak passes and the walls on the side of the Tartars; they say they are big, heavily bearded men who wear cut breeches, caps and curved swords; and a Portuguese who had been taken captive inland told me that he had heard the Chinese call these people Alimenes.
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this blackletter print is garbled); long s normalized, the Tironian sign for 'and' given as 'e', a few contractions (de, per, pro, terra) expanded, other abbreviation marks kept as printed
passages.speaker: Gaspar da Cruz, O.P. (Tractado, Évora 1569)
passages.caution: Third-hand report; the leap from 'Alimenes' to Germans is Cruz's guess.

passages.headline: Painted giants who guard the passes of Tartary
passages.people: Door-guardian figures in Canton, said to portray the king's frontier guards
passages.gloss: Describing officials' houses in Canton, Cruz notes huge gates painted with two giants holding staves. He saw four such figures in a temple, said to be portraits from life of men the king keeps to guard the weakest passes of Tartary, big-limbed and twelve or thirteen palms tall. What he saw were painted door gods; the frontier story is what he was told.
passages.quote: tẽ na frõtaria hũas portas muy grandes como portas de hũa cidade, com dous gigantes pintados cõ hũs bastões nas mãos: eu vi quatro em hũ pagode (que he tẽplo de idolos) tirados polo natural dalgũs q̃ dizẽ ter el Rey q̃ lhe guardã os passos
passages.translation: on the front they have some very large doors, like the gates of a city, with two giants painted on them holding staves in their hands. I saw four in a pagoda (which is a temple of idols), portrayed from life of some whom they say the King keeps to guard for him the passes [that are weakest in Tartary; they are very big-limbed, perhaps twelve or thirteen palms tall].
passages.quote_note: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this blackletter print is garbled); long s normalized, the Tironian sign for 'and' given as 'e', a few contractions (de, per, pro, terra) expanded, other abbreviation marks kept as printed; the sentence ends on the next page (n44): 'mais fracos da Tartaria, sam muy mẽbrudos, poderã ser de doze ou treze palmos dalto', given in brackets in the translation
passages.speaker: Gaspar da Cruz, O.P. (Tractado, Évora 1569)
passages.caution: He saw paintings; the story that they depict real giant frontier guards is hearsay.

passages.headline: Ninety years of Tartar rule, 1206 to 1368
passages.gloss: In his outline of Chinese dynasties Semedo says that after two thousand years of regional lords, the Tartars began conquering China piece by piece in 1206 and ruled it for ninety years until 1368, when Hongwu ('Hum Vu') found them grown careless and hated, drove them out and even subjected their borderlands. The Tartars here are the Mongols of the Yuan dynasty.
passages.quote: Permanecieron en la China los señores de Estados particulares mas de dos mil años, hasta que el de 1206. de nuestra Redencion, los Tartaros (entonces con otro poder i govierno) empeçando a conquistarla por partes, la vinieron a dominar por espacio de noventa años, que fenecieron el de 1368. en que el Hum Vu cogiendolos ya floxos de cuidado, i de tirania encendidos
