passages.translation: The lords of particular states remained in China more than two thousand years, until in the year 1206 of our Redemption the Tartars (then with another power and government), beginning to conquer it piece by piece, came to rule it for the space of ninety years, which ended in 1368, when Hum Vu, catching them now slack in their care and inflamed with tyranny
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized against the page image; long s normalized, abbreviation marks (q̃, õ, ẽ) kept as printed
passages.speaker: Álvaro Semedo, S.J. (Spanish edition by Manuel de Faria e Sousa, Madrid 1642)
passages.caution: 1206 is the year Chinggis Khan was proclaimed, not the start of Mongol rule over all China (completed in 1279).

passages.headline: How the Tartar borderlands split into three kingdoms
passages.people: Tartars north of China (Mongols and the eastern Jurchen, later Manchus)
passages.gloss: Semedo's origin story for the new enemy: after expelling the Tartars, Hongwu made the Tartar borderlands tributary and divided them into states with titles. These grew until they split into three kingdoms, East, West and North. The western and northern ones broke away at once; the eastern one stayed loyal until the Chinese, for no reason, decided to crush it, and it turned on them. The eastern kingdom is the Jurchen (Manchu) state.
passages.quote: Quando el Hum Vu, Trõco de la Familia q̃ oy tiene el cetro Chino, sacudiò de su Imperio al Tartaro, … dexando avassallados los cõfines de la Tartaria, los reduxo a tributarios, dividiẽdolos en Estados de titulos i dignidades diferẽtes. Crecierõ ellos despues tãto, q̃ se separarõ en tres Reynos: uno al Oriente, otro al Ocaso, i al Norte otro.
passages.translation: When Hum Vu, the founder of the family that today holds the Chinese sceptre, shook off from his empire the Tartar [who had ruled it for ninety years], … leaving the borders of Tartary as vassals, he reduced them to tributaries, dividing them into states with different titles and dignities. These afterwards grew so much that they separated into three kingdoms: one to the East, another to the West, and another to the North.
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized against the page image; long s normalized, abbreviation marks (q̃, õ, ẽ) kept as printed
passages.speaker: Álvaro Semedo, S.J. (Spanish edition by Manuel de Faria e Sousa, Madrid 1642)
passages.caution: A simplified Chinese-court version of frontier history.

passages.headline: Captives sacrificed before the battle of 1618
passages.gloss: Semedo translates a memorial sent to the Wanli emperor by the President of the Council of War in 1618. It reports that the Tartars had massed to 'take this world of China', broke through the walls, seized Chinese prisoners and sacrificed them the day before the battle, acclaiming their own king as king of Beijing. Semedo says he translated it at the time and later found it printed in Europe.
passages.quote: En este tiempo con grã poder i multitud, entrando los muros, prendieron algunos de los nuestros para sacrificarlos; i sacrificaron el dia antes de la batalla con grãdes aclamaciones de su Rey, llamandole ya Rey de PeKim.
passages.translation: At this time, with great power and multitude, entering the walls, they seized some of our men in order to sacrifice them; and they sacrificed them the day before the battle, with great acclamations of their king, calling him already King of Peking.
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized against the page image; long s normalized, abbreviation marks (q̃, õ, ẽ) kept as printed
passages.speaker: President of the Chinese Council of War, memorial of 1618, as translated by Álvaro Semedo (Spanish edition, Madrid 1642)
passages.caution: A Chinese official's war report, written to alarm the emperor; Semedo only translates it.

passages.headline: Cannibal famine, mice and two suns: omens of the Tartar war
passages.people: Chinese court facing the Tartar (Manchu) invasion
passages.gloss: The same 1618 memorial explains the defeat by heaven's anger and lists recent prodigies: no rain in the capital province, famine so bad in another province that people ate one another, a plague of mice in Nanjing, fires in the palace and two suns in the sky, one eclipsing the other. It shows how the Ming court read the Tartar war as a sign of cosmic disorder.
passages.quote: the Prodigies, which we have lately all seen, do demonstrate no lesse, In the Province of Pekim the last yeare it raigned not at all … in the Province of Xankim, there was so great a dearth and famine, that the people did eat one another: and into Nankim came an infinite multitude of Mice … we saw two Sunnes together, and the one did Ecclipse the other.
passages.speaker: President of the Chinese Council of War, memorial of 1618, in Semedo's translation (English edition, London 1655)
passages.caution: Reported omens, not observed events. 'Xankim' is a slip in the English; the Spanish has Xantum (Shandong).

passages.headline: The famous Wall: 'more fame than effect'
passages.gloss: Ending his tour of the provinces with Liaodong, famous for ginseng, Semedo notes that as the frontier with the Tartars it is badly wasted and partly held by them. Here, he says, runs the celebrated wall of three hundred leagues, which has more fame than effect: for all its size the enemy has reduced it to a miserable state. The Wall is Chinese, and in his view failing.
passages.quote: Llamase Ginsem: pero por ser frontera a los Tartaros muy destruida, antes parte posseída dellos. Aqui es que se vè aquella tan celebre muralla corriendo por espacio de trecientas leguas, con màs fama que efecto: porque sin embargo de su grandeza i capazidad, la tiene el enemigo puesta en miserable estado.
passages.translation: It [the root] is called ginseng. But being the frontier with the Tartars, [the province] is much destroyed, and even partly possessed by them. Here is where one sees that so celebrated wall, running for the space of three hundred leagues, with more fame than effect: for in spite of its greatness and capacity, the enemy has put it in a miserable state.
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized against the page image; long s normalized, abbreviation marks (q̃, õ, ẽ) kept as printed
passages.speaker: Álvaro Semedo, S.J. (Spanish edition by Manuel de Faria e Sousa, Madrid 1642)

passages.headline: Beijing made capital to face the Tartars
passages.people: Ming emperors; Tartars on the northern border
passages.gloss: Semedo explains that Beijing, called Cambalu by the Muslims, became the court when Yongle ('Yunlo'), who lived in that region, seized the throne after Hongwu's death and moved the court from Nanjing, both to be among his own supporters and to stand up better to the neighbouring Tartars. The Mongol name Khanbaliq survives in 'Cambalud'.
passages.quote: tiene aora la soberania de gozar de la Corte en la ciudad del mismo nombre: el propio es Xunthienfu: Cambalud la llaman los Moros … un nieto suyo llamado Yunlo … como para poder mejor hazer rostro a los Tartaros confinantes, sacò la Corte de NamKim, i plantòla acà.
passages.translation: it now has the sovereign privilege of enjoying the Court, in the city of the same name; its proper name is Xunthienfu; the Moors call it Cambalu … a grandson of his named Yunlo … [both to trust those he had always dealt with] and to be better able to face the neighbouring Tartars, took the Court out of Nanjing and planted it here.
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized against the page image; long s normalized, abbreviation marks (q̃, õ, ẽ) kept as printed
passages.speaker: Álvaro Semedo, S.J. (Spanish edition by Manuel de Faria e Sousa, Madrid 1642)
passages.caution: Yongle was Hongwu's son, not his grandson ('nieto') as the Spanish says.

passages.headline: Portuguese cannon against the Tartars, 1621
passages.gloss: In 1621 the city of Macau sent the emperor three large cannon with gunners. One burst at a demonstration in Beijing, killing three or four men, but the guns were still sent to the Tartar frontier. The Tartars, not knowing the new weapon, came too close, were hit by a shower of iron fragments, and fled; afterwards they were more careful.
passages.quote: Todavia embiaronse a la frontera de los Tartaros, que no sabiendo de la nueva arma, i llegandose màs de lo que les convenia, provaron un rocîo de troços de hierro, de que cayeron muchos, i todos fueron huyendo. Despues se acautelaron.
passages.translation: Nevertheless they were sent to the frontier of the Tartars, who, not knowing of the new weapon and coming nearer than was good for them, tasted a shower of pieces of iron, from which many fell, and all fled. Afterwards they became cautious.
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized against the page image; long s normalized, abbreviation marks (q̃, õ, ẽ) kept as printed
passages.speaker: Álvaro Semedo, S.J. (Spanish edition by Manuel de Faria e Sousa, Madrid 1642)

passages.headline: The wonder-working magicians of Tartar times
passages.people: Mongol (Yuan) era magicians, as recalled by Semedo
passages.gloss: Discussing Chinese divination, Semedo says some are said to keep familiar spirits, but he never saw any. In the time of the Tartar, he adds, there were many deeply sunk in such arts, and according to Marco Polo they worked marvels; today nothing of the kind is clearly known. He is sceptical and leans on Marco Polo for the Mongol period.
passages.quote: Dizese, que algunos tienen Familiares, i q̃ los consultan. Destos no vi. Antiguamente en tiempo del Tartaro huvo muchos, i muy empantanados en esto: i, segun Marco Veneto, hazian maravillas. Oy no sè que aya cosa alguna destas con claridad.
passages.translation: It is said that some have familiar spirits and consult them. Of these I saw none. Anciently, in the time of the Tartar, there were many, and very deeply sunk in this; and, according to Marco Polo, they worked marvels. Today I do not know that there is any such thing clearly.
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized against the page image; long s normalized, abbreviation marks (q̃, õ, ẽ) kept as printed
passages.speaker: Álvaro Semedo, S.J. (Spanish edition by Manuel de Faria e Sousa, Madrid 1642)
passages.caution: Second hand from Marco Polo; Semedo says he saw none.

passages.headline: Christians backed the Tartars and lost
passages.people: Tartars (Mongol Yuan rulers); Christians and Muslims in China
passages.gloss: Semedo explains why Jesuits found no trace of the Christians Marco Polo described. When the Tartar ruled China there were many Christians with fine churches, favoured by him. When Hongwu fought to recover the kingdom, the Muslims sided with the Chinese and kept their liberties and mosques, while the Christians sided with the Tartar and went down with him: some died, some converted, some hid.
passages.quote: Quando el Tartaro dominò la China, avia en ella muchos Christianos, con Iglesias bien suntuosas, que se hallavan favorecidos dèl, como parece de las Relaciones del Veneto. … Los Christianos tomando la voz del Tartaro, i quedando èl perdido en aquella accion, precisamente quedaron tambien perdidos en su estado
passages.translation: When the Tartar ruled China there were many Christians in it, with quite sumptuous churches, who found themselves favoured by him, as appears from the accounts of the Venetian [Marco Polo]. … The Christians, taking the side of the Tartar, and he being lost in that action, necessarily were also lost in their standing
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized against the page image; long s normalized, abbreviation marks (q̃, õ, ẽ) kept as printed
passages.speaker: Álvaro Semedo, S.J. (Spanish edition by Manuel de Faria e Sousa, Madrid 1642)
passages.caution: Semedo's own reconstruction, built on Marco Polo and Jesuit reasoning.

passages.headline: Cathay is China: Goes reaches the Wall
passages.people: Tartars beyond the Wall; Muslim merchants of the caravan road
passages.gloss: Semedo retells how the Jesuit brother Bento de Goes, travelling from India to find Cathay, learned from a caravan that Cathay and China were the same land under different names. He then passed Turfan and Hami to 'Quiaicion' (Jiayuguan), where one sees the wall dividing the Chinese from the Tartars, and on to Suzhou. This settled that 'Cathay' was simply northern China.
passages.quote: i otra que la China era lo mismo que el Catayo: no aviendo diferencia en las tierras, si no en los nombres. … passò por estas poblaciones, Puchan, Turfan, Aramuth, Camul, Quiaicion (de donde se vè aquella repetida muralla, que divide a los Chinos de los Tartaros) Sucheu
passages.translation: and the other, that China was the same as Cathay, there being no difference in the lands, but only in the names. … he passed through these towns: Puchan, Turfan, Aramuth, Camul, Quiaicion (from where one sees that much-repeated wall that divides the Chinese from the Tartars), Suzhou
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized against the page image; long s normalized, abbreviation marks (q̃, õ, ẽ) kept as printed
passages.speaker: Álvaro Semedo, S.J. (Spanish edition by Manuel de Faria e Sousa, Madrid 1642)
passages.caution: Semedo retells Goes's journey from Jesuit papers; he did not travel it.

passages.headline: Royal palaces and tombs burned, 1635
passages.gloss: In his year-by-year mission history Semedo notes that in 1635 the Tartars raided widely and set fire to royal palaces and the tombs of ancient princes, adding (as a moralist) a second fire to the one in which the princes' souls already burned. Mandarins were punished for negligence. He does not name the place.
passages.quote: Los Tartaros discurrian con sus assaltos, haziendo varios desperdicios, i llegaron a hazer bolar en humo de horrible incendio los Palacios Reales, i los sepulcros de los antiguos Principes, que alli yazian
passages.translation: The Tartars roamed about with their assaults, causing various destruction, and went so far as to send up in the smoke of a horrible fire the royal palaces and the tombs of the ancient princes who lay there
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized against the page image; long s normalized, abbreviation marks (q̃, õ, ẽ) kept as printed
passages.speaker: Álvaro Semedo, S.J. (Spanish edition by Manuel de Faria e Sousa, Madrid 1642)
passages.caution: Based on mission letters; the site is not named.

passages.headline: A hundred thousand guards for the emperor's ploughing
passages.people: Chinese court fearing a Tartar (Manchu) attack
passages.gloss: When the Chongzhen emperor went out to plough a furrow at the temple of agriculture as an example to his people, the fear of a Tartar 'flood' was so great that a hundred thousand men guarded him, even though the temple lay inside the city's second wall. A vivid picture of a capital living under threat.
passages.quote: Tanto se temian entonces de la inundacion de los Tartaros, que con ser el sitio deste Templo en lo interior de la segunda muralla de la ciudad, assistieron a la guarda de la persona Real cien mil hombres
passages.translation: So much did they then fear the flood of the Tartars that, although the site of this temple is inside the second wall of the city, a hundred thousand men attended to guard the royal person
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized against the page image; long s normalized, abbreviation marks (q̃, õ, ẽ) kept as printed
passages.speaker: Álvaro Semedo, S.J. (Spanish edition by Manuel de Faria e Sousa, Madrid 1642)

passages.headline: Semur, a great city destroyed by the Tartars
passages.gloss: Near Mount Ararat, at the lake where ten thousand martyrs were said to have been crucified, Jordanus says there was once a very great city called Semur, destroyed by the Tartars. He adds that he had been over almost the whole of that country. Yule could not identify Semur; it records the ruin left by the Mongol conquest of Armenia a century earlier.
passages.quote: et vocatur pars illa montis Ararat; et fuit ibi civitas una quæ Semur vocabatur, magna valdè, quæ per Tartaros fuit destructa. Ego fui per totam terram istam, ferè.
passages.translation: and that part of the mountain is called Ararat; and there was a city there called Semur, very great, which was destroyed by the Tartars. I have been over almost the whole of that land.
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized against the page image
passages.speaker: Jordanus Catalani of Séverac, O.P. (Latin text, ed. Coquebert de Montbret, Recueil de voyages IV, Paris 1839)
passages.caution: He travelled the region, but the city's destruction is reported, not witnessed; the city is unidentified.

passages.headline: 'Saracenized Tartars' in Persia
passages.people: Tartars of the Ilkhanate (Mongols in Persia converted to Islam)
passages.gloss: Jordanus, who lived in Tabriz, lists Persia's peoples: Saracens (Muslims), 'Saracenized Tartars', and Christians of many sects, plus a few Jews. The phrase captures the Mongol rulers of Persia after their conversion to Islam around 1295. He calls their ruler simply 'the emperor of Persia'.
passages.quote: Ista Persida habitatur per Saracenos et per Tartaros saracenatos, atque per Christianos schismaticos diversarum sectarum, seu per Nestorianos, Jacobitas, Græcos, Georgianos, Armenos, et per paucos Judæos.
passages.translation: This Persia is inhabited by Saracens and by Saracenized Tartars, and by schismatic Christians of various sects, that is Nestorians, Jacobites, Greeks, Georgians and Armenians, and by a few Jews.
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized against the page image
passages.speaker: Jordanus Catalani of Séverac, O.P. (Latin text, ed. Coquebert de Montbret, Recueil de voyages IV, Paris 1839)

passages.headline: Licking fingers and wiping hands on their shoes
passages.people: Persians and Tartars, western and eastern
passages.gloss: After describing how Persians eat sitting on the ground, several from one dish, Jordanus says they lick their fingers instead of using a napkin and wipe the leftover grease on their shoes. The Tartars, western and eastern, do exactly the same, he adds; only the Indians eat cleanly, though also with their hands. A fastidious European's table report.
passages.quote: ligant digitos cum linguâ et labris, et mundant loco manutegnii, et posteà, si adhuc superest de pinguedine in manibus, mundant eas super calceos suos; et sic faciunt, per omnia, Tartari occidentales atque orientales, Indis exceptis, qui soli comedunt, licèt cum manibus, satis mundè.
passages.translation: they lick their fingers with tongue and lips and clean them instead of with a napkin, and afterwards, if any grease is still left on their hands, they wipe them on their shoes; and so do the western and eastern Tartars in everything, except the Indians, who alone eat quite cleanly, though with their hands.
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized against the page image
passages.speaker: Jordanus Catalani of Séverac, O.P. (Latin text, ed. Coquebert de Montbret, Recueil de voyages IV, Paris 1839)
passages.caution: 'ligant' is the printed spelling (for lingunt, 'lick').

passages.headline: Tartary begins at Tana on the Don
passages.gloss: In his closing table of distances Jordanus says it is a thousand miles by sea, always eastwards, from Constantinople to 'Tana or Tartary'. Tana was the Italian trading post at the mouth of the Don, in Golden Horde territory, so for a traveller of 1330 'Tartary' started at the Sea of Azov.
passages.quote: De Constantinopoli usque Tanan vel Tartariam sunt milliaria mille, semper eundo versùs orientem, per mare.
passages.translation: From Constantinople to Tana or Tartary is a thousand miles, going always towards the east, by sea.
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized against the page image
passages.speaker: Jordanus Catalani of Séverac, O.P. (Latin text, ed. Coquebert de Montbret, Recueil de voyages IV, Paris 1839)

passages.headline: The other two Tartar empires
passages.people: Golden Horde (Uzbek Khan) and Chagatai khanate
passages.gloss: Besides the Great Tartar of Cathay and the Tartar emperor of Persia, Jordanus has heard of two more Tartar empires: one 'now of Osbet' called Gatzaria, and one of 'Dua and Cayda', now of 'Elchigaday'. Yule's note identifies Osbet as Uzbek, khan of the Golden Horde (1313 to 1340), and Elchigaday as the Chagatai khanate, and explains that Chinggis Khan's conquests had split among his heirs. An early sketch of the divided Mongol world.
passages.quote: But other two empires of the Tartars, as I have heard, to wit, that which was formerly of Cathay, but now is of Osbet, which is called Gatzaria, and the empire of Dua and Cayda, formerly of Capac and now of Elchigaday, extend over more than CC days' journey.
passages.speaker: Jordanus Catalani, translated by Henry Yule (Mirabilia descripta, Hakluyt Society, London 1863)
passages.caution: Hearsay; several names are garbled, and the identifications are Yule's.

passages.headline: The Great Tartar: rich, just, and paying in paper
passages.people: The Great Tartar (the Yuan emperor of China)
passages.gloss: Jordanus opens his chapter on the Great Tartar by saying he reports only what trustworthy people told him: the Great Tartar is very rich, very just and very generous, rules four realms each as big as France, and feeds and clothes for life anyone who cannot earn a living. In his lands paper stamped with black ink passes for money and buys gold, silver, silk, gems and anything else. Paper money is the Yuan chao.
passages.quote: De Magno Tartaro, quod audivi à fide dignis narro: scilicet, quòd est ditissimus, justissimus, atque largus valdè. Iste habet quatuor regna sub se, æqualiter magna sicut regnum Franciæ, et benè habitata. … In dominio istius, currit, pro monetâ, papyrus signata cum encausto nigro, cum quâ habetur aurum, argentum, sericum, lapides pretiosi, et simpliciter omnia quæ vult homo.
passages.translation: Of the Great Tartar I relate what I have heard from trustworthy people: that he is very rich, very just and very generous. He has under him four kingdoms, each as large as the kingdom of France, and well peopled. … In his dominion paper stamped with black ink runs as money, with which one obtains gold, silver, silk, precious stones and simply everything a man wants.
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized against the page image
passages.speaker: Jordanus Catalani of Séverac, O.P. (Latin text, ed. Coquebert de Montbret, Recueil de voyages IV, Paris 1839)
passages.caution: Hearsay that closely echoes Marco Polo.

passages.headline: Hyemo, a city a day's ride across
passages.people: Subjects of the Great Tartar (Yuan China)
passages.gloss: Jordanus heard from people who had seen them that the Great Tartar's empire has very great cities, one called Hyemo which takes a full day on horseback to cross by a straight road through the middle. On the next page he adds that the emperor rules two hundred cities bigger than Toulouse. Yule guessed Hyemo might be Emil, a Mongol town built by Ögedei, but thought it more likely a vast Chinese city like Hangzhou.
passages.quote: In isto imperio, sunt civitates permaximæ, prout ab hiis qui viderunt audivi; nam est una quæ Hyemo vocatur quæ per quadrum, rectâ viâ, habet dietam unam cum equo transeundo per medium, rectâ viâ.
passages.translation: In this empire there are very great cities, as I have heard from those who have seen them; for there is one called Hyemo which, square as it is, takes a day's journey on horseback to cross through the middle by a straight road.
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized against the page image
passages.speaker: Jordanus Catalani of Séverac, O.P. (Latin text, ed. Coquebert de Montbret, Recueil de voyages IV, Paris 1839)
passages.caution: The city is unidentified; the identification offered is Yule's guess.

passages.headline: Monasteries, choirs and red hats like cardinals
passages.people: Buddhists under the Great Tartar (Yuan China)
passages.gloss: In the Great Tartar's empire, Jordanus was told, there are idol temples and monasteries of men and women just as in Europe; they chant in choir and say prayers exactly like Catholics, and the great 'pontiffs of the idols' wear red capes and red hats like cardinals. The splendour of their sacrifices is beyond belief. It is an early European comparison of Buddhist (probably Tibetan) monastic life with Catholic ritual.
passages.quote: In isto imperio, sunt templa idolorum, et monasteria hominum et mulierum, sicut inter nos; et ita tenent chorum, et dicunt orationes suas, rectè sicut nos; et pontifices majores idolorum portant cappas rubeas et capellos rubeos ad modum cardinalium nostrorum.
passages.translation: In this empire there are temples of idols, and monasteries of men and of women, as among us; and they keep choir and say their prayers just as we do; and the great pontiffs of the idols wear red capes and red hats in the manner of our cardinals.
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized against the page image
passages.speaker: Jordanus Catalani of Séverac, O.P. (Latin text, ed. Coquebert de Montbret, Recueil de voyages IV, Paris 1839)

passages.headline: Bodies kept at home; lords buried with horse and slaves
passages.gloss: Jordanus heard that in this empire the dead are neither burned nor buried, sometimes for ten years, because the family cannot yet afford the proper rites; the body is kept in the house and served food as if alive. Great lords are buried with a horse and with one or two of their favourite servants alive. The first part fits Chinese custom; the second, steppe Mongol practice.
passages.quote: Ibi, mortuos suos non comburunt; non etiam sepeliunt, aliquotiens per decem annos; … sed tenent eos in domibus, et ministrant sibi cibaria, sicut si esset vivus. Magni domini, cùm moriuntur, sepeliuntur cum equo uno, et cum uno vel duobus suis servitoribus vivis sibi magis dilectis.
passages.translation: There they do not burn their dead, nor even bury them, sometimes for ten years; … but they keep them in their houses and serve them food as if they were alive. Great lords, when they die, are buried with one horse and with one or two of their best loved servants alive.
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized against the page image; the editor's '(sic)' after 'vivus' omitted
passages.speaker: Jordanus Catalani of Séverac, O.P. (Latin text, ed. Coquebert de Montbret, Recueil de voyages IV, Paris 1839)
passages.caution: Hearsay mixing Chinese and Mongol customs.

passages.headline: The emperor's corpse relayed so no one finds the grave
passages.gloss: When the emperor dies, Jordanus heard, men carry the body with great treasure to a certain spot, drop it and run 'as if the devil were after them'; others then snatch it up and do the same, relay after relay, so that the burial place can never be found and the treasure never stolen. His death is kept secret until a successor is quietly enthroned. Secret Mongol royal burials are real; the relay detail is hearsay.
passages.quote: Cùm imperator moritur, portatur cum maximo thesauro, à quibusdam hominibus, usque ad certum locum, ubi deponunt corpus, et fugiunt quàm possunt, sicut si diabolus insequeretur eos; et sunt alii parati qui immediatè corpus rapiunt, et simili modo faciunt usque ad alium locum; … et hoc faciunt ne locus possit inveniri
passages.translation: When the emperor dies he is carried with a very great treasure by certain men to a certain place, where they set down the body and flee as fast as they can, as if the devil were chasing them; and others are ready who at once snatch up the body and do the same as far as another place; … and they do this so that the place cannot be found
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized against the page image
passages.speaker: Jordanus Catalani of Séverac, O.P. (Latin text, ed. Coquebert de Montbret, Recueil de voyages IV, Paris 1839)
passages.caution: Hearsay; compare Carpini and Marco Polo on the secret cemetery of the khans.

passages.headline: They always live in tents, not villages or cities
passages.gloss: In a chapter on the Tartars' outward appearance and way of life, the text says plainly that they always live in tents and never in villages or cities, because they are country herdsmen with vast flocks of sheep and goats, herds of cattle, camels and horses. They winter on the plains and follow the good pasture into the mountains in summer. The same chapter describes their bull-like singing of 'Alai alai'.
passages.quote: In tentorijs semper habitant, & non in villis, vel vrbibus. Pastores enim pecorum rurales sunt, ac gregibus ouium, & caprarum armentisque boum, & camelorum, & equorum superabundant. In hyeme manere consueuerunt in planicie, in æstate vero pascuarum vbertatem sectantur in montibus.
passages.translation: They always live in tents, and not in villages or cities. For they are country herdsmen of livestock, and abound in flocks of sheep and goats and in herds of cattle, camels and horses. In winter they are accustomed to stay on the plain; in summer they follow the richness of the pastures in the mountains.
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized against the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Vincent of Beauvais, Speculum historiale (Douai 1624), from material he says he received from Simon of Saint-Quentin
passages.caution: Attributed to Simon's eyewitness report through Vincent's editing.

passages.headline: Craftsmen spared when a city surrenders
passages.gloss: On their cunning in sieges: the Tartars promise much to a besieged town, and if it surrenders they say 'come out so we can count you after our custom'. When the people come out, the Tartars keep those they find to be craftsmen and those they want as slaves, and kill all the rest by smashing their heads with stones. This matches other sources on Mongol use of captive artisans.
passages.quote: Et siquidem illi se reddiderint eis dicunt illis. Exite ad nos, vt secundum morem nostrum numeremus vos, cumque ad eos exeunt, quos comperiunt esse artifices sibi reseruant, alios autem omnes præter illos quos sibi pro seruis retinere volunt, cum lapidibus super lapides excerebrant.
passages.translation: And if they surrender to them, they say to them: 'Come out to us, so that we may count you according to our custom.' And when they come out to them, those whom they find to be craftsmen they keep for themselves; all the others, except those they wish to keep as slaves, they kill by dashing out their brains with stones upon stones.
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized against the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Vincent of Beauvais, Speculum historiale (Douai 1624), from material he says he received from Simon of Saint-Quentin
passages.caution: Hostile report written to warn Christians; the same chapter repeats cannibalism charges.

passages.headline: Rebels against Prester John's son
passages.gloss: This origin story says that in 1202, 'according to some', the Tartars, living in Tartary 'which borders on India', rose against their lord King David, son of Prester John, emperor of India, killed him by treachery and went out to destroy peoples. The chapter goes on to have Chinggis Khan organise them by tens, hundreds and thousands. It is a crusader-era legend; the real event behind it is Chinggis Khan's overthrow of the Kereit ruler Ong Khan in 1203.
passages.quote: Anno Domini 1202. secundum quosdam, Tartari post occisionem Domini sui exierunt in populorum destructionem. Hi etenim post adhuc in terra sua videlicet Tartaria quæ affinis est Indiæ, residentes contra Regem Dauid Dominum suum videlicet presbyteri Ioannis quondam dominatoris & Imperatoris Indiæ filium conspirauerunt, eumque dolose machinando, interfecerunt.
passages.translation: In the year of the Lord 1202, according to some, the Tartars, after the killing of their lord, went out to destroy peoples. For while they were still living in their own land, namely Tartary, which borders on India, they conspired against King David their lord, son of Prester John, formerly ruler and emperor of India, and killed him by treacherous scheming.
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized against the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Vincent of Beauvais, Speculum historiale (Douai 1624), from material he says he received from Simon of Saint-Quentin
passages.caution: Legend; the text itself flags it as what 'some' say.

passages.headline: Friars look for Alexander's enclosed nations and find nothing
passages.people: Dominican friars in Georgia; the legendary peoples shut behind the Caspian mountains
passages.gloss: Scholastic histories said Alexander the Great had the Jews (in other versions Gog and Magog) shut up between the Caspian mountains, to break out at the end of the world. Vincent reports that Dominicans who lived seven years in Tiflis asked Georgians, Persians and Jews about it, and all said they knew nothing of it. The margin says the story 'appears to be a fable', and the next page adds that only Alexander's gates exist, one of which the Tartars broke.
passages.quote: Cum enim dicant historiæ nostræ scolasticæ, quod Alexander magnus Rex Macedonum oratione impetrauit à Domino reclusionem Iudæorum inter montes Caspios, ipsosque circa finem mundi prædicent exituros, Fratres nostri … per 7. annos commorati sunt, diligenter à Georgianis & à Persis, & etiam à Iudæis de inclusione illa inquisierunt, & dicunt omnes etiam Iudæi, quod nihil penitus inde sciunt
passages.translation: For whereas our scholastic histories say that Alexander the Great, king of the Macedonians, obtained from the Lord by prayer the shutting up of the Jews between the Caspian mountains, and predict that they will come out near the end of the world, our brothers [of the Order of Preachers, in the Georgian city of Tiflis near the Caspian mountains] stayed seven years, and diligently asked the Georgians and Persians, and even the Jews, about that enclosure; and all, even the Jews, say that they know nothing at all of it
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized against the page image; long s normalized
passages.speaker: Vincent of Beauvais, Speculum historiale (Douai 1624), from material he says he received from Simon of Saint-Quentin
passages.caution: The friars tested a legend and found no support; the passage does not itself call the Tartars the enclosed nations.

passages.headline: Why they are called Tartars: the horde that gave its name
passages.people: Tartars (Mongols, as told to a Dutch interpreter in Qing China)
passages.when: report written after 1656; story set c. 1187
passages.gloss: Johannes Melman, a Dutch East India Company interpreter in China from 1656, wrote down for Witsen what 'the most sensible Tartars' in Peking told him about their origins. The Scythians beyond Mount Imaus lived in seven hordes, one of them called Tartar; because the khan they elected came from that horde, all his subjects took the name Tartar and kept it.
passages.quote: Daerenboven bestonden de Scyten, ten tijde dezer verdeelinge, die achter de Berg Imaus zich onthielden, in zeven Horden, welke genoemt wierden, Tartar, Tangur, Cunat, Tateyr, Sonic, Mongli, en Tebeta … en om dat dezen gekoren Keizer uit de Horde der Tartaren was voort gekomen, zoo hebben alle zijne onderdanen dien naem van Tartar … aengenomen, en tot noch toe behouden.
passages.translation: Moreover, at the time of this division, the Scythians who lived beyond Mount Imaus consisted of seven hordes, which were called Tartar, Tangur, Cunat, Tateyr, Sonic, Mongli and Tebeta … and because this elected emperor had come from the horde of the Tartars, all his subjects took that name of Tartar … and have kept it to this day.
passages.speaker: Johannes Melman (Dutch East India Company interpreter), report printed by Nicolaes Witsen
passages.caution: The seven names closely match the list of Tartar nations in Hayton's Flower of the Histories of the East (1307), so book learning seems to be mixed into this 'Tartar' testimony.

passages.headline: Tartary: a European label for everything east of the Ob
passages.gloss: Introducing Siberia, Witsen explains his own usage: in Europe the name Tartary is commonly given to all lands east of the Ob and the Caspian Sea, and he uses it that way too, though strictly speaking Siberia does not lie in Tartary. A clear statement that 'Tartary' on his maps was a convention, not the name of a state.
passages.quote: gelijk met de naem Tartarye, meest doorgaens in Europa, alle Landen beoosten de Oby, en het Kaspische Meir, zoo als ik dezelve onder die benaming mede betrekke, bekent zijn; hoe wel dan eigentlijk genomen, dit Siberia in Tartarye niet en legt
passages.translation: just as, under the name Tartary, most commonly in Europe, all lands east of the Ob and the Caspian Sea are known, as I too include them under that name; although, properly speaking, this Siberia does not lie in Tartary
passages.speaker: Nicolaes Witsen

passages.headline: A silver bowl from a riverbank grave, and who could have made it
passages.gloss: When the Irtysh undercut its bank near Samarovsky Yam in 1688, a wooden coffin with old bones, silver arm-rings, a silver necklace and a silver bowl fell out. The governor of Siberia, Fyodor Golovin, later gave the bowl to Witsen. Witsen asks who made such silverwork, found in several graves there, since the present inhabitants do not know how to work silver.
passages.quote: een Graft, of houte Dood-kist, met gebeenderen eener voor lang verstorven Mensch, beneffens eenig Zilver-werk van Arm-ringen, en een Zilvere Halsband … Het verdient zijn aenmerkinge, waer, en by wien dit Zilver geschir, wiens gelijken meer worden gevonden te dier Oord in zommige Begraef-plaetzen, mag gemaekt zijn, om dat in deze gewesten tegenwoordig by de Inboorlingen, de konst van in Zilver te werken niet is bekent.
passages.translation: a grave, or wooden coffin, with the bones of a man long dead, together with some silverwork of arm-rings and a silver necklace … It deserves notice where, and by whom, this silver vessel, whose like is found more often in that region in some burial places, may have been made, because in these parts the art of working silver is not known among the natives today.
passages.speaker: Nicolaes Witsen
passages.caution: Witsen owned the bowl but had the story of its discovery from Golovin.

passages.headline: A gold sphinx from a Siberian kurgan, and Egyptians in Siberia?
passages.gloss: Witsen describes a small beaten-gold figure sent to him from Siberia, dug from an old burial under a kurgan: a lion or tiger body with a human head and spread wings. On the same page he wonders whether Egyptian idol-worship somehow reached Siberia, or whether Chinese settlers of Chinggis Khan's time left such things. A striking early report of Scythian-style gold from Siberian mounds, wrapped in pure speculation.
passages.quote: Een ander Afgoden-beeld, groot twee vinger-breet, van geslagen Goud, is my uit Siberien toegezonden, 't geen mede uit een oude Begravenis-plaets, daer men Menschen doods-beenderen by vond, onder een Kurgan, of groote heuvel is geligt, vertoont het Lichaem van een viervoetig Beest, als van een Tyger of Leeuw, heeft het hooft van een Mensch, en twee vleugelen
passages.translation: Another idol, two fingers' breadth in size, of beaten gold, was sent to me from Siberia; it too was lifted from an old burial place, where human bones were found with it, under a kurgan or great mound; it shows the body of a four-footed beast, like a tiger or lion, has the head of a man, and two wings
passages.speaker: Nicolaes Witsen
passages.caution: The object is real evidence; Witsen's Egyptian and Chinese explanations are his own guesses, which he himself calls a riddle.

passages.headline: The emperor of China is the 'Grand Cham of Tartary'
passages.gloss: In his opening words Nieuhof explains that the Company sent its envoys to Peking 'to the Grand Cham of Tartary, the now Emperour of China'. The old European title for the Mongol Great Khan is simply transferred to the new Manchu ruler of China, the Shunzhi emperor. This is the vocabulary later writers like Witsen and Dapper inherited.
passages.quote: with Credentials, and a considerable train of Attendants, to Peking in China, to the Grand Cham of Tartary, the now Emperour of China, impowering to negotiate concerning a Free and Mutual Commerce with them in his Kingdoms and Territories.
passages.speaker: Johan Nieuhof (English translation by John Ogilby, 1669)

passages.headline: The fall and sack of Canton, 1650
passages.gloss: Nieuhof tells how the Tartar army took Canton after a siege that, he says, lasted a whole year, helped by a bribed Chinese governor who opened a gate. Two Dutch gunners married to Chinese women had helped the defenders. The sack that followed lasted weeks. He arrived five years later, so this is what the townspeople told him.
passages.quote: It was upon the 24. of November, in the year 1650. when the Tartars upon this advantage rushed with their whole Army into the City … The whole Tartar Army being got into the City, the place was soon turned to a Map of misery … there was heard no other cry in the Streets, but Strike, Kill, and Destroy the Rebellious Barbarians
passages.speaker: Johan Nieuhof (English translation by John Ogilby, 1669)

passages.headline: A Tartar archer hits a palm-sized mark three times
passages.place: Guangdong, on the river north of Canton
passages.gloss: While the embassy camped ashore, the Tartar escort put on a display of arms. One bowman shot three arrows in a row through a target no bigger than a hand at thirty-five paces and was paid a small coin. A small eyewitness scene that matches the Manchus' fame as archers.
passages.quote: The Tartars in the mean time, to show some pastime, exercised their Arms before the Tent of the Embassadours, which was performed by them with much dexterity. Amongst the rest, there was one with a Bow and Arrow, who was so rare a Marks-man, that he shot thrice together through the white, no broader then the Palm of a Hand, at the distance of thirty five Paces
passages.speaker: Johan Nieuhof (English translation by John Ogilby, 1669)

passages.headline: At Nanjing the conquerors live in huts; the Chinese keep the stone city
passages.gloss: Describing the ruined Ming imperial palace at Nanjing, Nieuhof notes that the Tartar garrison settled near a temple and built themselves huts, leaving the Chinese to live and trade in the city. The palace buildings, of hard stone painted yellow, were Chinese work. On the same page he says the Tartars destroyed the palace out of hatred for the Ming family.
passages.quote: The Tartars seated themselves near to an Idol Temple called Paolinxi, where they built themselves several Hutts, leaving the Chineses to dwell in the City, and there to drive their Trade. The buildings are all of a hard sort of Stone, which the Natives have most curiously Painted with a Yellow Colour, that when the Sun reflects on them, they shine like Gold.
passages.speaker: Johan Nieuhof (English translation by John Ogilby, 1669)

passages.headline: A Tartar lady tries on the ambassador's hat
passages.gloss: Riding past the old imperial court at Nanjing, the Dutch were invited in by a Tartar lady of about forty, 'very debonair and free'. She came out to meet the ambassador, admired how their swords bent without breaking, put his hat on her own head and unbuttoned his doublet. She then served them a strong drink made of beans. A lively picture of a Manchu noblewoman's easy manners with strangers.
passages.quote: we past by the Gate of the old Imperial Court, where sat a great Tartar Lady, with her servants waiting upon her, about forty years of Age: She very civilly sent to our Interpreter to invite the Embassadours into her House … She was very debonair and free, looked upon our Swords, and much admired their bending without breaking: She took the Embassadours Hat, and put it on her own Head
passages.speaker: Johan Nieuhof (English translation by John Ogilby, 1669)

passages.headline: The Porcelain Tower: said to be built by Chinese on a Tartar's orders
passages.people: Tartars (an earlier conquest, and the Manchus)
passages.gloss: Nieuhof admired the nine-storey glazed Porcelain Tower of Nanjing and repeats what he was told: the Chinese built it at their own cost on the orders of a Tartar conqueror seven hundred years before, and the new Tartar conquerors chose to spare it. In fact the tower was built by the Ming Yongle emperor in the early 1400s, so the story he was told is wrong, but it shows buildings being linked to Tartar conquerors in popular memory.
passages.quote: This wonderful Pile (as they inform us) the Chineses built at their own charges, commanded by the insulting Conquerour the Tartar, to them a Pillar of Honour, to the Subdued of Obloquie, seven hundred years since, when in like manner, as lately, they over-ran all China
passages.speaker: Johan Nieuhof (English translation by John Ogilby, 1669)
passages.caution: The dating and the Tartar command are hearsay and do not match the tower's known Ming date.

passages.headline: A Tartar grandee eats half-raw pork at the council table
passages.people: Tartars (Manchu lords of the Qing council)
passages.gloss: At their first reception in Beijing the envoys sat with the council, whose Tartar members wore plain clothes and sat on a bench covered with old linen. The presiding lord grew hungry and ate half-raw pork 'more like a Butcher, then a Prince'. The Jesuit Adam Schall, dressed in Tartar fashion, interpreted. The Dutch were shocked by the lack of ceremony.
passages.quote: his Highness found himself hungry, and sent for a piece of Pork to satisfie his Appetite, which was half-raw, whereof he did eat most heartily, in a slovenly manner, that he looked more like a Butcher, then a Prince … When Dinner was brought up, his Highness and the rest of the Tartar Lords fell on again as greedily, as if they had eat nothing all that day
passages.speaker: Johan Nieuhof (English translation by John Ogilby, 1669)
passages.caution: Written with obvious Dutch disdain; a contrast with Chinese court manners rather than neutral description.

passages.headline: Golden roofs? No, glazed clay tiles
passages.gloss: Describing the palace where the 'Great Cham' now lived, Nieuhof explains that the roofs are covered with yellow glazed tiles that shine brighter than gold in the sun. This, he says, is why some people reported that the palace was roofed with pure gold, when in fact the tiles are made of clay.
passages.quote: All the Roofs of the Buildings are covered with Yellow glazed Pantiles, which shine, when the Sun reflects, brighter then Gold; which has made some believe and report, that the Roof of this Royal Palace was covered with pure Gold; whereas in truth the Tiles are only made of Clay, and Glaz'd and Neil'd over with Artificial Yellow
passages.speaker: Johan Nieuhof (English translation by John Ogilby, 1669)

passages.headline: Forced to wear the Tartar queue
passages.gloss: The general description explains that since the conquest the Chinese must shave their heads in the Tartar manner and keep only one lock hanging behind. Thousands, it says, chose death rather than lose their long hair. This is the Qing head-shaving order, told from the Chinese side.
passages.quote: since this Famous Empire fell under the Tyrannous yoke of the Tartars, and became subject to them, they have also submitted to the Tartarian mode of cutting and wearing the Hair: for now the Chineses do cut off all their Hair after the manner of their Conquerour, and reserve only one Lock, which hangs down behind
passages.speaker: Johan Nieuhof, general description of China (English translation by John Ogilby, 1669); this part is compiled, largely from Martino Martini

passages.headline: Horsemen raised to arms from the cradle
passages.gloss: A compiled portrait of the Tartar soldier: iron helmets with dyed horse-tail plumes, bows and sabres but no muskets, nearly all cavalry. They are pale, silent, trained to arms from infancy, unmatched archers, and eat any flesh half cooked. The same page calls them 'a Nation of Plunderers' and says few have any religion beyond some lamas.
passages.quote: They are whitish of Complexion, not talkative, but silent, and well composed, bred up to Arms from their very Cradles, which makes them such excellent Souldiers … They eat whatsoever they can get, but chiefly flesh, and that half roasted or boiled, being not curious of what sort it is, whether of Camels, Horses, or other Creatures.
passages.speaker: Johan Nieuhof, general description of China (English translation by John Ogilby, 1669); this part is compiled, largely from Martino Martini
passages.caution: Compiled, and mixes observation with hostile stereotypes about plunder and irreligion.

passages.headline: The Manchus called 'Kin', lords of the golden mountains
passages.gloss: The Dutch general description says the people of Niuche, 'properly East Tartary', are known to the Chinese and their neighbours as Kin, meaning gold, and are called lords of the golden mountains because the Chinese believe their land is rich in gold mines. Kin is the Jin, the dynastic name used by the Jurchen and again by the Manchus before 1636.
passages.quote: D'Inwoonders zijn by de Sinezen en Grens-buren met den naam van Kin bekent; dat Gout op Neêrduitsch te zeggen is. Gemeenlijk wordenze ook de Heeren en Meesters van de goude Bergen genoemt, dewijl het een gemeen gevoelen onder de Sinezen is, dat hun landschap, datze bezitten, zeer gout-rijke Mijnen in zich besloten houd
passages.translation: The inhabitants are known among the Chinese and their neighbours by the name of Kin, which in Dutch means Gold. They are also commonly called the Lords and Masters of the golden Mountains, because it is a common belief among the Chinese that the land they possess holds very gold-rich mines
passages.speaker: Johan Nieuhof, general description of China (Dutch, 1665); this part is compiled, largely from Martino Martini

passages.headline: 124 cities once, now 'movable cities'
passages.gloss: The Tartars say there were 124 cities in East Tartary under the Yuan (Mongol) dynasty. The author will not vouch for it, since the Tartars in China themselves could not tell him whether they still stand, only that there were many low huts and earthen walls. Their real towns, 'so to speak', move with them and their herds.
passages.quote: De Tarters verhalen, dat, onder de regeering van den Stam Ivena, in dit Oosterlijk Tartarye hondert en vier en twintigh steden lagen: dan of de zelve noch tegenwoordigh daar te vinden zijn, zou ik voor de waarheit niet derven na-zeggen … maar wel, dat 'er meenigte van lage hutten, en aerde wallen waren. Zy hebben, zoo te zeggen, beweeghlijke en verplaatzelijke steden
passages.translation: The Tartars relate that under the rule of the Yuan dynasty there lay in this East Tartary one hundred and twenty-four cities; but whether they are still to be found today I dare not affirm as true … but [they said] indeed that there were many low huts and earthen walls. They have, so to speak, movable and portable cities
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized; the two printed columns, interleaved in the OCR, are read in order
passages.speaker: Johan Nieuhof, general description of China (Dutch, 1665); this part is compiled, largely from Martino Martini
passages.caution: In this compiled part the 'me' may be Martini's voice rather than Nieuhof's.

passages.headline: Not caves but shining tents of waxed silk
passages.gloss: The Chinese, bitter enemies of the Niuche Tartars, mock them as cave-dwellers, but the text calls this false: they live in fine tents used instead of houses, made of silk or cloth coated with clear wax so they shine like mirrors and shed the rain. Great men have several tents joined so they look like one, for wives, servants and kitchen.
passages.quote: De Sinezen, die met recht op de Tarters van Niuche zeer gebeeten zijn; verdichten en drijven hen tot spot na, datze in holen en onderaartsche kuilen woonen; 't welk valsch is: want zy onthouden zich in zeer schoone en cierlijke Tenten … uit zijde stoffen of lakens, die met helder en doorschijnend wasch zoo aartigh en kunstig bestreeken zijn, datze in de Zon glinsteren en blinken als een spiegel
passages.translation: The Chinese, who with good reason are very bitter against the Tartars of Niuche, invent and mock them by saying that they live in caves and underground pits; which is false: for they keep themselves in very fine and handsome tents … of silk stuffs or cloths, so neatly and artfully coated with bright, translucent wax that they glitter and shine in the sun like a mirror
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized; the two printed columns, interleaved in the OCR, are read in order
passages.speaker: Johan Nieuhof, general description of China (Dutch, 1665); this part is compiled, largely from Martino Martini

passages.headline: Gog and Magog beyond the mountains, fires in the night
passages.place: Central Asia (placed by Kircher near Cathay and Tangut)
passages.people: Gog and Magog, identified with the Great Cham's realm
passages.gloss: This page is not by Nieuhof but from Athanasius Kircher's China Illustrata, bound into Ogilby's English volume. Kircher quotes an Arabic geographer on the cities of Gog and Magog beyond an unclimbable snowy mountain: people who climb it rarely return, and those who do report many fires at night. Kircher then fits this to the Great Cham's empire and Prester John.
passages.quote: On the other side of the Mountain are many Cities of Jagog and Magog. And it often happened, that the Inhabitants of this Region, out of a certain curiosity, ascend some part of it … but many never return … some that have return'd safe, relate, that in the Region on the other side of the Mountain in the night season, are many fires
passages.speaker: an Arabic geographer as quoted by Athanasius Kircher (appendix in Ogilby's 1669 volume, not by Nieuhof)
passages.caution: Not part of Nieuhof's text; a learned legend passed through several books.

passages.headline: The Emperor of China is not the Great Khan, only a small Manchu prince
passages.gloss: Dapper corrects a long European belief: the Tartar ruler in Peking is not the Great Cham of all Tartary but one of the smallest Tartar princes, whose grandfather was raised to kingship by the people of a small province of East Tartary called Muncheu (Manchu). The same page names the present emperor Konchi (Kangxi), a youth of about sixteen, son of the Shunzhi emperor.
passages.quote: Men zeid de Tartersche Vorst, die heden het gewest van Sina bezit, en sijn verblijf in de Hooft-stadt Peking heeft, de groote Cham en Heer van geheel Tartarije niet is, gelijk tot dus lang gelooft is; maer een van de kleinste Vorsten der Tarters: waer van sijn groot-vader d'eerste Koning van zijnen stam was, verheven tot die waerdigheid door d'inwoonders van zijn land
passages.translation: It is said that the Tartar prince who today possesses the land of China and resides in the capital Peking is not the Great Cham and lord of all Tartary, as has been believed until now, but one of the smallest princes of the Tartars, whose grandfather was the first king of his line, raised to that dignity by the inhabitants of his land
passages.speaker: Olfert Dapper, compiled general description of China

passages.headline: A city surrendered by treaty, but its towers pulled down
passages.gloss: Passing through Zwanjefoe (Quanzhou), the Dutch envoys learned that the city had never been taken by the sword: its commander handed it over to the Tartars by agreement, keeping his office. Even so, as a sign of victory, the Tartar had all the city's towers torn down except three. A small, precise record of what conquest meant for a Chinese city's skyline.
passages.quote: Noit is de Stadt door het zwaert, by de Tarters overwonnen, maer wierd, door den Krijgs-overste … met verdrag overgegeven … Ten teken evenwel der overwinning, liet de Tarter al de torens, behalve de voorzeide drie, afbreken en ten gronde slopen
passages.translation: The city was never conquered by the sword by the Tartars, but was handed over by its military commander … by treaty … As a sign of victory, however, the Tartar had all the towers, except the three mentioned before, torn down and razed to the ground
passages.quote_note: OCR normalized; the two printed columns, interleaved in the OCR, are read in order
passages.speaker: Olfert Dapper, from the journals of the second Dutch embassy (Jan van Kampen and Constantijn Nobel)
passages.caution: The envoys saw the city but the story of its surrender was told to them.

passages.headline: Stone houses burned by the Tartars, heads on stakes
passages.people: Tartars (Qing army), fighting the Zheng regime
passages.gloss: Going ashore with Bort's fleet after the joint Dutch and Qing attack on the island bases of the Zheng (Koxinga) regime, the Dutch found a walled town and its suburb packed with fine stone houses, all wrecked and burned by the Tartars. In a square lay stakes and human heads, which the enemies of the Tartars had displayed six years before, after a great Tartar defeat at sea, and which had now been thrown down and burned 'after the manner of the Tartars'.
passages.quote: Zoowel de voor als de bemuurde stad, was zeer dicht met ontelbare redelijke schoone steene huizen betimmert, welke alle door de Tartaren verwoest, en door den brant in d'assche gelegt wierden. Men zag aldaer op zeker plein eenige staken, en daer by verscheide menschen hoofden leggen
passages.translation: Both the suburb and the walled town were very densely built with countless fairly handsome stone houses, all of which were destroyed by the Tartars and laid in ashes by fire. On a certain square one saw some stakes, and beside them several human heads lying
passages.speaker: Olfert Dapper, from the journals of Balthasar Bort's fleet

passages.headline: Mourning in white: Tartar and Chinese customs compared
passages.gloss: The general description sets Tartar mourning beside Chinese. Tartar mourners wear a long white robe down to the feet, girded with a rope, and their oldest boots, and they leave hair and beard unshaven for the whole mourning period. The next page adds that Tartar women change their usual black clothing to white.
passages.quote: Al de Tarters, zoo wel die van den huize, als bloed-vrienden trekken in den rou tijd een lange rok van wit laken aen, die hen tot op de voeten hangt, en met een tou of wronge van een selfste stoffe toegegort is … 't Hair van de baert noch hooft word hen in al dien tijd niet geschooren.
passages.translation: All the Tartars, those of the household as well as blood relations, put on during mourning a long robe of white cloth hanging down to their feet, girded with a rope or twist of the same stuff … The hair of the beard and of the head is not shaved in all that time.
passages.speaker: Olfert Dapper, compiled general description of China
passages.caution: Compiled from earlier Jesuit writers, not observed by Dapper.

passages.headline: The Cheremis: 'Tartars' who speak Russian
passages.place: Middle Volga, between Nizhny Novgorod and Kazan
passages.gloss: Struys files the Cheremis under 'Tartars' (his chapter title calls them 'Tartares nommés Czérémisses'), yet on this page he says their everyday language is Russian and that they only understand, and in places speak, Tatar. They were in fact the Mari, a Finno-Ugric people. He also calls them rough and stupid, a sample of the book's contempt.
passages.quote: Ces peuples sont rudes, grossiers & stupides … Leur Langue ordinaire est la Moscovite, mais ils entendent le Tartare, & le parlent même en quelques endroits. Ils n'ont ni Prêtres ni Eglises, ni ne célèbrent aucun des mistéres de l'Evangile.
passages.translation: These peoples are rough, coarse and stupid … Their ordinary language is Muscovite [Russian], but they understand Tartar and even speak it in some places. They have neither priests nor churches, nor do they celebrate any of the mysteries of the Gospel.
passages.speaker: Jan Struys (French translation by Glanius, Amsterdam 1681)
passages.caution: Much of the Cheremis chapter follows Olearius, so this may be borrowed rather than observed.

passages.headline: A sacrifice thrown against a hide on a post
passages.gloss: On holy days the Cheremis tie the freshly flayed hide of a cow, sheep or horse to a post, roast the meat, and throw a dish of it and a cup of mead against the hide while murmuring prayers. The page adds that they revere the sun, fire and water above all visible things.
passages.quote: Ils ont pour cela des jours consacrés, ausquels ils commencent la cérémonie par attacher à un poteau, une peau de vache, de mouton ou de cheval écorché exprès: ils en mettent la chair sur la braise; & quand elle est rôtie, ils la coupent par petits morceaux, dont ayant rempli un plat, ils le prennent d'une main & une tasse d'hidromel de l'autre, puis jettent le tout contre la peau
passages.translation: For this they have holy days, on which they begin the ceremony by tying to a post the hide of a cow, sheep or horse flayed for the purpose; they put the meat on the coals, and when it is roasted they cut it into small pieces, fill a dish with them, take it in one hand and a cup of mead in the other, then throw the whole against the hide
passages.speaker: Jan Struys (French translation by Glanius, Amsterdam 1681)
passages.caution: Very close to Olearius's description of the Cheremis, so probably copied.

passages.headline: The newly married bride's horn with a bell
passages.gloss: Cheremis brides, the book says, wear a horn a yard long planted in the middle of the forehead, with a silk tassel and a little bell whose sound reminds the bride that she has just changed her state. The same paragraph then repeats a lurid slander about fathers and their daughters, likened to a tale told of Ceylon.
passages.quote: les nouvelles mariées ajoûtent un ornement qui leur est tout particulier: c'est une corne longue d'une aune qu'elles se plantent au milieu du front; au bout de laquelle il y a une houpe de soie, & au milieu de cette houpe une clochette, dont le bruit sert à faire souvenir la mariée qu'elle a depuis peu changé d'état.
passages.translation: newly married women add an ornament all their own: a horn a yard long, which they plant in the middle of the forehead; at its end is a silk tassel, and in the middle of this tassel a little bell, whose sound serves to remind the bride that she has lately changed her state.
passages.speaker: Jan Struys (French translation by Glanius, Amsterdam 1681)
passages.caution: Probably taken from Olearius. The horned bridal headdress is plausible; the slander that follows is not evidence of anything.

passages.headline: Kazan: wooden walls, a stone castle, and no Tatars allowed inside
passages.gloss: Struys walked through Kazan, capital of the former Tatar kingdom. The town wall is only timber but the castle is good stone. Russians and Tatars both live there under a Russian governor, but Tatars are barred from the castle on pain of death. A sharp picture of a conquered Tatar capital more than a century after the Russian conquest of 1552.
passages.quote: Ses murailles ne sont que de bois, mais celles du Château sont de bonne pierre & d'une épaisseur raisonnable … Ses habitans sont Moscovites & Tartares; lesquels obeïssent à un Gouverneur établi par le Grand Czar … Pour la garde du Château, les Tartares en sont exclus, & ils n'oseroient y entrer sur peine de la vie.
passages.translation: Its walls are only of wood, but those of the castle are of good stone and reasonably thick … Its inhabitants are Muscovites and Tartars, who obey a governor appointed by the Great Tsar … From the guard of the castle the Tartars are excluded, and they would not dare enter it on pain of death.
passages.speaker: Jan Struys (French translation by Glanius, Amsterdam 1681)

passages.headline: A Tatar khan's statue in Moscow before which the Tsar must bow
passages.people: Kazan and Crimean Tatars (the khan Mehmed Giray)
passages.gloss: Struys retells the Tatar raid that took Moscow and made the Grand Prince pay tribute. The elder of two Tatar brothers, 'Mendliguerits', had a statue of himself set up in Moscow before which the Tsar would have to prostrate himself whenever he sent the tribute. The story, told from older books, is about the 1521 raid of the Crimean khan Mehmed Giray and his brother Sahib Giray of Kazan.
passages.quote: Des deux Chefs Tartares qui étoient frères, l'aîné nommé Mendliguerits, avant que de quitter Moskou, s'y fit dresser une statuë devant laquelle l'Empereur seroit obligé de se prosterner
passages.translation: Of the two Tartar chiefs, who were brothers, the elder, named Mendliguerits, before leaving Moscow, had a statue of himself set up there, before which the Emperor would be obliged to prostrate himself
passages.speaker: Jan Struys (French translation by Glanius, Amsterdam 1681)
passages.caution: Book history, not observation; the details, including the statue, come from older written accounts and cannot be checked here.

passages.headline: A hill made of the bones of a Tartar emperor and seventy kings
passages.gloss: Passing a hill called Sariol-Kurgan, Struys records a Russian tradition: the place was once a plain where an Emperor of Tartary came with seventy kings and a countless army to seize Muscovy, and was beaten there with all his men. The mountain, the story ends, is made of their bones (the OCR of those last words is damaged). Cornelis de Bruyn heard a version of the same legend in 1703 (W251).
passages.quote: l'une appelée Sariol-Kurgan, si l'on en croit la tradition des Moscovites, a été faite d'une manière fort étrange. Ce lieu disent-ils, étoit autrefois une vaste plaine, où un Empereur de Tartarie étant descendu avec soixante & dix Rois & un armée innombrable pour se s'emparer de la Moscovie, il y fut battu & défait avec tous ceux qui l'accompagnoient
passages.translation: one of them, called Sariol-Kurgan, if one believes the tradition of the Muscovites, was made in a very strange way. This place, they say, was once a vast plain, where an Emperor of Tartary came down with seventy kings and a countless army to seize Muscovy, and was beaten and defeated there with all who accompanied him
passages.speaker: Jan Struys (French translation by Glanius, Amsterdam 1681)
passages.caution: A local legend told by Russians; a kurgan is a burial mound, but nothing here dates it or names its builders.

passages.headline: Ruins of an imperial city, its stones carried off to build Astrakhan
passages.place: Tsarev, lower Volga (probably the Golden Horde capital, New Sarai)
passages.gloss: Near Tsaritsyn Struys passed the ruins of Czaresgorod, the 'Imperial City', which he says Tamerlane destroyed. It had been built of hard stone, some remains of which could still be seen, but most of it had been carried off to Astrakhan to build that city. This matches the known reuse of brick and stone from the ruined Golden Horde capital, though Struys does not say who built it.
passages.quote: nous passâmes prés des ruines de Czaresgorod ou Ville Impériale, qui fut détruite par Tamerlan pendant la guerre dont nous avons ci-dessus parlé. Elle étoit bâtie de pierres dures dont on voit encore quelques restes, mais la plupart furent portées à Astracan, & servirent à la construire.
passages.translation: we passed near the ruins of Czaresgorod, or Imperial City, which was destroyed by Tamerlane during the war we spoke of above. It was built of hard stones, of which some remains are still seen, but most were carried to Astrakhan and served to build it.
passages.speaker: Jan Struys (French translation by Glanius, Amsterdam 1681)
passages.caution: Struys saw ruins from the river; the Tamerlane story and the stone reuse he had from others.

passages.headline: Kalmyks and Nogais: no fixed homes, and horsemeat softened under the saddle
passages.gloss: At Saratov Struys first met the Kalmyks, whom he calls the ugliest of men. Kalmyks and Nogais, he says, have no fixed dwellings and move camp as the grazing allows; they prefer horsemeat and eat it after softening it under the saddle. The saddle-meat story is an old European stereotype about steppe riders. On the same page he wrongly calls the Kalmyks Muslims; they were Buddhists.
passages.quote: Ils n'ont point de demeures fixes … mais de toutes les viandes, celle de cheval est plus à leur goût. Tout l'aprêt qu'ils y font, est de la mettre sous la selle, où étant un peu amollie par la chaleur du cheval, ils l'en retirent, & en font leurs meilleurs repas.
passages.translation: They have no fixed dwellings … but of all meats, horse is most to their taste. All the preparation they give it is to put it under the saddle, where, being a little softened by the horse's warmth, they take it out and make their best meals of it.
passages.speaker: Jan Struys (French translation by Glanius, Amsterdam 1681)
passages.caution: The saddle-meat tale is repeated from much older writers, and the page is openly hostile.

passages.headline: The vegetable lamb: 'I have seen several'
passages.gloss: On the salt steppe west of the Volga grows the 'Boranez', a fruit shaped like a lamb with feet, head and tail, covered in white down. Struys says the Tartars and Russians prize it and keep it in their houses, where he saw several, and that he had also seen one in Swammerdam's cabinet in Amsterdam. People in Astrakhan told him it grows on a stalk and dies when the grass around it is gone. This is the famous barometz legend, in real life probably a fern rhizome shaped to look like a lamb.
passages.quote: où croît le Boranez ou Bornitsch dont nous avons déjà parlé. Ce merveilleux fruit a la figure d'un agneau, avec les piés, la tête & la queue distinctement formés … Les Tartares & les Moscovites en font grand état, & la plupart le gardent avec soin dans leurs maisons où j'en ai vu plusieurs.
passages.translation: where the Boranez or Bornitsch grows, of which we have already spoken. This marvellous fruit has the shape of a lamb, with the feet, head and tail distinctly formed … The Tartars and the Muscovites think highly of it, and most keep it carefully in their houses, where I have seen several.
passages.speaker: Jan Struys (French translation by Glanius, Amsterdam 1681)
passages.caution: He saw objects sold as barometz; how it grows is hearsay, and the whole idea is a legend.

passages.headline: Nogai huts outside Astrakhan: round, of bark or reeds, covered with felt
passages.gloss: The Nogais, though natives of the land, may not live inside the walls of Astrakhan and build poor huts outside, later protected by palisades. The huts are round, about ten feet across, made of bark or woven reeds covered with roughly joined felt, with an opening in the roof that serves as chimney and is closed with felt to keep in the heat.
passages.quote: Les Tartares du Nagai quoique naturels du pays, n'ont pas la liberté de demeurer dans l'enceinte de la Ville … Leurs hutes sont bâties en rond & ont d'ordinaire dix piés de diamètre: elles ne sont faites que d'écorce d'arbre ou de roseaux entrelacés, ni couvertes que de feutre grossiérement joint. Le toit est ouvert en forme de trape, & leur tient lieu de cheminée
passages.translation: The Tartars of the Nogai, though natives of the country, are not free to live within the walls of the town … Their huts are built round and are usually ten feet across; they are made only of tree bark or woven reeds, and covered only with roughly joined felt. The roof is open like a trapdoor and serves them as a chimney
passages.speaker: Jan Struys (French translation by Glanius, Amsterdam 1681)
passages.caution: Some of this closely follows Olearius's description of the Nogai huts at Astrakhan.

passages.headline: Huts on wagons, and guns lent only for the winter
passages.gloss: In summer the Nogais, like the Kalmyks, move camp for food and fodder, carrying their goods on camels and setting their huts on great wagons made for the purpose. In winter they camp around Astrakhan for mutual defence against Kalmyk raids across the frozen Volga, and the Russian governor lends them weapons each winter and takes them back each summer, keeping one of their princes as hostage.
passages.quote: pour le transport de leurs meubles, ils ont des chameaux, & mettent leurs hutes sur de grands chariots faits exprès … Pour repousser les insultes qu'ils en reçoivent, le Gouverneur d'Astracan qui les protège, leur prête des armes tous les Hivers, & les reprend tous les Etés
passages.translation: for carrying their goods they have camels, and they put their huts on great wagons made for the purpose … To repel the attacks they suffer from them, the Governor of Astrakhan, who protects them, lends them arms every winter and takes them back every summer
passages.speaker: Jan Struys (French translation by Glanius, Amsterdam 1681)
passages.caution: How the governor handled weapons and hostages was information Struys had from others.

passages.headline: Astrakhan once belonged to the Nogai Tartars
passages.gloss: Struys explains that Astrakhan used to belong to the Nogai Tartars under a king, allied with the Cheremis and Kazan Tatars. After taking Kazan the Tsar marched on Astrakhan, took it just as easily and drove out the Tartars. The town, he adds, was then neither as fine nor as large as it later became under Russian rule.
passages.quote: Cette ville étoit autrefois aux Tartares du Nagai, qui obeïssoient à un Roi … La prise de Cazan ayant rendu le chemin libre, le Vainqueur alla devant Astracan qu'il emporta avec la même facilité, & dont il chassa les Tartares
passages.translation: This town formerly belonged to the Tartars of the Nogai, who obeyed a king … The capture of Kazan having opened the way, the victor went before Astrakhan, which he took with the same ease, and from which he drove out the Tartars
passages.speaker: Jan Struys (French translation by Glanius, Amsterdam 1681)
passages.caution: History from books; the Astrakhan khanate was ruled by a Chinggisid khan and conquered in 1556.

passages.headline: Captured in Daghestan: dragged behind horses, shot with blunted arrows
passages.people: Tartars of Daghestan (the men of 'Sultan Osmin')
passages.gloss: After a shipwreck on the Caspian coast, Struys and his companions were stripped by one band and then seized by another, who took them for spies of the rebel Razin. He describes being tied to horses' tails and driven barefoot through thorns, then bound to a tree and struck with arrows whose points had been blunted to make the torment last. Russian slaves of the prince vouched that they were Dutch, which saved their lives (two pages later).
passages.quote: ils nous attachèrent à la queue de leurs chevaux, nous faisant suivre à reculons & les piés nus, au travers des ronces & des épines dont le chemin étoit tout couvert … me rattacher à un arbre, où ils me percèrent à coups de flèches dont ils avoient émoussé le fer
passages.translation: they tied us to the tails of their horses, making us follow backwards and barefoot through the brambles and thorns with which the road was covered … tie me to a tree, where they pierced me with arrows whose iron they had blunted
passages.speaker: Jan Struys (French translation by Glanius, Amsterdam 1681)
passages.caution: His own ordeal, but told in a ghost-written book that heightens every drama.

passages.headline: Samoyed and Tungus country, 'situated in Tartary'
passages.place: Northern Siberia (east of the Vaygach Strait)
passages.people: Samoyeds and Tungus, in a land called Tartary
passages.gloss: The Latin title page of Gerritsz's 1612 collection announces Isaac Massa's description of the Samoyed and Tungus regions 'lying in Tartary', recently acquired by the Muscovite empire, with a Russian map translated into Latin. Here 'Tartary' is simply the name of the far north-east of Asia, not a kingdom.
passages.quote: Isaaci Massae Harlemensis Samoiediae atque Tingoessae, regionum ad Orientem ultra Fretum Weygats in Tartaria sitarum, nuperque Imperio Moscovitico adquisitarum descriptio
passages.translation: Isaac Massa of Haarlem's description of Samoyedia and Tingoesia, regions lying in Tartary to the east beyond the Vaygach Strait, and recently acquired by the Muscovite Empire
passages.speaker: Hessel Gerritsz, title page (Latin version by R. Vitellius)

passages.headline: Old maps of Tartary drawn before even the Russians knew it
passages.gloss: In his preface Gerritsz attacks a German doctor, Helisaeus Röslin, who claimed ships could sail round Nova Zembla to Cathay. Röslin's 'absurdities', he says, rest on maps of Tartary drawn in very old times, when the Russians themselves did not know the country. A sharp early warning that the big 'Tartary' of old maps was guesswork.
passages.quote: This was also done by a certain Heliseus Röslin, a doctor of Hanau … in which (after many absurdities which he grounds on the maps drawn of Tartary from very old times, when the Russians themselves were unacquainted with it) he says: that the nearer the pole the warmer it is in summer time
passages.speaker: Hessel Gerritsz, preface to the 1612 Dutch tracts (English translation by F. J. Millard in the 1878 facsimile edition)

passages.headline: The golden old woman and the monstrous people beyond the Ob
passages.gloss: Gerritsz explains that earlier knowledge of the road to the Ob came from a Russian itinerary published by Herberstein, into which 'innumerable fables' had been mixed: the Zolotaya Baba or golden old woman with her children, and monstrous people beyond the Ob. He offers Massa's newer information as a correction.
passages.quote: a travel from the Moscow to Colmogro, described by the Russians and thence on Petzora where the nations received the Christian faith in the year 1518, and further to the Ovy, and still a little further onward, in which innumerable fables have been mixed up of Slatababa, the golden old woman with her children, and the monstruous people beyond the Oby.
passages.speaker: Hessel Gerritsz, preface to the 1612 Dutch tracts (English translation by F. J. Millard in the 1878 facsimile edition)

passages.headline: Russian forts of timber beams filled with clay
passages.people: Russians building among Tartars, Poles and others
passages.gloss: Massa describes how Moscow secured Siberia: strongholds were built in the plain along the Ob from big beams cut in the nearby forests, then filled with clay, and garrisoned. Settlers followed, and mixed communities of Poles, Tartars, Russians and others grew into towns. A plain account of Russian-built wooden forts, not inherited cities.
passages.quote: First some castles were built, for which large beams were supplied from the neighbouring forests and then filled up with clay; then these strongholds were filled with soldiers, while many people were sent thither daily, and in time, formed large communities composed of Poles, Tartars, Russians and other nations.
passages.speaker: Isaac Massa's description of Siberia, as printed by Hessel Gerritsz in 1612 (English translation by F. J. Millard in the 1878 facsimile edition)

passages.headline: Tartars and Samoyeds who keep cattle and boats
passages.gloss: On the route down the Tura below Verkhoturye, Massa notes that the country is now inhabited by Tartars and Samoyeds who live by keeping cattle and also have boats. On the page before he mentions 'wild Tartars and Samoyeds' in the Ural forests who hunt costly furs for the Muscovites.
passages.quote: This place is now inhabited by Tartars and Samoyeds, who keep cattle as a means of subsistence, and have boats besides.
passages.speaker: Isaac Massa's description of Siberia, as printed by Hessel Gerritsz in 1612 (English translation by F. J. Millard in the 1878 facsimile edition)

passages.headline: Tobolsk, capital of the Siberian cities
