passages.people: Siberian Tatars and traders from further south
passages.gloss: Tobolsk, founded by the Russians in 1587, is described as the capital of the Siberian towns, seat of the Tsar's viceroy, where tribute from both sides of the Ob is collected and sent to Moscow. Tartars come from the south from far inside Tartary to trade. Massa adds a pointed comparison: would that the 'cruel Spaniards' had taken America as peacefully.
passages.quote: From Tinnen one reaches Tobolsca, the capital of the Siberian cities; there is the seat of Siberia and the supreme Viceroy of the Muscovites … Also Tartars from the south come at a great distance from Tartary, and many other nations who gradually arrive there, in proportion as the fame of the country spreads wider.
passages.speaker: Isaac Massa's description of Siberia, as printed by Hessel Gerritsz in 1612 (English translation by F. J. Millard in the 1878 facsimile edition)
passages.caution: Massa's picture of a peaceful conquest reflects his Russian informants' view.

passages.headline: Tomsk: a new Russian castle on a site named by the Tartars
passages.people: Tartars of the upper Ob (subjects of 'King Altijn')
passages.gloss: Boris Godunov ordered a town built on the upper Ob, and 'a fine castle was built with some other houses'. The Russians later heard that many Tartars had lived there, that the Tartars had named the place for its pleasantness, and that they had a king called Altijn. So the source credits the Russians with the building and the Tartars only with the earlier settlement and the name.
passages.quote: a fine castle was built with some other houses, so that it is now a fine city, called Toom, for they heard afterwards, that many Tartars had lived there, and it was reported those Tartars had given the city that name on account of its pleasantness. These Tartars had a king over them called Altijn
passages.speaker: Isaac Massa's description of Siberia, as printed by Hessel Gerritsz in 1612 (English translation by F. J. Millard in the 1878 facsimile edition)
passages.caution: 'Altijn' likely echoes the Altan Khan of western Mongolia; the name story is hearsay.

passages.headline: 'Om-om': the sound of bells beyond the Pesida
passages.people: unknown people reported by Tungus and Tartar guides
passages.gloss: Tungus sent east by the Russians met strangers who, by signs, said that thunder and a great noise of people were often heard across a river they called Pesida, repeating 'om-om'. The Muscovites decided this must be the sound of bells, and Massa guessed it was the edge of Cathay. A lovely example of how rumour pushed the map of 'Tartary' eastward.
passages.quote: only by signs and gestures, they made out so much that thunder was often heard on the other side by their saying: om-om; and also a dreadful noise and rumour of human beings; they pointed to the river, saying: Pesida … From the words om-om, the Muscovites afterwards came to the conclusion, that it must be the sound of bells
passages.speaker: Isaac Massa's description of Siberia, as printed by Hessel Gerritsz in 1612 (English translation by F. J. Millard in the 1878 facsimile edition)
passages.caution: Third-hand rumour interpreted by signs; nothing was found.

passages.headline: Kasimov: a Tatar town of wood with a mosque tower
passages.gloss: Sailing down the Oka, de Bruyn passed Kasimov, which had been the seat of a small Tatar khanate under Moscow. He found a fair-sized town with no walls, where every house and all four churches were of wood, and a mosque with a tower used by 'Turks and Tartars'.
passages.quote: Elle n'a point de murailles quoi qu'elle soit assez grande, toutes les maisons en sont de bois, aussi-bien que les quatre églises. Il y a une tour à une mosquée, qui sert aux Turcs & aux Tartares
passages.translation: It has no walls, although it is fairly large; all the houses are of wood, as are the four churches. There is a tower at a mosque, which serves the Turks and the Tartars
passages.speaker: Cornelis de Bruyn (French translation, Voyages de Corneille Le Brun, 1718)

passages.headline: Ruined cities between Kazan and Astrakhan, their stones reused
passages.place: Akhtuba (the Volga branch where the Golden Horde capital Sarai lay)
passages.gloss: Near Simbirsk de Bruyn was told of very old and important cities between Kazan and Astrakhan, among them 'Achtoeba'. Nothing of it remains, he says, because all its stones were carried away to build Astrakhan and other places. The name almost certainly points to the Akhtuba branch of the Volga, where the ruins of the Golden Horde capital lay; Struys (W249) reported the same stone-robbing in 1669.
passages.quote: Au reste on affirme qu'il y a des villes fort anciennes & fort considerables entre Casan & Astracan, & entr'autres Achtoeba … On sait aussi que la ville d'Achtoeba étoit située sur cette riviere, mais il n'en reste pas les moindres vestiges, toutes les pierres en aiant été transportées pour bâtir Astracan & quelques autres places.
passages.translation: Moreover, it is said that there are very ancient and very considerable cities between Kazan and Astrakhan, among others Achtoeba … It is also known that the town of Achtoeba stood on this river, but not the least trace of it remains, all the stones having been carried away to build Astrakhan and some other places.
passages.speaker: Cornelis de Bruyn (French translation, Voyages de Corneille Le Brun, 1718)
passages.caution: Hearsay; de Bruyn says he could learn nothing certain about these cities.

passages.headline: A hill heaped over a Tartar emperor by soldiers' helmets
passages.people: a legendary 'Emperor of Tartary' called Mammon
passages.gloss: Below Samara the Russians pointed out a round hill called Sanol Kiergan and told de Bruyn it was the tomb of a Tartar emperor named Mammon, who came up the Volga with seventy other Tartar kings to conquer Russia and died there. His soldiers filled their helmets and shields with earth to raise the mound. The name may echo Mamai, the Golden Horde warlord of the 1370s; Struys (W249) heard a version in 1669.
passages.quote: Les Russiens nous dirent que c'étoit le tombeau d'un Roi, ou d'un Empereur de Tartarie, nommé Mammon, qui avoit monté le Wolga avec 70. autres Rois Tartares, pour s'emparer de toute la Russie. Que ce Prince étant mort en ce lieu-là, les soldats … remplirent leurs casques & leurs boucliers de terre, pour lui dresser un tombeau, dont cette montagne avoit été formée.
passages.translation: The Russians told us it was the tomb of a king or emperor of Tartary named Mammon, who had come up the Volga with seventy other Tartar kings to seize all Russia. That this prince having died in that place, the soldiers … filled their helmets and shields with earth to raise him a tomb, from which this mountain had been formed.
passages.speaker: Cornelis de Bruyn (French translation, Voyages de Corneille Le Brun, 1718)
passages.caution: A folk legend told by Russian boatmen; the hill may be natural.

passages.headline: Tatar tents like parrot cages, carried on carts
passages.gloss: De Bruyn often walked out to the Tatar camp three or four versts from Astrakhan and drew it. Each family camped apart. The tents were built like parrot cages from laths three or four inches wide, covered with felt, camel hair or horsehair, with a smoke hole and a pole carrying a turnable sail against wind and sun. When they moved, they set the tents on two-wheeled carts.
passages.quote: Ils campent par troupes, chaque famille separée, & à quelque distance des autres. Leurs tentes sont faites comme des cages de perroquets, hormis qu'elles ne sont pas si élevées à proportion; formées de lattes de trois à quatre pouces de large, couvertes de feutre, de poil de chameau ou de crin de cheval … Quand ils changent de lieu, ils mettent leurs tentes sur des chariots
passages.translation: They camp in groups, each family apart and at some distance from the others. Their tents are made like parrot cages, except that they are not so tall in proportion; formed of laths three to four inches wide, covered with felt, camel hair or horsehair … When they change place, they put their tents on carts
passages.speaker: Cornelis de Bruyn (French translation, Voyages de Corneille Le Brun, 1718)
passages.caution: De Bruyn drew these tents himself (plates 36 and 37 in the book).

passages.headline: 'This is how Abraham lived'
passages.gloss: While he sketched, the Tatars crowded round him, as surprised by his clothes as he was by theirs. The women spun and carded wool for the tent felts and burned dried cow dung for fuel. He found their way of life close to that of the Arabs, and thought this must be how Abraham and the patriarchs lived, content in tents as Europeans are in palaces.
passages.quote: Leur manière de vivre approche assez de celle des Arabes, & ils paroissent aussi contens de leurs demeures, qu'on l'est parmi nous des Palais, & des plus belles maisons. Cela me remet dans l'esprit l'ancienne manière des Orientaux, & je m'imagine que c'est ainsi que vivoient Abraham & les autres Patriarches
passages.translation: Their way of life is quite close to that of the Arabs, and they seem as content with their dwellings as we are with palaces and the finest houses. This brings to my mind the ancient way of the Orientals, and I imagine that this is how Abraham and the other patriarchs lived
passages.speaker: Cornelis de Bruyn (French translation, Voyages de Corneille Le Brun, 1718)

passages.headline: Portrait of a Tatar noblewoman in a headdress of gold ducats
passages.gloss: De Bruyn painted a young Tatar woman of high rank in the governor's house. Under her veils she wore a pointed, mitre-shaped headdress covered in gold ducats and embroidered with pearls, silver chains with little boxes for prayer books, and hair bound with black ribbon. She came with three women attendants and a Tatar escort known to the governor.
passages.quote: Cette coifure étoit toute couverte de ducats d'or, comme il a déjà été dit, & pointue en forme de mitre, brodée d'un grand nombre de perles … Cette demoiselle étoit une des plus considerables d'entre les Tartares; & étoit accompagnée de trois femmes de sa suite, & conduite par un Tartare, connu du Gouverneur.
passages.translation: This headdress was entirely covered with gold ducats, as has already been said, and pointed like a mitre, embroidered with a great number of pearls … This young lady was one of the most considerable among the Tartars, and was accompanied by three women of her suite and escorted by a Tartar known to the governor.
passages.speaker: Cornelis de Bruyn (French translation, Voyages de Corneille Le Brun, 1718)
passages.caution: The portrait was engraved for the book.

passages.headline: 'Yurt' Tatars: named for being born there
passages.gloss: De Bruyn records the Russian name for the Tatars around Astrakhan, 'Jurtsge' (the Yurt Tatars), explaining it as 'because they were born there'. They paid no tribute to the Tsar but had to send a few hundred men to his wars, though they could field 20,000. On the same page he notes that Nogais tented near Terki and that Crimean Tatars came only to sell horses and cattle.
passages.quote: Les Russiens nomment les Tartares, qui habitent en ces quartiers-là, Jurtsge, parce qu'ils y sont nez. Aussi ne payent-ils aucun tribut au Czar; ils sont seulement obligés d'envoyer quelques centaines de leurs gens à la guerre, lors que ce Prince le souhaite.
passages.translation: The Russians call the Tartars who live in those parts Jurtsge, because they were born there. Nor do they pay any tribute to the Tsar; they are only obliged to send some hundreds of their people to war when that prince wishes it.
passages.speaker: Cornelis de Bruyn (French translation, Voyages de Corneille Le Brun, 1718)

passages.headline: Tobolsk: a stone monastery, and Muslim Tartars trading to China
passages.gloss: In the inserted Ides section, Tobolsk is a strong place with a great stone monastery with high towers, standing on a hill where the Irtysh and Tobol meet. The foot of the hill and the Irtysh bank are inhabited by Muslim Tartars and Bukharans who trade along the river among the Kalmyks and go on as far as China.
passages.quote: il arriva heureusement à Tobol ou Tobolskoi, place forte, où l'on trouve un grand monastere de pierre, garni de hautes tours … Le pied de cette montagne & le rivage de l'Irtis sont habités par des Tartares & des Bachares Mahometans, qui trafiquent beaucoup sur ce fleuve parmi les Kalmuques, & vont même delà jusques à la Chine.
passages.translation: he arrived safely at Tobol or Tobolsk, a strong place, where there is a great stone monastery with high towers … The foot of this hill and the bank of the Irtysh are inhabited by Muslim Tartars and Bukharans, who trade a great deal on this river among the Kalmyks, and even go from there as far as China.
passages.speaker: Evert Ysbrants Ides's route to China (1692-1695), summarized by the editors of the 1718 French edition of Le Brun and inserted in it
passages.caution: Not seen by de Bruyn; a summary of Ides inserted by the French editors.

passages.headline: Inside a Tatar mosque at Tobolsk
passages.gloss: Ides, curious to see Tatar worship, visited a mosque at Tobolsk with the governor, without whom he would not have been let in. The mosques had large open windows and carpeted floors with no other ornament; worshippers left their shoes at the door. The mufti was an Arab, and the Tatars honoured anyone who could read Arabic. Many Kalmyk slaves lived in the area.
passages.quote: Les Tartares, qui demeurent à Tobol, & à plusieurs lieues aux environs, sont tous Mahometans. Mr. Isbrants, étant curieux de voir leurs cérémonies, se rendit dans une de leurs mosquées, accompagné du Waiwode, sans quoi il n'auroit pû y être admis. Elles sont entourées de grandes fenêtres, qu'on laisse ouvertes, & le pavé en est couvert de tapis, sans autre ornement.
passages.translation: The Tartars who live at Tobolsk and for several leagues around are all Muslims. Mr Isbrants, curious to see their ceremonies, went to one of their mosques accompanied by the voevoda, without whom he could not have been admitted. They are surrounded by large windows, which are left open, and the floor is covered with carpets, with no other ornament.
passages.speaker: Evert Ysbrants Ides's route to China (1692-1695), summarized by the editors of the 1718 French edition of Le Brun and inserted in it
passages.caution: Ides's eyewitness visit, reported second-hand in this book.

passages.headline: Summer huts, winter log cabins, and fields of barley
passages.place: Baraba steppe, between the Irtysh and the Ob
passages.people: Barabinsky (Baraba Tatars), called a kind of Kalmyk
passages.gloss: The Ides section describes the Baraba people between Tara and the Ob. They live in villages, in light huts in summer and good wooden cabins in winter, 'like the Tartars of Siberia', and they plough and sow oats, barley and buckwheat. The same page says they drink a spirit distilled from mare's milk called kumis and carry a wooden idol, their 'Saitan', on the hunt.
passages.quote: C'est un peuple malin & belliqueux, qui habite dans des cabanes de bois, comme les Tartares de Syberie … Ils habitent dans des especes de villages, sous des huttes legeres en été, & en de bonnes cabanes de bois en hyver. Le labourage est en usage parmi eux, & ils sement de l'avoine, de l'orge, du sarazin &c.
passages.translation: They are a cunning and warlike people, who live in wooden cabins like the Tartars of Siberia … They live in kinds of villages, in light huts in summer and in good wooden cabins in winter. Ploughing is practised among them, and they sow oats, barley, buckwheat and so on.
passages.speaker: Evert Ysbrants Ides's route to China (1692-1695), summarized by the editors of the 1718 French edition of Le Brun and inserted in it
passages.caution: From the Ides material; the book calls them 'a kind of Kalmyk', though they are now counted as Siberian Tatars.

passages.headline: Mammoths that burrow underground and die in the light
passages.people: Yakuts, Tungus and Ostyaks (and Siberian Russians)
passages.gloss: The Ides section reports mammoth tusks and bones thawing out of riverbanks, and a member of the embassy who found a head with half-rotten flesh. The Yakuts, Tungus and Ostyaks say the mammoth lives underground, making the earth rise and sink as it moves, and dies as soon as it sees daylight. The Russians of Siberia think it was an elephant-like beast buried by Noah's Flood.
passages.quote: Les Jakutes, Tungufes, & Ostiaques, prétendent qu'ils ne sortent jamais du sein de la terre, sous laquelle ils vont de côté & d'autre. Ils disent même qu'on voit souvent la terre s'élever & s'affaisser lors qu'ils sont en mouvement … Ils assurent, qu'ils meurent aussi tôt qu'ils découvrent la lumière
passages.translation: The Yakuts, Tungus and Ostyaks claim that they never come out of the bosom of the earth, under which they go this way and that. They even say that one often sees the earth rise and sink when they are moving … They assure us that they die as soon as they see the light
passages.speaker: Evert Ysbrants Ides's route to China (1692-1695), summarized by the editors of the 1718 French edition of Le Brun and inserted in it
passages.caution: Native belief and Russian flood theory reported by Ides; the bones and tusks themselves were real finds.

passages.headline: The Su-Mongols, 'also called Tartars after the river Tartar'
passages.gloss: Back in Astrakhan in 1707, de Bruyn adds a note from older books: in 1246 the Tartars chose 'Kuine' (Güyük) as their ruler, calling themselves Moals or Mongals. Their land, Mongol, held four nations, among them the water Mongols, also called Tartars after a river Tartar that runs through their country. This is the explanation given by the friar John of Plano Carpini in the 1240s, repeated second-hand.
passages.quote: En l'an 1246, ils choisirent pour chef de la Tartarie un certain Kuine, qu'ils surnommérent Gog Cham, c'est-à-dire, Roi ou Empereur, se nommant eux-mêmes Moales ou Mongales … les Saniongals, ou Mongales marins, qu'on nomme aussi Tartares, d'après la riviere de Tartar, qui traverse leur pais
passages.translation: In the year 1246 they chose as head of Tartary a certain Kuine, whom they surnamed Gog Cham, that is, King or Emperor, calling themselves Moals or Mongals … the Saniongals, or sea Mongols, who are also called Tartars, after the river Tartar, which crosses their country
passages.speaker: Cornelis de Bruyn (Le Brun), repeating medieval sources, ultimately John of Plano Carpini
passages.caution: Copied from older books; 'Gog Cham' is presumably a garbled form of Güyük's name, not a link to Gog and Magog.

passages.headline: Kalmyks swim for bread thrown from the boat
passages.gloss: Sailing back up the Volga, de Bruyn saw Kalmyks fishing with lines along the bank, with two-humped camels around them, and threw them bread, which they swam out to fetch. Ashore, Kalmyk men and women could not stop staring at his clothes and handling them. His boat kept to the east bank to avoid the Tartars on the other side, whom he calls great thieves.
passages.quote: Nous vîmes plusieurs Calmuques le long du rivage pêchant à la ligne, & nous leur jettâmes dans l'eau, du pain qu'ils allèrent prendre à la nage. Il y avoit des chameaux à 2. bosses autour d'eux … nous trouvâmes plusieurs Calmuques tant hommes que femmes, qui ne pouvoient se lasser de regarder mon habillement
passages.translation: We saw several Kalmyks along the bank fishing with lines, and we threw bread into the water for them, which they swam out to fetch. There were two-humped camels around them … we found several Kalmyks, both men and women, who could not tire of looking at my clothes
passages.speaker: Cornelis de Bruyn (French translation, Voyages de Corneille Le Brun, 1718)

passages.headline: Houses built on wheels and covered in white felt
passages.gloss: Rubruck opens his description of the Tartars with their homes. The sleeping-houses sit on wheels, are made of interlaced wooden laths that rise to a smoke-hole like a chimney, and are covered with white felt smeared with lime, white earth or powdered bone so that they gleam. He stresses that the Tartars have no fixed dwelling and divide the steppe from the Danube eastward into seasonal pastures.
passages.quote: Les maisons où ils habitent pour dormir sont fondées sur des rouës … des pieces de bois entrelassées, & abboutissent en haut en vne ouuerture comme vne cheminée, & couurent cela de feutre blanc, qu'ils enduisent de chaulx ou terre
passages.translation: The houses in which they sleep are set on wheels … [made of] interlaced pieces of wood, and they come together at the top in an opening like a chimney, and they cover this with white felt, which they coat with lime or earth
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck (French translation by Pierre Bergeron, 1634)
passages.caution: A margin note has run into the line after 'rouës'; the omitted words are garbled.

passages.headline: Twenty-two oxen to pull one house
passages.gloss: Rubruck took a tape to a Mongol wagon-house. He measured one at twenty feet between the wheels, with the house overhanging them, and counted twenty-two oxen, eleven abreast on each side, hauling it, with an axle as thick as a ship's mast. On the same page he says the felt roof was painted and the door-felt embroidered with vines, trees, birds and beasts.
passages.quote: Ils ont de ces maisons-là de telle grandeur, qu'elles ont bien trente pieds de long : car i'ay pris la peine quelquefois d'en mesurer vne qui auoit bien vingt pieds d'vne rouë à l'autre : & quand ceste maison estoit posée dessus, elle passoit au delà des rouës. … & ay conté iusqu'à vingt-deux bœufs pour traisner vne de ces maisons, vnze d'vn costé, & vnze de l'autre.
passages.translation: They have some of these houses so large that they are a good thirty feet long: for I once took the trouble to measure one that was a good twenty feet from one wheel to the other, and when the house was set on it, it overhung the wheels. … And I counted up to twenty-two oxen drawing one of these houses, eleven on one side and eleven on the other.
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck (French translation by Pierre Bergeron, 1634)

passages.headline: A rich Tartar's camp looks like a big town
passages.gloss: The Mongol camp could look like a settlement. Each wife of a great lord had her own large house with a train of smaller wagon-houses (Rubruck says Batu's wives each had more than 200), and the wives' courts were pitched in a row from west to east, a stone's throw apart. The result, he says, resembles a large town, though few men live in it.
passages.quote: la premiere des femmes fait poser sa petite court vers l'Occident, puis toutes les autres en font de mesme chacune en son rang: si bien que la derniere se trouue à l'Orient, & l'espace d'entr'elles est enuiron vn iet de pierre: de sorte que la court d'vn de ces riches Tartares semble vn gros bourg, où il y aura toutesfois bien peu d'hommes.
passages.translation: the first wife has her little court set up to the west, then all the others do the same, each in her rank, so that the last is at the east, and the space between them is about a stone's throw: so that the court of one of these rich Tartars looks like a big town, although there will be very few men in it.
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck (French translation by Pierre Bergeron, 1634)

passages.headline: How kumiss is made, and what it tastes like
passages.gloss: Rubruck explains the Mongols' summer drink, fermented mare's milk. Foals are tethered on a line so the mares let themselves be milked; the milk is churned in a skin with a club until it bubbles like new wine and turns sour. He found it prickled the tongue, left a taste of almonds and could make a weak head drunk; a clear black kind, cara-cosmos, was kept for the great.
passages.quote: ils le versent dans vn outre, ou autre vaisseau, là où ils le battent & remuent tres-bien … cela commence à boüillir comme du vin nouueau, puis à s'aigrir, comme du leuain … cela pique la langue comme feroit du vin raspé quand on le boit. Lors que l'on a acheué de boire, cela laisse sur la langue vn goust d'amande, & resioüit grandement le cœur
passages.translation: they pour it into a skin or other vessel, where they beat and stir it very well … it begins to bubble like new wine, then to turn sour like leaven … it stings the tongue like rough wine when you drink it. When you have finished drinking, it leaves a taste of almonds on the tongue and greatly cheers the heart
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck (French translation by Pierre Bergeron, 1634)

passages.headline: The silver tree that poured four drinks at Karakorum
passages.people: Mongols (court of Möngke Khan); Guillaume Boucher, a Parisian goldsmith
passages.gloss: Beside Möngke's palace at Karakorum stood a great silver tree made by a captive Parisian goldsmith, Master Guillaume. Four silver lions at its foot and pipes hidden in the trunk delivered wine, kumiss, honey-mead and rice beer, and a silver angel on top blew a trumpet (worked by a man hidden inside) to call the servers. It is a vivid case of a Mongol showpiece built by a foreign craftsman.
passages.quote: ce M. Guillaume luy auoit fait vn grand arbre d'argent, au pied duquel estoient quatre lyons aussi d'argent, ayans chacun vne pipe ou canal d'où sortoit du lait de iument. Les quatre pipes estoient cachées dans l'arbre, montans iusqu'au sommet, & de là s'escoulans en bas. Sur chacun de ces muids ou canaux y auoit des serpens dorez dont les queuës venoient à enuironner le corps de l'arbre.
passages.translation: this Master Guillaume had made him a great silver tree, at whose foot were four lions, also of silver, each with a pipe or channel from which mare's milk flowed. The four pipes were hidden in the tree, rising to the top and flowing down from there. On each of these conduits were gilded serpents whose tails wound round the trunk of the tree.
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck (French translation by Pierre Bergeron, 1634)

passages.headline: Karakorum: worse than Saint-Denis, with two quarters and many temples
passages.gloss: Rubruck's famous verdict on the Mongol capital: apart from the Khan's palace, it is not as good as the French town of Saint-Denis, whose abbey is worth ten Mongol palaces. It has a Saracen quarter with markets and a Cathayan (Chinese) quarter of craftsmen, twelve idol temples, two mosques and a church. On the next page (n221) he adds earthen walls with four gates, each with its own market for grain, sheep, oxen and carts, or horses.
passages.quote: excepté le Palais du Cham, elle n'est pas si bonne que la ville de S. Denis en France, dont le Monastere vaut dix fois mieux que tout le Palais mesme de Mangu. Il y a deux grandes ruës, l'vne dite des Sarrasins, où se tiennent les marchez & la foire … Là sont douze temples d'Idolatres de diuerses nations; & deux mosquées de Sarrasins
passages.translation: except for the Khan's palace, it is not as good as the town of Saint-Denis in France, whose monastery is worth ten times more than the whole palace of Möngke itself. There are two main streets, one called the Saracens', where the markets and fair are held … There are twelve temples of idolaters of various nations, and two mosques of the Saracens
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck (French translation by Pierre Bergeron, 1634)

passages.headline: A Russian husband who built houses for the Tartars
passages.people: Tartars (Mongols); Paquette of Metz and her Russian husband
passages.gloss: At the Mongol court Rubruck met Paquette, a woman from Metz captured in Hungary, who had married a young Russian. She told him her husband was expert in building, 'an art much valued and needed among the Tartars', and that a Parisian goldsmith was working at Karakorum. The Mongols' building work, in other words, was often done by captives from conquered lands.
passages.quote: ayant vn ieune mary de Russie, dont elle auoit trois beaux enfans, & son mary s'entendoit fort aux bastimens, qui est vn art bien estimé & requis entre les Tartares. Elle nous donna encor aduis qu'à Caracarum il y auoit vn Orfeure Parisien, nommé Guillaume Boucher
passages.translation: having a young husband from Russia, by whom she had three fine children; and her husband was very skilled at building, which is an art much esteemed and in demand among the Tartars. She also told us that at Karakorum there was a Parisian goldsmith named Guillaume Boucher
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck, reporting what Paquette told him (French translation by Pierre Bergeron, 1634)

passages.headline: Cuman grave mounds, statues and brick towers on the steppe
passages.gloss: Crossing the steppe, Rubruck describes the tombs of the Cumans, the Turkic people the Mongols had conquered there. They raised a mound over the dead with a statue facing east holding a cup; for the rich they built little pointed houses, and he saw great brick towers and stone houses in a land without stone. The same page notes that nobody knew where Chinggis Khan was buried.
passages.quote: Pour les Comans, ils ont coustume d'esleuer vne motte ou tertre sur la sepulture du mort, & luy dressent vne statuë la face tournée à l'Orient … Aux riches & Grands ils dressent des pyramides, ou petites maisons pointuës, & ay veu en des endroits de grandes tours de brique, & en d'autres des maisons basties de pierres; encores qu'en ces quartiers là on n'y trouue point de pierres.
passages.translation: As for the Cumans, they are accustomed to raise a mound over the grave of the dead man and set up a statue for him facing east … For the rich and great they put up pyramids, or little pointed houses, and in some places I saw great towers of brick, and in others houses built of stone, although no stone is found in those parts.
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck (French translation by Pierre Bergeron, 1634)
passages.caution: These are Cuman (Qipchaq) monuments, not Mongol ones; Rubruck does not say who built the brick towers.

passages.headline: A shaman's night séance and a demon on the roof
passages.gloss: Rubruck describes how Mongol diviners answered the Khan's questions: meat is laid in the middle of the house at night, the shaman mutters charms, beats a drum on the ground, raves and is tied up, and the 'devil' comes in the dark to eat and give answers. He then repeats a story from the goldsmith Guillaume about a hidden Hungarian who heard the demon shrieking on the roof, unable to enter because a Christian was present.
passages.quote: celuy qui fait l'inuocation commence à murmurer ses charmes, & tenant vn tabourin en la main, le frappe fort contre terre, & se demene & agite en sorte qu'il deuient comme hors de soy, & commence à resver, puis il se fait lier bien serré; lors le diable vient durant l'obscurité de la nuict, & luy donne à manger de ces chairs
passages.translation: the one who performs the invocation begins to mutter his charms and, holding a drum in his hand, beats it hard against the ground, and throws himself about so that he becomes as if beside himself and begins to rave; then he has himself bound tight; then the devil comes in the darkness of the night and gives him some of the meat to eat
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck (French translation by Pierre Bergeron, 1634)
passages.caution: Rubruck did not attend such a séance; the roof-demon story comes secondhand from Master Guillaume, and he frames it all as devil-worship.

passages.headline: Round felt tents, some carried whole on carts
passages.gloss: Carpini gives his own short description of Mongol dwellings: round, tent-shaped, built of slender rods, with a round window at the top for light and smoke, a central fire, and felt walls, roof and door. Some can be taken apart and loaded on pack animals; others travel whole on carts pulled by one ox or by several.
passages.quote: Leurs logemens sont ronds, en forme de tentes, & faits auec des verges & bastons fort deliez; & au dessus, droit au milieu, y a vne fenestre ronde, par où la lumiere entre, & la fumée sort; car ils font tousiours leur feu au milieu: les parois & toits de ces logis sont couuerts de feutres … Quelques-vnes sont fort aisées à deffaire & refaire
passages.translation: Their dwellings are round, shaped like tents, and made with very slender rods and sticks; and on top, right in the middle, there is a round window through which the light comes in and the smoke goes out, for they always make their fire in the middle; the walls and roofs of these dwellings are covered with felts … Some are very easy to take down and put up again
passages.speaker: John of Plano Carpini (French translation by Pierre Bergeron, 1634)

passages.headline: A tent for two thousand people at Güyük's election
passages.gloss: At the assembly that elected Güyük Great Khan, Carpini found a huge tent of white purple cloth which he reckoned could hold more than two thousand people, ringed by a wooden palisade painted with figures. The chiefs changed the colour of their robes each day. A few pages on he describes another tent, the 'Golden Horde', on pillars covered with gold plates fixed with gold nails.
passages.quote: Nous trouuames là vne tente de pourpre blanc tres-grande, voire telle, à nostre aduis, qu'elle estoit capable de tenir plus de deux mil personnes. A l'entour d'icelle on auoit fait esleuer vn eschaffaut ou palissade de bois, remply de diuerses figures & peintures.
passages.translation: There we found a very large tent of white purple, so large, in our opinion, that it could hold more than two thousand people. Around it they had set up a scaffold or palisade of wood, covered with various figures and paintings.
passages.speaker: John of Plano Carpini (French translation by Pierre Bergeron, 1634)

passages.headline: A great man buried sitting in his tent, with a mare and foal
passages.gloss: Carpini describes the secret burial of a Mongol noble: he is buried out on the steppe with his tent, seated before a table with a bowl of meat and a cup of mare's milk, with a mare and foal and a saddled horse. Another horse is eaten and its skin, stuffed with straw, is raised on four poles, so the dead will have a home, milk and horses in the next world. His name may not be spoken for three generations.
passages.quote: on l'enterre secrettement en la campagne, auec sa loge, & est assis au milieu d'icelle, auec vne table deuant luy, & vn bassin plein de chair, & vne tasse de lait de iument; On enterre aussi auec luy vne iument, & son poulain; & vn cheual sellé & bridé: & mangent vn autre cheual, dont ils remplissent la peau de paille
passages.translation: they bury him secretly in the open country, with his tent, and he is seated in the middle of it, with a table in front of him and a bowl full of meat and a cup of mare's milk; they also bury with him a mare and her foal, and a horse saddled and bridled; and they eat another horse, whose skin they stuff with straw
passages.speaker: John of Plano Carpini (French translation by Pierre Bergeron, 1634)
passages.caution: Carpini did not witness a noble burial; he reports Mongol practice as described to him.

passages.headline: Men with ox feet and dogs' faces by the northern ocean
passages.people: Tartars (Mongol armies) and fabled northern peoples
passages.gloss: In his account of Mongol campaigns Carpini passes on marvels: far north, beyond the Samoyeds who live by hunting and wear only skins, the Tartars met at the Ocean monsters shaped like men but with ox feet and dogs' faces, who spoke a few words and then barked. On the facing page are the Parossites, with tiny mouths, who live only on the steam of boiled meat.
passages.quote: De là ils paruindrent iusqu'à la mer Oceane, où ils trouuerent des monstres, qui en tout le reste auoient forme d'hommes, mais ils auoient des pieds de bœuf, & le visage fait comme vn chien.
passages.translation: From there they came as far as the Ocean sea, where they found monsters which in every other respect had the form of men, but they had the feet of oxen and faces like a dog.
passages.speaker: John of Plano Carpini (French translation by Pierre Bergeron, 1634)
passages.caution: Carpini never went to the far north; these are travellers' tales in the classical tradition of dog-headed peoples.

passages.headline: A trading city drowned by diverting its river
passages.people: Tartars (Mongol armies); Khazar, Russian and Alan Christians; Muslim traders
passages.gloss: Carpini tells how the Mongols took the rich, crowded city of Orna, a port full of Christians and Muslim merchants: finding it hard to storm, they dammed the river that ran through it and drowned the city with everything in it. He goes on to the sack of Kiev and the Russian towns.
passages.quote: Aprés cela ils vindrent deuant la cité d'Orna qui estoit fort peuplée, & là y auoit plusieurs Chrestiens Gazares, Russes, Alans, & autres, & quelques Sarasins … Les Tartares voyans qu'il estoit difficile de la prendre de force, ils s'aduiserent d'arrester la riuiere qui passe par ceste ville, & ainsi la submergerent auec tout ce qui estoit dedans.
passages.translation: After that they came before the city of Orna, which was very populous, and there were many Christians there, Khazars, Russians, Alans and others, and some Saracens … The Tartars, seeing that it was hard to take by force, decided to stop the river that runs through the city, and so they drowned it with everything that was in it.
passages.speaker: John of Plano Carpini (French translation by Pierre Bergeron, 1634)
passages.caution: Carpini places Orna on the Don, but the story matches the Mongol flooding of Urgench in Khwarazm (1221), and historians have often suspected a confusion; treat the location as uncertain.

passages.headline: Bergeron's guesses: a river Tartar, or Syriac for 'abandoned'
passages.gloss: In his Traicté, Bergeron lists Hayton's seven Mongol nations and offers two origins for the name: a river called Tartar, or a Syriac word meaning 'the abandoned', favoured by those who made the Tartars descendants of the ten lost tribes of Israel. He reports claims that some northern hordes bore the tribal names Dan, Zabulon and Naphtali, but on the next page calls the theory weak, resting on an apocryphal book.
passages.quote: Le nom de Tartar, Tatar, ou Totar, vient du fleuue Tartar; ou du mot Totar, ou Tatar, qui en langage Syrien veut dire delaissez, ou abandonnez, suiuant l'opinion de ceux qui les veulent faire descendre des dix lignées Israëlites releguées en Medie, & depuis venuës au pays d'Arsareth.
passages.translation: The name Tartar, Tatar or Totar comes from the river Tartar, or from the word Totar or Tatar, which in the Syrian language means 'forsaken' or 'abandoned', according to the opinion of those who would make them descend from the ten tribes of Israel exiled in Media and afterwards come to the land of Arsareth.
passages.speaker: Pierre Bergeron (Traicté des Tartares, 1634)
passages.caution: Compiled speculation; Abel-Rémusat (W261) later dismissed both etymologies and the river Tartar as imaginary.

passages.headline: Gog and Magog shut behind a rock at the end of the world
passages.people: Tartars (Mongols), as imagined by medieval French chroniclers
passages.gloss: Bergeron retells what French chroniclers such as Joinville and Nangis had heard from envoys: the Tartars said that at the northern end of the earth a rock no one could pass shut in the peoples Gog and Magog, whom Bergeron equates with the Mongal of other writers and the Moal the Tartars call themselves, destined to come with Antichrist at the end of the world. Behind the rock lay the sandy desert where the Tartars lived as tributary herders until Chinggis roused them.
passages.quote: estoient enclos les peuples appellez Goths & Magoths (qui est le Gog & Magog de l'Escriture, & le Mongal des autres Escriuains, & le Moal des Tartares mesmes). Que ces gens-là deuoient venir à la fin du monde auec l'Antechrist.
passages.translation: the peoples called Goths and Magoths were shut in (who are the Gog and Magog of Scripture, the Mongal of other writers and the Moal of the Tartars themselves). And that these people were to come at the end of the world with Antichrist.
passages.speaker: Pierre Bergeron (Traicté des Tartares, 1634), paraphrasing Joinville, Nangis and other French chroniclers
passages.caution: Secondhand legend; the chroniclers' 'Tartar origin story' is already filtered through biblical expectation.

passages.headline: Crimean Tatar towns: Perekop, Bakhchysarai and ruined Caffa
passages.gloss: Bergeron sketches the Crimean khanate of his own day. The Tatars' chief fortress is Perekop on the canal across the isthmus, the khans' royal seat is at Bakhchysarai, and they hold other towns such as Crim, from which they are called Crimeans. The Turks hold Mangup and Caffa (ancient Theodosia), the old Genoese trading port, which he says now lies half deserted, with ruins of a very great city.
passages.quote: Or la principale ville ou forteresse de ces Precopites, située sur ce canal pour la garde du pays, est Precop, ou Perecop; le siege royal des Chans, ou Cans est à Bacasaray, ou Almasaray; & y a plusieurs autres villes de leur partage, comme Crim, dont ils sont surnommez Crimenses, ou Krimski
passages.translation: Now the chief town or fortress of these Precopites, set on this canal to guard the country, is Precop or Perekop; the royal seat of the Khans is at Bacasaray or Almasaray; and they have several other towns in their share, such as Crim, from which they are called Crimenses or Krimski
passages.speaker: Pierre Bergeron (Traicté des Tartares, 1634)
passages.caution: Compiled from other writers, not observed.

passages.headline: Crimean Tatar buildings of stone, timber and wattle
passages.gloss: The Dominican Jean de Luca, who worked in the Crimea, says the Tatars' buildings are not worth much: the best are of stone and mortar, many are of timber roofed with planks, and others are of stakes driven into the ground with branches woven between them and a straw roof. On the next page he adds round wicker summer houses on wheels, bought at market. A settled Tatar people, in short, living in ordinary villages.
passages.quote: Leurs Bastiments ne valent pas grand chose, les meilleurs sont faits ordinairement de pierres & de mortier; il y en a beaucoup de bois & couuerts de planches, d'autres de pieux fichez en terre
passages.translation: Their buildings are not worth much; the best are usually made of stone and mortar; many are of wood and roofed with planks, others of stakes driven into the ground
passages.speaker: Jean de Luca, Dominican (Relation des Tartares Percopites et Nogaies, printed by Thévenot)
passages.caution: Very poor OCR on this scan; the quoted words are clear but surrounding names are garbled.

passages.headline: The Crimean khan's walled palaces with iron gates
passages.people: Crimean Tatars (the khan and the sultan, his heir)
passages.gloss: De Luca says the Crimean khan has five palaces (serails) and his heir two, one in the town where he lives (Bakhchysarai, spelled 'Bach* serai' on the previous page). Each covers about a mile, with a high but weak wall, iron gates and gilded, painted rooms. On the same page he notes that Caffa, bigger than Messina, was built by the Genoese and is now held by a Turkish garrison.
passages.quote: Le Roy a cinq Serails, & le Sultan deux; l'vn en la Ville où il fait sa residence … Chacun de ces Serails a enuiron vn mille de circuit, & est entouré d'vne haute muraille, mais peu forte; les portes en sont de fer, les appartemens qu'elles ferment sont dorez & peints au dedans de belles couleurs.
passages.translation: The King has five palaces, and the Sultan two; one in the town where he resides … Each of these palaces is about a mile round and is surrounded by a high wall, but not a strong one; the gates are of iron, and the apartments they enclose are gilded and painted inside in fine colours.
passages.speaker: Jean de Luca, Dominican (Relation des Tartares Percopites et Nogaies, printed by Thévenot)
passages.caution: The town name after 'residence' and the other palace sites are unreadable in the OCR and are left out.

passages.headline: 'Tartars of Kin', lords of the golden mountains, now masters of China
passages.gloss: Introducing the Dutch embassy to Peking, Thévenot explains in a margin note who these new 'Tartars' are. Eastern Tartary is called Kin, 'gold', by the Chinese; its people are known as lords of the golden mountains; the country is bounded by another Tartar kingdom, Niulhan, to the north, by the Korean peninsula to the south and by a great river, the 'Linohang', to the west, and 'these Tartars are the ones who are now masters of China'.
passages.quote: La Tartarie Orientale est appellée Kin par les Chinois, c'est à dire l'or, on appelle communément ces Tartares les seigneurs des montagnes d'or, parce que leurs païs en sont fort riches.
passages.translation: Eastern Tartary is called Kin by the Chinese, that is to say gold; these Tartars are commonly called the lords of the golden mountains, because their countries are very rich in it.
passages.speaker: Melchisédech Thévenot (editor's margin note)
passages.caution: Editor's gloss built on Martini and other Jesuit writers; 'Kin' is the Jin dynasty name the Manchus first used (Later Jin).

passages.headline: A Tibetan king of Tartar descent in a four-storey castle
passages.people: Tibetans; the king, of the 'Tartars of Tangut'
passages.gloss: The Jesuit Johann Grueber crossed the 'sands of desert Tartary', the Kokonor lake and Tangut to Lhasa. As told to a Florentine visitor in 1665, the king descends from an ancient race of Tartars of Tangut and lives at Butala (the Potala), a castle on a high mountain built like a European house, four storeys of fine architecture. The same page reports the Grand Lama worshipped as a god and said to have risen from death seven times.
passages.quote: La ville capitale de ce royaume s'appelle Lassa; le Roy se nomme Teva, qui descend d'une race tres-ancienne des Tartares de Tangut. Il fait sa residence à Butala, chasteau basty sur une haute montagne à la façon des maisons d'Europe; il a quatre étages de fort bonne architecture.
passages.translation: The capital city of this kingdom is called Lassa; the King is named Teva, and descends from a very ancient race of the Tartars of Tangut. He lives at Butala, a castle built on a high mountain in the fashion of European houses; it has four storeys of very fine architecture.
passages.speaker: Johann Grueber, as reported by an unnamed Florentine interviewer (generally identified as Lorenzo Magalotti), French translation in Thévenot, 1696
passages.caution: Interview notes, translated; Grueber saw Lhasa, but the reporter wrote from conversation. 'Teva' is probably the Tibetan title Depa (the regent), not a personal name.

passages.headline: The Tatar horde revolts, and the Jin are 'Eastern Tartars'
passages.people: the Tatar tribe; the Jin (Jurchen) emperors; Mongols
passages.gloss: In the story of young Temüjin, Gaubil writes that 'the horde of the Tatars' rebelled against the Jin emperor, keeping the Tatars as one tribe distinct from the Mongols. His footnote explains that the Jin were 'Eastern Tartars' who ruled the steppe north and north-east of Liaodong and much of northern China, and to whom the petty princes of both Tartaries paid tribute.
passages.quote: La Horde des Tatars se révolta contre l'Empereur des Kin. … L'Empereur des Kin dont il est ici parlé, est l'Empereur des Tartares orientaux qui étoient alors maîtres de la Tartarie qui est au Nord, & Nord-Est du Leaotong
passages.translation: The horde of the Tatars revolted against the Emperor of the Kin. … The Emperor of the Kin spoken of here is the Emperor of the Eastern Tartars, who were then masters of the part of Tartary lying north and north-east of Liaodong
passages.speaker: Antoine Gaubil (text and his own footnote)

passages.headline: Ögedei puts walls round the camp at Karakorum, 1235
passages.gloss: The Chinese annals record that in spring 1235 Ögedei ordered walls built around the encampment of Holin (Karakorum) and a palace called Wan'an five li round. Gaubil elsewhere in the book says Holin is the Caracoram of other writers. It is a precise date for when the Mongol camp-capital became a walled town.
passages.quote: Au Printemps de l'an 1235 L'Empereur Ogotay ordonna de revêtir de murailles le campement de Holin, & de faire de cinq lis de tour le palais appellé Ouangan.
passages.translation: In the spring of the year 1235 the Emperor Ögedei ordered the camp of Holin to be enclosed with walls, and the palace called Ouangan to be made five li in circumference.
passages.speaker: Antoine Gaubil, translating the Chinese annals

passages.headline: A Chinese monk lays out the Mongols' new capital (Shangdu)
passages.people: Mongols (Möngke Khan); the Chinese monk Liu Bingzhong
passages.gloss: Finding Holin (Karakorum) inconvenient, Möngke had a new capital chosen in Tartary. The task went to a learned Chinese Buddhist monk, Lieoupingtchong (Liu Bingzhong), who picked a site east of Huanzhou; a city, imperial palace, temples, lords' palaces and courts were built inside high thick walls, and it soon filled with Chinese and Tartars. Gaubil notes it was later called Changtou (Shangdu, the Xanadu of legend).
passages.quote: Il ordonna de choisir un lieu en Tartarie qui seroit désormais la capitale de ses Etats. Ce soin fut donné à un Bonze Chinois appellé Lieoupingtchong. … On y bâtit une grande ville, un palais pour l'Empereur, des temples, des palais pour les Seigneurs, & des tribunaux. On l'investit de hautes & épaisses murailles.
passages.translation: He ordered a place in Tartary to be chosen that would henceforth be the capital of his states. This task was given to a Chinese monk named Lieoupingtchong. … A great city was built there, a palace for the Emperor, temples, palaces for the lords, and courts of justice. It was enclosed with high, thick walls.
passages.speaker: Antoine Gaubil, translating the Chinese annals

passages.headline: A Tibetan lama loots the Song tombs and builds a pyramid of bones
passages.people: Mongols (Yuan court of Khubilai); a Tibetan lama; Chinese
passages.gloss: Under Khubilai a Tibetan lama in favour with the Mongols dug up the tombs of the Song emperors near Shaoxing, reportedly finding much gold and jewels, and piled the bones with those of oxen and horses into a pyramid. The outraged local officials jailed him, but Mongol lords and court lamas got Khubilai to free him and return most of his treasure, which, Gaubil says, the Chinese never forgave.
passages.quote: Sa passion pour l'or & l'argent le porta jusqu'à déterrer les corps morts des Empereurs, & des Grands dont le tombeau étoit près de Chaohing. Il y trouva, dit-on, beaucoup d'or, d'argent, & de bijoux. De ces ossemens mêlés avec des os de bœuf, & de chevaux il fit une pyramide.
passages.translation: His passion for gold and silver drove him to dig up the dead bodies of the Emperors and great men whose tombs were near Shaoxing. He found there, it is said, much gold, silver and jewels. From these bones, mixed with the bones of oxen and horses, he made a pyramid.
passages.speaker: Antoine Gaubil, translating the Chinese annals
passages.caution: The Chinese histories were hostile to the lamas and to this episode; 'dit-on' marks the treasure as report.

passages.headline: One northern nation, parent of Huns, Turks, Mongols and Tartars
passages.place: Mongolia (north of Shaanxi, Shanxi and Beijing)
passages.people: Xiongnu (Hiong-nou), in Deguignes' view the ancestors of the Huns and later Tartars
passages.gloss: Deguignes opens his history of the ancient Huns with his big claim: a famous nation north of China's frontier provinces gave rise to the peoples later known as Huns, Turks, Mongols, Hungarians and Tartars. He lists the names the Chinese gave it over the dynasties, ending with Hiong-nou, which he thinks produced the name Hun.
passages.quote: Au Nord des frontières Septentrionales des Provinces de Chensi, de Chansi & de Petcheli, habitoit autrefois une Nation célèbre, qui a donné naissance à celles que nous avons connues depuis sous le nom de Huns, de Turcs, de Mogols, de Hongrois & de Tartares
passages.translation: North of the northern frontiers of the provinces of Shaanxi, Shanxi and Beizhili there once lived a famous nation, which gave birth to those we have since known under the names of Huns, Turks, Mongols, Hungarians and Tartars
passages.speaker: Joseph de Guignes
passages.caution: A scholarly theory, not a report; the Xiongnu-Hun link is still debated and 'Hungarians' in this list is Deguignes' own speculation.

passages.headline: A nation born of a princess and a wolf
passages.gloss: Retelling a Chinese legend of the Uighurs, Deguignes says a Hun ruler shut his two beautiful daughters in a tower in the north so that heaven might marry them. An old wolf howled round the tower and made its den at the foot, and the younger sister, taking it for the god, went down to it. He adds that the Uighurs were said to imitate wolf howls in their songs, and that their tents stood on unusually high wheels, so the Chinese called them Kao-tche, 'high carts'.
passages.quote: Un vieux loup rodoit nuit & jour autour de la prison des Princesses Tartares, il observoit cette tour en faisant des heurlemens épouvantables; enfin il établit sa tanière au pied. La plus jeune persuadée que ce loup, qui examinoit depuis si long-tems la tour, ne pouvoit être que la divinité à laquelle son père l'avoit consacrée, encouragea sa sœur à descendre avec elle.
passages.translation: An old wolf prowled night and day around the prison of the Tartar princesses; he watched the tower, howling frightfully, and finally made his den at its foot. The younger one, persuaded that this wolf, which had been watching the tower for so long, could only be the god to whom her father had dedicated her, urged her sister to go down with her.
passages.speaker: Joseph de Guignes, retelling a Chinese legend
passages.caution: Deguignes himself calls it the nation's 'fabulous origin'.

passages.headline: Balkh: stone and brick houses and a marble castle of the Uzbek khan
passages.gloss: Describing the Uzbek khanate of Balkh, Deguignes calls Balkh the most important town held by the 'Mahometan Tartars': large and populous, mostly built of stone or brick, with earth ramparts faced by a wall, a trading hub between Bukhara and India, and a khan's castle 'in the oriental style' built almost entirely of marble from nearby quarries. He also calls Balkh's Uzbeks the most civilised of the Muslim Tartars.
passages.quote: La ville de Balkh, à présent la plus considérable de toutes les villes que les Tartares Mahométans possedent, est grande & bien peuplée, la plupart de ses bâtimens sont bâtis de pierre ou de brique … Le château du Khan est un grand bâtiment à l'orientale, presque tout bâti de marbre dont on trouve des carrières fort belles dans les montagnes voisines.
passages.translation: The town of Balkh, at present the most considerable of all the towns the Mahometan Tartars possess, is large and well peopled; most of its buildings are built of stone or brick … The Khan's castle is a large building in the oriental style, almost entirely built of marble, of which there are very fine quarries in the neighbouring mountains.
passages.speaker: Joseph de Guignes
passages.caution: Deguignes never saw Balkh; the description is borrowed from earlier compilations and is not dated precisely.

passages.headline: Timur's 'Tartars' slip into Delhi and sack it
passages.gloss: After taking Delhi, Timur's wives wanted to see the city and its palace of a thousand columns; when a gate was opened for them, fifteen thousand 'Tartars' slipped in unnoticed. Fighting with the inhabitants, fires and looting followed, and Delhi was given over to plunder; Deguignes says some soldiers ended up with a hundred and fifty slaves each.
passages.quote: les Sulthanes, femmes de Tamerlan, ayant envie de voir cette belle ville & principalement un superbe palais qui étoit orné de mille colonnes, elles entrèrent avec toute leur cour, la porte de la ville fut ouverte, & quinze mille Tartares y pénétrèrent sans qu'on s'en apperçût. … Dehli fut entièrement livrée au pillage.
passages.translation: the Sultanas, Tamerlane's wives, wishing to see this fine city and above all a superb palace adorned with a thousand columns, went in with their whole court; the city gate was opened, and fifteen thousand Tartars got in without anyone noticing. … Delhi was given over entirely to pillage.
passages.speaker: Joseph de Guignes
passages.caution: The page presents the sack as a disorder the Tartar officers could not stop, which is the version given by Timur's own court historians.

passages.headline: The last Yuan heir falls back to Karakorum
passages.people: Mongols (Yuan dynasty, then the Northern Yuan)
passages.gloss: In the summary of the fall of the Mongol dynasty, the Ming founder takes Tatou (Dadu, the Mongol capital at Beijing), which the last Yuan emperor had abandoned, and the heir retreats to Holin, 'or Caracorom', founding a new dynasty in Tartary, the Northern Yuan. Karakorum here is still a working Mongol capital more than a century after its founding.
passages.quote: Le Prince héritier, fils de cet Empereur fugitif, se retira à Holin ou Caracorom, & fonda en Tartarie une nouvelle Dynastie appellée les Yuen du nord
passages.translation: The heir prince, son of this fugitive Emperor, withdrew to Holin or Karakorum, and founded in Tartary a new dynasty called the Northern Yuan
passages.speaker: Mailla's Histoire générale de la Chine (dynastic summary heading vol. 10)

passages.headline: The Manchu 'Tartars' take China and change nothing
passages.gloss: After the rebel Li Zicheng's defeat, a Manchu prince led an army 'of Tartars and many Chinese' through the provinces. The annals, as rendered here, claim the conquerors followed their emperor's line, kept the old tribunals in Peking and simply doubled the posts so that Tartars could hold half; 'China, in changing masters, changed neither its form nor its government'. The passage shows 'Tartar' used plainly for the Manchus.
passages.quote: Un des princes Man-tchéous se mit à la tête d'une armée formidable, composée de Tartares & d'un grand nombre de Chinois … La Chine, en changeant de maîtres, ne changea ni de forme ni de gouvernement.
passages.translation: One of the Manchu princes put himself at the head of a formidable army made up of Tartars and a great number of Chinese … China, in changing masters, changed neither its form nor its government.
passages.speaker: Joseph de Mailla (compiled from Chinese works, edited by Grosier)
passages.caution: An official, pro-Qing view of the conquest, written from Peking under the Manchu dynasty.

passages.headline: Khalkha princes spellbound by puppets at the emperor's feast
passages.people: Khalkha Mongols (Kalkas), their Grand Lama, and Manchu court
passages.gloss: An editor's note describes the great assembly at which the Khalkha khans submitted to the Kangxi emperor. At the feast, rope-dancers and puppets played 'much as in Europe', and the Khalkhas, who had never seen such a show, forgot to eat; only the Grand Lama stayed grave. The emperor then dressed the princes in Manchu robes, which they wore from then on before him.
passages.quote: Ce festin fut entremêlé de divertissemens exécutés par des danseurs de corde, qui firent divers tours de souplesse. Il y eut aussi des marionnettes, qui jouèrent à-peu-près comme en Europe. Les Kalkas, qui n'avoient jamais vu ce spectacle, oublioient de manger, par l'admiration qu'il leur causoit. Le grand Lama parut insensible à ces frivolités
passages.translation: The feast was interspersed with entertainments by rope-dancers, who performed various feats of agility. There were also puppets, which played much as in Europe. The Khalkhas, who had never seen this spectacle, forgot to eat, so much did it amaze them. The Grand Lama appeared untouched by these frivolities
passages.speaker: Editor's note (signed 'Editeur') in Mailla's Histoire générale de la Chine, drawing on the Jesuit Gerbillon's journal
passages.caution: The place and year are not printed on this page; they are those of the Khalkha submission that the note describes. Gerbillon was an eyewitness, but the Paris editor paraphrases him.

passages.headline: Mongol farmers in earthen houses near Hohhot
passages.gloss: Following the Kangxi emperor's march of 1696, the note describes hamlets of a few earthen houses lived in by Mongols who farmed the nearby fields, lining the road to greet the emperor with sheep, butter and cream. Near Kouei-hoa-tching (Hohhot) the garrison knelt on the road and some two hundred lamas in ceremonial dress, with rough musical instruments and banners, waited at the main temple. Not every 'Tartar' lived in a tent.
passages.quote: On passa devant plusieurs hameaux, composés de quelques maisons de terre, habitées par des Mongous qui cultivent les champs voisins. Ces pauvres habitans se rangeoient sur le chemin pour saluer l'empereur, auquel ils offroient des moutons, du beurre, de la crème & divers bois odoriférans.
passages.translation: We passed several hamlets made up of a few earthen houses, inhabited by Mongols who farm the neighbouring fields. These poor inhabitants lined up along the road to greet the emperor, offering him sheep, butter, cream and various fragrant woods.
passages.speaker: Editor's note in Mailla's Histoire générale de la Chine (Qing volume), narrating Kangxi's 1696 journey
passages.caution: The note does not name its source on this page; it reads like a Jesuit companion's journal retold by the Paris editor.

passages.headline: 'The stinking Tartars': what the Chinese called them
passages.people: Tatars / Tartars as named in Chinese sources; later Jurchen and Mongol rulers
passages.gloss: In his 'Observation' on d'Herbelot's article Tatar, Visdelou traces the Chinese names: first Tha-tche, then Tha-tha, commonly Tha-tçe, and in contempt Sao-tha-tçe, 'the stinking Tartars'. He says the Chinese added a character meaning raw hide to show how low they ranked these peoples, and that the Jurchen and Mongols, once they had conquered China, dropped the insulting character. The volume's index adds an older name, Kiuen, 'dog'.
passages.quote: Les Chinois les ont nommé au commencement Thatche, ensuite Tha-tha, & vulgairement Tha-tçe; enfin par mépris Sao-tha-tçe, c'est-à-dire les puants Tartares. … Aussi les Niou-tchin & les Moumgols, après avoir conquis la Chine, ont retranché cette lettre injurieuse
passages.translation: The Chinese first called them Thatche, then Tha-tha, and commonly Tha-tçe; finally, in contempt, Sao-tha-tçe, that is, the stinking Tartars. … So the Jurchen and the Mongols, after conquering China, removed this insulting character
passages.speaker: Claude de Visdelou (Observation on d'Herbelot)
passages.caution: The spellings Tha-tçe and Sao-tha-tçe are taken from the volume's own index; the OCR on this page garbles them.

passages.headline: Genghis Khan descended from a grey deer and a white she-wolf
passages.gloss: Visdelou compares the Mongol origin stories. A Chinese abridgement says the Mongols' 'secret memoirs' traced Chinggis's family to the mating of a grey deer and a white she-wolf, whose monstrous child was his twenty-fourth ancestor; on the same page is the story of the widow Alan-kouo conceiving by a golden light through the tent's smoke-hole. Visdelou notes the official Chinese genealogy says none of this and calls the wolf tale 'shameful and impossible'.
passages.quote: les mémoires secrets des Moumgols témoignent que la famille de Ki-o-uen étoit sortie de l'accouplement d'un cerf gris & d'une louve blanche, & que l'enfant monstrueux qui en nâquit fut le vingt-quatrième Ayeul de Tchim-khis-khan … elle ne parle nulle part de la dernière, qui est également honteuse & impossible.
passages.translation: the secret memoirs of the Mongols testify that the family of Ki-o-uen came from the coupling of a grey deer and a white she-wolf, and that the monstrous child born of it was the twenty-fourth ancestor of Chinggis Khan … it [the official history] nowhere mentions the last story, which is both shameful and impossible.
passages.speaker: Claude de Visdelou, citing Yuan Liaofan's Chinese abridgement ('Tuen-leao-fan'), which cites the Mongols' 'secret memoirs'
passages.caution: Visdelou reports the legend at third hand and rejects it.

passages.headline: Türk funerals: slashed faces and a stone for every man killed
passages.people: Tou-kiue (the ancient Turks), counted among the Tartars
passages.gloss: From the Chinese histories Visdelou describes the Tou-kiue (Göktürks): a gold wolf's head on their standard because they believed they sprang from a she-wolf, tallies notched on wood because they had no writing, and funerals where the body lay in a tent, relatives sacrificed sheep and horses and cut their faces so blood mixed with tears, and stones were piled on the grave, one for each man the dead had killed.
passages.quote: Dans leurs funérailles, on plaçoit le corps du mort sous une tente. … Alors ils se déchiquetoient le visage avec des couteaux, & de cette façon leur sang se mêloit avec leurs larmes … Ils amassoient des pierres sur le lieu de la sépulture & y plaçoient des marques. On y mettoit autant de pierres que le mort avoit tué d'hommes durant sa vie.
passages.translation: At their funerals the dead man's body was laid under a tent. … Then they slashed their faces with knives, and in this way their blood mingled with their tears … They heaped stones on the burial place and set markers there. They put as many stones there as the dead man had killed men during his life.
passages.speaker: Claude de Visdelou, translating the Chinese histories

passages.headline: The Mongol siege of the Jin capital: double walls, siege lines and 'cannon'
passages.people: Mongols (Moumgols) under Ögedei and Subutai; the Jin (Jurchen) court
passages.gloss: Translating the Chinese history 'word for word', Visdelou describes the Mongol siege of the southern Jin capital (called Nan-kim here, which he stresses is not our Nanking but Kaifeng). The city had a double wall, the outer 120 li round; Subutai battered it with every kind of engine 'and even cannon', and the defenders answered in kind, so he ringed it with siege lines 54,000 paces round. In twelve days of fighting, the dead were counted 'by millions'.
passages.quote: La Ville étoit ceinte d'une double muraille. L'extérieure avoit 120 Li, ou 43200 pas géometriques de tour … il fit battre les murailles avec toutes sortes de machines de guerre, & même des Canons; mais comme les assiegés resistoient avec les mêmes armes, le siège n'avançoit point.
passages.translation: The city was surrounded by a double wall. The outer one was 120 li, or 43,200 geometric paces, round … he had the walls battered with every sort of war machine, and even cannon; but as the besieged resisted with the same weapons, the siege made no progress.
passages.speaker: Claude de Visdelou, translating a Chinese history
passages.caution: 'Canons' is Visdelou's word for Chinese fire-weapons of 1232, which were not European-style cannon; the 'millions' of dead is annalistic exaggeration.

passages.headline: The Dzungars live in tents, visiting their villages two months a year
passages.gloss: In a note on the emperor's text, Amiot explains that the Eleuths camp in tents and spend only two or three months a year in their hamlets, villages and 'kinds of towns', and only the most important among them bother to go there at all. Every head of a family plants a standard before his tent, larger or smaller by rank.
passages.quote: Les Eleuths campent sous des tentes; ils ne sont dans leurs hameaux, villages & especes de villes, qu'environ deux ou trois mois de l'année; & encore n'y a-t-il que les plus considérables d'entr'eux, qui daignent s'y retirer. Chaque chef de famille arbore un etendart devant sa tente
passages.translation: The Eleuths camp under tents; they are in their hamlets, villages and sorts of towns only about two or three months of the year, and even then only the most important of them deign to withdraw there. Each head of a family raises a standard in front of his tent
passages.speaker: Joseph-Marie Amiot (note to his translation of the Qianlong emperor's monument on the conquest of the Eleuths)
passages.caution: Amiot never went to Dzungaria; he writes from Peking court information.

passages.headline: No towns on the Ili until the emperor built one for exiles
passages.gloss: The next note says the banks of the Ili had long been the favourite home of the Eleuth kings, but 'there were no towns': they camped in tents, moving from place to place. After the conquest the emperor had a town built there that grew daily, and it had become the place of exile for Chinese and Tartars convicted of crimes.
passages.quote: Les bords de la riviere d'Ily ont été depuis long-temps le séjour de prédilection des Rois des Eleuths. Il n'y avoit point de villes. Ils y campoient sous des tentes, tantôt dans un endroit & tantôt dans un autre. L'Empereur y a fait bâtir une ville qui devient chaque jour plus peuplée. C'est-là qu'on envoie aujourd'hui & les Chinois & les Tartares qui ont mérité la peine de l'exil.
passages.translation: The banks of the Ili river had long been the favourite residence of the Eleuth kings. There were no towns. They camped there in tents, now in one place, now in another. The Emperor has had a town built there which grows more populous every day. It is there that Chinese and Tartars who have deserved the penalty of exile are now sent.
passages.speaker: Joseph-Marie Amiot (note to the Eleuth monument)

passages.headline: The emperor: 'nearer to the dirty monkey than to man'
passages.people: Eleuths (Dzungars), described by the Qianlong emperor
passages.gloss: In his victory inscription the Qianlong emperor explains the Dzungars' revolt after his gifts by comparing them to beasts: closer to a filthy monkey than to man, and fiercer than bears and the Yu-ki. Amiot notes that he softened the monkey insult, and that the Yu-ki is a fabulous creature with a tiger's claws, a dragon's head and a fox's body.
passages.quote: Je savois que par la nature de leurs défauts, & de leurs vices, ils approchoient plus du sale Sapajou que de l'homme, dont ils ont cependant l'empreinte & dont ils portent l'auguste nom; mais, je l'avoue, je n'imaginois pas qu'ils pussent être plus féroces que les Ours, plus cruels & plus intraitables que les Yu-ki.
passages.translation: I knew that by the nature of their faults and vices they were closer to the dirty monkey than to man, whose stamp they bear and whose august name they carry; but, I admit, I did not imagine they could be fiercer than bears, crueller and more untameable than the Yu-ki.
passages.speaker: The Qianlong emperor (stone inscription), translated by Joseph-Marie Amiot
passages.caution: Imperial war propaganda, not description; Amiot says he toned down the original insult.

passages.headline: Torghuts, Eleuths and the four branches of the Dzungar nation
passages.gloss: The emperor's monument explains who the Torghuts were: one of the branches of the Eleuths. Four branches once made up the whole Dzungar ('Tchong-kar') nation; they split, the Eleuths dominated the rest, and in Kangxi's time the Torghut chief Ayuki fled with his people into Russian territory and settled on the 'Etchil', which Amiot's note identifies as the Volga.
passages.quote: Les Tourgouths sont une des branches des Eleuths. Quatre branches differentes formoient autrefois toute la nation de Tchong-kar. Il seroit difficile d'expliquer leur commune origine, sur laquelle d'ailleurs on ne sait rien de bien certain. Ces quatre branches se séparerent, & firent chacune une nation à part.
passages.translation: The Torghuts are one of the branches of the Eleuths. Four different branches once formed the whole nation of Dzungar. It would be hard to explain their common origin, about which nothing very certain is known. These four branches separated and each became a nation of its own.
passages.speaker: The Qianlong emperor (monument on the Torghut migration), translated by Joseph-Marie Amiot

passages.headline: Why the Torghuts left the Volga: conscription, hostages and religion
passages.gloss: The emperor gives the Torghuts' reasons for leaving Russia: the Russians kept demanding soldiers, had taken Ubashi's son as a hostage, and had a different religion and no regard for the Lamas' faith the Torghuts followed. On the same page they set out with wives, children and baggage, crossed the Kazakh country and the deserts by Lake Balkhash, and after eight months and more than ten thousand li reached the Ili frontier. The volume's preface puts their number at 500,000.
passages.quote: Les Russes ne cessant point d'exiger de lui qu'il leur fournît des soldats … en dernier lieu lui ayant enlevé son propre fils pour leur servir d'otage, étant outre cela d'une religion différente de la sienne, & ne faisant aucun cas de celle des Lamas dont les Tourgouths font profession, Oubaché & les siens se sont enfin déterminés à secouer un joug
passages.translation: The Russians never ceasing to demand soldiers from him … and lately having taken his own son from him as a hostage, being moreover of a different religion from his and making no account of the religion of the Lamas which the Torghuts profess, Ubashi and his people at last resolved to shake off a yoke
passages.speaker: The Qianlong emperor (monument on the Torghut migration), translated by Joseph-Marie Amiot
passages.caution: The emperor's version stresses a free and willing submission to himself; Amiot's own note (n438) adds that the nation reached Ili in rags, with nothing to live on.

passages.headline: 'Destroyed by the Manchu Tartars, not the Chinese'
passages.gloss: Amiot corrects the French traveller Chappe d'Auteroche, who had written that the Kalmyk nation was destroyed 'by the Chinese' after a ten-year war. It would be more exact, Amiot says, to say it was destroyed by the Manchu Tartars, since no Chinese took part, and the war lasted only about three and a half years. The distinction matters for anyone reading 'Tartar' in these sources.
passages.quote: Il eût été plus exact de dire: elle a été détruite par les Tartares Mantchoux; car aucun Chinois n'y a eu part: & la guerre qui a exterminé les Eleuths n'a duré qu'environ trois ans & demi, & non pas dix ans.
passages.translation: It would have been more exact to say: it was destroyed by the Manchu Tartars, for no Chinese had any part in it; and the war that exterminated the Eleuths lasted only about three and a half years, not ten.
passages.speaker: Joseph-Marie Amiot (remarks on Chappe d'Auteroche's Voyage en Sibérie)

passages.headline: Walled Muslim towns of Kashgar and Yarkand, unlike the Eleuths
passages.people: Muslim townspeople of 'Little Bukharia' under the two Khojas; contrasted with the Eleuths
passages.gloss: Amiot explains why the Muslim princes of Yarkand and Kashgar thought they could resist the Qing after the Eleuths fell: unlike the nomad Eleuths they had firearms, walled towns and strongholds, and Muslim neighbours to help them. The Qing generals took both towns; the younger Khoja's head was sent to Peking in a box and displayed over the palace's Wu Men gate.
passages.quote: Ils avoient par dessus les Eleuths l'avantage des armes à feu, ils avoient des villes murées, quelques places fortes, & ils pouvoient être secourus par les autres Mahométans leurs voisins.
passages.translation: They had the advantage over the Eleuths of firearms; they had walled towns and some strongholds, and they could be helped by the other Mahometans, their neighbours.
passages.speaker: Joseph-Marie Amiot (note to the Eleuth monument)
passages.caution: These town-dwellers are the Turkic Muslims of the Tarim oases, not Tartars in Amiot's usage; the passage is useful for the contrast.

passages.headline: Peking's walls under the Khitan, Jin and Mongols
passages.gloss: Answering a French author who claimed Peking was founded by Khubilai in 1267, a Peking missionary traces its walls through Chinese annals: 36 li round with eight gates as the Khitan southern capital, 75 li under the Jin, then six leagues and eleven gates when the Mongol Yuan 'repaired its ruins' in 1274. Here the northern conquerors rebuild an old Chinese city rather than create one.
passages.quote: Pe-king n'avoit alors que trente-six li de tour … & huit portes. Sous les Kin, dont il fut aussi la Capitale, il eut soixante-quinze li de tour, ou sept lieues & demie. Les Yuen, qui le nommerent d'abord la Capitale du milieu puis la grande Capitale, ne lui donnerent que six lieues de tour & onze portes, lorsqu'ils en reparerent les ruines en 1274.
passages.translation: Peking was then only thirty-six li round … with eight gates. Under the Kin, whose capital it also was, it was seventy-five li round, or seven and a half leagues. The Yuan, who first named it the Middle Capital and then the Great Capital, gave it only six leagues round and eleven gates when they repaired its ruins in 1274.
passages.speaker: Anonymous Peking missionary writing in the voice of a Chinese scholar (Remarques sur un écrit de M. P**, Mémoires vol. 2, 1777)
passages.caution: The figures come from Chinese geographical annals as the writer reads them; the Yuan in fact built a largely new city (Dadu) beside the old site.

passages.headline: The Manchus build stupas after adopting the lamas' religion
passages.gloss: Arguing against the idea that Chinese towers came from Bactria or Tibet, the writer jokes that the Chinese built them 'before the Mongols knew how to sneeze without looking at the sun'. As for the ta (stupa-pagodas), he says the Manchu Tartars took up the lamas' religion and its superstition of the ta, and had them built in chosen places to please the lamas and bring luck.
passages.quote: nous avions des leou avant que les Mongoux sussent eternuer sans regarder le soleil. Tout ce que nous dirons sur les ta, c'est que les Tartares Mantchoux, ayant pris la religion des Lama, ont adopté la superstition des ta, & en ont fait bâtir de diverses hauteurs dans les lieux qu'ils ont déterminés
passages.translation: we had leou [towers] before the Mongols knew how to sneeze without looking at the sun. All we will say about the ta is that the Manchu Tartars, having taken up the religion of the Lamas, adopted the superstition of the ta and had them built, of various heights, in places they chose
passages.speaker: Anonymous Peking missionary writing in the voice of a Chinese scholar (Remarques sur un écrit de M. P**, Mémoires vol. 2, 1777)
passages.caution: Polemical and dismissive of both Mongols and lamas.

passages.headline: Tartars wield brush and sabre and scorn trade
passages.people: Manchu banner people ('Tartares') in Qing China
passages.gloss: An essay on money-lending in China contrasts the two ruling peoples: the Chinese are no warriors and prize learning, while the Tartars aim to handle the brush as well as the sabre and write works of every kind in Manchu, but would think it beneath them to practise a craft or trade. The same page praises their energy and toughness and says they spend freely rather than save.
passages.quote: Nos Chinois ne sont pas guerriers, mais ils se piquent de sagesse & d'habileté.
