Les Tartares visent à manier aussi-bien le pinceau que le sabre; ils composent en Tartare des ouvrages dans tous les genres … Les Tartares croiroient s'avilir de faire un métier ou commerce, & nos Chinois regardent le triste métier des armes comme la derniere ressource du défaut de mérite.
passages.translation: Our Chinese are not warriors, but they pride themselves on wisdom and skill. The Tartars aim to handle the brush as well as the sabre; they compose works of every kind in Tartar [Manchu] … The Tartars would think it degrading to practise a craft or trade, and our Chinese regard the sad trade of arms as the last resort of those without merit.
passages.speaker: Anonymous Peking missionary (essay on interest on money in China, Mémoires vol. 4, 1779)
passages.caution: A generalisation about national character by a writer living in Peking.

passages.headline: Manchus are 'Eastern Tartars', Mongols 'Western Tartars'
passages.gloss: Parrenin, sending the Académie des Sciences his Manchu translation of a French anatomy commissioned by the Kangxi emperor, stops to explain what 'Tartar language' means: the language of the Manchus, who have reigned in China for eighty years and are called Eastern Tartars, not that of the Mongols, called Western Tartars and almost all tributaries of the emperor. The two languages, he says, are very different.
passages.quote: je parle de la langue des Mantcheoux qui régnent à la Chine depuis quatre-vingts ans, & qui s'appellent Tartares Orientaux. Je ne parle nullement de la langue des Mongols, qu'on nomme Tartares Occidentaux, & qui sont presque tous tributaires de l'Empereur. Ces deux langues sont très-différentes entr'elles.
passages.translation: I mean the language of the Manchus, who have reigned in China for eighty years and are called Eastern Tartars. I do not at all mean the language of the Mongols, who are called Western Tartars and are almost all tributaries of the Emperor. These two languages are very different from each other.
passages.speaker: Dominique Parrenin, letter to the Académie des Sciences (Peking, 1 May 1723 or 1725; the year is unclear in the OCR)

passages.headline: Why a Manchu prince could not write 'prendre'
passages.gloss: Parrenin reports a friendly debate with a Manchu prince who praised the Manchu alphabet over European letters. Parrenin challenged him to write the French words prendre, platine, griffon and friand; he could not, because Manchu cannot put two consonants together, so he had to write perendre, pelatine, feriand. Parrenin adds that the script lacks initial B and D, writing P and T instead.
passages.quote: Essayez, par exemple, si vous pourrez écrire ces mots: prendre, platine, griffon, friand. Il ne le put, parce que dans la langue Tartare on ne peut joindre deux consonnes de suite; il faut placer entre deux une voyelle, & écrire perendre, pelatine, feriand, gerifon, &c.
passages.translation: 'Try, for example, whether you can write these words: prendre, platine, griffon, friand.' He could not, because in the Tartar language two consonants cannot be joined in a row; a vowel must be placed between them, and one writes perendre, pelatine, feriand, gerifon, etc.
passages.speaker: Dominique Parrenin, letter to the Académie des Sciences

passages.headline: New towns in eastern Tartary, none in the west
passages.people: Manchus (Eastern Tartary); Mongol and other nomads (Western Tartary)
passages.gloss: In a report on the China missions presented in Rome, François Noël says Eastern Tartary (Manchuria) is filling up: the emperor is building towns there and villages are well peopled. Western Tartary has neither towns nor villages except toward the Uzbeks and the Caspian; its peoples, recently subjected to the emperor, own nothing but herds, and move on every three months or so when the grass is eaten.
passages.quote: La Tartarie orientale se peuple tous les jours. L'Empereur y fait bâtir des villes, & l'on y voit des villages fort peuplés. Pour la Tartarie occidentale, il n'y a ni villes ni villages que du côté des Yousbecks, & de la mer Caspienne … Toutes les richesses de ces Peuples ne consistent qu'en de nombreux troupeaux, avec lesquels ils errent de côté & d'autre.
passages.translation: Eastern Tartary is filling with people every day. The Emperor is having towns built there, and very populous villages can be seen. As for Western Tartary, there are neither towns nor villages except toward the Uzbeks and the Caspian Sea … All the wealth of these peoples consists only of numerous herds, with which they wander here and there.
passages.speaker: François Noël, Mémoire on the state of the China missions (presented in Latin at Rome, translated into French)
passages.caution: A general survey written for Rome, not a travel report; the year on the title is garbled in the OCR.

passages.headline: Mukden, capital of Eastern Tartary, where Chinese count as Tartars
passages.people: Manchus and the people of Liaodong
passages.gloss: Noël reports a plan to open a mission at Chin-yam (Shenyang, the Manchu Mukden), capital of Liaodong and all Eastern Tartary, where the emperor had set four supreme tribunals for the Tartars' affairs. He adds that Liaodong now counts as part of Tartary and its people are regarded 'not as Chinese, but as true Tartars'. The label followed political allegiance, not ancestry.
passages.quote: Chin-yam capitale de Leaoton, & de toute la Tartarie orientale. Cette ville est considérable, & l'Empereur y a établi quatre Tribunaux souverains pour y juger en dernier ressort toutes les affaires des Tartares; car le Leaoton passe aujourd'hui pour être de la Tartarie, & on n'en regarde plus les habitans comme Chinois, mais comme de véritables Tartares.
passages.translation: Chin-yam, capital of Liaodong and of all Eastern Tartary. This city is considerable, and the Emperor has set up four supreme tribunals there to judge in the last resort all the affairs of the Tartars; for Liaodong now passes for part of Tartary, and its inhabitants are no longer regarded as Chinese, but as true Tartars.
passages.speaker: François Noël, Mémoire on the state of the China missions

passages.headline: Peking: a Tartar city and a Chinese city
passages.gloss: Jean de Fontaney, one of the French Jesuits sent by Louis XIV, describes Peking as two joined cities, each four leagues round: the 'Tartar city', with the emperor's palace in the middle, and the 'Chinese city'. The streets were so crowded one could hardly walk. On the same page he describes the great bell of Peking set on a base of brick and stone.
passages.quote: Peking est composée de deux Villes: la premiere, au milieu de laquelle est le Palais de l'Empereur, s'appelle la ville des Tartares; & la seconde, la ville des Chinois. Elles sont jointes l'une à l'autre, & ont chacune quatre lieues de tour.
passages.translation: Peking is made up of two cities: the first, in the middle of which is the Emperor's palace, is called the city of the Tartars; and the second, the city of the Chinese. They are joined to each other, and each is four leagues round.
passages.speaker: Jean de Fontaney, letter to Père de La Chaise (Zhoushan, 15 February 1703)

passages.headline: Russian forts and towns built across 'Great Tartary'
passages.people: Russians (Muscovites); Eastern Tartars, subjects of the Qing
passages.gloss: Fontaney explains how the Muscovites had pushed from Moscow through Siberia along the Irtysh, Ob, Yenisei and Angara to the Selenga and the Amur ('Sangalien-oula' to the Tartars, the Black Dragon river to the Chinese), building forts and towns as they went. The nearest to China were Selenginsk, Nerchinsk and Albazin. In this corner of 'Tartary' the builders were Russians.
passages.quote: Les Moscovites ne se contenterent pas de faire ces découvertes; ils bâtirent de distance en distance des forts & des villes sur toutes ces rivieres, pour s'en assurer la possession. Les plus proches de la Chine étoient Selinga, Nipchou & Yacsa.
passages.translation: The Muscovites were not content with making these discoveries; they built forts and towns at intervals on all these rivers to secure possession of them. The nearest to China were Selinga, Nipchou and Yacsa.
passages.speaker: Jean de Fontaney, letter to Père de La Chaise (1703)

passages.headline: A palisade of wooden stakes around Liaodong
passages.gloss: On the imperial map survey of Tartary, Pierre Jartoux found the ginseng country walled off from the province of Liaodong by a barrier of wooden stakes (the Willow Palisade), patrolled by guards to keep Chinese from slipping out to dig the precious root. He adds that two or three thousand still sneaked through, risking their freedom.
passages.quote: Les endroits où croît le gin-seng, sont tout-à-fait séparés de la province de Canton, appelée Leaotong dans nos anciennes cartes, par une barrière de pieux de bois qui renferme toute cette Province, et aux environs de laquelle des Gardes rôdent continuellement pour empêcher les Chinois d'en sortir, et d'aller chercher cette racine.
passages.translation: The places where ginseng grows are entirely separated from the province of 'Canton', called Liaodong on our old maps, by a barrier of wooden stakes that encloses the whole province, around which guards patrol constantly to prevent the Chinese from leaving it and going to look for this root.
passages.speaker: Pierre Jartoux, letter from Peking, 12 April 1711
passages.caution: 'Canton' is an error in this reprint (the province meant is Guandong, i.e. Liaodong, not Canton in the south). The volume is a later Toulouse reprint.

passages.headline: Ten thousand Tartars sent to hunt ginseng
passages.gloss: Jartoux writes that the emperor, wanting Tartars rather than Chinese to profit from ginseng, ordered ten thousand Tartars in 1709 to gather it, each owing him two ounces of the best, with the rest bought at its weight in fine silver. His survey party met these herb-hunters in the wilderness; on the same page he describes their troops of a hundred men advancing in a line through the forest. The letter opens with a Tartar villager near the Korean border bringing him four whole plants in a basket.
passages.quote: L'Empereur souhaitant que les Tartares profitassent de ce gain, préférablement aux Chinois, avait donné ordre, cette même année 1709, à dix mille Tartares, d'aller ramasser eux-mêmes tout ce qu'ils pourraient de gin-seng, à condition que chacun d'eux en donnerait à Sa Majesté deux onces du meilleur, et que le reste serait payé au poids d'argent fin.
passages.translation: The Emperor, wishing the Tartars rather than the Chinese to profit from this trade, had ordered ten thousand Tartars that same year, 1709, to go and gather for themselves all the ginseng they could, on condition that each of them would give His Majesty two ounces of the best, and that the rest would be paid for at the weight of fine silver.
passages.speaker: Pierre Jartoux, letter from Peking, 12 April 1711

passages.headline: Eight banners each of Manchu, Mongol and 'Tartarized Chinese'
passages.gloss: A footnote to Parrenin's letters on the persecuted Christian princes of the Sunu family explains the Qing banner system: eight banners of Manchu Tartars, eight of Mongol Tartars and eight of 'Tartarized Chinese', each with its own coloured flag, its own quarter in the Tartar city of Peking and its own courts, apart from those of the ordinary people. 'Tartar' here is a legal status as much as an ancestry.
passages.quote: Il y a huit bannières de Tartares Mantcheoux, huit autres de Tartares Mongous, & huit de Chinois tartarisés. … Chaque bannière a son quartier dans la ville Tartare, & sa justice particulière indépendante de celle du peuple.
passages.translation: There are eight banners of Manchu Tartars, eight more of Mongol Tartars, and eight of Tartarized Chinese. … Each banner has its own quarter in the Tartar city, and its own justice, independent of that of the common people.
passages.speaker: Footnote in Parrenin's letter to Du Halde (Peking, 22 October, mid-1730s; probably added by the editors)

passages.headline: The emperor: 'We Manchus have our own rites'
passages.people: Manchus; the Yongzheng emperor and a Christian Manchu prince
passages.gloss: Parrenin translates the Yongzheng emperor's words to his ministers about a Manchu prince who had become Christian: every nation honours Heaven in its own way; the Manchu rite is the Tiaochin, when all burn incense and paper on New Year's day; Mongols, Chinese, Muscovites and Europeans each have their own. The prince, as a Manchu, should follow the Manchu rite. A footnote says the Tiaochin had no fixed form and each family did it its own way.
passages.quote: Le rite des Tartares Mantcheoux est le Tiaochin, il n'y a personne qui le premier jour de l'an ne brûle des odeurs & du papier, & cela pour honorer le Ciel. Nous autres Mantcheoux, nous avons nos rites particuliers; les Mongous, les Chinois, les Moscovites, les Européens, &c. ont aussi chacun le Tien qui lui est propre.
passages.translation: The rite of the Manchu Tartars is the Tiaochin: there is no one who does not burn incense and paper on the first day of the year, and that is to honour Heaven. We Manchus have our own particular rites; the Mongols, the Chinese, the Muscovites, the Europeans and so on also each have the Tien [Heaven] proper to them.
passages.speaker: The Yongzheng emperor, as translated by Dominique Parrenin (letter of 26 September 1727)
passages.caution: Parrenin's translation of an edict hostile to Christianity; 'Tiaochin' is his transcription of a Manchu household rite.

passages.headline: Jehol: the emperor's hunting palaces in 'Chinese Tartary'
passages.gloss: Amiot explains why the painter-brother Attiret was summoned north: some ten thousand Dzungars had fled their ruler's usurper with families and baggage to submit to the emperor, who settled them in 'Chinese Tartary' and ordered their leaders to Gé-hol (Jehol, modern Chengde), where he hunted each year and had palaces nearly as fine as those around Peking. Attiret, it was guessed, was wanted to paint the portraits of the leading newcomers at the ceremony.
passages.quote: L'Empereur leur ordonna de se rendre à Gé-hol, lieu de la Tartarie Chinoise où il va chaque année pour prendre le divertissement de la chasse, & où il a des palais presque aussi beaux que ceux qui sont aux environs de Peking.
passages.translation: The Emperor ordered them to go to Gé-hol, a place in Chinese Tartary where he goes every year for the pleasure of hunting, and where he has palaces almost as beautiful as those around Peking.
passages.speaker: Joseph-Marie Amiot, letter to Père de La Tour (Peking, 17 October 1754)

passages.headline: Tengri, sun and moon, and felt idols called ongon
passages.people: the 'Tatar' peoples of the steppe (Mongols and neighbours)
passages.gloss: In his opening survey d'Ohsson sums up the old steppe religion: a supreme being called Tangri, like the sky; worship of sun, moon, mountains, rivers and elements, with bows to the south and drink sprinkled to the heavens; and little wooden or felt figures, ongon, hung on the walls of their huts, bowed to and fed by smearing meat or milk on their mouths. The page before describes burial with a mare, a foal and a saddled horse.
passages.quote: Ils reconnaissaient un Etre Suprême, qu'ils désignaient ainsi que le ciel, par le nom de Tangri. … Leurs divinités étaient représentées par de petites figures de bois ou de feutre, nommées Ongon, qu'ils suspendaient aux parois de leurs huttes; ils s'inclinaient devant ces idoles, et leur offraient les prémices de leurs repas, en leur frottant la bouche avec de la viande ou du lait.
passages.translation: They acknowledged a Supreme Being, whom they called, like the sky, by the name Tangri. … Their divinities were represented by small figures of wood or felt, called Ongon, which they hung on the walls of their huts; they bowed before these idols and offered them the first portions of their meals, rubbing their mouths with meat or milk.
passages.speaker: Constantin d'Ohsson
passages.caution: A synthesis of Carpini, Rubruck and Persian sources, not a separate witness.

passages.headline: The Tatars: a separate nation that Chinggis crushed in 1202
passages.people: the Tatar tribe; Mongols under Temüjin
passages.gloss: D'Ohsson, following Rashid al-Din and the Chinese annals, treats the Tatars as a distinct people: seventy thousand households around Lake Buir by the Jurchen frontier, split into six feuding tribes and bitter enemies of the Mongols. In spring 1202 Temüjin attacked and defeated them. The name of this rival, crushed nation became the name Europeans used for the whole Mongol empire.
passages.quote: Cette nation, qui habitait le pays environnant le lac Bouyour, près de la frontière des Tchourtchés, comptait alors soixante-dix mille huttes, ou familles, et se divisait en six tribus … Il régnait une grande animosité entre eux et les Mongols.
passages.translation: This nation, which lived in the country around Lake Buir, near the frontier of the Jurchen, then numbered seventy thousand huts, or families, and was divided into six tribes … There was great hostility between them and the Mongols.
passages.speaker: Constantin d'Ohsson (from Rashid al-Din and the Chinese annals)

passages.headline: The Tatars take Sudak, the Crimean trading port
passages.people: Tatars (Mongol army of Jebe and Subutai); Qipchaqs
passages.gloss: In a note d'Ohsson translates the Arab historian Ibn al-Athir on the first Mongol raid into the western steppe. The 'Tatars' reached Sudak, a Qipchaq port on the Black ('Khazar') Sea where ships called and where Qipchaqs traded slaves and furs of fox, beaver and squirrel for cloth. They took the town; its people fled to the mountains or by sea to Seljuk Anatolia. The note then describes the Tatars' feigned retreat before crushing the Russians.
passages.quote: Les Tatares s'avancèrent jusqu'à la ville de Soudac, qui appartient aux Kiptchacs, et d'où ils tirent leurs grains; elle est située sur la Mer Khazarienne, et les vaisseaux y abordent. On y trouve des étoffes, que les Kiptchacs viennent acheter, donnant en échange des esclaves des deux sexes et des peaux de renard … Les Tatares s'emparèrent de Soudac, dont les habitants prirent la fuite
passages.translation: The Tatars advanced as far as the town of Sudak, which belongs to the Qipchaqs and from which they draw their grain; it lies on the Khazar Sea and ships put in there. Cloth is found there, which the Qipchaqs come to buy, giving in exchange slaves of both sexes and fox skins … The Tatars took Sudak, whose inhabitants fled
passages.speaker: Ibn al-Athir, translated by Constantin d'Ohsson (Note VII)
passages.caution: Ibn al-Athir wrote in Mosul from reports; d'Ohsson's own footnote explains that Crimea was then called Khazaria.

passages.headline: A 'magician' who dug up a jewel and won the Ilkhan's trust
passages.people: Mongols of the Ilkhanate (Abaqa and Ahmad Tegüder)
passages.gloss: In a footnote from the Syriac chronicler Bar Hebraeus, d'Ohsson tells of Abd al-Rahman, a slave's son who escaped the sack of Baghdad, worked as a carpenter in Mosul, and then claimed spirits had taught him magic. Taken to the Mongol ruler Abaqa, he asked to be brought to the treasure castle of Tala, paced the ground, pointed to a spot, and there a ring with a precious stone was dug up. From then on he was believed to command demons, and under Ahmad he ran the whole kingdom.
passages.quote: il se mit à mesurer le sol de côté et d'autre; puis il indiqua un endroit où l'on devait creuser, et se tint lui-même à quelque distance. En creusant on trouva un anneau, où il y avait une pierre d'un grand prix; on le porta à Abaca. Ce fait ayant confirmé les paroles du prétendu magicien, on ajouta foi à tout ce qu'il disait
passages.translation: he began to measure the ground this way and that; then he pointed to a spot where they should dig, and himself stood some distance away. Digging, they found a ring set with a stone of great value; it was taken to Abaqa. This having confirmed the words of the so-called magician, everything he said was believed
passages.speaker: Constantin d'Ohsson, summarising Bar Hebraeus (footnote)
passages.caution: A hostile anecdote from a Christian chronicler about a Muslim favourite; d'Ohsson calls him a 'so-called' magician.

passages.headline: 'Tartar' is a European blanket name borrowed from one tribe
passages.people: the peoples of high Asia called 'Tartares' by Europeans; the Tatar tribe
passages.gloss: Rémusat opens by defining his subject. The peoples between India, China and Persia, the Sea of Japan, the Caspian and the Arctic are known by the 'vulgar and collective' name of Tartars, a word unknown to many of the peoples it is applied to. It seems to be a corruption of Tatar, the name of one tribe so powerful and famous that it was stretched to cover the others when all of Tartary united under Chinggis Khan's house.
passages.quote: sont connus sous le nom vulgaire et collectif de Tartares. Cette dénomination, entièrement inconnue à plusieurs des nations auxquelles les Européens l'appliquent, paroît être une altération de Tatar, nom particulier d'une tribu qui, par sa puissance et sa célébrité, a mérité qu'on l'étendît aux autres.
passages.translation: are known by the vulgar and collective name of Tartars. This name, entirely unknown to several of the nations to which Europeans apply it, seems to be an alteration of Tatar, the particular name of a tribe which, by its power and fame, earned the extension of its name to the others.
passages.speaker: Jean-Pierre Abel-Rémusat

passages.headline: The 'river Tartar' is imaginary
passages.gloss: Rémusat reviews earlier guesses about the name Tatar and dismisses them. Bergeron's river Tartar (taken from Matthew Paris) is 'entirely imaginary' in the light of better geography; his Syriac 'abandoned' and lost-tribes theory is 'more untenable still'; Fischer's claim that the Chinese called all neighbours Ta-ta is false; and Muslim writers' ancestor 'Tatar, brother of Mongol' is a genealogical invention modelled on the Bible.
passages.quote: Bergeron propose, d'après Matt. Paris, le nom d'une rivière Tartar ou Tatar, sur les bords de laquelle habitoit la tribu en question; mais des notions plus exactes acquises sur la géographie de ces contrées, permettent de regarder la rivière Tartar comme entièrement imaginaire.
passages.translation: Bergeron proposes, after Matthew Paris, the name of a river Tartar or Tatar, on whose banks the tribe in question lived; but more exact knowledge of the geography of these regions allows us to regard the river Tartar as entirely imaginary.
passages.speaker: Jean-Pierre Abel-Rémusat

passages.headline: A Chinese portrait of the Tatars: wool tents, hot stones, tree burials
passages.people: Tha-tche (Tatars, as Chinese writers used the name)
passages.gloss: Rémusat translates a Chinese geography, the Kouang-iu-ki, on the Tha-tche (Tatars): they follow rivers and pastures with their herds, dress in hides, make tents of coarse wool, cure illness by burning the sick part with a heated stone, sing and dance at funerals, and some place the corpse in a tree and burn the bones three years later. Rémusat judges such Chinese portraits 'not lacking in accuracy and fidelity'.
passages.quote: Les Tha-tche suivent les rivières et les lieux fertiles en pâturages … Ils font leurs tentes avec de grosses étoffes de laine. … Lorsqu'ils sont malades, ils font chauffer une pierre, et se brûlent eux-mêmes (la partie malade). Aux funérailles, ils accompagnent le mort en chantant et en dansant. Quelques-uns placent le cadavre sur un arbre, et, trois ans après, ils recueillent les os et les brûlent.
passages.translation: The Tha-tche follow the rivers and the places rich in pasture … They make their tents of coarse woollen cloth. … When they are ill, they heat a stone and burn themselves (on the sick part). At funerals they accompany the dead singing and dancing. Some place the corpse in a tree, and three years later they gather the bones and burn them.
passages.speaker: The Chinese geography Kouang-iu-ki, translated by Abel-Rémusat
passages.caution: A Chinese outsider's summary that lumps northern peoples together; Rémusat warns that Chinese writers confuse nations with similar ways of life.

passages.headline: Russian labels: the Tatars of Tobolsk, Tomsk, the Ob and Krasnoyarsk
passages.gloss: Rémusat explains the Siberian 'Tatars': southern Siberia is full of Turkic nations, partly descended from armies the Mongols brought in the thirteenth century and partly older inhabitants. The Russians who conquered them in the late sixteenth century call most of them simply Tatars, adding the name of the town or district where they live: Tatars of Tobolsk, of Tom, of the Ob, of Krasnoyarsk.
passages.quote: Les Russes qui les ont soumis à la fin du xvi.e siècle, les désignent, pour la plupart, par le nom commun de Tatars, auquel ils ajoutent celui de la ville ou du canton où ils les trouvent fixés. C'est ainsi qu'ils distinguent les Tatars de Tobolsk, de Tom, de l'Obi, de Krasnoyar, ceux du Tchoulim
passages.translation: The Russians, who subdued them at the end of the sixteenth century, call most of them by the common name of Tatars, to which they add the name of the town or district where they find them settled. Thus they distinguish the Tatars of Tobolsk, of the Tom, of the Ob, of Krasnoyarsk, those of the Chulym
passages.speaker: Jean-Pierre Abel-Rémusat

passages.headline: The 'plateau of Tatary' that exists only in their heads
passages.people: Uighurs (a Turkic people of the eastern Tian Shan)
passages.gloss: Some 18th-century writers had argued that all Old World civilisation began on a high plateau in the middle of Tatary. Klaproth, discussing the Uighurs, says their little kingdom never counted for much and gives no support to that idea, and he says bluntly that the plateau exists only in the brains of those who believe in it.
passages.quote: L'hypothèse favorite de ceux qui veulent que toute la civilisation de l'ancien continent soit venue du plateau de la Tatarie, qui n'existe que dans leur cerveau, ne reçoit donc aucun appui de la part des Ouigour, dont le petit royaume ne s'est jamais élevé à une certaine importance politique
passages.translation: The favourite hypothesis of those who would have all the civilisation of the Old World come from the plateau of Tatary, which exists only in their brains, therefore receives no support from the Uighurs, whose little kingdom never rose to any political importance
passages.speaker: Julius Klaproth
passages.caution: Klaproth is arguing against earlier scholars (notably Bailly); this is his judgement, not an observation.

passages.headline: The 'High Carts' people and their felt tents on wheels
passages.people: Gaoche (Kao-tche), a Turkic people Klaproth counts as a branch of the Uighurs
passages.gloss: Retelling Chinese histories, Klaproth explains that one nomadic branch of the Uighurs was called Kao-tche, 'High Carts', probably because the wheels of the carts carrying their felt tents were taller than those of other Turkic tribes. Their main camp lay between the Tula, Orkhon and Selenga rivers.
passages.quote: Elle porta, dans le IIIe siècle de notre ère, le nom de Kao tchhe ou de Chariots élevés, vraisemblablement parceque les roues des chariots, qui portaient ses tentes de feutre, étaient plus hautes que celles des autres peuplades turques.
passages.translation: In the 3rd century of our era it bore the name Kao-tche, or High Carts, probably because the wheels of the carts that carried its felt tents were higher than those of the other Turkic tribes.
passages.speaker: Julius Klaproth, summarising Chinese dynastic histories

passages.headline: Shooting arrows at the thunder
passages.gloss: From Chinese annals Klaproth lists the customs of the High Carts people: bride-price paid in oxen and horses, weddings feasted on curdled mare's milk and roast meat, and a terror of lightning. When a bolt struck they shrieked, shot arrows at the sky and moved camp, then came back the next year to burn a ram in a pit while their sorceresses performed.
passages.quote: Quand la foudre tombait, les Kao tchhe poussaient des cris affreux, tiraient des flèches contre le ciel, quittaient leur camp et le transportaient plus loin. L'année suivante, quand leurs chevaux étaient bien gras, il y revenaient en grand nombre, faisaient une fosse dans laquelle ils brûlaient un bélier : les sorcières exécutaient alors leurs prestiges.
passages.translation: When lightning struck, the Kao-tche let out terrible cries, shot arrows against the sky, left their camp and moved it further off. The next year, when their horses were well fattened, they came back in great numbers and dug a pit in which they burned a ram; the sorceresses then performed their magic.
passages.speaker: Julius Klaproth, translating Chinese dynastic histories
passages.caution: Chinese court historians wrote about northern neighbours with open disdain ('a barbarous and cruel people'), and Klaproth passes this on.

passages.headline: Ask a Kazan Tatar if he is a Tatar
passages.gloss: In a long footnote Klaproth explains that the khanates of Kazan, Astrakhan and Crimea were called Tatar because their rulers descended from Chinggis Khan, even though their subjects were Turks. He adds that a so-called Tatar of Kazan or Astrakhan will deny being a Tatar, calls his language 'Turki', and hears 'Tatar' as an insult meaning brigand.
passages.quote: Qu'on demande, cependant, à un soi-disant Tatar de Kazan ou d'Astrakhan, s'il est un Tatar; il répondra négativement ; il appellera l'idiome qu'il parle turki, et jamais tatari. N'ayant pas oublié que ses ancêtres ont été subjugués par les Mongols ou Tatars, il regarde ce dernier nom comme une injure équivalente au mot brigand.
passages.translation: Yet ask a so-called Tatar of Kazan or Astrakhan whether he is a Tatar: he will say no; he will call the language he speaks Turki, and never Tatari. Not having forgotten that his ancestors were subjugated by the Mongols or Tatars, he regards that name as an insult equal to the word brigand.
passages.speaker: Julius Klaproth (footnote)
passages.caution: Klaproth gives this as general experience, not a dated conversation. Later, many Volga Muslims did come to use 'Tatar' as their own name.

passages.headline: 'The Mongols are the true Tatars'
passages.people: Mongols; Turkic peoples wrongly called Tatars
passages.gloss: Klaproth opens his essay on the Tatars by calling it a common error to mix up Tatars and Turks. In the age of Mongol power, he says, only the Mongols bore the name; only in the last few centuries has it spread to all the eastern Turks and even to unrelated peoples. He asks scholars to drop the habit.
passages.quote: C'est une erreur généralement adoptée que de confondre les Tatars et les Turcs … car dans le tems de la puissance des Mongols, qui sont les véritables Tatars, ce nom ne fut donné qu'à eux. … Je veux tâcher d'éclaircir cette confusion, et j'invite tous les savans à abolir un abus qui occasionera toujours des méprises dans les recherches ethnographiques.
passages.translation: It is a generally accepted error to confuse the Tatars with the Turks … for in the time of the power of the Mongols, who are the true Tatars, that name was given to them alone. … I wish to try to clear up this confusion, and I invite all scholars to abolish an abuse that will always cause mistakes in ethnographic research.
passages.speaker: Julius Klaproth
passages.caution: Modern historians treat the medieval Tatars as a separate steppe confederation that Chinggis Khan destroyed, so Klaproth's simple equation of Mongols and Tatars goes too far.

passages.headline: White, wild and black Tatars
passages.people: Tatar tribes of the early 13th century (Mongols and Onggut)
passages.gloss: Klaproth summarises a Song Chinese general's account of the northern tribes before Chinggis Khan's rise. The 'White Tatars' cut their cheeks and were probably Turks, the 'Wild Tatars' were slaves to them, and the 'Black Tatars' were the tribe into which Temujin, the future Chinggis Khan, was born.
passages.quote: Tatars blancs, ceux-ci n'avaient rien de rebutant dans leur extérieur; cependant ils se faisaient des incisions dans les joues (se tatouaient, comme cela se pratique encore aujourd'hui parmi les Toungouses). … La seconde tribu mentionnée par Meng koung est celle des Tatars sauvages. Ceux-ci étaient stupides et servaient d'esclaves aux premiers. La troisième était celle des Tatars noirs, parmi laquelle Tchinghiz khan naquit
passages.translation: White Tatars: these had nothing repulsive in their appearance; yet they made cuts in their cheeks (tattooed themselves, as the Tungus still do today). … The second tribe mentioned by Meng Hong is that of the Wild Tatars. These were stupid and served as slaves to the first. The third was that of the Black Tatars, among whom Chinggis Khan was born
passages.speaker: Julius Klaproth, summarising the Chinese account he credits to the general Meng Hong (d. 1246)
passages.caution: The Chinese report (the Mengda beilu of 1221) is now usually credited to the envoy Zhao Gong rather than Meng Hong; its labels reflect a Chinese outsider's view.

passages.headline: The 'piebald horde' of Siberia
passages.gloss: A 'piebald horde' was famous in 16th-century Siberia, and some doubted it existed because people thought its members were themselves spotted. Klaproth says the name only described their horses, and quotes the explorer Messerschmidt's diary: in 1721 the governor of Tomsk still claimed the Kistym Tatars had been piebald people who slowly 'degenerated' into white ones.
passages.quote: la horde bigarrée, … dont on a souvent révoqué en doute l'existence, parce qu'on croyait que les hommes qui la composaient étaient eux-mêmes bigarrés, tandis qu'il ne s'agissait que de leurs chevaux. … le woiewode de Tomsk assura: « Qu'on appelait les Tartares de Kistym la horde bigarrée (piegaga ou piestra orda), qu'ils étaient bigarrés, mais qu'ils avaient successivement dégénéré, en devenant blancs.
passages.translation: the piebald horde, … whose existence has often been doubted because people believed that the men who made it up were themselves piebald, whereas it concerned only their horses. … the voevoda of Tomsk asserted 'that the Kistym Tartars were called the piebald horde (pegaya or pestraya orda), that they had been piebald, but had gradually degenerated by becoming white.'
passages.speaker: Julius Klaproth, quoting D. G. Messerschmidt's manuscript journal (10 October 1721) reporting the voevoda of Tomsk
passages.caution: Klaproth himself rejects the spotted-people story as an 'extravagant idea'; the voevoda was repeating local lore.

passages.headline: Alak-tsin, a town where every pot is silver
passages.people: a tribe of the 'Tatar people' in Abu'l-Ghazi's history
passages.gloss: In his chapter on the Tatar people, the Khivan khan and historian Abu'l-Ghazi describes a great town and many villages on a 'Bitter Sea' fed by the Uighur river (Klaproth identifies it as the Yenisei). The people shift their dwellings often, own only dapple-grey horses, mine silver nearby and cook in silver pots. Klaproth gives his own new translation because the old French version garbled the passage.
passages.quote: Sur les bords de cette mer est située une grande ville et beaucoup de villages. Les habitans changent souvent de demeure; ils possèdent de nombreux troupeaux, et une quantité considérable de chevaux. … Tous sont pommelés … Le nom de la ville est Alak-tsin; dans son voisinage il y a des mines d'argent. Chez ce peuple toutes les marmites et les jattes sont d'argent.
passages.translation: On the shores of this sea stands a great town and many villages. The inhabitants often change their dwellings; they own numerous herds and a considerable number of horses. … All are dapple-grey … The name of the town is Alak-tsin; near it there are silver mines. Among this people all the cooking pots and bowls are of silver.
passages.speaker: Abu'l-Ghazi Bahadur Khan (Genealogy of the Turks, 1660s), translated by Julius Klaproth
passages.caution: Abu'l-Ghazi wrote four centuries after the events from Rashid al-Din and oral tradition; the silver pots are hearsay, and Klaproth is unsure where the 'Bitter Sea' was.

passages.headline: Log houses roofed with birch bark
passages.people: Boma, the 'Piebald Horse' people of southern Siberia
passages.gloss: Klaproth translates the Chinese encyclopedist Ma Duanlin on a northern people called the Piebald Horses. They built houses of logs laid one on another like the curb of a well, roofed them with birch bark, slept on hay, did not ride but drank mare's milk and fattened black-maned horses to eat. Klaproth notes that Ostyaks and Samoyeds still build this way and thinks the people were one of those tribes.
passages.quote: Leurs habitations sont faites avec des arbres posés les uns sur les autres, comme on fait les clôtures des puits. Le toit est couvert d'écorce de bouleau. La terre, le bois, l'herbe ou la paille leur servent de tapis, et l'endroit où ils dorment est couvert de foin. D'autres n'ont pas de demeure fixe.
passages.translation: Their dwellings are made of trees laid one upon another, as the curbs of wells are made. The roof is covered with birch bark. Earth, wood, grass or straw serve them as carpets, and the place where they sleep is covered with hay. Others have no fixed dwelling.
passages.speaker: Ma Duanlin (Chinese encyclopedist, c. 1300), translated by Julius Klaproth
passages.caution: The link Klaproth draws between these Piebald Horses and the later 'piebald horde' of Siberia is his own suggestion.

passages.headline: Who dug the old graves and mines of Siberia?
passages.people: the 'Chud', a vague name for unknown ancient peoples
passages.gloss: Russians called the old graves and ancient mine shafts found across Siberia 'Chudic', and some scholars built on the word a theory of a highly civilised Chud people who once worked the Altai mines. Klaproth answers that the adjective simply means 'foreign' or 'unknown', as vague as 'Scythian' or 'barbarian', and links the theory to Bailly's dreams of a civilised plateau of Tatary, which he says does not exist.
passages.quote: Il y a même eu des savans qui croyaient qu'une partie de la Sibérie avait été autrefois habitée par des Tchoudes, que ce peuple était très-civilisé, qu'il exploitait les mines des montagnes d'Altai et autres. Toutes ces hypothèses ne sont fondées que sur l'adjectif tchoudique, dont on se sert en Russie et en Sibérie pour désigner les anciens tombeaux et les galeries de mines
passages.translation: There have even been scholars who believed that part of Siberia had once been inhabited by Chuds, that this people was highly civilised, and that it worked the mines of the Altai and other mountains. All these hypotheses rest only on the adjective 'Chudic', which is used in Russia and Siberia to designate the ancient tombs and mine galleries
passages.speaker: Julius Klaproth

passages.headline: Stone statues left by Cumans and other Turks
passages.people: ancient Turkic peoples of South Siberia; Cumans of the steppe
passages.gloss: Presenting drawings of inscribed stone columns near Abakan on the upper Yenisei, Klaproth notes that they closely resemble the stone statues scattered over the steppe north of the Caucasus. Those, he says, are the only monuments the Cumans and other Turkic peoples left behind there.
passages.quote: D'ailleurs, ces mêmes statues ressemblent beaucoup à celles qu'on voit assez fréquemment dans les vastes plaines situées au nord du Caucase, entre la mer Noire et la mer Caspienne, et qui sont les seuls monumens que les Comans et autres peuples turcs nous ont laissés de leur séjour dans ces contrées.
passages.translation: Moreover, these same statues closely resemble those seen fairly often on the vast plains north of the Caucasus, between the Black Sea and the Caspian, which are the only monuments that the Cumans and other Turkic peoples have left us of their stay in those regions.
passages.speaker: Julius Klaproth (paper read to the Asiatic Society, 2 December 1822)
passages.caution: Klaproth worked from drawings made by others (Müller's artist Lursenius, Strahlenberg, Pallas), not from the stones themselves.

passages.headline: Siberian inscriptions that look European
passages.gloss: Klaproth admits that the letters on the inscribed stones of South Siberia look more European than Asian, with shapes like Greek and Slavonic letters. He warns that this does not mean they were carved after the Russian conquest, since many stand on ancient gravestones. The script was still undeciphered in his day.
passages.quote: En examinant les caractères de ces inscriptions, on ne peut pas se dissimuler qu'ils ont plutôt un air européen qu'asiatique. On y reconnaît facilement plusieurs lettres grecques et esclavonnes. Cependant on ne peut raisonnablement conclure pour cela que ces inscriptions soient postérieures à la conquête de la Sibérie par les Russes
passages.translation: On examining the characters of these inscriptions, one cannot hide from oneself that they look more European than Asian. One easily recognises several Greek and Slavonic letters. Yet one cannot reasonably conclude from this that these inscriptions are later than the Russian conquest of Siberia
passages.speaker: Julius Klaproth
passages.caution: These are the Yenisei runic inscriptions, later shown (1893) to be in an Old Turkic script; the likeness to Greek letters is only in shape.

passages.headline: A Qing view of Russia: the White Khan took Kazan and Tobolsk
passages.people: Russians as seen by the Qing court; Kazan and Siberian khanates
passages.gloss: Klaproth translates the entry on Russia from the official Manchu imperial geography of China. It calls the Tsar the 'Tsagan khan' (White Khan, a Mongol title), places his residence at Moscow, and says the Russians seized the lands of Kazan and Tobolsk about 160 years earlier. It shows how the fall of the Tatar khanates looked from Beijing.
passages.quote: Le roi des Oros est le Tsakhan khan; il réside dans une ville appelée Moskowa, qui n'est pas trop éloignée de la mer du nord-ouest. … Leurs khans ont régné pendant vingt-trois générations, durant une période de plus de trois cent cinquante ans. Il y a cent soixante ans qu'ils s'emparèrent des territoires de Kazan et de Tobolsk.
passages.translation: The king of the Oros [Russians] is the Tsagan khan; he lives in a town called Moscow, not very far from the north-western sea. … Their khans have reigned for twenty-three generations, over a period of more than three hundred and fifty years. It is a hundred and sixty years since they seized the territories of Kazan and Tobolsk.
passages.speaker: Official Qing (Manchu) geography of the empire, translated by Julius Klaproth
passages.caution: Tobolsk itself was a Russian foundation of 1587 beside the old Tatar capital Sibir; the Chinese text uses it as the name of the region.

passages.headline: Nomads of Bishbalik in felt tents
passages.gloss: Klaproth translates the Ming dynasty's geography on the land of Bishbalik, north of the Tian Shan. It says the people had no houses, lived in felt tents, kept cattle, sheep, camels and horses, farmed little, lived on meat and milk, and spoke a Turkic dialect called Uighur. The same book notes that under the Mongols there had been a town of Bishbalik with a viceroy and military farming colonies.
passages.quote: Les habitans sont nomades, n'ont pas de maisons, et vivent sous des tentes de feutre. Ils s'occupent presqu'exclusivement de l'entretien des bœufs, des moutons, des chameaux et des chevaux. Ils n'ont que peu d'agriculture, et se nourrissent de la chair et du laitage de leurs troupeaux, qui leur fournissent l'habillement nécessaire. Leur langue est un dialecte du turc
passages.translation: The inhabitants are nomads, have no houses, and live under felt tents. They occupy themselves almost entirely with keeping oxen, sheep, camels and horses. They have little agriculture and live on the meat and milk of their herds, which also supply the clothing they need. Their language is a dialect of Turkish
passages.speaker: Ming dynasty imperial geography, translated by Julius Klaproth
passages.caution: This scan is volume 2 (1826) despite its IA label; the OCR is rough.

passages.headline: Flood geology and the 'Plateau of Tartary'
passages.gloss: Humboldt explains how a geographic guess became a myth. If the highest lands had been the first to emerge from the waters, they must also have received the first seeds of civilisation; 'diluvial' geology built on ancient myths encouraged this, and so the vaguely named Plateau of Tartary gained a 'moral interest'. Travel, measurement and the study of Asian languages, he says, have corrected these exaggerations.
passages.quote: Les hautes régions qui les premières avaient été abandonnées par les eaux, devaient aussi avoir reçu les premières des germes de civilisation. Des systèmes de géologie diluvienne, fondés sur des mythes anciens et sur des traditions locales, favorisaient ces aperçus. … donnait à ce grand massif, à ce plateau continu, vaguement appelé Plateau de la Tartarie, un intérêt moral et une importance particulière.
passages.translation: The high regions that had been the first to be left by the waters must also have been the first to receive the seeds of civilisation. Systems of diluvial geology, founded on ancient myths and local traditions, favoured these views. … gave this great massif, this continuous plateau vaguely called the Plateau of Tartary, a moral interest and a special importance.
passages.speaker: Alexander von Humboldt

passages.headline: The ancient people who 'taught us everything except their name'
passages.people: an imagined lost people of Tartary
passages.gloss: Humboldt says the high plains of Tartary are no longer seen as the cradle of human civilisation and of the arts and sciences. He borrows d'Alembert's joke about the vanished ancient people imagined by Bailly: they taught us everything except their name and the fact that they existed. Solid research, he adds, has shown that learning reached the lands between the Pamirs, China and the Altai late.
passages.quote: Ces plaines élevées de la Tartarie ne sont plus regardées comme le berceau de la civilisation humaine, le site primitif des sciences et des arts. Il a disparu, ce peuple ancien qui, selon une expression heureuse de d'Alembert, « Nous a tout appris, excepté son nom et son existence. »
passages.translation: These high plains of Tartary are no longer regarded as the cradle of human civilisation, the original home of the sciences and arts. It has vanished, that ancient people which, in d'Alembert's happy phrase, 'taught us everything except its name and its existence.'
passages.speaker: Alexander von Humboldt, quoting Jean d'Alembert's letter to Voltaire

passages.headline: 'The high plains of Tartary' are not the centre of Asia
passages.gloss: Explaining why he calls his book 'Central Asia', Humboldt warns that terms like 'Central Asia' and 'High Asia' are used loosely. Travellers from India who cross the Himalaya to the sacred lakes of Tibet, on the plateau once called 'the high plains of Tartary', are in fact as far from the true centre of Asia as a Siberian at Tobolsk.
passages.quote: Lorsque les voyageurs de l'Inde franchissent la chaîne de l'Himalaya … et arrivent aux deux Lacs Sacrés, sur le plateau que l'on a cru devoir nommer jadis « les hautes plaines de la Tartarie, » ils marchent sans doute vers l'Asie centrale, mais ils se trouvent encore … aussi éloignés du centre de l'Asie que le sont des habitants de la Sibérie sous le parallèle de Tobolsk
passages.translation: When travellers from India cross the Himalaya … and reach the two Sacred Lakes, on the plateau that people once saw fit to call 'the high plains of Tartary', they are no doubt heading towards Central Asia, but they are still … as far from the centre of Asia as are the inhabitants of Siberia on the parallel of Tobolsk
passages.speaker: Alexander von Humboldt

passages.headline: Marco Polo: all who meet a khan's funeral are killed
passages.people: Mongol grand khans (the house of Chinggis)
passages.gloss: Discussing where Marco Polo's 'Altai' was, Humboldt quotes Polo's story that Chinggis Khan and all his descendants were carried back to be buried in the Altai, however far away they died, and that everyone met on the road was killed to serve the dead khan in the next life. In a note he compares this to Herodotus' account of Scythian royal funerals some 1,700 years earlier.
passages.quote: « Tchinghiz lui-même et tous ses descendants, dit Marco-Polo, ont leur sépulture dans l'Altai. On les porte vers ce lieu, et fussent-ils morts à quarante journées de distance. Tous ceux qui se trouvent sur la route au passage du corps des grands-khans, sont impitoyablement mis à mort pour servir leur souverain et maître dans l'autre vie. »
passages.translation: 'Chinggis himself and all his descendants,' says Marco Polo, 'are buried in the Altai. They are carried there even if they died forty days' journey away. All those who happen to be on the road as the body of the great khans passes are mercilessly put to death, to serve their sovereign and master in the other life.'
passages.speaker: Marco Polo, quoted in French by Alexander von Humboldt
passages.caution: Polo was repeating what he was told; Humboldt uses the passage to locate Polo's 'Altai' (the mountains of northern Mongolia), not to vouch for the killings.

passages.headline: Sheep sacrificed to a 'volcano' in Lake Alakol
passages.people: caravan travellers between Semipalatinsk and Yarkand (Tatar informants)
passages.gloss: At Orenburg in 1829 Humboldt copied a caravan report from the papers of General Gens. It described a high mountain rising like an island in Lake Alakol that had once spewed fire and still caused storms that troubled caravans, so travellers sacrificed sheep to it as they passed. Humboldt believed the report came from a Tatar informant.
passages.quote: nous vîmes une très-haute montagne qui a autrefois vomi du feu. Présentement encore, ce mont qui s'élève dans le lac comme une petite île, occasionne des tempêtes violentes qui incommodent les caravanes : c'est pourquoi on sacrifie en passant quelques moutons à cet ancien volcan.
passages.translation: we saw a very high mountain that once spewed fire. Even now this mountain, which rises in the lake like a small island, causes violent storms that trouble the caravans: that is why, in passing, people sacrifice a few sheep to this old volcano.
passages.speaker: an anonymous caravan itinerary (Semipalatinsk to Yarkand) from General Gens's papers, quoted by Alexander von Humboldt
passages.caution: A later informant, the mullah Sayfulla, knew nothing of a fire mountain or of sacrifices to it, and said the offerings were made at a hot spring instead; Humboldt prints both versions.

passages.headline: The storm cave of Oufbe
passages.gloss: An old Tatar mullah of Semipalatinsk, who had travelled to Kulja, told the Kazan orientalist Kazim-Beg of a huge cave on the caravan road past Lake Alakol, called Oufbe in Tatar. It blew out storms lasting two days, strong enough to fling things into the lake; nobody dared go in, and only God knew how deep it was. Caravans waited a week for the winds to pass.
passages.quote: est une grande caverne souterraine; elle porte le nom tatar d'Oufbé. Quelquefois, et principalement en hiver, elle produit des tempêtes violentes qui durent pendant deux jours. L'entrée de cette caverne ressemble à celle d'un vaste caveau, et personne n'ose y entrer, ni même y regarder de bien près. Sa profondeur est inconnue à tout le monde, à l'exception de Dieu (Allah).
passages.translation: there is a great underground cave; it bears the Tatar name Oufbe. Sometimes, and chiefly in winter, it produces violent storms that last for two days. The entrance of this cave looks like a vast vault, and no one dares to enter it or even look at it closely. Its depth is unknown to everyone except God (Allah).
passages.speaker: Mullah Sayfulla Kazi of Semipalatinsk, reported in a letter by Mirza Kazem-Beg, translated by Alexander von Humboldt
passages.caution: Third-hand: Humboldt prints Kazem-Beg's English letter in French, and Kazem-Beg himself only guessed that fire had once come out of the cave. The pass is known for violent winds.

passages.headline: Nobody yet knew where Karakorum lay
passages.gloss: In a footnote Humboldt lists the rival guesses for the ruins of Karakorum, Mongke Khan's capital: Klaproth put it at one set of coordinates, Abel-Remusat at one of two named ruins, and d'Anville had it two degrees too far south-east. He adds that Wilhelm Schott thought the name meant 'black town' or 'black residence'. The site was still unidentified in his day.
passages.quote: Klaproth place les ruines de Kara-Khorum lat. 46° 41', long. 100° 24'. … Abel-Rémusat croit Kara-Khorum identique ou avec Talarho-kara-balgasoun (long. 100° 44', lat. 47° 32') ou avec Baisiri-bouritou (long. 100° 36', lat. 48° 24'). … M. Schott, auquel on doit d'ingénieuses et savantes recherches sur les langues tartares, pense que Kara-Koroum signifie ville ou résidence noire.
passages.translation: Klaproth places the ruins of Karakorum at latitude 46° 41', longitude 100° 24'. … Abel-Remusat believes Karakorum identical either with Talarho-kara-balgasun (long. 100° 44', lat. 47° 32') or with Baisiri-buritu (long. 100° 36', lat. 48° 24'). … Mr Schott, to whom we owe ingenious and learned research on the Tartar languages, thinks that Karakorum means black town or black residence.
passages.speaker: Alexander von Humboldt (footnote)
passages.caution: Longitudes are reckoned from Paris. The ruins of Karakorum were identified beside Erdene Zuu monastery only in 1889.

passages.headline: Kuznetsk, a Russian town among 'blacksmith Tatars'
passages.people: Kuznetsk Tatars (Turkic iron-smiths of the Tom valley)
passages.gloss: Describing the Kuznetsk mountains, Humboldt notes that the Russian town of Kuznetsk on the Tom was founded in 1618 in the midst of Tartars, or Turks, who worked iron. A footnote explains the name: the Russians called them 'Kuznetsk Tatars', from kuznets, blacksmith. He adds that the first Russian foundations of Tobolsk, near the old Tatar capital of Isker or Sibir, and of Tiumen were only some thirty years older.
passages.quote: la ville de Kousnetsk (au milieu de Tartares ou Turcs forgerons en fer) fut fondée en 1618, c'est-à-dire déjà 31 ou 32 ans après les premières fondations russes de Tobolsk (près de l'ancien Isker et Sibir) et de Tiumen.
passages.translation: the town of Kuznetsk (in the midst of Tartars, or Turks who were iron-smiths) was founded in 1618, that is, already 31 or 32 years after the first Russian foundations of Tobolsk (near the old Isker and Sibir) and of Tiumen.
passages.speaker: Alexander von Humboldt

passages.headline: Ablai-kit: a Kalmyk monastery with a printing press
passages.when: mid-17th century; ruins seen by Russians in the 18th century
passages.gloss: Near the upper Irtysh stand the ruins of Ablai-kit, a Buddhist monastery that the Kalmyk prince Ablai founded in the mid-17th century, with a Mongol-Tibetan library and a woodblock press. Manuscripts from it were sent to Paris under Peter the Great. Humboldt notes that half-torn leaves of Tibetan books could still be found scattered in the steppe grass around the ruins.
passages.quote: qu'un prince kalmuk Ablai avait fondé au milieu du dix-septième siècle et enrichi d'une bibliothèque mongolo-tubétaine comme d'une imprimerie xylographique. … Encore aujourd'hui on trouve éparses dans l'herbe de la steppe, autour des ruines d'Ablaikit, des feuilles à demi-déchirées de livres tubétains.
passages.translation: which a Kalmyk prince, Ablai, had founded in the middle of the 17th century and endowed with a Mongol-Tibetan library and a woodblock printing press. … Even today one finds half-torn leaves of Tibetan books scattered in the steppe grass around the ruins of Ablai-kit.
passages.speaker: Alexander von Humboldt
passages.caution: Humboldt passed nearby in 1829 but does not say he visited Ablai-kit itself; the detail about the leaves comes from reports.

passages.headline: The 'palaces' of Semipalatinsk were lama cells
passages.gloss: The town of Semipalatinsk ('seven palaces') took its name from old ruins. Humboldt, who saw them, thought they were a Buddhist establishment like Ablai-kit, whose painted cells had housed lamas. He compares the little roadside shrines of the Volga Kalmyks near Sarepta: cages on tall poles holding an idol and a few religious books.
passages.quote: Il est probable que les Palates dont j'ai vu les ruines à Semipolatinsk, étaient un établissement tout semblable dont les cellules, jadis couvertes de peintures, servaient d'habitation à des lamas. Dans la steppe des Kalmuks du Wolga, voisine de Sarepta, colonie des frères Moraves, on trouve en plein champ des cages surmontées de poteaux élevés et renfermant, près d'une idole du culte bouddhistique, une petite collection de livres religieux.
passages.translation: It is probable that the Palaty whose ruins I saw at Semipalatinsk were a very similar establishment, whose cells, once covered with paintings, served as dwellings for lamas. In the steppe of the Volga Kalmyks, near Sarepta, the Moravian Brethren's colony, one finds out in the open fields cages topped by tall posts and containing, beside a Buddhist idol, a small collection of religious books.
passages.speaker: Alexander von Humboldt (footnote)
passages.caution: Humboldt saw the Semipalatinsk ruins; his identification of them as a lama monastery is his inference.

passages.headline: Kazan in 1761: well-built wooden houses and honoured Tatars
passages.gloss: Chappe spent several days in Kazan fixing its position by the stars. He found a town that kept a remnant of its former wealth though its trade had nearly died, with houses mostly of wood but very well built. Tatars made up a large part of the population and, he says, far from being persecuted, were treated with great respect and were loyal to the empress.
passages.quote: Elle conserve encore un reste de son ancienne opulence, quoique son commerce soit presqu'éteint. Les maisons, quoiqu'en bois pour la plupart, y sont très bien bâties. … Les Tartares forment une grande partie des Habitants de Cazan; mais loin d'y être persécutés, ils y sont traités avec les plus grands égards; aussi sont-ils très attachés à leur Souverain. Ils ont conservé l'innocence de leurs mœurs, leur probité, leur bonne foi
passages.translation: It still keeps a remnant of its former opulence, although its trade is almost extinct. The houses, though mostly of wood, are very well built. … The Tartars make up a large part of the inhabitants of Kazan; but far from being persecuted there, they are treated with the greatest regard; and so they are very attached to their sovereign. They have kept the innocence of their manners, their probity, their good faith
passages.speaker: Jean Chappe d'Auteroche
passages.caution: Chappe stayed only a few days; his praise of Tatar honesty is a traveller's general impression.

passages.headline: Pipes, Chinese tobacco and watermelon with Kazan's Tatar governor
passages.people: a Tatar prince serving as governor of Kazan
passages.gloss: On arriving at Kazan Chappe was received by the governor, a Tatar prince. They sat round a table covered with a fine carpet; four long pipes and a porcelain jar of Chinese tobacco were set out, then local liqueurs, preserves, fruit and a watermelon so delicious that Chappe ate nothing else and took home seeds, which failed to grow in France.
passages.quote: J'arrivai à Cazan le premier Octobre. Un Prince Tartare en étoit le Gouverneur … nous nous assimes autour d'une table couverte d'un beau tapis : on y plaça quatre grandes pipes & un vase de porcelaine rempli de tabac de la Chine : je fumai quelques instants. On servit aussi-tôt des liqueurs du pays; des confitures, avec des fruits & un melon d'eau
passages.translation: I arrived at Kazan on the first of October. A Tartar prince was its governor … we sat down round a table covered with a fine carpet: four large pipes were placed on it and a porcelain jar full of Chinese tobacco; I smoked for a few moments. Then local liqueurs were served, preserves with fruit, and a watermelon
passages.speaker: Jean Chappe d'Auteroche

passages.headline: How Siberia's Tatar khanate fell
passages.people: Siberian Tatars under Khan Kuchum; Yermak's Cossacks
passages.gloss: Opening his description of Tobolsk, Chappe tells how Siberia, ruled by a Tatar prince of the Uzbek line, was conquered by the Cossack brigand Yermak. Helped by the Stroganov family, Yermak sailed down the Tagil and Tura rivers, took Tiumen, surprised 'Tobolsk', captured the twelve-year-old son of Khan Kuchum and sent him to Moscow, buying the tsar's pardon with the gift of Siberia.
passages.quote: Elle étoit gouvernée par un Prince Tartare de la Famille des Usbeks. … Il s'embarqua avec sa troupe sur la riviere Tagil, qu'il descendit jusqu'à son embouchure dans la riviere Tura. Continuant ensuite sa route sur cette derniere riviere, il s'empara de la Ville de Tumen, surprit celle de Tobolsk, fit prisonnier le fils du Kan Zutchuin, âgé de douze ans, & l'envoya à Moscou
passages.translation: It was ruled by a Tartar prince of the family of the Uzbeks. … He embarked with his band on the river Tagil, which he descended to its mouth in the river Tura. Continuing down that river, he seized the town of Tiumen, surprised that of Tobolsk, took prisoner the twelve-year-old son of Khan Kuchum, and sent him to Moscow
passages.speaker: Jean Chappe d'Auteroche
passages.caution: Second-hand history with a slip: Yermak took the Tatar capital Isker (Sibir) in 1582, and Tobolsk was built nearby by the Russians only in 1587. 'Zutchuin' is Khan Kuchum.

passages.headline: Welcomed at the Tatar village of Birna
passages.gloss: After a near-fatal sledge accident, Chappe reached Birna, a Tatar village. Villagers came out a verst to meet him with signs of friendship, led him to their headman (chosen, he says, for his merit without any election) and gave him a meal of honey, butter and vegetables. Their houses were as clean as Siberian ones were dirty; they lived much like their neighbours except that they were Muslims.
passages.quote: J'arrivai enfin à Birna; ce Village est habité par des Tartares. Plusieurs étoient venus au-devant de moi à un werst de leur Village … Ils m'avoient fait préparer une espece de dîner qui consistoit dans du miel, du beurre & quelques légumes. Leurs maisons sont aussi propres que celles des Sibériens le sont peu. Au reste, ils vivent à-peu-près de la même façon, excepté qu'ils sont Mahométans.
passages.translation: At last I reached Birna; this village is inhabited by Tartars. Several had come out a verst from their village to meet me … They had prepared a kind of dinner for me consisting of honey, butter and a few vegetables. Their houses are as clean as those of the Siberians are not. For the rest, they live in much the same way, except that they are Mahometans.
passages.speaker: Jean Chappe d'Auteroche

passages.headline: Tatar women's sugar-loaf caps, and equal marriages
passages.gloss: Chappe describes the dress of the Tatars of Birna: the men in wool tunics, long robes and boots with shaved heads, the women in shorter robes and tall sugar-loaf caps sewn with copper coins and glass beads. Wives shared most of their husbands' work and were treated gently, with 'perfect equality' between them, which he contrasts with the seclusion of Siberian Russian wives.
passages.quote: L'habillement des femmes Tartares differe peu de celui des hommes : il est plus court, & la ceinture est par-dessus la robe. Leur coeffure est un bonnet, souvent fait en pain de sucre; il est couvert de copecks & de grains de verre … Elles partagent la plupart des travaux de leurs maris : ceux-ci les traitent avec douceur : une parfaite égalité regne entre eux.
passages.translation: The dress of Tartar women differs little from that of the men: it is shorter, and the belt is worn over the robe. Their headdress is a cap, often shaped like a sugar loaf, covered with kopecks and glass beads … They share most of their husbands' work; the husbands treat them gently; a perfect equality reigns between them.
passages.speaker: Jean Chappe d'Auteroche
passages.caution: A one-day visit; the plate 'Tartares des environs de Kazan' in the same volume illustrates the dress.

passages.headline: Steppe nomads who flee from smallpox
passages.people: 'wandering Tartars' of the steppe south of Siberia
passages.gloss: Chappe was told by several people that the nomadic 'Tartars' south of Siberia hardly knew smallpox and dreaded it so much that a sick person was left alone in a tent with food while the camp moved elsewhere. Those who came into Siberia caught it at once, and many died. Chappe says he checked the story as best he could but could only rest it on trustworthy witnesses.
passages.quote: Différentes personnes m'ont attesté le fait singulier, que les Tartares vagabonds situés au Midi de la Sibérie ne connoissent presque point cette cruelle maladie. Ils en ont une si grande horreur, que si quelqu'un en est attaqué, on le laisse seul dans une tente, avec des provisions de vivres, & l'on va camper ailleurs. Les Tartares qui pénetrent dans la Sibérie en sont attaqués presque aussi-tôt
passages.translation: Various people assured me of the singular fact that the wandering Tartars south of Siberia hardly know this cruel disease at all. They have such a horror of it that if someone catches it, he is left alone in a tent with provisions, and the others go and camp elsewhere. The Tartars who come into Siberia are attacked by it almost at once
passages.speaker: Jean Chappe d'Auteroche
passages.caution: Hearsay, as Chappe admits. 'Tartares vagabonds' probably means Kazakh and other nomads of the steppe frontier.

passages.headline: Nomads who asked to be fired on
passages.gloss: Back in Paris Chappe heard from the Chevalier de Saint-Pierre that a large band of Tartars once approached a Russian fort on the Siberian lines. Warned that they would be fired on unless they withdrew, they held a council and sent word asking the commander to fire. After the first cannonade killed several of them they held another council and asked again, and only left after the third.
passages.quote: Un gros détachement de ces Tartares s'approcha, il y a quelques années, des lignes de Sibérie; le Commandant d'un des Forts Russes les ayant apperçus, & ignorant l'intention de ces Tartares en troupe, leur fit savoir qu'il feroit faire feu sur eux, s'ils ne se retiroient. Ces Tartares s'assemblent, & après avoir tenu conseil, ils envoient prier le Commandant d'ordonner qu'on fit feu; on le fit.
passages.translation: A large detachment of these Tartars approached the Siberian lines a few years ago; the commander of one of the Russian forts saw them and, not knowing what this band of Tartars intended, let them know he would open fire on them if they did not withdraw. The Tartars gathered, held a council, and sent to ask the commander to order the firing; it was done.
passages.speaker: Jean Chappe d'Auteroche, retelling a story from the Chevalier de Saint-Pierre
passages.caution: A second-hand anecdote told in Paris, used by Chappe to argue that some nomads did not know firearms; nothing confirms it.

passages.headline: Hunting the vegetable lamb around Kazan
passages.gloss: Chappe searched everywhere around Kazan for the famous Borametz, the 'vegetable lamb' described in Abbe Lambert's natural history: a plant shaped like a lamb, with fleece, a little blood and flesh, that grazed the grass around it and died when the grass dried. He could not find it, nobody in Kazan knew it, and he calls it a ridiculous fable.
passages.quote: Je cherchai par-tout dans les environs de Cazan la fameuse plante nommée Borametz, dont parle M. l'Abbé Lambert dans son Histoire Civile & Naturelle. … cette plante ressemble à un agneau, elle en a toutes les parties avec une toison délicate, dont les femmes se servent pour couvrir leur tête. … Malgré mes soins je ne pus jamais me procurer cette plante inconnue à Cazan.
passages.translation: I searched everywhere around Kazan for the famous plant called Borametz, of which the Abbe Lambert speaks in his Civil and Natural History. … this plant resembles a lamb; it has all its parts, with a delicate fleece which women use to cover their heads. … Despite all my efforts I could never obtain this plant, which is unknown at Kazan.
passages.speaker: Jean Chappe d'Auteroche, summarising the Abbe Claude-Francois Lambert
passages.caution: Chappe tested the legend and rejected it. He adds that a plant shown under that name at the King's Garden in Paris, which some authors class among the mosses, has nothing to do with the fable.

passages.headline: A Kalmyk idol that gave communion to the sick
passages.gloss: Chappe brought back Kalmyk Buddhist idols from Tobolsk and had their meaning explained by Kalmyk envoys and later by a Kalmyk lama in St Petersburg. Of the copper figure Otschirbany he writes that the god was sent from heaven to fight demons who had stopped the sun and moon, and that a channel ran from its mouth to its anus so that lamas could drop a sacred pill through it into a sick person's mouth.
passages.quote: Ce Dieu est du troisieme ordre. Il fut envoyé du Ciel pour combattre de mauvais génies qui avoient arrêté le Soleil & la Lune. … La bouche de cette Divinité communique avec l'anus par un canal perpendiculaire. Les Lamas ou Prêtres en font usage pour donner la communion aux malades.
passages.translation: This god is of the third order. He was sent from heaven to fight evil spirits that had stopped the Sun and Moon. … The mouth of this divinity connects with the anus by a vertical channel. The lamas or priests use it to give communion to the sick.
passages.speaker: Jean Chappe d'Auteroche, from explanations given by Kalmyk envoys at Tobolsk
passages.caution: Otschirbany is Vajrapani. Chappe owned and described the figure, but the ritual comes through interpreters and may be misunderstood.

passages.headline: Kalmyks and Mongols as heirs of Chinggis Khan's Tartars
passages.gloss: After recounting how China destroyed the Zunghar Kalmyk state in 1757, Chappe says the other Kalmyk branches kept the courage they had under Chinggis Khan, whose conquests were made with these peoples, and that the Mongols between China and Siberia descend from the same Tartars. Here 'Tartar' means the Mongol-speaking peoples as a whole.
passages.quote: Plusieurs autres branches des Calmouks habitent encore dans cette partie de l'Asie. Ils ont conservé le courage & la bravoure qu'ils avoient du temps de Gengis-kan & de ses Successeurs. C'est avec ces Peuples que ces Princes firent tant de conquêtes & donnerent la loi à l'Asie. Les Mongales situés entre la Chine & la Sibérie descendent des mêmes Tartares, & ils ne sont pas moins courageux.
passages.translation: Several other branches of the Kalmyks still live in that part of Asia. They have kept the courage and bravery they had in the time of Chinggis Khan and his successors. It was with these peoples that those princes made so many conquests and laid down the law to Asia. The Mongols situated between China and Siberia descend from the same Tartars and are no less courageous.
passages.speaker: Jean Chappe d'Auteroche
passages.caution: Chappe learned of the Zunghar collapse from Kalmyk refugees and Russians in Siberia; his view of the Kalmyks as Chinggis Khan's own army is a loose generalisation.

passages.headline: Votyaks are not Tartars
passages.gloss: Stopping at the Votyak hamlet of Sowialova, Chappe notes that some authors had counted the Votyaks among the Tartars, but that he could see no connection between the two peoples. It is a small example of a traveller correcting the catch-all use of the word.
passages.quote: Sowialova est un Hameau habité par des Wotiakes. La singularité de ce Peuple & de leur habillement me détermina à m'y arrêter une partie de la journée. Quelques Auteurs ont placé les Wotiakes au nombre des Tartares, mais je n'ai reconnu aucun rapport entre ces deux Nations.
passages.translation: Sowialova is a hamlet inhabited by Votyaks. The peculiarity of this people and of their dress made me decide to stop there part of the day. Some authors have placed the Votyaks among the Tartars, but I recognised no relation between these two nations.
passages.speaker: Jean Chappe d'Auteroche

passages.headline: Clean houses and full granaries: Tatar farmers
passages.people: Muslim Tatars of the Urals and Volga region
passages.gloss: In a short 'Note on the Tartars' written as he crossed from Yekaterinburg towards Kazan, Lesseps says the cleanliness inside Tatar houses astonished him after a year among Kamchadals and Koryaks. These Tatars, he stresses, were settled farmers, rich in grain and cattle, and Muslims.
passages.quote: Je dirai seulement de ces derniers, que la propreté de l'intérieur de leurs habitations m'a étonné, sans doute parce que je m'étois un peu trop familiarisé avec le défaut contraire parmi les Kamtschadales, Koriaques, &c. Ces Tartares sont sédentaires, agriculteurs & riches en blés & en bestiaux; ils professent la religion Mahométane.
passages.translation: I will only say of the latter that the cleanliness of the inside of their dwellings astonished me, no doubt because I had grown rather too used to the opposite fault among the Kamchadals, Koryaks and so on. These Tartars are settled, farmers, and rich in grain and cattle; they profess the Mahometan religion.
passages.speaker: Jean-Baptiste Barthelemy de Lesseps

passages.headline: Tobolsk after the great fire
passages.gloss: Lesseps reached Tobolsk, the Siberian capital between the Irtysh and the Tobol, soon after a fire had burned most of it. The lower town had only wooden houses, which went first; the upper town on its hilltop had several fine stone buildings, but the fire reached them too and left only walls. On the next page he describes silent townspeople already rebuilding houses and shops in stone.
passages.quote: Cette capitale, située entre ces deux fleuves, doit avoir été une des plus belles villes de Sibérie, mais elle venoit d'être la proie d'un incendie qui en avoit réduit en cendres la plus grande partie. Précédemment elle étoit divisée en deux, la ville basse & la ville haute: l'une bâtie sur la plate-forme d'une montagne, présentoit plusieurs beaux édifices en pierre; l'autre n'avoit que des maisons de bois
passages.translation: This capital, situated between these two rivers, must have been one of the finest towns in Siberia, but it had just fallen prey to a fire that had reduced most of it to ashes. Formerly it was divided in two, the lower town and the upper town: the one, built on the flat top of a hill, had several fine stone buildings; the other had only wooden houses
passages.speaker: Jean-Baptiste Barthelemy de Lesseps

passages.headline: A Yakut prince's winter house of timber and earth
passages.gloss: A Yakut prince at Amga, owner of two thousand horses, showed Lesseps his 'yurt'. Its walls were upright logs set side by side and plastered with clay, leaning inwards to carry a low-pitched roof. One half housed the family in bunk-like compartments, the other was a byre for cows and calves, with a round wooden hearth in the middle.
passages.quote: Des poutres posées debout les unes à côté des autres, & recouvertes de terre grasse, en forment les murs, qui ne s'élèvent point perpendiculairement comme les nôtres. Plus rapprochés vers le haut, ils supportent un toit dont l'inclinaison est peu rapide … De l'autre côté de la yourte demeurent les bêtes, les vaches, les veaux, c'est tout simplement une étable.
passages.translation: Beams set upright side by side and covered with clay form its walls, which do not rise vertically like ours. Drawing closer together towards the top, they carry a roof with a gentle slope … On the other side of the yurt live the animals, the cows and calves; it is quite simply a byre.
passages.speaker: Jean-Baptiste Barthelemy de Lesseps
passages.caution: The Yakuts are a Turkic people, but Lesseps does not call them Tartars.

passages.headline: Everyone who enters churns the kumiss
passages.gloss: In a corner of the Yakut house hung a leather bag of mare's milk. Everyone who came in, above all the women, stirred it with a plunger for a few minutes before doing anything else, which produced the sour but pleasant drink Lesseps calls koumouiss. Left to ferment longer, it became strongly intoxicating.
passages.quote: Dans un coin de la yourte est à demeure un paquet de cuir; chaque jour on y verse du lait de jument qu'on agite avec un bâton pareil à celui qui sert à battre le beurre. Tous ceux qui entrent, les femmes sur-tout, ne manquent jamais, avant de vaquer à d'autres travaux, de battre ce lait pendant quelques minutes; de-là provient cette boisson aigrelette & cependant agréable, qu'on nomme koumouiss.
passages.translation: In a corner of the yurt a leather bag is kept permanently; every day mare's milk is poured into it and stirred with a stick like the one used to churn butter. Everyone who comes in, the women above all, never fails to churn this milk for a few minutes before turning to other work; from this comes the sourish yet pleasant drink called kumiss.
passages.speaker: Jean-Baptiste Barthelemy de Lesseps

passages.headline: A Yakut prince buried with his favourite horses
passages.gloss: Lesseps had been shown old Yakut coffins hung in trees, but says the Yakuts now buried their dead like Christians. At a prince's funeral his favourite horse and the best of his herd, richly harnessed, were tied to two carved or painted posts by the grave and killed over his body. Their hides and heads were then hung in nearby trees as a 'mausoleum', and the mourners roasted and ate the two horses on the spot.
passages.quote: Si c'est un prince, on le revêt de ses plus riches habits & de ses plus belles armes. … Le cheval favori du prince & le meilleur du haras, tous deux richement harnachés … marchent à côté du convoi. Arrivés au lieu de la sépulture, ils sont attachés à deux poteaux plantés auprès de la fosse. Pendant qu'on inhume leur maître, on les égorge sur son corps,
passages.translation: If it is a prince, he is dressed in his richest clothes and finest weapons. … The prince's favourite horse and the best of his herd, both richly harnessed … walk beside the procession. On reaching the burial place they are tied to two posts planted by the grave. While their master is buried, they are slaughtered over his body,
passages.speaker: Jean-Baptiste Barthelemy de Lesseps
passages.caution: Lesseps describes the rite from what his Yakut host and others told him, not from a funeral he attended.

passages.headline: Yakuts who look and talk like Tartars
passages.gloss: Lesseps notes that the Yakuts are strong and tall, that their features resemble those of the Tartars, and that people say the two languages are closely related. He only vouches for the fact that Yakuts speak very briefly and do not run their words together.
passages.quote: Les Yakoutes sont robustes & généralement grands; l'ensemble de leurs traits a quelque analogie avec la figure des Tartares; on dit même que les deux idiomes se rapportent beaucoup.
