Tout ce que je puis affirmer, c'est que les Yakoutes ont la parole extrêmement brève, & qu'ils ne lient point leurs mots.
passages.translation: The Yakuts are robust and generally tall; their features as a whole bear some likeness to those of the Tartars; it is even said that the two languages are closely related. All I can affirm is that the Yakuts speak extremely briefly and do not run their words together.
passages.speaker: Jean-Baptiste Barthelemy de Lesseps
passages.caution: The language link was hearsay to Lesseps; Yakut (Sakha) is indeed a Turkic language, related to Tatar.

passages.headline: 'Manchu Tartars' who conquered China
passages.gloss: At Irkutsk, explaining the history of Russia's trade with China, Lesseps dates its beginnings to the invasion of the 'Manchu Tartars', who ravaged northern China for a long time and finally conquered the whole empire. Here 'Tartar' plainly means the Manchus.
passages.quote: Les relations primitives datent du milieu du dernier siècle, vers l'époque de l'invasion des Tartares Mantchoux, qui, après avoir ravagé pendant long-temps les provinces septentrionales de l'empire Chinois, finirent par le subjuguer entièrement.
passages.translation: The first relations date from the middle of the last century, around the time of the invasion of the Manchu Tartars, who, after ravaging the northern provinces of the Chinese empire for a long time, ended by subjugating it entirely.
passages.speaker: Jean-Baptiste Barthelemy de Lesseps

passages.headline: Mongol middlemen in the smuggling trade
passages.gloss: In a footnote on the Russian crown's monopoly of the Beijing caravans, Lesseps says private merchants soon slipped free of it by trading secretly with China through Mongol Tartars, who charged them dearly for their services.
passages.quote: Les particuliers ne tardèrent pas à se dégager des entraves tyranniques du monopole impérial; ils parvinrent à entretenir des relations secrètes en Chine par la voie des Tartares Mongols; qui leur vendirent cher leur entremise.
passages.translation: Private traders soon freed themselves from the tyrannical shackles of the imperial monopoly; they managed to keep up secret dealings with China through the Mongol Tartars, who sold them their services dearly.
passages.speaker: Jean-Baptiste Barthelemy de Lesseps (footnote)

passages.headline: Eski-Krim: from 'Cimmerium' to a wretched market town
passages.gloss: Peyssonnel identifies the town the Tatars call Eski-Krim ('Old Crimea') with Ptolemy's Cimmerium and argues that its name, which the Tatars gave to the whole peninsula, is Cimmerium disfigured. Now only a miserable market town, it seemed to have once been large and flourishing, with monuments from remote antiquity, the Middle Ages and the Genoese period.
passages.quote: La Ville appellée aujourd'hui par les Tartares Eski-Krim, est certainement l'ancienne Cimmerium de Ptolémée … son nom de Krim, qui est aussi celui de la presqu'Isle de Crimée, est visiblement le mot Cimmerium … défiguré par les Tartares. Cette Ville qui n'est plus qu'un misérable Bourg, paroît avoir été autrefois vaste & florissante. Il y a encore plusieurs monumens des siècles reculés, du moyen âge & du temps des Génois.
passages.translation: The town that the Tartars today call Eski-Krim is certainly the ancient Cimmerium of Ptolemy … its name Krim, which is also that of the peninsula of Crimea, is plainly the word Cimmerium … disfigured by the Tartars. This town, now no more than a wretched market town, appears once to have been large and flourishing. There are still several monuments of remote ages, of the Middle Ages and of the Genoese period.
passages.speaker: Charles de Peyssonnel
passages.caution: Peyssonnel lived in Crimea but does not say he saw these ruins. His Cimmerium etymology is a guess; Eski-Krim is the medieval Solkhat or Qirim, the Golden Horde's seat in Crimea, and Qirim is usually explained from Turkic.

passages.headline: No towns, only felt tents: Cumans like the Nogais
passages.gloss: Writing of the Cumans who held the land between the Danube, the Black Sea and the Dniester in the 13th century, Peyssonnel says they had no towns, villages or fixed homes and lived always in movable felt tents. He adds from his own knowledge that they were just like the Nogais of his day, whom he considers almost the same nation.
passages.quote: Ces Barbares n'avoient encore ni Villes, ni Villages, ni Habitations fixes; ils étoient sans cesse campés sous des Tentes de feutre, qu'ils transportoient d'un lieu dans un autre; ils étoient parfaitement semblables aux Nogaïs d'aujourd'hui, qui sont à peu près la même Nation.
passages.translation: These barbarians still had neither towns, nor villages, nor fixed dwellings; they were constantly camped under felt tents, which they carried from place to place; they were exactly like the Nogais of today, who are almost the same nation.
passages.speaker: Charles de Peyssonnel
passages.caution: The first part rests on medieval sources; the comparison with the Nogais is Peyssonnel's own.

passages.headline: Shooting backwards while fleeing, 'as the Tartars still do'
passages.people: Cumans; Crimean and Nogai Tatars of the 18th century
passages.gloss: Telling how Cuman horsemen raided the Latin crusaders besieging Adrianople in 1205, Peyssonnel describes their tactic of fleeing while loosing arrows backwards without stopping, 'as the Tartars of today still do'. The Latins could not catch them, because the Cumans were more lightly armed and had faster, better-trained horses.
passages.quote: Les Comains prirent la fuite, en se contentant de faire de temps en temps quelques décharges de flèches, par derrière, sans arrêter leur marche, comme font encore les Tartares d'aujourd'hui. Les Latins ne purent atteindre ces ennemis, qui étoient armés plus légèrement qu'eux, & avoient des Chevaux plus vîtes, & mieux exercés à la course.
passages.translation: The Cumans took flight, contenting themselves with loosing a volley of arrows behind them from time to time without halting, as the Tartars of today still do. The Latins could not overtake these enemies, who were more lightly armed than they and had faster horses, better trained for running.
passages.speaker: Charles de Peyssonnel

passages.headline: Yedisan, the 'Seven Thousand' horde that made a khan
passages.place: Yedisan (between the Dniester and the Southern Bug)
passages.people: Yedisan Nogais, subjects of the Crimean khan
passages.gloss: Correcting a Moldavian chronicler, Peyssonnel explains that the name Yedisan belongs only to the plains beyond the Dniester, taken from one of the four Nogai hordes under the Crimean khan. Yedi-san means 'seven thousand', the horde's original number of men. He adds that this horde alone, in revolt, deposed Khan Alim Girai and put Qirim Girai on the throne, events he witnessed and reported to the French court in 1759.
passages.quote: Cette Horde s'appelle Iedsan, ou Iedi-San, c'est-à-dire, sept mille, parce qu'elle étoit originairement composée de sept mille hommes … Cette seule Horde révoltée a dépossédé Alim Gueraï Khan, & placé sur le Trône Crim Gueraï Khan qui règne aujourd'hui. On voit les détails de cet événement dont j'ai été témoin, dans la Relation que j'en ai envoyée à la Cour en 1759.
passages.translation: This horde is called Yedsan or Yedi-San, that is, seven thousand, because it was originally made up of seven thousand men … This one horde, in revolt, deposed Alim Girai Khan and placed on the throne Qirim Girai Khan, who reigns today. The details of this event, which I witnessed, can be seen in the report I sent to the Court in 1759.
passages.speaker: Charles de Peyssonnel

passages.headline: Hire a 'Tartar' to handle your journey
passages.gloss: In practical advice for travellers, Jaubert says that in Turkey one can make a deal with a 'Tartar' who will supply everything needed on the road, but warns never to pay him the whole sum in advance; in Persia the custom was unknown. In the Ottoman Empire a 'Tatar' was a government courier, and Jaubert himself travelled with one, Omar, who renamed himself Aly in Persia.
passages.quote: Dans le premier de ces pays, on peut faire marché avec un Tartare qui se charge de vous fournir tout ce qui est nécessaire; mais il faut se garder de le payer d'avance en totalité. En Perse, cet usage est inconnu.
passages.translation: In the first of these countries one can strike a bargain with a Tartar who undertakes to supply you with everything necessary; but take care not to pay him the whole in advance. In Persia this custom is unknown.
passages.speaker: Pierre-Amedee Jaubert
passages.caution: Here 'Tartar' is an Ottoman job title, not an ethnic label.

passages.headline: Kurds who claim Mongol and Uzbek ancestors
passages.gloss: Jaubert reports that the Kurds, settled or nomadic, claim descent from the Mongols and Uzbeks whose sudden raids so often shook Asia. He rejects the claim on the evidence of their large eyes, aquiline noses, fair skin and height, which he thinks 'belie this Tartar origin'.
passages.quote: Ces peuples, soit qu'ils mènent une vie sédentaire ou qu'ils errent dans les campagnes, se prétendent issus des Mongols et des Uzbeks, dont les irruptions soudaines ont si souvent troublé l'Asie. Mais la grandeur et la beauté de leurs yeux, leur nez aquilin, la blancheur de leur teint et l'élévation de leur taille, démentent cette origine tartare.
passages.translation: These peoples, whether they lead a settled life or wander the countryside, claim descent from the Mongols and the Uzbeks, whose sudden incursions have so often disturbed Asia. But the size and beauty of their eyes, their aquiline noses, the fairness of their complexion and their tall stature belie this Tartar origin.
passages.speaker: Pierre-Amedee Jaubert
passages.caution: Jaubert argues from looks alone, a method of his time; the claimed ancestry reflects the prestige of Mongol and Uzbek descent.

passages.headline: Khoy, 'the Turkestan of Persia'
passages.gloss: Jaubert describes Khoy in Persian Azerbaijan as a fairly new town with regular fortifications, few mosques or large houses, tree-shaded streets and a good caravanserai for merchants. Its 25,000 inhabitants said they were of Tartar origin, which earned the district the nickname 'the Turkestan of Persia'.
passages.quote: La ville de Khoï, qui n'est pas fort ancienne, a des fortifications régulières. On n'y voit pas un grand nombre de mosquées ni de maisons considérables; mais les rues sont ombragées d'arbres, et l'on y trouve un assez beau caravanséraï spécialement réservé pour les marchands. On peut évaluer à vingt-cinq mille âmes la population de cette ville, dont les habitans se disent aussi d'origine tartare
passages.translation: The town of Khoy, which is not very old, has regular fortifications. One does not see many mosques or large houses there; but the streets are shaded with trees, and there is a rather fine caravanserai reserved especially for merchants. The population of this town may be put at twenty-five thousand souls, whose inhabitants also say they are of Tartar origin
passages.speaker: Pierre-Amedee Jaubert
passages.caution: The nickname comes from the Ottoman geographer Katib Celebi (Jihannuma), whom Jaubert cites.

passages.headline: Turkish as 'a dialect of Tartar'
passages.gloss: In a note drawn from his own Turkish grammar, Jaubert calls Turkish a dialect of 'Tartar' brought to Constantinople by the Ottomans in 1453, later enriched with Arabic and Persian words. For him 'Tartar' is the name of the whole Turkic language family.
passages.quote: Comme la langue turque est écrite et parlée dans plusieurs provinces de la Perse, nous croyons devoir insérer ici quelques réflexions extraites d'une grammaire que nous avons composée il y a quelque temps … Cette langue, disons-nous, est un dialecte du tartare, apporté par les Ottomans à Constantinople en 1453.
passages.translation: Since the Turkish language is written and spoken in several provinces of Persia, we think we should insert here some reflections taken from a grammar we composed some time ago … This language, we say, is a dialect of Tartar, brought by the Ottomans to Constantinople in 1453.
passages.speaker: Pierre-Amedee Jaubert (footnote from his Turkish grammar)
passages.caution: Turkic speech reached Anatolia with the Seljuks in the 11th century; 1453 is only the Ottoman capture of Constantinople.

passages.headline: 'The ferocity of Tartar blood' in a Persian prince
passages.gloss: Describing the Shah's eldest son, Mohammad Ali Mirza, Jaubert notes that he was born of a Khwarazmian slave woman and says 'the ferocity of Tartar blood' had shown in him since childhood, though he was also precociously brave. Here 'Tartar' marks a mother from Khwarazm, south of the Aral Sea, and carries the old stereotype of Tartar savagery.
passages.quote: Mehemed-Aly-Mirza, que les partisans de son compétiteur appellent Myr-Aly-Khan, fils aîné de Feth-Aly-Chah, est né d'une esclave khouarezmienne; et la férocité du sang tartare, qui coule dans ses veines, s'est fait reconnaître en lui dès son enfance.
passages.translation: Mohammad Ali Mirza, whom the partisans of his rival call Mir Ali Khan, eldest son of Fath Ali Shah, was born of a Khwarazmian slave woman; and the ferocity of the Tartar blood that flows in his veins showed itself in him from childhood.
passages.speaker: Pierre-Amedee Jaubert
passages.caution: Court gossip dressed in a racial stereotype; the Qajar dynasty was itself of Turkic origin.

passages.headline: The Shah's falcons from beyond Astrakhan
passages.people: Qajar court; falcon-rearing peoples north-east of Astrakhan
passages.gloss: Invited to hunt with Fath Ali Shah near Sultaniyeh, Jaubert notes that the Persians kept up falconry, an expensive taste he thinks they probably got from the Tartars. The Shah's many falcons came from the lands north-east of Astrakhan, each with its own name and trainer.
passages.quote: leur vient probablement des Tartares. Le Chah possède un grand nombre d'oiseaux de cette espèce, provenant des pays situés au nord-est d'Astrakhan, et qui sont dressés avec beaucoup d'art. Chaque faucon a son nom propre et un instituteur particulier.
passages.translation: probably came to them from the Tartars. The Shah owns a great number of birds of this kind, from the countries north-east of Astrakhan, which are trained with much art. Each falcon has its own name and its own trainer.
passages.speaker: Pierre-Amedee Jaubert
passages.caution: The Tartar origin of Persian falconry is Jaubert's guess.

passages.headline: Turkmen slave raids on the road to Mashhad
passages.gloss: In the appended notice on Mazandaran, Colonel Trezel explains why pilgrims to Mashhad gathered at Astarabad in caravans of seven or eight hundred. Turkmen raiders roamed the plains, plundered everything and carried off men and even children able to keep up, sending them to herd flocks around Bukhara and Samarkand; Sunni Turkmen, he says, were driven against Shia Persians by hope of plunder and by religion.
passages.quote: Les Turkomans rodent sur toutes ces plaines, pillent tout ce qu'ils trouvent, et emmènent en esclavage les hommes et les enfans même en état de suivre leurs courses. Ils les envoient garder leurs troupeaux dans les plaines de Bokhara et de Samarcand. Ces peuples sont animés contre les Persans par l'espoir du pillage et par la différence des opinions religieuses, parce qu'ils sont sunnys.
passages.translation: The Turkmen roam all these plains, plunder everything they find, and carry off into slavery the men, and even the children able to keep up with their raids. They send them to guard their flocks on the plains of Bukhara and Samarkand. These peoples are driven against the Persians by hope of plunder and by difference of religious opinion, because they are Sunnis.
passages.speaker: Colonel Camille-Alphonse Trezel (Notice sur le Ghilan et le Mazenderan, printed with Jaubert)
passages.caution: Trezel reports what he learned in Persia; he did not enter Turkmen country, and he does not call the Turkmen Tartars.

passages.headline: 'Do not call our lord a Christian, nor us Tartars'
passages.people: Mongols (Moal) of Sartaq's court, Golden Horde
passages.gloss: As Rubruck left Sartaq's camp, the secretary Coiac and other court scribes warned him not to say their lord was a Christian: he was a Moal. Rubruck explains that the Mongols treat 'Christian' as the name of a nation and are so proud that they want their own name, Moal, above every other, and will not be called Tartars either, because the Tartars had been a different people.
passages.quote: « Nolite dicere quod dominus noster sit christianus. Non est christianus, sed Moal »; quia enim nomen christianitatis videtur eis nomen cujusdam gentis. In tantam superbiam sunt erecti, quod quamvis forte aliquid credant de Christo, tamen nolunt dici christiani, volentes nomen suum, hoc est Moal, exaltare super omne nomen, nec volunt vocari Tartari. Tartari enim fuerunt alia gens de quibus sic didici.
passages.translation: 'Do not say that our lord is a Christian. He is not a Christian but a Moal'; for the name of Christianity seems to them the name of some nation. They are raised to such pride that, though they may perhaps believe something about Christ, they will not be called Christians, wishing to exalt their own name, that is Moal, above every name; nor will they be called Tartars. For the Tartars were another people, about whom I learned as follows.
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck (Latin text ed. Michel and Wright, 1839)

passages.headline: The 'water Mongols' who called themselves Tartars
passages.gloss: In his commentary d'Avezac summarises Carpini's account of the four peoples who once lived in Mongolia: the Yeka Mongal ('great Mongols'), the Su-Mongal ('water Mongols') who called themselves Tartars after a river named Tatar in their land, the Merkit and the Mecrit. He confirms that Yeka and Su do mean 'great' and 'water'.
passages.quote: En ce pays étaient autrefois quatre peuples, savoir: les Yeka Mongal ou grands Mongals; les Su-Mongals ou Mongals aquatiques, lesquels se donnaient à eux-mêmes le nom Tartares, d'après un fleuve appelé Tatar qui coulait en leur pays; les Merkit; et enfin les Mécrit.
passages.translation: In that country there were formerly four peoples, namely: the Yeka Mongal or great Mongols; the Su-Mongal or water Mongols, who gave themselves the name Tartars after a river called Tatar that flowed through their country; the Merkit; and lastly the Mecrit.
passages.speaker: Armand d'Avezac (editor's commentary), paraphrasing John of Plano Carpini
passages.caution: The 'river Tatar' is Carpini's explanation, repeated by d'Avezac; such a river is not otherwise attested and the name's origin remains uncertain.

passages.headline: 'No abiding city': entering another world
passages.gloss: Three days after leaving the Crimean port of Soldaia (Sudak), Rubruck met the first Tartars and felt he was entering another world. His opening line about them turns a verse from the Letter to the Hebrews ('here we have no abiding city, but we seek one to come'): the Tartars have no abiding city anywhere, and know nothing of the city to come.
passages.quote: Postquam ergo recessimus de Soldaia tertia die invenimus Tartaros, inter quos cum intravi visum fuit michi recte quod ingrederer quoddam aliud seculum, quorum vitam et morem vobis describo prout possum. Nusquam habent manentem civitatem, sed futuram ignorant.
passages.translation: So on the third day after we left Soldaia we came upon the Tartars, and when I went in among them it truly seemed to me that I was entering another world. I will describe their life and customs to you as best I can. Nowhere do they have an abiding city, and of the city to come they know nothing.
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck

passages.headline: Felt houses thirty feet wide, pulled by 22 oxen
passages.gloss: Rubruck describes the Mongol felt houses built on a frame of rods and carried whole on carts. He measured one cart's wheel track at 20 feet, with the house overhanging by at least 5 feet each side, and counted 22 oxen pulling one house, in two rows of eleven, with an axle as big as a ship's mast and a driver standing in the doorway.
passages.quote: Et faciunt tales domus ita magnas quod habent aliquando triginta pedes in latitudine. Ego enim mensuravi semel latitudinem inter vestigia rotarum unius bige .xx. pedum, et quando domus erat super bigam excedebat extra rotas in utroque latere .v. pedibus ad minus. Ego numeravi in una biga .xxij. boves trahentes unam domum, undecim in uno ordine secundum latitudinem bige, et alios .xj. ante illos.
passages.translation: And they make these houses so large that they are sometimes thirty feet across. I once measured the width between the wheel tracks of one cart at 20 feet, and when the house was on the cart it overhung the wheels on each side by at least 5 feet. I counted 22 oxen drawing one house on one cart, eleven in a row across the width of the cart and another eleven in front of them.
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck

passages.headline: Cuman mounds, stone statues and brick towers
passages.gloss: Among the burial customs he saw on the steppe, Rubruck notes that the Cumans raised a great mound over the dead and set up a statue facing east holding a cup at the navel. For the rich they built small pointed 'pyramids', and in places he saw tall towers of baked brick and even stone houses, though no stone was found there. He also saw a newly dead man with the hides of sixteen horses hung on tall poles around him.
passages.quote: Comani faciunt magnum tumulum super defunctum, et erigunt ei statuam versa facie ad orientem, tenentem ciphum in manu sua ante umbilicum. Fabricant etiam divitibus piramides, id est domunculas acutas, et alicubi vidi magnas turres de tegulis coctis, alicubi lapideas domos, quamvis lapides non inveniuntur ibi. Vidi quemdam noviter defunctum, cui suspenderant pelles .xvj. equorum, ad quodlibet latus mundi quatuor, inter perticas altas
passages.translation: The Cumans raise a great mound over the dead man and set up a statue to him, its face turned to the east, holding a cup in its hand in front of the navel. For the rich they also build pyramids, that is, small pointed houses, and in some places I saw great towers of baked tiles, in others stone houses, although stones are not found there. I saw one man newly dead for whom they had hung the hides of sixteen horses, four towards each quarter of the world, between tall poles
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck
passages.caution: On the same page Rubruck says the burial places of Mongol nobles were kept secret and guarded.

passages.headline: First taste of kumiss, and a moving city of carts
passages.gloss: Rubruck says that in two months between Soldaia and Sartaq's camp they never slept under a roof and saw no village, nor any trace of a building, except great numbers of Cuman tombs. One evening his guide gave him kumiss; he broke into a sweat from horror and novelty, but found it very tasty. Next morning the carts of the commander Scatatai, loaded with houses, looked to him like a great city coming towards him.
passages.quote: Illo sero dedit nobis garcio, qui ducebat nos, bibere cosmos, ad cujus haustum totus sudavi propter horrorem et novitatem, quia nunquam biberam de eo. Valde tamen sapidum videbatur michi, sicut vere est. Mane ergo obviavimus bigis Scatatay honustis domibus, et videbatur michi quod obviaret michi civitas magna.
passages.translation: That evening the lad who was guiding us gave us kumiss to drink, and at the first draught I sweated all over from horror and novelty, for I had never drunk it before. Yet it seemed to me very tasty, as indeed it is. In the morning we met Scatatai's carts loaded with houses, and it seemed to me that a great city was coming to meet me.
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck

passages.headline: Karakorum: smaller than the town of Saint-Denis
passages.gloss: Rubruck's verdict on the Mongol capital, where he spent the spring of 1254: apart from the khan's palace it was not as good as the little town of Saint-Denis outside Paris, and the abbey of Saint-Denis was worth ten times more than that palace.
passages.quote: De civitate Caracaron noveritis quod, excluso palatio ipsius Chan, non est ita bona sicut burgus Sancti Dyonisii, et monasterium Sancti Dyonisii in decuplo valet plus illo palatio.
passages.translation: As for the city of Karakorum, you should know that, leaving aside the Khan's own palace, it is not as good as the town of Saint-Denis, and the monastery of Saint-Denis is worth ten times more than that palace.
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck

passages.headline: Karakorum's quarters, temples and mud wall
passages.people: Muslim merchants, Chinese craftsmen and Mongol court scribes
passages.gloss: Rubruck describes Karakorum as two quarters: one of Muslims (Saracens) with the markets, where merchants gathered because of the court, and one of 'Cathayans' (northern Chinese), who were all craftsmen. Outside them stood the large palaces of the court secretaries. There were twelve temples of various idolaters, two mosques and one church; a mud wall with four gates enclosed the town, each gate with its own market for grain, sheep and goats, oxen and carts, or horses.
passages.quote: Sarracenorum in quo sunt nundine, et multi mercatores confluunt ibi propter curiam … alius est vicus Catharanorum, qui omnes sunt artifices. Extra istos vicos sunt magna palatia, que sunt scriptorum curie. Sunt ibi duodecim ydolatrie diversarum nationum, due mahummerie in quibus clamatur lex Machometi, una ecclesia cristianorum in extremitate ville. Villa clausa est muro luteo, et habet .iiijor. portas.
passages.translation: [one quarter] of the Saracens, where the markets are, and many merchants gather there because of the court … the other is the quarter of the Cathayans, who are all craftsmen. Outside these quarters are large palaces belonging to the court secretaries. There are twelve idol temples of different nations, two mosques in which the law of Mahomet is proclaimed, and one Christian church at the far end of the town. The town is enclosed by a mud wall and has four gates.
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck
passages.caution: The printed text reads 'Catharanorum'; one manuscript has 'Cataianorum', i.e. people of Cathay (northern China).

passages.headline: The silver tree made by a Paris goldsmith
passages.people: Mongke Khan's court; the Parisian goldsmith William Buchier
passages.gloss: At Karakorum Mongke had a large walled court beside the town wall with a great palace where he held drinking feasts twice a year. Because it was unseemly to carry skins of milk and drink into the hall, Master William of Paris, a goldsmith captured in Hungary and working for the khan, made at the entrance a great silver tree with four silver lions at its roots, from which mare's milk flowed through a pipe.
passages.quote: Ipse Mangu habet apud Caracarum magnam curiam juxta muros ville … Ibi est unum magnum palatium, in quo tenet potationem suam bis in anno … In introitu illius magni palatii, quia turpe erat ibi inferre utres cum lacte et aliis potibus, fecit ei magister Willielmus parisiensis unam magnam arborem argenteam, ad cujus radices sunt quatuor leones argentei, habentes unum cannale, et vomentes omnes lac album jumenti.
passages.translation: Mongke himself has at Karakorum a great court next to the town walls … There is a great palace in which he holds his drinking feast twice a year … At the entrance of this great palace, since it was unseemly to bring in skins of milk and other drinks, Master William of Paris made him a great silver tree, at whose roots are four silver lions with a pipe, all spouting white mare's milk.
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck
passages.caution: Rubruck names the maker as a Parisian captive craftsman; the Mongols' showpiece was European and Chinese workmanship.

passages.headline: Prester John: 'ten times more than the truth'
passages.gloss: Rubruck traces the legend of Prester John to a Nestorian shepherd-lord of the Naimans who made himself king after the death of the Kara-Khitai ruler. The Nestorians called him King John and said ten times more about him than was true, as they make great rumours out of nothing. Rubruck crossed his pastures and found that nobody knew anything of him except a few Nestorians.
passages.quote: Mortuo Con cham, elevavit se ille nestorinus in regem et vocabant eum nestorini regem Johannem, et plus dicebant de ipso in decuplo quam veritas esset. Ita enim faciunt nestorini venientes de partibus illis: de nichilo enim faciunt magnos rumores … Sic ergo exivit magna fama de illo rege Johanne; et ego transivi per pascua ejus, nullus aliquid sciebat de eo nisi Nestoriani pauci.
passages.translation: When Con Khan died, that Nestorian raised himself up as king, and the Nestorians called him King John and said ten times more about him than the truth. For that is what Nestorians coming from those parts do: they make great rumours out of nothing … So the great fame of this King John went out; and when I crossed his pastures, nobody knew anything about him except a few Nestorians.
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck

passages.headline: Bone skates, but no monsters
passages.gloss: From informants at Mongke's court Rubruck learned of northern peoples: the Orengai, who tied polished bones under their feet and sped over snow and ice fast enough to catch birds and beasts. He also asked about the monstrous races described by Isidore and Solinus; his informants said they had never seen any such thing, which, he writes, 'we much wonder whether it is true'.
passages.quote: Sunt etiam ibi Orengai, qui ligant ossa limata sub pedibus suis, et impellunt se super nivem congelatam, et super glaciem cum tanta velocitate ut capiant aves et bestias. … Quesivi de monstris, sive de monstruosis hominibus, de quibus narrat Ysodorus et Solinus. Ipsi dicebant michi quod nunquam viderunt talia, de quo multum miramur si verum sit.
passages.translation: There are also the Orengai, who tie polished bones under their feet and push themselves over the frozen snow and over the ice so fast that they catch birds and beasts. … I asked about the monsters, or monstrous men, that Isidore and Solinus tell of. They told me they had never seen such things, at which we much wonder whether it is true.
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck
passages.caution: Rubruck's doubt runs both ways: he is surprised the monsters of the old books were not confirmed.

passages.headline: Derbent: the Iron Gate, its towers cut down by the Tartars
passages.gloss: Returning south along the Caspian, Rubruck passed Derbent, the 'Iron Gate'. The town ran more than a mile between mountain and sea, with a strong castle on top, very strong walls without ditches and towers of large polished stones; but the Tartars had cut down the tops of the towers and the battlements to the height of the walls. The land within, he says, used to be like a paradise.
passages.quote: Fortissimos muros habet sine fossatis, et turres de lapidibus magnis et politis; sed Tartari destruxerunt summitates turrium et propugnacula murorum, equantes turres muro. Infra illam civitatem solebat terra esse sicut paradisus.
passages.translation: It has very strong walls without ditches, and towers of large polished stones; but the Tartars destroyed the tops of the towers and the battlements of the walls, levelling the towers with the wall. Within that city the land used to be like a paradise.
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck

passages.headline: Ruined walls from mountain to mountain: 'Alexander's barriers'
passages.gloss: A day beyond Derbent Rubruck crossed a valley where the foundations of walls ran from one mountain to the next. He identifies them with the barriers of Alexander meant to hold back 'wild peoples', and explains these rationally as the shepherds of the wilderness kept out of the farmland and cities. He adds that he could learn nothing certain about the other barriers where Jews were said to be enclosed.
passages.quote: In crastino transivimus per vallem quamdam, in qua apparebant fundamenta murorum de uno monte ad alium, et per summitates montium nulla erat via. Ista solebant esse claustra Alexandri, feras gentes chohibentia, hoc est, pastores de solitudine, ut non possent ingredi super terras cultas et civitates.
passages.translation: The next day we crossed a valley in which the foundations of walls could be seen running from one mountain to another, and over the mountain tops there was no road. These used to be the barriers of Alexander, holding back the wild peoples, that is, the shepherds of the wilderness, so that they could not come into the cultivated lands and the cities.
passages.speaker: William of Rubruck
passages.caution: The walls were real, probably part of the Sasanian (6th-century) defences around Derbent; crediting them to Alexander is legend, which Rubruck repeats.

passages.headline: Carpini: no towns except Karakorum, which he never saw
passages.gloss: Describing the Mongol homeland, Carpini says there is little wood, so everyone from the emperor down cooks on fires of cattle and horse dung, and hardly a hundredth of the land is fertile. With few streams and very rare rivers there are no villages and no towns, except one said to be fairly good, called Karakorum. The friars did not see it, though they were half a day's journey away at the Sira Ordo, the imperial camp.
passages.quote: Sed aquæ et rivi ibidem sunt pauci, flumina verò rarissima: undè ibidem villæ non sunt, nec aliquæ civitates, exceptà unà quæ dicitur satis bona, quæ Caracaron nominatur; nos autem non vidimus illam, sed fuimus propè ad dimidiam dietam cùm apud Syram ordam essemus
passages.translation: But waters and streams there are few, and rivers very rare: so there are no villages there, nor any cities, except one which is said to be quite good, called Karakorum; we did not see it, but we were about half a day's journey from it when we were at the Sira Ordo
passages.speaker: John of Plano Carpini (Latin text ed. d'Avezac, 1839)
passages.caution: Carpini's statement about Karakorum itself is hearsay, as he says.

passages.headline: Ox-footed men with dogs' faces
passages.gloss: Telling of Mongol campaigns in the far north, Carpini says the army passed the Samoyeds, who lived by hunting in tents of hide, and came to a land by the Ocean where they found monsters, 'as we were firmly told', with human bodies but ox feet and dogs' faces, who spoke two words like men and barked at the third.
passages.quote: Indè ultrà procedentes venerunt ad quandam terram super Oceanum, ubi invenerunt quædam monstra, ut nobis firmiter dicebatur, quæ per omnia formam humanam habebant sed pedes desinebant in pedes bovinos, et humanum caput habebant sed faciem habebant ut canis; duo verba loquebantur more humano et tercio latrabant ut canis
passages.translation: Going on further they came to a land on the Ocean, where they found certain monsters, as we were firmly told, which had human form in every way except that their feet ended in the feet of oxen, and they had human heads but faces like dogs; they spoke two words in the human way and at the third barked like a dog
passages.speaker: John of Plano Carpini
passages.caution: Carpini marks it as hearsay ('ut nobis firmiter dicebatur'); it echoes the dog-headed races of classical and medieval lore.

passages.headline: Prince Michael refuses to bow to Chinggis Khan's image
passages.people: Mongols of the Golden Horde; Russian princes
passages.gloss: Carpini tells how Michael of Chernigov, a great Russian prince, came to submit to Batu. He was first made to pass between two fires, then told to bow southwards to the image of Chinggis Khan. He answered that he would gladly bow to Batu and his servants, but not to the image of a dead man, since Christians may not; after repeated refusals he was kicked in the chest until he died.
passages.quote: undè nuper contigit quod Michael, qui fuit unus de magnis ducibus Rusciæ, cùm ivisset ad reddendum se Bati, fecerunt eum priùs inter duos ignes transire; post hoc dixerunt ei quod ad meridiem Chingis-can inclinaret: qui respondit quòd Bati et servis suis etiàm inclinaret libenter, sed imagini hominis mortui non inclinaret, quià non licet hoc facere christianis
passages.translation: So it recently happened that Michael, one of the great dukes of Russia, when he went to submit to Batu, was first made to pass between two fires; after this they told him to bow to the south to Chinggis Khan. He answered that he would willingly bow to Batu and even to his servants, but he would not bow to the image of a dead man, because Christians may not do so
passages.speaker: John of Plano Carpini
passages.caution: Carpini reports this as recent news, not as something he witnessed; Michael was later venerated as a martyr, so the story also served Christian purposes.

passages.headline: Jordanus on the 'Great Tartar' of China
passages.people: Mongol emperor of China and his subjects
passages.gloss: The Dominican bishop Jordanus, who never went to China, repeats what 'trustworthy people' told him of the Great Tartar: very rich, just and generous, with paper money and monasteries like Europe's. Some subjects keep their dead unburied at home for up to ten years, serving them food as if alive, and great lords are buried with a horse and one or two favourite servants alive.
passages.quote: De Magno Tartaro, quod audivi à fide dignis narro … Ibi, mortuos suos non comburunt; non etiam sepeliunt, aliquotiens per decem annos … sed tenent eos in domibus, et ministrant sibi cibaria, sicut si esset vivus. Magni domini, cùm moriuntur, sepeliuntur cum equo uno, et cum uno vel duobus suis servitoribus vivis sibi magis dilectis.
passages.translation: Of the Great Tartar I tell what I heard from trustworthy people … There they do not burn their dead; nor do they bury them, sometimes for ten years … but they keep them in their houses and serve them food as if they were alive. Great lords, when they die, are buried with one horse and with one or two of their favourite servants alive.
passages.speaker: Jordanus Catalani of Severac (Mirabilia descripta, c. 1330), in the 1839 edition
passages.caution: Explicit hearsay: Jordanus served in India and never reached China.

passages.headline: A 13th-century poem calls the Tartars cannibals
passages.gloss: In his notes d'Avezac prints lines, copied by Thomas Wright from a Cotton manuscript, of John of Garland's poem On the Triumphs of the Church. It paints the Tartars as Satan's household and the Church's plague who eat human flesh: no lion eats a lion and no wolf tears a wolf, but these men roast human limbs on spits. D'Avezac traces the poet's 'reliable' information to atrocity letters from priests in central Europe.
passages.quote: Gens est sæva nimis, Sathanæque domestica, pestis Ecclesiæ, fidei dissona, cædis amans. … Esuriens hominem corrodit homo; leo nullus Carne leonina viscera laxa replet; Non lupus ungue lupum lacerat; gens ista colurnis In veribus vertit membra veruta foco.
passages.translation: A people exceedingly savage, of Satan's household, a plague to the Church, at odds with the faith, in love with slaughter. … Hungry, man gnaws man; no lion fills its slack belly with lion's flesh; no wolf tears a wolf with its claw; this people turns limbs spitted on hazel skewers over the fire.
passages.speaker: John of Garland (De triumphis Ecclesiae, 13th century), quoted by Thomas Wright in Armand d'Avezac's notes
passages.caution: War propaganda built on rumour; Garland never met a Mongol. The poem's Latin is quoted from a single manuscript copy and the OCR is rough.

passages.headline: Natigay, the felt household god with a wife and children
passages.gloss: In the Latin Marco Polo of the Society's first volume, the chapter on Tartar customs describes their god Natigay (here 'Naagay'), lord of the earth who guards children, herds and crops. Every household made him of felt and cloth, with a felt wife and children beside him. At meals they smeared fat on the idols' mouths and threw broth out of the door for them before eating. The same page describes kumiss, called 'chenus'.
passages.quote: Lex autem eorum talis est; quia ipsi habent suum deum qui vocatur Naagay, et dicunt quod ille est deus terrenus vel deus terræ qui custodit eorum filios et eorum bestias et blada … Et faciunt istum deum de feltro et panno, et credunt quod iste deus eorum habeat uxorem et filios … Quando comedunt ipsi accipiunt carnes pingues et ungunt illi suo idolo os, et uxori et filiis idoli
passages.translation: Their law is this: they have their god called Naagay, and they say he is an earthly god, or god of the earth, who guards their children, their beasts and their crops … They make this god of felt and cloth, and believe this god of theirs has a wife and children … When they eat, they take fat meat and smear the mouth of their idol with it, and of the idol's wife and children
passages.speaker: Marco Polo (Latin version printed by the Societe de Geographie, 1824)
passages.caution: From volume 1 of the same series (1824), not the 1839 volume.

passages.headline: How the map of Tartary was put together
passages.gloss: The atlas foreword, summarising du Halde, says the Jesuits' manuscript maps passed through d'Anville's hands before engraving. For the general map of Tartary he used the travel memoirs of Father Gerbillon checked against the sheet maps, and for the lands between Tibet, Tartary and the Caspian, where the missionaries had only imperfect information, he combined their notes with whatever else he could learn.
passages.quote: elles ont passé par celles de Mr. d'Anville … qui en a formé ensuite les Cartes générales. Il s'est servi pour celle de la Tartarie des Mémoires du Pere Gerbillon, en les comparant avec les Cartes particulières … comme les Missionaires avaient eu quelques connoissances, quoi qu'imparfaites des Pays situez entre le Thibet, la Tartarie & la Mer Caspienne, Mr. d'Anville en a fait usage
passages.translation: they passed through the hands of Mr d'Anville … who then made the general maps from them. For that of Tartary he used the memoirs of Father Gerbillon, comparing them with the particular maps … as the missionaries had some knowledge, though imperfect, of the countries lying between Tibet, Tartary and the Caspian Sea, Mr d'Anville made use of it
passages.speaker: Foreword (Avertissement) of the 1737 atlas, summarising du Halde's preface
passages.caution: The foreword separates surveyed provinces from compiled areas; the far west of 'Tartary' on these maps rests on report and inference, not measurement.

passages.headline: Bukhara, 'twice the size of Moscow', in Great Tartary
passages.gloss: The Relation opens by noting that geographers count Bukharia as part of Great Tartary, because 'the Tartars, or rather the Kalmyks' had invaded part of it; the author insists it is a separate state, just as China remained China under its Tartar conquerors. Great Bukharia has several towns, each with its own khan, of which Bukhara is said to be twice as large as Moscow.
passages.quote: Les Géographes regardent ordinairement la Boucharie, comme faisant partie de la Grande Tartarie. En effet les Tartares, ou pour mieux dire les Calmuques, en ont envahi une partie … Il y a plusieurs Villes dans la Grande Boucharie, & elles ont chacune son Cham, ou Régent. Les principales sont: Bouchara, qu'on dit être deux fois plus grande que la ville de Moscou en Russie
passages.translation: Geographers usually regard Bukharia as part of Great Tartary. Indeed the Tartars, or rather the Kalmyks, have invaded part of it … There are several towns in Great Bukharia, and each has its own khan or regent. The chief ones are Bukhara, which is said to be twice as large as the city of Moscow in Russia
passages.speaker: Anonymous author of the 'Relation de la Boucharie' printed in the atlas
passages.caution: The author says he knew Little Bukharia at first hand but reports Great Bukharia (Bukhara) from hearsay ('qu'on dit').

passages.headline: Stone houses and mud-brick ovens in Little Bukharia
passages.people: Bukharans (townspeople of Little Bukharia) under Kalmyk rule
passages.gloss: The anonymous author, who says he lived in Little Bukharia, describes its townspeople's houses as built of stone and fairly good, with few furnishings: no tables or chairs, only Chinese chests on which mattresses were laid. Slaves bought from the Kalmyks, Russians and others cooked in iron pots set into a hearth, and some houses had small ovens of clay or unbaked brick, like their walls.
passages.quote: Les maisons des Bouchars sont de pierre, & passablement bonnes. Leurs meubles sont en petit nombre, & de peu d'ornement. Ils n'ont ni tables ni chaises. … Il y en a qui ont aussi de petits fours, qui se font, comme le reste de leurs murailles, de terre grasse ou de briques crues.
passages.translation: The houses of the Bukharans are of stone and passably good. Their furniture is scanty and plain. They have neither tables nor chairs. … Some also have small ovens, which are made, like the rest of their walls, of clay or of unbaked bricks.
passages.speaker: Anonymous author of the 'Relation de la Boucharie'
passages.caution: The text says both stone houses and walls of clay or mud brick; which was usual is not clear.

passages.headline: Cutting out the illness with a knife
passages.gloss: The Relation describes the Bukharans' cure for sickness: a mullah reads from a book, blows on the patient several times and makes passes with a sharp knife around his face, believing this cuts the root of the illness, which they hold to be the Devil's work. The dead, it adds, are buried with a Koran on the chest in a pleasant grove fenced with a hedge or palisade.
passages.quote: Lorsqu'un Bouchar tombe malade, voici le remede dont il se sert; Un Mula lui lit un passage de quelque livre, souffle à plusieurs reprises sur lui, & d'un couteau bien aiguisé fait plusieurs gesticulations tout autour du visage du Malade. Ils s'imaginent que par cette opération ils coupent la racine de la maladie, qu'ils disent d'ailleurs être l'ouvrage du Diable.
passages.translation: When a Bukharan falls ill, this is the remedy he uses: a mullah reads him a passage from some book, blows on him several times, and with a well-sharpened knife makes various passes all round the sick man's face. They imagine that by this operation they cut the root of the illness, which they say is the work of the Devil.
passages.speaker: Anonymous author of the 'Relation de la Boucharie'
passages.caution: An outsider's description of a healing rite, written with some condescension.

passages.headline: Kasimov, the old seat of Tatar khans
passages.people: Tatars of Kasimov (the Kasimov khanate on the Oka)
passages.gloss: Pallas notes that the Russian town of Kasimov is built entirely of logs, even its streets are paved with timber, although good building stone lies all along the Oka. The Tatar rulers who once lived here did use the stone, and he found the remains of their court: a gate with Arabic inscriptions, a long stone residence and a mausoleum. The descendants of the old Tatar townspeople still lived in their own quarter as prosperous fur traders.
passages.quote: Zu denen Zeiten, da Kasimof noch der Wohnplatz Tatarischer Beherrscher gewesen, hat man diesen Vorrath von Steinen nicht völlig so ungebraucht gelassen, und die Stadt hat noch izt schöne Ueberbleibsel tatarischer Gebäude aufzuweisen, welche erhalten zu werden verdienten. … Dieser Platz scheint würklich das Hoflager der hiesigen Chane gewesen zu seyn
passages.translation: In the days when Kasimov was still the residence of Tatar rulers, this store of stone was not left so wholly unused, and the town still has fine remains of Tatar buildings which deserve to be preserved. … This place really seems to have been the court of the local khans.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)

passages.headline: A stone minaret and a khan's tomb at Kasimov
passages.gloss: In the Tatar quarter Pallas measured a tall round tower (a minaret, which he calls Misgir) of dressed limestone, all that stood of a ruined mosque (Metsched) built of large bricks. On the next page he describes the plain stone mausoleum of the khans with a small prayer room, and reports that the owner of the land had pulled down the carved gate and the khan's house and burned much of the stone for lime.
passages.quote: stehet noch izt in dem höchsten Theil der Stadt, ein hoher und starker, rund aufgeführter Thurn oder Misgir, von einem zerstöhrten Bethause… Das alte Bethaus, oder Metsched, hat aus Ziegeln bestanden, welche über 13 Zoll groß sind; der Thurn aber ist aus lauter glattgehauenen und ziemlich grossen Baustücken… erbaut.
passages.translation: there still stands in the highest part of the town a tall, strong, round-built tower or Misgir, from a ruined house of prayer… The old house of prayer, or Metsched, was of bricks more than 13 inches long; but the tower is built entirely of smoothly dressed and fairly large blocks of stone.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)

passages.headline: Tombstones of Bolgars or Tatars at Bolgari
passages.people: Volga Bulgars and Tatars of the Golden Horde period
passages.gloss: In December 1768 Pallas visited the ruins of Bolgari on the Volga, which he calls the former capital of the Bolgars, with a rampart about six versts round, a stone minaret and vaulted buildings. The old gravestones there carry mostly Arabic and a few Armenian inscriptions, dated by the Muslim calendar from 619 to 742 (about 1222 to 1341). He reads them as the graves of Bolgars or Tatars of every rank, and notes that some of the dead came from Shemakha and Shirvan, a sign of long-distance trade.
passages.quote: Man hat bey Bolgari eine Menge alter Grabsteine mehrentheils mit arabischen, jedoch auch einige mit armenischen Aufschriften gefunden… Die Innschriften enthalten nichts, als einen mahometanischen Denkspruch, … den Namen des Verstorbenen und dessen Abstammung oder Würde. Es sind theils vornehme Bolgaren oder Tataren beyderley Geschlechts, theils Geistliche, theils Gemeine und vielleicht Kaufleute.
passages.translation: At Bolgari a great number of old gravestones have been found, mostly with Arabic but also some with Armenian inscriptions… The inscriptions contain nothing but a Muslim motto, … the name of the deceased and his descent or rank. They are partly noble Bolgars or Tatars of both sexes, partly clergy, partly common people and perhaps merchants.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)
passages.caution: Pallas relies on translations of the inscriptions made earlier on Peter the Great's orders; the dates are his conversion of Hijri years.

passages.headline: The brick ruins of Saraichik on the Ural River
passages.gloss: At the Cossack outpost of Saraichik on the Yaik (Ural) River, Pallas walked the ruins of what he calls a Nogai city, whose people were said to have migrated to Khiva. Inside a rampart four to five versts round he saw foundations and vaults of brick houses, fragments of glazed, porcelain-like pottery in white, blue and yellow, and small copper and silver coins ruined by the salty soil.
passages.quote: Innerhalb dem Wall befinden sich viele Spuren, Grundlagen und Gewölber von gemauerten Gebäuden, nach welchen mitten in der Stadt einige sehr ansehnliche Wohnungen müssen gestanden haben. Die Ziegel, deren man sich bedient hat, sind länglicht und ziemlich groß gestrichen… Von altem Geschirr findet man itzt fast nichts mehr, als Stücke von zerbrochenem Porcellanartigen Irdenzeug, welches eine starke und schöne Glasur hat
passages.translation: Within the rampart there are many traces, foundations and vaults of masonry buildings, from which it appears that some very handsome dwellings must have stood in the middle of the town. The bricks used are oblong and moulded fairly large… Of old vessels one now finds almost nothing but pieces of broken porcelain-like earthenware with a strong and fine glaze.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)

passages.headline: Ruins of a great 'Nogai city' on the Akhtuba
passages.people: Tatars (Pallas says Nogais); the Golden Horde
passages.gloss: Near the old saltpetre works of Selitrennoi Gorodok on the Akhtuba, Pallas found a stretch of ten versts covered with brick rubble, building traces and walled graves of what he calls a large Nogai town. On the highest mound stood the ruins of a walled palace or castle and of a khan's mausoleum, from whose vaults treasure hunters were said to have dug riches and coffins covered in silver. Modern archaeology identifies this site with Sarai, the capital of the Golden Horde.
passages.quote: in welcher man längst der Achtuba, ein auch wohl zwey Werste breit, nichts als Ziegelschutt und Spuren von Gebäuden oder ausgemauerten Gräbern einer hier sonst gestandnen ansehnlichen Nagaischen Stadt sieht.
passages.translation: in which, along the Akhtuba, for a width of one or even two versts, one sees nothing but brick rubble and traces of buildings or of walled graves of a considerable Nogai town that once stood here.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)
passages.caution: Pallas calls the town Nogai; the silver coffins are hearsay about earlier treasure digging.

passages.headline: Glazed tiles and bricks carted off to Astrakhan
passages.gloss: Pallas says he had never seen such splendour in any Tatar ruin: brick walls laid with great regularity, the joints inlaid with green, yellow, white and blue glazed ornaments, and a facade with mosaic tiles. He blames time and plunder for the damage, adding that whole boatloads of bricks had been shipped to Astrakhan, and that to get a thousand whole bricks the workers smashed two thousand because the mortar was so hard.
passages.quote: Die äussere Seite der Mauern ist von aussen nicht nur Felderweise in allen Steinfugen mit glasurten Thonzierrathen von grüner, gelber, weisser und blauer Farbe in dreyeckigten und andern Figuren eingelegt… Aber die Zeit und noch mehr der Geitz des Pöbels hat diese denkwürdigen Ueberbleibsel des Alterthums vorlängst in Steinhaufen verwandelt.
passages.translation: The outer face of the walls is not only inlaid, panel by panel in all the joints, with glazed clay ornaments of green, yellow, white and blue colour in triangular and other figures… But time, and still more the greed of the rabble, long ago turned these memorable remains of antiquity into heaps of stones.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)

passages.headline: A saint's mound that heals the sick
passages.gloss: Half a verst from the ruins stood a large, dug-out burial mound where the local Tatars went on pilgrimage, saying a Muslim saint lay buried there. They told Pallas the saint still worked miracles, healed the sick and appeared to them in dreams. Pallas reports this as their belief and dismisses it as the fruit of imagination.
passages.quote: Obgedachte Tataren behaupten, daß der heilige noch itzt Wunder thue, Kranke heile, und ihnen zuweilen im Schlaf erscheine; womit es eben so, wie mit so vielen andern heiligen Erscheinungen und Wundern, welche die Einbildungskraft unter den Menschen in wenig aufgeklärten Zeiten so fruchtbar gebahr, beschaffen seyn wird.
passages.translation: The said Tatars maintain that the saint still works miracles, heals the sick and sometimes appears to them in their sleep; which will be the same case as with so many other holy apparitions and miracles that imagination bore so fruitfully among men in unenlightened times.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)

passages.headline: Tatar tents that ride on two-wheeled carts
passages.gloss: Along the Akhtuba Pallas saw the camps of the Kundurov Tatars, Nogais from the Kuban who had stayed behind when many Kalmyks fled east in 1771. Unlike Kalmyk tents, their round felt-and-reed huts could not be taken apart and were small enough to set whole onto a tall two-wheeled cart (arba), which they covered like a parasol. He compares them to the wagon-dwelling 'Hamaxobii' of the ancient geographers and quotes Horace on the Scythians whose carts drag their wandering homes.
passages.quote: Ihre Jurten sind in der Gestalt und Bauart, von denen bey Kalmücken und andern asiatischen Nomaden gebräuchlichen sehr verschieden. Sie können nicht stückweise aus einander genommen werden, sind aber desto leichter gebaut und nur so groß, daß sie über einen grossen Karren gesetzt werden können
passages.translation: Their yurts are very different in shape and construction from those used by the Kalmyks and other Asian nomads. They cannot be taken apart piece by piece, but are all the more lightly built and only so large that they can be set over a big cart.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)

passages.headline: How a Kalmyk felt tent is put together
passages.gloss: Pallas gives a step-by-step account of the Kalmyk tent, keyed to an engraved plate: folding lattice walls of willow rods tied into a circle, a wooden crown ring lifted on long roof rods, the frame painted red, and a large cut felt thrown over the roof like a raincoat. In summer the sides stay open; in cold weather they are wrapped in felt or reed mats.
passages.quote: Alsdenn ist das Gerüste, dessen Theile roth angefärbt zu seyn pflegen fertig. Ueber das Dach desselben wird ein grosser, darnach zugeschnittener Filz, wie ein Regen-Mantel herum gelegt, und mit darüber geschlungenen Seilen befestigt. Die Seiten bleiben im Sommer offen, wenn es aber kalt ist, so werden Stücken Filz, oder Schilfmatten, oder auch beyde darum gelegt
passages.translation: Then the frame, whose parts are usually painted red, is finished. Over its roof a large felt, cut to fit, is laid round like a raincoat and fastened with ropes slung over it. The sides stay open in summer, but when it is cold pieces of felt or reed mats, or both, are laid around them.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)

passages.headline: Kalmyk women pitch the tent and saddle the horse
passages.gloss: Pallas describes the inside of the tent, with its iron tripod over the fire and cast-iron pans bought from Russian ironworks, then the division of labour. Men only make and mend the tents; women milk, dress hides, sew, strike and raise the tent, and even saddle the husband's horse.
passages.quote: Die häusliche Arbeit liegt bloß dem weiblichen Geschlecht ob. Die Männer bemühen sich in nichts, als in Ausbesserung und Verfertigung der Hütten… Das Weibsvolk muß die Hütte abnehmen, alle Sachen aufpacken, und auch die Hütte wieder aufstellen. Sogar muß das Weib dem Manne das Pferd satteln und vor die Hütte führen, wenn er verreisen will.
passages.translation: Housework falls on the female sex alone. The men busy themselves with nothing but mending and making the huts… The women must take down the hut, pack up everything and put the hut up again. The wife must even saddle her husband's horse and lead it to the hut when he wants to ride out.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)

passages.headline: A brick 'Tatar prayer-house' whose builders were forgotten
passages.place: Kazakh steppe between the Ui and Tobol
passages.gloss: Pallas rode out into the steppe beyond the Orenburg line to see a building the Russians called the Tatar Koshena. It was a square brick shrine with a pointed Gothic portal and a twelve-sided funnel dome, standing in a Kazakh cemetery. He thought it was not very old, yet neither the Kazakhs nor the Bashkirs remembered who had built it. On a following page he notes it is all of red brick, much like ordinary European brick.
passages.quote: Es ist noch in vollkommen gutem Zustand und scheint, wenigstens dem darinn befindlichen Holzwerk nach, von keinem ausserordentlichen Alterthum zu seyn. Gleichwohl ist unter den Kirgisen sowohl, als Baschkiren das Angedenken ihrer Auferbauung verloschen.
passages.translation: It is still in perfectly good condition and, at least to judge by the woodwork inside, seems to be of no extraordinary antiquity. Nevertheless the memory of its building has been lost among the Kirgis as well as the Bashkirs.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)

passages.headline: Horsehair and bullets left at a holy place
passages.place: Kazakh steppe between the Ui and Tobol
passages.people: Kazakhs (Kirgis) and Tatars of Pallas's escort
passages.gloss: At the same brick shrine birch poles were hung with tufts of horsehair and rags, and the ledges held pebbles, lead bullets, an arrow and gunpowder. Pallas explains that the Kazakhs believe leaving hair from a horse's tail at a holy place helps the horse, and that leaving some small thing is a general Tatar custom. The Tatars of his own escort added offerings after praying.
passages.quote: Die Kirgisen nehmlich glauben, daß es ihrem Pferde zuträglich ist, wenn etwas Haar von deßen Schweif an einem so heiligen Ort zurück gelassen wird, und überhaupt ist es eine tatarische Gewohnheit bey solchen Bethäusern, oder andern heiligen Plätzen, die sie der Andacht wegen besuchen, irgend etwas, so sie bey sich führen, zurück zu lassen.
passages.translation: For the Kirgis believe that it is good for their horse if some hair from its tail is left at so holy a place; and in general it is a Tatar custom, at such prayer-houses or other holy places they visit out of devotion, to leave behind something they carry with them.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)

passages.headline: The 'Seven Palaces' were mud-brick and Bukharan
passages.gloss: The fortress of Semipalatinsk ('seven palaces') on the Irtysh was named after ruins twelve versts upstream, famous in earlier travel books. Pallas went to see them: the remains of a few buildings of slate slabs set in clay and of unburnt brick, one a windowless hut, laid out without order. He judged the work poor and plainly Bukharan, and counted the seven 'palaces' only by including rubble heaps.
passages.quote: Gegenwärtig ist nur noch von dreyen Gebäuden verfallenes Mauerwerk vorhanden; die Lage der übrigen läst sich nur noch aus dem Schutt schliessen; die Bauart ist schlecht und leicht vor Bucharisch zu erkennen, auch sind die Gebäude ohne einige Ordnung angelegt gewesen.
passages.translation: At present only decayed masonry of three buildings remains; the position of the rest can only be inferred from the rubble; the building style is poor and easily recognised as Bukharan, and the buildings were laid out without any order.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)
passages.caution: The identification as Bukharan is Pallas's judgement from the building style; modern scholars link the site to a Zunghar (Oirat) Buddhist monastery.

passages.headline: Ablaikit, a walled Kalmyk temple in the steppe
passages.gloss: Pallas sent his student Sokolov to measure the ruins of Ablaikit, seventy versts from Ust-Kamenogorsk, and printed an abstract of his report with plans. It was a Buddhist temple and residence built by the Kalmyk prince Ablai, surrounded by a wall of stacked slate slabs that climbed over the crags, with a temple on a burnt-brick platform. Kazakhs and Russian hunting parties had since wrecked much of it.
passages.quote: Ablaikit liegt ausser der Gränze des rußischen Reichs, in der sonst von den Ssungorischen Kalmücken bewohnten, nunmehr aber den Kirgisen der mitlern Horde zu Theil gewordnen Wüste… Die historischen Umstände von dessen Erbauung durch einen Kalmückischen Fürsten Ablai, und von der erfolgten Zerstörung dieses Wohnsitzes
passages.translation: Ablaikit lies outside the border of the Russian Empire, in the desert formerly inhabited by the Zunghar Kalmyks but now fallen to the Kirgis of the Middle Horde… The historical circumstances of its building by a Kalmyk prince, Ablai, and of the later destruction of this residence
passages.speaker: Student N. Sokolov's description, abridged by P. S. Pallas
passages.caution: Second-hand: Pallas prints his student's report; the history of Ablai comes from G. F. Müller's earlier study.

passages.headline: The Tomsk Tatars call themselves Chat
passages.gloss: Stopping in the Muslim Tatar village of Kaltai near Tomsk, Pallas notes that the six or seven hundred Tatar families of the Tomsk area call themselves Tschaty and differ little from the Kazan Tatars in dress, customs and religion. Their women wear a closed cap over the veil, and girls wear up to thirty braids at their wedding.
passages.quote: Die hier wohnenden Tataren, deren in und um Tomsk in allem etwan sechs bis sieben hundert Familien wohnen, nennen sich Tschaty und sind in ihrer Tracht und Sitten, so wie in der Religion, von den Casanischen wenig unterschieden.
passages.translation: The Tatars living here, of whom about six to seven hundred families in all live in and around Tomsk, call themselves Tschaty and differ little from those of Kazan in their dress and customs, as in their religion.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)

passages.headline: Birch-bark summer yurts and earth-covered winter huts
passages.people: Baptised Siberian Tatars of the Krasnoyarsk district
passages.gloss: East of Tomsk, Pallas describes the dwellings of baptised Tatars: summer yurts of poles or bent birch rods shaped like a Kalmyk tent but covered with boiled and stitched white birch bark, and winter huts of thin birch logs shaped like a box, heaped with earth for warmth, with a clay-and-brushwood fireplace and a square smoke hole.
passages.quote: Die hiesigen getauften Tataren wohnen im Sommer in elenden Jurten, die theils aus spitz zusammen gestüzten Stangen, theils aus Birkenstäben die von der Erde herauf um einige grosse Reife befestigt und gebrochen, die Gestalt eines Calmückischen Zeltes vorstellen, und mit stark gekochten und zusammen genehten weissen Birkenrinden gedeckt werden, bestehen.
passages.translation: The baptised Tatars here live in summer in wretched yurts made partly of poles leaned together to a point, partly of birch rods fixed and bent from the ground up around some large hoops, which take the shape of a Kalmyk tent and are covered with strongly boiled, sewn-together white birch bark.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)

passages.headline: Kachin weddings and the bride who must lie flat
passages.gloss: Pallas reports that the Kachin Tatars, rich herders who had not taken up farming or Christianity, keep one wife, court for years, and hold two weddings. The groom's father must set up a new yurt for the couple, while the bride's father supplies the household goods. After the betrothal the father-in-law never sees his son's wife again, and if they meet she must throw herself flat on the ground until he has passed.
passages.quote: Die erste Hochzeit wird beym Brautvater, die andre beym Bräutigam gefeyert, wo des Bräutigams-Vater dem jungen Paar eine neue Jurte aufstellen muß… Ausser bey der ersten Freywerberey sieht der Schwiegervater seines Sohns Frau niemals wieder, geht nie in die Jurte des Sohns und geschieht es ja, daß er seiner Schwiegertochter begegnet, so will die Gewohnheit, daß sich diese platt auf die Erde niederwirft
passages.translation: The first wedding is held at the bride's father's, the second at the groom's, where the groom's father must set up a new yurt for the young couple… Except at the first wooing the father-in-law never sees his son's wife again, never goes into the son's yurt, and if he does meet his daughter-in-law, custom requires that she throw herself flat on the ground.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)

passages.headline: A Kachin shaman in ribbons and printed cotton
passages.gloss: Pallas saw a young Kachin shaman perform at the Karysh mine. The man was said to have been mad, or to have played mad, for years before taking up the craft, and still sometimes 'witched' all night until he collapsed. As a beginner he had no drum, only a paddle-shaped rattle stick; a shaman earned the right to a drum by sacrificing a horse and stretching its hide over it.
passages.quote: Ich habe den Aufzug eines jungen Katschinzischen Zauberers, der viele Jahre, ehe er das Handwerk angefangen, närrisch gewesen oder sich närrisch angestellt hatte, in Karysch gesehn… Er gauckelte ohne Mütze und hatte nur bunt ausgenähte lederne Strümpfe und am Leibe einen engen, ganz beschmutzten Kittel, von bunt gedrucktem baumwollenen Zeuge (Kitaika) an
passages.translation: I saw the costume of a young Kachin sorcerer, who for many years before taking up the trade had been mad or had pretended to be mad, at Karysh… He performed his tricks without a cap and wore only brightly embroidered leather stockings and on his body a tight, very dirty smock of brightly printed cotton cloth (kitaika).
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)

passages.headline: Feeding butter to a stone woman's mouth
passages.people: Heathen Tatars of the Abakan (Beltirs and other Khakas)
passages.gloss: On the Abakan steppe, crowded with ancient slab-fenced graves that the Tatars said were set up long before the Kirgis, Pallas found carved standing stones. One, a tall bellied stone with a large open-mouthed woman's face, was called Kurtejak-tash, the 'woman stone'. Hunters heading out for sable prayed to it for luck and smeared fat or butter into its mouth.
passages.quote: Diese Wake ist unter den Nahmen Kurtejaktasch (Weiberstein) oder Ulu-Kurtejak (das grosse Weib) bey den heydnischen Tataren dieser Gegend bekannt, und wird sonderlich im Herbst, von den auf die Zobeljagd vorbey reisenden Heyden, fleißig um Glück angesprochen und mit etwas Fett oder Butter, welches die Anbeter in den ofnen Mund des Gesichts andächtig schmieren, gefuttert.
passages.translation: This stone is known among the heathen Tatars of this region by the name Kurtejak-tash (woman stone) or Ulu-Kurtejak (the great woman), and especially in autumn it is earnestly asked for luck by the heathens travelling past to the sable hunt, and fed with a little fat or butter, which the worshippers devoutly smear into the open mouth of the face.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)

passages.headline: A model farm run by a Tatar general
passages.people: Kazan Tatars (Muslim estate owner and peasants)
passages.gloss: Passing through villages owned by Major General Tevkelev, a Muslim of Tatar descent whose serfs were all Tatars, Pallas praises the order and cleanliness of the grain stores, sheaves, fields and even the peasants' households as an example of good husbandry, unusual in the region. The general was away celebrating the Tatar ploughing festival, Saban.
passages.quote: Die drey letztern Dörfer gehören dem Generalmajor Tewkelef, welcher tatarischer Herkunft und der mahometanischen Religion zugethan ist, auch lauter Tataren zu seinen zahlreichen Unterthanen hat.
passages.translation: The last three villages belong to Major General Tevkelev, who is of Tatar descent and an adherent of the Muslim religion, and has nothing but Tatars among his numerous subjects.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)

passages.headline: Thirty 'Tartarian' languages from the Black Sea to Japan
passages.people: Peoples of Siberia and 'Tartary' (Turkic, Mongolic, Uralic and others)
passages.gloss: Strahlenberg announces the first part of his planned work: a comparative table of thirty languages spoken between the Black Sea and the Sea of Japan, which he calls the 'Tartarian' languages. He explains that the many peoples of Siberia and Tartary each have their own language besides the main languages used among them, and a footnote adds that they therefore cannot all properly go under the name of Tartars.
passages.quote: Das erste nun, ist ein Specimen Harmoniae linguarum Tartaricarum, bestehend in 30 Sprachen, die sich anheben von dem Schwartzen und sich endigen bey dem Japanischen Meer. … (indem unterschiedliche Völckerschaften in Siberien und der Tartarey vorhanden sind, welche nebst denen Haupt-Sprachen, so unter ihnen gebräuchlich sind, ihre eigene oder particuliere daneben haben)
passages.translation: The first, then, is a Specimen of the Harmony of the Tartarian Languages, consisting of 30 languages, which begin at the Black Sea and end at the Sea of Japan. … (since various peoples live in Siberia and Tartary who, besides the main languages in use among them, have their own particular ones as well)
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (Vorbericht, Stockholm 1726)
passages.caution: The OCR of this copy is badly garbled Fraktur; the quote has been restored letter by letter from the damaged text, so check the scan.

passages.headline: Tatar and Mongol, the two sons of one khan
passages.gloss: Commenting on the new French edition of Abulghazi's 'Genealogical History of the Tatars' (Leiden 1726), Strahlenberg retells its origin story: a khan (Alenzie or Alinja Khan) had two sons, Tatar and Mungel, both of Turkish descent, whose followers split into two branches named after them. It is a Central Asian Muslim tradition, passed on through the Swedish prisoners' translation.
passages.quote: weil der Alenzie-Chan zwey Söhne gehabt, einen Tater den andern Mungel, so zwar beyde Türckischer descendence, wie der Autor recht zeiget, so haben sich solche doch von Stund an in diese beyde branches getheilet, indem jener mit seinem Türckischen Volck gegen Osten gegangen, welche hernach von ihm den Nahmen angenommen, der Mungel aber in Westen mit den Seinigen geblieben
passages.translation: since Alenzie Khan had two sons, one Tater, the other Mungel, both indeed of Turkish descent, as the author rightly shows, these nevertheless divided at once into these two branches, the former going east with his Turkish people, who afterwards took their name from him, while Mungel stayed in the west with his own people
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (Vorbericht, Stockholm 1726), paraphrasing Abulghazi Bahadur Khan
passages.caution: The OCR of this copy is badly garbled Fraktur; the quote has been restored letter by letter from the damaged text, so check the scan. The legend is Abulghazi's (17th century), as read by Strahlenberg.

passages.headline: 'Kalmyk' means the ones who stayed behind
passages.gloss: Strahlenberg rejects the view, in the French edition of Abulghazi, that 'Kalmyk' was an insult aimed at their religion. He says the name was given to them in the Tatar language and means a people that remained behind, from 'kal' (I stay) and 'umak' (tribe). A similar 'those who remained' explanation is still often repeated today.
passages.quote: den Nahmen von Kallmack erhalten, welches kein Scheltwort ihrer Religion halber ist, wie der Autor … remarquiret … sondern es bedeutet und heisset ein Volck oder Geschlecht, so nach- oder dableibet, denn Kall oder Call, heisset ich bleibe da oder nach, und Amack oder Umack ein Geschlecht, daher per syncop: Kallmack oder Kallmuck.
passages.translation: received the name Kallmack, which is not a term of abuse on account of their religion, as the author remarks … but it means and signifies a people or tribe that stays behind or remains there, for Kall or Call means 'I stay there or behind', and Amack or Umack a tribe; hence by syncope Kallmack or Kallmuck.
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (Vorbericht, Stockholm 1726)
passages.caution: The OCR of this copy is badly garbled Fraktur; the quote has been restored letter by letter from the damaged text, so check the scan.

passages.headline: Prester John was really the Dalai Lama
passages.people: Kalmyks and Mongols; medieval European envoys
passages.gloss: Strahlenberg offers one example of how getting a name right can clear up history: the famous 'great priest John'. He says this priest, who sits between India and China in the land of Tangut, is the one Kalmyks and Mongols call Dalai Lama, with the added title 'Jegan', meaning holy. On the next page he claims the thirteenth-century friar envoys Carpini and Rubruck turned that title into the Christian name John, which is why the king of Portugal later sought Prester John in India and then in Abyssinia.
passages.quote: von dem sogenannten großen Priester Johann; dieser, welcher seinen Sitz zwischen Indien und China im Lande Tan-guht … hat, wird von allen Kalimucken, Mungalen und … Dalai Lama genannt … woraus nun klärlich zu ersehen, daß dieser Nahme sowol von den Indianern, als auch von den Kalmücken und Mungalen hergekommen
passages.translation: of the so-called great Priest John; he who has his seat between India and China in the land of Tangut … is called Dalai Lama by all Kalmyks, Mongols and … from which it is now clearly to be seen that this name came from the Indians as well as from the Kalmyks and Mongols
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (Vorbericht, Stockholm 1726)
passages.caution: The OCR of this copy is badly garbled Fraktur; the quote has been restored letter by letter from the damaged text, so check the scan. The Jegan/Johannes derivation is Strahlenberg's own theory.

passages.headline: Gog and Magog from a khan's name?
passages.gloss: Strahlenberg criticises the French editor of Abulghazi for suggesting that the biblical names Gog and Magog came from a khan called Budenür-Mogack, an idea also found in Pétis de la Croix. He insists that the Tatar original text, under an Arabic name, shows something quite different. It shows how European scholars tried to fit the peoples of Tartary into biblical prophecy.
passages.quote: item pag. 148 praesumiret, der Nahme Gog & Magog entstehe von einem Könige oder Chan, der Budenür-Mogack geheissen, (welches, wo mir recht ist, La Croix in seinen Remarquen auch anführet) da doch der Tatarsche Grund-Text unter einem Arabischen Nahmen solches ganz anders beweiset.
passages.translation: likewise on p. 148 he presumes that the name Gog and Magog comes from a king or khan called Budenür-Mogack (which, if I am right, La Croix also cites in his remarks), whereas the Tatar original text, under an Arabic name, proves it quite otherwise.
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (Vorbericht, Stockholm 1726)
passages.caution: The OCR of this copy is badly garbled Fraktur; the quote has been restored letter by letter from the damaged text, so check the scan.

passages.headline: Marco Polo's lost city of Campion
passages.place: Gansu corridor (western end of the Great Wall)
passages.gloss: Strahlenberg says he asked every nation in Tartary about Marco Polo's city of Campion, shown on old maps, and found no one who had heard of it. He concludes the name was mispronounced and that it must be the city at the western entrance of the Chinese Wall, which the Tatars call Camtzi, where all caravans must stop and wait for permission to enter China.
