passages.quote: ob gleich bey allen Nationen in der Tatarey von dem Nahmen der Stadt Campion, wie eben uns Marcus Paulus und andere alte Mappen darlegen, ziemliche Nachfrage gethan, ich dennoch keine einzige gefunden, die mir weder aus alter noch neuer Zeit, davon Unterricht geben können … welche im Gebürge und beym Eingange der Chinaeischen Mauer Westlicher Seiten lieget, die von den Tatern in Stelle vor Campion, Camtzi … genant wird
passages.translation: although I made considerable inquiry among all the nations of Tartary about the name of the city of Campion, as Marco Polo and other old maps set it before us, I nevertheless found not a single one who could inform me about it from old or recent times … [the city] which lies in the mountains at the entrance of the Chinese Wall on the western side, which the Tatars call Camtzi instead of Campion
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (Vorbericht, Stockholm 1726)
passages.caution: The OCR of this copy is badly garbled Fraktur; the quote has been restored letter by letter from the damaged text, so check the scan.

passages.headline: Kazan, called 'Shahr-i Bolgar' by Turks and Tatars
passages.gloss: In a note on old place names, Strahlenberg observes that Turks and Tatars still call Kazan 'Schaire Bolgar', the Bolgar capital, although it was only taken by Tsar Ivan Vasilievich, and his father Vasily already bore the title 'lord of the Bolgars'. He uses this to argue that 'Bolgar' in Russian titles covered all the peoples living along the Volga.
passages.quote: da nemlich die Stadt Casan anjetzo von den Türcken und Tatern, Schaire Bolgar, d. i. die Bolgarische Haupt-Stadt genannt wird, selbe aber allererst von Iwan Wasiliowitz dem 2ten eingenommen, dessen Vater Wasili Iwanowitz aber bereits den Titul, Herr über Wolgarski, gebraucht
passages.translation: since the city of Kazan is at present called by the Turks and Tatars 'Schaire Bolgar', that is, the Bolgar capital, though it was only taken by Ivan Vasilievich the Second, whose father Vasily Ivanovich already used the title 'Lord over Wolgarski'
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (Vorbericht, Stockholm 1726)
passages.caution: The OCR of this copy is badly garbled Fraktur; the quote has been restored letter by letter from the damaged text, so check the scan. Strahlenberg counts Ivan the Terrible (Ivan IV) as Ivan II.

passages.headline: Timur's carved inscription in the steppe
passages.gloss: Among the illustrations promised for his book, Strahlenberg lists a monument that Timur (Tamerlane) had carved on a mountain when his army marched into Tartary, recording the day and year he stood there, still to be seen some 80 or 90 miles south of Tobolsk. He also promises copies of runic-looking epitaphs and metal plates and medals dug out of grave mounds in the steppes.
passages.quote: wie Timur-Beck (oder der sogenannte Tamerlan) in die Tatarey mit seiner Armee marchiret, und bey einem gewissen Gebürge eine Zeitlang gestanden, daß derselbe den Tag und das Jahr seiner Anwesenheit daselbst eingraben und hauen lassen, welches Monument noch diese Stunde, etwa 80 oder 90 Meil Weges von der Stadt Tobolski in Süden, daselbst zu sehen ist
passages.translation: how Timur Beg (or the so-called Tamerlane) marched into Tartary with his army and stayed a while by a certain mountain, so that he had the day and year of his presence carved and cut there, which monument is still to be seen there to this hour, about 80 or 90 miles' journey south of the city of Tobolsk
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (Vorbericht, Stockholm 1726), citing Pétis de la Croix's History of Timur
passages.caution: The OCR of this copy is badly garbled Fraktur; the quote has been restored letter by letter from the damaged text, so check the scan. The inscription story comes from Pétis de la Croix's translation; the distance is Strahlenberg's.

passages.headline: A Tobolsk mullah's book of Tatar history
passages.people: Bukharan and Tatar Muslims of Tobolsk
passages.gloss: While making his map as a prisoner, Strahlenberg befriended the Bukharan and other Muslim residents of Tobolsk. Their chief priest showed him two manuscripts from the city of Turkestan, one on the Persian dynasties and one on Tartary, called 'Chingis' or 'Kitap' (book). On the next page he tells how a Tatar explained it word by word in Russian and two Swedish officers wrote it down in German: this became the German text of Abulghazi's history.
passages.quote: Weil ich mich aber absonderlich an ihren vornehmsten Priester, Agun Asbackewitz genannt, so ein gar freundlicher Mann war, adressirte, wurden mir … auch zweene Manuscripta von ihm hervor gezeiget, eines betreffend die Persischen Dynastien, das andere aber die Tatarey, welches letztere er nur Tzingis oder Zingis, item: Kitap oder Buch nannte; beyde aber aus der Stadt Turckestan erhalten hatte
passages.translation: But because I addressed myself especially to their chief priest, called Agun Asbackewitz, who was a very friendly man, he showed me … two manuscripts, one concerning the Persian dynasties, the other Tartary, which latter he called only Tzingis or Zingis, or Kitap, that is, book; both of which he had obtained from the city of Turkestan
passages.speaker: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (Vorbericht, Stockholm 1726)
passages.caution: The OCR of this copy is badly garbled Fraktur; the quote has been restored letter by letter from the damaged text, so check the scan.

passages.headline: 'Tartar houses' with a window of ice
passages.people: Voguls (Mansi), whom Brand calls the first Siberian Tartars
passages.gloss: Travelling up the Chusovaya toward the Urals, the embassy stayed in villages of the Voguls, whom Brand calls the first Siberian Tartars. He says they live in Tartar houses with a fireplace, and once the wood has burned down to coals the smoke hole in the roof is closed with a sheet of ice that lets in the daylight. They sit and sleep cross-legged on a broad bench running round the room.
passages.quote: welche die ersten Siberischen Tartarn so Wogultski genennet werden, und ein Heydnisches, aber dabey sehr superstitiöses Volck … wie sie denn auch in solchen tartarischen Häusern wohnen, die doch mit einem Camin gemacht, das Rauch-Loch, welches oben im Dach ist, wird so bald das Holtz zu Kohlen gebrennet ist, mit einer Decke von Eiß zu gedecket, wodurch das Tages-Licht hinein fället
passages.translation: who are the first Siberian Tartars, called Wogultski, and a heathen but very superstitious people … and they also live in such Tartar houses, which are however made with a fireplace; the smoke hole at the top of the roof is covered, as soon as the wood has burned to coals, with a cover of ice, through which the daylight falls in
passages.speaker: Adam Brand (Neu-vermehrte Beschreibung, Lübeck 1734)

passages.headline: A hunting dog buried like a man, with its own little house
passages.gloss: Brand watched the Voguls mourn a large hunting dog that had died suddenly. They lamented its virtues, buried it like a person with a pillow of wood under its head, and built a small wooden house six or seven feet high on four posts over its grave. He adds that this is said to be an age-old custom among them.
passages.quote: endlich bestätigten sie ihn gleich einen Menschen zur Erde, legten ihm ein darzu verfertigtes Holtz unter das Haupt, damit er sanft liegen möchte, und baueten nachmahls ein apartes Häuslein von Holtz, auff sein Grab, 6. biß 7. Fuß hoch, stehend auf vier Pfälen
passages.translation: finally they laid him in the earth like a human being, put a piece of wood made for the purpose under his head so that he might lie softly, and afterwards built a separate little wooden house over his grave, six to seven feet high, standing on four posts
passages.speaker: Adam Brand (Neu-vermehrte Beschreibung, Lübeck 1734)

passages.headline: 'We see so many poor Russians who believe in Christ'
passages.gloss: When the travellers urged the Voguls to give up their 'errors' and accept Christ, they gave a sharp reply: they saw every day many poor Russians who believed in Christ and could barely earn a crust of bread, and as for salvation, they would live and die as their ancestors had. Brand adds that they neither farm nor trade and live by hunting sable and elk.
passages.quote: was das zeitliche Wohlseyn anlangt, sehen wir täglich vor unsern Augen so viel arme Russen, welche, ob sie wohl an Christum glauben, dennoch kaum ein Stuck Brodt erübrigen können, was aber die ewige Wohlfahrt anlangt, müsten sie fernerhin also leben und sterben, wie ihre Vor-Eltern, sie möchten gut oder übel geglaubt haben.
passages.translation: as for well-being in this life, we see daily before our eyes so many poor Russians who, though they believe in Christ, can scarcely spare a piece of bread; as for eternal welfare, they must go on living and dying as their forefathers did, whether they had believed well or badly.
passages.speaker: Adam Brand (Neu-vermehrte Beschreibung, Lübeck 1734)

passages.headline: Tyumen, a walled town of Tatar traders
passages.gloss: Reaching Tyumen on 25 June 1692, Brand found a large town with a rampart and walls, mostly fallen into decay. Most of its people were born Tatars who had settled there, many baptised into the Russian faith and the rest Muslims, who traded far into the Kalmyk lands and Bukhara and paid tribute to the tsar. He calls them a courteous people.
passages.quote: gelangten wir in die Stadt Tumeen an, so ein ziemlich groß begriffener Ort, und mit Wall und Mauren umgeben, aber mehrentheils verfallen, die Einwohner dieser Stadt aber sind meistentheils gebohrne Tartarn, so sich allhier gesetzet, wovon ihrer viel den Rußischen Glauben angenommen, die andern aber den Mahometischen Glauben haben, diese Leute treiben in frembde Oerter, als in Kalmucker und Bugarien Lande, grosse Handelung
passages.translation: we reached the town of Tyumen, a fairly large place surrounded with rampart and walls, but mostly decayed; the inhabitants of this town are mostly born Tartars who have settled here, many of whom have taken the Russian faith, the others the Muslim faith; these people carry on great trade in foreign places, such as the Kalmyk and Bukharan lands
passages.speaker: Adam Brand (Neu-vermehrte Beschreibung, Lübeck 1734)

passages.headline: Prayers in a Tatar mosque at Tobolsk
passages.gloss: At Tobolsk the governor's learned son took the envoy's party to a Tatar mosque. Brand describes a plain room with large open windows and carpets, the worshippers leaving their shoes at the door and sitting cross-legged in rows, a white-robed chief priest in a turban, a loud call, kneeling, and the priest looking over his right and then his left shoulder.
passages.quote: daß er uns in eine tartarische Mosquee, Meschets oder Kirche führte, die ringsherum grosse Fenster hatte, welche alle offen stunden, der Boden war mit Tapeten belegt, ohne daß andere Zierrathen darin zu sehen waren, die Leute so hinein giengen, liessen vor der Thüre ihre Schuhe oder Bismacken stehen, und setzen sich ordentlich in gewissen Reyhen mit unter sich geschlagenen Füssen nieder
passages.translation: that he took us into a Tartar mosque, Meschet or church, which had large windows all round, all standing open; the floor was laid with carpets, with no other ornaments to be seen; the people who went in left their shoes or boots before the door and sat down in orderly rows with their feet crossed under them
passages.speaker: Adam Brand (Neu-vermehrte Beschreibung, Lübeck 1734)

passages.headline: A ruined city of the Tartar king 'Utai-chan'
passages.place: Inner Mongolia (between the Nen River and the Great Wall)
passages.people: Tartars (Mongols) as remembered by Chinese informants
passages.gloss: On 10 October 1693 the caravan reached a large, old, deserted city called Taimingzinz, with two sealed towers, fallen masonry, and life-size stone statues of people and idols and huge stone lions, all carved so true to life that, Brand says, few such are found in Europe. The Chinese told him a Tartar king named Utai-chan had ruled there centuries before, until a Chinese king took it and drove the Tartar out; stone towers on the hills, they said, marked Tartar graves.
passages.quote: Den 10 Octobris kamen wir an eine grosse, alte und verwüstete Stadt Taimingzinz genannt, in derselben stehen 2. Thürme … Die Chineser erzehlten, daß dieser Ort vor viel 100. Jahren, als zur selben Zeit ein Tartarischer König, Utaichan genannt, allda regieret, durch einen Chinesischen König erobert, und der Tartar vertrieben worden
passages.translation: On 10 October we came to a great, old and ruined city called Taimingzinz, in which stand two towers … The Chinese told us that this place, many hundreds of years ago, when a Tartar king called Utaichan reigned there, was conquered by a Chinese king and the Tartar driven out
passages.speaker: Adam Brand (Neu-vermehrte Beschreibung, Lübeck 1734)
passages.caution: Brand saw the ruins; the story of Utai-chan is what his Chinese guides told him.

passages.headline: The 'city of idols' and its tower of bells
passages.place: Inner Mongolia (between the Nen River and the Great Wall)
passages.gloss: Four days later the embassy passed another ruined city, Burgankoron ('idol city'), said to have been home only to the highest pagan priests. In the middle stood a tall octagonal stone tower hung with countless little bells that rang in the wind; inside were thousands of small Chinese idols, and holes in its sides were stuffed with writings in Mongol or 'East Tartar' left by passing lamas.
passages.quote: Mitten in der Stadt stund ein hoher steinerner achteckigter Thurm, daran unzehlich viel Glöcklein hingen, welche, wann sie vom Winde gerührt, ein überaus laut Gethön verursachten. in diesem Thurm war ein Eingang, worin wir viele 1000 kleine Chinesische Götzen, von vielerley Gestalt fanden. An der Seite des Thurms waren viel Löcher, diese lagen voll Schrifften, welche auf Mongalisch oder Ost-Tartarische Sprache geschrieben waren
passages.translation: In the middle of the city stood a tall octagonal stone tower on which hung countless little bells which, when stirred by the wind, made a very loud ringing. In this tower was an entrance, in which we found many thousands of small Chinese idols of many shapes. On the side of the tower were many holes, full of writings in the Mongol or East Tartar language
passages.speaker: Adam Brand (Neu-vermehrte Beschreibung, Lübeck 1734)

passages.headline: A Mongol nun's prophecy of a war in heaven
passages.place: Inner Mongolia (between the Nen River and the Great Wall)
passages.people: Mongols or 'Tartars' near the Great Wall
passages.gloss: Near the Great Wall Brand met Mongols or Tartars of the Dalai Lama's faith, who kept images in their houses with little pots of food and drink before them and set a white cock on the coffin at burials. Asked whom she worshipped, a Mongol nun telling her beads answered that it was the god whom 'our' God had thrust out of heaven, who would return and throw the Christians' God down.
passages.quote: Eine Mongalische Nonne, welche, mit einem Pater Noster in der Hand, continuirlich das Maul rührete, fragte man, wen sie anbetete, sie gab zur Antwort, den Gott, welcher von unsern Gott aus dem Himmel gestossen worden, und würde ihr Gott wieder im Himmel kommen, und wieder unsern Gott vom Himmel herunter werffen
passages.translation: A Mongol nun, who with a rosary in her hand kept moving her lips continually, was asked whom she worshipped; she answered: the god who was thrust out of heaven by our God, and her god would come back into heaven and throw our God down from heaven again
passages.speaker: Adam Brand (Neu-vermehrte Beschreibung, Lübeck 1734)
passages.caution: A single conversation, probably through interpreters; the words may be garbled in translation.

passages.headline: Kumis in golden bowls at the emperor's feast
passages.gloss: At the Kangxi emperor's banquet for the Russian envoy, after a meal of nearly three hours, two great golden bowls of kumis, which Brand says is a Tartar drink made from mare's milk, were brought to the emperor. The envoy was called up to the throne and ordered to drain one bowl completely; the embassy staff were then served kumis too, followed by tea boiled in milk.
passages.quote: wurden dem Bogdegan zwey grosse güldene Schalen mit einem Tranck, (welcher auf tartarisch Kumis genannt wird, und der von Pferde-Milch abgezogen seyn solle,) überreichet, welcher gleich darauf den Herrn Envoye vor sich auf seinen Thron entbiethen ließ
passages.translation: two great golden bowls with a drink (which in Tartar is called kumis, and is said to be made from mare's milk) were handed to the Bogdikhan, who immediately afterwards had the envoy summoned before him on his throne
passages.speaker: Adam Brand (Neu-vermehrte Beschreibung, Lübeck 1734)

passages.headline: The emperor of China as a 'Mongol or East Tartar'
passages.people: Manchus (called 'Mongal or East Tartar' by Brand)
passages.gloss: Brand gives a close portrait of the Kangxi emperor seen at the audience, and labels him a 'Mongal or East Tartar'. Kangxi was in fact a Manchu. The confusion shows how Europeans of the 1690s used 'Tartar' as one label for the Manchu rulers of China and the Mongols.
passages.quote: welcher ein Mongal oder Ost-Tartar ist, braun von Gestalt, und seines Alters 45. biß 50. Jahr, schön von Taille und hatte grosse schwartze Augen, eine gebogne Nase, einen über die Lippen herabhangenden schwartzen Knebel-Bahrt, hingegen wenig Bahrt an dem Kinn, dabey war die Haut seines Gesichts sehr pockengrübicht
passages.translation: who is a Mongol or East Tartar, brown of complexion, about 45 to 50 years old, well built, with large black eyes, an aquiline nose, a black moustache hanging over his lips but little beard on his chin, and the skin of his face much pitted by smallpox
passages.speaker: Adam Brand (Neu-vermehrte Beschreibung, Lübeck 1734)
passages.caution: Kangxi was born in 1654, so he was about 39, not 45 to 50; Brand's 'Mongal' is a mislabel for Manchu.

passages.headline: A palace hall covered with felt 'in the Tartar manner'
passages.gloss: Describing the palace hall where the embassy was feasted, Brand notes a building of fired brick about 30 fathoms long with yellow glazed roof tiles bearing lions and dragons, paper windows, twelve gilded pillars and an open painted roof. One surface (the OCR word is garbled, probably the floor) was covered with felt in the Tartar manner and decorated with foliage and figures, a steppe touch in a Chinese palace.
passages.quote: so war selbiger ein viereckigtes Gebäu, ohngefehr 30 Klafter lang, und 10. Klafter breit von Mauersteinen aufgeführet, und das Dach war mit gelben verglasurten Ziegeln bedecket … war nach der tartarischen Art mit Filtz bedecket, und mit Laubwerck und Figuren ge-
passages.translation: it was a four-sided building, about 30 fathoms long and 10 fathoms wide, built of bricks, and the roof was covered with yellow glazed tiles … was covered with felt in the Tartar manner, and with foliage and figures
passages.speaker: Adam Brand (Neu-vermehrte Beschreibung, Lübeck 1734)
passages.caution: The noun before 'war nach der tartarischen Art' is garbled in the OCR; check the scan.

passages.headline: Where the name 'Tartary' came from: a river, a province or a Syriac word
passages.gloss: Before describing China, the enlarged 1734 edition inserts a compiled chapter on Tartary 'from the most approved historians'. It offers three origins for the name: a river called Tartar, a province of that name mentioned by Hayton, or a Syriac word 'Tartaroye' meaning a numerous nation. It then divides Tartary into old and new, little and great, stretching from Jesso (Hokkaido) to the Sea of Azov, Poland and Russia.
passages.quote: Die Tartarey, welche etwan von dem Fluß Tartar …, oder nach Haithony Bericht von einer also genannten Provintz, oder von dem syrischen Wort Tartaroye, welches eine zahlreiche Nation bedeutet, seinen Nahmen bekommen, wird von einigen in die alte und neue Tartarey, item in die kleine und grosse, oder in dieß- und jenseits des Bergs Imaus gelegene, eingetheilet
passages.translation: Tartary, which got its name perhaps from the river Tartar …, or according to Hayton's account from a province so called, or from the Syriac word Tartaroye, which means a numerous nation, is divided by some into old and new Tartary, likewise into little and great, or into that lying on this side and beyond Mount Imaus
passages.speaker: Compiled chapter in the 1734 enlarged edition of Brand's journey (from earlier historians)
passages.caution: Book learning added to the 1734 edition, not something Brand learned on the road.

passages.headline: Pit houses of the Baraba Tatars
passages.people: Baraba Tatars (Siberian Tatars between Tara and Tomsk)
passages.gloss: Crossing the Baraba steppe between Tara and Tomsk, Lorenz Lange's party met the Baraba Tatars, whom he calls heathens living wretchedly. Their winter dwellings were dug into the ground, raised about an ell above it with stakes and roofed with straw; inside each stood a small wooden idol in human shape, dressed in rags, called Shaitan, to whom they promised a cap or collar in return for good hunting.
passages.quote: Im Winter bewohnet diese Wüsteney eine Horde von Tartaren, welche von denen Russen Barabinsky Tartaren genennet werden … In ihren Wohnungen, welche in der Erde gegraben, und oberhalb ungefehr eine Elle mit Staqueten erhöhet, und mit Stroh bedecket sind, halten sie einen kleinen aus Holz geschnittenen Abgott, in der Gestalt eines Menschen.
passages.translation: In winter this wilderness is inhabited by a horde of Tartars whom the Russians call Baraba Tartars … In their dwellings, which are dug into the earth and raised about an ell above it with stakes and covered with straw, they keep a small idol carved from wood in the shape of a man.
passages.speaker: Lorenz Lange (journal of his 1715 journey to China, printed by Weber)
passages.caution: Cited from the 1744 reissue, which reprints the 1721 text page for page with clearer OCR.

passages.headline: Kalmyk leather huts shaped like a hooped petticoat
passages.gloss: Weber's informant Poussett described the Kalmyk caravan that came to trade at Astrakhan each year, grazing its way along the Volga. They carried leather huts called 'Kubiten' (kibitkas), which looked like a whalebone hooped petticoat; they raised them on poles, cooked inside, and closed the top hole when the fire was out to keep warm at night. Each morning the houses were loaded back onto the pack animals.
passages.quote: Sie hätten eine Art Hütten von Leder, die einer jupe de baleine ähnlich sähen, und Kubiten genennet würden, diese stelleten sie mit Stangen auf, machten Feuer und Essen darinn, und stopfeten wenn das Feuer ausgebrannt, oben das Loch zu, und wärmeten sich auf solche Art des Nachts. Des Morgens lüden sie ihre Häuser auf die Last-Thiere und jagten weiter fort.
passages.translation: They had a kind of leather huts, which looked like a whalebone petticoat and were called Kubiten; these they set up with poles, made fire and food inside, and when the fire had burned out stopped up the hole at the top, and so kept warm at night. In the morning they loaded their houses onto the pack animals and moved on.
passages.speaker: Friedrich Christian Weber (Das veränderte Russland), reporting Poussett of Astrakhan
passages.caution: Cited from the 1744 reissue, which reprints the 1721 text page for page with clearer OCR.

passages.headline: 'They have no town': low log houses and summer tents
passages.people: Baraba people (described as a kind of Kalmyk) and Siberian Tatars
passages.gloss: An anonymous description of the Kalmyks printed by Weber says the Baraba people, whom it calls a kind of Kalmyk paying tribute both to the tsar and to the Zunghar khan, live like the Siberian Tatars in low wooden houses built close to the ground, with a smoke hole closed once the fire burns down. They have no town or fixed dwelling: in summer light huts and tents, in winter their warm wooden houses. It adds that they grow oats, barley and buckwheat but spit out rye bread.
passages.quote: Sonsten ist diese Nation ein böses und streitbar Volk, wohnet wie die Siberischen Tartarn in hölzernen Häusern, welche ganz niedrig auf die Erde gezimmert … Sie haben keine Stadt noch andere beständige Wohnung, sondern wohnen des Sommers in leicht aufgeschlagenen Hütten und Gezelten, die sie gar hurtig wissen abzubrechen und aufzuschlagen. Des Winters aber ziehen sie in ihre warme hölzerne Wohnungen.
passages.translation: Otherwise this nation is a wicked and warlike people, and lives like the Siberian Tartars in wooden houses built quite low on the ground … They have no town or other fixed dwelling, but live in summer in lightly pitched huts and tents, which they know how to strike and set up very quickly. In winter, however, they move into their warm wooden dwellings.
passages.speaker: Anonymous description of the Kalmyks, printed in Weber
passages.caution: Cited from the 1744 reissue, which reprints the 1721 text page for page with clearer OCR. The author is not named.

passages.headline: Beijing's 'Tartar cities' and a wall built by earlier Tartars
passages.people: Manchus (the ruling 'Tartars') and the earlier Mongol (Yuan) rulers
passages.gloss: The description of China printed with Lange's journal explains that Beijing is three cities in one: an outer suburb now called the Chinese city, and two 'Tartar cities', inside which lies the emperor's city with its yellow or red wall. The outer earthen rampart, it says, was built about 500 years earlier by the western Tartars when they ruled China for some thirty years, and is now almost fallen.
passages.quote: Die Stadt Pekin ist dreyfach: erstlich die Vorstadt, die man heut zu Tage die Sineser-Stadt nennet: die andern zwo sind der Tartaren Städte, und innerhalb dieser, des Kaysers Stadt oder die Stadt mit der gelben oder rothen Mauer, in welcher des Kaysers Pallast ist. Die Vorstadt hat einen Wall, denn die Chineser Tuchin oder die erdene Mauer nennen, ist ohngefehr vor 500. Jahren gemacht worden, von denen Westwerts gelegenen Tartaren
passages.translation: The city of Peking is threefold: first the suburb, which is nowadays called the Chinese city; the other two are the cities of the Tartars, and within these the emperor's city, or the city with the yellow or red wall, in which the emperor's palace stands. The suburb has a rampart, which the Chinese call Tuchin or the earthen wall, made about 500 years ago by the Tartars living to the west
passages.speaker: Description of China printed with Lange's journal in Weber
passages.caution: Cited from the 1744 reissue, which reprints the 1721 text page for page with clearer OCR. The history of the rampart is garbled: Mongol rule of China lasted about ninety years, not thirty.

passages.headline: A khan's burial mound heaped up with helmets and shields
passages.gloss: Sailing down the Volga below Simbirsk in May 1703, the traveller saw a high, almost treeless round hill called Sariolkiergan. Russians told him it was the tomb of a Tatar king named Mamon (Mamai), who had come up the Volga with seventy Tatar princes to conquer Russia, and that his soldiers had carried the earth for the mound in their helmets and shields. It is a local legend about a kurgan, reported as hearsay.
passages.quote: Die Russen berichteten uns, daß daselbst das Begräbniß eines Tartarischen Königs oder Kaysers, Namens Mamon, wäre, welcher mit siebenzig andern Tartarischen Prinzen die Wolga herauf gekommen, in der Absicht, sich von ganz Rußland zu bemeistern. Weil aber dieser Prinz hier gestorben, hätten seine in grosser Menge mitgebrachte Soldaten ihm zu Ehren dieses Grabmahl errichtet, und in ihren Sturm-Hauben und Schildern die Erde zu diesem Berge angetragen.
passages.translation: The Russians told us that there lay the tomb of a Tartar king or emperor named Mamon, who had come up the Volga with seventy other Tartar princes, intending to make himself master of all Russia. But because this prince died here, the soldiers he had brought in great numbers raised this tomb in his honour, and carried the earth to this hill in their helmets and shields.
passages.speaker: Journal of an unnamed painter-traveller (evidently Cornelis de Bruyn, 1703) printed in Weber, Das veränderte Russland
passages.caution: Cited from the 1744 reissue, which reprints the 1721 text page for page with clearer OCR. A legend told by Russians; no Mamai burial is known there.

passages.headline: Fireproof cloth from a Tatar prince
passages.gloss: The traveller reports a quarrel between two Tatar princes of the Kazan region, father and son, which almost came to battle over a woman until Prince Golitsyn, governor of Kazan and Astrakhan, made peace. In thanks the Tatar prince gave Golitsyn a large piece of cloth that would not burn, said to be still made in Cathay between China and Bukhara. The traveller, who had himself once brought asbestos stone from Cyprus, received a piece.
passages.quote: worauf der Tartarische Prinz diesem Scheids-Mann unter andern Sachen ein grosses Stück unverbrennlichen Leinwands schenket, wovon der Herr Poppe und ich wiederum von diesem etwas bekommen. Er sagte mir, daß es zu Katai, zwischen China und Bucharen, noch würklich gemacht würde.
passages.translation: whereupon the Tartar prince gave this arbitrator, among other things, a large piece of incombustible linen, of which Mr Poppe and I in turn received some from him. He told me that it was still actually made in Cathay, between China and Bukhara.
passages.speaker: Journal of an unnamed painter-traveller (evidently Cornelis de Bruyn, 1703) printed in Weber, Das veränderte Russland
passages.caution: Cited from the 1744 reissue, which reprints the 1721 text page for page with clearer OCR.

passages.headline: A Tatar camp near Astrakhan, 'as Abraham must have lived'
passages.gloss: Visiting the Tatar camp a short mile from Astrakhan, the traveller found families camped apart in tents shaped like parrot cages, very clean and well furnished. They lived from their herds, burned dried cow dung stacked around the tents like peat, and, he thought, lived as contentedly in their tents as Europeans in palaces. He sketched a finely dressed young woman and compared their life to the Arabs and the biblical patriarchs.
passages.quote: Ihre Zelte sind wie die Papageyen Bauer, nur nach Proportion nicht so hoch, sehr reinlich und mit guten Meublen versehen… Ihre Wärme schaffen sie sich von Küh-Mist, den sie trucknen und zu recht machen, wie wir unsern Torff, und in Hauffens um ihre Zelte legen. Ihre Lebens-Art kommt mit der Arabischen ziemlich überein
passages.translation: Their tents are like parrot cages, only not so high in proportion, very clean and provided with good furniture… They get their warmth from cow dung, which they dry and prepare as we do our peat, and lay in heaps around their tents. Their way of life agrees fairly well with the Arabs'
passages.speaker: Journal of an unnamed painter-traveller (evidently Cornelis de Bruyn, 1703) printed in Weber, Das veränderte Russland

passages.headline: Four Mongol peoples, one of them called Tartars after a river
passages.gloss: After the Astrakhan Tatars, the text turns to the history of the Mongols, retelling medieval reports: the khan's seal read 'One God in heaven and one Khan on earth', and Batu's army counted 160,000 Tartars and 440,000 Christians and others. It then lists four Mongol peoples, including the 'Saniongals' or water Mongols (the Su-Mongals of Carpini), who were also called Tartars after the river Tartar.
passages.quote: Dieses Mongalen Land lieget nach Osten und ist … vier unterschiedene Völcker bewohnet; nemlich die … die Saniongals oder See-Mongalen, welche auch nach den … Tartar, Tartern genennet werden; die Merkates … Diese vier Völcker waren in der Sprache und Lebens-Art … ziemlich ähnlich, hatten aber jede ihr eigen Ober-Haupt.
passages.translation: This Mongol land lies to the east and is inhabited by four different peoples, namely the … the Saniongals or water Mongols, who are also called Tartars after the [river] Tartar; the Merkits … These four peoples were fairly similar in language and way of life, but each had its own chief.
passages.speaker: Compiled historical note in the de Bruyn extract printed in Weber (after Plano Carpini)
passages.caution: Book learning from medieval sources, not observation; the OCR has gaps.

passages.headline: Gog and Magog on the Onon River
passages.gloss: An anonymous description of the Mongols printed next in Weber sets out their lands, from Lake Khövsgöl east to the sand desert, to the Argun, and north-west to the rivers Onon and Sikoi, a country which, it says, has been said since ancient times to be inhabited by Gog and Magog. The same description goes on to the lamas, the Dalai Lama and whether he could be Prester John.
passages.quote: ferner biß an das Land Argun, und von dort wiederum Nord-west biß an den Fluß Onon und Sikoi, welches wie man von Alters hersaget, von Gog und Magog bewohnet wird.
passages.translation: further to the land of Argun, and from there again north-west to the rivers Onon and Sikoi, which, as has been said from ancient times, is inhabited by Gog and Magog.
passages.speaker: Anonymous description of the Mongols, printed in Weber

passages.headline: 'You are both right': a Sunni and a Shia before the judge
passages.people: Muslim Tatars and Persians at Astrakhan
passages.gloss: Poussett told Weber that a Persian and a Muslim Tatar at Astrakhan had quarrelled over religion and taken their complaint to the Russian commandant. When he learned that the Tatar had called the prophet Ali, and the Persian the prophet Muhammad, a cheat and a vagabond, the commandant shrugged and ruled that he could punish neither, since both were right. Poussett also praised the Astrakhan Tatars' orderly life and hospitality.
passages.quote: daß der Tartar den Prophet Aly, und hinwiederum der Persianer den Propheten Mahomet, vor einen Betrüger und Landstreicher gescholten, so ziehet der Commendant die Schulter, und spricht das Urthel: Ihr Herren, ich kan weder einen noch den andern von euch strafen, denn ihr habt alle beyde recht.
passages.translation: that the Tartar had abused the prophet Ali, and the Persian in turn the prophet Muhammad, as a cheat and vagabond, the commandant shrugs his shoulders and pronounces judgement: Gentlemen, I can punish neither the one nor the other of you, for you are both right.
passages.speaker: Friedrich Christian Weber (Das veränderte Russland), reporting Poussett of Astrakhan
passages.caution: Cited from the 1744 reissue, which reprints the 1721 text page for page with clearer OCR. Two words ('Persianer', 'Betrüger') are damaged in this copy and read from the 1721 edition (T0707 n187).

passages.headline: Frozen half-moon dumplings for winter journeys
passages.people: Bukharans of Little Bukhara (Turkic Muslims of the Tarim oases, then under Zunghar rule)
passages.gloss: Part 2 of Weber's work prints an account 'Of Tartarian Bukhara' by an author who says he had been in Little Bukhara himself. He notes that the men's dress differs little from the Tartar, that they eat with their fingers and wooden spoons, drink tea with milk, salt and butter, and fill half-moon-shaped pastries with chopped meat, which they freeze and carry in a sack on long winter journeys to boil into soup.
passages.quote: Sie füllen mit denselben eine Art Pasteten, die wie ein halber Mond gestaltet sind. Auf weiten Reisen, insonderheit in Winter, nehmen sie einen guten Vorraht von diesen Pasteten mit, und tragen sie bey sich in einem Sakke. Wenn nun diese Speise vorher an der Luft rechtschaffen durchgefroren ist, so wird sie in einem siedenden Wasser gekocht, und eine ziemlich gute Suppe davon gemacht.
passages.translation: They fill a kind of pastry, shaped like a half moon, with it. On long journeys, especially in winter, they take a good supply of these pastries with them and carry them in a sack. When this food has first frozen thoroughly in the air, it is cooked in boiling water, and a fairly good soup is made of it.
passages.speaker: Anonymous account 'Von der Tartarischen Bucharey' in Weber, part 2 (1739)
passages.caution: The author is not named; he says he had visited Little Bukhara.

passages.headline: Marco Polo's northern Tartars read as Siberia
passages.people: Tartars of the far north (Marco Polo's 'northern Tartars')
passages.gloss: The compiler admits that older books say almost nothing about Siberia, and turns to Marco Polo, who 'entered Tartar service' but never crossed the land himself. He is sure Polo's northern country is what is now called Siberia, and quotes him on its Tartars: ruled by a king of the great khan's line, keeping the old Tartar customs, worshipping an earth god called Natigai, living in no towns but in the open country, and eating only milk and meat.
passages.quote: In den inwendigen mitternächtlichen Ländern wohnen viele Tartarn, deren König von dem Geschlecht des grossen Kaisers derer Tartaren abstammet; und selbige behalten noch die Sitten und Gewonheiten der alten Tartarn. Sie sind alle abgöttisch, beten einen Gott an, den sie Natigai nennen … Sie wohnen weder in Städten noch Flecken, sondern auf dem Felde zwischen Bergen und Felsen.
passages.translation: In the inner northern lands live many Tartars, whose king descends from the family of the great emperor of the Tartars; and they still keep the manners and customs of the old Tartars. They are all idolaters and worship a god whom they call Natigai … They live neither in towns nor in villages, but in the open country between mountains and rocks.
passages.speaker: Marco Polo, quoted in German by the anonymous compiler
passages.caution: A thirteenth-century report of the Mongol north, applied by the compiler to Siberia in 1720.

passages.headline: Krasnoyarsk, where twenty horses stood saddled day and night
passages.people: Kirgiz (Yenisei Kyrgyz) raiders; Mongols and their subject 'Tartars'
passages.gloss: The compiler describes Krasnoyarsk as a large town heavily garrisoned with Cossacks and cavalry against raids by the Kirgiz, so that twenty saddled horses had to stand day and night on the market square before the governor's house. The garrison also guarded the western side against the Mongols and 'the Tartars under them', and the town's name is explained as 'red whirling-river town'.
passages.quote: Krasnajar ist eine grosse Stadt, von dem Czar starck mit Cosaken und Reuterei besetzet, gegen dem Einfall der Kirgisen, um deren willen auf dem Markt vor des Gouverneurs Haus Tag und Nacht 20. Pferde gesattelt stehen müssen
passages.translation: Krasnoyarsk is a large town, strongly garrisoned by the tsar with Cossacks and cavalry against the incursions of the Kirgiz, on whose account twenty horses must stand saddled day and night in the market before the governor's house
passages.speaker: Anonymous compiler (Der allerneueste Staat von Siberien, Nuremberg 1720)
passages.caution: Compiled from reports of Swedish prisoners and travellers, not seen by the compiler.

passages.headline: Vogul log rooms with an ice skylight, retold
passages.gloss: The chapter on the 'Siberian Tartars' called Voguls repeats, almost word for word, Adam Brand's description of their houses, with one change: the compiler says they are square wooden rooms like those of Russian peasants rather than 'Tartar houses'. The smoke hole is still sealed with a lid of ice that lets in daylight.
passages.quote: Ihre Wohnungen sind viereckigte hölzerne Kammern, wie die Russischen Bauren haben. An statt des Ofens haben sie Camin oder Feuer-Herd, worauf sie Holz brennen und darbei ihre Speise kochen. Das Rauch-Loch, so oben im Tach ist, wird, so bald das … zu Kohlen gebrennet ist, mit einem Deckel von Eiß
passages.translation: Their dwellings are square wooden rooms such as the Russian peasants have. Instead of a stove they have a fireplace or hearth, on which they burn wood and cook their food. The smoke hole at the top of the roof, as soon as the [wood] has burned to coals, [is covered] with a lid of ice
passages.speaker: Anonymous compiler (Der allerneueste Staat von Siberien, Nuremberg 1720)
passages.caution: Copied from Adam Brand's journal (1698; see W274), with small changes.

passages.headline: Felt yurts that no wind can overturn
passages.place: Khalkha Mongolia (between Selenginsk and the Tola River)
passages.gloss: Crossing northern Mongolia with the Russian caravan, Lange describes how the Mongols live from their herds: hides for boots and harness, dung for fuel on the treeless steppe, sheepskins for coats, and sheep's wool for the felts that cover their yurts and beds. He finds the felt huts better than European tents: warm in winter, cool in summer with the side walls removed, proof against wind and rain.
passages.quote: Aus der Schafswolle machen sie die Filze oder Woilokken, womit ihre Jurten oder Hütten überzogen, und ihr Lager gemacht ist. Diese Filzhütten dienen ihnen wider die Kälte, und sind im Sommer, wenn man die Seitenwände abnimmt, viel schattiger und kühler als unsere Gezelte. Der Wind kann sie nie umwerfen, und kein Regen schlägt durch.
passages.translation: From the sheep's wool they make the felts or voiloks with which their yurts or huts are covered and their beds made. These felt huts protect them against the cold, and in summer, when the side walls are taken off, are much shadier and cooler than our tents. The wind can never blow them over, and no rain comes through.
passages.speaker: Lorenz Lange (journal of 1727 to 1728, translated and abridged by P. S. Pallas, 1781)

passages.headline: A steppe where hardly anyone is sober in summer
passages.place: Khalkha Mongolia (between Selenginsk and the Tola River)
passages.gloss: Lange (as abridged by Pallas) notes that the Mongols live mainly on brick tea boiled with milk and butter, bought from the Chinese, and in the milking season distil milk brandy and drink it warm, so that apart from girls and children one rarely meets a sober person in their camps. They also make small cheeses and air-dry strips of meat for the hungry winter.
passages.quote: Vom Frühling bis in den Herbst, so lange das Vieh häufige Milch giebt, ziehen sie häufigen Milchbranntewein ab, und trinken ihn gleich warm auf, daher man in selbiger Zeit, ausser Mädchen und Kindern, selten einen nüchternen Menschen in den mongolischen Lägern antrifft.
passages.translation: From spring until autumn, as long as the cattle give plenty of milk, they distil a great deal of milk brandy and drink it straight away while warm, so that at that time, apart from girls and children, one seldom meets a sober person in the Mongol camps.
passages.speaker: Lorenz Lange (journal of 1727 to 1728, translated and abridged by P. S. Pallas, 1781)
passages.caution: A generalisation by a Russian caravan official, abridged by Pallas; not a measured observation.

passages.headline: Urga, the moving camp that became a walled town
passages.people: Khalkha Mongols and their Jebtsundamba Khutukhtu
passages.gloss: In a footnote Pallas explains that on the Tola River stands the now fixed court of the Khutukhtu (the Mongol high lama) and the Mongol princes: a place enclosed by wooden walls with several temples and dwellings. It used to be a moving camp called Urga, he says, but is now called Küree, a word meaning a walled place, and Chinese governors live there to watch over the Mongol princes. This is the origin of today's Ulaanbaatar.
passages.quote: An demselben ist gegenwärtig das unveränderliche Hoflager des Kutuchta und der mongolischen Häupter, als ein fester, mit hölzernen Wänden umgebner Platz, mit verschiedenen Tempeln und Wohnungen angelegt. Man nennt daher dieses Hoflager, welches sonst, da es noch ein wandelbares Lager vorstellte, Urga oder Gergö hieß, nunmehr Kurö
passages.translation: On it now stands the permanent court of the Khutukhtu and the Mongol chiefs, laid out as a fixed place surrounded by wooden walls, with various temples and dwellings. This court, which formerly, when it was still a moving camp, was called Urga or Gergö, is therefore now called Kurö
passages.speaker: P. S. Pallas (editor's footnote, 1781)

passages.headline: Isker, the khan's capital: 'if one can call it a town'
passages.gloss: Müller visited the remains of Isker, the capital Yermak's Cossacks entered in 1582, on a steep height of the Irtysh above Tobolsk. He describes a small round hill protected on the landward side by a triple rampart and ditches, the river and a ravine guarding the other sides, and an interior only a few dozen fathoms across, room for little more than the khan, his family and servants. Part of it had fallen into the river.
passages.quote: Die Ueberbleibsel dieser ehmahligen Haupt-Stadt des Landes, wenn man anders einen Ort, so wie dieser gewesen zu seyn scheinet, eine Stadt nennen kann, sind noch heut zu Tage zu sehen.
passages.translation: The remains of this former capital of the land, if one can indeed call a place such as this seems to have been a town, can still be seen today.
passages.speaker: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Sammlung Russischer Geschichte, vol. 6, 1761-1762)

passages.headline: Houses of wood or unburnt brick, leaving no trace
passages.gloss: Inside the ramparts of Isker Müller found no remains of houses, only uneven ground and some pits that might have been cellars. He concludes that any buildings must have been of wood in the Siberian Tatar manner, or of unburnt brick in the Bukharan way, since nothing of them survives, and notes that some pits were dug later by treasure seekers, not always in vain.
passages.quote: Wenn solches ist, so müssen sie nach Sibirisch-Tatarischer Art nur von Holze, oder nach Bucharischer Gewohnheit von ungebrannten Ziegeln, gebauet gewesen seyn, weil nichts davon mehr bemerket wird. An einigen Orten sind Gruben, welche zu Kellern gedienet haben können. Man sagt aber auch, daß einige Gruben in neuern Zeiten gemacht seyn, weil man daselbst Schätze gesuchet
passages.translation: If so, they must have been built only of wood in the Siberian Tatar manner, or of unburnt bricks after the Bukharan custom, since nothing more is to be seen of them. In some places there are pits which may have served as cellars. But it is also said that some pits were made in recent times, because people searched for treasure there
passages.speaker: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Sammlung Russischer Geschichte, vol. 6, 1761-1762)

passages.headline: Chimgi-Tura, the old Tatar court at Tyumen
passages.gloss: Müller identifies the first seat of the Siberian Tatar princes with Tyumen. The remains of the old Tatar court, a small entrenchment between two ravines of the Tyumenka stream, were still visible, and the local Tatars still called the fort and the Russian town Chimgi or Chimgi-Tura, without knowing why. Müller argues the name comes from 'Chingidin', given by the founder Taibuga in honour of Chinggis Khan.
passages.quote: Man siehet daselbst noch die Ueberbleibsel des ehmahligen Tatarischen Hoflagers, das in einer kleinen Verschanzung bestanden, und zwischen zwo Klüften des Baches Tümenka, welcher durch die Stadt in die Tura fällt, gelegen gewesen. Die dortigen Tataren nennen diese Festung, und hiernächst auch die dabey erbauete Stadt Tümen, noch heutzutage Tschimgi, oder Zimgitura. Warum? wissen sie nicht.
passages.translation: There one still sees the remains of the former Tatar court, which consisted of a small entrenchment and lay between two ravines of the Tyumenka stream, which flows through the town into the Tura. The Tatars there still call this fortress, and after it the town of Tyumen built beside it, Chimgi or Chimgi-Tura. Why, they do not know.
passages.speaker: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Sammlung Russischer Geschichte, vol. 6, 1761-1762)

passages.headline: 'Turali': the Tatars who lived in towns
passages.people: Tyumen and Tobolsk Tatars, as named by the Bashkirs
passages.gloss: Discussing the word 'tura' (town or fortress in Tatar and Bukharan), Müller reports that the Bashkirs call the Tyumen Tatars, and after them the Tobolsk Tatars, only 'Turali'. On the next page he gives the Bashkirs' explanation: these Tatars had lived since ancient times in towns and fortresses, or at least in fixed places, while the Bashkirs often moved their dwellings about the steppe.
passages.quote: Man kann hier leicht auf die Gedanken kommen, da Tura in der Tatarischen und Bucharischen Sprache eine Stadt, oder Festung, bedeutet, daß vielleicht der Fluß Tura von dieser alten Tatarischen Festung Tschimgi den Nahmen empfangen. Die Baschkiren haben für die Tümenischen Tataren, und nach selbigen auch für die Tobolskischen, keinen andern Nahmen, als daß sie solche Turali nennen
passages.translation: One may easily think here, since Tura in the Tatar and Bukharan language means a town or fortress, that perhaps the river Tura received its name from this old Tatar fortress of Chimgi. The Bashkirs have no other name for the Tyumen Tatars, and after them for the Tobolsk Tatars too, than to call them Turali
passages.speaker: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Sammlung Russischer Geschichte, vol. 6, 1761-1762)

passages.headline: 'Sibir' was not the Tatars' name for their capital
passages.gloss: Müller corrects a common belief that 'Sibir' is the Tatar word for the capital. When he asked the Tobolsk Tatars, they did not know the word at all; they called the place Isker. He thinks the name Sibir arose in Russia, taken from the Permians or Zyrians who first brought news of the land, and was only later attached to the Tatar capital.
passages.quote: Man glaubt insgemein, Sibir sey die Tatarische Benennung des Orts, welche soviel, als eine Hauptstadt, oder Residenz, bedeute. Fraget man aber die Tobolskischen Tataren nach diesem Umstande, so ist ihnen solcher ganz unbekannt. Sie nennen vielmehr den Ort Isker
passages.translation: It is commonly believed that Sibir is the Tatar name of the place, meaning a capital or residence. But if one asks the Tobolsk Tatars about this, it is quite unknown to them. They call the place Isker instead
passages.speaker: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Sammlung Russischer Geschichte, vol. 6, 1761-1762)

passages.headline: A bird that cried 'Chinggis'
passages.people: Mongols (their own tradition of Chinggis Khan)
passages.gloss: A learned Mongol lama gave Müller a story from Tibetan and Mongol books about the rise of Chinggis Khan. A khan's son and nine nobles fled rather than become monks; the peoples they met joined them and chose the son as khan. As the nine debated his new name, a small bird landed nearby and cried 'Chinggis, Chinggis', and so he was named. Müller calls the story very fabulous but prints it because nothing like it had been published.
passages.quote: Zu derselben Zeit sey ein kleiner Vogel angeflogen gekommen, welcher in der Nähe der Rathsversammlung sich niedergesetzet, und mit vernehmlicher Stimme Tschingis, Tschingis, geschrieen. Alsobald habe man einmüthig beschlossen, diesen von dem Vogel angestimmten Nahmen dem Chane beyzulegen.
passages.translation: At that same time a little bird came flying up, settled near the council, and cried out in a clear voice, 'Chinggis, Chinggis'. At once they unanimously decided to give the khan this name that the bird had sung.
passages.speaker: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Sammlung Russischer Geschichte, vol. 6, 1761-1762), reporting a Mongol lama's account

passages.headline: Gold in the old graves: 'from whom but the former Tatars?'
passages.people: The 'former Tatars' (the Mongol empire of Chinggis Khan)
passages.gloss: Arguing that the history of Chinggis Khan belongs to Siberian history, Müller points to the antiquities of southern Siberia: old entrenchments across the steppes, many memorial stones and statues, and graves from which gold and silver had been dug. He asks from whom such treasure could come but the former Tatars, to whom the riches of China, Persia, Russia, Poland, Bohemia and Hungary had fallen as plunder. On the next page he adds that the poorer old graves near Baikal show the earliest owners lived simply.
passages.quote: was für Kostbarkeiten an Gold und Silber hat man nicht aus den Gräbern hervorgeholet? von wem können dieselbe anders, als von den ehmahligen Tataren, herstammen, indem bekannt ist, daß alle Schätze von China, Persien, Rußland, Polen, Böhmen, Ungarn, ihnen zum Opfer werden müssen?
passages.translation: what treasures of gold and silver have not been brought out of the graves? From whom can they come but from the former Tatars, since it is known that all the treasures of China, Persia, Russia, Poland, Bohemia and Hungary had to fall to them as prey?
passages.speaker: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Sammlung Russischer Geschichte, vol. 6, 1761-1762)
passages.caution: Müller's inference; modern archaeology dates many Siberian gold-bearing kurgans far earlier (Scythian and Hunnic periods).

passages.headline: A Christian city seen in the sky above Tobolsk
passages.gloss: Müller relays, somewhat apologetically, the omens that the Siberian chronicles say foretold the end of Tatar rule. The Tatars living around the site of later Tobolsk often saw a Christian city with churches and bell towers in the air and heard bells ringing. He says he tells it only to stay faithful to his source.
passages.quote: Wird man es mir wohl zu gute halten, wenn ich solche erzähle? Ich thue es aus keiner andern Ursache, als weil ich mich nicht gerne von meinem Originale entferne. Oft sollen die umher wohnenden Tataren über dem Orte, wo jetzt die Stadt Tobolsk stehet, eine Christliche Stadt mit Kirchen und Glockenthürmen in der Luft gesehen, und dabey auch ein Geläute von Glocken gehöret haben.
passages.translation: Will I be forgiven for telling them? I do it for no other reason than that I do not like to depart from my original. The Tatars living round about are often said to have seen, above the place where the town of Tobolsk now stands, a Christian city with churches and bell towers in the air, and to have heard bells ringing too.
passages.speaker: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Sammlung Russischer Geschichte, vol. 6, 1761-1762), retelling the Siberian (Remezov) chronicle

passages.headline: Yermak's body that bled for six weeks
passages.gloss: Following the Remezov chronicle, whose author wanted Yermak made a saint, Müller tells how Tatars found the drowned Cossack leader by his armour. When a murza tried to strip it, blood ran from the corpse's mouth and nose as from a living man, so the Tatars laid the body naked on a scaffold and everyone who passed shot an arrow into it, and each time fresh blood flowed. Birds would not touch it, and after six weeks troubling dreams led the Tatars to bury him.
passages.quote: Alsobald lief dem Todten aus Mund und Nase häufiges Blut, nicht anders, als von einem lebendigen Menschen … Sie legten zu solchem Ende den Leichnam ganz entkleidet auf ein Gerüste, da denn ein jeder, der herzukam, oder vorüber gieng, einen Pfeil nach demselben abschoß, wovon jedes mahl frisches Blut aus der Wunde lief.
passages.translation: At once much blood ran from the dead man's mouth and nose, just as from a living person … For this purpose they laid the body quite naked on a scaffold, and everyone who came up or passed by shot an arrow at it, and each time fresh blood ran from the wound.
passages.speaker: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Sammlung Russischer Geschichte, vol. 6, 1761-1762), retelling the Siberian (Remezov) chronicle
passages.caution: A hagiographic chronicle story; Müller notes its author wished Yermak to be canonised.

passages.headline: A Tatar funeral feast of thirty oxen for Yermak
passages.gloss: In the same chronicle story, the Tatars repented of mistreating Yermak's body, wished they had made him their king, and buried him under a spreading pine at the Begishev burial ground, holding a memorial feast 'after the Tatar custom' at which thirty oxen and ten rams were eaten. They shared out his weapons and clothes, and one coat of mail was offered to a famous Ostyak idol.
passages.quote: Man habe ihn an dem Begischewischen Begräbniß-Orte unter einer krauß-astigen Fichte zur Erden bestattet, und zu seinem Gedächtnisse nach Tatarischem Gebrauche ein Todtenmahl angestellet, auf welchem 30 Ochsen und 10 Hammel verzehret worden.
passages.translation: They buried him at the Begishev burial ground under a pine with crooked branches, and in his memory held a funeral feast after the Tatar custom, at which 30 oxen and 10 rams were consumed.
passages.speaker: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Sammlung Russischer Geschichte, vol. 6, 1761-1762), retelling the Siberian (Remezov) chronicle

passages.headline: A Kalmyk ruler who searched for the legendary valley of Ergene Kon
passages.gloss: Discussing Abulghazi's legend that the ancestors of the Mongols lived shut in the valley of Ergene Kon until a whole mountain was melted to let them out, Müller adds a curious report he had been assured of: the Zunghar ruler Galdan Tseren, having heard the story from Bukharans, searched for such a valley as a refuge for his treasure and family, and was said to have found one somewhere in his lands.
passages.quote: Es ist merkwürdig, daß, wie man mich versichert, der Calmückische Beherrscher Galdanzerin nach langem Suchen eine dergleichen Ebene zwischen dem Gebürge, wie Irgene-Kon von Abulgasi beschrieben ist … innerhalb den Gränzen seines Gebiets, man weiß nur nicht wo, soll gefunden haben
passages.translation: It is remarkable that, as I am assured, the Kalmyk ruler Galdan Tseren after long searching is said to have found such a plain among the mountains, as Ergene Kon is described by Abulghazi … within the borders of his territory, only no one knows where
passages.speaker: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Sammlung Russischer Geschichte, vol. 6, 1761-1762)

passages.headline: 'When a European speaks of Tatars, no one knows who is meant'
passages.people: 'Tatars' as a European catch-all; Mongols of Batu
passages.gloss: Fischer complains that Europeans mispronounce the name as 'Tartar', perhaps imagining it comes from Tartarus, an allusion he says is common in old and new histories. Worse, they give it to every Asian people beyond Persia and India up to the Pacific, however different in looks, way of life, religion and language. He even doubts whether any single people ever properly bore the name, noting that Batu's army that invaded Hungary were Mongols, not Tatars.
passages.quote: Vielleicht haben sie sich eingebildet, daß der name von Tartarus herkomt. … Solcher gestalt geschiehet es, daß wenn ein Europäer von Tataren redet, man nicht weiß von wem die rede ist. Weil dieser name so gar allgemein ist, so habe ofters bei mir angestanden, ob auch jemals ein besonder volk auf dem erdboden gewesen sei, das den eigentümlichen namen Tatar geführet.
passages.translation: Perhaps they imagined that the name comes from Tartarus. … So it happens that when a European speaks of Tatars, one does not know whom he means. Because this name is so very general, I have often hesitated whether there was ever a particular people on earth that bore the proper name Tatar.
passages.speaker: Johann Eberhard Fischer (Sibirische Geschichte, introduction, 1768)

passages.headline: The Mongols disliked the name; the Chinese called all outsiders 'Ta-ta'
passages.people: Mongols; peoples beyond the Great Wall
passages.gloss: Fischer notes that in Europe and western Asia 'Tatar' (or 'Tarter') is better known than 'Mongol', although Chinggis Khan was a Mongol and not a Tatar. The mix-up, he says, is as old as the Mongol empire, and the Mongols themselves did not like to be called Tatars. He suggests the usage may come from the Chinese, who called all peoples living beyond their Great Wall 'Tata'.
passages.quote: Wiewol die Mogolen selbst es nicht gerne höreten, wenn man sie mit dem namen Tatar belegete … Die ursache solcher benennung mag wol von den Schinesern herrüren, als welche allen ausserhalb ihrer großen mauer wonhaften und an Schina grenzenden völkern den namen Tata zu geben pflegen
passages.translation: Although the Mongols themselves did not like to hear it when they were given the name Tatar … The cause of such naming may well come from the Chinese, who are accustomed to give the name Tata to all peoples living outside their great wall and bordering on China
passages.speaker: Johann Eberhard Fischer (Sibirische Geschichte, introduction, 1768)

passages.headline: Prester John was a mishearing
passages.people: Tibetans and Mongols; medieval European travellers
passages.gloss: Like Strahlenberg before him, Fischer explains the legend of Prester John as a European mistake: the first Europeans in Tibet and Mongolia misheard a title, their fancy shaped it into 'Prêtre Jean' or 'Juan', and so it spread through the world. They forgot that Tibetans and Mongols spoke neither French, Italian nor Portuguese, and were pleased to find what they hoped for; later came strange etymologies and fables of an Indian 'Johannes Presbyter'.
passages.quote: der name Pretre Jean oder Juan, ist von den erstern Europäern, die dorthin gekommen, unrecht gehöret, hernach von ihrer fantasei übel gebildet, und so weiter in die welt geschikket worden. Diesen guten leuten fiele nicht ein, daß die Tibetaner und Mogolen, unter denen sie sich befanden, weder französisch, noch italiänisch noch portugiesisch verstunden
passages.translation: the name Prêtre Jean or Juan was wrongly heard by the first Europeans who came there, then badly shaped by their fancy, and so sent out into the world. It did not occur to these good people that the Tibetans and Mongols among whom they found themselves understood neither French, nor Italian, nor Portuguese
passages.speaker: Johann Eberhard Fischer (Sibirische Geschichte, introduction, 1768)
passages.caution: Fischer's explanation, following Strahlenberg; not a proven derivation.

passages.headline: 'Kam', the Tatar word for a shaman since Rubruck's day
passages.people: Kacha Tatars, Teleuts, Chulym and Baraba Tatars; medieval Mongols
passages.gloss: Comparing medieval reports with what he saw in Siberia, Fischer notes that the soothsayers Carpini and Rubruck described among the Mongols, who beat drums and went out of themselves, can still be seen among the Yakut shamans. In a footnote he adds that Rubruck's word 'Cham' for such a seer is still used by the Tatars of the Kacha, the Teleuts, and the Chulym and Baraba Tatars for their sorcerer-priests.
passages.quote: Rubruquis sagt Chap. 19, das wort Cham bedeute einen weißager, und alle leute von dieser sorte werden unter den Mogols Cham genannt… Dieser name ist noch heutiges tages gebräuchlich bei den Tataren am Katscha-fluß, bei den Teleuten, Tschulümern und Barabinen, und wird ihren zauberpriestern gegeben.
passages.translation: Rubruck says, chapter 19, that the word Cham means a soothsayer, and that all people of this sort are called Cham among the Mongols… This name is still in use today among the Tatars on the Kacha river, among the Teleuts, the Chulym people and the Baraba people, and is given to their sorcerer-priests.
passages.speaker: Johann Eberhard Fischer (Sibirische Geschichte, introduction, 1768) (footnote)

passages.headline: Felt temples on the Volga, stone temples in Mongolia
passages.people: Volga Kalmyks; Khalkha and Inner Mongols
passages.gloss: Opening his chapter on Buddhist temples, Pallas contrasts the Volga Kalmyks, who because of their wandering life still kept their images in portable sacred felt tents, which he compares to the Tabernacle of the Israelites in the desert, with the Mongols under Chinese rule, who had long had permanent temples, some of stone. He adds that under the Mongol khans who ruled China, buildings for Lamaist worship were raised in the eastern Mongol steppes, but after the empire broke up the Mongols returned to a moving life.
passages.quote: die wolgischen Kalmücken aber halten, wegen ihrer unstäten Lebensart, ihren Götzendienst noch izt, so wie sonst auch die Mongolen thaten, in beweglichen heiligen Filzhütten, (Burchanin-Orgö) welche der Stiftshütte, bey denen in der Wüste, noch nomadisch lebenden Israeliten verglichen werden könten … Die Mongolen, welche unter China stehn, haben vorlängst an verschiednen Orten ihres Landes beständige und zum Theil von Stein erbaute Tempel gehabt
passages.translation: but the Volga Kalmyks, because of their unsettled way of life, still keep their idol worship, as the Mongols also formerly did, in movable sacred felt huts (Burchanin-Orgö), which could be compared to the Tabernacle of the Israelites still living as nomads in the wilderness … The Mongols who are under China have long had permanent temples in various places of their land, some of them built of stone
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (Sammlungen historischer Nachrichten über die mongolischen Völkerschaften, part 2, 1801)

passages.headline: A brick bell tower and brick monastery near the half-ruined city of Taimingtschin
passages.place: Inner Mongolia (Naun, Locho and Sharamurin rivers)
passages.gloss: From reports, Pallas lists the temples of eastern Mongolia: a remarkable brick tower called Chonchotu with many idol figures and iron bells, and on the Locho a monastery of many brick temples, less than thirty versts from the half-deserted city of Taimingtschin and forty from an old earth fortress. A footnote sends the reader to Ides's and Witsen's accounts of this ruined 'city of the gods' (Burchan-Chotton) and its idol tower, the same ruins Adam Brand described.
passages.quote: ordentliche Tempel und an lezteren Bach auch ein merkwürdiger Thurn von Ziegeln, mit vielen Götzenfiguren und eisernen Glocken, Chonchotu genant, am Flusse Locho selbst aber, unterhalb dem Bach Elbingol, ein mit vielen Tempeln aus Ziegeln erbautes Kloster … nicht dreißig Werste von der halbwüsten Stadt Taimingtschin und etwan vierzig von einer am Locho vorhandnen alten Erdfestung
passages.translation: proper temples, and on the latter stream also a remarkable tower of bricks with many idol figures and iron bells, called Chonchotu; but on the Locho river itself, below the stream Elbingol, a monastery built with many temples of brick … not thirty versts from the half-deserted city of Taimingtschin and about forty from an old earth fortress on the Locho
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (Sammlungen historischer Nachrichten über die mongolischen Völkerschaften, part 2, 1801)
passages.caution: Pallas says he had only imperfect reports of these distant places.

passages.headline: Tatar songs 'like the Scottish Highlanders''
passages.people: Crimean, Nogai, Kazan, Bashkir and Siberian Tatars; Mongols
passages.gloss: Pallas dismisses Mongol music as wailing and inharmonious and claims the Mongols passed this 'corrupted taste' to the Crimean Tatars, outdone only by Nogai songs. By contrast, he says, the Kazan Tatars, the Bashkirs and the 'unmixed' Siberian Tatars have quite tolerable melodies, much like the songs of the Scottish Highlands. He adds that the Mongols can write down music in Tibetan letters with lines showing rising and falling notes.
passages.quote: eben diesen verdorbenen Geschmack haben die Mongolen den Krymischen Tataren mitgetheilt, deren elendes Geschrey, durch die Nogaischen Gesänge noch weit übertroffen wird, da doch die Kasanischen und Baschkirischen, wie auch die Sibirischen unvermischten Tataren ganz erträgliche Melodien haben, welche sehr nach den Gesängen der Schottischen Hochländer arten.
passages.translation: the Mongols have passed on this same corrupted taste to the Crimean Tatars, whose miserable screeching is far surpassed by the Nogai songs, whereas the Kazan and Bashkir, and also the unmixed Siberian Tatars, have quite tolerable melodies, which very much resemble the songs of the Scottish Highlanders.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (Sammlungen historischer Nachrichten über die mongolischen Völkerschaften, part 2, 1801)
passages.caution: A personal and prejudiced judgement of taste, not a description of how the music works.

passages.headline: What the Kalmyks call Tatars, Russians and themselves
passages.gloss: Pallas ends his notes on Mongol learning with a list of Kalmyk names for peoples and places. The Kalmyks call the Tatars 'Manggot', a word meaning a goblin, which the Buryats and Mongols apply to the Russians instead; the Kalmyks call Russians 'Orross' and themselves 'Oelöt' or 'Chalmik'. The list also gives Tobolsk as 'Toboltora' and Bukhara as 'Chotton', 'the towns'.
passages.quote: Manggot, die Tataren, welchen Namen aber, der einen Kobolt bedeutet, die Buraten und Mongolen den Russen beylegen; Orroß werden leztere hingegen von den Kalmücken … genannt … sich selbst endlich Oelöt oder Chalmik
passages.translation: Manggot, the Tatars, a name which, however, means a goblin, and which the Buryats and Mongols give to the Russians; the latter, on the other hand, are called Orross by the Kalmyks … and themselves, finally, Oelöt or Chalmik
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (Sammlungen historischer Nachrichten über die mongolischen Völkerschaften, part 2, 1801)

passages.headline: A seal, not a signature
passages.people: Mongol and Tatar peoples of Asia
passages.gloss: In a footnote to a pass issued by the Tibetan Panchen Lama that he found among the Kalmyks, stamped with a red seal, Pallas explains that the Mongol and Tatar peoples of Asia confirm letters and documents not by signing their names but by printing the mark of their seal or signet ring (tamga) in colour beneath them; without it, even a signed name is not considered valid.
passages.quote: Die Mongolischen sowohl, als tatarischen Völker Asiens pflegen ihre Briefe und Handschriften nicht mit Unterschrift des Namens, sondern durch das mit Farbe darunter abgedrukte Zeichen ihres Signets oder Petschierrings (Tamga) zu bekräftigen, ohne welches selbst die Namensunterschrift nicht für gültig gehalten wird.
passages.translation: The Mongol as well as the Tatar peoples of Asia are accustomed to confirm their letters and manuscripts not by signing their name, but by the mark of their signet or seal ring (tamga) printed underneath in colour, without which even a signature is not considered valid.
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (Sammlungen historischer Nachrichten über die mongolischen Völkerschaften, part 2, 1801) (footnote)

passages.headline: Scholars who moved Atlantis to Spitsbergen
passages.people: Mongol and Tibetan Buddhists; European theorists
passages.gloss: Pallas rejects the theory, pushed by the Augustinian friar Georgi, that Tibetan and Mongol Buddhism grew out of Nestorian Christianity or Manichaeism, calling it a heap of rubble glued together in a polemical spirit. He lumps it with other learned fantasies: the Chinese and Indians as an Egyptian colony, the Lapps as Israelites, pagan gods as biblical patriarchs, and the recent placing of Atlantis and the first seat of all learning as far north as Spitsbergen.
passages.quote: Mit dergleichen gelehrtem Schwall sind wohl eher die Chineser und Indianer zu einer ägyptischen Colonie, die Lappländer zu Israeliten, die Götzen des Heydenthums zu Patriarchen der Bibel gemacht, und noch neulich die Atlanten und mit ihnen, der erste Sitz aller Wissenschaften bis nach Spitzbergen verlegt worden
passages.translation: With such learned bombast the Chinese and Indians have before now been made into an Egyptian colony, the Lapps into Israelites, the idols of heathendom into patriarchs of the Bible, and only recently the Atlanteans, and with them the first seat of all learning, have been moved as far as Spitsbergen
passages.speaker: Peter Simon Pallas (Sammlungen historischer Nachrichten über die mongolischen Völkerschaften, part 2, 1801)
passages.caution: Pallas does not name the Atlantis author; it fits J.-S. Bailly's northern Atlantis letters of 1779.

passages.headline: Bakhchysarai, Eski-Krim and Kefa: where the Crimean khans lived
passages.gloss: Zuev, back from an Academy journey to the Crimea, sketches the khanate's capitals. The khans had lived for over 200 years at Bakhchysarai, having moved there from Eski-Krim (Staryi Krym), the old Genoese city, after Mengli Giray took the sea ports and expelled the Genoese; at first the Tatars had been at Kozlov (Yevpatoria). Under the current khan Şahin Giray the residence had moved to Kefa, the old Theodosia. He adds that rich Tatars and murzas mostly live in the country, not in towns.
passages.quote: Die Residenz der krimmischen Chans war sonst in Baktschisarai, in welcher Stadt sie über 200 Jahr ihren Sitz gehabt haben. Sie ward dahin von Eski-Krim (Alt-Krim), der Hauptstadt der Genueser, bald nachdem Mengli-Girei Chan alle Seeplätze erobert, und die Genueser aus ihren Besitzungen vertrieben hatte, verlegt.
passages.translation: The residence of the Crimean khans was formerly at Bakhchysarai, in which town they had their seat for over 200 years. It was moved there from Eski-Krim (Old Crimea), the capital of the Genoese, soon after Mengli Giray Khan had conquered all the sea ports and driven the Genoese out of their possessions.
passages.speaker: Vasily Zuev (Sujef), 'Nachrichten von der Krim', in Neue Nordische Beyträge vol. 4 (1783), edited by P. S. Pallas
passages.caution: Pallas notes that Zuev's historical information is not entirely reliable; Mengli Giray took Kaffa with Ottoman help in 1475.

passages.headline: Genoese forts razed by Tatars, rebuilt by Turks
passages.gloss: Zuev credits the Crimean fortresses to three builders: the Genoese fortified the towns, the Tatars razed the walls when they took them, and the Turks later restored the fortifications at Kefa, Kerch and Kozlov and built Arabat and Perekop. At Perekop a broad, deep, stone-lined ditch cut the isthmus from sea to sea behind an earth rampart, while the fortress itself had become heaps of brick, bombs and cannonballs.
passages.quote: Alle diese Oerter waren, so lange die Genueser sie beherrschten, wohl befestigt, die Tatarn schleiften aber, bey der Einnahme derselben, die Festungswerke. Wie sie nachher den Türken unterwürfig wurden, stellten selbige in Kefa, Kertsch und Koslow die Festungswerke wieder her, und legten die Festung Arabat … wie auch Perekop an
passages.translation: All these places were well fortified as long as the Genoese ruled them, but the Tatars razed the fortifications when they took them. When they later became subject to the Turks, these restored the fortifications at Kefa, Kerch and Kozlov and built the fortress of Arabat … as well as Perekop
passages.speaker: Vasily Zuev (Sujef), 'Nachrichten von der Krim', in Neue Nordische Beyträge vol. 4 (1783), edited by P. S. Pallas

passages.headline: A quarter of an hour to eat hundreds of roast oxen
passages.gloss: Describing the khan's duty to join Ottoman wars with 100,000 men, Zuev reports how the Tatar army was welcomed on reaching the Turkish camp: hundreds of roasted oxen and two or three thousand sheep on spits were laid out in rows on the open field with heaps of bread, and at a cannon shot the Tatars fell on the food and ate it all within a quarter of an hour. He adds that they carried no provisions, lived on plunder in enemy country, and were cruel foes, a judgement coloured by long wars.
passages.quote: es wurden den Tag nach der Ankunft des Heers einige hundert gebratene Ochsen, und zwey bis dreytausend Schaafe, auf Spießen, in verschiednen Reihen, auf freyem Felde ausgestellet, und zwischen selbigen große Haufen Brod aufgeworfen; sobald alles fertig war, ward durch einen Kanonenschuß das Signal gegeben, worauf die Tatarn auf die Speisen zufielen, und selbige in solcher Geschwindigkeit verzehrten, daß in einer Viertelstunde nichts mehr übrig war.
passages.translation: the day after the army arrived, several hundred roasted oxen and two to three thousand sheep on spits were set out in several rows on the open field, with great heaps of bread thrown up between them; as soon as all was ready, the signal was given by a cannon shot, whereupon the Tatars fell upon the food and devoured it so quickly that within a quarter of an hour nothing was left.
passages.speaker: Vasily Zuev (Sujef), 'Nachrichten von der Krim', in Neue Nordische Beyträge vol. 4 (1783), edited by P. S. Pallas
passages.caution: Hearsay about earlier campaigns, written in the year Russia annexed the Crimea; the remarks on Tatar cruelty reflect Russian hostility.

passages.headline: Steppe full of ancient graves of the 'Chud', an unknown people
passages.people: Unknown ancient builders ('Chud'); Sagai and other steppe Tatars living there now
passages.gloss: Crossing the 'Tatar steppe' to the Abakansk fort on the Yenisei, the botanist Sievers found the whole area full of ancient grave monuments of a people still unknown, whom Siberians simply called Chud. He saw no inscriptions on the many standing stones. Nearby, he notes, Abakansk had been built in the previous century with palisades and five small cannon against raids by Tatars and Kirgiz.
passages.quote: Auf der ganzen tatarischen Steppe und hier herum ist alles voll von uralten Grabmälern von einer bis jetzt unbekannten Nation, die nur schlechthin in Sibirien Tschudi genannt werden. An den vielen aufgerichteten Steinen sah ich nirgends Inschriften.
passages.translation: On the whole Tatar steppe and round about here everything is full of very ancient grave monuments of a nation unknown until now, which in Siberia are simply called Chud. On the many standing stones I saw inscriptions nowhere.
passages.speaker: Johann Sievers, letters from Siberia, in Neueste Nordische Beyträge vol. 7 (1796), edited by P. S. Pallas

passages.headline: Birch-bark yurts gleaming white on the Sagai steppe
passages.gloss: Staying some days with the Tatars by Lake Ilkul on the Sagai steppe, Sievers praises their fine horses and cattle, sold to merchants as far as Moscow, notes that traders always bring brandy because 'one bargains better with a drunk Tatar than a sober one', and says he saw no sign of religion. Their yurts, he writes, were clean and roomy and all built of birch bark, shining a dazzling white against the green meadows and hills.
passages.quote: Ihre Jurten sind reinlich, geräumig, und alle von Birkenrinde gebauet, die bey Sonnenschein eine blendende Weisse in … der Ferne von sich geben und aufs Angenehmste mit dem … Grün der Wiesen und Berge contrastiren.
passages.translation: Their yurts are clean, roomy, and all built of birch bark, which in sunshine give off a dazzling whiteness into the distance and contrast most pleasantly with the green of the meadows and hills.
passages.speaker: Johann Sievers, letters from Siberia, in Neueste Nordische Beyträge vol. 7 (1796), edited by P. S. Pallas
passages.caution: The OCR here interleaves two columns; the quoted pieces are on this page but their order was restored.

passages.headline: Pyramids of poles covered with hides
passages.gloss: The mine official Shangin, travelling in the high Altai, describes the local 'mountain Tatars' as herders who do no farming. Their huts, apart from the elders', are wretched: a few poles set up in a pyramid and covered with hair felts or, more often, animal hides, because they make no felt themselves. Since they move often with their herds, empty pole pyramids stand in many places.
passages.quote: sie stellen einige Stangen … zusammen, und bedecken sie mit Haarfilzen, noch gewöhnlicher aber mit Thierfellen, weil … selbst keine … verfertigen
passages.translation: they set up a few poles … together and cover them with hair felts, but still more commonly with animal hides, since … make none themselves
passages.speaker: Peter Ivanovich Shangin, journal of an Altai journey (translated by P. S. Pallas), Neue Nordische Beyträge vol. 5 (1793)
passages.caution: The scan's left margin is cropped, so several words are lost; the gaps are marked.

passages.headline: Burial on a scaffold, and a horse left to starve
passages.gloss: Shangin admits he could learn little reliable about their burials; Cossacks told him they sometimes burned their dead, which he doubted. What he was sure of is that they never bury them in the ground: he found many corpses in full dress with their riding gear in caves and on high open rocks, and they also lay the dead on a scaffold of brushwood on tall poles, wrapped in skins with saddle and harness under the head. Often a horse is tied beside it until it drops from hunger.
passages.quote: So viel ist gewiß, daß sie selbige nie in die Erde vergraben … Sie machen auch wohl auf hohen Stangen, von Strauchwerk, ein Gerüst, und legen die Leiche, mit Fellen bekleidet darauf, Sattel und Zeug unter den Kopf und bedeckt mit Haarfilzen. Dazu wird oft noch ein Pferd … welches endlich vor Hunger umfällt.
passages.translation: This much is certain, that they never bury them in the earth … They also make a scaffold of brushwood on high poles and lay the corpse on it, dressed in skins, with saddle and harness under the head and covered with hair felts. Often a horse is added as well … which finally drops from hunger.
passages.speaker: Peter Ivanovich Shangin, journal of an Altai journey (translated by P. S. Pallas), Neue Nordische Beyträge vol. 5 (1793)
passages.caution: Cropped margin; a few letters at line starts restored and one gap marked.

passages.headline: Khanbalik and Ordu-Balik: the 'king's city' and the 'royal camp'
passages.people: Mongols of the Yuan dynasty; Persian and Arab writers
passages.gloss: Stritter's description of Beijing explains that the Inner City was part of the city built by Kublai, the 'Kambalu' of Marco Polo, from the Mongol 'Khan' and 'balga' or 'balgasun' (town), meaning the king's city, which Persians and Arabs turned into Khanbalik. It adds that eastern writers used the name for any royal residence, including towns in Tartary, and that Orda-Balik or Ordu-Balik likewise meant 'the royal camp'.
passages.quote: Was jetzt von Chan Balik u. s. w. ist gesagt worden, gilt auch von Orda Balik, Ordu Balik, oder Orda und Ortu, welche Wörter im Mongolischen königlich bedeuten. So nannte man Orda-Balgasun, Ordo Balga, Ordo Balk, das königliche Hoflager.
passages.translation: What has now been said of Khan Balik and so on applies also to Orda Balik, Ordu Balik, or Orda and Ortu, which words mean royal in Mongolian. Thus the royal camp was called Orda-Balgasun, Ordo Balga, Ordo Balk.
passages.speaker: J. G. Stritter, description of Peking, in Neue Nordische Beyträge vol. 2 (1781)
